bottom = np.zeros(len(loc))
for k in ["U", "P", "S"]:
    a2.bar(loc.index, loc[k], bottom=bottom, color=cols[k], width=0.7, edgecolor=style.SURFACE, label=names[k])
    for x, b, v in zip(loc.index, bottom, loc[k]):
        if v >= 7:
            a2.text(x, b + v / 2, f"{v:.0f}", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=7.2, color="white")
    bottom += loc[k].values
a2.set_xticks(loc.index, [f"'{y % 100:02d}" for y in loc.index], fontsize=8)
a2.set_ylim(0, 100)
a2.set_yticks([])
a2.grid(False)
a2.spines["left"].set_visible(False)
a2.set_title("QB location (FTN)", fontsize=9.5)
a2.legend(loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, -0.1), ncol=2, fontsize=7, frameon=False, handlelength=1.0,
          columnspacing=0.8)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=1.0)
plt.show()








Figure 11.14: The quarterback moves back. Left: share of NFL regular-season runs and passes snapped to a quarterback in the shotgun, 2006–2025 (nflverse play-by-play shotgun flag; the rest are under center or, in recent seasons, a few percent from the pistol). Right: where the quarterback lined up, 2022–2025, from FTN’s play-by-play charting (which records under center, shotgun and pistol separately). The shotgun peaked in 2023 and fell back in 2025, when under center rose to about a third of plays. Different sources, so different panels.





In 2006 offenses were in the shotgun on about one play in five. By 2023 it was about 72%. Over the same years the I-formation’s share of plays fell from about 11% in 2016 to about 6% in 2022, as far as the formation labels in the public data go.18 The causes overlap, but there are five worth knowing.

Passing became more valuable than running. After the 1978 rule changes, and again as offenses learned to throw efficiently, a pass gained more on average than a run. In the EPA terms you met in Downs, Distance, and Field Position, NFL dropbacks (sacks and scrambles included) averaged about +0.04 expected points per play in 2025 and designed runs about −0.05; across 2006–2025 it was about +0.03 against −0.07, and dropbacks came out ahead in every one of those seasons.19 Expected Points and Success Rate shows how analysts measure that gap, and why it’s smaller than it looks (runs are less risky, and they set up the pass). An offense that passes more wants more receivers, and the second back is the first player to go.
The shotgun is a better place to pass from. Five yards back, the quarterback takes a shorter drop and never has to turn his back on the defense. He sees the coverage from the snap and has more time before the rush arrives. The shotgun was used in the NFL as early as 1960 and revived by Tom Landry’s Cowboys in 1975, but for decades it was a third-down formation;20 the history chapters follow it.
Spreading the defense makes running easier, too. Three or four receivers pull defensive backs out wide, which leaves fewer defenders near the ball. An offense in the shotgun with 11 personnel can often run against six defenders in the box instead of seven or eight: the same count you did for the iso, now tilted toward the offense. Spread formations are the next chapter.
College stopped producing under-center quarterbacks. By the 2010s most college offenses, and many high schools, played almost entirely from the shotgun. Quarterbacks arrived in the NFL having rarely taken a snap under center, and NFL coaches built around what their quarterbacks did best.
A fullback is an expensive specialist. A roster spot used on a lead blocker is one not used on a receiver or tight end who can play every down. Many NFL teams stopped carrying a true fullback at all.







ImportantWhy it exists



The shotgun won the passing game; the classic formations kept the running game’s advantages. Under center, the quarterback can hand off to a back already running downhill, toward the line, and fake a handoff with his back to the defense. In the shotgun, many runs start sideways, and a play fake is less convincing because the defense can see the ball the whole time. Each formation is a bundle of trade-offs, and the NFL’s long move to the shotgun traded the run game’s angles for the passing game’s vision. The 2025 turn back toward under center is offenses deciding they gave up too much.

text:
Where the classic formations survive
The I-formation isn’t dead. It has retreated to the places where its advantages matter most, and in 2025 it started coming back out. Look at what lining up under center tells you now:


Show the Python
s = recent[recent.season == 2025]
locs = [("U", "under\ncenter"), ("P", "pistol"), ("S", "shotgun")]
pass_rate = [s[s.qb_loc == k]["pass"].mean() * 100 for k, _ in locs]
drop = s[s["pass"] == 1]
pa_rate = [drop[drop.qb_loc == k]["is_play_action"].astype(float).mean() * 100 for k, _ in locs]
uc = lambda x: (x.qb_loc == "U").mean() * 100   # noqa: E731
situ = [("all plays", uc(s)), ("1 yard or\nless to go", uc(s[s.ydstogo <= 1])),
        ("inside the\nopp. 2", uc(s[s.yardline_100 <= 2]))]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(6.6, 2.7))
colors = [style.DEFENSE, style.THIRD, style.OFFENSE]
for ax, vals, title in [(axes[0], pass_rate, "Pass rate"), (axes[1], pa_rate, "Play-action share\nof dropbacks")]:
    ax.bar(range(3), vals, color=colors, width=0.62)
    for i, v in enumerate(vals):
        ax.text(i, v + 2, f"{v:.0f}%", ha="center", fontsize=8, color=style.INK)
    ax.set_xticks(range(3), [n for _, n in locs], fontsize=7.5)
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=9)
axes[2].bar(range(3), [v for _, v in situ], color=[style.MUTED, style.DEFENSE, style.DEFENSE], width=0.62)
for i, (_, v) in enumerate(situ):
    axes[2].text(i, v + 2, f"{v:.0f}%", ha="center", fontsize=8, color=style.INK)
axes[2].set_xticks(range(3), [n for n, _ in situ], fontsize=7.5)
axes[2].set_title("Snapped under center", fontsize=9)
for ax in axes:
    ax.set_ylim(0, 100)
    ax.set_yticks([])
    ax.grid(False)
    ax.spines["left"].set_visible(False)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=1.2)
plt.show()








Figure 11.15: What lining up under center means in the 2025 NFL (regular season, FTN charting via nflverse). Left: how often the offense passed from each quarterback location. Middle: of the dropbacks from each location, the share that used a play-action fake. Right: the share of plays snapped under center, overall and on short yardage (1 yard or less to go) and inside the opponent’s 2-yard line. Under center is a running alignment, it is the home of play-action, and it is the default when the offense needs a yard.





Three things stand out, and they’re where the classic formations live now: two situations (short yardage and play-action) and one kind of team (the few that still build around a fullback).
Short yardage. With a yard or less to go, NFL offenses lined up under center on about 63% of plays in 2025, nearly twice their overall rate. When the offense needs one yard, the quick snap, the downhill handoff and the extra blockers of the I and the goal-line formation are worth more than the quarterback’s view of the coverage. (The sneak and the tush push start from under center too.)
Play-action. About four of every five dropbacks from under center in 2025 used a play fake, against about one in ten from the shotgun. That’s no coincidence. A quarterback who turns his back to the defense and puts the ball in a running back’s belly is selling the run with his whole body, and a two-back formation that usually runs is the best advertisement for a fake. The formation’s predictability is the bait. Play-Action, Bootlegs, and Screens shows what the fake does to the defense.
Notice the middle bar in each panel, too. The pistol isn’t under center, so the next chapter files it with the shotgun, but in 2025 it behaved like a cousin of this chapter’s formations: offenses passed on only about 29% of pistol snaps, and about half of those dropbacks used a play fake. That’s what you’d expect from an alignment built to keep the running back directly behind the quarterback: a downhill run and a believable fake, from a few yards back.
21 personnel. A few NFL teams still build around a fullback, and they’re among the most interesting offenses in the league.


Show the Python
t = (recent[recent.season == 2025].groupby("posteam")
     .agg(uc=("qb_loc", lambda x: (x == "U").mean() * 100), two=("two_back", lambda x: x.mean() * 100)))
lg = recent[recent.season == 2025]
lg_uc, lg_two = (lg.qb_loc == "U").mean() * 100, lg.two_back.mean() * 100
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.9))
hot = {"LA": "Rams", "SEA": "Seahawks", "BUF": "Bills", "SF": "49ers", "BAL": "Ravens", "MIA": "Dolphins",
       "NE": "Patriots", "WAS": "Commanders", "KC": "Chiefs", "CIN": "Bengals", "DET": "Lions", "PHI": "Eagles"}
ax.scatter(t.uc, t.two, s=[34 if k in hot else 18 for k in t.index],
           color=[style.OFFENSE if k in hot else style.BASELINE for k in t.index], zorder=3,
           edgecolor="white", lw=0.6)
OFFS = {"LA": (-0.8, 0.0, "right"), "SEA": (0.0, 1.2, "center"), "BUF": (0.0, -1.3, "center"),
        "SF": (-1.4, 0.0, "right"), "BAL": (0.9, 0.0, "left"), "MIA": (-0.9, 0.0, "right"),
        "NE": (0.0, 1.2, "center"), "WAS": (0.0, 1.0, "center"), "KC": (0.9, 0.0, "left"),
        "CIN": (0.0, -1.1, "center"), "DET": (0.9, 0.0, "left"), "PHI": (0.9, 0.0, "left")}
for k, name in hot.items():
    dx, dy, ha = OFFS[k]
    ax.text(t.loc[k, "uc"] + dx, t.loc[k, "two"] + dy, name, fontsize=7.5, ha=ha, va="center", color=style.INK)
ax.axvline(lg_uc, color=style.INK_2, lw=0.9, ls=(0, (4, 3)), zorder=1)
ax.axhline(lg_two, color=style.INK_2, lw=0.9, ls=(0, (4, 3)), zorder=1)
ax.text(lg_uc + 0.4, 34.6, f"league {lg_uc:.0f}%", fontsize=7, color=style.INK_2, va="top")
ax.text(63.5, lg_two + 0.5, f"league {lg_two:.0f}%", fontsize=7, color=style.INK_2, ha="right", va="bottom")
ax.set_xlim(4, 64)
ax.set_ylim(8, 35)
ax.set_xlabel("snapped under center (% of plays)", fontsize=8)
ax.set_ylabel("two or more backs (% of plays)", fontsize=8)
ax.tick_params(labelsize=8)
ax.set_title("Under center and two-back usage by team, 2025", fontsize=10)
plt.show()








Figure 11.16: Who still plays classic football: each NFL team’s 2025 share of plays snapped under center (across) against its share with two or more players in the backfield besides the quarterback, usually two backs (up). Dashed lines are the league rates. The Rams, Seahawks and Bills led the under-center revival; the Dolphins, Ravens, Seahawks, Bills, Patriots and 49ers used the most two-back sets. Regular season, runs and passes; FTN charting via nflverse.





The two axes don’t always go together, which is the interesting part. The Rams were the league’s most under-center team in 2025 (about 59% of plays) but used two backs only a little more than average; their under-center snaps were mostly one-back looks with two or three tight ends. The Dolphins were the opposite: more two-back plays than anyone, mostly from the shotgun and pistol. The teams in the top right, the Seahawks, Bills, 49ers and Patriots, with the Ravens just over the under-center line, are the ones still playing something close to classic football, a fullback and a tailback behind a quarterback under center, on a quarter of their snaps or more.






NoteFilm room: San Francisco 49ers, 2017–2025



Kyle Shanahan’s 49ers have been the NFL’s leading 21-personnel team for most of his tenure, with fullback Kyle Juszczyk (Personnel has the numbers). Much of it comes from the I and offset I: Juszczyk lines up behind the quarterback, leads on a linebacker or the edge defender on running plays, and on play-action slips out into the flat as the defense crashes on the run. In 2025 the 49ers were under center on about 46% of plays, well above the league’s 34%, and had two backs on the field on about a quarter.21
The 49ers’ version of the I isn’t the 1970s version, though. Juszczyk motions out of the backfield, lines up as a wing or in the slot, and returns to the I on the next play, so the defense can’t key on where he stands. The formation is classic; the way it’s used is modern.
What to notice: when the 49ers line up in the I, watch where the fullback’s path ends. His first steps are designed to look the same on the run and on the fake. If he hits someone, it’s a run; if he crosses the formation as if to block the backside end, brushes past him and keeps going to the flat, it’s the bootleg, and the defense has been fooled by its own expectations.








NoteFilm room: Baltimore Ravens 2024, Patrick Ricard and Derrick Henry



The 2024 Ravens (head coach John Harbaugh, offensive coordinator Todd Monken, an era that ended after 2025) paired Lamar Jackson with Derrick Henry, who ran for 1,921 yards, second in the league, behind Patrick Ricard, an undrafted defensive tackle from Maine turned 300-pound fullback.22 Baltimore had two or more backs on the field on about a quarter of its 2024 plays, against a league rate of about 18%. A defense built to stop Jackson’s passing sits in nickel; the Ravens line up with two backs, and the nickel back suddenly has a 300-pound fullback coming at him. If the defense answers with linebackers, Jackson throws over them: the personnel dilemma, delivered from a formation that has been around since the 1950s.
What to notice: in a classic two-back formation, find the fullback and do the count: blockers against defenders in the box. If the defense matched the count with a defensive back where a linebacker should be, the offense has the matchup it wanted; if it matched it with a linebacker, look for the throw over him.



The 2025 under-center revival
The shotgun’s share fell from 72% in 2023 to 66% in 2025, and FTN’s charting has offenses under center on 33.6% of plays in 2025, up from 27.3% in 2023.23 The reason is the same arms race that sent personnel heavier (Personnel told that half): defenses spent the early 2020s getting lighter and playing more two-deep safety looks to stop the pass, which left fewer big bodies near the line. Offenses answered by getting bigger and putting the quarterback back under center, where the run game has its best angles and play-action its best disguise. The offensive side of the ledger pushed the same way. Wide zone and play-action from under center, the Shanahan and McVay style, kept producing: in 2024 and 2025, dropbacks from under center averaged about +0.14 expected points per play against about +0.03 from the shotgun.24 (That gap flatters under center, whose passes come on downs when the defense is braced for a run, but that is exactly the point of the formation.) And the quarterbacks who run those offenses are comfortable under center. Sean McVay’s Rams were under center on about 59% of their 2025 snaps, the most in the league, and their quarterback, Matthew Stafford, was the league’s MVP. The champion Seahawks, under offensive coordinator Klint Kubiak in 2025, were second, at about 53%.
Whether the turn lasts depends on the defense’s answer, and in 2025 defenses were already answering by playing more base. The old formations didn’t come back because they were old. They came back because, for now, they’re the right answer to what defenses are doing. That’s the pattern of this entire book.

title: Classic Formations: I, Power I, Pro Set, Singleback, and Their Ancestors
section: The classic formations on one page
text:
The classic formations on one page
Here are all eleven, reduced to what you’ll actually see on a broadcast: the line, the quarterback and the backfield. The backfield is the fingerprint, so it’s what to memorize.


Show the Python
names = ["T-formation", "Pro set", "I-formation", "Offset I", "Power I", "Singleback", "Ace", "Wishbone",
         "Flexbone", "Wing-T", "Goal line"]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 4, figsize=(6.6, 4.2))
for ax, name in zip(axes.flat, names + ["Shotgun"]):
    pl = SHOTGUN if name == "Shotgun" else players_of(name)
    pl = [q for q in pl if abs(q.w) <= 8.0]
    p = ring_by_body(Play(pl, None, los=35, to_go=None))
    p.draw(ax=ax, lateral=(-8.6, 8.6), window=(-8.6, 1.6), title=False)
    hide_yard_numbers(ax)
    sub = "11 · gun" if name == "Shotgun" else FORMS[name][0]
    ax.set_title(f"{name}  ({sub})", fontsize=7.6, color=style.INK, loc="left", pad=2)
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.01, right=0.99, top=0.95, bottom=0.01, hspace=0.32, wspace=0.06)
plt.show()








Figure 11.17: The eleven classic backfields, with the shotgun for comparison (last panel). Only the players within about eight yards of the ball are shown: the line, the quarterback (Q), the backs (aqua rings) and any tight ends or wings (gold rings). Read them back to front: under center or not, how many backs, stacked, side by side or offset. Two spots look identical here and differ only in who stands there: the Wing-T’s wingback (W, a running back) and the goal-line set’s wing (H, a tight end). On a broadcast the picture can’t tell you which; the personnel can.






What the backfield looks like on TV
Every diagram in this chapter is drawn from above, the way coaches draw them and the way the All-22 film shows them. The broadcast mostly isn’t. The main sideline camera sits high on one side of the field, looking across it, so the direction the offense is moving runs left to right across your screen and the width of the field is squashed into the up-down direction. That flips the picture in a way worth knowing before you try to name a backfield live.


Show the Python
CAM = np.array([-1.0, -52.0, 24.0])      # (d, w, height) in yards: high on the offense's left sideline
LOOK = np.array([-2.5, 0.0, 0.0])


def tv_project(pts):
    """Pinhole projection of (d, w, z) points onto the camera's screen; returns screen (x, y), depth."""
    f = LOOK - CAM
    f /= np.linalg.norm(f)
    r = np.cross(f, [0.0, 0.0, 1.0])
    r /= np.linalg.norm(r)
    u = np.cross(r, f)
    v = np.atleast_2d(pts) - CAM
    depth = v @ f
    return np.c_[(v @ r) / depth, (v @ u) / depth], depth


def tv_panel(ax, name):
    pl = [q for q in players_of(name) if abs(q.w) <= 9.0]
    for d in range(-15, 11, 5):                      # yard lines, and the line of scrimmage
        xy, _ = tv_project(np.array([[d, -20.0, 0.0], [d, 20.0, 0.0]]))
        ax.plot(xy[:, 0], xy[:, 1], color=style.BASELINE, lw=0.8, zorder=1)
    xy, _ = tv_project(np.array([[0.0, -20.0, 0.0], [0.0, 20.0, 0.0]]))
    ax.plot(xy[:, 0], xy[:, 1], color=style.OFFENSE, lw=1.2, zorder=1)
    cols = []
    for q in pl:
        foot, dep = tv_project(np.array([q.d, q.w, 0.0]))
        head, _ = tv_project(np.array([q.d, q.w, 2.0]))
        cols.append((dep[0], q, foot[0], head[0]))
    for dep, q, foot, head in sorted(cols, key=lambda c: -c[0]):      # far players first
        wid = 0.75 * (head[1] - foot[1]) / 2.0
        ring = RB_RING if q.pos in ("RB", "FB") else TE_RING if q.pos == "TE" else "white"
        ax.add_patch(FancyBboxPatch((foot[0] - wid / 2, foot[1]), wid, head[1] - foot[1],
                                    boxstyle=f"round,pad=0,rounding_size={wid * 0.45}", fc=style.OFFENSE,
                                    ec=ring, lw=1.8 if ring != "white" else 0.6, zorder=3))
        if q.label:
            ax.text(foot[0], foot[1] + 0.62 * (head[1] - foot[1]), q.label, ha="center", va="center",
                    fontsize=6.5, color="white", fontweight="bold", zorder=4)
    ax.set_facecolor(style.TURF)
    xs = [c[2][0] for c in cols]
    ys = [c[2][1] for c in cols] + [c[3][1] for c in cols]
    return (min(xs), max(xs), min(ys), max(ys))


def tv_frame(ax, ext, title):
    x0, x1, y0, y1 = ext
    padx, pady = 0.12 * (x1 - x0), 0.25 * (y1 - y0)
    ax.set_xlim(x0 - padx, x1 + padx)
    ax.set_ylim(y0 - pady, y1 + pady)
    ax.set_xticks([])
    ax.set_yticks([])
    for sp in ax.spines.values():
        sp.set_visible(False)
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=9.5, fontweight="bold", color=style.INK, loc="left")


fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 2.4))
exts = [tv_panel(ax, n) for ax, n in zip(axes, ["I-formation", "Pro set"])]
ext = (min(e[0] for e in exts), max(e[1] for e in exts), min(e[2] for e in exts), max(e[3] for e in exts))
for ax, t in zip(axes, ["I-formation: a row", "Pro set: a stack"]):
    tv_frame(ax, ext, t)
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.01, right=0.99, top=0.88, bottom=0.03, wspace=0.05)
plt.show()








Figure 11.18: The same backfields as the broadcast’s sideline camera sees them (a simple perspective sketch: camera high on the offense’s left sideline, near the line of scrimmage, offense moving left to right; bodies are drawn as plain columns). The offensive line, which runs across the field, is squashed into a column at the right of each panel. Left: the I-formation. The stacked backs, one directly behind another from above, become a row strung out across the screen: quarterback, fullback, tailback, each farther from the line. Right: the pro set. The side-by-side backs are at the same depth, so they stand at the same spot left to right, one nearer the camera (lower on the screen and bigger) and one farther (higher and smaller), and they can hide behind each other. From the sideline, an I looks like a row and split backs look like a stack.





So on the live shot, a row of helmets behind the quarterback is an I, one helmet seven yards back is a singleback, and two backs stacked one above the other on screen are split backs. An offset fullback is the second helmet sitting a little above or below the tailback’s. The end-zone replay or the skycam behind the offense shows the backfield the way this chapter draws it; use it to check your call.

title: Classic Formations: I, Power I, Pro Set, Singleback, and Their Ancestors
text:
Watch for it on Sunday






TipWatch for it: name that formation



For ten snaps in a row, before the ball is snapped, say three things out loud and then a name.

Under center or gun? Look at the quarterback’s hands. Under center means this chapter’s formations; pistol or shotgun means the next chapter’s.
One back or two (or three)? Count the players strung out behind the quarterback (on the sideline camera, a row is an I and a stack is split backs). Name the shape by where they stand: a tight end directly behind the quarterback still makes it an I. A tight end off the line beside a tackle (an H-back) is a tight end for the personnel count.
Stacked, split or offset? Two backs in a line is an I; side by side is a pro set; one a yard to the side is an offset I. Three backs is a Power I, a wishbone or a T, and in the NFL that means short yardage.
Where are the tight ends? One on each side with one back is an ace. Three tight ends and no receivers is goal line.
Count. Blockers (linemen, tight ends and any back who isn’t getting the ball) against the defenders in the box. One more defender than blockers says the defense is braced for the run.
Name it, then guess. Under center with two backs: lean run (about three plays in four), and if it’s a pass, expect a play fake. Under center with one back: still run-leaning (about three passes in eight in neutral situations) and still play-action heavy. Note which way an offset fullback points and whether the play went that way.
Log it. Add a formation column to your prediction log next to personnel: “21, I, UC” or “12, ace, UC.” After ten snaps, check how often your run/pass guess was right from under center versus from the gun.

title: Classic Formations: I, Power I, Pro Set, Singleback, and Their Ancestors
text:
Predict the play






TipPredict the play 1: the offset fullback



Second-and-4 at your own 40, first quarter, tied. The offense has come out like this against a base 4-3:


Show the Python
off = players_of("Offset I")
off = [q.moved(w=-1.6) if q.key == "FB" else q for q in off]
dfn = base43(off, fix={"MIKE": dict(w=0.6), "SAM": dict(d=4.0, w=6.6)})
q1 = ring_by_body(Play(off, dfn, los=50, to_go=4))
fld = q1.draw(lateral=(-17.5, 17.5), window=(-9.0, 14.5), title=False)
hide_yard_numbers(fld.ax)
plt.show()








Figure 11.19: Drill 1: second-and-4. Offense: tight end Y (gold ring) on the right, backs ringed aqua, receivers X and Z. Defense: E = end, T = tackle, S/M/W = linebackers, C = cornerbacks, FS/SS = safeties.





What formation and personnel is this? Run or pass? And which side is the fullback set up to lead to?






TipAnswer





An offset I, offset weak (a “Weak I”), with 21 personnel. Two backs (fullback and tailback) and one tight end, so two receivers. The fullback is offset to the left, away from the tight end: that’s “weak.”
Run or pass: lean run. Two backs stacked behind an under-center quarterback ran about three times in four in neutral situations, and second-and-4 is a comfortable running down. If it’s a pass, expect a play fake.
Which side: the left. The offset fullback is already behind the left guard, in position to lead on a weak-side run (an iso into the bubble over the Will, as in the iso diagram) or to pick up a blitzing linebacker from that side on play-action. Whether this offense actually runs toward its offset is a tendency, not a rule, and smart offenses break it on purpose. There’s no league-wide number to look up: the public charting data records how many backs there are, not which way the fullback is offset; that takes tracking data (Tracking Data and the Big Data Bowl works with it). Log it for the team you’re watching instead.











TipPredict the play 2: second-and-goal at the 1



The offense has the ball on the defense’s 1-yard line, second down. It sends in three tight ends, a fullback and a tailback; the defense answers with its goal-line package.


Show the Python
q2 = ring_by_body(Play(players_of("Goal line"), gl_def, los=109, to_go=None))
fld = q2.draw(lateral=(-13.0, 13.0), window=(-9.0, 8.5), title=False)
hide_yard_numbers(fld.ax)
plt.show()








Figure 11.20: Drill 2: second-and-goal at the 1. The offense is in its goal-line formation; the tight end H is a wing behind and outside Y. The defense has five linemen, three linebackers and three defensive backs; its two safeties (SS, FS) are only about four yards deep.





Count the blockers and the defenders in the box. Who wins the count, and so how does the offense try to score? If it throws, who is the likeliest target?






TipAnswer





The defense wins the count, eleven to nine, and at the goal line it always will: nobody has to stay deep. The offense’s blockers are the five linemen, the three tight ends and the fullback; the quarterback and the tailback don’t block.
So the offense doesn’t try to block everyone. It tries to win one gap. Expect a run aimed at a single spot with extra bodies there (a double team and the fullback leading into the hole) or a quarterback sneak behind the center. A tailback who needs one yard only has to fall forward.
If it throws: a play fake and a tight end, because eleven defenders committed to the run is exactly what the fake exploits. The likeliest target is the wing (H) or the tight end on the side away from the fake: he blocks for a count, as he would on a run, then slips into the end zone while the linebackers and safeties step up. Watch the two safeties: if both crash at the snap, the tight end is alone.











TipPredict the play 3: the I against eight in the box



First-and-10 at midfield, second quarter. The offense is in the I with 21 personnel. The defense, in its base 4-3, has walked the strong safety down beside the linebackers, leaving one safety deep.


Show the Python
off = players_of("I-formation")
dfn = base43(off, shell="single_high", fix={"SS": dict(d=5.5, w=8.8), "SAM": dict(d=4.0, w=5.6),
                                            "MIKE": dict(w=0.6), "FS": dict(d=13.5)})
q3 = ring_by_body(Play(off, dfn, los=60, to_go=10))
q3.highlight("SS", "FS", color=style.DEFENSE)
fld = q3.draw(lateral=(-17.5, 17.5), window=(-9.0, 16.0), title=False)
hide_yard_numbers(fld.ax)
plt.show()








Figure 11.21: Drill 3: I-formation (21 personnel) against a base 4-3 with the strong safety (SS) walked down outside the Sam linebacker on the tight end’s side, leaving one deep safety (FS) in the middle of the field. The cornerbacks (C) are about seven yards off the two receivers.





Do the count. Why did the defense bring the safety down, and what is the offense likely to try?






TipAnswer





The count is eight against seven. The offense has seven blockers (five linemen, the tight end and the fullback). In the box the defense has four linemen, three linebackers and the strong safety: eight. The I’s whole advantage was a hat on a hat with a lead blocker; the safety takes that away by giving the defense one more player than the offense can block. It came down because the formation says run.
What the offense is likely to try: the run is still the most common call. If it runs, it often runs away from the extra man, to the left here: the safety walked down on the tight end’s side, so a run the other way makes him chase across the formation, and he arrives late. But this is also the picture play-action was invented for. Single-high, with the safety in the middle, means each cornerback is alone on his side, with no safety beside him. If the defense is playing man coverage behind the safety (Cover 1), that’s a one-on-one outside; if it’s zone with the corners dropping deep (Cover 3), the fake pulls the linebackers up and opens the window behind them for a crossing route. Either way, the run fake is what moves the eight defenders.

title: Classic Formations: I, Power I, Pro Set, Singleback, and Their Ancestors
text:
Takeaways

The classic formations are defined by the backfield. Read them back to front: quarterback under center or not, how many backs, and whether they’re stacked (I), side by side (pro set), offset (offset I) or three wide (T, wishbone, Power I).
Each formation is an answer to a problem, and every answer has a price. The I gives the tailback a lead blocker and a running start but is slow to the edge and obvious; the pro set is balanced and quick-hitting but has no deep tailback; the singleback and ace trade the fullback for a tight end or receiver; the wishbone and flexbone are built to read a defender instead of blocking him; the Wing-T lives on misdirection; the goal-line formation trades all its space for blockers.
They’re one family. The T’s three backs were stacked (I), split (pro set), spread (flexbone), scattered for misdirection (Wing-T) or traded for receivers (singleback). Knowing the tree helps you name the shape.
Count, every time. Blockers (everyone but the quarterback and the ball carrier) against defenders in the box. A hat on a hat favors the run; one extra defender is the defense’s answer; at the goal line the defense always wins the count, so the offense picks one gap instead.
Formation follows personnel. 21 usually means an I, offset I or pro set; 12 an ace; 11 a singleback or a shotgun look; three backs or three tight ends mean short yardage. Name the shape by where players stand, the personnel by who they are.
Two-back, under-center football faded because passing won, and it survives where running and faking matter most. In 2025, under center meant run about 70% of the time, play-action on about four of five dropbacks, and it was the default on short yardage. The under-center share rose to about a third of plays as offenses got bigger against lighter defenses.

text:
Connections
Builds on: Personnel (who is on the field, and why 21 and 12 personnel matter), Formation Rules and the Language of Alignment (seven on the line, the X/Y/Z letters, under center, shotgun and pistol, strong and weak side), and The Twenty-Two (running backs, fullbacks and tight ends).
Sets up: Spread Formations (the shotgun branch of the tree), A First Look at Defense (the box and base defense, the defense’s answer to these formations), and Motion and Shifts as Weapons (what the H-back’s motion becomes). Later: The Language of the Run Game and Gap and Power Runs (the lead block, iso, counter trey and Lombardi’s sweep, drawn block by block), Option Football (the split-T, the veer and the triple option from the wishbone and flexbone), Perimeter Runs and Misdirection (the Wing-T’s series), Play-Action, Bootlegs, and Screens, and the history in The Single Wing to the Scoring Drought, 1978 and the Passing Revolution and The College Laboratory (the wishbone and flexbone lineage).
Case studies: the Shanahan tree (the 49ers’ fullback and the under-center revival) and the Ravens with Lamar Jackson.






NoteGo deeper




Tim Layden, Blood, Sweat and Chalk (2010): readable chapters on the T, the wishbone, the one-back offense and the Wing-T, built from interviews with the coaches who drew them.
Vince Lombardi with W. C. Heinz, Run to Daylight! (1963): a week inside the Packers, with Lombardi explaining his sweep in his own words.
Chris B. Brown, The Art of Smart Football (2015) and his Smart Football site (https://smartfootball.com): essays on the I, the flexbone and the shotgun’s takeover.

“Split-T formation,” Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Split-T_formation (Don Faurot, Missouri, first used in 1941; “the offensive line was spread out over almost twice as much ground”; the quarterback ran toward the unblocked defender and pitched to the trailing halfback if he closed; “what may have been the first option offense in football, which was a precursor of the wishbone, veer, and some modern run-first spread offenses”).↩︎
“Veer,” Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Veer (Bill Yeoman ran it at Houston “beginning in the mid-1960s”; a triple option with a dive course, a pitch course and a lead blocker); “Wishbone formation,” Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wishbone_formation (Bellard “tried to merge his old high school tactics with Stallings’ triple option out of the Slot-I formation and Homer Rice’s variations of the Veer, an offensive formation created by Bill Yeoman”).↩︎
“Elroy Hirsch,” Pro Football Hall of Fame: https://www.profootballhof.com/players/elroy-hirsch/ (66 catches, 1,495 yards and 17 touchdown catches in 1951); “Elroy Hirsch,” Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elroy_Hirsch (Shaughnessy, the Rams’ head coach, moved Hirsch to end after he signed in 1949; the Rams often split him wide and later moved him permanently to end, “the first flanker”; the article also notes the dispute, since Don Hutson’s Packers and the 1940s Bears and Washington had split backs wide before).↩︎

title: Spread Formations: 2x2, Trips, Bunch, Empty, and the Condensed Revolution
text:
What makes a formation “spread”
Third-and-6, midway through the second quarter. The offense breaks the huddle and the running back doesn’t stop behind the quarterback. He keeps jogging, out past the right tackle, and settles in the slot just inside the tight end, who is himself standing ten yards from the ball. Nobody is left beside the quarterback. Five players are spread across the width of the field, and the defense starts to move: a linebacker drifts out after the running back, a safety creeps down toward the line, a cornerback points and shouts. The analyst says “empty set, they’re going to make the defense show its hand.” Two series later the same offense lines up with all three of its wide receivers squeezed in tight, the nearest one barely four yards outside the tackle, and the analyst says “look how condensed they are.” Same team, same players, opposite pictures. This chapter explains both: what the spread formations are, why spreading players across the field makes a defense commit, and why so many of the best NFL offenses then pulled their receivers back in.
You’ll be able to…
Three ideas from Formation Rules and the Language of Alignment run through this chapter, so here they are in one line each. Seven players must be on the line of scrimmage, and only the two at the ends of that line can catch a pass; everyone else is a yard or more behind it, “off the line.” The letters name spots, not body types: X is the receiver on the line on one side, Z the receiver off the line on the other, Y usually the tight end, H a slot receiver or second back. A split is how far a receiver lines up from the ball or the nearest lineman, and a slot receiver is one who lines up between the outside receiver and the line. And remember the last chapter’s rule: personnel is who is on the field. Formation, this chapter’s subject, is where they stand.
A formation is a picture of where the eleven offensive players stand at the snap. For most of football history that picture was compact: the receivers lined up a few yards outside the tackles, the quarterback was under center, and two backs stood behind him. The classic formations, the I, the pro set and the singleback, are all built that way, and they are built to run the ball with as many blockers near it as possible.
A spread formation does the opposite. It takes the players who can catch passes and spreads them out across the width of the field, toward both sidelines, usually with the quarterback a few yards back in the shotgun so he can see it all. Nothing about the personnel has to change. The same eleven players can line up either way:
Show the Python
tight = check_legal(line5() + [P("QB", "QB", UC, 0, "Q"), P("RB", "RB", TB_D, 0, "R"),
                               P("Y", "TE", LINE_D, TE_W), P("H", "WR", OFF_BALL, WING_W + 0.4),
                               P("Z", "WR", OFF_BALL, 10.5), P("X", "WR", LINE_D, -9.0)])
d_tight = [D("WDE", "DE", 1.0, -5.0, "E"), D("WDT", "DT", 1.0, -0.7, "T"), D("SDT", "DT", 1.0, 2.35, "T"),
           D("SDE", "DE", 1.0, 5.7, "E"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -2.6), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, 1.4),
           D("SS", "SS", 6.8, 3.9), D("NB", "NB", 4.0, 8.2, "$"), D("LCB", "CB", 6.0, -9.5),
           D("RCB", "CB", 6.5, 11.5), D("FS", "FS", 13.0, -1.0)]
spread = form("2x2")
d_spread = [D("WDE", "DE", 1.0, -4.6, "E"), D("WDT", "DT", 1.0, -0.7, "T"), D("SDT", "DT", 1.0, 2.35, "T"),
            D("SDE", "DE", 1.0, 4.6, "E"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -2.0), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, 2.0),
            D("NB", "NB", 5.0, -8.2, "$"), D("SS", "SS", 7.5, 7.6), D("LCB", "CB", 7.0, -15.5),
            D("RCB", "CB", 7.0, 15.5), D("FS", "FS", 13.0, 0.0)]
LAT, WIN = (-18, 18), (-8.5, 14.6)
fig, axes = grid(1, 2, LAT, WIN)
for ax, off, dfn, head in [(axes[0, 0], tight, d_tight, "Tight"), (axes[0, 1], spread, d_spread, "Spread (2x2)")]:
    p = ring_bodies(Play(off, dfn, los=40, to_go=None))
    fld = p.draw(ax=ax, lateral=LAT, window=WIN, title=False)
    hide_yard_numbers(ax)
    shade_box(ax, p, fld)
    put(ax, p, fld, f"{box_count(p)} in the box", 9.8, -9.5, size=8,
        weight="bold", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK)
    title(ax, head)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()








Figure 12.1: The same 11 personnel (one back, R, aqua ring; one tight end, Y, gold ring; three wide receivers, X, Z and H), lined up two ways against the same nickel defense. Left: a tight formation, receivers close to the line; the defense can keep seven players in the box (shaded: the area near the ball where run defenders stand). Right: a spread 2x2, two receivers on each side out toward the sidelines; defenders have to go with them, and only six are left in the box. Offense: Q = quarterback; the five linemen are unlettered (the center is the middle one). Defense: E = end, T = tackle, M and W = linebackers, $ = nickel back (the fifth defensive back), C = cornerback, FS and SS = safeties.
Look at what the spread did to the defense without anybody running a step. On the left, the defense can keep seven players in the box: the area near the ball, roughly between the ends of the offensive line and within about seven yards of it, where the defenders who stop runs stand. (The full definition, and the habit of counting the box before every snap, belong to A First Look at Defense.) On the right, the offense has put four players out toward the sidelines. Each of them is a threat to catch a pass, so each needs a defender somewhere near him, and those defenders have to come from somewhere. They come out of the box. Now there are six.
That is the first and most basic reason spread formations exist. The field is 53⅓ yards wide, and a spread formation makes the defense defend all of it. Every defender who leaves the middle to cover a receiver out wide is a defender who isn’t there to tackle a runner or to rush the quarterback.
There are three more reasons, and they are what the rest of this chapter is about.
Spreading out makes the defense declare itself. When receivers stand close together, defenders can stand close together too, in a clump that hides what they plan to do. When the receivers spread out, the defenders have to spread with them, and where they go is information. A cornerback who follows a receiver all the way across the field is probably playing man-to-man, each defender assigned to one receiver, rather than zone, each defender assigned to an area of the field (both are introduced properly in A First Look at Defense). A safety who walks down toward a slot receiver has told you he isn’t going to be deep. A linebacker who stays in the box has told you somebody outside is uncovered or covered by someone farther away. The quarterback reads all of that before the snap. So can you.
Spreading out creates space. A receiver near the sideline with one defender in front of him and nobody else within fifteen yards is in a one-on-one race. A quick throw to him, or a run through a box with six defenders instead of eight, gives the ball carrier room to make one man miss.
Spreading out simplifies the quarterback’s job. With receivers spaced widely, each pass-catcher occupies his own patch of grass, and the quarterback can see who is open by seeing where the defenders aren’t.

title: Spread Formations: 2x2, Trips, Bunch, Empty, and the Condensed Revolution
text:
ImportantWhy it exists



Spread formations exist to make the defense cover the whole field and tell you how it plans to do it. They trade blockers near the ball for space away from it. What the offense gives up is the old advantages of tight formations: extra blockers at the point of attack (the spot where the run is aimed), a quarterback under center who can hand off and fake quickly, and a run game that can simply outnumber the defense. A spread offense can still run, often very well, but it runs by making the box lighter, not by bringing more bodies to it.



Formation, not philosophy
A spread formation is a picture at the snap: receivers out wide. A spread offense is a whole philosophy, born mostly in college, built on those pictures. Every NFL team uses spread formations every week; only some would call their offense a spread offense. This chapter is about the pictures. The philosophy has its own chapter in The College Laboratory, and the systems that grew out of it, like the Air Raid, are installed in Part 4.






CautionCommon misconception



“Spread means pass.” Spreading out makes the defense lighter in the box, which is good for running. Many college spread offenses were built to run first, and in the NFL, 11-personnel formations with three receivers spread out are only slightly pass-leaning (about 56% pass in neutral situations, as Personnel showed). The one spread formation that really does mean “pass,” the empty backfield, is the exception, and we’ll measure it below.

title: Spread Formations: 2x2, Trips, Bunch, Empty, and the Condensed Revolution
section: The question every spread formation asks
text:
The question every spread formation asks
Spread formations work because they force the defense to answer a question it would rather not answer. Here is the cleanest version of it. The offense lines up in a 2x2 (two receivers on each side). On the right, the slot receiver is the tight end, Y. The defense has a cornerback on each outside receiver, a fifth defensive back (the nickel back, $) on the left slot, and two safeties deep. Who covers Y?


Show the Python
def dilemma(w_out):
    dfn = [D("WDE", "DE", 1.0, -4.6, "E"), D("WDT", "DT", 1.0, -0.7, "T"), D("SDT", "DT", 1.0, 2.35, "T"),
           D("SDE", "DE", 1.0, 4.6, "E"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, -1.4),
           D("WILL", "WILL", 4.3, 7.0) if w_out else D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, 2.4),
           D("NB", "NB", 5.0, -8.2, "$"), D("LCB", "CB", 7.0, -15.5), D("RCB", "CB", 7.0, 15.5),
           D("FS", "FS", 12.0, -9.0), D("SS", "SS", 12.0, 9.0)]
    p = ring_bodies(Play(form("2x2"), dfn, los=40, to_go=None))
    p.highlight("WILL", color=style.DEFENSE)
    if w_out:
        p.handoff("RB", t=0.5)
        p.run("RB", [(1.5, 2.0), (6.0, 2.4), (10.5, 1.6)], delay=0.15)
    else:
        p.route("Y", r.hitch(6))
        p.pass_to("Y", t=1.3)
    return p


LAT, WIN = (-18, 18), (-7.5, 14.0)
fig, axes = grid(1, 2, LAT, WIN)
for ax, w_out, head in [(axes[0, 0], False, "W stays inside"), (axes[0, 1], True, "W walks out")]:
    p = dilemma(w_out)
    fld = p.draw(ax=ax, lateral=LAT, window=WIN, title=False)
    hide_yard_numbers(ax)
    shade_box(ax, p, fld)
    n = box_count(p)
    put(ax, p, fld, f"{n} in the box", 9.6, -1.0, size=7.6, weight="bold", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK)
    put(ax, p, fld, "run it" if w_out else "throw to Y", 9.6, -10.0 if w_out else 12.6, size=7.6,
        weight="bold", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK)
    title(ax, head)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()








Figure 12.2: The slot question. Same offense, same defense, one decision: what does the linebacker W do about the slot receiver Y? Left: W stays in the box. The box has six defenders, but Y has nobody within seven yards of him, so the quarterback throws him a quick pass: a hitch, six yards up the field and a turn back to the ball. Right: W walks out over Y to take that throw away. Now the box has five defenders against five offensive linemen, and the offense hands the ball off. Shaded rectangle = the box; the safeties (FS, SS) are deep, 12 yards off the ball.





If the linebacker stays inside, the box is solid against the run but the tight end is alone, and a five-yard throw to him is as easy as a handoff. If he walks out, he takes the throw away and leaves five defenders in the box to face five blockers. Every lineman now has someone to block, and the first defender the running back has to beat is a safety twelve yards away. The defense can’t be right both ways, because one player can’t stand in two places. The offense watches where he stands and does the other thing.
That defender, the one stuck between the box and a slot receiver, is so important that he has his own names. A defender who stands halfway between the end of the line and the slot is “at the apex” (the point of the triangle the three of them make), and the man outside the box but inside a receiver is the overhang defender, because he hangs over the edge of the box. The passing game builds whole plays around reading him. (The name for a defender with two jobs and time for only one is a conflict defender; you’ll meet him again in RPOs, run-pass options in which the quarterback decides after the snap whether to hand off or throw, and which turn this exact question into a play.) For now, notice that the formation created the question. In the tight formation there was no slot receiver, so there was no question.
The defense isn’t helpless, of course. It can bring a safety down to help, which leaves less help deep. It can play a coverage in which the outside cornerback and the linebacker trade responsibilities. It can disguise its answer and change it at the snap. Those are the defense’s moves, and Parts 5 to 7 are full of them. But every one of them costs something somewhere else on the field, and the spread’s whole idea is to make the defense pay that cost on every snap.






NoteMadden vs. real life



In Madden, the defense lines itself up: you pick a play, and the computer slides every defender into place against whatever formation the offense shows. Real defenses have to do that themselves, in about the ten seconds between the offense breaking the huddle and the snap. They do it with rules agreed in advance: “against 2x2, the nickel takes the slot to the field and the Will takes the other one; against trips, the safety rotates down.” The middle linebacker and the safeties shout those adjustments to everyone else, and they all have to hear and agree. That’s why offenses love formations the defense hasn’t prepared for, and why a defense that sees a formation it didn’t practice sometimes ends up with two players covering one receiver and nobody on another.

title: Spread Formations: 2x2, Trips, Bunch, Empty, and the Condensed Revolution
text:
Counting receivers: #1, #2, #3
You met the coaches’ counting system in Formation Rules, and every formation name in this chapter is built on it, so here it is again with a name. Receiver numbering counts the receivers from the sideline in, separately on each side of the ball. The widest receiver on a side is #1, the next one in is #2, the next is #3. It doesn’t matter whether he’s a wide receiver, a tight end or a running back who has lined up out wide: if he’s out of the backfield, he gets a number. A back standing beside or behind the quarterback isn’t counted until he leaves.
Why number them instead of using names? Because the defense doesn’t care who the receivers are; it cares where they are. A coverage rule like “the nickel back takes #2” works against any formation and any personnel. The numbers also give a formation its name: two on each side is “2x2,” three on one side and one on the other is “3x1.” The side with more receivers is the passing strength you met in the last chapter.
Two wrinkles, because defenses don’t all count the same way. Many coverage systems give an offset back (one standing to one side of the quarterback) the next number on his side before the snap, #3 beside two receivers, because he can release there in a step. And the count is redone after every motion: a receiver who motions across the formation changes both sides’ numbers, so the player who was “#2 right” in the huddle can be “#3 left” at the snap. That re-counting, under a play clock, is one reason offenses motion so much.
Here are the four formations you’ll see most, all with the same 11 personnel:


Show the Python
fig, axes = grid(2, 2, PLATE_LAT, PLATE_WIN, extra=0.42)
fig.set_size_inches(6.6, fig.get_size_inches()[1] + 0.3)
plate(axes[0, 0], "2x2", "2x2 (doubles)", "2 + 2")
plate(axes[0, 1], "3x1", "3x1 (trips)", "1 + 3")
plate(axes[1, 0], "trey", "3x1 with the TE attached (trey)", "1 + 3")
plate(axes[1, 1], "empty", "Empty (3x2)", "2 + 3, nobody in the backfield")
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.01, right=0.99, top=0.92, bottom=0.12, hspace=0.55, wspace=0.05)
ring_legend(fig)
plt.show()








Figure 12.3: The core spread formations, all from the same 11 personnel (one back, R; one tight end, Y; three wide receivers, X, Z and H) with the quarterback (Q) in the shotgun. The numbers count each side’s receivers from the sideline in; the back beside the quarterback isn’t counted. Top left: 2x2, two on each side. Top right: 3x1 (trips), three detached receivers on the right and X alone on the left. Bottom left: the same 3x1 count with the tight end attached to the line, which many teams call ‘trey’ instead of trips. Bottom right: empty, the back has left the backfield, so all five receivers are out, three to one side and two to the other (3x2).





The names vary by team. One staff’s “Doubles” is another’s “Deuce” or “Spread”; “Trips” is also “Trio,” “Tre” or “Triangle,” and whether the tight end attached to the line makes it “trips” or “trey” depends on whose playbook you’re reading. The counting doesn’t vary, which is why this book uses the numbers.






CautionCommon misconception



“Trips means three wide receivers.” It means three receivers on one side, whatever their position. In the plate above, the third receiver in trips is a tight end, and in empty the third man on the right is the running back. Personnel counts bodies; formations count spots. When the broadcast says “11 personnel, trips right,” that’s two separate facts: who is on the field, and where three of them are standing.

title: Spread Formations: 2x2, Trips, Bunch, Empty, and the Condensed Revolution
text:
2x2: balance
A 2x2 formation, also called doubles, has two receivers on each side of the ball. In the most common NFL version the outside receivers (#1s, X and Z) stand on the line near the sidelines and the inside receivers (#2s, the slots) stand off the line, a few yards inside them. The slots must be off the line: if a slot receiver stood on the line, the outside receiver would be “covered” (no longer at the end of the line) and couldn’t legally catch a pass. That’s the covered receiver rule, and it’s why you’ll almost always see a slot receiver a step behind the receiver outside him.
The 2x2’s virtue is balance. The defense can’t tell from the alignment which side the play is going to, because the two sides look alike. The offense can run the same route combination to both sides, called a “mirrored” concept, and let the quarterback pick whichever side the defense covers worse. Or it can run two different combinations and pick based on what the defense shows. Against a defense with two deep safeties, a 2x2 asks each safety to help on his own side, two receivers apiece, and a defense that wants to bring an extra defender into the box has to decide which side gets less help.
What 2x2 gives up is concentration. Because the formation is balanced, the defense can be balanced too: it can play the same coverage to both sides with the same number of defenders, and nothing about the alignment forces it to shift. The formations that follow all trade some of that balance for an advantage somewhere specific.

title: Spread Formations: 2x2, Trips, Bunch, Empty, and the Condensed Revolution
text:
3x1: the overload
Put three receivers on one side and one on the other, and you have a 3x1 formation, almost universally called trips. It’s the formation of the opening play in What a Play Really Is, “Gun Trips Right,” and it’s one of the most common pictures in the NFL.
Trips does two things at once. On the three-receiver side, the trips side, it puts more receivers than the defense normally has defenders, so the defense has to send help. On the other side, the backside, it leaves one receiver, often the offense’s best, alone with one cornerback.
To see the problem, you need a way to count a side. Here’s the one this book uses, every time:

Count the receivers on that side (#1, #2, #3).
Count the underneath defenders who could cover them: everyone on that side who stands outside the box, including an apex or overhang defender walked out toward a slot. Defenders inside the box don’t count; they’re there for the run.
Note the deep safety on that side separately, as help over the top (“+ safety”). He’s too deep to stop a quick throw, but he matters on anything thrown down the field.

If step 1 beats step 2, the offense has a numbers advantage underneath, and a quick throw to that side is waiting. The defense has to choose which side’s problem to solve:


Show the Python
def trips_d(rotate):
    common = [D("WDE", "DE", 1.0, -4.6, "E"), D("WDT", "DT", 1.0, -0.7, "T"), D("SDT", "DT", 1.0, 2.35, "T"),
              D("SDE", "DE", 1.0, 4.6, "E"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, -0.6),
              D("LCB", "CB", 7.0, -15.5), D("RCB", "CB", 7.0, 15.5), D("NB", "NB", 5.0, 11.6, "$")]
    if rotate:
        return common + [D("WILL", "WILL", 4.4, 6.6), D("SS", "SS", 7.5, 9.2), D("FS", "FS", 12.0, -9.0)]
    return common + [D("WILL", "WILL", 4.4, 6.6), D("SS", "SS", 12.0, 9.5), D("FS", "FS", 12.0, -9.0)]


LAT, WIN = (-18, 18), (-7.4, 16.5)
fig, axes = grid(1, 2, LAT, WIN)
for ax, rot, head in [(axes[0, 0], False, "Stay balanced"), (axes[0, 1], True, "Rotate to trips")]:
    p = ring_bodies(Play(form("3x1"), trips_d(rot), los=40, to_go=None))
    if rot:
        p.drop("FS", (14.0, 0.5))
        p.highlight("X", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK)
    fld = p.draw(ax=ax, lateral=LAT, window=WIN, title=False)
    hide_yard_numbers(ax)
    if rot:
        put(ax, p, fld, "X alone:\none-on-one", -4.8, -11.5, size=7.2, weight="bold", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK)
        put(ax, p, fld, "3 receivers vs\n4 defenders", -4.8, 11.5, size=7.2)
    else:
        put(ax, p, fld, "1 receiver vs\nC + safety", -4.8, -11.5, size=7.2)
        put(ax, p, fld, "3 receivers vs\n3 + safety", -4.8, 11.5, size=7.2)
    title(ax, head)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()








Figure 12.4: Trips makes the defense choose. Left: the defense stays balanced with two deep safeties. Counted the three-step way, the three receivers on the right face three underneath defenders (the cornerback C, the nickel back $ and the linebacker W, walked out to the apex over Y) plus a deep safety, and the lone receiver X on the left has his cornerback and a safety over the top. Right: the defense rotates toward trips. The left safety (FS) moves to the deep middle and the right safety (SS) comes down between H and Y, so the trips side now has four underneath defenders against three receivers, but X is one-on-one with no safety on his side of the field. Either way the defense has given something up.





If the defense stays balanced, the trips side is three receivers against three defenders underneath and one safety, and the offense can attack it with combinations designed to put two receivers on one defender. If the defense rotates, it gets an extra man to the trips side, but the backside receiver is now alone on what coaches call an island, one-on-one with nobody behind his cornerback. That’s why offenses so often put their best receiver at the single-receiver spot in 3x1. They’re betting he wins one-on-one, and if the defense refuses that bet by keeping a safety on his side, the trips side is short-handed.
Many modern defenses have a third answer. They keep both safeties deep before the snap, so the picture still looks balanced, and then let the backside safety leave X to his cornerback and drift across to help on the trips side’s #3 if he runs deep. Coaches call it poach, and it and its cousins are the subject of Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage. It looks like a better deal, but count it: X is still on an island. Every answer to trips spends the backside safety somewhere.
The trade-off for the offense is that trips announces its strength. The defense knows which side has the numbers and can tilt its coverage, its front and its blitzes (extra pass rushers; see A First Look at Defense) toward it. Trips also leaves the backside thin for the run game: with only one receiver over there, the defense can squeeze its run defenders toward the trips side without worrying much about a quick throw the other way. Offenses answer by running away from trips, toward the single receiver, where the defense has thinned out; the run game chapters show how.
Trips also interacts with the hash. With the ball on a hash mark, one side of the field is about six yards wider than the other (the field side and the boundary side). Most offenses put trips to the field side, where three receivers have room to spread out, and leave the single receiver to the short side. When an offense puts trips into the boundary, squeezing three receivers into the narrow side, it’s usually a deliberate surprise: the defense’s rules for the field and the boundary may not fit.

title: Spread Formations: 2x2, Trips, Bunch, Empty, and the Condensed Revolution
text:
Empty: everyone out
An empty formation has nobody in the backfield but the quarterback. All five eligible receivers are out, most often three on one side and two on the other, so it’s also called 3x2 (and “5-wide” on broadcasts). As the plates above showed, empty usually isn’t a special personnel grouping. The running back and tight end simply line up as receivers. In 2025, about 72% of NFL empty snaps came from ordinary 11 personnel.1
Empty is the spread taken to its limit, and it does three things nothing else does.
It shows the quarterback everything. With five receivers spread out, the defense has to put someone near each of them, and the quarterback can often make a good guess at man coverage or zone before the snap by watching who goes where. Where a defender lines up isn’t enough on its own (a linebacker walked out over the back can be playing a zone area just as easily as the back himself), but how he lines up and moves is. A defender who presses the receiver or sits on his inside shoulder with his eyes on him is usually in man; one who stands off with his eyes on the quarterback is usually in zone. And if the back motions and a linebacker has to run across the field with him, that’s a strong man tell, the trick Motion and Shifts builds on.
It isolates the backs and tight ends. A running back split out wide is often covered by a linebacker, who is bigger and slower than the defensive backs. If the defense brings in more defensive backs to cover him, it is smaller everywhere else.
It exposes the blitz. Five receivers out means only the five offensive linemen are left to block. If the defense shows six pass rushers, everyone in the stadium can count: five blockers, six rushers, one man free. The protection decides which man: it usually blocks from the inside out and leaves the widest rusher, because he has the longest way to run. The quarterback knows it in advance, so the answer is built into the play: get the ball out before the free man arrives, to a receiver running into the space a blitzer just left. Coaches call that a hot route, and a receiver who sees the blitz and cuts his route short for it is making a sight adjust; you’ll hear both words on broadcasts.


Show the Python
emp = form("empty")
d_emp = [D("WDE", "DE", 1.0, -4.6, "E"), D("WDT", "DT", 1.0, -0.7, "T"), D("SDT", "DT", 1.0, 3.0, "T"),
         D("SDE", "DE", 1.0, 5.0, "E"), D("WILL", "WILL", 1.6, -2.4), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 1.6, 0.8),
         D("LCB", "CB", 3.0, -15.5), D("NB", "NB", 3.5, -9.0, "$"), D("SS", "SS", 4.5, 6.2),
         D("DB", "DB", 4.0, 10.9, "D"), D("RCB", "CB", 3.0, 15.5)]
p = ring_bodies(Play(emp, d_emp, los=40, to_go=None))
# Inside-out protection: five blockers each step to one rusher; the widest rusher (the end on the left)
# is the sixth man, and nobody has him. Drawn the playbook way: each rusher's arrow stops at his blocker.
for ol, dk, w_meet in [("LT", "WILL", -3.1), ("LG", "WDT", -1.3), ("C", "MIKE", 0.4),
                       ("RG", "SDT", 2.2), ("RT", "SDE", 3.9)]:
    d_ = p.players[dk]
    p.rush(dk, pts=[(0.05 - d_.d, w_meet - d_.w)])
p.rush("WDE", pts=[(-1.5, -0.7), (-5.0, 1.2), (-6.4, 3.4)])
p.dropback(1.0)
p.route("H", r.slant(1.0, 6.0))
p.pass_to("H", t=0.85)
p.highlight("WDE", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK)
fld = p.draw(lateral=(-18, 18), window=(-8.0, 9.0), title=False)
hide_yard_numbers(plt.gca())
put(plt.gca(), p, fld, "free rusher", -4.4, -7.9, size=7.6, weight="bold", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK)
put(plt.gca(), p, fld, "5 blockers vs 6 rushers", -4.2, 8.4, size=7.4, color=style.INK)
put(plt.gca(), p, fld, "ball out fast", 6.2, -4.4, size=7.6, weight="bold", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK)
plt.show()








Figure 12.5: Empty against a six-man pressure. The defense lines up six players at the line of scrimmage (four linemen and both linebackers, M and W) and plays man-to-man with no deep safety: C = cornerbacks, $ = nickel back, D = dime back (a sixth defensive back), SS = safety. The five offensive linemen each take one rusher (each of those rushers’ arrows stops at the lineman who blocks him); the sixth, the widest rusher, the end on the left (ringed), is left free on purpose. The quarterback doesn’t wait for him: H runs a quick slant (a sharp cut toward the middle) into the space the blitzing linebacker W just left, and the ball comes out within about a second of the snap. That’s the hot throw. With five receivers and five blockers, every extra rusher the defense sends is one fewer defender in coverage.





The trade-offs are just as clear. Empty leaves nobody to pick up a blitzer, so the quarterback has to throw quickly and accurately every time the defense brings pressure, and some of those throws are short of the first-down marker. It makes the run game nearly disappear: there’s no back to hand off to, so the only run left is the quarterback himself. And it is the most predictable formation in the spread family, because everyone knows what it’s for.
How predictable? Here is the empty-backfield rate in the NFL over the last decade, measured two ways, and what offenses did from it. (Empty is the only formation in this chapter the free play-by-play data can see; there’s no free season-by-season count of 2x2 against 3x1.2)


Show the Python (load play-by-play, participation and FTN charting data)
from gridiron.data import nfl, pbp

SEASONS = list(range(2016, 2026))
COLS = ["season", "season_type", "game_id", "play_id", "posteam", "down", "ydstogo", "play_type", "pass",
        "shotgun"]
plays = pbp(SEASONS, columns=COLS)
plays = plays[(plays.season_type == "REG") & plays.play_type.isin(["pass", "run"]) & plays.down.notna()]

# Source 1, 2016-2022: Next Gen Stats formation labels in the participation file ("EMPTY" is one label).
part = nfl().load_participation(list(range(2016, 2023))).to_pandas()
ngs = plays.merge(part[["nflverse_game_id", "play_id", "offense_formation", "offense_personnel"]],
                  left_on=["game_id", "play_id"], right_on=["nflverse_game_id", "play_id"])
ngs = ngs[ngs.offense_formation.notna()].copy()
ngs["is_empty"] = ngs.offense_formation == "EMPTY"

# Source 2, 2022-2025: FTN charting counts the offensive players in the backfield (not the QB);
# zero means empty. From 2023 the participation file's formation labels no longer include EMPTY.
ftn = nfl().load_ftn_charting(list(range(2022, 2026))).to_pandas()
fx = plays.merge(ftn[["nflverse_game_id", "nflverse_play_id", "n_offense_backfield"]],
                 left_on=["game_id", "play_id"], right_on=["nflverse_game_id", "nflverse_play_id"])
fx = fx[fx.n_offense_backfield.notna()].copy()
fx["is_empty"] = fx.n_offense_backfield == 0

ngs_rate = ngs.groupby("season").is_empty.mean() * 100
wildcat_rate = (ngs.offense_formation == "WILDCAT").groupby(ngs.season).mean() * 100
ftn_rate = fx.groupby("season").is_empty.mean() * 100
recent = fx[fx.season >= 2023]

# Empty rate within 11 personnel (participation personnel strings, e.g. "1 C, 2 G, 1 QB, 1 RB, 2 T, 1 TE, 3 WR").
pers = nfl().load_participation([2024, 2025]).to_pandas()[["nflverse_game_id", "play_id", "offense_personnel"]]
f11 = fx.merge(pers, left_on=["game_id", "play_id"], right_on=["nflverse_game_id", "play_id"],
               suffixes=("", "_p"))
f11 = f11[f11.offense_personnel.notna()]
cnt = lambda col, pos: f11[col].str.extract(rf"(\d+) {pos}\b")[0].fillna(0).astype(int)
f11["is11"] = ((cnt("offense_personnel", "RB") + cnt("offense_personnel", "FB")) == 1) & \
              (cnt("offense_personnel", "TE") == 1) & (cnt("offense_personnel", "WR") == 3)
e11 = f11[f11.is11].groupby("season").is_empty.mean() * 100
s11 = f11.groupby("season").is11.mean() * 100
empty_pass = recent[recent.is_empty]["pass"].mean() * 100
other_pass = recent[~recent.is_empty]["pass"].mean() * 100




Show the Python
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.0))
ax.plot(ngs_rate.index, ngs_rate.values, color=style.SERIES[0], lw=2.2, marker="o", ms=4,
        label="Next Gen Stats formation label")
ax.plot(ftn_rate.index, ftn_rate.values, color=style.SERIES[2], lw=2.2, marker="s", ms=4, ls=(0, (4, 2)),
        label="FTN backfield count")
ax.annotate("2022: both sources\n8.1%", xy=(2022, ftn_rate[2022]), xytext=(2019.6, 4.2), fontsize=7.5,
            color=style.INK_2, arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=style.BASELINE, lw=0.8))
for yr in (2016, 2021, 2025):
    v = (ngs_rate if yr <= 2022 else ftn_rate)[yr]
    ax.text(yr, v + (0.55 if yr < 2025 else -1.25), f"{v:.1f}%", ha="center", fontsize=7.5, color=style.INK)
ax.set_ylim(0, 12)
ax.set_xlim(2015.5, 2025.5)
ax.set_xticks(SEASONS, [str(s) for s in SEASONS], fontsize=8)
ax.set_ylabel("share of plays (%)", fontsize=8)
ax.legend(fontsize=7.5, loc="upper left", ncol=2)
ax.set_title("Empty-backfield rate by season", fontsize=10)
plt.show()








Figure 12.6: How often NFL offenses lined up with an empty backfield, regular-season runs and passes, 2016–2025 (course calculation from nflverse data). Through 2022 the formation label comes from Next Gen Stats; from 2022 on, from FTN’s charted count of players in the backfield. The two sources overlap in 2022 and agree (8.1% each), so the series can be read as one. Empty has stayed between about 7% and 9.5% of plays for a decade: a specialty tool, not a base formation.







Show the Python
def situation(row):
    if row.down == 1:
        return "1st down"
    if row.down == 2:
        return "2nd down"
    if row.down == 4:
        return "4th down"
    return ("3rd & 1–3" if row.ydstogo <= 3 else "3rd & 4–6" if row.ydstogo <= 6
            else "3rd & 7–10" if row.ydstogo <= 10 else "3rd & 11+")


recent = recent.assign(sit=recent.apply(situation, axis=1))
order = ["1st down", "2nd down", "3rd & 1–3", "3rd & 4–6", "3rd & 7–10", "3rd & 11+", "4th down"]
g = recent.groupby("sit").is_empty.agg(["mean", "size"]).reindex(order)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 2.9))
ax.bar(range(len(order)), g["mean"] * 100, color=style.SERIES[0], width=0.62)
for i, (k, row) in enumerate(g.iterrows()):
    ax.text(i, row["mean"] * 100 + 0.4, f"{row['mean'] * 100:.0f}%", ha="center", fontsize=8, color=style.INK)
allr = recent.is_empty.mean() * 100
ax.axhline(allr, color=style.INK_2, lw=1, ls=(0, (4, 3)))
ax.text(-0.42, allr + 0.6, f"all plays {allr:.0f}%", fontsize=7.5, color=style.INK_2, ha="left")
ax.set_xticks(range(len(order)), [f"{k}\n(n={int(row['size']):,})" for k, row in g.iterrows()], fontsize=7.5)
ax.set_ylim(0, 22)
ax.set_ylabel("plays in empty (%)", fontsize=8)
ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
ax.set_title("Empty-backfield rate by down and distance, 2023–2025", fontsize=10)
plt.show()








Figure 12.7: When offenses go empty: the share of plays with an empty backfield by down and distance, 2023–2025 regular seasons (FTN charting via nflverse). Empty is rare on first down and most common on third down with more than ten yards to go, the down and distance on which the offense most needs a completion and the run is least of a threat. The dashed line is the rate across all plays.





Two numbers tell the story. First, empty is a specialty formation: between about 7 and 9.5 percent of plays, every season for a decade, with no steady trend either way. Second, it is overwhelmingly a passing formation: in 2023–2025, more than 94% of NFL plays from empty were dropbacks, against about 58% from everything else.3 Offenses save it for third down, and especially third-and-long, when they need a completion and a run would rarely get the yards anyway.
What about the dip to a decade low in 2025? It came in the same season that 11 personnel, the grouping most empty snaps come from, fell to a decade low of its own (Personnel tells that story). But the mix explains only a little of it. Offenses also went empty less often from 11 personnel: about 10.6% of 11-personnel snaps were empty in 2024, and 8.6% in 2025.4 One season is a blip until the next one confirms it.
That predictability is the price, and it’s why empty is a tool rather than a base formation. If empty is almost always a pass, the defense can rush the passer without worrying about the run. Offenses that use it a lot find ways to make it less predictable, and the best way is a quarterback who is dangerous running the ball. The Buffalo Bills under Josh Allen have gone empty on about 10% of their plays since 2019, against a league rate of about 8%, and in 2023 about one in eight of their empty snaps was a designed run, nearly all by Allen, more than twice the rate for the rest of the league.5 Why that works is the second drill at the end of the chapter.
