12  Spread Formations: 2x2, Trips, Bunch, Empty, and the Condensed Revolution

title: Spread Formations: 2x2, Trips, Bunch, Empty, and the Condensed Revolution
text:
Clusters: bunch and stack
Spreading receivers apart is one idea. Putting them close together on purpose is another, and it’s just as old. Here are the four variations you’ll see most, again all from one personnel group:


Show the Python
fig, axes = grid(2, 2, PLATE_LAT, PLATE_WIN, extra=0.42)
fig.set_size_inches(6.6, fig.get_size_inches()[1] + 0.3)
plate(axes[0, 0], "bunch", "Bunch", "3x1, clustered", at={"Y": (-3.9, 7.0), "Z": (-3.9, 10.4)})
plate(axes[0, 1], "stack", "Stack", "2x2, one behind the other", at={"Y": (-2.5, 13.2)})
plate(axes[1, 0], "nub", "Trips nub", "TE alone on the left")
plate(axes[1, 1], "quads", "Quads", "4x1, empty")
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.01, right=0.99, top=0.92, bottom=0.12, hspace=0.55, wspace=0.05)
ring_legend(fig)
plt.show()








Figure 12.8: Four variations, again all 11 personnel, with each side’s receivers numbered. Top left: bunch, three receivers in a tight triangle on the right (H on the line, Y and Z a yard or two behind and either side of him); counted by width, the point man H is #2. Top right: stack, two receivers one directly behind the other (Z on the line, Y behind him); with no difference in width, the man on the line counts first. Bottom left: trips nub, three receivers to the right and only the tight end on the left, attached to the line with nobody outside him. Bottom right: quads, four receivers on the right (the back, R, among them) and X alone on the left, with nobody beside the quarterback.





A bunch is three receivers clustered in a tight triangle, usually within two or three yards of each other: one on the line (the “point”), the other two just off it, one inside and one outside. A stack is two receivers lined up one directly behind the other, the front man on the line and the back man a yard or two behind. Both are legal for the same reason as everything else in this chapter: only one receiver in each cluster is on the line, and he’s the end of it.
Clusters are where numbering gets awkward, so it’s worth a rule. Count by width, as always: in the bunch above, Z is the widest (#1), the point man H is #2 and Y, tucked inside, is #3. In a stack the two receivers share a width, and most staffs count the man on the line as #1 and the man behind him as #2. Don’t expect the numbers to hold for long, though. Many defenses facing a cluster number it after the snap, by who releases where (“whoever goes out is #1”), which is exactly the kind of on-the-fly agreement the cluster is designed to strain.
Why would an offense that wants space squeeze its receivers together? Three reasons, and they all have to do with defenses that play man-to-man.
Traffic. In man coverage, each defender follows one receiver wherever he goes. When three receivers start within two yards of each other and then run in different directions, their paths cross, and the defenders chasing them have to get around each other and around the other receivers. A defender who is a step late is a receiver who is a step open. Watch the ringed safety:


Show the Python
bunch_off = form("bunch")
bunch_def = [D("WDE", "DE", 1.0, -4.6, "E"), D("WDT", "DT", 1.0, -0.7, "T"), D("SDT", "DT", 1.0, 2.35, "T"),
             D("SDE", "DE", 1.0, 4.6, "E"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, -0.5), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, 3.0),
             D("LCB", "CB", 6.5, -16), D("RCB", "CB", 5.0, 12.2), D("NB", "NB", 4.2, 9.6, "$"),
             D("SS", "SS", 5.2, 6.2), D("FS", "FS", 14.0, 0.0)]
bp = Play(bunch_off, bunch_def, los=40, to_go=None)
bp.route("H", [(0, 0), (5.5, 0), (10.5, 5.5)])                # point man climbs, then breaks to the corner
bp.route("Z", [(0, 0), (2.2, 0), (5.2, -5.0)])                # outside man cuts in, under the point man
bp.route("Y", [(0, 0), (2.4, 4.4), (3.2, 9.3), (6.2, 10.8)])  # inside man to the flat, crossing under both
# Man defenders, drawn by hand. The nickel and the corner chase their men; the safety on Y can't go
# straight through the bunch, so he bends back over the top of the traffic and arrives late.
bp.path("NB", [(5.6, 10.0), (7.2, 10.6), (9.0, 12.4)], absolute=True, speed=5.8, delay=0.2)    # trails H
bp.path("RCB", [(4.2, 11.0), (3.0, 8.4), (2.6, 6.4)], absolute=True, speed=5.4, delay=0.25)    # chases Z
bp.path("SS", [(5.4, 7.0), (6.8, 8.4), (5.0, 11.4), (3.4, 14.4), (2.2, 16.6)], absolute=True, speed=5.4,
        delay=0.35)
bp.dropback(1.5)
bp.pass_to("Y", t=1.0)
T_CATCH = next(t for t in np.arange(1.0, 3.0, 0.05)
               if np.linalg.norm(bp.ball_position(t) - bp.position("Y", t)) < 0.3)
BUNCH_T = [0.0, 0.6, 1.2, float(np.ceil(T_CATCH * 10) / 10)]
SS_GAP = float(np.linalg.norm(bp.position("SS", BUNCH_T[-1]) - bp.position("Y", BUNCH_T[-1])))
assert SS_GAP > 2.5, SS_GAP                                     # the caption says "about three yards away"
BUNCH_NOTES = ["Snap: each defender has\none receiver in the triangle",
               "H climbs, Z cuts under him,\nY heads out: the paths cross",
               "The safety on Y has to bend\nover the top of the traffic",
               "The ball reaches Y with his\ndefender three yards away"]
animated(bp, BUNCH_T, BUNCH_NOTES, lateral=(-5.0, 23.0), window=(-8.0, 15.0),
         rings=(("Y", TE_RING), ("SS", style.DEFENSE)))





  
  Your browser does not support the video tag.



Figure 12.9: Bunch against man coverage (simulated, BDB-format tracking). Ringed: the tight end Y and the safety (SS) assigned to him. 1: each receiver in the bunch has one defender: the cornerback (C) on Z, the nickel ($) on H, the safety on Y. 2: H climbs, Z cuts inside underneath him and Y heads for the flat, so their paths cross right at the line, where the defenders have to get through them. 3: the safety can’t go straight to Y; H and the defenders chasing H and Z are in his way, so he has to bend back over the top of them. 4: the ball arrives at Y in the flat with his defender still about three yards away. Nobody blocked anybody; the alignment did the work.




The receivers never touched the defenders, and that matters. Running into a defender on purpose to knock him off a receiver, after the snap and before the pass is touched, more than a yard past the line of scrimmage, is offensive pass interference.6 Read that rule closely and you can see how bunch plays are built. Contact within a yard of the line isn’t pass interference, which is one reason the crossings in a bunch release happen right at the line, as they do in the strip above. Past that yard, the receivers’ own paths have to do the work: each one runs his route exactly as drawn, and if a defender has to go around him, that’s the defender’s problem. Officials have to judge the difference between a receiver running his route (“natural pick,” or “rub”) and a receiver who goes looking for a defender to block, and the second one draws a flag. The full family of rub routes is in Dropback Concepts.
Free releases. A cornerback who wants to jam a receiver at the line (to press him) has to line up right in front of him. In a stack, only the front receiver can be pressed; the man behind him starts with a free run. In a bunch, the two back receivers are shielded in the same way. That makes clusters a favorite answer to defenses that press.
Communication. Clustered receivers force defenders to decide, at the snap, who takes whom. Many defenses don’t try to follow their man through the traffic; they agree to switch (coaches also say “swap”), so the defender nearest the receiver going out takes him and the defender nearest the receiver going in takes that one. Switching works, but it takes two defenders who see the same thing at the same time and talk. Every time a defense has to communicate under stress, it can get it wrong.
What clusters give up is width. Three receivers within three yards of each other can be covered by fewer zone defenders than three receivers spread across the field, because a zone defender standing in the right spot can cover two of them. That’s why bunch and stack are at their best against man coverage, and why you’ll see them most in the red zone and on third-and-short, where defenses play the most man. They aren’t useless against zone, though: three receivers released from one spot can flood one defender’s area at three depths (short, middle and deep), and he can only cover one of them.
Andy Reid’s Kansas City Chiefs are the best-known modern users, stacking and bunching receivers (often with Travis Kelce in the cluster) as an answer to man coverage; both of their fourth-quarter touchdowns in Super Bowl LVII came from a stack with a receiver tucked behind another, though the trick that beat the man coverage was the return motion you’ll meet in Motion and Shifts.7

title: Spread Formations: 2x2, Trips, Bunch, Empty, and the Condensed Revolution
text:
Lopsided: nub and quads
Two more names describe formations by what’s missing.
A nub side is a side of the formation where a tight end is the only receiver, attached to the line with no wide receiver outside him. “Trips nub” (the bottom-left plate above) puts three receivers to one side and only the tight end on the other. It’s a clever shape, because it splits the formation’s identity in two. The tight end side is the strong side for the run game (it has the extra blocker), while the trips side is the receiver strength (it has the extra pass-catchers). Remember the common defensive rule from Formation Rules: front to the tight end, coverage to the passing strength. Trips nub is built to make that rule hurt. The front leans one way and the coverage the other, so a defense that sets its front to the tight end is under-manned against the receivers, and a defense that rotates its coverage to the receivers is light against a run to the tight end.
The defense’s usual answer is to keep the backside cornerback on the nub side anyway, lined up over or just outside the tight end five to seven yards deep. From there he can come up and force a run to that side or run with the tight end if he goes deep. Other defenses send that cornerback across to the trips side and give the tight end to a linebacker or safety. Either way the defense has had to decide, which is the point of the formation.
Quads puts four receivers on one side. Only five players can be eligible, and the line needs an eligible end on each side if the offense wants to be able to throw to both, so quads almost always means empty: four receivers on one side, one on the line on the other, nobody beside the quarterback (the 4x1 above). Keep a back beside the quarterback and the arithmetic breaks: with nobody on the other side, the tackle becomes that end of the line, both remaining players on the line have to stand on the quads side, and the inner one is covered and ineligible. It’s the most extreme overload in football, and it’s rare: you’ll see it in two-minute drills, on trick plays, and from offenses testing whether the defense has a rule for it. Its value is the question it asks. A defense that hasn’t practiced against four receivers on one side has to improvise, and improvised coverage is how receivers get open.

title: Spread Formations: 2x2, Trips, Bunch, Empty, and the Condensed Revolution
text:
The condensed revolution
Everything so far might suggest the answer is always “spread out more.” For about a decade, that was roughly where NFL offenses were heading. Then, in the late 2010s, some of the most successful offenses in the league started doing something that looked like going backward: they pulled their receivers in.
A condensed formation lines its receivers up close to the offensive line, with reduced splits (inside the painted numbers) or even tight ones (a few yards outside the tackle or tight end), instead of out near the sidelines. The personnel is the same; the receivers just stand closer to the ball. (Coaches have a dialect for this. Besides the plus and minus splits you met in Formation Rules, you’ll hear “reduced,” “squeeze” and “nasty,” the last one for a receiver only two or three yards outside the tackle or tight end.) Sean McVay’s Los Angeles Rams made it their signature in the late 2010s, Kyle Shanahan’s San Francisco 49ers took it furthest, and much of the league followed: by Next Gen Stats’ count, condensed alignments went from about 11% of NFL plays in 2016 to outnumbering wide ones in 2023.8
That raises a question of words. Is a condensed trips formation a “spread” formation? The cleanest way to think about it is as two separate dials. One dial is the count: how many receivers stand on each side (2x2, 3x1, empty). The other is the width: how far from the ball they stand (spread or condensed). Any count can be set at any width:


Show the Python
CONDENSED_W = {"2x2": {"X": -9.0, "H": -5.9, "Y": 5.9, "Z": 9.0},      # the same players, pulled in
               "3x1": {"X": -9.0, "Y": 5.6, "H": 8.0, "Z": 10.6}}


def condense(name):
    return check_legal([p.moved(w=CONDENSED_W[name][p.key]) if p.key in CONDENSED_W[name] else p
                        for p in form(name)])


DIAL_LAT, DIAL_WIN = (-SIDELINE, SIDELINE), (-6.6, 2.6)
fig, axes = grid(2, 2, DIAL_LAT, DIAL_WIN, extra=0.42)
for r_i, name in enumerate(["2x2", "3x1"]):
    for c_i, width_name in enumerate(["spread", "condensed"]):
        ax = axes[r_i, c_i]
        p = ring_bodies(Play(form(name) if width_name == "spread" else condense(name), None, los=40,
                             to_go=None))
        fld = p.draw(ax=ax, lateral=DIAL_LAT, window=DIAL_WIN, title=False)
        hide_yard_numbers(ax)
        for sgn in (-1, 1):
            w0 = sgn * (SIDELINE - 13.0)
            shade(ax, p, fld, [(-6.4, w0 - 1.0), (2.4, w0 - 1.0), (2.4, w0 + 1.0), (-6.4, w0 + 1.0)],
                  style.MUTED, alpha=0.10, lw=0.4)
        widest = max(abs(q.w) for q in p.players.values() if q.side == "off")
        title(ax, f"{name}, {width_name}", f"widest: {widest:.1f} yd from the ball")
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.01, right=0.99, top=0.9, bottom=0.12, hspace=0.6, wspace=0.05)
ring_legend(fig)
plt.show()








Figure 12.10: Two dials. Rows: the count (2x2 on top, 3x1 below). Columns: the width (spread on the left, condensed on the right). Same 11 personnel and the same quarterback in the shotgun in all four; only the receivers’ distance from the ball changes. In the condensed versions the outside receivers stand nine to ten and a half yards from the ball, well inside the painted numbers (grey bands, 12 to 14 yards in from each sideline, with the ball in the middle of the field). Broadcasters say ‘spread’ loosely for the whole family; in this book 2x2, 3x1 and empty name the count, and spread and condensed name the width.





So a condensed 3x1 is still a 3x1, and still part of the shotgun, three-receiver family the NFL lives in; it just isn’t wide. Broadcasters will call all four of these pictures “spread” at some point. When this book says spread or condensed, it means the width dial.
If the condensed pictures remind you of the tight formation in the very first figure of this chapter, they should. On paper the alignments are close. The difference is in who is standing there and what they’re for:

Different bodies. The old tight formations got their blockers by bringing in a fullback or a second tight end, and the defense answered with linebackers. A condensed formation is usually 11 personnel: three wide receivers. The defense still has to stay in nickel to cover them, so the extra defender near the ball is a nickel back (about 195 pounds) rather than a linebacker. (In 2018, defenses had five or more defensive backs on the field for about 94% of the Rams’ snaps, as Personnel showed.)
Different threats. A fullback or second tight end in a tight formation is mostly a blocker. A wide receiver in a condensed split can block, but he can also run past the defender in front of him or across the field, so every defender near him has to respect both.
One picture for everything. The point of condensing isn’t to run the ball more; it’s to run the ball and throw it from a picture that doesn’t tell the defense which. The four reasons below are all versions of that.


1. Room to the outside
You met the basic trade in Formation Rules, as a tell: a reduced split often means a route toward the sideline or a block on the inside. Here’s why it works. A receiver lined up near the sideline has little grass outside him, and the cornerback covering him knows it. The cornerback can line up inside the receiver and let the sideline guard the outside, like a twelfth defender. A throw to that receiver on an outside-breaking route also has to travel across most of the field. Move the receiver in toward the ball and the grass outside him becomes his, and the same route turns into a shorter, safer throw:


Show the Python
def split_view(w_x, cb_w):
    """Left half of a 2x2 (the right half is off the picture, so legality isn't checked here)."""
    off = [Player("LT", "LT", "off", LINE_D, -2 * OL_SPLIT, label=""),
           Player("LG", "LG", "off", LINE_D, -OL_SPLIT, label=""), Player("C", "C", "off", LINE_D, 0.0, label=""),
           P("QB", "QB", GUN, 0, "Q"), P("X", "WR", LINE_D, w_x), P("H", "WR", OFF_BALL, w_x / 2 - 1.0)]
    dfn = [D("WDE", "DE", 1.0, -4.6, "E"), D("WDT", "DT", 1.0, -0.7, "T"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -2.8),
           D("NB", "NB", 5.0, w_x / 2 - 1.6, "$"), D("LCB", "CB", 7.0, cb_w), D("FS", "FS", 13.0, -9.5)]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=40, to_go=None)
    p.route("X", r.out(10.0, 7.0))
    p.pass_to("X", t=1.75)
    p.highlight("X", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK)
    return p


LAT, WIN = (-SIDELINE, 2.0), (-7.0, 15.5)
fig, axes = grid(1, 2, LAT, WIN)
for ax, (w_x, cb_w, head) in zip(axes.flat, [(-16.5, -15.6, "Wide split"), (-8.5, -9.8, "Condensed split")]):
    p = split_view(w_x, cb_w)
    fld = p.draw(ax=ax, lateral=LAT, window=WIN, title=False)
    hide_yard_numbers(ax)
    shade(ax, p, fld, [(0.0, w_x - 0.8), (14.5, w_x - 0.8), (14.5, -SIDELINE), (0.0, -SIDELINE)],
          style.OFFENSE, alpha=0.10)
    (td, tw), (cd, cw) = p.pass_target_spot()
    throw = float(np.hypot(cd - td, cw - tw))
    left_after = SIDELINE + cw
    put(ax, p, fld, f"throw about {throw:.0f} yd\n{left_after:.0f} yd to the sideline\nafter the catch",
        12.6, -13.0, size=7.0, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, weight="bold")
    title(ax, head)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()








Figure 12.11: The same route from two splits, left half of the field, ball in the middle. X runs an out: ten yards straight up, then a sharp cut toward the sideline (the dashed line is the ball). Left: X lines up wide, outside the numbers, about ten yards from the sideline. The cornerback (C) sits on his inside, the catch comes about three yards from the sideline with nowhere to run afterward, and the throw from the quarterback (Q) is long. Right: X condensed, about eight and a half yards from the ball. The cornerback has to move outside him to protect the open grass (shaded), which opens the inside, and if X still runs the out, the throw is several yards shorter and he has about ten yards of room after the catch. On a hash, the boundary-side receiver has even less room than the left panel shows.





That doesn’t contradict the last chapter’s split ladder. A receiver on the numbers, about 12 to 14 yards from the sideline, does have room to break either way; it’s a receiver outside the numbers, or one pinned into the short side of the field when the ball is on a hash, who has lost most of his outside room. Condensing goes the other direction: it turns “some room outside” into “more room outside than the cornerback can protect from where he’s standing.”


2. The two-way go
That leads to the second reason. A receiver with room on both sides of his defender has what coaches call a two-way go: he can break inside or outside, and the defender has to guess. Against a receiver near the sideline, the defender doesn’t guess; he takes away the inside and lets the sideline squeeze everything that breaks outside. Against a receiver with a two-way go, a defender who leans one way gets beaten the other.


Show the Python
LAT, WIN = (-SIDELINE, 2.2), (-2.6, 10.0)
fig, axes = grid(1, 2, LAT, WIN, extra=0.42)
for ax, (w_x, head) in zip(axes.flat, [(-17.0, "Near the sideline: one way"), (-8.0, "Room both ways: two-way go")]):
    off = [P("X", "WR", LINE_D, w_x), Player("C", "C", "off", LINE_D, 0.0, label="")]
    cb_w = w_x + (1.0 if w_x < -12 else 0.0)
    p = Play(off, [D("CB", "CB", 1.4, cb_w)], los=40, to_go=None)
    fld = p.draw(ax=ax, lateral=LAT, window=WIN, title=False)
    hide_yard_numbers(ax)
    if w_x < -12:
        branch(ax, p, fld, [(-0.7, w_x), (3.2, w_x), (7.4, w_x + 5.5)], color=style.MUTED, ls=(0, (2, 2)), lw=1.3)
        branch(ax, p, fld, [(-0.7, w_x), (3.2, w_x), (6.6, w_x - 6.2)])
        shade(ax, p, fld, [(-2.0, -SIDELINE), (9.5, -SIDELINE), (9.5, -SIDELINE + 2.0), (-2.0, -SIDELINE + 2.0)],
              style.DEFENSE, alpha=0.12)
        put(ax, p, fld, "sideline\n= help", 1.2, -SIDELINE + 3.6, size=7.0, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK)
        put(ax, p, fld, "taken\naway", 8.3, w_x + 6.4, size=7.0, color=style.INK_2, boxed=False)
        put(ax, p, fld, "inside\nleverage", 1.3, w_x + 4.4, size=7.0, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, boxed=False)
    else:
        branch(ax, p, fld, [(-0.7, w_x), (3.2, w_x), (7.2, w_x + 5.5)], ls=(0, (3, 1.5)))
        branch(ax, p, fld, [(-0.7, w_x), (3.2, w_x), (7.2, w_x - 5.5)], ls=(0, (3, 1.5)))
        put(ax, p, fld, "in", 7.2, w_x + 6.9, size=7.4, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, boxed=False, weight="bold")
        put(ax, p, fld, "out", 7.2, w_x - 7.0, size=7.4, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, boxed=False, weight="bold")
        put(ax, p, fld, "head-up:\nmust guess", 1.4, w_x + 4.4, size=7.0, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, boxed=False)
    title(ax, head)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.8)
plt.show()








Figure 12.12: The two-way go. Left: a receiver outside the numbers, near the sideline. His defender (C) sits on his inside shoulder (inside leverage) and takes away everything breaking in (grey dotted, ‘taken away’); everything breaking out (solid) runs toward the sideline, which squeezes it. One way to go, and the defender knows which. Right: a receiver in the slot or with a condensed split. With room on both sides, his defender lines up head-up and has to guess; the receiver can break in or out (both dashed options), and whichever way the defender leans, the receiver goes the other. The lineman on the right of each panel is the center, for scale.





The defender’s position relative to the receiver, inside him, outside him or straight in front, is called his leverage, and the quick passing game is largely a contest of reading it. The point here is about the formation: where a receiver lines up decides how many ways he can go, and so how much the defender has to guess. Slot receivers have always had two-way gos. Condensed splits give one to the outside receivers too.
The two-way go matters most against man coverage with no help nearby, which is why you’ll hear it so much on third down. If the defense has a safety or a linebacker helping inside, the cornerback can play outside leverage, give up the inside to his helper and stop guessing. Taking that help away, by spreading the other defenders out or pulling them toward the run, is the offense’s job.


3. Crack blocks
The third reason is the run game. A receiver who lines up close to the formation is already inside the cornerback and right next to the defenders he wants to block, close enough to hit them from the side. A crack block is a wide receiver blocking back toward the ball, on a nickel back, linebacker or safety who is watching the play and not him. It’s one of the most effective blocks in football, because the defender is looking the other way and the receiver gets a running start. From a wide split it takes too long: by the time the receiver gets back inside, the play is over. From a condensed split he’s there in a step or two.
If that sounds like a cheap shot, the rulebook agrees with you halfway. A crack block is legal, but only if it’s above the waist and not to the head or neck: a receiver who lines up more than two yards outside the tackle and blocks back toward the ball near the line may not go low, and doing it costs 15 yards.9 So the receiver needs to get his eyes and hands on the front of the defender, chest-high, which is one more reason he wants to start close to him. Perimeter Runs and Misdirection has the full rule.
Here’s the classic version, a toss (the quarterback pitches the ball underhand to a back who is already running wide) with the receiver cracking inside and a pulling lineman (one who leaves his spot at the snap and runs along the line to block somewhere else) replacing him on the cornerback. Coaches call that pairing crack-and-replace. Here the guard pulls; in other versions, like the one in Perimeter Runs, the tackle does:


Show the Python
crack_off = check_legal(line5() + [P("QB", "QB", UC, 0, "Q"), P("RB", "RB", -6.0, 0.0, "R"),
                                   P("X", "WR", LINE_D, -8.6), P("H", "WR", OFF_BALL, -5.6),
                                   P("Y", "TE", LINE_D, TE_W), P("Z", "WR", OFF_BALL, 8.6)])
crack_def = [D("WDE", "DE", 1.0, -4.1, "E"), D("WDT", "DT", 1.0, -0.7, "T"), D("SDT", "DT", 1.0, 2.35, "T"),
             D("SDE", "DE", 1.0, 4.2, "E"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -2.6), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, 1.6),
             D("NB", "NB", 4.4, -6.6, "$"), D("LCB", "CB", 6.5, -10.2), D("RCB", "CB", 6.5, 10.0),
             D("FS", "FS", 12.0, -7.0), D("SS", "SS", 12.0, 7.0)]
cp = Play(crack_off, crack_def, los=40, to_go=None)
cp.path("QB", [(-0.6, -0.8)], speed=3.0)
cp.pitch("RB", t=0.35)
cp.run("RB", [(-5.8, -3.5), (-4.4, -7.4), (-1.6, -9.2), (2.6, -8.8), (8.5, -9.0), (13.0, -10.0)],
       absolute=True, speed=7.6)
cp.block("X", pts=[(2.4, 1.0)], speed=6.0)                     # crack down on the nickel
cp.path("NB", [(-0.6, -0.9)], speed=3.0, delay=0.2)            # nickel steps up to force and is met
cp.pull("LG", [(-1.3, -2.4), (-0.1, -7.4), (3.1, -9.6)], speed=7.4)   # guard pulls and "replaces" on the corner
cp.path("LCB", [(-3.1, -1.4)], speed=4.0, delay=0.3)           # corner comes up to force the play
cp.block("H", pts=[(2.4, -0.6), (3.8, 1.6)], speed=5.0)        # H climbs past the end, seals the linebacker
cp.path("WILL", [(-0.8, -1.2)], speed=4.0, delay=0.2)
cp.path("WDE", [(-0.1, -0.3)], speed=2.0)                     # end widens to keep contain
cp.block("LT", pts=[(0.3, -0.7)])                              # reach the end
cp.block("C", pts=[(0.4, -1.0)])                               # cut off the backside-shaded tackle
cp.block("RG", target="MIKE", speed=3.4)                       # climb to the Mike
cp.path("FS", [(-3.5, -2.8)], speed=5.5, delay=0.4)
CRACK_T = [0.0, 0.6, 1.4, 2.4]
CRACK_NOTES = ["Condensed: X starts inside\nthe cornerback",
               "Toss; X cracks the nickel,\nthe guard pulls",
               "The guard 'replaces' X\non the cornerback",
               "The back cuts up between the\nblocks; only the safety is left"]
animated(cp, CRACK_T, CRACK_NOTES, lateral=(-18.5, 9.0), window=(-8.0, 14.5),
         rings=(("X", style.OFFENSE_DARK), ("LG", style.OFFENSE_DARK)))





  
  Your browser does not support the video tag.



Figure 12.13: Crack toss from a condensed formation (simulated, BDB-format tracking). 1: X lines up only about eight and a half yards from the ball, outside the nickel back ($) and inside the cornerback (C). 2: the quarterback tosses the ball to the running back (R) heading left; X blocks down (cracks) on the nickel and the left guard pulls around the end. 3: the guard blocks the cornerback, the man X would have blocked from a wide split; H blocks the linebacker W; the left tackle reaches the end, the center cuts off the defensive tackle and the right guard climbs to the middle linebacker. 4: the back turns upfield between X’s crack block and the guard’s block, with only the deep safety left to beat. The ringed players are the two whose jobs the condensed split makes possible.




Notice the defender who got blocked. The nickel back was lined up to stop the toss, watching the ball, and the receiver he was “covering” turned around and hit him from the side. If the nickel starts watching the receiver instead, the receiver runs past him on a pass. That’s the condensed formation’s version of the slot question from earlier in the chapter: a defender who has to worry about the receiver and the run can’t do both. The rest of the perimeter run game, including the jet sweep (a receiver running across the formation at full speed who takes a handoff and keeps going to the edge), is in Perimeter Runs and Misdirection.


4. Everything looks the same
The last reason is the subtlest, and for many coaches the most important. When receivers stand close to the formation on every play, a run and a pass start from the same picture. The receiver who cracks on a run is lined up exactly where he lines up to run a route on play-action (faking the handoff, then throwing). The defense can’t read the play from the splits. The condensed formations of the late-2010s Rams and 49ers were built around exactly that: outside zone runs (on which the whole line steps sideways together and the back aims for the edge), crack blocks and play-action passes, all from one look. The condensed split is also the ideal launch point for a favorite play-action pass of those offenses: the receiver starts inside the cornerback and just outside the linebackers, the linebackers step up to stop the fake run, and he crosses the field behind them. A linebacker or safety who guessed “run” because the receivers were tight was guessing wrong half the time.
Two more things come with the tight picture. A receiver eight yards from the ball can motion across the formation in about a second, so condensed splits and pre-snap motion go naturally together. And the more often the offense lines up this way, the less any single snap gives away.


What condensed gives up
Nothing in football is free, and condensing has two clear costs.
It brings the defense in too. Defenders line up on receivers, so when the receivers move in, the defenders move in, and the box can get more crowded, not less. The spread’s first benefit, thinning the box, runs backward. Condensed offenses accept that because the receivers now block those extra defenders, but a condensed formation against a defense that plays it well can feel very crowded.
It gives up horizontal stretch. A spread formation makes defenders cover sideline to sideline; a condensed one lets them stay closer together, so one defender can sometimes cover two receivers, and quick throws to the outside, like screens to a receiver near the sideline, have less room. The horizontal stretch, making defenders cover too much width, is one of the passing game’s basic weapons, and condensing trades some of it for the other advantages.






ImportantWhy it exists



Condensed formations exist because the spread taught defenses to play wide. Once defenses learned to spread out and play the receivers from the inside, using the sideline as help, the open space moved: it was now outside the receivers and in the run fits near the ball (each run defender’s assigned gap, which a block from an unexpected angle can wipe out). Condensing puts the receivers where the new space is, and where they can block the defenders who are watching the ball. It trades width for angles. It’s the same idea as the spread, making the defense defend space it would rather not, aimed at a different patch of grass.

title: Spread Formations: 2x2, Trips, Bunch, Empty, and the Condensed Revolution
text:
Specialty looks
Three more formations deserve names, not because you’ll see them every drive but because when you do see them, they’re asking a specific question, and you can answer it before the snap.

Wildcat: a direct snap to someone else
In the wildcat, the ball is snapped directly to a running back (or a receiver, or a tight end) standing where the shotgun quarterback would be, while the real quarterback lines up as a receiver or leaves the field. Usually another back or receiver runs in motion across the formation at the snap, so the player who takes the snap can hand it to him, fake to him, or keep it himself.


Show the Python
wc = check_legal(line5() + [P("RB", "RB", GUN, 0, "R"), P("QB", "QB", OFF_BALL, -11.8, "Q"),
                            P("X", "WR", LINE_D, -16), P("Y", "TE", LINE_D, TE_W),
                            P("F", "RB", OFF_BALL, 9.0, "F"), P("Z", "WR", OFF_BALL, 15.5)])
wd = [D("WDE", "DE", 1.0, -4.6, "E"), D("WDT", "DT", 1.0, -0.7, "T"), D("SDT", "DT", 1.0, 2.35, "T"),
      D("SDE", "DE", 1.0, 5.6, "E"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -2.6), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, 1.6),
      D("SAM", "SAM", 4.2, 7.4), D("LCB", "CB", 6.5, -16), D("NB", "NB", 5.5, -11.8, "$"),
      D("RCB", "CB", 6.5, 15.5), D("FS", "FS", 12.5, 0.0)]
wp = Play(wc, wd, los=40, to_go=None)
wp.motion("F", to=(-2.6, 1.2))
wp.run("F", [(-2.2, -3.0), (-0.6, -9.0), (3.2, -13.0), (8.5, -14.5)], absolute=True)
wp.pull("LG", [(-1.5, 1.4), (-1.5, 4.0), (1.3, 4.9)])          # the power puller leads up through the hole
wp.highlight("RB", color=RB_RING)
wp.highlight("F", color=RB_RING)
wp.highlight("QB", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK)
fld = wp.draw(lateral=(-19.5, 19.5), window=(-8.0, 14.5), title=False)
ax = plt.gca()
hide_yard_numbers(ax)
branch(ax, wp, fld, [(GUN, 0.0), (-3.4, 2.6), (-1.8, 4.0), (6.2, 4.0)], color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, lw=2.4)
put(ax, wp, fld, "keep", 7.2, 4.0, size=7.4, boxed=False, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, weight="bold")
put(ax, wp, fld, "give", 9.6, -14.5, size=7.4, boxed=False, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, weight="bold")
put(ax, wp, fld, "QB split\nout wide", -4.6, -11.8, size=7.2)
plt.show()








Figure 12.14: A typical wildcat. The running back (R) stands in the shotgun spot and takes the snap; the quarterback (Q) is split out on the left as a receiver, and the nickel back ($) has gone out with him. A second back (F) runs in motion from the right (dashed) and crosses in front of R at the snap. R either hands it to him on a sweep to the left (give) or keeps it and runs off tackle to the right behind the pulling left guard (keep), a power play. Because the quarterback has drawn a defender out of the box, the offense has one more blocker or runner near the ball than a normal handoff would give it. Defense: E = end, T = tackle, W, M and S = the Will, Mike and Sam (strongside) linebackers, C = cornerbacks, FS = free safety.





Why snap to a running back? Think about a normal handoff. The quarterback takes the snap, hands the ball off, and then does nothing useful for the run: he’s one of the offense’s eleven players, but he isn’t blocking anybody. The defense, meanwhile, has all eleven of its players available to tackle. In the wildcat, the player who takes the snap is himself a running threat. And the quarterback, now split out wide, still needs a defender on him, because he is still an eligible receiver: leave him alone and the offense can throw to him, or toss him the ball back for a pass of his own. So the offense has one more player who matters to the run and the defense has one fewer to stop it. The motion man adds a second runner, so the defense can’t key on one ball carrier.
The wildcat’s ancestor is the single wing, the direct-snap formation that ruled football before the T-formation. Its modern NFL moment came in 2008, when the Miami Dolphins used it to stun the New England Patriots (the story is in the film room below), and for a season or two teams all over the league copied it. Then it faded, for a reason worth remembering: the player taking the snap usually couldn’t throw. Once defenses stopped respecting the pass, they put an extra player in the box, and the wildcat’s one-player advantage disappeared. It survives today in short bursts, as a short-yardage or goal-line package, or built around a player who really can both run and throw. In Next Gen Stats’ formation labels it never reached even one play in a hundred in any season from 2016 to 2022.10


Unbalanced line: tackle over
An unbalanced line puts more offensive linemen on one side of the center than the other. The common way, tackle over, moves one tackle to line up next to the other one, so one side has three linemen outside the center and the other side has only a guard.


Show the Python
def unbal(over):
    q, rb = P("QB", "QB", UC, 0, "Q"), P("RB", "RB", TB_D, 0, "R")
    if over:
        ol = [Player("LG", "LG", "off", LINE_D, -OL_SPLIT, label=""), Player("C", "C", "off", LINE_D, 0, label=""),
              Player("RG", "RG", "off", LINE_D, OL_SPLIT, label=""), Player("RT", "RT", "off", LINE_D, 2 * OL_SPLIT, label=""),
              Player("LT", "LT", "off", LINE_D, 3 * OL_SPLIT, label="")]
        skill = [q, rb, P("Y", "TE", LINE_D, 4 * OL_SPLIT + 1.0), P("X", "WR", LINE_D, -10.0),
                 P("H", "WR", OFF_BALL, -6.0), P("Z", "WR", OFF_BALL, 13.0)]
    else:
        ol = line5()
        skill = [q, rb, P("Y", "TE", LINE_D, TE_W), P("X", "WR", LINE_D, -12.0),
                 P("H", "WR", OFF_BALL, -7.5), P("Z", "WR", OFF_BALL, 12.0)]
    return check_legal(ol + skill)


ud = [D("WDE", "DE", 1.0, -4.6, "E"), D("WDT", "DT", 1.0, -0.7, "T"), D("SDT", "DT", 1.0, 2.35, "T"),
      D("SDE", "DE", 1.0, 5.6, "E"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -2.6), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, 1.6),
      D("SAM", "SAM", 4.2, 7.2), D("LCB", "CB", 6.5, -11.0), D("NB", "NB", 5.5, -7.0, "$"),
      D("RCB", "CB", 6.5, 12.5), D("FS", "FS", 12.0, 0.0)]
LAT, WIN = (-16, 16), (-8.5, 13.5)
fig, axes = grid(1, 2, LAT, WIN)
for ax, over, head in [(axes[0, 0], False, "Balanced"), (axes[0, 1], True, "Tackle over")]:
    p = Play(unbal(over), ud, los=40, to_go=None)
    p.highlight("Y", color=TE_RING)
    if over:
        p.highlight("LT", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK)
    fld = p.draw(ax=ax, lateral=LAT, window=WIN, title=False)
    hide_yard_numbers(ax)
    put(ax, p, fld, "2 linemen | 2 linemen" if not over else "1 lineman | 3 linemen", -4.4, 0.0,
        size=7.0, color=style.INK_2)
    put(ax, p, fld, ("right side:\n4 blockers vs 4" if over else "right side:\n3 blockers vs 4"), 9.8, 8.6,
        size=7.0, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK if over else style.INK, weight="bold" if over else "normal")
    title(ax, head)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()








Figure 12.15: Balanced and unbalanced, against the same defensive front. Left: a normal line, two linemen on each side of the center, with the tight end (Y, gold ring) on the right. Counting the right side of the center, three blockers (the right guard, the right tackle and Y) face four defenders (the tackle T, the end E and the linebackers M and S). Right: tackle over. The left tackle (dark ring) lines up outside the right tackle, so the right side has three linemen plus the tight end, and the left side has only the guard. X lines up on the line on the left to keep seven on the line; he is now the left end. If the defense doesn’t shift its front, the right side is now four blockers against four defenders: everyone has a man, and the back runs behind them. Q = quarterback, R = running back; linemen unlettered; S = Sam linebacker; C = cornerbacks; $ = nickel back.





The point is arithmetic. A defense lines up its front by counting blockers on each side of the center. If one side suddenly has an extra lineman and the defense doesn’t notice or doesn’t shift, the offense has a blocker for every defender on that side, and it runs there. The defense’s simplest answer is to declare the extra-lineman side its strong side and slide its whole front a gap over, which works if everyone sees it in time, and can open a hole somewhere else or leave a pass-rusher out of position if they don’t.
Moving the left tackle isn’t the only way to get there. An offense can also bring in a sixth offensive lineman to stand next to a tackle, which gives the same extra blocker without weakening the other side of the line.
Two rules keep the look honest. Linemen wear numbers 50 to 79 and are ineligible, so a tackle who moves to the end of the line is still just a blocker, which is why a tight end usually lines up outside him if the offense wants to threaten a pass that way. And the line still needs seven men, so the side left with only a guard needs a receiver on the line at its end, like X in the picture. (A lineman can become eligible by reporting to the referee, a different trick.)


Swinging gate: make the defense follow
The swinging gate is a trick alignment you’ll see mostly on extra points and two-point tries. The snapper stays over the ball, with the holder behind him, and most of the other linemen line up in a group far out to one side.


Show the Python
gate_off = check_legal([
    P("X", "WR", LINE_D, -13.0), Player("C", "C", "off", LINE_D, 0.0, label=""),
    Player("G1", "LG", "off", LINE_D, 9.6, label=""), Player("G2", "LT", "off", LINE_D, 11.2, label=""),
    Player("G3", "RG", "off", LINE_D, 12.8, label=""), Player("G4", "RT", "off", LINE_D, 14.4, label=""),
    P("T2", "TE", LINE_D, 16.2, "Y"),
    P("HOLD", "QB", -7.0, 0.0, "P"), Player("K", "K", "off", -9.5, -1.6, label="K"),
    P("T1", "TE", -2.2, 11.2, "U"), P("W1", "WR", -2.2, 14.4, "Z")])
gate_def = [D("D1", "DE", 1.0, -3.0, "E"), D("D2", "DT", 1.0, -1.0, "T"), D("D3", "DT", 1.0, 1.0, "T"),
            D("D4", "DE", 1.0, 3.0, "E"), D("D5", "LB", 1.0, -5.0, "LB"), D("D6", "LB", 1.0, 5.0, "LB"),
            D("D7", "CB", 4.5, -13.0, "C"), D("D8", "CB", 4.0, 10.6, "C"), D("D9", "SS", 5.5, 13.2, "SS"),
            D("D10", "CB", 4.0, 16.0, "C"), D("D11", "FS", 8.0, 12.0, "FS")]
gp = Play(gate_off, gate_def, los=95, to_go=None)
fld = gp.draw(lateral=(-16.5, 21.0), window=(-11.5, 10.0), title=False)
ax = plt.gca()
hide_yard_numbers(ax)
shade(ax, gp, fld, [(-3.4, 8.4), (2.4, 8.4), (2.4, 17.6), (-3.4, 17.6)], style.OFFENSE, alpha=0.08, ls=(0, (3, 2)))
put(ax, gp, fld, "the 'gate': 5 on the line,\n2 behind (7 players)", -5.4, 13.0, size=7.2)
put(ax, gp, fld, "4 defenders\nfollowed", 7.8, 18.0, size=7.2, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK)
plt.show()








Figure 12.16: A swinging gate on an extra-point try. Only the snapper (the lone lineman at the ball) is over the ball, with the holder (P, usually the punter) and kicker (K) behind him. Four linemen and a tight end stand on the line far to the right, with a second tight end (U) and a receiver (Z) behind them: the ‘gate,’ seven players in all. A receiver (X) on the line on the far left gives the formation its seventh man on the line, so it’s legal. Here the defense has sent only four players out to the gate (two cornerbacks, C, and two safeties, FS and SS), so the gate’s six blockers can take all four while Z carries the ball; if more defenders follow, the offense shifts back into its normal kicking formation (the gate ‘swings shut’). Defense at the ball: E = ends, T = tackles, LB = linebackers.





The gate asks the defense a yes-or-no question. If the defense lines up to block the kick and ignores the group out wide, the offense snaps the ball to the holder, who throws to or pitches to the gate, where there are more offensive players than defenders: in the picture, six blockers for four defenders, and a seventh man to carry the ball. If the defense sends people out to cover the gate, the gate “swings shut”: the linemen run back to their normal spots and the team kicks, or the offense uses the defense’s confusion to run a play from the normal formation. Either way the defense has to recognize it, count it, and adjust in a few seconds, which is exactly the kind of pressure every formation in this chapter is designed to create.11

title: Spread Formations: 2x2, Trips, Bunch, Empty, and the Condensed Revolution
text:
Where spread formations came from
The full story belongs to Part 11, but three sentences explain why the NFL looks the way it does. Spreading receivers out is almost as old as the forward pass: Dutch Meyer’s TCU teams of the 1930s and 1940s used what he called the “spread formation,” and from the late 1950s on, the run and shoot and later the Air Raid turned the idea into whole offenses, mostly in high school and college.12 The NFL came to it slowly, then all at once, as a generation of quarterbacks and receivers arrived having played nearly every snap in the shotgun with three or four receivers out, and as offenses like the 2007 Patriots (see the film room) showed what it could do; by the late 2010s the shotgun 11-personnel spread was the league’s default, and the condensed formation was the next move in the same back-and-forth. The College Laboratory and The Modern Era tell it in full.

title: Spread Formations: 2x2, Trips, Bunch, Empty, and the Condensed Revolution
text:
Film room






NoteFilm room: New England Patriots 2007



The 2007 Patriots went 16–0 in the regular season and scored 589 points, at the time an NFL record. Tom Brady threw 50 touchdown passes (also a record then), Randy Moss caught 23 of them (a single-season record), and Wes Welker caught 112 passes.13 The offense, coordinated by Josh McDaniels, lived in spread formations: by the play-by-play data’s shotgun flag, the Patriots were in the shotgun on about half their plays, more than any other team and nearly twice the league rate of about 27%.
The spread was built around two very different receivers, and it shows the two halves of this chapter. Moss was the deep threat outside, exactly the kind of receiver a 3x1 leaves on the island: a defense that rotated its safety away from him left him one-on-one with a cornerback, and a defense that kept a safety over him was short-handed everywhere else. Welker worked from the slot, where he had a two-way go on most snaps and could break inside or outside depending on how the defender played him.14
What to notice: when an offense puts one receiver alone on one side and three on the other, find the safeties. Where they go before the snap tells you which bet the defense is making, and which receiver the quarterback will look at first.








NoteFilm room: Los Angeles Rams 2018



Sean McVay’s 2018 Rams went 13–3 and reached Super Bowl LIII, and as Personnel showed, they used 11 personnel on about 93% of their plays. With the personnel never changing, the variety had to come from formation and motion, and the Rams’ signature was the condensed formation: receivers lined up close to the formation, so tight that about 60% of the Rams’ formations were less than 20 yards wide at the snap, against 37% for the next-tightest team. (For scale: a 2x2 with both outside receivers on the numbers and the ball in the middle is about 25 to 30 yards wide from one outside receiver to the other.)
The tight splits made the run game and the passing game look alike. On outside zone runs, the receivers were close enough to block the linebackers and safeties at the edge; on play-action and bootlegs, the same receivers released into routes from the same spots, and defenders who had been hit by those receivers on the previous run had to guess.15
What to notice: before the snap, measure the outside receiver against the numbers painted on the field. If he’s well inside them, look for a crack block on a run or an outside-breaking route on a pass, and watch the cornerback: if he widens to protect the outside, the inside is open.








NoteFilm room: Miami Dolphins 2008, the Wildcat



On September 21, 2008, the Miami Dolphins, who had gone 1–15 the year before, traveled to New England and beat the Patriots 38–13. Running back Ronnie Brown took direct snaps in a formation the Dolphins called the Wildcat and scored four rushing touchdowns, and threw a touchdown pass from it as well. Miami stacked two of this chapter’s tricks: the Wildcat line was unbalanced, and the handful of plays (a power, a counter, a sweep to Ricky Williams coming across in motion, a reverse and a couple of passes) all started from the same picture. The loss ended New England’s 21-game regular-season winning streak, and Miami went on to win the AFC East at 11–5.16
The idea came to Miami through quarterbacks coach David Lee, who had run a version of it at the University of Arkansas with Darren McFadden. The name has a longer and disputed history: several high school and college coaches ran direct-snap formations under the same name in the late 1990s and 2000s, and all of them were rediscovering the single wing.17
What to notice: when a running back walks up to the shotgun spot and the quarterback jogs out wide, count the box. The wildcat’s edge is one extra runner; if the defense has one extra defender inside, it has taken that edge away, and the offense’s best play may be to shift back out of it.

title: Spread Formations: 2x2, Trips, Bunch, Empty, and the Condensed Revolution
text:
Watch for it on Sunday






TipWatch for it: formation and leverage




Name the formation. As the offense breaks the huddle, count receivers on each side, from the sideline in: 2x2, 3x1, empty (3x2), or a variation (bunch, stack, nub, quads). Is anybody beside the quarterback?
Find the strength. Which side has more receivers? Is the tight end on the same side or the other one (a nub)? A split strength means the defense has to pick one.
Check the splits. Use the painted numbers as your ruler. An outside receiver on or outside the numbers is a normal or wide split; one clearly inside the numbers (a high camera shows it best) is condensed, and one within a few yards of the tackle or tight end is tight. Condensed splits mean crack blocks, outside-breaking routes, play-action crossers and rubs; wide splits mean the offense wants the defense spread thin.
Count each side, three steps. Receivers on that side; underneath defenders outside the box on that side (an apex defender counts); then the deep safety as “+ safety.” More receivers than underneath defenders is a quick throw waiting to happen; a lone receiver with no safety on his side is on an island.
Count the box. Did the spread pull defenders out? Six or fewer in the box against a spread formation is an invitation to run.
Look for specialty clues. The quarterback split out wide: wildcat. Three linemen on one side of the center: unbalanced. Linemen standing far out on an extra point: swinging gate.
Log it. Add a “formation” column to your prediction log beside personnel: for example “11, 3x1 right, condensed.” After a half, check how often empty meant pass.

title: Spread Formations: 2x2, Trips, Bunch, Empty, and the Condensed Revolution
text:
Predict the play






TipPredict the play 1: count the sides



Second-and-6 at midfield. The offense is in 11 personnel and lines up like this; the defense is in nickel with two deep safeties.


Show the Python
dd = [D("WDE", "DE", 1.0, -4.6, "E"), D("WDT", "DT", 1.0, -0.7, "T"), D("SDT", "DT", 1.0, 2.35, "T"),
      D("SDE", "DE", 1.0, 4.6, "E"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, -1.2), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, 2.6),
      D("LCB", "CB", 7.0, -15.5), D("RCB", "CB", 7.5, 15.5), D("NB", "NB", 4.6, 11.6, "$"),
      D("FS", "FS", 12.0, -9.0), D("SS", "SS", 12.5, 9.5)]
q = ring_bodies(Play(form("3x1"), dd, los=60, to_go=6))
fld = q.draw(lateral=(-18, 18), window=(-7.5, 14.5), title=False, width_in=5.2)
hide_yard_numbers(plt.gca())
shade_box(plt.gca(), q, fld)
plt.show()








Figure 12.17: Drill 1. Defense: E = end, T = tackle, M and W = linebackers, $ = nickel back, C = cornerbacks, FS and SS = safeties (both about 12 yards deep). Shaded rectangle = the box. Offense: X, H and Z are wide receivers, Y the tight end (gold ring), R the running back (aqua ring), Q the quarterback. The thick gold line across the field, in all three drills, is the line to gain.





Name the formation and number the receivers. Where does the offense have more receivers than defenders, and what’s the likely play?






TipAnswer





3x1 (trips right). On the right, Z is #1, H is #2 and the tight end Y is #3; on the left, X is #1. The back beside the quarterback isn’t numbered.
Count the right side, three steps: three receivers; two underneath defenders outside the box (the cornerback on Z and the nickel on H); and the safety, twelve yards deep, as “+ safety.” The linebacker W is inside the box, so he doesn’t count, and the third receiver, Y, has nobody within about seven yards. That’s three against two underneath.
The likely play: a quick throw to the trips side, to Y or on a screen to the three-receiver side, before the defense can bring the safety down or widen W. If W walks out before the snap, the box drops to five and the run looks better: that’s the slot question from earlier in the chapter. Either way, the defense’s alignment has handed the offense a numbers advantage, and good offenses check to it.











TipPredict the play 2: empty with a running quarterback



Third-and-4 at the opponent’s 40. The offense has a quarterback who’s one of the league’s best runners. It goes empty, and the defense matches with six defensive backs.


Show the Python
ed = [D("WDE", "DE", 1.0, -4.6, "E"), D("WDT", "DT", 1.0, -1.6, "T"), D("SDT", "DT", 1.0, 1.6, "T"),
      D("SDE", "DE", 1.0, 4.6, "E"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 5.0, 0.0),
      D("LCB", "CB", 7.0, -15.5), D("NB", "NB", 5.5, -9.0, "$"), D("DB", "DB", 5.5, 7.6, "D"),
      D("SS", "SS", 7.5, 10.8), D("RCB", "CB", 7.0, 15.5), D("FS", "FS", 13.0, -3.0)]
q = ring_bodies(Play(form("empty"), ed, los=70, to_go=4))
fld = q.draw(lateral=(-18, 18), window=(-7.5, 14.5), title=False, width_in=5.2)
hide_yard_numbers(plt.gca())
shade_box(plt.gca(), q, fld)
plt.show()








Figure 12.18: Drill 2. Empty 3x2 against a dime defense (six defensive backs). Defense: E = end, T = tackle, M = linebacker, C = cornerbacks, $ = nickel, D = dime back, FS and SS = safeties. Shaded rectangle = the box.





Is this a pass? What does the defense’s alignment invite, and why?






TipAnswer





Probably a pass, but watch for a quarterback run. League-wide, empty is nearly always a dropback, and third-and-4 is a passing down. That’s the default.
What the alignment invites: count the box. Four linemen and one linebacker: five defenders inside, against five offensive linemen. Every box defender has a blocker. The other six defenders are spread out over the five receivers: the strong safety has walked up over the tight end, and the free safety is alone, thirteen yards deep. If the quarterback is a real running threat, a quarterback draw (he drops back as if to pass, then runs up the middle) has the numbers: every box defender blocked, and the quarterback against defensive backs who are backing up to cover receivers. If the coverage is man, it’s even better, because the man defenders turn and run with their receivers, their backs to the quarterback. That’s the arithmetic behind the Bills’ empty runs with Josh Allen.
The defense’s dilemma: to take the draw away it needs a sixth defender in the box, and the only place to get one is from coverage over five receivers. That’s what empty is for.











TipPredict the play 3: everybody’s tight



First-and-10 at the offense’s own 35. The offense lines up in 11 personnel with the quarterback under center and the receivers squeezed in.


Show the Python
cd = [D("WDE", "DE", 1.0, -4.1, "E"), D("WDT", "DT", 1.0, -0.7, "T"), D("SDT", "DT", 1.0, 2.35, "T"),
      D("SDE", "DE", 1.0, 6.0, "E"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -2.4), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, 1.6),
      D("NB", "NB", 4.2, -4.9, "$"), D("LCB", "CB", 6.5, -6.6), D("RCB", "CB", 6.5, 6.6),
      D("FS", "FS", 12.0, -7.5), D("SS", "SS", 12.0, 7.5)]
q = ring_bodies(Play(crack_off, cd, los=45, to_go=10))
fld = q.draw(lateral=(-SIDELINE, SIDELINE), window=(-8.0, 13.0), title=False, width_in=6.5)
hide_yard_numbers(plt.gca())
plt.show()








Figure 12.19: Drill 3. A condensed 2x2 with the ball in the middle of the field: X and Z about eight and a half yards from the ball, H and the tight end Y inside them, the quarterback (Q) under center and the back (R) behind him. The defense has lined up as if the receivers were still wide: both cornerbacks (C) are a couple of yards inside the receivers they cover, with a nickel back ($), two linebackers (W, M) and two deep safeties (FS, SS).





Where is the open grass, and what kinds of play does this formation set up? What would you expect the cornerbacks to do about it, and what does that set up?






TipAnswer





The open grass is outside the receivers: about 18 yards between each outside receiver and his sideline, and the cornerbacks, lined up inside them, aren’t protecting any of it.
What it sets up right now:

Outside-breaking routes: an out (straight up, then a sharp cut to the sideline), a corner (up, then angling toward the back corner of the end zone) or a fade (a deep throw toward the sideline). With the cornerback inside him, the receiver doesn’t even need his two-way go; he has a one-way go to the side the defender isn’t protecting.
Play-action. It’s first down, the quarterback is under center and the receivers are tight: the defense has to respect the run. A fake handoff pulls the linebackers forward, and the receivers can release behind them or outside the cornerbacks.

What the corners should do: widen and play outside leverage, protecting the grass. (Good defenses do this before the offense can punish them; the drill shows a defense that hasn’t.) But look at what that creates. With the corners outside the receivers, X and Z are now outside the nickel and the linebackers and inside the cornerbacks, exactly the picture the crack toss started from. X can crack down on the nickel while a pulling lineman takes the cornerback. And with the corners guarding the outside, the inside opens for slants and digs (a dig is a route that goes straight up the field, then cuts flat across it). The defense can take away one thing; the formation has set up the other.

title: Spread Formations: 2x2, Trips, Bunch, Empty, and the Condensed Revolution
text:
Takeaways

A formation is where the players stand, and a spread formation puts the pass-catchers across the width of the field. It makes the defense defend all 53⅓ yards, thins the box and forces defenders to show where they’re going. Personnel doesn’t change; one grouping can line up a dozen ways.
Count receivers from the sideline in, side by side: #1, #2, #3. That count names the formation (2x2, 3x1, empty 3x2, quads 4x1) and sets the defense’s coverage rules. Then count each side in three steps (receivers, underneath defenders outside the box, the deep safety) to see where the offense has the numbers.
Every spread formation asks the defense a question it can’t answer both ways. Cover the slot or stay in the box; help the trips side or the lone receiver; match an empty set with defensive backs or keep a sixth man inside. The offense does whatever the defense didn’t.
Clusters and lopsided formations have specific jobs. Bunch and stack beat man coverage and press with traffic and free releases; nub splits the formation’s strength; quads asks a question most defenses haven’t practiced. Empty shows the quarterback everything but is more than 94% pass.
Count and width are two separate dials. 2x2, 3x1 and empty describe the count; spread and condensed describe the width. Condensed splits are the modern counter-move: pulling receivers in gives them room outside, a two-way go, angles for crack blocks and a way to make runs and passes look alike, at the cost of some width and a more crowded box. It differs from the old tight formations because the bodies are wide receivers, so the defense has to stay small.
Specialty looks (wildcat, unbalanced, swinging gate) are arithmetic tricks. Each one adds a blocker or a runner somewhere the defense hasn’t counted. Count the defense’s answer before the snap.

Connections
Builds on: Personnel (who is on the field; this chapter is where they stand), Formation Rules and the Language of Alignment (seven on the line, the X/Y/Z/H letters, splits and strength), and What a Play Really Is (“Gun Trips Right” as one chunk of a play call).

History and case studies: The College Laboratory (where the spread offense grew up), The Modern Era (the spread, the condensed counter and the defenses in between), Belichick’s Patriots: the Game-Plan Offense and Defense and the Shanahan tree.






NoteGo deeper




Chris B. Brown, The Art of Smart Football (2015) and The Essential Smart Football (2012): short, clear essays on the spread, the run and shoot, the Air Raid and why formations create mismatches.
Tim Layden, Blood, Sweat and Chalk (2010): the stories behind the single wing, the spread and the Wildcat, told through the coaches who built them.
Pat Kirwan, Take Your Eye Off the Ball (2010; 2nd ed. 2015): a former NFL coach on reading formations and counting the defense before the snap.
The 2025 NFL Big Data Bowl data on Kaggle includes a receiver-alignment label (“2x2,” “3x1,” “3x2” and so on) and full tracking for every play of the first nine weeks of the 2022 season. Counting 2x2 against 3x1, and measuring each team’s receiver splits from the tracking coordinates, is a good first project; the web edition of this chapter has starter code under “Show the Python” (not run when the book is built).



Show the Python (measure receiver splits from real tracking; not run in the build)
import pandas as pd
from gridiron import bdb

plays = pd.read_csv("data/bdb/plays.csv")
print(plays["receiverAlignment"].value_counts(normalize=True).round(3))   # 2x2, 3x1, 3x2 ...

trk = bdb.load_tracking("data/bdb/tracking_week_*.csv")
players = pd.read_csv("data/bdb/players.csv")[["nflId", "position"]]
snap = trk[trk["frameType"] == "SNAP"]
ball = snap[snap["displayName"] == "football"][["gameId", "playId", "y"]].rename(columns={"y": "ball_y"})
wr = snap.merge(players, on="nflId").query("position == 'WR'").merge(ball, on=["gameId", "playId"])
wr["split"] = (wr["y"] - wr["ball_y"]).abs()                 # yards from the ball, across the field
widest = wr.groupby(["gameId", "playId", "club"])["split"].max()
print(widest.groupby("club").median().sort_values())        # the most condensed offenses come first

title: A First Look at Defense
text:
The defense’s problem: eleven players against a play it hasn’t seen
Second-and-7, early in the second quarter. The offense jogs out of the huddle with three wide receivers, and before the quarterback has his hands under the center the analyst has already said three things: “They stay in their nickel. Six in the box. Two high.” Then the ball is snapped, a linebacker who looked like he was going to rush the passer turns and runs backward, and the quarterback throws the ball away. “They showed blitz and dropped out of it.” To a casual fan that is a stream of jargon. To the analyst it is a quick inventory: who the defense sent onto the field, how many of them are waiting for a run, how many are guarding the deep part of the field, and how many came after the quarterback. That inventory is what this chapter teaches. It is a first look, deliberately shallow, so the chapters on the run and pass games can talk about defenders by name. The full treatment of each idea comes later: fronts in Part 5, coverages in Part 6, pressure in Part 7.
You’ll be able to…
Start with the asymmetry. The offense knows what it is going to do. Its play-caller chose a play, the quarterback told ten teammates, and every one of them knows where the ball is supposed to go (What a Play Really Is). The defense does not. Its coordinator called his own play at the same moment, blind, and everything after that is reaction. A defense is eleven people trying to be ready for a run in either direction, a short pass, a long pass and a quarterback scramble, all at once, without knowing which.
They cannot be ready for everything equally, because there are only eleven of them. Every defender placed near the ball to stop a run is a defender not standing 15 yards deep to stop a long pass. Every defender sent after the quarterback is one fewer covering a receiver. So a defensive call is a set of bets about where to spend eleven players, and almost everything you can read about a defense is a clue to how those players were spent. This chapter breaks the spending into five questions, in the order you can answer them on a broadcast (the sections teach them in a slightly different order, because man and zone has to come before the safeties make sense):
A real defensive call names the plan in a few words: one for the front (where the linemen and linebackers line up, taught in Part 5 starting with Defensive Line Play), one for the coverage (how the players behind them split up the receivers; Part 6), and sometimes a pressure (who rushes; Part 7). The package is usually settled a few seconds earlier, as players run on and off, and the call then assumes it.

title: A First Look at Defense
text:
Who is on the field? The package: how many big run-stoppers, how many fast pass defenders. You can answer it as players run on.
How many are near the ball? The box count, compared with the offense’s blockers.
Who is stuck in between? The apex or overhang defender, half run-stopper, half pass defender.
How many safeties are deep? One or two: the shell, the best pre-snap hint about the coverage.
After the snap: how many rush, and how do the rest cover? Four rushers or five and more (a blitz); man or zone behind them.

title: A First Look at Defense
section: Packages: who comes onto the field
text:
Packages: who comes onto the field
A defensive package is the group of eleven defenders on the field for a given snap. Football players are specialists: a 320-pound defensive tackle and a 190-pound cornerback are both “defense,” but they are built for opposite jobs (The Twenty-Two walks through every position). A package is the defense’s choice of how many of each body type to use, and teams name packages mostly by counting one group: the defensive backs (DBs), the cornerbacks and safeties of the secondary. Linemen and linebackers make up the rest, and since there are always eleven, more DBs means fewer big players.

Base: the 4-3 and the 3-4
A base defense is the traditional starting package: four defensive backs and seven bigger players in the front seven. There are two classic ways to split those seven, and their names are simply the counts:

The 4-3: four defensive linemen and three linebackers (the Sam, Mike and Will of The Twenty-Two).
The 3-4: three defensive linemen and four linebackers. The two outside linebackers often stand on the line of scrimmage, at the ends of the line, and on most pass plays they rush the quarterback like defensive ends.

Both were built for an older offense, one with two running backs or two tight ends, where the main threat was a run and the third wide receiver did not exist. The 4-3 became the NFL’s standard in the late 1950s; it is usually credited to Tom Landry, the New York Giants’ defensive coach (what we would now call the coordinator), who made it the Giants’ base defense in 1956, and after the Giants won the championship that year much of the league copied it.1 The 3-4 grew out of the college “Oklahoma 5-2” of Bud Wilkinson, a front with five linemen and two linebackers behind them. Count it and you can see the family resemblance: stand the 5-2’s two end men up off the ground, call them linebackers, and the same seven players are three linemen and four linebackers. In the NFL, Chuck Fairbanks’s 1974 New England Patriots are usually named as the first team to play the 3-4 regularly, and it was the league’s dominant base defense around 1980.2
For a first look, the difference that matters is smaller than the names suggest. In both, the defense usually rushes four players on a pass (the 3-4’s fourth rusher is an outside linebacker standing up instead of a lineman with his hand on the ground), and both put seven players near the ball against the run. The labels have blurred, too: most NFL defenses now line up in both kinds of front, sometimes in the same game (“now every team is ‘multiple,’” as one analyst put it more than a decade ago),3 so calling a team “a 3-4 team” today mostly tells you what bodies it drafts: stand-up edge rushers rather than four big linemen. What really separates the fronts, which linemen take on which blockers and who is responsible for which gap, is the subject of Even Fronts and Odd and Hybrid Fronts, and Appendix C has a one-page comparison card. For now: the digits count linemen and linebackers, and the base package always has four defensive backs.






CautionCommon misconception



“A 3-4 defense rushes three.” Almost never on a passing down. The 3-4’s outside linebackers are usually its best edge rushers (The Twenty-Two), so a 3-4 team usually rushes four. In its base package, that is the three linemen and one outside linebacker. On passing downs the nose tackle usually comes off for a nickel back, and the four rushers are the two remaining linemen and both outside linebackers: that is the 2-4-5 nickel you will see in the table below.4 (A lineman dropping into coverage while a linebacker rushes in his place is a deliberate disguise, which comes up at the end of this chapter.) The labels describe how the defense lines up, not how many come after the quarterback. Count rushers after the snap instead.




Nickel and dime: taking linebackers off the field
The trouble with base defense starts with the third wide receiver. Against an offense with three receivers, a base defense has four DBs for three receivers plus a tight end and a back who can also run routes. Someone from the front seven, usually a linebacker, has to line up across from the third receiver, the one in the slot (the gap between the offensive line and a wide receiver). That linebacker might weigh 240 pounds; the slot receiver might run the 40-yard dash a few tenths of a second faster. That is a mismatch the offense will find on every snap.
The answer is a substitution. Take a linebacker off the field and send in a fifth defensive back. That package is the nickel, and the fifth DB, usually a cornerback who specializes in covering slot receivers, is the nickel back or slot cornerback. Take out a second linebacker for a sixth DB and you have the dime. The names are coins: a nickel is five cents, so the fifth DB is “the nickel,” and a dime is two nickels, so the sixth is “the dime.”
Which linebacker comes off? Usually the Sam. He is the biggest of the three, built to take on a tight end at the line, and the weakest in coverage (The Twenty-Two). The Will, lighter and faster, stays on, and since the nickel back now has the slot, the Will slides back inside to play beside the Mike. Watch for that in the figure below: the ringed linebacker in the base panels is stranded out toward the slot; in the nickel panel a defensive back has his job and both linebackers are back in the middle.
You won’t always catch the substitution, and jersey numbers no longer settle who is who (most positions can now wear most numbers; see The Twenty-Two). The quickest check is the second row, the players standing 4 or 5 yards off the ball. Base has three linebackers there, though against three receivers one may have walked out toward the slot, as in the figure below; nickel has two inside, and the player out over the slot is visibly smaller; dime has one.


Show the Python
def base_43():
    return four_down() + [D("SAM", "SAM", 4.0, 6.6, "S"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, 1.0, "M"),
                          D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -7.4, "W")] + corners() + two_high()


def base_34():
    """Three linemen (two ends on the tackles' inside shoulders, a nose on the center), two outside
    linebackers standing up on the edges, two inside linebackers. Against three receivers the
    weak-side inside linebacker has to widen toward the slot."""
    return [D("LDE", "DE", 1.0, technique("4i", -1), "E"), D("NT", "NT", 1.0, 0.0, "N"),
            D("RDE", "DE", 1.0, technique("4i"), "E"),
            D("ROLB", "OLB", 1.0, technique("9"), "B"), D("LOLB", "OLB", 1.0, technique("5", -1) - 1.4, "B"),
            D("MIKE", "ILB", 4.5, 1.8, "M"), D("WILL", "ILB", 4.5, -7.4, "W")] + corners() + two_high()


def dime_d():
    return [D("SDE", "DE", 1.0, technique("7"), "E"), D("SDT", "DT", 1.0, technique("3"), "T"),
            D("WDT", "DT", 1.0, technique("3", -1), "T"), D("WDE", "DE", 1.0, technique("5", -1) - 0.8, "E"),
            D("MIKE", "MIKE", 5.0, 0.0, "M"), D("NB", "NB", 5.0, -6.1, "$"), D("DM", "DB", 5.5, 7.0, "D")] \
        + corners() + two_high()


panels = [
    ("Base 4-3: 4 DL, 3 LB, 4 DB", base_43(), ["WILL"], "a linebacker\nmust cover the slot", (-4.9, -12.0)),
    ("Base 3-4: 3 DL, 4 LB, 4 DB", base_34(), ["WILL"], "a linebacker\nmust cover the slot", (-4.9, -12.0)),
    ("Nickel: 4 DL, 2 LB, 5 DB", nickel_d(), ["NB"], "the nickel back\ntakes the slot", (-4.9, -12.0)),
    ("Dime: 4 DL, 1 LB, 6 DB", dime_d(), ["NB", "DM"], "a sixth DB, the\ndime, replaces a LB", (-4.9, 11.0)),
]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(6.6, 5.0))
for ax, (ttl, dfn, ring, txt, at) in zip(axes.flat, panels):
    p = Play(off_11(), dfn, los=35, to_go=None)
    p.highlight(*ring)
    fld = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=(-18.5, 18.5), window=(-7.5, 15.5))
    say(fld, p, *at, txt, fontsize=6.3)
    panel_title(ax, ttl)
fig.tight_layout(h_pad=0.8, w_pad=0.5)
plt.show()








Figure 13.1: The same offense (11 personnel: one back, one tight end, three wide receivers) against four packages. In both base defenses (top) the four defensive backs are already spent on the two outside receivers and the two deep safeties, so a linebacker (ringed, the Will) has to walk out toward the slot receiver, H. Nickel (bottom left) takes a linebacker off, usually the Sam, and sends in a fifth defensive back ($, the nickel back) to take the slot; the Will slides back inside beside the Mike. Dime (bottom right) replaces a second linebacker with a sixth (D, the dime back), leaving one linebacker (M). Labels: E = defensive end, T = defensive tackle, N = nose tackle, B = outside linebacker standing on the line, S/M/W = Sam, Mike and Will linebackers, CB = cornerback, FS/SS = safeties.





The idea is older than most fans assume. The usual account credits Jerry Williams, a Philadelphia Eagles assistant, with putting a fifth defensive back on the field around 1960, and George Allen, then a Chicago Bears assistant, with giving it the name “nickel” (and, by some accounts, with taking the credit). Don Shula and his defensive coordinator Bill Arnsparger made nickel and dime packages a routine part of the Miami Dolphins’ defense in the 1970s.5 As with most “who invented it” stories in football, treat the details as contested; the coin joke has outlived everyone’s claim to it.
The packages keep going in both directions. A table is the quickest way to hold them:



Table 13.1: Defensive packages from heaviest to lightest. Personnel numbers (21, 12, 11) are the offense’s backs-then-tight-ends code from Personnel; the DL-LB splits vary by team.











Package
Typical make-up (DL-LB-DB)

What it is for
