title: Gap Schemes: Power, Counter, Duo, Trap, Wham, Iso, and the Draw
text:
Predict the play






TipPredict the play



Drill 1. One puller: which play? Second-and-7, shotgun, the back offset to the right. Figure 63.9 shows the first half-second. One guard is pulling. Is this power, counter or trap? Say which defender the offense is letting through on purpose, who will block him, and where the back will run.


Show the Python
off = line() + [te(+1), O("QB", "QB", -5.0, 0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -5.0, 1.8, "R")]
dfn = [dl("PE", "5", -1), dl("DT", "3", -1), dl("NT", "1", +1), dl("BE", "5", +1),
       D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.6, -1.2, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.6, 2.4, "W"),
       D("FS", "FS", 11.0, -5.0, "FS"), D("SS", "SS", 11.0, 5.0, "SS")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=40, to_go=7, title="Drill 1: one puller. Which play?")
go_to(p, "LG", (1.3, -1.0), via=[(-0.1, -1.2)])                   # releases inside, past the 3
go_to(p, "C", (0.3, 0.45), via=[(-0.45, 0.15)])                   # back block on the 1
go_to(p, "RT", (1.3, 2.3), via=[(-0.1, 2.7)])                     # releases inside
go_to(p, "LT", (0.3, -4.1), via=[(-0.3, -3.6)])                   # the 5
go_to(p, "Y", (0.35, 4.35), via=[(-0.3, 4.75)])                   # down on the end
go_to(p, "RG", (-2.3, -0.9), "path", via=[(-1.6, 1.3), (-2.3, 0.4)])   # pulls left, flat and short
go_to(p, "DT", (-1.0, -2.4), "path", speed=3.0)                   # nobody touches him
go_to(p, "RB", (-4.3, 0.2), "run", via=[(-4.8, 1.2)])             # across the quarterback's face
p.highlight("RG", color=PURPLE)
f = draw(p, width_in=5.0, lateral=(-7.6, 7.6), window=(-7.0, 12.8))
plt.show()








Figure 17.13: Drill 1: the first half-second (shotgun, the back offset right). Look at the left side of the defensive line.











TipAnswer





Trap left. The 3-technique on the left is being let through on purpose: the left guard in front of him has released inside him, toward the Mike, without touching him, and nobody else is coming at him from the front. The right guard’s pull is the giveaway that he will be trapped: it is short and flat, aimed at the space behind the center, not a long run to the edge. The guard will hit the 3 from the inside, where he is not looking, and the back will cut just inside the trap block, through the B gap on the left, with the left guard and right tackle already climbing to the two linebackers.
How to rule out the others: on power the 3 would get a down block (here nobody touches him), and a fullback or H-back would be heading for the edge to kick out the end man (nobody is). On counter the back would step away from the play first and two blockers would pull; here the back goes straight across the quarterback’s face, to the left, and only one guard pulls. The one thing that beats this call is a disciplined 3-technique who reads the guard’s inside release and squeezes down into the hole before the trapper arrives.











TipPredict the play



Drill 2. Third-and-long. Third-and-11 from midfield. The offense is in the shotgun with three receivers and a tight end split out; the defense shows a dime package (six defensive backs) with two deep safeties, four linemen in wide alignments, and one linebacker seven yards deep (Figure 63.10). The offense is going to hand the ball off. Which run from this chapter has the best chance, and what would ruin it?


Show the Python
off = line() + [O("QB", "QB", -5.0, 0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -5.0, 1.6, "R"), O("X", "WR", -0.7, -15.0, "X"),
                O("H", "WR", -1.5, -9.0, "H"), O("Y", "TE", -1.5, 9.0, "Y"), O("Z", "WR", -0.7, 15.0, "Z")]
dfn = [D("LE", "DL", 1.0, -5.6, "E"), dl("LT3", "3", -1), dl("RT3", "3", 1), D("RE", "DL", 1.0, 5.6, "E"),
       D("MIKE", "MIKE", 7.0, 0.5, "M"), D("NB", "NB", 6.0, -9.0, "NB"), D("DB", "DB", 6.0, 9.0, "DB"),
       D("LCB", "CB", 8.0, -15.0, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 8.0, 15.0, "CB"),
       D("FS", "FS", 14.0, -8.0, "FS"), D("SS", "SS", 14.0, 8.0, "SS")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=60, to_go=11, title="Drill 2: 3rd and 11. Which run?")
f = draw(p, width_in=6.2, lateral=(-17.6, 17.6), window=(-7.6, 16.6))
plt.show()








Figure 17.14: Drill 2: third-and-11 (yellow line). Shotgun, the back beside the quarterback, the tight end (Y) in the slot; a dime defense with four rushers aligned wide, one linebacker (M) about seven yards deep, and two safeties 14 yards deep.











TipAnswer





The draw. Everything in the picture is a draw invitation. The defense has five men in the box against five offensive linemen, the rushers are lined up wide so they can get to the quarterback, and the only linebacker will drop into a zone at the snap. If the line sets up to pass, the wide ends will rush upfield and outside, the 3-techniques will rush through the B gaps, and the middle of the field, the A gaps, will be empty except for the linebacker, who will be backpedalling. Hand the ball off late, after the rush has committed, and the back is running at a linebacker who is turned the wrong way and safeties 14 yards deep.
Why not duo, which this chapter called a two-high play against light boxes? Because duo needs the linebacker to fill: the back reads him and the double teams come off onto him. On third-and-11 this linebacker will be running backward at the snap, and a play built to catch a man running away from it is the draw.
Will it get 11 yards? Probably not, and the offense knows it: as the draw section showed, third-and-long runs rarely convert and usually lose expected points. A draw here is a conservative call (no sack, no interception, a shorter punt) and a warning shot to the pass rush.
What would ruin it: the linebacker coming forward at the snap, a blitz up the middle, or a “spy” assigned to sit in the middle and watch the back. Any defender who stays home in the A gaps is standing exactly where the draw needs to go, and nobody is assigned to block him.











TipPredict the play



Drill 3. Two pullers, one decision. Counter right. Figure 63.11 freezes the play as the two pullers arrive: the left guard, whose job is the end man, and the left tackle behind him, who was going to turn up inside the kick-out. The end has crashed hard inside as the right tackle blocked down, and the Mike is scraping outside. What should the guard do, what should the tackle behind him do, where should the back go, and who is left for the back to beat?


Show the Python
off = [O("RG", "RG", -0.7, 1.6, "RG"), O("RT", "RT", -0.7, 3.2, "RT"), O("LG", "LG", -1.6, -0.6, "LG"),
       O("LT", "LT", -2.9, -2.4, "LT"), O("RB", "RB", -4.8, -0.6, "R")]
dfn = [dl("DT", "3", 1), D("PE", "DL", 0.45, 4.35, "5"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.6, 0.2, "W"),
       D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.6, 2.8, "M"), D("SS", "SS", 7.0, 9.0, "SS")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=40, to_go=None, title="Drill 3: two pullers, one decision")
go_to(p, "RT", (0.4, 2.8), via=[(-0.3, 3.05)])
go_to(p, "RG", (3.7, 0.6), via=[(-0.2, 1.6)])
go_to(p, "MIKE", (3.6, 5.6), "path", speed=4.0)
go_to(p, "SS", (4.4, 8.0), "path", speed=4.0)
go_to(p, "LG", (-1.7, 3.0), "path", via=[(-1.9, 1.4)])
go_to(p, "LT", (-2.8, 1.0), "path", via=[(-3.0, -0.4)])
go_to(p, "RB", (-3.4, 1.4), "run")
p.highlight("LG", color=PURPLE); p.highlight("LT", color=PURPLE)
f = draw(p, width_in=4.8, lateral=(-4.4, 12.4), window=(-7.0, 9.6))
ghost(f, p, (1.2, 5.2), (0.8, 4.85))
plt.show()








Figure 17.15: Drill 3: the moment of decision on counter right. The right tackle has blocked down on the 3; the end (5) has crashed inside behind him from his alignment (dashed square); the pulling left guard and left tackle (purple rings) and the back are arriving. The right guard is climbing to the Will. Outside, the Mike is scraping and the strong safety (SS) is coming down.











TipAnswer





Log him and bounce, and the tackle follows the log outside. The end has taken away the inside: there is no room to kick him out, because he is already standing where the hole was supposed to be, and the guard cannot get his head inside him. So the guard takes his outside shoulder, gets his head and body outside him and seals him in (a log block). The pulling tackle, who was going to turn up inside the kick-out, now has no inside to turn up into, so he follows the log outside and takes the first defender to show, usually the Mike scraping over the top. The back, reading the guard’s helmet, bounces outside the log behind the tackle.
The defender left over is the strong safety, coming down outside, and he is the back’s to beat. That is not an accident: a defense that tells its end to spill the ball outside is counting on a fast defender outside to meet it there, the alley player (Run Fits and Box Math explains who that is and why). The offense’s counter-move is to block that man, often with a wide receiver’s crack block (a receiver cutting back inside to block a defender from the side, which Perimeter Runs and Misdirection covers).

title: Gap Schemes: Power, Counter, Duo, Trap, Wham, Iso, and the Draw
text:
Takeaways

A gap scheme blocks men, not areas, and aims at a hole chosen in advance. The core gap run is down blocks (the inside wall), a kick-out (the outside wall) and a puller through the middle; the rest of the family drops or swaps one part. The hole moves only as far as the end man forces it, and the back runs to the side of the kick-out man’s helmet (kick or log).
Power is the template. Block down, kick out with the fullback, lead with the backside guard, hinge the backside, and leave the backside end unblocked. It turns a play side of three blockers against four defenders into five against four, with the spare man doubling the 3 and then climbing. It does not add a blocker to the box; it moves one.
The rest of the family varies one thing. Counter changes the back’s first step and pulls two (guard kicks, tackle wraps). Duo pulls nobody and drives two double teams into a light box. Trap and wham leave a lineman unblocked and hit him from the side, with a guard or a tight end. Iso sends a fullback at one linebacker. Pin-and-pull and the sweep take the same blocks outside. The draw blocks the rush where it wants to go.
Every gap run names who is left free. Usually it is a defender far from the hole (the backside end); the offense bets he arrives late, or reads him with the quarterback.
Coaches choose by front, shell, personnel and line. Gap schemes like angles, seven-man boxes and big static fronts; zone likes movement; duo and zone like light boxes; most teams run both from the same looks. The rules travel from front to front, which is why a backside 3-technique turns power into dart.
Follow the guard. A puller runs to the hole. Find the backside guard on every run (in the shotgun, usually the one on the back’s side), and you will call the direction of most gap plays before the back gets there.

title: Gap Schemes: Power, Counter, Duo, Trap, Wham, Iso, and the Draw
text:
Connections
Builds on: The Language of the Run Game (down blocks, pulls, kick-outs, lead blocks, hat math) and Zone Running (the other family, and the contrast that runs through this chapter); Classic Formations (the I-formation and the fullback) and How to Watch a Broadcast (stance tells and the prediction log).
Sets up:

Option Football: the quarterback who reads the defender power leaves unblocked, plus QB power and QB counter, where the quarterback carries the ball behind these same blocks.
Perimeter Runs and Misdirection: crack and seal blocks on the edge, jet sweeps, and the Wing-T’s buck sweep, a gap-scheme cousin of the Lombardi sweep.
Play-Action, Boots and Screens: pulling guards on pass plays, and why linebackers who read guards are vulnerable to them.
Run Fits and Box Math: the defense’s half of this chapter: who fills which gap against power, and the spill-or-box decision that decides kick or log.
Constraint Theory and Sequencing: power, counter, trap and the boot as a sequence in which each play punishes the defense’s answer to the last.

See also (case studies): The Ravens’ Lamar Jackson Run Game and The Eagles: Trenches and the Tush Push.
If you want to go deeper: Chris B. Brown’s The Art of Smart Football and his Grantland “Draw It Up” columns (the wham piece cited here is a model of the form); Vince Lombardi and W. C. Heinz, Run to Daylight! (1963), for the sweep in its inventor’s words; and any coaches’ clinic talk on “gap, down, backer” rules, which are the grammar of every play in this chapter.






NoteGo deeper



Finding gap runs in real tracking data. The play diagrams and both animations here are gridiron simulations written in NFL Big Data Bowl coordinates. The 2025 Big Data Bowl release (2022 season, weeks 1–9) labels every run with PFF’s primary run concept, so you can count how often each concept was called (the first print below), pull every power or counter play, find the pulling guard by his first-second movement, and draw the real version of Figure 17.4. The data needs a free Kaggle login, so this code (in the web edition, under “Show the Python”) is not run when the book is built.


Show the Python (real Big Data Bowl tracking; not run in the build)
import pandas as pd
from gridiron import bdb, show_animation

plays = pd.read_csv("data/bdb/plays.csv")
print(plays["pff_runConceptPrimary"].value_counts().head(12))      # how often each concept was called

counters = plays[plays["pff_runConceptPrimary"].astype(str).str.upper().str.contains("COUNTER")]
g, pl = counters.iloc[0][["gameId", "playId"]]
trk = bdb.load_tracking("data/bdb/tracking_week_*.csv")
one = bdb.prepare(trk, plays, game_id=g, play_id=pl)

# the puller is the offensive lineman who moves farthest sideways in the first second after the snap.
# BDB tracking has no position column, so take the linemen from players.csv first.
players = pd.read_csv("data/bdb/players.csv")
linemen = set(players.loc[players["position"].isin(["T", "G", "C"]), "nflId"])
snap = one[one["frameType"] == "SNAP"]["frameId"].min()
ol = one[one["nflId"].isin(linemen) & one["frameId"].between(snap, snap + 10)]
print(ol.groupby("displayName")["y"].agg(lambda s: abs(s.iloc[-1] - s.iloc[0])).sort_values().tail(2))
show_animation(one, times=[0.0, 0.6, 1.3, 2.3])                    # the same moments as the simulated counter

“Gap, down, backer” (sometimes “gap, down, linebacker” or “GDL”) is the standard play-side rule for power and counter in coaching manuals and clinic talks. One coaching write-up states it as: gap, “if there is somebody in your immediate backside gap, block them”; down, “if there is somebody over or inside shoulder of the linemen in your backside gap, block them”; backer, “if there is nobody in the gap or down, head to the linebacker”: Chris Haddad, “How To Install Gap Scheme Runs Into Your Offense,” Viqtory Sports, https://www.viqtorysports.com/the-gap-scheme-how-its-run-in-every-offense/. For power’s assignments in general, see Chris B. Brown, The Art of Smart Football (2015).↩︎

title: Option Football: Reading Defenders Instead of Blocking Them
text:
The option principle: read one, block the rest
Second-and-6, midway through the first quarter. The offense is in the shotgun with the running back standing beside the quarterback. At the snap the line surges to the right, the quarterback puts the ball in the back’s stomach, and the two of them ride together toward the line for a heartbeat. The defensive end on the left side sees the handoff coming and crashes down the line to make the tackle. He gets there, too: he hits the running back square, a perfect form tackle. Except the back does not have the ball. The quarterback pulled it out at the last instant and is running around the left end, through the exact patch of grass the defensive end just left, and nobody is within ten yards of him. The replay shows something even stranger: nobody blocked that end. On purpose. This chapter explains why leaving a defender alone can be smarter than blocking him, and how to see the decision coming before the quarterback makes it.
You’ll be able to:
How to read the diagrams. Offense is blue circles, defense orange squares; left and right mean the offense’s left and right. Q is the quarterback and R the running back; Y is a tight end, H a slot receiver and Z a wide receiver on the right; in flexbone pictures B is the B-back (the fullback), A an A-back (a slotback), and X and Z the two wide receivers. LT, LG, C, RG and RT are the linemen. Defensive linemen are labelled by technique number; S, M and W are the Sam, Mike and Will linebackers; NB is the nickel back (a fifth defensive back who lines up over a slot receiver), CB a cornerback, and SS and FS the strong and free safeties. Lines ending in a short bar are blocks, thin arrows are paths without the ball (fakes, motion, rushers), thick dark arrows are ball carriers, and the dashed green line from the quarterback is his eyes: the defender he is reading. Dashed arrows are a play’s branches: the paths the ball can take depending on the read. Rings: orange marks the defender to watch (usually the read key), green follows the ball in the animations, and purple marks a blocker to follow (a puller, or a back who has become a blocker). Receivers who do not matter to the play are often left out of the box-sized pictures.
Start from the arithmetic of 03-01: on a normal handoff the quarterback becomes a spectator, so some defender is always free. The only question is which one.
An option answers that question in the offense’s favour. The offense chooses the free defender in advance and leaves him unblocked on purpose. Then the quarterback, holding the ball, watches what that defender does after the snap and hands the ball to whichever runner the defender is not playing. The defender is not blocked, but he is not free either: whatever he does, he is wrong. If he tackles the running back, the quarterback has the ball. If he takes the quarterback, the running back has it. The read did the work of a blocker, and the blocker the offense saved is now blocking someone else.
That is the whole idea, and everything else in this chapter is detail. Option coaches say it in one line: you don’t block him, you read him. The defender the quarterback watches is the read key (also called the read defender).

title: Option Football: Reading Defenders Instead of Blocking Them
text:
Which defender gets read?
Usually the end man on the line of scrimmage: the outermost defensive player lined up on the line on one side of the formation. Coaches shorten it to EMOLOS or EMOL, and you will see both in coaching material. “On the line” means within about a yard of the ball, in a lineman’s stance or standing up; a linebacker four yards deep is off the line and doesn’t count, however far outside he stands.
Why him? Because he is the cheapest defender to leave alone. He is at the edge of the formation, so a blocker would have to travel to reach him; he is usually a big, fast pass rusher who is hard to block anyway; and on most runs he is the man whose job is to chase the play from behind or to squeeze it from outside. If the offense can make his decision for him, the five linemen can spend their blocks inside, where the double teams are.


Show the Python
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 3.6))
for ax, walked in zip(axes, (False, True)):
    off = gun(extra=(O("Y", "TE", -0.7, 4.8, "Y"),))
    dfn = front7()
    if walked:
        dfn = [q.moved(d=1.0, w=6.6) if q.key == "SAM" else q for q in dfn]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=None)
    p.highlight("BE", color=style.DEFENSE)
    p.highlight("SAM" if walked else "PE", color=style.DEFENSE)
    f = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=(-9.0, 9.5), window=(-6.5, 8.6), title=False)
    say(f, p, 3.0, -6.4, "end man\n(left)", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
    if walked:
        say(f, p, 3.6, 6.6, "end man\n(right)", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
        point_to(f, p, (-3.4, 5.8), (1.0, 4.0), "the 5 is now\ninside him", fontsize=6.6)
    else:
        say(f, p, 2.7, 4.3, "end man\n(right)", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
        say(f, p, 6.4, 6.6, "Sam: off the line,\ndoesn't count", fontsize=6.6)
    ax.set_title("Sam walked up: he's the end man" if walked else "Four on the line",
                 fontsize=9, loc="left", color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()








Figure 18.1: Finding the end man on the line of scrimmage (ringed), shotgun with one tight end on the right. Left: the defense has four linemen and nobody else on the line. On the left, the side with no tight end, the 5-technique is the end man. On the right, the 5-technique is inside the tight end, so he is still the last defender on the line on that side; the Sam linebacker is outside him but four yards deep, off the line, so he does not count. Right: the defense walks the Sam up to the line outside the tight end. Now he is the end man on that side, and the 5-technique is not. The count changes with every alignment, which is why the quarterback (and you) must find the end man again before every snap.





The end man is the usual read key, not the only one. Later in the chapter you will see plays that read a defensive tackle (the midline), the play-side end instead of the backside one (the inverted veer), and two defenders one after the other (the triple option). The principle is the same every time: pick a defender the offense would struggle to block, and make his choice the wrong one.


What the option costs






ImportantWhy it exists



Option football exists because an offense that blocks every defender it can reach still leaves the defense a free man, and the option turns that man into a non-factor without spending a blocker on him. It also attacks the defense where it is strongest: the best pass rushers usually line up on the edge, and the option makes the best of them guess. The trade is real, though. The quarterback has to be a genuine running threat, or the defender simply ignores him. He takes hits, often from big men, on plays where he keeps the ball, and sometimes on plays where he doesn’t. Every exchange between quarterback and back is a chance to fumble (the numbers section near the end puts a figure on the cost). And because the defense decides who gets the ball, the offense cannot always put the ball in its best player’s hands.








NoteMadden vs. real life



In a video game, an option play is a button press: you decide who gets the ball. In real football, the defense decides. The quarterback’s job is not to choose who gets the ball but to see, in a fraction of a second, which choice the defender has already made, and to take the other one. Good option quarterbacks talk about it this way: the defender tells them what to do. That is also why option plays are so hard to call against: a defensive coordinator who guesses right on the read defender only changes which runner gets the ball.

title: Option Football: Reading Defenders Instead of Blocking Them
section: The mesh: deciding in half a second
text:
The mesh: deciding in half a second
On most read plays the quarterback and the running back meet just after the snap, the quarterback holding the ball in the back’s stomach while both move toward the line. That meeting is the mesh (or mesh point), which you met in 03-02. Don’t confuse it with the passing concept called mesh, which you will meet in 04-04; same word, different thing.
The mesh is a ride, not a handoff. The quarterback puts the ball in the back’s belly, the back closes his arms softly over it, and the quarterback “rides” him for a step or two, with his eyes not on the back but on the read key. At the end of the ride he either lets go (the give) or pulls the ball back out and runs (the keep). Those are the quarterback’s two answers on every read, and the vocabulary is simply give / keep (coaches also say pull for the keep).
The ride has a deadline. The ball meets the back at the quarterback’s back hip, and the ride carries it forward across his body; option coaches teach that the decision must be made before the ball passes his front hip. A quarterback who reads past that point, and the back who clamps down on the ball too early, cause most mesh fumbles: both men think they own it.1
What is the quarterback looking for? Not where the defender is, but what he can do next, which coaches teach him to judge from two things: the defender’s shoulders (turned down the line toward the back, or still square to the line of scrimmage) and his distance to the back:

If the read key can tackle the running back, because he is crashing down the line toward the mesh or squeezing inside, the quarterback keeps. The defender has taken himself out of the quarterback’s path.
If the read key can’t tackle the running back, because he stays wide, sits, or rushes upfield outside, the quarterback gives. The defender is in position to tackle the quarterback, so the quarterback is the wrong man to carry it.

Teams differ on which answer is the default. A give read says: hand it off unless the defender clearly takes the back away. A pull read says the opposite. Most teams teach the give as the default, because the running back is the designated ball carrier and a hesitant keep is the worst outcome of all: a quarterback who isn’t sure should give.
Why does the ride matter? Because the defender has to commit too. A read key who sees the handoff immediately can stop, wait, and play whoever comes out with the ball. The ride hides the ball and buys time: by the time the defender knows who has it, he is already moving toward one of them.

title: Option Football: Reading Defenders Instead of Blocking Them
text:
The zone read
The first option play most NFL fans saw, and still the most common, is the zone read, which broadcasters usually call the read option. You already know its pieces from 03-02. The line blocks inside zone to one side, every lineman stepping play-side and double-teaming to the linebackers. As in plain inside zone, the defender farthest from the play on the backside, usually the backside end, is not on anyone’s list. On plain inside zone he is a problem the quarterback can only fake at. On the zone read, he is the read key.
The two branches play out like this.


Show the Python
def zone_read_play(keep):
    off = gun(extra=(O("Y", "TE", -0.7, 4.8, "Y"),))
    p = Play(off, front7(), los=35, to_go=None)
    # defenders first (blocks aim at where they end up)
    go_to(p, "BT", (1.3, -2.1), "path", speed=0.8)
    go_to(p, "PT", (1.4, 0.9), "path", speed=0.8)
    go_to(p, "PE", (1.4, 4.3), "path", speed=0.8)
    go_to(p, "WILL", (3.5, -0.9), "path", speed=2.6, delay=0.3)
    go_to(p, "MIKE", (3.6, 2.4), "path", speed=2.6, delay=0.3)
    go_to(p, "SAM", (3.7, 5.8), "path", speed=2.6, delay=0.3)
    # inside zone right
    go_to(p, "LT", (0.45, -2.75), speed=1.6)
    go_to(p, "LG", (2.2, -1.0), speed=2.6, via=[(-0.3, -1.4), (0.6, -1.5)])
    go_to(p, "C", (0.5, 0.45), speed=1.6)
    go_to(p, "RG", (2.3, 2.1), speed=2.6, via=[(-0.3, 1.9), (0.7, 2.0)])
    go_to(p, "RT", (0.55, 3.75), speed=1.6)
    go_to(p, "Y", (2.4, 5.3), speed=2.6, via=[(0.0, 4.7)])
    # the mesh: the back rides across the quarterback's face
    go_to(p, "RB", (-3.9, 0.7), "run", speed=3.5, delay=0.25, via=[(-4.3, -0.4)])
    go_to(p, "QB", (-5.2, 0.0), "path", speed=0.5)
    if keep:   # a real crash: flat down the line, a yard deep, at the back's near hip
        go_to(p, "BE", (-1.2, -2.2), "path", speed=4.0, delay=0.15)
        go_to(p, "BE", (-1.4, -0.6), "path", speed=2.5)
        go_to(p, "RB", (3.0, 2.8), "run", speed=6.5, via=[(-1.2, 2.3)])
        go_to(p, "QB", (6.5, -7.0), "run", speed=6.8, delay=0.2,
              via=[(-4.9, -1.0), (-3.6, -3.6), (-1.0, -6.1)])
    else:
        go_to(p, "BE", (-0.9, -5.6), "path", speed=2.6, delay=0.15, via=[(0.4, -4.5)])
        p.handoff("RB", t=0.85)
        go_to(p, "RB", (6.0, 2.9), "run", speed=6.8, via=[(-1.2, 2.3)])
        go_to(p, "QB", (-3.6, -4.1), "path", speed=4.5, delay=0.2, via=[(-4.9, -1.4)])
    return p


TIMES_ZR = [0.0, 0.85, 2.4]
NOTES_ZR = ["Q catches the snap and\nlooks at the end", "End crashes at the back:\nQ pulls the ball", "Q runs where the\nend used to be",
            "Same snap, same look", "End stays wide:\nQ gives", "Back on the zone track;\nthe end is too wide"]
option_animation([zone_read_play(True), zone_read_play(False)], TIMES_ZR, lateral=(-10.5, 8.0),
                 window=(-6.8, 7.8), notes=NOTES_ZR, rows=["End crashes: keep", "End stays: give"],
                 rings=(("BE", style.DEFENSE),))





  
  Your browser does not support the video tag.



Figure 18.2: The zone read, two branches of the same play (the line zones right; the quarterback reads the backside end, ringed in orange; the green ring follows the ball). Top, the end crashes: at the mesh he is already sliding down the line at the running back, so the quarterback keeps and runs where the end used to be, with nobody left on that side to tackle him. Bottom, the end stays home: he shuffles wide and keeps his eyes on the quarterback, so the quarterback gives, the back runs the inside-zone track, and the end is now a yard or more too wide to tackle him. Simulated in Big Data Bowl coordinates; the box only, receivers and deep safeties left out.




If the end crashes (top row of Figure 18.2), he has done exactly what he would do against plain inside zone: chase the running back from behind, down the line. Against a handoff, that is the play that catches the cutback. Against the zone read, it leaves the whole backside empty. The quarterback pulls the ball, the end tackles a back with no ball, and the quarterback runs around him.
If the end stays home (bottom row), he takes the quarterback away, so the quarterback gives. Now the end is a step or two wider than he would have been on a normal run, which means the back’s cutback lane, the best part of inside zone, is wider too. Either way the offense got what it wanted from the one defender it didn’t block.
Count the hats to see why this matters. In the picture the defense has seven in the box (four linemen, three linebackers) and the offense has six blockers (five linemen and the tight end). On a plain handoff, that’s one defender free, and inside zone picks the backside end to be him. On the zone read, the free man is “blocked” by the read, and the box is seven against seven. Remember 03-01’s lesson: the defense can always bring one more defender than the offense can block, and the read is the offense’s way of getting that man back. Expect the defense to answer by bringing yet another one, usually a safety, which is the plus-one idea that 05-05 builds.
What the zone read gives up. The keep only gains one man. The quarterback who pulls the ball runs into the next defender out. In Figure 18.2 the left guard has climbed to the Will, so that man is outside the picture: a slot defender (the nickel back lined up over a slot receiver) or a safety coming down. If nobody accounts for him, the quarterback is running into a free tackler. That is why zone-read teams add an arc block (a tight end running past the read end to block the next man) or have a receiver block the force defender (the defender whose job is to turn outside runs back inside), and why the quarterback has to be a runner who can make that man miss, and why he is exposed even on a give: he can be hit while carrying out his fake (see “Hit the quarterback,” under How defenses answer the option below).






CautionCommon misconception



“The quarterback decides whether to run.” On a true read, he doesn’t; the read key does. The quarterback’s skill is in seeing the decision early and riding the mesh long enough to make the defender commit. That is why the best option quarterbacks are not always the fastest ones: a quarterback who reads the end cleanly and keeps only when the end is truly gone gains more than a faster one who guesses.

title: Option Football: Reading Defenders Instead of Blocking Them
section: The defense strikes back: the scrape exchange
text:
The defense strikes back: the scrape exchange
If the offense reads one defender, the defense can answer by making that defender lie. The classic answer is the scrape exchange, which 03-02 previewed. The end crashes down hard on the running back, every time, showing the quarterback a “keep” read. Meanwhile a linebacker who would normally fill inside instead loops around behind the end (a scrape, in linebacker language: a sideways run behind the line to a gap outside; 05-04 teaches it) to the spot where the quarterback will be running. The end and the linebacker have exchanged jobs: the end takes the back, the linebacker takes the quarterback.


Show the Python
p = Play(gun(extra=(O("Y", "TE", -0.7, 4.8, "Y"),)), front7(), los=35, to_go=None)
go_to(p, "BE", (-2.4, -2.1), "path", speed=4.0)
go_to(p, "WILL", (-0.6, -6.1), "path", speed=5.5, via=[(3.4, -4.8), (1.2, -6.0)])
for k, end in [("LT", (0.4, -2.6)), ("C", (0.4, 0.5)), ("RT", (0.4, 3.7))]:
    go_to(p, k, end)
go_to(p, "LG", (3.2, -1.6), via=[(-0.3, -1.4), (0.8, -1.5)])
go_to(p, "RG", (3.4, 1.8), via=[(-0.3, 1.9), (0.8, 2.0)])
go_to(p, "Y", (3.2, 5.6), via=[(0.0, 4.7)])
go_to(p, "RB", (1.0, 2.6), "path", via=[(-4.3, -0.4), (-3.6, 0.9)])   # the back's fake (no ball)
p.read("BE")
p.highlight("WILL", color=style.DEFENSE)
f = draw(p, lateral=(-11.5, 8.0), window=(-7.0, 7.5), title=False, width_in=5.4)
branch(f, p, [(-5.0, 0.0), (-4.6, -1.1), (-3.3, -3.7), (-1.2, -5.7)], color=GREEN, label="keep",
       label_at=(-3.0, -6.6), fontsize=7)
tackle_x(f, p, -0.9, -6.4)
point_to(f, p, (-5.4, -4.6), (-2.4, -2.1), "end crashes:\nQ reads 'keep'", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK,
         fontsize=6.8)
point_to(f, p, (5.7, -8.8), (3.4, -4.8), "Will scrapes over\nthe top to the QB", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK,
         fontsize=6.8)
point_to(f, p, (6.6, 1.0), (3.3, -1.4), "LG climbs to\nan empty spot", fontsize=6.6)
point_to(f, p, (-5.8, 4.6), (-3.2, 1.5), "R: fake, no ball", fontsize=6.6)
f.ax.set_title("The scrape exchange", fontsize=10, loc="left", color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")
plt.show()








Figure 18.3: The scrape exchange against the zone read (line zoning right; the quarterback reads the backside end). The end crashes inside at the running back (thin arrow: the back carries out a fake without the ball), so the quarterback reads ‘keep.’ But the Will linebacker (ringed) was never going inside: at the snap he scrapes over the top of the end to the outside, and arrives where the quarterback is running, while the left guard climbs to the spot the Will has left. The read was right and the play still fails, because the defense swapped jobs between the two men the quarterback could see.





The scrape exchange is clever because it beats the quarterback while he does everything right. He read the end correctly; the end really could not tackle the quarterback. The defense simply put someone else there. A cousin of the same idea, the gap exchange, has two defenders swap gaps after the snap in other ways (a linebacker replacing a slanting lineman, for instance); it is built from the defense’s side in Run Fits, along with the other ways a defense “fits” an option play.
The defense pays for the exchange, too. The scraping linebacker is no longer filling his gap inside, so the give is now running at one fewer defender, and a running back who sees the crashing end can cut back into the space the linebacker left. And a defense that exchanges every time is predictable, which is exactly what the offense’s counters feed on.
The offense’s replies are the chapter in miniature, each one a different way of turning the exchange against itself:

Bash (03-02): swap the runners. The back runs wide around the read end and the quarterback, if he keeps, runs the inside-zone track. The read flips with them: if the end squeezes, give; if he widens with the back, keep. Here is why that hurts an exchange. The exchange is a plan made before the snap, built on where the runners usually go: the end crashes at the inside runner, and the Will races to the spot a yard or two outside the end where a zone-read keep arrives. Against bash, the end crashes as planned, which is now a squeeze, so the quarterback gives. The ball goes to the back on a much wider path, bending around the spot the Will is racing to rather than through it, and the Will has to turn and chase a running back in space from inside, instead of meeting a quarterback head-on. If the end refuses to crash and widens with the back, the quarterback keeps on the inside track the Will has just left. Bash doesn’t make the scraper vanish; it makes the defense’s plan point the wrong way.
Arc (03-02): send a tight end or H-back past the read end to block the scraper. The quarterback keeps into a lane with a blocker already in it.
Read someone else. Leave the end blocked and read the linebacker instead, or read a defensive tackle (the midline, below). The defense’s exchange only works if it knows who is being read.
Throw it. If the linebacker is scraping outside at the snap, the space he left behind him is open for a quick pass. Packaging a throw with the read is the run-pass option (RPO), which gets its own chapter.

The defense, in turn, has answers to those. Option football is a conversation, and in the eras this chapter visits (1960s Houston, the college spread offenses of the 2000s, 2010s Baltimore) it was usually the offense who spoke last.

title: Option Football: Reading Defenders Instead of Blocking Them
section: Inverted veer: the quarterback goes inside
text:
Inverted veer: the quarterback goes inside
The zone read sends the back inside and the quarterback outside. The inverted veer (also called the power read) flips them: the back goes outside on a sweep path, the quarterback is the inside runner, and the read is the play-side end, the defender right where the play is going.


Show the Python
dfn = [D("PE", "DE", 1.0, technique("5", 1) + 1.4, "5"), D("PT", "DT", 1.0, technique("3", 1), "3"),
       D("BT", "DT", 1.0, technique("1", -1), "1"), D("BE", "DE", 1.0, technique("5", -1), "5"),
       D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, 2.4, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -2.0, "W"), D("NB", "NB", 4.0, 8.4, "NB")]
p = Play(gun(extra=(O("H", "WR", -1.5, 10.2, "H"),)), dfn, los=35, to_go=None)
go_to(p, "RT", (0.5, 2.6), via=[(-0.4, 3.0)])                              # down on the 3
go_to(p, "RG", (3.7, -1.2), via=[(-0.2, 1.9), (0.4, 2.0), (1.2, 1.0)])     # double the 3, then climb to the Will
go_to(p, "C", (0.4, -0.5))                                                 # back on the 1
go_to(p, "LT", (0.3, -3.6), via=[(-0.6, -3.4)])                            # hinge on the backside end
go_to(p, "LG", (3.4, 2.6), "pull", via=[(-1.6, -1.2), (-1.8, 1.4), (0.2, 3.4)])
go_to(p, "H", (3.3, 9.0), via=[(1.2, 9.9)])                                # slot blocks the nickel inward
p.highlight("PE", color=style.DEFENSE)
f = draw(p, lateral=(-7.5, 14.5), window=(-7.5, 8.6), title=False, width_in=5.8)
read_line(f, p, (-4.4, 0.3), (0.4, 5.6))
branch(f, p, [(-5.0, -1.6), (-4.7, 0.6), (-4.2, 5.0), (-3.0, 9.0), (-1.0, 12.0), (4.8, 12.4)],
       color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, label="give if the end\nsqueezes", label_at=(-5.9, 11.3), fontsize=6.8)
branch(f, p, [(-5.0, 0.0), (-3.6, 0.6), (-1.9, 2.5), (-0.6, 4.7), (5.6, 4.8)], color=GREEN,
       label="keep if the end\nwidens", label_at=(6.2, 2.4), fontsize=6.8)
point_to(f, p, (-2.6, -5.0), (-1.7, -1.2), "LG pulls", fontsize=6.8)
point_to(f, p, (6.2, 10.6), (2.4, 9.3), "H blocks\nthe nickel", fontsize=6.6)
f.ax.set_title("Inverted veer (power read)", fontsize=10, loc="left", color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")
plt.show()








Figure 18.4: The inverted veer (power read) to the right. The line blocks power: the right tackle and right guard double-team the 3-technique, then the guard climbs to the Will; the center blocks back on the 1-technique; the left guard pulls across for the Mike. The slot receiver (H) blocks the nickel back inward, so the edge outside him is clear. The play-side end (ringed) is left unblocked and read (dashed green eyes line). The back sweeps wide across the quarterback’s face. If the end squeezes inside to take the quarterback, the quarterback gives and the back bends outside the slot’s block; if the end widens with the back, the quarterback keeps and runs inside him, between the end and the tackle’s down block, behind the pulling guard.





Why build it this way? Three reasons, each a trade.
It puts the bigger runner inside. Many running quarterbacks are big, strong men (Cam Newton, Jalen Hurts, Josh Allen), better suited to running through a crease behind a pulling guard than to outrunning a safety on the edge. The inverted veer gives them the inside track and a lead blocker: power blocking, with the quarterback as the ball carrier.
It attacks the edge with the back. The running back, already moving sideways at full speed, gets the ball going outside a defender who has just stepped inside. Defenses are taught to “squeeze” plays inside-out with their end; the inverted veer makes that squeeze the wrong answer.
It saves the blocker the play needed most. On power as 03-03 drew it, the fullback or H-back kicks out the play-side end and the pulling guard leads through the hole for a linebacker. The inverted veer doesn’t block the end at all; it reads him. The guard still pulls for the linebacker, but the back who would have been the kick-out man is now a second runner, attacking the edge.
What it gives up: the back is running sideways, not downhill, so if the read is wrong (the quarterback gives when the end was actually wide), the back is running at a defender with no momentum and loses yards. And the quarterback is a ball carrier between the tackles, in traffic, on every keep.
Inverted veer or bash? Both put the back outside and the quarterback inside, so they are easy to merge. Two things separate them. Which end is read: bash reads the backside end, away from the line’s flow, while the inverted veer reads the play-side end, the man the play is aimed at. What the line does: bash is zone blocking with everyone stepping the same way; the inverted veer is power blocking, down blocks and a guard pulling across the formation. Look for the puller: if one crosses the center toward the read end, it is a power read. Many NFL teams also hand the outside role to a receiver instead of the back, a jet motion man sprinting across the formation at the snap (a “jet” power read); the read is the same, and 03-05 builds the jet sweep it borrows from.
The name comes from the older veer (next section), in which the back is the inside runner and the quarterback the outside one. Turn it inside out and you have the “inverted” version. Who invented the play is unclear; it was made famous by TCU in 2009 and by Gus Malzahn’s Auburn offense with Cam Newton in 2010, when Newton won the Heisman Trophy and Auburn the national championship, and in Malzahn’s circle it also went by dash read.2

title: Option Football: Reading Defenders Instead of Blocking Them
section: Speed option: straight at the edge
text:
Speed option: straight at the edge
The fastest of the option plays, and the simplest to watch, is the speed option. There is no handoff and no mesh. The quarterback takes the snap and runs straight at the end man on the line of scrimmage, with the running back trailing him, ready for a pitch: a one-handed, underhand toss, sideways or backward, to the trailing back (the pitch man). The back keeps a pitch relationship with the quarterback: typically about four or five yards outside him and a yard or so deeper, so that a toss can reach him without traveling forward (coaches differ on the exact spacing; the one fixed rule is that the end man must not be able to tackle both runners).3 The end man has two runners coming at him. If he takes the quarterback, the quarterback pitches; if he takes the back, the quarterback keeps and turns up inside him.


Show the Python
off = gun(rb_w=1.6, extra=(O("H", "WR", -1.5, 12.2, "H"), O("Z", "WR", -0.7, 16.0, "Z")))
dfn = [D("PE", "DE", 1.0, technique("5", 1) + 0.6, "5"), D("PT", "DT", 1.0, technique("3", 1), "3"),
       D("BT", "DT", 1.0, technique("1", -1), "1"), D("BE", "DE", 1.0, technique("5", -1), "5"),
       D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, 1.8, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -2.2, "W"),
       D("NB", "NB", 4.5, 11.6, "NB"), D("RCB", "CB", 6.5, 16.0, "CB")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=None)
go_to(p, "RT", (3.8, 2.6), via=[(-0.3, 3.9), (0.9, 3.4)])      # skips the end, climbs to the Mike
go_to(p, "RG", (0.4, 2.9), via=[(-0.4, 2.2)])                  # reach the 3
go_to(p, "C", (0.4, 0.2), via=[(-0.4, 0.4)])                   # reach the 1
go_to(p, "LG", (3.6, -2.0), via=[(-0.4, -1.2)])                # climbs to the Will
go_to(p, "LT", (0.3, -4.3), via=[(-0.6, -3.8)])                # hinge: wall off the backside end
go_to(p, "H", (3.6, 11.0), via=[(1.0, 10.9)])                     # inside-out onto the nickel
go_to(p, "Z", (5.6, 16.0))
go_to(p, "QB", (-1.6, 6.0), "run", via=[(-4.4, 1.6), (-2.8, 4.4)])
go_to(p, "RB", (-2.8, 10.0), "path", via=[(-5.6, 3.6), (-4.4, 7.6)])
p.read("PE")
p.highlight("PE", color=style.DEFENSE)
f = draw(p, lateral=(-7.0, 19.5), window=(-7.5, 10.0), title=False, width_in=5.8)
pitch_arc(f, p, (-1.6, 6.2), (-2.8, 9.7))
branch(f, p, [(-2.8, 10.0), (0.2, 9.4), (6.6, 9.0)], color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, label="pitch if the\nend takes Q",
       label_at=(-5.8, 12.4), fontsize=6.8)
branch(f, p, [(-1.6, 6.0), (-0.2, 4.0), (6.2, 3.9)], color=GREEN, label="keep if the end\nwidens to the back",
       label_at=(7.7, 4.4), fontsize=6.8)
f.ax.set_title("Speed option", fontsize=10, loc="left", color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")
plt.show()








Figure 18.5: Speed option to the right from the shotgun (the receivers on the left are out of the picture). The line reaches to the right and leaves the end man (ringed) unblocked; the left tackle walls off the backside end and the left guard climbs to the Will. The slot receiver (H) blocks the nickel defender, the next man outside, from the inside out, and the Z blocks the cornerback. The quarterback (thick arrow, he has the ball) attacks the end man’s outside shoulder, forcing him to choose, with the running back (thin arrow) about four yards outside and a yard deeper. If the end takes the quarterback, the ball is pitched (dashed brown arc) and the back runs inside the slot’s block; if the end widens to take the back, the quarterback keeps and cuts up inside him.





The speed option exists to get the ball to the edge fast, against a defense that is outnumbered there. Count it in Figure 18.5: on the right side the offense has the quarterback, the back and two blockers (H and Z) against the end, the nickel and the cornerback. The end is read, the other two are blocked, and the two runners face nobody until a linebacker or the safety arrives from inside. The play is over before the defense can rally.
Its costs are the pitch and the quarterback. Two rules shape the pitch. A toss that goes sideways or backward is a backward pass, and if nobody catches it, it is a live ball, like a fumble, that either team can recover. A toss that drifts forward is a forward pass, and that is worse, not safer: a forward pass is legal only from behind the line of scrimmage, and an option quarterback who has reached the end man is often at or past the line when he pitches. A forward pitch from there is an illegal forward pass, five yards and the loss of the down.4 So the pitch must go back, and a backward ball on the ground belongs to whoever falls on it. Option teams drill the pitch endlessly, and a quarterback who pitches under pressure, falling, with a defender hitting him, is the play’s weak point. That is the other cost: on the pitch branch, the end man has been invited to hit the quarterback, and he will, every time, often just after the ball is gone.

title: Option Football: Reading Defenders Instead of Blocking Them
section: Veer and the triple option: two reads, three runners
text:
Veer and the triple option: two reads, three runners
Everything so far has had two possible ball carriers. The older option plays had three, and that is where the modern idea came from.
The veer came from Bill Yeoman’s University of Houston teams in the mid-1960s. Yeoman had a weak offensive line that could not block a dive play straight up; his solution, first used in the middle of a losing 1965 season that he expected to get him fired, was to stop blocking the first defensive lineman outside the play-side tackle and read him instead.5 The play-side tackle releases inside to a linebacker, which makes the down lineman a free man, and the quarterback either gives to a back diving just inside that defender or keeps the ball. Yeoman ran it from split backs (two running backs side by side behind the quarterback, the pro set’s backfield in 02-03): the play-side halfback was the dive, and the other halfback swung out behind the quarterback to trail him.6 Yeoman’s Houston teams ran it for two decades, and it spread across college football in the 1970s.
So be precise about the words. The veer is a blocking-and-read rule: release the play-side tackle, read the first man outside him, give to the dive or keep. Put a pitch man behind the quarterback, so a keep can become a pitch, and the veer becomes the triple option: the same first read with a second one bolted on. The triple is the play the wishbone (1968) and later the flexbone of 02-03 were built to run, and the version drawn here is the flexbone one. It has three runners:

the dive: the fullback (the flexbone’s B-back) driving straight at the play-side guard’s outside hip;
the quarterback, who rides the dive, then, if he keeps, runs down the line toward the edge;
the pitch man: an A-back who went in motion before the snap and is now trailing the quarterback in pitch relationship.

And it has two read keys. The first, the dive key, is the first defensive lineman on or outside the play-side tackle; the second, the pitch key, is the next defender outside him, often an outside linebacker or a safety who has come down. Everyone else is blocked. Option coaches turn that into a count, numbering the defenders from the inside out on the play side: #1 is the dive key and #2 the pitch key, both “blocked” by the quarterback’s reads; #3 is the run-support defender who shows up in the alley (the gap between the pitch key and the sideline), and the play-side A-back arcs to block him; #4 is the deep defender, usually the cornerback, and the receiver takes him.7 Count #1 to #4 in the next picture and every defender on that side is accounted for.


Show the Python
def triple_play(react):
    off = flexbone()
    dfn = [D("PE", "DE", 1.0, technique("5", 1), "5"), D("PT", "DT", 1.0, technique("1", 1), "1"),
           D("BT", "DT", 1.0, technique("3", -1), "3"), D("BE", "DE", 1.0, technique("5", -1), "5"),
           D("SAM", "SAM", 1.0, 8.6, "S"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, 1.6, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -2.6, "W"),
           D("SS", "SS", 8.0, 9.6, "SS"), D("FS", "FS", 12.5, -2.0, "FS"),
           D("RCB", "CB", 6.0, 12.6, "CB"), D("LCB", "CB", 6.0, -12.6, "CB")]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=None)
    check_legal(off)
    p.motion("LA", to=(-3.6, -1.6))                                   # pitch man in motion
    if react:   # this branch: the dive key squeezes the dive, the pitch key attacks the quarterback
        go_to(p, "PE", (0.6, 3.3), "path", speed=3.8, delay=0.1)
        go_to(p, "SAM", (-0.6, 6.3), "path", speed=3.6, delay=0.55)
        go_to(p, "MIKE", (3.4, 2.4), "path", speed=2.4, delay=0.3)
        go_to(p, "WILL", (3.0, -1.2), "path", speed=2.4, delay=0.3)
        go_to(p, "SS", (3.0, 9.2), "path", speed=5.0, delay=0.3)         # fills the alley hard
        go_to(p, "RCB", (4.5, 14.1), "path", speed=2.0, delay=0.3)
        go_to(p, "PT", (1.4, 0.9), "path", speed=0.8)
    go_to(p, "RT", (2.6, 2.3), via=[(0.0, 2.6)], speed=3.0)            # veer release to the Mike
    go_to(p, "RG", (0.6, 1.1), speed=1.6)                             # down on the 1
    go_to(p, "C", (2.2, -1.3), via=[(0.2, -0.4)], speed=2.5)           # climbs to the Will
    go_to(p, "LG", (0.5, -1.9), speed=1.6)
    go_to(p, "LT", (0.5, -3.6), speed=1.6)
    if react:   # arc meets the safety in the alley; the receiver walls the corner off outside
        go_to(p, "RA", (2.7, 10.0), via=[(-0.6, 7.4), (0.6, 10.4)], speed=5.0)
        go_to(p, "RW", (3.3, 12.9), speed=2.5)
    else:       # arc around the pitch key (never touch him) to the safety; the receiver takes the corner
        go_to(p, "RA", (4.8, 10.8), via=[(-0.9, 8.0), (0.3, 11.4), (2.6, 11.7)], speed=5.0)
        go_to(p, "RW", (4.6, 12.4), speed=2.5)
    go_to(p, "FB", (0.6, 2.2), "run", speed=6.0, via=[(-2.6, 1.6)])     # the dive
    go_to(p, "QB", (-2.6, 1.0), "path", speed=3.0)                      # open to the mesh
    go_to(p, "QB", (-2.5, 1.5), "path", speed=1.2)                      # ride
    if react:
        go_to(p, "QB", (-0.8, 5.9), "path", speed=5.5, via=[(-2.1, 3.5)])   # pull, attack the pitch key
        go_to(p, "LA", (6.4, 11.6), "run", speed=7.0,
              via=[(-4.3, 2.0), (-3.6, 6.5), (-2.2, 9.6), (-0.4, 11.4)])
        p.pitch("LA", t=1.45)
    return p


p = triple_play(react=False)
p.highlight("PE", color=style.DEFENSE); p.highlight("SAM", color=style.DEFENSE)
f = draw(p, lateral=(-13.5, 15.5), window=(-6.5, 11.0), title=False, width_in=6.3)
read_line(f, p, (-2.5, 1.5), (1.0, 4.0))
read_line(f, p, (-2.5, 1.5), (1.0, 8.6))
branch(f, p, [(-3.6, -1.6), (-4.3, 2.0), (-3.7, 6.2), (-2.4, 8.8)], color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, lw=1.6)
for n, (d, w) in {"1": (2.6, 4.2), "2": (2.6, 7.6), "3": (9.4, 8.4), "4": (7.4, 11.4)}.items():
    say(f, p, d, w, n, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=8.5, weight="bold")
say(f, p, 7.9, -7.0, "1 = dive key (first read)\n2 = pitch key (second read)\n3 = alley: the A-back's block\n"
    "4 = deep: the receiver's block", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
point_to(f, p, (-5.3, 4.2), (-2.4, 1.7), "dive", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
point_to(f, p, (-5.0, -5.6), (-2.6, -3.4), "pitch man's\nmotion", fontsize=6.8)
point_to(f, p, (-4.6, 11.4), (-2.6, 8.8), "pitch path", fontsize=6.8, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK)
point_to(f, p, (5.6, 4.6), (0.2, 11.1), "A-back arcs around\nthe Sam to the safety", fontsize=6.6)
f.ax.set_title("Triple option from the flexbone", fontsize=10, loc="left", color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")
plt.show()








Figure 18.6: The triple option from the flexbone, to the right: the assignments. Before the snap the backside A-back (A, left) goes in motion (thin dashed path) to a spot behind the quarterback; he will be the pitch man. The B-back dives at the right guard’s outside hip. The right tackle ‘veer releases’ inside to the Mike, leaving the 5-technique unblocked as the first read (the dive key, #1). The Sam, standing on the line outside him, is left unblocked too, as the second read (the pitch key, #2): the play-side A-back arcs well outside him, never touching him, to block the safety (#3, the alley defender), and the receiver Z blocks the cornerback (#4, the deep defender). Count them: every defender on the right side is blocked or read.





The quarterback’s two decisions come one after the other, both in less than two seconds:

At the mesh, read the dive key. If he squeezes inside to tackle the dive, pull the ball. If he stays outside, or rushes upfield, give to the dive: it is going straight up the field just inside him.
If he kept, run at the pitch key. If the pitch key attacks the quarterback, pitch. If he widens to take the pitch man, keep and turn up inside him.

Notice the order. The first read decides most snaps: if the dive key does not squeeze, the ball goes to the dive and the second read never happens. That is the triple’s most common result and much of its point. A fullback who gains four yards every time he is given the ball lets the offense run the play all day, and the only way to stop him is to squeeze the dive key inside, which opens the keep and the pitch.
Here is one branch, in motion: the dive key takes the dive and the pitch key takes the quarterback.


Show the Python
option_animation([triple_play(react=True)], [-0.6, 0.85, 1.45, 2.5], lateral=(-8.0, 16.0), window=(-6.5, 10.0),
                 notes=["A-back in motion:\nthe pitch man", "Dive key squeezes the\ndive: Q pulls",
                        "Pitch key takes Q:\nQ pitches", "A-back outside the\nlast defender"],
                 rings=(("PE", style.DEFENSE), ("SAM", style.DEFENSE)), ncols=2)





  
  Your browser does not support the video tag.



Figure 18.7: The triple option, one branch, in motion (simulated, Big Data Bowl coordinates; the green ring follows the ball). 1: the backside A-back’s motion puts him behind the quarterback at the snap. 2: at the mesh the dive key (the 5, ringed) squeezes down on the B-back, so the quarterback pulls the ball. 3: the quarterback runs at the pitch key (the Sam, ringed); the Sam comes up to tackle him, so the quarterback pitches. 4: the pitch man has the ball in the alley, between the other A-back’s block on the safety (who filled hard) and the Z’s block on the cornerback.




The triple option is a machine for one thing: making a defense play eleven men against eleven with every assignment perfect, every snap. Against it, a defense needs someone for the dive, someone for the quarterback and someone for the pitch, on both sides of the formation, and it needs them to do their job and nothing else. That idea, “assignment football,” is how coaches describe defending it. A defender who does two jobs (who tackles the dive and tries to get the quarterback) is doing neither. One player out of place and the ball goes to the man he should have had.
Why isn’t it everywhere, then? Because its costs are steep, and steeper the higher the level:

The quarterback takes a hit on nearly every play, from the dive key on the pull and from the pitch key on the pitch. College option quarterbacks are built for that and are replaceable; NFL franchise quarterbacks are neither.
The classic flexbone version needs under-center snaps and three backs in the backfield, which tilts the offense toward the run and makes passing harder (though option teams hit big play-action passes because the safeties have to play the run). The dive needs the quarterback right behind the center, so he can open, put the ball in the B-back’s belly a step later and ride him downhill. Spread teams get a shotgun triple another way: a zone read with a pitch man added behind it, a slot in motion or a second back, so a keep can still become a pitch. Even Washington’s 2012 NFL offense mixed in what NFL.com called “double- and triple-option play calls,”8 and Navy itself has moved much of its option game into the shotgun.9
It is hard to come from behind with: it runs clock and gains yards in chunks, not in bursts of passing.
NFL defenders are fast enough to cover mistakes. A pitch key who is a step slow in college is a step fast in the NFL.

The triple option lives on where its trade still pays: at the service academies, in many high schools, and for eleven seasons (2008–2018) at Georgia Tech under Paul Johnson, whose flexbone teams 02-03 introduced. The full college story, from the split-T to the wishbone to the spread option, is told in The College Laboratory.






NoteFilm room: Navy 2015



The triple option’s best recent showcase is Navy under Ken Niumatalolo, with Keenan Reynolds at quarterback. Reynolds closed his career in the Military Bowl on December 28, 2015, a 44–28 win over Pittsburgh in which Navy ran for 417 yards. His 88th career touchdown that day set the FBS record, and his 4,559 career rushing yards were then the most by a quarterback in FBS history.10
What to notice on a Navy or Army broadcast: for the first second, ignore the ball and watch #1, the dive key. If he stays outside, the B-back is through the line before the quarterback has turned around. If #1 squeezes, watch the quarterback come off the mesh and run at #2, with the pitch man about four yards outside him and a yard deeper. And watch the play-side A-back: on a well-run triple he runs past the pitch key without touching him.

title: Option Football: Reading Defenders Instead of Blocking Them
section: Midline: reading the man in the middle
text:
Midline: reading the man in the middle
The option doesn’t have to read someone on the edge. The midline option reads the first defensive lineman outside the center, often a 3-technique, the defensive tackle on the guard’s outside shoulder. The guard in front of him leaves him alone and climbs to a linebacker. The dive back runs at the A gap, right at the center’s hip, and the quarterback reads the tackle.


Show the Python
dfn = [D("PE", "DE", 1.0, technique("5", 1) + 0.9, "5"), D("PT", "DT", 1.0, technique("3", 1), "3"),
       D("BT", "DT", 1.0, technique("1", -1), "1"), D("BE", "DE", 1.0, technique("5", -1), "5"),
       D("SAM", "SAM", 4.5, 5.8, "S"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, 1.6, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -2.6, "W")]
off = [q for q in flexbone() if q.key not in ("LW", "RW")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=None)
go_to(p, "RG", (3.6, 1.6), via=[(0.3, 1.2)])                    # climb to the Mike
go_to(p, "RT", (0.5, 4.7))                                      # block the end
go_to(p, "C", (0.4, -0.6))                                      # back on the 1
go_to(p, "LG", (3.6, -2.4), via=[(0.3, -1.4)])
go_to(p, "LT", (0.4, -3.6))
go_to(p, "RA", (3.7, 6.3), via=[(0.2, 7.0)])                    # outside the 5, lead up on the Sam
p.read("PT")
p.highlight("PT", color=style.DEFENSE)
f = draw(p, lateral=(-8.5, 9.5), window=(-6.8, 9.5), title=False, width_in=5.4)
branch(f, p, [(-4.6, 0.0), (-2.6, 0.6), (0.4, 0.9), (6.2, 0.6)], color=style.OFFENSE_DARK,
       label="give if the 3\nstays put", label_at=(7.3, -1.6), fontsize=6.8)
branch(f, p, [(-1.9, 0.0), (-2.5, 0.6), (-1.4, 2.0), (-0.6, 2.45), (0.8, 3.6), (6.2, 3.7)], color=GREEN,
       label="keep if the 3\nsqueezes", label_at=(7.3, 5.4), fontsize=6.8)
f.ax.set_title("Midline option", fontsize=10, loc="left", color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")
plt.show()








Figure 18.8: The midline option from the flexbone, to the right. The 3-technique (ringed) is read: the right guard leaves him and climbs to the Mike, the right tackle blocks the end, and the center blocks back. The B-back dives at the A gap. If the 3-technique squeezes inside to tackle the dive, the quarterback keeps and runs just outside him, through the B gap; if he stays in his gap or rushes upfield, the quarterback gives and the B-back hits the A gap. The play-side A-back releases outside the 5-technique and leads up on the Sam.





Why read a tackle? Two reasons. First, the 3-technique is often the defense’s best interior player, a penetrator who is very hard to block one-on-one (03-01 explains why the position became a star’s job). Leaving him unblocked and reading him neutralizes him the same way the zone read neutralizes an edge rusher. Second, the midline beats defenses that load up on the edge to stop the outside options: if the pitch and the keep outside are covered, the ball goes up the middle. Option teams use the midline as a change-up when defenses crowd the edges: it reads a different man and attacks the middle.
The cost: the read is in the middle of the line, among bodies, with almost no time. A dive back in the A gap is at the line in about a second, and a defensive tackle who reads the play can split the difference (step inside and tackle the quarterback a step later). The give is a chain-mover by design, a dive into the A gap for a few yards; the keep is different, because a clean read puts the quarterback through the line with the linebackers already blocked, and it can go the distance.

title: Option Football: Reading Defenders Instead of Blocking Them
section: Designed quarterback runs: adding a blocker
text:
Designed quarterback runs: adding a blocker
Everything above reads a defender. The other way to make the quarterback count in the run game is simpler: give him the ball on purpose. On a designed quarterback run there is no read. The quarterback is the ball carrier from the start, and that changes the arithmetic in the offense’s favour, because the running back is free to block. On a normal run, the back is the ball carrier and the quarterback watches. On a quarterback run, the quarterback carries and the back blocks: the offense has gained a hat.


Show the Python
dfn = [D("PE", "DE", 1.0, technique("5", 1), "5"), D("PT", "DT", 1.0, technique("3", 1), "3"),
       D("BT", "DT", 1.0, technique("1", -1), "1"), D("BE", "DE", 1.0, technique("5", -1), "5"),
       D("SAM", "SAM", 1.0, 7.4, "S"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, 2.4, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -2.4, "W")]
p = Play(gun(rb_w=1.6, extra=(O("Y", "TE", -0.7, 4.8, "Y"),)), dfn, los=35, to_go=None)
go_to(p, "Y", (0.4, 4.2), via=[(-0.3, 4.6)])                  # down on the 5
go_to(p, "RT", (0.4, 2.6), via=[(-0.3, 3.0)])                 # down on the 3
go_to(p, "RG", (3.7, -1.6), via=[(-0.2, 1.8), (0.6, 1.0)])    # climbs to the backside Will
go_to(p, "C", (0.4, -0.5))                                    # back on the 1
go_to(p, "LT", (0.3, -3.6), via=[(-0.6, -3.4)])               # hinge
go_to(p, "LG", (3.6, 3.0), "pull", via=[(-1.6, -1.2), (-1.8, 2.0), (0.4, 4.6)])
go_to(p, "RB", (0.3, 6.8), via=[(-3.6, 4.0)], speed=5.0)       # kick out the Sam
go_to(p, "QB", (6.6, 5.9), "run", via=[(-4.0, 0.4), (-2.6, 3.0), (-0.7, 5.75), (1.0, 5.9)])
p.highlight("RB", color=PURPLE)
f = draw(p, lateral=(-8.5, 10.0), window=(-8.0, 9.5), title=False, width_in=5.4)
x0, y0 = _P(f, p, 6.0, -5.2)
x1, y1 = _P(f, p, 0.0, 8.5)
from matplotlib.patches import Rectangle
f.ax.add_patch(Rectangle((min(x0, x1), min(y0, y1)), abs(x1 - x0), abs(y1 - y0), fc=GREEN, alpha=0.07,
                         ec=GREEN, lw=0.8, ls=(0, (3, 2)), zorder=1))
say(f, p, 7.4, -5.6, "7 in the box\nv 7 blockers", color=GREEN, fontsize=7.2, weight="bold")
point_to(f, p, (-6.4, 7.0), (-3.4, 4.2), "R: now a blocker", color=PURPLE, fontsize=6.8)
point_to(f, p, (-6.6, -3.0), (-5.3, -0.6), "Q: the ball carrier", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
point_to(f, p, (-3.6, -5.6), (-1.7, -1.2), "LG pulls", fontsize=6.8)
f.ax.set_title("QB power: the back becomes a blocker", fontsize=10, loc="left", color=style.INK,
               fontweight="bold")
plt.show()








Figure 18.9: QB power to the right, from the shotgun with one tight end (11 personnel; wide receivers out of the picture). It is the power play of 03-03 with the quarterback as the ball carrier: the tight end and right tackle block down, the right guard climbs, the center blocks back, the left guard pulls through the hole for the Mike, and the running back, freed from carrying the ball, kicks out the Sam on the edge (purple ring: the back is now a blocker). The quarterback (thick arrow) runs just outside the tight end’s down block and inside the kick-out. Seven defenders in the box (shaded) against seven blockers: a hat on every hat. On a handoff, the same front would leave one man free. The deep safety is out of the picture.





There are four designed quarterback runs you will see most weeks.

QB power (Figure 18.9): the power play, with the backside guard pulling through the hole and the running back as a lead or kick-out blocker. It is a short-yardage and red-zone favourite, because on third-and-2 the extra hat is worth more than anything a running back can do with the ball.
QB counter (Figure 63.4): the quarterback steps one way, as if running with the back’s flow, then follows two linemen pulling the other way: one kicks out the end, the other leads through the hole (03-03’s counter blocking). The back often runs the opposite way as a decoy or blocks the backside end the pulling tackle left.
QB draw (Figure 18.11): a run disguised as a pass. The line shows pass protection, the quarterback shows a drop, and only when the pass rushers have charged upfield and the linebackers have turned to cover receivers does he run up the middle, through the space they left. It is strongest against man coverage, where defenders have their backs to the quarterback.
QB sweep: the quarterback runs wide, with pulling linemen or the back leading him around the edge. It is the outside version of QB power, built for a quarterback with a running back’s speed.



Show the Python
def qb_counter():
    dl = [D("PE", "DE", 1.0, technique("5", 1) + 0.6, "5"), D("PT", "DT", 1.0, technique("3", 1), "3"),
          D("BT", "DT", 1.0, technique("1", -1), "1"), D("BE", "DE", 1.0, technique("5", -1), "5")]
    lbs = [D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, 2.4, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -2.2, "W")]
    p = Play(gun(rb_w=-1.6), dl + lbs, los=35, to_go=None)
    # the defense: the end squeezes, the tackles are driven, the linebackers step up
    go_to(p, "PE", (0.6, 5.3), "path", speed=1.2, delay=0.3)
    go_to(p, "PT", (1.0, 1.0), "path", speed=0.9, delay=0.2)
    go_to(p, "BT", (0.9, -0.5), "path", speed=0.5)
    go_to(p, "BE", (-0.2, -4.6), "path", speed=2.0)
    go_to(p, "MIKE", (3.3, 1.8), "path", speed=1.4, delay=0.4)
    go_to(p, "WILL", (3.5, -1.6), "path", speed=1.4, delay=0.4)
    # the offense
    go_to(p, "RT", (0.4, 1.6), via=[(-0.3, 2.8)], speed=1.8)                     # down on the 3
    go_to(p, "RG", (2.4, -0.8), via=[(-0.2, 1.6), (0.6, 0.8)], speed=2.4)       # climbs to the Will
    go_to(p, "C", (0.2, -0.4), speed=1.0)                                       # back on the 1
    go_to(p, "LG", (-0.1, 4.3), "pull", via=[(-1.7, -1.2), (-1.9, 2.4)], speed=5.0)        # kick out the end
    go_to(p, "LT", (2.1, 2.6), "pull", via=[(-2.3, -3.0), (-2.6, 1.6), (-0.6, 3.1), (1.0, 3.0)], speed=6.5)  # wrap
    go_to(p, "RB", (-1.0, -4.2), via=[(-4.2, -3.0), (-1.8, -4.0)], speed=4.5)  # fill for the pulled tackle
    go_to(p, "QB", (-5.6, -0.9), "path", speed=2.4)                             # step left with the back
    go_to(p, "QB", (4.0, 3.0), "path", speed=5.0, delay=0.3, via=[(-4.6, 0.4), (-2.6, 2.2), (-0.8, 2.9)])
    return p


fig = strip([qb_counter()], [0.8, 2.0], lateral=(-6.5, 7.5), window=(-6.8, 5.5),
            notes=["Q steps left with the back;\nthe guard and tackle pull right",
                   "The guard kicks out the end, the\ntackle wraps; Q follows through"],
            rings=(("LG", PURPLE), ("LT", PURPLE)), ncols=2)
plt.show()








Figure 18.10: QB counter to the right, from the shotgun with the back on the left, in two moments (simulated, Big Data Bowl coordinates; purple rings mark the two pullers, the green ring the ball; faint trails show where each player has been). 1, the quarterback has taken a short step left with the back, selling a run that way, while the left guard and left tackle pull to the right behind the line; the right tackle blocks down on the 3-technique, the right guard climbs to the Will and the center blocks back. 2, the left guard has kicked out the play-side end, the left tackle has wrapped through the hole for the Mike, and the quarterback follows him through the space the right tackle’s down block left. The back fills on the backside end for the pulled tackle.







Show the Python
dl = [D("PE", "DE", 1.0, technique("5", 1), "5"), D("PT", "DT", 1.0, technique("3", 1), "3"),
      D("BT", "DT", 1.0, technique("1", -1), "1"), D("BE", "DE", 1.0, technique("5", -1), "5")]
lbs = [D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, 2.4, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -2.2, "W")]
p = Play(gun(rb_w=1.6), dl + lbs, los=35, to_go=None)
for k, rush in [("PE", (-4.6, 6.4)), ("PT", (-1.5, 2.4)), ("BT", (-1.5, -1.4)), ("BE", (-4.6, -6.4))]:
    go_to(p, k, rush, "path", speed=4.0)
go_to(p, "MIKE", (6.2, 3.8), "path"); go_to(p, "WILL", (6.2, -3.8), "path")
for k, end in [("LT", (-3.6, -5.4)), ("LG", (-2.3, -1.4)), ("C", (-2.0, 0.0)), ("RG", (-2.3, 2.4)), ("RT", (-3.6, 5.4))]:
    go_to(p, k, end)
go_to(p, "RB", (-3.0, 6.6), "path", via=[(-4.0, 3.6)])
go_to(p, "QB", (-6.5, 0.0), "path", speed=3.0)
f = draw(p, lateral=(-9.0, 9.5), window=(-8.5, 8.0), title=False, width_in=4.8)
branch(f, p, [(-6.5, 0.0), (-4.8, 0.2), (-1.0, 0.6), (5.6, 0.8)], color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, label="then run",
       label_at=(6.3, -1.8), fontsize=6.8)
say(f, p, -7.0, -3.4, "Q shows\na drop", fontsize=6.6)
say(f, p, 3.6, 6.9, "LBs drop\nto cover", fontsize=6.6, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK)
f.ax.set_title("QB draw", fontsize=10, loc="left", color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")
plt.show()








Figure 18.11: QB draw. The line sets as if to pass and lets the four rushers charge upfield into their pass blocks; the linebackers, reading pass, drop to cover receivers. The quarterback shows a drop, then runs up the middle, through the space the rushers and linebackers have left.





QB power or power read? The names sit side by side, and a beginner (or a broadcaster) can merge them. The power read is an option: two runners, one unblocked end, and the quarterback decides after the snap who carries. QB power has no read at all: the quarterback carries every time, and the back, who on the power read was a runner, is now the man who blocks the end. Same blocking up front, a different job for the back.
Two more versions matter in the NFL. The first adds a blocker without a back: from empty (no back beside the quarterback, five receivers spread wide; 02-04), the defense has to send defenders out with the receivers, the box thins to five linemen against five or six defenders, and a quarterback draw or counter makes the quarterback the extra hat by himself. The numbers section below counts how often NFL designed runs come from empty. The second is the quarterback zone: the quarterback runs the inside-zone track himself with the back leading him, or, in the version coaches call dart, with the backside tackle pulling across to lead him through the hole.
The simplest designed quarterback run of all is the sneak, where the quarterback follows his center for a yard; its pushed-from-behind version, the tush push, has its own story in Red Zone, Goal Line, and Short Yardage.






ImportantWhy it exists



Designed quarterback runs exist because a quarterback carrying the ball turns the running back into an extra blocker: ten men block for the ball carrier instead of nine, which no handoff can do. On short yardage and near the goal line, where the defense crowds the box and every inch is contested, that extra hat is often the difference. The cost is the quarterback’s body, and NFL teams pay their quarterbacks too much to spend it twenty times a game. So designed quarterback runs are a spice, used when the extra blocker matters most and rationed the rest of the time.

title: Option Football: Reading Defenders Instead of Blocking Them
text:
How defenses answer the option
You have met the scrape exchange. Defenses have five broader answers, and you will see all of them on a Sunday when an option team is in town.
Assignment football. Every option has a fixed number of ball carriers, and the defense assigns one defender to each: someone for the dive (or the back), someone for the quarterback, someone for the pitch. The rule is discipline. The defender assigned to the quarterback takes the quarterback even when the ball was given, every time, and trusts that his teammate has the back.
Make the read hard. The read key does not have to commit. A defensive end can slow-play or feather the read: shuffle down the line with his shoulders square, inside enough to threaten the back and outside enough to threaten the quarterback, giving the quarterback a muddy picture until the last instant. A slow-playing end wants the quarterback to give, so the defense can tackle the back with the linebackers inside, or to hesitate, which kills the play.
So what does the quarterback do? The rule “if he can tackle the back, keep” doesn’t settle it, because a slow-player is built to sit exactly between can and can’t: he can reach either runner, a step late. This is where the shoulder-and-distance read from the mesh section earns its keep: shoulders turned down the line toward the back mean pull; shoulders still square and upfield mean give. Against a true slow-play, most offenses fall back on their default, the give, because a give into a slow-playing end gives the back a one-on-one with a man moving sideways, and a late, hesitant keep is the worst outcome on the menu. The offense’s longer answers are the ones you have met: an arc block, so a keep has a blocker in front of it; bash or the power read, so the end’s in-between spot is the wrong spot; or simply block the end and run the ball somewhere else.
Out-number it. Every read gains the offense a man (the triple option, with two reads, gains two). The defense can bring one more into the box, usually by rolling a safety down, and get its plus-one back. That is the box-count battle of 05-05, and it is why option offenses work best when the passing game keeps the safeties deep.
Spy the quarterback. Against a quarterback who runs, a defense can assign one defender, often a linebacker or a safety, to do nothing but shadow him: a spy (10-02 uses him on third down). The spy takes the quarterback on every keep and every designed run, which frees the rest of the defense to play the back, at the cost of one fewer man in coverage or in the box.
Hit the quarterback. The bluntest answer is also legal. Since 2013, NFL officials have treated a quarterback who is carrying out a read-option fake as a runner: as the league’s vice president of officiating, Dean Blandino, put it in a 2013 rules video, “the quarterback can be hit like a runner until he’s clearly out of the play.”11 A defense facing a read offense will tell its read key to hit the quarterback whenever he can, ball or no ball, to make every keep, and every fake, cost something.

title: Option Football: Reading Defenders Instead of Blocking Them
text:
Where option came from, briefly
Option football is older than the forward pass’s dominance, and almost all of it was invented in college, by coaches who had worse players than their opponents and needed arithmetic to win.

The split-T option, 1941. Missouri’s Don Faurot widened the T-formation’s line splits and built a series of plays (a dive, a quarterback keep and a “running pitchout”) that together worked like the modern option. Bud Wilkinson learned it from Faurot in the Navy during the war and took it to Oklahoma, whose split-T teams won a record 47 straight games from 1953 to 1957.12
The veer, 1965, Bill Yeoman at Houston, as above, and the wishbone, 1968, Emory Bellard at Texas (02-03): the triple option’s two great formations.
The zone read, early 1990s. At Glenville State, a small college in West Virginia, Rich Rodriguez’s quarterback Jed Drenning fumbled a handoff on a zone play in practice in 1991, picked the ball up, saw the end crashing inside, and ran where the end had been. Rodriguez saw that the mistake was a play.13 He took it to Tulane and West Virginia, and Urban Meyer’s spread-option offenses at Utah and Florida (shotgun, three or four receivers spread wide, and the quarterback’s legs as the run game’s extra threat) made it national.
The pistol, 2005, Chris Ault at Nevada (02-02): shotgun depth for the quarterback’s read, with the back directly behind him so the run can go either way. In 2009 Ault’s Nevada became the first team in NCAA history with three 1,000-yard rushers in one season; one of them was the quarterback, Colin Kaepernick.14

The whole lineage, from the single wing through the spread option and the RPO, is in The College Laboratory.
