title: Pass Protection: Slides, Man Schemes, and Who Blocks the Extra Guy
text:
Watch for it on Sunday






TipWatch for it



Before the snap.

Count the blockers you can see. Five linemen, plus a back beside the quarterback, plus any tight end on the line. Empty backfield means five-man protection: someone is hot.
Count the threats. How many defenders are standing within a couple of yards of the line? Six or seven at the line against five or six blockers means a hot throw is in the plan, or the defense is bluffing.
Listen and look for the Mike call. The center or quarterback points at a linebacker. If a defender moves after that, watch for a second call.
Find the help. A tight end next to a tackle may mean that side’s edge rusher is getting a chip. A back offset to one side more often shows his check side, the side he will watch for a blitzer (usually the man side, away from the slide), and maybe chip after. Neither is a guarantee: a late call can send him across the quarterback’s face.

After the snap: rushers versus blockers.

Watch the linemen’s first step. All five the same way: slide. The center and his two neighbours one way, the other two straight back at the man in front of them: half-slide. Each to a different defender: man.
Count, in the first second, how many rushed and how many blocked. Four rushers against six blockers? Look for the spare men helping. Six against six? Everyone has a man.
Watch the back’s first step. Forward into a gap: he has a blitzer. Out to the flat: his man dropped (check-release). A shove on an end and then out: a chip.
Watch the tackles’ sets. Deep and backward (vertical), angled out (45-degree), or forward at the line (jump, and expect a quick throw).
If a rusher comes free, guess who owned him. Was he the widest man, unblocked on purpose, with the ball out fast to the space he left? That was the plan. Was he an inside man, a linebacker through an A gap, with two blockers on someone else? That was a bust, probably a bad count. Check the replay. And look at the ball: a free man by design should be met by a quick throw. If the widest man came free and the ball was not out, the quarterback or the hot receiver missed it; if an inside man came free, suspect the protection first.
Note the time. Count “one-Mississippi” from the snap. Pressure inside about two and a half seconds is almost always the protection’s problem: the average throw is out by then. Past three seconds, where the EPA chart above peaked and started to fall, the quarterback owns part of it. These are rules of thumb from that chart, not laws.

For your prediction log: for one quarter, write down rushers and blockers on every dropback (for example, “4 v 6”) and whether anyone came free. By the end you will know whether that defense wins by numbers or by stunts.

text:
Predict the play






TipPredict the play 1: seven at the line





Show the Python
dfn = [D("LE", "DE", 1.0, -5.0, "E"), D("NT", "DT", 1.0, -2.4, "3"), D("DT", "DT", 1.0, 2.4, "3"),
       D("RE", "DE", 1.0, 5.0, "E"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 1.8, 0.95, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 1.8, -0.95, "W"),
       D("NB", "NB", 2.0, -7.6, "NB"), D("LCB", "CB", 6.0, -13.5, "C"), D("RCB", "CB", 6.0, 14.0, "C"),
       D("SS", "SS", 6.5, 10.0, "SS"), D("FS", "FS", 13.0, 1.0, "FS")]
p = Play(empty_3x2(), dfn, los=40, to_go=7)
p.highlight("MIKE", "WILL", "NB", color=PURPLE)
fld = draw(p, width_in=6.4, lateral=(-15.6, 15.6), window=(-6.8, 14.6), ol_fs=6.2)
plt.show()








Figure 21.17: Third-and-7. The offense is in an empty 3x2 formation: five blockers. The defense has two 3-techniques, shows both linebackers standing in the A gaps on either side of the center, and has walked the nickel back (NB) up over H. The three defenders who might or might not rush are ringed.





How many can the offense block, how many might come, and where should the ball go if they all do?






TipAnswer





Five blockers, up to seven rushers, so the ball must come out fast, with a hot answer on each side. Count it: four defensive linemen, two linebackers in the A gaps and the walked-up nickel make seven possible rushers against an empty protection’s five. If all seven come, two are free; there is no protection that blocks seven with five.
Which two is the offense’s choice. Inside-out, the five linemen take the two A-gap linebackers and the two 3-techniques first, because their paths are shortest, and the fifth blocker goes to one of the ends. The offense picks the end by working the protection toward the side with more threats. The left has four possible rushers (the Will, a 3-technique, the end and the nickel), the right only three, so the line works left and the left tackle takes the left end. The two men left over are then the widest on each side: the nickel on the left and the right end on the right, each with the longest way to go.
Two free rushers need two answers. On the left, H is hot: if the nickel comes, H runs into the space he left. On the right, count the coverage as well as the rush, which is the first thing a quarterback coach asks. If seven rush, only four defenders are left to cover five receivers, so someone is uncovered; as drawn, nobody is over R. The quarterback’s throw depends on who actually comes, and it has to be out in about a second.
Two cautions. First, this is exactly the look that attacks the Mike call: with two linebackers in the A gaps, the offense must decide before the snap which one the line will count, and the defense will try to make him wrong. Second, the defense may not bring them all. Showing seven and rushing four, with the A-gap linebackers dropping out, is a staple of simulated pressure. Then the hot throw is thrown into a linebacker who never left. Good quarterbacks check where the threat goes at the snap, not where it stood.











TipPredict the play 2: two on the edge





Show the Python
off = line() + gun(-1.5) + [O("X", "WR", -0.7, -13.5), O("H", "WR", -1.4, -8.5), O("Y", "TE", -1.4, 8.5),
                            O("Z", "WR", -0.7, 13.5)]
dfn = [D("LE", "DE", 1.0, -5.0, "E"), D("NT", "DT", 1.0, -0.7, "1"), D("DT", "DT", 1.0, 2.35, "3"),
       D("RE", "DE", 1.0, 5.0, "E"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, 1.4, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 1.4, -6.6, "W"),
       D("NB", "NB", 3.0, -8.9, "NB"), D("LCB", "CB", 6.5, -13.5, "C"), D("RCB", "CB", 6.5, 13.5, "C"),
       D("SS", "SS", 6.0, 8.5, "SS"), D("FS", "FS", 13.0, 0.0, "FS")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=40, to_go=6)
p.highlight("WILL", "NB", color=PURPLE)
p.highlight("RB")
fld = draw(p, width_in=6.4, lateral=(-15.6, 15.6), window=(-6.8, 14.6), ol_fs=6.2)
for wg in (0.8, 2.4, 4.0):
    gap_oval(fld, p, wg, width=1.4, height=1.2, alpha=0.42)
say(fld, p, -3.2, 6.2, "slide right", color=GREEN, weight="bold")
plt.show()








Figure 21.18: Third-and-6. The offense is in 11 personnel with the back to the quarterback’s left and has called a half-slide right (the slide side’s gaps are shaded), so the back’s job is the left side. The Will linebacker has walked up to the line outside the left end, and the nickel back has crept down outside him, both ringed. The back is ringed in green.





(a) If both the Will and the nickel blitz from the left, whom does the back block, and who is the quarterback’s problem?
(b) Now a post-snap read. Suppose that instead the Mike comes through the right A gap untouched, while the center has turned left to help the left guard on the 1-technique. Was the Mike free by design, or was it a bust? And whose was he?






TipAnswer





(a) The back takes the Will; the nickel is the quarterback’s, and the throw goes to H. On the left, the man side, the left tackle has the end and the left guard has the 1-technique. That leaves two potential rushers, the Will and the nickel, and one back. Block inside-out: the Will is closer to the quarterback’s path, so he is the back’s; the nickel, wider and deeper, has the longer way to go and is left free by design. His blitz empties the area over H, so H is the hot receiver, and the quarterback has to see the nickel come and throw at once.
The offense had other options before the snap: the quarterback could have re-declared the protection, sliding the line left toward the threat and sending the back right, or kept the tight end in. Notice why it might not bother: the right side has only three rushers for three sliding linemen, and a quick throw to H against a blitzing nickel is often the best play on the field. If the nickel doesn’t come, the back’s man (the Will) still might, and if neither comes, the back releases and five receivers are out.
(b) A bust, and the Mike was the center’s. In a half-slide right, the center owns the right A gap, whoever comes through it. He may “look for work” and help a neighbour only once nobody has come into his gap; turning left first left his own gap empty. Every tell in the “Watch for it” list points the same way: the free man came from the inside, through an A gap, the shortest path, while two blockers were on one defender. A free man by design is the widest man, and the ball is already on its way to the space he left.











TipPredict the play 3: the star on the edge





Show the Python
off = line() + gun(1.6) + [O("Y", "TE", -0.7, 4.8), O("X", "WR", -0.7, -13.5), O("H", "WR", -1.4, -8.5),
                           O("Z", "WR", -1.4, 13.0)]
dfn = [D("LE", "DE", 1.0, -5.0, "E"), D("NT", "DT", 1.0, -0.7, "1"), D("DT", "DT", 1.0, 2.35, "3"),
       D("RE", "DE", 1.0, 7.2, "99"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, 1.6, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -2.4, "W"),
       D("NB", "NB", 5.0, -8.1, "NB"), D("LCB", "CB", 6.5, -13.5, "C"), D("RCB", "CB", 6.5, 13.0, "C"),
       D("SS", "SS", 12.0, 8.0, "SS"), D("FS", "FS", 12.0, -8.0, "FS")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=30, to_go=10)
p.highlight("RE", color=PURPLE)
fld = draw(p, width_in=6.4, lateral=(-15.6, 15.6), window=(-6.8, 14.6), ol_fs=6.2)
point_to(fld, p, (4.6, 10.0), (1.0, 7.2), "their best pass rusher,\nwide outside the tight end")
plt.show()








Figure 21.19: Second-and-10. The defense’s best pass rusher (99, ringed) lines up wide outside the offense’s right tight end. The offense has the tight end on the line next to the right tackle and the back offset to the right of the quarterback, with two receivers to the left.





Where is the protection’s help going, and what does the offense give up to send it?






TipAnswer





99 belongs to the right tackle, and the help comes on top: chips from the tight end and the back. The price is receivers and time. Everything about the offense’s alignment points at the right edge. Expect a half-slide left: the center, left guard and left tackle slide left and own the gaps on that side (the 1-technique, the Will and the left end), while on the man side the right guard takes the 3-technique and the right tackle takes 99 man to man, big on big. Then the help. The tight end chips 99 from the inside as he releases. The back, offset to that side, checks his linebacker (the Mike) first; if the Mike doesn’t come, he chips 99 too and releases (check, chip, release). If the offense wants a full-time double team instead, it is the tackle and the tight end together, a seven-man protection.
What the offense will not do is leave 99 to the tight end and the back. You never leave a star alone with a back; help means in addition to the tackle.
The cost is visible too. With two players spending time on 99, only three receivers (X, H and Z) are out on time, and the tight end and back arrive late, so expect a throw to the receivers who are on time, or a two- or three-man route combination with lots of protection behind it. The defense’s answer is just as predictable: move 99 around (inside, to the other side, standing up over a guard) or run stunts with him, so that the offense’s help is in the wrong place. That cat-and-mouse is where The Pass Rush picks up the story.

title: Pass Protection: Slides, Man Schemes, and Who Blocks the Extra Guy
text:
Takeaways

Protection is counting. The offense always blocks with five and may add a back or tight ends; every added blocker is one fewer receiver. Block inside-out, and if someone must go unblocked, make it the widest man and make him the quarterback’s.
Two ways to assign blockers. Slide protection blocks gaps, so it absorbs stunts and surprises but leaves an end for the back. Man protection (BOB) blocks men, so it matches big on big but has to chase movement. The half-slide, the everyday six-man protection, does both. Slide toward the inside trouble, and never leave a star edge rusher alone with a back.
The Mike call makes six blockers one mind. Naming a reference defender sets every assignment (the center works toward him, the man side counts out from him, the back takes the next man); two blockers counting from different men produce a free rusher without the defense sending an extra man. Defenses move after the call to make it wrong.
Backs and tight ends decide after the snap. Check-release turns a blocker into a receiver when his man doesn’t come; a chip gives help on the way out. Max protect buys time with up to eight blockers; empty and scat buy receivers with five, and a blitz means a hot throw or a sight adjust into the space the blitzer left.
The pocket is a cup. The interior holds firm; the tackles give ground with a kick slide (vertical, 45-degree, or a jump set for quick throws) and push the edge past the quarterback, who steps up. Punch wins control, the anchor stops power, and switching beats stunts.
Measure pressure, not just sacks, and share the blame. Pressure rate is steadier than sack rate; pressure climbs with time to throw; and sack rate depends on the quarterback and the play call as much as on the line.

title: The Quick Game: Slant-Flat, Stick, Snag, Quick Screens, and Beating Press
text:
What the quick game is
Third-and-6, midway through the second quarter. Before the snap the slot defender creeps toward the line, and both linebackers walk up into the gaps beside the center. Six defenders are now standing within a yard or two of the ball, and the broadcast’s analyst says the word you have heard a thousand times: blitz. The ball is snapped. The quarterback takes one big step back from the shotgun, plants, and throws. The outside receiver, who had run three steps upfield and cut sharply inside, catches it eight yards downfield and falls forward for a first down. The play took about two seconds. Nobody touched the quarterback, and the replay doesn’t even bother to show the rush. How did the quarterback know where to throw before the blitz got to him? Why was the receiver open at all, with so many defenders so close? And why do so many drives, even for the best quarterbacks in the league, live on throws that travel five yards? This chapter is about the family of plays that answers all three questions: the quick game.
You’ll be able to…
The quick game is the set of pass plays built to get the ball out in roughly 2.5 seconds or less. Three things make a pass play “quick,” and they go together:
Nothing in the rulebook defines it, and teams draw the line in different places, but analysts usually treat throws out in under 2.5 seconds as “quick.” In 2025 about half of all NFL pass attempts came out that fast; the median attempt left the quarterback’s hand at 2.5 seconds.1 That’s the first thing to understand about the quick game: it is not a gadget or a change-up. It is a large share of everything an NFL offense throws.

title: The Quick Game: Slant-Flat, Stick, Snag, Quick Screens, and Beating Press
text:
A short drop. From under center, the quarterback takes three steps back (a three-step drop); from the shotgun, already five yards deep, he takes one step (some teams teach three quick, short steps that cover the same ground). There’s no time to drift, reset or scan.
Short routes. Most receivers break at five or six yards or less: slants, hitches, flats, short outs. One receiver often runs deep, but mainly to drag a defender out of the way.
A throw timed to the break. The ball leaves as the quarterback’s back foot lands, aimed at the spot where the receiver will be when he makes his cut. If the throw is late, the play is usually dead.

title: The Quick Game: Slant-Flat, Stick, Snag, Quick Screens, and Beating Press
text:
Why it exists: three jobs
The quick game survives in every playbook, from the old 49ers to the modern Chiefs, because it does three jobs no other part of the offense does as cheaply.
Job 1: beat the pass rush with the clock. A pass rush is a race. Four rushers against five blockers usually need well over two and a half seconds to get home, if they get there at all; a blitzer nobody blocks can arrive in about two. The quarterback can win that race in two ways: block long enough for the deep routes to develop, or throw before the rush matters. The quick game is the second way. It can’t be sacked if the ball is already gone, and it doesn’t need the offensive line to win, only to hold for a heartbeat. The linemen block it differently, too. A quick throw is released low and early, from a quarterback only a step or two behind them, so they meet the rushers aggressively at the line (the jump set of Pass Protection) to keep the defenders’ hands down and out of the throwing lanes. A defensive lineman who gets his arms up in the gap the slant is thrown through is the quick game’s most common way to lose a ball: the batted pass.
Pass Protection showed one half of the clock’s bargain: the longer the ball stays in the quarterback’s hand, the more often the rush gets to him (under one throw in ten is pressured when it comes out in under two seconds; about half when it is held three and a half seconds or more). Here is the other half, the price of throwing early.


Show the Python
bins = [0, 2.0, 2.5, 3.0, 3.5, 99]
labels = ["< 2.0", "2.0–2.5", "2.5–3.0", "3.0–3.5", "3.5 +"]
a = ATT25.copy()
a["bucket"] = pd.cut(a["time_to_throw"], bins, labels=labels, right=False)
g = a.groupby("bucket", observed=True).agg(n=("epa", "size"), pressured=("was_pressure", "mean"),
                                           air=("air_yards", "mean"), comp=("complete_pass", "mean"))
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.4, 3.0))
cols = [style.OFFENSE, style.OFFENSE] + [style.BASELINE] * 3
for ax, col, fmt, top, title in ((axes[0], "air", "{:.1f} yd", 14, "How deep the throw went"),
                                 (axes[1], "comp", "{:.0%}", 1.0, "How often it was caught")):
    vals = g[col].values
    ax.bar(range(len(g)), vals, color=cols, width=0.62, zorder=2)
    for i, v in enumerate(vals):
        ax.text(i, v + top * 0.02, fmt.format(v), ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=7.6, color=style.INK)
    ax.set_xticks(range(len(g)), list(g.index), fontsize=7.6)
    ax.tick_params(axis="x", length=0, pad=3)
    ax.set_ylim(0, top * 1.12)
    ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=9, loc="left")
    ax.set_xlabel("Seconds from snap to throw", fontsize=8)
axes[0].set_yticks([0, 5, 10], ["0", "5 yd", "10 yd"])
axes[1].set_yticks([0, 0.5, 1.0], ["0%", "50%", "100%"])
for ax in axes:
    ax.tick_params(axis="y", labelsize=7.6)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=1.6)
plt.show()








Figure 22.1: The price of a fast throw. Every bar is a group of 2025 regular-season pass attempts sorted by time from snap to throw. Left: how far past the line of scrimmage the ball traveled, on average. Right: how often it was caught. The two blue bars, throws out in under 2.5 seconds, are the quick game’s territory: they go less than half as far as the slowest throws, and they are caught far more often. Sacks are not throws, so they are left out.





Fast and short come as a package: the quick throws went only three to seven yards past the line of scrimmage on average, against eleven or twelve for the slow ones.
Job 2: keep the offense on schedule. A first down takes ten yards in three plays, and the plays that kill drives are the ones that lose yards or gain none: sacks, incompletions, and the third-and-long that follows them. Coaches call staying ahead of the chains being on schedule: roughly, gaining four or more on first down and half the remaining distance on second. Quick throws are completed far more often (in 2025, about 72% of attempts out in under 2.5 seconds were caught, against 57% of the rest) and almost never end in a sack, so they keep the offense in second-and-5 instead of second-and-10.2 By success rate (the share of plays with positive EPA, meaning plays that left the offense better off than before the snap), quick throws succeeded on about 51% of attempts, slower throws on about 45%.
Job 3: stretch the run game sideways. Bill Walsh, who built the most influential short passing offense in NFL history, started from a team that couldn’t run the ball well enough to control a game, so he used short, high-percentage throws to do the running game’s job; his throws have often been described as extended handoffs.3 A five-yard pass to a receiver near the sideline gets the ball to a fast player in space, away from the big defenders in the middle, and lets him run. In 2025 about 59% of the receiving yards on quick completions came after the catch, against about 38% on slower ones.4 That is the defining fact of the quick game: the throw is short and the run after it does most of the work. It also means that a defense that wants to stop the quick game has to tackle in space, on the edges of the field, where it has the fewest defenders.






ImportantWhy it exists, and what it costs



The quick game trades depth for certainty: a high chance of a small gain, a near-zero chance of a sack and a receiver running before the defense is set, in place of the big gain through the air. The bill comes in three parts. First, the defense can squeeze it. If an offense never threatens deep, defenders creep closer and the short windows shrink; quick game works best when the defense still has to respect the deep ball. Second, it needs yards after the catch: a five-yard throw that is tackled at five yards on third-and-7 is a punt. Third, it gets harder as the field shrinks: near the goal line there is less room to run after the catch. The rest of this chapter is about how good offenses keep the bargain on their side.



A short history: the rest of the Walsh story
You met the start of this story in Passing Fundamentals: Bill Walsh, an assistant on Paul Brown’s Cincinnati Bengals in 1970, building a passing game of short, timed throws around Virgil Carter, a quarterback who was accurate but had no deep arm, and Carter leading the NFL in completion percentage in 1971.5 Two details sharpen it. Carter was never supposed to be the starter: the Bengals’ brilliant young quarterback, Greg Cook, had wrecked his throwing shoulder as a rookie in 1969, so Walsh built the offense around the quarterback he had, not the one he wanted. And Carter, who had studied statistics in college and took an MBA during his playing career, co-wrote one of the first academic papers to estimate the expected points value of field position: the same idea this book uses as its scorecard.6
In San Francisco from 1979, with Joe Montana, the approach became the backbone of three Super Bowl champions (after the 1981, 1984 and 1988 seasons).7 Its signature was the slant to Jerry Rice, thrown on rhythm before the cornerback could react and turned into a long touchdown by Rice’s speed: Rice caught a record 22 touchdown passes in just 12 games in 1987.8 The family of offenses descended from Walsh’s ideas came to be called the West Coast offense, a label with a tangled history that Offensive Systems and Languages untangles.
A rule change helped. In 1978 the NFL barred defenders from contacting receivers more than five yards past the line of scrimmage; until then a defensive back could keep bumping a receiver well down the field.9 Receivers who could no longer be mugged at eight and ten yards made short timing routes far more reliable, and passing numbers rose across the league. Walsh arrived in San Francisco a year later.

title: The Quick Game: Slant-Flat, Stick, Snag, Quick Screens, and Beating Press
section: Rhythm: the drop and the throw are one motion
text:
Rhythm: the drop and the throw are one motion
Watch a quick throw from the end-zone camera and you’ll notice that the quarterback never seems to decide anything. He catches the snap, takes his steps, and the ball is gone on the last one. That is a rhythm throw: a pass thrown on the last step of the drop, with no hitch or hesitation, so the ball arrives just as the receiver breaks.
The rhythm is the whole point. The quarterback’s drop and the receiver’s route are designed together, step for step: a three-step drop under center, or a one-step drop from the shotgun, is timed to a receiver who breaks at about five or six yards (Passing Fundamentals lays out the matched pairs). When the quarterback’s back foot hits, the receiver is making his cut, and the ball leaves. If the quarterback has to hitch (take an extra reset step) or look somewhere else, the timing is gone and a different, slower play has begun.
You’ll meet three different clocks in this chapter, and they measure different things:

About 1 to 1.5 seconds is the design: from the shotgun, a rhythm throw against a receiver who gets a clean release leaves the hand about then.
2.5 seconds is the analysts’ line, the cut-off the data in this chapter uses to call a throw “quick.” It sits well past the design time because real plays lose a beat here and there: a receiver delayed by a jam, a quarterback who waits half a second for a defender to commit, a snap that comes late in his hands. A 2.1-second slant against press is still a quick-game throw; it just shows you the press cost the receiver a step.
“One-thousand-two” is the couch rule in the “Watch for it” box at the end: if the ball is gone before you finish saying it, you saw the quick game working as designed.

What does a late quick throw look like? The quarterback’s last step lands and the ball doesn’t come out: he hitches, or his shoulders turn to another receiver, and the slant runner is already two or three steps past his break, drifting into the linebackers. When the throw finally comes, the defender who was a step behind is now at the catch point. That is when you see the batted balls, the contested catches and the interceptions on short routes.
That has a consequence that shapes the whole quick game: the quarterback has almost no time to read the defense after the snap. He gets one look, at one defender, and has to know in advance what that defender’s answer means. Most of the “reading” therefore happens before the snap. To see how, we need one more piece of vocabulary.

title: The Quick Game: Slant-Flat, Stick, Snag, Quick Screens, and Beating Press
text:
Leverage: the pre-snap read
Look at any cornerback before the snap and ask a simple question: is he lined up inside the receiver, outside him, or straight in front of him? That position is his leverage, and it is the most important thing a quarterback looks at before a quick throw.


Show the Python
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.5, 3.2))
for ax, shade in ((axes[0], -1.5), (axes[1], 1.5)):
    p = Play([O("X", "WR", LINE_D, -15.0)], [D("LCB", "CB", 6.0, -15.0 + shade, "CB")], los=40, to_go=None)
    p.highlight("LCB")
    if shade < 0:
        p.route("X", r.slant(stem=2.5, length=9))
    else:
        p.route("X", r.quick_out(depth=5.0, width=6.0))
    fld = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=(-25.0, -4.0), window=(-3.5, 12.5), show_ruler=False)
    if shade < 0:
        taken(fld, p, [(-0.7, -15.0), (5.0, -15.0), (4.7, -20.0)])     # the square quick out he sits on
        say(fld, p, 8.2, -8.9, "slant: open,\nhe has to cross\nX's path to\nget there", color=READ_GREEN,
            fontsize=7, weight="bold")
        say(fld, p, 9.0, -20.4, "out: he's\nalready there", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
        say(fld, p, 2.6, -21.3, "CB outside", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
        panel_title(ax, "Outside leverage: throw inside")
    else:
        taken(fld, p, [(-0.7, -15.0), (2.5, -15.0), (7.0, -10.0)])     # the slant he sits on
        say(fld, p, 9.0, -20.4, "quick out:\nopen, he is\non the wrong\nside", color=READ_GREEN,
            fontsize=7, weight="bold")
        say(fld, p, 9.4, -9.0, "slant: he's\nalready there", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
        say(fld, p, 2.6, -9.0, "CB inside", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
        panel_title(ax, "Inside leverage: throw outside")
legend(fig, ["route", "taken"], y=0.08)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=1.0, rect=(0, 0.07, 1, 1))
plt.show()








Figure 22.2: Leverage, from the quarterback’s side of the ball. Left: the cornerback lines up a yard and a half outside the receiver, protecting the sideline (outside leverage). Routes toward the sideline run into him; a route that breaks inside, like the slant, starts on the side he isn’t on. Right: the cornerback lines up inside the receiver (inside leverage), protecting the middle; now the quick out is the route that starts on the open side. Throw away from leverage.





Why would a defender give anything away on purpose? Because he can’t take everything away, so he takes away what his teammates can’t help him with. A defender usually lines up on the side where he has no help, and funnels the receiver toward the side where he does. A cornerback with a safety deep in the middle and linebackers underneath often plays outside leverage: his teammates can help on routes inside. A corner whose help is outside plays inside leverage, and that help can be a teammate sitting in the flat in front of him or simply the sideline. Coaches call the sideline the cornerback’s twelfth man, because a receiver near it has nowhere to go but inside or straight up. So leverage is not just one man’s position. It is a clue to the whole coverage behind him.
The receiver’s split, how far from the ball he lines up, feeds the same read from the other side. Split wide, near the sideline, he has little room to break outside, so the corner can shade him inside and let the sideline do the rest. A receiver who reduces his split, lining up closer to the ball, has room both ways, and a defender who sees a reduced split starts expecting an outside-breaking route.
The quarterback’s rule is short: throw away from leverage. A route that breaks toward the side the defender isn’t on gains a step at the break, because the defender has to cross the receiver’s path, or run around him, to get there. That’s the core of the pre-snap read: a look at the defense’s alignment before the snap (leverage, the cushion, meaning how far off the receiver the defender stands, the safeties, the box) that tells the quarterback which side, or which receiver, a play should go to. Many quick-game calls are drawn with a concept on each side of the formation for exactly this reason: the quarterback picks the side whose leverage he likes before the ball is snapped, then reads one defender on that side after it. The coordinator calls the play; the quarterback chooses the side, at the line, inside the rules the offense has practiced all week (many teams pre-set a default, such as “work the side with the extra receiver,” for when both look equal).
Three numbers belong in every pre-snap read of a single receiver:

Inside, outside or head-up? Head-up (straight in front of the receiver) is a defender who hasn’t given a side away. It is common in press coverage, and the release section below shows how a receiver deals with it.
How deep? A defender seven or eight yards off can’t stop a short throw from being caught; he can only tackle the catch. One pressed up at the line (in press coverage: a yard or so away, ready to jam the receiver at the snap) can disrupt the route itself.
Where is his help? A deep safety over the top lets a cornerback sit on short routes. No safety at all means the cornerback has to protect against the deep ball first.







CautionCommon misconception



“The quarterback reads the coverage after the snap.” For deep dropback passes, mostly yes. For the quick game, the important decision is made before the snap and the post-snap read is a single glance at a single defender. When you see a quarterback throw the instant his foot lands, he isn’t guessing; he made the decision ten seconds earlier, from the alignment, and the snap merely confirmed it.

title: The Quick Game: Slant-Flat, Stick, Snag, Quick Screens, and Beating Press
text:
Slant-flat: the high-low
Now the concepts. A pass concept is a set of routes designed to work together, usually to put one defender in a position where he can’t be right. Every quick concept in this chapter is built on one of the two stretches from Passing Fundamentals: a high-low (one receiver above a defender, one below him) or a horizontal stretch (one inside him, one outside him). The defender being stretched is the one the quarterback watches.
The simplest quick concept in football is slant-flat. The outside receiver runs a slant: three hard steps upfield, then a sharp break inside at about 45 degrees. The inside receiver runs to the flat, the area near the sideline just past the line of scrimmage. Between them stands one defender, usually the slot defender or an outside linebacker, whose job in most zone coverages is to guard the short area outside: the flat defender (or, in Cover 3 language, the curl-flat defender). He is the read.
The quarterback’s thought process is one sentence long: “If the flat defender widens, throw the slant; if he sits, throw the flat.” He doesn’t have to diagnose the coverage, find the safeties or work through five receivers. He has to watch one man take one step. That’s why slant-flat is often the first pass concept a young quarterback learns, and why it survives at every level of the sport.
Notice what each route is doing to the defender. The flat route is a low threat: it pulls him toward the sideline and forward. The slant is a high threat: it attacks the space behind him and inside him. It is the same high-low as the curl-flat read in Passing Fundamentals, squeezed into three steps. He can’t be in both places, and he has to commit in about half a second. If he widens, he has opened the door the slant runs through. If he stays put, or sinks into the slant’s path, the inside receiver catches the ball in the flat with no one within five yards, which on most downs is a fine result: a “long handoff” to the edge.






TipWatch for it: what the read defender can do



Coaches describe the one defender’s choice with a handful of verbs. You’ll see them through the rest of this chapter:








He…
What he does
Throw to




widens
runs toward the sideline with the outside or flat route
the route inside him or behind him


sits
holds his spot
the route he isn’t standing on


sinks
drops deeper, under the higher route (coaches say he robs it)
the low route in front of him


jumps (or drives)
runs forward at the short route
the route behind him


carries
runs up the field with a vertical route
the short route he left


bails
turns and runs deep at the snap (as Cover 3 cornerbacks do)
the short route in front of him



A defense that wants to take slant-flat away coaches its flat defender to sink under the slant and trusts a cornerback squatting in the flat to take the other route, which is why slant-flat struggles against Cover 2.




Show the Python
def slant_flat_play(nb_widens=True):
    off = spread()
    dfn = cover3(nb_side=-1)
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=40, to_go=10)
    protect(p)
    p.dropback(1.5)
    p.route("X", r.slant(stem=3.0, length=10.0))
    p.route("H", r.path((1.0, 1.8), (2.6, 8.5)))
    p.route("Z", r.go(16.0))
    p.route("Y", r.hitch(6.0))
    p.drop("LCB", (14.0, -18.0), speed=5.5)
    p.drop("RCB", (14.0, 18.0), speed=5.5)
    p.drop("FS", (15.0, -1.0))
    p.drop("WILL", (6.8, -3.6), delay=0.15)
    p.drop("MIKE", (6.8, 3.6), delay=0.15)
    p.drop("SS", (6.0, 10.5), delay=0.1)
    if nb_widens:
        p.path("NB", [(-1.6, -3.4), (-2.3, -7.4)], speed=7.0, delay=0.05)
        p.pass_to("X", t=1.0)
    else:
        p.path("NB", [(1.2, -1.2), (2.0, -1.5)], speed=4.0, delay=0.15)
        p.pass_to("H", t=1.0)
    return p


sf = slant_flat_play()
t_catch = catch_time(sf)
_trk = tracking(sf)
_cx = _trk[(_trk["displayName"] == "X") & np.isclose(_trk["time"], t_catch)]
catch_d = float(_cx["x"].iloc[0]) - sf.los
notes = ["The $ is the only defender between\nX and H. He can't cover both.",
         "H bursts to the flat; the $ widens\nwith him, leaving the slant open.",
         "The ball leaves on X's break, behind\nthe $ and in front of the W.",
         f"Caught about {catch_d:.0f} yards deep,\nwith room to run."]
play_movie(sf, [0.0, 0.5, 1.0, t_catch], notes=notes, lateral=(-24.5, 2.5), window=(-8.0, 12.5),
           rings=(("NB", style.THIRD),), throw_t=1.0)





  
  Your browser does not support the video tag.



Figure 22.3: Slant-flat against a Cover 3 look, the offense’s left side (simulated, BDB-format tracking). The ringed defender, the nickel back ($), is the quarterback’s only read. He stands between two receivers going in two directions: X’s slant above and inside him, H’s flat below and outside him. Here he widens with H, so the ball goes to X on the slant, into the space between the $ and the Will linebacker (W). Had he stayed inside, the throw would have gone to H in the flat. The ball is out about one second after the snap; faint lines are where each player has been, brown dashes the ball in flight. (Simulated tracking: positions generated by this book’s gridiron library in the same format as the NFL’s public Big Data Bowl tracking data.)




What does slant-flat give up? Depth. The best case is a slant caught at seven or eight yards with room to run; the usual case is a flat route for four or five. It also needs the cornerback to cooperate: against a corner who sits low in the flat (as in Cover 2, where corners squat short), the flat is covered by a second man and the slant must fit into a tighter window. That’s where the other concepts come in.

title: The Quick Game: Slant-Flat, Stick, Snag, Quick Screens, and Beating Press
text:
Stick: the in-out
Stick is one of the most-called quick concepts in the NFL, and you met it in What a Play Really Is as that chapter’s one example play. Here is why it is so popular. Slant-flat stretches the flat defender vertically; stick stretches him horizontally, inside and outside, at a depth that usually reaches the line to gain on second or third and medium.
Three receivers on one side. The outside man (#1) runs off, deep: a go route or a fade that carries the cornerback away. One man runs to about six yards, at or just past the line to gain, and sticks: he settles in the open space and turns to face the quarterback, or, against man coverage, breaks away from his defender. One man runs to the flat, getting to the numbers or wider. The stick sits inside the flat defender; the flat route goes outside him.
Which man runs which route depends on the formation, and you’ll see both versions on Sundays. In the trips version you met in What a Play Really Is (sometimes called Y-stick), the tight end is #3, the innermost receiver, and runs the stick, while #2 runs an arrow to the flat outside him. In the 2x2 version drawn below, the classic NFL drawing, the tight end is #2 and runs the stick, and the running back comes out of the backfield to the flat. The rule underneath is the same: the stick runner settles inside the flat defender, and the flat comes from whoever is outside or under him.


Show the Python
def stick_play(nb_widens):
    off = spread(rb_w=1.5)
    dfn = cover3(nb_side=1)
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=40, to_go=6)
    protect(p)
    p.dropback(2.0)
    p.route("Z", r.go(16.0))
    p.route("Y", r.stick(7.5))
    p.route("RB", r.path((0.5, 4.5), (1.4, 8.5), (5.2, 11.8), (6.8, 13.6)), side=1)
    p.drop("RCB", (13.5, 17.5))
    p.drop("MIKE", (7.2, 2.6), delay=0.15)
    p.highlight("NB")
    p.pass_to("Y" if nb_widens else "RB", t=1.4)
    return p


fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.5, 3.05))
for ax, widen in zip(axes, (True, False)):
    p = stick_play(widen)
    fld = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=(-11.5, 25.5), window=(-8.5, 15.5), show_ruler=False)
    if widen:
        branch(fld, p, [(5.0, 7.2), (3.6, 11.0), (3.0, 13.0)], color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.4)
        opening(fld, p, (5.9, 8.4), (3.4, 4.8))
        say(fld, p, 11.0, 7.0, "stick: open in\nthe space he left", color=READ_GREEN, fontsize=7, weight="bold")
        say(fld, p, 3.8, 21.4, "$ widens", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
        panel_title(ax, "$ widens: throw the stick")
    else:
        branch(fld, p, [(5.0, 7.2), (6.0, 8.2)], color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.4)
        opening(fld, p, (1.8, 14.4), (3.0, 4.6))
        say(fld, p, 11.0, 7.0, "$ sits inside,\nunder the stick", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
        say(fld, p, -3.2, 16.0, "flat: open", color=READ_GREEN, fontsize=7, weight="bold")
        panel_title(ax, "$ sits: throw the flat")
legend(fig, ["route", "react", "pass", "window"], y=0.09)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.8, rect=(0, 0.08, 1, 1))
plt.show()








Figure 22.4: Stick from 2x2, run to the offense’s right against a Cover 3 look: Z clears out deep, Y (a tight end split into the slot) runs six yards and settles, and the running back runs to the flat. The ringed nickel back ($) is the read, and the two panels are his two choices. Left: he widens toward the back in the flat, so the stick is open in the space he left. Right: he sits, staying inside under the stick, so the back is alone in the flat at the numbers. The Mike linebacker (M) drops to the middle and is too far inside to help on the stick in time; the cornerback goes deep with Z.





The stick route itself is the clever part. It isn’t a hitch with a fixed landmark; it’s a rule. Against zone, the receiver finds the soft spot between the flat defender and the next defender inside (the Mike linebacker here) and sits in it, facing the quarterback, so the ball can be thrown the moment he settles. Against man coverage, there is no soft spot to find, because a defender is following him, so he breaks away from that defender’s leverage, in or out. That’s an option route in miniature, and it is why the quarterback and the stick runner rehearse it endlessly: both of them have to see the same thing.
Stick is everywhere because it does three things at once: it puts the ball at or near the line to gain on the downs where five or six yards matter most; it works against nearly every zone, because nearly all of them have one defender responsible for both the area inside and the area outside at that depth; and the clear-out by #1 keeps a deep threat on the field, so the cornerback can’t come up and sit on everything short.

title: The Quick Game: Slant-Flat, Stick, Snag, Quick Screens, and Beating Press
text:
Snag: the triangle
Slant-flat stretches one defender up and down; stick stretches him side to side. Snag does both at once by putting three receivers in a triangle, so two defenders are stuck guarding three spots. (Some teams call it spot.)


Show the Python
off = spread(rb_w=1.5)
dfn = cover3(nb_side=1)
p = Play(off, dfn, los=40, to_go=10)
protect(p)
p.dropback(2.0)
p.route("Z", r.path((4.0, 0.0), (5.5, -1.5), (5.2, -3.5)))
p.route("Y", r.path((5.5, 0.0), (8.5, 0.0), (14.0, 6.5)))
p.route("RB", r.path((0.5, 5.5), (2.0, 10.0), (2.7, 13.5), (6.0, 16.5)), side=1)
p.drop("RCB", (12.5, 17.5))
p.drop("MIKE", (7.0, 3.0), delay=0.15)
p.highlight("NB")
fld = draw(p, lateral=(-19.0, 26.0), window=(-8.5, 20.5), show_ruler=False)
triangle(fld, p, [(12.5, 15.5), (4.5, 11.5), (1.0, 18.0)])
say(fld, p, 13.4, 13.0, "corner (high)", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
point_to(fld, p, (2.2, 9.6), (4.6, 11.5), "snag", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
say(fld, p, -0.6, 21.2, "flat (low)", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
say(fld, p, 16.0, -10.2, "The reads\n"
    "vs Cover 3 (this look), watch the $:\n"
    "   $ widens?  Snag, inside him.\n"
    "   $ sits on the snag?  Flat.\n"
    "vs Cover 2, watch the cornerback:\n"
    "   CB squats in the flat?  Corner.",
    color=READ_GREEN, fontsize=6.8, ha="center")
legend(fld.fig, ["route", "drop", "triangle"], y=0.07)
plt.show()








Figure 22.5: Snag to the offense’s right against a Cover 3 look. Z, the outside receiver, pushes upfield five yards and settles just inside where he started (the snag). Y, from the slot, runs a corner route over the top, toward the sideline about fifteen yards deep. The running back runs to the flat. Together they make a triangle (shaded): a high-low on the cornerback (corner route over, flat under) and an in-out on the flat defender (snag inside, flat outside). The receivers on the other side are left out. The quarterback’s reads are in the box: against this look, the $.





Snag is read against the coverage the quarterback identified before the snap. Against Cover 3, the look drawn here, the cornerback has a deep third and bails, so the corner route is covered before it starts. The quarterback’s eyes go straight to the flat defender, the $, exactly as in stick: if he widens to the flat, throw the snag inside him; if he sits on the snag, throw the flat. Against Cover 2, the cornerback squats in the flat with a safety deep behind him, and the read moves to the top of the triangle: if the corner squats on the flat route, the corner route goes over his head into the hole in front of the safety; if he sinks under the corner route, the flat is open.
So why call snag instead of stick? Against Cover 3 they are close cousins that read the same man. Snag’s extra is the corner route. Stick’s flat route runs straight into a Cover 2 cornerback squatting in the flat; snag throws over him. A quarterback who isn’t sure before the snap whether he will see Cover 3 or Cover 2 has an answer to both in one call.
Because the triangle combines both kinds of stretch, a single adjustment can’t take it away; the triangle read becomes a whole family in the next chapter, with deeper routes and more time.

title: The Quick Game: Slant-Flat, Stick, Snag, Quick Screens, and Beating Press
text:
Spacing: five windows
Every concept so far stretches one or two defenders. Spacing stretches the whole underneath coverage: four or five receivers settle at about the same depth, five or six yards, at even intervals across the field, each in the gap between two zone defenders. You saw the geometry in Passing Fundamentals’s horizontal stretch (five receivers against Cover 3’s four underneath defenders). As a called concept it adds two things.
First, one route goes underneath. Almost every spacing call sends one receiver, often the back or the innermost slot, on an arrow or flat route to the sideline at two or three yards. Without it, the curl-flat defender can sit at five yards on the hitch and nobody punishes him; with it, he is in a high-low as well. Second, the quarterback works one half of the field. He can’t watch five receivers in a second and a half, so before the snap he picks a side, usually the one where the offense has more receivers than the defense has underneath defenders, and after it he reads one man on that side.


Show the Python
off = spread(rb_w=1.5)
dfn = cover3(nb_side=1, extra={"SS": (7.5, -11.5), "WILL": (7.5, -4.0), "MIKE": (7.5, 3.5), "NB": (7.0, 11.0),
                                 "LCB": (11.5, -17.5), "RCB": (11.5, 17.5), "FS": (14.5, 0.0)})
p = Play(off, dfn, los=40, to_go=10)
protect(p)
p.dropback(2.0)
p.route("X", r.hitch(6.2))
p.route("Z", r.hitch(6.2))
p.route("H", r.path((6.5, 0.0), (7.0, -1.2)))     # settles inside, in the gap between the SS and the W
p.route("Y", r.path((6.5, 0.0), (7.0, -1.8)))     # settles inside, between the M and the $
go_to(p, "RB", (2.4, 15.5), kind="route", via=[(-3.6, 4.0), (0.2, 9.5)])
for k in ("SS", "WILL", "MIKE", "NB"):
    q = p.players[k]
    p.zone((q.d, q.w), (3.5, 6.0))
p.highlight("NB")
fld = draw(p, lateral=(-25.0, 25.0), window=(-8.5, 19.0))
for k in ("X", "H", "Y", "Z"):
    opening(fld, p, tuple(p._cur(k)), (2.4, 2.8))
opening(fld, p, (2.4, 15.5), (2.4, 2.8))
branch(fld, p, [(7.0, 11.0), (5.2, 14.0)], color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.3)
branch(fld, p, [(7.0, 11.0), (7.4, 8.6)], color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.3)
say(fld, p, 14.6, 9.6, "$ widens to the flat?\nthrow Z's hitch or Y.\n$ sits on Z? the flat.",
    color=READ_GREEN, fontsize=6.8, weight="bold")
say(fld, p, -5.4, 13.0, "his side: 3 receivers\nvs 2 defenders", color=READ_GREEN, fontsize=7)
say(fld, p, -5.4, -13.0, "the other side: 2 vs 2", color=style.INK_2, fontsize=7)
legend(fld.fig, ["route", "zone", "react", "window"], y=0.07)
plt.show()








Figure 22.6: Spacing against a Cover 3 look, drawn at the moment the quarterback’s back foot lands. The four underneath zone defenders have finished their drops (their areas shaded orange); the corners and the deep safety are on their way to their deep zones. Five receivers sit at five or six yards, each in a gap between two defenders or between a defender and the sideline, and the running back runs an arrow to the right flat underneath. Before the snap the quarterback picked the right half: there, three receivers (Y, Z and the back) face two underneath defenders (M and the ringed $). After the snap he reads the $ alone. On the left, two receivers face two defenders; he doesn’t look there unless the right is taken away.





Spacing is the quick game’s answer to a defense that plays zone and refuses to rush more than four. Its weakness is the mirror image: against man coverage there are no gaps to sit in, so the receivers have to beat their men, and the sitting routes turn into breaks away from leverage, the same rule as the stick route.
Spacing is an old idea, and a natural fit for the Air Raid offenses of Hal Mumme and Mike Leach in college football, which spread receivers across the whole width of the field and made the quick game one of their foundations;10 The College Laboratory tells that story.

title: The Quick Game: Slant-Flat, Stick, Snag, Quick Screens, and Beating Press
section: Speed out: beating a soft corner to the sideline
text:
Speed out: beating a soft corner to the sideline
Not every quick throw is a two-man read. The speed out is a single receiver’s route, thrown on timing against one particular look: a cornerback playing well off, with inside leverage, who is backing up at the snap. (Names vary by system: some playbooks call this five-yard rounded cut the quick out and save “speed out” for a deeper rounded out off a longer drop. The route here is the short one.)


Show the Python
off = spread()
dfn = cover3(nb_side=1, cb_d=8.0, cb_out=-1.0,
             extra={"SS": (12.0, -9.0), "FS": (12.0, 11.8), "NB": (5.0, 6.8), "MIKE": (4.5, 1.8)})
p = Play(off, dfn, los=40, to_go=10)
protect(p)
p.dropback(1.5)
p.route("Z", [(0, 0), (3.0, 0.0), (4.1, 0.25), (4.8, 0.9), (5.15, 1.8), (5.2, 2.9), (5.0, 4.6), (4.7, 7.0)],
        speed=7.5)                                   # a rounded break: the turn is spread over several steps
p.route("Y", r.seam(14.0))
p.drop("RCB", (11.0, 14.6), delay=0.1)
p.drop("FS", (14.8, 12.6))
p.pass_to("Z", t=0.8)
p.highlight("RCB")
fld = draw(p, lateral=(-6.5, 25.5), window=(-8.5, 17.5))
vbracket(fld, p, 12.0, -0.7, 8.0)
say(fld, p, 5.4, 12.5, "8-yard\ncushion", fontsize=7, ha="left")
point_to(fld, p, (13.0, 19.6), (8.0, 14.0), "CB inside Z\n(inside leverage),\nbacking up", fontsize=7)
point_to(fld, p, (1.2, 22.4), (4.1, 15.9), "rounded\nbreak", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
say(fld, p, -6.4, 11.5, "ball out as the drop\nlands, before the break", color=style.BALL, fontsize=7)
say(fld, p, 15.2, 6.0, "seam holds\nthe safety", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
plt.show()








Figure 22.7: The speed out to the offense’s right against a two-high look. The cornerback lines up eight yards off Z and slightly inside him, and backs up at the snap. Z runs four or five hard steps and rounds his break toward the sideline without slowing down (the curve, not a square corner); the quarterback throws as his one-step drop lands (from under center, on his third step), before Z has even turned, aiming at the sideline. Y’s seam route keeps the safety on that side deep and out of the throw. The pass travels farther than any other quick throw, so it needs an accurate, strong arm.





Why would a cornerback line up inside in the first place? The leverage rule answers it: he lines up where he has no help. Against a two-high look nobody sits in the deep middle, so the routes that hurt him are the post and the dig, breaking inside toward all that open grass, while the sideline protects his outside. (In a quarters-style coverage there’s a second reason: the safety on that side is reading the slot, so the corner is effectively alone on Z, backing up to stay on top of him.)
Why does the speed out beat that? Because the cornerback’s alignment has already made a promise. Lined up inside and eight yards off, he is protecting the middle of the field and the deep ball, and the sideline in front of him is the one area he has conceded. A receiver who runs at him hard and rounds his break toward the sideline, without the throttle-down of a square cut, gets there first. The ball has to beat the corner’s break, which is why the speed out is a timing route: the quarterback lets it go before the receiver turns, to a spot, and trusts him to be there.
It is also the quick throw that most exposes a quarterback’s arm. The ball travels from the middle of the field to the sideline, the longest flight in the quick game, and a throw that floats lets a defender close on it. The dangerous defender is usually not the corner on top but one underneath: a Cover 2 cornerback squatting in the flat, or a Cover 3 curl-flat defender who sinks and widens under the out (the $ in the figure, if he reads it). An interception there has an open field in front of it, which is why coaches call the out a risky throw for a weak arm and why the speed out is a pre-snap call against one look, not a throw into any coverage.

title: The Quick Game: Slant-Flat, Stick, Snag, Quick Screens, and Beating Press
section: Two more pairs: double slants and hitch-seam
text:
Two more pairs: double slants and hitch-seam
Two last concepts round out the core of the quick game. Each pairs two receivers on one side.
Double slants: both receivers run slants, one shallower and quicker, the other a step deeper, so their paths stack one above the other as they cross in front of the linebackers. (Teams differ on which one goes underneath; many NFL playbooks have the inside man run the deeper slant instead.) Against zone, that is a high-low on the hook defender in the middle. Against man coverage, the version drawn below, it is even better. Two receivers break inside at the same moment, each defender is trying to keep his own man from getting across his face, and the one defender man coverage usually keeps in the middle as a helper (the “hole” or “rat” player, built in Man Coverage) faces the same high-low as a zone hook defender: he can drive on the low slant or sink under the high one, not both. The two paths also cross close to each other, and the defenders have to fight through that traffic; deliberately running into a defender to block him is a foul once it happens more than a yard past the line, the rub route question settled in the next chapter.11
Hitch-seam: the outside receiver runs a hitch (five or six yards, stop, turn back to the quarterback) and the inside receiver runs a seam straight up the field. It is a high-low on the flat defender. Against Cover 3 that defender is usually coached to carry a slot receiver who goes vertical, running up the field with him until the deep defender takes over, which is exactly why the hitch underneath him is usually the throw. The seam is the punishment if he doesn’t carry: it also threatens the deep middle safety, who can’t take a seam on both sides of the field. Offenses keep him honest by running seams from both slots, or by having the quarterback look the safety off (stare at one seam to pull him there) before throwing.


Show the Python
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.5, 3.0))
# -- double slants vs press man: the defenders shade outside, then trail
off = [q for q in spread() if q.key in ("X", "H", "LT", "LG", "C")]
dfn = [D("LCB", "CB", 1.2, -15.6, "CB"), D("NB", "NB", 1.4, -9.6, "$"), D("WILL", "WILL", 6.0, -4.6, "W"),
       D("FS", "FS", 13.0, -1.0, "FS")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=40, to_go=None)
p.route("X", r.slant(stem=3.0, length=10.0))
p.route("H", r.path((1.5, 0.0), (4.0, -3.5), (4.5, -5.5)))
p.highlight("WILL")
fld = draw(p, ax=axes[0], lateral=(-24.0, 1.5), window=(-3.0, 15.0), show_ruler=False)
branch(fld, p, [(1.2, -15.6), (2.8, -15.6), (6.4, -12.6)], color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.3)
branch(fld, p, [(1.4, -9.6), (1.8, -9.4), (2.4, -6.6)], color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.3)
say(fld, p, 12.0, -10.0, "X: slant, a step\ndeeper (high)", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
say(fld, p, -1.6, -12.4, "H: quick\nslant (low)", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
say(fld, p, 9.4, -1.8, "W in the\nhole: can't\ntake both", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
say(fld, p, 6.0, -20.0, "CB and $\nchase from\nbehind", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
panel_title(axes[0], "Double slants vs press man")
# -- hitch-seam vs cover 3
off = [q for q in spread() if q.key in ("X", "H", "LT", "LG", "C")]
dfn = [D("LCB", "CB", 7.0, -16.0, "CB"), D("NB", "NB", 5.0, -7.2, "$"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -2.2, "W"),
       D("FS", "FS", 13.0, 0.0, "FS")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=40, to_go=None)
p.route("X", r.hitch(5.5))
p.route("H", r.path((10.0, 0.4), (16.0, 0.4)))
p.drop("LCB", (13.0, -17.5))
p.drop("WILL", (6.5, -3.0), delay=0.1)
p.drop("FS", (14.5, -2.0))
p.highlight("NB")
fld = draw(p, ax=axes[1], lateral=(-24.0, 1.5), window=(-3.0, 15.0), show_ruler=False)
branch(fld, p, [(5.0, -7.2), (6.0, -10.5)], color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.3)
opening(fld, p, (5.2, -15.0), (2.4, 3.2))
opening(fld, p, (11.0, -8.6), (3.4, 3.0))
say(fld, p, 2.0, -20.2, "hitch: open if\nthe $ carries\nthe seam", color=READ_GREEN, fontsize=7, weight="bold")
say(fld, p, 12.4, -13.6, "seam: open if\nthe $ jumps\nthe hitch", color=READ_GREEN, fontsize=7, weight="bold")
panel_title(axes[1], "Hitch-seam vs Cover 3")
legend(fig, ["route", "drop", "react", "window"], y=0.09)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=1.0, rect=(0, 0.08, 1, 1))
plt.show()








Figure 22.8: Two quick pairs, both on the offense’s left. Left: double slants against press man coverage, with one helper, the Will linebacker (W, ringed), sitting in the middle. H runs a quick, flat slant underneath him; X a deeper slant above him. The cornerback and the nickel back start on the receivers’ outside shoulders, so both slants break away from them and they chase from behind (dashed), and the one helper in the middle can’t take both. Right: hitch-seam against a Cover 3 look. X runs a hitch underneath the bailing cornerback, H a seam straight up the field. The ringed flat defender ($) can stay low on the hitch or carry the seam, not both: if he carries the seam, throw the hitch; if he jumps the hitch, throw the seam behind him.





Seven concepts, and notice how few ideas they really contain. Five of them (slant-flat, stick, snag, double slants and hitch-seam) pick one defender, put two receivers on opposite sides of him (above and below, or inside and outside), and ask the quarterback to watch that one man and throw to the one he doesn’t take. Spacing does the same thing to the whole underneath coverage at once, with the quarterback choosing a half of the field before the snap. The speed out skips the post-snap read entirely: it beats one cornerback’s alignment. In every case the quarterback’s eyes are on one player or one alignment, which is why he can run the quick game at full speed.

title: The Quick Game: Slant-Flat, Stick, Snag, Quick Screens, and Beating Press
text:
Beating press: the receiver’s side
Everything so far assumed the receivers get into their routes on time. The defense’s most direct answer to the quick game is to make sure they don’t. In press coverage, a cornerback lines up right on the receiver, a yard or so away, and tries to jam him at the snap: punch him, reroute him, knock him off his path. Its opposite, off coverage, is a defender who starts five to ten yards away and gives ground (Coverage Fundamentals covers both from the defender’s side).
Press attacks the quick game where it lives: the timing. A slant that should break at three steps breaks at five because the receiver spent two of them fighting through a jam, and the quarterback, whose back foot has already landed, is left holding the ball with a rush closing in. That is why press and the quick game are a matched pair in every game plan: the defense presses to wreck the rhythm, and the offense answers with receivers who can beat press quickly and routes that use the press defender’s own position against him.
The rules frame the fight. Within five yards of the line of scrimmage, an NFL defender may contact a receiver in front of him; beyond five yards, until the ball is thrown, contact that impedes the receiver is illegal contact or defensive holding.12 Either foul costs the defense five yards and gives the offense an automatic first down, which on third-and-8 is a gift. So press is a five-yard fight, and the receiver’s goal is to get through those five yards on his path and on time. Here is how he does it, from the receiver’s side of the ball.

Release: getting off the line
A release is a receiver’s first moves off the line against a pressing defender: footwork to make the defender commit, and hands to keep the defender’s hands off him. The defender wants to get his hands on the receiver’s chest and mirror him; the receiver wants to make him move first, then go the other way.


Show the Python
LAT_R, WIN_R = (-23.0, -7.0), (-3.6, 11.5)


def press_panel(ax, title, x_pts, cb0, cb_pts, labels):
    off = [O("X", "WR", LINE_D, -15.0)]
    dfn = [D("CB", "CB", cb0[0], cb0[1], "CB")]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=40, to_go=None)
    p.route("X", x_pts, absolute=True)
    fld = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=LAT_R, window=WIN_R, show_ruler=False)
    branch(fld, p, [cb0] + cb_pts, color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.4)
    for txt, at, col in labels:
        say(fld, p, at[0], at[1], txt, color=col, fontsize=6.8)
    panel_title(ax, title, fs=8.5)


OD, DD = style.OFFENSE_DARK, style.DEFENSE_DARK
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(6.5, 5.3))
press_panel(axes[0, 0], "1. Inside release",
            [(-0.5, -16.4), (0.2, -15.6), (1.0, -14.4), (2.6, -13.6), (7.5, -9.0)], (1.1, -15.4),
            [(1.0, -16.6), (2.0, -15.6), (5.2, -12.0)],
            [("jab out", (-2.0, -19.0), OD), ("swipe, slip\ninside", (1.0, -11.0), OD), ("slant", (8.9, -11.2), OD),
             ("CB bites on\nthe jab, then\nchases", (6.0, -19.4), DD)])
press_panel(axes[0, 1], "2. Outside release",
            [(-0.5, -13.6), (0.2, -14.4), (1.2, -16.4), (4.0, -17.0), (10.2, -17.2)], (1.1, -14.6),
            [(1.0, -13.4), (2.6, -14.8), (8.6, -15.9)],
            [("sell\ninside", (-2.0, -11.4), OD), ("burst\noutside", (1.4, -20.1), OD), ("go", (10.0, -19.4), OD),
             ("CB bites inside,\nthen trails", (5.4, -11.6), DD)])
press_panel(axes[1, 0], "3. Stem and stack, then break",
            [(1.4, -16.4), (5.0, -16.8), (7.6, -15.2), (8.6, -15.0), (9.4, -11.0)], (1.1, -15.0),
            [(2.6, -15.6), (6.2, -15.1)],
            [("release\noutside", (0.8, -19.2), OD), ("stem at his\noutside shoulder", (4.6, -20.0), OD),
             ("stack: back\non top of him", (8.0, -19.6), OD), ("break", (10.2, -9.6), OD),
             ("CB now\nbehind X", (3.2, -12.4), DD)])
press_panel(axes[1, 1], "4. Double move (slant-and-go)",
            [(2.4, -15.0), (3.6, -13.8), (4.4, -14.4), (7.5, -14.9), (10.8, -15.6)], (5.6, -15.6),
            [(4.6, -12.6)],
            [("fake the\nslant", (2.0, -11.0), OD), ("go", (10.4, -12.4), OD),
             ("CB drives\non the slant", (7.0, -19.4), DD)])
legend(fig, ["route", "react"], y=0.035)
fig.tight_layout(h_pad=1.4, w_pad=1.0, rect=(0, 0.03, 1, 1))
plt.show()








Figure 22.9: Four ways a receiver (X) beats a cornerback (CB), drawn from above on the offense’s left: three against a cornerback pressing him, and one against a cornerback sitting on short routes. Blue is the receiver’s path, orange dashes the cornerback’s reaction. 1. Inside release: a hard jab step outside makes the cornerback step that way too; the receiver swipes the cornerback’s hands down and slips inside, onto a slant. 2. Outside release: he sells inside with a step, the cornerback steps with him, and the receiver bursts outside and up the sideline, with the cornerback trailing on his inside hip. 3. Stem and stack: after the release, the receiver runs his stem straight at the cornerback’s outside shoulder, as if going deep, then moves back directly in front of him (the stack) before breaking. 4. The double move: against a cornerback playing off and waiting for the short route, he fakes a quick slant, the cornerback drives on it, and the receiver turns up the field behind him.





The inside and outside releases are mirror images of one idea: make the defender declare first. Attack one side hard enough that he has to move his feet or reach to stop it, then go to the other side. The hands matter as much as the feet: receivers swipe the defender’s hands down, chop at his wrists or rip an arm through under his, to keep him off the chest. A defender who lands a two-hand jam controls the receiver; one who whiffs has to turn and chase.
Which release a receiver uses is not his whim. On a quick route, the route decides. A three-step slant needs an inside release, a fade or go route an outside one, because there is no time to go one way and come back. (On longer routes there is, which is why panel 3 shows a receiver releasing outside and breaking inside: the stem buys the time.) That’s why the pre-snap read includes the press corner’s leverage: a corner pressing with inside leverage is daring the receiver to win inside, so the quarterback may prefer the fade or a quick out to that side, and the slant to the other.
A corner pressing head-up, square in front of the receiver, hasn’t given a side away; he plans to mirror whichever way the receiver goes. The receiver’s answer is to make him declare anyway: a quick flurry of short, choppy steps in place, or a jab one way and then the other, until the corner’s hips or hands commit, and then a release to the side he left. Against a patient head-up corner that takes an extra beat, so quarterbacks often treat that matchup as a coin flip and look for a better one on the other side.


Stem and stack: setting up the break
Once he is off the line, the receiver still has to get open at the top of the route. The stem is the part of the route between the release and the break, and good receivers treat it as a weapon rather than a run-up. By aiming the stem at one of the defender’s shoulders, the receiver tells him what the route “is”: run at his outside shoulder at full speed and the defender has to worry about the go route and turn his hips to run, which makes a break inside much harder for him to match.
Against a defender trailing in man coverage, the receiver also wants to stack him: get directly in front of him, on his line, so the defender is behind the receiver and can’t see or reach the ball without going through him. A stacked defender can’t undercut a throw, can’t play the receiver’s hands, and has to guess which way the break will go. The best route runners win most of their battles here, in the yard or two between “released” and “broken,” and that’s why coaches say a route is won before the break, not at it.


The break and the catch point
The break is the cut itself, and its quality decides how much separation the receiver has when the ball arrives. A sharp break (sink the hips, plant, explode the other way) creates space against a defender who is mirroring. A rounded break keeps speed, as in the speed out, and works against a defender who is backing up. Either way, on a quick throw the ball is usually already in the air.
Then comes the catch point: the moment the ball and the receiver’s hands meet. If the release, stem and break were good, it’s an easy catch with the defender a step or two away. If not, it’s a contested catch: a catch made with a defender close enough to touch the ball or the receiver’s hands. FTN’s charters flagged about 14% of 2025 targets as contested; only about 42% of those were caught, against about 71% of the rest.13 The quick game is designed to avoid contested catches: a well-run slant-flat or stick throws to the receiver who is not covered. When a quick throw becomes a contested catch, usually against press-man coverage with no open receiver, the offense is relying on a receiver who can win at the catch point, and on a quarterback willing to throw him the ball anyway. Throws placed where only the receiver can reach them, like the back-shoulder throw, are how good pairs make those catches more likely.


The double move: punishing the defender who guesses right
The quick game creates its own counter. A cornerback who has watched film of an offense throwing slant after slant and hitch after hitch learns to sit on those routes, and to jump them the instant the receiver breaks. That is exactly the defender a double move is built for. The receiver fakes a quick route, the quarterback often pump-fakes (starts his throwing motion without letting go) as if throwing it, and when the defender drives on the fake, the receiver turns up the field behind him. The common forms are named for their two parts: slant-and-go (the sluggo), out-and-up, hitch-and-go, the stutter-go (a fake stop), and the stick-nod, in which the stick runner fakes settling and then breaks up the field, the counter to a flat defender who has learned to drive on the stick.
The double move is the quick game’s insurance policy: without it, a defense could squeeze the short routes harder every week; with it, every corner who jumps a slant risks a long touchdown. The cost is time. A double move takes three seconds or more, so offenses tend to call it with an extra blocker, after they have thrown the short version often enough to bait the defender.

title: The Quick Game: Slant-Flat, Stick, Snag, Quick Screens, and Beating Press
text:
Quick screens: now and bubble
The quick game has two close cousins that aren’t really passes in the usual sense. Both are screens, throws to a receiver behind or at the line of scrimmage with teammates blocking in front of him, and both are thrown the instant the ball is snapped. (Slower screens to running backs and tight ends, with linemen releasing to block, are in Play-Action, Bootlegs, and Screens.)
A now screen goes to an outside receiver. He takes a step back (or none) and catches the ball a second after the snap, while the receiver inside him blocks the nearest defender. Teams call versions of it a smoke screen or a quick screen; the names vary by playbook (some use “smoke” for the version with no blocker at all), but the idea is the same.


Show the Python
off = spread()
dfn = cover3(nb_side=-1, cb_d=8.0, cb_out=0.5,
             extra={"NB": (5.0, -7.8), "SS": (12.0, 9.0), "FS": (12.0, -9.0)})
p = Play(off, dfn, los=40, to_go=10)
protect(p)
p.route("X", [(0, 0), (-1.0, 0.3)], speed=3.0)
p.run("X", [(5.5, 1.2)], delay=0.15)
go_to(p, "H", (3.3, -8.6), kind="block")
p.pass_to("X", t=0.35)
p.drop("LCB", (6.5, -15.2), delay=0.25)
p.highlight("LCB")
fld = draw(p, lateral=(-25.0, 7.5), window=(-8.5, 15.5))
vbracket(fld, p, -17.8, -0.7, 8.0)
say(fld, p, 3.6, -21.4, "8-yard\ncushion:\nfree yards", fontsize=7)
say(fld, p, 0.9, -11.2, "H blocks\nthe $", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
say(fld, p, -3.6, -11.0, "ball out at once:\nno drop, no read", color=style.BALL, fontsize=7)
bracket(fld, p, 6.8, -5.6, 5.6, "6 in the box", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7, dy=1.1)
legend(fld.fig, ["route", "block", "run", "pass"], y=0.07)
plt.show()








Figure 22.10: A now screen against off coverage, the offense’s left side. The cornerback lines up eight yards off X, so X catches the ball about a second after the snap and is already running before the cornerback can close. H blocks the slot defender ($), the only other defender nearby. The box holds six defenders, so outside it on this side the defense has just the cornerback and the $ underneath, with a safety twelve yards deep. The quarterback can decide this before the snap from the cushion alone.





The now screen exists to punish one thing: a defender playing far off the ball. An eight-yard cushion is eight yards the defender has to cover before he can make a tackle, and a receiver who catches the ball at the snap gets to spend those yards running instead. Many offenses attach the now screen to ordinary plays as an extra option (coaches say they tag it on), so that the quarterback, seeing the cornerback backed up eight yards, can throw it as a free five yards instead of running the called play. The ball comes out at once for a rules reason too: the receivers who block for it may not block a defender more than a yard past the line before the pass is thrown, the same one-yard limit that governs rubs.
The bubble screen is the inside version. A slot receiver drifts a step or two back and then out toward the sideline, a path that looks like a bubble when you draw it, and catches the ball already running, while the receivers outside him turn and block.


Show the Python
def trips_right():
    """11 personnel, gun trips right: Y (the tight end, #3) and H (#2) off the ball, Z (#1) on the line."""
    return line5() + [O("QB", "QB", GUN, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", GUN, -1.5, "R"), O("X", "WR", LINE_D, -15.0),
                      O("Y", "TE", OFF_BALL, 8.5), O("H", "WR", OFF_BALL, 13.0), O("Z", "WR", LINE_D, 19.0)]


dfn = [D("WDE", "DE", 1.0, -4.6, "E"), D("WDT", "DT", 1.0, -0.8, "T"), D("SDT", "DT", 1.0, 2.4, "T"),
       D("SDE", "DE", 1.0, 5.0, "E"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -2.2, "W"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, 2.6, "M"),
       D("NB", "NB", 5.5, 12.0, "$"), D("RCB", "CB", 7.0, 21.2, "CB"), D("LCB", "CB", 7.0, -16.0, "CB"),
       D("SS", "SS", 12.0, 12.0, "SS"), D("FS", "FS", 12.0, -8.0, "FS")]
p = Play(trips_right(), dfn, los=40, to_go=10)
protect(p)
p.route("H", [(0, 0), (-1.6, 2.0), (-1.8, 4.0)], speed=6.0)
p.run("H", [(1.5, 1.2), (5.8, 1.6), (10.8, 1.8)])
go_to(p, "Z", (5.0, 20.8), kind="block")
go_to(p, "Y", (4.2, 11.4), kind="block")
p.pass_to("H", t=0.45)
p.highlight("H")
fld = draw(p, lateral=(-10.5, 26.0), window=(-8.5, 19.5))
bracket(fld, p, 15.6, 7.0, 22.5, "outside the box: 3 offensive players vs 2 defenders\n(the safety starts 12 yards deep)",
        fontsize=7, dy=1.3)
say(fld, p, -5.6, 12.0, "bubble: a step\nback, then out", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
legend(fld.fig, ["route", "block", "run", "pass"], y=0.07)
plt.show()








Figure 22.11: A bubble screen to the trips side, on the offense’s right. H, the middle of three receivers (#2), bows back and out and catches the ball on the run, already moving toward the sideline. Z (#1) blocks the cornerback and Y, the tight end on the inside (#3), blocks the slot defender ($). Outside the box on that side the offense has three players (two blockers and the ball carrier) against two defenders; the third, the safety (SS), starts twelve yards deep. Before the snap, the quarterback counted those numbers.





Coaches who throw these screens on almost every snap, as many college offenses do and some NFL offenses do, often teach the decision with three words: numbers, leverage, grass.

Numbers: count the defenders outside the box on one side and compare them with the offense’s players there. Three against two is a screen. This is the box count seen from the other side: every defender a defense puts in the box to stop the run is one fewer outside it.
Leverage: can the blockers get between their defenders and the ball carrier? A defender lined up inside, near the ball, is easy to block from the outside; one lined up wide is not.
Grass: how much space is there between the ball carrier and the nearest unblocked defender? A safety twelve yards deep is twelve yards of grass.

That is why quick screens are often thought of as part of the run game, and why they are so often packaged with runs. If the defense puts a seventh or eighth man in the box to stop the run, someone outside the box has left, and the screen to that side gets better. When the quarterback decides between the run and the screen after the snap, by reading a defender, the play becomes a run-pass option, and the bubble attached to a run is one of the most common RPOs in football (bubble RPO).
One rule detail makes the bubble unusual. Because it is often thrown sideways or slightly backward, a bubble that is thrown behind the receiver is a backward pass, and a backward pass that hits the ground is a live ball, not an incompletion: either team can recover it.14 That’s why you sometimes see a defender scoop up a dropped bubble and run the other way, and why offenses want the throw to be clearly forward or clearly caught.
