section: Under center or shotgun: two kinds of fake
text:
Under center or shotgun: two kinds of fake
The quarterback’s starting spot changes what the fake can be, and you can see the difference from the couch in the first half-second.


Show the Python
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 3.5))
for ax, uc in zip(axes, (True, False)):
    off = [q for q in (ace_tight() if uc else spread(rb_w=-2.0)) if q.key in (*dict(OL), "QB", "RB")]
    dfn = [q for q in even_front() if q.key in ("PE", "PT", "BT", "BE", "MIKE", "WILL")]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=None)
    zone_steps(p)
    if uc:
        go_to(p, "QB", (-3.3, 1.6), via=[(-2.5, -0.5)], speed=3.0)
        go_to(p, "QB", (-7.4, -1.4), speed=4.0)
        go_to(p, "RB", (-1.8, 4.7), via=[(-4.4, 2.3)])
    else:
        go_to(p, "QB", (-5.4, 0.7), speed=2.0)
        go_to(p, "QB", (-7.0, 0.2), speed=3.0)
        go_to(p, "RB", (-2.2, 4.0), via=[(-3.7, 1.1)])
    p.read("RB", key="MIKE")
    fld = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=(-8.5, 8.5), window=(-10.5, 7.2))
    if uc:
        badge(fld, p, -2.6, 3.0, 1)
        say(fld, p, -3.6, -5.6, "back to the\ndefense", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
        badge(fld, p, -8.8, -2.8, 2)
        say(fld, p, -8.2, -5.0, "turn, find the\ndefense, set", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
        panel_title(ax, "Under center: a full fake")
    else:
        badge(fld, p, -3.6, 2.2, 1)
        badge(fld, p, -8.2, 1.4, 2)
        say(fld, p, -8.2, -4.8, "eyes downfield\nthe whole time", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
        panel_title(ax, "Shotgun: a ride and a pull")
    say(fld, p, 5.3, 5.0, "M reads\nthe back", color=GREEN, fontsize=6.6)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()








Figure 24.3: Two kinds of fake. Left, under center: the quarterback opens, turns his back to the defense and extends the ball to the back on the outside-zone path (1), then turns around, finds the defense and sets up seven or eight yards deep (2). For about a second he cannot see the field. Right, shotgun: the back runs across the quarterback’s face, the quarterback rides the ball into his belly (1) and pulls it, never turning his head away from the defense (2). The fake is quicker, but it looks less like a real handoff, and the defense knows most shotgun snaps are passes.





Under center, the quarterback takes the snap, turns and carries out the same footwork as a real handoff, often with his back fully to the defense, and the running back’s path is identical to the run. It is the most convincing fake in football, because it is the run for the first second. The cost is that the quarterback loses sight of the defense, then has to whip around, find his receivers and throw, often with a defensive lineman closing. Plays from under center are therefore usually built with a simple read the quarterback can find quickly after he turns.
From the shotgun, the back runs across the quarterback’s face and the quarterback “rides” the ball into his belly for a beat, the same handoff exchange (the mesh) as a shotgun run. The quarterback never stops seeing the defense, and the throw can come sooner. But a shotgun fake looks less like a run, partly because defenses know that most shotgun plays are passes.
The numbers make the split vivid. In 2025, 82% of all dropbacks from under center used play-action, against 10% from the shotgun. Under center has become, in effect, the play-action formation, which is a big reason it came back into fashion.5 And play-action from under center was the most productive kind of dropback in football. Over 2022–2025:



Table 24.1: EPA per dropback by the quarterback’s alignment and whether he faked a handoff, 2022–2025 regular seasons (FTN charting via nflverse). Under-center dropbacks without a fake are a small, unusual group (2,559 plays against 9,730 with a fake).





Dropback from…
No fake
Play-action
Boost




Under center
+0.08
+0.13
+0.05


Shotgun
-0.00
+0.08
+0.09






Does the “Boost” column mean the shotgun fake is better? No. The shotgun’s no-fake column is dragged down by the obvious passing downs: 38% of shotgun dropbacks without a fake came on third or fourth down, against 7% of shotgun fakes. Compare first and second downs only and the two boosts are about the same (+0.04 from the shotgun, +0.05 from under center). The verdict: both fakes help, and the full fake from under center, the one that looks most like a run, is the most productive dropback an offense has.






NoteMadden vs. real life



In Madden, play-action is a menu category: pick a play with “PA” in the name and the game handles the fake. In real football the fake is a skill that the quarterback, the back and the linemen rehearse every week, and it degrades if any one of them gets lazy. Quarterbacks are graded on their fakes. Running backs are coached to carry out the fake for several steps after the quarterback has pulled the ball, often running into the line with an empty hand, because a linebacker who sees the back stop knows instantly.

title: Play-Action, Bootlegs, and Screens
section: Where the fake sends the ball: three windows
text:
Where the fake sends the ball: three windows
What does the quarterback do with the second the fake bought? Look at where play-action completions end up. Over 2022–2025, play-action passes traveled about as far in the air as other passes (7.8 yards on average, against 7.7), but receivers gained 6.4 yards after the catch on them, against 4.9 on other passes.6 The fake’s main gift is not depth. It is catching the ball with nobody in front of you, because the people who would have been in front of you stepped up.
That points to the three places a play-action pass usually goes:

Behind the linebackers, in the middle. The window in Figure 24.1: crossing routes, digs and shallow crosses that cross the field 5–15 yards deep through the space the linebackers just vacated.
Behind the safeties. If a safety reads run and comes down to help, the deep post or the corner route behind him is open. This is the shot play, below.
To the side the defense left. Move the quarterback the other way with the ball, and the whole defense’s flow is pointing at the wrong sideline. This is the bootleg.

title: Play-Action, Bootlegs, and Screens
section: The bootleg: move the launch point away from the flow
text:
The bootleg: move the launch point away from the flow
You met the bootleg in Zone Running as outside zone’s partner, and its ancestor, the Wing-T’s waggle, in Perimeter Runs and Misdirection. Here is the full play.
A bootleg is a play-action pass in which the quarterback fakes a run one way and then rolls out the other way with the ball, toward a group of receivers set up at three depths on that side. Nobody recorded who named it, but the usual story is that the quarterback hides the ball against his hip or thigh as he rolls away, the way a Prohibition bootlegger hid a bottle.7 Two things make it work at once:

The run fake pulls the linebackers and safeties toward the run side, and it pulls the one defensive lineman nobody blocks, the end on the far side, down the line after the back.
The rollout moves the quarterback’s launch point away from that side, so the pass rush, which is aimed at where he was, has to turn around and chase.

The classic route combination is a flood of the boot side at three depths (the flood idea of Dropback Concepts): a short route to the flat (the area near the sideline just past the line), a crosser coming all the way across the field from the other side at about 6–10 yards, and a deep route, often a deep crosser called the over route, 15–20 yards down. A receiver on the boot side runs deep straight away to clear out the cornerback. That gives the quarterback a simple read on the move: deep if it is there, crosser if the linebackers are trailing, flat if anyone comes at him.
Watch it move.


Show the Python
def boot_play():
    p = Play(ace_tight(), even_front(cb_w=10.0), los=35, to_go=10)
    zone_steps(p)
    # the fake: reverse out, ball to the back on the outside-zone path, then boot left and set to throw
    go_to(p, "QB", (-3.3, 1.6), via=[(-2.5, -0.5)], speed=4.0)
    go_to(p, "QB", (-6.0, -8.0), speed=6.2, via=[(-5.0, -3.0)], delay=0.05)
    go_to(p, "RB", (-1.0, 6.8), via=[(-4.3, 2.4), (-1.9, 4.9)], speed=6.0)
    # U shows the cut-off block he makes on the real run, then lets the end go and releases to the flat
    go_to(p, "U", (-0.1, -4.5), "block", speed=2.0)
    go_to(p, "U", (3.0, -15.0), "route", via=[(-0.4, -6.6), (0.8, -9.2)], delay=0.15)
    # Y sells his outside-zone block for a beat, then crosses behind the linebackers' flow
    go_to(p, "Y", (-0.1, 5.4), "block", speed=3.0)
    go_to(p, "Y", (10.0, -15.0), "route", via=[(5.5, 2.5), (7.6, -3.0), (9.2, -9.0)], delay=0.25, speed=6.5)
    go_to(p, "Z", (18.0, -13.0), "route", via=[(10.0, 8.0), (14.5, 1.0)])           # deep over
    go_to(p, "X", (19.5, -15.0), "route", via=[(8.0, -10.5)], speed=6.5)             # clear-out
    # the defense believes the run
    go_to(p, "PE", (1.6, 4.4), speed=2.0)
    go_to(p, "PT", (1.1, 2.0), speed=1.5)
    go_to(p, "BT", (0.9, -0.9), speed=1.5)
    go_to(p, "BE", (-1.8, 0.6), via=[(0.6, -3.2), (-0.8, -1.4)], speed=4.2)          # chases the fake ...
    go_to(p, "BE", (-4.2, -5.0), speed=4.4, delay=0.15)                              # ... then turns, too late
    go_to(p, "MIKE", (2.9, 3.6), speed=4.0)                                          # step up, flow ...
    go_to(p, "MIKE", (5.6, -4.0), speed=4.2, delay=0.35)                            # ... then turn and chase
    go_to(p, "WILL", (3.0, -0.6), speed=4.0)
    go_to(p, "WILL", (5.8, -8.5), speed=4.6, delay=0.35)
    go_to(p, "SAM", (2.8, 7.2), speed=3.0)
    go_to(p, "SAM", (4.6, 3.5), speed=3.5, delay=0.3)
    go_to(p, "SS", (7.5, 6.5), speed=4.5)
    go_to(p, "SS", (10.0, -1.0), speed=5.0)
    go_to(p, "FS", (10.5, -7.8), speed=3.0)                                          # a step up on the fake ...
    go_to(p, "FS", (16.5, -11.0), speed=5.5)                                         # ... then over the over route
    go_to(p, "LCB", (18.5, -16.0), speed=6.2, via=[(8.0, -11.2)])                    # runs with the clear-out
    go_to(p, "RCB", (12.0, 6.0), speed=4.5)
    throw_at(p, "Y", 3.2)
    return p


bp = boot_play()
T_THROW = [e[2] for e in bp.ball_events if e[0] == "pass"][0]
play_movie(bp, [0.6, 1.7, 2.2, 3.2],
           notes=["the fake: line steps right, Y and U\nshow blocks, LBs step up and flow",
                  "QB pulls it and boots left;\nthe end (ringed) chased the fake",
                  "Y crosses behind the LBs; X has\ntaken the CB deep, FS sits on Z",
                  "deep is covered, so the ball\ncomes down to the Y: room to run"],
           frame_rings=[(("MIKE", style.DEFENSE), ("WILL", style.DEFENSE)),
                        (("BE", style.DEFENSE),),
                        (("Y", style.THIRD), ("FS", style.DEFENSE)),
                        (("Y", style.THIRD),)],
           lateral=(-19.5, 12.5), window=(-9.5, 21.0), throw_t=T_THROW)

Figure 24.4: The outside-zone bootleg, frame by frame (simulated, BDB-format; faint lines show each player’s path so far). The offense shows the same two-tight-end look and the same first steps as outside zone right (03-02). (1) The line steps right, the back takes the fake, the Y and U show their run blocks, and the Mike and Will (ringed) step up and flow with it. (2) The quarterback has pulled the ball and is rolling left; the backside end (ringed) chased the fake and is now behind him. (3) The Y, who started on the right side as a blocker, is crossing behind the linebackers, who are turning to chase; on the left, X’s deep clear-out has taken the cornerback away, the U is in the flat, and Z’s deep over route has the free safety (ringed) sitting on it, so the deep throw is not there. (4) The quarterback comes down to his second read and the ball goes to the Y on the move, with room to run.




Look at frame 2 of Figure 24.4. Every defender’s momentum is going one way and the quarterback is going the other. The Y has already slipped past the two linebackers who stepped up; they are still facing the line, and by frame 3 they are chasing him from behind. The cornerback on the boot side has turned and run with the clear-out, and the backside end, the one man whose job was to stay home, chased the fake and is behind the play.
Now count the quarterback’s options. All three receivers are on his side of the field, at three depths, and he is moving toward them, which shortens every throw. The read is usually high to low. First the over route, if nobody deep is on it: the cornerback has gone with the clear-out, so the man to check is the safety on that side (in Figure 24.4 the free safety has stayed over it, so the quarterback moves on). Then the crosser, if the linebackers are trailing him. Then the flat, if a defender comes up to stop the quarterback. If nobody comes up at all, he can run.
Why the defense struggles. It is not that the defenders are fooled for long. It is that the linebackers and the unblocked end are fooled at the start, when the decisive steps happen, and then the play moves away from them. A defense that has been flowing hard to stop outside zone has been flowing correctly, every time, for three quarters. The bootleg makes the correct reaction to the run the wrong reaction to the play.
What the bootleg gives up. The quarterback is throwing on the run, to only half the field, with fewer receivers than a dropback (three, usually, sometimes four). Moving the launch point also moves it away from most of the protection: on most boots, nobody is blocking the man the quarterback is running toward. And the direction matters. Every boot in this chapter goes left, which for a right-handed quarterback is the harder way: rolling right, a right-hander’s body is already turned the way he throws, but rolling left he has to open his hips and shoulders back toward the receiver before he can throw. Quarterbacks drill it (“flip the hips”) because outside zone goes both ways, and so must its boot.

The naked bootleg: nobody blocks the end
That last point is the bootleg’s central bet, and the naked version makes it explicitly. A naked bootleg assigns no one to block the defender on the boot side, usually the backside end. On the real outside zone run from this formation, the U cuts that end off (03-02). On the naked boot the U shows that block for a beat, then lets the end go and releases to the flat, so nobody blocks him. The whole line and the back go with the run fake. The play is betting that the end, seeing a run and no blocker, will chase the back down the line, as he does on the real run.


Show the Python
def naked(bites):
    p = Play(ace_tight(), even_front(cb_w=10.0), los=35, to_go=10)
    zone_steps(p)
    go_to(p, "QB", (-3.3, 1.6), via=[(-2.5, -0.5)], speed=3.4)
    go_to(p, "QB", (-6.2, -8.0), speed=4.8, via=[(-5.0, -3.0)], delay=0.05)
    go_to(p, "RB", (-1.0, 6.8), via=[(-4.3, 2.4), (-1.9, 4.9)], speed=6.0)
    go_to(p, "U", (-0.1, -4.5), "block", speed=2.0)            # show the cut-off block ...
    go_to(p, "U", (3.0, -15.0), "route", via=[(-0.4, -6.6), (0.8, -9.2)], delay=0.15)   # ... then the flat
    go_to(p, "Y", (-0.1, 5.4), "block", speed=3.0)
    go_to(p, "Y", (10.6, -14.0), "route", via=[(5.5, 2.5), (8.0, -3.0), (10.2, -8.0)], delay=0.25, speed=6.5)
    go_to(p, "Z", (17.0, -6.0), "route", via=[(10.0, 8.0), (15.5, 1.0)])
    go_to(p, "X", (17.0, -10.0), "route")
    go_to(p, "MIKE", (2.9, 3.6), speed=4.0)
    go_to(p, "WILL", (3.0, -0.6), speed=4.0)
    go_to(p, "SAM", (2.8, 8.2), speed=3.0)
    if bites:
        go_to(p, "BE", (-2.4, 1.0), via=[(0.4, -3.5), (-1.5, -2.6)], speed=4.2)
    else:
        go_to(p, "BE", (-4.4, -6.4), via=[(0.0, -5.0), (-2.6, -5.8)], speed=3.6)
    return p


T_NB = 1.8
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 4.7))
for ax, bites in zip(axes, (True, False)):
    p = naked(bites)
    fld = moment(ax, p, T_NB, lateral=(-18.5, 11.5), window=(-10.0, 17.5), rings=(("BE", style.DEFENSE),),
                 plans=("U", "Y", "Z", "X"), mark_r=0.75)
    q = p.position("QB", T_NB)
    if bites:
        plan(fld, p, "QB", T_NB, color=style.OFFENSE)
        branch(fld, p, [(-6.2, -8.0), (-4.2, -11.6), (0.5, -13.2), (4.5, -13.6)])
        say(fld, p, -2.2, -15.4, "keeper", color=GREEN, fontsize=7, weight="bold")
        say(fld, p, -5.2, 5.4, "end chased\nthe fake", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
        say(fld, p, -8.6, -2.4, "Q: the edge\nis his", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
        panel_title(ax, "The end bites: throw or run")
    else:
        u = p.position("U", T_NB + 0.6)
        throw_arrow(fld, p, tuple(q), tuple(u))
        say(fld, p, -7.6, -12.6, "end stayed\nhome", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
        say(fld, p, -8.6, 1.4, "Q: throw the\nflat now", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
        panel_title(ax, "The end stays home: get rid of it")
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()








Figure 24.5: The naked bootleg’s bet, frozen 1.8 seconds after the snap (faint lines: where players have been; arrows: where the receivers are going). The quarterback has faked outside zone right and is rolling left; the U showed his cut-off block and released, so nobody is assigned to the backside end (ringed). Left: the end chased the fake down the line, so he is behind the quarterback, who has the edge: he can throw to any of his three receivers (U in the flat, Y crossing, Z deep) or, if nobody comes up, keep it and run (green dashes: the keeper). Right: the end stayed home and is attacking the quarterback. Now there is no time to read high to low; the quarterback throws to the flat at once (or throws the ball away).





When the bet wins (left panel of Figure 24.5), the naked boot is one of the easiest plays in football: the quarterback is alone on the edge with three receivers and a defense running the wrong way. When it loses (right panel), the quarterback has turned his back on a free defender. That is why the flat route is always there and always first if the end stays home: it is the boot’s built-in hot throw, and the quarterback learns to check the end before anything else. It is also why offenses run naked boots after the end has been chasing outside zone all day, not before.


Keepers, protected boots and leaks
Three variations answer the obvious questions a defense asks of the bootleg.
What if nobody covers the quarterback? Then he runs. A keeper is a quarterback run off a run fake: he shows the handoff, keeps the ball and goes around the end the fake drew inside. On a bootleg it is built in (the green branch in Figure 24.5): if the end chased and the flat defender has run with the flat route, the quarterback’s best option is often the empty grass in front of him. Some teams also call keepers as designed runs, and some playbooks simply call the whole bootleg a “keep.” Either way, a quarterback who will run makes the defense pay for chasing the receivers.
What if the end stops chasing? Then the offense blocks him. A protected bootleg sends a blocker to meet the end on the boot side: a guard pulling from the line, as the Wing-T’s waggle did (Figure 24.6, left), or, very often in today’s NFL, a fullback, H-back or tight end coming across behind the line, the same block that kicks out the end on split zone. The price is a tell: a blocker running the “wrong” way, away from the run fake, is the first thing a linebacker who keys the guards and the backfield will see.
What if the whole defense starts flowing to the boot? Then throw back the other way. A leak is a late release by a tight end or back who first sells a block, then slips into the space the defense has abandoned. On a bootleg, the classic leak is the tight end on the run-fake side, who blocks the end for a count as if the run were real, then releases into the flat on his side, the side the quarterback just ran away from. It is a change-up, not a staple, because the throw is hard: the quarterback has to stop his roll, reset his feet and throw back across the field, against his own momentum, to the side he has been moving away from.


Show the Python
def boot_variant(kind):
    p = Play(ace_tight(), even_front(cb_w=10.0), los=35, to_go=10)
    zone_steps(p, keys=("LT", "C", "RG", "RT") if kind == "protect" else ("LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT"))
    go_to(p, "QB", (-3.3, 1.6), via=[(-2.5, -0.5)], speed=3.4)
    go_to(p, "QB", (-6.2, -8.0), speed=4.8, via=[(-5.0, -3.0)], delay=0.05)
    go_to(p, "RB", (-2.0, 5.4), via=[(-4.3, 2.4)], speed=6.0)
    go_to(p, "U", (-0.1, -4.5), "block", speed=2.0)            # show the cut-off block ...
    go_to(p, "U", (3.0, -15.0), "route", via=[(-0.4, -6.6), (0.8, -9.2)], delay=0.15)   # ... then the flat
    go_to(p, "Z", (17.0, -8.0), "route", via=[(10.0, 8.0), (15.5, 1.0)])
    go_to(p, "X", (17.0, -10.0), "route")
    go_to(p, "MIKE", (2.9, 3.6), speed=4.0)
    go_to(p, "WILL", (3.0, -0.6), speed=4.0)
    go_to(p, "SAM", (2.8, 8.2), speed=3.0)
    if kind == "protect":
        go_to(p, "Y", (-0.1, 5.4), "block", speed=3.0)
        go_to(p, "Y", (10.6, -14.0), "route", via=[(5.5, 2.5), (8.0, -3.0), (10.2, -8.0)], delay=0.25, speed=6.5)
        go_to(p, "LG", (-0.6, -5.0), "pull", via=[(-1.8, -2.2), (-1.6, -4.0)], speed=4.5)
        go_to(p, "BE", (1.2, -6.6), speed=2.0)          # will not chase: squeezes upfield and outside
    else:   # the coverage has learned to flow to the boot; the Y blocks, then leaks the other way
        go_to(p, "Y", (0.5, 5.4), "block", speed=1.0)
        go_to(p, "Y", (7.0, 12.0), "route", via=[(0.6, 8.8)], delay=0.6, speed=6.5)
        go_to(p, "PE", (0.9, 5.2), speed=2.0)
        go_to(p, "PE", (-4.0, -2.0), speed=5.0, delay=0.1)
        go_to(p, "BE", (-0.2, -5.4), speed=2.0)
        for k, step in (("MIKE", (5.0, -4.0)), ("WILL", (5.0, -9.0)), ("SAM", (5.2, 1.0))):
            go_to(p, k, step, speed=4.5, delay=0.2)
        go_to(p, "SS", (13.0, -1.0), speed=5.0)
        go_to(p, "RCB", (14.0, 3.0), speed=5.5)
        go_to(p, "FS", (14.0, -10.0), speed=4.0)
        go_to(p, "LCB", (12.0, -14.5), speed=4.5)
        throw_at(p, "Y", 3.3)
    return p


fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 4.8))
for ax, kind in zip(axes, ("protect", "leak")):
    p = boot_variant(kind)
    if kind == "protect":
        t = 1.3
        fld = moment(ax, p, t, lateral=(-18.5, 15.0), window=(-10.0, 18.0), rings=(("LG", PURPLE),),
                     plans=("U", "Y", "Z", "X", "QB"), mark_r=0.75)
        say(fld, p, -7.8, -12.6, "LG pulls and\nkicks out the end", color=PURPLE, fontsize=6.8)
        say(fld, p, -7.6, 6.6, "a guard pulling away\nfrom the fake: a tell", color=style.INK_2, fontsize=6.6)
        panel_title(ax, "Protected boot")
    else:
        t = 2.1
        fld = moment(ax, p, t, lateral=(-18.5, 15.0), window=(-10.0, 18.0), rings=(("Y", style.THIRD),),
                     plans=("U", "Z", "X", "QB", "Y"), mark_r=0.75)
        te = [e[2] for e in p.ball_events if e[0] == "pass"][0]
        throw_arrow(fld, p, tuple(p.position("QB", te)), tuple(p.position("Y", 3.3)))
        say(fld, p, -3.0, 10.6, "Y: block,\nthen leak", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
        say(fld, p, -8.3, -13.4, "the coverage flowed\nto the boot (left)", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.6)
        panel_title(ax, "Boot leak: throw it back")
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()








Figure 24.6: Two answers to two defensive adjustments, each frozen mid-play (faint lines: where players have been; arrows: where they are going). Left, a protected bootleg at 1.3 seconds: against an end who will not chase, the left guard pulls (purple ring) on his way to kick him out, so the quarterback has a blocker on the boot side; the cost is that the pulling guard tips off linebackers who read the guards. Right, a boot leak at 2.1 seconds: against a defense that has learned to flow to the boot, the quarterback still rolls left and the receivers still flood that side, dragging the coverage with them (the defenders’ faint orange trails all lead left), but the Y (green ring) blocked the end for a count and is now releasing into the right flat, where nobody is left; the quarterback will throw back across the field (dashed brown).





Each of these is a reply to a defensive reply. None is a great play on its own; together, they make chasing, staying home and flowing all wrong some of the time, which is all an offense needs.
How much of this do offenses actually run? FTN charts whether the quarterback threw from outside the pocket. From 2022 to 2025, the quarterback was out of the pocket on 30% of play-action dropbacks, against 15% of the rest, and those include scrambles; the difference is mostly designed boots and rollouts.

title: Play-Action, Bootlegs, and Screens
section: The shot play: the fake that goes deep
text:
The shot play: the fake that goes deep
The third window in the list above is behind the safeties. A shot play is a play built to throw deep, usually 20 or more yards downfield, and called in a situation the offense picked for it. Most shot plays share three features, and each has a reason.

Play-action, because the deepest defender that matters is a safety, and a safety who reads run takes a step or two forward. A deep throw needs only that. A safety who starts 13 yards deep normally backpedals at the snap and is 15 or 16 yards deep when the receivers get to him. One who steps up on the fake is at 11 or 12 and has to stop and turn before he can run. That is about four yards of cushion gone, and a receiver at full speed covers four yards in under half a second: the difference between a breakup and a touchdown.
Extra blockers, often max protect with seven or eight men in protection, because a deep route takes three seconds or more to develop.
Only two or three receivers, which is the price of the extra blockers. They are paired so that the one safety cannot cover both: in the classic yankee concept, a deep post from one side and a deep over route from the other.



Show the Python
p = Play(i_form(), even_front(cb_w=13.5, shell="one"), los=35, to_go=None)
p.players["LCB"] = p.players["LCB"].moved(w=-14.5)
p.players["RCB"] = p.players["RCB"].moved(w=14.5)
zone_steps(p, step=(0.2, 0.3))
p.block("Y", pts=[(0.2, 0.2)])
go_to(p, "QB", (-3.0, 0.9), via=[(-2.4, -0.4)], speed=3.0)
go_to(p, "QB", (-8.0, -0.6), speed=4.0)
go_to(p, "RB", (-2.3, 1.6), via=[(-4.4, 0.9)])
go_to(p, "FB", (-2.6, -2.4), "block")

go_to(p, "LCB", (25.0, -3.0), via=[(13.5, -12.8)], speed=7.0)                  # trails the post, a step behind
go_to(p, "RCB", (19.2, -6.0), via=[(11.6, 12.9), (16.3, 5.0)], speed=7.0)      # chases the over across the field
p.pass_to("X", t=2.9)
fld = draw(p, width_in=6.2, lateral=(-18.5, 18.5), window=(-10.0, 31.5))

say(fld, p, -8.2, 7.4, "eight blockers,\ntwo receivers", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
say(fld, p, 5.4, -9.4, "LBs and SS\nattack the fake", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
say(fld, p, -5.0, 12.4, "Cover 1: each CB\nruns with his man", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)

              loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, 0.0), ncol=3, fontsize=7, frameon=False)

Figure 24.7: A play-action shot from the I formation against Cover 1 (man coverage with one deep safety) and eight defenders near the box. Eight blockers stay in: the five linemen, the Y, the fullback and, after his fake, the running back. Only two receivers go out: X on a deep post and Z on a deep over route (the yankee pairing). Each cornerback runs with his man (solid orange): the left one trails the post, the right one chases the over across the field from behind. The fake pulls the linebackers and the strong safety forward, and the free safety, the only deep help, takes two steps up (dashed orange) before he can retreat. He is the read: if he stays on the post, throw the over in front of him (green dashes: the other throw); if he drives on the over, throw the post behind him.





The defense in Figure 24.7 is the picture offenses want for a shot: one deep safety, the other safety down near the box, and linebackers who attack the run. Against Cover 1 (man coverage with one deep safety, built in Man Coverage), the corners are in man coverage and the yankee routes run away from them, so the free safety alone has to help on two deep routes. (Against Cover 3, where the cornerback on the over’s side bails into a deep third, the over attacks that corner’s zone and the read shifts to him, but the idea is the same: make one deep defender choose.) That defense is built to stop the run, and the offense has usually spent the game showing it run looks from this exact formation. Situations matter as much as looks. Coaches like shots on second-and-short (an incompletion leaves a manageable third-and-short), right after a turnover or a big play (the defense is rattled and expects conservatism), and when the defense has just moved a safety down to stop the run.
Downs, Distance, and Field Position showed that NFL offenses mostly run on second-and-short. That is one reason the shot works when it comes: a defense that has seen second-and-short handed off fifty times believes the fake.
What the shot play gives up. Two receivers against at least three deep defenders (both corners and the free safety), with every linebacker whose man stays in to block free to drop or to rush, is a long-odds play on any single snap, and it has no answer if both routes are covered except a throwaway, a scramble or a sack. Coaches accept a low completion rate for the size of the prize: one completion can be worth more expected points than a whole series of short gains.

24  Play-Action, Bootlegs, and Screens

title: Play-Action, Bootlegs, and Screens
text:
Screens: let them come
Now the opposite trick. Play-action pretends to be a run so the defense steps forward. A screen pretends to be a normal pass so the defense rushes in, then throws the ball to a receiver at or behind the line with blockers already set up in front of him. The rushers who came after the quarterback are now behind the play. The defenders left in front are outnumbered by linemen.
The quick wide receiver screens, the now screen and the bubble screen, were in The Quick Game: the ball comes out at the snap and the blockers are other receivers. This section is about the screens that use the offensive linemen as blockers, which changes everything about their timing.
The one-yard rule from the start of the chapter shapes how they are blocked. In the NFL it covers every forward pass, including one caught behind the line, so screen linemen release flat, sideways along the line, set up a wall where the receiver will catch the ball, and turn upfield to block only once the ball is in the air. (College is different: its limit is three yards and covers only passes that cross the line, so college screen blockers can be well downfield before the throw.)8 Every screen in this section follows that pattern: in the diagrams, a dashed block is the climb that happens after the throw.

The slow screen
The original is the running back’s screen, the slow screen (also called the RB screen). It is “slow” because it is built on patience: everyone on the offense pretends, for a count or two, that this is an ordinary dropback.


Show the Python
def slow_screen(p):
    """RB slow screen to the left: the line sets, the LT, LG and C release, the back slides out behind them."""
    for k in ("RG", "RT"):
        p.block(k, pts=[(-1.2, 0.0)])
    # each sets and punches for a beat (the delay), then releases: the first man out takes the widest threat,
    # the next the man inside him, the center peels back for the first chaser
    # NFL rule 8-3-1: no lineman more than a yard past the line before the throw, so they release flat
    go_to(p, "LT", (0.8, -8.8), "block", via=[(-1.7, -3.6)], speed=4.2, delay=0.8)
    go_to(p, "LG", (0.8, -5.2), "block", via=[(-1.7, -1.8)], speed=4.2, delay=0.8)
    go_to(p, "C", (-1.4, -3.4), "block", via=[(-1.6, 0.0)], speed=3.0, delay=0.8)
    go_to(p, "RB", (-4.2, -2.6), speed=2.0)                                  # pretend to block ...
    go_to(p, "RB", (-3.3, -7.0), "route", delay=0.8, speed=3.5, via=[(-4.6, -5.0)])  # ... then slide out
    go_to(p, "RB", (8.0, -6.3), "run", delay=0.12, via=[(1.0, -6.6)])
    go_to(p, "QB", (-9.4, 0.4), speed=2.0)
    go_to(p, "X", (16.0, -15.5), "route")
    go_to(p, "H", (4.4, -11.4), "block", speed=3.0)
    kf, _, _ = p._compile()
    t_catch = float([a.t1 for a in p.actions if a.key == "RB" and a.kind == "route"][-1]) + 0.05
    throw_at(p, "RB", t_catch)
    return p


p = slow_screen(Play(spread(), nickel(), los=35, to_go=None))
for k, end in (("WDE", (-7.4, -2.6)), ("WDT", (-7.0, -0.2)), ("SDT", (-1.0, 2.0)), ("SDE", (-1.2, 4.4))):
    go_to(p, k, end, "rush", speed=3.6)
fld = draw(p, width_in=6.2, lateral=(-19.5, 17.5), window=(-11.5, 17.5))
for k, end in (("WILL", (3.1, -8.2)), ("MIKE", (3.4, -4.8)), ("SS", (5.4, -11.6)), ("LCB", (13.0, -16.0))):
    q = p.players[k]
    branch(fld, p, [(q.d, q.w), end], color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.4)
badge(fld, p, -2.6, 2.4, 1)
badge(fld, p, 0.9, -2.8, 2)
badge(fld, p, -10.2, 2.2, 3)
say(fld, p, -10.0, 7.4, "drift back: pull\nthe rush deeper", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
say(fld, p, -7.8, -14.2, "R: block a count,\nthen slide out", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
say(fld, p, -9.7, -4.6, "rushers let through", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
point_to(fld, p, (8.2, -4.0), (0.8, -8.8), "three linemen out in front,\nwithin a yard of the line",
         color=GREEN, fontsize=6.8, shrink=6)
fld.ax.legend(handles=[LEGEND["block"], LEGEND["run"], LEGEND["pass"], LEGEND["react"]], loc="upper center",
              bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, 0.0), ncol=4, fontsize=7, frameon=False)
fld.ax.text(0.5, -0.085, "Who blocks whom: LT \u2192 Will (the widest threat), LG \u2192 Mike, C \u2192 the first chaser,\n"
            "H \u2192 the safety over him; X runs his corner off.", transform=fld.ax.transAxes, ha="center", va="top",
            fontsize=7, color=style.INK_2)
plt.show()








Figure 24.8: The running back slow screen to the left, against a four-man rush (all eleven jobs). (1) The linemen set as if pass-blocking and give a soft punch, and the back pretends to block. (2) On a count of about one-and-a-half to two, the LT, LG and C let their rushers go and release flat to the left, staying within a yard of the line until the ball is thrown; the back slides out behind them. (3) The quarterback drifts back to pull the rushers deeper and lofts the ball over them, about two and a half seconds after the snap. The RG and RT keep blocking their men; the key under the field says who blocks whom in front of the back.





Walk through Figure 24.8 in order, because the order is the play.
Sell the dropback. For the first second and a half, nothing looks unusual. The linemen pass-set, the back steps up as if to pick up a blitzer, and the receivers run their routes, and those routes have a job: pulling the cornerback and safeties deep and away from where the ball is going.
Let them go. Then the three linemen on the screen side deliberately lose. Each gives his rusher a punch, then lets him run past toward the quarterback, and releases to the side. Line coaches teach the release with a count (it varies by team, but roughly “one-thousand-one, one-thousand-two”), because a lineman who leaves too early tips the play off and one who leaves too late is still in the backfield when the ball arrives. They release flat, along the line (the one-yard rule), each to a spot a few yards outside where the back will catch it, with a rule for whom to block: the first one out takes the widest threat, the next one the next defender inside, the center the first defender chasing from behind.
Pull the rush deep, then throw over it. The quarterback keeps drifting back, eight, nine, ten yards, dragging the rushers with him, then floats the ball over their heads to the back, who has slid out behind the released linemen. The deeper the rushers chase, the farther they are from the catch.
What the slow screen gives up. It is a timing play with a lot of moving parts and a low margin for error. If a rusher is not fooled (a defensive end who sees the tackle let go and stops to sit in the throwing lane, which coaches call “smelling” the screen), the ball can be batted or intercepted near the line. If the released linemen miss their spots, the back is running into a crowd. And it gives up the whole downfield passing game for one snap: the quarterback has one place to throw. When the screen is sniffed out, the quarterback’s best play is usually to throw the ball into the ground at the back’s feet. That is legal, because the back is an eligible receiver right there (intentional grounding, the foul for throwing the ball away under pressure, applies only to a pass that is not in the direction and vicinity of an eligible receiver), and an incompletion is much better than a sack or a tipped interception.9
(For the stat sheet: a screen thrown forward, even from behind the line, is an ordinary pass, with an attempt, passing yards and receiving yards, which is how this chapter’s play-by-play data can count screens at all. One thrown backward is a lateral, as The Quick Game showed.)


Swing and flare: not screens
Casual viewers call any short pass to a running back a screen. Most of them are not, and the difference tells you what the offense was thinking.


Show the Python
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 4.4))
for ax, screen in zip(axes, (False, True)):
    p = Play(spread(), nickel(), los=35, to_go=None)
    if screen:
        slow_screen(p)
    else:
        pass_set(p)
        p.dropback(1.6)
        p.route("RB", r.swing(9.0), side=-1)
        go_to(p, "RB", (6.0, -11.5), "run", delay=0.1, via=[(1.0, -11.0)])
        go_to(p, "H", (14.0, -9.0), "route")
        go_to(p, "X", (16.0, -15.5), "route")
        p._compile()
        t_c = float([a.t1 for a in p.actions if a.key == "RB" and a.kind == "route"][0])
        throw_at(p, "RB", t_c)
    fld = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=(-19.5, 11.0), window=(-11.5, 17.5))
    if screen:
        say(fld, p, 10.6, -6.4, "three linemen\nin front", color=GREEN, fontsize=6.8, weight="bold")
        te = [e[2] for e in p.ball_events if e[0] == "pass"][0]
        say(fld, p, -10.0, 4.6, f"ball out\nat ~{te:.1f} s", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.6)
        say(fld, p, -9.2, -12.4, "R: blocks a count,\nthen settles in", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.6)
        panel_title(ax, "Slow screen: blockers out front")
    else:
        q = p.players["SS"]
        branch(fld, p, [(q.d, q.w), (1.6, -11.0)], color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.5)
        say(fld, p, -3.4, 4.6, "the line keeps\npass-blocking", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.6)
        say(fld, p, -9.6, -12.0, "R leaves at the snap;\ncaught on the move", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.6)
        say(fld, p, 4.6, -15.6, "SS comes\nto meet him", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.6)
        panel_title(ax, "Swing route: no blockers")
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()








Figure 24.9: Swing route or screen? Same formation, same defense, two different plays. Left, a swing route: the linemen stay in pass protection, nobody releases, and the back leaves at the snap, bows backward and out toward the sideline and catches the ball on the move, with the safety over the slot coming to meet him (dashed orange). He has to beat that man himself. Right, the slow screen of the figure above: the back first sets as if to block, the left side of the line releases in front of him, and when he catches it he has three blockers between him and the defense.





A swing route is a running back’s route that bows backward and then out toward the sideline, so he catches the ball on the move behind or at the line. A flare is a quicker, flatter release toward the sideline that bends slightly upfield; many playbooks use the two words for the same thing. Either way, it is a pass route: the line keeps blocking and nobody releases in front of the back. Its purposes are different from a screen’s. It is an outlet when the downfield routes are covered (a checkdown the quarterback can always find), a way to pull a linebacker wide and open the middle for another route, and a way to get a fast back the ball in space against a slower linebacker.
The tell on a broadcast is the offensive line. If linemen leave their rushers and slide out to one side before the ball is thrown, it is a screen (or a run). If the line is still pass-blocking when the back catches it, it was a route. The second tell is the back’s first steps. A swing back leaves at the snap and runs his path. A screen back waits: he sets as if to block, then slips out and settles behind the released linemen. Don’t rely on timing: a swing can be thrown at once or late as a checkdown.

title: Play-Action, Bootlegs, and Screens
text:
The screen family
Once you see the slow screen’s logic (let the rush come, release the linemen, throw behind them), the rest of the family is variations on who catches it and where the blockers go.

Tunnel and jailbreak: screens to a wide receiver


Show the Python
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 3.25))
for ax, kind in zip(axes, ("tunnel", "jail")):
    p = Play(spread(), nickel(), los=35, to_go=None)
    if kind == "tunnel":
        for k in ("LT", "LG", "C"):
            p.block(k, pts=[(-1.2, 0.0)])
        # a quick pass set, then out along the line; they climb only once the ball is thrown (dashed)
        go_to(p, "RT", (0.6, 7.4), "block", via=[(-1.0, 4.2)], speed=5.0)
        go_to(p, "RG", (0.6, 4.2), "block", via=[(-0.9, 2.4)], speed=4.5)
        go_to(p, "Y", (4.4, 14.0), "block", speed=4.5)                          # an eligible: may go downfield
        go_to(p, "Z", (-0.8, 11.2), "route", via=[(3.0, 15.4)], speed=5.5)     # sell upfield, come back inside
        go_to(p, "Z", (11.0, 10.6), "run", delay=0.1, via=[(3.0, 10.4)])
        p._compile()
        te = throw_at(p, "Z", float([a.t1 for a in p.actions if a.key == "Z" and a.kind == "route"][0]) + 0.05)
        p.path("QB", [(-0.8, 0.0)], speed=2.0)
        go_to(p, "SDE", (-3.6, 4.4), "rush", speed=3.4)
        go_to(p, "SDT", (-3.4, 1.4), "rush", speed=3.4)
        fld = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=(-6.8, 20.5), window=(-9.0, 15.0))
        for k, end in (("NB", (3.4, 8.2)), ("MIKE", (3.8, 4.4)), ("RCB", (7.6, 15.0))):
            q = p.players[k]
            branch(fld, p, [(q.d, q.w), end], color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.3)
        after_throw(fld, p, "RT", (2.6, 8.0))
        after_throw(fld, p, "RG", (3.0, 4.4))
        say(fld, p, 9.0, 13.4, "the tunnel", color=GREEN, fontsize=7, weight="bold")
        say(fld, p, -5.6, 12.0, "Z: two steps up,\nthen back inside", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.6)
        say(fld, p, -6.4, 4.6, f"ball out at ~{te:.1f} s", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.6)
        panel_title(ax, "Tunnel screen")
    else:
        # the screen-side linemen never pass-set: they sprint out along the line at the snap
        go_to(p, "LT", (0.6, -12.0), "block", via=[(-0.4, -6.2)], speed=5.5)
        go_to(p, "LG", (0.6, -8.4), "block", via=[(-0.4, -4.2)], speed=5.5)
        go_to(p, "C", (0.5, -4.6), "block", via=[(-0.3, -1.6)], speed=5.0)
        for k in ("RG", "RT"):
            p.block(k, pts=[(-1.2, 0.0)])
        go_to(p, "H", (2.0, -9.4), "route", speed=6.0)                          # a two-step stem upfield ...
        go_to(p, "H", (-1.8, -10.4), "route", speed=4.0)                        # ... then back behind the line
        go_to(p, "H", (10.0, -10.6), "run", delay=0.1, via=[(2.0, -10.2)])
        p._compile()
        te = throw_at(p, "H", float([a.t1 for a in p.actions if a.key == "H" and a.kind == "route"][-1]) + 0.05)
        go_to(p, "X", (3.0, -15.4), "block", speed=4.0)
        p.path("QB", [(-0.8, 0.0)], speed=2.0)
        for k, end in (("WDE", (-3.8, -2.2)), ("WDT", (-3.8, -0.4))):
            go_to(p, k, end, "rush", speed=4.5)
        fld = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=(-20.5, 6.8), window=(-9.0, 15.0))
        for k in ("WDE", "WDT"):
            q = p.players[k]
            ring(fld, p, q.d, q.w, r_=1.2)
        for k, end in (("SS", (3.6, -12.4)), ("WILL", (4.0, -8.6)), ("MIKE", (4.4, -4.8))):
            q = p.players[k]
            branch(fld, p, [(q.d, q.w), end], color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.3)
        after_throw(fld, p, "LT", (2.6, -12.2))
        after_throw(fld, p, "LG", (3.0, -8.6))
        after_throw(fld, p, "C", (3.4, -4.8))
        say(fld, p, 9.4, -5.4, "linemen sprint out\nat the snap, flat", color=GREEN, fontsize=6.8, weight="bold")
        say(fld, p, -7.0, -6.0, "rushers\nleft free", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
        say(fld, p, -6.6, -14.6, f"ball out at ~{te:.1f} s", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.6)
        panel_title(ax, "Jailbreak screen")
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.6, rect=(0, 0.06, 1, 1))
legend(fig, ["block", "after", "run", "pass", "react"], ncol=5, y=0.06)
plt.show()








Figure 24.10: Two wide receiver screens that use the offensive line. Left, a tunnel screen to Z: Z takes two hard steps upfield to back his cornerback off, then comes back inside toward the ball and catches it behind the line. The Y (an eligible receiver, so he may go downfield) blocks out on the cornerback; the RT and RG show a quick pass set, release outward along the line, and climb to the nickel and the Mike once the ball is thrown (dashed); Z runs up the ‘tunnel’ between them. Right, a jailbreak screen to H: at the snap the LT, LG and C skip pass protection entirely and sprint out flat to the left, while H takes two steps upfield and comes back behind the line for the throw; the linemen turn upfield to block only after it (dashed). The two rushers they would have blocked are left free (ringed). X blocks his cornerback.





A tunnel screen goes to an outside receiver who comes back inside, toward the ball. The receiver’s first steps upfield matter: the cornerback, seeing a receiver attack him, backs up, and that cushion is the space the receiver catches the ball in. Two linemen show a quick pass set, then release outward along the line to wall off the defenders inside, and a teammate (here the Y, a tight end in the slot, a natural blocker) blocks the cornerback from the outside. The receiver catches it in the gap between them and runs up the “tunnel.”
A jailbreak screen gets its name from what the line does: at the snap, the linemen on the screen side do not pass-block at all, they break out and sprint toward the screen side, leaving their rushers free. That makes it a quick screen, thrown in about a second, because nobody is blocking those rushers. Its advantage over the now and bubble screens of 04-03 is size: instead of a receiver trying to block a defender, a 310-pound lineman arrives in space against a 190-pound cornerback.
Both screens obey the one-yard rule the same way the slow screen does. The linemen sprint sideways, along the line, and the ball comes out about a second after the snap, so they are barely a yard past the line when it is thrown; only then do they turn upfield onto the linebackers and safeties. That is why the receiver’s two steps upfield matter on both: they buy the second the linemen need to get across.



Table 24.2: The two wide receiver screens side by side, as this book names them.











Tunnel screen
Jailbreak screen




Who catches it
An outside receiver
Usually a slot receiver (here H)


His path
Two steps upfield, then back inside between blockers
A step or two up, then back behind the line


The linemen
Two or three show a quick pass set, then release outward
The screen-side linemen sprint out at the snap: no pass set at all


Who blocks the corner
A teammate outside him (here the Y)
A teammate outside him (here X)


Ball out
About a second
About a second






Playbook names in this family vary a lot. Some teams call the tunnel screen a jailbreak, and some call any screen with the whole line releasing a “jailbreak.” The features in Table 24.2 are what matter: who catches it, which way he runs, and whether the linemen sell pass first.


Tight end and middle screens


Show the Python
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 4.1))
for ax, kind in zip(axes, ("te", "mid")):
    if kind == "te":
        p = Play(spread(y_inline=True), nickel(extra={"NB": (5.0, 8.4), "RCB": (7.0, 15.0)}), los=35, to_go=None)
        for k in ("LT", "LG", "C"):

        go_to(p, "RG", (0.5, 3.6), "block", via=[(-1.6, 1.8)], speed=2.4)

        go_to(p, "Y", (-2.4, 8.4), "route", delay=0.2, speed=3.5)               # ... then slide out

        p._compile()
        throw_at(p, "Y", float([a.t1 for a in p.actions if a.key == "Y" and a.kind == "route"][0]) + 0.05)
        go_to(p, "SDE", (-5.4, 2.6), "rush", speed=3.4)
        go_to(p, "SDT", (-5.0, 1.0), "rush", speed=3.4)
        fld = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=(-6.8, 18.5), window=(-11.0, 15.5))
        for k, end in (("NB", (3.2, 7.8)), ("MIKE", (3.6, 3.8)), ("RCB", (11.0, 15.0))):

        p = Play(spread(), nickel(), los=35, to_go=None)

        go_to(p, "RT", (-3.2, 5.0), "block", speed=2.6)
        # set, let the tackles through, then shuffle up to the line in front of the catch (dashed: after the throw)
        go_to(p, "LG", (0.5, -2.2), "block", via=[(-1.7, -1.6)], speed=2.0)
        go_to(p, "C", (0.5, 0.2), "block", via=[(-1.7, 0.0)], speed=2.0)
        go_to(p, "RG", (0.5, 2.6), "block", via=[(-1.7, 1.6)], speed=2.0)
        go_to(p, "RB", (-4.2, -1.6), speed=2.0)
        go_to(p, "RB", (-2.6, -0.4), "route", delay=0.7, speed=2.5)
        go_to(p, "RB", (9.0, -0.3), "run", delay=0.1)
        go_to(p, "QB", (-9.0, 0.6), speed=2.2)
        p._compile()
        throw_at(p, "RB", float([a.t1 for a in p.actions if a.key == "RB" and a.kind == "route"][0]) + 0.05)
        for k, end in (("WDE", (-4.4, -6.2)), ("SDE", (-4.4, 6.2)), ("WDT", (-7.2, -1.4)), ("SDT", (-7.2, 2.0))):
            go_to(p, k, end, "rush", speed=3.6)
        fld = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=(-12.5, 12.5), window=(-11.0, 15.5))
        for k, end in (("WILL", (3.8, -2.6)), ("MIKE", (4.0, 1.8))):
            q = p.players[k]
            branch(fld, p, [(q.d, q.w), (q.d + 2.0, q.w)], color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.3)
        after_throw(fld, p, "LG", (5.4, -2.6))
        after_throw(fld, p, "C", (5.6, 1.6))
        after_throw(fld, p, "RG", (3.6, 5.6))
        say(fld, p, -9.6, -8.0, "tackles push\nthe ends wide", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.6)
        say(fld, p, 10.6, 6.4, "G, C, G: a wall at the\nline, then up to the LBs", color=GREEN, fontsize=6.6,
            weight="bold")
        say(fld, p, -9.4, 6.4, "DTs let\nthrough", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.6)
        panel_title(ax, "Middle screen")
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.6, rect=(0, 0.06, 1, 1))
legend(fig, ["block", "after", "run", "pass", "react"], ncol=5, y=0.06)
plt.show()








Figure 24.11: Two more members of the family (receivers not involved in the play stand still). Left, a tight end screen: the Y blocks the end for a count, then slides out to the right flat behind the line; the RG and RT set, release outward along the line and, once the ball is thrown, climb to the Mike and the nickel (dashed); Z runs his cornerback off. Right, a middle screen to the back: the tackles push the ends wide and past the quarterback; the guards and center set, let the defensive tackles through, and form a wall at the line in front of the back, climbing to the linebackers only once the ball is thrown (dashed); the back slips into the middle behind the rushers, in the space they left.





The tight end screen is the slow screen run with a tight end: he blocks the end for a count, which is exactly what defenders expect a tight end to do, then slides out behind the line on his side. It is a good call against defenses that bring the edge rusher hard, because the rusher is the man the tight end just let go. The middle screen puts the back in the middle of the field instead of the flat. The tackles push the ends wide, as they do on any dropback; the guards and center let the defensive tackles through, set up a wall at the line, and climb to the linebackers as the ball is thrown; the back slips into the space the defensive tackles just left. It punishes interior pass rushers who get upfield fast, and linebackers who drop deep on passing downs.






ImportantWhy screens exist



Every good pass rush has the same weakness: its rushers are trying to get upfield as fast as possible, toward the quarterback. A screen uses that against them. It turns the rushers’ speed into distance from the ball, and it turns the five biggest people on the field, who are usually stuck at the line, into blockers in open space. The price is that a screen gives up the rest of the passing game for one snap, needs precise timing from seven or more players, and turns into a loss, or worse, if the defense recognizes it.

title: Play-Action, Bootlegs, and Screens
text:
Screens punish pressure
The logic of the screen predicts something you can check: screens should get better the more defenders rush. Every extra rusher is one more defender running away from the ball, and one fewer defender in front of it.
Watch it against a six-man blitz. In Figure 24.12 the defense shows pressure before the snap: both linebackers walk up into the gaps beside the center (a double A-gap mug, built in Blitz and Man Pressure), and behind them the defensive backs play man coverage. The free safety has come down to about eight yards to cover the running back man-to-man, so nobody is left deep. Six rushers, five protectors plus the back.


Show the Python
def screen_vs_blitz():
    dfn = nickel(extra={"MIKE": (1.5, 0.8), "WILL": (1.5, -0.8), "WDT": (1.0, -2.6), "LCB": (6.0, -15.5),
                        "RCB": (6.0, 15.5)},
                 shell="zero")
    p = Play(spread(), dfn, los=35, to_go=8)
    for k in ("RG", "RT"):
        p.block(k, pts=[(-1.4, 0.0)], speed=1.5)
    go_to(p, "LT", (-1.4, -3.4), "block", speed=1.6)
    go_to(p, "LT", (0.8, -9.8), "block", delay=0.45, speed=5.0)     # flat release: within a yard at the throw
    go_to(p, "LG", (-1.4, -1.8), "block", speed=1.6)
    go_to(p, "LG", (0.8, -4.6), "block", delay=0.45, speed=5.0)
    go_to(p, "C", (-1.3, 0.0), "block", speed=1.6)
    go_to(p, "C", (0.6, -6.2), "block", delay=0.45, speed=5.0, via=[(-0.4, -4.4)])
    go_to(p, "RB", (-4.2, -2.0), speed=2.0)
    go_to(p, "RB", (-3.0, -7.4), "route", delay=0.35, speed=3.4, via=[(-4.4, -4.6)])
    go_to(p, "RB", (9.0, -9.0), "run", speed=6.0, via=[(-1.5, -8.0), (3.0, -8.0)])
    go_to(p, "QB", (-8.6, 0.2), speed=2.6)
    go_to(p, "QB", (-10.4, 0.8), speed=1.6)
    p.pass_to("RB", t=2.0)
    go_to(p, "X", (15.0, -15.5), "route")
    go_to(p, "H", (5.0, -9.4), "route")
    go_to(p, "Y", (8.0, 9.0), "route")
    go_to(p, "Z", (12.0, 15.0), "route")
    # the rush: the screen side lets them through; they converge on the quarterback
    go_to(p, "WILL", (-7.6, -3.2), "rush", speed=4.4, via=[(-1.0, -0.5)])
    go_to(p, "MIKE", (-7.4, 2.4), "rush", speed=4.2, via=[(-1.0, 0.1)])
    go_to(p, "WDT", (-9.0, -0.8), "rush", speed=4.4, via=[(-1.0, -2.4)])
    go_to(p, "WDE", (-6.4, -4.6), "rush", speed=4.2, via=[(-1.6, -4.6)])
    go_to(p, "SDT", (-0.4, 2.0), speed=1.2)
    go_to(p, "SDE", (-0.6, 4.4), speed=1.2)
    # man coverage: each defender runs with his receiver; the free safety has the back
    go_to(p, "LCB", (15.0, -15.0), speed=6.5)
    go_to(p, "SS", (6.0, -9.0), speed=5.0)
    go_to(p, "NB", (9.0, 8.5), speed=6.0)
    go_to(p, "RCB", (12.5, 14.5), speed=5.5)
    go_to(p, "FS", (5.0, -5.0), speed=1.6)
    go_to(p, "FS", (4.6, -8.0), speed=5.0)
    # once the ball is out (2.0 s) the released linemen turn upfield (rule 8-3-2 lets them advance now)
    kf, _, _ = p._compile()
    for k, end in (("LT", (4.4, -10.6)), ("LG", (3.6, -6.8)), ("C", (3.0, -8.6))):
        go_to(p, k, end, "block", delay=max(0.0, 2.05 - float(kf[k][-1, 0])), speed=4.5)
    return p


sp = screen_vs_blitz()
play_movie(sp, [0.0, 0.9, 2.0, 3.0],
           notes=["six show blitz: the Mike and\nWill stand in the A gaps",
                  "LT, LG, C let them go and\nrelease; the back slides out",
                  "four rushers converge;\nthe throw goes over them",
                  "linemen turn upfield in front\nof him; every blitzer is behind"],
           frame_rings=[(("MIKE", style.DEFENSE), ("WILL", style.DEFENSE)),
                        (("RB", style.THIRD),), (("RB", style.THIRD),), (("RB", style.THIRD), ("FS", style.DEFENSE))],
           lateral=(-20.0, 8.0), window=(-11.8, 10.6), throw_t=2.0)





  
  Your browser does not support the video tag.



Figure 24.12: The slow screen against a six-man blitz, frame by frame (simulated, BDB-format). (1) Six defenders show blitz; the Mike and Will (ringed) stand in the A gaps. (2) The LT, LG and C let their men go and release left along the line; the back (ringed), who appeared to pick up a blitzer, slides out behind them. (3) Four rushers converge on the quarterback, who throws over them. (4) The ball is out, so the linemen have turned upfield in front of the back, and the only defender left to beat is the free safety (ringed), the man assigned to cover him. Every blitzer is behind the play.




The data agrees, strikingly. FTN’s charters count the pass rushers on every dropback, so we can split pass attempts by how many came after the quarterback.


Show the Python
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 3.7))
xs = [3, 4, 5, 6]
lab = {3: "3", 4: "4", 5: "5", 6: "6+"}
ax.axhline(0, color=style.BASELINE, lw=1, zorder=1)
series = [("Other passes", SCR[~SCR["screen"]].set_index("rushers"), style.SERIES[1]),
          ("All screens", SCR[SCR["screen"]].set_index("rushers"), style.SERIES[0]),
          ("RB screens", RBS, style.SERIES[2])]
for name, df, col in series:
    df = df.reindex(xs)
    ax.plot(xs, df["epa"], color=col, marker="o", ms=6, mec=style.SURFACE, mew=1.2, lw=2, zorder=3)
    ax.annotate(name, (6, df["epa"].iloc[-1]), xytext=(8, 0), textcoords="offset points", va="center",
                fontsize=7.5, color=style.INK_2)
    if name != "Other passes":
        for x_, (n_, e_) in zip(xs, zip(df["n"], df["epa"])):
            off = (0, -12) if name == "All screens" else ((-20, -2) if x_ == 4 else (0, 8))
            ax.annotate(f"n={int(n_):,}", (x_, e_), xytext=off, textcoords="offset points", ha="center",
                        fontsize=6.3, color=style.MUTED)
ax.set_xticks(xs, [lab[x] for x in xs])
ax.set_xlim(2.7, 6.9)
ax.set_ylim(-0.25, 0.2)
ax.set_xlabel("Pass rushers on the play", fontsize=8, color=style.INK_2)
ax.set_ylabel("EPA per pass attempt", fontsize=8, color=style.INK_2)
ax.tick_params(labelsize=7.5)
ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
ax.set_title("The more they rush, the better the screen", fontsize=10)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 24.13: Screens get better as the rush gets bigger. EPA per pass attempt by the number of pass rushers, 2022-2025 regular seasons: screens of every kind (blue), running back screens alone (green) and every other pass (orange). Against three rushers (with eight defenders in coverage), screens are among the worst plays in football; against six or more, they beat ordinary passes. The six-plus group is small (labelled counts), so read its exact height loosely and its direction firmly. Data: nflverse play-by-play with FTN charting via nflreadpy.





Read Figure 24.13 from left to right. Against a three-man rush, all screens averaged -0.18 EPA per attempt: the defense has eight players in coverage and no rushers to fool, so the screen is just a short pass into a crowd. Against six or more rushers they averaged +0.03, better than other passes against the same pressure. Running back screens, the purest version of the idea, climb the most steeply.
Coverage matters too. Against man coverage, the defender assigned to the back (usually a linebacker or, as in Figure 24.12, a safety) has to chase him, which means running straight into the released linemen. That is why screens pair so well against Cover 0 blitzes (man coverage with nobody deep, as in Figure 24.12) and Cover 1 blitzes. Against zone, the danger is an underneath defender who simply sits in the flat where the screen is going and waits for it.
Two cautions about the chart. First, selection: offenses call screens when they expect pressure, and a screen called into a blitz is likely to be the right call at the right moment, so these averages flatter screens a little. Second, the typical screen is not a great play: across all rush counts, screens averaged -0.07 EPA per attempt, below ordinary passes. Screens are not an engine of an offense. They are a tax on pressure: a play that makes blitzing expensive, so that the defense rushes four more often, which helps every other pass the offense throws. Screens made up about 8% of pass attempts in 2025, and 38% of screens over 2022–2025 went to running backs.

title: Play-Action, Bootlegs, and Screens
text:
How defenses fight back
None of this is free for the offense, because defenses coach against every one of these plays. The answers belong to the defensive chapters, but here is the shape of each, so you can spot it on Sunday.

Against the fake: linebackers are taught to read through their key. A guard who fires out but stops at the line, or a guard pulling the “wrong” way, says pass or boot even when the back says run; some teams have their linebackers cross-key, each watching the guard on the far side as well as his own. On obvious passing downs, many simply give ground first and react to the run late. (Linebackers builds this.)
Against the boot: the backside end is assigned to stay home (his checklist is boot, counter, reverse), and the flat defender on the boot side sinks under the over route instead of jumping the flat. Coverages with a middle-of-the-field robber or match rules that pass the crosser from one defender to the next take away the boot’s middle read. (Run Fits and Box Math and Man Coverage.)
Against the screen: a defensive lineman who feels his blocker let go is taught to stop rushing and turn to find the back (“smell” it), and a rusher who sees a back slip out can peel off and chase him. Defenses that expect a screen on third-and-long call a coverage that keeps an underneath defender home rather than blitzing. (Blitz and Man Pressure.)

Each of those answers costs the defense something on another play: an end who stays home is not chasing the run, and a lineman who stops to smell the screen is not rushing the passer. The offense’s reply to the reply is the subject of Constraint Theory.

24  Play-Action, Bootlegs, and Screens

title: Play-Action, Bootlegs, and Screens
text:
A short history
Play-action is as old as the legal forward pass (1906): as soon as a team could throw, faking a run first was the obvious way to make a defense hesitate.10 What changed over the twentieth century was how systematically offenses built it in. The Wing-T of the 1950s made the run fake and the bootleg (its waggle) part of a series in which every play looked like the others, the idea you met in 03-05.
The modern NFL bootleg game runs through Mike Shanahan and Gary Kubiak in Denver. Kubiak was the Broncos’ offensive coordinator from 1995 through 2005 under Shanahan, alongside Alex Gibbs’s outside zone run game of 03-02, and John Elway, in the last four seasons of his career, made faking outside zone and rolling away from it a staple. The pairing became a coaching tree’s signature. Kyle Shanahan, Mike’s son, was the Atlanta Falcons’ offensive coordinator in 2016, when Matt Ryan, throwing off play-action and boots, was named the league’s MVP. Kyle took the system to San Francisco as head coach in 2017, and Sean McVay and Matt LaFleur, who had coached on his offensive staffs in Washington (and, for LaFleur, Atlanta), carried it to the Rams and the Packers.11
Then the data caught up with the coaches. In 2018 Sean McVay’s Rams went 13–3 and reached the Super Bowl with Jared Goff throwing off play-action more than any quarterback in the league, on about 35 percent of his dropbacks.12 In the same year Baldwin and Hermsmeyer published the analyses described above, showing that play-action’s value did not depend on the run game. The league was already moving that way: by Football Outsiders’ count, play-action rose from 18 percent of dropbacks in 2016 to 24 percent in 2018.13 (Other charting services count fakes differently, so their percentages are not comparable year to year.) In FTN’s charting the league used play-action on 21% of dropbacks in 2022 and 23% in 2025, with the return of the under-center formation (see Classic Formations) helping push it up.
Screens are just as old, and no one owns them. The screen game most associated with the modern NFL is Andy Reid’s. Reid learned the West Coast offense under Mike Holmgren in Green Bay, and from his first years as a head coach in Philadelphia (from 1999) his teams threw running back screens as a core play, not a gimmick, with Brian Westbrook as their best-known weapon in the 2000s. He took the same habits to Kansas City in 2013.14






NoteFilm room: Los Angeles Rams 2018



The season: the one in the history above. Notice the formation: the Rams faked nearly always from the same 11-personnel, tight-split sets they used for their outside zone runs with Todd Gurley (see the film room in Spread and Modern Formations). The “run look” was not two tight ends; it was whatever the Rams ran from.
What to notice:

The match. Line steps, back’s path and receivers’ splits are identical on the run and the fake. Try to call run or pass from the first step; you will be wrong often, and so were linebackers.
The crossers. A large share of the big plays are receivers running across the field at 10–15 yards, behind linebackers who stepped up: the window of Figure 24.1.
The boots. Goff rolling away from outside zone with the flat, crosser and over routes, often after pre-snap motion has moved a receiver to the boot side.
What went wrong in the Super Bowl: the Rams scored three points. New England packed the middle of the field, where the crossers run, and pressured Goff on about 43 percent of his dropbacks, much of it with stunts that had time to develop because Goff was holding the ball.15 A play-action game still needs time and room to throw.









NoteFilm room: Seattle Seahawks 2025



The season: Klint Kubiak’s one year as Seattle’s offensive coordinator, with Sam Darnold at quarterback, ending in a 29–13 win over New England in Super Bowl LX.16 Kubiak is Gary Kubiak’s son, and his offense was the Denver tree in its 2025 form: outside zone from tight formations and the boots and play-action that pair with it. In FTN’s charting, Seattle’s play-action dropbacks averaged +0.40 EPA, against +0.02 on its other dropbacks, the biggest gap in the league (Figure 24.14).
What to do: watch any Seahawks game from 2025 and keep two counts: how many dropbacks start with a run fake, and how many of those move the quarterback out of the pocket. Then watch the linebackers on each fake with this chapter’s checklist. Kubiak was hired as the Raiders’ head coach for 2026, so this was one season’s offense, not Seattle’s current one.








NoteFilm room: Kansas City Chiefs 2022–2025, the screen game



The record: in FTN’s charting, the Chiefs threw 327 screens over the four seasons, more than any other team, and averaged +0.11 EPA on them, when the league average screen was worth -0.07. Most teams use screens as a tax on pressure; Reid’s offense gets value from them.
What to notice:

The sell. Watch the Chiefs’ linemen on a running back screen: they pass-set, punch and give ground as if in a real protection before releasing. A lazy release is the most common way screens die, and Kansas City’s rarely look lazy.
The variety. Running back slow screens, tunnel screens to receivers, tight end screens, screens off play-action and screens after motion: the defense cannot simply key one look.
The timing against pressure. Watch what the Chiefs call on downs when an opponent has been blitzing; the screen is often the punishment.

The numbers: who fakes, and does it work?
Now the league-wide picture. In 2025 offenses used play-action on 23% of dropbacks, and those dropbacks averaged +0.12 EPA, against +0.02 for dropbacks without a fake; their success rate was 49% against 45%. Figure 24.14 breaks that down by team.


Show the Python
t = team25.sort_values("rate")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 5.6))
y = np.arange(len(t))
ax.axvline(0, color=style.BASELINE, lw=1, zorder=1)
ax.hlines(y, t["epa_no"], t["epa_pa"], color=style.GRID, lw=2.4, zorder=2)
ax.scatter(t["epa_no"], y, s=30, color=style.SERIES[1], zorder=3, label="No run fake", edgecolor=style.SURFACE, lw=0.6)
ax.scatter(t["epa_pa"], y, s=30, color=style.SERIES[0], zorder=4, label="Play-action", edgecolor=style.SURFACE, lw=0.6)
ax.set_yticks(y, t.index, fontsize=6.4)
ax.tick_params(axis="x", labelsize=7.5)

ax.set_xlim(float(min(t["epa_pa"].min(), t["epa_no"].min())) - 0.05, xmax + 0.12)
for yi, (rate, team) in enumerate(zip(t["rate"], t.index)):
    ax.text(xmax + 0.1, yi, f"{100 * rate:.0f}%", fontsize=6.4, color=style.INK_2, va="center", ha="right")
ax.text(xmax + 0.1, len(t) - 0.2, "PA rate", fontsize=7, color=style.INK_2, va="bottom", ha="right",
        fontweight="bold")
ax.set_ylim(-0.8, len(t) + 0.4)
ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
ax.set_xlabel("EPA per dropback", fontsize=8, color=style.INK_2)
ax.set_ylim(-0.8, len(t) + 1.6)
ax.legend(loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.42, 1.0), ncol=2, fontsize=7.5, frameon=False)
ax.set_title("Most offenses are better when they fake", fontsize=10)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 24.14: Play-action by team, 2025 regular season. Each row is a team: EPA per dropback without a run fake (orange) and with one (blue); the line between them is the boost the fake gave that team. The right-hand column is the team’s play-action rate (share of its dropbacks that began with a fake). Teams are sorted by that rate; where a team shows one dot (KC), the two sit on top of each other: the fake made no difference. Data: nflverse play-by-play with FTN charting via nflreadpy; dropbacks include sacks and scrambles.





Three things stand out in Figure 24.14.
Most teams were better with the fake. 22 of 32 offenses averaged more EPA on play-action dropbacks than on their others. That is a single season, and some teams’ play-action samples are only a hundred-odd plays, so individual gaps bounce around from year to year. The league-wide pattern does not.
The heaviest users build their passing game on their run game. McVay’s Rams led the league at 35% and Ben Johnson’s Bears were next at 31%. Several other offenses from the Shanahan family tree sat in the top half (McDaniel’s Dolphins, LaFleur’s Packers, Kubiak’s Seahawks), though Shanahan’s own 49ers ranked only 21st in 2025. These are offenses whose runs and passes are designed to look alike before and just after the snap.
Some offenses barely fake, and not all of them suffer for it. The lowest rates belong to offenses built around a shotgun quarterback who wins from the pocket, where a fake looks less like a run. The Chiefs ranked 32nd in play-action rate but 13th in EPA per dropback, above the league’s middle. Low use is a style, not a mistake: a fake is worth most when it looks like your real run, and some offenses’ real runs are not the ones defenses fear.
Why doesn’t everyone fake on every snap, if it is worth that much? Because a fake only works while the defense must respect the run (part of the measured boost belongs to the friendly early-down situations offenses pick for it). On third-and-9, nobody bites.

title: Play-Action, Bootlegs, and Screens
text:
Watch for it on Sunday






TipWatch for it: the linebackers’ feet



Before the snap

Under center? About four of every five under-center dropbacks begin with a run fake. When the quarterback lines up under the center, think run or play-action, not dropback.
The run look. Whatever formation this offense runs its main run from (often 12 personnel, or 11 personnel with the receivers in tight splits) is the formation it fakes from.
The down and distance. First-and-10 and second-and-short are play-action downs; third-and-long is not.

At the snap: watch the linebackers’ feet, not the ball

Did they step forward? Count the steps. Two steps up on a fake is a win for the offense. The main broadcast shot is usually framed on the box, so the linebackers are in it; the replay from the end zone, behind the offense, shows their first steps best.
Did the guard in front of them fire out low, or pop up? If he popped up and they stayed home, the fake did not work, and the throw will be harder.

In the first two seconds

Did the quarterback turn his back to the defense (under-center fake) or ride the back (shotgun)?
Did he roll away from the fake? Find the backside end: did he chase (the boot wins) or stay home (watch for the quick throw to the flat, or a protected boot with a pulling guard or a back coming across)?
Only two receivers out, eight in to block? Count the receivers who release. Two out with a hard fake on an early down is a shot play: look deep, at the single safety.
A tight end who blocks on the run-fake side, then slips out late while everyone else floods the other way: that’s the leak.
Linemen leaving their rushers and sliding out to one side before the throw? It’s a screen. Which ones released, and to which side? Did the rushers run past the back?

After the play (on the replay)

How many yards did the crosser gain after the catch? That is the space the linebackers left.
On a screen, count the blockers in front of the catch and the rushers behind it.

For your prediction log (How to Watch a Broadcast): on every under-center snap, write run, PA or boot before the snap. Then, when the defense blitzes on a passing down, write screen? and see how often you are right.
