28  Defensive Line Play: Techniques, One-Gap and Two-Gap

title: Defensive Line Play: Techniques, One-Gap and Two-Gap
text:
One-gap: attack a gap
Now the big choice. In a one-gap defense, each defensive lineman is responsible for exactly one gap. He lines up in it or shaded toward it (that is what an odd number or an “i” usually signals), and at the snap he attacks it. His goal is penetration: getting across the line of scrimmage and into the offense’s backfield before the play can develop, through his gap. If a blocker gets in his way, he defeats the blocker while staying in his gap; he does not need to read where the ball is going first, because the other gaps belong to somebody else.
How does he attack it? Watch three things, the same three a defensive line coach teaches first. His stance: shaded toward his gap, with the hand and foot on the gap side slightly back, so his first step goes straight into the gap instead of at the blocker. His key: he does not wait for the quarterback’s cadence (the defense never knows the snap count), so he watches the ball, or the blocker’s hand beside it, and moves the instant it moves. And his hat and hands: helmet into the gap he owns, hands on the blocker’s near shoulder or chest, pads lower than the blocker’s, so that even if the blocker gets to him he is driving through the gap rather than standing in front of the man.
That last point, staying in his gap, is what makes one-gap football work: the gaps add up. Seven gaps across a line with one tight end, seven defenders in the box, one defender for each. The linemen take the gaps they are aligned in; the linebackers behind them take the rest. Everybody has one job and can play it fast. (Change the formation and the count changes with it: no tight end means six gaps, two tight ends mean eight, and the defense adds or removes a box defender to keep one man per gap. The full accounting is Run Fits and Box Math.)


Show the Python
GAPS = [(-4.0, "C"), (-2.4, "B"), (-0.8, "A"), (0.8, "A"), (2.4, "B"), (4.0, "C"), (5.95, "D")]


def owners(f, p, groups):
    """Under the gap letters: a bar spanning the gap(s) each player owns, with his label beneath it."""
    for w0, w1, lab in groups:
        bracket(f, p, -3.0, w0 - 0.35, w1 + 0.35, lw=1.6)
        say(f, p, -3.75, (w0 + w1) / 2, lab, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7, weight="bold")


fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 3.9))
# one-gap 4-3
dfn = front([("LE", "5", -1), ("L1", "1", -1), ("R3", "3", 1), ("RE", "9", 1)],
            lbs=[("WILL", 4.5, -2.4, "W"), ("MIKE", 4.5, 0.8, "M"), ("SAM", 4.3, 4.0, "S")])
p = Play(line("short") + [te(+1)], dfn, los=35, to_go=None)
for k, w in [("WILL", -2.4), ("MIKE", 0.8), ("SAM", 4.0)]:
    go_to(p, k, (2.0, w), "path")
f = draw(p, ax=axes[0], lateral=(-8.0, 8.6), window=(-5.0, 7.2), title=False)
for w, g in GAPS:
    gap_tag(f, p, -2.2, w, g)
owners(f, p, [(w, w, lab) for w, lab in zip([g[0] for g in GAPS], ["5", "W", "1", "M", "3", "S", "9"])])
axes[0].set_title("One-gap 4-3: seven gaps, seven men", fontsize=8.8, loc="left", color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")
# two-gap 3-4
dfn = front([("LE", "4", -1), ("NT", "0", 1), ("RE", "4", 1)],
            lbs=[("MIKE", 4.6, -1.8, "M"), ("WILL", 4.6, 1.8, "W")],
            others=[("LOLB", 0.9, -5.6, "E"), ("ROLB", 0.9, 6.5, "E")])
p = Play(line("short") + [te(+1)], dfn, los=35, to_go=None)
f = draw(p, ax=axes[1], lateral=(-8.0, 8.6), window=(-5.0, 7.2), title=False)
for w, g in GAPS:
    gap_tag(f, p, -2.2, w, g)
owners(f, p, [(-4.0, -2.4, "4"), (-0.8, 0.8, "0"), (2.4, 4.0, "4"), (5.95, 5.95, "E")])
say(f, p, 5.75, 0.0, "M and W: read, then fill", color=GREEN, fontsize=6.9, weight="bold")
say(f, p, 2.4, -5.6, "sets the\nedge", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.6)
axes[1].set_title("Two-gap 3-4: three men, six gaps", fontsize=8.8, loc="left", color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.7)
plt.show()








Figure 28.3: Who owns which gap, against the same offense (one tight end, so seven gaps: two A, two B, two C and a D on the tight-end side). The row under the gap letters says who owns each one. Left, a one-gap 4-3 (with the 3 toward the tight end, this is the Over front of Even Fronts): each of the seven defenders in the box has one gap. The linemen take the gaps they are shaded into (5, 1, 3, 9) and the three linebackers (arrows) fill the three left over. Right, a two-gap 3-4: the nose (0) and the two ends (4, head-up on the tackles) each own the two gaps on either side of their blocker (the wide bars), and the edge player on the right (E) takes the D gap. Three players cover six gaps, so the left edge player can set the edge and both inside linebackers can read the play and fill wherever the ball goes, as long as the linemen in front of them keep the blockers busy. This is the basic accounting; real defenses add wrinkles to both pictures.





Here is a one-gap 3-technique doing his job. The offense runs outside zone to the right, the run from Zone Running in which every lineman steps to the play side and tries to get his head outside the defender in front of him. For the right guard, that means reaching the 3-technique: stepping sideways to get from the 3’s inside shoulder to his outside shoulder, against a man who is already outside him. The 3-technique’s answer is to be faster: to be through the gap before the reach can land. (If the guard does get there first, the 3 plays the reach the way every defender does, the subject of Fighting the blocks, below.)


Show the Python
def one_gap_play():
    off = line("full") + [te(+1), O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -7.0, 0, "R")]
    dfn = front([("LE", "5", -1), ("L1", "1", -1), ("R3", "3", 1), ("RE", "9", 1)],
                lbs=[("WILL", 4.6, -2.6, "W"), ("MIKE", 4.6, 1.2, "M")])
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=None)
    # the line steps right (outside zone): the guard steps sideways to reach the 3 and is late
    go_to(p, "RG", (-0.6, 2.25), speed=1.2)
    go_to(p, "RG", (-1.3, 2.75), speed=1.6)
    go_to(p, "RT", (-0.1, 4.4), speed=3.4)              # uncovered: steps play side, then climbs
    go_to(p, "RT", (2.1, 3.9), speed=3.0)
    go_to(p, "Y", (0.0, 6.0), speed=2.0); go_to(p, "RE", (1.0, 6.6), "path", speed=1.0)
    go_to(p, "C", (-0.5, 0.85), speed=2.0); go_to(p, "LG", (-0.4, -0.75), speed=2.0)
    go_to(p, "LT", (-0.5, -2.35), speed=2.0)
    go_to(p, "L1", (0.95, 0.15), "path", speed=1.0); go_to(p, "LE", (0.6, -3.2), "path", speed=1.2)
    # the 3-technique: get-off into the B gap, past the guard's hip, into the back's track
    go_to(p, "R3", (-0.45, 3.05), "path", speed=4.4, via=[(0.4, 2.85)])
    go_to(p, "R3", (-3.55, 3.45), "path", speed=4.8, via=[(-2.0, 3.4)])
    go_to(p, "MIKE", (3.0, 3.6), "path", speed=4.0, delay=0.2); go_to(p, "WILL", (3.6, 0.2), "path", speed=4.0, delay=0.25)
    go_to(p, "QB", (-3.0, 0.7), "path", speed=3.0)
    go_to(p, "RB", (-5.15, 3.8), "run", speed=6.4, via=[(-6.6, 1.4)])
    p.handoff("RB", t=0.55)
    go_to(p, "RB", (-5.05, 3.85), "run", speed=0.8)
    return p


def mark_tfl(fld, play, t, i):
    if t >= 1.1:
        spot(fld, play, -4.3, 3.65, ms=9)


P_ONE = one_gap_play()
animation_or_strip([(P_ONE, 0.0, ""), (P_ONE, 0.2, ""), (P_ONE, 0.6, ""), (P_ONE, 1.15, "")],
                   notes=["the 3 on the RG's outside\nshoulder: he owns the B gap",
                          "get-off: first step into\nthe B gap, low",
                          "past the guard's hip before\nthe reach can land",
                          "in the back's path, 4 yards\ndeep: tackle for loss"],
                   rings=(("R3", style.DEFENSE),), lateral=(-5.4, 8.6), window=(-8.6, 6.2), after=mark_tfl,
                   width_in=5.2)





  
  Your browser does not support the video tag.



Figure 28.4: A one-gap 3-technique against outside zone to the right (simulated, in Big Data Bowl tracking coordinates; faint lines are each player’s path so far). 1: the 3 (ringed) is on the right guard’s outside shoulder; his gap is the B gap. 2: the get-off, the defender’s first-step explosion at the snap. The defense never knows the snap count, so he watches the ball and moves the instant it moves; his first step is already into the B gap while the guard is still stepping sideways to reach him and the tackle steps past him to climb to the Mike. 3: he is past the guard’s hip before the guard can get his head across: penetration. 4: he meets the running back about four yards behind the line, in the back’s path to the outside, before the back can turn upfield (X).




Why it exists. One-gap play turns the defense’s linemen loose. A lineman who doesn’t have to read before he moves gets a half-step head start on every snap, and on the line half a step is everything: the blocker who is reaching or pulling or setting for a pass is moving sideways or backward while the defender is moving forward. The results are the plays fans remember, tackles for loss, sacks, a running back hit as he takes the handoff, and they wreck an offense’s plans in a way a two-yard gain never does. One-gap play also fits the players the modern game produces. A lineman who wins by quickness, the Donald type, is wasted standing still with his hands on a blocker; turn him loose in a gap and he is the most disruptive player on the field.
What it costs. Three things.

A wrong guess is a big hole. A one-gapper who penetrates past the play, or gets moved out of his gap by a double team, leaves his gap empty, and nobody else was assigned to it. A run that gets through a vacated gap is usually not a short gain, because the next defender is a linebacker who was busy with his own gap.
Offenses build plays to punish it. An aggressive penetrator is exactly what the trap in Gap and Power Runs is designed for: let him into the backfield unblocked, then hit him from the side with a pulling lineman, and run the ball through the space he left. Draws and screens work on the same idea: invite the rush, then go where it was.
It needs everyone else to be right. One-gap defense is only as good as its accounting. If one linebacker fills the wrong gap, there are two defenders in one gap and none in another. That is why one-gap teams spend so much practice time on run fits, the subject of Run Fits and Box Math.

Where it came from. For much of football’s history, defensive linemen were taught to read and react. The great attacking interior linemen changed that by being too quick to keep at home. The best known story is Pittsburgh’s in 1974: late that season the Steelers began lining Joe Greene up at the center, his stance tilted at about 45 degrees toward the A gap, so he could knife through before anyone could block him. Accounts differ on whose idea it was: the Hall of Fame credits Greene, other histories credit his line coach, George Perles. The Steelers called it the stunt 4-3 (a period name: today “stunt” usually means the looping pass-rush games of The Pass Rush, which this was not). It began as a practice-field experiment, got its first heavy use late that regular season, and carried the Steelers through the 1974 playoffs to their first Super Bowl win.7 Two decades later the Tampa Bay Buccaneers of Tony Dungy and Monte Kiffin built a whole defense around a one-gap 3-technique, Warren Sapp, who was the NFL’s Defensive Player of the Year in 1999.8

title: Defensive Line Play: Techniques, One-Gap and Two-Gap
section: Two-gap: control the man, then pick a side
text:
Two-gap: control the man, then pick a side
The other answer is older, heavier and quieter. In a two-gap defense, a lineman lines up head-up on a blocker (a 0, a 2, a 4: the even numbers) and is responsible for the gaps on both sides of him. At the snap he does not attack a gap. He attacks the man: strikes him with both hands inside the blocker’s chest, straightens his arms to keep the blocker off his body (coaches call it locking out), and stands him up at the line of scrimmage. Then, with the blocker held at arm’s length, he looks into the backfield, sees which side the ball is going, and throws the blocker the other way to make the tackle.
Coaches have a rule for how a two-gapper knows which way to go: read the blocker’s head. A blocker who wants to wall a defender off from one side has to get his helmet to that side of him. Say the center’s helmet slides to the right of the nose (the offense’s right, as always in this book): the center is trying to keep him from going right, which means the ball is going right. So the two-gapper “plays across the face”: he keeps his arms locked, works to the side the blocker’s head went (right), throws the blocker the other way (left), and is standing in the right A gap when the ball arrives. The block tells him where the ball is going before he ever sees the ball.
Head-up is the natural spot for this, because the defender starts with a gap on each side and the blocker in the middle. A shaded player can be asked to two-gap too, and some 4-3 teams ask exactly that of a 1 or a 4i. He plays it the same way, by striking and controlling the man he is shaded on, but his near gap is already his and his far gap is the hard one: to reach it he has to work back across the blocker’s face, so his alignment is a lean, not a commitment. That is why “odd number or an i” is only a hint about the job.


Show the Python
def two_gap_play(side=+1):
    """3-4 with a 0 nose and 4-technique ends against inside zone right. The center and right guard
    double the nose and the left guard climbs; the back hits the right A (side=+1) or cuts back to
    the left A (side=-1)."""
    off = line("full") + [O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -6.6, 0, "R")]
    dfn = front([("LE", "4", -1), ("NT", "0", 1), ("RE", "4", 1)],
                lbs=[("MIKE", 4.6, -2.2, "M"), ("WILL", 4.6, 2.2, "W")])
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=None)
    # the strike: nose and center meet, the nose locks out and drives him back a step
    go_to(p, "C", (-1.3, 0.0), speed=1.2, via=[(-0.6, 0.0)])
    go_to(p, "NT", (0.75, 0.0), "path", speed=1.6)
    go_to(p, "NT", (0.6, 0.05), "path", speed=0.6)
    # the right guard doubles the nose (the drive man, from the side); the left guard climbs to the Mike
    go_to(p, "RG", (-0.35, 1.0), speed=2.2, via=[(-0.55, 1.4)])
    go_to(p, "LG", (2.75, -2.6), speed=3.6, via=[(0.5, -1.6)])
    go_to(p, "MIKE", (3.85, -1.75), "path", speed=2.0, delay=0.2)
    # the ends hold up the tackles
    go_to(p, "LT", (-0.2, -3.2), speed=1.2); go_to(p, "LE", (1.0, -3.2), "path", speed=0.5)
    go_to(p, "RT", (-0.3, 3.4), speed=1.2); go_to(p, "RE", (1.0, 3.4), "path", speed=0.5)
    go_to(p, "QB", (-3.4, 0.4), "path", speed=3.6)          # opens to the play side for the handoff
    go_to(p, "QB", (-4.7, -1.9), "path", speed=2.4)         # then carries out his fake
    if side > 0:   # the hole never opens; the free Will fills it
        go_to(p, "NT", (0.55, 0.3), "path", speed=0.5, delay=0.1)
        go_to(p, "WILL", (-0.75, 2.45), "path", speed=5.0, delay=0.15)
        go_to(p, "RB", (-2.55, 1.9), "run", speed=5.6, via=[(-4.0, 0.6), (-3.2, 1.2)])
    else:          # cutback: the nose throws the center right and takes the left A
        go_to(p, "NT", (-0.25, -1.05), "path", speed=3.4, delay=0.3)
        go_to(p, "C", (-1.45, 0.45), speed=1.4, delay=0.3)
        go_to(p, "WILL", (2.6, 0.8), "path", speed=3.0, delay=0.4)
        go_to(p, "RB", (-2.25, -1.3), "run", speed=5.6, via=[(-4.0, 0.6), (-3.2, 0.1)])
    p.handoff("RB", t=0.45)
    return p


def two_gap_marks(fld, play, t, i):
    """Both A gaps marked while the nose still owns them; the locked-out arms; an X at the tackle."""
    if t < 0.2:
        for w in (-0.8, 0.8):
            gap_tag(fld, play, -3.2, w, "A", fontsize=7)
    (nd, nw), (cd, cw) = play.position("NT", t), play.position("C", t)
    if 0.3 <= t and abs(nw - cw) < 0.5 and nd - cd > 1.2:      # arms locked out on the center
        for off in (-0.38, 0.38):
            xs, ys = _P(fld, play, np.array([nd - 0.7, cd + 0.5]), np.array([nw + off, cw + off]))
            fld.ax.plot(xs, ys, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, lw=3.2, solid_capstyle="round", zorder=11)
    if t >= 1.1:
        if play.position("RB", 2.0)[1] > 0:
            spot(fld, play, -1.65, 2.2, ms=9)
        else:
            spot(fld, play, -1.25, -1.2, ms=9)


P_TWO_R, P_TWO_L = two_gap_play(+1), two_gap_play(-1)
animation_or_strip([(P_TWO_R, 0.0, ""), (P_TWO_R, 0.45, ""), (P_TWO_R, 1.25, "ball right"),
                    (P_TWO_L, 1.25, "ball left")],
                   notes=["0-technique on the C:\nboth A gaps are his",
                          "strike and lock out; the RG\ncomes over to double him",
                          "he gives no ground: the RG is\nstuck, the W is free to tackle",
                          "same start, back cuts left:\nhe sheds the C and tackles"],
                   rings=(("NT", style.DEFENSE),), lateral=(-5.8, 5.8), window=(-7.8, 6.4), after=two_gap_marks,
                   width_in=5.0)





  
  Your browser does not support the video tag.



Figure 28.5: A two-gap nose tackle in a 3-4 against an inside zone run, the same start with two endings (simulated, Big Data Bowl coordinates). 1: the nose (ringed) is a 0-technique, head-up on the center, responsible for both A gaps (green). Nobody covers the guards. 2: the strike. Both hands inside the center’s chest, arms locked out (the two short bars), the center held a yard off his body and pushed back a step. The right guard comes over to double-team him, as the zone rules tell him to, while the left guard climbs to the Mike. 3: the back aims at the right A gap. The nose gives no ground, so the hole never opens, and the right guard can’t leave the double team to block the Will: the Will, unblocked, fills and makes the tackle (X). 4: the same play, but the back cuts back to the left A gap, so the nose throws the center off to the right and makes the tackle in the left A himself. Either way the offense spent two blockers on one man and the run went nowhere.




Why it exists. Look back at the right half of Figure 28.3. If one lineman can be responsible for two gaps, three linemen can hold six of them, and the defense has players left over. In the classic two-gap 3-4, the two inside linebackers have no gap of their own to rush to at the snap. They read the play and fill wherever the ball goes, and the two-gappers’ job is to make that possible. Three linemen can’t occupy five blockers just by standing there: the guards are uncovered, and if nothing stops them they climb straight to the linebackers. What stops them is the nose. A nose who can’t be moved by the center alone forces a guard to stay and help him, as in Figure 28.5, so at most one blocker gets up to the linebackers, and the 4s keep the tackles from climbing at all. That is the two-gapper’s real product: not tackles, but clean linebackers. And because he doesn’t commit before the snap, the offense can’t build its blocking around where he will go.
Two-gapping matters even more in the modern NFL than its reputation suggests. Defenses now keep two deep safeties on many snaps to stop the pass, which leaves only six men in the box against an offense that may have six or seven blockers (A First Look at Defense has the numbers). With six defenders and seven gaps, the accounting of one-gap football does not add up. The usual fix is to ask a big nose to play both A gaps, so six men can cover seven gaps. That is one of the ideas behind the light-box fronts of Vic Fangio and his followers, taken up in Odd and Hybrid Fronts and the case study Fangio’s Two-High Revolution and Macdonald’s Answer.
What it costs.

Rare bodies. Holding a 310-pound center at arm’s length while a guard hits you from the side takes size and strength that very few people have: two-gap noses are typically well over 320 pounds, and the pool of such players who can also move is small.9
No head start. Reading before moving means the two-gapper is always reacting. He rarely makes a tackle behind the line and rarely gets a sack. On a pass his job is mostly to push the center straight back into the quarterback’s lap, collapsing the middle of the pocket so the quarterback can’t step up, which matters but doesn’t show up as a sack. That is why classic two-gap noses often leave the field on third down for a lighter, quicker pass-rush package.
His value hides. The stat sheet credits the man who makes the tackle, not the man who made the tackle possible. A great two-gapper can have a quiet box score in a game he dominated.







CautionCommon misconception



“A 3-4 means two-gap, and a 4-3 means one-gap.” It is a decent first guess, nothing more. The classic 3-4s of the 1970s through the 2000s, Bill Parcells’s and Bill Belichick’s among them, did two-gap with big ends and a big nose. But Wade Phillips, son of the Bum Phillips who devised the technique numbers, spent decades running an attacking, one-gap 3-4: when he took over the Houston Texans’ defense in 2011, the team’s own preview called it “his one-gap scheme,” and the line coach explained that it was “not like a two-gap type defense where you need that 350-pound nose man to be able to just clog up and take on two blocks.”10 And plenty of 4-3 teams ask a nose to two-gap. The number of linemen tells you how many there are; their first step tells you how they play.








NoteMadden vs. real life



In Madden, a defensive lineman is mostly someone you steer at the quarterback, and the run defense takes care of itself. On a real early down, a lineman’s job is mostly the gap: hold it, or attack it, exactly as the call says. A nose tackle who abandons both A gaps to chase a sack can give up a 20-yard run even if he beats his man, which is why defensive line coaches grade every snap on assignment before they grade it on result.

title: Defensive Line Play: Techniques, One-Gap and Two-Gap
text:
Fighting the blocks
Whichever style he plays, a defensive lineman has to beat whatever block the offense throws at him, and the offense has a whole vocabulary of them. You learned them from the blocker’s side in 03-01. Here are the defender’s answers to the three that matter most, the down block, the reach and the double team, and the one principle underneath all of them: fight pressure with pressure. Whatever direction a block is pushing you, push back into it. A blocker pushes you where the offense wants you, toward the hole’s edge or out of your gap, so leaning into the pressure is how you stay where the defense wants you.


Show the Python
DD = 2.6
SPAN = 8.6


def r_down(p):
    go_to(p, "RT", (1.45, 2.75), via=[(0.2, 3.05)])
    go_to(p, "D3", (2.6, 3.4), "path", speed=1.0)
    go_to(p, "D5", (1.3, 4.0), "path", speed=1.5)
    go_to(p, "RG", (0.45, 4.35), "pull", via=[(-1.8, 2.0), (-1.85, 3.9)])


def r_reach(p):
    go_to(p, "RG", (1.3, 2.75), via=[(0.2, 2.2)])
    go_to(p, "RT", (2.5, 5.3), via=[(0.3, 4.2)])
    go_to(p, "D3", (1.7, 4.0), "path", speed=1.5)
    go_to(p, "RB", (-1.4, 6.2), "run", via=[(-4.6, 2.4), (-3.4, 4.6)])


def r_double(p):
    go_to(p, "C", (1.45, 0.3))
    go_to(p, "RG", (1.45, 1.2), via=[(0.2, 1.4)])
    go_to(p, "M", (4.3, 1.9), "path", speed=2.0)


PLATES = [
    ("1. Down block", "the 3 fights pressure; the 5\nsqueezes and waits for the puller",
     [D("D3", "DL", DD, T("3"), "3"), D("D5", "DL", DD, T("5") + 0.5, "5")], r_down, -1.2, ("C", "LG", "LT")),
    ("2. Reach", "step with him, outside arm free,\npress him back: don't get hooked",
     [D("D3", "DL", DD, T("3"), "3"), O("RB", "RB", -5.2, 0.2, "R")], r_reach, -1.6, ("C", "LT", "LG")),
    ("3. Double team", "sink, lean into the drive man,\nkeep both blockers: the Mike runs free",
     [D("D1", "DL", DD, T("1"), "1"), D("M", "LB", 5.5, 1.0, "M")], r_double, -3.4, ("RT",)),
]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(6.6, 3.4))
for ax, (ttl, note, extra, build, w0, drop) in zip(axes, PLATES):
    ol = [q for q in line("short") if w0 + 0.8 <= q.w <= w0 + SPAN - 0.8 and q.key not in drop]
    p = Play(ol + extra, None, los=35, to_go=None)
    build(p)
    f = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=(w0, w0 + SPAN), window=(-6.4, 7.4), title=False)
    if build is r_down:
        say(f, p, 4.6, 4.6, "eyes inside:\npuller?", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.5)
        say(f, p, -2.9, 2.9, "puller", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.5)
    if build is r_reach:
        dashed(f, p, [(-3.9, 1.9), (-1.8, 2.4), (0.3, 2.45)], color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, lw=1.2)
        say(f, p, -2.6, 0.7, "wanted", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.5)
    if build is r_double:
        say(f, p, 5.6, -1.3, "free", color=GREEN, fontsize=7, weight="bold")
        say(f, p, -1.9, -0.4, "post", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.5)
        say(f, p, -1.9, 2.1, "drive", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.5)
    ax.set_title(ttl, fontsize=9, loc="left", color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")
    ax.text(1.0, 1.035, "play \u2192", transform=ax.transAxes, ha="right", va="bottom", fontsize=7,
            color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontweight="bold")
    ax.text(0.5, -0.02, note, transform=ax.transAxes, ha="center", va="top", fontsize=6.9, color=style.INK_2)
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.01, right=0.99, top=0.9, bottom=0.17, wspace=0.08)
plt.show()








Figure 28.6: The defender’s answers, play going right in every panel (defenders drawn a little deeper than real so each path shows; blue bars are blocks, the blue path with a bar is a pulling lineman, orange arrows the defender’s response). 1, Down block: the tackle blocks down on the 3-technique while the guard pulls. The 3 fights the pressure, pushing back outward so he isn’t washed inside; the 5, left without a blocker, squeezes down the line, hip to hip with the tackle, to shrink the hole, with his eyes inside for the puller coming to kick him out. 2, Reach: the guard tries to get his head outside the 3, and the tackle climbs past. The 3 steps with him, keeps his outside arm free and presses him back toward the backfield, so the runner, who wanted to turn up just outside the guard (dashed), has to keep running sideways instead; the 3 does not run around the block. 3, Double team: the center and guard combine on the 1-technique. The guard, hitting him from the side, is the drive man; the center, in front, is the post. The 1 sinks his hips, leans into the drive man, gives no ground and keeps both blockers on him, so the Mike behind him is free to fill.






Against a down block
A down block hits a defender from the side: the blocker outside him comes inside, at an angle, to drive him toward the center and seal the inside of the hole. Two defenders are involved, and they have opposite jobs.

The man being down-blocked (the 3-technique in panel 1) feels pressure from his outside. If he gives way, he is washed down the line and the hole doubles in size. So he fights pressure: drops his outside shoulder into the blocker and pushes back outward, holding his gap and never slipping behind the block. A few defenses let a dominant player fight across the blocker’s face and into the hole himself; if he doesn’t win that fight, he has given up the inside.
The man left alone (the 5 in panel 1) has just seen the tackle in front of him leave. A blocker who vanishes is a warning, not a gift. On a gap-scheme run like power, the tackle blocks down because someone else is coming for the end: a pulling guard or a fullback, to kick him out. So he squeezes: steps down the line, hip to hip with the down-blocker, shrinking the hole, with his eyes inside for the puller. When the puller arrives, the defense’s call decides what he does next. He can keep his outside arm free and force the ball back inside (box or squeeze), or attack the puller’s inside shoulder and pile up the hole, pushing the ball outside to a teammate waiting there (spill, the “wrong-arm” you met in 03-03). Which one, and who is waiting, is the heart of Run Fits and Box Math.

There is a cousin of this rule that every defensive line coach teaches: if nobody blocks you, something is coming. A lineman who is let through untouched should close inside at once and get small: turn his shoulders and drop his pads, so a blocker coming from the side has only a narrow shoulder to hit and can’t knock him out of the gap. The likeliest explanation is a trap block from the side, the gap play built to catch penetrators. But coaches say “trap or read,” because there is a second explanation. On an option play the offense leaves an end unblocked on purpose and lets the quarterback read him (Option Football): if the end closes inside, the quarterback keeps the ball and runs where he was. How does a lineman know which it is? Partly from what he sees (a quarterback holding the ball in the back’s belly with his eyes on him is reading him; a guard pulling toward him is trapping him), and mostly from the call. The call tells him in advance whether he takes the back or the quarterback, and against option teams defenses often swap those jobs between the end and a linebacker, the scrape exchange of 03-04, precisely so the read is wrong.


Against a reach
A reach block is the blocker trying to get his head and body outside a defender who is already a step to the play side of him, and seal him inside. The defender’s whole job is not to let that happen, and he has the head start. A one-gapper fast enough to be through his gap before the blocker arrives beats the reach before it starts, as in Figure 28.4. Once the blocker has got to him, every defender, one-gap or two-gap, does the same thing: he steps with the blocker, keeps his outside arm free (so there is always an arm between the blocker and the sideline), and presses the blocker back into the backfield. Panel 2 shows the effect: the runner, who wanted to turn upfield just outside the guard, has to keep running sideways. Every yard he goes sideways is a yard of pursuit for the rest of the defense.
The mistake to avoid is the one that looks most athletic: running around the block. A defender who loops around the blocker’s back to get outside him has left his gap. On outside zone, that is exactly the hole the runner is looking for when he cuts back. The rule coaches use is to beat the block through the blocker, not around him.


Against a double team
The double team, or combo block, is the hardest thing a defensive lineman faces and the most important to survive. Two blockers want two things from him: to move him off the ball, and then, once the linebacker behind him commits, for one of them to come off and block that linebacker. The defender’s goal is to deny both.

Don’t get moved. He widens his base, sinks his hips, and fights the pressure of the blocker coming from the side. Coaches call that blocker the drive man (he does the moving) and the one in front of the defender the post man (he stops him from going forward). The defender drops the hip nearest the drive man and leans into him, so the pair can’t turn his shoulders and walk him out of his gap. Giving up a yard backward is how a double team creates the hole.
Keep both blockers. The longer he keeps both men busy, the longer the linebacker behind him goes unblocked. The double team’s second blocker is supposed to climb to the second level; a defender who stays heavy on him keeps him from leaving.
If he is losing, make a pile. A lineman being driven back is taught to drop his hips, even to go to a knee in the gap, so that the bodies pile up where the hole was supposed to be. It looks like losing. It is a win if the running back has nowhere to go.

A few great linemen split double teams, slipping between the two blockers into the backfield, and it is a spectacular play when it works. It is also a gamble. If he doesn’t get through, he has turned his shoulders and left his gap, and the double team walks him out of it.


Against blocks going away
When the play goes away from a defender, his blocker uses a cut-off block (or the whole backside line scoops), stepping toward the play to get between him and the ball. Here he does chase. He flattens down the line, staying at about the depth of the ball, so that if the runner cuts back he is waiting. Backside blockers on zone runs often cut him instead, diving at his thighs to put him on the ground; he plays the cut with his hands, pushing the blocker’s shoulders down and away, and keeps his feet free. But the defender farthest from the play has a different rule, and it comes next.

title: Defensive Line Play: Techniques, One-Gap and Two-Gap
section: Setting the edge and keeping contain
text:
Setting the edge and keeping contain
The last man on the line on each side has a special job. Inside him, his teammates can count on someone being in the gap next to them. Outside him there is nobody, just the sideline. If a run gets outside him, it gets outside everybody.


Show the Python
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 4.3))
# set the edge
off = line("full") + [te(+1), O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -6.6, 0, "R")]
dfn = front([("LE", "5", -1), ("L1", "1", -1), ("R3", "3", 1)],
            lbs=[("WILL", 4.6, -2.6, "W"), ("MIKE", 4.6, 1.2, "M")],
            others=[("E", 1.0, T("9") + 0.9, "E")])
p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=None)
go_to(p, "Y", (-0.15, 6.0), via=[(-0.45, 5.5)])
go_to(p, "RT", (0.4, 2.95), via=[(-0.2, 3.0)])
go_to(p, "E", (0.15, 7.7), "path", speed=1.4)
go_to(p, "RB", (2.4, 3.7), "run", via=[(-5.0, 2.4), (-3.0, 4.3), (-1.6, 4.0)])
go_to(p, "MIKE", (3.3, 3.4), "path"); go_to(p, "WILL", (3.2, 1.4), "path")
p.highlight("E", color=style.DEFENSE)
f = draw(p, ax=axes[0], lateral=(-4.6, 11.4), window=(-9.6, 6.8), title=False)
dashed(f, p, [(-3.0, 4.3), (-1.4, 8.6), (3.4, 9.4)], color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, lw=1.3)
say(f, p, 4.9, 8.6, "hooked: ball\ngets outside", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.7)
say(f, p, -6.6, 6.6, "edge set:\nback turns up\ninside the Y,\ninto pursuit", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.7)
axes[0].set_title("Setting the edge", fontsize=9, loc="left", color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")
# contain
off = line("full") + [O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -6.6, 0, "R")]
dfn = front([("LE", "5", -1), ("L1", "1", -1), ("R3", "3", 1)],
            lbs=[("WILL", 4.6, -2.6, "W"), ("MIKE", 4.6, 1.2, "M")])
p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=None)
for k in ("LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT"):
    p.block(k, pts=[(0.3, 1.0)])
go_to(p, "RB", (-3.0, 4.2), "run", via=[(-5.4, 2.0)])
go_to(p, "QB", (-5.6, -6.6), "path", via=[(-4.4, -0.6), (-6.4, -3.4)])
go_to(p, "LE", (-4.4, -7.4), "path", via=[(0.2, -4.9), (-2.8, -6.6)])
go_to(p, "MIKE", (3.0, 2.8), "path"); go_to(p, "WILL", (3.2, 0.4), "path")
p.highlight("LE", color=style.DEFENSE)
f = draw(p, ax=axes[1], lateral=(-11.4, 4.6), window=(-9.6, 6.8), title=False)
dashed(f, p, [(0.45, -3.6), (0.27, -2.4), (0.27, 0.9)], color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, lw=2.0, dash=(0, (2.5, 1.6)))
say(f, p, 2.5, -2.3, "crashes?", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7.2, weight="bold")
say(f, p, -8.1, -2.2, "QB boots away\nfrom the fake", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.7)
say(f, p, -2.0, -9.2, "contain:\nstays outside\nthe QB", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.7)
say(f, p, -3.5, 3.0, "run fake", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.7)
axes[1].set_title("Keeping contain", fontsize=9, loc="left", color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()








Figure 28.7: The edge defender’s two jobs. Left, setting the edge against a run to the right (outside zone or a toss): the tight end tries to reach the edge player outside him (E, ringed, a 9-technique outside linebacker). The E steps with him, keeps his outside arm free, and drives him back into the backfield, so the runner cannot get outside and has to turn up inside the tight end (the solid path), back toward the Mike and Will chasing from inside. The dashed path is what happens if the E is hooked: the ball gets outside everybody. Right, contain against a play-action bootleg: the run fake goes right (the line’s short blocks to the right are part of the fake) and the quarterback rolls out left. The backside end (5, ringed) does not chase the fake down the line; he shuffles along behind the line and stays outside the quarterback. If he had crashed down the line after the fake (dashed), the quarterback would be outside him with nobody in front.





To set the edge is to be that last man and win: take on the blocker coming at you (a tight end, a tackle, a pulling guard, a fullback) at or near the line of scrimmage, with your outside arm free, and don’t let him push you back or get his head outside you. Then the run has only one place to go, back inside, toward the linebackers and safeties chasing it. A defense talks about a hard edge (the defender holds his ground at the line and turns the ball in quickly) and a soft edge (he gets pushed back or upfield, and the runner gets around him). Setting a hard edge is one of the least glamorous and most valued skills an edge player has, and it is a big part of why teams still want 270-pound defensive ends when a 245-pound linebacker might rush the passer just as well. On a given play, the player who turns the ball back inside is also called the force defender; who that is, and how it changes with the coverage, is in Run Fits and Box Math.
The end who did both jobs as well as anyone was Reggie White, the “Minister of Defense,” who played for the Eagles and the Packers and retired with 198 sacks, then the NFL record (Bruce Smith later passed him). In Super Bowl XXXI, after the 1996 season, he sacked Drew Bledsoe three times, a Super Bowl record that has since been tied but never broken, as Green Bay beat New England 35–21.11 If you find his games, watch the runs at him rather than the sacks: the blocker in front of him going backward, White’s outside arm free, and the ball carrier turning back inside. That is a hard edge, from a man who was also one of the great pass rushers of his era: proof that an edge player doesn’t always have to choose between the two jobs.
Contain is the edge player’s other rule, and its spirit is the same: nothing gets outside me, but with an emphasis on patience. On the backside of a run, the end who has contain does not chase the play flat down the line. He trails it at about the depth of the ball, because the plays most likely to come back his way are the ones designed to punish a chasing end: the bootleg, the reverse, the quarterback keeping the ball on a read (Perimeter and Misdirection has those plays from the offense’s side). Not every call keeps the end outside, though: against teams that run the read option, the end is often told to crash on the running back while a linebacker loops outside him to take the quarterback, the scrape exchange from the trap-or-read discussion above, a swap built to confuse the read. Contain still belongs to somebody; the call says who. On a pass rush, contain means the ends rush outside the tackles but not past the quarterback’s depth. An end who loops too far upfield opens a lane between himself and the quarterback, and a mobile quarterback steps up and runs through it. You will hear analysts call this rush-lane discipline; how pass rushers balance it against getting home is in The Pass Rush.
Both jobs ask a fast, aggressive player to be patient on a down when patience isn’t rewarded with a statistic. That is exactly why offenses attack them. A defensive end who gets a little too eager for the sack or the tackle for loss is the end the bootleg is built for.

title: Defensive Line Play: Techniques, One-Gap and Two-Gap
text:
Line movement: slants and angles
So far the linemen have played from where they lined up. But the alignment the offense sees before the snap doesn’t have to be the one it blocks after the snap. Defenses can move their linemen at the snap, and the two basic movements are the slant and the angle.


Show the Python
GAPS = [(-4.0, "C"), (-2.4, "B"), (-0.8, "A"), (0.8, "A"), (2.4, "B"), (4.0, "C"), (5.95, "D")]
LB_DASH = (0, (1.5, 2.0))


def base43():
    """A 4-3 front, linemen drawn a little deeper than real (2.2 yd) so their movement arrows show."""
    dl = front([("LE", "5", -1), ("L1", "1", -1), ("R3", "3", 1), ("RE", "9", 1)],
               lbs=[("WILL", 5.9, -2.6, "W"), ("MIKE", 5.9, 1.0, "M"), ("SAM", 5.7, 4.6, "S")])
    return [q.moved(d=2.2) if q.d == 1.0 else q for q in dl]


fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 3.7))
p = Play(line("short") + [te(+1)], base43(), los=35, to_go=None)
for k, end in [("RE", (1.75, 4.2)), ("R3", (1.75, 0.95)), ("L1", (1.75, -2.25)), ("LE", (1.85, -5.4))]:
    go_to(p, k, end, "path", speed=3.0)
f = draw(p, ax=axes[0], lateral=(-7.6, 8.4), window=(-3.8, 8.0), title=False)
for w, g in GAPS:
    gap_tag(f, p, -2.4, w, g, fontsize=7.5)
for k, end in [("SAM", (3.4, 5.95)), ("MIKE", (3.4, 2.4)), ("WILL", (3.4, -0.8))]:
    q = p.players[k]
    dashed(f, p, [(q.d - 0.7, q.w + 0.3 * np.sign(end[1] - q.w)), end], color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, lw=1.3,
           dash=LB_DASH)
say(f, p, 4.0, -5.9, "flat: across,\nnot upfield", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.7)
axes[0].set_title("Slant (weak): the whole line steps over", fontsize=8.6, loc="left", color=style.INK,
                  fontweight="bold")
p = Play(line("short") + [te(+1)], base43(), los=35, to_go=None)
go_to(p, "R3", (0.15, 0.85), "path", speed=3.0)
f = draw(p, ax=axes[1], lateral=(-7.6, 8.4), window=(-3.8, 8.0), title=False)
for w, g in GAPS:
    gap_tag(f, p, -2.4, w, g, fontsize=7.5)
dashed(f, p, [(5.2, 1.4), (3.4, 2.4)], color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, lw=1.3, dash=LB_DASH)
point_to(f, p, (4.0, -1.6), (1.2, 1.55), "45\u00b0: across\nand upfield", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK,
         fontsize=6.7, shrink=3)
axes[1].set_title("Angle: one man, into the next gap", fontsize=8.6, loc="left", color=style.INK,
                  fontweight="bold")
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()








Figure 28.8: Two ways to move the line at the snap, from the same 4-3 front (pre-snap alignments shown, linemen drawn a little deeper than real so the arrows show; orange arrows are the movement). Left, a slant to the weak side (away from the tight end): every lineman steps hard across the face of the man in front of him into the next gap over, gaining very little ground, so the arrows run almost along the line: the 9 into the C gap, the 3 into the A gap, the 1 into the left B gap, and the left end widens to keep contain. The linebackers replace them (dashed arrows): the Sam takes the D gap the 9 left, the Mike the right B gap, the Will the left A gap. Right, an angle: just the 3-technique moves, at about 45 degrees, into the A gap and on into the backfield; the Mike replaces him in the B gap. A slant moves the whole picture sideways; an angle moves one or two men while they keep attacking.





A slant is a called movement in which the linemen step hard across the face of the blocker in front of them at the snap, into the next gap over, usually all in the same direction, gaining only a little ground: the slanter’s job is to arrive in the next gap, not to go deep. The linebackers move the opposite way to fill the gaps the line just left, so the whole front’s gap assignments shift by one. An angle is a shorter movement, typically by one or two linemen: a step at about 45 degrees into the adjacent gap that moves the defender over while he keeps going upfield. Think of the slant as relocating the line, and the angle as a penetrator changing lanes. (The words are not standardized. Some staffs call every movement a slant, some have names for a slant toward the tight end and a slant away from him, and inward and outward moves by pairs of linemen are often called a pinch and an open. The footwork varies by staff too: the clinic source cited here starts the slant with a roughly 45-degree step that gains a little ground, and nearly every coach warns that a lineman who moves purely sideways can be caught by the blocker and pushed along the line. What separates the two movements is where the lineman is headed, across the line or through it.)12
Why move? Because the offense’s blocking is decided before the snap. Every offensive lineman has looked at the front and decided whether he is covered or uncovered, who doubles whom and who climbs to which linebacker. Movement changes the answers after it is too late to change the call. A slant can turn a covered lineman uncovered and an uncovered one covered in a single step. A double team aimed at a 3-technique hits air when the 3 angles into the A gap. A pulling guard runs into a defender who wasn’t in his path a moment ago. Movement is also how a defense of quick, lighter linemen deals with bigger blockers: they can’t win a head-on shove, so they don’t take one. As one college staff put it in a coaching clinic, “we use a lot of slants up front (gap control) to try and keep the offensive linemen occupied, which then will allow our linebackers the freedom to roam and get to the ball.”13
What it costs. Movement is a bet on where the play is going, and whether the bet pays depends on the blocking scheme as much as the direction.

Against gap schemes, slanting toward the run is the jackpot. Power and counter are built on pre-snap assignments and pullers aimed at where the defenders were; a front that slants into the play’s path arrives at the hole before the blockers do, and the puller finds a defender where his gap was supposed to be. Slant away from a gap play and every defender has stepped out of the gap the ball is coming through, with the replacing linebackers a step farther from it.
Against zone, slanting toward the run gains less than it looks. Zone linemen block whoever arrives in their area, so a slanting defender just runs into the next blocker’s arms (Zone Running explains why), and the play side gets crowded without getting stopped. The real danger is behind the slant: every lineman has left a gap, and the zone back’s cutback is aimed at exactly those gaps. Against zone, a slant lives or dies on the linebackers replacing the gaps the line left.
Either way, the linebackers have to move with the line every time. If one of them forgets the slant was called, two players fill one gap and the other is empty.

When two linemen go further and loop around each other on a pass rush, the movement becomes a stunt, which belongs to The Pass Rush.
How do the linemen know, and can you see it coming? The call comes from the sideline to the defense’s green-dot player, usually a linebacker, who relays it in the huddle or, against a fast offense, with a word or a hand signal at the line. It includes the front (where each lineman lines up), whether each plays one gap or two, and any movement, and it can be changed at the line when the offense shifts. From the stands or the couch you can sometimes see it leak. Look for the tells you learned for offensive linemen in How to Watch a Broadcast, applied to the other side of the ball: a lineman whose stance is cheated (weight leaning, back foot staggered toward the gap he is about to take, his body tilted the way Joe Greene’s was), a lineman who widens or tightens his alignment just before the snap, or a linebacker creeping toward the gap he will have to replace. Good defenses know this and try to give the same look on every snap, so treat any tell as odds, not a promise.

title: Defensive Line Play: Techniques, One-Gap and Two-Gap
text:
Putting a front together
Step back and the parts fit together. A defensive coordinator calling a front is choosing, for each lineman, three things you can now name:

Where he lines up (his technique), which tells the offense who is covered and shapes its blocking.
How he plays it: one-gap (attack the gap he is in) or two-gap (control the man and read).
Whether he moves: straight ahead, or a slant or an angle into another gap at the snap.

Different answers to those questions are what separate the fronts in the rest of this part: the even fronts with their 3-techniques and wide ends (Even Fronts), the odd and tite fronts with their 0s and 4is (Odd and Hybrid Fronts), and the linebackers whose jobs change with every one of these choices (Linebackers and the Second Level). A defense can also mix them: two-gap the nose, one-gap the 3-technique, angle the end. The modern NFL front is less a system than a menu.

title: Defensive Line Play: Techniques, One-Gap and Two-Gap
text:
Film room






NoteFilm room: Tampa Bay Buccaneers, Super Bowl XXXVII (2002 season)



The game: Super Bowl XXXVII, January 26, 2003: Tampa Bay 48, Oakland 21. The Buccaneers’ defense, built by Tony Dungy and coordinator Monte Kiffin around a one-gap four-man line and still run by Kiffin in Jon Gruden’s first season, intercepted the league MVP, Rich Gannon, a Super Bowl-record five times and returned three of them for touchdowns.14 Warren Sapp played the 3-technique, and the design of that whole defense, a fast, light front backed by linebackers who ran to the ball, starts with him.
What to notice:

Find Sapp before each snap. He moves to whichever side the front’s rule puts the 3-technique; note where the tight end is, see whether you can work out the rule, and notice which guard has a one-on-one problem.
His first step. Count how often he is across the line of scrimmage before the guard in front of him has finished his first step. That is one-gap penetration at its purest.
What happens behind him. When an offense spends a second blocker on him, look for the linebacker that blocker would have taken, and watch him run free.









NoteFilm room: New England Patriots, 2004–2010 seasons



The player: Vince Wilfork, a first-round pick in 2004 who played nose tackle in Bill Belichick’s two-gap 3-4 for his first seven seasons: as a rookie he shared the job with the veteran Keith Traylor, and from 2005 it was his alone. (In 2010 he spent some weeks at end, and in 2011 the Patriots went to a four-man front.)15 He was a Pro Bowler five times and won two Super Bowls, XXXIX and XLIX.
What to do: pick any Patriots early-down base snap from those seasons in which Wilfork lines up over the center. Ignore the ball and watch only him and the center.

The strike: both hands inside, arms locked, the center held off his body.
The double team: when a guard comes over, does Wilfork give ground? Usually he doesn’t, and the linebacker behind him is unblocked.
The shed: watch him throw the blocker to the side the ball isn’t going. Then check the box score; his name often isn’t in it.









NoteFilm room: Los Angeles Rams, Super Bowl LVI (2021 season)



The game: Super Bowl LVI, February 13, 2022, at SoFi Stadium: Rams 23, Bengals 20. Cincinnati got the ball back with 1:25 left needing a field goal to tie. Facing third-and-1 near midfield, the Bengals ran Samaje Perine, and Aaron Donald and nose tackle Greg Gaines tackled him for no gain. On fourth-and-1, Donald got to Joe Burrow and wrapped him up as he threw; the pass fell incomplete, and the Rams won.16
What to notice: two snaps, one player, both phases of the game. On third down, a run: watch Donald’s get-off, his first step at the instant the ball moves, and where he is relative to the line when the back arrives. On fourth down, a pass: the same first step, and the same result, a quarterback with no time. It is the best two-play summary of why teams pay a one-gap 3-technique more than almost anyone else on the defense.








NoteFilm room: Philadelphia Eagles 2011



The season: Jim Washburn’s first year coaching the Eagles’ defensive line, and the clearest look at a full-time wide-9 front. The Eagles tied for the league lead with 50 sacks, and Jason Babin, whom Washburn had also coached in Tennessee, had 18 of them.17
What to notice: the ends’ alignment, well outside the tight end on that side (or where one would be), in sprinter’s stances; how quickly they are upfield; and then, on running plays, the space inside them. Watch which linebacker has to fill the lane between the end and the 3-technique, and how often he gets there in time. The pass rush and the run lanes come from the same alignment: that is the trade this chapter has been describing, on the field for a whole season.

title: Defensive Line Play: Techniques, One-Gap and Two-Gap
text:
Watch for it on Sunday






TipWatch for it



Before the snap: find the 3-technique.

Look at the guards. Is there a defensive tackle on a guard’s outside shoulder? That is the 3-technique, and his side of the line is where the defense has put its quickness. Is he toward the tight end or away from him? That is the front’s rule, and it will usually hold all game. Is there one big man right over the center? That is a 0 nose, likely playing both A gaps.
Look at the ends. On the tackle (a 4i, 4 or 5)? Standing up just outside the tight end (a 9)? Way out wide, a couple of yards past the tight end or where one would be, in a sprinter’s stance (a wide-9)? Wider ends mean more pass rush and bigger run lanes inside them.
Don’t try to measure a yard on the live shot. As in 03-01, ask whose shoulder the defender is on: the guard’s outside shoulder is a 3, the tackle’s inside shoulder a 4i, his outside shoulder a 5. The end-zone replay, shot straight down the line, shows it best.

At the snap: the first step.

Does the lineman’s first step go into a gap, upfield (one-gap), or into the blocker, with his hands, standing him up (two-gap)?
Does the whole line step sideways together at the snap? That is a slant; look for the linebackers to shift the other way. One man darting into the next gap and on upfield while the rest go straight is an angle.

After the play: where did the run go?

Which way did the run go relative to the 3-technique: at him, or away? Did he get into the backfield, get double-teamed, or get trapped?
Did the run get outside the edge? If it did, ask who had the edge on that side and whether he got hooked. On a bootleg or scramble, ask who had contain.

For your prediction log (How to Watch a Broadcast): before each early-down snap, note which side the 3-technique is on. After the play, note whether the run went toward him or away from him. A few quarters of that will tell you something about both coordinators.

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 3.2))
fronts = [("Front A", front([("L4", "4i", -1), ("NT", "0", 1), ("R4", "4i", 1)],

           [("L1", "340 lb"), ("R3", "285 lb")])]
for ax, (ttl, dfn, wts) in zip(axes, fronts):
    p = Play(line("short") + [te(+1), O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -6.0, 0, "R")], dfn, los=40,
             to_go=10)

    for key, txt in wts:

    ax.set_title(ttl, fontsize=9, loc="left", color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.7)
plt.show()








Figure 28.9: Drill 1: two fronts against the same offense. Front A: five men on the line, an edge player (E) at each end, two 4i-techniques and a 0 nose between them, two inside linebackers. Front B: a four-man front shaded 5, 1, 3, 9, with a 340-pound 1-technique and a 285-pound 3-technique, and three linebackers.











TipAnswer





Front A is a mix: the nose two-gaps, the 4is most likely one-gap. The 0 is head-up on the center with no gap of his own, and he is 330 pounds: everything about him says control the center and play both A gaps. The 4is are shaded into the B gaps, so the likeliest job is to own those (some defenses ask them to play the C gap as well; their first step will tell you). Add it up: the nose holds two gaps, the 4is one each, the edge players the outside gaps, and one inside linebacker fills the gap left over inside the tight end. The other linebacker is the free one. That is the point of this front, which you will meet as the tite front in Odd and Hybrid Fronts: one big two-gapper lets six men cover seven gaps against the run, so the defense can keep two safeties deep.
Front B is shaded like a one-gap front, but look at the nose. The 3-technique is a classic penetrator (285 pounds, in the B gap): expect him to attack. The 1-technique is shaded too, but 340 pounds is an anchor’s body, not a penetrator’s. Whatever the call says about his gaps, his job is to take on the center and the guard and not move, which keeps a blocker off the Mike. So: the 3 and the ends attack their gaps, the nose holds his ground, and if the nose eats a double team, the Mike is the man who runs free.
The lesson: alignment is a strong hint and body type is another. Wade Phillips ran a one-gap defense out of 3-4 looks for decades, and many 4-3 teams ask a big shaded nose to anchor or play both A gaps. Confirm it with the first step after the snap: into the gap, or into the man.











TipPredict the play



Drill 2. The slant meets the run. First-and-10. The offense runs inside zone to the right. At the snap, the defense’s four linemen all slant to the right, toward the tight end, and the picture below is the first half-second; the linebackers have not moved yet. Where is the run most likely to go now, and which defenders does the defense need to be right?


Show the Python
off = line("full") + [te(+1), O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -7.0, 0, "R")]
dfn = front([("LE", "5", -1), ("L1", "1", -1), ("R3", "3", 1), ("RE", "9", 1)],
            lbs=[("WILL", 4.6, -2.6, "W"), ("MIKE", 4.6, 1.0, "M"), ("SAM", 4.4, 4.6, "S")])
dfn = [q.moved(d=2.1) if q.d == 1.0 else q for q in dfn]    # linemen drawn a little deep so the slant shows
p = Play(off, dfn, los=40, to_go=10, title="Drill 2: inside zone right meets a slant right")
for k in ("LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT", "Y"):
    p.block(k, pts=[(0.3, 0.7)])
for k, end in [("LE", (1.5, -2.45)), ("L1", (1.5, 0.85)), ("R3", (1.5, 4.0)), ("RE", (1.4, 7.0))]:
    go_to(p, k, end, "path", speed=3.0)
go_to(p, "RB", (-4.6, 1.6), "run", via=[(-6.2, 0.6)])
go_to(p, "QB", (-3.2, 0.5), "path", speed=3.0)
f = draw(p, width_in=5.5, lateral=(-9.0, 10.4), window=(-8.6, 7.8))
say(f, p, 6.3, 0.0, "linebackers: not yet moved", fontsize=6.9)
plt.show()








Figure 28.10: Drill 2: the first half-second. The offense’s line steps right for inside zone and the back aims at the right guard’s outside hip; the defense’s linemen (orange arrows; drawn a little deeper than real) all slant one gap to the right at the snap, the end outside the tight end widening. The linebackers have not moved yet.











TipAnswer





Most likely back to the left, on the cutback, and the linebackers decide it. The slant ran the same way as the play. Inside zone’s blockers are happy about that at first: each one simply rides the man who slanted into his area (the right guard takes the 1 who came into the right A gap, the right tackle the 3 who went to the right C). But look at what moved. The 3 left the right B gap, which is exactly the gap the back is aiming at, and the 1 left the left A gap. The 5 left the left C gap for the left B.
Replacing those gaps is the linebackers’ job, and they have to move the opposite way from the line. The Sam has to get into the right B gap the 3 vacated. If he doesn’t, the back runs through it untouched. If he does, the back does what inside zone teaches him: he bends the run back toward the gaps the slant emptied. The Mike has the left A and the Will the left C the 5 left. If either flows right with the line instead of filling behind it, the cutback lane is empty and the next defender is a safety. That is the bet every slant makes against zone: the line wins the first half-second, and the linebackers have to win the rest.











TipPredict the play



Drill 3. Who has contain? Third-and-7. The offense is in the shotgun with an empty backfield (five receivers spread wide, not shown) and a quarterback who likes to run. The defense rushes four: a wide-9 on the right, a 5 on the left, and two tackles inside. Which rushers have contain, how should they rush, and where is the quarterback most likely to escape if somebody gets it wrong?


Show the Python
off = line("full") + [O("QB", "QB", -5.0, 0, "Q")]
dfn = front([("LE", "5", -1), ("L1", "1", -1), ("R3", "3", 1)]) + [D("RE", "DL", 1.0, T("wide9") - 1.0, "w9")]
dfn = [q.moved(d=1.9) for q in dfn]                         # drawn a little deep so the first steps show
p = Play(off, dfn, los=40, to_go=7, title="Drill 3: four rushers, one mobile quarterback")
for k, end in [("LE", (-1.2, -5.2)), ("L1", (0.5, -0.85)), ("R3", (0.5, 2.5)), ("RE", (-1.4, 6.6))]:
    go_to(p, k, end, "path", speed=3.0)
for k in OL_KEYS:
    p.block(k, pts=[(-1.0, 0.0)])
f = draw(p, width_in=5.4, lateral=(-9.6, 10.6), window=(-9.4, 8.4))
say(f, p, -7.2, 3.8, "a quarterback\nwho likes to run", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
plt.show()








Figure 28.11: Drill 3: third-and-7, shotgun, empty backfield, a mobile quarterback. The defense rushes four (orange arrows show the first steps; linemen drawn a little deeper than real): the wide-9 on the right, the 5 on the left, a 3 and a 1 inside. Everyone else drops into coverage (not shown).











TipAnswer





The two ends have contain: the 5 on the left and the wide-9 on the right. Their rule is to rush outside the tackles but not past the quarterback’s depth. If either one runs a wide arc around the tackle and keeps going, he ends up behind the quarterback, and the space between him and the defensive tackle next to him becomes a running lane. A mobile quarterback steps up into the pocket and out through that lane, usually for a first down on third-and-7.
The wide-9 is the likeliest to get it wrong, because his whole alignment is built for a long, fast arc to the quarterback. Against a runner he has to flatten his rush earlier and stay level with the quarterback. The two inside rushers have the opposite job: push the middle of the pocket back into the quarterback so he can’t step up. A four-man rush against a mobile quarterback is a box: two sides that must hold, and a front that must squeeze. When one side bursts, look for the quarterback there. Defenses facing a real runner often go further: all four rushers stay level with the quarterback and squeeze him instead of racing to him (a mush rush), or one defender is held back to shadow him (a spy). The Pass Rush has the rest of this, including the stunts that trade one rusher’s lane for another’s.

title: Defensive Line Play: Techniques, One-Gap and Two-Gap
text:
Back to the replay
The chapter opened with two great defensive linemen on the same afternoon. Now you can name them.

Lined up just outside the right guard and gone past him before the guard finished his first step: a one-gap 3-technique. His alignment gave him a single blocker and the B gap; his get-off beat the reach before it landed; he was through the gap and in the back’s path before the play could develop. That is penetration, and the analyst’s “he lives in the backfield” is its signature.
The biggest man on the field, over the center, a guard comes over to help, and he stays where he is: a two-gap nose. The center and guard double-teamed him, he gave no ground, and when the back arrived he shed one blocker to the side the ball went and made the tackle. “He ate up two blockers” is the other half of the story: on a play he doesn’t finish himself, that guard never reaches the linebacker, who does.

One wins by going and one by staying, and both are doing the same arithmetic: making the offense’s blockers add up to less than the defense’s gaps.

28  Defensive Line Play: Techniques, One-Gap and Two-Gap

title: Defensive Line Play: Techniques, One-Gap and Two-Gap
text:
Takeaways

Alignment is a job description. The nose (0 or 1) anchors against double teams and wants mass; the 3-technique is the likeliest to get a guard one-on-one and wants quickness; the 4i, 4 and 5 want length to control a tackle; the 9 and the wide-9 want speed, and the wider the end, the more pass rush and the bigger the run lane inside him.
One-gap attacks. Each lineman owns one gap and attacks it, aiming for penetration. It wins with quickness, creates sacks and tackles for loss, and turns the linemen loose, but a wrong guess leaves an empty gap, and traps, draws and screens are built to punish it.
Two-gap controls. A head-up lineman strikes the blocker, locks out, reads (the blocker’s head tells him where the ball is going) and sheds to the ball’s side. One man covering two gaps, and forcing a second blocker to stay on him, keeps the linebackers clean, at the cost of rare bodies, little pass rush, and a stat sheet that hides his value.
Fight pressure with pressure. Against a down block, the man blocked fights back outward and the man left alone squeezes and looks for the puller (or, if nobody blocks him at all, asks “trap or read?”); against a reach, step with the blocker and keep the outside arm free; against a double team, lean into the drive man, give no ground and keep both blockers.
The edge is everybody’s boundary. Setting the edge turns runs back inside; contain keeps the quarterback and the misdirection plays from getting outside. Both ask an aggressive player for patience.
Movement changes the picture after the snap. Slants shift the whole line a gap; angles move one man while he keeps attacking. Both beat pre-snap blocking assignments, especially gap schemes, and both are bets on direction that the linebackers have to back up, above all against zone’s cutback.

Linebackers and the Second Level: the players who fill the gaps the line leaves, and replace them after a slant.
Run Fits and Box Math: spill and squeeze, force, and how eleven gap assignments add up.
The Pass Rush: the same linemen on passing downs, rush moves, stunts, and why pressure matters more than sacks.

See also (case study): Fangio’s Two-High Revolution and Macdonald’s Answer, for what happens to defensive line play when a defense keeps two safeties deep and asks six men to hold the box.
If you want to go deeper: Pro Football Focus’s “Defensive Prototypes” series (one article per technique, with player examples); Chris B. Brown’s The Art of Smart Football on how fronts and run schemes answer each other; and any Patriots game from the late 2000s and any Rams game from 2018, watched for nothing but the man over the center and the man outside the guard.






NoteGo deeper



Penetration, measured. Tracking data turns this chapter’s distinction into a number. A one-gap penetrator is behind the line of scrimmage a second after the snap; a two-gapper is at it. In the two simulated plays above, here is how far each ringed defender is past the line (negative numbers mean he is in the offense’s backfield), computed from their Big Data Bowl-format tracking frames exactly as you would from real data:


Show the Python (depth past the line of scrimmage, from tracking frames)
def depth_table(plays, times=(0.3, 0.6, 1.0)):
    rows = []
    for name, play, key in plays:
        trk = play.to_tracking()
        los = trk.loc[(trk["displayName"] == "football") & (trk["time"] == 0.0), "x"].iloc[0]
        me = trk[trk["displayName"] == key].set_index("time")
        rows.append({"defender": name, **{f"+{t:.1f} s": round(float(me.loc[round(t, 1), "x"] - los), 1)
                                          for t in times}})
    return pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("defender")


from IPython.display import Markdown


def as_markdown(df):
    """A small table as a Markdown pipe table (no index column), which prints cleanly in every format."""
    cols = list(df.columns)
    rows = ["| " + " | ".join(cols) + " |", "|" + "|".join([":--"] + ["--:"] * (len(cols) - 1)) + "|"]
    rows += ["| " + " | ".join(str(v) for v in r) + " |" for r in df.itertuples(index=False)]
    return Markdown("\n".join(rows))


as_markdown(depth_table([("one-gap 3-technique (simulated)", P_ONE, "R3"),
                         ("two-gap nose (simulated)", P_TWO_R, "NT")]).reset_index())

The same calculation on real frames is a few lines with gridiron.bdb. The 2025 Big Data Bowl release (2022 season, weeks 1–9) has every player’s location ten times a second, and its players file has his position label, so you can find each interior defensive lineman on each run and measure how deep he is at one second. Aggregated by player, it separates the penetrators from the anchors, with two caveats. Position labels are rosters, not jobs: filtering on “DT” and “NT” misses 3-4 ends who play a 4i or a 3 and edge players who slide inside on passing downs. And depth alone can’t tell a penetrator from a defender the offense let through: an unblocked man on a trap, an option read or an influence block shows up deep in the backfield too. The data needs a free Kaggle login, so this cell is not run when the book is built.


Show the Python (real Big Data Bowl tracking; not run in the build)
import pandas as pd
from gridiron import bdb

plays = pd.read_csv("data/bdb/plays.csv")
players = pd.read_csv("data/bdb/players.csv")[["nflId", "position", "displayName"]]
runs = plays[plays["isDropback"] == False]                       # not a dropback: designed runs (plus kneels)
trk = bdb.load_tracking("data/bdb/tracking_week_*.csv")
if "position" not in trk:                                        # 2025 tracking has no position column:
    trk = trk.merge(players[["nflId", "position"]], on="nflId", how="left")   # take it from players.csv

out = []
for g, pl in runs[["gameId", "playId"]].itertuples(index=False):
    one = bdb.prepare(trk, plays, game_id=g, play_id=pl, label="position")
    los = one.loc[(one["side"] == "ball") & (one["time"] == 0.0), "x"].iloc[0]
    at1 = one[(one["time"].round(1) == 1.0) & one["position"].isin(["DT", "NT"])]
    out += [{"nflId": r.nflId, "depth": r.x - los} for r in at1.itertuples()]

depth = (pd.DataFrame(out).merge(players, on="nflId")
         .groupby("displayName")["depth"].agg(["mean", "count"]).query("count >= 50").sort_values("mean"))
depth.head(10)    # the deepest penetrators (most negative = furthest into the backfield)

title: Even Fronts: 4-3 Over, Under, Wide-9, and the 46 Bear
text:
What makes a front “even”
First-and-10. The offense breaks the huddle with its tight end on the right. Before the quarterback reaches the line, the defensive tackle who had drifted up over the right guard while the offense huddled jogs across to the left guard, the other tackle slides the opposite way, and a linebacker who had been off the ball walks up and plants himself on the line just outside the tight end, hand on his knees. The middle linebacker is pointing and shouting one word. Two plays later the tight end lines up on the left, and this time the tackles don’t trade places at all, and the linebacker outside the tight end stays five yards back. Nobody on the broadcast mentions it. The defense has just played two different fronts, chosen by one word and the position of one offensive player, and each was a bet about where the run would go. This chapter teaches you to read that bet.
You’ll be able to:
How to read the diagrams. Offense is blue circles, defense orange squares, and plays go up the page. Left and right always mean the offense’s left and right. LT, LG, C, RG and RT are the offensive linemen (T, G and C in the smallest pictures), Y and U are tight ends, Q the quarterback, R the running back and F a fullback. Defensive linemen are labelled with their technique number: 5w is a loose 5, a yard or so wider than a normal 5 on the tackle’s outside shoulder, and w9 a wide-9. M, W and S are the Mike, Will and Sam linebackers; SS and FS are the safeties and $ a nickel back. Green letters are gaps, never players. Unless a picture says otherwise, the tight end, and so the offense’s strength, is on the right.
A First Look at Defense counted the front by its players: a 4-3 has four linemen and three linebackers. Coaches count it a second way, by where the linemen stand, and the second count is the one that tells the offense what it is up against.
Show the Python
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 2.9))
dfns = [("Even: 5, 3, 3, 5 (four down)",
         [D("LE", "DE", 1.0, T("5", -1), "5"), D("LT3", "DT", 1.0, T("3", -1), "3"),
          D("RT3", "DT", 1.0, T("3", 1), "3"), D("RE", "DE", 1.0, T("5", 1), "5")]),
        ("Odd: 4, 0, 4 (three down)",
         [D("LE", "DE", 1.0, T("4", -1), "4"), D("NT", "DT", 1.0, 0.0, "0"), D("RE", "DE", 1.0, T("4", 1), "4")])]
for ax, (ttl, dl) in zip(axes, dfns):
    p = Play(line("short") + [te(+1)], dl, los=35, to_go=None)
    f = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=(-6.6, 7.6), window=(-3.4, 4.2), title=False)
    ring(f, p, "C", color=GREEN if "Even" in ttl else style.DEFENSE_DARK, r=0.9)
    say(f, p, 3.0, 0.0, "center free" if "Even" in ttl else "center covered",
        color=GREEN if "Even" in ttl else style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7, weight="bold")
    title(ax, ttl)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.8)
plt.show()








Figure 29.1: Even and odd, the coach’s way of counting. Left, an even front in its balanced form: four linemen set in pairs, two on each side of the ball, and nobody head-up on the center (green ring), so here the center is the free man, able to help a teammate or climb to a linebacker. Right, an odd front: a nose head-up on the center, splitting the line into a middle man and a pair on either side. Fronts are named after this picture as much as after the head count.
An even front sets its down linemen in pairs, two on each side of the ball, with nobody head-up on the center. In practice that means a four-man line, the family of fronts that grew up around the 4-3. An odd front puts a man on the center (the nose of a 3-4, or the middle man of a five-man line) and is the subject of Odd and Hybrid Fronts.
Why does the center matter so much? Because of what you learned about covered and uncovered linemen in 03-01. An offensive lineman with nobody on him, head-up or on a shoulder, is the offense’s spare part: he can double-team a neighbor or climb to a linebacker. In an odd front the nose covers the center from the first instant, and the spare parts are the guards. An even front has only two defensive tackles for the three interior offensive linemen, the center and the two guards, so one of those three is always uncovered. Which one is the even front’s first decision. In the balanced front of Figure 30.1 it is the center. In the two fronts this chapter is built around, a tackle sits on one of the center’s shoulders, which covers him, and the free man is a guard instead. Every even front is a decision about which lineman to leave free, and where to put the linebacker who has to deal with him.
The perfectly balanced version in Figure 30.1 (a 3-technique on each guard, an end on each tackle) exists, and you will see it on passing downs, when it gives each of the two best interior rushers a guard to himself. On early downs, most even fronts are unbalanced on purpose. One tackle slides in to a 1-technique, shaded on a shoulder of the center, and the other stays a 3-technique, outside a guard. Now the line leans: the 3-technique’s side has its linemen spread wide, the 1-technique’s side has them pinched in toward the ball, and the guard between the 1 and the end on that side has nobody on him. Which way the line leans, toward the offense’s strength or away from it, decides which guard that is, and it is the difference between the two fronts this chapter is built around.

title: Even Fronts: 4-3 Over, Under, Wide-9, and the 46 Bear
text:
CautionCommon misconception



“Even and odd just mean four linemen or three.” That’s the fan’s shortcut and it usually works. But the coaches’ test is the center and the pairs, and the two counts can disagree: the bear front later in this chapter has four men with their hands down and a nose head-up on the center, and a 3-4 team can put a fourth player’s hand on the ground without changing who covers whom. When the counts argue, believe the alignment. (The bear is in this chapter anyway, for history rather than taxonomy: it grew out of a 4-3 team’s playbook. By the alignment test it is an odd front.)

title: Even Fronts: 4-3 Over, Under, Wide-9, and the 46 Bear
section: Setting the front: the strength call
text:
Setting the front: the strength call
A front leans toward or away from something, so before it can line up, the defense needs a word for which side is which. That word is the strength, the side the defense calls strong, from Formation Rules and Vocabulary. For fronts, the usual rule is simple: the strength is the tight end’s side. The tight end is a sixth blocker attached to the line, so his side has one more gap (the D gap outside him) and one more man to block with. Runs go there more often, and the front wants to know about it.
When there is no tight end, or one on each side, defenses fall back on other rules. Common ones are the field (the wide side of the field when the ball is on a hash), the running back (the side he is offset to in the shotgun), or the side with more receivers. Which rule a team uses, and in what order, is in its playbook, and the call before the snap says which one applies. Two tight ends on the same side make that side strong twice over. A tight end who is detached, split a few yards off the line or in the slot, usually stops counting: he is no longer a blocker attached to the tackle, so many defenses treat him as a receiver and set the front by their next rule.
That last case is why many defenses keep two strengths. The run strength, usually the tight end’s side, sets the front: where the linemen and linebackers go. The pass strength, the side with more receivers, sets the coverage. Against a tight end on the right and three receivers on the left, the front can lean one way and the coverage the other. In this chapter “strength” means the run strength unless it says otherwise.
The call is relative, and that is the whole point. The defense does not call “3-technique on the left guard.” It calls something like “Over” and lets the formation decide which guard: Over means the line leans toward the strength, Under means it leans away from it.1 A Mike linebacker shouting “Strong right! Over!” is translating one word into eleven alignments for this particular snap.

The 4-3 Over

for ax, (ttl, dfn, free, owners) in zip(axes, [
        ("4-3 Over: lean toward the TE", over_front(+1), "LG", ["5", "W", "1", "M", "3", "5", "S"]),
        ("4-3 Under: lean away from it", under_front(+1), "RG", ["5", "3", "W", "1", "M", "5", "S"])]):

    f = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=(-7.6, 8.4), window=(-5.0, 6.6), title=False)
    gap_row(f, p, owners)
    ring(f, p, free, color=GREEN, r=1.05)
