title: Odd and Hybrid Fronts: 3-4, Okie, Tite, and Modern Nickel Fronts
text:
Predict the play






TipPredict the play



Drill 1. Name it, then pick a run. First-and-10 from the offense’s own 35. The offense is in the shotgun with three receivers and an attached tight end (Y). The defense is in nickel. Name the front. How many defenders are in the box, and how many blockers does the offense have? If you were calling the run, would you run inside zone, or something else?


Show the Python
off = gun11(y_attached=True)
dfn = [D("LE", "OLB", 1.0, -5.3, "E"), D("L4", "DL", 1.0, T("4i", -1), "4i"), D("NT", "DL", 1.0, 0.0, "0"),
       D("R4", "DL", 1.0, T("4i", 1), "4i"), D("RE", "OLB", 1.0, 6.1, "E"),
       D("MIKE", "LB", 4.7, 0.8, "M")] + secondary(nickel_w=-6.2, high=11.5, safety_w=7.6)
p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=10, title="Drill 1: first-and-10, nickel")
f = draw(p, width_in=5.0, lateral=(-11.6, 11.6), window=(-7.0, 13.4))
hands(f, p, ("L4", "NT", "R4"))
plt.show()








Figure 30.12: Drill 1: the defense’s alignment before the snap (dark dots are hands on the ground). Two safeties deep, a nickel ($) over the slot on the left, and the corners on the wide receivers (outside the picture).











TipAnswer





A tite. Three hands down inside the tackles (a 4i, a 0 and a 4i) with a stand-up edge on each side make five on the line, and one linebacker stands behind them: the coach’s 3-3-5, the Penny of the Fangio tree.
Six in the box against six blockers (five linemen and the tight end), with two safeties deep and the nickel outside the box. On paper that is a light box, and analysts will tell you to run against light boxes. But this light box was built to be run into. Inside zone aims at the play-side B gap, where the 4i is; the nose and the 4is will occupy all five offensive linemen, and the Mike will fill his gap unblocked, as in Figure 30.4.
The better calls test what the tite gives up. Outside zone or a toss to the tight-end side attacks the empty C gap: the right tackle is uncovered, so he can help the tight end on the edge or climb to the only linebacker, and the Mike and the strong safety have to beat the ball to the alley. A run with the quarterback reading the backside edge (a zone read) turns the unblocked edge into a wasted defender. Or don’t run at all: a single linebacker in a light box is exactly the defender an RPO or a quick throw underneath attacks. The defense has dared you to run inside; the smart offense declines.











TipPredict the play



Drill 2. Choose your front. You coordinate the defense. This week’s opponent runs outside zone more than any other play, from tight formations with the quarterback under center, and its tight end is an excellent blocker. Here are two fronts you could show on first down. Which would you rather be in, and where will the run most likely go against each?


Show the Python
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 3.5))
OFF_UC = line("short") + [te(+1), O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -7.0, 0, "R")]
fA = [D("LE", "OLB", 1.0, -5.6, "E"), D("L4", "DL", 1.0, T("4i", -1), "4i"), D("NT", "DL", 1.0, 0.0, "0"),
      D("R4", "DL", 1.0, T("4i", 1), "4i"), D("RE", "OLB", 1.0, 6.1, "E"), D("MIKE", "LB", 4.7, 0.8, "M")]
fB = front([("LE", "5", -1), ("L1", "1", -1), ("R3", "3", 1), ("RE", "9", 1)],
           lbs=[("WILL", 4.7, -2.0, "W"), ("MIKE", 4.7, 1.6, "M")])
for ax, dfn, hd, ttl in [(axes[0], fA, ("L4", "NT", "R4"), "Front A: tite"),
                         (axes[1], fB, ("LE", "L1", "R3", "RE"), "Front B: wide four-man")]:
    p = Play(OFF_UC, dfn, los=35, to_go=None)
    f = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=(-8.0, 8.8), window=(-8.4, 6.8), title=False)
    hands(f, p, hd)
    ax.set_title(ttl, fontsize=9, loc="left", color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.7)
plt.show()








Figure 30.13: Drill 2: two fronts against the same under-center, one-tight-end formation. Front A: the tite: a 0 and two 4is between two stand-up edges, the right edge on the tight end’s outside shoulder (a 9), one linebacker. Front B: a four-man even front aligned wide: a 3-technique on the right guard’s outside shoulder, a 1 on the center, a 5 on the left tackle and a defensive end (9) on the tight end, with two linebackers.











TipAnswer





Front B is the better bet against this opponent, though neither is free. Outside zone lives on reach blocks. In Front B, the defenders on the play side are all outside the men who must reach them: the 3 outside the right guard, the end outside the tight end. Those are the hardest reaches in football, and a quick 3-technique can be through the B gap before the guard gets there (the one-gap animation in Defensive Line Play). If the reaches fail, the back can’t get outside and has to cut up early, into two linebackers.
In Front A, the trouble is the gap nobody is in. The play-side C gap, between the right tackle and the tight end, is empty, so the right tackle is uncovered: he can help the tight end, an excellent blocker, on the edge, or climb straight to the only linebacker. The 4i and the nose, big men built to hold ground, have to chase the play sideways. Everything rests on one edge against two blockers, with one linebacker and a safety coming from depth to fill the alley. Expect the ball to bounce outside if the edge is reached, or to cut back if the Mike over-runs it.
What Front B gives up: the interior. Against the same team’s inside zone, the 1 and the 3 can be doubled and the doubles can climb to two linebackers. That is why defenses facing an outside-zone team mix fronts by down and formation instead of living in one, and why the tite’s teams widen their edges (or switch to four-man fronts) against wide-zone offenses.











TipPredict the play



Drill 3. Which 3-4 is it? Two snaps from the same 3-4 defense against the same formation, and the linemen line up in exactly the same place both times: a nose head-up on the center and the ends head-up on the tackles. The pictures freeze each snap a quarter-second after the ball moves. Where a lineman has moved, a dashed outline shows where he started. For each snap, say whether the front is playing two-gap or one-gap, and which linebackers you expect to be free.


Show the Python
STEPS3 = {False: {"LE": (0.72, -3.2), "NT": (0.72, 0.0), "RE": (0.72, 3.2)},
          True: {"LE": (0.62, -2.4), "NT": (0.62, 0.8), "RE": (0.62, 4.0)}}
START3 = {"LE": (1.0, -3.2), "NT": (1.0, 0.0), "RE": (1.0, 3.2)}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(6.0, 4.6))
for ax, snapB in [(axes[0], False), (axes[1], True)]:
    dfn = front([("LE", "4", -1), ("NT", "0", 1), ("RE", "4", 1)],
                others=[("LOLB", 1.0, -6.2, "E"), ("ROLB", 1.0, 6.2, "E")])
    dfn = [q.moved(d=STEPS3[snapB][q.key][0], w=STEPS3[snapB][q.key][1]) if q.key in START3 else q for q in dfn]
    p = Play(line("short") + [te(+1)], dfn, los=35, to_go=None)
    f = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=(-8.0, 8.0), window=(-2.0, 2.8), title=False, width_in=6.0)
    for k, (d0, w0) in START3.items():
        d1, w1 = STEPS3[snapB][k]
        (x0, y0), (x1, y1) = _P(f, p, d0, w0), _P(f, p, d1, w1)
        if snapB:   # where he started (dashed) and the step that took him into the gap
            ax.add_patch(RegularPolygon((float(x0), float(y0)), 4, radius=0.94, orientation=np.pi / 4,
                                        fc=style.SURFACE, ec=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.1, ls=(0, (2, 1.6)), zorder=6))
            (xe, ye) = _P(f, p, d0 + 0.62 * (d1 - d0), w0 + 0.62 * (w1 - w0))
            ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((float(x0), float(y0)), (float(xe), float(ye)), arrowstyle="-|>",
                                         mutation_scale=12, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, lw=1.8, zorder=13))
        else:       # hands on the blocker's chest
            (xc, yc), (xd, yd) = _P(f, p, 0.06, w1 - 0.6), _P(f, p, 0.06, w1 + 0.6)
            ax.plot([float(xc), float(xd)], [float(yc), float(yd)], color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, lw=5.0,
                    solid_capstyle="butt", zorder=12)
    ax.set_title("Snap A" if not snapB else "Snap B", fontsize=9, loc="left", color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")
fig.tight_layout(h_pad=0.8)
plt.show()








Figure 30.14: Drill 3: the interior of two snaps, a quarter-second after the ball is snapped (the linebackers, behind them, are not shown). Both snaps started from the same alignment: a 0 and two 4s, each nose to nose with a blocker. Snap A: each lineman is still nose to nose with his blocker, hands on his chest (dark bars). Snap B: each lineman has stepped diagonally, all toward the tight end (arrows from the dashed outlines where they started), and is now in the seam beside his blocker.











TipAnswer





Snap A is two-gap. The alignment couldn’t tell you, but the first step can: each lineman has stepped straight into the blocker in front of him and put his hands on his chest, about to lock out and read. That means three linemen are holding six gaps, the edge on the tight end has the D gap, and both inside linebackers are free: they have no gap of their own at the snap and will read and fill wherever the ball goes. If the linemen win, nobody blocks either of them.
Snap B is one-gap, from the same head-up alignment. Every lineman has slanted into a gap beside his blocker, all toward the tight end: the left end into the B gap, the nose into the A gap toward the tight end, the right end into the C gap. Every lineman has one gap, so the linebackers have one each too: the Mike the B gap toward the tight end, the Will the other A gap, exactly the assignments of the right half of Figure 30.3. Nobody is free, but everybody is fast. One-gap teams usually line up shaded, as in that figure, but plenty of them line up head-up and slant, precisely so that the alignment gives nothing away. That is why the first step, not the alignment, is the tell.

title: Odd and Hybrid Fronts: 3-4, Okie, Tite, and Modern Nickel Fronts
text:
Back to the broadcast
The chapter opened with a graphic that said 3-4 and a picture that kept changing. Now you can read both.

The graphic says 3-4, and you count four on the line, two standing: that is the 3-4 team’s 2-4-5 nickel, its nose on the bench and its two outside linebackers on the edges. The roster says 2-4-5; the football is a four-man line.
Next snap, five across the line, three of them enormous and wedged inside the tackles, one linebacker behind them: a tite, built by sending the nose back on for a linebacker, the coach’s 3-3-5. A multiple defense like Georgia’s can reach the same picture without substituting at all, by shifting a four-man line into it at the last moment.
The inside run into a wall, the linebacker never touched: the tite’s whole purpose. A nose and two 4is occupy all five offensive linemen, the doubles can’t climb, and the one linebacker fills his gap unblocked and makes the tackle. That is how six defenders stop a run aimed at six blockers: one of them, the nose, is doing the work of two.

title: Odd and Hybrid Fronts: 3-4, Okie, Tite, and Modern Nickel Fronts
text:
Takeaways

Find the center. A defender head-up on the center makes the front odd; nobody there makes it even. The odd fronts are built around a heavy nose who takes two blockers so somebody else can run free.
The 3-4 Okie is one alignment played two ways. Two-gap (head-up, control and read) keeps the inside linebackers clean at the cost of rare bodies and little pass rush; one-gap (shaded, attack) turns the 3-4 into an aggressive front, often an Under with a standing Sam. The first step tells you which.
The stand-up edge is the 3-4’s great legacy. Standing gives him vision, width and the option to drop, which makes the defense’s rush uncertain; the price is leverage against the run.
The tite walls off the middle. A 0 and two 4is leave the offense’s uncovered linemen stuck on doubles that can neither move them nor climb, so a light box with two safeties deep can still stop inside runs; the one linebacker owns the last gap, unblocked. It gives up pass rush, the perimeter (an empty C gap against outside zone) and the space underneath.
Fronts choose what to stop. Line up on or inside blockers to beat double teams (inside runs); line up outside them, with every outside gap filled, to beat reaches (outside zone). No front does both, so defenses change fronts by opponent, by situation and by shifting at the snap.
Nickel labels are roster labels. As roster counts, 4-2-5, 2-4-5 and 3-3-5 describe nearly the same box count and pass rush; what differs is whether the edges are listed as ends or linebackers. (When a coach calls a 3-3-5, he means the tite.) Count hands, not names, and read alignment before dialect.

title: Odd and Hybrid Fronts: 3-4, Okie, Tite, and Modern Nickel Fronts
text:
Connections
Builds on: Defensive Line Play (techniques, one-gap and two-gap, the edge) and Even Fronts (the four-man fronts and their strength rules), with A First Look at Defense (base, nickel, the box) and Zone Running (inside and outside zone) as the background.
Sets up:

Linebackers and the Second Level: the players these fronts are built to keep clean, and what they do with the freedom.
Run Fits and Box Math: the full eleven-man accounting behind every front in this chapter, the plus-one, and how two-high light-box defenses fit the run.
The Pass Rush and Zone Blitz and Simulated Pressure: the stand-up edge’s other job, and how standing edges and five-man lines become four-man rushes from unexpected places.
History: Arnsparger’s 53 in The 1978 Liberation, and the 3-4’s revival and the hybrid edge in Dynasties and Counterpunches.

See also (case study): Fangio’s Two-High Revolution and Macdonald’s Answer, the tite front and the light box as the run-defense half of the two-high era.
If you want to go deeper: Cody Alexander’s MatchQuarters site and books (defensive structure, including the tite and four-down fronts, from a coach’s view); Chris B. Brown’s The Art of Smart Football and his Grantland and Smart Football writing on the 3-4 and its noses; and the 2024 Eagles’ or 2021 Georgia Bulldogs’ games, watched for nothing but the three men inside the tackles.






NoteGo deeper



Measuring the wall. The tite’s promise is that nobody climbs: every offensive lineman is still engaged with a defensive lineman a second after the snap, so the linebacker behind them is untouched. Tracking data can test that. A simple measure is the distance from the linebacker to the nearest offensive blocker: two players whose centres are about a yard apart are in contact, so anything under about 1.5 yards means a blocker has reached him. Here it is at three moments for the Mike in the simulated tite play above, and, for contrast, for the Mike in the same inside zone against a four-man front that leaves the play-side guard uncovered (a 1 on the center and a 3 on the left guard), so that the guard can climb. Both are computed from Big Data Bowl-format frames (simulated, BDB-format):


Show the Python (nearest blocker to the linebacker, from tracking frames)
def nearest_blocker(play, key, times=(0.5, 1.0, 1.5)):
    trk = play.to_tracking()
    me = trk[trk.displayName == key].set_index("time")
    ol = trk[trk.displayName.isin(OL_KEYS + ("Y",))]
    out = {}
    for t in times:
        m = me.loc[round(t, 1)]
        o = ol[ol.time.round(1) == round(t, 1)]
        out[f"+{t:.1f} s"] = f"{np.hypot(o.x - m.x, o.y - m.y).min():.1f} yd"
    return out


def even_iz():
    """Inside zone right against a four-man front: 3 on the left guard, 1 on the center's right shoulder,
    5s on the tackles. The right guard is uncovered: he helps on the 1, then climbs to the Mike."""
    dfn = [D("LE", "DE", 1.0, T("5", -1), "5"), D("L3", "DL", 1.0, T("3", -1), "3"),
           D("R1", "DL", 1.0, T("1", 1), "1"), D("RE", "DE", 1.0, T("5", 1), "5"),
           D("WILL", "LB", 4.7, -1.6, "W"), D("MIKE", "LB", 4.7, 1.6, "M")]
    p = Play(gun11(y_attached=True), dfn, los=35, to_go=10)
    go_to(p, "C", (-0.35, 0.0), speed=1.4); go_to(p, "R1", (0.9, 0.9), "path", speed=0.5)
    go_to(p, "RG", (-0.2, 1.2), speed=2.0); go_to(p, "RG", (2.9, 1.9), speed=3.2)
    go_to(p, "MIKE", (3.6, 2.2), "path", speed=2.2, delay=0.35)
    go_to(p, "LG", (-0.3, -2.0), speed=1.6); go_to(p, "RT", (-0.3, 3.4), speed=1.6)
    go_to(p, "RB", (-1.9, 1.5), "run", speed=6.0, via=[(-4.7, -0.2), (-3.8, 1.0)])
    p.handoff("RB", t=0.5)
    return p

title: Linebackers: Keys, Flow, Tackling, and the Hardest Job on the Field
text:
The hardest job on the field
Second-and-7, early in the first quarter. The offense hands the ball to its running back, whose first step is a jab to his left. The middle linebacker, facing him, does not step to his right, the way the back seems to be going. He goes the other way, toward the side the back is leaving, running hard just behind his own defensive line, and he arrives in the hole a step before the pulling guard who was supposed to block him. No gain. On the replay the analyst ignores the back completely and draws a circle around the offense’s left guard: “Watch the guard. He pulls, and the Mike is gone before the back even gets the ball.” What did the linebacker see, and how did he see it so fast? This chapter is about the few square yards between the offensive tackles where most runs are won or lost, and the players who live there.
You’ll be able to:
How to read the diagrams. Offense is blue circles, defense orange squares, and plays go up the page. Left and right always mean the offense’s left and right. LT, LG, C, RG and RT are the offensive linemen (T, G and C in the smaller pictures), Y and U tight ends, Q the quarterback, R or T the running back, F a fullback, and X, Z and H wide receivers (H in the slot). Defensive linemen are labelled with their technique number; M, W and S are the Mike, Will and Sam linebackers, $ is a nickel back, CB a cornerback and FS and SS the safeties. Dotted green lines are a defender’s eyes: who he is watching. Green letters are gaps, never players. Unless a picture says otherwise, the tight end, and so the offense’s strength, is on the right.
A linebacker lines up behind the defensive line, about four or five yards off the ball, at what coaches call the second level of the defense: the linemen are the first level, the safeties the third. You met the three classic linebackers in The Twenty-Two: the Mike in the middle, the Sam on the strong (tight end’s) side and the Will on the weak side. In Even Fronts you saw where they stand in a 4-3, and that each front leaves one guard uncovered and puts a linebacker over him.
This chapter is about off-ball linebackers: the ones who stand off the line of scrimmage, behind the linemen. The name “outside linebacker” can mean two different players, and it is worth sorting out now. In a 4-3, the Sam and the Will are outside linebackers in the old sense: off the ball, on either side of the Mike. In a 3-4, “outside linebacker” usually means a stand-up edge (Odd and Hybrid Fronts), an edge rusher who lines up on the line and rushes the passer; that is a different job, and this chapter mostly leaves it alone. When it says inside linebackers, it means the off-ball linebackers in the box: the Mike and the Will in a 4-3, the two linebackers of a nickel defense, the two inside linebackers of a 3-4 (whom staffs name differently: Mike and Will is common).
Why call it the hardest job? Put yourself in his cleats for the first second of a play.
The position grew out of a lineman standing up. In the early 1950s most NFL defenses played a five-man line with a middle guard over the center. The Chicago Bears’ middle guard, Bill George, kept hitting the center and then watching passes sail over his head, so during a 1954 game against the Philadelphia Eagles he started dropping back off the line at the snap, and two plays later he intercepted a pass, the first of his career. He kept doing it. A five-man line with its middle man standing up is a four-man line with a linebacker in the middle. Nobody can be sure which middle guard first stood up, but George is the usual answer, and he is often credited, by accident, with the 4-3 as well.1 Two years later Tom Landry, coaching the New York Giants’ defense, built a 4-3 around a rookie from West Virginia, Sam Huff, and in 1960 CBS wired Huff with a microphone for a half-hour special, The Violent World of Sam Huff. The middle linebacker became the most famous defensive player in football, and has stayed near the top ever since: Dick Butkus, Ray Nitschke, Mike Singletary, Ray Lewis, Brian Urlacher, Luke Kuechly.2
This chapter takes the linebacker’s job apart in the order he does it: where he stands, what he looks at, which way he goes, how he gets there, how he tackles, and what he does when it’s a pass. Then it explains why the position looks so different today from the one Sam Huff played.

title: Linebackers: Keys, Flow, Tackling, and the Hardest Job on the Field
text:
He has two jobs that point in opposite directions. Against a run he has a gap to fill, and it is in front of him: he has to go forward, fast, because the running back reaches the line about a second after the snap. Against a pass he has a zone to drop to or a man to cover, and that is behind him or beside him. Every snap, he has to choose before he can be sure.
He is the one who gets blocked by someone twice his size. Defensive linemen are big men fighting big men. A linebacker weighs about 225 to 245 pounds, and the man coming to block him, a guard who has climbed off a double team, weighs 315. He cannot win that collision by force. He wins by getting to the spot first, or by meeting the block on his own terms and getting off it.
He tackles in space. A defensive lineman makes his tackles in a crowd, with the runner barely moving. A linebacker meets the ball carrier after he has come through the line, at full speed, with room to cut both ways.
He covers people who are faster than he is. Running backs and tight ends run routes against him on every pass play, and offenses spend whole weeks scheming to get their best receiver matched up with a linebacker.
He often runs the defense. In most NFL defenses the Mike linebacker hears the call in his helmet radio, relays it to the other ten, and adjusts it to the formation, all in the 15 seconds before the snap.

p = Play(line("short") + [te(+1), O("H", "WR", -1.5, -9.4, "H")],
         [q.moved(d=4.6, w=-6.3) if q.key == "WILL" else q for q in over_front(+1)], los=35, to_go=None)
f = draw(p, ax=axes[2], lateral=(-11.8, 7.0), window=WIN, title=False)
ghost(f, p, 4.5, -2.0, "W")
dashed(f, p, [(4.5, -2.85), (4.55, -5.4)], color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, lw=1.1)
say(f, p, 6.9, -6.3, "halfway to\nthe slot", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.6)
title(axes[2], "Walked out (apex)")
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.5)
plt.show()








Figure 31.1: Three places a linebacker stands. Left, stacked: each linebacker directly behind a defensive lineman (here a 3-3 stack, with a nose on the center and two 5-techniques), so a blocker coming for the linebacker has to get past the lineman first, and the pair can split the two gaps either side of the lineman any way they like. Middle, open: the Will of a 4-3 Over over the uncovered left guard (green ring), the ‘bubble’ from 05-02. He can see everything, and the guard can come straight for him (dashed). Right, walked out: the same Will moved out of the box to stand halfway between the left tackle and a slot receiver (H), an apex, ready to cover him. The dotted square is where he stood in the middle picture.





Stacked. In a stack alignment the linebacker lines up directly behind a defensive lineman, four or five yards deep. The lineman is his shield. A blocker who wants the linebacker has to go around the lineman to get to him, and by then the linebacker has seen the play. The stack also hides the defense’s intentions: a lineman and the linebacker behind him own the two gaps on either side of that lineman between them, and the offense cannot tell before the snap which man will take which. On one snap the lineman slants left and the linebacker fills right; on the next, the reverse. The left panel of Figure 31.1 is the extreme version, a 3-3 stack, with all three linebackers hidden behind all three linemen; you met it as the 3-3-5 front in Odd and Hybrid Fronts. Four-man fronts usually stack at most one linebacker (in many Under fronts, the Will behind the 3-technique) and play the others open or over a shaded lineman.
The cost of the stack is that his own lineman is in his way. To get to either gap he has to go around his own man, so he is a step slower to it than a linebacker standing over open grass, and if the lineman in front of him gets driven backward, the linebacker is caught in the pile (coaches say “in the wash”).
Open. The opposite is to stand over an uncovered offensive lineman, a guard nobody is lined up on. That is the middle panel, and it is the bubble you met in Even Fronts: every even front leaves one guard uncovered and puts a linebacker over him. The linebacker gets a clear view of the whole backfield, and nobody is in his way when he goes. The cost is that nobody is in the guard’s way either. He can climb straight up to the linebacker at the snap, so the open linebacker has to be quick enough to beat him to a spot two yards away.






NoteGo deeper



Coaches number linebacker spots the way they number linemen’s techniques, often with a zero added: a linebacker in a 30 is lined up on the guard’s outside shoulder, the spot behind a 3-technique, and one in a 10 is on the center’s shoulder, over the A gap. You won’t hear it on a broadcast, but it is how a linebacker coach talks, and it tells you that linebacker alignments are as precise as the line’s.


Depth. Off-ball linebackers usually stand about four to six yards deep, a little deeper against a team that likes play-action or against a running back aligned deep behind the quarterback, a little shallower on short yardage. The trade is simple. Every yard closer to the line is a step quicker to the hole and a step closer to the blockers; every yard deeper is more time to read and less time to get there.

The apex and the walk-out
The right panel of Figure 31.1 is the third alignment, and the modern one. An apex is the spot halfway between the last man in the box (a tackle or tight end) and a slot receiver, a few yards off the ball. A First Look at Defense introduced the defender who stands there, the overhang defender, usually a nickel back. When a linebacker goes there instead, coaches call it a walk-out: he walks out of the box before the snap to stand over or near the slot receiver.


Show the Python
off = line("short") + [O("QB", "QB", -5.0, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -5.0, -1.6, "R"),
                       O("X", "WR", -0.7, -16.0, "X"), O("H", "WR", -1.5, -9.0, "H"),
                       O("Y", "TE", -1.5, 9.0, "Y"), O("Z", "WR", -0.7, 16.0, "Z")]
dfn = [D("WE", "DE", 1.0, -5.0, "5"), D("NT", "DT", 1.0, T("1", -1), "1"), D("DT", "DT", 1.0, T("3", 1), "3"),
       D("SE", "DE", 1.0, 5.0, "5"), D("MIKE", "LB", 4.8, 0.4, "M"),
       D("SAM", "LB", 5.0, 6.1, "S"), D("WILL", "LB", 5.0, -6.1, "W"),
       D("LCB", "CB", 7.0, -16.0, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 7.0, 16.0, "CB"),
       D("FS", "S", 12.5, -8.5, "FS"), D("SS", "S", 12.5, 8.5, "SS")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=None)
p.highlight("SAM", "WILL", color=style.DEFENSE)
f = draw(p, width_in=6.4, lateral=(-19.5, 19.5), window=(-7.4, 15.6), title=False)
lane(f, p, -4.6, 4.6, -0.2, 6.6, color=style.MUTED, alpha=0.08, ls=(0, (2, 2)))
say(f, p, 2.9, -1.2, "the box: five", color=style.INK, fontsize=6.8, weight="bold")
say(f, p, 8.3, -6.1, "apex: halfway between\ntackle and slot", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
dashed(f, p, [(4.1, 6.2), (1.9, 5.6)], color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, lw=1.3)
dashed(f, p, [(5.9, 6.3), (8.0, 7.3)], color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, lw=1.3)
say(f, p, 2.3, 10.4, "run: downhill,\noutside-in", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
say(f, p, 9.4, 11.6, "pass: wall the slot's\ninside route, sink", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
plt.show()








Figure 31.2: A base 4-3 against a 2x2 formation (two receivers on each side; the tight end, Y, is detached as the right slot). With only four defensive backs, one answer is to walk both outside linebackers out of the box (ringed) to apex alignments, halfway between each tackle and slot receiver, about five yards deep. The box (shaded) now holds five defenders: four linemen and the Mike, alone in the middle. Each walked-out linebacker has two jobs (shown for the Sam): on a run, come downhill from the outside in, keeping the ball inside him (he is usually the force or alley player on his side); on a pass, wall off the slot receiver’s inside route and sink under the curl. He cannot be early for both.





Figure 31.2 shows why a walk-out happens. The offense has spread four receivers across the field, two on each side. A base 4-3 has only four defensive backs: two cornerbacks on the wide receivers and two safeties deep. Somebody has to stand near the two slot receivers. The defense has three answers: walk the outside linebackers out, as here; rotate a safety down over one slot and keep one linebacker in the box (a single-high look); or take a linebacker off and bring in a nickel back, which the defense can only do before the snap, by substitution or a pre-planned check.
Why walk out? Because leaving him inside is worse. A linebacker left in the box against a slot receiver is eight or nine yards from a man he may have to cover, which is an easy completion every time the quarterback looks at him. From the apex, he can still come downhill at the edge of the box against a run, outside-in, keeping the ball inside him, and he can get under or in front of the slot receiver’s route against a pass. (Whether he squeezes the run or bounces it outside is the call’s decision, built in Run Fits and Box Math.)
What does it cost? Count the box. Five defenders against five offensive linemen and a running back: the box is now light, and every run defender can be blocked. And each walked-out linebacker is now the defense’s conflict defender: if he comes inside for the run, the slot receiver behind him is open; if he widens for the pass, the edge of the box is open. The offense can read him after the snap and throw or run accordingly, which is exactly what the RPOs of Part 4 are built to do.
That is the problem that pushed linebackers off the field. A defense that expects the slot receiver to run routes would rather have a defensive back at the apex, a nickel back who can cover him, and it takes a linebacker off to make room. The last section of this chapter follows that trade to its end. For now, notice the walk-out as a tell: when a linebacker walks out with a receiver, the defense has told you it is short of defensive backs for this formation, and the offense will usually try to find out whether he can cover.

31  Linebackers: Keys, Flow, Tackling, and the Hardest Job on the Field

title: Linebackers: Keys, Flow, Tackling, and the Hardest Job on the Field
section: Keys: what a linebacker looks at
text:
Keys: what a linebacker looks at
Here is the problem with standing five yards off the ball. Things happen faster than a linebacker can see all of them. At the snap, eleven offensive players move at once; the running back has the ball, or doesn’t, half a second later; the linebacker has to be moving in the right direction by then. He cannot watch eleven people. So he watches one or two.
A key is the offensive player a defender watches at the snap to learn what the play is and where it is going. (It is the defense’s version of an idea; don’t confuse it with an option play’s read key, which is the defender a quarterback watches.) For an inside linebacker, the two classic keys are the guards and the near running back, and coaches talk about reading “through” the guard to the back: eyes on the guard’s first step, the back in the edge of the picture.
Which guard? The simplest rule is the guard nearest him, the one he is lined up on or over. Many teams have their inside linebackers read both guards, the near one first, because the far guard’s pull is the single most valuable thing a linebacker can see (the Mike in Figure 31.3, below, reads his near guard and sees the far one pull). You’ll hear the versions by name: a “guard read” or “high hat, low hat” read; a “triangle” of the near guard, the far guard (or the near tackle) and the near back (not the quarterback’s triangle read of Part 4); and a “flow” or “backfield” read, which watches the backs and trusts the linemen in front to keep the guards off.

What the guard tells him
Offensive linemen can’t hide what kind of play it is, because the physics of blocking and the rules tell them how to move (a lineman may not go downfield on a pass, a rule the play-action section below puts to work). A guard’s first step is the most honest signal on the field.








The guard’s first step
What it means
The linebacker’s reaction




Fires forward, pads low (“low hat”)
Run, and the guard is blocking the man in front of him or doubling a lineman
Downhill: attack his gap


Comes straight up at the linebacker
Run, and the linebacker is the guard’s target; the ball is coming near him
Beat the guard to the spot, or take him on and keep his gap


Blocks down, inside, away from the linebacker
A gap-scheme run coming to the linebacker’s side; a puller, a fullback or the tackle is coming to kick out or lead
Squeeze toward the down block and find the puller or the kick-out


Opens his hips and steps back and flat behind the line, either direction
A pull: a gap-scheme run (power, counter, trap) going where he goes
“Pull, follow”: flow with him, inside-out


Steps sideways and reaches, the whole line stepping together
Zone: the run will go the way the line is stepping
Flow with the line, inside-out (next section)


Steps back and sits, hands up (“high hat”)
Pass protection
Pass: get to his drop or his man


High hat, but the back stays square in front of the quarterback, or the linemen set softly and let the rushers by
A draw or a screen
Get depth slowly, eyes on the back; don’t run away from it



The “high hat, low hat” read is the same one How to Watch a Broadcast gave you for spotting run and pass from the couch. The linebacker uses it a quarter-second after the snap, from five yards away.
The last row is where reading gets hard. A draw is built to look like a pass: the linemen set, the quarterback drops, and then he hands the ball to a back who waited. A linebacker who reads “high hat, pass” and sprints to his zone is running away from it. The tells are small: the back stays square in front of the quarterback instead of stepping up to block or releasing; the guards set but don’t punch, inviting the rushers upfield; the quarterback’s drop is a little too quick. So linebackers are taught to open to their drop with their eyes still on the back for a beat. A screen shows the same high hat first, then the linemen let their rushers through and release, running sideways after a pass set, while the back slips out behind them. Linemen running flat after setting to pass is the screen’s signature.
The pull is the most valuable signal of all, because the gap-scheme runs of Gap and Power Runs need a pulling lineman to get an extra blocker to the hole, and that lineman has to run there. Wherever he is going, the ball is going too. That is the read in the chapter’s opening scene, and Figure 31.3 plays it out, jab step and all.


Show the Python
def power_vs_over():
    off = line("short") + [te(+1), O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0, "Q"), O("FB", "FB", -4.5, 0, "F"),
                           O("RB", "RB", -7.0, 0, "T")]
    p = Play(off, over_front(+1), los=35, to_go=None)
    # play side: the right guard and tackle block the 3, Y blocks down on the end; the center blocks back,
    # the left tackle hinges
    go_to(p, "Y", (-0.3, 3.95), "block", speed=1.6); go_to(p, "SE", (1.0, 3.65), speed=0.6)
    go_to(p, "RT", (-0.35, 3.0), "block", speed=1.2); go_to(p, "RG", (-0.35, 2.0), "block", speed=1.2)
    go_to(p, "DT", (1.0, 2.45), speed=0.4)
    go_to(p, "C", (-0.35, -0.6), "block", speed=1.2); go_to(p, "NT", (1.0, -0.7), speed=0.4)
    go_to(p, "LT", (-0.9, -3.6), "block", speed=1.2); go_to(p, "WE", (0.5, -3.7), speed=1.0)
    # the left guard pulls (first step back and flat), around the double team and up into the hole;
    # the fullback kicks out the Sam
    go_to(p, "LG", HOLE_G, "pull", speed=5.5, via=[(-1.6, -1.0), (-2.2, 2.6)])
    go_to(p, "FB", (-0.2, 7.1), "block", speed=5.4, via=[(-2.4, 3.4)])
    go_to(p, "SAM", (1.2, 7.7), speed=3.0, delay=0.3)
    # the back: a jab step to his left (the lie), then the handoff and downhill behind his guard
    go_to(p, "QB", (-2.6, -0.6), speed=2.5)
    go_to(p, "RB", (-6.75, -0.6), "run", speed=2.6)
    go_to(p, "RB", (-2.7, 4.6), "run", speed=6.5, via=[(-4.6, 2.4)])
    p.handoff("RB", t=0.75)
    # the linebackers: the Mike flows on the pull, straight for the hole; the Will follows the guard
    go_to(p, "MIKE", HOLE_M, speed=6.0, delay=0.2, via=[(3.6, 2.6)])
    go_to(p, "WILL", (1.9, 3.1), speed=4.6, delay=0.3, via=[(4.0, 0.6)])
    return p


HOLE_M, HOLE_G = (0.7, 5.5), (-0.75, 5.35)


MIKE_TRIP = path_len([(4.5, 0.8), (3.6, 2.6), HOLE_M])
GUARD_TRIP = path_len([(-0.7, -1.6), (-1.6, -1.0), (-2.2, 2.6), HOLE_G])


def key_marks(fld, play, t, i):
    if t < 0.05:
        for k, g in (("MIKE", "LG"), ("MIKE", "RG"), ("WILL", "LG")):
            eyes(fld, play, play.position(k, t), play.position(g, t))
        # the race: each man's whole trip to the hole, from his snap spot
        dashed(fld, play, [(4.5, 0.8), (3.6, 2.6), HOLE_M], color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, lw=1.0)
        dashed(fld, play, [(-0.7, -1.6), (-1.6, -1.0), (-2.2, 2.6), HOLE_G], color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, lw=1.0)
        say(fld, play, 5.9, 3.3, f"Mike: {MIKE_TRIP:.0f} yd", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.4)
        say(fld, play, -3.3, -2.6, f"guard: {GUARD_TRIP:.1f} yd", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.4)


P_POWER = power_vs_over()
animation_or_strip([(P_POWER, 0.0, ""), (P_POWER, 0.5, ""), (P_POWER, 0.9, ""), (P_POWER, 1.4, "")],
                   notes=["eyes on the guards (dotted);\ndashed: the race to the hole",
                          "the left guard pulls: the Mike's\nfirst step goes with him",
                          "Mike flows over the top;\nthe back's jab step was the lie",
                          "Mike meets the puller at the\nline: hole full, back stopped"],
                   rings=(("MIKE", style.DEFENSE), ("LG", style.THIRD)), lateral=(-6.2, 9.6), window=(-7.9, 7.6),
                   after=key_marks, width_in=6.0)





  
  Your browser does not support the video tag.



Figure 31.3: The key read: the guard pulls, the Mike flows (simulated play in Big Data Bowl tracking coordinates; faint lines are each player’s path so far). Power to the right from an I-formation against a 4-3 Over, with the tailback’s jab step to the left first, as in the chapter’s opening. 1: at the snap the Mike (orange ring) reads both guards, the Will the left guard (green ring); dotted lines are their eyes, and the dashed lines show the race each man is about to run to the hole, about six yards for the Mike against nearly eight for the pulling guard, whose first step goes backward. 2: the right guard fires out (run) and the left guard pulls (where); the Mike’s first step goes with the puller, not with the back. 3: the Mike runs just behind his own linemen, inside the ball, while the Will follows the guard as the backup; the fullback kicks out the Sam. 4: the Mike reaches the hole first and meets the puller at the line instead of two yards past it, so the hole is full and the back, a step behind his guard, has nowhere to go. A Mike who had watched the back would have been a step late, and the guard would have blocked him at linebacker depth.




Notice three things about the picture. First, the Mike’s two guards told him two truths in the first quarter-second: the right guard, nearest him, fired out low (it’s a run), and the left guard pulled (it’s going right). Second, the Mike’s first step in panel 2 goes sideways, with the puller. A linebacker who reads a pull does not charge at the line; he runs with the puller, just behind his own linemen, until he sees the hole. Third, he wins the race because his trip is shorter and starts just as soon. The guard has to step back, run behind the center and around the double team, nearly eight yards; the Mike has about six, and he leaves the moment the guard does. If he waits to see where the back goes, he arrives with the guard, and the guard is there to block him. That is the case for keys in one sentence: the linemen tell the truth sooner than the ball does.


What the back tells him
The near back is the second key. His first two steps say three things: direction (left, right, or straight ahead), speed (a sprint sideways or a patient downhill track) and depth (does he get deeper, for a toss or a pitch, or come straight at the line). If he steps up to block, or swings out of the backfield to the flat, it is a pass. If there is a fullback, he is the most honest back of all: on an iso or a lead play, he runs straight at the linebacker he is going to block, which tells that linebacker where the ball is going.
Why not just read the back? Because the back can lie and the linemen mostly can’t. Offenses build whole plays on the backfield lie. The counter starts with the back stepping away from the play while the guard and tackle pull toward it; a linebacker who believes the back takes a false step and is out of position before he knows it. Play-action shows him a back who seems to have the ball. That is why most coaches teach the guards as the primary key and the back as the confirmation: if they say the same thing, go; if they disagree, believe the linemen.
Keys also depend on the defense. Linebackers in a two-gap 3-4, who sit behind big linemen and are protected from blockers, often read the guards almost exclusively. Linebackers in an attacking one-gap 4-3 (the Tampa 2 teams of the 2000s are the classic case) often read the backfield flow and trust their linemen to hold the guards. And a Sam on the line’s strong side, or a walked-out apex player, keys the tight end or tackle in front of him and the near back, because the play coming his way starts out there: a tight end who blocks down means the ball is coming outside him, one who releases means pass, and from the apex the eyes go on through to the slot receiver.






ImportantWhy it exists



Keys exist because a linebacker who waits to be sure is always late. The back reaches the line in about a second; a linebacker four or five yards away needs most of that second to get there. So he decides from the first step of one or two blockers, who have to show their intent early. The price is that the offense knows what he is looking at. Counters, traps, play-action and screens are all, in part, plays built to show a linebacker’s key a lie.








CautionCommon misconception



“Great linebackers just follow the ball.” Watch the replay of a linebacker making a tackle for no gain, and then watch his first step: almost always it came before the ball went anywhere, and it went where a lineman was going. The ball is the last thing a good linebacker looks at, not the first. Linebackers who “see the ball” are usually the ones a counter or a play-action pass catches out.

title: Linebackers: Keys, Flow, Tackling, and the Hardest Job on the Field
text:
Flow: fast and slow
Keys tell a linebacker what the play is. Flow tells him how to move. In coaches’ language, flow is the direction and speed of the backfield action at the snap: where the backs (and, on zone, the whole line) are going, and how fast. Staffs use different words, but nearly all of them sort it into two kinds.


Show the Python
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 4.3))
LAT, WIN = (-8.6, 10.6), (-8.6, 9.2)
off = line("short") + [te(+1), O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -7.0, 0, "R")]
# fast flow: outside zone right
p = Play(off, over_front(+1), los=35, to_go=None)
for k in OL_KEYS + ("Y",):
    q = p.players[k]
    go_to(p, k, (q.d + 0.2, q.w + 1.1), "block", speed=2.0)
go_to(p, "QB", (-2.6, 1.6))
go_to(p, "RB", (-1.6, 6.2), "run", via=[(-5.7, 3.0)])
go_to(p, "MIKE", (2.9, 5.0), via=[(4.0, 2.6)])
go_to(p, "WILL", (5.5, -0.5), via=[(5.0, -1.4)])          # shuffle over the top, deeper than the Mike
go_to(p, "SAM", (1.6, 7.9))
f = draw(p, ax=axes[0], lateral=LAT, window=WIN, title=False)
dashed(f, p, [(-2.8, 4.6), (0.0, 1.6), (3.0, 0.0)], color=style.OFFENSE, lw=1.2)
say(f, p, 7.1, 4.6, "run with it,\ninside the ball", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.7)
say(f, p, 7.1, -3.6, "Will: over the top,\nbehind the Mike,\nfor the cutback", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK,
    fontsize=6.6)
say(f, p, 2.6, -3.0, "cutback lane", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.4)
title(axes[0], "Fast flow: outside zone")
# slow flow: inside zone right
p = Play(off, over_front(+1), los=35, to_go=None)
for k in OL_KEYS + ("Y",):
    q = p.players[k]
    go_to(p, k, (q.d + 0.5, q.w + 0.4), "block", speed=2.0)
go_to(p, "QB", (-2.6, 0.9))
go_to(p, "RB", (-1.4, 2.3), "run", via=[(-4.6, 1.2)])
go_to(p, "MIKE", (2.5, 1.5))
go_to(p, "WILL", (2.6, -1.4))
f = draw(p, ax=axes[1], lateral=LAT, window=WIN, title=False)
say(f, p, 7.1, 0.0, "press the gap,\nstay square", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.7)
say(f, p, -4.4, 4.6, "downhill at\nthe B gap", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.6)
title(axes[1], "Slow flow: inside zone")
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()








Figure 31.4: Two kinds of flow against a 4-3 Over (the offensive line, the backfield and the linebackers move; the defensive line is left standing). Left, fast flow: outside zone to the right; the line steps sideways and the back sprints flat for the tight end’s outside leg. The Mike runs with it, just behind his line and a step behind the ball; the Will shuffles over the top, deeper than the Mike and behind the end of the cutback lane (dashed blue), so a back who cuts back runs into him; the Sam stays outside the ball to turn it back in. Right, slow flow: inside zone, the back coming straight downhill at the B gap. Both linebackers press forward into their gaps, square to the line, and wait for the back to commit. Running sideways here would open the gap they just left.





Fast flow is the ball going sideways in a hurry: outside zone, a toss, a sweep, the back sprinting flat for the edge. The linebacker’s job is to run with it, and to run with it correctly. Correctly means inside-out: a yard or so behind his own linemen and a step behind the ball, so that the ball is always a little outside him. (You will see the phrase again; it is the linebacker’s master rule.) If the back keeps going, the linebacker can keep up and fill as soon as he turns upfield. If the back stops and cuts back, which is what outside zone is designed to make him do (see Zone Running), the linebacker is still inside him and can stop. The backside linebacker, the Will in Figure 67.1, shuffles over the top: behind the Mike and a little deeper, ending up behind the spot where a cutback would come through. He is the cutback player: if both linebackers race to the sideline, the back has the whole field behind them.
Slow flow is the ball coming straight at the line, or coming slowly: inside zone, an iso, a draw, a delayed handoff, the counter’s first step. Now the linebacker presses: he steps forward into his gap, square to the line, shoulders parallel to it, and makes the back declare first. The worst thing he can do against slow flow is to run sideways, because every inside run is built around a back who reads the linebackers and cuts into the gap one of them just left.
There is a third case, and coaches have a phrase for it: split flow, the backs going in opposite directions (one back left, the other right, or a back one way and the quarterback the other). Split flow is the offense saying misdirection. A linebacker who sees it plays his gap and does not chase either one until the ball shows.

title: Linebackers: Keys, Flow, Tackling, and the Hardest Job on the Field
section: Fitting the run: fill, plug, scrape and run-through
text:
Fitting the run: fill, plug, scrape and run-through
Once a linebacker knows it’s a run and where it’s going, he has to get into the right gap. The defense’s plan for who takes which gap is the run fit, and its full arithmetic is the subject of Run Fits and Box Math. What a linebacker does to get to his gap has four common names, and you will hear all four on broadcasts and in coaches’ interviews.


Show the Python
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(6.6, 6.4))
LAT, WIN = (-7.8, 9.4), (-8.2, 8.8)
ofb = line("short") + [te(+1), O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0, "Q"), O("FB", "FB", -4.5, 0, "F"), O("RB", "RB", -7.0, 0, "T")]
one = line("short") + [te(+1), O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -7.0, 0, "R")]
# fill vs iso: the hole is the strong A gap, open in the Over because the 1 is shaded the other way
p = Play(ofb, over_front(+1), los=35, to_go=None)
p.highlight("MIKE", color=style.DEFENSE)
go_to(p, "C", (-0.2, -0.45), "block"); go_to(p, "RG", (-0.2, 1.95), "block")
go_to(p, "FB", (0.4, 0.9), "run", speed=5.5)
go_to(p, "RB", (-1.4, 0.9), "run", via=[(-4.6, 0.4)])
go_to(p, "MIKE", (1.7, 0.9))
f = draw(p, ax=axes[0, 0], lateral=LAT, window=WIN, title=False)
say(f, p, 6.6, 4.4, "meet the fullback\nin the hole", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.7)
title(axes[0, 0], "Fill")
# plug: the 3-technique slants inside, the Mike plugs the B gap
p = Play(one, over_front(+1, mike_w=2.4), los=35, to_go=None)
p.highlight("MIKE", color=style.DEFENSE)
go_to(p, "DT", (1.0, 0.95))
go_to(p, "MIKE", (2.0, 2.45))
go_to(p, "RB", (-1.6, 2.3), "run", via=[(-4.6, 1.2)])
f = draw(p, ax=axes[0, 1], lateral=LAT, window=WIN, title=False)
gap_tag(f, p, 0.2, 2.45, "B", fontsize=6.6)
say(f, p, 6.6, 4.4, "straight into the\ngap the 3 left", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.7)
point_to(f, p, (2.8, -2.6), (1.25, 1.5), "the 3 slants\ninside", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.4)
title(axes[0, 1], "Plug")
# scrape: the end squeezes, the Mike scrapes outside him
p = Play(one, over_front(+1), los=35, to_go=None)
p.highlight("MIKE", color=style.DEFENSE)
go_to(p, "SE", (0.6, 2.9))
go_to(p, "RB", (-2.6, 6.1), "run", via=[(-5.8, 2.8)])
go_to(p, "MIKE", (2.0, 4.4), via=[(3.9, 2.6)])
go_to(p, "SAM", (1.8, 6.6))
f = draw(p, ax=axes[1, 0], lateral=LAT, window=WIN, title=False)
say(f, p, 6.6, 2.6, "over the top\nof his linemen", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.7)
point_to(f, p, (2.9, -2.4), (0.75, 2.75), "the end\nsqueezes", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.4)
say(f, p, 3.6, 7.6, "Sam:\nD gap", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.2)
title(axes[1, 0], "Scrape")
# run-through: the Will beats the climbing guard through the A gap
p = Play(one, over_front(+1, will_w=-2.5), los=35, to_go=None)
p.highlight("WILL", color=style.DEFENSE)
go_to(p, "WILL", (-2.0, -2.7))
go_to(p, "RB", (-3.6, -2.2), "run", via=[(-5.6, -0.8)])
f = draw(p, ax=axes[1, 1], lateral=LAT, window=WIN, title=False)
dashed(f, p, [(0.2, -1.4), (2.0, -1.6), (3.2, -1.9)], color=style.OFFENSE, lw=1.3)
spot(f, p, -2.75, -2.55, ms=8)
say(f, p, 6.6, 3.0, "through the B gap before\nthe guard gets there", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.6)
title(axes[1, 1], "Run-through")
fig.tight_layout(h_pad=0.8, w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()








Figure 31.5: Four ways a linebacker fits a run (the ringed linebacker acts in each panel). Fill: on an iso the fullback leads into the strong A gap, open in the Over because the nose is shaded the other way, while the center and right guard block the two tackles; the Mike attacks downhill and meets the fullback in the hole, as close to the line as he can. Plug: the 3-technique slants inside, and the Mike, stacked behind him, steps straight forward into the B gap the 3 left, where the back is aiming. Scrape: on an outside run the end squeezes down inside, and the Mike runs sideways behind his linemen to the C gap outside the end, while the Sam keeps the D gap outside him. Run-through: the Will, over the uncovered left guard (the bubble), attacks through the B gap outside the guard at the snap, before the guard can climb to him (dashed blue: where the guard was heading), and meets the back in the backfield (X).






Fill. To fill is to attack downhill into the gap the run is aimed at and meet whatever comes through it, a lead blocker or the back, as close to the line of scrimmage as possible. It is the general verb: “the Mike filled the hole.” The closer to the line he meets the play, the less room the back has to choose a different hole, so coaches measure fills in yards: a fill at the line of scrimmage is a good play even if the linebacker doesn’t make the tackle, because it forces the back to stop or bounce.
Plug. To plug is to step straight forward into a gap directly in front of you and close it with your body. It is the inside linebacker’s partner to the defensive line’s slant (05-01): when the 3-technique slants into the A gap, the B gap he left behind needs a body, and the linebacker stacked behind him plugs it. Plugs are short and violent, and they usually end in a collision with a lineman.
Scrape. To scrape is to run sideways, behind and close to your own defensive linemen (“over the top” of them), to a gap farther outside. It is how a linebacker gets to an outside gap without getting caught in the traffic at the line, and it is the move you saw in fast flow. Scraping linebackers stay square to the line, shuffling or crossing over, so that they can turn upfield and fill the instant the back commits. The defense’s answer to the zone read, below, is built on it.
Run-through. A run-through is the aggressive version of a fill: the linebacker attacks through his gap at the snap (or on his first key), before the blocker assigned to him can climb, and meets the play in the backfield. “Run-through linebacker” is also a compliment, for the kind of player who does it naturally. It wrecks zone schemes, whose climbing linemen need a fraction of a second to come off their double teams, and it makes tackles for loss. It is also the fit most vulnerable to misdirection: a linebacker who runs through a gap on a counter step or a play-action fake is out of the play, or out of his coverage.

The call and the front decide a lot (a defense whose linemen slant and stunt asks its linebackers to plug and scrape behind them; one that wants plays in the backfield against a zone team asks them to run through), but from the couch you can usually match the fit to what the run looks like:







What the run shows the linebacker
The fit it usually calls for




A fullback or lead blocker coming straight at him (iso, lead)
Fill: meet the lead blocker in the hole, at the line


His own lineman slanting away, leaving the gap in front of him empty
Plug that gap


The ball going outside, or the end in front of him squeezing inside (and the zone read, below)
Scrape over the top to the outside gap


Zone blocking, with linemen who need a moment to climb to him, and a call that says go
Run-through before they arrive



The first step, and the block he can’t avoid. None of these starts with a lunge. A linebacker’s first step is a short read step (some coaches say “pop step”): a few inches, downhill, that keeps him moving without committing him. His second step is the one that tells you what he saw. The cardinal sin is the false step, a first step the wrong way, which is exactly what counters and play-action are built to draw. And sometimes a climbing lineman gets to him anyway. Then he does not run around the block, which would open the gap behind him (unless the call tells him to). He meets the blocker with his hands, a punch to the chest, keeps his gap-side arm free, and gets off the block toward his gap. Which shoulder he takes the blocker on with, keeping the ball inside him (box, or squeeze) or bouncing it outside (spill), is a whole-defense decision, and Run Fits and Box Math builds it.






NoteMadden vs. real life



In Madden, the linebacker you control can run anywhere and the computer fills the gap you left. On a real field, every linebacker’s gap is somebody else’s assumption. If the Mike scrapes outside when the call told him to plug, the gap he was supposed to fill is empty, and the defensive lineman next to it, who slanted away because the Mike would be there, is now on the wrong side of the ball. That is why coaches care more about a linebacker being in the right gap than about him making the tackle, and why “he was out of his gap” is one of the harshest things a linebacker coach says on film.



The scrape against the zone read
The scrape has its most famous use against the zone read. On a zone read the offense leaves the backside end unblocked and the quarterback reads him: if he stays wide, hand off; if he crashes down on the back, keep the ball and run where the end was. The defense’s answer, the scrape exchange from Option Football, has the end crash on the back on purpose and the linebacker behind him scrape around him to the spot where the quarterback will keep. The quarterback reads “keep” correctly and runs into the linebacker.
That chapter showed the trade. Here is the linebacker’s side of it, because the scrape is easy to draw and hard to time.


Show the Python
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 4.4))
LAT, WIN = (-13.2, 6.6), (-7.6, 8.4)
off = line("short") + [te(+1), O("QB", "QB", -5.0, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -5.0, -1.9, "R"),
                       O("H", "WR", -1.5, -10.0, "H")]
dfn = nickel_front(mike=(4.7, 1.4), will=(4.7, -2.2)) + [D("NB", "NB", 4.6, -8.0, "$")]
for ax, good in zip(axes, (True, False)):
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=None)
    p.highlight("WILL", color=style.DEFENSE)
    go_to(p, "WE", (-2.3, -2.4))
    go_to(p, "RB", (-3.0, 3.4), "run", via=[(-4.0, -0.4)])
    if good:
        go_to(p, "QB", (1.0, -6.6), "run", via=[(-4.3, -2.6), (-2.0, -5.2)])
        go_to(p, "WILL", (0.9, -5.6), via=[(3.3, -4.6)])
        go_to(p, "NB", (2.4, -8.0))
    else:
        go_to(p, "QB", (2.6, -4.3), "run", via=[(-4.3, -2.6), (-1.6, -5.8), (0.2, -5.3)])
        go_to(p, "WILL", (0.6, -8.4), via=[(3.0, -6.0)])
        go_to(p, "NB", (2.6, -9.2))
    f = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=LAT, window=WIN, title=False)
    # the left tackle is uncovered (the end he would block is being read), so he climbs to the Will
    dashed(f, p, [(0.1, -3.2), (2.4, -2.9), (3.9, -2.4)], color=style.OFFENSE, lw=1.2)
    if good:
        spot(f, p, 1.25, -6.25, ms=8)
        say(f, p, 6.8, -5.4, "tight over the end,\non the QB's inside hip", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.6)
        title(ax, "On time and inside-out")
    else:
        say(f, p, 6.8, -5.4, "too wide, too fast:\nthe QB cuts inside", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.6)
        title(ax, "Overrun")
    say(f, p, -4.6, -9.4, "end crashes:\nQB keeps", color=style.INK_2, fontsize=6.4)
    say(f, p, 2.6, -0.4, "LT climbs", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.2)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()








Figure 31.6: The Will’s scrape on a zone read, from the linebacker’s side (the line zones right; the quarterback reads the left end, who crashes down on the back, so the quarterback keeps). Left, a good scrape: the Will runs tight over the top of the end, a step behind him, and arrives on the quarterback’s inside hip with the nickel back ($) outside: the keeper has nowhere to go but toward the help. Right, an overrun: the Will scrapes too wide and too fast, gets outside the quarterback, and the quarterback cuts back inside him, into the space the crashing end left. In both, the left tackle (dashed blue), uncovered because the end he would block is being read, climbs toward the spot the Will left: the scrape has to beat him there.





The scraper has three things to get right. Timing: he has to leave at the snap, before the read, because a quarterback keeps the ball and is past the line in about a second and a half. Path: tight to the crashing end, so that the quarterback can’t run between them and the uncovered left tackle, climbing at the snap, can’t get to him first; coaches tell scrapers to “rub the end’s hip.” Leverage: he has to arrive inside the quarterback, on his inside hip, with a teammate (the nickel back or a safety in Figure 31.6) outside, so that the quarterback’s only way out is toward that teammate. An overrun, on the right, is the scraper’s classic mistake: he gets to the spot so eagerly that he passes it, and an athletic quarterback cuts back underneath him into the hole the end left. Offenses fight back by giving the scraper something else to worry about, like a tight end or H-back who arcs around the end to block him, which is why the scrape exchange is a call the defense mixes in, not something it can do every snap.

title: Linebackers: Keys, Flow, Tackling, and the Hardest Job on the Field
text:
Getting there: pursuit angles
Most runs don’t end in the hole. The back gets through, or bounces outside, and the play becomes a footrace in which several defenders who started in different places converge on one runner. How they converge is the difference between a five-yard gain and a fifty-yard one.
A pursuit angle is the path a defender takes to a ball carrier who is already moving. The instinct, for anyone who has never been coached, is to run at the runner. That is almost always wrong.


Show the Python
def intercept(R0, vR, L0, sL):
    """Earliest time t at which a defender from L0 at speed sL can reach the runner R0 + vR t."""
    d = np.asarray(R0, float) - np.asarray(L0, float)
    a = vR @ vR - sL ** 2
    b = 2 * d @ vR
    c = d @ d
    if abs(a) < 1e-9:
        return -c / b
    disc = b * b - 4 * a * c
    ts = [(-b - np.sqrt(disc)) / (2 * a), (-b + np.sqrt(disc)) / (2 * a)]
    return min(t for t in ts if t > 0)


R0, L0 = np.array([0.5, 6.0]), np.array([2.0, 1.5])
uR = np.array([1.0, 0.45]) / np.hypot(1.0, 0.45)
vR, sL = 7.0 * uR, 7.5
inside = np.array([-0.45, -0.9])                     # meet him a step inside, not on his outside hip
t_meet = intercept(R0 + inside, vR, L0, sL)
MEET = R0 + vR * t_meet + inside
# the chase: always aimed at the runner's current spot
dt, chase = 0.01, [L0.copy()]
for k in range(int(1.9 / dt)):
    tgt = R0 + vR * (k * dt)
    v = tgt - chase[-1]
    chase.append(chase[-1] + sL * dt * v / np.linalg.norm(v))
chase = np.array(chase)
# keep chasing (off the picture) until he is within arm's reach (1 yard): when, and how far downfield?
c_, t_ = chase[-1].copy(), len(chase) * dt
while np.linalg.norm(R0 + vR * t_ - c_) > 1.0:
    v = R0 + vR * t_ - c_
    c_ += sL * dt * v / np.linalg.norm(v)
    t_ += dt
CATCH_T, CATCH_D = t_, (R0 + vR * t_)[0]
GAP = {t: float(np.linalg.norm(R0 + vR * t - chase[int(round(t / dt))])) for t in (0.5, 1.0, 1.5)}
# the overrun: aimed too far ahead, so that he arrives outside the back
over_end = R0 + vR * t_meet + np.array([-0.6, 3.4])
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.4, 4.9))
p = Play([O("RB", "RB", R0[0], R0[1], "R")],
         [D("MIKE", "LB", L0[0], L0[1], "M"), D("CB", "CB", 8.0, 15.5, "CB")], los=35, to_go=None)
f = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=(-3.0, 19.0), window=(-2.4, 15.0), title=False)
P = lambda q: _P(f, p, q[0], q[1])  # noqa: E731
rb_end = R0 + vR * 1.8
solid(f, p, [tuple(R0), tuple(rb_end)], color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, lw=2.4)
xs, ys = _P(f, p, chase[:, 0], chase[:, 1])
ax.plot(xs, ys, color=style.MUTED, lw=1.6, zorder=4)
solid(f, p, [tuple(L0), tuple(MEET)], color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.8)
dashed(f, p, [tuple(L0), tuple(over_end)], color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, lw=1.3)
cut0 = R0 + vR * (t_meet + 0.05)
dashed(f, p, [tuple(cut0), tuple(cut0 + np.array([3.6, -2.6]))], color=style.OFFENSE, lw=1.3)
for k in range(1, 4):                       # half-second ticks
    t = 0.5 * k
    for q, col in ((R0 + vR * t, style.OFFENSE_DARK), (chase[min(int(t / dt), len(chase) - 1)], style.MUTED)):
        x, y = P(q)
        ax.plot([x], [y], marker="o", ms=3.2, color=col, zorder=6)
    if t < t_meet:
        x, y = P(L0 + (MEET - L0) * t / t_meet)
        ax.plot([x], [y], marker="o", ms=3.2, color=style.DEFENSE, zorder=6)
for t in (0.5, 1.0, 1.5):                   # same moment, two men: how far apart the chaser still is
    (x0, y0), (x1, y1) = P(R0 + vR * t), P(chase[int(round(t / dt))])
    ax.plot([x0, x1], [y0, y1], color=style.INK_2, lw=0.8, ls=(0, (1, 1.2)), zorder=5.5)
    xr, yr = P(R0 + vR * t + np.array([0.0, 0.9]))
    ax.text(xr, yr, f"{t:.1f} s: {GAP[t]:.1f} yd", fontsize=6.0, color=style.INK_2, ha="left", va="center",
            zorder=9, bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.12", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none", alpha=0.85))
spot(f, p, MEET[0], MEET[1], ms=9)
solid(f, p, [(8.0, 14.6), (MEET[0] + 1.6, MEET[1] + 2.2)], color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.4)
point_to(f, p, (2.0, 11.4), tuple(chase[45]), "chase (grey):\naimed at the man", color=style.INK_2, fontsize=6.8)
say(f, p, MEET[0] - 0.4, MEET[1] - 4.6, "angle: aimed where\nhe will be, a step inside", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK,
    fontsize=6.8)
say(f, p, over_end[0] - 1.9, over_end[1] + 1.2, "overrun", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
say(f, p, cut0[0] + 4.4, cut0[1] - 2.8, "cutback", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
say(f, p, 12.7, 15.6, "leverage player:\nstays outside", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
say(f, p, -0.9, 9.4, "the back bounces\noutside", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
plt.show()








Figure 31.7: Pursuit angles (geometry computed for a back running 7 yards a second as he comes out of his cut and a linebacker running 7.5; dots on each path mark every 0.5 seconds). The back has bounced outside to the right and turned upfield; the Mike starts inside him and a little downfield. Grey, the chase: aimed at where the back is at every instant. The dotted ties join where the two men are at the same moment, labelled with the time and the gap: he is still two yards behind after a second and a half. (The grey path crosses the back’s, but later, after the back has gone.) He doesn’t get within reach until well past 20 yards downfield. Orange, the angle: aimed at where the back will be, a step inside him, he meets him at the X after about a second and a quarter. Dashed orange, the overrun: aimed too flat and too far outside, he gets outside the ball, and the back cuts back inside him (dashed blue) into open field. The cornerback (CB) is the leverage player: he stays outside the back and squeezes him inside, toward the Mike.





Figure 31.7 makes the point with real geometry. A linebacker who runs at the back (the grey path) is always aiming at a spot the back has already left. In this example the linebacker is the faster man, and he is still two yards behind after a second and a half; he gets within arm’s reach only after 3.6 seconds, 23 yards downfield. Against a back who is as fast as he is, or faster, which in the open field is most backs, he never catches him at all. A linebacker who aims at where the back will be (orange) cuts the distance he has to run and meets the back in about a second and a quarter. That is a pursuit angle. The catch is the dashed path: aim too far ahead, and the linebacker gets outside the back, who simply plants his foot and cuts back behind him. Every defender who has been run past has done one of those two things: chased, or overrun.
The rule coaches give for it is inside-out again: take the angle that keeps the ball carrier a step outside you, never inside. If you are inside him, he can only go one way, outside, and outside is where the next defender is.
That next defender is the leverage player: the man on the outside whose job is to keep the ball inside, turning the runner back toward the pursuit. In Figure 31.7 it is the cornerback; on other plays it is the end who set the edge, an outside linebacker, a safety who came down. (The defense names him in advance, as its force player, in Run Fits and Box Math.) Put the two together and you have the shape of good team pursuit: one defender outside the ball, squeezing it in, and everyone else inside-out on it, each a little deeper and farther inside than the man in front, so that whichever way the runner cuts, someone is already there. Coaches drill it constantly, and it is one of the clearest things you can see on the end-zone replay: on a good defense, the arrows all converge.

title: Linebackers: Keys, Flow, Tackling, and the Hardest Job on the Field
section: Tackling, and why tackles get missed at the second level
text:
Tackling, and why tackles get missed at the second level
Then the linebacker has to bring the man down. Tackling has changed more in the last decade than in the fifty years before it, for two reasons: safety, and the realization that the old way missed too many tackles.
The old way, the one a lot of fans still picture, was a head-on collision: eyes up, head across the runner’s body (“head across the bow”), drive through him. It produces highlight hits. It also uses the head as the first point of contact, and it fails whenever the runner moves at the last moment, because a tackler who commits his whole body to one spot can’t adjust.
The modern approach is leverage tackling, and its most influential teachers were Pete Carroll’s Seattle Seahawks. In 2014 they made a 20-minute instructional video of their shoulder tackling, borrowed from rugby, and that August the league sent it, with a letter from Carroll, to coaches and parents at every level of the game; a second video in 2015 named its basic tackle the hawk tackle.3 The ideas fit together:

Leverage first. The tackler approaches with the runner on one side of him, usually inside-out, so the runner’s only escape is toward the sideline and the next defender. The pursuit angle in Figure 31.7 is the start of the tackle, not something separate from it.
The near shoulder to the near thigh. The target is the runner’s thighs (“eyes through the thighs,” in Seattle’s coaching points), not his chest; the shoulder makes contact and the head goes to the side, behind the runner on a tackle from an angle, out of the line of contact. The legs are what carry the ball, and they can’t dodge as easily as a torso can.
Wrap and roll. Arms around the thighs, keep the feet moving, and roll the runner to the ground, taking him toward the help rather than trying to drive him backward.
Breakdown in space. Within a couple of yards of the runner, the tackler shortens his steps and lowers his hips, so he can move either way with the runner’s last cut.

The rules have pushed in the same direction. In March 2024 the league banned the hip-drop tackle, in which a tackler grabs a runner from behind and swings his hips and weight down onto the runner’s legs, with a 15-yard penalty; the details are in Contact Rules and Penalties.4 For the 2026 season the league and the players’ union added a three-strike system: a player called for three of five fouls (hip-drop, horse-collar, launching, hits on a defenseless player and blindside blocks) in a season is suspended for a game.5 Most of those fouls are committed by defenders tackling in pursuit, which is the linebacker’s daily life.

Why the second level is where tackles are made, and missed
Where on the field do linebackers actually tackle people? nflverse’s play-by-play records who made the tackle on every play, so we can ask the data. Figure 31.8 sorts every designed run from 2021 to 2025 by how far the runner got before he was brought down, and shows who made the tackle.


Show the Python
style.apply()
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.2, 3.6))
ax.axvspan(1.5, 4.5, color=style.GRID, alpha=0.55, lw=0, zorder=0)
order = ["Defensive line", "Outside linebacker (mostly edge)", "Inside linebacker", "Defensive back"]
cols = {"Defensive line": style.SERIES[3], "Outside linebacker (mostly edge)": style.SERIES[4],
        "Inside linebacker": style.SERIES[1], "Defensive back": style.SERIES[0]}
xs = np.arange(len(BIN_LABELS))
LABEL_Y = {"Defensive line": SHARE["Defensive line"].values[-1] - 2.5,
           "Outside linebacker (mostly edge)": SHARE["Outside linebacker (mostly edge)"].values[-1] + 1.0,
           "Inside linebacker": SHARE["Inside linebacker"].values[-1] + 2.5}
for g in order:
    lw = 2.6 if g == "Inside linebacker" else 1.6
    ax.plot(xs, SHARE[g].values, marker="o", ms=3.5, lw=lw, color=cols[g], zorder=3)
    ax.text(xs[-1] + 0.15, LABEL_Y.get(g, SHARE[g].values[-1]), g, va="center", fontsize=7.4, color=style.INK_2)
ax.set_xticks(xs, BIN_LABELS)
ax.set_xlabel("Yards gained on the run")
ax.set_ylabel("Share of tackles (%)")
ax.set_xlim(-0.3, len(BIN_LABELS) + 1.6)
ax.set_ylim(0, 85)
ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
ax.text(3.0, 80, "the second level (3-9 yards)", ha="center", fontsize=7.6, color=style.INK_2)
ax.spines["left"].set_visible(False)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 31.8: Who makes the tackle, by how far the run got. Every regular-season designed run from 2021 to 2025 that ended in a tackle (no scrambles, touchdowns or penalties), grouped by the yards gained, with the share of tackles made by each position group (the first tackler listed in nflverse play-by-play, matched to the team’s roster position that season). Inside linebackers are those listed ILB, MLB or LB; outside linebackers are those listed OLB, mostly 3-4 edge rushers but also some off-ball 4-3 outside linebackers, so the inside-linebacker line is a floor for off-ball linebackers. The defensive line makes most of the tackles at or near the line. The inside linebackers’ share holds at a fifth to a quarter out to 9 yards and peaks on runs of 5 to 9, as the line’s share collapses. Past 10 yards it is the defensive backs’ tackle.





Read the chart from left to right and you can watch the three levels hand the runner along. Runs stopped at or near the line are the defensive line’s: about two in five of those tackles. The inside linebackers’ share barely moves, a fifth to a quarter of the tackles on every run up to 9 yards, and it peaks, at about a quarter, on runs of 5 to 9 yards, just where the line’s share collapses. They never top the chart, because they share the second level with everyone else who flows to the ball, and because the roster labels undercount them. Past 10 yards the run has beaten them, and it is a defensive back’s tackle. Across all runs, inside linebackers made 22% of the tackles; their median tackle came on a run of 3 yards, against 2 for linemen and 5 for defensive backs.6
One thing in the chart deserves a second look: defensive backs already make 31% of the tackles on runs of only 5 or 6 yards. Those tackles split almost evenly among cornerbacks (39%), free safeties (31%) and strong safeties (30%). The corners are the leverage players on outside runs, turning the ball back in, as in Figure 31.7; the safeties are the eighth man in the box when a single-high defense rotates one down, or the “big nickel” safety playing linebacker. The second level isn’t only linebackers any more, which is where the end of this chapter is heading.
The chart is also a warning about the statistic fans quote most. A linebacker’s tackle total counts every tackle the same, but a tackle five yards downfield is a run that beat the defense first, and the best fill of the game, the one that meets the fullback at the line and makes the back bounce into a teammate, often goes in the box score under someone else’s name. Coaches grade linebackers on whether they were in their gap on time; the tackle is a by-product.
Missed tackles are not in the play-by-play, but Pro Football Reference charts them for every defender, and nflverse carries the numbers. Per hundred tackle attempts from 2021 to 2025 (runs and passes together), defensive linemen missed 7.2, inside linebackers 7.5, outside linebackers 8.4, safeties 8.5 and cornerbacks 9.9.7 The farther from the line a defender usually tackles, the more often he misses. A lineman tackles a back who is still in a crowd, barely moving, with nowhere to go. Past the line the runner is moving at full speed, with room to cut both ways, and the tackler is often coming off a block, from an angle, alone. The runner chooses his cut after seeing the tackler commit; the tackler has to commit first.
Two things stand out. Inside linebackers make their tackles in far more space than linemen do and miss barely more often: that is what leverage tackling, and all the drilling behind it, buys. (Take away one direction with your angle, and you only have to win the other.) And the misses that hurt are the ones past the line, because the cost of a miss grows with the space behind it: a lineman who misses leaves the back a crowd, a linebacker who misses leaves him a safety ten yards away.
For a play-by-play look, the 2024 Big Data Bowl was about tackling, and its data marks every missed tackle on nine weeks of 2022 plays. This chapter’s source includes code (not run here, because the data isn’t downloaded) that counts missed-tackle rates by position from it.


Show the Python (missed tackles by position, Big Data Bowl 2024 data; not run here)
# Data: https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/nfl-big-data-bowl-2024/data (tackles.csv, players.csv).
# Check the year's data dictionary; column names below are from the 2024 release.
import pandas as pd
tackles = pd.read_csv("data/bdb2024/tackles.csv")      # gameId, playId, nflId, tackle, assist, forcedFumble, pff_missedTackle
players = pd.read_csv("data/bdb2024/players.csv")      # nflId, position, ...
t = tackles.merge(players[["nflId", "position"]], on="nflId")
by_pos = t.groupby("position").agg(made=("tackle", "sum"), assists=("assist", "sum"),
                                   missed=("pff_missedTackle", "sum"))
by_pos["miss_rate"] = by_pos.missed / (by_pos.made + by_pos.assists + by_pos.missed)
print(by_pos.sort_values("miss_rate", ascending=False))

# To watch one of them: gridiron.bdb.prepare(tracking, plays, game_id, play_id) and show_animation().
