title: Cover 2 and Tampa 2
section: Why classic Tampa 2 faded, and what survived
text:
Why classic Tampa 2 faded, and what survived
In 2005 the Buccaneers had the NFL’s best total defense and the Bears the second-best.16 By 2006 a long list of teams (Buffalo, Minnesota, Kansas City, Detroit and others) had imported the system, often by hiring coaches from Dungy’s and Kiffin’s staffs. A decade later almost none of them played it as a base defense. What happened?
The rules leaned against it. The coverage depended on squeezing receivers’ releases and on underneath defenders who could disrupt routes as they crossed their zones. After the 2003 AFC Championship Game, in which New England’s physical defensive backs (Ty Law above all) took apart Peyton Manning’s Colts, the league made downfield contact past 5 yards a “point of emphasis” for the 2004 season (a rule the league tells officials to enforce more strictly that year), and the flags for illegal contact more than doubled, from 79 in 2003 to 191 in 2004.17 Physical zone coverage became expensive. (There’s an irony in it: the Colts’ complaints drove the change, and Dungy was the Colts’ head coach.) Dynasties and Counterpunches tells the story of that rule and the passing boom that followed.
Offenses learned to live in the seam. A Tampa 2 Mike carrying a tight end up the middle was a fair fight in 1999. Against a 6-foot-6 tight end who ran like a receiver, or a slot receiver lined up as the inside man in a trips formation, it wasn’t. Offenses also learned to attack the hole the Mike vacates, with digs and curls that sit down 12 to 15 yards deep in front of him, and to flood the sideline holes the squat corners leave. Peyton Manning, who practised against Dungy’s Tampa 2 every day in Indianapolis, became one of the best at taking it apart (that, too, is in Dynasties and Counterpunches).
The Mikes were rare. A middle linebacker who can stop the run between the tackles and also run 20 yards with a receiver is one of the rarest athletes in the sport. Teams that copied the scheme without one found out quickly what Cover 2 without a deep middle defender looks like.
Light boxes met better run games. A two-deep, four-rush defense lives with six or seven defenders near the line. That was survivable when offenses lined up in two-back formations and ran into the teeth of it; it was less survivable against spread formations that thinned the box further and against run games designed to exploit it.
Then the league went one-high, and then two-high again, but differently. Through the early 2010s the fashionable answer to everything was Pete Carroll’s Seattle Cover 3, a single-high defense with press corners and an eighth defender near the line (The Cover 3 Family). (Gus Bradley, Seattle’s defensive coordinator from 2009 to 2012, had coached linebackers under Kiffin in Tampa.) When two-high defense came back after 2018, it came back as quarters and match coverage: two safeties who read the receivers in front of them and fit the run, not two safeties guarding halves while the Mike runs the middle (Quarters and the Two-High Match Family).

What survived
A great deal, just not under its old name.

Cover 2 itself. It never left. Next Gen Stats counted 13.9 percent of 2025 dropbacks as Cover 2 (the source is in the note on 2-Man’s situations), and the FTN charting in nflverse labels even more; it remains a standard call on long yardage, at the end of halves, and as a change-up for defenses whose base is something else.
The Mike who carries the seam. “The middle defender carries #3 vertical” (if the third receiver from the sideline runs straight up the field, the middle linebacker runs with him) is now a rule in Cover 3 match and quarters, the descendants of spot-drop zone. Any time you see a linebacker turn and run with a tight end up the middle of the field in a modern zone, that’s the Tampa 2 Mike’s job inside a newer coverage (Cover 3 match).
Two-high pictures that become three-deep. The Tampa 2’s real trick was showing two deep safeties and playing with three deep defenders after the snap. Modern defenses do the same thing by rotating a safety instead of running the Mike, and that is the whole subject of Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage.
Cover 2 as half a coverage. Cover 6 plays quarters to one side and Cover 2 to the other, squat corner and all; split-field defenses use the Cover 2 half to the short side of the field or against a formation’s lone receiver (Quarters and the Two-High Match Family).
2-Man on third down, as the chart above shows.
The people. The Tampa staffs of 1996–2008 seeded a generation of NFL coaches. Lovie Smith and Rod Marinelli took the system to Chicago and Detroit; Mike Tomlin, Tampa Bay’s defensive backs coach from 2001 to 2005, and Raheem Morris, who worked his way up the same secondary, became head coaches.18 The approach (simple calls, fast players, eyes on the quarterback, rally to the ball) outlived the coverage, and a branch of the tree, Matt Eberflus, ran some of the most Cover 2-heavy defenses of the charting era in Indianapolis and Chicago.19







TipWatch for it on Sunday: the squat-corner spotter



On every passing down for one quarter, look at the cornerbacks first.

Before the snap. Corners 5 to 7 yards off, a step outside the wide receiver, flat-footed, shoulders turned in toward the ball? Two safeties deep (12 to 14 yards) and wide (outside the hashes)? Think Cover 2. Corners pressed on the receiver’s inside shoulder on third-and-long? Lean 2-Man, but confirm it after the snap. Corners 7 or 8 off with two safeties deep? It may be quarters (Quarters and the Two-High Match Family), or a Cover 2 that squats only at the snap (Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage).
At the snap. Does the corner punch the receiver and then stop, hips square, eyes on the quarterback, while the receiver runs past? Cover 2. Does he turn his hips and run with him, eyes on the receiver? 2-Man (or a disguise into something else).
One second later. Find the Mike. Did he stop at 10 yards, eyes on the quarterback? Cover 2. Is he still running straight down the middle at 15? Tampa 2.
When the ball is thrown. Where did it go? A sideline throw between the corner and the safety, or a seam between the safeties, is the offense attacking exactly the holes this chapter mapped. A completed 6-yard out on third-and-12, followed by an immediate tackle, is the coverage winning.

ruler(fld, pr1, widths=True)
plt.show()








Figure 36.9: First-and-10 at midfield, ball in the middle of the field. Two safeties deep. The left corner is 5 yards off X, a step outside him; the right corner is 8 yards off Z, nearly head-up. The cornerbacks and safeties are ringed. Use the depth numbers on the left and the hash marks along the bottom.





The two corners disagree. Which coverages fit this picture, which side would you attack with smash or a hole shot, and what would you check in the first second after the snap?






TipAnswer





Several coverages fit; the left side means the same thing in all of them. A two-high shell with one squat corner could be plain Cover 2 (the right corner will squat at the snap), Cover 6 (Cover 2 on the left, quarters on the right; see Quarters and the Two-High Match Family), or Cover 3 with a cloud rotation to the left, where the left safety runs to the deep outside third and the other safety spins to the middle (The Cover 3 Family).
Attack the left. In every one of those, the left corner is a flat defender with a safety coming from inside and deep to cover the sideline behind him. Smash (hitch by X, corner route by H) or a go route by X with H up the seam attacks exactly that grass. Smash is a high-low on the squat corner whatever the coverage behind him; that’s why it’s a favourite call against a squat corner you can see.
Then check, in the first second: does one safety race to the middle of the field? Then it’s cloud Cover 3, the deep middle is closed, and the hole shot is against a safety running to his third. Do both safeties stay on their sides? Then it’s Cover 2 or Cover 6, and the right corner tells you which: squatting at the snap means Cover 2, backpedalling to a deep quarter means Cover 6.











TipPredict the play 2: the tight end up the middle





Show the Python
off = offense("gun_trips")
dfn = c2_shell(off, corner_d=5.5)
mv = {"NB": (5.0, 9.5), "MIKE": (4.5, 2.0), "WILL": (5.0, -4.0)}
dfn = [p.moved(d=mv[p.key][0], w=mv[p.key][1]) if p.key in mv else p for p in dfn]
pr2 = Play(off, dfn, los=40, to_go=7)
pr2.route("Y", r.path((2.0, 0.6), (12.0, -3.5), (22.0, -4.0)))
pr2.highlight("MIKE", "Y")
fld = pr2.draw(lateral="full", window=(-7.5, 24))
no_numbers(fld.ax)
ruler(fld, pr2, widths=True)
plt.show()








Figure 36.10: Second-and-7. Trips to the offense’s right: Z (#1), H (#2) and the tight end Y (#3), in-line. The defense shows a two-high shell with squat corners. On this play Y will run straight up the middle of the field. The Mike (M) and Y are ringed.





(a) If this is plain Cover 2 played by the book, who has Y? (b) What would you watch in the first second to know whether it’s Tampa 2? (c) The defense has seen this formation all game. What might it have changed, and where would you look for it before the snap?






TipAnswer





(a) By the book, almost nobody. The Mike drops to the hole at 10 to 12 yards and watches Y run past him. The trips-side safety has three receivers in his half, and the outside two are running routes he can’t ignore; the far safety is guarding the left half and X. Y ends up in the deep middle, between the two safeties: thin spot ③. This is the classic way to attack Cover 2 from trips.
(b) The Mike. At one second, is he still running, opening toward the trips side and getting on top of Y? That is Tampa 2: the Mike carries #3 up the pipe, which is exactly the throw it was built to take away. Then the question becomes who is running up the middle. A big, slow tight end against a fast linebacker is a fair fight; a fast tight end or a slot receiver against a linebacker 15 yards downfield is not. And the dig by H, sitting down at 12 to 14 yards where the Mike used to be, is open underneath him.
(c) Look at the backside safety, the one on X’s side. He has only X in his half, and his corner is already sitting short on X’s side, so the most common adjustment is to give him #3: he cheats a couple of yards toward the middle before the snap, or he drifts there at the snap, and Y’s seam runs into him. Other defenses hand #3 to the Mike every snap, or check out of Cover 2 entirely against trips (Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage). A backside safety narrower than his partner is your pre-snap hint.











TipPredict the play 3: third-and-8, two-high, corners outside





Show the Python
off = offense("gun_2x2")
pr3 = Play(off, c2_shell(off, corner_d=5.0, safety_d=13.0), los=45, to_go=8)
pr3.highlight("LCB", "RCB", "NB", "WILL", "MIKE")
fld = pr3.draw(lateral="full", window=(-7.5, 17.5))
no_numbers(fld.ax)
ruler(fld, pr3, widths=True)
plt.show()








Figure 36.11: Third-and-8. Two safeties 13 yards deep. Both corners are 5 yards off, a step outside their receivers; the Will (W) is 5 yards off over the slot receiver H and the nickel ($) over the tight end Y. The ringed defenders are the five possible man defenders. The quarterback is a good runner.





Cover 2 or 2-Man? Which is more likely, what single thing would you watch in the first second, and how would you design the pass so the quarterback has an answer either way?






TipAnswer





You can’t be sure, and that is the point of the alignment. Third-and-8 is where 2-Man peaks, but even there Cover 2 is called about twice as often: on third or fourth and 7 to 10, the charting behind the down-and-distance chart has Cover 2 on roughly 12 to 17 percent of dropbacks and 2-Man on 6 to 10. And the corners are showing Cover 2’s alignment, off and outside, not the press-inside look of a 2-Man lean. So the base rate says Cover 2, with 2-Man very much alive.
Watch the corners’ hips and eyes. If a corner opens his hips and runs with his receiver, eyes on him, it’s 2-Man. If he stays square, eyes on the quarterback, and lets the receiver go, it’s Cover 2.
Design for both. Offenses facing this picture often put a zone-beater on one side and a man-beater on the other and let the quarterback pick after the snap: smash to one side (it beats the squat corner in zone), and a rub or an out-breaking route to the other (it beats a man defender playing inside leverage). And if it is 2-Man and nobody is open, the quarterback’s legs are the answer: five defenders have their backs to him, unless the one on the running back has been told to rush or spy. Throwing deep is the one thing not to do: two safeties are waiting there either way.

title: Cover 2 and Tampa 2
text:
Takeaways

Cover 2 is two deep and five under. The safeties each guard a deep half; the corners guard the flats; three linebackers (or two and a nickel) guard the hook-curl zones and the hole. It takes away the short throws and everything over the top, and it costs a defender in the box.
The hard (squat) corner is the tell. Five to seven yards off, outside leverage, eyes inside; at the snap he jams, sinks and sits in the flat. When you see two of them with two deep safeties, think Cover 2, then confirm it after the snap: a corner whose hips turn to run with the receiver is playing 2-Man.
Cover 2’s thin spots are known by heart: the hole shot along the sideline, the smash corner over the squat corner (the same grass, reached from inside), the deep middle between the safeties, and the intermediate sideline hole. Deep passes go to the middle against Cover 2 about one time in three, as often as or more often than against any other coverage in the charting data.
Tampa 2 sends the Mike down the middle: five underneath at the snap, then four under and three deep. It closes the deep middle, needs a rare linebacker, opens the intermediate middle (dagger and levels live there), and is Cover 2’s best answer to trips. It was the identity of Dungy and Kiffin’s Buccaneers, Dungy’s Colts and Lovie Smith’s Bears.
2-Man keeps the two deep safeties and plays man underneath, in trail technique with inside leverage. It’s a long-yardage and end-of-half call, vulnerable to scrambles, rubs and out-breaking routes.
Classic Tampa 2 faded (contact rules, seam-stretching offenses, rare Mikes, light boxes, the move to Cover 3 and then to quarters), but its pieces survive: Cover 2 as a call, the seam-carrying middle defender, two-high pictures that become three-deep, and a large coaching tree.

title: Quarters and the Two-High Match Family: Cover 4, Cover 6, Palms
text:
Quarters in one picture: four deep, but not really
Second-and-8 near midfield. The offense comes out with three wide receivers and a tight end, two receivers on each side. Before the snap the broadcast’s high camera shows both safeties standing only about 9 or 10 yards deep, one over each slot receiver, and both cornerbacks backed off 7 or 8 yards. It looks soft. The offense hands the ball off on an inside run, and the first defender to hit the running back, four yards downfield, is one of those safeties, arriving at full speed from a spot that looked like pass coverage. Two plays later the offense fakes the same run and throws deep, and the same safety is running stride for stride with the tight end up the seam. How can one player be a deep pass defender and a run stopper on the same snap? And why did NFL defenses, which spent the 2010s crowding an eighth man into the box, spend the next six years taking him back out? The answer is a coverage with a misleading name: quarters.
You’ll be able to…
Start with the name, because it misleads almost everyone. Quarters, also called Cover 4, is a two-high coverage in which four defenders, the two cornerbacks and the two safeties, each start with a deep quarter of the field, a lane about 13 yards wide (hence the “4” in the numbering system). If that were the whole story, quarters would be a passive coverage: four defenders guarding deep grass, three underneath, plenty thrown in front of them. But each of those four deep defenders has a rule that tells him whom to cover once the receivers start running, and two of those rules point the safeties forward, not back. Here are the alignment and the rules against the NFL’s most common formation, a 2x2 set with the tight end attached.
Show the Python
off = pro_2x2()
p = Play(off, quarters_vs(off), los=35, to_go=None)
for w in (-19.0, -6.5, 6.5, 19.0):
    p.zone((18.0, w), (7.0, 12.2), "deep ¼")
for key, txt in (("X", "#1"), ("H", "#2"), ("Y", "#2"), ("Z", "#1")):
    p.note(txt, at=(p.players[key].d - 3.2, p.players[key].w))
p.highlight("FS", "SS", "LCB", "RCB")
fld = p.draw(lateral="full", window=(-7.5, 22.5))
no_numbers(fld.ax)
ruler(fld, p, widths=True)
say(fld, p, "CB: MOD on #1\n(man if he goes deep)", (12.0, -18.3), fs=6.6)
say(fld, p, "CB: MOD on #1", (11.5, 20.5), fs=6.6)
say(fld, p, "FS: read #2", (12.6, -7.0), fs=6.6)
say(fld, p, "SS: read #2", (12.6, 7.0), fs=6.6)
say(fld, p, "$: wall #2,\nthen the flat", (2.6, -11.0), fs=6.6)
say(fld, p, "W: run, then hook", (7.0, -4.6), fs=6.3)
say(fld, p, "M: run, then Y's flat", (7.0, 5.4), fs=6.3)
say(fld, p, "E: edge,\njams Y", (-2.5, 9.6), fs=6.3)
plt.show()








Figure 37.1: Quarters against a 2x2 formation (11 personnel, tight end attached on the right). The shaded ovals are the four deep quarters each defender starts with, but the labels are what matter: each defender’s rule. The corners (CB) play MOD on the outside receiver, #1: man-to-man if he runs deep. The safeties (FS, SS) read the inside receiver on their side, #2: H on the left, the tight end Y on the right. On the slot side the nickel ($) at the apex walls off #2 and then takes the flat. The tight end’s side has no apex defender, so the Mike plays the run first and then becomes the first man to the flat if Y releases outside; the Will plays the run, then the hook. The end outside Y sets the edge and can jam him. Notice how shallow the safeties are, about 9 or 10 yards, and how narrow: the free safety a few yards inside the slot, the strong safety just outside the tight end. Cover 2 safeties stand at 12 to 14 yards and wider.
Go around the picture one position at a time.
Now count the defenders against the two receivers on one side. On the slot side: the corner, the safety, the apex defender and, a step inside, a linebacker. On the tight end’s side: the corner, the safety, the Mike and the end. Four players against two receivers, with the back as a possible third. Coaches like to say quarters is really “four over two” on each side, not four deep, and that everyone deep is also, depending on what the receivers do, a man defender or a run defender. That is what makes quarters a pattern-matching coverage, and the purest one in common use.

title: Quarters and the Two-High Match Family: Cover 4, Cover 6, Palms
text:
The corners line up 7 or 8 yards off the outside receiver (#1), square or with a slight outside shade, eyes on him. Their rule, MOD, gets its own section below. The short version: if #1 runs deep, the corner has him man-to-man; if #1 runs a short route, the corner lets him go and drops into his deep quarter.
The safeties are the heart of the coverage. They line up 8 to 10 yards deep (some teams 10 to 12): a few yards inside a slot receiver, or over or just outside an attached tight end, who is already inside the box. That’s much shallower and narrower than a Cover 2 safety, who has to reach the sideline and so stands at 12 to 14 yards, outside the hash. The quarters safety doesn’t have a sideline to reach. His real job is to read the inside receiver.
The apex defender, here the nickel back on the slot side, stands between the tackle and the slot, 4 or 5 yards deep. Against a pass his first job is to wall #2: get in the slot receiver’s path from the inside and keep him from running freely up the seam, so the safety behind has time to read him. Then he takes the first receiver who comes to the flat, the running back included.
The linebackers read run first. Against a pass they drop to the hook zones and take the running back if he runs up the middle. On the tight end’s side there is no apex defender, so the strong-side linebacker (here the Mike) is the first man to the flat if the tight end releases outside.
The front rushes four. The end outside the tight end is the edge (contain) player against runs to his side, and he can jam the tight end on his way out.








NoteMadden vs. real life



In a video game’s play menu, “Cover 4” usually draws four blue deep zones and three short ones, and the defenders drop to them like spot-drop zone players. If the real coverage worked that way it would be a prevent defense (the soft, everyone-deep look teams use to protect a late lead, covered in Clock and Game Management): four defenders guarding grass 15 yards deep while the offense completes everything underneath. Real quarters is a read coverage. The deep quarters are starting points; the receivers’ first steps decide who covers whom, and the two safeties spend the first second of every snap deciding whether they are deep defenders at all. If you remember one thing from this chapter, make it this: quarters safeties play the inside receiver, not a zone.








ImportantWhy it exists



What it solves. A defense wants two things that normally conflict: two safeties deep, so the offense can’t hit an explosive pass over the top, and an extra run defender, so it can’t run the ball down its throat. Quarters gets both from the same two players. Standing at 9 or 10 yards instead of 13, a safety is close enough to the line to fit a run in time and deep enough to carry a receiver up the seam.
What it gives up. The shallow, inside-leaning safeties are reading, and anything that makes them read wrong hurts: a run fake, a receiver whose release looks like a block, a route that starts one way and ends another. With only three defenders underneath, the short outside throws (the quick out, the hitch, the flat) belong to the offense unless a corner or an apex defender takes them away. Quarters trades a few easy short completions for no deep ones, and asks its safeties to be right.

section: The read safety: one key, three answers
text:
The read safety: one key, three answers
The quarters safety is the clearest example of a read safety: a safety whose job is decided after the snap by a single key receiver, usually #2 on his side. Coaches teach it as three answers to one question, what did #2 do?


Show the Python
def read_panel(ax, branch):
    off = pro_2x2()
    p = Play(off, quarters_vs(off), los=35, to_go=None)
    p.highlight("SS")
    if branch == "vert":
        p.route("Y", r.seam(18)); p.route("Z", r.go(18))
        p.drop("SS", (19.0, 5.2), speed=5.0); p.drop("RCB", (19.5, 16.3), speed=5.0)
        p.drop("MIKE", (8.0, 3.5))
        title, txt, at = "#2 goes vertical: carry him", "SS: man on #2", (11.5, 9.6)
    elif branch == "out":
        p.route("Y", r.flat(2.0, 7.0)); p.route("Z", r.dig(12, 8))
        p.drop("SS", (8.4, 11.0), speed=5.0); p.drop("RCB", (14.5, 15.0), speed=3.5)
        p.drop("MIKE", (3.2, 10.0), speed=4.5)     # first man to the flat on the tight end's side
        title, txt, at = "#2 goes out: help on #1", "SS: bracket #1\ninside", (16.5, 7.0)
    else:
        p.block("Y", "SDE")
        p.block("RT", "MIKE"); p.block("RG", "SDT"); p.block("C", "WDT")
        p.run("RB", [(1.5, 1.6), (5.2, 3.8)], speed=6.0); p.handoff("RB", 0.6)   # aimed at the C gap
        p.drop("SS", (5.6, 5.8), speed=5.5); p.drop("RCB", (9.5, 15.4), speed=1.0)
        title, txt, at = "#2 blocks: run, fill the alley", "SS: alley\nplayer", (15.5, 6.5)
    fld = clip(p.draw(ax=ax, lateral=(-3.5, 21.5), window=(-6.5, 22.5), title=False))
    no_numbers(ax)
    say(fld, p, "#2", (-3.2, 4.8), fs=6.5)
    say(fld, p, "#1", (-4.0, 15.0), fs=6.5)
    if branch == "out":
        say(fld, p, "M: first man\nto the flat", (5.8, 7.0), fs=6.0)
    say(fld, p, txt, at, fs=6.6, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, weight="bold")
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=8.2, loc="left", color=style.INK)


fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(6.6, 4.3))
for ax, b in zip(axes, ("vert", "out", "run")):
    read_panel(ax, b)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.5)
plt.show()








Figure 37.2: The strong safety’s three answers to one key, the tight end Y (#2), on the offense’s right. Left: Y releases straight up the seam, so the safety (ringed) turns and covers him like a man defender, while the corner goes deep with Z. Middle: Y releases to the flat, so the safety has no #2 to cover; he works to the outside receiver (#1) and sits inside him, taking away Z’s in-breaking route (here a dig) while the corner stays over the top: a bracket. The Mike, the first man to the flat on the tight end’s side, runs to Y. Right: Y fires out low to base-block the end outside him, a block that says run, so the safety comes downhill to fill the alley outside the tight end and becomes the defense’s extra run defender. Same alignment, three jobs; the receiver chose.






#2 goes vertical: carry him. If the inside receiver runs up the seam, the safety covers him, man-to-man, as deep as he goes. With the corner on #1, every vertical route on that side has a defender on top of it.
#2 goes short or out: help on #1. If #2 runs to the flat or breaks off a short route, the safety has nobody to cover, so he turns to the outside receiver and sits inside him. Now #1 has the corner outside and over the top and the safety inside: a bracket, two defenders on one receiver. The dig and the post, the routes that hurt quarters corners most because they break away from the corner’s outside position, run straight into the safety. (If #2 runs inside, across the field, many systems tell the safety to pass him to the linebackers and look for work: #1 breaking in, or a crossing route coming from the other side.)
#2 blocks: it’s a run, so fill. If #2 is a tight end who blocks, or a slot receiver who steps up to block the apex defender, and the linemen in front of the safety fire out low, the safety reads run and comes downhill. In the language of Run Fits and Box Math, he becomes the alley player: he fills the lane between the edge and the box, inside-out, and he is the defense’s plus-one.

What counts as “vertical”? Most staffs draw the line where the corner’s rule does, at about 5 yards. A #2 who breaks out or in before that is short; a #2 still pushing upfield past it is vertical, and the safety stays on top of him until he breaks. If he then curls or digs at 10 or 12 yards, the safety sits over it with a hook defender underneath. Exact depths vary by staff.
Why does one receiver make such a good key? Because #2’s release tells the safety, almost instantly, both run-or-pass and where the danger is. A receiver who blocks is the strongest run signal there is; one who releases vertical is the danger; one who runs to the flat isn’t a deep threat, so the deep threat must be the outside man. Good safeties check it against the linemen in front of them: low hats confirm the run, but a #2 who “blocks” while the linemen pop up tall to pass-protect is selling a fake, a chip before a release or a play-action block. That check takes a beat, and it is the read’s weak spot, as the bootleg section will show.
That also explains where the safety stands. He has to be shallow enough to fill the alley before the running back gets through it, and deep enough to turn and run with a tight end up the seam without being beaten over the top. Nine or ten yards is the compromise. TCU’s Gary Patterson, one of the coaches who made quarters famous in college football, taught his safeties not to backpedal at the snap at all but to shuffle flat-footed and read, because a safety rocking backward can’t come forward in time.1 Watch one quarters safety for a whole game on the All-22 film (the high, wide camera coaches use) and you’ll be surprised how rarely he ends the play deep.

Four verticals: the stress test quarters was built for
The best way to see why match rules matter is the play that broke spot-drop zones in the 1980s and 1990s: four verticals, four receivers running straight up the field. Against spot-drop Cover 3, four vertical routes meet three deep defenders, and one of them has to guard two receivers (Cover 3 shows the seam opening). Against quarters, the rules simply add up.


Show the Python
off = spread_2x2()
p = Play(off, quarters_vs(off, {"NB": (4.8, 6.2), "WILL": (4.8, -6.2), "MIKE": (4.8, 0.0)}), los=35, to_go=None)
p.route("X", r.go(22)); p.route("Z", r.go(22)); p.route("H", r.seam(21)); p.route("Y", r.seam(21))
p.dropback(2.5)
protect(p)
p.drop("LCB", (22.5, -14.6), speed=5.5); p.drop("RCB", (22.5, 14.6), speed=5.5)
p.drop("FS", (21.0, -8.0), speed=5.5); p.drop("SS", (21.0, 8.0), speed=5.5)
p.drop("WILL", (8.0, -9.0)); p.drop("NB", (8.0, 9.0)); p.drop("MIKE", (7.0, 0.0))
p.highlight("LCB", "RCB", "FS", "SS")
fld = p.draw(lateral="full", window=(-8.5, 25.0))
no_numbers(fld.ax)
ruler(fld, p)
say(fld, p, "corners: #1 deep", (13.5, -21.0), fs=6.6)
say(fld, p, "safeties: #2 deep", (13.0, 0.0), fs=6.6)
say(fld, p, "$, W: wall,\nthen sink", (14.0, 12.0), fs=6.4)
plt.show()








Figure 37.3: Four verticals against quarters from a spread 2x2 (the tight end flexed out as the right slot). Each corner (CB) takes #1 deep, man-to-man, because #1 went vertical; each safety (FS, SS) takes #2 deep, because #2 went vertical. The apex defenders (W on the left, $ on the right) wall the slots for a step or two, then sink under the outside receivers. Four vertical routes, four deep defenders, each on top of a receiver.





Notice what the defense didn’t need: a decision. Nobody had to choose between two receivers; the rules assigned one defender to each. That doesn’t make four verticals hopeless. Every deep defender is now man-to-man with nobody in the deep middle, so a great outside receiver against a corner (a fade, a back-shoulder throw) can still win, and the running back checking down against three underneath defenders is the offense’s release valve. Offenses also built concepts aimed straight at the safety’s read: dagger (a deep dig behind a clearing seam) and scissors (a post by #1 crossing a corner route by #2), both in Dropback Concepts, and the weaknesses section below adds three more.

section: The corner’s rule: MOD and MEG
text:
The corner’s rule: MOD and MEG
The safety’s rule only works if the corner’s rule fits with it. Quarters teams use two, and the names come from the playbook vocabulary that spread out of Nick Saban’s defenses (more on that history below).
MOD, short for man only deep, is the standard quarters corner rule. The corner covers #1 man-to-man if #1 runs a deep route. If #1 breaks his route off short, about 5 yards or less (a hitch, a quick out, a slant, a shallow cross), the corner doesn’t chase him. He passes him to the underneath defenders and drops into his deep quarter, looking for the next threat to come into it. “Deep” here means anything past that 5-yard line, so a 12-yard dig or a curl counts: the corner stays on it. That is nearly word for word the rule Cameron Soran decoded from Saban’s playbooks, which also give the other two clauses of the same call. The safety: take all of #2 vertical; if #2 isn’t vertical, bracket #1. The apex defender: take the first man to the flat, rerouting #2 first if he starts vertical.2
MEG, short for man everywhere he goes, is the other rule. The corner covers #1 on every route, short or deep, no exceptions. You met MEG in Cover 3 as the backside corner’s rule in a trips check; it shows up wherever a defense needs one corner to take care of his man alone so that the defenders around him can do something else.


Show the Python
def modmeg_panel(ax, kind):
    off = spread_2x2()
    mv = {"NB": (4.8, -6.4)}
    if kind == "MEG":
        mv["LCB"] = (1.0, -14.1)                     # MEG from press, inside shade on X
    p = Play(off, quarters_vs(off, mv), los=35, to_go=None)
    p.route("X", r.slant(2, 6)); p.route("H", r.path((10, 0), (18, 5.5)))
    if kind == "MOD":
        p.highlight("LCB", "FS")
        p.drop("LCB", (15.5, -15.6), speed=4.0)
        p.drop("FS", (16.5, -13.2), speed=5.0)
        p.drop("NB", (5.0, -10.0)); p.drop("WILL", (6.5, -4.0))
        title = "MOD: #1 breaks short, so the corner zones off"
        lab = [("slant: left to\nthe underneath\ndefenders", (9.0, -21.0)),
               ("corner route:\nCB and FS\nboth on it", (20.5, -12.5))]
    else:
        p.highlight("LCB", "NB")
        p.drop("LCB", (3.8, -12.3), speed=5.0); p.drop("LCB", (6.6, -10.6), speed=5.0)
        p.drop("FS", (16.5, -14.5), speed=5.0)
        p.drop("NB", (10.0, -12.0), speed=5.0); p.drop("WILL", (6.0, -4.5))
        title = "MEG: the corner goes wherever #1 goes"
        lab = [("CB alone\non the slant", (9.0, -21.0)),
               ("$ freed: sinks\nunder the corner\nroute; FS over it", (20.5, -11.5))]
    fld = clip(p.draw(ax=ax, lateral=(-25.0, 3.5), window=(-6.5, 24.0), title=False))
    no_numbers(ax)
    for txt, at in lab:
        say(fld, p, txt, at, fs=6.6)
    say(fld, p, "#1", (-3.0, -15.0), fs=6.5); say(fld, p, "#2", (-3.8, -9.0), fs=6.5)
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=8.0, loc="left", color=style.INK)


fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 4.2))
for ax, k in zip(axes, ("MOD", "MEG")):
    modmeg_panel(ax, k)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.8)
plt.show()








Figure 37.4: MOD and MEG against the same two routes, offense’s left side: X (#1) runs a quick slant, H (#2) a corner route toward the sideline. Left, MOD: X broke inside at 2 yards, so the corner (CB, ringed) lets him go to the underneath defenders (the nickel, $, drives on the slant) and drops into his deep quarter, right where H’s corner route is heading. The free safety (FS, ringed) carries H because H went vertical. Two defenders on the corner route, and the slant left to the defender in front of it. Right, MEG, played here from press: the corner stays with X on the slant by himself, with no inside help (the cost). In exchange the nickel (ringed) isn’t needed on the slant, so he is free to sink under H’s corner route while the free safety stays over it (the benefit). Both rules double one route; they differ in who is left alone.





The trade is clear in the two panels.

MOD keeps the corner deep and gives the defense extra help on the dangerous routes. Short routes by #1 are left to the defenders already in front of them (the apex defender, the linebackers), who can rally and tackle for a short gain. The corner, freed from the short route, becomes a second defender on whatever goes deep on his side, often #2 breaking outside, as here. The cost: the short throw to #1 is there if the underneath defenders are slow to it, and a receiver who fakes short and goes deep (a stop-and-go, a slant-and-go) can catch a MOD corner who passed him off too early.
MEG locks the corner on his man and frees someone else. In the figure the freed player is the nickel; in the trips checks of Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage it is a whole safety, who leaves his side to help elsewhere. The cost: the corner is on an island with no inside help, and every route that breaks away from him, especially a slant or a dig against an off corner, is his problem alone. MEG needs a corner the defense trusts.

A defense picks between them by situation and by personnel. A team with one great corner might play him MEG on the opponent’s best receiver and MOD on the other side. Against a lone receiver in a trips formation, MEG on the backside corner is the standard way to free the backside safety. And in the red zone MEG becomes more common, because MOD’s escape hatch is gone: with the end line 10 or 15 yards away there is no deep quarter to retreat into, so the short routes are the dangerous ones, and a corner who passes them off has nothing left to guard.






NoteGo deeper: rules that agree with each other



The rules fit together like a contract. MOD says “I’ll let #1 go if he’s short”; the apex and hook defenders say “we’ll take what comes short, outside and inside”; the safety says “if #2 isn’t vertical, I’ll bracket #1,” covering the one thing MOD gives up deep. Change one clause, from MOD to MEG for example, and every other clause shifts with it. That is why match defenses talk so much before the snap.

title: Quarters and the Two-High Match Family: Cover 4, Cover 6, Palms
section: Quarters against the run: the safeties fit from depth
text:
Quarters against the run: the safeties fit from depth
Now the part of quarters that made it a run defense. Look back at the alignment: four defensive linemen and two linebackers in the box, six defenders, against five offensive linemen and a tight end, six blockers. By the box count of A First Look at Defense that is a light box: every run defender can be blocked and nobody is left over. A defense playing one-high would usually have walked its strong safety down to make it seven against six.
Quarters gets its seventh (and sometimes eighth) run defender from 9 or 10 yards away: when #2 blocks and the linemen fire out low, the safety comes downhill into the alley. College coaches with a 4-3 front call it a “nine-man front,” seven defenders near the line plus two safeties who arrive when the play is a run.


Show the Python
def run_play():
    off = pro_2x2()
    p = Play(off, quarters_vs(off), los=35, to_go=None)
    # inside zone right: the line steps right; Y base-blocks the end; the center and right tackle climb
    p.block("LT", "WDE"); p.block("LG", "WDT"); p.block("RG", "SDT"); p.block("Y", "SDE")
    p.block("C", "WILL", speed=2.6); p.block("RT", "MIKE", speed=2.6)
    p.run("RB", [(-4.6, 0.2), (-1.0, 2.6), (2.0, 4.6), (4.0, 6.5)], delay=0.25, speed=6.2, absolute=True)
    p.handoff("RB", 0.6)
    p.route("X", [(2.0, 0.0)], speed=3.0); p.route("Z", [(2.5, 0.0)], speed=3.0)   # stalk blocks
    p.route("H", r.seam(18))                                                     # H releases
    for k, to in (("WDE", (1.2, -4.6)), ("WDT", (1.3, -1.6)), ("SDT", (1.3, 2.0)), ("SDE", (1.4, 6.2))):
        p.path(k, [to], absolute=True, speed=1.0)
    p.path("MIKE", [(3.6, 2.6)], absolute=True, speed=2.0); p.path("WILL", [(3.8, 0.4)], absolute=True, speed=2.0)
    p.drop("SS", (5.2, 7.6), speed=4.6, delay=0.45)      # reads Y's low block: run, so fill the alley
    p.drop("FS", (16.0, -8.8), speed=5.0, delay=0.2)     # reads H's release: pass, so stay with him
    p.drop("RCB", (5.5, 13.6), speed=2.2, delay=0.4)     # Z blocks him: the corner comes up outside-in
    p.drop("LCB", (9.0, -15.4), speed=2.0); p.drop("NB", (6.0, -8.0), speed=2.0)
    p.highlight("SS", "FS")
    return p


run_c4 = run_play()
RUN_T = [0.0, 0.5, 1.3, 2.1]
if PDF:
    strip(run_c4, RUN_T, ["Snap · six in the box against six blockers", "+0.5 s · Y blocks low: the SS reads run",

          ghosts=("SS", "FS"), lateral=(-20, 20), window=(-8.0, 18.5),
          notes_at={0: [("6 v 6", (-3.4, -6.5))], 2: [("H released:\nFS stays deep", (13.0, -14.0))],
                    3: [("alley", (8.0, 11.5))]})
    plt.show()
else:

Figure 37.5: Quarters against inside zone, frame by frame (simulated). Snap: six defenders in the box against six blockers, with both safeties (ringed) 9 to 10 yards deep. +0.5 s: the tight end Y (the strong safety’s #2) fires out low to block the end, and the line steps right: run. +1.3 s: the strong safety (SS) is already coming downhill into the alley outside the tight end, while the free safety (FS), whose #2 (H) released up the field, stays with him: H took the FS out of the run fit. +2.1 s: the ball carrier (R, with the brown ball beside him) bends the run outside and the SS meets him three or four yards downfield. The dashed outlines show where the safeties stood at the snap. The run went toward Y, so losing the FS cost the defense nothing here; the text explains why the offense would rather run the other way.




Three things in that play are worth slowing down for.
The trigger is a read, not a call. The strong safety didn’t know before the snap that this would be a run. He found out from Y’s block in the first half-second, and he went. That is the difference between quarters and the rotation of Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage, where a safety is told before the snap to come down at the snap, read or no read. The called rotation arrives sooner, and it is wrong whenever the guess is wrong. The read arrives later, and an honest pass never pulls it forward, because #2 running a route is a pass read. Its weak spot is the dishonest run look, a play-action fake and a #2 who pretends to block, which is exactly what the bootleg flood below attacks.
He meets the back past the line of scrimmage. From 9 or 10 yards the safety is a beat later than a linebacker at 4 or 5, so he typically makes the play three to five yards downfield, roughly the bargain Run Fits and Box Math describes for the two-high light box: give up a four-yard run, never a forty-yard pass.
The other safety went with his receiver. The free safety’s #2, H, released up the field, a pass read, so the free safety stayed with him and was out of the run fit. Here that cost the defense nothing, because the run went toward Y and the safety who filled was the play-side one. Now flip it: run the same play to the left, toward H. H releases, the free safety (now the play-side safety) goes with him, and the only safety left to fill is the strong safety, on the backside, arriving late through traffic. That is the offense’s main weapon against quarters’ run defense, and it costs the offense little, one fewer blocker on the perimeter (the nickel is left unblocked, so the back has to beat him). Offenses with a good slot receiver run the ball away from the tight end for exactly this reason, and RPOs go one step further by letting the quarterback read that safety and throw to the receiver if he comes down anyway.
Had H blocked instead, the free safety still wouldn’t have raced to the ball. With the run going away from him he is the cutback player, filling late and inside-out in case the back reverses course, and the first defender who has to see a bootleg or a reverse coming back his way. Outside the safeties, the end sets the edge on the tight end’s side and the corner comes up once Z blocks him; on the slot side the nickel is both the force player and the first man to the flat, the overhang defender job (the defender outside the box, over the slot). Names vary by staff; the geometry, an outside defender who forces and a safety who fills inside him, doesn’t.






ImportantWhy it exists: run support from the secondary



What it solves. Most of the time a defense that wants an extra run defender has to show him: a safety walked down to 7 or 8 yards before the snap, which tells the offense to throw. Quarters hides the extra defender inside a two-high picture and lets the offense’s own blocking call him into the fit. Every running play is met by six defenders in the box plus one or two who arrive late from depth, and every pass that looks like a pass is met by two safeties who never left.
What it gives up. Time and certainty. The safety arrives after the back has crossed the line, so quarters gives up more yards per run than an eight-man box, and he must tackle in space with nobody behind him. And anything that disguises the read attacks the coverage at its heart.

title: Quarters and the Two-High Match Family: Cover 4, Cover 6, Palms
section: Cover 6: quarters on one side, Cover 2 on the other
text:
Cover 6: quarters on one side, Cover 2 on the other
Quarters works beautifully when each side of the formation has two receivers. Formations don’t always cooperate. Against trips, one side has three receivers and the other a lone receiver, and on the lone receiver’s side there is no #2 at all: a read-#2 safety has nothing to read. The most common fix is to split the field. Cover 6 plays quarters on one half of the field and Cover 2 on the other, which is why coaches also call it quarter-quarter-half (the corner and safety each take a quarter on one side; one safety takes the whole half on the other). The number is dialect, not law: in Vic Fangio’s system the split-field family is Cover 6 and Cover 8, and his Cover 8 flips the halves, putting the Cover 2 half toward the passing strength (Coverage Fundamentals has the dialect notes).
Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage shows Cover 6 in its most common NFL use, against a 2x2 set split by field position (quarters to the wide side, Cover 2 to the short side). Here it is against a 3x1 trips set, one of the formations that calls for it, with the split made by formation: quarters to the three receivers, Cover 2 to the lone receiver.


Show the Python
off = offense("gun_trips")
mv = {"RCB": (7.5, 17.6), "SS": (9.5, 8.6), "NB": (4.6, 7.5), "MIKE": (4.8, 2.4), "WILL": (4.8, -2.2),
      "LCB": (5.5, -16.2), "FS": (12.5, -7.0)}
p = Play(off, quarters_vs(off, mv), los=35, to_go=None)
p.zone((18.0, -13.0), (8.0, 25.0), "deep ½")
p.zone((18.0, 6.5), (7.0, 12.0), "¼"); p.zone((18.0, 19.0), (7.0, 12.0), "¼")
p.zone((3.8, -20.0), (4.0, 8.0), "flat")
p.highlight("LCB", "RCB", "FS", "SS")
fld = p.draw(lateral="full", window=(-7.5, 25.5))
no_numbers(fld.ax)
ruler(fld, p, widths=True)
(x0, y0), (x1, y1) = fld.xy(*p.to_abs(-6.5, 0.0)), fld.xy(*p.to_abs(24.5, 0.0))
fld.ax.plot([x0, x1], [y0, y1], color=style.INK_2, lw=1.0, ls=(0, (6, 4)), zorder=2)
say(fld, p, "COVER 2 HALF", (23.6, -6.5), fs=7.5, weight="bold")
say(fld, p, "QUARTERS", (23.6, 5.0), fs=7.5, weight="bold")
for txt, key in (("#1", "Z"), ("#2", "H"), ("#3", "Y")):
    q = p.players[key]
    say(fld, p, txt, (q.d - 2.6, q.w), fs=6.6)
say(fld, p, "CB: squat,\nthe flat", (8.6, -20.6), fs=6.4)
say(fld, p, "FS: deep half\nover X", (15.2, -7.0), fs=6.4)
say(fld, p, "W: curl/hook", (7.4, -4.6), fs=6.4)
say(fld, p, "CB: MOD on #1", (11.0, 20.6), fs=6.4)
say(fld, p, "SS: read #2", (12.3, 9.4), fs=6.4)
say(fld, p, "$: wall #2", (2.7, 10.8), fs=6.4)
say(fld, p, "M: carry #3\nif vertical", (7.6, 3.2), fs=6.4)
plt.show()








Figure 37.6: Cover 6 against 3x1 (trips right, the tight end Y attached as #3). The dashed line splits the two halves. Right, toward the three receivers, quarters: the corner plays MOD on #1 (Z), the strong safety reads #2 (H), the nickel ($) walls #2 from the apex, and the Mike carries #3 (Y) if he runs up the middle. Left, toward the lone receiver X, Cover 2: the corner squats 5 yards off with outside leverage to take the flat and short outside throws, the Will takes the curl and hook, and the free safety (FS) stands deeper and wider, 12 to 13 yards deep a few yards outside the hash, to take the whole deep half over X. Before the snap the halves already disagree: one shallow corner and one deep, one deep wide safety and one shallow inside one. That asymmetry is the Cover 6 tell.





Why put Cover 2 on the lone receiver? Look at what the two defenders on that side are doing to X. The squat corner sits in front of him, taking away the quick out, the hitch and the flat; the half-field safety sits over the top of him, taking away the go route. X is bracketed under and over by two defenders, which is more help than most single receivers ever see. That matters because offenses put their best receiver alone on the backside of trips precisely to get him a one-on-one matchup. Cover 6 says no.
The cost is on the trips side, where four defenders (corner, safety, nickel and Mike) handle three receivers who can all run deep. Nobody is uncovered: the corner has #1, the safety #2 and the Mike #3 if he runs up the middle. The problem is the matchup. If #2 and #3 both go vertical, the safety takes #2 and the Mike is left running down the seam with a tight end or a slot receiver, a race most linebackers lose. That is the trips problem in its purest form, and two-high defenses carry other answers to it, such as poach (the backside safety leaves the lone receiver to his corner and comes across to help on #3), which Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage covers in detail. Cover 6 is the simplest answer: give the lone receiver to two defenders, and trust four on three.
Cover 6 is also how Cover 2 survived: too easy to attack as a whole defense (Cover 2 and Tampa 2), it still earns its keep as half of one, aimed at the short side or a lone receiver. By NFL Next Gen Stats’ count, Cover 6 was 9.2% of coverages in 2025.3 After the snap the corners give it away, one squatting and one bailing; the Watch-for-it box at the end has the full sequence.

title: Quarters and the Two-High Match Family: Cover 4, Cover 6, Palms
section: Palms: the corner who traps the out
text:
Palms: the corner who traps the out
Quarters has one obvious soft spot: the flat, in the first second after the snap. The apex defender’s rule makes him the owner of the flat, but he starts inside #2, walling him off the seam, 4 or 5 yards from where a quick out breaks. On a throw that comes out in about a second he can’t widen in time. The corner is 8 yards deep playing #1, and the safety is reading #2 from 9. So a quick throw to #2 breaking toward the sideline lands in front of everyone. Offenses learned to throw it all day: the slot receiver’s quick out, the “now” throw to the flat (a cousin of the now screen), the out by the slot in a smash-type concept.
Palms is the answer. The same coverage goes by 2-read and, because of what the corner does, trap coverage. Different staffs use different names and slightly different rules, but the core is one adjustment on one side of the field: the corner reads #2 instead of #1.

If #2 breaks out quickly (inside the first 5 yards or so), the corner leaves #1 and jumps #2’s out or flat route. He was 6 or 7 yards deep, square or a little outside #1, with his eyes turned in to #2, so he comes forward and outside-in onto the throw instead of chasing it. That is the trap.
The safety, seeing #2 go out, takes #1 deep: he’s now the deep defender over the outside receiver whom the corner just left. In Saban’s version the safety’s rule reads: take #1 vertical if #2 is out in the first 5 yards; otherwise, take all of #2 vertical, and if #2 isn’t vertical, bracket #1.4
If #2 goes vertical, the safety carries #2 and the corner plays #1 man to man, in most versions without the MOD release, so a short route by #1 runs into a corner who is already shallow and squeezing.



Show the Python
def palms_play():
    off = spread_2x2()
    p = Play(off, quarters_vs(off, {"LCB": (6.3, -15.9)}), los=35, to_go=None)
    p.route("H", r.out(5.5, 6)); p.route("X", r.path((3, 0.6), (24, 1.4)))
    p.route("Y", r.seam(16)); p.route("Z", r.hitch(6))
    p.route("RB", r.flat(1.5, 5), side=1)
    p.dropback(2.5); p.pass_to("H", t=1.05)
    protect(p)
    p.drop("LCB", (6.6, -15.8), speed=1.0)                                    # sits and reads #2
    p.path("LCB", [(4.4, -15.0)], absolute=True, speed=4.6, delay=0.45)      # #2 out: drive on it, outside-in
    p.drop("FS", (19.0, -14.6), speed=6.0, delay=0.25)                        # #2 out: take #1 vertical
    p.drop("NB", (5.6, -8.4), speed=3.0); p.drop("NB", (4.4, -11.6), speed=3.5)   # walls H inside, late to widen
    p.drop("WILL", (8.0, -4.0)); p.drop("MIKE", (6.5, 4.0))
    p.drop("SS", (15.0, 6.5)); p.drop("RCB", (8.5, 15.6), speed=2.0)
    p.highlight("LCB", "FS")
    return p


palms = palms_play()
PALMS_T = [0.0, 0.6, 1.4, 2.0]
h6, x6 = palms.position("H", 0.6), palms.position("X", 0.6)
if PDF:
    strip(palms, PALMS_T, ["Snap · it looks like quarters", "+0.6 s · #2 breaks out; CB reads him",
                           "+1.4 s · CB drives on it; FS takes X", "+2.0 s · thrown into the CB"],
          ghosts=("LCB", "FS"), lateral=(-25, 11.5), window=(-9.0, 23.0),
          notes_at={1: [("#2", (float(h6[0]) - 2.6, float(h6[1]))), ("#1", (float(x6[0]) - 2.8, float(x6[1])))],
                    2: [("$ walled H inside:\ntoo late to widen", (-5.4, -10.0))]})
    plt.show()
else:
    show_animation(palms, times=PALMS_T)





  
  Your browser does not support the video tag.



Figure 37.7: Palms on the offense’s left, frame by frame (simulated). Snap: the picture is quarters, except that the corner (CB, ringed) is a yard or so shallower than usual, square to slightly outside X, with his eyes turned in to H, the #2 receiver. +0.6 s: H breaks to the sideline on a quick out at 4 yards; the corner’s eyes are on him, and the free safety (FS, ringed) sees it too. +1.4 s: the corner has left X and is driving forward, outside-in, onto the out; the free safety has turned and is taking X deep. The nickel ($), who walled H from the inside, is still yards away from the flat. +2.0 s: the quarterback, who saw an off corner before the snap and thought the out would be open, has thrown it, and the ball arrives with the corner already in the throwing lane. The dashed outlines show where the corner and safety stood at the snap.




Watch the timing. The out route is a rhythm throw: the quarterback decides before the snap, takes his drop and lets it go as #2 breaks, about a second after the snap. He threw it because the corner looked like a quarters corner, off and playing the outside receiver. Why would he fall for it if there is a tell? Because the tell is a yard of depth and a turn of the head, often disguised until the snap, and a rhythm throw is decided before the snap: the quarterback isn’t re-reading the corner as he lets it go. A Palms corner’s eyes were on #2 from the start, and he started forward the moment #2 broke. Against a throw that travels 15 or more yards across the field, a defender coming downhill onto the route gets to the catch point first. That’s how quick outs become interceptions returned the other way.
Palms also cleans up two routes that trouble Cover 2. Against smash (a hitch by #1, a corner route by #2), #2’s corner route starts vertical, so the safety carries it, and the hitch runs into the corner, who is manned up on #1 and sitting on it. Against a slot’s flat route paired with a curl by #1, the corner jumps the flat and the safety, who no longer has a vertical #2, drives on the curl from inside.






ImportantWhy it exists: taking away the throw quarters gives up



What it solves. Quarters concedes quick outside throws to #2. Palms puts a defender on them without adding one: the corner, who would have been 8 yards deep over a #1 who isn’t going deep, trades jobs with the safety, who would have had nothing to do once #2 went to the flat.
What it gives up. The trap is a guess about the route, and good offenses bait it. A #2 who breaks out and then turns up the sideline (an out-and-up, or a wheel) runs right past the jumping corner, and the safety is busy with #1. A #1 who runs a double move against a safety coming from inside can win too. And the corner who reads #2 is, for a moment, not watching #1 at all, so a fast #1 on a quick slant inside him can be open in the first second. Defenses mix Palms with plain quarters for exactly this reason: a corner who always traps gets beaten by the play designed for him.


How do you spot it? Before the snap, barely: the Palms corner is often a yard or two shallower than the other corner, with his shoulders and eyes turned in toward the slot. After the snap it’s unmistakable: the corner comes forward toward #2 while the safety on that side runs outward and deep over #1, and the two cross like a pair of scissors. Palms is usually played to one side, often the short side of the field or a 2x2 side, while the other half plays its own call, which makes it another piece of the split-field toolbox.

title: Quarters and the Two-High Match Family: Cover 4, Cover 6, Palms
section: Who decides: calls, checks and motion
text:
Who decides: calls, checks and motion
Three coverages that look alike before the snap raise an obvious question: how do eleven defenders know which one they’re in? Usually in two layers. The sideline sends in a call for the family, and the players on each side check within it once they see the formation. The corner and safety on a 2x2 side might play quarters or Palms depending on the receivers’ splits; a 3x1 set might turn the call into Cover 6 or a trips check such as poach. A safety or the Mike makes the strength call, by shout and hand signal, so both halves agree where the split is.
Motion tests all of that, because motion changes who is #2. Receivers are recounted from the sideline after every move. If H motions from the left slot across to the right, the free safety’s side suddenly has one receiver and no #2 to read, and the right side has three. The defense has a second or two to re-declare: the strength flips, the free safety becomes a lone-receiver-side player (a Cover 2 half, or a poach player watching #3), and the apex defender usually slides over with the motion, a bump that keeps everyone in his zone. Get the re-declaration wrong and two defenders take the same receiver while the new #2 runs free. That is a big reason offenses motion so much against split-field defenses (Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage has the offense’s side, Motion and Shifts as Weapons the defense’s answers).

section: Why two-high match took over the NFL, 2018 to 2025
text:
Why two-high match took over the NFL, 2018 to 2025
None of this was new in 2018. What changed is how much NFL defenses used it. NFL Next Gen Stats (the league’s tracking-data arm) measures how often defenses play a split-safety (two-high) coverage after the snap: 32.9% of dropbacks in 2018, 37.8% in 2021, 40.4% in 2024 and 42.0% in 2025, the highest since its tracking began. Quarters was the biggest single piece: Cover 4 alone was 17.2% of 2025 coverages by Next Gen Stats’ count, against a 2018–2024 average of 13.9%, with Cover 2 at 13.9% and Cover 6 at 9.2%.5
You can rebuild the trend yourself from the free nflverse data, which carries a coverage label on each charted play. The labels come from charting: people watching film of every play and tagging it, here with the coverage they think the defense played. Coverage is tagged essentially only on passing plays (dropbacks, plays where the quarterback drops back to pass), because on a run nobody can tell what the coverage would have become. That human judgment is the caveat.


Show the Python
from gridiron.data import nfl

part = nfl().load_participation(list(range(2018, 2026))).to_pandas()
cv = part[part["defense_coverage_type"].notna()].copy()
gid = cv["nflverse_game_id"].str.split("_", expand=True)          # e.g. 2024_02_SF_MIN
cv["season"], cv["week"] = gid[0].astype(int), gid[1].astype(int)
cv = cv[cv["week"] <= np.where(cv["season"] <= 2020, 17, 18)]    # regular season only
cv = cv[~cv["defense_coverage_type"].isin(["BLOWN", "COMBO", "PREVENT"])]
share = pd.crosstab(cv["season"], cv["defense_coverage_type"], normalize="index") * 100
two = share[["COVER_2", "2_MAN", "COVER_4", "COVER_6"]].sum(axis=1)
NGS = {2018: 32.9, 2021: 37.8, 2024: 40.4, 2025: 42.0}            # published, NFL.com (see notes)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(6.5, 5.4), sharex=True, gridspec_kw={"height_ratios": [1.15, 1]})
ax = axes[0]
ax.plot(two.index, two.values, marker="o", ms=4.5, color=style.SERIES[0], label="nflverse charting labels")
ax.scatter(list(NGS), list(NGS.values()), s=46, facecolor="white", edgecolor=style.SERIES[1], lw=1.6,
           zorder=3, label="NFL Next Gen Stats (published)")
for yr, v in two.items():
    ax.text(yr, v + (-2.0 if yr == 2024 else 1.0), f"{v:.0f}", ha="center", fontsize=7, color=style.SERIES[0])
ax.set_ylim(28, 47)
ax.set_ylabel("Two-high, % of dropbacks", fontsize=8.5)
ax.legend(loc="upper left", fontsize=7.5)
ax.set_title("Two-high coverage after the snap, 2018–2025 regular seasons", fontsize=10)
ax = axes[1]
for col, lab, c in (("COVER_2", "Cover 2", style.MUTED), ("COVER_4", "Quarters (Cover 4)", style.SERIES[2]),
                    ("COVER_6", "Cover 6", style.SERIES[3])):
    ax.plot(share.index, share[col], marker="o", ms=4, color=c, lw=1.8, label=lab + " (nflverse)")
ngs25 = {"Cover 4": 17.2, "Cover 2": 13.9, "Cover 6": 9.2}
ax.scatter([2025] * 3, list(ngs25.values()), s=40, facecolor="white", edgecolor=style.SERIES[1], lw=1.5,
           zorder=3, label="NGS 2025 (published)")
for lab, v in ngs25.items():
    ax.text(2025.17, v, f"{lab} {v}", fontsize=7, color=style.INK_2, va="center")
ax.legend(loc="upper left", fontsize=7.0, ncol=1)
ax.set_ylim(0, 31)
ax.set_ylabel("% of dropbacks", fontsize=8.5)
ax.set_xlim(2017.6, 2026.4)
ax.set_xticks(range(2018, 2026))
for a in axes:
    a.axvline(2022.5, color=style.INK_2, lw=1.0, ls=(0, (4, 3)))
axes[0].text(2022.58, 46.2, "source break:\nNGS charting → FTN charting", fontsize=7, color=style.INK_2, va="top")
fig.tight_layout(h_pad=0.8)
plt.show()








Figure 37.8: Top: share of charted regular-season dropbacks played as a two-high coverage after the snap (Cover 2, 2-Man, quarters or Cover 6), 2018–2025. Blue: the nflverse charting labels; orange rings: the figures NFL Next Gen Stats published. Both rise from about a third of dropbacks to over 40%. Bottom: the components, from the same labels. Here the source break matters: the coverage labels come from NGS charting through 2022 and from FTN Data charting from 2023 (dashed line), and the two charters sort two-high snaps differently. FTN calls far more of them Cover 2 and far fewer quarters than NGS did, and Next Gen Stats’ own counts for 2025 (orange rings at right) put quarters at 17.2%, against 10.0% in the FTN labels. Read each side of the line on its own: before it, quarters and Cover 6 climb steadily; after it, the total is consistent but the split between Cover 2 and quarters is a charting choice, not a trend.





The top panel is the trend, and the two sources agree on it: about a third of dropbacks in 2018, over 40% by 2022 and again in 2025, with a dip in 2024 that only the nflverse labels show.6 The bottom panel is a lesson in reading charting data. Through 2022 the components climb together; after the switch from NGS to FTN charting, quarters appears to collapse while Cover 2 soars. Nothing like that happened on the field. Two groups of charters drew the line between “two safeties guarding halves” and “two safeties reading #2” in different places, and NGS’s own 2025 counts, shown as rings, disagree with the FTN labels by close to a factor of two in both directions. Both are honest. Quarters and Cover 2 look alike before the snap and for a beat after it, and the difference is in rules a charter has to infer. Palms is the extreme case: on one snap it plays like quarters, on the next like a corner squatting in the flat, so where it lands depends on who is charting. Use the total, which is robust, and be careful with the split. (The nflverse data has the same kind of break in its man/zone labels, which is why Man Coverage doesn’t chart a man-coverage trend across 2022–2025.)
Why the rise? No single cause, but five reasons show up again and again in coaches’ and analysts’ explanations, and they reinforce each other.

Explosive passes became the thing to stop. The plays that decide games are the long completions (Expected Points and Success Rate shows why a 40-yard pass is worth so much more than a 4-yard run), and by the late 2010s passing was more efficient than ever. The 2018 season was the loudest version: Patrick Mahomes threw 50 touchdown passes in his first year as a starter, and the Rams beat his Chiefs 54–51 on a Monday night in November.7 Two deep safeties are the most direct protection against the explosive pass, and quarters keeps two deep without giving up the run.
Match rules answered the spread passing game. Offenses built on putting two receivers in one zone defender’s area ran into zones that followed the receivers.
The extra run defender could come from depth. A defense that played one-high with an eighth man in the box was guessing run every snap, and run-pass options punished that guess (RPOs). Quarters’ read safeties are harder to put in conflict before the snap, because their run job is decided by the play itself.
Two-high pictures disguise everything. From a two-high shell a defense can play quarters, Cover 6, Palms, Cover 2 or 2-Man, or rotate into a one-high coverage at the snap. The more of those it plays, the less the quarterback learns before the snap (Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage).
Coaching trees and a college pipeline. Coaches who learned split-field quarters in college (more below) reached NFL staffs, and one tree in particular spread it: that of Vic Fangio, whose two-high defenses in Chicago (as coordinator) and Denver (as head coach, 2019–2021) became the model. His story is a case study: Fangio’s Two-High Revolution and Macdonald’s Answer.

There is a sixth condition that isn’t a cause so much as a price of admission: a four-man rush that can win. A light box and two deep safeties work only if four rushers can pressure the quarterback without help, because nobody else is coming. Quarters teams can blitz, usually with an apex defender or a linebacker, but every extra rusher comes out of the four-over-two, so much of their pressure is still four rushers chosen in a surprising way, a simulated pressure. The defenses that lived in two-high were also the ones with dominant interior rushers, a pattern you’ll see in the film room.
And offenses answered. If quarters invites the run against a light box, run it; if it reads #2, make #2 a blocker. The 2024 and 2025 seasons brought more two- and three-tight-end personnel and more snaps under center, the subject of The Modern Era.

A short history: from Cleveland to East Lansing and Iowa City
Four defenders deep is an old idea; prevent defenses have used it for decades. Quarters as a read coverage whose safeties fit the run is mostly a product of 1990s and 2000s college football, with one important root in the NFL.
That root is Cleveland. Nick Saban was Bill Belichick’s defensive coordinator with the Browns from 1991 to 1994, and the pattern-matching rules the two developed there, first for Cover 3 and then for the quarters family, went with Saban to Michigan State as head coach in 1995 and later to LSU and Alabama.8 Saban’s vocabulary is the one this chapter has been using (MOD, MEG, Palms), plus “Cover 7” for his quarters-based split-field family (Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage) and “Rip” and “Liz” in his match Cover 3 (Cover 3). One set of match rules, several coverages: that’s the Saban-Belichick inheritance. Like most who-invented-it stories, this one has rivals; other staffs were building match rules at the same time, and the coverage numbers themselves meant different things in different buildings.
Michigan State kept the quarters thread alive after Saban left. Under head coach Mark Dantonio, who had coached Saban’s secondary in East Lansing, and defensive coordinator Pat Narduzzi (2007–2014), the Spartans’ 4-3 quarters became one of the most studied defenses in the country (the film room has its best season). Narduzzi came to Cover 4 the hard way: in 2002, as a Northern Illinois assistant, he watched Miami (Ohio)’s Ben Roethlisberger throw for 525 yards against his defense’s two-deep look, and when he became Miami’s defensive coordinator the next year, by his own telling at a 2014 clinic, his answer was Cover 4.9
Iowa is the other long-running reference point. Norm Parker installed his 4-3 defense when Kirk Ferentz took over the program at the end of the 1990s, and Phil Parker (no relation), the defensive coordinator since 2012, kept it: a front that holds up against the run while the safeties play split-field quarters behind it, year after year.10 TCU’s Gary Patterson built a 4-2-5 (four linemen, two linebackers, five defensive backs) around the same idea. When NFL defenses went looking for a two-high answer to the spread offenses of the late 2010s, this is where the coaching knowledge was.

title: Quarters and the Two-High Match Family: Cover 4, Cover 6, Palms
text:
Where quarters breaks
The holes of quarters follow directly from its rules. An offensive coordinator facing a quarters team starts with three of them.

Light-box runs
You’ve already seen the first, in the run-fit section: six in the box against six blockers, with the safeties arriving late, and an offense that releases #2 or reads the safety with an RPO to take one of them away. The other lever is simpler: add a blocker. Two-tight-end and fullback sets make #2 a blocker who can block the safety, or put a seventh blocker against a six-man box so the box is outnumbered before anyone arrives from depth; the heavier personnel of 2024 and 2025 was partly this. The defense’s counters are a front that holds its gaps without help (which is why two-high defenses prize big interior linemen), safeties who tackle in space, and a willingness to give up four-yard runs. Run Fits and Box Math has the data on what runs against light boxes actually gain.


The bootleg flood
Play-action attacks any coverage whose defenders read the run. Quarters is special because its deep defenders read the run.


Show the Python
def boot_play():
    off = [q.moved(w=8.5) if q.key == "Z" else q for q in offense("ace")]   # Z in a tight split
    dfn = defense("4-3_over", "two_high", off)
    mv = {"LCB": (7.5, -16.4), "RCB": (7.5, 9.3), "FS": (9.5, -6.0), "SS": (9.5, 5.5), "WILL": (4.5, -4.2)}
    dfn = [q.moved(d=mv[q.key][0], w=mv[q.key][1]) if q.key in mv else q for q in dfn]
    dfn = [q.moved(label="CB") if q.pos == "CB" else q for q in dfn]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=None)
    for k in ("LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT"):
        p.block(k, pts=[(0.6, 1.4)])
    p.block("Y", pts=[(0.5, 0.8)])
    p.path("RB", [(-4.5, 2.6), (-2.0, 5.0)], absolute=True, speed=5.5)                # the run fake
    p.path("QB", [(-3.2, 1.0), (-6.0, -2.5), (-6.5, -6.5)], absolute=True, speed=5.0)   # fake, then boot left
    p.route("X", r.go(24))
    p.route("U", [(0.6, 0.6), (0.7, 0.9), (1.8, 2.6), (3.5, 8.0)], speed=6.0)   # sells the block, then the flat
    p.route("Z", r.path((4, -1.5), (12, -13), (13.5, -21)))             # deep over, across the field
    p.pass_to("Z", t=2.9)
    p.drop("FS", (6.0, -5.0), speed=3.5)              # U's block says run: he steps up...
    p.drop("SS", (6.5, 4.8), speed=3.5)               # ...and so does the SS, keyed on Y
    p.drop("LCB", (21.0, -16.4), speed=5.5)           # MOD: X went deep, so he goes too
    p.drop("RCB", (11.0, 7.0), speed=4.6); p.drop("RCB", (13.6, -5.0), speed=4.6)   # trails Z across
    p.drop("WILL", (3.4, -3.8), speed=3.0); p.drop("WILL", (3.6, -9.6), speed=4.0)
    p.drop("MIKE", (3.0, 2.6), speed=3.0); p.drop("SAM", (3.0, 7.4), speed=3.0)
    p.highlight("FS", "Z")
    return p


boot = boot_play()
fld = clip(boot.draw(lateral=(-25, 14), window=(-9.5, 24.5), title=False))
no_numbers(fld.ax)
ruler(fld, boot)
say(fld, boot, "FS: U's fake block says run,\nso he steps up; the over\nroute lands behind him", (18.4, 0.5), fs=6.3)
say(fld, boot, "CB: MOD, carries X", (22.6, -14.6), fs=6.3)
say(fld, boot, "deep", (16.0, -18.4), fs=6.0, color=style.OFFENSE)
say(fld, boot, "~12 yd", (15.4, -12.4), fs=6.0, color=style.OFFENSE)
say(fld, boot, "flat", (4.8, -12.6), fs=6.0, color=style.OFFENSE)
say(fld, boot, "U: fakes a\nblock, then\nleaks out", (-4.0, -10.8), fs=6.0)
say(fld, boot, "trailing CB", (14.6, -2.2), fs=6.0)
plt.show()








Figure 37.9: A bootleg flood against quarters. The offense is in 12 personnel (two tight ends, U on the left and Y on the right; Z in a tight split), so the defense is in its base 4-3, with a Sam linebacker (S) next to the strong safety (SS). The offense fakes an outside zone run to the right and the quarterback rolls left. Three receivers flood the left side at three depths (the blue tags): X runs deep and the corner (MOD) carries him; U fakes a block for a beat, then leaks out to the flat; Z runs a deep over route from the far side and is caught at about 12 yards. The free safety (ringed) reads U, his #2, and U’s fake block says run, so he steps up. The over route lands behind him and in front of the corner, with the corner from the other side trailing. The strong safety, keyed on Y’s block, stepped up too.





Walk through it from the defense’s side. The corner saw #1 go deep and went with him: correct, MOD. The Will stepped up on the fake, then chased U to the flat: correct. The free safety read #2, saw a block and came forward: correct by his rule, and wrong, because U’s block was a fake. An honest pass never fools a quarters safety; a pass dressed as a run can, because for a beat the fake and the real thing look the same. The over route, coming from the other side of the field, entered the space between the corner (deep with X) and the safety (up for the run) where nobody’s rule put a defender: three receivers at three depths on one side, against defenders whose first read sent them the wrong way. The fake has to hold one more defender. On a bootleg the end on the side the quarterback rolls to is usually left unblocked, so the quarterback is running toward a free rusher who must bite on the run fake too.
It isn’t that play-action is magic against quarters in particular. In the nflverse charting for 2023–2025, play-action raised the average result of a dropback against quarters by about as much as it did against Cover 3 or Cover 1.11 The point is which play-action. A run fake that pulls the safeties forward, paired with a deep crosser from the far side, attacks the exact gap between quarters’ corner rule and its safety rule. The defense’s counter is discipline in the read (safeties taught to key through the blocker to the linemen and the quarterback, not just #2’s first step) and calls that tell the safety on the bootleg side to stay deep no matter what, at the cost of the run fit.


The running back’s wheel
The third weakness hides in the rule for the apex defender: take the first man to the flat.


Show the Python
off = [q.moved(w=2.3) if q.key == "RB" else q for q in spread_2x2()]   # back offset to the QB's right
p = Play(off, quarters_vs(off, {"NB": (4.8, 6.2), "WILL": (4.8, -2.4), "MIKE": (4.8, 1.6)}), los=35, to_go=None)
p.zone((19.0, 20.5), (8.0, 9.0), "empty")
p.route("Z", r.dig(12, 12)); p.route("Y", r.slant(2, 6))
p.route("RB", [(-3.8, 8.0), (-1.2, 12.6), (2.0, 17.6), (8.0, 20.2), (20.0, 20.8)], absolute=True, speed=7.5)
p.dropback(2.5); p.pass_to("RB", t=2.2)
protect(p)
p.drop("RCB", (10.6, 14.6), speed=5.0); p.drop("RCB", (11.8, 10.2), speed=5.0)   # MOD: #1 went deep, stay on him
p.drop("SS", (13.6, 7.6), speed=4.0)                                          # #2 not vertical: bracket #1
p.drop("MIKE", (5.6, 4.0), speed=4.0); p.drop("WILL", (6.5, -2.0))
p.drop("NB", (5.4, 8.0), speed=3.0); p.drop("NB", (2.5, 12.5), speed=5.0)     # first man to the flat...
p.drop("NB", (4.0, 16.8), speed=5.0); p.drop("NB", (10.6, 19.0), speed=5.0)                                         # ...then chasing up the sideline
p.highlight("NB", "RB")
fld = clip(p.draw(lateral=(-5, 26.6), window=(-8.5, 25.0), title=False))
no_numbers(fld.ax)
ruler(fld, p)
say(fld, p, "SS: #2 not vertical,\nso bracket #1's dig", (16.8, 7.0), fs=6.3)
say(fld, p, "CB: dig > 5 yd,\nMOD stays on #1", (6.6, 10.6), fs=6.3)
say(fld, p, "$: first man to the flat,\nnow chasing from behind", (-5.0, 18.4), fs=6.3)
plt.show()








Figure 37.10: The running back’s wheel against quarters, offense’s right side. Z (#1) runs a dig, past 5 yards, so it counts as deep and the corner (MOD) stays on him and follows him inside. Y (#2) runs a quick slant inside, so the strong safety, with no vertical #2, works inside and over the top to bracket Z’s dig, and the Mike takes the slant. The running back (R, ringed, aligned to the quarterback’s right) releases to the flat; the nickel ($, ringed) takes him as the first man to the flat, and then the back turns up the sideline. The ball is caught about 15 yards downfield with the nickel chasing from behind and the deep outside quarter empty: the corner and the safety both went inside with the routes in front of them.





Each rule is reasonable on its own. Together, the routes in front of the corner and the safety pulled both of them inside, and the back’s route started as a flat route (the apex defender’s) and became a deep route down the sideline (nobody’s). The defender left with him is a nickel back or a linebacker, chasing a running back from behind, with an empty deep quarter in front of them. The wheel is the classic match-coverage beater because it changes category in the middle of the play: short when the rules assign it, deep when it’s caught.
Defenses answer by teaching the apex player to “carry” a flat route that turns up, and by telling the corner, when #1 goes inside, to look for something coming outside behind him; each answer loosens something else. The offense’s side of all this, the full menu of concepts aimed at quarters’ rules, is the job of Concepts Versus Coverages.
