title: Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage
text:
Measuring the lie
Can you count how often a defense lies? Broadcasters and charting services label the coverage after the snap, and the nflverse data used throughout this course carries those labels (2018–2025). What they don’t record is the picture the defense showed before the snap. For that you need tracking data: the safeties’ positions in the frames before the snap.
That is exactly what the 2025 Big Data Bowl asked for. Its theme was pre-snap behaviour, and it was the first edition whose tracking files included full pre-snap frames, from the first nine weeks of the 2022 season. The winning entry, by NYU students Smit Bajaj and Vishakh Sandwar, was called “Exposing Coverage Tells in the Pre-Snap.”14 NFL Next Gen Stats then built a pre-snap model of its own, crediting that project as inspiration. It classifies the shell a quarterback sees before the snap and compares it with the coverage after. In its words: “If a defense shows split-safety zone and rotates to single-high man (or spins to Cover 0), we flag it as disguised.”15 The article that introduced the model gave no league-wide disguise rate, we found no other published one, and the Big Data Bowl files cover only half of one season. So “how often does an NFL defense lie?” has no public league-wide answer yet (one analyst’s count for a single team is in the Film room below).
Here is how you would get one. First fix what “the shell” means: the picture once the offense is set and the quarterback starts his cadence, say two seconds before the snap. Then classify that picture with a simple rule (two or more defenders at least 10 yards deep and none of them near the middle means two-high), do the same at the snap, and compare both with the coverage the defense actually played. A defense that rotates during the cadence has still disguised, but the quarterback had time to see the truth; one that rotates at the snap did not give him that time.
The chart below runs that measurement on eight made-up defenses. We typed in how often each one disguises and how late it moves, simulated 90 plays for each as BDB-format tracking, and let the classifier score them, so the chart can only give back what we put in. Its job is to show what the measurement looks like and how to read it, not to tell you anything about real teams. Read each row from left to right: the hollow dot is how often the picture two seconds before the snap told the truth, the filled dot how often the picture at the snap did, and the bar between them is how much of the lie the defense gave away during the cadence.


Show the Python
rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
# hypothetical defenses: (share shown two-high, share disguised, share of disguises that move only at/after the snap)
DEFS = {"A": (0.50, 0.05, 0.5), "B": (0.55, 0.12, 0.4), "C": (0.45, 0.25, 0.1), "D": (0.60, 0.30, 0.2),
        "E": (0.65, 0.30, 0.5), "F": (0.70, 0.35, 0.9), "G": (0.75, 0.40, 0.6), "H": (0.75, 0.45, 0.9)}
N = 90
res, pid = [], 0
for name, (p_two, p_dis, p_late) in DEFS.items():
    n_dis = round(N * p_dis)
    for i in range(N):
        pid += 1
        shown_two = rng.random() < p_two
        disguised, late = i < n_dis, i < round(n_dis * p_late)
        kind = {(True, False): "stay2", (True, True): "rot1",
                (False, False): "stay1", (False, True): "spin2"}[(shown_two, disguised)]
        tau = rng.uniform(0.0, 0.3) if late else rng.uniform(-1.6, -0.6)
        trk = sim_play(kind, rng, tau=tau, play_id=pid)
        played = "two-high" if kind in ("stay2", "spin2") else "one-high"   # the post-snap label
        res.append((name, played,
                    shell_at(trk[np.isclose(trk["time"], -2.0)]),
                    shell_at(trk[np.isclose(trk["time"], 0.0)])))
chk = pd.DataFrame(res, columns=["defense", "played", "shell_early", "shell_snap"])
agree = (chk.assign(early=chk["shell_early"] == chk["played"], snap=chk["shell_snap"] == chk["played"])
            .groupby("defense")[["early", "snap"]].mean().mul(100))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.6))
y = np.arange(len(agree))[::-1]                   # Defense A at the top
ax.hlines(y, agree["early"], agree["snap"], color=style.BASELINE, lw=2.0, zorder=1)
ax.scatter(agree["early"], y, s=46, facecolor="white", edgecolor=style.SERIES[0], lw=1.6, zorder=2,
           label="2 seconds before the snap")
ax.scatter(agree["snap"], y, s=46, color=style.SERIES[0], zorder=3, label="at the snap")
ax.set_yticks(y, [f"Defense {d}" for d in agree.index], fontsize=8.5)
ax.set_xlabel("Plays where the pre-snap shell matched the coverage played (%)", fontsize=8.5)
ax.set_xlim(50, 101)
ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
ax.legend(loc="lower right", fontsize=8)
ax.set_title("Pre-snap shell vs coverage played (simulated defenses, BDB-format)", fontsize=10)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 38.9: Did the shell tell the truth? Eight made-up defenses (not real teams) whose disguise rates we chose, 90 simulated dropbacks each, listed from the least disguise (A) to the most (H). Hollow dots: how often the shell two seconds before the snap matched the coverage played. Filled dots: the same, measured at the snap. A and B are honest: they disguise on only 5% and 12% of plays, so their dots sit high (between about 88 and 98), though not at 100. C and D disguise often but rotate during the cadence: low hollow dots, long bars, and by the snap the picture is true again. F and H disguise often and move late: short bars, low scores. Those are the hardest to read. E and G sit in between. A filled dot can’t fall left of its hollow dot here, because the defenses only ever move toward the truth.





Two numbers, then, describe a defense’s disguise: how often it lies sets how low its early score can go, and when it moves decides whether the lie can be caught in time. With the real 2025 Big Data Bowl files, whose plays carry a charted post-snap coverage, the same code would give real values; the website’s “Show the Python” holds it, and Tracking Data and the Big Data Bowl runs it on real defenses.


Show the Python (the real version from Big Data Bowl 2025 files; not run here)
from gridiron import bdb

plays = pd.read_csv("data/bdb/plays.csv")        # pff_passCoverage is the post-snap label
trk = bdb.load_tracking("data/bdb/tracking_week_*.csv")
TWO_HIGH = {"Cover-2", "2-Man", "Quarters", "Cover-6 Right", "Cover 6-Left"}   # check the year's label list
ONE_HIGH = {"Cover-1", "Cover-3", "Cover-3 Seam", "Cover-3 Cloud Left", "Cover-3 Cloud Right",
            "Cover-3 Double Cloud", "Cover-1 Double", "Cover-0"}

out = []
for row in plays.dropna(subset=["pff_passCoverage"]).itertuples():
    one = bdb.prepare(trk, plays, game_id=row.gameId, play_id=row.playId)
    snap = one[one["frameType"] == "SNAP"]
    one["los"] = float(snap.loc[snap["side"] == "ball", "x"].iloc[0])
    one["ball_y"] = float(snap.loc[snap["side"] == "ball", "y"].iloc[0])
    played = ("two-high" if row.pff_passCoverage in TWO_HIGH
              else "one-high" if row.pff_passCoverage in ONE_HIGH else None)
    if played is None:
        continue
    out.append((row.defensiveTeam, played,
                shell_at(one[np.isclose(one["time"], -2.0)]), shell_at(one[np.isclose(one["time"], 0.0)])))
# ...then group by defensiveTeam and plot exactly as in the simulated chart above.

title: Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage
text:
Film room






NoteFilm room: Vikings 2023–2025 — Brian Flores and the defense that is both



Brian Flores became the Vikings’ defensive coordinator in 2023 and was still there in 2026. His defenses have been described as close to unreadable before the snap. The back seven (the linebackers and defensive backs, everyone behind the defensive line) move constantly, safeties change the shell during the cadence and again at the snap, and pressure comes from players who don’t look like rushers. In 2023 the Vikings blitzed on 50.7% of opponents’ dropbacks, the highest rate in the league. After a 23–17 Vikings win in Week 2 of 2024, 49ers quarterback Brock Purdy told Flores on the field, “The scheme, man, it’s crazy.”16
What to notice: CBS’s breakdown of that 49ers game shows the two halves of the trick. On one snap six Vikings stand on the line before the snap and the play becomes a four-man rush with seven in coverage. On another, a blitz look is real but the coverage behind it is split-field Cover 6 (both plays are in the same CBS piece). Watch the number of defenders at the line before the snap, then count the rushers after it. With Flores, the two numbers often differ.
What makes it work is the spread of possibilities behind one look. In the nflverse post-snap coverage labels for 2023–2025, the Vikings played two-high coverage more often than any other defense (51.4% of charted dropbacks, just ahead of Buffalo’s 50.5%) and Cover 0, man with no deep safety, at 5.8%, behind only Kansas City and level with Baltimore; the Chiefs under Steve Spagnuolo sit right beside them on both counts. The chart shows the menu, not the disguise: post-snap labels can’t say what the shell looked like. But the menu is what makes disguise pay. Against most defenses a quarterback who sees two-high can lean on the odds that it stays two-high; against a defense that lives at both ends, the odds are no help. (The blitz numbers are pressure disguise, the subject of Part 7; the logic is the same.)




Show the Python
from gridiron.data import nfl

part = nfl().load_participation([2023, 2024, 2025]).to_pandas()
cv = part[part["defense_coverage_type"].notna()
          & ~part["defense_coverage_type"].isin(["BLOWN", "COMBO"])].copy()
gid = cv["nflverse_game_id"].str.split("_", expand=True)        # e.g. 2024_02_SF_MIN
cv["week"] = gid[1].astype(int)
cv["defteam"] = np.where(cv["possession_team"] == gid[3], gid[2], gid[3])
cv = cv[cv["week"] <= 18]                                      # regular season only
cv["two_high"] = cv["defense_coverage_type"].isin(["COVER_2", "2_MAN", "COVER_4", "COVER_6"])
cv["zero"] = cv["defense_coverage_type"].eq("COVER_0")
team = cv.groupby("defteam")[["two_high", "zero"]].mean() * 100

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 4.0))
rest = team.drop(["MIN", "KC", "BUF"])
ax.scatter(*team.loc["BUF", ["zero", "two_high"]], s=30, color=style.INK_2, zorder=3)
ax.annotate("Bills", tuple(team.loc["BUF", ["zero", "two_high"]]), xytext=(7, 0), textcoords="offset points",
            ha="left", va="center", fontsize=8, color=style.INK_2)
ax.scatter(rest["zero"], rest["two_high"], s=26, color=style.MUTED, alpha=0.7, zorder=2)
ax.scatter(*team.loc["MIN", ["zero", "two_high"]], s=64, color=style.SERIES[1], zorder=3)

            textcoords="offset points", ha="right", va="center", fontsize=8.5, fontweight="bold", color=style.INK)

            textcoords="offset points", ha="right", fontsize=8.5, color=style.INK)

ax.set_xlabel("Cover 0 (no deep safety), % of charted dropbacks", fontsize=8.5)
ax.set_ylabel("Two-high after the snap, %", fontsize=8.5)
ax.set_ylim(team["two_high"].min() - 2.5, team["two_high"].max() + 3)
ax.set_title("Two-high and Cover 0 by defense, 2023–2025", fontsize=10)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 38.10: Post-snap coverage mix by defense, 2023–2025 regular seasons pooled: share of charted dropbacks played as a two-high coverage (Cover 2, 2-Man, quarters or Cover 6) against share played as Cover 0. Each dot is a defense; dashed lines are league medians. The Vikings lead the league in two-high, by less than a point over Buffalo (which plays very little Cover 0), and are tied in effect with Baltimore for second in Cover 0, behind Kansas City, which sits close by: both extremes from the same team. Source: nflverse participation data, charted for 2023–2025 by FTN Data (a football charting company); plays the charters marked as a blown coverage or a mix of coverages are left out.





A caution about the chart: the coverage labels are charted by people watching film, and the 2023–2025 seasons come from a different charting source than earlier years, so compare teams within these seasons rather than across the 2022/2023 break.17 The labels describe what was played after the snap; they can’t tell you what was shown before it. That is the job of the tracking data in the previous section.






NoteFilm room: Rams 2020 — Brandon Staley’s first year



Brandon Staley arrived in Los Angeles in 2020 as a first-time NFL defensive coordinator, from Vic Fangio’s staff in Denver, and took over a defense with two great individual players: Aaron Donald inside and Jalen Ramsey at cornerback. He built it around a two-high shell. Most snaps looked alike before the snap, and the coverage was decided at and after it: quarters and Cover 6 to the field or the boundary, rotations down into Cover 3 or a robber, and Ramsey moved around the formation, from outside corner to the nickel (“star”) spot, to follow the matchup.18 Three things made the light-box, two-high approach affordable. Donald’s four-man pass rush meant the Rams didn’t need to blitz more than an average defense (they sent five or more rushers on about a quarter of dropbacks, close to the league median). The front, with Donald inside, could hold up against the run with fewer defenders in the box, while the safeties fitted the run from depth (Run Fits and Box Math). And the defense was disciplined enough to rotate late.
What to notice: on a 2020 Rams passing down, find Ramsey first (outside or in the slot), then the two safeties: level and deep while the quarterback calls signals, with the rotation, if there is one, coming only as the ball moves. The results: the 2020 Rams finished the regular season first in the NFL in points allowed (18.6 a game), total yards allowed (281.9) and passing yards allowed (190.7).19 Staley was hired as the Chargers’ head coach after one season, and the Rams’ approach spread through his coaching tree and the league. Its parent, Fangio’s system, is the subject of Case Study: Fangio’s Two-High Revolution and Macdonald’s Answer.








NoteFilm room: Panthers under Ejiro Evero — the coin-flip rotation



Ejiro Evero, a safeties coach on Staley’s 2020 Rams staff, has run Carolina’s defense since 2023. His Panthers are the cleanest public example of this chapter’s main move: show two-high, then decide at the snap whether to stay there or rotate a safety down to a single-high, “closed-post” coverage. In Cody Alexander’s charting of the Panthers’ defense, published in April 2026, they stayed two-high 397 times and rotated 375 times, what he called “an almost perfect 1:1 ratio.” Cornerback Jaycee Horn described what that felt like from inside: “Everything is really out of a shell, not many tells or pre(-snap) things. It was just on the snap; everything happened.”20
What to notice: on a Carolina passing down, call the shell as the quarterback starts his cadence; it will almost always be two-high. Then, on the replay, watch the two safeties at the snap. Roughly half the time one of them comes down and the other runs to the middle; the rest of the time both stay deep. Nothing before the snap tells you which, and that is the design. It also gives you a benchmark for your own log below: one charted NFL defense built around disguise rotated out of its two-high shell on about half the snaps that started there.








TipWatch for it on Sunday: call it twice



For one quarter (two if you’re keen), on every obvious passing down, make two calls out loud and write them down.

Call 1, as the quarterback starts his cadence: the shell. One-high or two-high? Then the details that could change it: how deep is each safety, is one narrower or shallower, are the corners pressed or off? Which side is the formation’s strength?
Call 2, one second after the snap: what it became. Is the middle of the field closed (one safety in the post) or open (two safeties splitting the field)? Closed: Cover 1 if the corners turn and run with receivers, Cover 3 if they bail into deep thirds. Open: then the corners tell you which, squatting in the flats for Cover 2 (or that side of Cover 6), backpedalling with eyes on the quarterback for quarters, trailing their man for 2-Man. No safety deep at all: Cover 0. If the two safeties went to two different jobs, notice which one came down and where he landed.
Log the lie. Mark each play S (same) or R (rotated). By the end of the quarter you’ll have a disguise rate for that defense. For scale, the Panthers in the film room above rotated out of two-high on about half their two-high snaps. Also note whether the rotation started before the snap (you could see it coming) or at the snap (you couldn’t). Both count as a lie; only the second one worked.
Bonus: trips. When the offense shows 3x1, watch the backside safety. Did he stay home (stubbie), come across to #3 (poach), run to the deep middle (rotate), or come down (solo)? Then watch where the ball went.

Live, Call 1 needs a shot that shows the safeties: the wide pre-snap view some broadcasts use while the quarterback surveys the defense, or a high camera behind the offense. The standard live angle sits at the line and often cuts the safeties out of frame at the snap, so on many plays Call 1 has to wait for the replay. The high, wide replays (the closest a broadcast gets to the All-22 film coaches use) are the best place to check yourself: use the first replay to see the shell and the second to check the rotation.

Figure 38.11: Second-and-9, ball in the middle of the field, play clock at 3. The defense shows two-high; the two safeties are highlighted. Use the depth numbers on the left and the hash marks to size them up.





What will the shell turn into at the snap, and which side of the field should the quarterback be wary of?

Show the Python
answer(r"""
**Most likely a rotation to one-high zone, Cover 3, with the right safety (SS) coming down.**
The safety tells: the SS has crept to 10 yards and stands 5 yards from the middle, while the FS is
at 13.5 and 7 yards out. The SS is shallower and narrower, so he can reach the curl or the hole
quickly, and he has crept down as the play clock runs out (a timing tell). The FS is the deeper
one and can reach the deep middle. The corner tells: they are 8 yards off, outside and turned to
the quarterback, which is zone technique, the way deep-third corners line up, not the square,
pressed stance of man corners. You can't tell before the snap whether the SS will land in the curl
(a **buzz** rotation) or in the hole (a robber), and you don't need to: either way he lands in the
in-breaking lanes on the right.

For the quarterback, the danger is to the **right**: curls and digs on that side run straight into
the SS. The opportunities are the classic Cover 3 ones away from the rotation, such as stressing
the left [curl-flat defender](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-curl-flat-defender) with a curl-and-flat
combination, or the seam on the left between the deep middle and the deep third (the Cover 3
weaknesses listed with the robber rotation). Of course a disciplined defense could show exactly this and
stay two-high.
""")







TipAnswer





Most likely a rotation to one-high zone, Cover 3, with the right safety (SS) coming down. The safety tells: the SS has crept to 10 yards and stands 5 yards from the middle, while the FS is at 13.5 and 7 yards out. The SS is shallower and narrower, so he can reach the curl or the hole quickly, and he has crept down as the play clock runs out (a timing tell). The FS is the deeper one and can reach the deep middle. The corner tells: they are 8 yards off, outside and turned to the quarterback, which is zone technique, the way deep-third corners line up, not the square, pressed stance of man corners. You can’t tell before the snap whether the SS will land in the curl (a buzz rotation) or in the hole (a robber), and you don’t need to: either way he lands in the in-breaking lanes on the right.

The opportunities are the classic Cover 3 ones away from the rotation, such as stressing the left curl-flat defender with a curl-and-flat combination, or the seam on the left between the deep middle and the deep third (the Cover 3 weaknesses listed with the robber rotation). TipPredict the play 2: the safety who isn’t home





Show the Python

number_receivers(pr2)

Figure 38.12: Third-and-6. The offense shows detached trips (3x1) to the right and X alone on the left. The defense is two-high. Compare the two safeties’ widths, and look at where the left corner stands on X.





Which 3x1 check does this look like, and where would you throw?

Show the Python
answer(r"""
**Poach, or a rotation; either way, X is alone.** The left (backside) safety is only about 4 yards
from the middle, much narrower than the right safety at 9. A backside safety staying home to help
on X would be wider and square to X, so he isn't home: he is getting ready to go somewhere on the
trips side. Before the snap there are two candidates. In **poach** he reads #3 and carries him if
he goes up the middle. In a **rotation** to one-high he becomes the deep-middle safety and the
trips-side safety comes down. The clue here is that the right safety is still deep and wide, not
creeping down, which leans toward poach, but you confirm it after the snap: the poacher goes where
#3 goes; the rotating safety runs to the middle and stays there. The left corner fits both. He is
pressed a yard inside X (inside leverage), taking away the inside, which is what a corner does when
he expects no help over the top.

**Throw to X**, especially if X is the offense's best receiver. Against poach, X is one-on-one with no help. The classic poach beaters are a
[back-shoulder](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-back-shoulder-throw) fade or a go route outside (the corner gave up the outside to take away the inside),
or a [double move](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-double-move). Against the rotation, X still
faces his corner with the post safety starting far away. It's also worth sending #3 vertical
anyway, so the safety has to commit.
""")







TipAnswer





Poach, or a rotation; either way, X is alone. The left (backside) safety is only about 4 yards from the middle, much narrower than the right safety at 9. A backside safety staying home to help on X would be wider and square to X, so he isn’t home: he is getting ready to go somewhere on the trips side. Before the snap there are two candidates. In poach he reads #3 and carries him if he goes up the middle. In a rotation to one-high he becomes the deep-middle safety and the trips-side safety comes down. The clue here is that the right safety is still deep and wide, not creeping down, which leans toward poach, but you confirm it after the snap: the poacher goes where #3 goes; the rotating safety runs to the middle and stays there. The left corner fits both. He is pressed a yard inside X (inside leverage), taking away the inside, which is what a corner does when he expects no help over the top.
Throw to X, especially if X is the offense’s best receiver. Against poach, X is one-on-one with no help. The classic poach beaters are a back-shoulder fade or a go route outside (the corner gave up the outside to take away the inside), or a double move. Against the rotation, X still faces his corner with the post safety starting far away. It’s also worth sending #3 vertical anyway, so the safety has to commit.











TipPredict the play 3: the safeties spin with the motion





Show the Python
off, dfn = nickel_vs_2x2()
# Z must start off the line to go in motion, so Y steps up to be the end on the line (still 7 on it)
off = [p.moved(d=-0.7) if p.key == "Y" else p.moved(d=-1.5) if p.key == "Z" else p for p in off]
pr3 = Play(off, dfn, los=30, to_go=10)
pr3.motion("Z", pts=[(-1.5, -7.0), (-1.5, -17.0), (-1.5, -18.0)], speed=7.0)   # offsets from his start
pr3.motion("FS", to=(9.0, -8.0), speed=2.0)      # motion side: walks down toward the motion
pr3.motion("SS", to=(13.5, 1.0), speed=2.5)      # side the motion left: rotates to the post
pr3.highlight("FS", "SS", "RCB")
pr3.note("CB stays: deep third,\nno man", at=(11.0, 16.0))
fld = pr3.draw(lateral=(-22, 22), window=(-7.5, 17))
no_numbers(fld.ax)
ruler(fld, pr3)
plt.show()








Figure 38.13: First-and-10. Two-high before the motion. Z then motions across the formation from right to left. No defender follows him. The left safety (FS), on the side Z is heading to, walks down to about 9 yards; the right safety (SS) drifts toward the middle and gains depth; the right corner (CB) stays where he was, now over empty grass. Every arrow here is movement before the snap.





What did the motion tell the offense? And what could the defense still do to it at the snap, and how would the offense take that away?

Show the Python
answer(r"""
**It suggested one-high zone, Cover 3 rotating toward the motion.** Nobody went with Z across the
formation, and the right corner stayed home over empty grass: a corner with no man to cover is
playing a zone, here a deep third. The left safety coming down toward the motion while the right
safety rotates to the post is the defense moving to a single deep safety, with the FS as an
underneath (buzz or sky) defender on the side Z is going to. That is the
[spin](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-spin-safety-rotation-on-motion) from
[Motion and Shifts as Weapons](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-06-motion-and-shifts.qmd), and it
goes the default way: toward the motion, which is where the receivers now are.

**The catch:** a defense that knows you use motion to read it can spin on purpose and then rotate
*back* at the snap. That is late rotation used against the motion read, and it's a favourite of
heavy-disguise defenses. The offense's counter is in the timing: snapping the ball as Z passes the
quarterback (motion at the snap) leaves the safeties almost no time to re-rotate, so the picture
they show during the motion is much more likely to be the real one. It is still a strong hint, not
a certainty.
""")







TipAnswer





It suggested one-high zone, Cover 3 rotating toward the motion. Nobody went with Z across the formation, and the right corner stayed home over empty grass: a corner with no man to cover is playing a zone, here a deep third. The left safety coming down toward the motion while the right safety rotates to the post is the defense moving to a single deep safety, with the FS as an underneath (buzz or sky) defender on the side Z is going to. That is the spin from Motion and Shifts as Weapons, and it goes the default way: toward the motion, which is where the receivers now are.
The catch: a defense that knows you use motion to read it can spin on purpose and then rotate back at the snap. That is late rotation used against the motion read, and it’s a favourite of heavy-disguise defenses. The offense’s counter is in the timing: snapping the ball as Z passes the quarterback (motion at the snap) leaves the safeties almost no time to re-rotate, so the picture they show during the motion is much more likely to be the real one. It is still a strong hint, not a certainty.

title: Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage
text:
Takeaways

The shell is a hypothesis, not an answer. Defenses choose their alignment separately from their coverage, and the best ones show the same picture for many calls. Name the shell before the snap, and expect to check it one second after.
Disguise buys time, and it costs something. Every defender must line up where his real job is still reachable, so disguises leak: safety depth and width, corner technique and leverage, eyes, and above all the timing of movement. Late rotation hides the most and risks the most. Which safety rotates is set by the call, most often toward the strength or the motion.
Rotations run both ways. Two-high can become Cover 3 or a robber (taking away the middle throws two-high invites); one-high can bail into Cover 2 (taking away the outside throws one-high invites). Each rotation opens the area the quarterback ruled out.
Split-field coverage plays two coverages at once, one per half, keyed to strong and weak or (more in college, with its wide hashes) field and boundary. Each player’s job is simpler; the communication is harder, and motion across the split tests it. It is a big part of why two-high defenses spread through the NFL after 2018.
Trips forces a decision, and the decision is about #3: the backside safety comes across (poach), a linebacker takes him (solo), the trips side handles it four-on-three (stubbie), or the defense rotates. Whoever is left alone is where the offense will attack.
Offenses answer by forcing the defense to show earlier or by making the picture not matter: motion, tempo, hard counts, post-snap reads, play-action and RPOs that target the rotating safety, and quick throws.

title: The Pass Rush: Moves, Stunts, and Why Pressure Beats Sacks
text:
The rusher’s problem: a race and a fight
Third-and-8, early in the second quarter. The offense spreads four receivers and keeps the back in to block; the defense shows four linemen and nobody else near the line. At the snap the right defensive end takes three long strides up the outside, and the offensive tackle in front of him kick-slides back fast to stay between him and the quarterback. Then, with the tackle’s weight going backward, the end plants his outside foot and drives straight into the tackle’s chest. The tackle’s feet stop moving; he is walked backward three yards, into the spot where the quarterback wanted to set his feet. The quarterback throws a beat early, off his back foot, and the pass sails over a receiver who was about to come open. Incomplete. Punt. The box score records nothing for the end: no sack, no tackle, not even a hit. His position coach will grade it as one of his best plays of the day. This chapter is about why.
You’ll be able to:
How to read the diagrams. Offense is blue circles, defense orange squares, and left and right are the offense’s. The linemen are LT, LG, C, RG and RT; Q is the quarterback (usually drawn at his launch point, the spot he throws from) and R the running back. On defense, E is an edge rusher: a 4-3 defensive end with his hand down or a 3-4 outside linebacker standing up, since the rush is the same job. The defensive tackles are labelled by technique (1, 3), and the drills use the coverage labels from Part 06 (CB, NB, FS, SS, M and W for the linebackers). An orange arrow is a rusher’s path; a blue line ending in a short bar is a blocker’s set. The few other marks are explained with the first figure that uses them.
The quarterback in today’s NFL releases the ball a little under three seconds after the snap on average (Pass Protection has the numbers), and on a quick throw in well under two. An edge rusher who lines up outside the tackle has to cover an arc of about thirteen yards to reach the spot where the quarterback sets his feet; a defensive tackle in the middle has nine or so, straight ahead, but through the thickest traffic on the field. Unblocked, an edge rusher would cover his arc in roughly two seconds. He is never unblocked. A man who weighs about 315 pounds, who knows where the quarterback will be and only has to stay in the way, is standing on the path.
So a pass rush is two contests at once. It is a race: the rusher has to get to the quarterback before the ball leaves, and a rusher who arrives at 3.4 seconds against a quarterback who threw at 2.6 has done nothing, however good his move was. And it is a fight: to win the race he has to beat a blocker who is bigger, who has the inside position, and who is allowed to use his hands too. The rusher’s advantages are the two the blocker lacks. He knows the snap is coming and where he is going, and he moves forward, while the blocker moves backward.
There is a third fact, and it explains why defenses pay pass rushers so much: most of the time, the defense rushes only four. In FTN’s charting of the 2023–2025 regular seasons, 69% of dropbacks faced exactly four rushers and 26% faced five or more.1 A blitz can manufacture a free rusher by sending more men than the offense can block, but every extra rusher is one fewer defender in coverage, and the quarterback knows it. Four rushers against five or six blockers leaves seven defenders to cover at most five receivers. If those four can create pressure by themselves, the defense gets to the quarterback and covers everybody. That is the holy grail of defensive football, and this chapter is about how it is done: by moves, by plans, and by stunts.

title: The Pass Rush: Moves, Stunts, and Why Pressure Beats Sacks
text:
ImportantWhy it exists



A four-man rush is the balance point between coverage, which is expensive, and pressure, which is valuable. A team whose four can win their fights gets pressure without paying for it in coverage, which is why an edge rusher who wins them is usually the highest-paid player on his defense.

section: Get-off: the first step decides more than you think
text:
Get-off: the first step decides more than you think
The fight begins before anyone touches anyone. A rusher’s get-off is his first movement at the snap: how quickly he reacts to the ball moving and gets across the line of scrimmage.
Defenders are not allowed to move into the neutral zone before the snap, and unlike the offense they do not know the snap count. So a rusher does not listen to the quarterback’s cadence; he watches the ball, or the center’s hand on it, and goes the instant it moves. The offense’s weapons against this are a varied snap count (a “hard count” to draw a rusher offside, a quick count to catch him flat-footed) and, in a loud stadium, a silent count, which takes away the hard count but can leave the snap on a rhythm (the center looks back, the guard taps him, the ball comes on a set beat) that a good rusher learns to time. The rusher’s weapon is a stance with his weight already tilted forward and a first step that covers ground without popping up.
Why does a tenth of a second matter so much? Because of what it does to the meeting point.


Show the Python
p = Play(line(["RG", "RT"]) + [O("QB", "QB", -7.2, 0.0, "Q")], [D("RE", "DE", 1.0, 5.4, "E")], los=35, to_go=None)
ARC = [(1.0, 5.4), (-0.6, 6.3), (-2.8, 6.0), (-4.4, 4.8), (-6.2, 1.6)]
to(p, "RE", ARC[-1], "rush", via=ARC[1:-1])
to(p, "RT", (-2.5, 4.4))
fld = draw(p, width_in=5.4, lateral=(-2.2, 10.8), window=(-9.4, 3.2))


def along(pts, s):
    """The point a distance s (yards) along a polyline."""
    for a, b in zip(pts[:-1], pts[1:]):
        seg = float(np.hypot(b[0] - a[0], b[1] - a[1]))
        if s <= seg:
            f = s / seg
            return (a[0] + f * (b[0] - a[0]), a[1] + f * (b[1] - a[1]))
        s -= seg
    return pts[-1]


def run_dist(t, t0, acc=8.0, vmax=7.5):
    """Yards covered by time t for a rusher who starts at t0, accelerates at acc to vmax."""
    dt = max(0.0, t - t0)
    t_top = vmax / acc
    return 0.5 * acc * dt ** 2 if dt <= t_top else 0.5 * acc * t_top ** 2 + vmax * (dt - t_top)


FAST, SLOW = along(ARC, run_dist(1.2, 0.10)), along(ARC, run_dist(1.2, 0.40))
GAP_YD = run_dist(1.2, 0.10) - run_dist(1.2, 0.40)
ghost(fld, p, *FAST, "E")
ghost(fld, p, *SLOW, "E")
ghost(fld, p, -2.5, 4.4, side="off", alpha=0.35)
point_to(fld, p, (-4.6, 8.9), FAST, "fast get-off at 1.2 s:\nlevel with the tackle,\nturning the corner",
         color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, shrink=9)
point_to(fld, p, (0.9, 8.9), SLOW, "0.3 s slower:\nstill upfield of him", color=style.INK_2, shrink=9)
point_to(fld, p, (-5.6, 3.9), (-2.5, 4.4), "the tackle's set\nat 1.2 s", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, shrink=8)
say(fld, p, -7.6, 3.6, "flatten to the QB", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
plt.show()








Figure 39.1: Two edge rushers on the same arc against the same tackle, 1.2 seconds after the snap (the faint squares are where each rusher is at that moment; the line is the path both run; the faint circle is the tackle, who has kick-slid back to his set point). The rusher who moved the instant the ball did has already reached the tackle’s depth, his hips level with the tackle’s: the tackle has to open up and run with him, and is in trouble. The rusher who started three-tenths of a second later is still a couple of yards upfield of the tackle, where the tackle can meet him square and punch. Same speed, same path; the only difference is the first step.





At full speed an edge rusher covers about seven yards a second, so a tenth of a second at the snap is most of a yard on the arc. In Figure 39.1 the two rushers differ by three-tenths, and by 1.2 seconds that has become a 2.2-yard difference in where they meet the tackle. The quick one meets him level, at the tackle’s own depth, where the tackle has to turn his hips to run with him, and a blocker who turns his hips has given up the inside and lost most of his power. The slow one meets him in front, where the tackle is square, balanced and ready to punch. Same athlete, same path, a completely different fight.
That is why scouts time rushers’ first steps at the Combine (the league’s pre-draft testing event), why defensive line coaches drill get-off every day, and why the best rushers are often the first player on the field to move. Tracking data now measures it directly: Next Gen Stats times how long a rusher takes to cross the line of scrimmage after the snap and quotes it in its broadcasts and analysis.2 For a scale: the quickest single snaps it has highlighted are around a third of a second, best-ever reps. A lineman whose body starts about a yard behind the ball needs roughly half a second to cross it from a standstill, so most rushes take longer; the simulated rushers at the end of this chapter take half a second to eight-tenths.

title: The Pass Rush: Moves, Stunts, and Why Pressure Beats Sacks
text:
The arc and the corner
Before the moves, the geometry they are all trying to bend. An edge rusher’s basic path is the arc: a curve up the outside of the tackle and around him toward the quarterback. He aims it at a landmark, not at the blocker: the quarterback’s launch point, about seven or eight yards behind the line from the shotgun, which is why the diagrams put Q there. The tackle’s answer, as Pass Protection showed, is to kick-slide back and out, staying between the rusher and that spot, and to push the rusher past the quarterback if he keeps running. The pocket is a cup, and a rusher run around the rim of the cup ends up behind it, harmless.
How wide the rusher lines up is the first trade. A wide alignment like the wide-9 gives him a running start and room to build speed, at the cost of a longer arc and a soft spot inside him that draws and screens are built to punish; a tight alignment over the tackle gives him a shorter path and power, but no space to work.
The rusher wins the arc at one spot: the corner, the moment his hips draw level with the tackle’s. Before that, the tackle is in front of him and can punch and steer. Once the rusher’s hips are past, the tackle is beside or behind him, can only push, and any push sends the rusher where he wanted to go. (His last resort is to grab: a hold, ten yards if the official sees it.) That is why the last part of every good edge rush is a tight turn back toward the quarterback, flattening the arc once he is past the tackle rather than continuing upfield.
Two physical skills decide whether a rusher can do this, and you can see both on any broadcast replay. The first is bend: the ability to lean his whole body toward the inside, ankles flexed, shoulder almost at the turf, while running at full speed, so he can turn the corner tightly instead of drifting wide. The second is dip: dropping the shoulder nearest the tackle so the tackle’s reaching hands slide off it. Watch a great edge rusher win and you will see a body tilted at an angle that looks like it should fall over.
One coaching rule sits under all of it: rush half a man. A rusher never attacks the blocker’s whole chest, where the blocker is strongest; he attacks one half of him, a shoulder, so the blocker has to turn to stay in front. Every move below starts on a shoulder.
The tackle, of course, knows all this. If he gets deep enough fast enough, there is no corner to turn. He can also get it wrong in the other direction and overset: retreat wider or deeper than the rush in front of him needs, opening his hips to the outside too early, which leaves the space inside him empty. And so the rusher needs other ways to win: through the tackle, or back inside him. That is what the moves are.

title: The Pass Rush: Moves, Stunts, and Why Pressure Beats Sacks
text:
The moves
There are dozens of named pass-rush moves, and every rusher has his own blend, but almost all of them belong to a handful of families. Six are worth knowing by sight. In each panel of Figure 39.2 the rusher (E) lines up outside the right tackle; read the note under each panel for what the move attacks.


Show the Python
LAT_M, WIN_M = (-0.6, 8.6), (-6.4, 2.6)
MOVES = [
    ("1  Speed rush", (-2.6, 4.5), [(-0.5, 6.5), (-2.4, 6.4), (-3.6, 5.3)], (-5.2, 3.0),
     "Win the race to the corner, dip\nunder his hands, bend back.\nBeats a slow or short set.", "dip\nand bend"),
    ("2  Bull rush", (-1.6, 3.8), [(-0.8, 4.5)], (-3.3, 3.4),
     "Hands inside, chest to chest,\nwalk him into the QB. Beats a\nhigh set or one already bailing.", "drive\nthrough him"),
    ("3  Long arm", (-1.9, 3.9), [(-0.8, 4.9)], (-2.6, 4.6),
     "One arm locked out: he can't\nreach you. Drive him back,\nthen shed and go.", "arm\nlocked out"),
    ("4  Swim", (-2.2, 4.8), [(0.2, 6.2), (-1.0, 4.5), (-2.2, 3.0)], (-4.8, 1.6),
     "Jab outside, clear his hands,\narm over the top, inside.\nBeats a tackle who bites outside.", "over\nthe top"),
    ("5  Rip", (-2.4, 4.4), [(-0.6, 6.3), (-2.2, 5.8), (-3.4, 4.8)], (-5.1, 2.6),
     "Uppercut up through his outside\narm and shoulder, hips past.\nThe finish of most speed rushes.", "rip\nthrough"),
    ("6  Spin", (-2.7, 5.3), None, (-5.0, 2.0),
     "He oversets for the arc: plant,\nspin all the way round, inside.\nBig reward, big risk.", "spin\ninside"),
]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(6.6, 6.3))
for ax, (name, rt_end, via, end, note, tag) in zip(axes.flat, MOVES):
    p = Play(line(["RG", "RT"]), [D("RE", "DE", 1.0, 5.4, "E")], los=35, to_go=None)
    to(p, "RT", rt_end)
    if via is None:   # the spin: up the arc, a full turn, then back inside
        c, rr = np.array([-2.45, 5.85]), 0.5
        th0 = np.arctan2(6.35 - c[1], -2.0 - c[0])
        loop = [tuple(c + rr * np.array([np.cos(a), np.sin(a)])) for a in np.linspace(th0, th0 + 2 * np.pi, 14)]
        via = [(-0.6, 6.4), (-2.0, 6.35)] + loop[1:] + [(-3.2, 3.9)]
    to(p, "RE", end, "rush", via=via)
    fld = draw(p, ax=ax, title=False, lateral=LAT_M, window=WIN_M)
    if name.endswith("Bull rush"):
        pushed(fld, p, (-1.6, 3.8), (-4.3, 2.9))
        ghost(fld, p, -4.3, 2.9, side="off")
    elif name.endswith("Long arm"):
        pushed(fld, p, (-1.9, 3.9), (-3.7, 3.6))
        ghost(fld, p, -3.7, 3.6, side="off")
        arm(fld, p, (-2.6, 4.6), (-3.25, 4.0))
        dashed(fld, p, [(-2.6, 4.6), (-3.4, 5.25), (-4.3, 5.0), (-4.9, 3.9)], color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.6)
    elif name.endswith("Swim"):
        curl(fld, p, (-0.4, 5.7), (-1.9, 3.7), rad=0.8)
    elif name.endswith("Rip"):
        curl(fld, p, (-1.8, 5.9), (-3.0, 4.6), rad=-0.7)
    say(fld, p, *((-0.9, 7.3) if name.endswith("Long arm") else (-4.9, 6.2)), tag, color=ARM, weight="bold",
        fontsize=6.6)
    panel_title(ax, name)
    note_below(ax, note)
fig.tight_layout(h_pad=1.6, w_pad=0.7)
plt.show()








Figure 39.2: Six pass-rush moves against a right tackle (zoomed in on him; the quarterback is off the bottom-left of each panel, where the rush arrows are heading). The orange arrows show where the rusher goes; the arm work is in the note under each panel. New marks: a dashed dark-blue line ending in a bar is the blocker being driven backward, and a faint circle is where he ends up; a thick dark-orange stroke ending in a dot is the rusher’s arm; a curved orange arrow is a hand move. Bull rush: chest to chest, walking him backward. Long arm: the same push from arm’s length, with a dashed escape route once the tackle is driven back. Swim: sell outside, arm over the top, go inside. Rip: an uppercut through his outside arm to get the hips past. Spin: when he has overcommitted to the outside, spin back inside. Each move beats a different mistake.





The speed rush. The speed rush is the move everything else is built on: beat the tackle to the corner before he can get in front. Fast get-off, a curved path up the arc, a dip of the near shoulder as the tackle reaches for him, and a bend back toward the quarterback. It beats a tackle who sets too slowly or not deep enough, and it is the move tackles fear most, which is exactly why it makes every other move work: a tackle who is worried about speed retreats fast, and a man retreating fast is off balance in other ways. Its weakness is the one the pocket is built around: a tackle who gets deep enough simply runs the rusher past the quarterback.
The bull rush. The bull rush is the opposite idea. Instead of going around the blocker, the rusher goes through him: hands inside on the chest, hips low, legs churning, driving him straight back into the quarterback. A bull rush rarely produces a sack by itself; what it produces is a collapsing pocket. A quarterback who has a tackle or guard backing into his feet cannot step up, cannot finish his throwing motion and often cannot see. It beats a blocker who sets too high (pads up, so the rusher gets under him) or one whose weight is already going backward because he retreated too fast, since a man moving backward cannot plant and push. The blocker’s answer is the anchor: sink the hips, widen the base, and stop the slide. A bull rush against a blocker who anchors is a stalemate, and a stalemate is a win for the offense.
The long arm. The long arm is the bull rush with an escape hatch. The rusher locks one arm, fully extended, into the blocker’s chest (usually his inside arm into the outside half of the blocker’s chest, the near breastplate). Why can the blocker not just reach back? Because a punch is thrown with both hands and square shoulders, which keeps the elbows bent; one arm locked straight, with the rusher’s shoulder turned into it, reaches several inches farther. So the blocker’s hands fall short of the rusher’s body, the rusher controls the distance between them and drives the blocker back with it, and his other hand stays free to knock the blocker’s hands away and slip off the block when the moment comes. It has become one of the signature moves of the modern NFL edge rusher, because it works for long-armed athletes who are not giant men, and because it lets a rusher generate power without getting tied up chest to chest.
The swim. The swim move clears the blocker’s hands with one hand and throws the other arm over the top of his shoulder, like a swimmer’s overhand stroke, to get past him. On the edge it is usually an inside move: the rusher fakes outside to make the tackle widen, then swims back inside. In the middle it is a staple of quick, compact defensive tackles who meet guards almost at once. It needs timing and a blocker whose weight has gone the wrong way, and its risk is visible in the drawing: for a moment the rusher’s arm is up and his chest is open, and a blocker who is not fooled will drive right into it.
The rip. The rip move is an uppercut: the rusher drives his inside arm up under the blocker’s arm and through his armpit, lifting the arm off him and turning his own shoulder through the gap so his hips get past. It is the usual way a speed rush is finished, because at the corner the tackle’s outside hand is the last thing between the rusher and the quarterback, and the rip takes that hand away. A dip and a rip together are the most common sight on an edge sack.
The spin. The spin move is the showpiece. When the tackle has committed to the outside, the rusher plants his outside foot, turns his back to the blocker and spins all the way round, coming out back inside him toward the quarterback. Dwight Freeney made it famous with the Colts in the 2000s, and it carried him to the Hall of Fame.3 Done at the right moment, against a tackle who has overset, it leaves the blocker grabbing air. Done at the wrong one, against a blocker who stayed square, it spins the rusher out of the pocket, and for half a second he cannot even see the quarterback: big reward, big risk.
Telling them apart on the broadcast. The speed rush and the rip look like one motion: the rusher’s outside shoulder dips, his inside arm swings up through the tackle’s armpit, and he flattens toward the quarterback. In a bull rush the two men are chest to chest and the tackle’s helmet is snapped back; in a long arm there is daylight between them, one arm locked straight across it, and the tackle’s arms flailing short. A swim shows an arm going over the tackle’s shoulder, like a freestyle stroke, as the rusher goes inside; a spin shows the rusher’s back to the camera for an instant.






CautionCommon misconception



“Pass rushers win with strength.” Strength helps, especially in the bull rush and the long arm, but most rush wins are wins of timing and position: a quicker first step, hands that land before the blocker’s do, a move chosen for the set the blocker just showed. It is the mirror of Pass Protection’s point that most protection losses are losses of position.



Moves are counters to hands
Watch a pass rush closely and you will see that the rusher’s hands are busy before his feet have done anything clever. The blocker’s main weapon is his punch, a two-handed strike into the rusher’s chest to stop his momentum and steer him. Many moves are built specifically to beat that punch.
The two oldest are power moves. The club is a forearm or open-hand blow to the blocker’s shoulder or elbow that knocks his punch aside, usually to set up a rip or a swim. The push-pull (also called a snatch or a jerk) grabs the blocker, pulls him forward past the rusher just as he leans in, and lets go: the interior rusher’s signature move, because guards meet rushers almost at once and lean into them.


Show the Python
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 3.6))
for ax, name in zip(axes, ("1  Cross-chop", "2  Ghost")):
    p = Play(line(["RG", "RT"]), [D("RE", "DE", 1.0, 5.4, "E")], los=35, to_go=None)
    to(p, "RT", (-1.9, 3.9))
    if name.endswith("chop"):
        to(p, "RE", (-4.6, 3.0), "rush", via=[(-0.4, 5.6), (-1.6, 5.2), (-3.0, 4.6)])
    else:
        to(p, "RE", (-4.7, 3.1), "rush", via=[(-0.6, 5.8), (-1.6, 5.6), (-2.9, 5.0)])
    fld = draw(p, ax=ax, title=False, lateral=(-0.4, 9.0), window=(-6.4, 4.8))
    if name.endswith("chop"):
        arm(fld, p, (-1.9, 3.9), (-1.25, 4.55), lw=2.6, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK)
        curl(fld, p, (-0.2, 6.3), (-1.55, 4.15), rad=0.55, lw=1.8)
        say(fld, p, 2.9, 6.0, "outside arm\nchops down", color=ARM, weight="bold", fontsize=6.6)
        point_to(fld, p, (-3.9, 6.9), (-1.3, 4.5), "his punch,\nknocked down", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, shrink=4)
        say(fld, p, -5.2, 5.1, "rip past", color=ARM, fontsize=6.6)
    else:
        ghost(fld, p, -1.15, 4.75)
        arm(fld, p, (-1.9, 3.9), (-1.2, 4.7), lw=2.6, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK)
        point_to(fld, p, (-3.9, 6.9), (-1.2, 4.7), "his punch\nhits air", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, shrink=4)
        say(fld, p, 2.9, 6.0, "shoulder turned\naway, no contact", color=ARM, weight="bold", fontsize=6.6)
        say(fld, p, -5.2, 5.4, "bend\naround", color=ARM, fontsize=6.6)
    panel_title(ax, name)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.8)
plt.show()








Figure 39.3: Two modern hand moves against the tackle’s punch, in close-up (the tackle’s punch is drawn in dark blue). Cross-chop: as the tackle’s hands come out, the rusher swings his outside arm across his own body (curved arrow) and chops them down, then rips past while the tackle’s hands are out of position. Ghost: the rusher never touches him. At the instant of the punch he turns his inside shoulder away and dips it (the faint square is where his shoulder was), so the punch lands on air and the tackle lunges forward, off balance, as the rusher bends around him.





The cross-chop is the clearest example (Figure 39.3). As the tackle punches, the rusher swings his outside arm across his own body and chops down on the tackle’s hands or forearms, knocking the punch down and away, then rips or dips past while the tackle’s hands are out of position. It turns the blocker’s best tool into the reason he loses. On a replay it looks like a karate chop: the rusher’s arm sweeps across his chest and the tackle’s arms drop.
The ghost (rush move) goes one step further: no hand contact at all. A dip lowers the shoulder under hands that are already reaching; a ghost is timed to the punch. At the instant the tackle strikes, the rusher turns his inside shoulder away, so the punch lands on nothing and the tackle, having thrown his weight into a strike that hit air, lunges forward off balance as the rusher bends around him. On a replay, look for the tackle reaching at empty space, often falling forward. A ghost works best against a tackle who punches early and hard; a patient tackle who “catches” the rusher and strikes late gives it nothing to avoid, which is one reason many NFL tackles have stopped throwing one textbook punch at every rusher.
Rules shape this hand fight too. A rusher may use his hands on a blocker’s body, but thrusting them up into the blocker’s head or neck is a foul (an illegal use of hands, five yards and an automatic first down when the defense does it).4 That rule has a history you will meet below, and it is why the modern hand fight is aimed at the blocker’s hands, arms and chest.

title: The Pass Rush: Moves, Stunts, and Why Pressure Beats Sacks
section: The rush plan: setting up the move you want
text:
The rush plan: setting up the move you want
Here is the real secret of pass rushing, and the reason the moves above are only half the story. A tackle facing the same rusher thirty-odd times in a game is not guessing blindly; he is studying the rusher too, and he adjusts. So the best rushers do not just have moves. They have a rush plan: a planned sequence across the game that shows the blocker one move until he adjusts to stop it, then uses the counter his adjustment has opened.


Show the Python
PLAN = [
    ("He oversets: inside opens", (-2.9, 5.5), [(-0.6, 6.4), (-1.7, 6.0), (-2.2, 4.0)], (-5.0, 2.0),
     "Counter: back inside\n(spin or swim)"),
    ("He sets short: corner opens", (-1.3, 3.8), [(-0.6, 6.6), (-2.6, 6.4), (-3.8, 5.2)], (-5.3, 3.0),
     "Counter: speed around\nthe edge"),
    ("He bails: power opens", (-2.6, 4.4), [(-0.6, 6.3), (-1.4, 5.9)], (-1.95, 5.0),
     "Counter: speed-to-power\nthrough his chest"),
]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(6.6, 3.55))
for ax, (name, rt_end, via, end, note) in zip(axes, PLAN):
    p = Play(line(["RG", "RT"]), [D("RE", "DE", 1.0, 5.4, "E")], los=35, to_go=None)
    to(p, "RT", rt_end)
    to(p, "RE", end, "rush", via=via)
    fld = draw(p, ax=ax, title=False, lateral=LAT_M, window=WIN_M)
    if "inside" in name:
        x, y = _P(fld, p, -2.9, 3.0)
        ax.add_patch(Ellipse((float(x), float(y)), 2.2, 2.6, fc=RED, alpha=0.13, ec=RED, lw=0.9, ls=(0, (2, 1.5)),
                             zorder=1.5))
        say(fld, p, -4.6, 6.0, "inside is\nopen", color=RED, weight="bold", fontsize=6.6)
    elif "corner" in name:
        x, y = _P(fld, p, -2.6, 6.3)
        ax.add_patch(Ellipse((float(x), float(y)), 2.2, 2.6, fc=RED, alpha=0.13, ec=RED, lw=0.9, ls=(0, (2, 1.5)),
                             zorder=1.5))
        say(fld, p, -4.6, 1.6, "corner is\nopen", color=RED, weight="bold", fontsize=6.6)
    else:
        pushed(fld, p, (-2.6, 4.4), (-4.6, 3.7))
        ghost(fld, p, -4.6, 3.7, side="off")
        point_to(fld, p, (-5.3, 6.6), (-2.6, 4.4), "weight going\nback: no anchor", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK,
                 fontsize=6.4)
    panel_title(ax, name, size=7.8)
    note_below(ax, note, size=7.0)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()








Figure 39.4: Why a rush plan works: every way the tackle sets opens something else (zoomed on the right tackle; the quarterback is off the bottom-left). Left: after being beaten around the edge, he oversets, kicking wide at the snap to take the corner away; the space inside him (shaded) opens, and the rusher counters back inside with a spin or swim. Middle: worried about the inside, he sets short and square; now the corner is open and the speed rush wins it. Right: worried about speed, he bails straight back as fast as he can; his weight is going backward, so when the rusher turns into his chest he cannot plant and anchor, and is driven back (dashed): the speed-to-power. The blocker cannot protect all three at once, so the rusher’s job is to make him choose and then punish the choice.





The logic in Figure 39.4 is a triangle. Speed threatens the corner, so the tackle must get depth, and there are only two ways to get it fast. Get it by widening, and the inside opens for the spin or swim. Get it by retreating straight back at full speed, and his weight is going backward, which is exactly when power works. So he must stay balanced and patient, which slows his set, which brings speed back. A rusher with one great move can be planned for. A rusher with two that look the same for the first two steps cannot.
That is the job of speed-to-power, probably the single most important move in the modern edge rusher’s kit. It starts exactly like a speed rush: the same get-off, the same first steps up the arc. The tackle, seeing speed, kicks back fast. Then, two or three steps in, the rusher turns straight into him and converts all that speed into a bull rush, hitting him while his weight is still going backward, when he cannot anchor. It is the move in this chapter’s opening, and it works because of the speed rush: the more a tackle fears the corner, the faster he retreats, and the more his own momentum helps the rusher push him.
You can follow a rush plan from the couch. Early, many rushers show speed again and again, to make the tackle think about the corner. Once he starts bailing, the counters come: the inside spin, the speed-to-power, the long arm. A tackle who has been beaten inside starts to sit, and the speed rush is back on. The plan is built during the week from film of that specific tackle (his set depth, whether he punches early, whether he oversets after being beaten), so the same rusher may use a completely different plan the following Sunday.






NoteMadden vs. real life



In Madden a pass-rush move is a button press, and whether it works is mostly a matter of ratings. Real moves work or fail depending on what the blocker is afraid of, which depends on what the rusher showed him on the previous ten snaps. The spin that beats a tackle in the fourth quarter would have been stuffed in the first, before he had a reason to overset. Pass rushing is a conversation across a game, not a series of independent dice rolls.

title: The Pass Rush: Moves, Stunts, and Why Pressure Beats Sacks
section: Inside rushers: less room, shorter path
text:
Inside rushers: less room, shorter path
Everything above is described from the edge, where most sacks are recorded. Defensive tackles play a different version of the same game. An interior rusher has the shortest path to the quarterback, and pressure up the middle is the most destructive kind: the quarterback cannot step up into it and cannot see over it. But he also has the least room to work. A guard is on him almost immediately (there is no long arc to set up a move, only a yard or so of space), and he often faces two blockers. That is the four-against-five arithmetic from the start of the chapter: five linemen against four rushers leaves one blocker spare, and the spare is usually the center, who sits in the middle and can turn either way to help a guard. Interior rushers therefore win with fast, compact hands: a club or a push-pull the instant they meet the guard, a swim or a rip past him, a bull rush to push the pocket. When the ball is coming out too quickly to get home, they do the next-best thing and get their hands up into the throwing lane; a batted pass is an interior rusher’s win. And they are measured differently. A 3-technique who drives the guard back into the quarterback’s lap, forcing him to slide away from the pressure and into an edge rusher’s arms, may have done more than the edge rusher who gets credited with the sack.
The greatest interior rusher of the modern era made the case that a defensive tackle could be the most important player on the field. Aaron Donald, a 6-foot-1 defensive tackle the Rams drafted 13th overall in 2014, won Defensive Player of the Year three times (2017, 2018 and 2020) and had 20.5 sacks in 2018, astonishing for a player who lined up inside and was double-teamed constantly.5 What made him special was not size. It was get-off, hand speed and leverage: he was often past the guard before the guard had finished his first step, the one-gap penetration of Defensive Line Play applied to the pass, and his hands (the club, the push-pull, the swim) were too quick for a double team to land cleanly.

title: The Pass Rush: Moves, Stunts, and Why Pressure Beats Sacks
section: Stunts: winning with geometry instead of muscle
text:
Stunts: winning with geometry instead of muscle
Moves win one-on-one fights. A stunt, also called a pass-rush game or a twist, wins by making two blockers’ assignments collide. In a stunt, two or more rushers exchange gaps after the snap: one goes first to occupy blockers (the penetrator), and the other loops around behind him into the space he left (the looper). The defense still rushes four, still covers with seven; it just rearranges where the four go.
You saw the most common stunt from the offense’s side in Pass Protection, where the guard and tackle passed it off by switching. Here are the main families from the defense’s side.


Show the Python
DL_DEEP = 1.6   # depth at which the defensive linemen are drawn (the book default is 1.0), so the loops show
STUNTS = [
    ("T-E stunt", ["RG", "RT"], ["DT", "RE"], (-1.0, 7.0),
     {"DT": ([(0.4, 3.3)], (-0.5, 3.7)),
      "RE": ([(0.9, 5.5), (2.0, 4.6), (2.35, 3.2), (2.0, 1.7), (0.4, 0.9)], (-3.4, 0.7))},
     {"RG": ((-1.4, 2.6), []), "RT": ((-1.7, 4.6), [])}),
    ("E-T stunt", ["RG", "RT"], ["RE", "DT"], (-0.4, 7.6),
     {"RE": ([(0.5, 3.9)], (-0.3, 2.9)),
      "DT": ([(2.2, 2.6), (2.45, 3.9), (2.0, 5.2), (0.3, 5.7)], (-3.1, 4.6))},
     {"RG": ((-1.3, 1.9), []), "RT": ((-1.7, 3.5), [])}),
    ("Interior twist (T-T)", ["LG", "C", "RG", "RT"], ["DT", "NT"], (-3.0, 5.0),
     {"DT": ([(0.5, 1.4)], (-0.4, 0.95)),
      "NT": ([(2.2, -0.3), (2.45, 1.0), (2.3, 2.3), (0.6, 2.7)], (-3.2, 2.1))},
     {"LG": ((-1.5, -1.8), []), "C": ((-1.3, 0.1), []), "RG": ((-1.4, 1.35), []), "RT": ((-1.6, 3.4), [])}),
]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(6.6, 3.7))
for ax, (name, ol, dl, lat, paths, sets) in zip(axes, STUNTS):
    p = Play(line(ol), [q.moved(d=DL_DEEP) for q in four_down() if q.key in dl], los=35, to_go=None)
    for k in dl:
        via, end = paths[k]
        to(p, k, end, "rush", via=via)
    for k, (end, via) in sets.items():
        to(p, k, end, via=via)
    fld = draw(p, ax=ax, title=False, lateral=lat, window=(-5.0, 4.0))
    for n, k in enumerate(dl, 1):
        q = p.players[k]
        badge(fld, p, q.d + 1.35, q.w, str(n))
    panel_title(ax, name, size=8.0)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()








Figure 39.5: Three common stunts, each zoomed on the part of the line it attacks (the defensive linemen are drawn about half a yard deeper than in the book’s other diagrams, so the loops have room to show; the badge above each rusher gives the order he goes in). T-E: the 3-technique goes first and drives into the right tackle’s inside half, picking him; the guard follows the 3 outside, and the end loops in a tight hook behind the 3’s starting spot into the space the guard left. E-T: the mirror. The end crashes inside first and picks the guard, the tackle chases him inside, and the 3-technique loops around to the outside lane the tackle vacated. Interior twist (T-T): the 3-technique crashes through the right guard’s inside shoulder into the A gap, picking the guard and the center; the 1-technique wraps over the top behind him into the B gap the 3 left. In each, two blockers end up on one man (or on nobody), and the second rusher arrives where nobody is.





The T-E stunt. In a T-E stunt (tackle first, end second) the defensive tackle drives into the offensive tackle’s inside half to pick him, then takes over contain, and the end loops around behind him into the inside gap he vacated. The penetrator’s aiming point is the near hip of the far blocker (the offensive tackle, not the guard in front of him): he has to collide with both blockers, a legal pick, so they cannot switch cleanly. A penetrator who just runs around the tackle has wasted the stunt. If the guard follows the 3-technique outside and the tackle waits for the end on the outside, both block the wrong man, and the end walks through the gap.
The E-T stunt. The E-T stunt is the mirror: the end crashes inside first, picking the guard, and the tackle loops around him to the outside, taking over the end’s rush lane. It sends the looper wide, toward an offensive tackle who has just watched the end leave and may have turned inside to chase him.
Which one, when? Both hunt the same seam; the difference is who arrives second, unblocked or against the wrong man. Defenses usually make the best rusher the looper, so a star end means T-E (he loops inside onto a guard, who is slower than a tackle and rarely sees an end) and a quick, rangy 3-technique means E-T (he loops outside onto a tackle who is turned the wrong way). The matchup matters too: aim the looper at the weaker blocker, and the pick at the one who switches poorly.
The interior twist. Two defensive tackles can do the same thing in the middle, a T-T twist. In Figure 39.5 the 3-technique crashes through the right guard’s inside shoulder into the A gap, picking the guard and the center, and the 1-technique wraps over the top behind him into the B gap he left. It attacks the guards and center, the three men who are supposed to hold firm, and it is especially effective against centers who have to make the protection calls and then find a man.
The words overlap: many staffs say “stunt” for run-down line movement and “game” or “twist” for a pass-rush exchange, the penetrator is also the crasher or picker, and the looper the wrapper. Each stunt gets a code word (“Tex” is a common one for T-E), and many defenses run three-man games too. Most stunts come in the coordinator’s call, but many lines also have games they can check into at the line when they see a particular protection.

Why stunts work, and what they cost
Stunts exist because they create a mismatch or a free rusher without blitzing. Against man protection, the blockers have to recognise the stunt and pass it off in a split second; if either one hesitates, the looper is free. Against slide protection, as you are about to see, a stunt aimed the wrong way is simply absorbed, but one aimed at the right spot can still choose who blocks whom.
The animation shows a T-E against a slide going the other way. Compare it with the stunt figure in Pass Protection, where the right tackle took the crashing 3-technique: that line was in man protection and switched. Here the line is sliding, so the tackle steps inside to his gap and lets the 3-technique go by.


Show the Python
def te_vs_slide():
    """A four-man rush: T-E stunt on the right against a full slide left, the back assigned to the right end."""
    p = Play(line() + [O("QB", "QB", -5.0, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -5.0, 1.7, "R")], four_down(), los=35,
             to_go=None)
    timed(p, "QB", [(0.8, -6.8, 0.0), (2.0, -6.8, 0.0), (2.6, -7.0, -0.9)])
    # the slide: everyone steps left; the left side is blocked normally
    timed(p, "LE", [(0.5, -0.4, -5.8), (1.0, -1.8, -5.9), (1.6, -3.0, -5.4), (2.6, -4.6, -4.6)], "rush")
    timed(p, "LT", [(0.5, -1.5, -4.2), (1.0, -2.3, -4.6), (1.6, -3.0, -4.5), (2.6, -4.0, -3.9)], "block")
    timed(p, "LG", [(0.4, -1.2, -2.5), (0.8, -1.6, -2.7), (1.6, -2.0, -2.6), (2.6, -2.4, -2.5)], "block")
    timed(p, "NT", [(0.4, 0.0, -0.9), (0.8, -0.5, -1.0), (1.6, -1.0, -1.0), (2.6, -1.2, -1.0)], "rush")
    timed(p, "C", [(0.4, -1.3, -0.9), (0.8, -1.7, -1.0), (1.6, -2.2, -1.1), (2.6, -2.6, -1.1)], "block")
    timed(p, "RG", [(0.4, -1.3, 0.8), (0.8, -1.7, 0.6), (1.3, -2.1, 0.4), (2.6, -2.7, 0.35)], "block")
    timed(p, "RT", [(0.4, -1.2, 2.4), (0.8, -1.6, 2.15), (1.3, -1.9, 2.2), (1.8, -2.2, 2.3), (2.6, -2.7, 2.3)],
          "block")
    # the penetrator: the 3-technique crashes outside, through the space the RT stepped away from
    timed(p, "DT", [(0.4, 0.1, 3.4), (0.8, -0.8, 4.2), (1.3, -2.0, 4.4), (1.8, -3.1, 3.9), (2.2, -3.9, 3.0),
                    (2.6, -4.6, 2.2)], "rush")
    # the looper: the end jabs upfield, then loops behind the 3-technique into the B gap
    timed(p, "RE", [(0.4, 0.2, 5.6), (0.8, 0.6, 4.6), (1.3, -0.3, 3.2), (1.8, -0.8, 2.6), (2.6, -0.6, 2.7)], "rush")
    # the back steps up to take the end outside the tackle, and meets the 3-technique instead
    timed(p, "RB", [(0.4, -4.6, 2.4), (0.8, -4.1, 3.4), (1.3, -3.6, 4.0), (1.8, -4.5, 3.2), (2.2, -5.4, 2.3),
                    (2.6, -6.5, 1.1)], "block")
    return p


rush_animation(te_vs_slide(), [0.0, 0.4, 0.8, 1.3, 1.8, 2.6],
    notes=["snap: the line slides left;\nR has the right end", "line steps left; 3 crashes\noutside, E jabs upfield",
           "RT lets the 3 go;\nE loops behind him", "RT picks up the E;\nR meets the 3, not the E",
           "a 300-lb tackle\non a 210-lb back", "R driven back, Q slides away:\nnobody free, still pressure"],
    lateral=(-2.6, 8.4), window=(-8.6, 2.6), ncols=3, rings=(("DT", PURPLE), ("RE", style.THIRD)),
    final_links=(("RT", "RE", GREEN), ("RB", "DT", RED)))





  
  Your browser does not support the video tag.



Figure 39.6: A T-E stunt against slide protection (simulated; zoomed on the offense’s right side, linebackers and coverage not shown because they drop). The line slides left, toward the 1-technique shaded in the left A gap, so each lineman steps left and owns the gap to his left: the right guard owns the right A gap, the right tackle the B gap, and the back’s job is the right end. The 3-technique (ringed in purple) crashes outside, out of the tackle’s gap and into the back’s area; the end (ringed in green) jabs upfield and loops behind him into the B gap. The slide does its job: the tackle keeps his gap and picks up the looping end, so nobody is free. (The right guard, with nobody in his gap, does what slide rules tell him: he looks the way the slide is going and helps the center on the 1-technique, so he never sees the stunt behind him.) But the stunt has changed the matchup: the back, set to block a 250-pound end, meets a 300-pound defensive tackle at full speed and is driven back toward the quarterback, who has to slide away. Dotted lines in the last frame: who finished on whom.




Notice what the stunt did and did not do in Figure 39.6. It did not produce a free rusher: the slide protection handled it exactly as designed, because the right tackle owned a gap, not a man, and simply took whoever came into it. That is slide protection’s strength: gaps do not move. What the stunt did instead was choose the matchup. The protection had assigned the back to the end. The stunt swapped the end for a defensive tackle who outweighs the back by ninety pounds, and the back lost. No one was unblocked, and the quarterback was still pressured.
Run the same T-E into the slide side, where the center, guard and tackle are all stepping toward it, and it dies: the guard owns the B gap the end loops into, the tackle owns the C gap the 3-technique crashes into, and each blocker simply takes the man who arrives. So defenses aim stunts away from the slide, at the man side of a half-slide, or at a specific blocker: a slow-footed guard, a rookie tackle, a back who has to take a lineman.
How does the defense know which way the slide will go before the snap? It mostly doesn’t know; it bets on clues. Film shows how an offense protects from each formation and each back alignment, so the back’s spot is a clue to the offense’s habits. Before the snap the center points out the linebacker he is counting from, which hints at the slide’s direction. And many defenses simply shift or align late, so the slide is called against a picture that changes. Line coaches talk about stunts the way offensive coordinators talk about plays, as weapons chosen for a particular opponent.
Stunts have three costs, and they are why defenses do not stunt on every snap.

They take time. The looper runs a longer path than a straight rush, so a stunt usually arrives later, about two and a half seconds or more after the snap. Against a quick throw, a stunt is a defense that rushed two men late and two men sideways. Stunts belong on long-yardage downs, when the quarterback must hold the ball for routes to develop.
They give up the one-on-one. The penetrator’s job is to occupy blockers, not to win, so a great rusher who is asked to penetrate on a stunt is a great rusher not rushing. Defenses often build stunts so their best player is the looper.
They open lanes. Two rushers crossing paths leave, for a moment, a space where neither of them is, and a quarterback who can run will find it. That is the next subject.

title: The Pass Rush: Moves, Stunts, and Why Pressure Beats Sacks
text:
Rush lanes and contain
A four-man rush is not four men running at the quarterback. It is four men each responsible for a lane, and the lanes together form a box around him.
A rush lane is the path to the quarterback that one rusher owns. The two ends usually own the outside lanes and have contain: they rush outside the tackles but must not run past the quarterback’s depth, because the space behind them would become a running lane. The two interior rushers own the middle and have the job of pushing the pocket straight back, so the quarterback cannot step up. If every rusher stays in his lane, the quarterback has nowhere to go: forward is the interior push, sideways is the edge rushers, backward is a longer throw. If one rusher leaves his lane, there is a hole.


Show the Python
LANES = {"LE": [(1.0, -5.4), (-1.2, -6.5), (-4.6, -6.1), (-6.7, -2.0)], "NT": [(1.0, -0.7), (-5.0, -0.7)],
         "DT": [(1.0, 2.35), (-5.0, 1.0)], "RE": [(1.0, 5.4), (-1.2, 6.5), (-4.6, 6.1), (-6.7, 2.0)]}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 4.1))
for ax, lost in zip(axes, (False, True)):
    p = Play(line() + [O("QB", "QB", -7.0, 0.0, "Q")], four_down(), los=35, to_go=None)
    for k, sp in {"LT": (-3.4, -4.3), "LG": (-1.9, -1.8), "C": (-1.6, 0.0), "RG": (-1.9, 1.8), "RT": (-3.4, 4.3)}.items():
        if not (lost and k == "RT"):
            to(p, k, sp)
    if lost:   # the right tackle rides the end past the quarterback
        to(p, "RT", (-6.4, 5.7), via=[(-2.4, 5.0)])
    for k, pts in LANES.items():
        if lost and k == "RE":
            to(p, "RE", (-9.3, 4.4), "rush", via=[(-1.2, 6.5), (-5.0, 6.8), (-8.0, 6.2)])
        else:
            to(p, k, pts[-1], "rush", via=pts[1:-1])
    fld = draw(p, ax=ax, title=False, lateral=(-11.6, 11.6), window=(-11.6, 3.0), ol_fs=5.4)
    ppy = fld.pts_per_yard()
    for k, pts in LANES.items():
        xs, ys = _P(fld, p, np.array([q[0] for q in pts]), np.array([q[1] for q in pts]))
        ax.plot(xs, ys, color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.9 * ppy, alpha=0.13 if not (lost and k == "RE") else 0.05,
                solid_capstyle="round", solid_joinstyle="round", zorder=1.4)
    for sgn in (-1, 1):
        (x0, y0), (x1, y1) = _P(fld, p, -7.0, sgn * 2.6), _P(fld, p, -7.0, sgn * 8.6)
        ax.plot([x0, x1], [y0, y1], color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, lw=1.0, ls=(0, (2, 2)), zorder=2)
    if lost:
        dashed(fld, p, [(-7.0, 0.6), (-5.4, 2.4), (-3.0, 4.1), (1.8, 4.2)], color=RED, lw=2.0)
        point_to(fld, p, (-2.4, 9.0), (-2.2, 4.12), "escape\nlane", color=RED, fontsize=7.0)
        say(fld, p, -10.0, 8.2, "too deep", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.6)
        point_to(fld, p, (-6.0, 9.0), (-6.4, 5.9), "tackle rides\nhim past", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.4)
        panel_title(ax, "One lane lost")
    else:
        say(fld, p, -8.7, -5.6, "contain line:\nnot past the QB", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.4)
        say(fld, p, -3.5, 0.15, "push the\npocket", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.4)
        panel_title(ax, "Lanes kept: the QB is boxed in")
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.8)
plt.show()








Figure 39.7: Rush lanes (shaded) for a four-man rush, with the quarterback at his launch point. The arrows show each rusher’s lane, not the hand fight; in a real rush every one of them is engaged with a blocker along the way. Left: lanes kept. The ends rush outside the tackles and stop at the quarterback’s depth (the dashed contain line), the inside rushers push the pocket straight back, and the quarterback is boxed in. Right: one lane lost. The right end, chasing the sack, runs his arc past the quarterback’s depth; the right tackle rides him past (that is the tackle’s job), and the space they have both left becomes an escape lane (red). A quarterback who can run climbs and slips out underneath them, often past the line of scrimmage before anyone can turn around. A right-handed quarterback escapes to his right most readily, which is why this side’s contain matters most.





The trade in Figure 39.7 is the oldest one in pass rushing. A rusher who stays disciplined in his lane gives the quarterback nowhere to go, but he also gives up some of his own chance to get home. A rusher who abandons his lane for the sack, whether by running too far upfield, spinning inside out of an outside lane, or looping on a stunt, may get there, or may open the door. Against a quarterback who will stand in the pocket, the gamble usually pays. Against one who runs, it often doesn’t. Defenses guard the contain on the quarterback’s throwing-arm side hardest (the offense’s right, for a right-hander), because he can escape that way and still throw on the run.
Stunts make the lanes move. On a T-E, the penetrator crashing outside takes over the outside lane and with it contain, while the end who usually has contain loops inside. If the penetrator does not get there, or gets there too deep, the edge is open. That is part of why stunts are rarer against running quarterbacks, and why the stunts defenses do run against them are often the ones that keep a fast player outside.
