title: The Pass Rush: Moves, Stunts, and Why Pressure Beats Sacks
section: The mush rush: squeezing instead of racing
text:
The mush rush: squeezing instead of racing
Keeping lanes is ordinary discipline: every good four-man rush does it, and every end in it is still trying to beat his tackle to the corner and then stop at the quarterback’s depth. Against a quarterback who is a real threat to run, defenses often go further and change what the rush is for. In a mush rush (some staffs say cage rush), the ends stop trying to win the corner at all. Each one stays on his tackle’s outside shoulder, in front of him, and pushes him straight back, with a bull rush or a long arm, until the tackle is standing beside the quarterback. The inside rushers do the same to the guards. The pocket is squeezed from all sides rather than raced into, and the goal is no longer to sack him quickly. It is to make sure that when the routes are covered and he looks for somewhere to run, there is nowhere to go.


Show the Python
p = Play(line() + [O("QB", "QB", -6.2, 0.0, "Q")], four_down() + [D("MIKE", "MIKE", 5.0, 0.0, "M")], los=35,
         to_go=None, title="The mush rush: a cage, not a race")
to(p, "C", (-1.6, 0.0))
p.highlight("LE", "RE", color=PURPLE)
fld = draw(p, width_in=5.6, lateral=(-11.5, 11.5), window=(-10.2, 8.4), ol_fs=5.8)
for sg in (-1, 1):
    pushed(fld, p, (-0.7, sg * 3.2), (-5.3, sg * 3.4))      # tackles walked back
    ghost(fld, p, -5.3, sg * 3.4, side="off")
    dashed(fld, p, [(1.0, sg * 5.4), (-0.6, sg * 5.0), (-4.3, sg * 4.6)], color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.6, dash="solid")
    ghost(fld, p, -4.3, sg * 4.6)                           # end on the tackle's outside shoulder
    pushed(fld, p, (-0.7, sg * 1.6), (-3.0, sg * 1.7))      # guards walked back
    ghost(fld, p, -3.0, sg * 1.7, side="off")
dashed(fld, p, [(1.0, -0.7), (-1.7, -1.4)], color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.6, dash="solid")
dashed(fld, p, [(1.0, 2.35), (-1.7, 1.9)], color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.6, dash="solid")
ghost(fld, p, -1.7, -1.4)
ghost(fld, p, -1.7, 1.9)
cage = [(-4.3, -4.6), (-1.7, -1.4), (-1.6, 0.0), (-1.7, 1.9), (-4.3, 4.6), (-6.2, 4.2), (-8.2, 1.6), (-8.6, 0.0),
        (-8.2, -1.6), (-6.2, -4.2)]
xy = np.array([_P(fld, p, d, w) for d, w in cage], dtype=float)
fld.ax.add_patch(Polygon(xy, closed=True, fc=GREEN, alpha=0.10, ec=GREEN, lw=1.2, ls=(0, (3, 2)), zorder=1.5))
(xa, ya), (xb, yb) = _P(fld, p, 6.3, -2.2), _P(fld, p, 6.3, 2.2)
fld.ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((float(xa), float(ya)), (float(xb), float(yb)), arrowstyle="<|-|>", mutation_scale=9,
                                 color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, lw=1.3, zorder=9))
point_to(fld, p, (-6.6, -8.8), (-4.3, -4.6), "ends: on the tackle's\noutside shoulder,\ndrive him back",
         color=style.DEFENSE_DARK)
point_to(fld, p, (-6.6, 8.8), (-5.3, 3.4), "tackle walked back\nbeside the QB:\nno escape lane", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK)
point_to(fld, p, (3.0, -3.6), (-3.0, -1.7), "inside: drive the\nguards into his face", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK)
say(fld, p, 6.3, 5.4, "spy (optional):\nmirrors the QB", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
say(fld, p, -9.0, 4.0, "the cage", color=GREEN, weight="bold")
plt.show()








Figure 39.8: The mush rush against a quarterback who runs. Nobody goes around anybody: the ends (ringed) stay on the outside shoulders of their tackles and drive them straight back to the quarterback’s depth (dashed), and the inside rushers drive the guards back into his face. The cage (green outline) is made of driven-back blockers with rushers on their outside shoulders: it shrinks around him but never opens. Some defenses add a spy, a linebacker who stays at home and mirrors the quarterback side to side (M), as a last line if he does escape.





The word “mush” sounds passive, and the mush rush is often criticised as timid when it fails. But watch it work against a great runner and it is anything but. The rushers are still fighting their blockers; they are fighting them for position rather than for a path around them. The quarterback ends up throwing from a shrinking space with no lanes, or running into a defender who was waiting for exactly that.
The cost is the clock. A mush rush produces fewer quick pressures and fewer sacks, so the coverage behind it has to hold for four or five seconds instead of two and a half. Against a quarterback who is both a great runner and a patient passer, that is a miserable choice, which is why such quarterbacks are so hard to defend. Some defenses add the spy you met in Linebackers, a defender assigned only to mirror the quarterback; it buys insurance at the cost of a man in coverage or in the rush.






CautionCommon misconception



“A mush rush means the defense isn’t trying to get to the quarterback.” It means the defense has decided where it wants the quarterback to be, and has accepted that he will get there later. Against a quarterback who runs for a first down every time a lane opens, a sack is less valuable than an escape is costly.

title: The Pass Rush: Moves, Stunts, and Why Pressure Beats Sacks
section: Measuring a pass rush: why pressure beats sacks
text:
Measuring a pass rush: why pressure beats sacks
A sack, the quarterback tackled behind the line before he can throw, is the pass rush’s famous statistic, and for good reason: it is one of the most damaging plays in football. It costs yards, a down and often the drive, and sometimes the ball. The NFL has counted sacks officially only since 1982;6 the single-season record is the 23.0 that Myles Garrett set in 2025, breaking the 22.5 shared by Michael Strahan (2001) and T.J. Watt (2021).7
But as a way to judge a pass rush, sacks are a poor instrument, and the reason is simple arithmetic. A sack happens only when three things go right for the defense: a rusher gets to the quarterback (pressure), the quarterback fails to get rid of the ball or escape, and the rusher finishes the tackle. Only the first is mostly about the rush. So analysts split it in two:
\[\text{sacks} = \text{pressures} \times \text{the share of pressures that become sacks}\]
Pressure, as Pass Protection defined it, is any rusher forcing the quarterback to change what he wanted to do: a sack, a hit or a hurry. In FTN’s charting of the 2023–2025 regular seasons, quarterbacks were pressured on 30% of dropbacks and sacked on 6.6%, so only about 22% of pressures, roughly one in 5, became sacks.
Does a pressure that is not a sack matter? A great deal. Over the same seasons, a clean dropback was worth +0.23 expected points to the offense on average, a pressured dropback that did not end in a sack -0.07, and a sack -1.77. Quarterbacks completed 70% of their throws when clean and 47% when pressured.8 (Some of that gap is selection, since long-developing plays get pressured more often, but the direction is not in doubt.) The hurry that nobody counts turns a good play for the offense into a slightly bad one, on many more snaps than sacks ever do. So the question is what decides the conversion from pressure to sack, and whether it belongs to the rush at all.


Show the Python

Figure 39.9: Pressure and sacks, defense by defense: every team-season from 2023 to 2025 (regular season; pressure includes sacks, from FTN’s charting). Teams that pressure more do sack more, but look at the spread: at any pressure rate, sack rates differ by a factor of two. The faint rays show the conversion, the share of pressures that became sacks. The arrow follows the Cleveland Browns: in 2024 they had the highest pressure rate of any defense in these three seasons and an ordinary sack rate; in 2025 they pressured less often, converted far more of those pressures, and Myles Garrett set the single-season record. Data: nflverse play-by-play and participation via nflreadpy.





Three things stand out in Figure 39.9.
Pressure and sacks are related, but loosely. Across these team-seasons the correlation between a defense’s pressure rate and its sack rate is 0.59: real, but far from one. Two defenses that reach the quarterback equally often can finish with very different sack totals. The 2025 Broncos turned 28% of their pressures into sacks, 68 in all; the 2025 49ers turned 14% into sacks and finished with 20.
The best pressure team was not the best sack team. The 2024 Browns pressured opposing quarterbacks on 41.1% of dropbacks, the highest rate of any defense in these three seasons (far enough from the pack that some of it may be how FTN’s charters judged hurries that year; trust the ranking more than the decimal), and finished with 41 sacks, converting only 17%. In 2025, with largely the same star at the heart of the rush, they pressured less often (34.9%) and finished with 53 sacks, because 27% of their pressures became sacks. Context shaped both years: a wide, attacking front produces many hurries that arrive just as the ball leaves, and a team that trails often, as the 2024 Browns did, faces quarterbacks throwing quickly to catch up. But the data that follows says the conversion itself is mostly not something a defense keeps. Garrett’s record season was real, and so was his dominance the year before; the sacks just arrived in one year rather than the other.
So which number should you believe? The test is which one repeats. A measure of skill should carry over from one season to the next, because the players and coaches mostly carry over; a measure full of luck should not.


Show the Python

Figure 39.10: What carries over from one season to the next. Each row is a correlation between a measure in one season and the same team’s (or quarterback’s) measure the next season; the faint dots are the individual season pairs (2018-19 to 2021-22 from Next Gen Stats’ charting, 2023-24 and 2024-25 from FTN’s; the 2022-23 pair is left out because the source changes), and the large dot is their average. Read the averages and the pattern, not any single dot. A defense’s pressure rate repeats better than its sack rate, and even predicts next year’s sacks better than this year’s sacks do. A defense’s pressure-to-sack conversion does not repeat at all; a quarterback’s does. Data: nflverse play-by-play and participation via nflreadpy; quarterbacks with at least 100 pressured dropbacks in both seasons.





Figure 39.10 is the core of the case for pressure.9 On average, a defense’s pressure rate correlates about 0.31 with its own pressure rate the next season; its sack rate correlates only about 0.13 with next season’s sack rate. And this season’s pressure rate predicts next season’s sack rate (about 0.26) better than this season’s sack rate does. If you want to know which pass rush will get sacks next year, count its pressures this year, not its sacks. A caution on precision: with 32 teams, any one season pair carries a margin of roughly ±0.17, and the season pairs scatter widely. The gap between the two averages is about two of its own standard errors, so “pressure repeats better” is solid; exactly how much better is not.
The fourth row shows why. A defense’s conversion rate, the share of its pressures that become sacks, has essentially no carry-over (an average correlation of +0.00). A defense that converted a lot one year is no more likely than any other to convert a lot the next. Whatever drives the conversion, it is not something the defense keeps.
The fifth row says what it is, or at least who. A quarterback’s conversion rate, the share of the times he is pressured that end in a sack, does carry over, about 0.33 on average (noisier, because there are only twenty or thirty quarterbacks a season with enough pressures to measure). Some quarterbacks get rid of the ball, throw it away, step up or escape when the rush arrives, and some take the sack, year after year. How big is that? Among the 35 quarterbacks with at least 200 pressured dropbacks in 2023–2025, the conversion ran from 13% (Bo Nix) to 30% (Will Levis), with the middle half between 18% and 23%. The same rush, aimed at the quarterback at the top of that list, produces more than twice as many sacks. FTN’s charters also flag every sack they judge to be the quarterback’s fault, and they flagged about 34% of them, one in three.10 Quarterback Play has more on that spread. A pass rush’s sack total depends a great deal on which quarterbacks it happened to face, how often it faced them on third-and-long, and a large helping of luck about which pressures arrived a half-step before the throw. Pressure is the part of the sack the rush owns.






CautionCommon misconception



“Sacks tell you who the best pass rushers are.” They tell you who finished plays, which is real but partial. Many sacks are clean-up sacks: an interior rusher collapses the pocket, the quarterback slides away from him into an edge rusher, and the edge rusher gets the credit. Others are coverage sacks, where the quarterback held the ball for four or five seconds because nobody was open, and whoever arrived first got the stat. And some of the best rushes in a game, like the one that opened this chapter, produce a throw a beat too early and no statistic at all. Watch for who caused the pressure, not just who was standing over the quarterback.

title: The Pass Rush: Moves, Stunts, and Why Pressure Beats Sacks
section: Pass rush win rate, get-off and time to pressure
text:
Pass rush win rate, get-off and time to pressure
If sacks are too noisy and pressure is better, can we do better still? Pressure has its own flaw: it depends on the clock. A rusher who beats his man cleanly in 1.5 seconds against a quarterback who throws in 1.3 gets no pressure, and a rusher who is stonewalled for four seconds and then wanders in while the quarterback pats the ball gets one. Tracking data allows measures that do not depend on what the quarterback does.
Pass rush win rate. ESPN’s pass rush win rate (PRWR), introduced in 2018 by ESPN Analytics and built on Next Gen Stats tracking data, asks one question of every rush: did the rusher beat his block within 2.5 seconds of the snap?11 Its companion, pass block win rate, asks the reverse of every blocker. The fixed 2.5-second clock is the clever part. It sits a little before the average throw, ESPN found it best separated the rushers and blockers already known to be good, and it takes the quarterback out of the number: a quarterback who holds the ball cannot hand rushers late “wins,” and one who throws quickly cannot hide a rusher who was about to get home. ESPN publishes it as leaderboards ranked within position groups, so edge rushers are compared with edge rushers and interior linemen with interior linemen, because their jobs are so different. For a scale: when ESPN introduced it, four weeks into the 2018 season, the average edge rusher won about 22% of his rushes and the leaders were in the 40s. A rusher who wins one rush in three is very good; one in five is ordinary. Double teams get special care: since 2019, beating one blocker of a double team no longer counts as a win, which is why an interior rusher who wins often against constant doubles is so impressive.
Its limits are worth knowing. A “win” is not a pressure; a rusher can beat his man and still be too late or too wide to matter. A bull rush that walks the tackle into the quarterback without ever shedding him is the kind of rep a “did he beat his block” measure can miss. The model does not know each rusher’s assignment, so a penetrator on a stunt, whose job is to occupy blockers, can look like a loser while doing exactly what was asked. And the play-by-play data is not public, only the leaderboards, so you cannot rebuild it yourself. Use it the way you would use a scout’s opinion: an excellent tiebreaker between players, not a final verdict.
Get-off and time to pressure. Two simpler tracking measures bracket the rush. Get-off, as above, is how quickly a rusher crosses the line after the snap. Time to pressure is the seconds from the snap to the first pressure on the play. Together they separate the rushes that won from the ones that were handed something. A pressure inside about two and a half seconds, before most throws are due, is almost always a rush win. One after three and a half seconds, when every route has finished, is usually the coverage, the quarterback holding the ball, or both. In between is shared credit: the routes are just finishing, and the rush and coverage are working together. Here is how each is computed from tracking data, on a simulated four-man rush.


Show the Python
def measured_rush():
    """A four-man rush against five blockers: the right end wins with speed, the others are held up."""
    p = Play(line() + [O("QB", "QB", -5.0, 0.0, "Q")], four_down(), los=35, to_go=None)
    timed(p, "QB", [(0.9, -7.0, 0.0), (2.1, -7.0, 0.0), (2.8, -6.4, -1.4)])
    timed(p, "RE", [(0.1, 1.0, 5.4), (0.5, 0.0, 5.8), (0.95, -1.9, 6.2), (1.3, -3.2, 5.8), (1.7, -4.5, 4.7),
                    (2.0, -5.6, 3.0), (2.3, -6.3, 1.6), (2.8, -6.5, 0.1)], "rush")
    timed(p, "RT", [(0.4, -1.4, 3.7), (0.8, -2.2, 4.2), (1.2, -2.8, 4.3), (1.6, -3.2, 4.1), (2.0, -3.5, 3.9),
                    (2.8, -3.8, 3.6)], "block")
    timed(p, "LE", [(0.35, 1.0, -5.4), (0.8, 0.0, -5.8), (1.2, -1.3, -6.0), (1.8, -2.4, -5.6), (2.4, -3.0, -5.1),
                    (2.8, -3.2, -4.8)], "rush")
    timed(p, "LT", [(0.4, -1.4, -3.7), (0.9, -2.3, -4.4), (1.4, -3.0, -4.6), (2.0, -3.6, -4.2), (2.8, -3.9, -3.5)],
          "block")
    timed(p, "NT", [(0.25, 1.0, -0.7), (0.7, 0.0, -0.75), (1.2, -0.8, -0.8), (2.0, -1.25, -0.8), (2.8, -1.5, -0.8)],
          "rush")
    timed(p, "C", [(0.4, -1.3, -0.1), (1.0, -1.9, -0.2), (2.0, -2.3, -0.2), (2.8, -2.6, -0.2)], "block")
    timed(p, "LG", [(0.4, -1.2, -1.8), (1.0, -1.6, -1.6), (2.0, -2.1, -1.6), (2.8, -2.4, -1.6)], "block")
    timed(p, "DT", [(0.1, 1.0, 2.35), (0.5, 0.0, 2.3), (1.2, -0.9, 2.1), (2.0, -1.35, 2.0), (2.8, -1.7, 1.9)], "rush")
    timed(p, "RG", [(0.4, -1.3, 1.8), (1.2, -2.0, 1.9), (2.0, -2.3, 1.9), (2.8, -2.8, 1.9)], "block")
    return p


MR = measured_rush()
TRK = MR.to_tracking()               # simulated tracking in Big Data Bowl columns: frameId, time, x, y, ...
LOS_X = MR.los
RUSHERS = {"LE": "left end", "NT": "1-technique", "DT": "3-technique", "RE": "right end"}
frames = TRK[TRK["time"] >= 0]
qb = frames[frames["displayName"] == "QB"].set_index("time")[["x", "y"]]
GETOFF, DIST = {}, {}
for k in RUSHERS:
    r = frames[frames["displayName"] == k].set_index("time")[["x", "y"]]
    GETOFF[k] = float(r.index[r["x"] <= LOS_X + 1e-9][0])          # first frame on or past the line
    DIST[k] = np.hypot(r["x"] - qb["x"], r["y"] - qb["y"])
near = pd.concat(DIST, axis=1).min(axis=1)
TTP = float(near.index[near <= 2.0][0])                              # first frame within 2 yards of the QB
rt = frames[frames["displayName"] == "RT"].set_index("time")["x"]
re_ = frames[frames["displayName"] == "RE"].set_index("time")["x"]
WIN_T = float(re_.index[(re_ < rt - 0.5)][0])                        # the end half a yard deeper than his blocker
ALL_ACROSS = float(np.ceil(max(GETOFF.values()) * 10) / 10) + 0.3   # a beat after the last one crossed
strip(MR, [0.0, ALL_ACROSS, WIN_T, TTP],
      notes=["snap", "all four have crossed the line:\neach one's get-off is logged",
             f"+{WIN_T:.1f} s: the end gets past\nthe tackle: a rush 'win'",
             f"+{TTP:.1f} s: within 2 yards\nof the QB: pressure"],
      lateral=(-8.0, 8.0), window=(-9.4, 2.6), ncols=2, rings=(("RE", style.THIRD),))
plt.show()








Figure 39.11: A four-man rush measured from tracking data (simulated, BDB-format; receivers and coverage not shown). 1: the snap. 2: under a second later all four rushers have crossed the line; each one’s get-off is the frame he crossed it. 3: the right end gets past the right tackle (deeper than him, toward the quarterback): his rush is won, well inside the 2.5-second window pass rush win rate uses. 4: the end reaches two yards of the quarterback, this chapter’s working definition of pressure for the measurement, and the quarterback has to move. The other three rushers are still in front of their blockers.







Show the Python
style.apply()
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 2.9))
END_Y = {}
for k, name in RUSHERS.items():
    col = style.SERIES[1] if k == "RE" else style.MUTED
    d = DIST[k][DIST[k].index <= 2.8]
    ax.plot(d.index, d.values, color=col, lw=2.2 if k == "RE" else 1.3, zorder=3)
    ax.plot([GETOFF[k]], [float(DIST[k].loc[GETOFF[k]])], "o", ms=5, color=col, mec="white", mew=0.7, zorder=4)
    END_Y[k] = float(d.values[-1])
ys_lab, last = {}, None
for k in sorted(END_Y, key=END_Y.get):            # spread the end labels so none overlap
    y = END_Y[k] if last is None else max(END_Y[k], last + 0.62)
    ys_lab[k], last = y, y
for k, name in RUSHERS.items():
    ax.text(2.84, ys_lab[k], name, fontsize=7.2, color=style.SERIES[1] if k == "RE" else style.INK_2, va="center")
ax.axhline(2.0, color=style.SERIES[7], lw=1.0, ls=(0, (3, 2)), zorder=2)
ax.text(0.05, 2.25, "pressure: within 2 yards", fontsize=7, color=style.SERIES[7], va="bottom")
ax.axvspan(0, 2.5, color=style.SERIES[0], alpha=0.06, zorder=0)
ax.text(1.25, 9.6, "pass rush win rate's 2.5-second window", fontsize=7,
        color=style.SERIES[0], ha="center", va="top")
ax.axvline(TTP, color=style.SERIES[1], lw=1.0, ls=(0, (1, 1.5)), zorder=2)
ax.text(TTP - 0.05, 8.3, f"time to pressure\n{TTP:.1f} s", fontsize=7, color=style.SERIES[1], ha="right", va="center")
ax.set_xlim(0, 3.45)
ax.set_ylim(0, 10)
ax.set_xlabel("seconds after the snap", fontsize=8)
ax.set_ylabel("yards to the QB", fontsize=8)
ax.tick_params(labelsize=7.6)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 39.12: The same simulated rush as numbers: each rusher’s distance from the quarterback, frame by frame (ten per second). For the first half-second or so the distances rise or hold steady, because the quarterback is dropping back as fast as the rushers are closing. The dots mark each rusher’s get-off, the frame he crossed the line. The dashed horizontal line is the two-yard pressure threshold used here; the right end crosses it first, which is the play’s time to pressure. The shaded band is pass rush win rate’s 2.5-second window: the end beat his blocker inside it, so his rush counts as a win, while the other three never beat theirs.





In this simulated play the rushers’ get-offs range from 0.5 to 0.8 seconds, the right end beats his tackle at 1.4 seconds, and the time to pressure is 2.4 seconds, inside two and a half: a rush win by the stopwatch too. On a real play the definitions need more care than a two-yard circle (data providers use their own rules for what counts as pressure, and real players are not points), but the logic is exactly this, and it is the logic you will build on real Big Data Bowl frames in Tracking Data and the Big Data Bowl.


Show the Python (the same measurements on a real Big Data Bowl play)
# Run this after downloading a Big Data Bowl edition (see 13-05). Column names differ by year;
# gridiron.bdb.prepare() normalizes direction (offense moving +x) and labels each player 'off', 'def' or 'ball'.
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from gridiron import bdb

trk_all = bdb.load_tracking("data/bdb/tracking_week_1.csv")
plays = pd.read_csv("data/bdb/plays.csv")
players = pd.read_csv("data/bdb/players.csv")[["nflId", "position"]]
one = bdb.prepare(trk_all, plays, game_id=2022091100, play_id=55).merge(players, on="nflId", how="left")
after = one[one["time"] >= 0]
los_x = float(one.loc[(one["time"] == 0) & (one["side"] == "ball"), "x"].iloc[0])
qb = after[after["position"] == "QB"].set_index("time")[["x", "y"]]
rushers = after[(after["side"] == "def") & after["position"].isin(["DE", "DT", "NT", "OLB"])]
for nfl_id, r in rushers.groupby("nflId"):
    r = r.set_index("time")
    crossed = r.index[r["x"] <= los_x]                      # get-off: first frame on or past the line
    dist = np.hypot(r["x"] - qb["x"], r["y"] - qb["y"])     # distance to the passer, frame by frame
    close = dist.index[dist <= 2.0]                         # a simple pressure rule; providers use their own
    print(r["displayName"].iloc[0], "get-off", crossed.min() if len(crossed) else None,
          "within 2 yd at", close.min() if len(close) else None)

title: The Pass Rush: Moves, Stunts, and Why Pressure Beats Sacks
text:
Where the moves came from
The modern pass rusher’s ancestor is Deacon Jones, the Los Angeles Rams’ defensive end of the 1960s, a ferocious speed rusher who is credited with coining the word “sack” for what he did to quarterbacks. His signature weapon was the head slap: a blow to the side of the blocker’s helmet at the snap to stun him for an instant, then go around him. The NFL banned the head slap in 1977, and blows to the head have been illegal for rushers ever since.12 A year later the 1978 rule changes went the other way for blockers, letting them extend their arms and open their hands on pass blocks (The 1978 Liberation tells that story). Together, the two changes turned the pass rush into what it is now: a fight between the rusher’s hands and the blocker’s, aimed at arms and chests, where technique and timing matter as much as violence.
Then came the player who made offenses rebuild their protections around him: Lawrence Taylor, the Giants’ outside linebacker from 1981, rushing from a two-point stance on the edge of a 3-4 with a speed no blocker of the time could match (Pass Protection told how offenses answered him with extra blockers). In 1986 he had 20.5 sacks and was the league’s Most Valuable Player, the last defensive player to win the award,13 and the value of the left tackle, who blocks a right-handed quarterback’s blind side, rose with him. Defenses still like a great rusher on that side, but many of today’s best flip sides from week to week, or snap to snap, to hunt whichever tackle is weaker.
Reggie White, “the Minister of Defense,” showed what power and hands could do. After fifteen seasons, most of them with the Eagles and the Packers, he retired as the NFL’s career sack leader, with 198 (Bruce Smith later passed him, finishing with 200), and his signature, the “hump” move, was a club-and-lift: a forearm club up under the blocker’s arm that lifted and threw him aside, a rip and a bull rush in one violent motion.14 In the 2000s Dwight Freeney’s spin move made a smaller, quicker body type dangerous on the edge. And in the 2010s Aaron Donald proved that the most dangerous rusher on the field could line up inside.
Today’s edge rushers study tackles’ sets on film like quarterbacks study coverages, and the hand fight has become its own discipline: the long arm, the cross-chop, the ghost. T.J. Watt tied the sack record in 2021 and won Defensive Player of the Year; Myles Garrett broke it in 2025 and won the award unanimously.15 And Micah Parsons, the Cowboys’ first-round pick in 2021, made a different point: drafted as an off-ball linebacker, he became one of the league’s most feared rushers by lining up all over the front, over a guard one snap and wide on the edge the next, so that protections could never be sure where to slide. Dallas traded him to Green Bay just before the 2025 season, for two first-round picks and defensive tackle Kenny Clark.16

title: The Pass Rush: Moves, Stunts, and Why Pressure Beats Sacks
text:
Film room






NoteFilm room: Cleveland Browns 2025 — Myles Garrett’s record



The play to find. Week 18 of 2025, the Browns at Cincinnati, fourth quarter, 5:16 left: Garrett sacks Joe Burrow for his 23rd sack of the season, the one that broke the record.17 He was playing in Jim Schwartz’s attacking front (Schwartz was the Browns’ defensive coordinator from 2023 to 2025), which lines its ends up wide and sends them upfield.18
What to notice: then pick any Browns passing down from that season and watch only Garrett and the man blocking him.

The alignment. Which side is he on, and how wide? Wide means a long arc and a running start.
The get-off. Count how often he is the first player on the field to move, and where he meets the tackle: in front of him, or level with him at the corner.
The first move, then the second. Note what he shows in the first quarter and what he does in the fourth. Look for the speed-to-power: three steps of speed, then straight into the tackle’s chest.
The help, and his answer. Count how often the offense chips him with a back or tight end or slides its protection toward him, and watch how he beats the chip: by rushing through the chipper’s outside shoulder, or by starting wider so the back cannot reach him. Every extra man on Garrett is a one-on-one for someone else.
The finish. On his sacks, notice how many came quickly (a rush win) and how many came after the quarterback had held the ball (a coverage or clean-up sack).









NoteFilm room: Super Bowls LIX and LX — pressure with four



The games. The last two Super Bowls were won by defenses that got to the quarterback without blitzing. In Super Bowl LIX (February 2025) the Eagles rushed four or fewer on 44 of Patrick Mahomes’s 45 dropbacks and sacked him 6 times, 6 of them with four or fewer rushers. In Super Bowl LX (February 2026) the Seahawks rushed four or fewer on 46 of Drake Maye’s 54 dropbacks and sacked him 6 times, 5 of them with four or fewer.19 Mike Macdonald’s Seattle defense has a reputation for four-man simulated pressures, in which a lineman drops and a linebacker or defensive back rushes in his place (Zone Blitzes and Simulated Pressure shows how). Macdonald himself pushed back on that in November 2025 (“We do not run a lot of simulated pressures”),20 and the Super Bowl bears him out: FTN’s charters counted a blitzer on only 4 of Seattle’s 46 four-man rushes. Mostly, its four were its front four, winning.
What to notice:

Count the rushers on every dropback. Almost always four. Then count the coverage behind them: seven men for at most five receivers.
Look for the stunts. On long downs, watch for two rushers crossing paths, and ask which blocker the looper was aimed at.
Time the pressure. Count from the snap to the moment the quarterback has to move, and see how many pressures arrive before the receivers have finished their routes.

The Eagles’ game is studied in the Eagles case study, and Seattle’s defense, built by Mike Macdonald, in Fangio’s Two-High Revolution and Macdonald’s Answer.

title: The Pass Rush: Moves, Stunts, and Why Pressure Beats Sacks
text:
Watch for it on Sunday






TipWatch for it



Before the snap.

Find the best rusher and his alignment. Wide outside the tackle (built for speed), tight over him (power and inside moves), or standing up over a guard (he is being moved around to beat the protection).
Count the rushers you expect and the blockers you see. Four rushers against five or six blockers means the defense is trusting its four; look at the coverage behind them.
Check the down and distance. Third-and-long is when stunts and patient rushes have time to work; on third-and-2 the ball will be out too fast for either.
Is the quarterback a runner? If so, expect the ends to rush with discipline, and maybe a spy.
Where is the help? Find the back and any tight end. One aligned near the best rusher probably means a chip, and at the snap the linemen’s first steps tell you slide or man (all five stepping the same way is a slide). Stunts and the best rusher’s moves are aimed away from the help.

After the snap: the stopwatch drill.

Count the seconds from the snap to the first pressure (“one-Mississippi”), or use a stopwatch on a replay. Under about two and a half seconds is a rush win. Past three and a half, the coverage or the quarterback owns most of it. In between, they share it.
Note whether the ball was already out. A rusher who arrives just after the throw has still done his job if he made the quarterback throw early; a rusher who arrives after a five-second hold was handed it.
Name the move. Around the corner (speed and rip), through the chest (bull or long arm), or back inside (swim, spin). In the fourth quarter, look for the counter to whatever worked in the first.
Watch for crossing paths. Two rushers swapping lanes is a stunt; find the looper, and see which blocker he was aimed at, and whether the blockers passed it off.
Check the lanes. If the quarterback escapes, freeze the replay and find the rusher who left his lane.

For your prediction log: for one quarter, write down on every dropback the number of rushers, your stopwatch time to pressure (or “none”), and whether the ball was out first. You will see which defenses win early and which only win late.

Predict the play






TipPredict the play 1: third-and-long against five





Show the Python
def quiet_line():
    """The five linemen with only the center labelled: on full-width drills the two-letter labels overprint."""
    return [q.moved(label="C" if q.key == "C" else "") for q in line()]


def empty_3x2():
    return quiet_line() + [O("QB", "QB", -5.0, 0.0, "Q"), O("X", "WR", -0.7, -15.0), O("A", "WR", -1.4, -9.5),
                     O("Y", "TE", -1.4, 6.5), O("H", "WR", -1.4, 10.5), O("Z", "WR", -0.7, 15.0)]


dfn = four_down() + [D("WILL", "WILL", 5.0, -6.0, "W"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.8, 4.6, "M"),
                     D("NB", "NB", 5.0, 10.0, "NB"), D("LCB", "CB", 6.5, -15.0, "CB"),
                     D("RCB", "CB", 6.5, 15.0, "CB"), D("FS", "FS", 13.0, -7.0, "FS"), D("SS", "SS", 13.0, 7.0, "SS")]
p = Play(empty_3x2(), dfn, los=40, to_go=11)
p.highlight("DT", "RE", color=PURPLE)
fld = draw(p, width_in=6.4, lateral=(-17.0, 17.0), window=(-7.0, 14.6))
plt.show()








Figure 39.13: Third-and-11. The offense is in an empty formation, three receivers right and two left, so only the five linemen can block. The defense shows four linemen (a 1-technique shaded to the center’s left, a 3-technique to the right, an end outside each tackle), two linebackers walked out over the slot receivers, and two deep safeties. The two defenders on the right side of the line are ringed.





Is this a good down for a stunt? If so, which one, aimed where, and what is the defense risking?






TipAnswer





Yes: this is the down stunts are made for, and a T-E on the right, with the 3-technique picking the right tackle and the end looping inside, is the natural call. The clock: on third-and-11 the quarterback needs routes that get past the line to gain, so he will usually hold the ball two and a half seconds or more, long enough for a looper to arrive. The numbers: five blockers against four rushers gives the offense one spare man, but against this front the spare is the left guard, uncovered on the far side. Aim the stunt at the right guard and right tackle, away from him, and those two must pass it off alone. The choice: T-E rather than E-T if the end is the better rusher, because the looper is the man who arrives free.
Two cautions. If the offense slides its five-man protection toward that side, the center, right guard and right tackle all step that way and own those gaps, and the stunt is absorbed. You cannot see that from the pre-snap picture, which is why defenses study how a team protects from empty before calling it. And the stunt moves the right side’s contain from the end to the 3-technique: against a quarterback who runs, a washed-out 3-technique turns third-and-11 into a scramble. Against a pocket passer, most defenses happily take that risk.











TipPredict the play 2: the quarterback who runs





Show the Python
off = quiet_line() + [O("QB", "QB", -5.0, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -5.0, -2.0, "R"), O("X", "WR", -0.7, -15.0),
                      O("H", "WR", -1.4, -9.5), O("Y", "TE", -0.7, 4.8), O("Z", "WR", -1.4, 15.0)]
dfn = [D("LE", "DE", 1.0, -5.4, "E"), D("NT", "DT", 1.0, -0.7, "1"), D("DT", "DT", 1.0, 2.35, "3"),
       D("RE", "DE", 1.0, 7.1, "w9"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.6, 1.3, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.6, -3.0, "W"),

       D("FS", "FS", 12.5, -6.5, "FS"), D("SS", "SS", 12.5, 6.5, "SS")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=40, to_go=6)
p.highlight("QB")
fld = draw(p, width_in=6.4, lateral=(-17.0, 17.0), window=(-7.0, 14.6))
plt.show()








Figure 39.14: Third-and-6. The offense is in the shotgun with three wide receivers, a tight end, and a back beside a quarterback (ringed in green) who is one of the league’s most dangerous runners. The defense is in a nickel with four linemen, including a wide-9 end (w9) on the right.





How do you expect the four to rush, which of them has the hardest job, and what is the defense giving up?






TipAnswer





Expect a mush rush. On third-and-6, a quarterback who runs does not need a receiver to get open; he needs one lane. So the defense’s first priority is that no lane opens, and its second is the sack.
The wide-9 end has the hardest job, because his alignment is built for the long, fast arc that runs an end past the quarterback and opens the escape lane in Figure 39.7, on the quarterback’s throwing-arm side at that. Expect him to tighten his alignment before the snap, or, if he stays wide, to rush through the tackle’s outside half rather than around him. The other side is less of a worry: the back, lined up on the quarterback’s left, will likely chip the left end or stay in to block, and the tight end beside the right tackle can chip the wide-9 on his way out, which is one more reason that end cannot win with speed alone. Expect fewer stunts, and don’t be surprised if a linebacker mirrors the quarterback instead of covering anyone: a spy.
The price is time: the coverage, with six or seven men, must hold for four seconds or more, and if anyone breaks contain, the play you will see is the one the defense feared most, a quarterback through the hole and past the line to gain.











TipPredict the play 3: the counter





Show the Python
p = Play(line(["RG", "RT"]), [D("DT", "DT", 1.0, 2.35, "3"), D("RE", "DE", 1.0, 5.4, "E")], los=35, to_go=None)
to(p, "RT", (-1.2, 3.7))
to(p, "RG", (-1.5, 1.8))
to(p, "DT", (-0.4, 2.2), "rush")
to(p, "RE", (-0.9, 6.6), "rush", via=[(0.2, 6.2)])
fld = draw(p, width_in=5.0, lateral=(-0.8, 10.6), window=(-7.2, 3.4))
ghost(fld, p, -0.9, 6.6, "E")
point_to(fld, p, (-3.6, 6.6), (-1.2, 3.7), "the tackle sets short\nand square, sitting inside", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK)
say(fld, p, -5.6, 1.4, "QB this way", color=style.INK_2, fontsize=6.6)
plt.show()








Figure 39.15: Fourth quarter. The defense’s best rusher (E) has beaten this right tackle inside twice today with a spin, once for a sack. On this snap the tackle has set short and square, sitting inside, determined not to be spun again; the right guard has the 3-technique in front of him. The picture is about 0.8 seconds after the snap: the faint square is where the rusher is now, early in his arc.





What move is coming, and what can the offense do about it, this snap and the next?






TipAnswer





The speed rush, around the corner: a dip and rip. This is the rush plan paying off from the other direction. Twice the rusher won inside, so the tackle has stopped bailing: he is sitting short and square to protect the inside. But a tackle who has not gained depth has no time to get back to the corner, and the rusher meets him level before he can turn and run. The spin is the wrong answer now; that is exactly the move the tackle is sitting on.
The offense has fewer answers on this snap than you might think. The right guard cannot help outside, because the 3-technique is on him. The quarterback’s best move is to step up into the pocket, so the rusher’s arc carries him past behind. Next snaps: the tackle varies his sets (a jump set at the line, or a 45-degree set instead of sitting) so the rusher cannot read the set and pick the counter; the offense chips the rusher with a back or tight end on the way out; and the play caller calls quick throws, so the ball is gone before any move can finish. That is the conversation across a game in miniature: the rusher made the tackle afraid of one thing, and now the offense has to change the question.

title: The Pass Rush: Moves, Stunts, and Why Pressure Beats Sacks
text:
Back to the replay
Return to the play that opened the chapter. Third-and-8, four rushers, an end who took three strides up the arc and then drove straight into the tackle: speed-to-power, set up by every speed rush he had shown before. The tackle, fearing the corner, had kicked back fast, so his weight was going backward when the end turned into him, and he could not anchor. The pocket collapsed from the side, the quarterback threw early, and the pass sailed.
The box score has nothing for the end. FTN’s charters would mark that dropback as pressured. Pass rush win rate might well count it as a win, though a bull rush that never sheds the blocker is the kind of rep a beat-the-block measure can miss. And a stopwatch would put the pressure at about two seconds, early enough that it was entirely the rush’s doing. That is the whole chapter in one snap: the moves, the plan that set them up, and the reason a coach values the hurry that nobody counts more than the sack total everybody does.

title: The Pass Rush: Moves, Stunts, and Why Pressure Beats Sacks
text:
Takeaways

The rush is a race and a fight. A rusher must beat a bigger blocker before the ball is out, a little under three seconds on average. Get-off decides where they meet: a tenth of a second is most of a yard, and meeting the tackle level at the corner instead of in front of him is the difference between winning and losing.
Each move punishes a mistake. Speed beats a slow set; the bull rush and long arm beat a high, light or retreating one; the swim, rip and spin beat a blocker who has committed. Cross-chops and ghosts beat the punch itself.
The best rushers have a plan. They show one move until the tackle adjusts, then use the counter his adjustment opens; speed-to-power works because tackles fear speed.
Stunts win with geometry. T-E, E-T and interior twists exchange rushers to beat man blocking or choose matchups against slides, at the cost of time and of lanes.
Four rush lanes make a box. Ends keep contain, the middle pushes the pocket; against a quarterback who runs, the mush rush squeezes instead of racing and accepts a longer clock.
Count pressure, not sacks. Pressure carries over from season to season and predicts future sacks; the share of pressures that become sacks mostly does not, except as a trait of the quarterback. Pass rush win rate, get-off and time to pressure use tracking data to take the quarterback out of the measure.

title: Blitzing: Numbers, Overloads, A-Gap Mugs, and Cover 0
text:
Why blitz at all: buying a rusher with a defender
Third-and-6 near midfield. As the offense settles at the line, two linebackers walk forward and plant themselves in the gaps on either side of the center, close enough to touch him. A safety starts creeping down from 12 yards toward the slot receiver. The center points at one of the linebackers and shouts a number; the quarterback steps up behind him, points at the other one and shouts a word. At the snap, the linebacker the center pointed at turns and runs backward into coverage, and the center is left blocking air. The other one hits the gap. The running back steps up to meet him, and from the far edge the slot cornerback comes untouched, sprinting at the quarterback’s back. The quarterback never looks at him. He has already thrown, on his third step, a quick hitch to the slot receiver the cornerback left behind, who catches it in front of the safety still running down from 12 yards. Nine yards, first down. The announcer says the defense “brought the house and got burned.” It didn’t, quite: six rushed against six blockers, and the cornerback was left unblocked on purpose, by the offense. To see why, you have to count the way coaches do.
You’ll be able to:
How to read the diagrams. Offense is blue circles, defense orange squares, and left and right are the offense’s. The linemen are LT, LG, C, RG and RT (on the wide figures only the center is labelled); Q is the quarterback and R the running back; X, Z, H, Y and A are receivers. On defense, E is an end and the defensive tackles are labelled by technique (1 shaded on the center, 3 on a guard’s outside shoulder, 0 head-up on the center); M and W are the Mike and Will linebackers, NB the nickel back, CB the cornerbacks, FS and SS the safeties. A solid orange arrow is a rusher; a faded orange arrow is a conditional rusher, who comes only if the man he is covering stays in to block; a dashed orange line is a defender dropping or rotating into coverage; a dotted orange line joins a man defender to his receiver. A blue line ending in a short bar is a block. A red ring marks the unblocked rusher, and a dashed red arrow is the path he takes. A purple ring marks the player to watch: the one the caption is about. A dashed brown arrow is the throw.
Every defense starts each passing down with the same budget: eleven players, split between rushing the quarterback and covering receivers. The offense spends its own budget first, in the huddle: five linemen who must block, plus however many backs and tight ends it keeps in, and everybody else runs a route. Most of the time the defense rushes four and covers with seven (The Pass Rush explains why that is the balance point). A blitz moves one or more players from the coverage column to the rush column.
What does the defense want from that trade? Not sacks, mostly. It wants time taken away. The quarterback in today’s NFL typically needs about two and a half seconds to let the ball go on an ordinary dropback; a blitz is an attempt to make that impossible, to put a rusher in his lap before the routes have finished, so that he has to throw early, throw somewhere he didn’t want to, or hold the ball and get hit. In FTN’s charting of the 2023–2025 regular seasons the median pass against four rushers came out after 2.5 seconds; against six it was 2.2, and against seven 2.0.1 Those few tenths are the whole point: they are the difference between a quarterback who can wait for a deep route to clear and one who cannot.
The price is paid in the back end: each extra rusher is one fewer defender in coverage, one less helper over the top and one fewer tackler for a receiver who catches a short ball. A blitz is a bet that the time it removes is worth more than the coverage it costs, and the last third of this chapter shows how often that bet pays.
How often do defenses make it? In FTN’s charting, about one dropback in four: 25% of regular-season dropbacks from 2022 through 2025 faced five or more rushers (20% in 2022, 27% in 2025; part of that rise may be the charters rather than the coaches, so read the trend loosely).2 And most of those blitzes are small: 77% of them sent exactly five. Only 6% of all dropbacks faced six or more. The all-out, everybody-comes blitz that broadcasts love to replay is the rare, high-stakes end of a mostly modest habit.

ImportantWhy it exists



The blitz exists because a defense that cannot win with four still needs the quarterback to throw before his receivers are ready. Adding rushers is the bluntest way to shorten his clock. What it gives up: a defender in coverage for every rusher it adds, which is why most blitzes add one, and why almost every blitz is designed around a quick throw the defense knows is coming.

title: Blitzing: Numbers, Overloads, A-Gap Mugs, and Cover 0
section: Blitz math: three counts and one question
text:
Blitz math: three counts and one question
Coaches on both sides of the ball think about a blitz as a short piece of arithmetic. You can do it from the couch, and once you can, a blitz stops being a blur.
Count 1: rushers against blockers. How many defenders can rush, and how many blockers does the offense have? Five linemen always block; a running back or tight end may stay in to make six or seven. If the rushers outnumber the blockers, somebody comes free by arithmetic. If they don’t, nobody should, and a free man means somebody made a mistake or the defense has outsmarted the rules.
Count 2: coverage defenders against receivers. Whatever is left after the rush has to cover whoever is left after the protection. Seven rushers leaves four defenders for, say, four receivers: man on everyone, no help anywhere. Five rushers against a six-man protection leaves six defenders for four receivers: room for a deep safety and a spare man underneath.
Count 3: by side. The first two counts are totals, but blocking happens in places. A protection that has six blockers for six rushers can still lose if four of those rushers arrive on a side with three blockers. Hold that thought for the section on overloads; it is the key to most clever blitzes.
The question: who is the unblocked rusher? When the rushers outnumber the blockers, one man will come untouched. This chapter calls him the unblocked rusher: the rusher the protection leaves alone on a particular snap. Pass Protection called a man left alone on purpose a free rusher and gave the offense’s rule for choosing him: block inside-out. The inside rushers have the shortest path to the quarterback, so the blockers take them first and leave the widest man, whose path is longest, because the ball can be out before he arrives. A second rule works the same way: most protections count only the box (the defenders lined up between the tackles and a few yards deep), so a nickel, corner or safety who blitzes from outside it is the quarterback’s to beat, with the ball, not the line’s to block. For the rest of the chapter, “the widest man” is shorthand for all of this: the rusher the offense chooses to leave, because he has the farthest to run. The defense knows these rules too, and the whole art of blitz design is to defeat them: to make the man who comes free the one with the shortest path, or one the quarterback cannot see, or one nobody expected to rush at all.
Put the counts together and you get a small table that every coordinator carries in his head.

Blitz math. Seven-man protections and three-man rushes follow the same logic. The “free by arithmetic” column is only the floor: overloads and mugs try to free a rusher even when the numbers match.

Two rows deserve a second look. In the third, five against five, nobody is free, but there is no spare blocker either, so one confused assignment produces a man nobody blocks. In the fifth, six against six, the offense has “enough,” yet the defense still has five defenders for four receivers: man on everyone with one spare. That is the shape of most real blitzes. The defense does not usually try to out-number the protection. It tries to make it guess.
Where does the quarterback throw when somebody does come free? To the hot receiver, and which one depends on the coverage behind the blitz:

If a defender left a receiver or an area to rush, throw there. Against zone it is the area the blitzer was guarding; against man it is the receiver he was covering, until someone rotates over. This is why the hot throw is usually on the same side the free rusher comes from: the free rusher is the blitzer, and the receiver he left is standing right where he started. The quarterback is not throwing at the rusher; he is throwing to the man the rusher left, before the rusher arrives.
If every receiver is still covered (a man blitz in which the extra rusher had no receiver of his own), there is no hole. Throw to the matchup you like, on a route that breaks away from the defender’s leverage.

Every blitz design, read from the defense’s side, is also a guess about where that throw will go, and many of them are built to take it away.






CautionCommon misconception



“The unblocked guy means somebody missed a block.” Sometimes. Just as often, the offense left him on purpose, because its protection had more rushers than blockers and its rules chose him: the widest man. Whether the play was a bust or a success depends on what the quarterback did: if he threw hot before the unblocked rusher arrived, the protection worked exactly as designed. The tell is the quarterback’s timing. A ball out on the third step, to a receiver who was already looking for it, was planned.

title: Blitzing: Numbers, Overloads, A-Gap Mugs, and Cover 0
section: Man pressure, part 1: the Cover 1 blitz
text:
Man pressure, part 1: the Cover 1 blitz
Most blitzes travel with man coverage, and the reason is the hole. In a zone, each defender guards an area; send one of them after the quarterback and his area is empty, and the hot throw goes straight into it. In man coverage it depends on who blitzes. If the blitzer is the spare defender, the one with no receiver of his own, every receiver is still covered and the defense has lost only a helper. If he is a man defender, his receiver is uncovered until someone rotates over to him: a hole, but a brief one, and the blitz families later in the chapter are largely about who rotates and how fast. Either way, when the defense blitzes, man coverage behind it roughly doubles. In FTN’s charting of 2023–2025, defenses played man on 33% of labelled dropbacks with four or fewer rushers, and on 60% when they sent five or more.3 The rest are zone blitzes, the subject of Zone Blitzes, Fire Zones, and Simulated Pressure, whose whole design problem is filling the hole the blitzer leaves.
The everyday man pressure is the Cover 1 blitz: man coverage on every eligible receiver, one deep safety in the middle as help, and the spare defenders sent after the quarterback. Its most common form is a five-man pressure: exactly five rushers, the four linemen plus one linebacker or defensive back.


Show the Python
off = line("C") + [O("QB", "QB", -5.0, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -5.0, 2.0, "R"), O("X", "WR", -0.7, -16.0),
                   O("H", "WR", -1.2, -10.0), O("Y", "TE", -0.7, -4.8), O("Z", "WR", -0.7, 16.0)]
dfn = [D("LE", "DE", 1.0, -6.6, "E"), D("NT", "DT", 1.0, -0.7, "1"), D("DT", "DT", 1.0, 2.35, "3"),
       D("RE", "DE", 1.0, 5.4, "E"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.4, 0.6, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.6, 3.4, "W"),

       D("SS", "SS", 5.4, -5.2, "SS"), D("FS", "FS", 13.5, 0.0, "FS")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=40, to_go=7)
for d_, t_ in (("LCB", "X"), ("RCB", "Z"), ("NB", "H"), ("SS", "Y"), ("WILL", "RB")):
    p.man(d_, t_)
to(p, "MIKE", (-2.4, 0.9), "rush", via=[(0.4, 0.8)])
to(p, "RB", (-3.0, 1.0))
p.zone((14.6, 0.0), (5.0, 22.0), label="deep middle")
for k in ("LE", "NT", "DT", "RE"):
    q = p.players[k]
    to(p, k, (-0.9, q.w + (0.5 if q.w > 0 else -0.5)), "rush")
fld = draw(p, lateral=(-19.5, 19.5), window=(-7.5, 18.5))
dashed(fld, p, [(4.6, 3.4), (1.6, 4.4), (-0.8, 4.4), (-2.6, 3.4)], color=style.DEFENSE, lw=2.4, dash="solid",
       alpha=0.42)
ring(fld, p, "MIKE", color=PURPLE)
say(fld, p, 9.7, 7.6, "W has R in man. If R stays\nin to block, W has no one to\ncover, so he rushes ('hug')",
    fontsize=6.6)
say(fld, p, -3.4, -2.6, "M blitzes;\nR steps up", fontsize=6.6, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK)
say(fld, p, 11.0, -9.6, "5 rush (6 with the hug) v 6 block\n5 in man, 1 deep (FS)", fontsize=7.0, weight="bold",
    color=style.INK)
plt.show()








Figure 40.1: A Cover 1 blitz against 11 personnel (one back, one tight end, three receivers), third-and-7. Five defenders are in man coverage (dotted lines): the cornerbacks (CB) on X and Z, the nickel (NB) on the slot H, the strong safety (SS) on the tight end Y, and the Will (W) on the running back. The free safety (FS) has the deep middle. The fifth rusher is the Mike (M, ringed purple), who blitzes through the right A gap; the back’s rule is to stay in and block the first linebacker who comes, so he steps up to meet him. Now the Will’s man is blocking, so the Will has no one to cover: under the hug rule he rushes too (the faded arrow), making six rushers against six blockers. Everyone is accounted for, but only if every blocker gets his man.





Walk through Figure 40.1 with the three counts. Rushers against blockers: five against six (the five linemen and the back), so on paper the offense can block everyone. Coverage against receivers: five defenders in man on five eligible receivers, plus the free safety deep. The side count: the Mike comes through the right A gap, on the back’s side, so the back has a short, straight trip to meet him. (Picking up a linebacker is easy when the back is lined up on his side and hard when he has to cross the formation to get there; keep that in mind for the bear pressure later.)
Then the twist that makes this a real blitz rather than a five-man rush the offense handles easily. When the back stays in to block, the Will, who was assigned to him in man coverage, has nobody to cover. Most defenses tell him to hug: to rush the moment he sees his man block. Now it is six against six. Everyone is still accounted for, but the offense has no spare blocker left at all, and the coverage still has a deep safety. If any blocker hesitates, two blockers take the same man, or the back meets the Mike a yard too late, someone comes through clean. The rule cuts the other way too: if the back releases into a route instead, the Will must peel off and cover him, and a back swinging out of the backfield past a linebacker who started toward the quarterback is one of the oldest blitz-beaters there is. (The hug is one kind of delayed blitz, a rusher who comes a beat after the snap. Some linebackers delay on purpose, waiting until the blockers have picked their men and then running through whatever gap is left.)
That is the design philosophy of the Cover 1 blitz: keep the safety, make the protection perfect. It is cheap in coverage, because the deep middle stays protected and every receiver has a man, and it is cheap in risk, because a receiver who beats his man still has a safety coming. Its weakness is that it does not guarantee anything. A good protection blocks it, a good quarterback reads it as man coverage and throws to the matchup he likes, and the defense has spent a linebacker to get a rush that would have been blocked anyway.






NoteMadden vs. real life



In Madden a blitz is a play you pick from the menu, and every player runs exactly the path drawn on it. Real blitzes have rules inside them. The Will in Figure 40.1 does not know before the snap whether he is a rusher or a cover man; the back decides that for him, after the snap, by blocking or by running a route. Many blitzes branch like this (“if your man blocks, rush; if he releases, cover him”), which is why the same call can produce five rushers on one snap and six on the next. Nobody learns those rules on the field. The coordinator radios one word to the green-dot defender (What a Play Really Is explains the helmet radio), he repeats it in the huddle, and each player already knows his branch of it, because the call and its rules were installed in meetings and practice all week.








NoteGo deeper: blitz dialects



Every staff has its own words. The hug is also called a “green dog” or an “add-on” rusher. A “dog” is still a linebacker blitz in many playbooks (the history section has where that comes from). “Cat” is the nickel in many playbooks (hence cat blitz), but in others “cat” or “cougar” means a corner blitz. When a broadcaster or a coach uses a name, ask who came and from where; that is what the name is trying to say.

title: Blitzing: Numbers, Overloads, A-Gap Mugs, and Cover 0
section: Man pressure, part 2: the Cover 0 blitz
text:
Man pressure, part 2: the Cover 0 blitz
Take the deep safety away and you have the Cover 0 blitz: man coverage on every eligible receiver, nobody deep, and every defender not covering someone sent after the quarterback. Man Coverage built Cover 0 from the coverage side: the safety’s job disappears, so he and the spare man become rushers. Here is the same idea from the rush side, against the formation that makes the arithmetic starkest: an empty backfield, where the five linemen are the only blockers.


Show the Python
off = line("C") + [O("QB", "QB", -5.0, 0.0, "Q"), O("X", "WR", -0.7, -15.5), O("A", "WR", -1.4, -9.5),
                   O("Y", "TE", -1.4, 5.8), O("H", "WR", -1.4, 10.0), O("Z", "WR", -0.7, 15.5)]
dfn = four_down() + [D("MIKE", "MIKE", 1.6, -2.4, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 1.6, 0.8, "W"),
                     D("LCB", "CB", 1.3, -14.0, "CB"), D("NB", "NB", 3.0, -8.0, "NB"),
                     D("SS", "SS", 3.0, 4.3, "SS"), D("FS", "FS", 3.0, 8.5, "FS"), D("RCB", "CB", 1.3, 14.0, "CB")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=40, to_go=4)
for d_, t_ in (("LCB", "X"), ("NB", "A"), ("SS", "Y"), ("FS", "H"), ("RCB", "Z")):
    p.man(d_, t_)
# inside-out: each lineman takes the man inside him, the widest rusher is left
for blk, rsh, spot in (("LT", "LE", (-1.5, -3.7)), ("LG", "MIKE", (-1.4, -1.9)), ("C", "NT", (-1.3, -0.3)),
                       ("RG", "WILL", (-1.3, 1.3)), ("RT", "DT", (-1.4, 2.9))):
    to(p, rsh, (spot[0] + 0.8, spot[1]), "rush")
    to(p, blk, spot)
p.dropback(1.0)
p.route("H", [(0, 0), (6.0, 0), (5.8, 4.0)])
p.route("Z", [(0, 0), (8, 0.8), (19, 1.6)])
p.pass_to("H", t=1.3)
fld = draw(p, lateral=(-19.0, 19.0), window=(-9.0, 20.5))
dashed(fld, p, [(1.0, 5.4), (-2.8, 4.0), (-5.8, 1.0)])
ring(fld, p, "RE")
point_to(fld, p, (-5.9, 10.8), (-3.2, 3.7), "unblocked by design:\nthe widest rusher,\nunder 2 s to the QB",
         color=RED, shrink=4)
say(fld, p, 15.0, 0.0, "nobody deep", fontsize=7.6, weight="bold", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK)
say(fld, p, -3.4, 14.6, "inside leverage:\nthe out is open", fontsize=6.6)
say(fld, p, 12.4, 11.6, "fade: win at the line,\nnobody behind", fontsize=6.6)
say(fld, p, 10.6, -9.8, "6 rush v 5 block\n5 in man, 0 deep", fontsize=7.0, weight="bold", color=style.INK)
say(fld, p, -5.6, -5.8, "line blocks inside-out", fontsize=6.6, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK)
plt.show()








Figure 40.2: A Cover 0 blitz against an empty formation (five receivers, so only the five linemen can block), third-and-4. The defense rushes six: the four linemen plus the Mike and Will, who were standing in the gaps. Five defenders play man on five receivers with nobody deep, each a step or two inside his receiver (inside leverage: no one is in the middle to help, so they take the inside away). The line blocks inside-out, each lineman taking the gap to his inside, and leaves the widest rusher, the right end (ringed red), unblocked; with a clear path he arrives in a little under two seconds. The quarterback must beat him: here with a quick out by H, run a yard past the sticks and thrown on rhythm at about 1.3 seconds, toward the sideline his defender’s inside leverage concedes. Z’s fade is the shot: if he wins at the line, there is nobody behind him.





The math in Figure 40.2 is brutal. Six rushers against five blockers: one is free by arithmetic, and the line’s inside-out rule makes it the right end, the widest man. Five defenders against five receivers: nobody left over, nobody deep. The quarterback has the time it takes that end to arrive, a little under two seconds. He cannot read the coverage, because there is nothing to read: everybody is in man. He has to pick the matchup before the snap, take a short drop and throw on rhythm.
Where? Look at how the defenders line up. With nobody in the middle of the field behind them, a man defender who lets his receiver cut inside has given up a catch with open grass in front of it and nobody coming to tackle. So Cover 0 defenders take inside leverage: they line up toward the middle and dare the receiver to go outside. That makes the classic answers outside-breaking quick routes (the quick out, the speed out, a whip or pivot route that fakes in and breaks out) and, for the brave, the fade: a receiver who beats a pressed corner at the line has nobody between him and the end zone. The figure shows both. The out is the safe hot throw; the fade is the throw that turns a third-and-4 into a touchdown. Defenses choose how tight to play it. “Zero press” puts everyone up close to deny every quick throw and lives with the fade; “off zero” gives a few yards of cushion against the fade and rallies to the short throw. Both are common, and the cushion you see before the snap tells you which throw the defense fears more.
Why would a defense take that deal? Because the arithmetic cuts both ways. The offense has to be perfect too: the right protection, a quarterback who sees it, a receiver who wins quickly, and a throw on time with a rusher arriving. Any one of those failing is a sack, an incompletion or worse. In the charted seasons, Cover 0 got the ball out fastest of any coverage and also gave up a 20-yard play on about one dropback in seven between the 20-yard lines, the highest rate of any coverage (Man Coverage has the chart): it compresses the play into a single high-stakes moment. Even an all-out blitz is not a free-for-all, either. The edge rushers still keep contain (they stay outside the quarterback so he cannot escape around them, the rush-lane discipline of The Pass Rush), because a quarterback who slips out of a zero has nobody deep to stop him; against a fast quarterback, many defenses give up a rusher to spy him (shadow him from a few yards off) instead. Not every Cover 0 is an all-out blitz, either. Of the dropbacks FTN labelled Cover 0 in 2023–2025, 50% had six or more rushers, but 23% had four or fewer, the “zero lurk” or “zero hole” versions in which the spare men sit in the middle and wait for the hot throw instead of rushing.






ImportantWhy it exists: the Cover 0 blitz



The Cover 0 blitz exists to end the play before it starts. It guarantees an unblocked rusher against any protection the offense has not built to beat it, and it covers every receiver, so the quarterback must win a race and a matchup at once. It belongs where the field is short and the throw has to be quick anyway (third-and-short, fourth down, the red zone) and where surprise is high. What it gives up: every margin. One missed tackle, one blown assignment, one receiver who wins at the line or one quarterback who escapes the pocket is a touchdown.

title: Blitzing: Numbers, Overloads, A-Gap Mugs, and Cover 0
section: Overloads: winning the count on one side
text:
Overloads: winning the count on one side
Here is where blitz design gets clever. The offense can almost always match the defense’s total: six rushers against a six-man protection, everyone accounted for. But blockers block where they stand. An overload blitz sends more rushers at one side of the protection than the blockers on that side can handle, so that a man comes free there even though the totals match.
The natural target is the half-slide, the NFL’s everyday six-man protection. Recall how it works: the center and the two linemen on one side slide that way and own gaps (the slide side), the two linemen on the other side block the man in front of them (the man side), and the back takes the next threat on the man side. That makes the man side the thin side. It has three blockers (guard, tackle, back), the same as the slide side, but the back is the smallest of them and the last to know what is coming. Either side can be overloaded, since each has only three blockers, but the man side is the favourite target. An overload aims four rushers at it.
Count the overload in Figure 40.3 by side. Left of the center: two rushers (the 1-technique and the left end) against three blockers (center, left guard, left tackle). Right of the center: four rushers (the Will, the 3-technique, the right end and the safety) against three (right guard, right tackle, back). Six against six in total, and still one free, because the protection put its extra blocker where the defense wasn’t.


Show the Python
def overload_play():
    off = line() + [O("QB", "QB", -5.0, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -5.0, 2.0, "R"), O("Y", "WR", -1.2, 8.6)]
    dfn = four_down() + [D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, 2.4, "W"), D("SS", "SS", 7.6, 6.4, "SS"),
                         D("NB", "NB", 4.6, 9.4, "NB")]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=40, to_go=None)
    p.motion("WILL", to=(1.4, 0.8), speed=2.2)
    p.motion("SS", to=(4.2, 6.9), speed=2.4)
    timed(p, "QB", [(0.5, -6.3, 0.0), (1.45, -6.3, 0.0), (1.8, -7.2, -0.5)])
    # slide side: the line steps left; only two rushers come there
    timed(p, "LE", [(0.5, -0.4, -5.7), (1.0, -1.6, -5.6), (1.8, -2.6, -5.0)], "rush")
    timed(p, "LT", [(0.5, -1.4, -4.1), (1.0, -2.1, -4.5), (1.8, -2.9, -4.2)], "block")
    timed(p, "LG", [(0.4, -1.2, -2.3), (1.0, -1.7, -2.2), (1.8, -2.0, -1.9)], "block")
    timed(p, "NT", [(0.4, 0.1, -0.9), (1.0, -0.4, -0.9), (1.8, -0.8, -0.9)], "rush")
    timed(p, "C", [(0.4, -1.3, -0.8), (1.0, -1.5, -0.9), (1.8, -1.8, -0.9)], "block")
    # man side: guard on the 3, tackle on the end
    timed(p, "DT", [(0.4, 0.1, 2.2), (1.0, -0.5, 2.1), (1.8, -0.9, 2.0)], "rush")
    timed(p, "RG", [(0.4, -1.2, 1.9), (1.0, -1.5, 1.9), (1.8, -1.9, 1.8)], "block")
    timed(p, "RE", [(0.5, -0.3, 5.4), (1.0, -1.0, 5.1), (1.8, -1.3, 4.9)], "rush")
    timed(p, "RT", [(0.5, -1.4, 3.7), (1.0, -1.9, 3.9), (1.8, -2.3, 3.7)], "block")
    # the overload: Will up the A gap (shortest path), safety off the edge
    timed(p, "WILL", [(0.35, 0.3, 0.8), (0.9, -2.4, 0.7), (1.45, -5.5, 0.25), (1.8, -6.6, -0.3)], "rush")
    timed(p, "SS", [(0.4, 1.8, 7.5), (0.9, -1.0, 7.5), (1.3, -2.4, 7.2), (1.8, -2.6, 7.1)], "rush")
    # the back's mistake: he steps outside to the safety
    timed(p, "RB", [(0.3, -4.7, 2.7), (0.9, -3.9, 5.4), (1.3, -3.7, 6.0), (1.8, -3.8, 6.0)], "block")
    # the hot route that never gets thrown: Y's quick slant into the space the safety left
    timed(p, "Y", [(0.5, 1.8, 8.7), (0.9, 3.4, 6.9), (1.5, 5.4, 4.0), (1.8, 6.2, 2.9)], "route")
    timed(p, "NB", [(0.5, 4.8, 8.9), (0.9, 5.0, 7.8), (1.5, 6.4, 5.4), (1.8, 7.0, 4.2)], "path")
    return p


blitz_animation(overload_play(), [-1.6, 0.0, 0.6, 1.0, 1.45, 1.8],
    notes=["W walks into the A gap;\nSS creeps down outside", "snap: the line slides left,\naway from both of them",
           "R drifts outside,\ntoward the safety", "R takes SS; W is in\nthe A gap untouched",
           "W arrives: shortest path.\nY is open, too late", "sack, from a rusher\nthe rules said was R's"],
    lateral=(-7.2, 11.2), window=(-8.6, 9.2), ncols=3, rings=(("WILL", RED), ("RB", PURPLE)))





  
  Your browser does not support the video tag.



Figure 40.3: An overload blitz against a half-slide, and a back who picks the wrong man (simulated; zoomed on the offense’s right side; the far-left receivers and their defenders are off the frame). Before the snap the Will (W, ringed red) walks into the right A gap and the strong safety (SS) creeps down outside the right tackle. The protection slides left, away from them: the center, left guard and left tackle block the left A, B and C gaps, where only two rushers come. On the man side, the right guard takes the 3-technique, the right tackle the end, and the back (R, ringed purple) has ‘the next threat’. There are two: the Will inside and the safety outside. The rule says inside first. The walk-up came too late for the quarterback to reset the slide toward it, so the back has to get it right. His eyes go to the safety, the more obvious threat; he steps out to take him, and the Will runs untouched up the A gap, the shortest path on the field, and reaches the quarterback in about a second and a half, before the hot slant to Y can be thrown.




The back’s mistake made it worse, but notice that even a perfect back could only choose which man came free. Had he taken the Will, the safety would have been unblocked instead: the widest man, the one the offense is happy to give up. That is Figure 40.4.
So the overload is not really a way to win the count; it is a way to choose the battle. Handled correctly, it produces a free rusher from the edge and a quick throw, the trade the offense wanted. Handled wrongly (a slide the wrong way, a back who looks outside first, a quarterback who misses the hot throw), it produces a free rusher up the middle, the trade the defense wanted.


Show the Python
p = Play(line() + [O("QB", "QB", -5.0, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -5.0, 2.0, "R"), O("Y", "WR", -1.2, 8.6)],
         four_down() + [D("WILL", "WILL", 1.4, 0.8, "W"), D("SS", "SS", 4.2, 6.9, "SS"),
                        D("NB", "NB", 4.6, 9.4, "NB")], los=40, to_go=7)
to(p, "WILL", (-1.7, 0.4), "rush")
to(p, "RB", (-2.6, 0.2))
for blk, rsh, spot in (("LT", "LE", (-1.8, -4.6)), ("LG", None, (-1.6, -2.2)), ("C", "NT", (-1.4, -0.9)),
                       ("RG", "DT", (-1.4, 1.9)), ("RT", "RE", (-1.9, 4.3))):
    if rsh:
        to(p, rsh, (spot[0] + 0.9, spot[1] + (0.3 if spot[1] > 0 else -0.3)), "rush")
    to(p, blk, spot)
p.dropback(1.2)
to(p, "Y", (5.0, 5.2), "route", via=[(1.8, 8.6)])
p.man("NB", "Y")
p.pass_to("Y", t=1.1)
fld = draw(p, lateral=(-8.2, 12.2), window=(-8.8, 10.2))
dashed(fld, p, [(4.2, 6.9), (1.2, 7.3), (-2.4, 6.4), (-4.4, 3.7)])
ring(fld, p, "SS")
ring(fld, p, "WILL", color=PURPLE)
point_to(fld, p, (-7.3, 5.6), (-3.9, 4.4), "free by design: the widest man", color=RED, shrink=3)
say(fld, p, -6.4, -5.0, "slide side:\n3 block, 2 rush", fontsize=6.6, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK)
say(fld, p, -4.9, 9.6, "man side:\n3 block, 4 rush", fontsize=6.6, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK)
point_to(fld, p, (-3.5, -2.9), (-2.6, 0.2), "R: inside first", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, shrink=6)
say(fld, p, 8.3, 3.6, "hot slant:\nball out ~1.1 s", fontsize=6.6, color=style.BALL)
plt.show()








Figure 40.4: The same overload, played by the rules. The back takes the inside threat, the Will in the A gap, because inside rushers have the shortest path. That leaves the safety (ringed red) unblocked: the widest man, roughly two seconds from the quarterback. The quarterback knows it from the pre-snap picture, so he throws hot: a quick slant by Y into the space the safety left, out of his hand at about 1.1 seconds. The protection did not block everyone. It chose who would be free, and the quarterback beat him.





That is why the offense’s real weapon against overloads is information, before the snap. The quarterback and center watch for the overload forming (a linebacker walking into a gap, a safety creeping down, a nickel inching toward the line) and move the protection toward it: they reset the Mike identification so that the slide, and its three blockers, go to the loaded side, and the thin man side faces the lighter one. The defense’s answer to that is timing. It disguises the overload until the last second, shows it to one side and brings it from the other, or walks the safety down so late that the protection cannot be reset without a timeout. In one snap you are watching both sides try to make the other side’s count wrong.

title: Blitzing: Numbers, Overloads, A-Gap Mugs, and Cover 0
text:
The blitz families: who comes
Ask a defensive coach about a blitz and he will usually name it by who comes and from where. The names vary from staff to staff, but most blitzes belong to a handful of families, and each family has its own reason to exist. The families overlap (a nickel off the edge is both a nickel blitz and edge pressure), so use the rule coaches use: name it for the surprise. One defensive back coming is a nickel or safety blitz; two or more rushers built to win the same edge is edge pressure.
Nickel (cat) blitz (panel 1 of Figure 40.5). In today’s NFL the most common extra rusher is not a linebacker at all but the slot cornerback. A nickel blitz sends him, usually off the edge from his slot alignment, while a safety rotates down to take the receiver he left; many defenses’ code word for the nickel is “cat,” so coaches often call it a cat blitz. Why him? Because he lines up outside the box, where the protection does not count him, and because he is fast: five or six yards outside the tackle, running at full speed, he can arrive as quickly as a linebacker from inside. The trade is in coverage, and it is the “brief hole” from earlier in the chapter: the safety rotating down to the slot has to cover a quick receiver in space from a long way off, and until he gets there the slot receiver is exactly the hot throw the offense will look for. Someone also has to take the other slot, and in many defenses that is a linebacker, a mismatch the offense will happily throw at.


Show the Python
LAT_F, WIN_F = (-13.0, 13.0), (-7.6, 14.4)


def fam_offense(te=False, rb_w=2.0):
    out = line("C") + [O("QB", "QB", -5.0, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -5.0, rb_w, "R"), O("H", "WR", -1.2, -9.4)]
    out += [O("Y", "TE", -0.7, 5.0)] if te else [O("Y", "WR", -1.2, 9.4)]
    return out


def short_rush(p, keys):
    for k in keys:
        q = p.players[k]
        to(p, k, (-0.3, q.w + (0.3 if q.w > 0 else -0.3)), "rush")


def short_sets(p, keys=OL_KEYS):
