title: Zone Blitzes, Fire Zones, and Simulated Pressure
section: Simulated pressure: four that look like six
text:
Simulated pressure: four that look like six
The fire zone still sends five. The modern form of the zone blitz goes one step further: send only four, from unexpected places, and keep seven in coverage. That is simulated pressure, a four-man rush built to look like a blitz: one or more players the protection expects to rush drop into coverage, and one or more it expects to cover rush instead, so the defense gets a blitz’s confusion with seven players still in coverage. You will hear it shortened to sim pressure or “sim,” and many coaches call it a creeper, because an off-ball defender “creeps” into the rush to replace the lineman who drops. Ted Nguyen of The Athletic puts the broadcast version simply: multiple defenders on the line showing blitz, but the defense rushes only four and drops seven.2
Why would four ever be enough against six blockers? Because a protection puts specific blockers on specific possible rushers. If the right four come, at least one blocker has nobody, and one of the four may face a back instead of a lineman. The defense hasn’t out-numbered the offense; it has out-positioned it, with seven men still covering five receivers.


Show the Python
def creeper_play():
    # the pressure look: Mike mugged in the right A gap, the nickel creeping down over H
    p = Play(spread(), nickel(MIKE=(1.5, 0.8)), los=40, to_go=7)
    p.motion("NB", to=(2.6, -7.6), speed=1.6)
    p.dropback(2.0)
    # protection: a half-slide toward the mugged Mike. C, RG, RT slide right; LG and LT block man;
    # the back checks the Will, then the nickel
    timed(p, "C", [(0.5, -1.4, 0.7), (1.2, -1.6, 1.4)], "block")     # nobody comes: he helps on the 3-tech
    timed(p, "RG", [(0.5, -1.6, 2.1)], "block"); timed(p, "RT", [(0.6, -1.9, 4.2)], "block")
    timed(p, "LG", [(0.5, -1.6, -0.9)], "block")
    timed(p, "LT", [(0.5, -1.8, -3.6), (1.3, -2.0, -2.2)], "block")   # his end drops: he turns in to help
    timed(p, "RB", [(0.7, -4.4, -2.0), (1.5, -4.6, -3.4)], "block")   # Will drops: late to the nickel
    # four rushers: the nickel off the left edge and three linemen
    timed(p, "NB", [(0.6, 0.6, -7.4), (1.3, -3.6, -6.8), (1.8, -6.2, -4.0), (2.1, -6.8, -1.3)], "rush")
    timed(p, "LDT", [(0.45, -0.7, -0.9), (2.0, -1.0, -1.0)], "rush")
    timed(p, "RDT", [(0.45, -0.8, 2.0), (2.0, -1.0, 2.0)], "rush")
    timed(p, "RDE", [(0.6, -1.1, 4.9), (2.0, -1.8, 4.5)], "rush")
    # seven in coverage: Cover 3 behind it. The left end drops into H's slant window, the Will runs
    # to the curl-flat the nickel left, the Mike backs out to the hook, the SS takes the right curl-flat
    timed(p, "LDE", [(0.35, 1.6, -5.4), (1.3, 5.4, -5.6), (2.0, 5.8, -5.8)], "drop")
    timed(p, "MIKE", [(1.3, 6.6, 1.2), (2.0, 7.4, 1.0)], "drop")
    timed(p, "WILL", [(1.3, 7.0, -9.5), (2.0, 8.0, -11.0)], "drop")
    timed(p, "SS", [(1.3, 7.5, 10.5), (2.0, 8.0, 11.5)], "drop")
    timed(p, "LCB", [(2.0, 16.0, -15.5)], "drop"); timed(p, "RCB", [(2.0, 16.0, 15.5)], "drop")
    timed(p, "FS", [(2.0, 16.5, 0.0)], "drop")
    # routes: H converts to a quick slant (his defender, the nickel, is the blitzer)
    p.route("H", r.path((2.3, 0.0), (5.3, -2.4))); p.route("X", r.go(19)); p.route("Z", r.curl(12))
    p.route("Y", r.seam(18))
    p.highlight("LDE", color=PURPLE)
    return p


cr = creeper_play()
CR_T = [-0.1, 0.8, 1.3, 2.1]
animation_or_strip(cr, CR_T, ["1.  −0.1 s · The look: six at or near the line", "2.  +0.8 s · Mike backs out, end drops",
                              "3.  +1.3 s · H's quick slant is covered", "4.  +2.1 s · Four rush; the nickel gets the sack"],
                   web_times=[-1.2, 0.8, 1.3, 2.1],
                   ghosts=("LDE", "MIKE", "NB"), ghost_t=0.0, rings=[("LDE", PURPLE)], window=(-9.0, 18.5),
                   lateral=(-18.5, 18.5),
                   notes_at={2: [("C: no one to block", (-5.6, 6.5), (-1.6, 1.4))],
                             3: [("back: late", (-7.0, -11.0), (-4.6, -3.4))]},
                   legend=STRIP_KEY)
plt.show()





  
  Your browser does not support the video tag.



Figure 41.5: A creeper from the nickel (a frame strip; a video on the web). (1) Six at or near the line: four linemen, the Mike (M) mugged in the right A gap and the nickel ($) crept down over the slot receiver (H). The line half-slides right, toward the Mike; the back’s rule is the Will, then the nickel. (2) The Mike backs out to the hook and the left end (purple ring) drops. (3) The nickel’s blitz turns H’s route into a quick slant (a sight adjust), but the end sits in that window, so the quarterback holds the ball. Cover 3 behind: three deep, four under. (4) Four rushed against six blockers, and the nickel gets the sack.




Look at what the creeper did to each blocker. The center slid toward the Mike, and the Mike left: one blocker gone. The left tackle set up for the end, and the end dropped, so he did what his rule says and turned in to help the guard; that is exactly why the edge was empty. The back’s rule was “the Will, then the nickel.” On paper the nickel was covered. But the back had to wait to see whether the Will came, and by the time he turned outside the nickel was on top of him at full speed. Nobody’s rule was wrong; the defense simply chose the order in which the offense would find out. Four rushers against six blockers, and the offense ended up with one back against a running start, while the quick slant that should have punished the nickel’s blitz ran into the end.
That is the deal simulated pressure offers, and it explains why it spread through the NFL in the 2020s:

It keeps seven in coverage. A creeper has four underneath, or five with two deep safeties, so the fire zone’s holes mostly close.
It wins one-on-ones instead of numbers: a nickel against a back, a defensive tackle against a center who just helped somebody else.
It attacks the rules without the risk. If the protection guesses right, it is a normal four-man rush with a funny-looking front; if wrong, a free rusher or a hot throw into a dropper, at no extra cost.
It looks identical to the real thing. The same pressure look can hide a creeper, a fire zone or a Cover 0 blitz, so the offense can never safely ignore it.

Nothing about a sim requires Cover 3 behind it. With two deep safeties the arithmetic is four rush, five under, two deep, and the dropper becomes one of five underneath players instead of four:


Show the Python
dfn = nickel(WILL=(3.4, -2.3), FS=(13.0, -9.0), SS=(13.0, 9.0), LCB=(6.0, -15.0), RCB=(6.0, 15.0))
p = Play(spread(), dfn, los=35, to_go=None)
to(p, "LDE", (-2.4, -4.8), "rush"); to(p, "RDT", (-2.2, 2.3), "rush"); to(p, "RDE", (-2.4, 4.8), "rush")
to(p, "WILL", (-2.4, -0.8), "rush", via=[(1.0, -2.0), (-0.3, -1.0)])
drop_to(p, "LDT", (5.5, 1.0), via=[(2.6, 0.5)])
drop_to(p, "MIKE", (7.0, 5.5)); drop_to(p, "NB", (7.0, -8.0))
drop_to(p, "LCB", (4.5, -14.0)); drop_to(p, "RCB", (4.5, 14.0))
drop_to(p, "FS", (16.0, -9.5)); drop_to(p, "SS", (16.0, 9.5))
p.route("H", r.slant(2, 6))
p.highlight("LDT", color=PURPLE)
fld = p.draw(width_in=6.4, lateral=(-21, 21), window=(-6.5, 20.0), title=False)
clean(fld.ax)
for c, sz in (((5.5, 1.0), (4, 6)), ((7.0, 5.5), (5, 6)), ((7.0, -8.0), (5, 6)), ((4.5, -14.0), (4, 6)),
              ((4.5, 14.0), (4, 6))):
    zone_patch(fld, p, c, sz)
for c in ((16.5, -9.5), (16.5, 9.5)):
    zone_patch(fld, p, c, (6, 17), alpha=0.05)
point_to(fld, p, (8.8, -2.4), (5.5, 1.0), "tackle drops to\nthe middle hook", color=PURPLE)
point_to(fld, p, (-4.6, -6.0), (-1.2, -1.05), "Will through the\nA gap he left", color=RED)

say(fld, p, 10.6, 12.0, "five under", color=style.INK_2, fontsize=6.8)
plt.show()








Figure 41.6: Simulated pressure with two-high coverage behind it (illustrative). Before the snap the Will (W) has walked up toward the line on the left and both safeties are deep. At the snap the 1-technique tackle (purple ring) drops into the middle hook and the Will comes through the A gap the tackle just left. Four rush (both ends, the 3-technique and the Will); five play underneath (the corners in the flats, the nickel, the dropping tackle and the Mike); two play deep halves. Count to eleven: 4 + 5 + 2. The quick slant against the Will’s blitz now runs into a 300-pound lineman, and both deep halves are still covered.






The price of the creeper
If the exchange confuses no one, a creeper is just a four-man rush with a good rusher playing a hook zone, and a defensive tackle is a real liability if a receiver runs into his area with room to work. It is also hard to teach: the four rushers have to keep their rush lanes (The Pass Rush) from odd starting places, or the quarterback escapes through the gap the dropper left. The defenses that do it best have edge players who can drop, safeties and nickel backs who can rush, and linemen mobile enough to look at home in a hook zone.


What the charting data says
In public data the closest thing to a simulated-pressure flag comes from FTN, a football-data company whose charters watch every play and record, for every dropback, how many players rushed and how many of those were blitzers. FTN doesn’t publish a definition, but the counts behave as if a blitzer is a rusher who isn’t one of the usual linemen and edge rushers: an off-ball linebacker or a defensive back. Four rushers with at least one blitzer means somebody who usually rushes didn’t. It’s an imperfect proxy, and it errs both ways. It misses sims in which the dropper and his replacement are both linemen or edge rushers (say, an end drops and a stand-up outside linebacker beside him rushes, since neither counts as a blitzer). And it counts some plain four-man rushes as sims, such as a three-lineman front whose fourth rusher is simply an off-ball linebacker every snap, with no one dropping. With that caution, here is what each kind of rush bought in 2023–2025.3


Show the Python
order = ["four", "sim", "blitz"]
names = {"four": "Four, no off-ball\nrusher", "sim": "Four, incl. an\noff-ball rusher", "blitz": "Five or more\n(a blitz)"}
cols = {"four": style.MUTED, "sim": style.SERIES[1], "blitz": style.INK_2}
metrics = [("press", "Pressure rate", True), ("sack", "Sack rate", True), ("epa", "EPA per dropback", False),
           ("man", "Man coverage behind it", True)]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(6.6, 2.5), sharey=True)
ys = np.arange(len(order))[::-1]
for ax, (m, title, is_pct) in zip(axes, metrics):
    vals = np.array([RT.loc[k, m] for k in order])
    n = np.array([RT.loc[k, "n"] for k in order])
    if m == "epa":
        err = 1.96 * np.array([RT.loc[k, "epa_se"] for k in order])
    elif m == "man":
        err = None
    else:
        err = 1.96 * np.sqrt(vals * (1 - vals) / n)
    ax.barh(ys, vals, color=[cols[k] for k in order], height=0.62, xerr=err,
            error_kw=dict(ecolor=style.INK, lw=0.8, capsize=2))
    span = 0.19 if m == "epa" else max(vals) * 1.5
    for y, v, e in zip(ys, vals, err if err is not None else [0] * 3):
        txt = f"{v:+.3f}" if m == "epa" else (f"{100 * v:.1f}%" if m == "sack" else f"{100 * v:.0f}%")
        ax.text(max(v, 0) + e + 0.04 * span, y, txt, va="center", ha="left", fontsize=7.0, color=style.INK)
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=8.2)
    ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
    ax.tick_params(axis="x", labelsize=6.8)
    if m == "epa":
        ax.axvline(0, color=style.BASELINE, lw=0.8)
        ax.set_xlim(-0.06, 0.13)
        ax.set_xticks([-0.05, 0, 0.05, 0.1])
    else:
        ax.set_xlim(0, span)
        ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(plt.FuncFormatter(lambda x, _: f"{100 * x:.0f}%"))
axes[0].set_yticks(ys)
axes[0].set_yticklabels([names[k] for k in order], fontsize=7.4)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()








Figure 41.7: What each kind of rush buys, all NFL regular-season dropbacks 2023–2025 charted by FTN. ‘Four, incl. an off-ball rusher’ is four rushers of whom at least one is an off-ball linebacker or a defensive back (the closest public proxy for simulated pressure); ‘Four, no off-ball rusher’ is a normal four-man rush. It produced pressure and sacks at nearly the rate of five-plus blitzes, while the coverage behind it was man about as often as behind a normal four-man rush (most of the time it was zone), not the majority-man of the blitz. EPA per dropback is from the offense’s side: lower is better for the defense. Whiskers are 95% confidence intervals; the simulated-pressure sample is small, so read the EPA gap as suggestive, not settled. Man/zone shares come from the charters’ coverage labels, which have shifted between seasons; compare the rows, not the levels. Source: nflverse play-by-play, participation and FTN charting data.





Three things stand out. First, the proxy for simulated pressure got the quarterback under pressure on 36% of dropbacks, close to the 39% of a real blitz and well above the 27% of a normal four-man rush; its sack rate (7.9%) matched the blitz’s (8.0%). Second, it got there with zone coverage behind it most of the time: the coverage was man on 35% of these plays, about the same as behind a normal four-man rush (33%) and far below the 60% behind a blitz. That is the creeper’s whole promise, in two numbers: blitz-like pressure, four-man-rush coverage. Third, offenses did worst against it, in expected points added (EPA) per dropback, though the sample is small (simulated pressure by this definition was only 4.7% of dropbacks) and the uncertainty is wide. Defenses also choose when to call it, and that choice is part of what the number measures.
If simulated pressure is this good, why isn’t it called more often? Partly because the proxy undercounts it, but mostly because it works only as a surprise: its value depends on the offense having to respect the blitz, which is why the teams that sim the most also blitz a lot, or at least show it.

title: Zone Blitzes, Fire Zones, and Simulated Pressure
section: Where it came from: Miami, Cincinnati, and “Blitzburgh”
text:
Where it came from: Miami, Cincinnati, and “Blitzburgh”
Who invented the zone blitz depends on whom you ask, and the honest answer is that it grew in stages, with each coach building on the last.
Bill Arnsparger’s Dolphins. Arnsparger was Don Shula’s defensive coordinator in Miami in two stints (1970–73 and 1976–83), a quiet, meticulous coach whose units were famous for being greater than their parts: the “No-Name Defense” of the early 1970s and the “Killer B’s” of the 1982 Super Bowl team.4 In the early 1970s he used linebacker Bob Matheson, who could rush like an end or cover like a linebacker, as a defensive end in the 4-3; with Matheson on the line, the defense could send five and still cover with six without the offense knowing which five. The package was known as the “53” defense, after Matheson’s jersey number.5 “With Bob there, with linebacking skills, we were able to rush five guys and cover with six,” Arnsparger later explained. “That’s what you need to run a zone blitz.” His catchphrase for what he was after was “safe pressure.”6 Some histories therefore date the zone blitz to Arnsparger’s Miami defenses of the early 1970s. Others point instead to the blitzes and zone-based defenses he tinkered with in the late 1970s and early 1980s, in his second Miami stint, as the more direct ancestor of what came next.7
Dick LeBeau’s Bengals. Dick LeBeau had been a Hall of Fame cornerback for the Lions (1959–72, 62 interceptions) before he started coaching. He became Cincinnati’s defensive coordinator in 1984, facing Bill Walsh’s 49ers and the precise, quick passing games spreading through the league, offenses that ate man-coverage blitzes alive with hot throws.8 He had already been experimenting. Before the 1983 season, while still the Bengals’ defensive backs coach, he put in a package that showed blitz and then had veteran cornerback Ken Riley sit down in a zone with a safety rotating behind him. “We ran the zone blitz and the quarterback just threw the ball straight to Ken Riley,” he remembered of an exhibition game.9 Around the time he became coordinator he visited Arnsparger, by then the head coach at LSU, and came away with the “safe pressure” idea, which he built into a system: linebackers and defensive backs rushing from many angles, linemen dropping, zone coverage behind. The arrival of safety David Fulcher in 1986, a big man who could rush and cover, let him expand it.
Blitzburgh. The scheme became famous in Pittsburgh. Bill Cowher’s Steelers hired Dom Capers as defensive coordinator in 1992 (he stayed through 1994, then left to become the first head coach of the Carolina Panthers) and LeBeau as defensive backs coach; LeBeau was coordinator in 1995–96 and again from 2004 to 2014.10 Cowher called the scheme “a collaboration between myself and Dom Capers and Dick LeBeau.” With a 3-4 front whose outside linebackers could both rush and drop, the 1994 Steelers led the NFL in sacks with 55, a franchise record, and the city got a nickname.11 LeBeau’s own description, decades later, is still the best one-sentence summary of the idea: “It’s a zone area where you would blitz a guy that normally doesn’t blitz and make the quarterback figure out what’s going on.”
Both origin stories are true in their way; this book gives Arnsparger the idea and LeBeau the system. From Pittsburgh it spread with the coaches: Capers took it to Carolina, and in the 1990s and 2000s the fire zone became a standard call for almost every NFL defense, especially once Nick Saban and Bill Belichick’s pattern-matching rules, worked out in the early 1990s, gave the three underneath defenders a better way to handle routes than spot-dropping: the seam-flat and middle-hook rules described earlier in this chapter.12






NoteFilm room: Steelers, Super Bowl XLIII (Feb. 1, 2009) — the rusher who dropped



The most famous coverage drop in Super Bowl history came straight out of the zone-blitz mindset. Last seconds of the first half, Arizona at Pittsburgh’s 1-yard line. The Steelers, with LeBeau as coordinator, showed a big blitz, and outside linebacker James Harrison, that season’s Defensive Player of the Year and the Steelers’ most dangerous edge rusher, was one of the players the Cardinals had to account for. Kurt Warner, expecting pressure, threw a quick slant to Anquan Boldin, and Harrison, who had dropped instead of rushing, was standing in the lane. He caught it at the goal line and ran 100 yards for a touchdown. “We had a play call where we were basically on a max blitz,” Harrison said afterward. “Kurt had to get it out, so he had to throw a quick slant in or out, and I guessed on in.” Accounts differ on exactly what Harrison’s assignment was and how much of the drop was his own read.13
What to notice: the play is the zone blitz’s logic in pure form. The quarterback reacted to the pressure he expected, threw the hot route to the spot the blitz should have emptied, and a man he had counted as a rusher was standing in it.

title: Zone Blitzes, Fire Zones, and Simulated Pressure
text:
The modern sim defenses
By the 2020s the fire zone was standard equipment, and offenses had answers to it: quick throws, empty sets, protections that counted the zone-blitz exchanges. The frontier moved to four-man simulated pressure, often with two-high coverage behind it, not just Cover 3. Three defenses of the 2020s are worth knowing.






NoteFilm room: Ravens 2023 — Mike Macdonald’s lie about who is coming



Mike Macdonald was Baltimore’s defensive coordinator in 2022 and 2023 before becoming the Seahawks’ head coach in 2024. His 2023 Ravens became the model modern pressure defense without being a heavy-blitz defense at all: they blitzed on about 21.5% of dropbacks, below the league average, by one count in December. What they did instead was lie. Macdonald “leaned into simulated pressures, making it look like they’re blitzing when they’re not, or disguising where exactly the pass rush is coming from,” and he was willing to drop 355-pound nose tackle Michael Pierce or 338-pound Travis Jones into coverage.14 Cody Alexander’s charting that October ranked Baltimore among the league’s heaviest users of simulated pressure, with “a deep bag of simulated pressures at their disposal” and a defense “not afraid to drop interior defensive linemen.”15 The Ravens finished 2023 with 60 sacks, the most in the NFL, and allowed 16.5 points a game, the fewest.16
What to notice: on a Ravens third down from 2023, find the biggest man in coverage after the snap. Kyle Hamilton, a 6-foot-4 safety, is often the rusher you didn’t expect; a defensive tackle is often the dropper. Macdonald’s Seattle defenses carried the same ideas into his head-coaching years: the 2025 Seahawks allowed the fewest points in the league (17.2 a game) and won Super Bowl LX, 29–13 over New England. How his defense combines this pressure with a two-high coverage shell is the second half of Case Study: Fangio’s Two-High Revolution and Macdonald’s Answer. As head coach he kept calling the defensive plays himself, with Aden Durde as his coordinator.17








NoteFilm room: Vikings 2023–2024 — Brian Flores and the blitz you have to respect



Brian Flores, Minnesota’s defensive coordinator since 2023 (and still in 2026), shows the other half of the bargain: a creeper only fools an offense that fears the blitz, and nobody had more reason to fear it than Flores’s opponents. In 2023 the Vikings rushed five or more on 51% of dropbacks in FTN’s charting, the most in the league. In 2024 they blitzed less and simmed more: by the FTN proxy, 11.3% of their dropbacks were four-man rushes including an off-ball rusher, the second-highest rate in the NFL behind Tampa Bay (12.1%), coached by Todd Bowles, another longtime pressure designer.18 Sports Info Solutions found that through Week 8 of 2024 the Vikings got pressure on 35% of dropbacks when they rushed four or fewer, sixth in the league, and on 34% when they blitzed, 27th: the four-man rushes from blitz looks were doing more work than the blitzes.19
What to notice: a Vikings passing down often starts with six, seven, even eight defenders near the line. Count them, then count the rushers. Every call starts from the same picture; that is the point.


Steve Spagnuolo, Kansas City’s coordinator since 2019 and the architect of the 2007 Giants’ pass rush, belongs on the list too: better known for his man-coverage blitzes (Blitzing), his 2023 Chiefs were also one of the league’s heavier sim users (sixth by the FTN proxy, at 6.8%) and finished with 57 sacks, second only to Baltimore.

text:
Third down: when to blitz in zone and when in man
Fire zones and sims are calls, not a defense, and the cleanest pattern in when they’re called is on third down. On third-and-short a fire zone hands the offense exactly what it wants, a short throw in front of three underneath defenders, so a defense that blitzes there usually plays man. On third-and-long the short throw it concedes is short of the line to gain, and zone pressure becomes far more common.


Show the Python
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.0, 2.6))
xs = np.arange(len(ZB))
ax.bar(xs, ZB["zone"], color=[style.MUTED, style.MUTED, style.SERIES[1], style.SERIES[1]], width=0.6)
for x, (z, n) in zip(xs, ZB[["zone", "n"]].itertuples(index=False)):
    ax.text(x, z + 0.015, f"{100 * z:.0f}%", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=8, color=style.INK)
    ax.text(x, 0.02, f"n = {n:,}", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=6.8, color="white")
ax.set_xticks(xs)
ax.set_xticklabels([f"3rd and {d}" for d in ZB.index], fontsize=8)
ax.set_ylim(0, 0.62)
ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(plt.FuncFormatter(lambda y, _: f"{100 * y:.0f}%"))
ax.set_ylabel("Blitzes with zone behind", fontsize=8)
ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 41.8: On third-and-long, a blitz comes with zone coverage behind it (fire zones and other zone pressures) far more often than on third-and-short or medium, where man coverage dominates. Share of five-plus-man rushes on third down played with zone coverage, by yards to go, NFL regular seasons 2023–2025 pooled. The n at the foot of each bar is the number of plays in that group. The charters’ man/zone labels shift between seasons, so the levels are rough, but the pattern (lowest at 4–6 yards, highest at 11-plus) holds in each season. Source: nflverse participation and FTN charting data.





Read it with the “count to eleven” table in mind. On third-and-1 to 3, only 27% of blitzes came with zone behind them; on third-and-11 or more, 47%. Man was most dominant of all at 4 to 6 yards (zone on only 20%).20 That is the fire zone’s bargain showing up in the data: three underneath defenders are a fine trade when the offense needs 12 yards and a poor one when it needs four. Why is third-and-short a little less man-heavy than third-and-medium? The data can’t say, but our reading is the run: on third-and-1 to 3 the offense may well hand off, so some of those pressures are run-and-pass calls with slanting linemen and zone behind them, while at 4 to 6 yards it almost always throws, and a quick throw against three underneath defenders is exactly what converts. (Simulated pressure, which keeps four underneath, is less tied to distance.) Third downs get their own chapter in Third Down: The Money Down.

title: Zone Blitzes, Fire Zones, and Simulated Pressure
text:
Watch for it on Sunday






TipWatch for it



Before the snap: read the pressure look.

Count the players at or near the line. Six or more means a pressure look. Is it two linebackers mugging the A gaps, a safety walked down beside an end, a nickel creeping toward the slot?
Count the deep players. Two safeties deep and the corners off means at most five rushers in any sound call, and probably four. One deep safety leaves room for a fire zone or a Cover 1 blitz; none, with corners pressed, warns of Cover 0.
Find who could drop. Stand-up edge players and any lineman in a two-point stance are the likely droppers; a lineman with his hand down, weight forward, is probably rushing.
Watch the offense react. A center pointing and re-pointing, a back moving to the other side, a tight end staying in: the offense is changing its protection to answer what it sees.

After the snap: who dropped?

Find the lineman who dropped into coverage, and then find who replaced him as a rusher. That pair is the zone blitz. The broadcast’s high replay angle shows it best.
Count the rushers. Five with three deep is a fire zone; four, with one of them a linebacker or defensive back and a lineman in coverage, is a simulated pressure; five or six with man coverage is an ordinary blitz.
Follow the ball. Did the quarterback throw hot? Was a dropper in the lane? If the quarterback completed it, where was the hole: behind the dropper, over a dropping tackle, or the receiver a blitzing corner left?
Find the blocker who blocked nobody. On a sim pressure there is usually one: a center or tackle standing with his hands up and no one in front of him. He is the measure of how well the lie worked.

For your log: on every third-and-6-or-more for one quarter, write down the number at the line before the snap, the number who rushed, and whether a lineman dropped. A defense whose two numbers often differ is a sim defense.

text:
Predict the play






TipPredict the play 1: six at the line, two deep





Show the Python
p1 = Play(spread(), nickel(LDT=(1.0, -2.35), MIKE=(1.9, -0.9), WILL=(1.9, 0.9), FS=(13.0, -8.0), SS=(13.0, 8.0),
                           LCB=(8.0, -16.0), RCB=(8.0, 16.0)), los=40, to_go=9)
fld = p1.draw(lateral=(-22, 22), window=(-7.5, 17.0), title=False)
clean(fld.ax)
plt.show()








Figure 41.9: Third-and-9. The offense is in the 2x2 shotgun with the back beside the quarterback. The defense shows six at the line (four linemen, the Mike (M) and Will (W) mugging the two A gaps) with the nickel over H. Behind them: two safeties 13 yards deep and both corners 8 yards off their receivers.





How many will rush, who is most likely to drop, and what should the quarterback be careful about?






TipAnswer





Most likely four or five, not six, and at least one of the mugged linebackers will drop. Count to eleven. Two deep safeties and two off corners are four defenders playing deep or soft. A defense that sent six of the other seven would have one man underneath and soft corners: a Cover 0 blitz without the press coverage Cover 0 needs. So the likely calls are a simulated pressure (four rush, one lineman dropping, two deep behind) or a fire zone with a safety rotating down at the snap.
The likely droppers are one of the two mugged linebackers (they can’t both rush and leave the middle empty) and probably a lineman, who replaces him underneath.
The quarterback’s danger is the hot throw: a dropper is very likely to land in the short middle, right where the slant against a linebacker blitz goes. Better: quick hitches or outs against corners 8 yards off, or a route that sits in the hole behind a dropping lineman. One last look before the ball is snapped: if both safeties drive down late, it’s a Cover 0 blitz after all (a late spin some defenses keep for third-and-long), and now the hot throw is exactly right.











TipPredict the play 2: 0.7 seconds after the snap





Show the Python
def dropper_play():
    p = Play(spread(), nickel(), los=35, to_go=10)
    p.dropback(2.0)
    for k, w in zip(["LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT"], (-3.9, -1.2, 0.0, 1.8, 3.8)):
        timed(p, k, [(0.6, -1.6, w)], "block")
    timed(p, "RB", [(0.7, -4.2, -2.6)], "block")
    timed(p, "WILL", [(0.7, 0.1, -2.9)], "rush"); timed(p, "LDE", [(0.7, -0.6, -4.6)], "rush")
    timed(p, "LDT", [(0.7, -0.5, -0.5)], "rush"); timed(p, "RDE", [(0.7, -0.6, 4.6)], "rush")
    timed(p, "RDT", [(0.35, 1.6, 2.6), (0.7, 3.4, 3.0), (1.5, 5.0, 2.6)], "drop")
    timed(p, "MIKE", [(0.7, 6.4, -1.8)], "drop"); timed(p, "NB", [(0.7, 6.0, -10.0)], "drop")
    timed(p, "SS", [(0.7, 7.0, 10.0)], "drop")
    timed(p, "LCB", [(0.7, 10.0, -15.5)], "drop"); timed(p, "RCB", [(0.7, 10.0, 15.5)], "drop")
    timed(p, "FS", [(0.7, 14.5, 0.0)], "drop")
    p.route("X", r.go(19)); p.route("Z", r.dig(12, 9)); p.route("Y", r.seam(18)); p.route("H", r.slant(2, 6))
    return p


p2 = dropper_play()
snapshot(p2, 0.7, ghosts=("RDT", "WILL"), ghost_t=0.0,
         rings=[("RDT", PURPLE), ("WILL", RED)], lateral=(-21, 21), window=(-8.0, 17.0))
plt.show()








Figure 41.10: Second-and-10. The picture is 0.7 seconds after the snap; the dashed outlines show where the defenders started. The 3-technique tackle (purple ring) has turned and is dropping. The Will (red ring) is rushing through the left B gap, between the guard and the tackle. One safety is in the middle of the field and the corners are bailing.





What is this, what is probably behind it, and where should the ball go?






TipAnswer





A simulated pressure: four rush (the Will and three linemen), and a tackle drops. Count the rushers: the left end, the 1-technique, the right end and the Will, four in all, with one of them a linebacker and one of the linemen going the other way. With the middle of the field closed and the corners bailing, the coverage behind it is most likely Cover 3: three deep, four under, with the dropping tackle as one of the underneath players, walling off the short middle around 4 to 6 yards.
Throw away from the dropper, and over him. A tackle can’t get much deeper than 5 or 6 yards before the throw, so the window behind him, an in-cut at 10 to 14 yards on the right side, is open, and so are the classic Cover 3 holes on the far side. Not the quick slant inside off the Will’s blitz: that is the throw the dropper is there for.











TipPredict the play 3: third-and-2





Show the Python
p3 = Play(spread(), nickel(MIKE=(1.3, 0.8), WILL=(3.0, -3.0), NB=(1.5, -8.8), LCB=(1.2, -15.0), RCB=(1.2, 15.0),
                           SS=(6.0, 7.0)), los=50, to_go=2)
p3.highlight("LCB", "RCB", "NB")
fld = p3.draw(lateral=(-22, 22), window=(-7.5, 17.0), title=False)
clean(fld.ax)
plt.show()








Figure 41.11: Third-and-2 near midfield. Six defenders at or near the line and one safety deep in the middle. Look at the three ringed defenders, both corners and the nickel: where are they standing relative to their receivers, and how far off?





If this is a blitz, will the coverage behind it be zone (a fire zone) or man? And what’s the offense’s answer?






TipAnswer





Man, most likely a Cover 1 blitz. Two reasons. The situation: on third-and-short a fire zone gives up exactly what the offense needs, a short throw in front of three underneath defenders, so defenses that blitz on third-and-1 to 3 play man behind it about three times in four (the third-down chart above). The picture: the corners are pressed, a yard off and square to their receivers, and the nickel is tight on the slot. Those are man techniques (Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage), and one deep safety is the Cover 1 shell.
The answer is the man-beater: quick throws that win against tight man coverage, such as a slant, a rub or pick concept where two receivers cross, or a back-shoulder fade (thrown to the outside shoulder, away from a defender who is running with the receiver), timed to come out before the extra rusher arrives, with the protection set to leave the free man (if there is one) on the side away from the throw. A smart defense knows the offense expects man here, which is exactly when a sim with zone behind it is worth calling.

title: Zone Blitzes, Fire Zones, and Simulated Pressure
text:
Takeaways

A blitz trades coverage for pressure; the zone blitz tries not to. It rushes a defender the protection didn’t count and drops one it did (a lineman, the dropper), so the rush is confusing and the coverage behind it is still zone.
The fire zone is the standard form: five rush, three under, three deep. It refuses the deep ball and accepts short throws; its holes live next to the slowest dropper and move with each variant.
Protections and hot reads lose to rules, not people. The Mike call, the slide and the hot are predictions keyed to who rushes. A pressure look gets the offense to commit; the zone blitz brings rushers from wherever it didn’t, and drops a man into the hot throw’s lane.
Simulated pressure (the creeper) does it with four. Four rushers from unexpected places, seven in coverage: it wins one-on-ones and makes blockers block air without paying in coverage. In 2023–2025 charting it produced blitz-like pressure and sack rates with four-man-rush coverage behind it.
It only works if the blitz is real. Creepers fool offenses that must respect a blitz, so the best sim defenses (Macdonald’s Ravens and Seahawks, Flores’s Vikings) also show, and sometimes bring, everything.
Count to eleven. Rushers plus underneath plus deep equals eleven. Count the deep players before the snap to cap the rush, and count the rushers after it to name what you saw.

title: What Beats What: Reading Coverage and Pass Concepts Versus Coverages
text:
The question under every pass
Third-and-7, early in the second quarter. Before the snap the broadcast’s high camera shows two safeties, one on each side of the field, about 13 yards deep. The quarterback takes the snap, drops, and stares at the left side of the field, shoulders turned that way, as if he is about to throw the seam route over there. The right-hand safety, who reads the quarterback, takes two steps toward the middle to help. Then the quarterback turns his head, resets his feet and throws to the right: a 16-yard completion to a receiver standing all alone in the space that safety had been guarding. On the replay the analyst circles the safety and says, admiringly, “he looked him off.” A few plays later the same analyst says something else you have heard a hundred times: “That’s a great call against that coverage.” What does it mean for a play to be “great against” a coverage? How does the quarterback know, in the second and a half he has, which coverage it is? And if offenses know which plays beat which coverages, why doesn’t every pass work? This chapter puts the two halves of the book you have read so far, the pass concepts of Part 4 and the coverages of Part 6, on the same field.
You’ll be able to…
Every pass play starts with a question the quarterback has to answer faster than any other decision in sport: what coverage is this? Not because coaches love labels, but because the coverage decides where the empty grass will be. Cover 2 leaves the sideline between its squatting corner and its deep safety; Cover 3 leaves the flats and the seams; quarters leaves the space behind its read safeties’ eyes; man leaves whoever loses his one-on-one. Know the coverage and you know, roughly, where the ball should go before the receivers have finished their first steps.
Quarterback Play showed the quarterback’s clock: a drop timed to the depth of the routes, a progression run one look at a time, a key defender answering each look. It left one thing out on purpose, because Part 6 had not yet taught the coverages: how he decides which defender is the key, and which side to look at first. That is the coverage read. Coaches teach it in many dialects, but nearly all of them reduce to four steps, in order.
Here are all four in one play, from the quarterback’s side.
Show the Python
def read_play():
    p = Play(spread(), nickel("c2", MIKE=(4.5, 4.4)), los=LOS, to_go=6)
    presnap(p)
    protect(p)
    p.dropback(2.5)
    # smash to the right: Z hitch settling at 7 (sticks + 1), Y corner route; the left side holds the free safety
    timed(p, "Z", [(0.95, 7.4, 15.0), (1.3, 6.8, 14.6)], "route")
    timed(p, "Y", [(1.35, 10.0, 9.4), (2.4, 16.5, 16.5), (2.9, 19.0, 18.5)], "route")
    timed(p, "X", [(2.9, 20.0, -15.5)], "route")
    timed(p, "H", [(2.9, 19.0, -8.2)], "route")
    timed(p, "RB", [(0.6, -4.2, -3.4), (1.4, -1.0, -7.0), (2.0, 0.2, -9.0)], "route")
    # the rotation: two-high becomes Cover 3, the strong safety skying down to the hitch side
    timed(p, "FS", [(1.0, 15.0, -3.0), (2.0, 17.0, -0.8), (2.9, 18.0, 0.0)], "drop")
    timed(p, "SS", [(0.8, 11.5, 10.0), (1.6, 10.0, 11.6), (2.6, 8.8, 12.4)], "drop")
    timed(p, "RCB", [(1.0, 8.5, 16.5), (1.8, 13.5, 16.6), (2.4, 16.5, 16.6), (2.9, 18.0, 17.0)], "drop")
    timed(p, "LCB", [(1.8, 13.0, -16.4), (2.9, 18.0, -16.8)], "drop")
    timed(p, "NB", [(1.4, 8.0, -11.5)], "drop")
    timed(p, "WILL", [(1.4, 8.5, -4.0)], "drop")
    timed(p, "MIKE", [(1.4, 8.5, 5.0)], "drop")
    p.pass_to("Z", t=1.4)
    p.highlight("FS", "SS", "RCB")
    return p


rp = read_play()
RT = [-1.0, 0.6, 1.4, 2.55]
animation_or_strip(rp, RT, ["1.  −1.0 s · Shell: two-high. Guess: Cover 2",
                            "2.  +0.6 s · Rotation: the middle closes",
                            "3.  +1.4 s · New key, the SS: still inside. Throw",
                            "4.  +2.55 s · Caught under the corner"],
                   ghosts=("FS", "SS", "RCB"), ghost_t=-1.0, window=(-9.0, 22.0),
                   per_panel={0: dict(look=(13.0, 16.0), notes=[("smash right:\nhitch + corner", (17.5, 11.0))]),
                              1: dict(notes=[("FS to the\nmiddle", (19.0, -6.0)), ("SS comes down", (16.0, 11.5))]),
                              2: dict(look=(14.3, 15.3), look_off=(-1.2, -2.6),
                                      notes=[("CB bails\nwith Y", (19.0, 11.0))]),

                                      notes=[("deep third\ntaken", (19.5, 10.5))])})

Figure 42.1: How the quarterback reads coverage, in four moments of one simulated play (a frame strip; a video on the web). Third-and-6, and the call is smash to the right: Z runs a hitch that settles at 7 yards, past the line to gain, and Y a corner route over him. Panel 1, before the snap: two safeties 13 yards deep (ringed) and squatting corners 5 yards off. The hypothesis is Cover 2, so the quarterback’s eyes start on the right corner, the Cover 2 key, expecting him to squat on the hitch and give up the corner route. Panel 2, 0.6 seconds after the snap: the free safety (FS) has turned for the deep middle and the strong safety (SS) is coming down toward the flat on the smash side (a sky rotation: the strong safety down, the free safety to the middle). The middle has closed: this is Cover 3, and the hypothesis is dead. Panel 3, the key changes: the right corner, now a deep-third defender, bails with Y’s corner route, as every Cover 3 corner does, so watching him tells the quarterback nothing. The decision passes to the strong safety, who is now the curl-flat defender on that side. He is still working out from the middle, inside the hitch, so the ball comes out at 1.4 seconds as Z turns. Panel 4: Z catches it under the bailing corner, with the strong safety about three yards away and arriving after the ball. The dashed outlines show where the safeties and the right corner stood before the snap.
Notice what the quarterback did not do. He did not decide where to throw before the snap and then throw there; that is how the rotation in Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage produced its interception. He also did not wait to see a receiver come open, which would have been too late: Z’s hitch is only open for the half-second before the strong safety arrives. He let one defender make the decision for him. Against Cover 2 that would have been the corner; once the coverage rotated to Cover 3, it became the strong safety rolling down to the flat. Either way the concept was built so that whatever that defender did, one of the two routes would be on the wrong side of him.
That is also why smash survived the rotation. Smash is built first of all to beat Cover 2, but its hitch sits under a Cover 3 corner who must bail and outside a flat defender who has to come from the middle of the field to reach it. The quarterback didn’t need to change the play. He needed only to know which half of it the coverage had handed him, and which defender now held the answer. (Had the strong safety sprinted straight to the hitch, the hitch would have been dead, and the throw would have been the corner route in the hole between him and the bailing corner, or nothing at all on this side.)

title: What Beats What: Reading Coverage and Pass Concepts Versus Coverages
text:
Shell, before the snap. First, though, the protection: how many defenders could rush, and who is his hot receiver if one more comes than he can block (Pass Protection). Then the coverage: one deep safety or two? Corners pressed or off? Is anyone creeping? Which side is the field side (the wide side of the field, away from the hash the ball sits on), since many defenses set their rotation and their coverage by it? This produces a hypothesis: “two-high, corners squatting, probably Cover 2.”
Rotation, at the snap. Did the safeties stay where they were, or did one spin to the middle and the other come down? Is the middle of the field open or closed? Did anyone extra rush? This confirms or overturns the hypothesis.
Key defender, after the snap. Given the coverage, which single defender decides whether the called concept works? For smash against Cover 2 it is the cornerback; for flood the curl-flat defender; for dagger the safety and then the linebacker; for four verticals the deep middle safety.
Throw. Read that defender and throw where he isn’t. If the answer is “nowhere,” move to the next read, and eventually to the checkdown.






Step 1: the shell, and what it is worth
The pre-snap read is worth more than its reputation suggests, even in an era of disguise. First, it narrows the menu. A defense showing two deep safeties and two off corners is very unlikely to be in Cover 0 one second later; a defense showing one safety in the middle and pressed corners is unlikely to end up in quarters. Each shell makes some coverages easy to reach and others a long run away, and as Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage showed, every defender has to stand where his real job is still reachable. Second, the shell sets up everything that has to be decided before the ball moves: the protection, which side the progression starts on, whether to take a shot (the alert, later in this chapter) and whether to change the play. How much the quarterback may change varies by team. In most NFL offenses the play-caller chooses the concept, and the quarterback’s freedom at the line is to flip it to the other side, to pick between two plays called together, or, in a check-with-me system, to choose from a short menu the coaches built for that week.
What the shell can’t do is name the coverage. The quarterback treats it as a short list ranked by likelihood: “two-high: Cover 2, quarters or 2-Man, unless they rotate.” The rest of the read decides between them.


Step 2: rotation, and the one-second answer
The single most useful question after the snap is the one you can ask from your couch: one second after the snap, how many safeties are deep in the middle of the field? One, and the middle is closed: Cover 1 or Cover 3 (or a fire zone, which is Cover 3 behind a blitz). Two, splitting the field, and it is open: Cover 2, Tampa 2, 2-Man, quarters or Cover 6. None: Cover 0, and the ball should already be on its way. Then the corners separate the members of each family: in the closed family, corners who turn and run with their receivers mean Cover 1 and corners who bail with their eyes on the quarterback mean Cover 3; in the open family, corners who squat in the flats mean Cover 2 (or the Cover 2 side of Cover 6), corners who backpedal and read mean quarters, and corners who trail their man mean 2-Man.
The quarterback answers that question with his first glance after the snap, often while he is still dropping. He does not need to see every defender. He needs the two safeties, because they are the ones a disguise moves, and the corner on the side he is reading. He can see them over linemen who are taller than he is because the safeties stand 10 to 15 yards deep, far above the line of helmets, and because from the shotgun he starts 5 yards behind the line with his eyes already up the field, instead of turning his back on the defense to drop from under center.
Against split-field coverage, Cover 6 for example (quarters on one half, Cover 2 on the other), “the” coverage doesn’t exist. The quarterback reads each half as its own coverage and works the half his concept is on: smash to the Cover 2 side, dagger or a quick out by #2 to the quarters side. Offenses that expect split-field coverage often call a different concept to each side and let the quarterback pick a half from the safeties’ alignment before the snap, which is the “man side, zone side” idea later in this chapter applied to two zones.


Step 3: the key defender for each coverage
Once the coverage has a name, the key defender follows from the concept and the coverage together. The table pairs each coverage with the defender quarterbacks are usually taught to read against it and where the ball tends to go. It is a summary of Part 6 from the offense’s side.



Table 42.1: The quarterback’s key against each coverage family. Typical, not universal: staffs teach different keys for the same coverage, and the concept called changes which defender matters.











Coverage (one second after the snap)

Cover 0

the free rusher, if any (the hot read)

Cover 1

the receiver who beats his man; crossers and rubs; away from the robber

the curl-flat defender (for smash and hitches too: the corner always bails); the post safety for seams
the flat or the curl behind him; the seams; the hitch under a bailing corner; flood

closed
the seam-flat defender (did he carry #2?)
the flat he left; post-wheel; the checkdown

The key is almost always one of three kinds of defender: the conflict defender the concept was built against (the corner in smash, the curl-flat defender in flood), the safety who reads the quarterback (the post safety against four verticals, the robber against in-cuts), or, against man, the matchup itself, the receiver’s defender, read by his leverage and the help behind him.

section: Moving a defender with your eyes: the look-off
text:
Moving a defender with your eyes: the look-off
Every defender in the second category has a weakness built into his job. A post safety, a robber, a Tampa 2 Mike and most zone linebackers are taught to watch the quarterback, because the quarterback’s eyes and shoulders tell them where the ball is going before it leaves his hand. That makes them movable.
A look-off is the quarterback deliberately looking at one receiver or area, often turning his shoulders that way too, to pull a defender who reads his eyes toward it, and then throwing somewhere else, into the space that defender left. It is the quarterback’s half of the disguise contest: the defense lies with its alignment before the snap; the quarterback lies with his head after it.


Show the Python
def lookoff_play():
    dfn = nickel("man", SS=(9.5, 1.0), WILL=(4.0, 6.5), MIKE=(4.5, -1.0))
    p = Play(spread(rb_w=1.6), dfn, los=LOS, to_go=9)
    presnap(p)
    protect(p)
    timed(p, "RB", [(0.7, -4.6, 3.0)], "block")
    p.dropback(3.0)
    # Z: dig from the right at 12; H: a flat in-cut from the left at 11; X and Y run vertical
    timed(p, "Z", [(1.6, 12.0, 15.0), (2.4, 12.5, 10.0), (3.0, 12.5, 6.5)], "route")
    timed(p, "H", [(1.45, 9.5, -9.2), (2.2, 10.6, -5.6), (2.95, 10.8, -3.2)], "route")
    timed(p, "X", [(3.0, 19.0, -15.6)], "route")
    timed(p, "Y", [(0.8, 5.0, 10.5), (3.0, 18.5, 11.5)], "route")
    # man defenders trail their receivers
    timed(p, "RCB", [(1.6, 11.0, 15.6), (2.4, 11.2, 12.0), (3.0, 11.0, 9.0)], "path")
    timed(p, "NB", [(1.45, 8.6, -9.9), (2.2, 9.4, -7.6), (2.95, 9.8, -5.8)], "path")
    timed(p, "LCB", [(3.0, 17.8, -16.2)], "path")
    timed(p, "WILL", [(0.8, 4.6, 9.0), (3.0, 16.0, 9.6)], "path")
    timed(p, "MIKE", [(0.7, 2.5, 1.2), (1.5, 3.0, 2.4)], "path")      # the back blocks: the Mike sits
    # the robber follows the quarterback's eyes to the right, then has to come back
    timed(p, "SS", [(0.6, 10.0, 2.0), (1.5, 11.0, 4.6), (1.95, 11.3, 5.4), (2.95, 11.0, 2.2)], "drop")
    timed(p, "FS", [(1.5, 15.5, 1.2), (3.0, 17.5, 2.0)], "drop")
    p.pass_to("H", t=1.95)
    p.highlight("SS")
    return p


lp = lookoff_play()
LT = [0.0, 1.5, 1.95, 3.0]
animation_or_strip(lp, LT, ["1.  Snap · Cover 1, the SS in the hole as robber",
                            "2.  +1.5 s · Eyes right on Z's dig: the robber follows",
                            "3.  +1.95 s · Eyes snap left: throw to H",
                            "4.  +3.0 s · Caught where the robber was"],
                   ghosts=("SS",), ghost_t=0.0, window=(-9.0, 21.0),
                   per_panel={0: dict(notes=[("robber", (13.0, -2.5), (9.5, 1.0))]),
                              1: dict(look=(12.0, 12.5), notes=[("robber drifts\nwith the eyes", (16.5, 9.5))]),
                              2: dict(look=(10.5, -5.0)),
                              3: dict(opens=[((10.8, -3.0), (3.6, 5.0))],
                                      notes=[("too late", (15.5, 4.5), (11.0, 2.4))])})

Figure 42.2: A look-off against Cover 1 robber, simulated. Panel 1: man coverage, with the corners pressed, the nickel ($) on H, the Will on Y and the Mike on the back, one deep safety, and the strong safety (SS, ringed) sitting in the hole as a robber, free to jump any in-breaking route. The back stays in to block, so the Mike, who has him in man, has nobody to cover: he sits at the line, ready to rush late (the ‘hug’ of Blitz and Man Pressure). Panel 2, 1.5 seconds after the snap: the quarterback’s eyes and shoulders are on Z’s dig coming in from the right, and the robber, who reads the quarterback, has drifted with them. Panel 3: the eyes snap back to the left and the ball comes out to H, breaking flat across the field on his in-cut, with the nickel trailing him from outside. Panel 4: H catches it at 11 yards in the space the robber left; the robber, coming back, is about five yards short, and the nickel is still a step and a half behind. The dashed outline shows where the robber started.




Why does the robber bite? Because his job is to be right about in-breaking throws, and the best evidence he has is the quarterback. A robber who ignores the quarterback’s eyes and simply sits in the middle is easy to throw around; one who reads them gets interceptions. The look-off turns his best evidence into bad evidence. The same logic works on the deep middle safety against four verticals (Cover 3 drew it: the quarterback looks at one seam, the safety leans, the ball goes to the other) and on a Tampa 2 Mike deciding which seam to carry. The play in this chapter’s opening is the two-high version. A read safety in quarters or Cover 2 also helps toward wherever the quarterback is looking, so eyes on the left seam pull the right-hand safety a step inside, and the throw goes to the right, into the space he left. The robber is drawn here because with only one eye-reader on the field the mechanism is easiest to see.
What a look-off costs. Time, mostly. Holding a defender with your eyes takes a beat, perhaps three to five tenths of a second, and every beat is one more for the pass rush. So the look-off is usually built into the play’s timing rather than added to it: the first read of a progression doubles as the look-off for the second, as in the figure, where the quarterback had a real reason to look at Z’s dig before coming back to H. It also takes a quarterback who can reset his feet and throw accurately to the other side of the field without a wasted step. A look-off by a quarterback whose feet don’t follow his eyes is just a late throw.
The defense’s answer. Coaches teach the eye-readers to “read through” the quarterback: to take their cue from his shoulders and the way his feet are pointing rather than his helmet, because a quarterback can turn his head cheaply but has to set his feet to throw. Defenses also mix in defenders who don’t read the quarterback, such as a robber who reads a receiver instead, so a look-off aimed at the wrong defender moves nobody. And they disguise who the eye-reader is. A quarterback who looks off a safety who wasn’t reading him has wasted his beat.






NoteMadden vs. real life



In a video game, defenders mostly react to the ball and to their assignments, and where your quarterback’s helmet points is rarely part of the contest. On a real field it is one of the most important things he does. NFL coaches grade a quarterback’s eyes on film the way they grade his footwork, and the most-praised quarterbacks are the ones whose eyes move defenders. A quarterback who stares at his first read is said to be “staring down” the receiver, and safeties feast on it.



Watching a look-off from the couch
The look-off is one of the few post-snap skills you can see on a broadcast without the All-22 film. Watch the quarterback’s helmet, not the ball. If his head goes to one side and the ball comes out to the other, ask who moved while his head was turned. On the replay from behind the offense, find the safety or linebacker who took a step toward where the quarterback looked. That step is what the look-off bought.

title: What Beats What: Reading Coverage and Pass Concepts Versus Coverages
text:
What beats what: the matrix
Now the question the chapter’s title promises. A coverage beater is a pass concept whose routes are arranged to attack the known weak spots of a particular coverage, so that if the defense plays that coverage, at least one receiver should come open. Smash against Cover 2 is the textbook case. The phrase is used loosely on broadcasts, often with a confidence the football doesn’t support, so here is a tighter version: a beater raises the odds against its coverage. It doesn’t guarantee anything, and it is usually worse against other coverages. That trade is the subject of the next section; first, the map.
Don’t memorise the grid below; learn to rebuild it. Every cell follows from two questions you already know how to ask. Where are this coverage’s thin spots? (Part 6.) Which defender does this concept put in a bind, and does this coverage give that defender help? (Part 4.) Read across a row to see where a concept lives and dies: smash is great against Cover 2 and bad against 2-Man; four verticals destroys spot-drop Cover 3 and runs into a wall against 2-Man and Cover 3 match. Read down a column to see a coverage’s menu of problems: quarters suffers against dagger and scissors, man coverage against mesh. After the grid, this section walks the columns one coverage family at a time, with a picture for each.
Two limits of the grid are worth knowing before you use it. It grades dropback concepts against coverages, so it leaves out the two things that most often change a column. Play-action shifts every column a little toward the offense, because a run fake pulls the eye-reading linebackers and safeties forward, out of the windows behind them; that is why yankee, the one play-action row, grades so well against single-high coverage. And an RPO sidesteps the grid altogether by reading one defender’s run-or-pass reaction rather than the coverage (Run-Pass Options). The grid also doesn’t grade the run, which is where most of the coverages that look weak in it earn their keep, as the end of this section shows.


Show the Python
MCOVS = ["Cover 0", "Cover 1", "2-Man", "Cover 2", "Cover 3", "Cover 3\nmatch", "Quarters", "Cover 6", "Fire\nzone"]
GRADES = {   # +2 strong edge to the offense ... -2 strong edge to the defense (typical, not measured)
    #                                  C0  C1  2M  C2  C3  C3m  Q  FZ      (Cover 6 is computed below)
    "Quick game (stick, slant-flat)": [+1, 0, 0, 0, +1, 0, +1, 0],
    "Smash":                          [0, -1, -2, +2, +1, 0, 0, 0],
    "Flood (sail)":                   [-1, -1, -1, +1, +2, 0, +1, +1],
    "Levels / drive":                 [+1, +1, 0, +1, +1, 0, -1, 0],
    "Dagger":                         [-1, 0, -1, +1, 0, 0, +2, -1],
    "Y-cross":                        [-1, +1, 0, 0, +2, +1, 0, -1],
    "Mesh":                           [+2, +2, +1, 0, 0, 0, 0, -1],
    "Four verticals":                 [0, 0, -2, +1, +2, -1, -1, +1],
    "Post-wheel":                     [0, +1, -1, 0, +1, +2, +1, 0],
    "Scissors":                       [-1, 0, -1, +1, 0, 0, +2, -1],
    "Yankee (play-action shot)":      [0, +1, -1, -1, +2, +1, -1, -1],
    "Screens":                        [+1, 0, 0, -1, 0, 0, 0, +2],
}
# Cover 6 = quarters on one half, Cover 2 on the other: the mean of those two grades, rounded toward 0
for k, g in GRADES.items():
    g.insert(7, int(np.trunc((g[3] + g[6]) / 2)))
G = np.array(list(GRADES.values()))
MCOL = [style.DEFENSE, "#f6b89c", "#efeeea", "#9ec5f4", style.OFFENSE]

                color="white" if abs(v) == 2 else style.INK)

ax.set_yticks(range(len(GRADES)), list(GRADES), fontsize=8)

ax.set_yticks(np.arange(-0.5, len(GRADES)), minor=True)
ax.grid(which="minor", color=style.SURFACE, lw=2)
ax.grid(which="major", visible=False)

    s.set_visible(False)

    ax.annotate("", (x0, -1.75), xytext=(x1, -1.75), annotation_clip=False,
                arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=style.INK_2, lw=0.8))

                                                                        "· even / depends", "− edge defense",
                                                                        "−− defense favoured"])]

fig.tight_layout(rect=(0, 0.04, 1, 1))
plt.show()








Figure 42.3: The concept-by-coverage matrix: the book’s summary, cell by cell, of which side a concept usually favours against each coverage when both are run as drawn. Blue is an edge for the offense, orange an edge for the defense, grey even or ‘depends’. These are typical grades from coaching wisdom and the reasoning of Parts 4 and 6, not measured values (the data chart later in the chapter shows how small measured edges are). The Cover 6 column is a blend of its two halves, the Cover 2 grade and the quarters grade averaged, with half-steps rounded toward grey, because the quarterback has to find the half his concept is on.






Against Cover 2: attack the sideline and the middle
Cover 2 has two deep defenders and five underneath, and its corners squat. That gives it two permanent thin spots: the sideline strip between the squatting corner and the deep-half safety, 12 to 20 yards deep, and the deep middle between the two safeties. Smash attacks the first, four verticals and dagger the second.


Show the Python
p = Play(spread(), nickel("c2", WILL=(4.5, -4.2), NB=(4.5, 6.6), MIKE=(4.5, 1.2)), los=LOS, to_go=8)
protect(p)
p.dropback(2.5)
p.route("Z", r.hitch(6.0))
route_to(p, "Y", (10.5, 9.2), (18.0, 20.0))
p.route("X", r.hitch(6.0))
route_to(p, "H", (10.5, -9.2), (18.0, -20.0))
route_to(p, "RB", (-4.6, -4.5), (-3.6, -11.5))
p.drop("RCB", (6.0, 18.2)); p.drop("LCB", (6.0, -18.2))
p.drop("SS", (17.5, 14.5)); p.drop("FS", (17.5, -14.5))
p.drop("NB", (8.5, 8.0)); p.drop("MIKE", (9.0, 0.5)); p.drop("WILL", (8.5, -8.0))
p.highlight("RCB")
p.pass_to("Y", t=1.9)
fld = draw(p, lateral=(-23.5, 23.5), window=(-8.0, 23.5))
opening(fld, p, (16.5, 18.0), (4.6, 5.6))
num(fld, p, 1, (19.6, 21.0)); num(fld, p, 2, (6.6, 13.3)); num(fld, p, 3, (-5.4, -11.8))
point_to(fld, p, (21.8, 5.0), (17.0, 17.0), "corner route lands behind\nthe CB, ahead of the late SS", color=GREEN)
say(fld, p, 3.0, 20.6, "CB squats\non the hitch", color=DD, fontsize=6.6)
say(fld, p, 21.6, -14.0, "mirror smash:\npick a side", color=OD, fontsize=6.6)
plt.show()








Figure 42.4: Smash against Cover 2 (a recap of the animation in Cover 2 and Tampa 2), run to both sides so the quarterback can pick one before the snap. On the right, Z runs a hitch at 6 yards and Y a corner route over him. The ringed corner, a Cover 2 hard corner, squats on the hitch, as his rules tell him to. The strong safety (SS) has the deep half behind him and does widen toward the corner route as it breaks, but he started 13 yards deep and 8 yards inside, near the hash, so he arrives late and the ball lands in the gap between the two (green). Progression, high to low: (1) the corner route if the corner sits, (2) the hitch if he sinks, (3) the back as the checkdown.





The reasoning is the one Cover 2 and Tampa 2 built move by move: the corner’s rule (squat on anything short in the flat) and the safety’s rule (stay deeper than anything in your half) are both sound, and smash places one route on each side of the line between them. The corner can’t be under the hitch and over the corner route at once, and the safety, starting near the hash, is a long way from the sideline. Flood earns a “+” here for the same reason, one step weaker: its sail route lands in the same hole, but its third route, in the flat, is exactly what the squatting corner is waiting for, so the defense covers one of flood’s three levels for free.
Four verticals attacks the other thin spot. With both seams running straight up the middle third of the field, each deep-half safety has a seam inside him and a go route outside him, and he can’t honour both; a quarterback who reads one safety throws to whichever receiver that safety doesn’t take. Tampa 2 exists to fix exactly this (the Mike runs down the middle and carries one seam), which is why four verticals is only a “+” against Cover 2 in the matrix: the Tampa version takes away one of the throws. NFL versions also build a choice into each seam (a route conversion): against two deep safeties the seam runners bend away from the safeties or split them, and against one they stay straight, which is part of why the concept survives a disguised coverage. The hole shot, a go route caught along the sideline behind the squatting corner, is the outside version of the same attack.
Against Cover 2 the offense gives up two things: the quick game to the outside, because the corners are sitting on it, and the screen, because the corner is also the force player and is standing right where a screen to the outside wants to go. Hence the grey and orange in those cells.


Against Cover 3: three under the deep ones, four across the front
Cover 3 is the opposite shape: three deep and four underneath. Its weaknesses, taught in Cover 3, are horizontal and vertical at once. Four underneath defenders can’t cover five short zones across the field, so the flats are thin; three deep defenders can’t cover four vertical routes, so the seams are thin. Flood attacks the first, four verticals the second.


Show the Python
def flood_play():
    dfn = nickel("one", NB=(5.0, 8.6), SS=(6.0, -8.8))
    p = Play(spread(rb_w=1.6), dfn, los=LOS, to_go=10)
    presnap(p)
    protect(p)
    p.dropback(2.5)
    timed(p, "Z", [(3.2, 21.0, 15.8)], "route")                                      # go: clears the corner
    timed(p, "Y", [(1.4, 9.5, 9.6), (2.1, 12.5, 14.5), (2.7, 13.5, 18.0), (3.4, 13.2, 18.6)], "route")  # sail
    timed(p, "RB", [(0.5, -3.8, 4.4), (1.3, 0.2, 10.0), (2.1, 1.6, 15.5), (2.7, 2.0, 18.0), (3.4, 2.2, 19.4)],
          "route")                                                                    # flat
    timed(p, "X", [(1.6, 12.0, -15.0), (2.1, 10.6, -14.0)], "route")                # curl
    timed(p, "H", [(2.7, 17.0, -7.6)], "route")                                     # seam: holds the FS
    timed(p, "RCB", [(1.0, 11.0, 16.2), (2.0, 17.5, 16.6), (2.8, 19.5, 16.6), (3.5, 18.0, 17.3)], "drop")
    timed(p, "NB", [(0.8, 7.5, 10.4), (1.5, 7.5, 13.2), (2.1, 6.0, 15.4), (2.7, 4.6, 16.8), (3.4, 6.5, 18.0)],
          "drop")
    timed(p, "MIKE", [(1.4, 8.5, 4.6), (2.7, 9.5, 7.6)], "drop")
    timed(p, "WILL", [(1.4, 8.5, -4.5)], "drop")
    timed(p, "SS", [(1.4, 8.5, -12.0), (2.1, 9.5, -13.0)], "drop")
    timed(p, "FS", [(1.4, 16.0, 0.0), (2.7, 17.5, 1.5)], "drop")
    timed(p, "LCB", [(1.4, 14.0, -16.0), (2.7, 17.0, -16.0)], "drop")
    p.pass_to("Y", t=2.0)
    p.highlight("NB")
    return p


fp = flood_play()
z1, y1, r1 = (fp.position(k, 1.0) for k in ("Z", "Y", "RB"))
animation_or_strip(fp, [0.0, 1.0, 2.0, 3.55],
                   ["1.  Snap · Cover 3: three deep, four under",
                    "2.  +1.0 s · Z clears the corner, Y stems",
                    "3.  +2.0 s · $ widens to the flat: throw the sail",
                    "4.  +3.55 s · Caught between $ and the corner"],
                   ghosts=("NB",), ghost_t=0.0, lateral=(-19, 22.5), window=(-8.0, 24.0),
                   per_panel={0: dict(notes=[("curl-flat\ndefender", (12.0, 11.5), (5.0, 8.6))]),
                              1: dict(notes=[("go", (12.5, 19.5), tuple(z1)), ("sail", (12.5, 6.0), tuple(y1)),
                                             ("flat", (-5.0, 10.0), tuple(r1))]),
                              2: dict(look=(20.0, 18.0), look_off=(-1.6, -2.2)),
                              3: dict(opens=[((13.2, 18.2), (4.0, 4.6))],
                                      notes=[("sail: 13 yd", (16.5, 11.0), (13.5, 17.6))])})

Figure 42.5: Flood against Cover 3, simulated (a frame strip; a video on the web). Panel 1: one deep safety, corners off, and the nickel ($, ringed) as the right curl-flat defender, the conflict defender for a flood to the right. Panel 2: Z’s go route carries the corner deep, because a Cover 3 corner may never let anyone behind him; Y stems up the field for his sail route; the back releases toward the flat. Panel 3, 2.0 seconds, as the quarterback reaches the top of his drop: the nickel, seeing the back come into the flat underneath him, widens for it, and the quarterback throws the sail behind him. Panel 4: Y catches it 13 yards downfield, in the space between the nickel and the corner, who is only now coming down from 19 yards deep. Three receivers at three depths against two defenders: the corner can take only the top one, and whichever of the lower two (the sail and the flat) the curl-flat defender takes, the other is open.




Flood is the purest Cover 3 beater because it uses Cover 3’s own rules against it. The corner’s rule (never let anyone behind you) means the go route takes him out of the play without a fight. The curl-flat defender’s rule (cover the curl, break to the flat) gives one man two receivers. The only help could come from the hook defender inside him or the post safety, and both are watching other routes. Four verticals works on the same arithmetic one level deeper: four vertical routes, three deep defenders, and a post safety who can be moved with the quarterback’s eyes. Y-cross and yankee attack the same single deep safety from across the field. In Y-cross the tight end runs a deep crosser behind the hook linebackers, who have dropped to 8 or 10 yards facing the quarterback and can’t see him go by, while a post or a go route holds the safety in the middle. The crosser comes out on the far side, 15 to 18 yards deep, in the space between the curl-flat defender (too shallow) and the corner (too deep, and occupied by the outside receiver). Every Cover 3 defender is where his rule says, and none of them has the crosser. Yankee does the same thing off play-action, with a post and a deep over route and a run fake that pulls the linebackers even further forward.
What Cover 3 does well doesn’t show in the grid at all, which is why its column has no orange. The grid grades pass concepts, and Cover 3’s strengths lie elsewhere: an eighth defender near the line against the run, and three deep defenders who never let anyone behind them, so it gives up very few explosive passes. What it concedes is the short and intermediate throw. In the charting data later in this chapter, every route type succeeds slightly more often than its own average against Cover 3. The defense’s bet is that a steady diet of 6-yard completions costs less than a light box or a busted deep ball.


Against quarters: make the safety’s eyes cost him
Quarters is built to stop most of what beats Cover 2 and Cover 3. It has four defenders who can play deep, so four verticals runs into four men; its safeties read the inside receiver and come down hard on anything short, so slants and short in-cuts thrown inside are dangerous. (The quick game still grades “+” against it because of the quick out by #2, thrown outside, away from those safeties, before the defender over the slot can widen.) Its weakness is the reverse of its strength. A read safety’s job is decided by one receiver, #2, and a route combination that tells him the wrong thing takes him out of the play.


Show the Python
def dagger_play():
    dfn = nickel("two", FS=(11.0, -7.0), SS=(11.0, 7.0), LCB=(7.5, -16.0), RCB=(7.5, 16.0),
                 WILL=(4.5, -4.5), NB=(5.0, 6.6), MIKE=(4.5, 1.2))
    p = Play(spread(rb_w=1.6), dfn, los=LOS, to_go=10)
    presnap(p)
    protect(p)
    timed(p, "RB", [(0.9, -4.2, 2.6), (1.6, -2.0, 6.0), (2.4, 0.0, 9.5)], "route")   # check, then release
    p.dropback(3.0)
    # dagger on the left: H straight up the seam, X a deep dig behind him
    timed(p, "H", [(1.2, 8.0, -9.0), (2.0, 14.0, -8.8), (3.2, 21.5, -8.4)], "route")
    timed(p, "X", [(1.9, 15.0, -15.0), (2.6, 16.0, -9.5), (3.3, 16.3, -3.0), (4.0, 16.5, 1.6)], "route")
    # the right side: Y up the seam holds the strong safety (a vertical #2 must be carried); Z go
    timed(p, "Y", [(1.2, 8.0, 9.0), (2.0, 14.0, 8.6), (3.2, 21.0, 7.6)], "route")
    timed(p, "Z", [(3.3, 22.0, 15.4)], "route")
    # the free safety carries the seam (H is #2 and vertical); the Will walls H, then sinks;
    # the corner plays X from outside and can only trail the dig
    timed(p, "FS", [(0.8, 11.5, -7.6), (1.8, 15.5, -7.6), (3.2, 20.0, -7.2)], "drop")
    timed(p, "WILL", [(0.8, 6.0, -6.5), (1.5, 8.0, -7.4), (2.6, 9.0, -6.6)], "drop")
    timed(p, "LCB", [(1.4, 11.5, -15.8), (2.0, 14.5, -15.4), (2.8, 15.0, -11.5), (3.3, 15.0, -7.0),
                     (4.0, 15.2, -2.6)], "drop")
    timed(p, "MIKE", [(1.2, 7.0, 0.8), (2.6, 9.0, 1.6)], "drop")
    timed(p, "SS", [(0.8, 11.5, 7.4), (1.8, 15.0, 7.0), (3.2, 19.5, 5.8), (4.0, 21.0, 5.4)], "drop")
    timed(p, "NB", [(1.0, 6.5, 8.0), (2.6, 9.0, 8.8)], "drop")                  # walls Y, then sinks
    timed(p, "RCB", [(1.6, 14.0, 16.6), (3.3, 21.0, 17.6)], "drop")
    p.pass_to("X", t=2.3)
    p.highlight("FS", "WILL")
    return p


dp = dagger_play()
animation_or_strip(dp, [0.0, 1.2, 2.3, 3.7],
                   ["1.  Snap · Quarters: the safeties read #2",
                    "2.  +1.2 s · #2 goes vertical: the FS carries him",
                    "3.  +2.3 s · The Will sinks short: throw the dig",
                    "4.  +3.7 s · Caught between the levels"],
                   ghosts=("FS", "WILL", "LCB"), ghost_t=0.0, lateral=(-21, 21), window=(-8.5, 25.5),
                   per_panel={0: dict(notes=[("reads #2", (14.5, -12.0), (11.0, -7.0))]),
                              1: dict(look=(12.0, -9.0), look_off=(1.4, 2.4)),
                              2: dict(look=(16.0, -3.0), look_label=""),
                              3: dict(opens=[((16.2, -1.0), (4.0, 6.5))])})
