Figure 42.6: Dagger against quarters, simulated (a frame strip; a video on the web), run to the left this time. Panel 1: quarters from a nickel, the safeties 11 yards deep over the slot receivers, reading #2 (the free safety reads H). Panel 2: H (#2) goes straight up the seam, so by rule the free safety (ringed) carries him deep. The Will (ringed) walls H for a few steps and then sinks to his hook spot; the corner plays X from outside, as quarters corners do. Panel 3, 2.3 seconds: X breaks inside on a deep dig. The safety is gone with the seam, the Will has stopped at 9 yards, and the corner, outside, can only trail. The quarterback, whose eyes went from the safety to the Will, throws as X breaks. Panel 4: the dig is caught at about 16 yards in the middle of the field, under the safeties and over the linebackers. On the right, Y runs up the seam too, and that matters: a quarters safety must carry a vertical #2, so Y holds the strong safety on his side. Had Y stopped short, the strong safety would have been free to drive inside and rob the dig, which is why dagger is usually paired with a backside vertical.




Quarterback Play used this same matchup to show a progression in real time; here, look at it as a lesson about rules. The free safety did exactly what quarters asks: #2 went vertical, so he carried #2. The Will did what he was taught: wall the seam, then sink to his landmark. The corner played the outside receiver from outside, which is what lets quarters take away the deep outside. Every rule was obeyed, and together they left the middle of the field empty at 16 yards for a receiver breaking in from the outside. That is the general shape of attacking quarters: make #2 tell the safety something, then throw where the safety’s answer took him from. It is also why the backside matters: a defense that expects dagger can rob the dig with the other safety, if his own #2 stays short and frees him to look inside.
Scissors makes the safety’s answer cost him in a different way. Here #1 runs a post and #2 a corner route, so their paths cross at 10 to 12 yards. Each defender started with leverage, on the side his help isn’t: the safety inside #2, the corner outside #1. Once #2 goes vertical the safety must carry him, and when #2 breaks for the sideline the safety has to chase him outward, across the path of the post. The corner, playing #1 from outside, has to cross inward to follow the post. Both defenders are now chasing receivers who broke away from their leverage, and they have to run through each other to do it, a rub at depth. Well-coached quarters teams answer by trading the routes as they cross (the corner takes the corner route, the safety the post), but that takes a word and a split-second decision at full speed, and the hesitation is the window. The quick out by #2 attacks quarters underneath, in the first second, before the apex defender can widen (Quarters and the Two-High Match Family); the running back’s wheel and the bootleg flood do it at the edge.
The concepts quarters likes follow from the same rule. Levels and drive send two receivers from one side across the middle at two depths, the deeper one a dig at about 12 yards, and in both #2 breaks inside instead of going up the seam. In levels #2 runs the dig himself, straight at the read safety who was watching him all along. In drive #2 runs the shallow cross, which by rule frees the safety to stop backing up and drive on the next route coming inside: #1’s dig. Either way the deep in-cut meets a safety coming downhill with his eyes on it. That is the “−” in the quarters column. The same concepts grade “+” against Cover 0, Cover 1 and Cover 2 because their crossers and in-cuts run through traffic against man and settle between spot-dropping linebackers against Cover 2.
What quarters gives the offense for free, if it chooses to take it, is not in the matrix at all: runs. With two safeties at 10 to 12 yards and only six or seven defenders near the line, the box is light, and Run Fits and Box Math showed why a light box invites the offense to hand the ball off. Some of the best answers to two-high coverage aren’t passes.


Against man: run away, run through traffic
Man coverage has no zones to stretch, so the stretches of the zone concepts don’t apply. Smash against Cover 1 is just two one-on-ones, and both favour the defense. The slot defender on Y plays with outside leverage, because his help (the free safety) is inside, so the corner route breaks straight into the side he is protecting. And the corner on Z, with nobody running deep behind him to worry about, can sit on the hitch. Flood against man is three one-on-ones near a sideline, which crowds the space the receivers need. Man coverage loses in three different ways: traffic (receivers whose paths cross, so a defender chasing one runs into the other: mesh and every rub), leverage (routes that break away from the side the defender is protecting: the out against inside leverage, the slant against outside leverage), and talent (a receiver who simply beats his man). Mesh, the purest man-beater, gets the double “+” in the Cover 0 and Cover 1 columns; the figure in the two-way section below shows it.
2-Man is the exception that explains the rule. With two deep safeties over the top, the underneath defenders can trail their receivers with inside leverage and give up nothing deep, so the vertical concepts (four verticals, smash’s corner route, yankee) all run into a defender underneath and a safety above. It is the most orange column of the matrix for that reason: almost every concept built to stretch a zone is worse against it. Its weaknesses are short and outside, away from the trailing defenders: outs, stops and the flat route break away from their inside leverage, while slants break straight into it, which is why the quick game, a mix of both, grades only even. The other weakness is the quarterback’s legs: with every defender’s back turned to him, a scramble often gains more than any throw.


Against pressure: get it out, or throw it where they left
The last column is the one that answers Zone Blitzes, Fire Zones, and Simulated Pressure. Against any blitz the first answer is time: the deep concepts (dagger, scissors, yankee) need three seconds or more, so dagger and scissors grade orange against both Cover 0 and fire zones. Yankee grades even against Cover 0 for one reason: it is a play-action call with seven or eight blockers, so it can block an all-out blitz more often than a five-man dropback protection can, and a post and a deep over route against man with no safety behind them are a touchdown if the ball gets out. If the protection breaks, the quarterback, with his back half-turned on the fake, is hit before he can throw: grey means “depends.” The second answer depends on what is behind the blitz.

Cover 0 has nobody deep and everybody in man. The answer is the quick man-beater (mesh, slants, a rub) or the hot throw to the receiver whose defender blitzed, thrown before the extra rusher arrives. A one-on-one go route with no safety behind it is a touchdown if the ball can get out, which is why the cell for four verticals is grey rather than orange.
A fire zone has three deep and three underneath. It is built to take away the hot throw: the dropper lands in the window a hot slant or a quick in-cut wants. So the answers are the throws it can’t cover with three underneath: the seams, which the seam-flat defenders have to carry alone (four verticals and flood grade “+”), the window behind the dropper (a lineman can’t get much deeper than 5 or 6 yards in time), and screens, thrown behind rushers who have committed to the quarterback. Why does four verticals get a “+” here while dagger, which also sends a seam, gets a “−”? Timing. Four verticals throws the seam on rhythm, at the top of the drop, before the fifth rusher arrives, and it reads one defender who is alone. Dagger’s dig breaks at 15 or 16 yards behind the seam and needs a beat longer, and the middle dropper and the hook defender are sitting exactly where the dig crosses.



If the grid is this one-sided, why play Cover 3 or 2-Man?
Read the matrix literally and two coverages look like mistakes. Cover 3 is beaten by flood, four verticals, Y-cross and yankee and has no orange cell at all. 2-Man is orange almost everywhere, so why doesn’t every defense play it on every down? Yet in the charting data Cover 3 is the most common coverage in the league, on 32% of charted dropbacks from 2018 to 2022, and 2-Man is one of the rarest, on 2%.1
The grid grades pass concepts against coverages and nothing else, and each coverage pays its way somewhere the grid can’t see.

Cover 3 is cheap and sound. With one safety deep, the other can stand near the line as an eighth defender against the run, and three deep defenders who never let anyone behind them mean few explosive passes. It concedes completions underneath and dares the offense to string them together without a mistake. It is simple, so it is rarely blown, and it is the base that Cover 3 match, the fire zones and the rotations of Part 6 are built on.
2-Man is expensive. It needs underneath defenders who can trail receivers all over the field, it leaves only five or six defenders near the line against the run, and with every back turned to the quarterback it invites scrambles. So it is a passing-down call. On third-and-7 or longer in those seasons it was 6% of charted dropbacks, still a small share. Played on every down, it would be run on and scrambled against; played rarely, it ambushes the vertical concepts offenses like to call on third-and-long.

A coverage’s real value is its whole column, plus the run game, plus how often it gets blown, weighted by the situations in which the defense chooses to play it. That is the defense’s half of the bet.


A short history: why the matrix keeps changing
The idea of choosing a pass play to beat a particular coverage is as old as coverages that could be studied. Sid Gillman, who coached the Los Angeles Rams in the late 1950s and the AFL’s Chargers in the 1960s, is usually credited with two of its foundations: studying opponents on film, cut up and spliced by play, and designing pass patterns to stretch a defense across the whole field, vertically and horizontally, so that zone defenders faced more receivers than they could cover. Bill Walsh, who said that much of what he did derived from Gillman, built those ideas into the West Coast offense’s progressions.2 The rules then tilted the field. In 1978 the NFL allowed defenders to contact a receiver only within the first five yards past the line of scrimmage, which made it far harder for defenses to disrupt routes and far more valuable for offenses to read coverage and throw on time (1978 and the Passing Revolution tells that story).3
The defense’s side of the history is the story of Part 6 told backwards. Four verticals against spot-drop Cover 3, a staple of the run-and-shoot and BYU passing games by the 1980s, helped produce pattern-matching Cover 3, usually traced to Nick Saban and Bill Belichick in Cleveland in the early 1990s (Cover 3).4 Smash and the quick out by #2 helped produce Palms, the quarters check that traps them. And the spread offenses of the 2000s and 2010s, which could create a one-on-one or a numbers advantage against any single coverage, helped push NFL defenses toward the disguised two-high shells that spread after 2018 (Fangio’s Two-High Revolution and Macdonald’s Answer). The matrix in this chapter is a snapshot of the mid-2020s. Its rows and columns will look different in ten years, because both sides are always working on the cells that hurt them.

42  What Beats What: Reading Coverage and Pass Concepts Versus Coverages

title: What Beats What: Reading Coverage and Pass Concepts Versus Coverages
text:
Why “beaters” are bets
If offenses know which concept beats which coverage, why doesn’t every pass work? Because a beater only beats the coverage the defense actually plays, as it actually plays it, and four things stand between the call sheet and that coverage.
1. The defense chose its coverage too, and it hid it. The play-caller picks a concept before the snap, often before the huddle breaks, from a guess about the coverage. The defensive coordinator picks the coverage at the same time, from a guess about the concept, and then disguises it. Neither sees the other’s card. A smash call that meets Cover 2 looks brilliant on the replay; the same call against 2-Man looks like a mistake, and the play-caller is the same man with the same information. The rotation at the start of this chapter is the everyday version: the offense called a Cover 2 beater and got Cover 3. Keep that in mind when a broadcast calls a completion “a great call against that coverage.” The analyst is grading the call with the answer key in hand; the honest version is “that was a good bet, and it paid.”
2. Coverage labels hide different rules. “Cover 3” names a family, not a set of instructions. Against spot-drop Cover 3, four verticals is a math problem the defense loses; against Cover 3 match, whose seam-flat defenders carry the slot receivers, it meets four defenders deep and the math is gone. The label in the matrix is the same; the behaviour after the snap is not. Quarters, Cover 6 and Palms look identical before the snap and play completely differently against the same concept. Every match coverage is a set of if-then rules (Quarters and the Two-High Match Family), and the “beater” depends on which rules this staff teaches.
3. Execution and talent. A beater produces a window; somebody still has to hit it. The window in the smash plate is about five yards wide and opens for perhaps half a second. A protection that breaks at 2.2 seconds, a corner route run a yard too flat, a ball thrown a beat late, a defender who is simply faster than the diagram assumed: each closes it. And the reverse happens constantly. Great receivers beat good coverage with bad matchups, and great quarterbacks complete throws into coverages the play was not designed for. That is why the best players change the matrix, which describes average players.
4. Situation and the second read. The defense doesn’t play coverages at random; it plays them by down, distance, field position, personnel and score (Tendencies, PROE, and Charting). On third-and-long, a defense can sit back in deep coverage and concede the short throw, so a concept can “beat” the coverage and still lose the down if its open receiver is two yards short of the sticks. Beating the coverage and moving the chains are different things.

What the data say: the edges are real, and small
You can’t count concepts in public data: play-by-play records where the ball went, not what was drawn. But you can count something close to the matrix’s ingredients. Next Gen Stats charting in nflverse records, for many dropbacks, the coverage the defense played after the snap and the route run by the receiver who was targeted. Here is the success rate (the share of plays with positive expected points added) for each common route against each coverage, over five regular seasons.


Show the Python
cmap = LinearSegmentedColormap.from_list("od", [style.DEFENSE, "#f3f2ee", style.OFFENSE])
norm = TwoSlopeNorm(vcenter=SR_MEAN, vmin=0.28, vmax=0.68)
CLAB = ["Cover 0", "Cover 1", "2-Man", "Cover 2", "Cover 3", "Quarters\n(Cover 4)", "Cover 6"]
RLAB = ["Hitch / curl", "Out", "Slant", "Crosser", "In / dig", "Corner", "Post", "Go / fade"]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 4.4))
ax.imshow(SR.values, cmap=cmap, norm=norm, aspect="auto")
for i in range(len(ROUTES)):
    for j in range(len(COVS)):
        v, n = SR.values[i, j], NN.values[i, j]
        if n < 100:
            ax.add_patch(plt.Rectangle((j - 0.5, i - 0.5), 1, 1, fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none"))
            ax.text(j, i, f"n={n}", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=6.5, color=style.MUTED)
            continue
        ax.text(j, i, f"{100 * v:.0f}%", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=8,
                color="white" if abs(v - SR_MEAN) > 0.12 else style.INK)
ax.set_xticks(range(len(COVS)), CLAB, fontsize=7.8)
ax.set_yticks(range(len(ROUTES)), RLAB, fontsize=8)
ax.xaxis.tick_top()
ax.tick_params(length=0, labelcolor=style.INK)
ax.set_xticks(np.arange(-0.5, len(COVS)), minor=True)
ax.set_yticks(np.arange(-0.5, len(ROUTES)), minor=True)
ax.grid(which="minor", color=style.SURFACE, lw=2)
ax.grid(which="major", visible=False)
for s in ax.spines.values():
    s.set_visible(False)
ax.set_ylabel("Route run by the targeted receiver", fontsize=8, color=style.INK_2)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 42.7: Success rate of targeted passes by the route the targeted receiver ran and the coverage the defense played after the snap, NFL regular seasons 2018–2022 (sacks excluded; a play is a success if it added expected points). Blue is above the average for these throws, orange below. Cells with fewer than 100 targets are greyed out and show only their count. The columns are the coverages the charters record, so Cover 6 appears and the matrix’s Cover 3 match and fire-zone columns don’t (charting files them under Cover 3). Compare along a row: most of the colour difference down the chart is between routes (go routes fail more often against everything), while within a route the coverage moves success rate by roughly 5 to 25 points. Hitches and curls succeed most against the spot-drop zones (Cover 2, Cover 3), where receivers settle in windows between underneath defenders, and least against 2-Man, where a trailing defender is on their hip with a safety behind him; corner routes do worst against man (Cover 1); go routes succeed most against Cover 2, the hole shot. No cell is near certainty. Source: nflverse play-by-play and participation data (Next Gen Stats coverage and route labels), course calculation.





Read it the way an analyst would. Across 63,058 targeted throws, the average success rate is 52%. The best cell is 63% and the worst 28%, but most of that spread is between routes, not between coverages: go routes are orange in every column because deep throws fail more often whatever the coverage, and hitches are blue in most. Within one route, the gap between its best and worst coverage runs from 6 points (crossers) to 24 (hitches). So read along a row.
Along the rows, some of the matrix’s logic shows clearly. A hitch or curl thrown against Cover 2 succeeds 63% of the time and against 2-Man only 38%: against Cover 2 the receiver settles in a window between underneath defenders who dropped to landmarks, while against 2-Man a defender is trailing on his hip with a safety over the top. Go routes do best against Cover 2 (43%), the hole shot behind a squatting corner, and worst against quarters (31%), which has a deep defender for every vertical route (only Cover 0, at 28%, is lower). Corner routes are a poor bet against Cover 1 (40%).5
Other cells seem to contradict the matrix, and each one teaches something about reading data like this.

The smash corner against Cover 2 succeeds only 49% of the time, below the chart’s average. But a corner route is a 20-yard throw toward the sideline, caught about half the time against most coverages, and success rate counts every incompletion as a failure. The corner route’s own average is 45%; against that baseline, Cover 2 is one of its better columns.
Slants and digs against Cover 3 succeed more often than average (61% and 58%), although four underneath defenders should make inside throws risky. Every route does a little better than its own average against Cover 3, the coverage that concedes underneath to protect against the deep ball, and a quarterback throws the slant against Cover 3 only after he has seen the hook defender leave its window. The cell records the result of a read, not of a call.
Crossers against man (Cover 1 53%, Cover 0 50%) succeed at about the crosser’s usual rate, with no sign of mesh’s double plus. The label lumps shallow crossers together with deep ones, and success rate calls a 6-yard catch on third-and-8 a failure however open the receiver was. It is also possible that the man-beater’s edge is simply smaller than coaching lore says, which is this section’s point.

Two cautions apply to every cell. First, the chart shows only the route thrown to, and the quarterback chooses that route after seeing the coverage, so every cell is already the result of someone’s read. Second, success rate punishes deep routes, which fail more often and win bigger. Neither caution changes the headline: even the best matchups fail more than a third of the time. A coverage beater moves the odds by a few points per throw. That still matters. Over a season of about 600 dropbacks, three points per throw is about 18 more successful plays, roughly one a game, which is why coordinators spend their week on it (The Game-Planning Week).


Calling against a menu, not a coverage
So a play-caller doesn’t pick the beater for the coverage; he picks the concept with the best expected result against the coverages this defense is likely to play in this situation. That is a weighted average, and you can do it with the matrix. Suppose that on second-and-7, film study says a defense plays Cover 3 35% of the time, Cover 1 25%, quarters 25% and Cover 2 15%. Score each grade as a number from −2 to +2, weight it by how often the coverage comes, and add. (This treats ordinal grades as if they were measurements: nobody knows that a “++” is exactly twice a “+”. It is a heuristic for organising a judgment, not a forecast of yards, and the ranking it produces matters more than the decimals.)



Table 42.2: A play-caller’s arithmetic: matrix grades weighted by a hypothetical defense’s second-and-7 coverage mix.

Flood wins on average, because the most common coverage is the one it beats. But notice the last column. Flood is bad against man, and one snap in four is man. Mesh and dagger never go below zero. If the down is third-and-7 and a bad play ends the drive, a careful coordinator may prefer the call with no bad outcome to the one with the best average. That is the logic of the next section.

title: What Beats What: Reading Coverage and Pass Concepts Versus Coverages
section: Two-way concepts: an answer for man and an answer for zone
text:
Two-way concepts: an answer for man and an answer for zone
A two-way concept has an answer built in for both man and zone coverage, so it isn’t a bad call whatever the defense plays. There are two ways to build one. The routes themselves can work against both (crossing routes rub against man and settle into holes against zone), or a receiver can change his route after the snap according to the coverage, the option route of Passing Game Fundamentals, whose runner breaks away from his defender against man and sits down in the window against zone. Mesh is the classic of the first kind.


Show the Python
def mesh_base(dfn, zone=False):
    q = Play(spread(rb_w=1.6), dfn, los=LOS, to_go=3)
    protect(q)
    q.dropback(2.5)
    if zone:   # the same crossers, settling in the first window past each hook defender
        route_to(q, "H", (3.8, -9.0), (6.4, -6.0), (6.6, 0.3))
        route_to(q, "Y", (2.6, 8.4), (5.2, 5.0), (5.8, -7.8))
    else:
        route_to(q, "H", (3.8, -9.0), (6.4, -6.0), (6.8, 9.5))
        route_to(q, "Y", (2.6, 8.4), (5.2, 5.0), (5.6, -10.5))
    route_to(q, "X", (10.0, -15.0), (16.5, -20.5)); route_to(q, "Z", (10.0, 15.0), (16.5, 20.5))
    route_to(q, "RB", (-3.4, 5.0), (0.2, 9.5), (1.2, 12.5))
    return q


fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(6.5, 8.4))
m = mesh_base(nickel("man", WILL=(4.2, 2.0), MIKE=(4.2, -1.6)))
for d_, t_ in (("LCB", "X"), ("RCB", "Z"), ("NB", "H"), ("SS", "Y"), ("WILL", "RB")):
    m.man(d_, t_)
m.rush("MIKE", pts=[(-4.0, 2.6)], speed=4.0)
m.highlight("NB", "SS")
fld = draw(m, ax=axes[0], lateral=(-23.5, 23.5), window=(-7.5, 19.5), width_in=6.5)
for d_, t_ in (("LCB", "X"), ("RCB", "Z"), ("NB", "H"), ("SS", "Y"), ("WILL", "RB")):   # bolder man lines
    (x0, y0), (x1, y1) = _P(fld, m, m.players[d_].d, m.players[d_].w), _P(fld, m, m.players[t_].d, m.players[t_].w)
    axes[0].plot([float(x0), float(x1)], [float(y0), float(y1)], color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.4, ls=(0, (1, 1.6)),
                 zorder=7)
opening(fld, m, (6.2, 0.0), (2.8, 4.4))
say(fld, m, 10.0, -0.5, "mesh point: chasers\nrun into traffic", color=OD, fontsize=6.6)
say(fld, m, 15.0, 9.0, "man answer: throw the\ncrosser who comes out clean", color=GREEN, fontsize=6.8,
    weight="bold")
axes[0].set_title("Against Cover 1 (man): the rub", loc="left", fontsize=9.5, fontweight="bold")
# the zone panel is drawn after the drops: defenders at their landmarks, dashed outlines where they began
Z_PRE = {"LCB": (7.0, -15.8), "RCB": (7.0, 15.8), "FS": (13.5, 0.0), "NB": (5.0, -10.4), "SS": (6.0, 10.0),
         "WILL": (4.5, -2.6), "MIKE": (4.5, 1.8)}
Z_POST = {"LCB": (14.5, -16.5), "RCB": (14.5, 16.5), "FS": (15.5, 0.0), "NB": (7.5, -12.8), "SS": (7.5, 12.8),
          "WILL": (7.5, -4.5), "MIKE": (7.5, 4.5)}
z = mesh_base(nickel("one", **Z_POST), zone=True)
z.highlight("WILL", "MIKE")
fld = draw(z, ax=axes[1], lateral=(-23.5, 23.5), window=(-7.5, 19.5), width_in=6.5)
for k, (d0, w0) in Z_PRE.items():
    (x0, y0), (x1, y1) = _P(fld, z, d0, w0), _P(fld, z, *Z_POST[k])
    axes[1].plot([float(x0), float(x1)], [float(y0), float(y1)], color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.0, ls=(0, (3, 2)),
                 zorder=3)
    ghost_marker(axes[1], float(x0), float(y0), z.players[k].label, fld.pts_per_yard())
opening(fld, z, (6.6, 0.3), (2.6, 5.0)); opening(fld, z, (5.8, -7.8), (2.4, 3.6))
say(fld, z, 17.6, 0.0, "zone answer: the crossers sit\nin the windows between defenders", color=GREEN,
    fontsize=6.8, weight="bold")
axes[1].set_title("Against Cover 3 (zone): sit in the holes", loc="left", fontsize=9.5, fontweight="bold")
fig.tight_layout(h_pad=1.2)
plt.show()








Figure 42.8: Mesh as a two-way concept, third-and-3. Top, against Cover 1 (a recap of the animation in Dropback Concepts): H and Y cross over the ball at 5 to 6 yards, H a step higher, so the defenders chasing them in man, the nickel ($) and the strong safety (SS), both ringed, have to get around one receiver to stay with the other (dotted lines are the man assignments). The Mike blitzes, so this is Cover 1 with five rushers; the back releases to the flat and the Will, who has him in man, goes with him. The quarterback throws to whichever crosser comes out of the traffic first. Bottom, the same play against Cover 3, drawn after the drops: each defender stands at the spot he dropped to, with a dashed outline where he started. Nobody is chasing, so each crosser settles in the first window past a hook defender (ringed) and turns to face the quarterback (green). The outside receivers’ corner routes do a different job in each picture: against man they take the two corners away from the crossers; against Cover 3 they pull the deep-third corners toward the sidelines. The back in the flat is the outlet.





Notice what the two-way concept costs. Against zone, mesh’s crossers are fine, settling for five or six yards in front of defenders who rally to them; they are not a zone beater the way flood is. In the matrix, mesh is grey across the zone columns: never bad, rarely great. That is the trade. A two-way concept gives up some of the ceiling of a pure beater to raise the floor. On third-and-3, where five or six yards is a first down and a bad call ends the drive, that is a bargain. On first-and-10, where a coordinator can afford a swing for a big gain, he may prefer the pure beater and accept that it will sometimes meet the wrong coverage.
There are three common ways offenses build two-way plays:

Routes that work against both. Mesh, drive and the shallow cross rub against man and find holes against zone. So does a slant run inside a defender with outside leverage.
Choices inside one route. The option route, a seam route that stays straight against one deep safety and bends into the open middle against two (a route conversion), and the hitch that turns into a fade against press: each receiver reads the coverage after the snap, and the quarterback reads the same thing.
A man side and a zone side. Put a zone beater on one half of the field (curl-flat, smash) and a man-beater on the other (a rub, a slant-flat), and let the quarterback choose his half from the man/zone read: the man/zone indicator on a motion before the snap, or the corners’ first steps after it. This is called a half-field or combination call, and many third-down playbooks are built from them.

All three ask more of the quarterback and the receivers than a single beater does, because now both of them must read the coverage the same way, at speed. When they disagree, the result is the interception where the receiver turned out and the ball went in. That is why two-way concepts are a veteran offense’s tool and why young quarterbacks are often given simpler, single-answer calls.

title: What Beats What: Reading Coverage and Pass Concepts Versus Coverages
text:
The defense answers back
If the offense’s job is to call the concept that beats the defense’s coverage, the defense’s job is to play a coverage that beats the offense’s concept, or at least doesn’t lose to it. Defenses fight the matrix in three ways.
Change the coverage’s rules against a known concept. This is the match idea from Part 6 seen as a counter. The clearest example is four verticals against Cover 3. Spot-drop Cover 3 loses to it by arithmetic; Cover 3 match changes one rule, the seam-flat defender’s, and the arithmetic is gone.


Show the Python
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.5, 4.6))
for ax, kind in zip(axes, ("spot", "match")):
    q = Play(keep(spread(rb_w=1.6), -30, 1.0), keep(nickel("one", NB=(5.0, -8.6), SS=(6.0, 8.6)), -30, 1.0),
             los=LOS, to_go=None)
    route_to(q, "X", (8.0, -15.8), (24.0, -16.8)); route_to(q, "H", (6.0, -8.0), (24.0, -6.2))
    q.drop("LCB", (22.0, -17.0)); q.drop("FS", (18.5, -1.0)); q.drop("WILL", (9.0, -3.8))
    if kind == "spot":
        q.drop("NB", (11.0, -13.0))
    else:
        q.path("NB", [(17.5, -7.2)], absolute=True)
    q.highlight("NB")
    fld = draw(q, ax=ax, lateral=(-24.5, 3.0), window=(-6.5, 27.0), width_in=3.25, rule=False)
    if kind == "spot":
        opening(fld, q, (17.0, -6.8), (4.0, 4.0))
        point_to(fld, q, (-3.4, -12.4), (5.0, -8.6), "$ runs to his\ncurl spot", color=DD, fontsize=6.2)
        say(fld, q, 24.6, -11.0, "seam open between\nthe CB and the FS", color=GREEN, fontsize=6.2)
        say(fld, q, 21.5, -1.6, "FS: two seams,\none man", color=DD, fontsize=6.0)
        ax.set_title("Spot-drop Cover 3", loc="left", fontsize=9, fontweight="bold")
    else:
        point_to(fld, q, (-3.4, -12.4), (5.0, -8.6), "$ walls H and\ncarries him", color=DD, fontsize=6.2)
        say(fld, q, 24.6, -11.0, "a defender under the\nseam, the FS over it", color=DD, fontsize=6.2)
        ax.set_title("Cover 3 match", loc="left", fontsize=9, fontweight="bold")
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.8)
plt.show()








Figure 42.9: The defense’s counter to four verticals, left half of the field (H’s and X’s routes; the right side is the mirror image). Left, spot-drop Cover 3: the nickel ($, ringed) runs to his curl landmark, wide and about 11 yards deep, so H’s seam runs past him on the inside and arrives in the gap between the deep-third corner and the free safety (green). That gap exists because the free safety has two seams to cover, this one and its mirror on the right, and can’t take both. Right, Cover 3 match: the same nickel reads #2 (H) and, because H goes vertical, walls him and carries him up the seam. Now the seam has a defender underneath it and the free safety over it, and the ball has nowhere to go. One rule changed; the concept’s best throw disappeared. (Cover 3 draws both as moving plays.)





Match rules invite their own answers, and they are the counter-counters in the table below. A seam-flat defender who carries #2 vertically is not in the flat, so the back or a quick out by #1 is open underneath him. And route combinations that make two defenders’ rules collide create holes that no single rule covers. The cleanest is post-wheel, and it is why that concept gets the only “++” in the Cover 3 match column: #1 runs a post, and the corner, whose rule is to carry a vertical #1, goes inside with him; #2 starts toward the flat, so the seam-flat defender, by rule, goes with him underneath; then #2 turns up the sideline. The corner is inside, the seam-flat defender is trailing from below, and nobody is over the top of the wheel. A switch release does something similar at the snap: #1 and #2 cross, the outside receiver running inside and the slot outside, so the corner and the seam-flat defender each have to decide in their first step who is now #1 and who is #2. If they hesitate, or both take the same man, the other is free (Cover 3 draws both).
The same move, changing the rules, works against smash. Smash beats Cover 2 because the corner sits on the hitch and the safety starts too far inside for the corner route. Palms keeps the two-high picture but changes who covers whom on that side, and both defenders read #2. If #2 goes vertical, the safety carries him, and the corner, freed of any deep worry, plays #1 man to man, which means sitting on any short route by #1. If #2 instead breaks short to the flat, the corner jumps him and the safety takes #1. Against smash, #2’s corner route starts vertical, so the first rule applies.


Show the Python
pre = {"RCB": (6.5, 16.0), "SS": (11.0, 7.5), "NB": (4.5, 6.6)}
q = Play(keep(spread(), -6.0, 30), keep(nickel("two", FS=(11.0, -7.5), SS=pre["SS"], RCB=pre["RCB"],
                                            LCB=(7.5, -16.0), NB=pre["NB"], WILL=(4.5, -4.2), MIKE=(4.5, 1.2)),
                                     -6.0, 30), los=LOS, to_go=8)
protect(q)
q.dropback(2.5)
q.route("Z", r.hitch(6.0))
route_to(q, "Y", (10.5, 9.2), (18.0, 20.0))
q.path("SS", [(13.0, 9.4), (19.5, 18.0)], absolute=True)       # #2 vertical: the safety carries him, over the top
q.path("RCB", [(6.2, 15.6)], absolute=True)                     # #1 short: the corner sits on the hitch
q.drop("NB", (6.5, 10.0)); q.drop("MIKE", (8.5, 2.0)); q.drop("WILL", (8.0, -4.5))
q.highlight("RCB", "SS")
fld = draw(q, lateral=(-8.0, 25.0), window=(-8.0, 26.0))
say(fld, q, 22.0, 12.5, "#2 went vertical:\nthe SS carries the\ncorner route", color=DD, fontsize=6.8)
say(fld, q, 2.6, 21.0, "#1 stopped short:\nthe CB sits on\nthe hitch", color=DD, fontsize=6.8)
say(fld, q, 21.0, 0.5, "both smash throws covered:\nwork back to the checkdown", color=GREEN, fontsize=6.8)
for k, txt in (("Z", "#1"), ("Y", "#2")):
    pl = q.players[k]
    say(fld, q, pl.d - 2.4, pl.w, txt, fontsize=6.4)
plt.show()








Figure 42.10: Smash against Palms: the defense wins. Same two-high look before the snap, same smash to the right. But in Palms the corner and safety on this side both read #2 (Y). Y starts vertical, so by rule the strong safety (SS, ringed) carries him, and when Y breaks for the corner the safety is already over the top of him and inside, running with him toward the sideline. Z (#1) stops for his hitch, and the corner (CB, ringed), who no longer has to worry about anything deep, sits on it. Both of smash’s throws are covered, and the quarterback has to come off them to the other side of the field or the checkdown. The left side of the field is left out.





Why does the matrix call smash “even” against quarters but a loss against Palms, if a vertical #2 makes Palms play like quarters? Because plain quarters handles smash in much the same way, which is why that cell is grey, not blue. What Palms adds is the trap on the other branch: if the offense answers with a quick out by #2, the corner, reading #2 from the start, jumps it.
Take the beater’s target away directly. Brackets, robbers and lurkers put an extra defender where a known concept wants to throw (Man Coverage). A defense that expects mesh on third-and-short can sit a linebacker at the mesh point, at five yards over the ball, so the crossers run into him instead of past each other. A defense that expects dagger can rob the dig with a safety who ignores the seam: usually the backside safety, freed when his own #2 stays short, or a poach call that sends him across on purpose.
Make the coverage hard to identify. Disguise and late rotation don’t change the matrix; they hide which column the offense is in until it’s too late to use it. That is why a beater called before the snap is a bet and a beater chosen after the snap, by a quarterback reading the key defender, is much closer to a sure thing.
And the offense answers the answers. Every counter has a hole of its own, and the defense’s counter becomes the next concept’s target:



Table 42.3: Counters and counter-counters. Each answer creates the next question, which is why the matrix is never finished.

Which side is ahead at any moment depends on who has the newer answer and the better players. That back-and-forth over many plays, how a coordinator sets up one call with another, is the subject of Constraint Theory: How Plays Talk to Each Other.

title: What Beats What: Reading Coverage and Pass Concepts Versus Coverages
section: The alert: calling the shot before the snap
text:
The alert: calling the shot before the snap
One more pre-snap tool turns the coverage read into a big play. An alert (many staffs say shot alert) is a pre-planned exception to the called play: if the quarterback sees a particular look before the snap, he throws to the alert receiver first, usually on a deep route; if he doesn’t see it, he runs the play as called. The play-caller builds it in; the quarterback decides at the line.
The classic trigger is a single deep safety with the offense’s best receiver isolated on the other side of the field, one-on-one against a corner with no help leaning his way. That is the situation in which a deep throw has the best odds and the highest payoff: the receiver only has to beat one man, and if he does, nobody is behind the corner. Other alerts are keyed to Cover 0 (any one-on-one deep with no safety at all), to a pressed corner whose leverage gives away the throw (one shaded inside with no deep help is conceding the fade or the back-shoulder throw outside; one shaded outside with no inside help is conceding the slant), or to a safety cheating down into the box against play-action. A shot play from Play-Action, Bootlegs, and Screens is called to take a deep shot; an alert is a shot that the defense has to give.
Why not just call the deep shot? Because the deep shot is a bad play against most coverages and a great one against a few, and the alert lets the offense take it only when the coverage shows that it is one of the few. The called play underneath is the insurance. What it costs is that the quarterback makes the decision before the snap, which is exactly the moment the defense is lying to him. Alerts are therefore built around looks that are hard to fake: a single safety who can’t get back to the alert side in time, whatever he does at the snap, or a corner pressed with no help. If the safety rotates over at the snap, a good quarterback abandons the alert and goes back to the play.

title: What Beats What: Reading Coverage and Pass Concepts Versus Coverages
section: Putting it together: identify, then predict
text:
Putting it together: identify, then predict
Everything above reduces to a routine you can run on any passing play, live or on the replay: the quarterback’s four steps, minus the throwing. Call the shell and your two likeliest coverages; watch the safeties at the snap; let the corners name the coverage within its family; find the defender the routes are putting in conflict (two receivers to one sideline at two depths means a high-low on that side’s corner or curl-flat defender; a slot running up the seam means somebody’s rule about #2 is being tested); then say the open receiver out loud before the ball is thrown. The checklist in “Watch for it on Sunday” below is the pocket version.
The four animated plays in this chapter are drills for exactly this. Run them again (on the website they are videos; in print, cover panels 3 and 4 with your hand) and, at panel 2, name the coverage and the open receiver before you look.

title: What Beats What: Reading Coverage and Pass Concepts Versus Coverages
text:
Film room
The famous concept-against-coverage plays have homes of their own in this book: the Chiefs’ “Jet Chip Wasp” on third-and-15 in Super Bowl LIV is drawn in Case Study: Andy Reid’s Chiefs, and the Super Bowl XLIX interception at the goal line, a rub concept met by a defense ready for it, in Case Study: Belichick’s Patriots and the Game Plan. Here are three more recent pictures of this chapter’s ideas.






NoteFilm room: Chiefs, Super Bowls LVII and LVIII — the man-beater, and its counter



In Super Bowl LVII (February 12, 2023, the 2022 season) the Eagles played a lot of man coverage against Kansas City, and two of the Chiefs’ fourth-quarter touchdowns, the go-ahead score and the one that followed it, came from the same idea. On both, a receiver went in motion across the formation and then, as the ball was snapped, turned and ran back the way he had come. Kadarius Toney scored on the first; Skyy Moore on the second, after his defender started across the formation with him. “As soon as I went in motion and I saw him come in motion with me, I knew I had him,” Moore said afterwards. Andy Reid’s name for Toney’s play was “Corn Dog.”6
That is a man-beater in its purest form: it attacks the one thing man coverage must do, follow a receiver, and uses the defender’s own movement against him. A year later, in overtime of Super Bowl LVIII (February 11, 2024), the Chiefs ran the same motion on first-and-goal from the 3-yard line. This time the call, “Tom and Jerry,” was built on the assumption that the 49ers would be ready for it. “We built corn dog in saying, for sure they’ll cover corn dog,” Reid said. The first answer on the play was a shovel pass to running back Jerick McKinnon underneath; when the 49ers converged on the shovel and played man on the outside, Patrick Mahomes threw to Mecole Hardman, breaking back to the flat, for the championship-winning touchdown.7
What to notice: the play-caller designed for the defense’s counter to the beater, not for the beater itself. Note too that return motion only works against a defender who travels with the motion man; a defense that bumps, banjos or simply zones off the motion takes the edge away. On any goal-line snap, watch the first defender to react to a motion. If he follows, it’s man, and the motion man’s turn back is the throw.








NoteFilm room: Seahawks 2025 — two-high, and what offenses could do about it



Mike Macdonald’s 2025 Seahawks won Super Bowl LX playing more two-high coverage than any other playoff team: from Week 14, when safety Julian Love returned to the lineup, through the Super Bowl, Next Gen Stats counted split-safety coverage on 54.8% of their opponents’ pass plays, and Seattle won all eight of those games. Across the league, offenses converted 29.0% of dropbacks into first downs against split-safety coverage in 2025, tied for the lowest rate since at least 2018.8 (For a rough comparison from a different charting source, FTN’s 2025 labels in nflverse give a first-down rate of 29% against two-high and 34% against single-high coverage.9)
What to notice: this is the matrix’s quarters column in real life, and its Cover 6 column, which plays quarters on one half. Against two-high, the concepts that work are the ones that make a read safety pay for his rule (dagger, scissors, the quick out to #2) and, above all, the run, because two safeties 12 yards deep leave a light box. The league noticed: in 2025, offenses used fewer than three wide receivers on 41.7% of plays, the highest share since Next Gen Stats began counting in 2016.10 Bigger personnel is partly a run-game answer to two-high coverage. When you watch a two-high defense, count the run calls before you count the beaters.








NoteFilm room: Matthew Stafford, 2025 — the quarterback who beat two-high



Matthew Stafford won the 2025 MVP award with a league-leading 46 touchdown passes.11 In the nflverse charting, he was also among the best quarterbacks in the league against two-high coverage: on 249 dropbacks against Cover 2, 2-Man, quarters or Cover 6 he averaged +0.26 expected points added per dropback, third best of the 25 quarterbacks with at least 150 such dropbacks, against a league average of +0.02.12
What to notice: what a quarterback brings to the matrix. Two-high coverage is built to take away the deep throw and the easy read; it is beaten by a quarterback who identifies the coverage at the snap, moves a safety with his eyes and throws on time into a window between the levels: the dig behind a read safety, the seam the Mike didn’t carry. On a Rams passing down from 2025, watch Stafford’s helmet in the first second after the snap. It often goes where the ball isn’t going.

title: What Beats What: Reading Coverage and Pass Concepts Versus Coverages
text:
Watch for it on Sunday






TipWatch for it



Predict the open man. For one quarter, on every dropback pass, make the coverage call and then a prediction, before the ball is thrown.

Before the snap: shell (one-high or two-high), corners (press or off), and the two coverages you think are most likely. Is a receiver isolated against a single safety? That’s an alert candidate.
One second after the snap: how many safeties in the middle? Then the corners: squat (Cover 2), bail (Cover 3), read (quarters), trail (man). Say the coverage out loud.
Name the conflict defender on the side the routes are going: the corner (two receivers at two depths outside), the curl-flat defender (three at three levels), the read safety (a slot going up the seam), the matchup (crossers against man).
Predict the open receiver from what that defender does, before the throw. Then watch.
Watch the quarterback’s helmet. Did he look one way and throw the other? Who moved?

For your log: coverage called, receiver predicted, receiver thrown to. Score yourself on the predictions. Over a quarter you’ll find that you get Cover 3 and Cover 2 right far more often than quarters and match coverages, which is exactly the point of those coverages.

Predict the play






TipPredict the play 1: the isolated receiver





Show the Python
off = line() + [O("QB", "QB", -5.0, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -5.0, -1.6, "R"), O("X", "WR", -0.7, -15.0),
                O("Y", "TE", -1.5, 7.5), O("H", "WR", -1.5, 11.5), O("Z", "WR", -0.7, 17.0)]
dfn = [D("LDE", "DE", 1.0, -5.5, "E"), D("LDT", "DT", 1.0, -0.7, "T"), D("RDT", "DT", 1.0, 2.35, "T"),
       D("RDE", "DE", 1.0, 5.5, "E"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -3.0, "W"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, 1.8, "M"),
       D("SS", "SS", 4.0, 7.6, "SS"), D("NB", "NB", 2.0, 11.2, "$"), D("RCB", "CB", 1.5, 16.6, "CB"),
       D("LCB", "CB", 1.2, -14.0, "CB"), D("FS", "FS", 14.0, 4.5, "FS")]
p1 = Play(off, dfn, los=55, to_go=7)
p1.highlight("LCB", "FS")
fld = draw(p1, lateral=(-22, 22), window=(-7.5, 18.0))
for k, t in (("Z", "#1"), ("H", "#2"), ("Y", "#3")):
    pl = p1.players[k]
    say(fld, p1, pl.d - 2.6, pl.w, t, fontsize=6.4)
say(fld, p1, 16.0, 13.0, "called: flood to the trips side", color=OD, fontsize=6.8)
point_to(fld, p1, (7.5, -12.0), (1.2, -14.0), "press, shaded\ninside X", color=DD, fontsize=6.4)
point_to(fld, p1, (10.0, 8.8), (14.0, 4.5), "one safety, cheated\ntoward trips", color=DD, fontsize=6.4)
plt.show()








Figure 42.11: Second-and-7 near midfield. The offense is in trips to the right (#1, #2 and #3 labelled; #3 is Y, the tight end, flexed out off the line) with X alone on the left. The defense shows one deep safety, who is standing 4 or 5 yards toward the trips side, and man-looking corners: the left corner presses X from a shade inside him. The called play is a flood to the trips side.





Before the snap: does the quarterback stay with the called play, or is there a better throw?






TipAnswer





This is the textbook alert: throw to X first. One deep safety, already leaning toward the trips, means X is one-on-one with no help on his side. The corner pressing him is shaded inside, so he is taking away the slant and conceding the outside: the alert throw is a fade or a back-shoulder throw up the left sideline. If X wins at the line, the throw has a high chance of a big gain, and the safety, 4 or 5 yards the wrong way and 14 deep, can’t get there in time.
The insurance: if the safety rotates back toward X at the snap, or the corner bails off the press, the alert is off and the quarterback works the flood to the trips side, where three receivers now face a defense that has shifted its help that way. And the defense knows all of this: a single safety cheating to trips is sometimes bait for exactly this throw, with a rotation back at the snap. That is why an alert is decided before the snap but confirmed in the first half-second after it.











TipPredict the play 2: 1.1 seconds into four verticals





Show the Python
def p2_play():
    p = Play(spread(rb_w=1.6), nickel("c2", WILL=(4.5, -4.2), NB=(4.5, 6.6), MIKE=(4.5, 1.2)), los=LOS, to_go=8)
    protect(p)
    p.dropback(3.0)
    for k, s in (("X", -1), ("Z", 1)):
        timed(p, k, [(2.6, 18.0, s * 16.0)], "route")
    for k, s in (("H", -1), ("Y", 1)):
        timed(p, k, [(2.6, 18.0, s * 7.5)], "route")
    timed(p, "RB", [(0.8, -4.0, 2.8), (1.5, -2.5, 5.5)], "route")
    timed(p, "MIKE", [(1.1, 10.5, 3.6)], "drop")                  # the Tampa Mike runs the middle, leaning right
    timed(p, "FS", [(1.1, 16.0, -10.5)], "drop"); timed(p, "SS", [(1.1, 16.0, 10.5)], "drop")
    timed(p, "LCB", [(1.1, 6.0, -18.0)], "drop"); timed(p, "RCB", [(1.1, 6.0, 18.0)], "drop")
    timed(p, "WILL", [(1.1, 8.5, -11.5)], "drop"); timed(p, "NB", [(1.1, 8.5, 12.0)], "drop")
    p.highlight("MIKE", "FS", "SS")
    return p


p2 = p2_play()
fld = snapshot(p2, 1.1, ghosts=("MIKE", "FS", "SS", "LCB", "RCB"), ghost_t=0.0, lateral=(-22, 22),
               window=(-9.5, 20.0))
ruler(fld, p2)
plt.show()








Figure 42.12: Second-and-8. The offense runs four verticals. The picture is 1.1 seconds after the snap; dashed outlines show where the ringed defenders started. Both corners squatted at about 6 yards. The two safeties have widened to about 10 or 11 yards outside the middle and 16 deep. The Mike (M, ringed) has turned and is running down the middle of the field, drifting toward the right-hand seam.





What is the coverage, which defender should the quarterback read, and where will the ball go?






TipAnswer





Tampa 2. Two safeties splitting the field (middle open), corners squatting in the flats (Cover 2 corners), and the Mike running down the middle: that is the Tampa 2 Mike, whose job is to carry the most dangerous seam and close the gap between the safeties that four verticals is built to hit.
Read the Mike, then a safety. The Mike can only carry one seam. Whichever he takes, the other seam is a one-on-one high-low on that side’s safety: the seam inside him and the go route outside him. If the safety stays inside on the seam, the go route is open along the sideline behind the squatting corner (the hole shot); if he widens toward the go route, as these two already have, the seam splits the gap between him and the Mike. Here the Mike has opened toward Y’s seam on the right, so the throw is H’s seam on the left, between the Mike and the free safety. This is where the look-off earns its keep: a quarterback who wants that throw holds his eyes on Y’s seam for a beat to keep the Mike drifting right, and many offenses coach the seam runners to bend away from the Mike as well. If the quarterback can’t decide in time, the back underneath, past the two hook defenders who have dropped deep under the verticals, is the checkdown. This is why four verticals is only a “+” against Cover 2 in the matrix, not a “++”: the Tampa Mike takes away half of the concept.











TipPredict the play 3: you call it





Show the Python
p3 = Play(spread(), nickel("two", LCB=(6.0, -15.8), RCB=(6.0, 15.8), MIKE=(4.5, 4.4)), los=60, to_go=7)
fld = draw(p3, lateral=(-22, 22), window=(-7.5, 17.0))
plt.show()








Figure 42.13: Third-and-7 near midfield, your offense in its 2x2 set. The defense shows two-high with both corners 6 yards off. Film study says that on third-and-medium against this formation it played Cover 2 30% of the time, quarters 35%, 2-Man 20%, and rotated to Cover 3 the other 15%.





You have four concepts on the call sheet: smash, flood, dagger and mesh. Using the matrix grades (reprinted below), which has the best expected result? Which has the safest floor? Which would you call, and why?



Table 42.4: The four rows of the matrix you need, with this defense’s coverage mix.

Quarters (35%)
2-Man (20%)
Cover 3 (15%)

TipAnswer





Weight each grade by the coverage mix (Cover 2 30%, quarters 35%, 2-Man 20%, Cover 3 15%):

Smash: +2, 0, −2, +1 → 0.60 + 0 − 0.40 + 0.15 = +0.35, worst case −2 (2-Man).
Flood: +1, +1, −1, +2 → 0.30 + 0.35 − 0.20 + 0.30 = +0.75, worst case −1.
Dagger: +1, +2, −1, 0 → 0.30 + 0.70 − 0.20 + 0 = +0.80, worst case −1.
Mesh: 0, 0, +1, 0 → +0.20, worst case 0.

Dagger has the best average, because the most likely coverage, quarters, is the one it was built to beat, and it is decent against Cover 2 too. Flood is a close second. Mesh never loses but rarely wins big. Smash, the famous Cover 2 beater, is the worst choice here: this defense plays enough 2-Man to punish it.
What a coordinator would add. Third-and-7 is a long-ish third down, and route depth matters as much as the grade. Dagger’s dig, at 15 or 16 yards, is past the sticks. Mesh’s crossers settle at 5 or 6 yards against zone, short of the line to gain, so its “safe floor” is less safe than it looks: a completed mesh crosser that is tackled a yard short still ends the drive. But dagger needs about three seconds, so the call depends on the protection and on whether this defense blitzes on third down; against a pressure-heavy defense the slightly quicker flood, or a two-way call, might be safer. And the 20% of 2-Man is the danger in every choice except mesh: if the 2-Man share were higher, or the down shorter, mesh’s floor would start to look like the smart call. The matrix doesn’t make the decision; it organises it.

title: What Beats What: Reading Coverage and Pass Concepts Versus Coverages
text:
Takeaways

The quarterback reads coverage in four steps: the shell before the snap (a hypothesis), the rotation at it (the middle open or closed one second later), the key defender after it (the one the concept puts in conflict), and the throw that defender leaves. The look-off is the same read run in reverse: move the key defender with your eyes, then throw where he was.
Every cell of the concept-by-coverage matrix follows from two questions: where are this coverage’s thin spots, and does it give help to the defender this concept attacks? Smash beats Cover 2 at the sideline; flood and four verticals beat Cover 3’s arithmetic; dagger and scissors make quarters’ read safeties pay for their rule; mesh beats man with traffic; quick throws, seams and screens beat pressure. Against split-field coverage, read each half on its own. The grid leaves out the run game, which is where Cover 3 and the two-high shells earn their keep.
Beaters are bets. Disguise hides the coverage, match rules change what a label means, execution and talent widen or close windows, and the defense chooses by situation too. In charting data the edges are real but small: even the best route-against-coverage matchups fail more than a third of the time.
Two-way concepts trade ceiling for floor. Built-in answers for man and for zone mean the call is never bad, at the cost of rarely being great; they rule third down.
The matrix is never finished. Every defensive counter (Cover 3 match, Palms, Tampa 2, robbers) opens something new, and the offense’s next concept attacks it. The shot alert lets the offense take a deep shot only when the coverage gives it.
Watching: call the coverage one second after the snap, find the conflict defender, and predict the open man before the throw.

title: Constraint Theory: How Plays Talk to Each Other
text:
Every play is an answer to a question
Second quarter, first-and-10 near midfield. For the fourth time today the offense comes out with two backs behind the quarterback and a tight end on the right, and for the fourth time every lineman takes the same step to his right at the snap. The first three times, the back ran behind that wall of blockers for 6, 4 and 9 yards, and by now the linebackers are flying to the right before the ball is even handed off. This time the quarterback fakes the handoff, turns his back to all of them and rolls left. The defensive end on that side has crashed down the line chasing the running back, and there is nobody within ten yards of the quarterback. His tight end is alone in the left flat. Twenty-two yards. “They set that up,” says the analyst. What does that actually mean? How does one play set up another, and if the bootleg is that good, why didn’t they call it on the first snap?
You’ll be able to:
How to read the diagrams. Offense is blue circles, defense orange squares, and left and right are always the offense’s. Q is the quarterback, R the running back, F the fullback, Y the tight end, and X and Z the wide receivers; H is a slot receiver and U a second tight end. C is the center (the other linemen are labelled only where they matter). On defense, E and T are the ends and tackles, S, M and W the Sam, Mike and Will linebackers, $ the nickel back, CB the cornerbacks and FS and SS the safeties. Lines ending in a bar are blocks, arrows are paths, the thick dark arrow is the ball carrier, and a dashed brown arrow is the throw. A red ring marks the defender a play is built to punish, a purple ring a blocker or dropper to watch, and a green ring the ball carrier to follow. In the defense’s pictures a dashed brown ring marks a defender who is threatening to blitz before the snap.
Start with what a defense is trying to do on every snap. It has eleven players and the offense has eleven, but the offense knows where the ball is going and the defense doesn’t. So the defense guesses, in an educated way. It studies the offense all week, learns what the offense likes, and on Sunday it leans. A linebacker who knows the offense runs outside zone half the time from this formation takes his first step toward the play side a little faster. A safety who has seen the tight end block on every snap creeps down to help against the run. A defensive end on the far side, told the cutback is where this offense hurts people, chases hard down the line.
Each of those leans makes the defense better against what the offense usually does. Each one also makes it worse against something else. The linebacker flying to the play side has left the middle of the field. The safety creeping down has nobody behind him. The end chasing down the line is no longer outside the quarterback. An offense that can see those leans, and that has a play aimed at each one, wins the argument.
That is the core of what coaches call constraint theory. Every offense has a small number of base plays: the handful of runs and passes it builds itself around, calls most often, and wants to be good at whatever the defense does. For a Shanahan-family offense the base play is outside zone; for a gap-scheme team it might be power; for a spread passing team it might be a quick-game concept or the inside-zone RPO. Then it has constraint plays: plays whose main job is to punish the defense for over-playing the base play. A constraint play works best exactly when the defense cheats against the base play, and its mere existence is what keeps the defense from cheating too much. The word comes from what it does to the defense: it constrains how far the defense can lean.1
The two kinds of play need each other. Without the constraint plays, the defense cheats freely and the base play dies. Without the base play, the constraint plays have nothing to punish: nobody chases a fake of a play that’s never run. This is why coaches talk about plays “talking to each other.” A good offense is not a list of good plays. It’s a set of plays in which each one’s weakness is another one’s strength.
You won’t often hear “constraint play” on a sideline or in a clinic talk. Coaches say the same thing in their own dialects: complementary plays, answers, if-then calls (“if the Will flows, then counter”), or the “play-pass off” a run. When a coordinator says a play “keeps them honest,” he is describing a constraint play.

43  Constraint Theory: How Plays Talk to Each Other

title: Constraint Theory: How Plays Talk to Each Other
text:
ImportantWhy it exists



A defense that knows what’s coming wins. Constraint plays exist so that the defense can never fully commit to stopping the base play: every lean has a price, and the offense collects it. The trade is that a constraint play is a specialist. It is usually a worse play than the base play when the defense hasn’t cheated (a bootleg into an end who stayed home is a sack waiting to happen, a counter into linebackers who didn’t flow runs straight into them), so it can’t become the offense’s main course. It lives on the base play’s reputation, and the base play lives on its protection. (If that sounds like it contradicts the receiver-run and play-action numbers from earlier chapters, where these plays win on average, hold the thought: the section “Why not just run the constraint play more?” below shows why their averages should look better anyway.)










NoteMadden vs. real life



In a video game you can find a play that works and call it until it stops working, and often it never does, because the computer’s defense doesn’t keep a scouting report on you. Real defenses do. They watch every snap you have run this season, they know what you like from every formation, and they adjust between series, at halftime and during the week. There is no best play in real football, only a best play given what the defense is doing about the others. That is also why the answer to “if the bootleg is so good, why not run it every time?” is the same as the answer to “why not throw deep every time?”: the defense would stop leaning, and the play would turn back into an ordinary one, or worse.








CautionCommon misconception



“Constraint plays are trick plays.” A few are (a flea-flicker, in which the back takes a handoff and pitches the ball back to the quarterback, who throws deep, is a constraint on safeties who come up to stop the run), but most are ordinary, bread-and-butter football: the bootleg, the screen, the draw, the counter, the quick throw behind a blitzing linebacker. What makes a play a constraint is not that it’s unusual. It’s that its job is defined by another play.

section: The constraint tree: outside zone and its family
text:
The constraint tree: outside zone and its family
The cleanest place to see constraint theory is the offense that has made it a way of life: the outside-zone system of Mike Shanahan’s Broncos in the 1990s (built with his offensive line coach Alex Gibbs, whose story is in Zone Running) and of his son Kyle’s 49ers today, and the many coaches who came out of it. Its base play is outside zone (wide zone), the run you met in that chapter: every lineman steps hard to one side, the back aims at the tight end’s outside leg, and the defense has to run sideways with the play or get outflanked. Outside zone trains a defense, snap after snap, to flow: to run hard to the play side. Every constraint play in the system is designed around a defender who has learned that lesson too well. How many plays is that? Fewer than a Madden menu suggests: a few base runs and a few base passes, each with a small family of answers like the one below. The exact count varies by staff, but the point of the system is that it is small enough to practice until every play looks the same for its first second.


Show the Python
fig = plt.figure(figsize=(6.6, 6.4))
cv = fig.add_axes([0, 0, 1, 1]); cv.set_xlim(0, 100); cv.set_ylim(0, 97); cv.axis("off")
axf = fig.add_axes([0.25, 0.555, 0.50, 0.425])
p = Play(offset_i(), base_43(), los=35, to_go=None)
for k in ("LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT"):

def box(x, y, w, h, title, body, num):

                                fc=style.SURFACE, ec=GREEN, lw=1.3, zorder=2))

            color=style.INK, zorder=3)

            zorder=3, linespacing=1.2)

                fontweight="bold", zorder=4, bbox=dict(boxstyle="circle,pad=0.18", fc=RED, ec="white", lw=0.6))


def arrow(x0, y0, x1, y1):
    cv.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((x0, y0), (x1, y1), arrowstyle="-|>", mutation_scale=11, color=style.DEFENSE,
                                 lw=1.3, zorder=1))


def why(x, y, text):
    cv.text(x, y, text, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=6.5, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, style="italic",
            zorder=3, linespacing=1.15, bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.2", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none"))


W, H, YB = 22.5, 16, 33
xs = [12.5, 37.5, 62.5, 87.5]
box(xs[0], YB, W, H, "Bootleg", "fake right, roll left\nbehind a blocker (the\nprotected boot); crossers\nopen behind the flow", "1")
box(xs[1], YB, W, H, "Naked boot", "same fake; nobody\nblocks the end: he is\nbehind a quarterback\nrolling away", "2")
box(xs[2], YB, W, H, "Counter", "line and back start\nright; the ball comes\nback left behind a\npulling guard", "3")
box(xs[3], YB, W, H, "Play-action shot", "same fake, seven\nblock; throw deep\nbehind the safety\nwho came down", "4")
box(xs[1], 8.0, W, 12.5, "Keeper", "on the naked: nobody\nstayed outside, so\nthe quarterback runs", None)
top = 52.5
for x, txt in zip(xs, ["linebackers\nflow hard", "backside end\nchases the back", "backside linebacker\nover-runs the play",
                       "safety races\ndown to the run"]):
    arrow(50 + (x - 50) * 0.35, top, x, YB + H / 2 + 0.9)
    why(50 + (x - 50) * 0.70, top - 5.6, txt)
arrow(xs[1], YB - H / 2 - 0.6, xs[1], 8.0 + 6.25 + 0.9)
why(xs[1] + 14.5, 19.4, "the flat defender\nruns with the receivers")
cv.text(76, 8.5, "Every arrow is the defense cheating\nto stop the base play. If nobody\ncheats, the base play gets its yards,\nwhich is why the defense cheats.",
        ha="center", va="center", fontsize=7.2, color=style.INK, linespacing=1.25,
        bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.5", fc=style.OFFENSE_TINT, ec="none"))
plt.show()








Figure 43.1: The constraint tree around outside zone (illustrative). Top: the base play, outside zone right, with four defenders numbered by how they learn to cheat against it. Below: the play that punishes each cheat. (1) Linebackers who flow hard with the line leave the middle behind them: the bootleg. (2) A backside end who chases the back down the line ends up behind a quarterback rolling away from him: the naked boot. (3) A backside linebacker who over-runs the play leaves the cutback side empty: the counter. (4) A safety who races down to help against the run leaves the deep middle open: the play-action shot. The keeper hangs off the naked boot: if the defender on that side runs with the receivers, nobody is left to stop the quarterback from running. The arrows also run backwards: if the defense cheats on none of them, outside zone gets its yards.





Read Figure 43.1 one branch at a time, starting from what the defense does wrong.
(1) Linebackers flow hard: the bootleg. Outside zone punishes slow linebackers; a linebacker who doesn’t beat his blocker to the play side gets sealed inside and the back runs past him. So linebackers learn to fly. The bootleg fakes outside zone one way and rolls the quarterback out the other way, behind a blocker (a pulling guard or the fullback) who takes care of the defensive end on that side; that blocker is why 04-05 also called it the protected boot. Receivers cross the field to meet him at three depths, and the crossing routes come open behind the linebackers who just ran the other way. The defense’s lesson (“flow fast”) is the very thing the bootleg cashes in.
(2) The backside end chases: the naked boot. On outside zone, the defensive end on the far side (the backside) has two jobs that pull against each other. He is the man who stops the cutback: if he stays put, the back has a lane back to his side. But he is also the last defender on that edge, so his coaching, which you met in 03-05, is to squeeze while checking boot, counter, reverse: shuffle down the line a yard or two to shrink the cutback lane, keep his shoulders square and his eyes on the quarterback, and stay at the edge until he is sure the ball has gone the other way. That is the disciplined version, and it is hard to play. When the cutback has been hurting the defense, the end starts to crash instead: he turns his shoulders, flattens down the line and chases the back. Figure 43.2 shows the difference. Crashing is the cheat. The naked bootleg sends the quarterback right at the spot the crashing end just left, with no blocker for him (that’s the “naked”). The end who crashed is now behind a quarterback who is running away from him, and nobody else is close. If the end squeezed and stayed home instead, he is standing on the quarterback’s launch point, and the quarterback is in trouble, which is the price of a play that only works against a cheat.


Show the Python
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 3.5))
E0 = (1.0, technique("5", -1))                      # the end's alignment, a 5-technique
for ax, crash in zip(axes, (False, True)):
    e1 = (-2.2, 3.3) if crash else (0.4, -2.9)     # where he is when Q would start the boot
    dfn = shifted([q for q in base_43() if q.key not in ("LCB", "RCB", "SS", "FS")], WDE=e1)
    p = Play(offset_i(), dfn, los=35, to_go=None)
    oz_first_second(p, fake=True)
    go_to(p, "QB", (-5.8, -6.8), "run", via=[(-3.6, -1.8)], delay=0.1)
    p.highlight("WDE", color=RED)
    f = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=(-13.0, 6.5), window=(-8.6, 6.4))
    # where he started: a faint outline and a dashed arrow to where he is now
    was_here(f, p, *E0)
    ghost(f, p, [E0, (E0[0] - 0.2, E0[1] + 0.9), e1] if crash else [E0, e1], alpha=0.9, lw=1.5)
    panel_title(ax, "He crashes: the naked boot wins" if crash else "He squeezes: the naked boot dies", fontsize=8.2)
    if crash:
        point_to(f, p, (4.3, -8.8), e1, "turned and\nchased R: inside,\nbehind Q", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK)
        say(f, p, -7.4, -3.6, "nobody here", fontsize=6.6, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK)
    else:
        point_to(f, p, (4.3, -8.8), e1, "a yard down\nthe line, shoulders\nsquare, eyes on Q", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK)
        say(f, p, -7.4, -3.6, "Q rolls right at E", fontsize=6.6, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.8)
plt.show()








Figure 43.2: Two ways to play the backside end (E, red ring) against outside zone right, at the moment the quarterback (Q) would start a naked boot to the left. Left, he squeezes: he shuffles a yard or two down the line with his shoulders square and his eyes on the quarterback (his checklist is boot, counter, reverse), so he is still at the edge, right on the spot the quarterback wants to roll to. Right, he crashes: he turns and chases the back flat down the line, which stops the cutback but leaves him inside and behind the quarterback. The naked boot beats the crash and dies against the squeeze.





The keeper off the naked. Once the quarterback is outside with the ball, somebody on that side has to cover the receivers coming across, and somebody has to stop the quarterback from running. If the defender on that edge runs with the flat route, the quarterback keeps it and runs, often for a first down, because the rest of the defense is still on the other side of the field chasing the fake. The keeper is a constraint on a constraint: it punishes the defense’s answer to the naked boot.
(3) The backside linebacker over-runs: the counter. The back on outside zone has three choices (bang, bend, bounce), and the cutback lane is always there for the backside linebacker to fill. If that linebacker starts running with the flow too, to get to the play side faster, the backside goes empty. The counter starts exactly like outside zone (the line’s first steps, the back’s first step) and then brings the ball back the other way behind a pulling lineman. It’s the run version of the bootleg: it punishes everyone who went with the first step.
(4) The safety races down: the play-action shot. A safety in the box is an extra run defender, and against an outside-zone team the safety on the play side learns to come down fast: a 6-yard run turns into a 2-yard run if he arrives in time. The play-action shot fakes the same run, keeps seven or eight players in to block, and sends two receivers deep, often in a yankee combination (a post from one side, a deep crosser from the other). A safety who has come forward for the run can’t get back to either.
Notice what the arrows in Figure 43.1 all have in common: they start at the defense. A constraint play is defined by the defender it punishes, not by the offense’s drawing. That gives you a practical way to watch: find the defender who is cheating, and you’ve found the play that’s coming.






NoteGo deeper: the RPO as a built-in constraint



The RPO takes this idea to its logical end. Instead of calling the constraint play on a later snap, after the defense has shown its lean, it attaches the constraint to the base play on the same snap: the line blocks the run, and the quarterback watches one defender (the conflict defender) and throws behind him if he leans toward the run. The constraint is no longer a separate call that has to be timed; it’s a branch of the base play that fires automatically. That’s why RPOs are sometimes described as “constraint theory in one play.” The cost is that the read has to be fast and the pass has to be short (the ineligible-downfield rule sees to that), so RPOs don’t replace the deep constraints, like the shot play, that punish the safety.



Same look, four plays: the signature plate
Constraint plays only work if, for the first second, they look like the base play. A linebacker reads a guard’s helmet and the running back’s first two steps; if those match what he has seen on every outside zone, he moves. This is why Shanahan-family offenses are obsessive about one formation, many plays: the same personnel, the same alignment, the same line steps and the same back’s track, with the decision about which play it really is hidden until the defense has already reacted.
In Figure 43.3 below, cover the bottom three panels with your hand and look only at the top-left one. That is what the defense sees for the first half-second of every play in the figure: the same alignment, the same line stepping right (all but one guard, as you’ll see), the same back heading toward the tight end. A defender who waits to find out which play it is gets beaten by outside zone, because outside zone is a race to the edge. A defender who reacts at once gets beaten by one of the other three. The offense has made waiting and reacting both wrong.
How long does a defender have? Not long. A linebacker’s read happens in his first step or two, well under a second, and by the time he is sure, outside zone has already reached the edge. That is why “wait and see” is not an option for him.


Show the Python
LAT, WIN = (-14, 14), (-9, 20.5)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(6.4, 7.6))
# A. outside zone right
p = Play(offset_i(), base_43(), los=35, to_go=10)
oz_first_second(p)
go_to(p, "Y", (0.3, 5.8)); go_to(p, "FB", (3.0, 6.4), via=[(-2.6, 4.2)])
go_to(p, "RB", (5.0, 7.8), "run", via=[(-5.6, 1.6), (-2.6, 3.8), (0.0, 5.6)])
go_to(p, "Z", (5.0, 9.6)); p.route("X", [(0, 0), (8, 0)])
p.highlight("RB")

panel_title(axes[0, 0], "A. Outside zone right: the base play")
say(f, p, -4.6, -7.0, "line steps right;\nback presses Y's\noutside leg", fontsize=6.6)
# B. naked boot left (the end is drawn where his chase has taken him; the outline shows where he started)
E_CHASE = (-2.6, 3.0)
p = Play(offset_i(), shifted(base_43(), WDE=E_CHASE), los=35, to_go=10)
oz_first_second(p, fake=True)
go_to(p, "QB", (-6.2, -7.4), "run", via=[(-4.2, -2.0)], delay=0.1)
go_to(p, "FB", (2.6, -12.4), "route", via=[(-3.8, 2.4), (-2.8, -2.0), (-1.4, -7.0)], delay=0.2)
p.route("Y", [(0, 0), (1.2, -1.0), (5.0, -5.0), (8.0, -10.0), (8.5, -11.8)])
p.route("Z", [(0, 0), (10, -1.0), (11.5, -11.0), (12.5, -21.5)])
p.route("X", [(0, 0), (18.0, 0.0)])
p.highlight("WDE", color=RED); p.highlight("QB")
p.pass_to("Y", t=4.2)
