was_here(f, p, 1.0, technique("5", -1), to=(-1.6, 2.2))
panel_title(axes[0, 1], "B. Naked boot left")
point_to(f, p, (-7.0, 7.4), E_CHASE, "end chased\nthe fake", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK)
say(f, p, 17.0, -6.0, "X clears\nthe corner", fontsize=6.4, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK)
# C. counter left (the linebackers are drawn where their flow has taken them; outlines show where they started)
p = Play(offset_i(), shifted(base_43(), MIKE=(4.4, 3.6), WILL=(4.8, 0.4)), los=35, to_go=10)
go_to(p, "LT", (0.5, -1.5)); go_to(p, "LG", (0.4, -0.4))          # play side blocks down (a step right)
go_to(p, "C", (0.3, 1.9))                                         # back block on the 3-technique
go_to(p, "RT", (0.0, 3.0)); go_to(p, "Y", (0.3, 5.8))             # the back side hinges
go_to(p, "RG", (0.5, -4.4), "pull", via=[(-1.5, 2.0), (-3.0, 0.6), (-2.6, -3.0)])
go_to(p, "FB", (3.8, -0.6), "pull", via=[(-3.8, 1.9), (-3.6, -0.6), (-0.8, -2.8)])
go_to(p, "QB", (-4.1, -0.6), "path", speed=3.0)
go_to(p, "RB", (6.0, -3.2), "run", via=[(-7.0, 1.3), (-4.8, -0.9), (-1.0, -2.9)])
p.highlight("MIKE", "WILL", color=RED); p.highlight("RG", color=PURPLE); p.highlight("RB")
f = draw(p, ax=axes[1, 0], lateral=LAT, window=WIN)
was_here(f, p, 4.6, 1.0); was_here(f, p, 4.6, -2.6)
panel_title(axes[1, 0], "C. Counter left")
point_to(f, p, (12.8, 6.0), (5.2, 3.0), "linebackers\nflowed right", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK)
point_to(f, p, (-4.8, -9.6), (-2.8, -2.0), "RG pulls,\nkicks out E", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK)
# D. play-action shot
p = Play(offset_i(), base_43(), los=35, to_go=10)
oz_first_second(p, fake=True)
go_to(p, "LT", (-1.0, -3.4), via=[(-0.5, -1.8)])                 # one zone step, then hinge back on the end
go_to(p, "QB", (-6.6, -0.6), "path", speed=3.5, delay=0.1)
go_to(p, "Y", (0.3, 5.8)); go_to(p, "FB", (-1.5, 4.8), via=[(-2.8, 4.0)])
p.route("X", [(0, 0), (11.5, 0), (18.0, -7.0)])
p.route("Z", [(0, 0), (9, -0.5), (12.0, -12.0), (13.0, -19.5)])
go_to(p, "FS", (9.0, 1.5), "path"); go_to(p, "SS", (5.0, 5.5), "path")
p.highlight("FS", color=RED)
p.pass_to("X", t=3.0)
f = draw(p, ax=axes[1, 1], lateral=LAT, window=WIN)
panel_title(axes[1, 1], "D. Play-action shot")
point_to(f, p, (17.6, 7.4), (12.6, 0.2), "safety comes\ndown on the fake", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK)
fig.tight_layout(h_pad=0.8, w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()








Figure 43.3: One formation, four plays (a Shanahan-style plate; illustrative, not a specific team’s playbook). Where to look: compare the five linemen’s first steps and R’s first step across the panels. They match, except for the right guard in C. The offense is identical before the snap in all four panels: 21 personnel, an offset I with the fullback (F) offset to the tight end’s side, the receivers in tight splits. A: outside zone right, the base play; the fullback seals the Sam inside and the back presses the tight end’s outside leg, then bounces. B: naked boot left: the same line steps and the back’s same track without the ball, and F starts on his arc before slicing back to the flat. The quarterback (thick arrow) rolls away from the backside end (red ring, drawn where his chase took him; the dashed outline is where he started), X clears the corner, and the throw (dashed brown) goes to Y crossing underneath. C: counter left: the play-side linemen block down, which is a step to the right, so their first step matches the zone step; the back takes one step right; then the right guard (purple ring) pulls back to kick out the end, and the back cuts inside that block, behind the fullback, who leads onto the Will. The linebackers (red rings) are drawn where they flowed. D: play-action shot: the same fake, seven blockers (the left tackle takes one zone step and hinges back onto the end), a post (X) and a deep crossing route (Z); the free safety (red ring) came down on the fake, so the post is open behind him. For the first half-second the defense sees the same thing four times.





Look closely and the plays aren’t perfectly identical, which matters for the arms race. On the counter the right guard pulls left instead of stepping right, a clue for a linebacker disciplined enough to read the guard instead of the back. On the naked boot nobody blocks the backside end, and that is a louder clue than it sounds: on a real outside zone somebody, the backside tackle or a tight end, cuts or cuts off that end (the block the tight end showed and then abandoned on 04-05’s naked boot), so a well-coached end’s rule is “no cut, no block: think boot.” Defenses coach to those clues (“read the guard,” “if nobody blocks you, think boot”), and offenses answer by disguising the clue: the protected boot puts a blocker back on the end, and some counters pull a tight end instead of a guard. The game never ends; it just moves to smaller details.


Why not just run the constraint play more?
Here is the puzzle that comes with every constraint play. In Perimeter Runs and Misdirection you saw that an NFL receiver’s carry (jet sweeps, end-arounds, reverses) has been worth far more on average than a running back’s, every season from 2016 to 2025. In Play-Action, Bootlegs, and Screens you saw that play-action dropbacks beat ordinary dropbacks by a wide margin, season after season. If the constraint plays are that much better, aren’t coaches leaving points on the table by calling them so rarely?
Partly, maybe. But a simple model shows why a constraint play should look better on average than the base play even when a coach is calling it exactly the right amount. Imagine the offense chooses what share of its snaps to spend on the constraint play. As that share rises, the defense sees it more on film and respects it more: it cheats less against the base play. So the constraint play gets worse the more it’s called (fewer defenders are cheating for it to punish) and the base play gets better (fewer defenders are cheating against it).


Show the Python
style.apply()
A_C, S_C, A_B, S_B = 0.60, 3.0, 0.02, 0.30          # constraint and base play: value = intercept + slope x share
q = np.linspace(0, 0.30, 301)
C = A_C - S_C * q
B = A_B + S_B * q
V = q * C + (1 - q) * B
qs = round(float(q[np.argmax(V)]), 2)
Cs, Bs, Vs = A_C - S_C * qs, A_B + S_B * qs, qs * (A_C - S_C * qs) + (1 - qs) * (A_B + S_B * qs)
# the worked example: move one more percentage point of snaps from the base play to the constraint play
GAIN = 0.01 * (Cs - Bs)                 # the extra constraint call is worth more than the base call it replaces
COST = qs * S_C * 0.01                  # ... but every constraint call already being made loses a little
LIFT = (1 - qs) * S_B * 0.01            # ... and every base call gains a little
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 3.5))
ax.axhline(0, color=style.BASELINE, lw=0.9)
ax.plot(q * 100, C, color=style.SERIES[1], lw=2, label="constraint play (e.g. the bootleg)")
ax.plot(q * 100, B, color=style.SERIES[0], lw=2, label="base play (e.g. outside zone)")
ax.plot(q * 100, V, color=style.INK, lw=1.6, ls=(0, (4, 2)), label="offense's average over all snaps")
ax.plot([qs * 100], [Vs], "o", color=style.INK, ms=6, zorder=5)
ax.axvline(qs * 100, color=style.MUTED, lw=0.9, zorder=0)
ax.annotate("", (qs * 100 + 0.5, Cs), (qs * 100 + 0.5, Bs),
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="<->", color=style.INK, lw=1.4))
ax.annotate("at the best mix, the constraint\nplay still looks better per snap",
            (qs * 100 + 0.7, (Cs + Bs) / 2), xytext=(19.0, 0.36), fontsize=7.5, color=style.INK,
            ha="left", va="center", arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=style.INK_2, lw=0.7))
ax.annotate(f"the average peaks here,\nabout {qs:.0%} of snaps", (qs * 100, Vs), xytext=(19.0, -0.08),
            fontsize=7.5, color=style.INK, ha="left", va="center",
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=style.INK_2, lw=0.7))
ax.set_xlabel("share of snaps spent on the constraint play (%)", fontsize=8)
ax.set_ylabel("EPA per snap (illustrative)", fontsize=8)
ax.tick_params(labelsize=7.5)
ax.set_xlim(0, 30); ax.set_ylim(-0.32, 0.65)
ax.legend(loc="lower left", bbox_to_anchor=(0.0, 0.0), fontsize=7.5, frameon=False)
ax.set_title("Why a constraint play's average flatters it", fontsize=10)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 43.4: A toy model of the dose (made-up numbers chosen to make the shape visible, not estimates). As the offense calls the constraint play more often, the defense respects it more: the constraint play’s value per snap falls (orange) and the base play’s rises a little (blue). The offense’s average over all its snaps (dashed) peaks, at the dot, well before the two lines cross. At that best mix the constraint play is still worth more per snap than the base play (the bracket), yet calling it more would lower the average, because each extra call makes the defense respect it more on every snap, base plays included.





The dashed line in Figure 43.4 is what the offense actually cares about: its expected points per snap, counting every snap. It peaks at about 13% here, and at that peak the constraint play is still worth clearly more per snap than the base play. Why stop there? Work through what one more percentage point of constraint calls would do, with the toy numbers at the peak:

The gain. One snap in a hundred switches from the base play (worth +0.06) to the constraint play (worth +0.21). That adds +0.0015 EPA per snap, averaged over all snaps.
The cost. The defense, seeing the constraint a little more often, respects it a little more. Every constraint call the offense was already making (13% of snaps) loses about 0.03: -0.0039 per snap.
The side benefit. A defense respecting the constraint more cheats less against the base play, so every base call gains about 0.003: +0.0026 per snap.

Add them up and the net is roughly zero. That is what “the peak” means: the value of one more call (economists say “at the margin”) has fallen to nothing, even though the average constraint call is still worth far more than the average base call. The constraint play’s average includes all the early, profitable calls; the next call only gets the margin.
So “the constraint play averages more than the base play” is not, by itself, evidence that coaches are under-using it; a well-run offense should show exactly that gap.2 What the gap can’t tell you is whether a particular team is at its peak or short of it, and economists who study play-calling have argued both ways. A second reason the gap flatters constraint plays is selection: coaches call them when they see the defense leaning, so their average is built from good moments. That’s not cheating the numbers. That’s the job.

title: Constraint Theory: How Plays Talk to Each Other
text:
The illusion of complexity
Constraint theory says the plays must look alike. Turn that into a design principle for a whole offense and you get what coaches call the illusion of complexity: make a few plays look like many, and many plays look like one, so that the defense has to prepare for far more than the offense has to learn.3 It has two halves, and you have already seen one of them.
Many plays, one look. That’s Figure 43.3: four plays from one picture, so the picture tells the defense nothing.
One play, many looks. The other half runs the same play out of different formations, personnel groups and motions. The linemen’s assignments don’t change at all; only the costume does.


Show the Python
def gun_11():
    return line() + [O("QB", "QB", -5.0, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -5.2, -2.4, "R"), O("Y", "TE", -0.7, 4.8, "Y"),
                     O("H", "WR", -1.5, -7.0, "H"), O("X", "WR", -0.7, -10.5, "X"), O("Z", "WR", -1.5, 10.5, "Z")]


def wing_12():
    return line() + [O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -7.0, 0.0, "R"), O("Y", "TE", -0.7, 4.8, "Y"),
                     O("U", "TE", -1.5, 6.4, "U"), O("X", "WR", -0.7, -9.5, "X"), O("Z", "WR", -1.5, 10.5, "Z")]


def jet_11():
    return line() + [O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -7.0, 0.0, "R"), O("Y", "TE", -0.7, 4.8, "Y"),
                     O("H", "WR", -1.5, -6.5, "H"), O("X", "WR", -0.7, -10.5, "X"), O("Z", "WR", -1.5, 10.5, "Z")]


OZ_TRACK = [(-5.6, 1.6), (-2.6, 3.8), (0.0, 5.4)]
specs = [("21 personnel, offset I", offset_i(), OZ_TRACK, "defense: base 4-3, eight in the box"),
         ("11 personnel, shotgun", gun_11(), [(-4.2, 0.6), (-2.2, 3.6), (0.0, 5.4)],
          "defense: nickel, a slot corner on H"),
         ("12 personnel, wing right", wing_12(), OZ_TRACK, "defense: base, widen the edge to the wing"),
         ("11 personnel, motion away", jet_11(), OZ_TRACK, "defense: decide who travels with Z")]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(6.6, 4.6))
for ax, (ttl, off, via, dnote) in zip(axes.flat, specs):
    p = Play(off, [], los=35, to_go=None)
    for k in ("LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT"):
        p.block(k, pts=[(0.5, 2.0)])
    go_to(p, "Y", (0.3, 6.2))
    if "FB" in p.players:
        go_to(p, "FB", (2.6, 6.8), via=[(-2.6, 4.2)])
    if "U" in p.players:
        go_to(p, "U", (1.2, 8.0))
    if ttl.endswith("motion away"):
        p.motion("Z", to=(-3.6, -3.0))                 # the ball is snapped once Z has cleared the mesh
        go_to(p, "Z", (-3.8, -10.0), "path", speed=8.0)
    go_to(p, "RB", (3.4, 8.4), "run", via=via)
    p.highlight("RB")
    f = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=(-12.5, 12.5), window=(-8.6, 4.6))
    sx, sy = _P(f, p, 0.0, 5.6)
    ax.plot([sx], [sy], marker="X", ms=7, color=style.THIRD, mec="white", mew=0.7, zorder=9)
    panel_title(ax, ttl, fontsize=8)
    ax.text(0.5, -0.04, dnote, transform=ax.transAxes, ha="center", va="top", fontsize=7.0, color=style.INK_2,
            style="italic")
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.5, h_pad=1.4)
plt.show()








Figure 43.5: One play, four outfits: outside zone right from four different looks (illustrative). In every panel the five linemen take the same first step to the right (the short blocks ending in bars), the back aims at the same spot (the green X, just outside the tight end), and the blocking rules are identical. Only the dressing changes: two backs (21 personnel), three receivers from the shotgun (11), two tight ends with one on a wing (12), and three receivers with Z in motion across the formation away from the play, a decoy to pull defenders’ eyes and feet the wrong way. To the offense this is one play to learn. The grey note under each panel is what the defense has to change to match that look: four alignments to install and practice.





Why does this work so well? Because the burden falls unevenly. A defense doesn’t line up against a play; it lines up against a formation, with rules for who aligns where against two backs, against three receivers, against a wing, against motion. Every new look is something the defense has to install, practice and get right in a few seconds before the snap. The offense, meanwhile, practices one set of blocking rules. In Figure 43.5 the offense learned one play, and the defense had to learn four answers. Multiply by a game plan’s worth of plays and formations and the arithmetic gets lopsided fast: eight formations with three motions each is 24 pictures the defense must have an alignment for, and behind each picture could be any of a dozen core plays, so the defense prepares for close to three hundred combinations while the offense still practices a dozen plays.
The second payoff is that the outfits hide tells, the pre-snap clues you met in How to Watch a Broadcast. If an offense runs outside zone only from the offset I, the offset I is a tell. Spread the same play over four looks and every look carries several plays, so none of them gives the play away. This is a big part of why pre-snap motion has spread so fast: PFF charted a shift or motion on 63.9% of NFL plays in 2025, up from 38.4% in 2016.4 Motion is cheap dressing. It costs the offense almost nothing to learn and the defense a great deal to handle.
What it costs. The illusion has limits. A play still needs the right players to work: outside zone from an empty backfield is not outside zone. Every new outfit adds a little to the players’ memory load and to the chance of a busted alignment. And the outfits only stay an illusion if the plays inside them are mixed: a formation used for one play is just a tell with extra steps.






NoteFilm room: Los Angeles Rams 2018



Sean McVay’s 2018 Rams took the “one look” half of the illusion to an extreme. They used 11 personnel (one back, one tight end, three receivers) on about 93% of their plays, against a league median of about 65%, by this book’s count from nflverse data.5 A defense facing them could learn almost nothing from the substitution before each snap, because there was almost never a substitution: runs, play-action passes and dropbacks all came from the same eleven players, usually in a tight, condensed alignment, often with a receiver in motion. The constraint plays in 03-05’s film room (the jet sweeps that went for big gains) worked partly because they came out of the same look as everything else.
What to notice: when a team never changes personnel, stop looking at personnel and start looking at the details inside the look: the back’s depth, the receivers’ splits, which way the motion goes. That’s where a one-look offense hides, and where it sometimes leaks.

title: Constraint Theory: How Plays Talk to Each Other
text:
Sequencing: plays in an order
Constraint theory tells you which plays belong together. Sequencing is the order you call them in: show the defense a look, watch how it reacts, then call the play that beats that reaction. It turns a playbook into a conversation.
The idea is old. The Delaware Wing-T that you met in 03-05 was built as series football, and its coach, Harold “Tubby” Raymond, put the point bluntly: “The Wing-T is more than a formation. It is sequence football.”6 In the series the buck sweep comes first; the buck trap, the waggle and the counter are what the offense calls when the defense starts stopping the sweep. The mechanism is the defense’s key. Both guards pull on the buck sweep, so linebackers learn to read the guards and chase them; the rest of the series starts with the same backfield action and puts the ball where the chasing linebackers just left: inside on the trap, back the other way on the counter, and, on the waggle, a bootleg away from the sweep fake. To the linebacker reading the backfield, the constraint looks like the base play, which is the whole idea. Bill Walsh’s habit of scripting his first fifteen or so plays (the opening script that the next chapter takes apart) was partly a sequencing tool too: he planned in advance which looks to show early so he could see how the defense answered them and call the answers later.7
Sequencing comes in three shapes you can watch for.
1. Setting up the counter. Run the base play until the defense flows hard to it, then call the play that goes back against the flow. You don’t call the counter because the counter is good; you call it because the defense’s last three reactions say it will be.


Show the Python
def counter_play():
    p = Play(offset_i(labels=True), base_43(), los=35, to_go=None)
    # offense: the line's first steps look like outside zone right
    for k, e in (("LT", (0.6, -1.5)), ("LG", (0.5, -0.3)), ("C", (0.4, 1.0))):
        go_to(p, k, e, speed=1.6)
    go_to(p, "RT", (0.1, 3.6), speed=1.6); go_to(p, "Y", (0.4, 5.6), speed=1.8)
    go_to(p, "RG", (-0.5, 2.1), "block", speed=1.6)                 # the same first step as everyone else ...
    go_to(p, "RG", (0.1, -4.6), "pull", via=[(-1.5, 1.6), (-1.5, -2.8)], speed=5.5)   # ... then the pull
    go_to(p, "FB", (3.0, -1.4), "pull", via=[(-3.6, 0.2), (-3.3, -2.2), (0.2, -2.6)], speed=5.6, delay=0.35)
    go_to(p, "QB", (-2.7, 0.7), "path", speed=2.4)                 # opens to the right, like zone ...
    go_to(p, "QB", (-4.3, -0.4), "path", speed=2.6, delay=0.1)     # ... then turns back to meet the back
    go_to(p, "RB", (-7.0, 1.6), "run", speed=3.2)                  # one step with the zone flow
    go_to(p, "RB", (7.0, -3.4), "run", delay=0.15, speed=6.6, via=[(-4.6, -0.7), (-1.2, -3.0), (2.0, -3.1)])
    p.handoff("RB", t=1.17)
    # defense: the linebackers flow right with the line
    go_to(p, "MIKE", (3.9, 4.2), "path", speed=4.6); go_to(p, "WILL", (4.0, 1.6), "path", speed=4.6)
    go_to(p, "WILL", (3.0, -0.8), "path", speed=3.5, delay=0.1)
    go_to(p, "SAM", (3.0, 7.5), "path", speed=3.0)
    go_to(p, "WDE", (1.2, -4.2), "path", speed=1.0); go_to(p, "WDE", (0.6, -5.6), "path", speed=1.5, delay=0.2)
    go_to(p, "WDT", (1.0, 0.3), "path", speed=1.0); go_to(p, "SDT", (1.0, 3.2), "path", speed=1.0)
    go_to(p, "SDE", (1.2, 6.6), "path", speed=1.0)
    go_to(p, "SS", (6.0, 6.2), "path", speed=3.0); go_to(p, "FS", (10.0, -2.5), "path", speed=3.5, delay=0.6)
    return p


animation_or_strip(counter_play(), [0.3, 1.2, 1.8, 2.8],
                   ["every lineman, RG included, and R\nstep right; the linebackers start to flow",
                    "handoff going left; RG and F\npull back across",
                    "RG kicks out the end; F leads\nthrough; the Will is a step late",
                    "R is through the hole; the flow\nis on the wrong side"],
                   lateral=(-9.5, 9.5), window=(-8.5, 9.0),
                   rings=(("RB", style.THIRD), ("RG", PURPLE), ("FB", PURPLE)))





  
  Your browser does not support the video tag.



Figure 43.6: The counter, after the defense has learned to flow (simulated, BDB-format tracking; faint lines are each player’s path so far). The offense shows the outside-zone look from earlier in the game. (1) Every lineman, the right guard included, takes his first step to the right, and the back (green ring) steps right with them; the linebackers, trained by the earlier outside-zone runs, start to flow. (2) The back takes the handoff going left as the right guard and the fullback (purple rings) pull back across. (3) The guard kicks out the end on the left (the backside end of the zone fake, but the play-side end of the counter); the back cuts inside that block, the fullback leads through the hole, and the Will, who flowed, is a step late coming back. (4) The back is through the line on the side the linebackers just left.




2. Play-action off the base run. After the base run has gained yards from a look, call play-action from the same look within the next few snaps. This is the most common sequence in football, and the most watchable, because you can see it coming. Notice what 04-05 showed, though: linebackers bite on a good fake whether or not the run has been working. So coaches describe the sequence as being less about “earning” the fake with yards than about timing: a defense that has just been gashed is primed to come forward hard, its coaches have just told it to, and the offense knows that.
Is there any sign of that in the data? A little. On neutral first-and-10 snaps from 2022 to 2025, play-action passes called right after a run of 10 or more yards on the same drive averaged +0.21 EPA, against +0.11 for play-action at other times, and the gap showed up in 3 of the 4 seasons. Offenses did not call much more play-action at those moments (51% of dropbacks, against 47%), and the sample is small (581 snaps, so the gap is under two standard errors), so read it as consistent with the coaches’ timing story rather than as proof of it.8
3. The tendency breaker. The third shape needs two new words. A tendency is a pattern in what a team does in a given situation, formation or personnel group (running on four snaps in five from one look, throwing to the tight end on most third-and-shorts) that an opponent can find on film or in data and play against. A tendency breaker is a play called on purpose against your own tendency: a pass from the run look, a run from the empty backfield, a screen from the formation you always use for deep shots. It punishes an opponent who studied you, and it keeps the pattern honest for next week.
Put the three together and a drive starts to read like a conversation. Here is an illustrative one (not a real drive), with the defense’s side of the conversation in the last column:










Snap
Situation
The look
The call
What the defense learned




1

21 personnel, offset I
Outside zone right: +5
“This look means outside zone.”


3

Same look
Outside zone right: +7
Linebackers start flowing on the first step.


4

Same look
Counter left: +11
“Don’t over-run; the back side has to fill the cutback.”


6

Same look
Outside zone right: +5
Backside end starts crashing down the line to stop the cutback.

Same look
Naked boot left: +19
Too late.



(Snaps 2 and 5, a 6-yard gain each, came from other looks.) The offense ran one look five times and called three plays, and the order did the work. Snaps 1 and 3 taught the linebackers to flow, so snap 4’s counter went back against them. The counter taught the defense that the cutback side needed help, so on snap 6 the backside end stopped squeezing and started crashing down the line to take the cutback away, and that crashing end is exactly the man the naked boot on snap 7 is built to beat. Real defenses adjust like this between series, usually because a coach in the booth or on the sideline tablet tells them to; how that works in real time is in In-Game Adjustments.






CautionCommon misconception



“A balanced offense alternates run and pass.” Alternating is a pattern too, and patterns are what defenses hunt. An economic study of NFL play-calling found that teams were more likely to switch between run and pass from one play to the next than a truly unpredictable mix would be, which makes the next call easier to guess, not harder.9 Balance means the defense can’t tell from the look or the last play what comes next, not that the offense takes turns.








NoteFilm room: Kansas City Chiefs, Super Bowl LVII (2022 season)



Andy Reid’s offense is famous for the second half of the illusion of complexity, a huge menu of formations, shifts and motions dressing a stable core of concepts, and for sequencing that plays on what a defense did a few minutes earlier. The best-known example is the pair of fourth-quarter touchdowns in Super Bowl LVII against the Eagles, built on a return-motion play the team called “Corn Dog” (the full story is in Motion and Shifts): Kadarius Toney scored on it, and less than three minutes of game clock later Skyy Moore scored on a mirrored version to the other side. Both times the Eagles’ man defender went with the motion and the receiver was alone when he turned back.10
What to notice: the second call was the same play. Sequencing doesn’t always mean switching to a constraint. If the defense hasn’t fixed what beat it, the right next call is the same question again, and a staff that’s watching closely knows when a defense hasn’t adjusted. A year later, in Super Bowl LVIII, a renamed relative of the play produced the winning overtime touchdown: same idea, new clothes.

title: Constraint Theory: How Plays Talk to Each Other
text:
Tendencies and the self-scout
Every play an offense calls goes on film, and every opponent’s quality control coaches (the entry-level assistants from 01-04 who break film down into numbers) log it: down, distance, field position, personnel, formation, motion, run or pass, direction, result. From those logs come the tendencies a defense plays against on Sunday. A defense that knows an offense runs 80% of the time from a particular look can set its front, its linebackers’ keys and its safety’s depth to stop the run before the snap, and be right four times in five.
So offenses do the same thing to themselves. A self-scout is a team’s study of its own film and data, the way an opponent would study it, to find the tendencies it is giving away. Many teams do a formal one during the bye week, and the same questions come up in smaller ways all season.11 The questions are the opponent’s questions: What do we do from each personnel group and formation? Which way do we run when the back is offset left? What do we do after a motion? What do we call on second-and-long after a first-down run? Where are we a coin flip, and where are we a giveaway?
What a team does with the answers is a judgment call, and there are three choices:

Break it. Call a few tendency breakers from the giveaway look, so the next opponent’s numbers are muddier.
Hide it. Spread the giveaway play across more outfits (the illusion of complexity again) so no single look carries it.
Keep it as bait. Leave the tendency in place on purpose, let the opponent load up for it, and save the breaker for the moment it will hurt most: a big third down, the red zone, the playoffs.


Building a tendency table
You can run the opponent’s first question yourself. A tendency table cross-tabulates two things a defense can see before the snap (here, the offense’s personnel group and the quarterback’s alignment) and shows how often each combination produced a pass. Why the quarterback’s alignment and not the formation? Because it is the only formation information in the public data: nflverse records whether the quarterback was under center, in the shotgun or in the pistol, but not the receivers’ splits or the backfield set. A real tendency report charts far more: dozens of formation codes (2x2, 3x1, bunch, nub), the back’s offset, the motion and its direction, the hash and the field zone (“runs to the field,” “runs to the tight end,” “runs to the side the back is offset”). So whatever this table finds is a floor on what a pro staff gets from the look. To keep the situation from doing the talking (everyone throws on third-and-long), the table uses only neutral snaps: first and second down, the game reasonably close, outside the last two minutes of each half. The formal version of this filter, and expected-pass models that adjust for the situation play by play, are in Tendencies, PROE and Charting.12
The recipe, if you want to build one yourself (the code is under “Show the Python” on the website): load a season’s play-by-play with nflreadpy; join the participation file for personnel and the FTN charting file for the quarterback’s alignment, matching on game and play; keep the neutral first- and second-down snaps; then make a pivot table of the pass flag’s mean by personnel group and alignment, with a second pivot of counts so you can ignore cells with only a handful of snaps.


Show the Python
cmap = LinearSegmentedColormap.from_list("run_pass", [style.SERIES[1], style.DIVERGING[1], style.SERIES[0]])
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 2.9), sharey=True)
for ax, (rt, nn, ttl) in zip(axes, [(R_DET, N_DET, "Detroit Lions, 2024"), (R_NFL, N_NFL, "All 32 teams, 2024")]):
    vals = np.where(nn.values >= 15, rt.values, np.nan)
    ax.imshow(vals, cmap=cmap, vmin=0, vmax=1, aspect="auto")
    for i in range(vals.shape[0]):
        for j in range(vals.shape[1]):
            if nn.values[i, j] >= 15:
                ax.text(j, i - 0.12, f"{rt.values[i, j]:.0%}", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=9.5,
                        fontweight="bold", color=style.INK)
                ax.text(j, i + 0.24, f"n={int(nn.values[i, j]):,}", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=6.6,
                        color=style.INK_2)
            else:
                ax.add_patch(plt.Rectangle((j - 0.5, i - 0.5), 1, 1, fc=style.GRID, ec="none"))
                ax.text(j, i, "too few" if nn.values[i, j] else "none", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=6.6,
                        color=style.MUTED)
    ax.set_xticks(range(3), rt.columns, fontsize=7.6)
    ax.set_yticks(range(len(rt)), [f"{g} personnel" for g in rt.index], fontsize=7.6)
    ax.tick_params(length=0)
    for sp in ax.spines.values():
        sp.set_visible(False)
    ax.set_xticks(np.arange(-0.5, 3, 1), minor=True); ax.set_yticks(np.arange(-0.5, len(rt), 1), minor=True)
    ax.grid(False); ax.grid(which="minor", color=style.SURFACE, lw=2.5); ax.tick_params(which="minor", length=0)
    ax.set_title(ttl, fontsize=9.5)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=1.0)
plt.show()








Figure 43.7: A tendency table: how often the offense passed, by personnel group (rows) and quarterback alignment (columns), neutral situations of the 2024 regular season (first and second down, win probability 20–80%, outside the last two minutes of each half). Left, the Detroit Lions in Ben Johnson’s last season as their offensive coordinator; right, all 32 teams together. Blue cells lean pass, orange cells lean run, pale cells are close to a coin flip; grey cells had fewer than 15 snaps. League-wide, the quarterback’s alignment is a loud tell: about seven passes in ten from the shotgun, three in ten from under center, two to three in ten from the pistol. The Lions were much closer to even under center. Data: nflverse play-by-play, participation (personnel) and FTN charting (alignment) via nflreadpy.





The right-hand table in Figure 43.7 is the league’s starting point, and the loudest thing in it is not personnel at all: it’s where the quarterback stands. From the shotgun, offenses passed on about seven neutral snaps in ten; from under center, about three in ten; from the pistol (the quarterback a few yards back with the back behind him), even fewer. Personnel barely moves those numbers. A defense that saw nothing but the quarterback’s feet would already be well ahead of a coin flip.
Now the Lions. In 2024, Ben Johnson’s third and final season calling Detroit’s plays, they passed on 46% of their neutral 11-personnel snaps from under center, against 32% for the league, and on about four in ten from under center with two or three tight ends. That’s a self-scouted offense: the look that screams “run” for everyone else was close to much closer to even in Detroit, because Johnson used it for play-action as readily as for runs. The shotgun was more predictable (80% passes from 12 personnel), but only on 35 snaps; Detroit lived under center, where its pictures said the least. (The empty 21-personnel cells don’t mean the Lions left the family. The modern Shanahan-tree offenses mostly hide the same one-look, many-plays idea in 11 and 12 personnel under center, with a tight end or a receiver doing the fullback’s motion and blocking jobs.)


Show the Python (build any team’s tendency table)
# Change the team and season to build your own table (seasons 2022-2025 are loaded above).
rate, n = tendency_table(N, team="KC", season=2025, groups=("11", "12", "13"))
print((100 * rate).round(0).astype("Int64"))   # pass rate, %
print(n)                                        # snaps behind each cell: ignore cells with only a handful




How much does the look give away?
A table shows the pattern; the question a defensive coordinator cares about is how much it’s worth. So run the scout’s experiment honestly. For every neutral snap from 2022 to 2025, predict run or pass using only that team’s other games that season (as a scout would, from film he has already seen): if the team passed on more than half of its snaps from this personnel-and-alignment look elsewhere, guess pass. Compare that with a dumber guess that ignores the look and uses only the team’s overall lean.
League-wide, the overall lean alone called about 53% of neutral snaps correctly, barely better than a coin. (For a team close to 50/50 overall, it can even do worse than a coin: if the team passed on 52% of snaps in its other games but ran more often in this one, every guess in this game is “pass” and most are wrong.) The look called about 67%. Two pre-snap facts, personnel and where the quarterback stands, turn a coin flip into two right guesses in three. Figure 43.8 shows how much that varied by team.

Figure 43.8: How much each offense’s pre-snap look gave away, 2024 and 2025 regular seasons (neutral situations). For each snap, run or pass was predicted from the team’s other games that season, using either the team’s overall run/pass lean (grey) or the pass rate of that personnel-and-alignment look (blue). Lower blue dots are harder offenses to read. In 2024 the three least predictable offenses by this measure were Green Bay, the Rams and Detroit; for Green Bay the look was no help at all. Teams named in this chapter are in bold. The dark vertical line at 50% is a coin flip. Data: nflverse play-by-play, participation and FTN charting; course calculation.





The bottom of the 2024 chart reads like a family tree. Matt LaFleur’s Packers, Sean McVay’s Rams and Johnson’s Lions were the three hardest offenses to read from the look; Green Bay’s looks were actually worse than useless, because what the Packers did from a look in one game didn’t carry over to the next. In 2025 the Packers were near the bottom again, along with the Jets (whose looks were also worse than nothing, and whose offensive coordinator that season, Tanner Engstrand, had been Johnson’s passing-game coordinator in Detroit),13 Mike McDaniel’s Dolphins and Johnson’s new team in Chicago. Most of the hardest offenses to read share one family of ideas: under-center outside zone, bootlegs and play-action from shared looks, the Shanahan tree and its close relatives, built around exactly the idea in Figure 43.3. At the other end, the most predictable offenses let the look call about three snaps in four for the defense.
Two cautions keep this honest. First, “predictable” is not the same as “bad”: a good offense can tell you what’s coming and do it anyway (see the Eagles below), and an unpredictable offense can still be poor at executing. This chart measures what the look gave away, not what it cost. Across the 128 team-seasons from 2022 to 2025, how well the look predicted an offense and how many points per play that offense produced were essentially unrelated (correlation -0.02); the fuller version of that question is in 13-04. Second, a team’s measure moves from year to year with its quarterback, its injuries and its coordinator, so read the shape of the chart more than any single rank.






NoteFilm room: Philadelphia Eagles 2024 — a tendency they could afford



The 2024 Eagles show the other side of the self-scout. In neutral situations they lined up in the pistol with 11 personnel 46 times and passed on 7% of them: about as loud a tell as an offense gives. They kept it anyway. Saquon Barkley ran for 2,005 yards that season behind one of the league’s best lines, and the Eagles won Super Bowl LIX.14
Knowing “run” also didn’t tell a defense which run. The Eagles’ runs carried their own built-in answers: quarterback read keeps, RPO tags, and a mix of schemes and directions, so a defense that loaded up for “run” still had to guess where.
What to notice: a tendency costs you only if the defense can do something with it. Knowing the run is coming helps a defense that can win at the line; it doesn’t help much against a line and a back that win anyway. A self-scout doesn’t break every tendency. It asks which ones the next opponent can actually exploit, and spends its tendency breakers there.




Does breaking a tendency pay?
If tendencies help defenses, then plays that go against the look should do better than plays that go with it. The data lets you test that directly. Sort every neutral snap from 2022 to 2025 by what its look said (from the team’s other games, as above): “run” if the team passed less than 45% of the time from that look, “pass” if more than 55%. Then compare what happened when the offense did what the look said, and when it didn’t.

Figure 43.9: Does going against the look pay? NFL neutral-situation snaps, 2022–2025 regular seasons. Left: expected points added (EPA) per play, by what the team’s look said from its other games (‘run’ below a 45% pass rate, ‘pass’ above 55%) and what the offense actually did. A pass from a look that usually means run was worth about twice as much as a pass from a passing look; a run from a passing look was worth no more than a run from a running look. Right: the pass rows split by play-action. Without a run fake, a pass gained the same from either kind of look; with one, both did well. Passes from run looks were mostly play-action (the share is printed on each bar), and that explains their edge. Whiskers are 95% confidence intervals; the no-fake bar for run looks rests on few snaps, so its wide whisker means ‘about the same’ is a loose statement for that bar. Data: nflverse play-by-play, participation and FTN charting; course calculation.





The left panel of Figure 43.9 is half a yes. When the look said run and the offense threw, the pass was worth +0.12 EPA on average, against +0.06 for passes from passing looks. Breaking a run tendency with a pass paid. Breaking a pass tendency with a run did not: runs were worth about the same (-0.07 and -0.07) whatever the look said.
The right panel shows why. Split the passes by whether they started with a run fake, and the difference between the looks disappears: a dropback without a fake was worth about the same from a running look as from a passing look, and a play-action pass did well from both. What made passes from run looks better is that 75% of them were play-action, against 21% from passing looks. In other words, the profitable tendency breaker in the NFL is not “surprise, it’s a pass.” It’s “surprise, it’s a pass that looks like the run you expected.” That’s constraint theory and the illusion of complexity again, showing up in the averages.
Treat this as what it is, an average over four seasons and every team, not a controlled experiment. Coaches choose when to break tendencies, and they pick good moments, so some of the gain is selection. But the asymmetry is striking, and it fits what coaches say: the run-look pass is the tendency breaker worth having.






NoteFilm room: Detroit Lions 2022–2024 — Ben Johnson’s sequencing



Ben Johnson called Detroit’s plays for three seasons, and by 2024 the Lions were the NFL’s highest-scoring offense.15 His offense was built from the Shanahan-family ingredients in this chapter, under-center runs and play-action from the same looks, plus a taste for tendency breakers. The clearest example was the sixth offensive lineman. Detroit was one of the league’s heaviest users of a “jumbo” package with an extra lineman, a look that tells most defenses “run”: league-wide, offenses passed on about 28% of neutral snaps from it in 2022–2024. Detroit passed on 33% of its 99 neutral jumbo snaps in those seasons, and 82% of those passes were play-action: a run look hiding exactly the kind of pass Figure 43.9 found profitable. The most famous jumbo snap was the extreme version of the breaker. In a December 2023 game at Dallas the Lions tried to take the lead on a two-point pass to a tackle, Taylor Decker, from a heavy look that screams run; the officials ruled that the wrong tackle had reported as eligible, and the play was wiped out.16
What to notice: watch the snap after a Lions-style big run from under center. The offense knows the defense’s coaches have just told it to come up and stop the run, and that’s the moment the same look turns into play-action. Johnson took the approach with him to Chicago as head coach in 2025, where the Bears were second in the league in play-action rate (see 04-05) and, in Figure 43.8, among the harder offenses to read.

section: The defense’s version: one look, several answers
text:
The defense’s version: one look, several answers
Defenses play the same game from the other side. A defense has base calls too, the coverage and front it wants to be good at and calls most, and its own constraint plays: the blitz that punishes an offense for holding the ball (long play-action shots, slow-developing dropbacks, a protection that always slides the same way), and the drop that punishes a quarterback who expects a blitz and throws hot. It has tendencies the offense’s quality control coaches are hunting (does it blitz on third-and-medium? does the safety rotate toward the motion?), and it self-scouts and breaks them too.
The defensive form of the illusion of complexity is the one you met in Disguise, Rotation and Split-Field and Zone Blitzes and Simulated Pressure: show one picture before the snap and play several things after it. The offense has to decide its protection and its hot throws from the picture, so a picture that carries several defenses turns every one of those decisions into a guess.
Read Figure 43.10, below, as a constraint tree turned around. The defense’s base threat here is the Cover 0 blitz: six rushers, as many as the offense can block even with the back staying in, and nobody deep, so one missed assignment is a free rusher and the quarterback must get the ball out right now, often hot, to whoever the blitz left uncovered.
Count the threats in its top-left panel. Four linemen, two mugged linebackers and two walked-up defenders make eight possible rushers, and the offense has six blockers: five linemen and the back. It cannot block all eight, and it doesn’t try. That is the point of the look. The offense has to guess which six are coming, block those, and have a hot throw ready for anyone extra. An offense that has seen the Cover 0 version a few times learns to answer the pressure look the standard way: the quarterback identifies the Mike, the center and the back take the two mugged linebackers, and the quarterback is “hot” off any seventh rusher, throwing quick to the receiver that rusher left.


Show the Python
LAT, WIN = (-14.4, 14.4), (-8.8, 18.6)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(6.2, 5.6))
ax = axes.flat

for k in ("LDE", "LDT", "RDT", "RDE", "MIKE", "WILL"):

p.man("LCB", "X"); p.man("RCB", "Z"); p.man("NB", "H"); p.man("SS", "Y")

panel_title(ax[2], "B. Fire zone: 5 rush, 3 deep, 3 under")

for k in ("LDE", "RDE", "LDT", "MIKE"):
    p.rush(k)

p.drop("RCB", (14.0, 10.0), zone=(5, 7))
p.highlight("WILL", "RDT", color=PURPLE)

panel_title(ax[3], "C. Simulated pressure: 4 rush, 7 drop")
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.5, h_pad=0.7)
plt.show()








Figure 43.10: The defense’s version: one pressure look, three answers (illustrative). Top left, the look: both linebackers mugged in the A gaps and the nickel ($) and strong safety (SS) walked up beside the ends (dashed rings: all four are blitz threats), so eight defenders could rush against six blockers, with one deep safety. A: Cover 0, six rush (the four linemen and both mugged linebackers) and everyone else plays man (dotted lines), nobody deep; the free safety comes down late to take the back. B: a fire zone, five rush, including the nickel off the edge, while the left end (purple ring) drops into a short zone: three deep, three under. C: simulated pressure, four rush (one of them the Mike), the Will and the right defensive tackle (purple rings) drop, seven cover. The protection has to be set, and the hot throw chosen, before the offense knows which one is coming.





The fire zone and the simulated pressure are the defense’s constraint plays against that answer. They drop players into the windows where the hot throws go and bring rushers from where the protection isn’t looking, so the offense’s answer to the blitz becomes the defense’s opportunity.
The same structure holds for coverage shells. A two-high shell that can rotate to Cover 3 at the snap, or a single-high look that spins back to two deep, is one picture carrying several coverages, and it constrains the quarterback’s pre-snap read the way a run-and-boot look constrains a linebacker’s first step. The defenses that lean hardest on this, such as Brian Flores’s Vikings in 06-06’s film room, are the hardest to scout, because their tendencies are built to be coin flips.
The defense also has to self-scout. A defense that always rotates the safety toward the motion, or always blitzes on third-and-6, has handed the offense a free play: motion to set the rotation, or a screen against the blitz. The cure is the same as on offense: break it, hide it, or keep it as bait for one big moment.






TipWatch for it on Sunday: call the follow-up



Pick one offense for a quarter and keep a tiny log: the look (personnel and where the quarterback stands) and the play.
Before the snap

Is this a look you’ve already seen today? Say what it was used for last time.
If the last play from this look was a big run, say “play-action” out loud. It’s the most common follow-up in football, usually within the next few snaps.
Pick out the cheater: the linebacker flowing early, the backside end crashing down the line instead of squeezing, the safety creeping down. The next constraint play will be aimed at him.

After the snap

First step: did the line go the same way as the base play? If so, watch the ball, not the line.
Did the ball come back against the flow (counter), the quarterback roll away from it (boot), or the throw go over the safety who came down (shot)? Name the defender it punished.
On defense: when you see a pressure look on third down, count rushers at the snap. If a mugged linebacker drops, you’ve seen the defense’s constraint play against the hot throw.

Figure 43.11: Second-and-6, second quarter. The offense is back in its favorite look: 21 personnel, offset I, tight end right. The faint dashed arrows show what the defense did on the offense’s last three outside-zone runs to the right from this look: both linebackers flew to the play side at the snap, while the backside end (ringed) now plays boot, counter, reverse: he squeezes the cutback a yard down the line but keeps his shoulders square and his eyes on the quarterback, instead of crashing down the line as he did earlier in the game.





The defense has adjusted to the outside zone and to the boot. What does the offense call, and where does the ball go?






TipAnswer





A counter to the left (or another run back against the flow), not the naked boot. Two things have changed. The linebackers are flowing even harder, which is the counter’s cue: it starts like outside zone and brings the ball back to the side they just left. And the backside end has stopped crashing. He now plays boot, counter, reverse: he squeezes a yard, keeps his eyes on the quarterback and stays at the edge. That kills the naked boot, because he is standing on the spot the quarterback would roll to, facing him.
Is the end a problem for the counter, too? Partly: a disciplined boot-counter-reverse end is also a counter defender (it’s the C in his checklist). But a squeezing end is exactly the man the pulling guard is built to kick out, and the guard comes at him from inside, with a good angle. (If he squeezes so hard that he crosses the guard’s face, the guard logs him, sealing him inside, and the back bends outside instead.) The counter still wins here because the linebackers’ over-flow is the bigger cheat, and nothing else on the tree punishes it as directly. Expect the back to take one step right, then the right guard (or the tight end, in some versions) to pull back across, kick the end out, and the fullback to lead up onto the Will, who has to stop, turn and come back.
What about the protected bootleg, branch (1) on the tree? The linebackers are flying, and it puts a blocker on the end, so it’s a reasonable second answer, and partial credit if you said it. It is worse than the counter here because of where this end is: he is waiting at the quarterback’s launch point with his eyes on the quarterback, so the boot’s lone blocker meets a defender who expects him, the quarterback has to pull up early, and the crossing routes don’t get time to come open behind the linebackers.
If you said “naked boot,” that was the right answer a few snaps ago, when the end was crashing. The tree in Figure 43.1 is a map of which defender to punish; this defense moved, so the answer moved with it. If the end starts crashing again, the naked boot comes back.

f = draw(p, lateral=(-14.5, 14.5), window=(-8.6, 16.5), width_in=5.4)
say(f, p, 13.0, 4.0, "one deep", fontsize=6.8, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK)
plt.show()








Figure 43.12: First-and-10 at the opponent’s 38, early in the third quarter. Two snaps ago, from this exact look (12 personnel, under center, both tight ends attached to the line), the offense ran outside zone for 23 yards. In its neutral-situation film this season the offense has passed on about 30% of its snaps from this look. The defense has brought its strong safety (SS, ringed) down to about seven yards, and the free safety is the only deep defender.





Run or pass? If pass, what kind, and what is the defense afraid of?






TipAnswer





This is the snap for a play-action shot, and if it’s a pass it’s likely to go deep, though run is still the single most likely call. Start with the numbers: from this look the offense passes about three times in ten, so a pure tendency guess says run. That’s what the defense’s tendency report says too, and after a 23-yard run its coaches will have told it to stop the run, which is why the strong safety has come down to seven yards. That’s the lean.
Now think like the play-caller. The best time to break a tendency is when the defense is most committed to it. A play-action shot from the same look, with the same line steps and the same back’s track, attacks the one deep safety: one receiver deep down the middle to hold him, another on a deep crossing route behind the linebackers who come forward on the fake, seven or eight players blocking. Figure 43.9 is the case for it: passes from looks that usually mean run have been worth about twice as much as ordinary passes, almost entirely because they’re play-action.
A good defense knows this too, which is why many coordinators keep a safety deep for a snap or two after a big run even when the scouting report says run. That matters for the offense in two ways. If the quarterback has a check at the line and sees the defense back out of the eight-man look before the snap (the strong safety drifting back to two deep), he can check to the run, because the shot has lost its target. And if the defense disguises it and the free safety bails at the snap, the shot is covered on this play, but the offense has learned something for the next snap from this look: a defense that is guarding the deep middle has fewer men in the box, and the run is back on.











TipPredict the play 3: the third time they show it





Show the Python
p = Play(spread(), mug_look(), los=40, to_go=7)
f = draw(p, lateral=(-14.6, 14.6), window=(-7.6, 15.5), width_in=5.6)
threat(f, p, "MIKE", "WILL", "NB", "SS")
ghost(f, p, [(-1.0, -7.3), (1.0, -6.0), (4.2, -2.9)], color=style.OFFENSE, alpha=0.7)
point_to(f, p, (11.0, -6.0), (4.0, -3.2), "where the hot throw\nwent twice", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK)
plt.show()








Figure 43.13: Third-and-7. The defense shows the same pressure look for the third time today: both linebackers mugged in the A gaps and the nickel and strong safety walked up beside the ends (dashed rings: blitz threats), one deep safety. The first two times it was a six-man Cover 0 blitz, and both times the quarterback beat it with a quick throw to the slot receiver on his left (H), right where a blitzing Will had come from.





Six rushers again? What should the quarterback expect?






TipAnswer





Probably not six this time: expect a simulated pressure or a fire zone, with a defender dropping into H’s window. The defense’s base threat has been beaten twice in the same way: the offense now expects six, puts the center and the back on the two mugged linebackers and throws hot to the slot. That answer is exactly what the defense’s constraint plays are built to punish. The likeliest call drops one of the mugged linebackers (most likely the Will, on H’s side) straight into the short window the hot throw has been going to, and brings a rusher from somewhere the protection isn’t looking, such as the nickel off the edge (he’s walked up, so he can) or a lineman looping. Four or five rush; six or seven cover.
For the quarterback, the danger is throwing the same hot route on rhythm into a defender who is waiting for it. The better plan is to hold the ball a beat to see who actually comes, or to have a route behind the dropper. The defense can also bluff the other way and blitz six a third time, betting that the offense has adjusted already; that’s the coin flip the defense wants the quarterback to face. But after two clean hot completions, the sequencing logic points to the drop.

title: Constraint Theory: How Plays Talk to Each Other
text:
Takeaways

Base plays are what an offense wants to be good at; constraint plays punish the defense for stopping them. Every constraint play is defined by the defender it punishes: find the defender who is cheating and you’ve found the play that’s coming.
The two need each other. The base play keeps the defense leaning, the constraint plays limit the lean, and a constraint play’s average should look better than the base play’s even when it’s called the right amount, because each extra call costs a little on every other snap.
The illusion of complexity works from both ends. One play in many outfits gives the defense more to prepare; many plays from one look gives it nothing to read. Both hide tells.
Sequencing is the order of the conversation: the counter after the flow, play-action after the big run, the tendency breaker after a stretch of predictability. Sometimes the right follow-up is the same play again.
Tendencies are real and measurable. In neutral situations from 2022 to 2025, personnel plus the quarterback’s alignment called about two snaps in three correctly; the hardest offenses to read came mostly from the Shanahan family of offenses. Passes from run looks paid off, mostly because they were play-action.
Defenses play the same game: one pressure look or one shell carrying several calls, and their own self-scout.

text:
The idea is much older than the name; the name “constraint theory” was popularized by the coach and writer Chris B. Brown on his Smart Football site, for example in “Why Every Team Should Apply the Constraint Theory of Offense” (June 14, 2011), which separates an offense’s “base, core plays” from the “constraint plays” (bubble screens, play-action, bootlegs, draws, traps) that make defenders “pay for their impatience” when they cheat: https://web.archive.org/web/20110616214847/http://smartfootball.com/offense/why-every-team-should-apply-the-constraint-theory-of-offense.↩︎
The textbook game-theory version says something different: if both sides choose at random each snap and neither can learn from the other’s history, the offense’s best mix makes its plays equally valuable on average. Brian Burke laid out that argument for run-pass balance in “Game Theory and Run/Pass Balance,” Advanced NFL Stats, June 13, 2008: https://web.archive.org/web/20080920054748/http://www.advancednflstats.com/2008/06/game-theory-and-runpass-balance.html. The toy model here lets the defense learn how often the constraint comes from film, which is what leaves a gap in the averages. Which picture fits real play-calling better is exactly what the economists argue about.↩︎
The phrase is common shorthand in the Shanahan family of offenses, and its first use is not well documented. Robert Mays used it of Kyle Shanahan’s Falcons offense in “The NFL’s Newest Mastermind Eyes the Throne,” The Ringer, Jan. 30, 2017: https://www.theringer.com/2017/01/30/nfl/kyle-shanahan-atlanta-falcons-super-bowl-nfl-playoffs-4a40f26c05e2. Matt LaFleur used it on taking the Packers job in January 2019; Davante Adams said LaFleur “wants to bring in a new kind of innovative style – an illusion of complexity” (Rob Demovsky, ESPN, Jan. 28, 2019: https://www.espn.com/blog/green-bay-packers/post/_/id/46765/davante-adams-packers-offense-will-be-new-school-under-new-coach). Later profiles trace the phrase to the Washington staff (2010s) that included Kyle Shanahan, LaFleur and Sean McVay.↩︎
Daire Carragher, “NFL pre-snap motion usage reaches new highs across the NFL,” PFF, Feb. 23, 2026 (shift or motion on 38.4% of plays in 2016 and 63.9% in 2025): https://www.pff.com/news/nfl-pre-snap-motion-usage-reaches-new-highs-across-the-nfl. PFF’s series counts shifts as well as motion and is not comparable with FTN’s is_motion flag.↩︎
Course calculation from nflverse participation data, 2018 regular season, runs and passes with a recorded personnel grouping: the Rams were in 11 personnel on 92.7% of plays (about 1,040 plays); the median team was at about 65% and the next-highest team, Green Bay, at 76%.↩︎
Raymond’s line is quoted in Chris B. Brown, “The Making of a Modern-Day Guru,” Grantland, January 3, 2014: https://grantland.com/features/gus-malzahn-offensive-evolution/. See also Harold R. Raymond and Ted Kempski, The Delaware Wing-T: An Order of Football (Parker Publishing, 1986).↩︎
Bill Walsh with Brian Billick and James Peterson, Finding the Winning Edge (Sports Publishing, 1998), on scripting the opening plays; AP obituary via NFL.com (July 30, 2007), crediting Walsh with popularizing “the practice of scripting the first 15 offensive plays of a game”: https://www.nfl.com/news/hall-of-fame-coach-bill-walsh-who-won-three-super-bowls-with-th-09000d5d800879e1. Comparing only first-and-10 snaps keeps the down and distance the same, since a big run usually ends in a fresh first down.↩︎
Kenneth Kovash and Steven D. Levitt, “Professionals Do Not Play Minimax: Evidence from Major League Baseball and the National Football League,” NBER Working Paper 15347 (September 2009): https://www.nber.org/papers/w15347. They report negative serial correlation in NFL run-pass choices (teams switch more than an unpredictable mix would: other things equal, a team that has just passed is about 10 percentage points less likely to pass next) and argue that teams passed too rarely in the seasons studied (2001–2005); summary in the NBER Digest, October 2009: https://www.nber.org/digest/oct09/w15347.html.↩︎
“Corn Dog (American football),” Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corn_Dog_(American_football) (Toney 5-yard touchdown at 12:04 and Moore 4-yard touchdown at 9:22 of the fourth quarter; the Super Bowl LVIII version, renamed “Tom and Jerry,” for Mecole Hardman’s walk-off touchdown); Super Bowl LVII result, Kansas City 38, Philadelphia 35 (Feb. 12, 2023): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_LVII.↩︎
For example, Titans coach Mike Munchak on his staff’s 2012 bye week: “see what our tendencies are … how other teams look at us as an offense, defense, special teams” (“Titans Coaches Using Bye to Scout Own Team,” TennesseeTitans.com, Nov. 13, 2012: https://www.tennesseetitans.com/news/titans-coaches-using-bye-to-scout-own-team-8831526); and Matt LaFleur’s 2019 Packers, whose offensive and defensive staffs studied each other’s side of the ball over the bye for “a different perspective of how opponents would attack one side of the ball, where we think there could be holes or potential holes” (Mike Spofford, “Packers taking hard look at themselves over the bye,” Packers.com, Nov. 11, 2019: https://www.packers.com/news/packers-taking-hard-look-at-themselves-over-the-bye).↩︎

title: The Game Plan: A Week Inside an NFL Building
text:
What a game plan is, and why there has to be one
Sunday, 1:03 in the afternoon, first play of the game. The offense comes out in a formation you have not seen from it all season: two tight ends, both standing out where wide receivers usually stand, and a lone back behind the quarterback. The defense, caught in its heavy, run-stopping personnel, sends two linebackers trotting out to cover them. The ball goes to the tight end on the right for 11 yards. On the second play the offense is back in a normal look and runs the ball for three. “That first one was a script play,” says the analyst. “They drew that up on Tuesday.” Tuesday? Who decided, five days before kickoff, what the first play would be? Why that formation, why that tight end, why against those linebackers? And if they knew it would work, why not run it again on the second snap? This chapter is about the six days you don’t see, in which a staff takes one opponent apart and puts its pieces on a sheet of laminated paper.
You’ll be able to:
How to read the diagrams. Offense is blue circles, defense orange squares, and left and right are always the offense’s. Q is the quarterback, R the running back, Y and U the tight ends, X and Z the outside receivers and H a slot receiver; C is the center. On defense, E and T are the ends and tackles, S, M and W the Sam, Mike and Will linebackers, $ the nickel back, D a sixth defensive back (a “dime” back), CB the cornerbacks and FS and SS the safeties. Dotted lines join a man-coverage defender to his receiver. A red ring marks the matchup a plan is hunting (or a player who pays the bill for a choice), and a purple ring a defender the game plan moved.
Start with arithmetic. An NFL playbook holds hundreds of plays once you count every formation, motion and protection they can be run from. A team gets three real practices a week during the season, and only about one practice a week in pads: fourteen padded practices in the whole regular season.1 A player can learn and rehearse only so many new things in three days, and every snap of practice spent on one play is a snap not spent on another. So each week a staff has to choose, and what it chooses is the game plan: the slice of the playbook picked for one opponent, plus the rules for using it. Which runs and passes, from which formations, in which situations. Which coverages and pressures. Which of the opponent’s players to attack, and which to avoid.
What a Play Really Is drew the funnel: playbook, then game plan, then call sheet. This chapter is the middle step, and it is most of a coach’s working life. A game plan answers four questions, and the rest of the chapter takes them one at a time.

title: The Game Plan: A Week Inside an NFL Building
text:
What do they do? The opponent’s habits, by situation. That’s the tendency report, built by the quality control staff from film.
What do they do best, and who does it? The thing the opponent most needs to work: a run, a receiver, a pass rusher, a blitz. The plan either takes it away or protects against it.
Where can we win? The matchups: which of our players should beat which of theirs, and how to arrange the formation so those pairings happen.
What do they think we’ll do? The opponent has scouted us. The plan includes which of our own tendencies to keep, hide or break (the self-scout from Constraint Theory).







ImportantWhy it exists



A game plan exists because time is scarce and every opponent is different. Practicing everything means practicing nothing well; practicing the same thing every week means the opponent knows what’s coming. The plan is the compromise: a stable core of plays the team runs every week (so they are sharp) dressed and aimed differently for each opponent (so they are hard to scout). The trade is real. Every play in the plan gets practice time and can be called with confidence; every play left out is unavailable on Sunday, however well it might have worked. A coach who loves a play that isn’t in this week’s plan can’t call it. That is why what’s left out of a game plan matters as much as what goes in.








NoteMadden vs. real life



In a video game, every play in the book is available on every snap, and your players execute a play you’ve never called as well as one you call every week. Neither is true in real life. A play-caller chooses from a few dozen calls per situation that his players rehearsed on Wednesday, Thursday and Friday, and a play the players haven’t practiced this week is a play somebody is likely to get wrong. The coach’s real menu is not the playbook. It’s the practice schedule.

Figure 44.1: A typical game week for a Sunday game (illustrative; every staff varies the details). Read across for one group’s week and down for one day. The installs move from the most common situations to the rarest: first and second down on Wednesday, third down on Thursday, red zone and two-minute on Friday, when the special-teams plan is also finished. The quality control coaches start the opponent a week or more before anyone else, and the analytics staff’s work arrives as decisions made in advance (fourth downs, two-point tries) rather than plays. On a short week before a Thursday game the same work is squeezed into three days, mostly as meetings and walk-throughs.





Monday: close the last game, open the next one. The morning after a game belongs to the last game. Coaches grade every player on every snap, the players come in for treatment, a lift and a film session on what went wrong, and the staff decides what to fix. By the afternoon the coordinators have turned to the next opponent, and they are not starting from scratch. The quality control coaches have been breaking that opponent down for a week or more (more on that below), so the coordinators spend the day watching film with a stack of reports already beside them.
Tuesday: the coaches’ day. At most teams Tuesday is the players’ day off, and the longest day of the week for the coaches.2 This is when the first-and-second-down game plan gets built: which runs, which passes, from which formations, against which of the opponent’s fronts and coverages. It’s when the first draft of the opening script appears, and when the plays the players will see on Wednesday morning are drawn, named and loaded onto their tablets. Some coordinators sleep at the facility. John Wolford, then a Rams quarterback, described getting the week’s play calls on Tuesday night, “though oftentimes we do not get these until Wednesday morning.”3
Wednesday: install one, first and second down. The first practice day teaches the plays that will be called most. First and second down are roughly three of every four snaps an offense runs, so they get the first meetings, the first walk-through and the most practice repetitions. The defense mirrors it: its base fronts and coverages against this opponent’s base runs and passes. A scout team of backups runs the opponent’s plays, drawn from the quality control coaches’ cards, so the starters see what they’ll see on Sunday. A scout card is a drawing of one opponent play on a sheet of poster board: the scout quarterback holds it up in the huddle, each backup finds his assignment on it, and they line up and run it.
Thursday: install two, third down. Third down is its own game (see Third Down): the defense’s pressures and disguises come out, and the offense needs answers to each. Thursday adds the third-down plan, the protections against the opponent’s blitzes, and usually some changes to Wednesday’s plan after the staff has watched Wednesday’s practice film. A quarterback calls it the hardest day of the week: “Bodies are sore from yesterday, practice is more intense, and more information is thrown at you.”
Friday: install three, the rare situations. Red zone, goal line, two-minute drill and the four-minute offense (running out the clock with a lead) come last, in a shorter practice. These are the situations with the fewest snaps and the highest stakes per snap. The call sheet is finished, and the script is set. The third phase gets its plan too: the special-teams coordinator’s return and coverage schemes for this opponent’s kicker and punter, and any fake or punt-block chance he found on film.
Saturday: walk-through and travel. A light, helmets-only rehearsal, special situations, travel for road games, and meetings at the team hotel at night, where the players often walk through the opening script. Many head coaches also hold a game-management meeting late in the week: timeouts, challenges, the end of each half and the analytics staff’s decision card, so that the clock decisions on Sunday are rehearsed rather than improvised.
Sunday: the sheet. Everything above is now a few hundred calls on one or two laminated pages in the play-caller’s hand, plus a booth full of people charting what the opponent actually does. Only a fraction of those calls get used: in 2025 an offense ran about 60 plays a game (runs and passes, not counting kicks or plays wiped out by penalties), and many of those were the same favorite calls more than once.4 The sheet is big because nobody knows in advance which sixty will be needed.
Who decides? The coordinators build their sides of the plan and usually call them on Sunday, but the head coach signs off on the whole thing, and on the decisions that belong to the whole team (fourth downs, two-point tries, timeouts, how aggressive to be) he has the final word. A head coach who calls one side himself, as several do, is also that side’s coordinator in all but name.






ImportantWhy it exists: why the installs go in that order



The week runs from the most common situations to the rarest. First and second down get Wednesday, the freshest day with the most practice time, because they’re most of the game; red zone and two-minute get Friday’s short practice because they are a small share of snaps. The defense has the same calendar, for the same reason. The trade is plain: the situations that decide close games (a fourth-and-goal, the last two minutes) get the least rehearsal. Coaches cover that gap by keeping their red-zone and two-minute plans small and familiar, built from the same few concepts week after week, with a new wrinkle or two for the opponent.


Two weeks break the pattern. A short week before a Thursday game compresses everything into about three days. The players come in sore on Monday, there is no time for a real practice in pads, and the install happens mostly in meetings and walk-throughs, so game plans on Thursday nights are usually smaller and simpler. A bye week goes the other way: the players get several days off, and the staff turns its film study on itself. That’s when most teams do the formal self-scout from Constraint Theory, and it is often when they plan the tendency breakers for the rest of the season.

section: Film first: the breakdown and the tendency report
text:
Film first: the breakdown and the tendency report
Every game plan starts with film, and the film is broken down long before the coordinators see it. The quality control coaches (QC coaches) from What a Play Really Is take the opponent’s recent games (often the last four or five, plus any game against an offense or defense like their own, and last season’s meeting if the coordinator hasn’t changed) on coaches film, and tag every snap. A tag is a row in a database: down, distance, yard line, hash, quarter, score, personnel, formation, motion, the play (run direction, pass concept, protection), the defense’s front, coverage and pressure, and the result. A season of one team’s snaps is a thousand-plus rows, and a QC coach may tag several opponents at once, a week or two ahead.
Those rows become the tendency report: the written breakdown of what the opponent does in each situation, personnel group and formation. On offense it reads like “from 12 personnel, under center, on first down: run 68%, mostly outside zone to the tight end side; play-action off it when the strong safety walks down.” On defense it reads like “third-and-4 to 6: man coverage half the time, five-man pressure from the slot when we’re in empty.” The report comes with cut-ups: video playlists of every snap in one category (“all their third-and-medium blitzes,” “every red-zone snap against 3x1”) so a coordinator can watch the twenty plays behind a number rather than trust the number alone.
You can build a simple version of one yourself. Figure 44.2 is what a defensive tendency report’s first page might look like if it were built only from public charting data: the defense that won Super Bowl LX, Mike Macdonald’s 2025 Seahawks, as the Patriots’ staff might have summarized it before that game.5 This is not their report. It’s a reconstruction, and a real one would be much finer grained.


Show the Python
COLS = [("rush5", "5+ rushers"), ("man", "man coverage"), ("two_high", "two-deep shell")]
cmap = LinearSegmentedColormap.from_list("vs_lg", [style.SERIES[1], style.SURFACE, style.SERIES[0]])
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.6, 3.7))
