say(f, d1, R(-3), 7.5, "fielded 3 yards\ndeep", color=DC, fontsize=7)
say(f, d1, 25.5, -12.0, "coverage released\nat the landing", color=OC, fontsize=7)
clip_texts(f)
plt.show()








Figure 47.9: Drill 1: the kick comes down at the receiving team’s 4 (X), inside the landing zone, and rolls into the end zone (dotted), where the returner (KR) picks it up three yards deep. The coverage was released when the ball landed and is closing. Kneel or run?











TipAnswer





Run it out. The kick came down in the landing zone before rolling into the end zone, so a knee gives his team the ball only at the 20, and returns fielded in the end zone averaged about the 26 in 2025. If the same kick had landed in the end zone on the fly, the knee would be worth the 35, and he should almost always take it: those returns reached the 35 only 9% of the time. This is why kickers love the line drive that lands at the 3 and skips in: it forces the returner either to accept the 20 or to run out from deep in his end zone.











TipPredict the play



Drill 2. Twenty-two seconds. It’s the end of the first half. You have just kicked a field goal to go up 13-10 with 0:22 left, and you are about to kick off. The other team has one timeout and a dangerous returner (KR1, the deeper of the two). Under the 2026 rules, which of the four kicks in the picture do you want, and which must you avoid?


Show the Python
kick, ret = dynamic_units()
d2 = Play(kick, ret, los=KICK_X, to_go=None)
d2.highlight("KR1", "KR2", color=DC)
f = fix_field(d2.draw(orient="horizontal", lateral="full", window=(-11.0, 75.0), title=False, width_in=5.6))
band(f, d2, R(35), R(30), style.DEFENSE, 0.10)
band(f, d2, R(20), R(0), style.LINE_TO_GAIN, 0.12)
ball(f, d2, 0.0, 0.0)
for name, (d, w), rad, dw in [("A", (R(-6), 9.0), -0.10, 2.9), ("B", (R(4), -9.0), 0.10, -2.9),
                              ("C", (R(15), -16.0), 0.12, -2.9), ("D", (R(27), 13.0), -0.12, 2.9)]:
    arrow(f, d2, (0.6, 0.0), (d, w), style.BALL, lw=1.1, ls=(0, (2, 2)), ms=7, rad=rad)
    land(f, d2, d, w)
    say(f, d2, d, w + dw, name, color=style.BALL, fontsize=8, weight="bold")
say(f, d2, 7.5, -18.5, "0:22 left in the half\nKicking team leads 13-10\nReceiving team: 1 timeout",
    color=style.INK, fontsize=6.6, weight="bold")
say(f, d2, R(4.5), 13.0, "dangerous\nreturner", color=DC, fontsize=6.8)
clip_texts(f)
plt.show()








Figure 47.10: Drill 2: the kickoff after a field goal with 0:22 left in the first half; the kicking team leads 13-10 and the receiving team has one timeout. The kicker’s four options: A, into the end zone (touchback at the 35, no time off the clock); B, deep into the landing zone; C, a squib that hits the ground around the 15, away from the dangerous returner; D, short of the 20 or out of bounds. Which one?











TipAnswer





B or C: make them field it, and never D. A touchback (A) hands the receiving team the ball at its 35 with all 22 seconds on the clock, because the clock doesn’t start until the ball is touched in the field of play. From the 35, two quick sideline completions of 15 to 20 yards and a timeout can set up a long field goal. A kick that has to be returned does two things for you. It usually ends short of the 35 (around the 28-30 on average in 2025), and the clock runs from the moment the returner touches it, so a five- or six-second return leaves them about 16 seconds from somewhere near their 30: time for two or three plays, if they get out of bounds or use the timeout. Against a dangerous returner, many coaches choose C, a squib that bounces away from him, giving up a couple of yards for the near-certainty that there is no long return. What you must avoid is D: the ball at the 40 with 22 seconds left is a gift. The clock rules behind this are in Clock and Game Management.











TipPredict the play



Drill 3. Down eight, a minute left. You have just scored a touchdown, but the two-point try failed, and you trail by 8 with 1:01 left in the fourth quarter. You have no timeouts. Do you kick off deep or declare an onside kick? If you declare it, what will the receiving team put on the field, and what are your chances?


Show the Python
fig, (a1, a2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.5, 5.0))
WIN3 = (-9.0, 72.0)
kick, ret = dynamic_units()
d3 = Play(kick, ret, los=KICK_X, to_go=None)
d3.highlight("KR1", "KR2", color=DC)
g1 = fix_field(d3.draw(ax=a1, lateral="full", window=WIN3, title=False))
band(g1, d3, R(35), R(30), style.DEFENSE, 0.10)
band(g1, d3, R(20), R(0), style.LINE_TO_GAIN, 0.12)
ball(g1, d3, 0.0, 0.0)
say(g1, d3, 13.0, 0.0, "coverage on\ntheir 40", color=OC, fontsize=6.6)
say(g1, d3, R(12), 0.0, "returners deep", color=DC, fontsize=6.6)
clip_texts(g1)
a1.set_title("Deep kick", fontsize=8.5, loc="left", color=style.INK)
kick = [K_("K", -6.0, 0.0, "K")]
kick += [K_(f"C{i + 1}", -0.8, w) for i, w in enumerate([-23.5, -20.5, -14, -9, -4, 4, 9, 14, 20.5, 23.5])]
ret = [RT_(f"H{i + 1}", 13.0, w, "H") for i, w in enumerate([-19.5, -14, -9, -4, 1, 6, 11])]
ret += [RT_(f"B{i + 1}", 19.0, w) for i, w in enumerate([-12, -3])]
ret += [RT_("DR", 28.0, 4.0), RT_("KR1", R(18), 0.0, "KR")]
o3 = Play(kick, ret, los=KICK_X, to_go=None)
o3.highlight("KR1", color=DC)
g2 = fix_field(o3.draw(ax=a2, lateral="full", window=WIN3, title=False))
ball(g2, o3, 0.0, 0.0)
line_across(g2, o3, 10.0, style.INK_2, lw=1.0, ls=(0, (1.5, 1.5)))
say(g2, o3, 5.0, 0.0, "coverage beside\nthe ball", color=OC, fontsize=6.6)
say(g2, o3, 16.4, 6.5, "hands team (H)", color=DC, fontsize=6.6)
say(g2, o3, 40.0, 0.0, "nobody deep but\none returner", color=DC, fontsize=6.6)
clip_texts(g2)
a2.set_title("Declared onside kick", fontsize=8.5, loc="left", color=style.INK)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.8)
plt.show()








Figure 47.11: Drill 3: trailing by 8 with 1:01 left and no timeouts, the kicking team has to choose before it lines up, because the two kicks use different alignments. Left: the dynamic-kickoff alignment for a deep kick, coverage on the receiving 40. Right: a declared onside kick, coverage beside the ball and the receiving team ten yards away; told in advance, it sends out its hands team (H).











TipAnswer





Declare the onside kick. If you kick deep with no timeouts, the other team takes over and kneels; each kneel keeps the clock running and uses up to 40 seconds of play clock, so the game ends without you touching the ball again. Your only hope is to recover the kick. The receiving team knows it is coming (the kick had to be declared), so it puts its hands team on the field: receivers, tight ends, backs and defensive backs, players chosen for their hands rather than their blocking. Your kicker will aim a hard, hopping kick toward one sideline so his fastest players can get to it just past the 10-yard line. Your chances are poor: under the declared-onside rules, kicking teams recovered 6% of onside kicks in 2024 and 10% in 2025. And recovering is only step one: you would still need a touchdown and a two-point conversion in under a minute with no timeouts, so your real chance of winning is far smaller than the recovery rate. Poor beats zero, though. With more time and timeouts (say 3:30 and three timeouts) the answer flips: kick deep, play defense, and use the timeouts to get the ball back with good field position, because a failed onside kick hands the other team the ball near midfield. Where exactly the line falls is a win probability question.

title: Kickoffs, Returns, and the Dynamic Kickoff
text:
Takeaways

A kickoff is a free kick that trades field position after a score. For fifteen years the league made it safer by making it disappear, until only about a quarter of kickoffs were returned in 2023.
The dynamic kickoff (2024) took away the distance instead: the coverage stands on the receiving team’s 40, five yards from blockers in the setup zone, and nobody but the kicker and returners moves until the ball lands in the landing zone. Returns rose and kickoff concussions fell.
The rules keep moving. 2025: touchback to the 35, onside kicks declarable whenever trailing. 2026 (changed after the 2025 season): onside kicks declarable at any time, only five receivers on the restraining line with up to four floaters, and touchbacks on kicks from the 50 spotted at the 20.
The touchback math drives everything: in 2025 a returned kick started, on average, around the 29 to 31, short of the 35 a touchback gives, and the deeper the kick was fielded the worse the return did, because the coverage always starts at the 40. So kickers aim deep into the landing zone, returners should usually kneel on a ball that lands in the end zone, and they should run out one that rolled in.
A return is now a run play: ten blockers for eleven cover men, so the scheme leaves the kicker for the returner to beat and one backside cover man free, and spends the spare blocker on a double team (setup-zone players only) at the point of attack.
Onside kicks must be declared, so the hands team is always waiting and the surprise onside is gone. Recovery rates fell to around one in ten or worse.

Connections
Builds on: Field Goals, Extra Points, and the Punting Game (touchbacks, fair catches, muffs, the punt return and its wall), The Language of the Run Game (double teams, kick-outs, lead blocks, the point of attack and hat math, all reused in return blocking), the seal block from Perimeter Runs and Misdirection, and the expected-points curve in Downs, Distance, and Field Position.
Sets up:

Contact Rules and Penalties as Strategy and Officials, Replay, and the Rules of the Ball: the penalties that move a kickoff to the 50, and the rules on loose balls and touchbacks.
Clock and Game Management: kickoffs at the end of a half, onside decisions, and the fair-catch kick.
Win Probability and Decision Analysis: when an onside kick is worth it.
Appendix E, Rules, Timeline, and Coaching Trees: the kickoff rules in one table, current as of the 2026 season.

If you want to go deeper: the NFL’s own explainers at NFL Football Operations (operations.nfl.com), which post each season’s approved rule changes, and Rule 6 of the official rulebook itself, which is short and readable; The Ringer’s 2024 guide to the dynamic kickoff and Sports Illustrated’s “Happy Returns” (2024) for the coaches’ view; and nflverse play-by-play, where every kickoff’s description says where it was fielded and where it was returned to, so you can rebuild every chart in this chapter.






NoteGo deeper



From simulation to real tracking data. The return animation above is a gridiron simulation written in NFL Big Data Bowl coordinates. The 2022 Big Data Bowl was about special teams and released tracking data for every kickoff, punt and field goal from the 2018-2020 seasons, so you can draw real kickoffs with the same code. Those are traditional kickoffs, which makes them a good contrast with the simulated dynamic kickoff here. The data is on Kaggle and needs your own free login, so this code is not run when the book is built.


Show the Python (a real kickoff from Big Data Bowl 2022 files; not run in the build)
import pandas as pd
from gridiron import bdb, show_animation

plays = pd.read_csv("data/bdb2022/plays.csv")
games = pd.read_csv("data/bdb2022/games.csv")
trk = bdb.load_tracking("data/bdb2022/tracking2018.csv")   # one file per season: tracking2018/2019/2020.csv
ko = plays[(plays["specialTeamsPlayType"] == "Kickoff") & plays["gameId"].isin(trk["gameId"].unique())]
g, pl = ko.iloc[0][["gameId", "playId"]]
# In the 2022 files 'team' is home / away / football, so map it to club abbreviations for prepare()
abbr = games.set_index("gameId")[["homeTeamAbbr", "visitorTeamAbbr"]]
one = trk[(trk.gameId == g) & (trk.playId == pl)].copy()
home, away = abbr.loc[g]
one["club"] = one["club"].map({"home": home, "away": away, "football": "football"})
one = bdb.prepare(one, plays, game_id=g, play_id=pl)     # possessionTeam = the kicking team here
kick_frame = one.loc[one["event"] == "kickoff", "frameId"].min()
one["time"] = (one["frameId"] - kick_frame) / 10.0        # time from the kick, not from a snap
show_animation(one, times=[0.0, 2.0, 4.0, 6.0])

text:
NFL, 2026 Official Playing Rules, Rule 6-1-1 (free kicks; the kick after a safety may be a punt, dropkick or placekick from the 20) and Rule 11-4-3 (the fair-catch kick is a field-goal attempt from the spot of the fair catch): https://static.www.nfl.com/image/upload/fl_attachment/league/tqivdkzt9mu6wdgsh1ku.pdf, linked from https://operations.nfl.com/the-rules/nfl-rulebook/.↩︎
Course calculation: average nflverse expected points for first-and-10 plays outside the last two minutes of a half, 2023-2025 regular seasons, by yard line; the per-yard figure is the slope of a straight line fitted to the 20 through the 40. Single five-yard steps on the raw curve bounce around it (from the 30 to the 35 is about 0.2, from the 25 to the 30 about 0.3) because each yard line’s average is an estimate; the fitted slope is the steadier number, and it is the one this chapter uses.↩︎
The kickoff spot moved from the 40 to the 35 in 1974, to the 30 in 1994 and back to the 35 in 2011: “Kickoff (gridiron football),” Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kickoff_(gridiron_football); NFL Football Operations, “Evolution of the NFL rules”: https://operations.nfl.com/the-rules/evolution-of-the-nfl-rules/.↩︎
ESPN, “Proposal trying to make NFL kickoffs more like a punt play” (2018), which gives both figures from the competition committee’s Rich McKay: concussions “five times as likely to occur on kickoffs as on other plays” in 2017, and 71 kickoff concussions in 2015-17: https://www.espn.com/nfl/story/_/id/23385442/proposal-trying-make-nfl-kickoffs-more-punt-play. The 71 also appears in NFL.com, “Kickoff changes could include eliminating running start” (May 2, 2018): https://www.nfl.com/news/kickoff-changes-could-include-eliminating-running-start-0ap3000000930999.↩︎
The 2009 rule banned wedges of three or more blockers: “Kickoff (gridiron football),” Wikipedia (cited in the kickoff-spot note above). Two-man wedges stayed legal until the 2018 rules banned all wedges: CBS Sports, “NFL kickoffs will be undergoing these major rule changes for 2018”: https://www.cbssports.com/nfl/news/nfl-kickoffs-will-be-undergoing-these-major-rule-changes-for-2018.↩︎
Course calculation from nflverse play-by-play (regular season), done in the code cells of this chapter. Return rate = kickoffs with a listed returner, as a share of all kickoffs including onside kicks (25.2% in 2023, 32.9% in 2024, 74.6% in 2025, matching other published counts of about 22%, 33% and 75%). Drive start = the yard line of the receiving team’s next play, excluding onside kicks and return touchdowns. Touchback rate uses the pbp touchback flag. Onside recovery uses own_kickoff_recovery on kicks whose description says “onside.”↩︎
The kickoff touchback moved from the 20 to the 25 in March 2016 as a one-year trial, extended in 2017: FOX6, “One-year trial: NFL owners approve placing ball at 25-yard line after touchbacks”: https://www.fox6now.com/sports/one-year-trial-nfl-owners-approve-placing-ball-at-25-yard-line-after-touchbacks-vs-20; ProFootballTalk, “NFL owners extend trial period for touchbacks to 25”: https://nbcsports.com/nfl/profootballtalk/rumor-mill/news/nfl-owners-extend-trial-period-for-touchbacks-to-25.↩︎
Sports Illustrated, “The NFL’s New Kickoff Rules, Explained” (Sept 7, 2018): https://www.si.com/nfl/2018/09/07/nfl-kickoff-rule-changes-explained-onside-return-clarified.↩︎
The 2023 rule, approved May 23, 2023 as a one-year trial, let a receiver fair-catch a kickoff inside his 25 and take the ball at the 25: CBS Sports, “NFL approves one-year trial run for new fair catch rule”: https://www.cbssports.com/nfl/news/nfl-approves-one-year-trial-run-for-new-fair-catch-rule-that-could-have-dramatic-impact-on-kickoff-returns. The dynamic kickoff replaced it in 2024.↩︎
Course calculation (method in the earlier calculation note): 25.2% of 2023 regular-season kickoffs were returned, the lowest rate in the nflverse data back to 1999.↩︎
“Sam Schwartzstein,” Wikipedia (his XFL role and Stanford career; sources give his XFL title in slightly different forms): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Schwartzstein; the simulations: Sports Illustrated, in the next note.↩︎
Gilberto Manzano, “Happy Returns: NFL’s New Dynamic Kickoff ‘Will Look Weird’,” Sports Illustrated (Sept 5, 2024): https://www.si.com/nfl/happy-returns-new-dynamic-kickoff-will-look-weird.↩︎
On Fassel presenting the XFL-based model to the competition committee: Sports Illustrated (Cowboys Country), https://www.si.com/nfl/cowboys/news/dallas-cowboys-john-fassel-kickoff-overhaul-rule-changes-xfl. title: Contact Rules and Penalties as Strategy
text:
The rule book as a price list
Third-and-9, a minute left in the half. The quarterback takes a deep drop and heaves the ball 45 yards down the left sideline toward a receiver who is not open. The cornerback is with him stride for stride, the ball comes down a yard out of reach, and the crowd groans. Then a yellow flag lands on the grass. The corner had grabbed the receiver’s arm a split second before the ball arrived. Pass interference: first down, at the spot of the foul. A throw that was going nowhere has just gained 41 yards, and the rules analyst in the booth says the offense “knew exactly what it was doing.” Two questions hide in that sentence. Why would a coach call a throw he expects to be incomplete? And why is the same grab worth five yards if it happens one second earlier, before the ball is in the air? This chapter reads the rule book the way coaches do: as a list of prices.
You’ll be able to…
Every sport has rules about contact. Football has more of them than most, because almost every player on almost every snap is allowed to hit somebody. The rules don’t try to stop contact. They decide who may touch whom, where, and when, and they attach a price to each violation: five yards, ten, fifteen, a first down, the spot of the foul, a safety, an ejection.
Prices change behaviour. A cornerback knows that grabbing a receiver before the throw costs five yards and an automatic first down. On third-and-20 that price is ruinous: the defense was one incompletion away from a punt, and the grab hands the offense a fresh set of downs. On first-and-10, with the receiver running past him for a touchdown, the same grab is a bargain. An offensive lineman beaten by a pass rusher will often hold rather than let his quarterback be sacked, because ten yards cost less than a sack plus the chance of a fumble. A play-caller who knows that pass interference is enforced at the spot will throw deep into coverage, because the flag is one of the throw’s possible outcomes. None of this is cheating; it’s arithmetic. Coaches teach it, and the NFL’s competition committee, which proposes the rule changes the owners vote on each spring, adjusts the prices when it doesn’t like how teams respond.
This chapter takes the rules in four groups:
Then we price them with data: how often each foul is called, and what it does to expected points. (Officials, replay review and the rules of the ball itself, what counts as a catch or a fumble, are the next chapter, Officiating, Replay, and the Rules of the Ball.)

title: Contact Rules and Penalties as Strategy
text:
Contact on receivers, the rules that shape pass coverage and route design: illegal contact, defensive holding, and pass interference in both directions.
Blocking rules, which shape what linemen and receivers may do: holding, hands to the face, blocks in the back, cut and chop blocks, and the lineman’s one-yard limit on passes.
Player-safety rules, mostly written in the last twenty years to protect heads, knees and quarterbacks.
Enforcement, the mechanics that turn a flag into a new down and distance: accepting and declining, free plays, where the yards are walked off, and half the distance.








ImportantWhy it exists



Football’s contact rules exist to keep two contests fair at once. One is between the offense and the defense: without limits, defenders would tackle receivers before every pass and linemen would tackle pass rushers, and the passing game would die. The other is between the players and the damage they can do to each other. Most rule changes of the last half-century have pushed one or both of those two ways: toward offense (1978, 2004) and toward safety (2005 onward). Read any rule change by asking which contest it was protecting.

title: Contact Rules and Penalties as Strategy
section: The receiver’s first five yards: illegal contact and defensive holding
text:
The receiver’s first five yards: illegal contact and defensive holding
A pass play is a race. The receiver needs to reach a spot on the field at a set time, and the quarterback needs to throw it there before the rush arrives. A defender’s best weapon in that race is his hands: knock the receiver off his line, slow him, turn him, and the timing of the whole play breaks. The NFL rules allow exactly a little of that.
Here are the rules, as the NFL writes them for 2026:1

Within five yards of the line of scrimmage, a defender may chuck (jam, push, re-route) a receiver who is in front of him. That is what a press corner is doing at the snap.
Beyond five yards, while the quarterback is still in the pocket with the ball, a defender may not initiate contact with the receiver. He may use his hands only to protect himself, and contact that started inside the five yards has to end as the two of them leave the zone: he may not shove, hook or ride him past it. The foul is illegal contact: five yards and an automatic first down.
Anywhere on the field, before the pass is thrown, a defender may not grab, hook or tackle a receiver, or otherwise restrict him: defensive holding, also five yards and an automatic first down. Holding can happen inside the five yards too. A jam with open hands is legal; a fistful of jersey is not.
Once the ball is thrown, both of those rules hand over to the pass-interference rules, below.
The illegal-contact restriction lifts when the quarterback leaves the pocket, so on a scramble a defender may chuck a receiver beyond five yards. Holding is still holding, and once the ball is in the air pass interference applies again. “The pocket” here has an exact meaning: the rule book’s pocket area runs between where the two tackles lined up, from the line back to the offense’s end line, and the quarterback has left it once any part of him or the ball is outside it. Officiating, Replay, and the Rules of the Ball draws it as the tackle box.2

Defensive holding isn’t only about receivers. The rule bans a defender holding any offensive player other than the ball carrier, and the version you’ll see flagged most at the line is a defensive lineman grabbing a blocker on a stunt (a pass-rush game in which rushers cross), pinning a guard so the looping teammate can come free (The Pass Rush). Same price: five yards and an automatic first down.

Figure 48.1: The receiver’s rules by depth and by moment, on one go route. Left, before the throw: inside the first five yards (green) the corner (C) may jam X; past five yards, while the quarterback is in the pocket with the ball, contact that impedes him is illegal contact, and grabbing or restricting him anywhere is defensive holding. Both cost five yards and an automatic first down. Right, after the throw: the pass-interference rules take over. Contact more than a yard past the line that significantly hinders the receiver’s chance to catch a catchable ball is defensive pass interference, enforced at the spot. Had the corner turned and played the ball instead, the same collision would have been legal.





Two prices, five yards and a first down, look small next to pass interference, and they are meant to. The automatic first down is the expensive part. On first-and-10 a five-yard foul gives the offense first-and-5, a nice gain. On third-and-12 it erases the down: the defense had the offense behind the sticks and needed one stop, and now it starts the series over. (The numbers on this, down by down, are in What penalties cost, below.)

Why five yards, and the year it started to bite
Coverage Fundamentals told the origin: the five-yard zone dates from the 1978 “Mel Blount rule,” the same package that let offensive linemen extend their arms and open their hands in pass protection, and both halves pointed toward passing.3 (The 1978 Liberation tells that story in full.) What matters here is what came next. The rule sat on the books for 25 years without being enforced very hard. Defensive backs learned what officials would tolerate (a hand on the hip at eight yards, a tug at the top of the route), and by the early 2000s the best press teams were playing the 1977 game with 1978 rules. This film room is the game that ended that.






NoteFilm room: Patriots vs. Colts, 2003 AFC Championship (Jan. 18, 2004)



In the AFC Championship Game after the 2003 season, Bill Belichick’s Patriots beat Peyton Manning’s Colts 24–14 in Foxborough. Manning, that season’s co-MVP, threw four interceptions, three of them to cornerback Ty Law.4 On the film, New England’s defensive backs jam, ride and bump Indianapolis’s receivers well past five yards, all game, and few flags fly.
The Colts’ president, Bill Polian, sat on the competition committee. That off-season the committee made illegal contact and defensive holding beyond five yards a “point of emphasis”: officials were told to call the rule as written. Patriots fans call it the “Ty Law rule.” The flags came at once: by one count illegal-contact fouls rose from 79 in the 2003 regular season to 191 in 2004 (nflverse’s play-by-play, which records only one foul per play, has 49 and 123), and teams averaged about 225 passing yards a game in 2004, up from 214.5 Manning threw 49 touchdown passes in 2004, breaking Dan Marino’s single-season record.6
What to notice: the rule didn’t change; its price did. A rule that is called is a different rule from one that isn’t, which is why “points of emphasis” announced each summer are worth reading. On a broadcast, watch a press corner’s hands after the receiver’s fifth step. If they stay on him, the next flag is coming.




What the five-yard zone does to schemes
Coverage Fundamentals covered what the zone does to press (all of the jam has to land in about the first second, so pressed corners want a safety behind them) and to releases (stacks, bunches and motion that dodge the jam). Three more effects:

Zone defenders have to pass receivers off, not re-route them. A linebacker in a hook zone may not shove a crossing receiver at eight yards, so zone defense is about positioning, not collision. The jam that survives is the Cover 2 corner’s, which happens inside the five yards (Cover 2 and Tampa 2).
A scramble changes the rules. When the quarterback leaves the pocket, defenders may chuck receivers downfield again. Part of why the scramble drill (Quarterback Play) is hard to defend is that coverage gets messy; part of why it is not easier is that defenders get their hands back.
Smart fouls. A corner beaten off the line on a go route can grab the receiver before the throw and give up five yards and a first down rather than a touchdown. Nobody coaches it out loud, but everybody knows the price.

title: Contact Rules and Penalties as Strategy
text:
Pass interference, both ways
Once the ball is thrown, the question changes from “may he touch the receiver?” to “is he playing the ball?” Defensive pass interference (DPI) is contact by a defender, after the ball is thrown and more than one yard past the line of scrimmage, that significantly hinders an eligible receiver’s chance to catch the ball. The rule lists the usual acts: grabbing an arm or the jersey, cutting in front of the receiver without looking for the ball, hooking him, putting an arm across his body, tackling him early. And it lists what is not interference:7

contact when both players are making a genuine attempt to catch or bat the ball;
incidental contact, such as feet tangling, that doesn’t materially affect the receiver;
contact on a pass that is clearly uncatchable;
contact before the throw, which is illegal contact or holding instead (five yards), not DPI.

Offensive pass interference (OPI) is the mirror image, with one big difference: the offense’s restrictions start at the snap, not the throw. From the snap until the pass is touched, an offensive player more than a yard past the line may not initiate contact that hinders a defender. The two everyday versions are the push-off (a receiver extends his arm to create separation at the top of a route or at the catch point) and the illegal pick (a receiver blocks a defender downfield before the ball is thrown, to free a teammate). OPI costs ten yards from the previous spot, and the down is replayed.






CautionCommon misconception



“He grabbed the receiver, so it’s pass interference.” Only if the ball was in the air. The same grab a second before the throw is defensive holding (five yards and a first down); a hard shove at eight yards before the throw is illegal contact (same price). The difference matters enormously, because DPI is enforced at the spot. When a flag flies on a pass, look at whether the ball had left the quarterback’s hand at the moment of the foul, and you’ll know which of the three it is.



The one-yard strip, and who started the contact
Dropback Concepts introduced rub routes and warned that they can become illegal picks. Here is the rule that draws the line. Pass interference by either side can only happen more than one yard past the line of scrimmage.8 Two tests follow from that, one about where and one about who:

Inside the first yard, even a deliberate pick is legal. A receiver may release straight into the defender covering a teammate, and if the bump happens within a yard of the line there is no interference (a grab there can still be holding).
Beyond the first yard, the question is who initiated the contact. OPI needs the offensive player to do something: push off, or block or obstruct a defender before the ball is touched. A receiver who keeps running his route while a defender chasing someone else has to go around him, or runs into him, hasn’t fouled at any depth. That is the natural rub, and it is how mesh and other crossing concepts free receivers 5 or 6 yards downfield every week. If the receiver stops, turns his shoulders to the defender or extends his arms, he has started a block, and it’s OPI.

LAT, WIN = (2.0, 19.5), (-3.0, 10.0)
for i, ax in enumerate(axes):
    off = [O_("RT", "RT", -0.7, 3.2, ""), O_("H", "WR", -1.0, 9.0, "H"), O_("Z", "WR", -0.7, 14.0, "Z")]
    dfn = [D_("NB", "NB", 0.8, 9.3, "$"), D_("CB", "CB", 2.0, 15.0, "C")]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=40, to_go=None)
    if i == 0:                                  # deliberate pick inside the first yard
        p.route("Z", r.path((1.2, -3.6), (4.6, -9.4)))
        p.route("H", r.path((1.4, 2.4), (2.0, 7.0)))
    elif i == 1:                                # natural rub: Z just runs his crosser
        p.route("Z", r.path((3.8, -1.2), (4.3, -10.0)))
        p.route("H", r.path((5.0, 0.0), (5.3, 6.0)))
    else:                                       # Z stops and blocks at three yards
        p.route("Z", r.path((3.0, -0.5), (3.3, -2.7)))
        p.route("H", r.path((1.4, 2.4), (2.0, 7.0)))
    p.highlight("Z", "NB")
    f = p.draw(ax=ax, lateral=LAT, window=WIN, title=False)
    no_numbers(f.ax)
    band(f, p, 0, 1, LEGAL_T)
    line_across(f, p, 1.0, LEGAL, lw=0.9, ls=(0, (3, 2)))
    if i == 0:
        say(f, p, -1.9, 5.6, "1 yard", color=LEGAL, fs=5.8, style_="italic", box=False)
        arrow(f, p, (-1.4, 5.6), (0.85, 5.6), LEGAL, lw=0.8, ms=6)
        trail(f, p, [(0.8, 9.3), (0.55, 10.25)], style.DEFENSE, lw=1.6, ls=(0, (2, 1.2)))
        trail(f, p, [(2.0, 15.0), (2.6, 12.8), (3.8, 9.6)], style.DEFENSE, lw=1.6, ls=(0, (2, 1.2)))
        star(f, p, 0.5, 10.75, LEGAL, ms=10)
        say(f, p, 7.0, 10.8, "they meet half a yard\npast the line:\nlegal, even on purpose", color=LEGAL, fs=5.8)
        panel_title(ax, "1. Pick inside 1 yard: legal", fs=7.8)
    elif i == 1:
        trail(f, p, [(0.8, 9.3), (3.0, 9.5), (3.45, 10.2)], style.DEFENSE, lw=1.6, ls=(0, (2, 1.2)))
        star(f, p, 3.55, 10.6, LEGAL, ms=10)
        say(f, p, 7.5, 9.6, "Z keeps running; the\nnickel runs into him:\nlegal at any depth", color=LEGAL, fs=5.8)
        panel_title(ax, "2. Natural rub: legal", fs=7.8)
    else:
        trail(f, p, [(0.8, 9.3), (1.7, 10.0), (2.45, 10.6)], style.DEFENSE, lw=1.6, ls=(0, (2, 1.2)))
        trail(f, p, [(2.0, 15.0), (2.9, 14.2)], style.DEFENSE, lw=1.6, ls=(0, (2, 1.2)))
        star(f, p, 2.75, 11.15, FOUL, ms=10)
        flag(f, p, 4.4, 13.6)
        say(f, p, 7.3, 9.4, "Z stops and blocks him\n3 yards downfield\nbefore the throw: OPI", color=FOUL, fs=5.8)
        panel_title(ax, "3. Block at 3 yards: OPI", fs=7.8)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()








Figure 48.2: Two tests for a pick: where the contact happens and who starts it. In each panel the nickel ($) is in man coverage on the slot receiver H, and the outside receiver Z crosses his path. 1: Z’s slant crosses the nickel half a yard past the line, inside the one-yard strip (green), so even a deliberate bump is legal; the nickel is stuck, the corner (C) has followed Z inside, and H is alone in the flat. 2: Z runs a shallow cross and keeps running; the nickel, chasing H, runs into him about 3.5 yards downfield. Z didn’t start the contact, so this natural rub is legal at any depth. 3: Z runs 3 yards upfield, stops, squares up and blocks the nickel before the throw: offensive pass interference, ten yards from the previous spot.





Offenses coach the legal versions: make the contact happen at the line, or keep running the route and let the defender run into you. Officials, judging at full speed, look for the giveaways of a block (a receiver who stops, turns his shoulders or extends his arms). Stacks and bunches (Spread Formations) put receivers’ paths across defenders in the first step or two, where the strip makes it legal.
Defenses answer in three ways. They play zone against bunches, because a zone defender isn’t chasing anyone through traffic. They switch (or banjo) in man coverage, trading receivers by agreement so nobody has to chase through the cross (Man Coverage). And they align deeper: a defender who lines up four or five yards off the ball can’t be picked inside the first yard, because he’s not there yet, and has room to go over or under a crosser. When the officials do see a pick, it is OPI: ten yards from the previous spot, the down replayed, and any completion wiped out.


The spot foul: why DPI is football’s most expensive flag
Most fouls are enforced from the previous spot, where the ball was snapped. Defensive pass interference is different. In the NFL it is a spot foul: the offense gets an automatic first down at the spot where the foul happened, however far downfield that is. A foul 40 yards past the line is a 40-yard penalty. If the foul happens in the end zone, the ball goes to the 1-yard line, first and goal.9
College football does it differently. Under the NCAA rule, defensive pass interference is 15 yards from the previous spot and an automatic first down; only when the foul happens less than 15 yards downfield is it enforced at the spot.10 The high-school rule is also 15 yards. The NFL is the outlier, and it is the reason the most consequential judgment call in football carries no cap.


Show the Python
NEW_SPOT = style.SERIES[6]    # one colour for "the ball goes here" in both panels


def dpi_panel(ax, college):
    off = line5() + [O_("QB", "QB", -5.0, 0.0, "Q"), O_("X", "WR", -0.7, -15.0, "X")]
    dfn = [D_("CB", "CB", 1.0, -14.4, "C")]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=40, to_go=10)
    p.route("X", r.go(37.3))
    p.highlight("X", "CB")
    f = p.draw(ax=ax, orient="horizontal", lateral=(-21.5, 9.0), window=(-7, 47), title=False)
    no_numbers(ax)
    for yl, dd in ((30, 0.0), (40, 10.0), (50, 20.0), (40, 30.0), (30, 40.0)):
        say(f, p, dd, 7.2, str(yl), color=style.MUTED, fs=8, weight="bold")
    trail(f, p, [(1.0, -14.4), (20, -14.3), (36.5, -14.0)], style.DEFENSE, lw=1.2, ls=(0, (3, 2)))
    arrow(f, p, (-5.0, 0.0), (38.4, -15.0), style.BALL, lw=1.2, ls=(0, (2, 2)), rad=0.06)
    xg, yg = P_(f, p, 36.3, -13.9)                       # the corner at the moment of the grab
    ax.add_patch(Rectangle((xg - 0.75, yg - 0.75), 1.5, 1.5, fc="none", ec=style.DEFENSE_DARK, lw=0.9,
                           ls=(0, (2, 1.2)), zorder=7))
    star(f, p, 37.6, -14.4, FOUL)
    flag(f, p, 35.0, -10.8, s=1.3)
    new_d = 15.0 if college else 38.0
    line_across(f, p, new_d, NEW_SPOT, lw=2.4, ls="-", w0=-26.7, w1=26.7, z=6)
    say(f, p, new_d, -21.0 + 2.6, "new spot", color=NEW_SPOT, fs=6.4, weight="bold")
    ball(f, p, new_d, 0.0)
    arrow(f, p, (0.0, 4.9), (new_d, 4.9), style.INK, lw=1.4, ms=9, z=7)
    if college:
        say(f, p, new_d + 7.0, 2.0, "college: 15 yards from\nthe previous spot,\n1st-and-10 at own 45", fs=6.6, weight="bold")
    else:
        say(f, p, new_d - 9.5, 2.0, "NFL: first down at the\nspot of the foul,\n1st-and-10 at opp. 32", fs=6.6, weight="bold")
    say(f, p, 30.0, -19.4, "foul: 38 yards downfield", color=FOUL, fs=6.6)
    panel_title(ax, "College and high school: 15-yard cap" if college else "NFL: spot foul")


fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(6.5, 7.0))
dpi_panel(axes[0], False)
dpi_panel(axes[1], True)
fig.tight_layout(h_pad=0.8)
plt.show()








Figure 48.3: One foul, two rulebooks. Second-and-10 from the offense’s own 30 (offense moving right). X runs a go route, the ball is thrown deep, and the corner (C) grabs him at the catch point (dashed outline), 38 yards downfield, at the opponent’s 32. The purple line is where the ball is spotted afterwards. Top, NFL: a spot foul, so it is first-and-10 at the opponent’s 32, a 38-yard penalty. Bottom, college: 15 yards from the previous spot and an automatic first down, so first-and-10 at the offense’s own 45. The same grab is worth 23 more yards in the NFL.











ImportantWhy it exists: the spot foul



What it solves. The NFL’s logic is that a penalty should give back what the foul took away. A defender beaten deep who tackles the receiver before the ball arrives has prevented, quite possibly, a 40-yard completion. Cap the penalty at 15 yards and every beaten defender would happily pay it. With no cap, there’s nothing to gain by tackling a receiver who has beaten you; you have to play the ball.
What it costs. The penalty is huge and the call is a judgment. “Significantly hinders” is decided at full speed by an official who may be 20 yards away, and the difference between a legal, hand-fighting 50-50 ball and a 45-yard flag is sometimes a single tug. That combination makes DPI the call most likely to decide a game, and it is why fans and coaches keep proposing either the college cap or replay review for it. (The NFL tried replay once; see the film room below.)




What the spot foul does to offenses: throw deep, into coverage
Put the two rules together and an NFL offense has a reason to throw deep that a college offense doesn’t. Each deep pass has four kinds of outcome: a completion, an incompletion, an interception, and a defensive pass interference flag, which is, in effect, a long completion that also stops the clock. In the 2021–2025 regular seasons, throws travelling 15 or more yards in the air drew a DPI flag about 4.1 times per 100 throws, against about 0.9 for shorter ones, and those deep flags averaged 23 yards. Counting them in raises the expected points of an average deep throw from +0.38 to +0.45 per attempt.11


Show the Python

vals = [DPI_RATE["short"], DPI_RATE["deep"]]

    a1.text(b.get_x() + b.get_width() / 2, v + 0.12, f"{v:.1f}", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=8.5, color=style.INK)
a1.set_ylim(0, max(vals) * 1.3)
a1.set_ylabel("DPI flags per 100 throws", fontsize=8)
a1.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
a1.tick_params(labelsize=7.5)
a1.set_title("How often", fontsize=9)
bins = np.arange(0, DPI.penalty_yards.max() + 3, 3)
a2.hist(DPI.penalty_yards, bins=bins, color=style.SERIES[1], edgecolor=style.SURFACE, lw=0.6)
a2.axvline(15, color=style.INK, lw=1.2, ls=(0, (4, 2)))
ymax = a2.get_ylim()[1]
a2.text(21.0, ymax * 0.93, f"college cap: 15 yards\n{OVER15:.0%} of NFL flags were longer;\n{OVER30:.0%} were 30 yards or more",
        fontsize=7.5, color=style.INK, va="top")
a2.set_xlabel("Yards gained on the penalty", fontsize=8)
a2.set_ylabel("Flags", fontsize=8)
a2.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
a2.tick_params(labelsize=7.5)
a2.set_title("How far", fontsize=9)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=1.2)
plt.show()








Figure 48.4: Why NFL offenses throw deep into tight coverage. Left: defensive pass interference flags per 100 throws, short (under 15 air yards) and deep (15 or more), 2021-2025 regular seasons; a deep throw is several times as likely to draw one. Right: how long each accepted DPI was. The dashed line is the college cap of 15 yards; every flag to its right would have been worth less under college rules. Source: nflverse play-by-play, accepted DPI flags on scrimmage downs.





That’s why you see things that look like bad decisions: a quarterback throwing up a 50-50 ball to a receiver who is covered, or a back-shoulder throw (a ball thrown behind a receiver’s outside shoulder, so he turns back for it while the defender is still running) into a corner who has his back turned. Two of the outcomes (a catch or a flag) are big gains, one (an incompletion) costs a down, and only the interception is a disaster. Big, physical receivers are worth more in the NFL partly because they win those balls or draw the flag, and defensive backs are taught to turn and find the ball, because a defender who never looks back isn’t “playing the ball” and any contact gets flagged (Man Coverage).






NoteFilm room: Rams at Saints, 2018 NFC Championship (Jan. 20, 2019)



Late in the fourth quarter, the score tied at 20, New Orleans had third-and-10 at the Rams’ 13 with about 1:49 to play. Drew Brees threw to Tommylee Lewis near the right sideline, and Rams cornerback Nickell Robey-Coleman, who later said he had been beaten, hit Lewis well before the ball arrived, helmet to helmet. No flag. A flag would have meant a first down inside the 10, and with the Rams down to one timeout the Saints could have run the clock to about ten seconds before kicking. Instead they kicked a field goal on fourth down with 1:41 left, the Rams tied it, and they won 26–23 in overtime.12
The league admitted the call was missed. Two months later the owners approved a one-year experiment: pass interference, called or not, became reviewable by replay, by coach’s challenge or, in the last two minutes and overtime, by booth review. It was a mess. Replay officials, reluctant to re-referee a judgment call, overturned very few calls or no-calls, coaches stopped challenging, and the rule was allowed to lapse after the 2019 season.13
What to notice: the NFL’s experience is why “just review it” isn’t simple. Replay works for facts (was his foot down? where was the ball?) and struggles with degree (did he significantly hinder him?). Since 2025 replay assist may help on a short list of fouls, but pass interference is not among them; Officiating, Replay, and the Rules of the Ball covers what replay can and can’t do now.

title: Contact Rules and Penalties as Strategy
section: Blocking rules: holding, hands to the face, and where a block may land
text:
Blocking rules: holding, hands to the face, and where a block may land
Offensive holding is, in most seasons, the most-called foul in the NFL (false starts edged it in 2020 and 2023), and also the one that, by common agreement, officials could call on nearly every snap. Blocking means leverage and hands. The line between blocking a defender and holding him is about where the hands are and what they do.
Offensive holding is a blocker grabbing, hooking or tackling a defender, or restricting him with hands or arms outside his body’s frame. The rule’s working idea is the frame: the body of the defender below the neck that faces the blocker, in practice the chest plate between his shoulders. A blocker may put his hands inside the frame and push, steer and lock on, and the rule tells him to work his hands there. What he may not do is use his hands or arms to materially restrict the defender: grab and turn him, hook him, wrap him up, take him to the ground. The test is the effect, not the hand position (a grab inside the frame that jerks a rusher off his path is still holding), but most flagged holds are a hand outside the frame (cloth at the shoulder, the side of the jersey, an arm). Officials also look at where it happened: a hold away from the point of attack, or on a double team the defender didn’t split, is generally not called, because a defender who was never going to reach the play hasn’t been robbed of anything. The rule is aimed at holds that change the play. Holding costs ten yards: from the previous spot on a pass, and on a run usually from the spot of the foul (the enforcement section below explains why). If an offensive player holds in his own end zone, it is a safety (two points and the ball to the other team): the spot the ten yards would be walked from is behind his own goal line, and the rules don’t move the ball around inside an end zone, they award the points.14
Illegal hands to the face is the foul for pushing, punching or grabbing an opponent’s face mask, helmet or neck area with the hands. The rule’s test is forcible contact, direct or prolonged: a hand that slides up to the chin and comes straight back down isn’t called, while a palm that snaps a head back, or stays locked under a face mask, is. That line decides whether an edge rusher’s long-arm move becomes a flag. It goes both ways: a lineman who snaps a pass rusher’s head back with a palm to the face mask, or a pass rusher who does the same to a blocker. The stat sheet files it as illegal use of hands, and the price depends on who did it: ten yards against the offense, five yards and an automatic first down against the defense.


Show the Python
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 3.9))
ax.set_xlim(-10, 10); ax.set_ylim(-1.2, 11.2); ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.axis("off")
# body: legs, torso, shoulder pads, arms, helmet
for x0 in (-1.9, 0.3):

                            fc=FOUL_T, ec=style.BASELINE, lw=1.0, zorder=2))

                            fc=FOUL_T, ec=style.BASELINE, lw=1.0, zorder=2.5))

                            fc=LEGAL_T, ec=LEGAL, lw=1.4, zorder=3))
ax.add_patch(Rectangle((-0.6, 7.4), 1.2, 0.7, fc="#f3c9bf", ec=style.BASELINE, lw=0.8, zorder=3))
ax.add_patch(Circle((0, 9.2), 1.45, fc="#f3c9bf", ec=FOUL, lw=1.4, zorder=4))
for yy in (8.7, 9.2):

ax.plot([0, 0], [8.4, 9.6], color=FOUL, lw=1.2, zorder=5)

    ax.annotate(txt, xy=xy, xytext=xytext, fontsize=7.6, color=color, ha="center", va="center", zorder=8,
                arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=style.INK_2, lw=0.9, shrinkB=2),
                bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.3", fc=style.SURFACE, ec=style.BASELINE, lw=0.6))

callout("shoulder pads, sleeves:\ngrab and turn him = holding", (-3.9, 6.6), (-7.0, 8.8), FOUL)
callout("side or back of the jersey:\ngrab and pull = holding", (2.9, 3.0), (6.9, 3.6), FOUL)
callout("arms around him, or a\ntakedown: always holding", (-4.1, 3.4), (-7.2, 1.6), FOUL)
plt.show()








Figure 48.5: Where a blocker’s hands may go, seen from the blocker’s side. Inside the frame (the chest plate, between the shoulders), hands may push, steer and lock on: legal. Grabbing outside the frame (shoulder pads, sleeves, the sides and back of the jersey) to turn or restrict him is holding, ten yards against the offense. (Strictly, the test is whether the defender is materially restricted, wherever the hands are; outside the frame is where that usually happens.) Hands to the face mask, helmet or neck are illegal hands to the face for either side. The same rules govern a defender’s hands on a receiver before the throw, where the holding foul is five yards and a first down.






Why linemen hold, and why most holds aren’t called
Pass protection is a losing fight by design. A pass rusher has to beat one man for a moment; a blocker has to stay in front of him for two and a half seconds or more (Pass Protection). When a rusher wins the edge, the tackle’s last resort is his hands, and a grab at the back of the jersey as the rusher turns the corner is the hold you’ll see flagged most often. From the lineman’s side the trade is sometimes worth it: a sack loses yards, a down and sometimes the ball, while a hold costs ten yards and replays the down.
Officials could find a technical hold on most snaps, so the working standard is narrower: a grab that materially restricts a defender, at or near the point of attack, especially one that turns him, pulls him down or keeps him from the ball. That makes holding unusually sensitive to instructions. In 2020 the league’s officiating department told crews to call only “clear and obvious” fouls rather than “ticky-tack stuff,” and offensive holding flags fell from about 2.8 a game in 2019 to 1.8; they drifted back to about 2.5 by 2024 (the chart below shows it).15






NoteMadden vs. real life



In a video game, holding is a slider: turn it up and the game calls more of it. In the NFL, holding happens on most plays, in small ways, and the question is whether an official sees one that matters. That makes holding calls lumpy: they cluster on edge rushers who win, on run plays at the point of attack, and on crews and seasons with different standards. When the flag comes out, it is usually because a defender was turned, pulled down or had a clear path to the ball taken away by a hand outside the frame, not because a lineman touched a jersey.




Blocks that may not happen: in the back, low, and in pairs
Three more blocking rules shape how plays are drawn:

Block in the back. A block from behind, above the waist, on a player who is not the ball carrier. The NFL’s name for it is an illegal block above the waist, and it costs ten yards, enforced from the spot of the foul. The same block below the waist is clipping, fifteen yards. It is the classic foul on kick returns and on screens, where blockers are running toward defenders who have already passed them. It is why return men and screen blockers are coached to “see the numbers, don’t block them”: if you can read the defender’s jersey number on his back, let him go. One exception: in close-line play, the area around the line (roughly tackle to tackle, and up to three yards on the defense’s side), a lineman may block a defender from behind above the waist. That’s why a guard who catches a slanting tackle from behind on a down block isn’t flagged.
Cut blocks, with limits. A cut block (at the thighs or below, from the front) is legal on a scrimmage down only near the ball: inside the tight end box, an area that runs from two yards outside each tackle and five yards either side of the line of scrimmage. Outside the box, low blocks are illegal (except against the ball carrier or a player trying to catch a pass), and so is any low block after a change of possession or on a kick. Even inside the box, a low block from behind or from the side while the blocker is moving back toward his own goal line (a peel-back block) has been illegal since 2013.16 The box rule doesn’t care whether the play is a run or a pass, so cuts aren’t only a zone-running tool: a running back may cut a blitzing linebacker inside the box to protect his quarterback, and some quick-game protections have linemen cut the rushers in front of them so the passer can see and throw over them.
Chop block. Two blockers on the same defender, one high and one low at the thigh or below, together or in quick succession. The defender is held up by one and his legs taken out by the other, which is how knees get destroyed. The NFL narrowed the chop for years and banned it in every situation in 2016; it costs fifteen yards.



Show the Python

WIN = (-6.8, 6.8)

p.highlight("T1")

Figure 48.6: Three blocking rules on the field. 1, a legal cut: on an outside-zone run to the right, the backside left tackle (LT) dives at the knees of the 3-technique tackle (T) from the front, inside the tight end box (shaded: two yards outside each tackle, five yards either side of the line). The backside end (E) is left unblocked, as outside zone often does. 2, a chop block: the right guard (RG) engages the defensive tackle high (solid arrow) while the right tackle (RT) cuts the same man low (dashed arrow): fifteen yards. 3, a block in the back: H has caught a screen behind the line and turned upfield. The cornerback (C) slipped inside Z’s block and is chasing him; Z, now behind C in the direction C is running, shoves him in the back above the waist: ten yards, from the spot of the foul. Because the catch came first, Z’s block is not pass interference.







The lineman’s one-yard limit, enforced
The last blocking rule belongs to Run-Pass Options, which explains it in full: on a pass, an ineligible lineman whose entire body is more than a yard past the line when the ball is thrown is illegal man downfield, unless he got there while still blocking a defender he engaged at the line. Its price is five yards from the previous spot, with no loss of down, and a completed pass is wiped out. Note how that interacts with OPI. A lineman who goes downfield and blocks a defender before the pass can be flagged for pass interference instead (ten yards), and a receiver who blocks downfield before the throw is OPI too. That is why NFL RPOs keep everyone’s downfield blocking honest until the ball is out.
So how do screens work? On a bubble or tunnel screen (Play-Action, Bootlegs, and Screens) receivers block cornerbacks and linemen lead the runner downfield, and it isn’t a foul, because of timing. In the NFL both rules apply to every forward pass, even one caught behind the line, and both are about what happens before the throw. The OPI rule bans blocking more than a yard downfield “clearly prior to a pass being thrown,” so screen receivers are coached to get in the defender’s way without touching him and to start the block as the ball comes out. Linemen on a screen engage a rusher at the line, let him go, and then slide sideways (or wait) until the throw: the rule lets an ineligible player who made contact at the line drift past one yard as long as he moves sideways or back, not upfield, until the ball is thrown. Then everyone turns upfield, and the blocks that follow the catch are ordinary blocks, which is the situation in panel 3 of the figure above.17 (College is looser: its pass-interference rules cover only passes that cross the neutral zone, and its linemen get three yards rather than one.)
In the data, ineligible-downfield flags rose as RPOs spread through the league, from about 0.06 a game in 2015–2018 to 0.15–0.3 a game in most seasons since 2019 (2020, a light year for flags of every kind, was the exception). The timing fits, though the data can’t prove the RPO was the cause.

title: Contact Rules and Penalties as Strategy
section: Player safety: protecting the passer and the defenseless
text:
Player safety: protecting the passer and the defenseless
The rules in this section are newer, mostly 21st century, and they exist for a different reason: not to balance offense against defense but to keep players from being badly hurt, especially in the head, neck and knees. They also cost the most. Almost all of them are personal fouls, the rule book’s category (Rule 12, Section 2) for contact that is dangerous or has no football purpose. A personal foul costs 15 yards, with an automatic first down when the defense commits it, and the worst can bring an ejection, a fine or, from 2026, a suspension. An ejection (the rule book says disqualification) is for a flagrant foul, which the rules define as one that is “extremely objectionable, conspicuous, unnecessary, avoidable, or gratuitous”; the on-field officials make that call, and since 2026 league officiating staff may consult on it from New York.18

Roughing the passer
A quarterback in the act of throwing can’t protect himself. His eyes are downfield, his arm is cocked, his front leg is planted. Roughing the passer protects him in that posture and just after. The main ways to commit it:19

Late. Hitting him after the ball is clearly gone, once the defender has had a reasonable chance to stop (officials think in terms of a step or so).
High. Forcible contact to his head or neck with the helmet, shoulder or forearm, even if the rusher was wrapping him up.
Low. Forcible contact at or below the knees, unless the rusher was blocked into him. This is the “Brady rule,” tightened in 2009 after Tom Brady tore knee ligaments on a low hit in the 2008 season opener.
Heavy. Landing on him with all or most of the defender’s body weight, or driving him into the ground after the throw. It got a major emphasis in 2018, after Aaron Rodgers broke his collarbone when he was driven into the turf in 2017.
Stuffing him. Picking him up and slamming him, or wrestling him down after the throw.

The price is 15 yards and an automatic first down; if the pass is completed, the 15 yards are walked off from the previous spot or the end of the play, whichever helps the offense more, so a completion usually keeps its yards and gets the 15 on top. That makes roughing one of the most expensive defensive fouls (see the chart in What penalties cost), and also one of the most argued, because it asks an official to judge a 270-pound man’s momentum in half a second. Two roughing calls on consecutive days in October 2022, on Atlanta’s Grady Jarrett for his sack of Tom Brady and on Kansas City’s Chris Jones for a strip-sack of Derek Carr, set off a week of debate about whether the rule had gone too far.20
The protection shrinks when the quarterback leaves the pocket. If he keeps moving or throws on the run, he loses the one-step “late hit” protection and the protection against low hits, though the head-and-neck and body-weight rules still apply. If he stops and sets up to throw again, he gets all of it back.

Figure 48.7: The passer’s protected zones, as the rules describe them. Head and neck: no forcible contact with the helmet, face mask, shoulder or forearm, even on a sack. Knees and below: no forcible low hits unless the rusher has been blocked into him (the 2009 ‘Brady rule’). Between them is the legal target, but a rusher may not land on him with most of his body weight or drive him into the ground, and any hit once the ball is clearly gone is late. Each foul is 15 yards and an automatic first down.







The sliding quarterback and the defenseless player
When a quarterback runs, he becomes a runner and can be tackled like one, with one exception. If he slides feet first, he is giving himself up: the ball is dead the instant he touches the ground with anything but his hands or feet, and defenders must treat him like a runner already down by contact (down because an opponent touched him, the subject of the next chapter) and pull up. “Pull up” has a limit that decides most late-slide arguments on a broadcast: a defender who had already committed to the tackle before the slide began isn’t flagged for contact he couldn’t avoid, unless he hits the quarterback in the head or neck with his helmet, shoulder or forearm, or does something else needlessly rough. The rule also puts the burden on the quarterback: slide early, before a hit is imminent, or lose the protection. A quarterback who fakes a slide is treated as having slid (the ball is dead when he begins the fake), so he can’t use it to freeze a defender and keep running. The current rule treats a dive, feet or head first, the same way as a slide.21
The defenseless player rule generalises the idea. The rule book lists players who can’t protect themselves: a passer in the act of throwing or just after; a receiver trying to catch a pass (and until he has had time to protect himself after the catch); a runner already held up with his forward progress stopped (his advance halted, so the play is effectively over); a kicker or punter during the kick; a kick returner fielding the ball; a quarterback after a change of possession; a player on the ground; a player hit by an illegal blindside block (a block thrown while the blocker is moving toward or parallel to his own end line, with forcible contact from the helmet, forearm or shoulder; itself 15 yards); a receiver running his route when the defender comes from the side or behind; and a few others. Against them a defender may not make forcible contact to the head or neck with the helmet, face mask, shoulder or forearm, and may not launch (leave his feet and spring upward and forward into the player). The foul is unnecessary roughness, the catch-all personal foul that also covers late hits after the whistle and hits on players out of bounds: 15 yards, with an automatic first down when the defense commits it.22
The defenseless-player rule is why you see safeties aiming low, at a receiver’s thighs, on a pass over the middle instead of “lighting him up” high. It is a rule that changed how a position is played.


The 2018 helmet rule
In 2018 the NFL went further with the use of the helmet (2018 rule): it is a foul for any player, anywhere on the field, to lower his head to initiate and make contact with his helmet against an opponent. Unlike the defenseless-player rules, it covers runners and blockers as well as tacklers, and it applies to everyone on every play, not just to hits on certain players. The penalty is 15 yards, and a flagrant violation can be an ejection.23


Tackles that are banned: the horse-collar and the hip-drop
Two tackles are illegal by name:

Horse-collar tackle (banned in 2005). Grabbing the inside back or side collar of a runner’s shoulder pads or jersey and pulling him down, usually from behind. The runner’s legs fold under him as he falls backward, which breaks ankles and tears knee ligaments. The ban followed the 2004 season, in which Dallas safety Roy Williams’s horse-collar tackles injured several players, among them Philadelphia’s Terrell Owens.24 15 yards and an automatic first down.
Hip-drop tackle (banned in 2024). The tackler wraps the runner from behind or the side, swings his hips and legs off the ground, and drops his weight onto the runner’s legs at or below the knee. The league’s injury data showed the technique injuring runners at a far higher rate than ordinary tackles, and the owners banned it in March 2024, unanimously and over the objections of the players’ union, with a 15-yard penalty and an automatic first down.25



Discipline beyond the flag: the 2026 three-strike policy
A flag is only one price. Players are also fined, and the worst hits bring suspensions. For the 2026 season the league and the players’ union agreed on a three-strike policy for five listed fouls (hip-drop tackles, horse-collar tackles, launching, hits on a defenseless player, and blindside blocks): three violations bring a one-game suspension, and the strikes carry over into later seasons. Everyone started the 2026 regular season with a clean slate. Reports differ on one detail: the Associated Press describes three violations across the categories, while ProFootballTalk reads the policy as three violations of the same rule. Strikes come from the league’s discipline after review, not only from flags.26 The point is to reach the habits that flags and fines hadn’t changed, especially for the hip-drop, which is rarely flagged (below).

What they solve. Head, neck and knee injuries that a career, or a life, can’t recover from. What they change. Defensive backs tackle lower and play the ball instead of the man; rushers learn to hit the quarterback’s torso and roll off him; offenses gain yards on every borderline call, and a quarterback who slides gets a free end to his run. Each rule also creates a judgment call, and judgment calls on 15-yard fouls swing games. That tension, between protecting players and leaving the officials too much to decide, runs through every live rules debate.

section: How a flag becomes yards: enforcement
text:
How a flag becomes yards: enforcement
Now the mechanics. When a flag flies during a play, the officials answer a fixed sequence of questions. Learn them and you can usually announce the result before the referee does.

Accept or decline
Most fouls happen during a live play, and the play keeps going until it ends normally. Then the team that was fouled gets a choice: accept or decline. Accept, and the result of the play is usually wiped out and the penalty enforced. Decline, and the play stands as though no foul happened.27 In practice the head coach decides, quickly, with the referee explaining the options to the team captain or the coach on the sideline.
The choice is usually obvious (nobody declines a 40-yard DPI) but not always:

Third down, incomplete pass, offensive holding. Accept, and it’s third-and-18 from ten yards back. Decline, and it’s fourth-and-8: the offense will probably punt. Most defenses decline, because a stop now beats a long third down later. In 2021–2025 offenses converted third-and-16 to third-and-20 about 10% of the time; a declined penalty that forces the punt takes even that chance away.
Defensive offside on a touchdown pass. The offense declines and keeps the touchdown. A defensive personal foul on a touchdown isn’t lost, though: the rules carry it over to the try, so the offense can kick the extra point from closer or go for two from the 1. (A personal foul on a successful extra-point kick can be carried to the kickoff instead.)
A sack and a hold. If the offense held and the quarterback was sacked anyway for 9 yards, the defense can take the sack (and the down) or the 10 yards (and replay the down), whichever leaves the offense worse off.
Two fouls by the same team on one play don’t add up. The fouled team picks the one it wants enforced, and the other is dropped.
Fouls by both teams on the same play usually offset: the penalties cancel and the down is replayed.

Some fouls aren’t part of the choice in the usual way. Fouls after the play is over (a late hit, a taunt, a fight) are dead-ball fouls: the play’s result stands and the yardage is added on, from where the play ended. That’s how a 20-yard completion plus a late hit becomes 35 yards.28


Free plays
Free play is the accept-or-decline option seen from the other end, and The Pre-Snap Phase showed it in action. When a defender is offside at the snap, the play goes on with the flag already down. The offense can’t lose: if the play works, it declines the penalty and keeps the result; if it fails (incomplete, sacked, even intercepted), it takes the five yards. So quarterbacks are taught to snap fast and take a shot downfield.
The catch is that not every jump gives a free play. If a defender’s jump makes a nearby blocker flinch, or leaves him with an unblocked path to the quarterback, the officials blow the whistle at once: a neutral zone infraction, five yards, no play (encroachment if he touches someone). The free play happens when the jumper draws no reaction and isn’t running free, typically a wide end who jumps and is picked up by his tackle, or a twelfth defender still running off the field at the snap (What a Play Really Is). That’s also why the quarterback snaps it fast on a jump: the play has to start before anybody reacts.29


Show the Python
def free_play():
    off = offense("gun_2x2")
    dfn = defense("nickel", "single_high", off, press=True)
    dfn = [q.moved(label="C") if q.pos == "CB" else q for q in dfn]
    dfn = [q.moved(d=13.5, w=0.0) if q.key == "FS" else q.moved(d=2.5, w=-9.2) if q.key == "SS" else q for q in dfn]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=40, to_go=10)
    p.motion("WDE", to=(-0.2, -4.7), speed=2.4)                 # the jump: into the neutral zone
    p.route("X", r.go(32)); p.route("H", r.hitch(6)); p.route("Y", r.hitch(6)); p.route("Z", r.curl(12))
    p.dropback(2.5)
    p.pass_to("X", t=1.7)
    for k in ("LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT"):
        p.block(k, pts=[(-1.0, 0.0)])
    for k in ("SDE", "SDT", "WDT"):
        p.rush(k, pts=[(-1.6, 0.0)], speed=2.0)
    p.rush("WDE", pts=[(-1.6, 0.4)], speed=2.0)
    p.man("LCB", "X"); p.man("NB", "Y"); p.man("RCB", "Z"); p.man("SS", "H")
    p.drop("FS", (20.0, -6.0), speed=6.0)
    p.drop("MIKE", (6.0, 1.0)); p.drop("WILL", (6.0, -4.0))
    p.highlight("WDE", "X")
    return p
