Figure 48.8: A free play, simulated (BDB-format tracking generated by gridiron). Set: the left defensive end (E) is in his stance outside the left tackle. Snap: he has jumped into the neutral zone (dashed outline: where he was), but nobody flinched and the tackle is in front of him, so there is no whistle; the center snaps the ball before he can get back, he is offside, and the flag comes out while the play runs. The quarterback, knowing the offense can take five yards if this goes badly, throws deep to X against the press corner, a throw he would rarely risk on a normal second down. If X catches it, the offense declines the flag; if it falls incomplete or is intercepted, the offense accepts it and replays the down five yards closer. Had the tackle flinched, or had the end been running free at the quarterback, the officials would have blown it dead before the snap: a neutral zone infraction.






From which spot, and how far
If the penalty is accepted, the officials need a starting point and a distance:

The previous spot (where the ball was snapped) is the default for most fouls, including all pre-snap fouls, every foul during a pass play (offensive holding, offensive pass interference, defensive holding, illegal contact), and every offensive foul behind the line of scrimmage.
The spot of the foul is used for defensive pass interference (the spot foul) and for many offensive fouls on running plays and returns: a block in the back 20 yards upfield on a punt return is walked off from where it happened.
The end of the play is used for dead-ball fouls after the whistle, and is an option for a defensive personal foul such as roughing the passer on a completed pass (the offense gets whichever of the previous spot and the end of the play helps it more).

The middle bullet is the one fans get wrong, and it has a logic. On a run, the officials compare the foul with the end of the run. A hold that happens behind that point, but past the line, is walked off from the spot of the foul: the offense keeps the yards it gained up to the hold, which came before the foul could help, and loses everything after it plus ten yards. A hold beyond where the run ended couldn’t have helped the runner, so it is walked off from the end of the run, and the offense keeps the whole gain before paying ten yards. A hold behind the line of scrimmage goes back to the previous spot, as on a pass.30 The NFL calls this the three-and-one method; you only need the picture.


Show the Python
def yard_strip(ax, lo, hi, prev, half=6.75, num_w=-4.9):
    """A horizontal strip of field from yard line lo to hi (offense's own territory, moving right)."""
    los = 10 + prev
    f = Field(ax=ax, orient="horizontal", los=los, window=(10 + lo - los, 10 + hi - los),
              lateral=(FIELD_W / 2 - half, FIELD_W / 2 + half), to_go=None, numbers=False)
    p = Play([O_("Q", "QB", 0.0, 0.0, "")], [], los=los, ball_y=FIELD_W / 2, to_go=None)
    for yl in range(lo - lo % 10 + 10, hi, 10):
        say(f, p, yl - prev, num_w, str(yl) if yl else "G", color=style.MUTED, fs=7.5, weight="bold")
    return f, p


def run_row(ax, foul, end, new_spot, tag, note, from_spot):
    f, p = yard_strip(ax, 8, 56, 30, half=5.4, num_w=-3.8)
    line_across(f, p, 0.0, style.OFFENSE_DARK, lw=1.6, ls="-", w0=-5.4, w1=5.4)
    line_across(f, p, 10.0, style.LINE_TO_GAIN, lw=1.6, ls="-", w0=-5.4, w1=5.4)
    arrow(f, p, (0.0, 0.2), (end - 30, 0.2), style.OFFENSE, lw=1.6, ms=8)          # the run
    ball(f, p, end - 30, 0.2)
    star(f, p, foul - 30, -1.5, FOUL, ms=11)
    say(f, p, foul - 30 + 1.4, -1.5, note, fs=6.2, color=FOUL, ha="left", box=False)
    arrow(f, p, (from_spot - 30, 2.0), (new_spot - 30, 2.0), FOUL, lw=1.6, ms=8)
    x0, y0 = P_(f, p, new_spot - 30, 0.0)
    ax.plot([x0, x0], [y0 - 2.8, y0 + 2.8], color=FOUL, lw=1.8, zorder=6)
    say(f, p, (from_spot + new_spot) / 2 - 30, 3.7, tag, fs=6.6, color=FOUL, weight="bold")
    return f


fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 1, figsize=(6.5, 4.5))
run_row(axes[0], 38, 42, 28, "from the spot of the foul: 1st-and-12", "hold", 38)
run_row(axes[1], 46, 42, 32, "from the end of the run: 1st-and-8", "hold", 42)
run_row(axes[2], 28, 42, 20, "from the previous spot: 1st-and-20", "hold", 30)
for ax, t in zip(axes, ["1. Hold behind the end of the run, past the line",
                        "2. Hold beyond the end of the run",
                        "3. Hold behind the line of scrimmage"]):
    panel_title(ax, t, fs=8.2)
fig.tight_layout(h_pad=0.6)
plt.show()








Figure 48.9: Offensive holding on a run, three ways (offense moving right). First-and-10 at the offense’s own 30; the back runs to the 42. Top: a receiver holds a corner at the 38, past the line but behind where the run ended, so ten yards come off from the spot of the foul: first-and-12 at the 28. Middle: the hold is at the 46, beyond where the run ended; it couldn’t have helped the runner, so the ten yards come off the end of the run: first-and-8 at the 32. Bottom: a lineman holds behind the line, at the 28, so the penalty goes back to the previous spot: first-and-20 at the 20.





Then how far: five, ten or fifteen yards, or the spot. And then two adjustments near the goal lines:

Half the distance. A penalty may not move the ball more than halfway to the offending team’s goal line. Holding by the offense on its own 8 moves the ball to the 4, not to the end zone. A defensive personal foul with the ball on the opponent’s 6 moves it to the 3. Without the rule, a penalty could score points; with it, the ball keeps creeping toward the goal line but never gets there.31
Fouls in the end zone. Offensive holding in the offense’s own end zone is a safety: the spot the penalty would be walked from is already behind the goal line, so instead of moving the ball the rules give the defense two points. DPI in the end zone puts the ball on the 1, not in the end zone. The rule book awards a touchdown for a foul only in the rare case of a palpably unfair act (a player coming off the bench to tackle a runner headed for the end zone, say), and pass interference, however blatant, isn’t one.32



Show the Python
def strip_row(ax, prev, new_spot, tag):
    f, p = yard_strip(ax, -9, 42, prev)
    say(f, p, -5 - prev, -4.9, "end zone", color=style.INK_2, fs=6.8, style_="italic", box=False)
    line_across(f, p, 0.0, style.OFFENSE_DARK, lw=1.6, ls="-", w0=-6.7, w1=6.7)
    ball(f, p, 0.0, 0.0)
    arrow(f, p, (0.0, 2.6), (new_spot - prev, 2.6), FOUL, lw=1.6, ms=9)
    ball(f, p, new_spot - prev, 0.0)
    x0, y0 = P_(f, p, new_spot - prev, 0.0)
    ax.plot([x0, x0], [y0 - 3.4, y0 + 3.4], color=FOUL, lw=1.6, zorder=6)
    say(f, p, (new_spot - prev) / 2, 4.6, tag, fs=7.0, color=FOUL, weight="bold")
    return f


fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 1, figsize=(6.5, 4.6))
strip_row(axes[0], 35, 25, "10 yd")
strip_row(axes[1], 8, 4, "4 yd")
f, p = yard_strip(axes[2], -9, 42, 2)
say(f, p, -7.0, -4.9, "end zone", color=style.INK_2, fs=6.8, style_="italic", box=False)
line_across(f, p, 0.0, style.OFFENSE_DARK, lw=1.6, ls="-", w0=-6.7, w1=6.7)
ball(f, p, 0.0, 0.0)
arrow(f, p, (-0.3, 0.0), (-5.3, 0.0), style.OFFENSE, lw=1.3, ms=7)
draw_marker(axes[2], *P_(f, p, -6.0, 0.0), "off", "Q", f.pts_per_yard())
star(f, p, -6.0, 2.0, FOUL, ms=11)
flag(f, p, -3.4, 3.4, s=1.1)
say(f, p, 9.5, 2.6, "hold in his own end zone: safety", fs=7.0, color=FOUL, weight="bold")
for ax, t in zip(axes, ["1. Holding with the ball on the 35: the full 10 yards, to the 25",
                        "2. Holding on the 8: half the distance to the goal line, to the 4",
                        "3. Snap from the 2, hold in his own end zone: a safety"]):
    panel_title(ax, t, fs=8.2)
fig.tight_layout(h_pad=0.6)
plt.show()








Figure 48.10: The same offensive holding call, ten yards, at three spots near the offense’s own goal line (offense moving right). Top: from the 35 the full 10 yards apply, so the next snap is at the 25. Middle: from the 8, ten yards would carry the ball into the end zone, so it moves half the distance to the goal line, to the 4. Bottom: the ball is snapped from the 2 and the quarterback drops back into his own end zone; a hold there, four yards deep, is a safety: two points to the defense, and the offense must free-kick.







What down is it?
Last question: the down.

Fouls by the offense usually replay the down: second-and-10 becomes second-and-20 after a hold. A few also cost a down (an illegal forward pass, intentional grounding; see Officiating, Replay, and the Rules of the Ball).
Fouls by the defense come in two kinds. The pre-snap and procedural fouls (offside, encroachment, neutral zone infraction, too many men) replay the down unless the yards reach the line to gain. The contact and safety fouls (defensive holding, illegal contact, DPI, roughing the passer, unnecessary roughness and the other personal fouls, illegal hands to the face) carry an automatic first down, however short the yardage.
A half can’t end on an accepted defensive foul during a play. If time runs out on a play with a defensive foul and the offense accepts, it gets one untimed down.



Show the Python
steps = [
    ("1  When?", "Before the snap with a whistle (false start, encroachment, neutral zone infraction: no play)? During the play, including offside at the snap (a live-ball foul: the play runs)? Or after it ended (a dead-ball foul: late hit, taunt; the play stands)?"),
    ("2  Who?", "Offense or defense? If both, the fouls usually offset and the down is replayed."),
    ("3  Accept/decline?", "The fouled team compares the play's result with the penalty's result and keeps the better one."),
    ("4  Where, how far?", "Previous spot (pass plays, pre-snap fouls, offense fouls behind the line), spot of the foul (DPI; offense fouls past the line but behind the end of a run, and on returns), or end of the play (dead-ball fouls; offense fouls beyond the end of a run); 5, 10, 15 yards or the spot; half the distance near a goal line."),
    ("5  What down?", "Offense foul: replay the down (a few cost one). Defense contact or personal foul: automatic first down. Defense procedural foul: replay unless the yards reach the sticks."),
]
wrapped = ["\n".join(textwrap.wrap(body, 66)) for _, body in steps]
heights = [1.9 + 0.95 * (w.count("\n") + 1) for w in wrapped]      # 1 unit = 0.155 in
gap = 0.9
total = sum(heights) + gap * (len(steps) - 1)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 0.155 * total))
ax.set_xlim(0, 100); ax.set_ylim(0, total); ax.axis("off")
y1 = total
for i, ((head, _), body, h) in enumerate(zip(steps, wrapped, heights)):
    y0 = y1 - h
    ax.add_patch(FancyBboxPatch((1, y0 + 0.15), 98, h - 0.3, boxstyle="round,pad=0.15,rounding_size=0.6",
                                fc=style.SURFACE if i % 2 else style.OFFENSE_TINT, ec=style.BASELINE, lw=0.9))
    ax.text(3.5, (y0 + y1) / 2, head, fontsize=8.6, fontweight="bold", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, va="center")
    ax.text(32, (y0 + y1) / 2, body, fontsize=7.4, color=style.INK, va="center", linespacing=1.2)
    if i < len(steps) - 1:
        ax.annotate("", xy=(14, y0 - gap + 0.05), xytext=(14, y0 + 0.05),
                    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=style.INK_2, lw=1.0))
    y1 = y0 - gap
plt.show()

title: Contact Rules and Penalties as Strategy
text:
What penalties cost
Now price them. Every NFL game has about 13 fouls named in the play-by-play (both teams, accepted or declined, in 2025), and a handful of types account for most of them.


Show the Python
SHOW = [("Offensive Holding", "Offensive holding"), ("False Start", "False start"),
        ("Defensive Pass Interference", "Def. pass interference"), ("Defensive Holding", "Defensive holding"),
        ("Unnecessary Roughness", "Unnecessary roughness"), ("Roughing the Passer", "Roughing the passer"),
        ("Illegal Contact", "Illegal contact"), ("Offensive Pass Interference", "Off. pass interference")]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 4, figsize=(6.6, 3.7), sharex=True)
yrs = RATES.index.values
for ax, (col, name) in zip(axes.flat, SHOW):
    v = RATES[col].values
    ax.plot(yrs, v, color=style.SERIES[0], lw=1.8, marker="o", ms=2.6)
    ax.set_ylim(0, max(v) * 1.3)
    ax.set_title(name, fontsize=7.4, loc="left")
    ax.tick_params(labelsize=6.6)
    ax.set_xticks([2015, 2020, 2025])
    ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
    ax.text(yrs[-1] + 0.3, v[-1], f"{v[-1]:.2f}", fontsize=6.4, color=style.INK, va="center")
    ax.set_xlim(2014.5, 2027.2)
    if col == "Offensive Holding":
        ax.annotate("2020", xy=(2020, RATES.loc[2020, col]), xytext=(2016.2, RATES.loc[2020, col] * 0.55),
                    fontsize=6.4, color=style.INK_2, arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=style.INK_2, lw=0.7))
for ax in axes[:, 0]:
    ax.set_ylabel("flags per game", fontsize=6.8)
fig.tight_layout(h_pad=0.9, w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()








Figure 48.12: Flags per game (both teams) for eight common fouls, 2015-2025 regular seasons. Offensive holding and false starts are the two most common by far. Holding dropped sharply in 2020, when officials were told to call it less, and has since climbed back. Roughing the passer peaked in 2018-2021 after the body-weight emphasis and fell back from 2022. Illegal contact jumps around from year to year, as emphasis changes. Source: nflverse play-by-play, one foul per play (the play’s main foul), accepted or declined, all plays including kicks; each panel has its own scale.





How often a foul is called is half the story. The other half is what each one is worth. Because nflverse computes expected points before and after every snap, a penalty snap gets an EPA like any other: the value of the down, distance and yard line after the flag, minus the value before. (That includes the play the flag wiped out, which is gone; the EPA reflects only where the penalty left the ball.) Averaging by foul type gives a price list in points.


Show the Python
ORDER = ["Roughing the Passer", "Defensive Pass Interference", "Unnecessary Roughness", "Illegal Contact",
         "Defensive Holding", "Face Mask", "Neutral Zone Infraction", "Defensive Offside", "Illegal Use of Hands",
         "False Start", "Ineligible Downfield Pass", "Illegal Block Above the Waist", "Offensive Holding",
         "Offensive Pass Interference"]
NAMES = {"Illegal Use of Hands": "Hands to the face", "Illegal Block Above the Waist": "Block in the back",
         "Ineligible Downfield Pass": "Illegal man downfield", "Defensive Offside": "Offside (defense)",
         "Roughing the Passer": "Roughing the passer", "Defensive Pass Interference": "Defensive pass interference",
         "Unnecessary Roughness": "Unnecessary roughness", "Illegal Contact": "Illegal contact",
         "Defensive Holding": "Defensive holding", "Face Mask": "Face mask", "Neutral Zone Infraction": "Neutral zone infraction",
         "False Start": "False start", "Offensive Holding": "Offensive holding",
         "Offensive Pass Interference": "Offensive pass interference"}
MIXED = {"Illegal Use of Hands", "Face Mask", "Unnecessary Roughness"}
e = EPA_S.reset_index()
e = e[e.penalty_type.isin(ORDER) & (e.n >= 40)]
e = e[e.penalty_type.isin(MIXED) | (e.by_off == (e.penalty_type.map(EPA_T.by_off) > 0.5))].sort_values("epa")
labels = [NAMES[t] + ((" (offense)" if bo else " (defense)") if t in MIXED else "") for t, bo in zip(e.penalty_type, e.by_off)]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 4.6))
cols = [style.OFFENSE if bo else style.DEFENSE for bo in e.by_off]
ax.barh(labels, e.epa, color=cols, height=0.66)
for i, (ep, yd) in enumerate(zip(e.epa, e.yds)):
    ax.text(ep + (0.04 if ep >= 0 else -0.04), i, f"{ep:+.2f}  ({yd:.0f} yd)", va="center",
            ha="left" if ep >= 0 else "right", fontsize=7.2, color=style.INK)
ax.axvline(0, color=style.BASELINE, lw=1.0)
ax.set_xlim(e.epa.min() - 0.75, e.epa.max() + 0.75)
ax.set_xlabel("Average EPA for the offense when the foul is accepted", fontsize=8)
ax.tick_params(labelsize=7.4)
ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
ax.legend(handles=[Patch(color=style.DEFENSE, label="foul by the defense"), Patch(color=style.OFFENSE, label="foul by the offense")],
          loc="lower right", fontsize=7.5)
plt.show()








Figure 48.13: The average swing in expected points (EPA, from the offense’s point of view) when a foul is accepted, 2021-2025 regular seasons, scrimmage downs. Fouls by the defense (orange) help the offense; fouls by the offense (blue) hurt it. The number on each bar is the average penalty yardage. Illegal use of hands, face mask and unnecessary roughness can be committed by either side, so each appears twice, once per side (only cases with at least 40 accepted flags are shown). Source: nflverse play-by-play.





Four things stand out.

The automatic first down is worth more than the yards. Defensive holding and illegal contact are five-yard fouls, the same yardage as a false start, yet they swing about a point toward the offense while a false start costs about two-thirds of one the other way. Splitting the two-sided fouls by team shows the same thing: hands to the face is worth more against the defense (five yards and a first down) than offside is (five yards, no first down).
DPI and roughing the passer cost a defense more than a completed pass usually gains. The average completion in these seasons was worth about +0.80 EPA; a DPI flag averaged +1.74, and roughing +1.76.
Offensive holding is a drive-killer. At about -1.00 EPA, a hold costs a little over half of what a sack does (-1.78 on average), and holds are flagged about two and a half times a game.
The same five-yard foul is worth more on later downs. The table shows it.

                  "Average yards to go": t["togo"].map(lambda v: f"{v:.1f}"),
                  "Average EPA for the offense": t["epa"].map(lambda v: f"{v:+.2f}")})

On first-and-10 a defensive hold is a modest gain, first-and-5. On third-and-7 it erases a likely punt and hands the offense a fresh set of downs, so it’s worth about three times as much. That’s why defensive coordinators preach discipline on third down above all, and why an offense with a long third down will often throw toward the corner it thinks is most likely to grab.






NoteGo deeper: penalties in EPA work



Analysts don’t agree on how to treat penalty snaps. The usual “EPA per play” leaves out snaps that a penalty wiped out (nflverse marks them play_type == "no_play"), which drops most DPI flags and most holding calls from team numbers. Expected Points and Success Rate shows how much that choice shades run-versus-pass comparisons; the DPI flags alone make passing look a little better once they are counted. For your own work: say which choice you made, and remember that nflverse records one foul per play, so a play with two flags carries only one penalty type.
Labels move, too. The 2018 helmet foul appears in nflverse under its own name, “lowering the head to initiate contact,” at about 0.07 to 0.13 flags a game from 2018 to 2020, then fades in 2021 and vanishes from the labels after that.33 Whether those calls dried up or are now filed under another name (unnecessary roughness is the likely home), the series breaks there. Check a category’s history before you chart it.

title: Contact Rules and Penalties as Strategy
section: The rules keep moving: live debates
text:
The rules keep moving: live debates
Every spring the competition committee and the teams propose rule changes, and the owners vote; a change needs 24 of 32 votes. The rules in this chapter will keep changing, so here are the debates that were live going into the 2026 season. (For how these fit the long history of rule changes, see The 1978 Liberation and Dynasties and Counterpunches; for the timeline, Appendix E.)

The tush push. The tush push is a quarterback sneak with teammates shoving the quarterback from behind, the Eagles’ near-automatic short-yardage play (Red Zone, Goal Line, Two-Point Plays, and Short Yardage explains it). Pushing the runner has been legal since the NFL removed its ban in 2005; pulling him (a teammate grabbing his arm or jersey and hauling him forward) is still a foul, ten yards, and it’s the one to watch for in a tush-push pile. In 2025 Green Bay proposed banning it again; the proposal was tabled in the spring and a revised version failed 22–10 on May 21, 2025, two votes short of 24. The league tightened its officiating guidance on false starts and alignment instead. For 2026, no team proposed a ban, and the play is legal this season.34 The argument is about safety (a pile of linemen driving forward), about fairness (is a nearly unstoppable play bad for the game?) and about whether one team’s mastery of a play is a reason to outlaw it. The case study is The Eagles: Trenches, RPOs, and the Tush Push.
Is the hip-drop ban being enforced? The tackle was banned in 2024, but on-field flags have been extremely rare: nflverse’s play-by-play records 1 hip-drop flag in the 2024 regular season and 2 in 2025. The technique happens in a blur, from behind, in a pile, which is hard for an official to see live. The league has leaned on fines after the game instead, and the 2026 three-strike policy adds suspensions on top. Whether discipline after the fact changes behaviour as much as flags would is the open question.
Replay for judgment calls. After the 2019 pass-interference experiment failed, the NFL moved more carefully. Since 2025 replay assist may help the referee on objective facts and may overturn flags for hits on a defenseless player, face mask (grabbing and twisting or pulling the face mask), horse-collar, tripping (using a leg to trip an opponent) and roughing or running into the kicker (hitting a punter or kicker after the kick). It cannot add a foul that wasn’t called, and roughing the passer and pass interference are not on the list. In 2026 league officials may also be consulted on ejections for flagrant acts.35 Proposals for a full “sky judge” who could call fouls from the booth keep coming back.
College versus NFL. The college game caps DPI at 15 yards, gives linemen three yards downfield instead of one, and treats targeting (a forcible hit to the head) with automatic ejections. College offensive pass interference was cut from 15 yards to 10 for 2026.36 Each difference is a live argument for moving the NFL rule toward college, or the reverse; the full side-by-side table is in Appendix E and the history in The College Laboratory.







TipWatch for it on Sunday: the flag predictor



Every time a yellow flag flies, play referee before the referee does. Say your answers out loud, then check them against the announcement.

Where did the flag come from? The official’s position is a clue. A flag from deep downfield (the side judges, field judge or back judge) is usually pass interference, illegal contact or defensive holding. A flag from the officials at the line of scrimmage or behind the offense is usually holding, a false start or a foul on the quarterback. A flag thrown late, after the play, is usually a personal foul. (Who stands where is in Officiating, Replay, and the Rules of the Ball.)
Was the ball in the air? If a receiver was grabbed before the throw, guess holding or illegal contact (five yards, first down). After the throw, guess DPI and estimate the spot.
Accept or decline? Ask what the fouled team gave up on the play, and whether the next down (a punt down, say) already punishes the offense more than the yards would.
Enforce it. Which spot, how far, half the distance near a goal line, and what down. Say the new down and distance.
Free play? If a defender jumped and the ball was snapped anyway, watch the quarterback take his shot.
Keep score. By the end of a game you’ll be calling most flags right. For a running tally, log the penalties’ expected-points cost from the chart in What penalties cost: which team gave away more points in flags?

Predict the play






TipPredict the play 1: backed up, and a flag





Show the Python
off = offense("i_form")
dfn = defense("4-3_over", "single_high", off)

p.run("RB", [(3.0, -4.2), (6.4, -7.0), (13.0, -8.2)])
p.handoff("RB", t=0.8)
for k, pts in (("LT", [(0.8, -1.0)]), ("LG", [(0.8, -1.0)]), ("C", [(0.8, -1.0)]), ("RG", [(0.8, -1.0)]),
               ("Y", [(0.6, -0.8)]), ("FB", [(3.6, -4.4)])):
    p.block(k, pts=pts)
p.path("SDE", [(-2.5, -1.7)])
p.block("RT", pts=[(-0.7, -0.5)])
p.highlight("RT", "SDE")

no_numbers(f.ax)

say(f, p, -5.8, 10.2, "RT holds the end about\na yard behind the line", fs=6.6, color=FOUL)
f.ax.plot(*zip(P_(f, p, -4.9, 8.4), P_(f, p, -2.2, 3.0)), color=style.INK_2, lw=0.6, zorder=8)
say(f, p, 8.6, -11.8, "tackled at the 10", fs=6.6)
say(f, p, -7.4, -9.5, "own end zone", fs=6.6, style_="italic", color=style.INK_2)
plt.show()








Figure 48.14: First-and-10 at the offense’s own 4. The back runs left and is tackled at the 10, a 6-yard gain. On the backside, the defensive end beat the right tackle inside, and the tackle grabbed him a yard behind the line of scrimmage (the star): flag, offensive holding.





The defense has the choice. Does it accept or decline? If it accepts, where does the ball go and what are the down and distance? Then two variations: what if the tackle had held the end in the end zone, and what if a receiver had held a defender at the 9, five yards downfield?








TipAnswer





Accept. Declining leaves the run standing: second-and-4 at the 10. Accepting is far worse for the offense:

Which spot? The hold was behind the line of scrimmage, so it goes back to the previous spot, the 4, even though this was a running play.
How far? Ten yards from the 4 would put the ball in the end zone, so it moves half the distance to the goal line: to the 2.
What down? An offensive foul replays the down, and the line to gain stays at the 14: first-and-12 from the 2, with the offense now one more mistake from a safety and likely to punt from its own end zone.

Variation 1, the hold in the end zone: an offensive foul behind the offense’s own goal line is a safety if the defense accepts: two points and the ball back on a free kick. The defense takes it.
Variation 2, a receiver’s hold at the 9: that’s past the line but behind where the run ended (the 10), so it is walked off from the spot of the foul, the 9. Ten yards would be more than half the distance, so the ball goes halfway, to the 4½: first-and-9½. The offense keeps the five yards it gained before the hold, which is the logic of the run rule, and the defense would probably still accept, since it beats second-and-4 at the 10.

Figure 48.15: Fourth quarter, 0:04 left, the offense trails by 5 with the ball at the opponent’s 42 and no timeouts. Five receivers spread out; the defense rushes three and drops eight, the deepest three at the goal line and in the end zone.





What will the offense try, where will the ball be thrown, and why there rather than ten yards short, where a receiver might be open?








TipAnswer





A Hail Mary into the end zone: a long, high throw to a crowd of receivers, hoping one of them comes down with it. With four seconds left there is time for one play, and only a touchdown wins, so a completion short of the goal line ends the game as soon as the receiver is tackled. That is the main reason to throw into the end zone.
The rules add a bonus, and it comes from this chapter: a half can’t end on an accepted defensive foul. Pass interference anywhere gives the offense an untimed down at the spot, and the deeper the foul, the better that down: interference in the end zone puts the ball on the 1-yard line, a far better chance than any heave. It cuts the other way too. A half can end on an offensive foul, and any score on that play doesn’t count, so a receiver who shoves a defender to get to the ball has just ended the game. That’s why receivers are coached to box out for position, not push.37
That’s why the receivers converge on one spot and fight for position, and why defensive backs are coached to go for the ball (jump and bat it down) rather than for the receiver. Officials are reluctant to call interference in a crowd where everyone is jostling for a jump ball, but a defender who grabs or tackles a receiver before the ball arrives gives the offense its best chance of the day. The eight deep defenders are there to make sure nobody catches it and that nobody has to foul to prevent it.

Figure 48.16: Third-and-3 at midfield. The offense lines up in a tight bunch to the right. The defense shows press man coverage on all three bunch receivers (the ringed defenders, each a yard off the ball), with one deep safety.





What kind of route combination should the offense call here? Where must the contact happen for it to be legal? And what could the defense have done differently before the snap?








TipAnswer





A rub (pick) concept out of the bunch. Against press man, with three defenders lined up a yard off three receivers standing close together, the receivers’ release paths will cross the defenders’ paths almost at once. A classic call is one receiver releasing inside on a slant or in-breaking route, another breaking out to the flat, and the third pushing vertically to clear the area; one of the defenders chasing his man has to fight through a teammate’s release.
Legal if the contact happens within a yard of the line, or if the receiver just runs his route. Because the defenders are pressed, the crossing happens right at the line, inside the one-yard strip where pass interference can’t occur, so even a deliberate bump is legal there. (The rule says more than one yard, so contact at the line or a step past it is safe; officials judge it by eye at full speed, which is why offenses aim for contact at the line rather than at the edge of the strip.) Deeper than that, a receiver who keeps running his route and lets a defender run into him is still legal; one who runs three yards, stops and steps into a defender’s path has blocked him, and that is offensive pass interference, ten yards.
What the defense could have done: not press all three. Against bunches, defenses usually align at different depths (one defender pressed, the others four or five yards off), so nobody can be picked within the first yard; or they switch/banjo, trading receivers by agreement so no defender chases through the traffic; or they play zone, where nobody is chasing a man at all. Lining up pressed on a tight bunch is inviting the rub.

48  Contact Rules and Penalties as Strategy

title: Contact Rules and Penalties as Strategy
text:
Takeaways

The rule book is a price list, and teams shop. Five yards, ten, fifteen, the spot, a first down, a safety, an ejection: every foul has a price, and coaches decide when it’s worth paying (the beaten corner’s grab, the beaten tackle’s hold, the deep throw hunting a flag).
A receiver’s rules change with depth and with the throw. Inside five yards, jam him. Past five, hands off until the ball is in the air (illegal contact, defensive holding: five yards and a first down). After the throw, play the ball (DPI: a spot foul in the NFL, 15 yards in college). The offense’s restrictions start at the snap: deliberate picks are legal only inside the first yard, and beyond it the receiver must not start the contact.
The spot foul shapes offense. Because DPI has no cap in the NFL, deep throws into tight coverage carry a hidden bonus, and big receivers who win 50-50 balls or draw flags are worth more.
Blocking is about the frame. Hands inside the chest plate that push and steer are legal; grabbing that materially restricts a defender (usually a hand outside the frame), hands to the face, blocks in the back, cuts outside the tight end box and chop blocks are not. Holding is usually the most-called foul and the most sensitive to officiating emphasis.
Safety rules are expensive and contested. Roughing the passer, the defenseless player, the 2018 helmet rule, the horse-collar and hip-drop bans are mostly 15-yard personal fouls with an automatic first down; from 2026, repeat violations of five listed rules bring a suspension.
Enforce it yourself: accept or decline, which spot (previous spot for passes and anything behind the line; on runs, compare the foul with where the run ended), how far (half the distance near a goal line), what down. The automatic first down, not the yardage, is what makes a five-yard defensive foul worth a point.

title: Officiating, Replay, and the Rules of the Ball
text:
Seven officials, seven jobs
Fourth quarter, 1:41 left in a one-score game. A receiver dives along the sideline, the ball pinned to his chest, and tumbles out of bounds. The nearest official, a man in a black cap twenty yards downfield, waves both arms across his body: incomplete. The home crowd roars at the stadium screen, which is replaying the catch from a low angle. The losing coach grabs the red flag from his sock, then stops; he isn’t allowed to throw it. Thirty seconds later, with nobody on either sideline having asked, the official in the white cap walks to the middle of the field, clicks on his microphone and says: “After review, the ruling on the field is reversed. The receiver had control of the ball with both feet down in bounds. The pass is complete.” Who decided that? Why couldn’t the coach challenge? And what exactly did “control with both feet down” have to do with it? This chapter is about the people who run the game and the small set of rules that decide, on almost every close play, who has the ball.
You’ll be able to…
An NFL game is run by seven officials on the field, each wearing a number and, on his back, letters that name his job (R, U, DJ, LJ, SJ, FJ, BJ). A seven-person crew sounds like a lot until you count what happens on one snap: 22 players, most of them in contact, spread across 53 yards of width and up to 50 of depth, in about five seconds. So the crew splits the field and the players into pieces. Each official has a starting spot, a few players he is responsible for (his keys), an area to cover once the ball moves, and a short list of fouls that are his to call.
Show the Python
off = offense("singleback")
dfn = defense("4-3_over", "two_high", off)
p = Play(off, dfn, los=40, to_go=10)
fld = p.draw(lateral=(-31.5, 31.5), window=(-16.5, 29.5), title=False)
ax = fld.ax
no_numbers(ax)
ppy = fld.pts_per_yard()
CREW = {  # key: (name, (d, w) of the official, (d, w) of his label)
    "R": ("Referee", (-12.0, 5.5), (-14.4, 5.5)),
    "U": ("Umpire", (-11.0, -5.5), (-13.4, -5.5)),
    "DJ": ("Down judge", (0.0, -28.4), (-2.6, -24.0)),
    "LJ": ("Line judge", (0.0, 28.4), (-2.6, 24.0)),
    "SJ": ("Side judge", (20.0, -23.5), (17.6, -23.5)),
    "FJ": ("Field judge", (20.0, 23.5), (17.6, 23.5)),
    "BJ": ("Back judge", (25.0, 4.0), (27.4, 4.0)),
}
for key, (name, (d, w), (ld, lw)) in CREW.items():
    official(ax, *XY(fld, p, d, w), key, ppy, r=1.25)
    say(fld, p, ld, lw, name, color=style.INK, fs=7.0, weight="bold")
say(fld, p, 10.0, -27.6, "sideline", fs=6.2, box=False, rot=90)
say(fld, p, 10.0, 27.6, "sideline", fs=6.2, box=False, rot=90)
say(fld, p, 1.4, 12.0, "line of scrimmage", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fs=6.2)
say(fld, p, 11.4, -2.0, "line to gain", color=style.INK, fs=6.2)
marker_legend(ax)
plt.show()








Figure 49.1: Where the seven officials stand before a snap (white discs; an 11-personnel offense in blue against a 4-3 defense in orange). Two officials work behind the offense: the referee (R), on the side of a right-handed quarterback’s throwing arm, and the umpire (U) opposite him. Two straddle the line of scrimmage at the sidelines, just off the field: the down judge (DJ), on the side with the chain crew, and the line judge (LJ). Three work deep: the side judge (SJ) and field judge (FJ) about 20 yards downfield near each sideline, and the back judge (BJ) about 25 yards deep in the middle. Exact depths vary with the down, the distance and the formation.
Here is what each of them is watching. The table is the short version of the league’s own description of the positions;1 the habits behind it are what let you guess who threw a flag before the referee says.
Table 49.1: The seven officials: where they start, what they watch, and the calls you’ll most often see them make.












Official
Starts
Watches
Typical calls




Referee (R, white cap)
Offensive backfield, 10–12 yards deep, on the quarterback’s throwing-arm side
The quarterback and the backs; the snap
Roughing the passer, intentional grounding, fumble or pass by the quarterback; announces every foul and review


Umpire (U)
Offensive backfield, opposite the referee; on the defensive side for field goals and extra points
The center, guards and the men across from them
Holding (both sides) and false starts inside, illegal hands to the face; spots the ball; checks equipment


Down judge (DJ)
On the line of scrimmage at one sideline, with the chain crew
The line (who’s on it, who moved), the end and receivers on his side, his sideline
Offside, encroachment, false start, illegal formation or motion; forward progress and out of bounds on his side


Line judge (LJ)
On the line of scrimmage at the other sideline
The same as the down judge, on his side
The same, plus whether a pass was thrown from beyond the line


Side judge (SJ)
About 20 yards deep near the down judge’s sideline
Receivers on his side once they’re downfield
Pass interference, illegal contact, catch or no catch, out of bounds


Field judge (FJ)
About 20 yards deep near the line judge’s sideline
Receivers on his side once they’re downfield
The same; under one upright on kicks


Back judge (BJ)
About 25 yards deep in the middle
The tight end and inside receivers, the deep middle, the end line
Deep pass interference, catches in the end zone; under the other upright on kicks
A few things in that table explain a lot of what you see on Sundays.
The wing officials own the line of scrimmage. The down judge and line judge stand exactly on the line at the sidelines so they can look straight down it, the only place from which you can see who is offside and which receivers are on the line (the formation rules need seven). Most pre-snap fouls come from these two. After the snap they drift downfield and mark where a runner’s forward progress stopped: the official you see jog in and point his foot at the spot.
The umpire lives in the trenches, and he moved. For most of football history the umpire, the official responsible for the interior line, stood four or five yards behind the defensive line, in the middle of the linebackers, which is where the holding happens. It was also where umpires kept getting run over. In 2010 the NFL moved him to the offensive backfield, opposite the referee, where he watches the same linemen from behind.2 The trade was visibility for safety: from behind you see a lineman’s hands on a jersey less clearly. (Its side effect was a slower snap, because the umpire also spots the ball after most plays and now had farther to walk; the footnote has the brief exceptions the league tried for hurry-up situations.)
The deep officials are pass officials. The side judge, field judge and back judge are the reason a deep throw can be judged at all. Each takes a share of the receivers, keeps them between himself and the sideline or the end line, and rules on pass interference and illegal contact, catches and out of bounds. The seventh official, the side judge, was added in 1978, the same year the league loosened the rules on pass defense to open up the passing game: more passing meant more eyes downfield.3
Finding them on a wide shot. The letters are too small to read on most camera angles, so use geography. Behind the offense there are two officials: the one in the white cap is the referee, the other is the umpire. On the line at the two sidelines, the one by the chain crew and its sticks is the down judge, the other the line judge. Of the three deep officials, the one in the middle is the back judge; the deep wing on the chain crew’s side is the side judge, and the one on the far side is the field judge.
The referee is the boss, and the voice. The referee wears the white cap and leads the crew. His spot, behind and to the throwing-arm side of the quarterback, lets him watch the one player the rules protect most: he throws most roughing-the-passer flags and decides whether a quarterback who lost the ball was throwing it or fumbling it. Any official can throw a flag; the crew gathers, the one who saw the foul tells the referee, and the referee announces it. A flag “picked up” after that conference usually means another official had a better look.

title: Officiating, Replay, and the Rules of the Ball
text:
NoteMadden vs. real life



In a video game a foul is a fact: the code knows a lineman held, and a flag appears. On a real field, a foul exists only if an official in the right spot sees it. A hold on the far side of a run play can be in no official’s view, and a hold on the play side might be seen by two. That is why “they’re letting them play” is sometimes true, and why the same contact draws a flag in front of the line judge and not behind the umpire’s back. Officiating is a sample, not a census.



The crew in motion
Starting spots are only half of it. Watch a wide shot of a deep pass and you’ll see the crew move as a unit: the referee stays with the quarterback; the wing officials read the receivers on their side through the first few yards and then drift downfield, with the line judge usually staying on the line until the ball is thrown so he can judge whether it was thrown from beyond it; and the deep officials backpedal to stay deeper and wider than the receivers they’re judging, so that every catch is seen from the side or facing the receiver, never from behind him.


Show the Python
off = offense("gun_2x2")
dfn = defense("nickel", "two_high", off)
dfn = [q.moved(d=7.5) if q.key in ("LCB", "RCB") else q for q in dfn]
cm = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=10)
cm.dropback(2.5)
cm.route("X", r.go(20)); cm.route("H", r.seam(18)); cm.route("Y", r.seam(18)); cm.route("Z", r.fade(26))
cm.route("RB", r.flat(1.5, 6.0), side=-1)
cm.pass_to("Z", t=2.6)
for k in ("LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT"):
    cm.block(k, pts=[(-1.4, 0.0)])
for k in ("SDE", "SDT", "WDT", "WDE"):
    cm.rush(k, pts=[(-1.3, 0.0)])
cm.drop("FS", (19.0, -10.0)); cm.drop("SS", (21.0, 11.5))
cm.drop("MIKE", (8.0, 3.5)); cm.drop("WILL", (7.0, -2.6)); cm.drop("NB", (10.0, 7.5))
cm.path("LCB", [(12.0, -1.5)]); cm.path("RCB", [(10.0, 2.6), (19.0, 2.4)])
trk = cm.to_tracking(t_after=1.6)
trk = trk[trk.time <= 4.8]
OFFICIALS = {
    "R": ("R", [(0, -12.0, 5.5), (1.0, -12.5, 6.5), (3.0, -12.0, 6.5), (4.6, -10.5, 7.5)]),

    "DJ": ("DJ", [(0, 0.0, -28.4), (0.9, 0.0, -28.4), (2.6, 4.0, -28.4), (4.6, 10.0, -28.4)]),

         "the catch, seen facing the receiver"]

    lab = "snap" if abs(t) < 1e-6 else f"{t:+.1f} s"
    fld.ax.set_title(f"{lab}: {NOTES[i]}", fontsize=8.2 if PDF else 10, color=style.INK, loc="left")


T_CM, CATCH_T = 2.6, 4.7
qb_throw = cm.position("QB", T_CM)

    zd, zw = cm.position("Z", t)                         # ring the target receiver

    if t >= T_CM - 1e-6:                                 # the ball's flight, from the throw onward
        path_arrow(fld, cm, [tuple(qb_throw), tuple(z_catch)], color=style.BALL, lw=1.4, head=9, rad=-0.06)

Figure 49.2: A deep pass seen through the officials (simulated tracking in Big Data Bowl format; an illustrative play, not a real one). The target, the receiver Z on the right, is ringed in green. Snap: the crew in its starting spots. 1.2 s: the quarterback is in his drop and the receivers are climbing; the referee (R) watches the quarterback, the umpire (U) the linemen; the down judge (DJ) has begun to drift downfield with his receivers, while the line judge (LJ) holds the line to judge whether the pass is thrown from behind it. 2.6 s: the ball is thrown (dashed brown line) to Z down the right side; the line judge releases downfield and the field judge (FJ) backpedals to stay wider and deeper than the receiver. 4.7 s: the catch, judged by the field judge facing the receiver from downfield and outside, with the line judge trailing to mark the spot. Faint lines are each person’s path.






Who the officials are
NFL officials are mostly part-time, with other careers, working under a labor agreement with their union, the NFL Referees Association; the league’s full-time experiments of 2017, 2019 and 2020 were each dropped. Every official is graded by the league office on every play, and the grades matter: during the regular season a referee leads the same crew week after week, but in the playoffs the crews are broken up and rebuilt from the best-graded individuals at each position, and crew rosters change between seasons as officials retire or move. In 2026 a contract standoff had the league preparing replacement officials (and a one-year rule giving New York wider powers to fix their mistakes) until a seven-year deal was agreed in May, so the regular officials are working this season.4
Even the referee’s microphone has a history: referees were first wired for sound in 1975, under the league’s supervisor of officials Art McNally, who also oversaw the first replay system in 1986 and in 2022 became the first official in the Pro Football Hall of Fame.5

title: Officiating, Replay, and the Rules of the Ball
section: Replay: three doors into the booth
text:
Replay: three doors into the booth
Officials miss things: they watch a five-second play at full speed from one angle. Replay exists to fix the misses that matter most without stopping the game every few minutes, through three separate doors, each with its own rules about who may open it.
Who is in the booth. Two groups of people watch the video. In every stadium a replay official (with an assistant) sits in a booth upstairs with the broadcast feeds; he is an official, not a team employee. In New York, the league’s officiating command center (named Art McNally GameDay Central) watches every game at once. When a review happens, the final decision belongs to the league’s senior vice president of officiating or a designee in New York, consulting the replay official and the referee, who watches on a field-level monitor (a tablet at the sideline). So: the stadium booth starts most reviews, New York decides them, and the referee announces them.6
Each door was added to fix a problem the last one created:7

1986–1991: the first try. An official in the press box could stop the game to review a play; it was slow, overturned little, and was voted out.
1999: the challenge flag. Replay came back with a twist: the coaches would decide which plays to review, by throwing a red flag, and pay for a failed challenge with a timeout. The booth kept control of the final two minutes of each half. The reason: a review stops the clock for a couple of minutes, and a successful challenge costs nothing, so in a close finish a coach could have used a challenge as a free timeout.
2011 and 2012: automatic reviews of every scoring play and every turnover, so a coach no longer had to spend a challenge on the biggest calls.
2017: New York decides. The final say moved from the referee, who had watched replays under a curtained “hood” on the sideline, to New York, so the same few people judge every review.
2019: pass interference, for one season (the story is in Contact Rules and Penalties). Almost nothing was overturned.
2021: replay assist. The booth began fixing clear-cut objective facts on its own, without a formal stop, and its powers grew in 2024, 2025 and 2026 (below).

Every review uses the same standard: the ruling on the field is changed only on clear and obvious visual evidence. That produces the three outcomes in every announcement. Reversed means the video shows the call was wrong. Confirmed means the video shows it was right. Stands means the video doesn’t show enough either way, so the call on the field survives. For the game, “confirmed” and “stands” are the same: the play counts as called, and a coach who challenged loses his timeout either way. The difference is what the video showed, and that is what you can predict: when the camera can’t see the key moment (a ball at the bottom of a pile, a knee hidden by a body), the answer is almost always “stands”.

Door 1: the coach’s challenge
A coach’s challenge is the head coach asking for a review by throwing a red flag onto the field before the next snap. The rules make it scarce on purpose:8

Each team gets two challenges a game. Since 2024 it gets a third if either of the first two succeeds; before that, both had to succeed.
A team must have a timeout left to challenge, and it loses that timeout if the challenge fails.
A coach may not challenge after the two-minute warning of either half, in overtime, or any play the booth reviews automatically (a score, a turnover). A coach who throws his flag anyway is charged a timeout, or 15 yards if he has none left, but the booth still reviews the play if it would have anyway.
Only certain rulings are reviewable: whether a pass was caught, whether a runner was down, in bounds or across the goal line, the spot relative to the line to gain or the goal line, who recovered a loose ball, too many men on the field. Judgment fouls, holding or interference, are not. A flag elsewhere on the play doesn’t block a challenge: a coach can challenge a catch on a play that also had a holding call, and the foul is enforced (or declined) after the ruling is settled.

That third rule has a story. On Thanksgiving 2012, Houston’s Justin Forsett was clearly touched down early in what became an 81-yard touchdown run against Detroit. Lions coach Jim Schwartz, furious, threw his red flag, even though every touchdown was already reviewed by the booth. Under the rule of the time, an illegal challenge drew a 15-yard penalty and cancelled the automatic review, so the touchdown stood unreviewed, and Houston won 34–31 in overtime. The next spring the league changed the penalty to a charged timeout and kept the review.9
Why make challenges expensive? Because a free challenge would be thrown on every close play, and each review costs two or three minutes. The timeout charge turns a challenge into a bet (the chance of winning times what the reversal is worth, against the chance of losing times what a timeout is worth later), which the game-management staff upstairs must make in the few seconds before the next snap. It’s also why an offense that likes the call hurries to the line: once the ball is snapped, the play can’t be challenged (In-Game Adjustments and Tempo).
And it’s why challenges are rarer than you’d guess. In 2025 coaches threw 151 challenges in 272 regular-season games, about 0.28 per team per game, and won 52% of them; over 2016–2025 the success rate was 46%.10 A coach who is right about half the time, and is only betting on plays he’s fairly sure of, is telling you how hard it is to see a play clearly from the sideline in ten seconds.


Door 2: booth review
A booth review is started by the replay official in the stadium (or by New York), not by a coach. It covers:

every scoring play (touchdowns, field goals, safeties) and every try;
every turnover as ruled on the field (an interception, a fumble recovered by the defense or knocked through its end zone, a muffed kick recovered by the kicking team), and every ruling that the offense came up short on fourth down;
every reviewable play after the two-minute warning of each half and in overtime.

Most booth reviews never stop the game: a touchdown is looked at during the celebration, and if the video agrees, the game goes on. If the booth wants a closer look, it buzzes the referee and the game stops. A replay review of either kind ends the same way, with the referee at the middle of the field reading New York’s decision.
A reversal also fixes the clock. The clock is reset to the moment the ball should have been dead and then runs or stops as the correct ruling dictates: an incompletion reversed to a catch in bounds puts the ball where the play should have ended, with the clock running as it would have. After the two-minute warning, a reversal that turns a stopped clock into a running one also brings a 10-second runoff, which either team can avoid only by spending a timeout. Those runoffs, and the end-of-half arithmetic around them, belong to The Clock, the Two-Minute Drill, and Fourth Down.11


Door 3: replay assist
The newest door is the quietest. Replay assist lets the booth tell the crew about a clear-cut objective fact before the next snap, usually with no stoppage you’d notice: the ball was spotted a yard short of the line to gain, the runner’s knee was down before the ball came out, the receiver’s second foot landed out of bounds, two seconds should go back on the clock. It began in 2021 as a way to fix the obvious without a coach gambling a timeout on it.
If the booth can fix a wrong spot for free, why would a coach ever challenge one? Because replay assist acts only when the answer is clear at once, in the few seconds before the next snap. If the booth stays quiet, a coach who thinks a longer look would change the call still has his red flag; the rules say replay assist never takes that away.
Since 2024 it has had a little power over flags, always limited to the objective piece of a foul. In 2024 it could wipe out a roughing-the-passer flag for a hit to the head when the video showed no contact with the head or neck, a grounding flag when the passer was clearly outside the pocket, and a late-hit flag when the runner was clearly still in bounds; the judgment part of roughing (was the hit late?) is still not reviewable. In 2025 it added five more: a hit to a defenseless player’s head or neck, a face mask, a horse-collar tackle, tripping, and roughing or running into the kicker, each only when the video plainly shows the key contact never happened. It cannot add a foul that nobody called. And in 2026 its staff may consult with the crew on ejections for flagrant acts: football acts (a hit during the play so violent it warrants ejection, such as a launch into a defenseless receiver’s head) and non-football acts (a punch away from the play). Some reports describe that as replay ejecting players; the league’s official wording is only that it may consult.12
What the NFL still doesn’t have is a sky judge: an official in the booth with the power to call or wipe out any foul in real time. Spring leagues have used one (the USFL’s sky judge wiped out a wrong face-mask flag in a 2023 playoff game), and the idea has been proposed in the NFL since at least 2019.13 The objections are practical: it would slow the game, and it would make every play (on which, coaches like to say, somebody is holding) a candidate for a flag. So the league has expanded replay one narrow, objective slice at a time.


Show the Python
fig, ax = canvas(6.5, 6.4)
Q, A_B, A_C, A_R, A_N = "#efeee9", style.OFFENSE_TINT, style.DEFENSE_TINT, "#d4efe5", "#f3f2ee"
sx, ox, bx = 21, 60.5, 88.5                    # spine, outcomes column, replay-assist band
fbox(ax, sx, 92, 38, 5.6, "A close call on the field", fc=Q, tfs=8.2)
fbox(ax, sx, 74, 38, 16.5, "Is the ruling reviewable?",
     "catch or no catch, down or not,\nin or out of bounds, the spot at\nthe line to gain or goal line, a\nrecovery, a forward or backward pass",
     fc=Q, tfs=7.6, bfs=6.4)
fbox(ax, sx, 46, 38, 17.0, "Does the booth review it\nautomatically?",
     "a score, a try, a turnover,\nshort on fourth down, or any\nplay after the two-minute\nwarning or in overtime",
     fc=Q, tfs=7.6, bfs=6.4)
fbox(ax, ox, 74, 28, 16.5, "FINAL", "holding, pass interference\nand other judgment calls\ncan't be reviewed (a few\nlisted flags excepted: right)",
     fc=A_N, ec=style.BASELINE, tfs=7.8, bfs=6.3)
fbox(ax, ox, 46, 28, 17.0, "BOOTH REVIEW", "the replay official starts it\nif he wants a closer look;\nNew York decides. A coach's\nflag is illegal (a timeout)",
     fc=A_B, ec=style.OFFENSE, tfs=7.8, bfs=6.3)
fbox(ax, sx, 17.5, 38, 17.0, "COACH'S CHALLENGE", "red flag before the next snap;\nneeds a timeout and loses it if\nit fails; two a game, a third\nif either succeeds",
     fc=A_C, ec=style.DEFENSE, tfs=7.8, bfs=6.3)
farrow(ax, (sx, 89.0), (sx, 82.4))
farrow(ax, (sx + 19.2, 74), (ox - 14.2, 74), "no", toff=(0, 2.4))
farrow(ax, (sx, 65.6), (sx, 54.6), "yes", toff=(3.4, 0))
farrow(ax, (sx + 19.2, 46), (ox - 14.2, 46), "yes", toff=(0, 2.4))
farrow(ax, (sx, 37.4), (sx, 26.1), "no", toff=(3.0, 0))
# replay assist: a band beside every door
fbox(ax, bx, 46, 21, 70, "REPLAY\nASSIST",
     "alongside every door,\non any play, before\nthe next snap:\n\nfixes an objective\nfact that is clear\nat once (the spot,\ncatch, down, out of\nbounds, the clock)\n\nmay wipe out the\nobjective part of a\nlisted flag; never\nadds one\n\nusually no stoppage;\na coach may still\nchallenge",
     fc=A_R, ec=GREEN, tfs=7.8, bfs=6.3)
for y in (74, 46):
    ax.plot([ox + 14.3, bx - 10.7], [y, y], color=GREEN, lw=1.0, ls=(0, (2, 2)), zorder=1)
ax.plot([sx + 19.3, bx - 10.7], [17.5, 17.5], color=GREEN, lw=1.0, ls=(0, (2, 2)), zorder=1)
ax.text(50, 3.0, "2026: New York may also consult with the referee on ejections for flagrant acts.", ha="center",
        va="center", fontsize=6.8, color=style.INK_2,
        bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.35", fc=A_N, ec=style.BASELINE, lw=0.8))
plt.show()








Figure 49.3: Who can review a close call, as of the 2026 season. Ask two questions in order. First: is the ruling reviewable at all? Judgment fouls such as holding and pass interference are not, so the call on the field is final. Second, for a reviewable ruling: is it a play the booth reviews automatically (a score, a try, a turnover, short on fourth down, anything after the two-minute warning or in overtime)? If so the booth decides whether to look; if not, only a coach’s challenge can start a review. Replay assist (right) runs alongside every door: on any play, before the next snap, the booth may fix an objective fact that is clear at once, or wipe out the objective part of a short list of flags.





Now the opening play answers itself. With 1:41 left the game was past the two-minute warning, so the coach couldn’t challenge (had he thrown the flag, he’d have lost a timeout for nothing). The replay official in the stadium started the review, someone in New York decided it, and the referee only announced it. And “control with both feet down in bounds” is two of the three gates of the catch rule, which is next.


What actually gets reviewed
Play-by-play data records a review whenever one changes or stops the game, with the ruling that was reviewed and the result, so you can see where replay earns its keep.


Show the Python
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.9))
ys = np.arange(len(tab))
ax.barh(ys, tab["challenge"], color=style.DEFENSE, height=0.62, label="Coach's challenge")
ax.barh(ys, tab["booth"], left=tab["challenge"], color=style.OFFENSE, height=0.62, label="Booth review")
for y, (_, row) in zip(ys, tab.iterrows()):
    ax.text(row.n + 6, y, f"{100 * row.rev:.0f}% reversed", va="center", ha="left", fontsize=6.9,
            color=style.INK)
ax.set_yticks(ys, [LABELS[k] for k in tab.index], fontsize=7.2)
ax.set_xlim(0, tab["n"].max() * 1.32)
ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
ax.tick_params(axis="x", labelsize=7)
ax.set_xlabel("Reviews, 2021–2025", fontsize=7.6)
ax.legend(loc="lower right", fontsize=7.2)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 49.4: The twelve rulings reviewed most often, 2021–2025 (regular season and playoffs), split by who asked: a coach’s challenge (orange) or the booth (blue). The label gives the share of those reviews that reversed the call. Catch or no catch is by far the busiest question. Don’t read the reversal rates as ‘officials are usually wrong’: every bar is a selected sample. Coaches challenge only when their staff has seen a replay that looks wrong, and the play-by-play generally records a booth review only when it stopped the game, not the routine quick confirmations of every touchdown, so both kinds of review are weighted toward close calls. Source: nflverse play-by-play (the review text in each play’s description).





Two patterns are worth carrying into a game. Catch-or-no-catch rulings make up about 40% of all the recorded reviews, which is why the next section spends so long on the catch. And rulings of a catch are reviewed more than twice as often as rulings of incomplete (overturned at a similar rate: 54% against 49%), partly because the booth looks at every touchdown catch and partly by design: officials rule the play that keeps the ball alive when in doubt, for a reason the 2008 story below makes plain.

49  Officiating, Replay, and the Rules of the Ball

title: Officiating, Replay, and the Rules of the Ball
text:
The catch
Nothing in the rulebook has caused more arguments than the definition of a catch, because of the stakes. If it was a catch and the ball then comes loose, it’s a fumble: a live ball anyone can recover. If it wasn’t, it’s an incomplete pass: dead, and the offense keeps it. So the rule has to separate possessing a ball from merely touching it, at full speed, often while someone is hitting the receiver.
Today’s rule, rewritten in 2018, says a player has made a catch when, in bounds, he does three things in order:14

Control. He secures control of the ball in his hands or arms before it touches the ground.
Feet (or a body part) down. He touches the ground in bounds with both feet, or with any part of his body other than his hands (a knee, a hip, an elbow).
Time. After the first two, he makes an act common to the game: tucks the ball away, turns upfield, takes an extra step, reaches the ball toward the line, wards off a defender. Or he keeps control long enough that he could have.

Three clarifications do most of the work on replays.

Slight movement isn’t a loss of control, and a bobble he then secures is fine, as long as the ball never touches the ground in between.
The ground matters only before gate 3. If he finishes gate 3 on his feet (a third step, a turn, a reach) and then falls and the ball comes out, it was a catch and then a fumble, or simply a catch if he was down by contact. But if he is falling while he catches it, so that he hits the ground before he has had time for any football act, the ground is part of the catch: he must keep control when he lands. If the ball pops loose and touches the ground then, the pass is incomplete.
A tie goes to the offense. If an offensive and a defensive player catch the ball at the same moment and both keep it, it’s the offense’s ball. If one had it first and the other wrestled in, it belongs to the first.

An interception is judged by exactly the same three gates.


Show the Python
fig, ax = canvas(6.5, 5.9)
G, YES, NO = "#efeee9", "#d4efe5", "#fbe3e1"
cx, rx = 32, 80
fbox(ax, cx, 86, 46, 6.0, "The pass arrives", fc=G, tfs=8.2)
gates = [
    (71, "1. Control", "secured in his hands or arms before\nthe ball touches the ground? (slight\nmovement or a bobble he secures is fine)"),
    (51, "2. Feet down in bounds", "both feet, or any body part\nother than his hands?"),
    (31, "3. Time", "an act common to the game (tuck, turn\nupfield, extra step, reach, ward off),\nor control long enough to make one?"),
]
farrow(ax, (cx, 82.9), (cx, 78.4))
for i, (y, t, b) in enumerate(gates):
    fbox(ax, cx, y, 46, 13.4, t, b, fc=G, tfs=7.8, bfs=6.5)
    nxt = gates[i + 1][0] + 6.8 if i < 2 else 15.6
    farrow(ax, (cx, y - 6.8), (cx, nxt), "yes", toff=(3.4, 0))
fbox(ax, rx, 71, 30, 10.5, "INCOMPLETE", "he never secured it before\nit hit the ground", fc=NO, ec=RED)
fbox(ax, rx, 51, 30, 10.5, "INCOMPLETE", "out of bounds (in the\nend zone: no touchdown)", fc=NO, ec=RED)
fbox(ax, rx, 31, 30, 12.0, "HIT THE GROUND FIRST", "falling as he caught it, or\nlanding out of bounds: did he\nkeep control through it?", fc="#fdf3d8",
     ec=style.LINE_TO_GAIN, tfs=7.2)
fbox(ax, rx, 11, 30, 8.0, "INCOMPLETE", "the ball came loose", fc=NO, ec=RED)
for y in (71, 51):
    farrow(ax, (cx + 23.2, y), (rx - 15.2, y), "no", toff=(0, 1.9))
farrow(ax, (cx + 23.2, 31), (rx - 15.2, 31), "not yet", toff=(0, 1.9))
farrow(ax, (rx, 24.9), (rx, 15.1), "no", toff=(3.0, 0))
fbox(ax, cx, 9.5, 46, 12.0, "CATCH", "if the ball comes loose now: a fumble\n(live ball). If he's in the end zone,\nor reaches it over the line: touchdown", fc=YES,
     ec=GREEN, tfs=8.6)
farrow(ax, (rx - 15.2, 27.5), (cx + 23.4, 13.5), "yes, kept it", toff=(2.0, 2.2))
plt.show()








Figure 49.5: The catch rule as a replay official applies it (NFL rule since 2018). A pass must pass all three gates in order. Failing gate 1 or 2 means incomplete. At gate 3, a receiver who hasn’t yet had time for a football act when he hits the ground (or lands out of bounds) must keep control through it, or the pass is incomplete. Once gate 3 is passed, losing the ball means a catch and then a fumble. The same test decides an interception.






Why the rule was rewritten
For most of the 2010s the rule had an extra clause that produced some of the most hated rulings in league history. A receiver who went to the ground “in the process of the catch” had to keep control of the ball after hitting the ground, the so-called survive the ground requirement, no matter how many steps he had taken or how obviously he had possessed it. The clause was meant to make the rule objective: instead of asking officials to judge whether a player had possession long enough, it gave them a test they could see on video. The trouble was that the objective test kept ruling against what everyone watching had seen. Three plays made it untenable:15

Calvin Johnson, Lions at Bears, September 12, 2010. Trailing 19–14 with 31 seconds left, Johnson caught a pass in the end zone, landed with both feet and his backside, and put the ball down on the turf as he rolled to get up. Ruled incomplete; the booth upheld it. The Lions lost by five, and “the Calvin Johnson rule” entered the vocabulary.
Dez Bryant, Cowboys at Packers, divisional playoffs, January 11, 2015. On fourth-and-2 late in the game, Bryant caught a deep ball, took three steps as he fell, reached for the goal line, and the ball moved when it hit the turf at the 1. Ruled a catch, reversed on Green Bay’s challenge; the Packers won (the Film room below walks through it).
Jesse James, Patriots at Steelers, December 17, 2017. With 34 seconds left and Pittsburgh down 27–24, James caught a short pass a few yards from the goal line, went to a knee untouched (so he wasn’t down: in the NFL a runner needs contact, as the next section explains), and lunged across the goal line; the ball moved as it hit the turf. Ruled a touchdown, reversed by the booth. The Steelers lost the game and, as it turned out, home-field advantage in the playoffs.

The owners approved a rewrite 32–0 in March 2018. Here is precisely what changed. Under the old rule, a receiver who went to the ground “in the process of the catch” had to survive the ground however many steps or reaches he had made on the way down: falling cancelled them. Under the new rule, a football act made before the ball comes loose (a third step, a reach for the line, or time enough to make one) finishes the catch, even if he is falling, and only a receiver who hits the ground before he has made one must still survive it. (The 2018 announcement said “football move”; the rulebook says “act common to the game”.) The league’s football chiefs said publicly that Bryant’s and James’s catches would now count.16
Would Calvin Johnson’s? Try it with the gates. Control: yes, high in the end zone. Feet: both feet, then his backside. Time: the argument. He went to the ground as he caught it, so he must keep control through the landing unless he had time for a football act first. If you see him land, hold the ball, and only then use it to push himself up, he had the time, and it’s a touchdown today. If you see one continuous fall with the ball coming loose as part of it, it’s still incomplete. The league never ruled on it publicly, and that is the honest answer: it’s a judgment about time.
Name the trade: the old rule was objective and produced absurd results; the new one matches what people see, at the price of a judgment (“was that lunge a football act or part of the fall?”) at its center.






CautionCommon misconception



“The ball touched the ground, so it’s incomplete.” The ball is allowed to touch the ground during a catch, as long as the receiver keeps control of it, with his hands under it or the ball pinned to his body. What it can’t do is help him: a ball trapped against the turf with no hand under it, or one that pops loose when he lands before he has had time for a football act, is incomplete.




Sidelines and end zones
Two places put extra weight on gate 2. At the sideline, a receiver needs both feet (or another body part) down in bounds with control; one foot, as in college football, isn’t enough. Since 2008 there has been no “force-out” ruling either: a receiver pushed out of bounds in the air before getting both feet down has not caught the ball, however sure the official is that he would have landed in bounds (unless he had control and was held up and carried out).17 And because a toe-tap leaves no time for a football act, he must keep control as he falls out; a ball jarred loose when he hits the ground out of bounds is incomplete.
In the end zone, the catch is the touchdown, so the receiver must complete all three gates there; a runner who already has the ball only needs it to touch the plane of the goal line (the end zone is generous that way). A receiver who completes the catch short of the line and then reaches across has scored, which is how Jesse James’s play would be ruled today.

title: Officiating, Replay, and the Rules of the Ball
text:
Down, progress and the whistle
Most plays end with a ball carrier going down, and the NFL’s definition differs from college’s. A runner is down by contact when any part of his body other than his hands or feet touches the ground and he has been touched by an opponent. The order of those two can go either way. If nobody touched him, he isn’t down: a running back who slips on wet turf, or a returner who kneels to field a bouncing kick, may get up and keep running. But if a defender touches him while he is on the ground, he is down right there, which is why defenders are coached to “touch him down” rather than assume the play is over. In college football the runner is down as soon as his knee touches, contact or not.18 (A runner who slides feet-first or simply gives himself up is down where he does it; that’s how quarterbacks protect themselves.)
The order of events matters more than anything else on these plays. If the ball comes out before the knee (or elbow, or hip) touches after contact, it’s a fumble: live, and anyone’s. If the knee touches first, the runner was down and the ball coming out afterward doesn’t matter. On television these are separated by a few frames of video, which is why they’re among the most-reviewed rulings in the data above.


Show the Python
fig, ax = canvas(6.5, 2.5, xmax=100, ymax=39)
rows = [
    (31.0, [(10, "contact"), (31, "ball comes out"), (52, "knee down")], "FUMBLE", "live ball: anyone may recover", RED),
    (19.5, [(10, "contact"), (31, "knee down"), (52, "ball comes out")], "DOWN", "dead: ball spotted where it was\nwhen the knee touched", GREEN),
    (8.0, [(10, "slips, untouched"), (31, "knee down"), (52, "gets up, runs on")], "NOT DOWN", "unless touched while on the\nground (college: down)", style.OFFENSE_DARK),
]
ax.text(3, 37.0, "time →", fontsize=7.0, color=style.INK_2, ha="left", va="center")
for y, evs, verdict, sub, col in rows:
    ax.plot([3, 62], [y, y], color=style.BASELINE, lw=1.2, zorder=1)
    for i, (x, lab) in enumerate(evs):
        ax.plot(x, y, marker="o", ms=7, color=col if i == 1 else style.INK_2, zorder=3)
        ax.text(x, y + 2.6, lab, fontsize=6.9, ha="center", va="center", color=style.INK, zorder=4)
    ax.text(66, y + 1.3, verdict, fontsize=8.2, fontweight="bold", color=col, ha="left", va="center")
    ax.text(66, y - 1.4, sub, fontsize=6.5, color=style.INK_2, ha="left", va="top", linespacing=1.1)
plt.show()








Figure 49.6: Down or fumble? It depends on the order of three events: the defender’s contact, the ball coming loose, and the runner’s knee (or any body part other than a hand or foot) touching the ground. Top: the ball comes out first, so it’s a fumble and the ball is live. Middle: the knee touches first, after contact, so he’s down and the play is dead before the ball comes loose. Bottom: nobody touched him, so in the NFL he isn’t down; he can get up and keep running, unless a defender touches him while he’s on the ground (in college he’d be down at once). Either way, the ball is spotted where it was when he went down, not where his knee was.





Forward progress decides where the play ended. You met it in Downs, Distance, and Field Position: the ball is spotted at the farthest point it reached toward the goal line before the runner was stopped, not where he ended up after a pile drove him back. The same idea tells officials when to blow the whistle. A runner wrapped up and held upright, his legs still churning, has had his forward progress stopped even though he hasn’t gone down, and the officials will whistle the play dead rather than let a pile of defenders keep shoving him backward (or strip the ball from a man who has stopped moving forward). It also protects runners at the goal line: a back who gets the ball across the plane and is knocked back has scored. (Only being driven back counts: a quarterback who retreats on his own and is sacked is spotted where he goes down.) And it affects the clock: a runner stopped in bounds and then shoved out of bounds was down in bounds, so the clock keeps running, a detail that matters in the two-minute drill.

The whistle, and the 2008 lesson
The whistle is the one tool officials can’t take back. Once it blows, the play is dead, whatever happens next. (When one is blown by mistake with the ball still live, the team with the ball can usually take it where the whistle killed the play or replay the down; a pass in the air is simply replayed.)19 That used to put replay in an impossible position: if an official ruled a play over and the video showed a fumble, replay could fix the ruling but couldn’t know who would have recovered the ball.
The play that made everyone face this came on September 14, 2008. Denver trailed San Diego 38–31 with 1:17 left, second-and-goal at the 1. Jay Cutler dropped back, and the ball slipped out of his hand as he started to throw; a Charger fell on it. Referee Ed Hochuli ruled it an incomplete pass and blew his whistle. Replay showed a fumble, but because the whistle had already killed the play, the Chargers couldn’t be given the ball. Denver kept it at the 10, where Cutler had lost it, scored on fourth-and-goal with 29 seconds left, went for two, and won 39–38.20 Hochuli, one of the most respected referees of his era, publicly apologized.
Two things changed. In 2009 the owners passed what was quickly nicknamed the “Hochuli rule”: replay may now award the ball to the team that recovered it when the recovery is clear and in the immediate continuing action, even after a whistle.21 And the officials’ habit changed: on a bang-bang fumble, they are taught to hold the whistle, let the players finish the scramble for the ball, and rule a fumble when in doubt, because replay can turn a fumble back into a dead ball cleanly but can’t recreate a recovery that never happened. That is why you now see a defender scoop up a loose ball and run the other way while everyone else has stopped.

title: Officiating, Replay, and the Rules of the Ball
section: Pass or fumble: the quarterback’s arm
text:
Pass or fumble: the quarterback’s arm
A close cousin of down-or-fumble is pass-or-fumble, and it comes up every time a pass rusher hits a quarterback as he throws. The rule is about the arm. Once the quarterback, holding the ball, starts his arm moving forward to throw, anything that comes out is a forward pass, and if it hits the ground it’s incomplete. If he loses the ball before his arm starts forward, or while he is pulling it back down to tuck it after deciding not to throw, it’s a fumble.
The second half of that sentence was not always true. Until 2013 the rulebook had the tuck rule: if the quarterback started forward and then brought the ball back toward his body, it was still a pass until he had tucked it all the way in. It is remembered for the snowy January 2002 playoff in Foxborough, when Tom Brady lost the ball under Charles Woodson’s hit, the Raiders recovered, and replay called it an incomplete pass; New England kept the ball and won in overtime. The league abolished the rule in 2013.22 Today the same play is a fumble.
Who reviews it depends on the call on the field. When the field rules a fumble that the defense recovered, it’s a turnover, so the booth reviews it automatically. When the field rules an incomplete pass, there’s no turnover to trigger the booth, so before the two-minute warning the defense’s coach usually has to throw his red flag (unless replay assist steps in on the possession), which is the moment you see a coach grab it on a strip-sack ruled incomplete. Either way, watch the arm, not the ball: if the arm was coming forward with the ball in the hand, it’s a pass.
