title: Officiating, Replay, and the Rules of the Ball
section: A fumble through the end zone
text:
A fumble through the end zone
Now the harshest rule in the book. When a fumble goes out of bounds, the general rule is generous to the team that fumbled: it keeps the ball. If the ball went out going backward, it’s spotted where it went out; if it went out going forward, it comes back to the spot of the fumble, so that nobody gains yards by fumbling forward on purpose.
The exception is the opponent’s end zone. A fumble through the end zone, a ball fumbled forward into the end zone that goes out of bounds there, out the side or out the back, is a touchback: the defense gets the ball at its own 20, even though no defender ever touched it.23 A fumble that stays in the end zone is simpler: if the offense falls on it there, it’s a touchdown (on fourth down or late in a half, only the man who fumbled may, as the box below explains); if the defense does, it’s a touchback. And the mirror image works against the offense in its own end zone: a ball it fumbles there that goes out of bounds (or one it fumbles in the field that it sends back into its own end zone and out) is a safety, because the offense supplied the push that put the ball there.


Show the Python
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(6.5, 3.9))
cases = [
    ((-2.0, 18.0), (2.0, 19.2), [(2.0, 19.2), (3.2, 21.4), (4.0, 23.58), (4.3, 24.8)], "offense's ball\nat the 4", (2.0, 12.2), style.OFFENSE_DARK),
    ((-1.5, 18.5), (5.0, 21.0), [(5.0, 21.0), (7.8, 22.4), (11.5, 23.58), (12.2, 24.8)], "touchback:\ndefense's ball\nat its 20", (11.6, 14.2), RED),
    ((-1.0, 16.5), (2.0, 19.5), [(2.0, 19.5), (0.5, 21.6), (-2.0, 23.58), (-2.6, 24.8)], "offense's ball\nat the 8", (-4.6, 15.5), style.OFFENSE_DARK),
]
for ax, (start, fum, ballpath, verdict, vat, col) in zip(axes, cases):
    rb = O("RB", "RB", start[0], start[1], "R")
    q = Play([rb], [D("DB", "DB", fum[0] + 1.0, fum[1] - 2.3, "D")], los=104, ball_y="right", to_go=None)
    q.run("RB", [fum], absolute=True)
    fld = q.draw(ax=ax, lateral=(7.0, 29.5), window=(-6.5, 16.5), title=False)
    no_numbers(ax)
    say(fld, q, 2.0, 26.6, "out of bounds", fs=5.6, box=False, rot=90)
    for dd, lab in ((1.0, "5"), (-4.0, "10")):
        say(fld, q, dd + 0.6, 9.0, lab, fs=5.8, color=style.MUTED, box=False)
    xmark(fld, q, *fum)
    path_arrow(fld, q, ballpath)
    say(fld, q, vat[0], vat[1], verdict, color=col, fs=6.6, weight="bold")
    say(fld, q, 6.0, 12.0, "goal line", fs=5.8, color=style.INK_2)
    say(fld, q, 14.4, 11.0, "end line", fs=5.8, color=style.INK_2)
    say(fld, q, -0.9, 11.8, "line of scrimmage", fs=5.0, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK)
for ax, lab in zip(axes, ["Forward, out at the 2", "Into the end zone, out", "Backward, out at the 8"]):
    ax.set_title(lab, fontsize=7.8, color=style.INK, loc="left", fontweight="bold")
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.4)
plt.show()








Figure 49.7: Three fumbles out of bounds near the goal line, offense moving up the page. Left: the ball squirts forward and out at the 2: the offense keeps it, but back at the 4, the spot of the fumble, because a forward fumble can’t gain ground. Middle: knocked loose at the 1, it bounces into the end zone and out the side: a touchback, and the defense takes over at its own 20. Right: the ball goes backward and out at the 8: the offense keeps it where it went out. The X marks the fumble (D is the defender who knocked it loose), the dashed brown line the ball’s path.





Why would the rules punish the offense so hard? The logic is about territory, not possession. The end zone belongs to the defending team, and when a ball goes dead there because of something the other team did (a punt rolls through, a kickoff sails out the back), it’s a touchback, like the touchbacks on punts. A fumble into your end zone and out is treated the same way. The rule is consistent; it just doesn’t feel fair, because the defense did nothing to earn it. It is one of the most criticized rules in the book; the competition committee looked at softening it in 2017 and again in February 2024 and kept it both times, arguing that the ball carrier is responsible for the ball and that nobody had a workable alternative. It is unchanged in the 2026 rulebook.24
The rule shapes technique: it’s why a ball carrier stretching for the pylon is taking a real gamble, and why defenders near the goal line punch at the ball instead of wrapping up.






ImportantWhy it exists: the fourth-down fumble rule



On September 10, 1978, with the Raiders trailing the Chargers in the final seconds, Ken Stabler, about to be sacked, fumbled the ball forward; teammates batted and kicked it toward the goal line, and Dave Casper fell on it in the end zone for the winning touchdown. The “Holy Roller” was legal then. The next season the league made it impossible: on fourth down, and on any down after the two-minute warning, only the player who fumbled may recover and advance the ball. If a teammate recovers it, the ball comes back to the spot of the fumble (or the spot of recovery, if that is behind it).25 The rule exists to stop an offense from fumbling forward on purpose when it has nothing left to lose.

title: Officiating, Replay, and the Rules of the Ball
text:
Backward passes and forward passes
Football allows exactly one forward pass per play, and it must be thrown from behind the line of scrimmage. It allows any number of backward passes (also called laterals), from anywhere, by anyone, at any time. The two are treated very differently when they hit the ground:

A forward pass that hits the ground is incomplete. The ball is dead, and the offense keeps it.
A backward pass that hits the ground is still live, exactly like a fumble. Either team may recover it, and either team may advance it.

Which is which? The test is the ball’s direction: compare the yard line where it left the passer’s hand with the yard line where it is first touched (or first hits the ground). If the second is closer to the opponent’s goal, the pass was forward. If it’s the same yard line or behind, the pass was backward, so a pass thrown perfectly parallel to the line counts as backward.26 Notice that it’s the ball’s path that counts, not the players’ positions on the field. (This chapter calls the yard line where the ball leaves the passer’s hand the release line; that’s our label for the diagrams, not a rulebook term.)
The forward pass’s two limits are fouls of their own, and the line judge watches for the first. A forward pass is illegal if the passer’s entire body and the ball are beyond the line of scrimmage when he lets go, which is the call you see on a quarterback who scrambles up to the line and flips it at the last moment: one foot still behind the line keeps it legal. A second forward pass on the same play is illegal too. Either costs a loss of down and 5 yards.


Show the Python
off = offense("gun_2x2")
off = [q.moved(w=2.6) if q.key == "RB" else q for q in off]
lp = Play(off, None, los=40, to_go=None)
lp.path("RB", [(-6.0, 4.6), (-6.4, 7.8)], absolute=True)           # swings out to take the pitch
lp.path("H", [(-3.2, -10.2), (-5.1, -10.9), (-5.4, -10.6)], absolute=True)   # the bubble: bows back
fld = lp.draw(lateral=(-19.5, 19.5), window=(-12.0, 4.5), title=False)
ax = fld.ax
no_numbers(ax)
rel = (-5.4, 0.3)
x0, y0 = XY(fld, lp, rel[0], -18.0)
x1, y1 = XY(fld, lp, rel[0], 18.0)
ax.plot([x0, x1], [y0, y1], color=PURPLE, lw=1.2, ls=(0, (4, 3)), zorder=2)
say(fld, lp, -4.4, -15.6, "release line", color=PURPLE, fs=6.6, weight="bold")
for tgt, col, lab, lat in [((-6.6, 7.4), GREEN, "1  backward:\nlive if dropped", (-9.6, 7.6)),
                           ((-5.4, -10.6), GREEN, "2  parallel = backward:\nlive if dropped", (-8.8, -10.0)),
                           ((-0.9, 14.0), RED, "3  forward:\nincomplete if dropped", (1.9, 9.4))]:
    path_arrow(fld, lp, [rel, tgt], color=style.BALL, lw=1.5)
    say(fld, lp, lat[0], lat[1], lab, color=col, fs=6.6, weight="bold")
say(fld, lp, 1.0, -3.0, "line of scrimmage", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fs=6.2)
plt.show()








Figure 49.8: Forward or backward is decided by the yard line where the ball leaves the passer’s hand (dashed ‘release line’) and the yard line where it’s first touched. From the shotgun, the quarterback catches the snap five yards deep. A pitch to the running back (1), who has swung out to the right and slightly back, is caught behind the release line: a backward pass, live if it hits the ground. A bubble screen (2) to the slot receiver, who has bowed back from his alignment to the release line, is parallel, which counts as backward. A quick screen to the outside receiver (3) is caught about five yards ahead of the release line: a forward pass, incomplete (and dead) if it’s dropped.





Why does a dropped backward pass stay live? Because the rules treat it as the normal case. A backward pass is just a handoff through the air: the ball stays a runner’s ball, and if he doesn’t catch it, it’s loose, like any fumble. The forward pass is the special case, the one the rules ration (one per play, from behind the line) and give a special ending: when it fails, the play stops and the offense keeps the ball, paying with the down. The result shows up in three places on a broadcast:

Pitches and option plays. A pitch on the option is a backward pass. Drop it and you’ve fumbled, in effect, which is why option teams drill the pitch relentlessly.
Screens. Most shotgun screens are forward passes, caught closer to the line than the five or six yards deep where the quarterback let go. But a bubble or swing screen to a player who has drifted back level with the quarterback may be backward, so defenders are coached to scoop up every dropped screen and run: if it was backward, the ball is theirs. (The illegal-man-downfield rule applies only to a forward pass thrown beyond the line, so on a true backward pass linemen may already be blocking downfield.)
Last-play desperation. The multi-lateral kickoff return or final snap, the ball pitched backward again and again, is legal because every pitch is backward.

The most famous backward pass in NFL history came in a wild-card game on January 8, 2000, on a kickoff with 16 seconds left: Tennessee’s Frank Wycheck threw the ball across the field to Kevin Dyson, who ran 75 yards for the winning touchdown. Replay couldn’t show that the throw had gone forward, so the ruling of a legal lateral stood, and the “Music City Miracle” became the standard illustration of the rule.27

title: Officiating, Replay, and the Rules of the Ball
section: Intentional grounding and the tackle box
text:
Intentional grounding and the tackle box
Quarterback Play introduced the throwaway and the rule that limits it. Here is the full rule, and the reasoning behind it.
Intentional grounding is a foul when a passer who is facing an imminent loss of yardage because of the rush throws a pass that isn’t in the direction and vicinity of an eligible receiver. (The rulebook says originally eligible: eligible when the ball was snapped, so a lineman who has wandered downfield doesn’t count as a target.) Three conditions, all needed:28

Pressure. He must be facing a likely sack. A quarterback under no pressure who throws the ball into the turf has wasted a down, but he hasn’t grounded it.
No realistic target. The pass isn’t thrown near an eligible receiver. “Near” is a judgment, and throwing the ball well over the head of a covered receiver in the right part of the field counts.
Inside the tackle box. The tackle box, which the rulebook calls the pocket area, is the region between the outside edges of where the two offensive tackles lined up, running from the line of scrimmage all the way back to the offense’s own end line. It’s fixed by where the tackles aligned at the snap: a tight end lined up outside a tackle doesn’t widen it, and it doesn’t move when the quarterback does.

The exception is what makes the box matter: a passer who is or has been outside the tackle box may throw the ball away freely, as long as it lands at or beyond the line of scrimmage (extended to the sidelines), including out of bounds past it. Since the 2024 rulebook he counts as outside the box if any part of his body, or the ball, is outside it. And “has been” means what it says: a quarterback who escapes the box and then drifts back inside it keeps the exception for the rest of the play.
The penalty is built to cost about what the sack would have: loss of down and 10 yards from the previous spot, or loss of down at the spot of the pass if that is farther back, and a safety if he throws it from his own end zone. The other exception is the spike: a quarterback who throws the ball straight into the ground immediately after the snap, to stop the clock, loses only the down (more in The Clock, the Two-Minute Drill, and Fourth Down).


Show the Python
off = offense("gun_2x2")
off = [q for q in off if q.key in ("LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT", "Y")]
off = [q.moved(d=7.5, w=8.0) if q.key == "Y" else q for q in off]
gp = Play(off + [O("QB", "QB", -6.0, 0.0, "A")],
          [D("LB", "MIKE", 9.0, 9.2, "M"), D("E1", "DE", -4.8, -2.2, "E"), D("E2", "DE", -5.2, 2.0, "T"),
           D("E3", "DE", -6.4, 9.4, "E")],                     # closing on quarterback B
          los=14, ball_y="right", to_go=None)
fld = gp.draw(lateral=(-20.5, 27.2), window=(-14.5, 15.5), title=False)
ax = fld.ax
no_numbers(ax)
tackle_box(ax, fld, gp, -14.0)
qbB = (-7.5, 12.5)
draw_marker(ax, *XY(fld, gp, *qbB), "off", "B", fld.pts_per_yard())
path_arrow(fld, gp, [(-6.0, 0.0), (-1.0, -3.5), (6.0, -6.0)], color=RED, lw=1.6)
path_arrow(fld, gp, [(-6.0, 0.0), (5.0, 6.0), (11.0, 9.0)], color=GREEN, lw=1.6)
path_arrow(fld, gp, [qbB, (2.5, 24.4)], color=GREEN, lw=1.6)
path_arrow(fld, gp, [qbB, (-3.2, 24.4)], color=RED, lw=1.6)
say(fld, gp, 8.8, -8.5, "1  grounding: inside the box,\nthe line doesn't help (safety)", color=RED, fs=6.8, weight="bold")
say(fld, gp, 12.8, 5.0, "2  legal: near Y", color=GREEN, fs=6.8, weight="bold")
say(fld, gp, 5.4, 15.8, "3  legal: out of\nbounds past the line", color=GREEN, fs=6.8, weight="bold")
say(fld, gp, -11.0, 16.6, "4  grounding: short\nof the line (safety)", color=RED, fs=6.8, weight="bold")
say(fld, gp, -11.7, 0.0, "tackle box\n(back to the end line)", color=PURPLE, fs=6.4, weight="bold")
say(fld, gp, -3.0, -10.5, "goal line", fs=6.0)
say(fld, gp, 1.2, -16.0, "line of scrimmage", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fs=6.2)
say(fld, gp, -9.0, -12.0, "end zone", fs=6.4, color=style.INK_2)
xs_, ys_ = XY(fld, gp, 6.0, 25.3)
ax.text(xs_, ys_, "out of bounds", rotation=90, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=6.0, color=style.INK_2)
plt.show()








Figure 49.9: Intentional grounding backed up at the offense’s own 4, where the tackle box (shaded) runs back into the end zone. Quarterback A, inside the box and in his end zone, throws to an empty part of the field (1): grounding, and from the end zone that’s a safety. Throwing it over the covered tight end’s head instead (2) is a legal throwaway. Quarterback B has escaped the box with a defender closing: throwing it out of bounds past the line of scrimmage (3) is legal even though no one is near, but a throw that lands out of bounds short of the line (4) is grounding, also a safety from the end zone. Notice that throw 1 lands past the line too: inside the box, reaching the line doesn’t help.





Why draw the line at the box? A sack is something the defense earned. If a quarterback could always throw the ball into the ground to avoid one, the pass rush would lose much of its value, so inside the pocket, where the defense has him trapped, he must at least throw toward someone. A quarterback who has escaped the pocket has beaten the rush himself; letting him throw it away (provided it reaches the line, so he can’t just dump it at his feet) rewards the escape. The 2024 wording tilted that balance a little further his way.
The best-known grounding call of recent decades shows the safety clause at work: on New England’s first offensive play of Super Bowl XLVI, February 5, 2012, Tom Brady, pressured in his own end zone, threw deep down the middle to nobody. Grounding from the end zone is a safety, and the Giants led 2–0 before the Patriots had gained a yard. They won by four.29
The “has been outside” clause is the subtle part, and it’s easiest to see in motion.


Show the Python
off = offense("gun_2x2")
dfn = defense("nickel", "two_high", off)
dfn = [q.moved(d=6.0, w=-3.5) if q.key == "WILL" else q for q in dfn]
sp = Play(off, dfn, los=40, to_go=10)
for k in ("X", "Z"):
    sp.route(k, r.go(12))
for k in ("H", "Y"):
    sp.route(k, r.seam(11))
for dk, rk in (("LCB", "X"), ("RCB", "Z"), ("NB", "H"), ("SS", "Y")):
    sp.man(dk, rk)
for k in ("LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT"):                  # the line sets and holds
    sp.block(k, pts=[(-1.3, 0.0)])
sp.block("RB", pts=[(0.6, -2.2)])                        # the back stays in to block
# the quarterback: drops, is flushed well right (out of the box), then steps back up inside it
sp.path("QB", [(-2.0, 0.0), (-2.8, 8.5), (-1.0, 1.5)], speed=5.0)
sp.path("SDT", [(-0.4, 0.9)], absolute=True); sp.path("WDT", [(-0.4, -0.9)], absolute=True)
sp.path("WDE", [(-3.5, -4.5), (-7.0, -1.2), (-8.8, 0.6)], absolute=True, speed=5.5)   # flushes him, overruns
sp.path("SDE", [(-1.8, 4.6)], absolute=True)                                            # held up by the tackle...
sp.path("SDE", [(-6.0, 10.8)], absolute=True, delay=1.0)                                # ...then closes outside
sp.drop("MIKE", (6.0, 2.5)); sp.drop("FS", (13.0, -7.0))
trk = sp.to_tracking(t_after=2.4)
trk = trk[trk.time <= 4.6].copy()
T_THROW, LAND = 3.5, (2.5, -5.5)                         # lands past the line, in open grass
qb_at = sp.position("QB", T_THROW)
ball = trk.side == "ball"
pre = ball & (trk.time > 0.15) & (trk.time < T_THROW)       # carried in his right hand, not over his face
trk.loc[pre, "y"] -= 0.8
m = ball & (trk.time >= T_THROW)
tt = trk.loc[m, "time"].to_numpy()
T_FLIGHT = np.hypot(*(np.array(LAND) - qb_at)) / 16.0
f = np.clip((tt - T_THROW) / T_FLIGHT, 0, 1)
bd = qb_at[0] + f * (LAND[0] - qb_at[0])
bw = qb_at[1] + f * (LAND[1] - qb_at[1])
trk.loc[m, "x"], trk.loc[m, "y"] = sp.to_abs(bd, bw)
GNOTES = [("inside the box:\nthrow near a receiver", PURPLE), ("well outside:\nexception on", GREEN),
          ("back inside, but has\nbeen outside: still on", GREEN), ("lands past the line:\nlegal throwaway", GREEN)]


def g_decor(fld, t):
    tackle_box(fld.ax, fld, sp, -13.0, alpha=0.12)
    if t >= T_THROW:                                    # the ball's flight so far
        g = min(1.0, (t - T_THROW) / T_FLIGHT)
        end = (qb_at[0] + g * (LAND[0] - qb_at[0]), qb_at[1] + g * (LAND[1] - qb_at[1]))
        if g > 0.05:
            path_arrow(fld, sp, [tuple(qb_at), end], color=style.BALL, lw=1.6, head=10)


def g_notes(fld, i, t):
    txt, col = GNOTES[i]
    say(fld, sp, -10.8, -12.0, txt, color=col, fs=6.6 if PDF else 8.0, weight="bold")


show_scene(sp, trk, [0.4, 2.1, 3.4, 4.4], window=(-13.5, 15.5), lateral=(-19.5, 19.5), decor=g_decor,
           notes=g_notes)





  
  Your browser does not support the video tag.



Figure 49.10: Once outside, always outside (simulated tracking in Big Data Bowl format; an illustrative play). 0.4 s: the quarterback finishes his drop in the middle of the tackle box (shaded), so a throwaway must go near a receiver. 2.1 s: pressure flushes him to his right, well outside the box; the grounding exception is now on. 3.4 s: he steps back up inside the box, but he has been outside, so the exception stays on for the rest of the play. 4.4 s: he has thrown it away (dashed brown line) into open grass on the left, away from every receiver, and it landed past the line of scrimmage: legal, no flag. section: The measurement: chains, cameras, and the spot
text:
The measurement: chains, cameras, and the spot
Downs, Distance, and Field Position described the chain crew’s ritual: two sticks joined by ten yards of chain, carried onto the field to see whether the ball’s nose had reached the front stick. Since 2025 that walk is mostly gone. A virtual measurement, often called a Hawk-Eye measurement after the Sony system that does it, uses six 8K cameras around the stadium to measure the distance from where the ball sits to the line to gain, and hands the answer to the officials in about 30 seconds, while a virtual graphic of the measurement plays on the broadcast and the stadium screens. The chain crew stays on the sideline as the visible marker for players and coaches, and as a backup if the cameras fail.30


Show the Python
q = Play([], None, los=62.0, ball_y="middle", to_go=None)   # d = yards past where this series began
LTG, NOSE = 10.0, 9.85                                     # line to gain; the ball's nose, about 5 inches short
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.5, 4.0), gridspec_kw=dict(width_ratios=[1.25, 1]))


def ball_shape(ax, fld, w=0.0, scale=1.0):
    bx, by = XY(fld, q, NOSE - 0.155 * scale, w)
    ax.add_patch(Ellipse((bx, by), 0.19 * scale, 0.31 * scale, fc=style.BALL, ec="white", lw=0.6, zorder=9))


def ltg_line(ax, fld, w0, w1):
    (x0, y0), (x1, y1) = XY(fld, q, LTG, w0), XY(fld, q, LTG, w1)
    ax.plot([x0, x1], [y0, y1], color=style.LINE_TO_GAIN, lw=2.2, zorder=3)


# left: the chain crew's measurement on the field
ax = axes[0]
fld = Field(ax=ax, orient="vertical", los=69.0, window=(-8.0, 6.0), to_go=None,
            lateral=(MIDDLE - 6.5, MIDDLE + 6.5))
no_numbers(ax)
for ln in list(ax.lines):                       # the line of scrimmage Field draws is not part of this story
    if ln.get_color() == style.OFFENSE_DARK:
        ln.remove()
ltg_line(ax, fld, -6.5, 6.5)
ball_shape(ax, fld, scale=3.0)
for d_ in (0.0, LTG):
    ax.plot(*XY(fld, q, d_, 0.6), marker="s", ms=6, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, zorder=10)
ax.plot(*zip(XY(fld, q, 0.0, 0.6), XY(fld, q, LTG, 0.6)), color=style.INK_2, lw=1.0, ls=(0, (1, 1)), zorder=8)
ax.plot(*XY(fld, q, 3.0, 0.6), marker="D", ms=4.5, color=style.INK, zorder=10)
say(fld, q, 0.3, 3.2, "rear stick", fs=6.4)
say(fld, q, 3.0, 3.8, "clip laid on the\nnearest 5-yard\nstripe", fs=6.4)
say(fld, q, 11.0, 3.2, "front stick", fs=6.4)
say(fld, q, 10.9, -3.6, "line to gain", fs=6.4, color=style.INK)
say(fld, q, 8.0, -2.8, "the ball\n(not to scale)", fs=6.2, color=style.BALL, weight="bold")
ax.set_title("Until 2024: the chains walk out", fontsize=8.2, loc="left", fontweight="bold", color=style.INK)
# right: a close-up of the same spot, where the cameras measure
ax = axes[1]
fld = Field(ax=ax, orient="vertical", los=62.0 + LTG, window=(-1.0, 0.9), to_go=None,
            lateral=(MIDDLE - 0.95, MIDDLE + 0.95), hashes=False, numbers=False)
xl, yl = ax.get_xlim(), ax.get_ylim()           # Field pads half a yard; at this zoom, drop the pad
ax.set_xlim(xl[0] + 0.5, xl[1] - 0.5); ax.set_ylim(yl[0] + 0.5, yl[1] - 0.5)
ltg_line(ax, fld, -0.95, 0.95)
band = [XY(fld, q, *pt) for pt in [(NOSE - 0.33, -0.95), (NOSE - 0.33, 0.95), (NOSE + 0.33, 0.95), (NOSE + 0.33, -0.95)]]
ax.add_patch(Polygon(band, closed=True, fc=style.DEFENSE, alpha=0.10, ec="none", zorder=2))
ball_shape(ax, fld)
(mx, my0), (_, my1) = XY(fld, q, NOSE, 0.28), XY(fld, q, LTG, 0.28)
ax.annotate("", xy=(mx, my1), xytext=(mx, my0), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="<->", color=GREEN, lw=1.3,
                                                                 shrinkA=0, shrinkB=0), zorder=11)
say(fld, q, LTG + 0.5, 0.45, "measured: about\n5 inches short", fs=6.4, color=GREEN, weight="bold")
say(fld, q, LTG + 0.5, -0.5, "line to gain", fs=6.4, color=style.INK)
say(fld, q, NOSE - 0.62, 0.0, "the spot, chosen by eye\n(shaded: illustrative error)", fs=6.0,
    color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, weight="bold")
ax.set_title("Since 2025: cameras measure the gap", fontsize=8.2, loc="left", fontweight="bold",
             color=style.INK)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.8)
plt.show()








Figure 49.11: What changed in 2025, and what didn’t. Left, the old way: the chain crew carries the sticks onto the field. At the start of the series an official clipped the chain at the nearest 5-yard stripe; laying that clip back on the same stripe puts the rear stick exactly where the series began, so the front stick, ten yards on, can be compared with the nose of the ball (the ball is drawn larger than scale). Right, a close-up of the same spot, about two yards across: since 2025, six cameras around the stadium measure the gap between the ball’s nose and the line to gain, to a fraction of an inch. But in both, the ball sits where an official spotted it by eye (the shaded band is an illustrative margin of error, not a measured one): the cameras measure from that spot; they don’t choose it.





The change is a nice lesson in two words that sound alike. Precision is how finely you can measure; accuracy is whether you measured from the right place. The chains were not very precise (a clip laid by hand, a chain pulled taut by eye), and they were slow. The cameras are extremely precise. But they measure from the spot, and the spot is still a human judgment: an official running alongside the play, often looking through a pile of bodies, deciding where the ball’s nose was when forward progress stopped. A measurement precise to a fraction of an inch, taken from a spot that could be off by a foot, is only as accurate as the spot. That is why the spot itself can still be reviewed, but only in narrow cases: on a play that’s challenged or booth-reviewed, or through replay assist, the booth can move the spot when the video clearly shows where the ball was relative to the line to gain or the goal line. (Who decides to measure at all? The referee. A team’s captain can ask him for one, but it’s his call.)31






CautionCommon misconception



“The cameras decide first downs now.” They decide the measurement. The officials still spot the ball by eye, and the yellow line on your screen is still the broadcaster’s drawing, not an official mark. When a spot looks wrong, the cameras can’t help; only the replay booth’s look at the spot can.

title: Officiating, Replay, and the Rules of the Ball
text:
Reading the referee’s announcement
Every announcement follows the same grammar, and once you know it you can usually finish the referee’s sentence for him. For a foul, the order is: what the foul was, who committed it (offense or defense, and the player’s number), how much it costs and from where, and what happens to the down. For a review it’s: the outcome (stands, confirmed, reversed), the reason in a sentence, and the result (the new down, distance and spot, and anything about the clock).




Table 49.2: Six announcements decoded. The words in quotation marks are the typical form; referees vary the wording a little.










What the referee says
What it means




“Holding, number 72, offense. Ten-yard penalty. Repeat second down.”
An accepted offensive holding foul: 10 yards from the previous spot, and the down is played again.


“Pass interference, defense, number 24. Spot foul. Automatic first down.”
Defensive pass interference: the ball goes to the spot of the foul with a new set of downs.


“Offsetting fouls. Repeat third down.”
A foul by each team; they cancel and the down is replayed.


“Illegal formation, offense. The penalty is declined. Fourth down.”
The defense chose the play’s result over the yards (a third-down incompletion, say).


“After review, the ruling on the field stands. Third down.”
The video wasn’t clear enough to overturn the call, whichever way it was.


“After review, the ruling on the field is reversed. The runner’s knee was down before the ball came out. There is no fumble. Second down.”
The booth turned a turnover back into a tackle: the down-by-contact order of events.








The enforcement words (spot foul, declined, automatic first down) are taught in Contact Rules and Penalties. Before the announcement, the referee’s arm signal tells you most of it, and a few signals cover most flags: a hand gripping the other wrist for holding; both hands on the hips for offside or encroachment; forearms rolling over each other in front of the chest for a false start; both open hands pushed forward from the shoulders for pass interference; one wrist chopping the other above the head for a personal foul; and both arms, held parallel, waved diagonally across the body for intentional grounding.32

Do crews call games differently?
Each referee leads the same crew through a regular season, and fans and bettors love the idea that some crews are “flag-happy”. The data gives a measured answer. (The names are the referees who led each crew; Shawn Hochuli, for one, is Ed Hochuli’s son.)


Show the Python
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 4.3))
ys = np.arange(len(wide))
ax.axvspan(avg25 - 2 * se_crew, avg25 + 2 * se_crew, color=style.GRID, alpha=0.7, lw=0, zorder=0)
ax.axvline(avg25, color=style.MUTED, lw=1.0, ls=(0, (3, 2)), zorder=1)
for y, (name, row) in zip(ys, wide.iterrows()):
    ax.plot([row[2024], row[2025]], [y, y], color=style.BASELINE, lw=1.4, zorder=2)
    ax.plot(row[2024], y, "o", ms=6, mfc=style.SURFACE, mec=style.OFFENSE, mew=1.4, zorder=3)
    ax.plot(row[2025], y, "o", ms=6, color=style.OFFENSE, zorder=4)
ax.set_yticks(ys, wide.index, fontsize=7.2)
ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
ax.tick_params(axis="x", labelsize=7)
ax.set_xlabel("Accepted penalties per game", fontsize=7.6)
ax.text(avg25, len(wide) - 0.2, f"2025 average {avg25:.1f}", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=6.8,
        color=style.INK_2)
h = [Line2D([], [], marker="o", ls="", mfc=style.SURFACE, mec=style.OFFENSE, mew=1.4, ms=6, label="2024"),
     Line2D([], [], marker="o", ls="", color=style.OFFENSE, ms=6, label="2025")]
ax.legend(handles=h, loc="lower right", fontsize=7.2)
ax.set_ylim(-0.7, len(wide) + 0.4)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 49.12: Accepted penalties per game (both teams combined, every play) in games led by each referee’s crew, 2024 (hollow) and 2025 (filled), for the referees who led a crew in both seasons, sorted by 2025. The grey band is the range around the 2025 league average that a crew would land in from game-to-game randomness alone, about two standard errors for a 16-game sample. Most crews sit inside it, and the order reshuffles from one season to the next. Source: nflverse play-by-play and officials data (regular seasons).





In 2025 an average game had 12.8 accepted penalties, and the crews’ averages ran from 10.2 (Brad Allen’s crew) to 14.6 (Adrian Hill’s).33 That spread sounds large until you set it against the noise. A single game’s total varies a lot (the standard deviation was about 4.3 penalties), so a crew’s 16- or 17-game average would wander about ±2.2 around the league average by luck alone. Most crews sit inside that band. And the ranking usually doesn’t hold: the correlation between a crew’s 2024 and 2025 averages was 0.28, and across the ten seasons from 2016 to 2025 the year-to-year correlation was usually weak (median 0.28), occasionally strong (it ranged from -0.35 to 0.76). Only 12 of the 16 crews landed in the same half of the table both years.
So crews differ a little, and inconsistently. Teams are hardly more predictable: a team’s own rate of accepted fouls has a median year-to-year correlation of 0.32 over the same seasons. Most of a single game’s flag count, in other words, is noise: who happened to hold on which snap, in front of which official. And some of the variation is the league’s doing, not the crews’: the league-wide average swings with points of emphasis, from 11.2 to 13.5 per game across 2016–2025, which is why a preseason memo telling officials to watch for a particular foul can move the numbers for every crew at once.

title: Officiating, Replay, and the Rules of the Ball
text:
Film room






NoteFilm room: Cowboys at Packers, 2014 divisional playoffs, the catch that wasn’t



Find the play: January 11, 2015, fourth quarter, 4:42 left, fourth-and-2 at the Green Bay 32, Dallas down 26–21. Watch Dez Bryant and count the gates. Control: yes, above the cornerback. Feet: yes. Time: the argument. He takes three steps while falling and stretches the ball toward the goal line, and the ball hits the turf and moves as he lands. Under the 2014 rule, he was going to the ground in the process of the catch, so his three steps and his reach didn’t count; he had to keep control through the ground, and replay ruled he hadn’t. Under the 2018 rule, those steps and that reach are acts common to the game, made before the ball touched down, so the catch was complete before he landed. Watch the replay twice, once with each rule in your head, and you’ll understand why the league changed it.








NoteFilm room: Patriots at Jets, 2017, the touchback nobody recovered



October 15, 2017, fourth quarter, 8:31 left, the Jets down 24–14 at the New England 4. Austin Seferian-Jenkins catches a short pass and turns toward the goal line; as he dives for it, with a defender on him, the ball comes loose. Ruled a touchdown, it went to the booth as a scoring play. Replay ruled he lost the ball before crossing the line and didn’t regain control until he was out of bounds in the end zone: a fumble out of the end zone. That second point was the argument afterward; two former league officiating chiefs said they wouldn’t have overturned it, and the league stood by the call. No defender recovered anything, and the Patriots got the ball at their own 20. New England won by seven.34








NoteFilm room: the 2025 season, the cameras arrive



Pick any 2025 or 2026 game and wait for a close spot on third or fourth down. Watch the order of events: the official spots the ball by eye, the referee signals for a measurement, and within about half a minute the stadium screen shows the virtual line against the ball’s nose. The chain crew never leaves the sideline. Then watch the reactions: players and coaches now argue about the spot, the only human part left, and almost never about the measurement.

title: Officiating, Replay, and the Rules of the Ball
text:
Watch for it on Sunday






TipWatch for it: the ref’s mic



Every time a flag flies, or a ruling is close, make two calls before the referee turns on his microphone:

Name the official. Who threw it? A flag from the line of scrimmage at a sideline is the down or line judge (pre-snap foul, likely false start, offside or illegal formation). A flag from deep downfield is a side, field or back judge (likely pass interference or illegal contact). A flag from the backfield, near the quarterback, is the referee (roughing the passer, grounding) or the umpire (holding in the middle).
Name the foul or the ruling, and its result: how many yards, from where, and the down that follows.
On every review, predict the outcome: reversed, confirmed or stands. First ask who started it (a coach’s flag, or the booth: after the two-minute warning, a score, a turnover). Then ask which angle would settle it. If the decisive moment is hidden (a pile, a body in the way), say stands.
On every close catch, count the gates out loud: control, feet, time.

Keep a tally for one game, and add your review predictions to your prediction log. You’ll miss plenty at first; by the end of a season the official-then-foul habit will have you announcing it before the referee does.

title: Officiating, Replay, and the Rules of the Ball
text:
Predict the play






TipPredict the play 1: the sideline catch





Show the Python
off = [O("QB", "QB", -6.5, -1.0, "Q"), O("Z", "WR", -0.7, 13.0, "Z")]
dfn = [D("RCB", "CB", 15.0, 17.0, "C"), D("SS", "SS", 12.0, 7.0, "S")]
pp = Play(off, dfn, los=58, ball_y="right", to_go=6)
pp.route("Z", [(0, 0), (9.0, 0.5), (13.2, 8.8)], side=+1)
pp.path("RCB", [(13.3, 20.3)], absolute=True)                    # rallies down from deeper and drives him out
pp.pass_to("Z", t=1.6)
fld = pp.draw(lateral=(-3.0, 32.0), window=(-8.5, 22.5), title=False)
ax = fld.ax
no_numbers(ax)
official(ax, *XY(fld, pp, 19.6, 25.0), "FJ", fld.pts_per_yard(), r=1.3)
feet = [(12.6, 22.0), (14.0, 23.1)]                  # right foot, then left foot, both inside the line
for dd, ww in feet:
    ax.plot(*XY(fld, pp, dd, ww), marker="o", ms=5.5, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, zorder=11, mec="white", mew=0.6)
ball_at(fld, pp, 15.4, 25.6)
ax.annotate("", xy=XY(fld, pp, 12.3, 22.4), xytext=XY(fld, pp, 9.0, 25.0), zorder=11,
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, lw=0.8))
say(fld, pp, 8.0, 26.6, "both feet down\nin bounds", fs=6.6, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, weight="bold")
say(fld, pp, 12.0, 28.4, "ball shifts\nin his hands\nas he lands", fs=6.4, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, weight="bold")
say(fld, pp, 3.0, 24.6, "sideline", fs=6.0, box=False, rot=90)
plt.show()








Figure 49.13: Second quarter, 1:52 left. The receiver (Z) catches a pass running toward the right sideline at the opponent’s 38, gets his right foot down in bounds, then his left, and is knocked out of bounds by the cornerback. As he lands out of bounds the ball shifts in his hands, but his hands stay on it and it never touches the ground. The deep official on that side, about 20 yards downfield near the sideline (the far side from the chain crew), signals incomplete. The offense’s head coach reaches for his red flag.





Which official made the call? Can the coach challenge? Who decides, and what will the referee announce?






TipAnswer





The field judge, the deep wing on the far side from the chain crew. The coach can’t challenge: it’s after the two-minute warning, so only the booth can review it (his flag would just cost a timeout). The replay official starts the review, New York decides, the referee announces.
The review runs the gates. Control and feet: yes, both feet in bounds with the ball secured. Time: a toe-tap leaves no time for a football act, so he had to keep control through his landing out of bounds, and he did: a ball that shifts while his hands stay on it is slight movement, and it never touched the ground. So: “After review, the ruling on the field is reversed. The pass is complete,” dead where he went out. No 10-second runoff: a catch that ends out of bounds stops the clock anyway. (Had the ball come loose and hit the ground, it would “stand” or be “confirmed”: incomplete.)











TipPredict the play 2: reaching for the pylon





Show the Python
gl = [O(k, k, -0.7, w, "") for k, w in [("LT", -3.2), ("LG", -1.6), ("C", 0.0), ("RG", 1.6), ("RT", 3.2)]]
gl += [O("YL", "TE", -0.7, -4.8, "Y"), O("YR", "TE", -0.7, 4.8, "Y"), O("Z", "WR", -1.5, 17.0, "Z"),
       O("QB", "QB", -2.0, 0.0, "Q"), O("FB", "FB", -4.4, 0.0, "F"), O("RB", "RB", -6.8, 0.0, "R")]
pz = Play(gl, [D("SS", "SS", 3.5, 8.0, "S"), D("CB", "CB", 3.0, 20.5, "C")], los=107, ball_y="right", to_go=None)
pz.run("RB", [(-3.2, 4.0), (-1.6, 9.6), (2.0, 14.2)], absolute=True)       # bounces outside the tight end
pz.path("SS", [(2.6, 11.2)], absolute=True)
pz.path("CB", [(1.2, 15.8)], absolute=True)
fld = pz.draw(lateral=(-8.5, 30.0), window=(-8.5, 13.5), title=False)
ax = fld.ax
no_numbers(ax)
xmark(fld, pz, 2.0, 14.2)
path_arrow(fld, pz, [(2.0, 14.2), (4.8, 17.6), (7.5, 23.58), (8.0, 24.8)])
say(fld, pz, -2.5, 25.2, "sideline", fs=6.0, box=False, rot=90)
say(fld, pz, 3.6, 4.0, "goal line", fs=6.2)
say(fld, pz, 11.8, 12.0, "end line", fs=6.2)
ax.annotate("", xy=XY(fld, pz, 2.4, 13.6), xytext=XY(fld, pz, 4.6, 12.9), zorder=11,
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, lw=0.8))
say(fld, pz, 5.6, 12.2, "punched out\nat the 1", fs=6.6, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, weight="bold")
say(fld, pz, 8.6, 17.0, "out of bounds\nin the end zone", fs=6.6, color=style.BALL, weight="bold")
plt.show()








Figure 49.14: Third-and-goal from the 3, third quarter, the offense in a heavy goal-line set (two tight ends, a fullback). The running back (R) bounces outside and dives for the pylon, holding the ball out in his outside arm. At the 1 the cornerback (C), coming from outside, punches it loose; it bounces into the end zone and rolls out of bounds through the side of the end zone. Nobody touches it after the punch.





What’s the ruling, and who gets the ball where? What if the ball had gone out of bounds at the 1 instead?






TipAnswer





A fumble through the end zone: touchback, the defense’s ball at its own 20, though it never recovered anything. As a turnover, the booth reviews it automatically, asking in order: did the ball break the plane, or touch the pylon, while he still had it? (touchdown); was he touched and down before it came out? (fourth-and-goal at the 1); did the loose ball really go out in the end zone? (A loose ball that hits the pylon is out there too: touchback.)
Out of bounds at the 1 instead, the offense keeps it, back at the spot of the fumble: fourth-and-goal from the 1. A few feet of turf, worth several expected points: that’s why coaches tell runners to carry the ball high and tight near the goal line.











TipPredict the play 3: flushed and thrown away





Show the Python
gg = [O(k, k, -0.7, w, "") for k, w in [("LT", -3.2), ("LG", -1.6), ("C", 0.0), ("RG", 1.6), ("RT", 3.2)]]
gg += [O("QB", "QB", -5.0, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -4.6, -2.6, "RB")]
pg = Play(gg, [D("DE", "DE", 0.9, 4.6, "E"), D("DT", "DT", 0.9, -0.9, "T")], los=40, to_go=8)
pg.path("QB", [(-7.5, 1.0), (-8.0, 7.0), (-7.0, 12.5)], absolute=True)
pg.block("RB", pts=[(0.8, -0.8)])
fld = pg.draw(lateral=(-12.0, 30.5), window=(-14.0, 6.0), title=False)
ax = fld.ax
no_numbers(ax)
tackle_box(ax, fld, pg, -14.0)
official(ax, *XY(fld, pg, -11.5, 5.5), "R", fld.pts_per_yard(), r=1.15)
path_arrow(fld, pg, [(0.0, 5.2), (-4.6, 7.6), (-6.0, 10.6)], color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.4, ls="-", head=10)  # the end closes
path_arrow(fld, pg, [(-7.0, 12.5), (-1.0, 27.8)], color=style.BALL, lw=1.6)
ball_at(fld, pg, -1.0, 27.8)
say(fld, pg, -9.0, 22.0, "lands out of bounds,\na yard short of the line", fs=6.4, color=style.BALL, weight="bold")
say(fld, pg, -11.8, -4.8, "tackle box", color=PURPLE, fs=6.4, weight="bold")
say(fld, pg, 1.4, -7.0, "line of scrimmage", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fs=6.2)
say(fld, pg, 1.0, 25.4, "sideline", fs=6.0, box=False, rot=90)
plt.show()








Figure 49.15: Third-and-8 at the offense’s own 30. The quarterback is flushed from the pocket to his right, well outside the tackle box (shaded), with the end closing on him and his receivers covered downfield. Running toward the sideline, he throws the ball away; it lands out of bounds a yard short of the line of scrimmage. A flag flies from the backfield. The referee (R) is shown where he started the play, behind the quarterback on his throwing-arm side.





Who threw the flag, and for what? Where is the ball, and what down is it?






TipAnswer





The referee, for intentional grounding: he watches the quarterback, and grounding is his call. Pressure: the end was closing. No receiver near: nobody. The box: he was outside it, so the exception applies, but only if the ball reaches the line of scrimmage, and this one landed a yard short. (A yard past the line, it would have been a legal throwaway.)
The penalty is loss of down and 10 yards from the previous spot (the spot of the pass, about 7 yards back, isn’t farther), so the ball goes back to the 20 and it’s fourth-and-18: almost certainly a punt. “Intentional grounding, offense. Ten-yard penalty and loss of down. Fourth down.” Replay assist can’t save him: being outside the pocket isn’t what made this one grounding.

title: Officiating, Replay, and the Rules of the Ball
text:
Takeaways

Seven officials split the field and the players: the referee (white cap) the quarterback, the umpire the interior line, the down and line judges the line of scrimmage and sidelines, the side, field and back judges the receivers downfield. Where a flag came from tells you what it is likely to be.
Replay asks two questions in order. Is the ruling reviewable at all (judgment fouls aren’t)? Does the booth review it automatically (scores, tries, turnovers, short on fourth down, after the two-minute warning, overtime)? If not, only a coach’s challenge, paid for with a timeout, can open it. Replay assist runs alongside on clear objective facts and the objective part of a short list of flags. There is no sky judge.
Reversals need clear and obvious evidence, so a hidden moment usually “stands”; “stands” and “confirmed” leave the play exactly as called.
A catch is three gates: control, feet down, then time. Since 2018 a football act made on the way down finishes the catch; only a receiver who hits the ground before he’s had time for one must survive the ground. The rule now matches what people see, at the price of a judgment about time.
The order of events decides possession, and direction and territory decide the rest. Ball out before the knee is a fumble; an NFL runner needs to be touched to be down. A forward fumble out of bounds comes back to the spot of the fumble, but into the opponent’s end zone and out it’s a touchback. A pass that doesn’t go forward is a backward pass and stays live if dropped. Grounding is about the box and the line: once outside the box, a throwaway just has to reach the line.
Cameras measure, people spot, and crew differences in flags are small and unstable from year to year.

title: Officiating, Replay, and the Rules of the Ball
text:
Connections
Builds on: Contact Rules and Penalties (the fouls these officials call and how they’re enforced), Quarterback Play (the throwaway), Downs, Distance, and Field Position (the spot, forward progress, the chains) and What a Play Really Is (the staff who advise on challenges).
Sets up: The Clock, the Two-Minute Drill, and Fourth Down, where spikes, grounding, the booth’s control of the final two minutes and the value of a timeout spent on a challenge all become clock decisions; and Red Zone, Goal Line, Two-Point Plays, and Short Yardage, where forward progress and the goal-line spot decide the tush push and every fourth-and-inches. The rules’ history (the 1978 passing changes, the catch rule, replay) is placed in context in The 1978 Liberation and Appendix E, and Part 13 shows how to pull the review and penalty data behind this chapter’s charts yourself (nflverse in Python).






NoteGo deeper




The NFL Rulebook (NFL Football Operations, free online): Rule 7 (dead ball, down by contact), Rule 8 (passes, grounding, fumbles), Rule 15 (instant replay); the league also posts officiating videos.
Football Zebras (footballzebras.com), written by former officials and longtime followers of officiating: crew assignments, rule changes and play-by-play explanations of controversial calls.
nflverse (via nflreadpy): load_officials() for every game’s crew since 2015, and the play-by-play desc text for every recorded review and penalty, enough to rebuild this chapter’s charts.
Former NFL officiating chiefs (Mike Pereira, Dean Blandino) explain controversial calls on broadcasts every week: the fastest way to learn how the booth thinks.

title: Officiating, Replay, and the Rules of the Ball
text:
The positions and duties follow the NFL’s own descriptions (“Officials’ responsibilities and positions,” NFL Football Operations), as reproduced in Crescent City Sports, “Breakdown of duties for NFL game officials” (Oct. 20, 2019): referee and umpire 10–12 yards deep in the backfield, side judge and field judge 20 yards downfield, back judge 25 yards: https://crescentcitysports.com/breakdown-of-duties-for-nfl-game-officials/ ; “Official (American football),” Wikipedia, for the referee favoring the quarterback’s throwing arm and the seven abbreviations: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Official_(American_football).↩︎
The umpire was moved to the offensive backfield for the 2010 season after a run of injuries to umpires in the middle of the defense (five serious ones in 2009). Because walking up from the backfield to spot the ball slowed hurry-up offenses, from 2010 to 2015 he returned to the defensive side in the closing minutes of the game (Wikipedia gives the last five minutes; some accounts of the 2010 rule add the last two minutes of the first half); that exception was dropped in 2016, and since 2023 he works on the defensive side on field goals and extra points. “Official (American football),” Wikipedia (umpire): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Official_(American_football).↩︎
The NFL went to seven officials in 1978 by adding the side judge; the back judge and field judge exchanged titles in 1998 to match college and high-school usage; and the head linesman was renamed the down judge in 2017. “Official (American football),” Wikipedia (history): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Official_(American_football) ; “1998 NFL season,” Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1998_NFL_season. The 1978 changes to pass-defense rules are covered in The 1978 Liberation.↩︎

“Replay review in gridiron football,” Wikipedia (NFL section): the 1986–1991 system, the 1999 challenge system, automatic review of scoring plays (2011) and turnovers (2012), centralized decisions in New York (2017), and the one-season pass-interference review (2019): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Replay_review_in_gridiron_football.↩︎
NFL Rulebook (2026), Rule 15, Section 1: two challenges, each needing an available timeout; a timeout charged for an unsuccessful challenge; a third challenge if at least one succeeds; a team that challenges when it isn’t permitted to is charged a timeout, or 15 yards if it has no timeouts left; only the Replay Official may start a review after the two-minute warning, in overtime, on scores, tries, turnovers and a ruling of short on fourth down: https://operations.nfl.com/rules-officiating/2026-nfl-rulebook . 49  Officiating, Replay, and the Rules of the Ball

title: Early Downs and Field Zones: How Situation Shapes the Call
text:
The situation comes before the play
First quarter, no score, first-and-10 at the offense’s own 25. The back runs for two yards, and the analyst approves: they’re “establishing the run.” Next series, first-and-10 again, a quick throw gains nine, and now the analyst perks up: second-and-1 is “a free play,” the perfect time for a shot down the field. (That’s booth slang. On the field a free play is stricter: a snap on which the defense has jumped offside, so the offense can’t lose.) The offense hands the ball off again. A few series later the same offense faces third-and-3 at the other team’s 38, on a down where offenses threw 86% of the time when the ball sat in their own half, and this time it runs. Nothing about the players has changed. The situation has: which down it is, how far there is to go, and where the ball sits on a field that coaches carve into zones with names. This chapter teaches you to read those three things the way a play-caller does, and to check what the broadcast booth tells you against what teams actually do.
You’ll be able to…
How to read the diagrams. Offense is blue circles, defense orange squares, and left and right are always the offense’s. Q is the quarterback, R the running back, Y and U the tight ends, and X, Z and H the wide receivers; C is the center. On defense, E and T are the ends and tackles, S, M and W the Sam, Mike and Will linebackers, $ the nickel back, CB the cornerbacks and FS and SS the safeties. Lines ending in a bar are blocks, arrows are paths, and a dashed brown arrow is the throw. The yellow line is the line to gain. In the charts, “neutral situations” means what it meant in 01-02: outside the last two minutes of each half, with each team’s win probability between 20% and 80%, so that the score and the clock aren’t making the call.
A play-caller does not walk into a game with a list of “good plays” and pick his favorite. He walks in with a call sheet, the laminated card you see covering his mouth on the sideline, and that card is organized by situation. One box for first-and-10, one for second-and-long, one for second-and-short, a few for third down cut by distance, then boxes for the places on the field where the rules of the game change the math: backed up against your own goal line, coming out, the red zone, the goal line. A separate panel handles the clock: the two-minute drill and the four-minute offense, where the score and the time left are the situation.
One thing sits on top of the boxes: the opening script, a list of about 15 plays the play-caller picks before the game and calls in order on ordinary first and second downs. Bill Walsh’s 49ers made it famous, and The Game Plan shows how one is built. So many of a team’s first-quarter early downs come off a list written before the game, not off the situation boxes. Keep that in mind when this chapter measures what teams did early in games: some of it was planned, not reactive.
Strip away the score and the clock and three numbers define a situation: the down, the distance to the line to gain, and the yard line. This chapter is about all three on the first two downs of a series, and about the yard line everywhere.
Start with the downs. First and second down are the early downs: the snaps where the offense still has at least one more try in hand before the down that decides whether it punts. That one extra try is what makes them different. On third down the offense must gain the yards, and the defense knows it, so third down gets its own chapter (Third Down: The Money Down). On an early down nothing is forced. A play-caller can run, throw short, throw deep, fake one and do the other, and the defense has to be ready for all of it. Early downs are also most of the game: about three snaps in four are first or second downs.

title: Early Downs and Field Zones: How Situation Shapes the Call
text:
NoteMadden vs. real life



In a video game you see the same playbook menu on every snap, and the “situation” is something you notice if you feel like it. A real play-caller’s options are pre-filtered by situation before the game starts. On his own 2-yard line, half of his passing game is crossed off the sheet; on second-and-1 a box of deep shots appears that he would never call on second-and-11. When you hear a coordinator say “we were in a good situation for that call,” he means the call was on the right part of the sheet.

section: First down: the freest snap in football
text:
First down: the freest snap in football
If any snap is a true guess for the defense, it’s first-and-10. Here is how often offenses have thrown on it, in neutral situations, for every season the play-by-play covers. (Throughout this chapter a “pass” is a called pass, or dropback: the quarterback sets up to throw, so sacks and scrambles count as passes. A “run” is a designed run.)


Show the Python
fig, (a1, a2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.5, 2.9), gridspec_kw=dict(wspace=0.32))
yrs = TREND.index.values
a1.plot(yrs, TREND.values * 100, color=style.SERIES[0], lw=2, label="1st & 10")
a1.plot(yrs, TREND2.values * 100, color=style.SERIES[1], lw=2, label="2nd down (any distance)")
a1.set_ylim(35, 70)
a1.set_ylabel("Pass rate (%)", fontsize=8)
a1.axhline(50, color=style.BASELINE, lw=0.8, ls=(0, (3, 2)), zorder=1)
a1.text(2009.5, 50.4, "coin flip", fontsize=6.5, color=style.MUTED, va="bottom", ha="center")
a1.legend(loc="upper left", fontsize=7, handlelength=1.5)
a1.set_title("How often they pass", fontsize=9)
a2.plot(yrs, GAP[1].values, color=style.SERIES[0], lw=2, label="dropbacks")
a2.plot(yrs, GAP[0].values, color=style.SERIES[1], lw=2, label="designed runs")
a2.axhline(0, color=style.BASELINE, lw=1)
a2.set_ylabel("EPA per play, 1st & 10", fontsize=8)
a2.set_ylim(-0.2, 0.2)
a2.legend(loc="center right", fontsize=7, handlelength=1.5, bbox_to_anchor=(1.0, 0.62))
a2.set_title("What each one earned", fontsize=9)
for a in (a1, a2):
    a.set_xticks([2000, 2005, 2010, 2015, 2020, 2025])
    a.tick_params(labelsize=7)
    a.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
plt.show()








Figure 50.1: Left: how often offenses passed on first-and-10 (blue) and on second down (orange), neutral situations, every regular season from 1999 to 2025. A pass is a called pass, so sacks and scrambles count. First-and-10 has barely moved in 27 years; second down has drifted toward the pass. Right: what each choice earned on first-and-10, in EPA per play. A dropback beat a run in every one of the 27 seasons, by roughly 0.15 to 0.25 points a play. Source: nflverse play-by-play.





Two facts sit side by side in that chart, and the tension between them is the whole early-down debate.
The first fact: first-and-10 is a coin flip, and it always has been. In every season since 1999, offenses in neutral situations have thrown on between 44% and 48% of their first-and-10 snaps (46% in 2025). Over the same years the league remade itself: the shotgun went from a passing-down formation to the default, the spread arrived from college, the rules protected quarterbacks and receivers more every few years. Second down moved with it, from about 54% passes in the first five seasons of the data to about 59% in the last five. First down didn’t.1
The second fact: the pass has been the better bet on first-and-10 every single year. A dropback out-earned a designed run by between 0.14 and 0.26 points of EPA per play, and the run has averaged a loss of expected points in all 27 seasons. A tenth of a point per play, you’ll remember from 01-02, is roughly the gap between a good offense and an average one. So the obvious question: if passing on first down is that much better, why hasn’t anyone’s first-down pass rate moved?
There are four honest answers, and none of them is “coaches are fools.”

The averages aren’t a fair fight. First-down runs and passes are not run against the same defenses. Offenses call passes when the defense looks ready for the run, and many first-down passes are play-action, which borrows its value from the run’s existence. Take the run away and the pass faces a defense that knows it’s coming. This is the selection effect you met with box counts in A First Look at Defense, and Expected Points, EPA, and Success Rate will deal with it head on.
Balance is the point of first down. First-and-10 is the one snap where the defense can’t lean. A team that throws 80% of the time on first down has handed the defense a tendency, and the defense will play pass on first down until the edge is gone. In the language of 08-02, the run is what keeps the pass from being a guess the defense wins.
Coaches price risk, not just averages. A run almost never loses ten yards or the ball; a pass sometimes does both. EPA counts sacks and interceptions in its average, but a head coach who answers for every turnover on Monday weighs a disaster more heavily than a bonus. The economist David Romer found the same lean in NFL fourth-down decisions twenty years ago.2
Runs buy things EPA doesn’t price. A run keeps the clock moving when you’re ahead, keeps a pass rush from teeing off on every snap, and spares your quarterback a hit.

Weigh those and you get the position most analysts actually hold. It isn’t “never run.” It’s that the average first-down run has been a worse bet than the average first-down pass for a generation, that most teams could throw a little more on early downs before the pass’s edge wore off, and that the teams who do it well tend to have the better offenses. That “how much more than expected” idea has a name, pass rate over expected (PROE), and a chapter of its own (Tendencies: PROE, Personnel, Motion, and Coverage).






ImportantWhy it exists: balance on first down



First-and-10 is balanced because balance is what first down is for. It is the one snap where a defense has nothing to go on but the formation and the film, so a play-caller who keeps it near a coin flip forces the defense to defend everything, and makes every later down easier to call. The price is the gap in the chart: each first-down run called “to stay balanced” gives up, on average, a slice of expected points. The good offenses keep the balance and shrink the price, with runs that look exactly like their passes and passes that look exactly like their runs.



On schedule and behind schedule
Coaches don’t talk about first down in EPA. They talk about the schedule. An offense is on schedule when its early downs leave it a manageable next down: about 4 yards or more on first-and-10, then a little more than half of what’s left on second down, so that third down is short or never comes. It’s behind schedule when a short gain, a loss, a sack, an incompletion or a penalty leaves second-and-long or third-and-long. The yardage version of success rate from 01-02, 40% of the needed yards on first down and 60% on second, is the schedule turned into a number: 4 of the 10 on first down, then 60% of whatever is left (4 of the 6 after a 4-yard gain), which leaves a third-and-2.
Why 4 yards? Because of what each first-down result does to the rest of the series:


Show the Python
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 2.9))
xs = list(SCHED.index)
labs = ["loss"] + [str(g) for g in range(0, 10)] + ["10+"]
cols = [style.DEFENSE if g < 4 else style.OFFENSE for g in xs]
cols[-1] = style.THIRD

    ax.text(i, 4, nxt, ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=5.6, color="white", linespacing=1.0, zorder=4,
            fontweight="bold")

ax.set_ylabel("Series converted (%)", fontsize=8)

Figure 50.2: What a first-and-10 play sets up: the chance the series ends in a first down or a touchdown, by the yards the first-down play gained (neutral situations between the offense’s own 20 and the opponent’s 30, 2016-2025 regular seasons; plays that ended in a turnover are left out). A 0 includes incompletions; ‘loss’ includes sacks. Each bar is labelled with the second down it leaves. Every yard helps, by three or four percentage points of conversion; the costliest result is a loss. Coaches draw the ‘on schedule’ line at about 4 yards, where second down is 6 or shorter. Source: nflverse play-by-play.





Read the bars as the price of first down. A first-down play that loses yards (a sack, a run stuffed in the backfield) leaves a series that converts only 49% of the time; an incompletion or a no-gain run, 57%. After that there’s no cliff: every yard is worth three or four percentage points of conversion, and 4 yards gets the series to 71%. Coaches draw the line at about 4 because second-and-6 or shorter still leaves room for a run and a pass, and puts a third-and-short within one ordinary play. The EPA bookkeeping from 01-02 lands in nearly the same place: the smallest first-and-10 gain whose average EPA is positive is 5 yards. The coaches’ rule of thumb and the analysts’ model describe the same slope and draw the line within a yard of each other.
The bars also show what coaches fear most on first down, and it isn’t the incompletion. It’s the negative play. A sack or a tackle for loss (8% of these first downs) does more damage than an incompletion, because it spends the down and lengthens the distance. A holding penalty is worse still: first-and-20. That is why so much of the modern early-down passing game is built to be safe as well as productive (the quick game, screens, play-action with the quarterback rolling away from pressure) and why a quarterback who takes a sack on first down hears about it in the film room.






CautionCommon misconception



“Second-and-long is no big deal: you still have two downs.” Look at the bars again. A first-down play that gains nothing leaves a series that converts 57% of the time; a 4-yard gain leaves one that converts 71%. Either way the offense has two downs left, but two downs to gain ten yards is a much harder problem than two downs to gain six, and the defense knows it: on second-and-long it can start playing the pass.




“Establish the run”: what the claim says, and what survives
Every broadcast has an announcer who says a team needs to “establish the run”: run the ball early and often, and good things will follow. It is one of the oldest pieces of football wisdom, and it is really four different claims bundled together. The data treats them very differently.
Claim 1: running wears the defense down, so the runs get better as the game goes on. If that were true, early-down runs in close games should gain more in the fourth quarter than in the first. They barely do. From 2016 to 2025 they averaged −0.09 EPA in the first quarter and −0.07 in the fourth, a hair better and nowhere near closing the gap to passes, which averaged +0.10 and +0.09.3 Big, physical offenses do tire defenses on some days, and you’ll see it on individual drives. It just doesn’t show up as a rule.
Claim 2: you have to run to make play-action work. This one has been tested hardest, and it fails. Play-Action, Bootlegs, and Screens walks through the evidence: play-action passes beat ordinary dropbacks by about the same margin whether a team’s run game is good, bad or barely used. Linebackers react to the look of the run (the line’s first step, the back’s path) because reacting is their job, not because a running back has been gaining yards. What survives is the weaker point: the fake has to look exactly like your real run, so you need a real run to copy.
Claim 3: teams that run the ball win. This is the claim that keeps the phrase alive, because the correlation is real and enormous. Here it is, beside the version of it that matters:


Show the Python
fig, (a1, a2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.5, 2.9), sharey=True, gridspec_kw=dict(wspace=0.12))
for a, tab, title, xl in [(a1, WIN_RUNS, "By total runs in the game", "Designed runs called"),
                          (a2, WIN_H1, "By first-half early-down run rate", "Run rate on 1st and 2nd down, 1st half")]:
    xs_ = range(len(tab))
    a.bar(xs_, tab["mean"] * 100, color=style.SERIES[0] if a is a1 else style.MUTED, width=0.68, zorder=3)
    for i, v in zip(xs_, tab["mean"]):
        a.text(i, v * 100 + 1.5, f"{v * 100:.0f}", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=7, color=style.INK)
    a.set_xticks(list(xs_), [str(i) for i in tab.index], fontsize=6.6)
    a.set_xlabel(xl, fontsize=7.5)
    a.set_title(title, fontsize=8.6)
    a.axhline(50, color=style.BASELINE, lw=0.8, ls=(0, (3, 2)), zorder=1)
    a.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
    a.tick_params(axis="y", labelsize=7)
a1.set_ylabel("Won the game (%)", fontsize=8)
a1.set_ylim(0, 100)
plt.show()








Figure 50.3: Two ways to connect running and winning, every regular-season team-game from 2016 to 2025 (ties left out). Left: win rate by how many designed runs a team called in the game. Teams with 31 or more runs won more than four times in five. Right: win rate by how often the team ran on first and second down in the first half, split into five equal-sized groups. The line is flat: running a lot early told you nothing about who would win. The difference is direction. Teams run a lot because they are ahead (protecting a lead, running out the clock), not ahead because they ran. Source: nflverse play-by-play.





On the left, the famous version: teams that ran more than 30 times won 84% of their games; teams that ran 20 times or fewer won 20%. On the right, the version a play-caller can actually choose: how much a team leaned on the run on early downs in the first half, before the score had a say. Every fifth of that scale won about half its games.4
The left panel runs backward. A team that leads in the fourth quarter runs to drain the clock (the four-minute offense), and a team that trails throws to catch up. Across these games, a team’s fourth-quarter run rate correlated with winning at 0.67; its first-half early-down run rate, at 0.03 (a correlation runs from 0, no connection at all, to 1, a perfect one). Winning causes running. Running, by itself, doesn’t cause winning.
Claim 4: the run keeps the defense honest. This one survives, and it’s the reason the debate never ends. A defense that doesn’t have to respect the run can drop seven or eight players into coverage on every early down, rush four, and make the pass much harder. The run’s value isn’t only its own EPA; part of it shows up in the pass’s EPA. That is constraint theory again, and it explains why the best offenses of the analytics era did not simply stop running. It also explains what does make a run game worth leaning on: being efficient, not being frequent. A run that gains as much as a pass (because the defense is outnumbered, or because the quarterback is a running threat) is worth calling often. A run that’s merely “establishing” something is the price you pay for balance.


Show the Python

Figure 50.4: Every offense from 2016 to 2025 (320 team-seasons) on first and second down in neutral situations: how often it passed (across) and what it earned per play (up). The dashed lines are the averages. The cloud tilts up a little, since passing more goes with scoring more, but loosely: the best offenses of the decade sit on both sides of the average pass rate. The five labelled seasons are this chapter’s case studies. Source: nflverse play-by-play.





The chart is the debate in one picture. Passing more goes with better offense, but loosely (a correlation of 0.26 across these team-seasons, on that 0-to-1 scale): plenty of pass-happy teams were bad, and some of the best offenses of the decade ran more than average. What the offenses near the top of the chart share, whichever side of the average pass rate they sit on, is efficiency on both kinds of play, or a run game good enough that the usual price of running wasn’t there. The three film-room boxes take the labelled seasons one at a time.






NoteFilm room: Kansas City Chiefs and Los Angeles Rams, 2018



The season: a year the analytics argument still points to, because the two best offenses in football leaned on early-down passing. Kansas City (12–4) led the NFL with 565 points in Patrick Mahomes’s first season as a starter; the Rams (13–3), in Sean McVay’s second season, were second with 527.5 In neutral situations on first and second down, the Chiefs ranked 2nd in how often they passed and first in EPA per play; the Rams ranked only 11th in how often they passed but 3rd in what they earned, with a play-action game built to look exactly like their outside-zone runs (the Rams film room in 04-05 has the details). Part of how McVay made runs and passes look alike was sameness of personnel: the Rams lined up in 11 personnel (one back, one tight end, three receivers) on 93% of their runs and passes, the most in the league (the league average was 65%), so the defense never got a personnel clue about which was coming.6
The game: Monday night, November 19, 2018, moved from Mexico City to the Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum six days before kickoff because of the condition of the field in Mexico. The Rams won 54–51. Mahomes threw for 478 yards and six touchdowns, with three interceptions; Jared Goff threw for 413 and four touchdowns, and the two defenses scored three touchdowns between them on turnovers.7 Both offenses threw on about seven of every ten first downs that night.
What to notice: the Rams’ passing rate is the lesson. “Pass more on early downs” was never the whole recipe. The Rams were only a little above average in how often they threw; what set them apart was how much each early-down pass earned, and that their runs (2nd in early-down run EPA) were good enough that the defense had to honor them on every snap. Kansas City’s runs ranked 3rd. The best early-down offenses of 2018 were efficient at both, and leaned toward the pass.
And notice what didn’t spread. The league’s neutral first-and-10 pass rate in 2018 was 48%, the highest of the decade, and no season since has matched it (the flat blue line in the first chart). What the rest of the league copied from these two offenses was how they threw (play-action, motion, runs and passes from the same look), not how often.








NoteFilm room: Baltimore Ravens, 2019



The season: the counter-example every “pass more” chart has to answer. The 2019 Ravens went 14–2, led the NFL with 531 points and ran for 3,296 yards, the most by any team in NFL history, with Lamar Jackson setting the quarterback record of 1,206 rushing yards on his way to a unanimous MVP award.8 On first and second down in neutral situations they passed less often than any other team (32nd of 32), and they were first in EPA per play.
What to notice: their runs were first in the league in early-down EPA too (+0.09 per run, against a league average close to −0.08). A quarterback who is a real running threat changes the arithmetic of the run game: on option and quarterback-run plays the defense has to account for one more ball carrier, so the offense effectively gains a blocker (Option Football shows how). When a run is as good as a pass, “establishing” it costs nothing, and calling it often is simply good football. The Ravens weren’t proof that running wins; they were proof that efficient running wins.
The coda: in the divisional round, the Titans jumped ahead and beat them 28–12. Behind on the scoreboard, the Ravens threw on about three of every four early downs that night, and the offense built on the run’s threat looked ordinary. Situation decides even for the best run game in history. (The whole Baltimore era is a case study of its own.)
