title: Early Downs and Field Zones: How Situation Shapes the Call
text:
Second down: four buckets
Second down is where the schedule shows up. Whatever happened on first down sets the distance, and the distance sorts second downs into four buckets that call for different football:


Show the Python
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(6.5, 2.5), sharey=True, gridspec_kw=dict(width_ratios=[1.0, 1.2, 1.2],
                                                                                  wspace=0.10))
ys = np.arange(len(SB))[::-1]
a0, a1, a2 = axes
a0.barh(ys, SEC.pr.values * 100, color=style.SERIES[0], height=0.6, zorder=3)
for y_, v in zip(ys, SEC.pr.values):
    a0.text(v * 100 + 2, y_, f"{v * 100:.0f}%", va="center", fontsize=7, color=style.INK)
a0.set_xlim(0, 112); a0.set_xticks([0, 50, 100], ["0", "50", "100%"], fontsize=6.8)
a0.set_title("Pass rate", fontsize=8.5)
a0.set_yticks(ys, [f"2nd & {b}\nplay-action {PA2.loc[b]:.0%}" for b in SB], fontsize=6.8)
for a, tab, title, fmt, lim in [(a1, SEC_EPA, "EPA per play", lambda v: signed(v), (-0.2, 0.2)),
                                (a2, SEC_FD, "First down on the play", lambda v: f"{v:.0%}", (0, 0.8))]:
    for k, (col, lab) in enumerate([(style.SERIES[1], "run"), (style.SERIES[0], "dropback")]):
        vals = tab[k].values
        a.scatter(vals, ys, s=34, color=col, zorder=3, label=lab, edgecolor="white", lw=0.6)
    for y_, r0, r1 in zip(ys, tab[0].values, tab[1].values):
        a.plot([r0, r1], [y_, y_], color=style.BASELINE, lw=1.4, zorder=2)
    a.set_xlim(*lim)
    a.set_title(title, fontsize=8.5)
    a.tick_params(axis="x", labelsize=6.8)
    a.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
a1.axvline(0, color=style.BASELINE, lw=0.9)
a1.set_xticks([-0.1, 0, 0.1], [MINUS + "0.1", "0", "+0.1"])
a2.set_xticks([0.2, 0.4, 0.6], ["20%", "40%", "60%"])
a1.legend(loc="lower center", bbox_to_anchor=(1.05, -0.36), ncol=2, fontsize=7)
for a in axes:
    a.set_ylim(-0.6, len(SB) - 0.4)
plt.show()








Figure 50.5: Second down by bucket, neutral situations, 2021-2025 regular seasons. Left: how often offenses passed. Middle: EPA per play for designed runs (orange) and dropbacks (blue). Right: how often each one gained a first down on the spot. The pass earns more in every bucket, by the least on second-and-short, where runs convert two times in three. The play-action share is the percentage of each bucket’s passes that faked a handoff (FTN charting, 2022-2025). Source: nflverse play-by-play and FTN charting.






Second-and-short (1 to 3) is a running down in practice: offenses ran on 70% of these snaps (and on 77% of second-and-1s). It is also, in theory, the best passing down in football. The next two sections take both halves of that contradiction: why it’s a shot down, and why most teams run anyway.
Second-and-medium (4 to 6) is the true toss-up: offenses split almost exactly half and half, even though the pass has out-earned the run by a wide margin here too. An offense here is on schedule, and every call on the sheet is live.
Second-and-long (7 to 10) is the most common second down, the usual result of an incompletion or a short run. The offense is behind schedule, and its job is to get half of it back: a 5-yard gain turns third-and-long into third-and-short. Offenses throw about two times in three, and the pass is clearly the better bet.
Second-and-very-long (11 or more) follows a sack, a penalty or a loss. Offenses throw more than four times in five, and defenses play deep, conceding the short throw (the second drill in 01-02 shows that picture). The goal is a makeable third down, not the whole distance, which is where the draw and the screen earn their place.


Why second-and-short is a shot down
Every coach knows the logic, and you heard it from the analyst in the opening paragraph. On second-and-1 the offense has two downs to gain one yard. It can afford to spend one of them on a shot play, a pass aimed deep down the field, because if the shot falls incomplete it’s third-and-1, the easiest third down there is. Three things make the shot unusually good here, and the first one can be measured.
1. Failure is cheap. Losing a down costs less on second-and-short than anywhere else. From second-and-1, a series converted 94% of the time; from third-and-1, 81%. A wasted second down cost 13 percentage points of conversion. From second-and-5 or longer, a wasted down cost about 24 percentage points on average: from second-and-10 to third-and-10 is 57% to 33%. The same incompletion is about half as expensive on second-and-1.9
2. The offense’s own look pulls the defense into run mode. In the NFL a defense’s personnel follows the offense’s personnel, not the down. Teams often answer second-and-short with heavy personnel (two tight ends, or a fullback) and the quarterback under center, the same look they run from. Heavy personnel draws the defense’s base personnel; base personnel on a run-heavy down puts an eighth defender in the box, usually a safety walked down; and eight in the box leaves one deep safety to cover the whole middle of the field. Linebackers on short yardage are coached to attack the line the moment they see a run action, because a yard is all the offense needs. (Against three receivers, most defenses stay in nickel and walk a safety down instead. That one-high look invites the same shot.)
3. The fake is believable. Because the look is the run look, a run fake sells. On second-and-short, 42% of passes were play-action, against 24% on second-and-long and 13% on second-and-very-long.
Put those together and this is what the shot looks like:


Show the Python
LOS_SHOT = 55.0
def shot_play():
    off = line() + [O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -7.0, 0.0, "R"),
                    O("Y", "TE", -0.7, 4.8, "Y"), O("U", "TE", -0.7, -4.8, "U"),
                    O("X", "WR", -1.5, -15.0, "X"), O("Z", "WR", -1.5, 14.0, "Z")]
    dfn = [D("WDE", "DE", 1.0, -6.4, "E"), D("WDT", "DT", 1.0, technique("1", -1), "T"),
           D("SDT", "DT", 1.0, technique("3", 1), "T"), D("SDE", "DE", 1.0, 6.4, "E"),
           D("SAM", "SAM", 4.0, 6.0, "S"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.6, 0.8, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.6, -3.2, "W"),
           D("SS", "SS", 5.5, -7.2, "SS"), D("LCB", "CB", 6.5, -15.5, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 6.5, 14.5, "CB"),
           D("FS", "FS", 13.0, 0.5, "FS")]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=LOS_SHOT, to_go=1)
    # the line fires out as if it were a run, then holds its ground: eight men protect
    for k in ("LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT", "Y", "U"):
        p.block(k, pts=[(0.35, 0.0)], speed=1.2)
    for k, dw in (("WDE", (-0.6, 0.6)), ("WDT", (-0.6, 0.0)), ("SDT", (-0.6, 0.0)), ("SDE", (-0.6, -0.6))):
        p.rush(k, pts=[dw], speed=0.8)                           # the rushers are engaged at the line
    p.path("QB", [(-1.4, 1.0)], speed=4.0)                       # open to the back for the fake
    p.path("QB", [(-4.6, -0.8)], speed=4.2)                      # then set up deep
    p.path("RB", [(3.6, 1.4)], speed=5.5)                        # the fake: the same track as the run
    p.block("RB", pts=[(0.9, 0.5)], speed=2.0)                   # then he stays in to block
    p.route("X", [(11.0, 0.0), (28.0, 11.0)], frame="field")     # post from the left, breaking inside
    p.route("Z", [(7.0, -1.0), (17.0, -9.0), (20.0, -24.0)], frame="field")   # deep over (18-22 yards), from the right
    for k, to in (("SAM", (2.7, 5.0)), ("MIKE", (2.8, 1.4)), ("WILL", (2.8, -2.0)), ("SS", (3.0, -5.4))):
        st = p.players[k]
        p.path(k, [(to[0] - st.d, to[1] - st.w)], speed=2.4)      # the run fake pulls them up, hard
    for k, to in (("SAM", (7.5, 3.5)), ("MIKE", (8.0, -0.5)), ("WILL", (7.5, -5.0)), ("SS", (7.5, -10.0))):
        st = p._cur(k)
        p.path(k, [(to[0] - st[0], to[1] - st[1])], speed=4.0)    # ...then turn to chase, too late
    p.drop("FS", (16.0, -1.0), speed=3.0)
    p.drop("FS", (21.5, -3.5), speed=4.2)                         # he carries the post
    p.drop("LCB", (21.0, -18.0), speed=4.5)                       # deep third, outside and over the over
    p.drop("RCB", (17.5, 15.5), speed=4.5)
    p.pass_to("Z", t=3.1)
    return p


SHOT = shot_play()
animation_or_strip(
    SHOT, times=[0.0, 0.9, 3.1, 4.8],
    notes=["2nd & 1: run look, 8 in the box,\none deep safety (purple): Cover 3",
           "the fake: linebackers and the\nstrong safety (red) step up hard",
           "the throw: the free safety\nhas carried the post",
           "caught behind the linebackers,\nin front of the deep corner"],
    lateral=(-20.5, 20.5), window=(-10.0, 30.0), rings=[("FS", PURPLE), ("SS", RED)])





  
  Your browser does not support the video tag.



Figure 50.6: A second-and-1 shot against Cover 3 (illustrative; frame strip in print, video on the website). The offense shows its run look: two tight ends (Y and U), the quarterback under center, the back behind him. The defense answers with base personnel and eight men within a few yards of the ball, the strong safety (red ring) walked down on the left; only the free safety (purple ring) is deep, with the two corners bailing to the deep outside thirds. (1) The snap. (2) The quarterback fakes the handoff, and the linebackers and the strong safety step up hard to stop a run that isn’t coming. (3) Eight players stay in to block (max protection; some teams release a tight end late as an outlet), and only two go out: X on a post from the left, Z on a deep over route from the right, the yankee concept from 04-04. The free safety can’t cover both; he carries the post, and the ball is thrown. (4) Z catches it about 18 yards downfield, behind the linebackers and in front of the deep corner. If the throw had fallen incomplete, it would be third-and-1.




The read in the strip is the Cover 3 read: one deep safety, two deep routes, and he can only carry one. Many defenses play this same eight-man, one-high look as Cover 1, man-to-man with the free safety deep. Yankee still works against it, but for a different reason: the over route becomes a crosser running away from the defender chasing him, and the quarterback reads the man, not the safety. Either way, it’s the eight-man box that makes the shot.
And when teams take the shot, it pays. On second-and-1-to-3 from 2021 to 2025, passes that traveled 15 or more yards in the air averaged +0.29 EPA per attempt, against +0.03 for runs and +0.10 for shorter throws. Yet only about 5% of second-and-short snaps were a deep throw (231 in five seasons of neutral situations).10 Two cautions belong next to those numbers. A deep-throw average only counts passes that were thrown, not the sacks taken while waiting for a deep route to open, so the true value of calling the shot is lower. And the shot is a constraint play: it works because the defense is leaning toward the run. If every offense threw deep on every second-and-1, defenses would stop leaning, and the number would shrink. The case the data makes is narrower and still strong: most offenses could take this shot more often than they do before it stopped paying.






CautionCommon misconception



“An incomplete shot on second-and-1 is a wasted down.” It’s a spent down, and it was the cheapest down the offense will have all game. The offense still has third-and-1, converted more than two times in three, with fourth-and-1 behind it in much of the field. Compare that with an incompletion on second-and-10, which leaves third-and-10 and a series that converts about a third of the time.




Why most teams still run on second-and-short
If the shot is that cheap and that good, why did offenses still run on 70% of second-and-shorts? Four reasons, and each one is real.

The run usually just wins. A designed run on second-and-1-to-3 gained the first down on the spot 66% of the time, and 79% on second-and-1. That’s a fresh set of downs with no third down at all, and every coach values never having to face one.
The shot is expensive to call. It needs a long run fake or a deep drop, eight men in protection and three seconds or more, which means only two receivers and a real chance of the drive-killing negative play from the on-schedule section. A sack turns second-and-1 into third-and-8, which is no longer cheap at all.
The risk weighs more than the reward. Romer’s asymmetry again: an interception on a shot is replayed all week, a stuffed run is forgotten by the next series.
The defense doesn’t always cooperate. Some defenses answer second-and-short with two deep safeties precisely to take the shot away, and then the right call is the run, into a lighter box.

Second-and-short isn’t the only shot box on a call sheet, either. Most staffs also keep shots for sudden change, the first snap after a takeaway, while the defense that just ran onto the field is still settling (08-03’s call sheet has a box for it); for the first first down after crossing midfield; and for coming out, which you’ll meet below.


The second down after an incompletion
One more second-down habit is worth knowing, because it’s a tendency you can see from your couch. Second-and-10 comes about two ways: after a first-down incompletion, or after a first-down run that gained nothing. Same down, same distance, so it should be the same call. It isn’t. From 2021 to 2025, offenses threw on 83% of second-and-10s that followed a no-gain run, and on only 56% of those that followed an incompletion. The pattern holds a yard or three shorter, too: on second-and-7-to-9, teams threw 73% of the time after a first-down run and 56% after a first-down pass.11
Play-callers alternate. After a pass that didn’t work, there’s a pull toward a run, to avoid two incompletions in a row and a third-and-10, and to “get back on track” with a sure few yards. After a run that didn’t work, the pull goes the other way. It’s exactly the habit that 08-02’s misconception box warned about: alternating is a pattern too. A truly unpredictable caller’s next call wouldn’t depend on his last one, because if it did, the defense could guess the next play from the last. Economists who studied NFL play-calling found the habit in the data, and found that it costs something: the habit made plays less effective.12 That’s why defensive coordinators chart it, and now you can too.

section: Field zones: the map on the call sheet
text:
Field zones: the map on the call sheet
The down and distance tell a play-caller how much freedom he has. The yard line tells him what a mistake will cost and what success is worth, and the field is not uniform. Coaches divide it into zones, each with its own box on the call sheet:


Show the Python
LAT = (11.0, 42.3)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.7))
Field(ax=ax, orient="horizontal", los=60, window=None, to_go=None, numbers=False, hashes=False, lateral=LAT)
top, bot = LAT[1], LAT[0]
NAME_AT = {"backed up": 15.0, "coming out": 27.5, "open field": 52.5, "four-down\nterritory": 81.5,
           "red zone": 100.0}
PATCH = dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.15", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none", alpha=0.92)
SHOWN = {"backed up": "BACKED\nUP", "coming out": "COMING\nOUT", "open field": "OPEN FIELD",
         "four-down\nterritory": "FOUR-DOWN\nTERRITORY", "red zone": "RED ZONE"}
GOALS = {"backed up": "get out:\nno sack,\nno\nturnover", "coming out": "first first\ndown;\nflip the\nfield",
         "open field": "the whole menu;\nstay on schedule", "four-down\nterritory": "fourth down is\npart of the plan",
         "red zone": "touchdowns,\nnot field goals"}
for name, lo, hi in ZONES:
    x0, x1 = 110 - hi, 110 - lo
    ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x0, bot), x1 - x0, top - bot, fc=ZONE_COL[name], alpha=0.16, lw=0, zorder=0.5))
    fs = 6.6 if hi - lo <= 15 else 7.4

    ax.text(NAME_AT[name], (top + bot) / 2 - 5.0, GOALS[name], ha="center", va="center",
            fontsize=5.9 if hi - lo <= 15 else 6.3, color=style.INK_2, linespacing=1.05, zorder=6, bbox=PATCH)
ax.text(81.5, (top + bot) / 2 + 0.6, "(the fringe)", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=6.4, color=style.INK_2,
        zorder=6, bbox=PATCH)
# the open field crosses midfield: show its full extent so the strip past the 50 isn't an unnamed zone

for x, lab in [(20, MINUS + "10"), (35, MINUS + "25"), (60, "50"), (70, "+40"), (90, "+20")]:

    ax.text(x, (top + bot) / 2, t, rotation=90, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=6.3, color=style.INK_2)


def bracket(x0, x1, y, text, col=style.INK, fs=7.2):

bracket(10, 60, top + 2.4, "minus territory: your half (" + MINUS + "1 to " + MINUS + "49)")
bracket(60, 110, top + 2.4, "PLUS TERRITORY: their half (+49 to +1)")
ax.plot([75, 75], [bot, top], color=style.INK, lw=1.0, ls=(0, (1, 1.5)), zorder=3)
ax.text(75.7, top - 1.4, "field-goal\nrange begins\n(about +35)", ha="left", va="top", fontsize=5.8, color=style.INK_2,
        zorder=6, linespacing=1.0, bbox=PATCH)
ax.plot([45], [bot + 1.8], marker="^", ms=6, color=style.INK, zorder=6)
ax.text(46.4, bot + 2.4, "kickoff\ntouchback", ha="left", va="center", fontsize=5.9, color=style.INK_2, zorder=6,
        linespacing=1.0, bbox=PATCH)
ax.text(45, bot - 1.2, MINUS + "35", ha="center", va="top", fontsize=6.4, color=style.INK_2)   # the touchback spot
ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((38.0, top - 2.6), (56.0, top - 2.6), arrowstyle="-|>", mutation_scale=9,
                             color=style.OFFENSE, lw=1.5, zorder=6))
ax.text(47.0, top - 4.4, "offense moving this way", ha="center", va="top", fontsize=5.8, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK,
        zorder=6)
ax.set_ylim(bot - 5.5, top + 7.5)
plt.show()








Figure 50.7: The field as a play-caller sees it, offense moving left to right. Coaches number yard lines in their own half with a minus sign and in the opponent’s half with a plus sign, so ‘minus 25’ is the offense’s own 25 and ‘plus 35’ the opponent’s 35. Backed up runs from the goal line to the minus 10; coming out to about the minus 25; the open field to about the plus 40; four-down territory (the fringe) from there to the plus 20; the red zone inside it. The lines between zones vary by staff and by situation; these are typical. The small triangle marks where a kickoff that lands in the end zone has been spotted since 2025, the minus 35, and the dotted line where field-goal range typically begins for an NFL kicker, around the plus 35. ‘Flip the field’ means turning a punt from deep in your own end into one that pins the opponent deep in theirs.





Here is each zone in plain words. The names are the common ones; exact boundaries vary by staff, and the same staff will move them with the weather, the kicker and the score.13

Backed up: inside your own 10. A sack in the end zone, or a holding penalty there, is a safety: two points and the ball for the other team. Even the punt is cramped. A punter normally stands 14 or 15 yards deep; with the ball at the 2, the end line is only 12 yards back, so he sets up a step in front of it, the snap arrives sooner, and a blocked punt is a safety or a touchdown (Kicking and Punting). Many staffs split this zone again: a tight box for the minus 1 to about the minus 4 or 5, where even under-center play-action is rare and the sneak and quick-hitting runs dominate, and the rest of the zone out to the minus 10. That’s why 08-03’s call sheet draws “backed up” at the 5 and this chapter draws it at the 10: both are in use.
Coming out: roughly your own 10 to your own 25. The emergency is over, but the offense still wants its first first down, which moves the ball away from its goal line and turns a short punt into a long one (“flipping the field”).
Open field: roughly your own 25 to the opponent’s 40. Field position neither forces the offense’s hand nor tempts it. Since 2025, a kickoff that lands in the end zone comes out to the 35, and about two drives in three now start at the offense’s own 25 or better.14
Plus territory: the opponent’s half. Coaches write yard lines there with a plus sign (“plus 35”) and in their own half with a minus sign (“minus 25”), so you’ll hear a coordinator say “we got the ball in plus territory” after a turnover, often followed by that sudden-change shot. The plus side isn’t one zone: it holds the last ten yards of the open field and the next two zones.
Four-down territory, which coaches also call the fringe: roughly the opponent’s 40 to its 20. A punt from here buys little field (a little too long and it’s a touchback at the 20), and a field goal is long or uncertain, so the offense plans on using fourth down if it needs it.
The red zone, from 01-02: inside the opponent’s 20, where the field compresses and drives cash in or settle for three. It has zones of its own (inside the 10, the goal line), which belong to The Red Zone, Goal Line, and Short Yardage.

text:
How the call changes from zone to zone
You can watch the zones change behavior in the data. The top half of the next chart is first-and-10 all the way down the field; the bottom half is third-and-2-to-4, the short distances where, as you’ll see, the yard line matters most.


Show the Python
def by5(df, col):
    d_ = df.copy()
    d_["b"] = ((d_.yardline_100.clip(1, 99) - 1) // 5) * 5 + 3          # bin centres 3, 8, ..., 98
    t_ = d_.groupby("b")[col].agg(["mean", "size"])
    return 110 - t_.index.values, t_["mean"].values, t_["size"].values


fig, (a1, a2) = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(6.5, 4.4), sharex=True, gridspec_kw=dict(hspace=0.16))
f1 = N10[(N10.down == 1) & ((N10.ydstogo == 10) | (N10.goal_to_go == 1))]
for a in (a1, a2):
    shade_zones(a, alpha=0.08, labels=False)
x_, m_, n_ = by5(f1, "pass")
a1.plot(x_, m_ * 100, color=style.SERIES[0], lw=2, marker="o", ms=3.5, label="pass rate", zorder=3)
x_, m_, n_ = by5(f1, "shotgun")
a1.plot(x_, m_ * 100, color=style.SERIES[0], lw=1.3, ls=(0, (3, 2)), label="QB in the shotgun", zorder=3)
a1.set_ylim(15, 72)
a1.set_ylabel("1st & 10 (%)", fontsize=8)
a1.legend(loc="lower center", fontsize=7, ncol=2, bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, 0.0))
TOP_LAB = {"backed up": "BACKED\nUP", "coming out": "COMING\nOUT", "open field": "OPEN FIELD",
           "four-down\nterritory": "FOUR-DOWN\nTERRITORY", "red zone": "RED\nZONE"}
for name, lo, hi in ZONES:
    a1.text(110 - (lo + hi) / 2, 68.5, TOP_LAB[name], ha="center", va="top", fontsize=5.6, color=style.INK_2,
            fontweight="bold", linespacing=0.95)
t3b = N10[(N10.down == 3) & N10.ydstogo.between(2, 4)]
x_, m_, n_ = by5(t3b, "pass")
big = n_ >= 150
a2.plot(x_, m_ * 100, color=style.SERIES[1], lw=2, zorder=3)
a2.scatter(x_[big], m_[big] * 100, s=14, color=style.SERIES[1], zorder=4)
a2.scatter(x_[~big], m_[~big] * 100, s=14, facecolor=style.SURFACE, edgecolor=style.SERIES[1], zorder=4)
a2.axvline(60, color=style.INK_2, lw=0.8, ls=(0, (3, 2)))
a2.text(59, 62, "midfield", ha="right", va="bottom", fontsize=6.6, color=style.INK_2)
a2.set_ylim(60, 95)
a2.set_ylabel("3rd & 2–4: pass (%)", fontsize=8)
yardline_axis(a2)
for a in (a1, a2):
    a.tick_params(axis="y", labelsize=7)
    a.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
plt.show()








Figure 50.8: How the yard line changes the call, neutral situations, 2016-2025 regular seasons, offense moving left to right; each point is a 5-yard stretch of field. Top: on first-and-10 (first-and-goal inside the 10), how often the offense passed (blue) and how often its quarterback lined up in the shotgun (dashed). The pass rate is flat across the open field and falls off at both ends, backed up and near the opponent’s goal line; the shotgun disappears when the offense is backed up and, at the other end, only inside the 10. Bottom: on third-and-2-to-4, how often the offense passed. In its own half it threw about seven times in eight; past midfield the rate drops sharply, because fourth down is now part of the plan. Hollow points rest on fewer than 150 snaps. Source: nflverse play-by-play.






Backed up: get out, and don’t make it worse
Inside its own 10, an offense changes character. On first-and-10 there, teams passed 33% of the time, against 49% in the open field, and their quarterbacks were in the shotgun on 36% of snaps, against 46%. The passes they did call were built not to be sacked: the sack rate on first-down dropbacks fell from 4.8% in the open field to 2.7% backed up, which means quick throws, play-action with extra blockers, and quarterbacks told to throw the ball away rather than take the loss.15 Even the throwaway has a limit down there. A quarterback still inside the tackle box who throws the ball to no one to dodge a sack is guilty of intentional grounding, and from his own end zone that’s a safety too. A legal throwaway needs him outside the tackle box with the ball reaching the line of scrimmage (Officiating, Replay, and the Rules of the Ball draws it), which is one more reason backed-up passes are either quick or rolled out to the edge.16 The picture shows why the shotgun in particular goes away.


Show the Python
def backed_up_panels():
    LOSb = 12.0      # BDB x of the offense's own 2-yard line
    fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.5, 3.55), gridspec_kw=dict(wspace=0.04))
    # A: shotgun dropback
    off = line() + [O("QB", "QB", -5.0, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -5.0, -1.6, "R"), O("Y", "TE", -1.5, 7.0, "Y"),
                    O("H", "WR", -1.5, -7.5, "H"), O("X", "WR", -0.7, -12.5, "X"), O("Z", "WR", -0.7, 12.5, "Z")]
    dfn = [D("LE", "DE", 1.0, -4.6, "E"), D("LT_", "DT", 1.0, -1.4, "T"), D("RT_", "DT", 1.0, 2.4, "T"),
           D("RE", "DE", 1.0, 4.8, "E"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.6, 1.0, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.6, -2.5, "W")]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=LOSb, to_go=10)
    for k, w in zip(["LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT"], (-0.6, -0.2, 0.0, 0.2, 0.6)):
        p.block(k, pts=[(-1.0, w)])                     # pass sets
    p.block("RB", pts=[(-0.6, -1.8)])                   # the back stays in to protect
    p.dropback(2.0)
    p.rush("LE", pts=[(-3.5, -1.6), (-7.6, 3.6)])       # edge rushers loop to the quarterback
    p.rush("RE", pts=[(-4.0, 2.0), (-7.6, -3.8)])
    f1 = draw(p, ax=ax1, lateral=(-15.0, 15.0), window=(-12.0, 9.0))
    panel_title(ax1, "A. Shotgun at the 2")
    say(f1, p, -10.0, -9.5, "OWN END ZONE", fontsize=6.6, weight="bold")
    point_to(f1, p, (-9.2, 8.2), (-7.0, 0.6), "sacked here:\na safety, 2 points\nand the ball",
             color=style.DEFENSE_DARK)
    # B: under center, two tight ends, a handoff going forward
    off = line() + [O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -5.5, 0.0, "R"), O("Y", "TE", -0.7, 4.8, "Y"),
                    O("U", "TE", -0.7, -4.8, "U"), O("X", "WR", -1.5, -12.5, "X"), O("Z", "WR", -1.5, 12.5, "Z")]
    dfn2 = [D("LE", "DE", 1.0, -5.6, "E"), D("LT_", "DT", 1.0, -2.4, "T"), D("RT_", "DT", 1.0, 1.4, "T"),
            D("RE", "DE", 1.0, 5.6, "E"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.2, 1.0, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.2, -2.6, "W"),
            D("SAM", "SAM", 4.2, 5.2, "S")]
    q = Play(off, dfn2, los=LOSb, to_go=10)
    for k in ["LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT", "U", "Y"]:
        q.block(k, pts=[(1.0, 0.3)])
    q.path("QB", [(-0.8, 1.2)], speed=3.0)
    q.run("RB", [(3.6, 1.0), (8.5, 2.0)])
    q.handoff("RB", t=0.75)
    f2 = draw(q, ax=ax2, lateral=(-15.0, 15.0), window=(-12.0, 9.0))
    panel_title(ax2, "B. Under center at the 2")
    say(f2, q, -10.0, -9.5, "OWN END ZONE", fontsize=6.6, weight="bold")
    point_to(f2, q, (-9.0, 7.5), (-5.5, 0.0), "even the back\nstarts in the\nend zone", color=style.INK_2)
    say(f2, q, 4.6, -9.5, "3 yards here\nis a good play", fontsize=6.4, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK)
    return fig


backed_up_panels()
plt.show()








Figure 50.9: First-and-10 at the offense’s own 2 (illustrative). Left: from the shotgun, the quarterback takes the snap five yards behind the ball, three yards deep in his own end zone, and a normal dropback takes him deeper still. Any sack there is a safety, and so is a holding penalty by a blocker in the end zone. Right: under center, with two tight ends, the quarterback takes the snap just in front of his goal line and hands off going forward; even the running back, who lines up in the end zone, gets the ball near the goal line moving out. The call that gets three yards safely is worth more here than the call that might get twenty.





Here’s the puzzle: by EPA, the run is a worse bet backed up than anywhere else on the field (you’ll see it in the EPA chart at the end of the chapter), and the pass still comes out ahead on average, sacks and safeties included. Why run anyway? Partly the averages again: the backed-up passes that teams do call are the safe, quick, well-protected kind, chosen precisely because they rarely end in disaster, and a defense that expected more of them would make them harder. Partly the objective is different. Backed up, the first goal isn’t a big gain, it’s getting out: a few yards so the punter can stand at his normal depth, a first down so the next series starts with room. And partly it’s the asymmetry Romer described: a safety or an interception at your own 5 loses a game in a way a three-yard run never does. Backed-up football is the most conservative football you’ll see all day, and for most teams it’s also their least productive: on first-and-10 inside the 10, plays succeeded only 35% of the time, against 43% in the open field.


Coming out: the first first down
From its own 10 to about its own 25, an offense’s priority is the first first down, and you can put a number on why. From 2021 to 2025, after a punt from the offense’s own 10 to 15, the opponent’s next drive started, on average, at its own 43; after a punt from the own 25 to 30, at its own 28.17 One first down before the punt is worth about 15 yards of the opponent’s field position: that’s what “flipping the field” buys. You’ll see play-callers here lean on their most reliable first-down calls, the ones they trust not to go backward, but you’ll also see the quarterback come back out in the shotgun and a normal pass rate return: first-and-10 in this zone was a pass 47% of the time, against 33% backed up and 49% in the open field. Some staffs also keep a box of play-action shots for this zone, because defenses that just watched a backed-up offense run three times in a row are expecting a fourth.


The open field: the whole menu
From your own 25 out to about the opponent’s 40, the yard line stops mattering much. First-and-10 pass rates are flat across the whole stretch, and so are shotgun rates. This is where the base plays live, where sequencing does its work and where a play-caller’s balance on first down earns its keep. If you want to learn an offense’s personality, watch it here: the open field is where coaches call what they like, not what the field forces on them.


Plus territory and four-down territory: one more down to spend
Cross midfield and something changes that you can’t see on the field: the offense gains a down. Not officially, but in practice, because once a punt buys little and the kick is long, most offenses now plan to go for it on fourth-and-short. In 2025 teams went for it on 77% of fourth-and-1-to-3s between midfield and the opponent’s 21, against 33% in their own half between their 21 and midfield (outside the last two minutes of each half).18 Is going that often right? Public fourth-down models, such as Ben Baldwin’s open-source nfl4th, generally favor going for it on fourth-and-short across most of this part of the field, so the rise mostly reflects teams catching up with the math; The Clock, the Two-Minute Drill, and Fourth Down prices the decision case by case.19
The extra down changes third down. Look at third-and-2-to-4 first. (Third-and-1 is a running down everywhere, the quarterback sneak alone sees to that: offenses threw on only 24% of them, wherever the ball was. So the yard line’s effect shows a yard or three further out.) In its own half, an offense facing third-and-2-to-4 threw 86% of the time; past midfield, 73%. It is still a passing down, but the run comes back into play: with a fourth down in hand, third-and-3 becomes the first of two tries, and a run that gains two yards is no longer a failure, because it sets up fourth-and-1. Notice in the bottom panel of the chart where the switch flips: right at midfield, a little earlier than the “plus 40” that the textbook definition of four-down territory uses. On short yardage, today’s NFL treats the whole plus side as four-down territory.






NoteFilm room: Detroit Lions, 2023–2024



The seasons: Ben Johnson’s last two years as Detroit’s offensive coordinator under head coach Dan Campbell. The Lions went 12–5 in 2023 and reached the NFC Championship Game, losing 34–31 in San Francisco; in 2024 they went 15–2, took the NFC’s top seed, and led the league with 564 points before losing to Washington in the divisional round.20
What to notice, part 1: balanced and efficient. On early downs in neutral situations the Lions passed less often than most of the league (24th in 2023, 23rd in 2024) and were 5th and 6th in EPA per play. Like the 2018 Rams, they ran and faked from the same looks, so their run rate was a weapon rather than a price (Constraint Theory has their tendency table).
What to notice, part 2: they used the extra down. Campbell’s Lions were among the league’s most committed users of four-down territory. They went for it on fourth down 40 times in 2023 (2nd most in the league) and 33 times in 2024 (4th), converting 21 and 22. The fourth-down decision itself, and when it pays, is in The Clock, the Two-Minute Drill, and Fourth Down; the whole Detroit era is a case study.




The fringe of field-goal range, and the red zone
Somewhere around the opponent’s 35, a drive enters field-goal range, and the cost of a negative play changes again. A field goal is the yard line plus about 18 (the kick is spotted 8 yards behind the line, and the posts stand 10 yards deep, on the end line), so a sack at the plus 33 doesn’t just cost a down and seven yards; it can turn a 51-yard field goal into a 58-yarder or a punt. That’s why you’ll see quarterbacks near the edge of range throw the ball away rather than hold it, and play-callers avoid slow-developing dropbacks on third-and-long there: three points in hand are worth more than a small chance at a first down.
That line is moving outward. NFL kickers tried 266 field goals of 50 yards or more in 2025, against 150 in 2016, and made 69% of them, up from 57%.21 With a strong-legged kicker, “range” can start near the plus 40, and four-down territory shrinks with it, which is one reason the boundaries on the map are drawn loosely.
Inside the 20, the field shrinks. The back of the end zone works like an extra defender, there’s no room to throw over the top, and both pass rates and shotgun rates fall again as the goal line nears. How offenses and defenses play that compressed field is the next chapter but one, The Red Zone, Goal Line, and Short Yardage.


The defense reads the same map
This section has been told from the offense’s side, but the defensive coordinator’s call sheet carves up the same field. Backed up, the defense is the aggressive side: it expects a run or a quick throw, crowds the line, and is happy to pressure, because a sack or a holding flag might be a safety and even a short punt hands it good field position. In the open field it plays its base calls and its tendencies. In four-down territory a stop on third down isn’t a stop yet, so the defense is really defending two short-yardage snaps, and its third-down call can’t sell out against the run or the pass. Near the edge of field-goal range a sack is worth more than usual, because it can push the offense out of range. And on second-and-short, as the shot section showed, it mostly answers the offense’s personnel. The defense’s half of these situations gets its full treatment in the rest of Part 10.

section: Reading the numbers: down, distance, and yard line
text:
Reading the numbers: down, distance, and yard line
You’ve now seen the pieces one at a time. Two charts put them together, and they are the kind of chart you’ll meet in every analytics article about play-calling. Here is how to read them.


Show the Python
H = N5[N5.down <= 3].copy()
H["dist"] = H.ydstogo.clip(upper=15).astype(int)
HP = H.pivot_table(index="down", columns="dist", values="pass", aggfunc="mean")
HN = H.pivot_table(index="down", columns="dist", values="pass", aggfunc="size")
cmap = LinearSegmentedColormap.from_list("pr", [style.DEFENSE, "#fbe3d6", "#f6f4ee", style.OFFENSE_TINT,
                                                style.OFFENSE])
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 2.35))
for i, dn in enumerate([1, 2, 3]):
    for j, dist in enumerate(range(1, 16)):
        v, nn = HP.loc[dn, dist], HN.loc[dn, dist]
        rare = nn < 150
        ax.add_patch(Rectangle((j, 2 - i), 0.95, 0.92, fc=style.GRID if rare else cmap(float(v)), ec="white", lw=1.2))
        dark = (not rare) and (v >= 0.9 or v <= 0.15)      # white text only on the deepest cells
        ax.text(j + 0.475, 2 - i + 0.46, "·" if rare else f"{v * 100:.0f}", ha="center", va="center",
                fontsize=7.4, fontweight="bold", color="white" if dark else style.INK)
ax.set_xlim(-0.05, 15); ax.set_ylim(-0.05, 3)
ax.set_xticks([j + 0.475 for j in range(15)], [str(k) for k in range(1, 15)] + ["15+"], fontsize=7.2)
ax.set_yticks([2.46, 1.46, 0.46], ["1st down", "2nd down", "3rd down"], fontsize=7.8)
ax.xaxis.tick_top()
ax.xaxis.set_label_position("top")
ax.set_xlabel("Yards to go  (numbers are the % of snaps that were passes)", fontsize=7.6, labelpad=6)
ax.tick_params(length=0); ax.grid(False)
for sp in ax.spines.values():
    sp.set_visible(False)
plt.show()








Figure 50.10: How often offenses passed, by down (rows) and exact yards to go (columns, 15 or more grouped), neutral situations, 2021-2025 regular seasons. Blue cells lean pass, orange cells lean run; grey cells had fewer than 150 snaps. First down is almost always first-and-10; its other cells are mostly first-and-goal inside the 10 and first downs after a penalty. Read across a row to see how fast the pass takes over as the distance grows, and down a column to see what each lost down does at the same distance. Two details are real, not noise: second-and-10 is a less pass-heavy cell than second-and-9 (it usually follows an incompletion), and the 1-yard column is run-heavy on every down. Source: nflverse play-by-play.





A heatmap like this answers “what does the situation predict?” It shows the league’s habits, not what’s right. Three habits stand out. Across the second-down row, the pass takes over steadily from about second-and-4. Down the 1-yard column, the run dominates on every down. And across the third-down row, the switch is nearly instant: by third-and-4 almost everybody throws. Every one of those habits is a tendency a defense can lean on, which is why the interesting calls are the ones that land in the “wrong” color.


Show the Python
E = N10.copy()
E["b10"] = ((E.yardline_100.clip(1, 99) - 1) // 10) * 10 + 5
# third-and-short is thinner, so it is binned by field zone (the zone's middle yard line) instead
E["bz"] = E.yardline_100.map(lambda y: next((lo + hi) / 2 for _, lo, hi in ZONES if lo < y <= hi))
panels = [("1st & 10", E[(E.down == 1) & ((E.ydstogo == 10) | (E.goal_to_go == 1))]),
          ("2nd down", E[E.down == 2]), ("3rd & 1–3", E[(E.down == 3) & (E.ydstogo <= 3)])]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(6.5, 2.8), sharey=True, gridspec_kw=dict(wspace=0.08))
for a, (title, sub) in zip(axes, panels):
    shade_zones(a, alpha=0.08, labels=False)
    col_ = "bz" if title.startswith("3rd") else "b10"
    t_ = sub.groupby([col_, "pass"]).epa.mean().unstack()
    n_ = sub.groupby([col_, "pass"]).epa.size().unstack()
    t_ = t_.where(n_ >= 150)                    # leave out stretches with too few snaps to trust
    for k, col, lab in [(0, style.SERIES[1], "designed runs"), (1, style.SERIES[0], "dropbacks")]:
        a.plot(110 - t_.index.values, t_[k].values, color=col, lw=1.8, marker="o", ms=3, label=lab, zorder=3)
    a.axhline(0, color=style.BASELINE, lw=1)
    a.set_title(title, fontsize=8.6)
    a.set_xlim(10, 110)
    a.set_xticks([20, 40, 60, 80, 100], [MINUS + "10", MINUS + "30", "50", "+30", "+10"], fontsize=6.6)
    a.tick_params(axis="y", labelsize=7)
    a.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
axes[0].set_ylabel("EPA per play", fontsize=8)
axes[0].set_ylim(-0.25, 0.25)
axes[1].legend(loc="lower center", fontsize=7, ncol=2, bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, -0.36))
plt.show()
EF = {t: s.groupby(["b10", "pass"]).epa.mean().unstack() for t, s in panels}








Figure 50.11: What runs and dropbacks earned across the field, neutral situations, 2016-2025 regular seasons: EPA per play for designed runs (orange) and dropbacks (blue), by 10-yard stretch of field, offense moving left to right. On first and second down the dropback line sits above the run line almost everywhere; the gap is widest when the offense is backed up and closes near the opponent’s goal line, where the field is short and a run is as good as a pass. Third-and-1-to-3 is shown instead of all third downs so that runs and passes face the same distances; it is thinner, so each point there is a whole field zone. Runs have earned about as much as dropbacks or more, and clearly more in the red zone. Points resting on fewer than 150 snaps of either kind are left out, which is why the backed-up end of that panel is empty. Source: nflverse play-by-play.





A chart like this answers a different question: “what did each choice earn?” Read it in three steps. First, find the gap between the lines: on early downs the pass has earned more almost everywhere, by the most when the offense is backed up, where teams run the most. Second, find where the lines meet: close to the opponent’s goal line, where the defense has no deep space to protect and a run is as good as a pass. Third, remember what the chart can’t see. Every point mixes situations (the backed-up passes are the safe ones; the third-and-short runs include quarterback sneaks, the best short-yardage play in football), and every point is an average of what teams chose to do, not of what they would have earned doing more of it. The gap is a strong hint about where offenses are too cautious. It isn’t a play-call.






TipWatch for it on Sunday: the situation tag



This is the 01-02 forecaster, upgraded with the field. For one half of one game, before every snap:

Say the tag out loud: the down-and-distance bucket plus the zone. “Second and short, open field.” “First and ten, backed up.” “Third and three, four-down territory.”
Predict run or pass from the tag, then glance at the formation and change your guess if it tells you something. Mark both.
Flag the four situations this chapter gave you an edge in: second-and-10 after an incompletion (less pass than usual, though still slightly more likely a pass); second-and-short with one deep safety and eight defenders near the ball (shot alert: count the deep safeties before the snap); backed up (count the shotgun snaps, and expect a quick throw or a run); third-and-2-to-4 past midfield (still usually a pass, but the run comes back into play, and expect a fourth-down try if it fails).
At halftime, score yourself by tag, not just overall. You should be very good on third-and-long and second-and-very-long, decent backed up and in the red zone, and close to a coin flip on first-and-10 and second-and-medium. That isn’t a failure: first-and-10 is built to beat you.



What “good” looks like: the table below is what you’d score by always guessing the more common call for each tag, in neutral situations from 2021 to 2025. First-and-10 is split by the five zones; second down by its four buckets; third down by the cuts this chapter used (third-and-1 anywhere, third-and-2-to-4 on each side of midfield, and everything longer). Overall, that simple rule was right 66% of the time. Beat it on any tag and you’re reading something the down and distance alone don’t show.


Show the Python
rows = "| Tag | Pass rate | Guess | Right |\n|---|---:|:---:|---:|\n"
for t in TAG_ORDER:
    r_ = TAG_T.loc[t]
    rows += f"| {t} | {pct(r_.pr)} | {r_.guess} | {pct(r_.acc)} |\n"
display(Markdown(rows))

title: Early Downs and Field Zones: How Situation Shapes the Call
text:
Predict the play






TipPredict the play 1: first-and-10 at your own 3





Show the Python
LOS1 = 13.0
off = line() + [O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -5.5, 0.0, "R"), O("Y", "TE", -0.7, 4.8, "Y"),
                O("U", "TE", -0.7, -4.8, "U"), O("X", "WR", -1.5, -13.5, "X"), O("Z", "WR", -1.5, 13.5, "Z")]
dfn = [D("WDE", "DE", 1.0, -5.6, "E"), D("WDT", "DT", 1.0, technique("2i", -1), "T"),
       D("SDT", "DT", 1.0, technique("3", 1), "T"), D("SDE", "DE", 1.0, 5.6, "E"),
       D("SAM", "SAM", 3.6, 3.4, "S"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.2, -0.4, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.2, -3.6, "W"),
       D("SS", "SS", 5.0, 7.8, "SS"), D("LCB", "CB", 5.5, -13.5, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 5.5, 13.5, "CB"),
       D("FS", "FS", 12.0, -1.0, "FS")]
p1 = Play(off, dfn, los=LOS1, to_go=10)
f_ = draw(p1, lateral=(-17.5, 17.5), window=(-12.5, 14.5), width_in=5.6)
say(f_, p1, -9.5, -11.0, "OWN END ZONE", fontsize=7.0, weight="bold")
say(f_, p1, -3.6, 12.5, "goal line", fontsize=6.4)
plt.show()








Figure 50.12: First-and-10 at the offense’s own 3, second quarter, tied 7-7. The offense has two tight ends (Y and U) and a running back (R) in its own end zone, with the quarterback (Q) under center. The defense has seven men within five yards of the ball and the strong safety (SS) walked down outside the right tight end: eight near the line of scrimmage, one safety (FS) deep.





Run or pass? And name two calls this offense is very unlikely to make.






TipAnswer





Most likely a run, from exactly this kind of look; very unlikely: a shotgun dropback, or any play that asks the quarterback to hold the ball.
On first-and-10 inside their own 10, offenses in neutral situations passed only 33% of the time (2016–2025), against 49% in the open field. Two tight ends with the quarterback under center make a run more likely still. But even this run isn’t safe by default: the quarterback takes the snap in the field of play, and the handoff comes right around the goal line, so a defensive tackle who knifes into the backfield can make the tackle at the mesh for a safety. That’s why, backed up this tight, staffs cheat the back up a yard or two (he’s only two and a half yards deep in the end zone here) and call downhill runs that hit fast: a dive, an iso, duo, the quarterback sneak.
The calls to cross off are the ones that keep the ball behind the goal line for a long time: the quarterback in the shotgun (he’d start three yards deep in his own end zone), a deep dropback, a pass that needs four seconds to develop, and any run with a deep mesh or a long sideways path (a stretch, a toss, a counter with pulling linemen), which might be caught going sideways in the end zone. A sack or a holding penalty in the end zone is two points and the ball.
The surprise you’ll occasionally see: a play-action shot from this exact look, with both tight ends and the back staying in to block, because eight defenders near the line and one deep safety is exactly the picture a shot is built to beat. It is rare, and when it hits it can go 90-plus yards. The defense knows the odds, which is why it walked the strong safety down: it’s betting on the run, and accepting the risk of the shot.











TipPredict the play 2: second-and-10 after an incompletion





Show the Python
LOS2 = 45.0
off = line() + [O("QB", "QB", -5.0, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -5.0, -1.6, "R"), O("Y", "TE", -0.7, 4.8, "Y"),
                O("H", "WR", -1.5, -8.0, "H"), O("X", "WR", -0.7, -14.5, "X"), O("Z", "WR", -1.5, 14.0, "Z")]
dfn = [D("WDE", "DE", 1.0, -4.6, "E"), D("WDT", "DT", 1.0, technique("2i", -1), "T"),
       D("SDT", "DT", 1.0, technique("3", 1), "T"), D("SDE", "DE", 1.0, technique("6", 1) + 0.6, "E"),
       D("MIKE", "MIKE", 5.0, 1.8, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 5.0, -2.2, "W"), D("NB", "NB", 5.0, -8.5, "$"),
       D("LCB", "CB", 7.0, -14.5, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 7.0, 14.0, "CB"),
       D("FS", "FS", 12.5, -8.0, "FS"), D("SS", "SS", 12.5, 8.0, "SS")]
p2 = Play(off, dfn, los=LOS2, to_go=10)
f_ = draw(p2, lateral=(-18.5, 18.5), window=(-9.5, 15.0), width_in=5.6)
say(f_, p2, -6.2, -11.5, "last play: 1st & 10,\npass incomplete", fontsize=6.6)
plt.show()








Figure 50.13: Second-and-10 at the offense’s own 35, first quarter, tied. On first down the quarterback threw incomplete. The offense is in the shotgun with three receivers and a tight end (11 personnel), the back (R) beside the quarterback. The defense is in its nickel (five defensive backs) with two deep safeties: only six defenders are in the box, inside the tight end and within five yards of the ball.





Is a pass more or less likely here than on a typical second-and-10? What does the previous play tell you, and what does the defense tell you?






TipAnswer





Less likely than usual: still a pass more often than not, but only barely (56%), against 83% when the same second-and-10 follows a no-gain run.
Second-and-10 is usually a passing down, but which second-and-10 matters. From 2021 to 2025, offenses threw on 83% of second-and-10s that followed a no-gain run and on only 56% of those that followed an incompletion (4,179 snaps). After a failed pass, play-callers lean toward a run to avoid two straight incompletions and a third-and-10.
The defense adds a second reason. Two deep safeties and a nickel back leave six defenders in the box against six blockers (five linemen and the tight end), a light box that is all but inviting a run. Many offenses build this answer into the play itself, with a run-pass option or a quarterback check at the line: against six in the box, hand it off. The defense, for its part, knows that four or five yards here are not a disaster for it; what it can’t allow is the explosive pass that a single-high shell would risk.
If a pass does come, expect something quick that gets half the distance back: a 5-yard completion turns the down into third-and-5.











TipPredict the play 3: third-and-3 at the opponent’s 38





Show the Python
LOS3 = 72.0
off = line() + [O("QB", "QB", -4.0, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -7.0, 0.0, "R"), O("Y", "TE", -0.7, 4.8, "Y"),
                O("H", "WR", -1.5, -8.0, "H"), O("X", "WR", -0.7, -14.5, "X"), O("Z", "WR", -1.5, 14.0, "Z")]
dfn = [D("WDE", "DE", 1.0, -4.6, "E"), D("WDT", "DT", 1.0, technique("2i", -1), "T"),
       D("SDT", "DT", 1.0, technique("3", 1), "T"), D("SDE", "DE", 1.0, technique("6", 1) + 0.8, "E"),
       D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, 1.6, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -2.0, "W"), D("NB", "NB", 4.5, -8.5, "$"),
       D("SS", "SS", 6.0, 8.5, "SS"), D("LCB", "CB", 6.0, -14.5, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 7.0, 14.0, "CB"),
       D("FS", "FS", 13.0, 0.0, "FS")]
p3 = Play(off, dfn, los=LOS3, to_go=3)
f_ = draw(p3, lateral=(-18.5, 18.5), window=(-10.0, 16.0), width_in=5.6)
plt.show()








Figure 50.14: Third-and-3 at the opponent’s 38 (plus territory), second quarter, tied. The offense is in the pistol (the quarterback about four yards behind the ball with the back directly behind him) with three receivers and a tight end. The defense is in its nickel with one deep safety: six defenders in the box, with the nickel back ($) and the strong safety (SS) close enough to fill against a run.





Run or pass? Would your answer change if this were third-and-3 at the offense’s own 38?






TipAnswer





Still more likely a pass, about three times in four, but a run is far more likely than it would be in the offense’s own half, and if it fails, expect the offense to stay on the field for fourth down.
On third-and-2-to-4 from 2016 to 2025, offenses threw 86% of the time in their own half and 73% of the time past midfield. The yard line is the reason. At the opponent’s 38 a punt buys little and a field goal would be 56 yards (38 plus 18), so most offenses plan to use fourth down: in 2025 teams went for it on 77% of fourth-and-1-to-3s between midfield and the opponent’s 21. That makes this third down the first of two tries, and a run that gains two yards isn’t a failure; it sets up fourth-and-1. The pistol helps the run here too: the back gets the ball going downhill, and the quarterback can keep it.
It also explains why the conversion rate on these third downs barely changes between the two halves of the field (54% in the offense’s own half, 56% past midfield): the run isn’t a worse call, just a different one. At its own 38, with a punt coming if it fails, the offense would probably throw, about six times in seven, and the defense would know it.

title: Early Downs and Field Zones: How Situation Shapes the Call
text:
Takeaways

The situation comes before the play. A call sheet is organized by down and distance, field zone, and score and clock. On the early downs (first and second) nothing is forced, which is why they are where a play-caller’s philosophy shows.
First-and-10 is a coin flip, on purpose. Neutral first-down pass rates have sat near 46% for a quarter century, even though dropbacks have out-earned runs there every season. Balance keeps the defense guessing; the price is the gap. Good offenses shrink the price; they don’t abandon balance.
“Establish the run” is four claims. Running doesn’t measurably wear defenses down, play-action doesn’t need a successful run game, and teams run a lot because they’re winning, not the reverse. What survives: a run game the defense must respect makes the passing game better, and an efficient run game (2019 Ravens) is worth calling often.
Stay on schedule. About 4 yards on first down is the line between a series that usually converts and one that often doesn’t. The play that kills drives is the negative play, not the incompletion.
Second down comes in four buckets, and second-and-short is the cheapest down in football to spend on a shot: a failed shot costs about half what a wasted second-and-long does. Teams still mostly run there, because the run usually moves the chains and the shot carries sack and turnover risk; when they do take the shot, it usually pays. And the second-and-10 after an incompletion is less of a passing down than its down and distance say.
The field has zones. Backed up, offenses get conservative and leave the shotgun; coming out, they chase the first first down that flips the field; in the open field the whole menu is available; past midfield, fourth down becomes part of the plan, and on third-and-short the run comes back into play.

Connections
Builds on: Downs, Distance, and Field Position (the buckets, the third-down price list, expected points and EPA, the red zone) and Constraint Theory (base and constraint plays, tendencies). title: Third Down: The Money Down
text:
Why third down is the money down
Third-and-7, early in the fourth quarter, a three-point game. You can tell it matters before anyone lines up. The broadcast puts up a graphic of the offense’s third-down conversions so far. On the defensive sideline, two linebackers jog off and two defensive backs jog on, and a pass rusher who has been standing by the bench all series pulls on his helmet. The offense’s best receiver, who stood out wide on first and second down, now lines up in the slot. The quarterback looks to the sideline, then points at a safety creeping toward the line and shouts. At the snap that safety drops into the middle instead of rushing, four defenders rush, the slot receiver pushes eight yards upfield, looks at the defender in front of him and turns away from him toward the sideline, and the ball is already there. The chains move. Why did half the defense change before the play? What was the quarterback pointing at? Why eight yards, not seven, and why did the receiver seem to decide where to go after he started running? And why does the whole stadium seem to agree that this one snap is worth more than the two before it? This chapter is about third down, the down that decides drives, and about why everyone on the field plays it differently.
You’ll be able to…
How to read the diagrams. Offense is blue circles: the linemen (only the center, C, is labelled on wide pictures), Q the quarterback, R the running back, X and Z the outside receivers, H the slot receiver and Y the tight end. Defense is outlined orange squares: E and T the defensive ends and tackles, N a nose tackle, B a stand-up edge player, M the Mike and W the Will linebacker, $ the nickel back (the slot cornerback), D a dime back (the sixth defensive back), CB the cornerbacks, FS and SS the free and strong safety. A green ring marks the player to watch and a purple ring a spy. Blue arrows are routes, the thick dark-blue arrow a ball carrier’s path; solid orange arrows are rushers and dashed orange arrows zone drops, with the shaded ovals the zones; dotted orange lines join a man-coverage defender to his receiver. The thick orange line across the field is the line to gain, the blue line the line of scrimmage, and the small numbers on the left edge count yards past the line of scrimmage. Pictures of a moment in a simulated play show faint lines for where each player has been, and an × where a tackle is made. Left and right are the offense’s.
Start with what third down is. On first and second down a bad play is a setback; on third down it is usually the end of the drive. Convert, and the offense gets three more tries and keeps the ball. Fail, and outside field-goal range it punts, giving the ball away 40 yards downfield. That cliff is why the down gets its nickname.
Put a number on the cliff. In the 2021–2025 regular seasons, a converted third down was worth +1.8 expected points to the offense on average, and a failed one -1.3. The difference, about 3.0 points, rides on one snap.1 No other ordinary play swings that much so often: a first-and-10 that gains four yards or loses one leaves the drive alive either way. Third downs are only about 21% of all runs and passes, but they decide whether most drives become points or punts.
And the league converts them at a remarkably steady rate: between 39% and 42% in every season from 2016 to 2025, about two in five.2 Rule changes, the passing boom and the two-high defenses of the last decade have barely moved it. That stability is a clue. Third down is a contest both sides prepare for more than any other, and the offense’s gains and the defense’s answers have stayed roughly matched.
What makes third down special isn’t just the stakes; it’s the information. On first-and-10 the defense has to guard against everything, because the offense can do anything. On third-and-8 both sides know what the offense needs: eight yards, almost certainly through the air. Knowing that, the defense can specialise. It can take off run defenders and put on pass defenders, take off a big run-stopping tackle and put on a quick pass rusher, and set every underneath defender’s depth by the line to gain. The offense specialises too: its best receiver moves to where he can get a free release, its routes are cut to a depth measured from the sticks, and it calls the plays it has practised all week for exactly this distance. Third down is the down on which the situation tells both teams the most, so it is the down on which they each carry a separate plan.

title: Third Down: The Money Down
text:
NoteMadden vs. real life



In a video game you pick a play from a menu on every down, and the menu looks the same on third-and-8 as on first-and-10. In the NFL, third down has its own section of the call sheet, its own practice day (in a typical week the third-down plan is installed on Thursday, after the early-down plan; The Game Plan), its own personnel and often its own play-caller’s mindset. The plays on that page are sorted by distance: third-and-1, third-and-2 to 3, third-and-4 to 6, third-and-7 to 10, third-and-long. A coordinator calling a third-down play is choosing from a short list built for exactly this distance against exactly this opponent’s third-down habits, not from the whole playbook.

title: Third Down: The Money Down
text:
Four kinds of third down
A broadcaster will tell you “third and short” or “third and long.” Coaches cut it finer, because each distance changes what both sides can do. This book uses four buckets: short (1 to 3 yards), medium (4 to 6), long (7 to 10) and very long (11 or more). Start with how often each kind is converted, and how.


Show the Python
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.1))
xs = np.arange(len(LABS))
wbar = 0.38
for j, (kind, lab, col) in enumerate([("run", "Designed runs", style.SERIES[0]),
                                      ("drop", "Dropbacks (pass, sack, scramble)", style.SERIES[1])]):
    vals = CB["mean"][kind].reindex(LABS).values
    ns = CB["size"][kind].reindex(LABS).values
    x = xs + (j - 0.5) * (wbar + 0.03)
    ax.bar(x, vals, width=wbar, color=col, label=lab, zorder=3)
    for xi, v, n in zip(x, vals, ns):
        ax.text(xi, v + 0.012, f"{100 * v:.0f}", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=7.2, color=style.INK)
        ax.text(xi, -0.035, f"{n / 1000:.1f}k" if n >= 1000 else f"{n}", ha="center", va="top", fontsize=6.0,
                color=style.INK_2)
ax.set_xticks(xs, [f"3rd & {b}" for b in LABS], fontsize=7.8)
ax.tick_params(axis="x", pad=13, length=0)
ax.set_ylim(-0.075, 0.85)
ax.set_yticks([0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8])
ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(plt.FuncFormatter(lambda y, _: f"{100 * y:.0f}%"))
ax.tick_params(axis="y", labelsize=7.5)
ax.set_ylabel("Converted to a first down", fontsize=8)
ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
ax.axhline(0, color=style.BASELINE, lw=0.8, zorder=2)
ax.legend(loc="upper right", fontsize=7.5, frameon=False)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 51.1: Third-down conversion rate by yards to go and by play type, NFL regular seasons 2021–2025. Designed runs convert more often at 1 and 2 yards to go; from 4 yards on, dropbacks (passes, sacks and scrambles together) convert far more often, and a run on third-and-11 or more almost never does. The small number under each bar is the number of plays (k = thousand); runs are rare from 4 yards on, so those bars are mostly deliberate, low-risk calls. Source: nflverse play-by-play.





The chart has two sets of bars, designed runs and dropbacks, at each distance.3 On third-and-1, runs convert 73% of the time and dropbacks 59%. That isn’t because passing is worse; it’s because a run needs only a yard and gets it on a good push, while a pass can go wrong in more ways (a sack, a drop, an incompletion) that a run can’t. By third-and-3 the two are level, and from 4 yards on the pass is the only sensible way: runs on third-and-4 to 6 convert 36%, dropbacks 45%. Offenses know it, which is why they pass on 91% of third-and-4 to 6 snaps and 94% of third-and-7 to 10.
Each bucket has its own conversion rate and its own logic, and the rest of the chapter follows them (rates are for 2021–2025).
Short, 1–3 yards: converted 60%. A run can get it, so the offense’s whole menu is open and the defense has to defend both. It can’t fill the field with defensive backs, it usually plays tight man coverage because any completion converts, and it often packs the box. The offense’s best weapons are a power run, a quarterback sneak, or a quick throw that beats tight coverage before the rush arrives. (Third-and-1 and the sneak get their own chapter, Red Zone, Goal Line, Two-Point Plays, and Short Yardage.)
Medium, 4–6 yards: converted 44%. The most contested distance. The offense will almost certainly throw, but it doesn’t need to throw far: a 6-yard route run well converts. The defense plays tight man coverage, mixes in pressure, and leans on mugs and disguise to make the quarterback guess. It is the bucket of option routes, rubs and mesh on one side and of Cover 1 and A-gap mugs on the other.
Long, 7–10 yards: converted 31%. Almost always a pass, and one that has to travel past the defenders waiting at the sticks. Now the offense needs a route that takes time to run, and that time is what the defense attacks: this is where the blitz peaks, because a hot throw to beat it usually lands short of the line.
Very long, 11 or more: converted 15%. The defense can concede anything short and still win, so it drops more players into coverage, plays deep, and rallies to tackle. Some offenses take a shot; many take the safe completion, the screen or the draw, and play for a better punt or a field-goal try.
And the long kinds are common: 46% of third downs needed 7 yards or more. That is why coaches care so much about first and second down: a four-yard gain on first down doesn’t look like much, but it is the difference between a third down at the top of that list and one at the bottom (Early Downs and Field Zones).

section: The sticks route: a yard past the line
text:
The sticks route: a yard past the line
If the target is a known distance, aim past it. That is the whole idea behind a sticks route: a route whose depth is set by the line to gain, usually so the receiver breaks or settles a yard or two beyond it. On first-and-10 a curl might be run at 12 yards because that’s where it fits the defense. On third-and-6 the same receiver runs it at 7 or 8, because what matters now is that the catch is a first down at the catch, with no need for yards after it. Coaches teach it bluntly: get past the sticks before you break, and don’t break short of them.
Why a yard or two past, and not exactly on the line? Two reasons, both about the catch point.

Receivers drift back toward the ball. A receiver who breaks at 7 and turns back to the quarterback is caught at 6 and a half, short of a third-and-7. A route designed at 8 leaves room for that.
Defenders sit on the sticks. On third down the underneath defenders’ landmark is the line to gain (more below). A ball caught right on the line is caught in front of a defender who is already there and only has to tackle forward.

But a sticks route can’t go too far past the line, because every extra yard of depth costs completion probability: it takes the receiver longer to get there, and the quarterback has to hold the ball against the rush. The design problem of third-and-medium is to get a receiver open as close past the sticks as possible, as fast as possible. Against the man coverage defenses favour at those distances, that means beating a defender who knows where you’re going.

The answer to man: routes that choose
Here is a typical third-and-7 against Cover 1. The offense is in trips to the right; the defense plays man coverage with one deep safety and a robber. (Staffs call that low middle player a robber, a rat or a hole player depending on the playbook and how deep he sits; Man Coverage draws the versions.)


Show the Python
def cover1_play():
    dfn = four_down(rde=6.0) + [
        D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -2.2, "W"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, 2.6, "M"),
        D("NB", "NB", 4.0, 8.4, "$"), D("LCB", "CB", 1.2, -15.8, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 1.2, 16.8, "CB"),
        D("SS", "SS", 9.5, 3.0, "SS"), D("FS", "FS", 14.0, -1.0, "FS")]
    p = Play(trips(), dfn, los=45, to_go=7)
    p.route("X", r.go(19)); p.route("Z", r.go(18)); p.route("Y", r.seam(16))
    # route offsets are from H's alignment (1.5 yards off the line): a 9.5-yard stem breaks at 8 past the LOS
    p.route("H", r.out(9.5, 4)); p.route("RB", r.flat(1.0, 5), side=-1)
    p.dropback(2.0); p.pass_to("H", t=1.55)
    protect(p)
    for k in ("LDE", "LDT", "RDT", "RDE"):
        p.rush(k, pts=[(-1.6, 0.0)])
    for dk, ok in (("LCB", "X"), ("RCB", "Z"), ("NB", "H"), ("MIKE", "Y"), ("WILL", "RB")):
        p.man(dk, ok)
    p.drop("SS", (10.0, 4.0)); p.drop("FS", (17.0, 0.0))
    p.highlight("H")
    return p


p = cover1_play()
fld = p.draw(lateral=(-21, 23), window=(-9.5, 21.5), title=False)
clean(fld.ax); ruler(fld, p)
say(fld, p, 7.0, -7.5, "line to gain (3rd & 7)", color=style.INK_2, fontsize=6.5)
point_to(fld, p, (-5.0, 13.6), (8.0, 11.6),
         "H's option route: the nickel ($)\nis inside, so H breaks out at\n8 yards, one past the line")
point_to(fld, p, (11.8, -8.0), (9.6, 2.6), "robber (SS): sits inside,\nwaiting for the in-cut")
point_to(fld, p, (18.8, -9.0), (14.0, -1.0), "free safety: one man deep,\nheld in the middle by the seam")
point_to(fld, p, (-6.2, -11.5), (-4.0, -6.0), "checkdown: back\nin the flat, short\nof the line")
plt.show()








Figure 51.2: Third-and-7 against Cover 1 (illustrative). The offense is in trips to the right: Z (#1), H (#2) and the tight end Y (#3, attached to the line), with X alone on the left. The defense plays man coverage (dotted lines) with the free safety (FS) deep and the strong safety (SS) as a robber in the middle. Z and X run go routes that take their cornerbacks deep, and Y’s seam holds the free safety in the middle. H runs an option route set past the line to gain: the nickel back ($) lines up a yard and a half inside him, protecting the middle, so H pushes to 8 yards and breaks away from that leverage, toward the sideline, where the robber can’t help. The ball is out at about 1.6 seconds. The back checks for a blitzer, then releases to the flat as the checkdown.





The option route is the heart of it (Passing Game Fundamentals taught the rule). A man defender has to line up on one side of his receiver, and that side, his leverage, is the side he is protecting. Here the nickel sits inside H, taking away the quickest throws, the slant and the in-cut toward the middle. So H pushes to 8 yards, past the line, and breaks the other way, toward the sideline, where the nickel can’t get to him in time and the robber can’t help.
That inside alignment is a choice, not the default. With a robber in the middle, many defenses play the slot defender outside and funnel the receiver inside to the help; this one is taking away the quick slant instead. Against that outside alignment the rule sends H inside, straight toward the robber, and the quarterback has to see it and look elsewhere. And the rule has a third branch that coaches always teach: if the defender is soft, head-up, or dropping into a zone, sit it down in the open space past the sticks, face the quarterback and catch the ball. That is why the quarterback reads two things, not one: the nickel’s leverage and where the robber is standing. The receiver doesn’t guess; he reads, and the quarterback reads with him, which is why option routes go to the receivers a quarterback trusts most.
The rest of the concept exists to protect that one decision. The two go routes outside are clear-outs: they take the cornerbacks, who are in man coverage and must run with them, out of the area where H will break. Y’s seam up the middle gives the single deep safety something to worry about, so he can’t drift toward the sideline to help on H. And the back is the checkdown. If the defense blitzes, he blocks; if it doesn’t, he is the safe throw, short of the sticks, for when the option route is covered.
The option route is one of a family of third-down man-beaters, all of which do the same job by different means: give the receiver an advantage over a defender who has no help.

Rubs and bunches. Line receivers up close together, a bunch, and send them across each other’s paths. Each man defender has to fight through traffic to follow his receiver, while zone defenders would just swap receivers. (Dropback Concepts draws the concepts; where a rub becomes illegal offensive pass interference is in Contact Rules and Penalties as Strategy.)
Mesh. Two shallow crossers who brush past each other in the middle (mesh), with the same traffic problem for their defenders; the crossers usually settle a few yards past a third-and-medium line to gain.
Slants and quick outs. The fastest throws on the field, aimed at the receiver who has the leverage he wants before the snap. They beat a blitz too, because the ball is out before the rush arrives.
Matchups. The offense moves its best receiver to wherever the defense’s worst cover man will have to take him, usually the slot, against a linebacker or a safety. On third down, who covers whom often matters more than the concept, which is why defenses answer the best receiver with a bracket: two defenders on him, one under and one over, or one inside and one outside. “Take away their guy and make somebody else beat us” is a third-down plan in itself.
Empty. Five receivers spread across the field and nobody in the backfield (empty). It thins the box, forces the defense to show man or zone by how it lines up, and usually leaves a linebacker on a receiver. Offenses lined up in empty on 19% of third-down dropbacks in 2020–2022, against 12% on first and second down.4 The price is protection: with no back to block, a sixth rusher is the quarterback’s problem, and he has to throw hot.

Why does all this aim at man coverage? Because that is what defenses play on third-and-short and medium. In 2023–2025, charted third-down dropbacks at 1 to 3 yards to go were played in man coverage 58% of the time, and at 4 to 6 yards 58%; at 11 or more it fell to 26%.5 A zone defense on third-and-4 has defenders spread across the field waiting for the ball, and any route that finds the space between two of them, five yards deep, converts. Man coverage takes that space away by putting a defender on every receiver. The offense’s reply is to make that defender’s life as hard as possible for about a second and a half.
Man coverage has one more price on third down: flags. A man defender is attached to his receiver, and when he is beaten his last resort is a grab. On charted third-down dropbacks in 2023–2025, defenders were flagged for pass interference, defensive holding or illegal contact on 4.8% of snaps in man coverage, against 1.6% in zone, about three times as often. All three give the offense an automatic first down whatever the distance. Across 2021–2025, about one third-down snap in 25 (4.0%) ended in a first down by defensive penalty, pass interference and holding the most common.6 The conversion rates in this chapter leave those out, so they slightly understate how often drives survive third down, and every one of those flags is a quiet cost of playing man.






ImportantWhy it exists



The sticks route exists because on third down the distance is fixed in advance, so the offense can aim at one yard and give the receiver the right to choose his break. What it gives up: a route set to the sticks hands the defense a target depth too, and the two sides have been trading moves over that yard ever since. Defenders learn to sit at the sticks and drive on the break; receivers answer by selling the sit and turning upfield (a “stick-nod”), quarterbacks by throwing to the back shoulder, away from the defender’s drive. Defenses answer with man coverage from depth and safeties over the top, so that the receiver who turns upfield runs into help; offenses answer that with rubs. That steady trading of moves is why the league’s third-down rate barely moves.

Past the sticks: what the numbers say, and when it doesn’t matter
Every broadcaster has said it: “you have to throw it past the sticks on third down.” Here is how true that is.


Show the Python
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.0))

short = xs < 4
ax.axvspan(-0.5, 3.5, color=style.GRID, alpha=0.45, lw=0, zorder=0)
ax.text(1.5, 0.93, "thrown short of the line to gain", ha="center", fontsize=7.2, color=style.INK_2)
