ax.bar(xs, PS.conv.reindex(REL_LABS).values, width=0.62, color=style.SERIES[0], zorder=3,
       label="Converted (share of attempts)")
ax.plot(xs, PS.comp.reindex(REL_LABS).values, color=style.SERIES[1], lw=2, marker="o", ms=5, zorder=4,
        label="Completed")
for x, v in zip(xs, PS.conv.reindex(REL_LABS).values):
    if v > 0.25:   # inside the bar, clear of the completion line that meets the bar tops past the sticks
        ax.text(x, v - 0.03, f"{100 * v:.0f}", ha="center", va="top", fontsize=7, color="white", zorder=5)
    else:
        ax.text(x, v + 0.015, f"{100 * v:.0f}", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=7, color=style.INK)
ax.set_xticks(xs, REL_LABS, fontsize=7.2)
ax.set_xlabel("Where the ball was thrown, relative to the line to gain (yards)", fontsize=8)
ax.set_ylim(0, 1.0)
ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(plt.FuncFormatter(lambda y, _: f"{100 * y:.0f}%"))
ax.tick_params(axis="y", labelsize=7.5)
ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
ax.legend(loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, -0.24), ncol=2, fontsize=7.5, frameon=False)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 51.3: Where third-down passes were aimed, and what happened. Each bar is the share of attempts that converted, grouped by how far past (or short of) the line to gain the ball was thrown (air yards minus yards to go); the line is the completion rate for the same throws. Throws short of the line are caught more often but convert rarely, because the receiver still has to run for the rest; throws one or two yards past it convert most often; deeper throws are completed, and so convert, less often. Third-down aimed passes (sacks, scrambles and throwaways without a charted depth excluded), NFL regular seasons 2021–2025. Source: nflverse play-by-play.





The shape of the bars is the case for the sticks route.7 Throws aimed 10 or more yards short of the line to gain were completed 77% of the time and converted only 9%. Throws aimed one or two yards past it converted 63%, the best of any group. Past the line, the bar and the line meet: every completion there converts, so conversion simply tracks completion rate, and falls as the throws get deeper and harder to complete. Notice the dip for throws aimed right at the line (52%, with completions falling off too): that is very likely, at least in part, the sticks-sitting defender at work, and it is the reason the sticks route is set a yard or two beyond.
So the broadcasters are mostly right. But “past the sticks” is a rule about averages, and there are four situations in which a throw short of the line is the right one.

Third-and-short. Even a catch behind the line can convert when the line is only a yard or two away. Completed throws short of the sticks converted 80% of the time on third-and-1 and 69% on third-and-2, against 36% on third-and-7 to 10 and 11% on 11 or more. On third-and-1 a pass to the flat, caught a yard behind the line with nobody near the receiver, is a good play; it’s a run with a better start.
The receiver who will run after the catch. Screens and quick throws to the offense’s best open-field runner are short by design: the bet is on the yards after the catch, and against a defense playing deep it can be a good bet.
Four-down territory. When an offense near midfield has already decided it will go for it on fourth down if it needs to, third-and-6 is really “third-and-6 with two tries.” A five-yard completion that sets up fourth-and-1 is then a fine outcome (Early Downs and Field Zones has the field zones; The Clock, the Two-Minute Drill, and Fourth Down the decision).
Field-goal range and field position. On third-and-12 at the opponent’s 35, a 7-yard completion doesn’t convert, but it turns a 52-yard field-goal try into a 45-yard one. Deep in his own end, an offense facing third-and-15 may simply want a safe gain and a punt from further out.

How often do offenses throw past the line? It depends heavily on the distance: 78% of aimed passes on third-and-1 to 3 were thrown at or past it, 68% at 4 to 6, 52% at 7 to 10 and only 29% at 11 or more. The longer the distance, the more the defense can make the deep throw hard and the short throw easy, and the more often the quarterback takes the short one.






CautionCommon misconception



“A completion short of the sticks on third down is a quarterback mistake.” Sometimes. But on third-and-11 or more the defense’s whole design is to make the short completion the only open one, with everybody else deep and waiting at the line to gain. A quarterback who forces the ball into that coverage risks an interception to chase a first down that converts less than one time in five even when everything goes right. Taking the checkdown, getting five yards, and punting from further out is often the better play. The mistake is the other one: the third-and-5 checkdown that gets four, when a receiver was open at six.

section: Third-and-long: screens, draws and the punt
text:
Third-and-long: screens, draws and the punt
On third-and-12 the odds are poor whatever the offense calls: dropbacks converted 16% of third-and-11-or-more snaps in 2021–2025. Here a lot of offenses stop trying to win the down outright and start trying to win the possession: to avoid the sack, the interception and the holding penalty, and to make the punt that follows a little shorter. Two plays do most of that work, and both turn the defense’s third-and-long plan against it.
The screen lets the pass rush through and throws behind it. On third-and-long the defense’s rushers are going all-out for the quarterback and its coverage players are deep and facing the quarterback, so a back or receiver who catches the ball behind the line with linemen in front of him has room. The draw shows a pass, then hands the ball off up the middle, into the space the linebackers just left by dropping into coverage. Its mechanics, and Paul Brown’s Browns who made it famous, are in Gap Schemes. Here is why it lives on third down.


Show the Python
def draw_play():
    dfn = four_down(ldt=-2.35, rdt=2.35) + [
        D("MIKE", "MIKE", 6.0, 0.6, "M"), D("NB", "NB", 6.0, -9.5, "$"), D("DB", "DB", 6.0, 9.5, "D"),
        D("LCB", "CB", 8.0, -15.8, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 8.0, 15.8, "CB"),
        D("FS", "FS", 14.0, -8.0, "FS"), D("SS", "SS", 14.0, 8.0, "SS")]
    p = Play(spread(), dfn, los=40, to_go=12)
    # receivers sell the pass: verticals that pull the defensive backs away
    p.route("X", r.go(16.5)); p.route("Z", r.go(16.5)); p.route("H", r.seam(15)); p.route("Y", r.seam(15))
    # quarterback: a short drop as if to throw; the handoff comes at 0.9 s
    timed(p, "QB", [(0.6, -6.5, 0.0), (1.2, -6.5, 0.0)], "qbdrop")
    timed(p, "RB", [(0.55, -5.0, -1.6), (0.9, -5.6, -0.6), (1.5, -2.5, 0.3), (2.1, 1.5, 1.1),
                    (2.7, 6.0, 2.2), (3.3, 9.4, 2.5)], "run")
    p.handoff("RB", t=0.9)
    # line: pass sets, then each guard rides his tackle out and upfield from the inside shoulder;
    # the uncovered center climbs to the Mike and stays on him
    timed(p, "LT", [(0.6, -2.4, -4.6), (1.6, -3.4, -5.6)], "block")
    timed(p, "LG", [(0.6, -1.5, -1.9), (1.6, -2.0, -2.2)], "block")
    timed(p, "C", [(0.8, -0.2, 0.2), (2.2, 4.6, 0.4), (3.3, 5.0, 0.5)], "block")
    timed(p, "RG", [(0.6, -1.5, 1.9), (1.6, -2.0, 2.3)], "block")
    timed(p, "RT", [(0.6, -2.4, 4.6), (1.6, -3.4, 5.8)], "block")
    timed(p, "LDE", [(0.6, -1.6, -6.4), (1.6, -3.6, -6.8)], "rush")
    timed(p, "LDT", [(0.6, -0.8, -2.6), (1.6, -1.8, -3.2)], "rush")
    timed(p, "RDT", [(0.6, -0.8, 2.6), (1.6, -1.8, 3.2)], "rush")
    timed(p, "RDE", [(0.6, -1.6, 6.4), (1.6, -3.6, 6.8)], "rush")
    # the defense drops for the pass, then has to come back; the Mike is met by the center
    timed(p, "MIKE", [(0.9, 10.0, 0.4), (1.6, 10.0, 0.4), (2.3, 5.8, 0.4), (3.3, 5.8, 0.4)], "drop")
    timed(p, "NB", [(1.2, 10.5, -11.0), (2.0, 12.5, -10.5), (3.3, 10.2, 1.0)], "drop")
    timed(p, "DB", [(1.2, 10.5, 11.0), (2.0, 12.5, 10.5), (3.3, 11.6, 4.6)], "drop")
    timed(p, "FS", [(1.2, 17.0, -8.5), (2.0, 17.0, -8.0), (3.3, 12.4, 0.9)], "drop")
    timed(p, "SS", [(1.2, 17.0, 8.5), (2.0, 17.0, 8.0), (3.3, 10.6, 3.6)], "drop")
    timed(p, "LCB", [(1.6, 15.0, -15.8)], "drop"); timed(p, "RCB", [(1.6, 15.0, 15.8)], "drop")
    p.highlight("RB")
    return p


drw = draw_play()
DRAW_T = [0.0, 0.8, 1.7, 3.3]
if PDF:

                              "+1.7 s · handoff, through the vacated middle", "+3.3 s · tackled at 9–10: short of the sticks"],
                lateral=(-21, 21), window=(-9.0, 20.0), trails_from={3: 2.4},
                notes_at={1: [("linemen let the\nrushers upfield", (-5.5, 10.5), (-3.4, 6.6))],
                          2: [("Mike bailed\nto 10 yards", (5.8, 7.0), (9.4, 0.4)),
                              ("center climbs\nto the Mike", (3.0, -8.5), (2.8, 0.3))],
                          3: [("center on\nthe Mike", (3.0, -8.0), (5.0, 0.5)),
                              ("tackled at 9.5:\n2.5 yards short", (4.0, 12.5), (9.4, 2.5))]})
    plt.show()
else:
    show_animation(drw, times=DRAW_T)





  
  Your browser does not support the video tag.



Figure 51.4: A third-and-12 draw against a dime defense (simulated, illustrative). Snap: the defense has four rushers (both tackles lined up outside the guards, so nobody is over the center), one linebacker (M) and six defensive backs, two of them deep. +0.8 s: everything says pass. The quarterback has dropped, the linemen have set back as if to pass-block and let the rushers come upfield, the receivers are running deep, and the defense is dropping into coverage. +1.7 s: the back takes the handoff and heads up the middle, where the Mike was standing before he bailed to 10 yards; the guards ride the tackles outward, and the center, with nobody over him, climbs to the Mike. +3.3 s: the back has cut off the center’s block on the Mike and reached the defensive backs, who rallied down from the sticks (their trails from 2.4 s shown) and tackle him at about 9.5 yards, short of the line to gain (orange). The draw worked as designed and still didn’t convert: that is the bargain.




Watch what the defense’s third-and-long plan does to itself. It has taken off a linebacker for a sixth defensive back, so there is one fewer big body near the line. Its remaining linebacker drops to 10 yards at the snap, because that is where the passing windows are. Its rushers come upfield as fast as they can, because they are trying to reach a quarterback who is about to throw. The draw uses all three: the linemen let the rushers run themselves past the play, and the back runs into the space the dropping linebacker left. Against a defense playing the pass, it’s one of the few runs with numbers on its side.
And it still usually fails to convert. Designed runs on third-and-11 or more converted only 5% of the time in 2021–2025, because the defensive backs who dropped to the sticks are waiting there to tackle. So why call it? Partly because a 9-yard run on third-and-12 is a better outcome than a sack, an interception or an incompletion, especially near midfield, where it improves the punt or sets up a long field-goal try. Partly to protect the next third down: a defense that has been gashed by a draw rushes a half-step more carefully the next time, and its linebacker drops a half-step later. That is a constraint play, a call that exists to keep the defense honest against another (Constraint Theory).
The same logic explains the third-and-long screen, which also rarely converts but pays in the same currency. Both are cheap ways to lose the down safely, with a small chance of winning it big against a defense that guessed wrong.

title: Third Down: The Money Down
text:
The defense’s third-down package
When the defense knows the offense will throw, it changes the people on the field. That is a third-down package: the personnel and calls a team keeps for third down. On defense it means more defensive backs, faster pass rushers, and the pressures and disguises it has practised all week. On offense it means its best quick concepts, its protections for the opponent’s pressures, and the receivers and back it trusts most on the money down.
The defensive half is visible from your couch, and the data show it clearly.


Show the Python
ORDER = ["1–3", "4–6", "7–10", "11+"]
series = [("dime", "6+ defensive backs", style.SERIES[0], "o", "-"),
          ("blitz", "Blitz (5+ rushers)", style.SERIES[1], "s", "-"),
          ("cov0", "Cover 0", style.SERIES[2], "^", "-"),
          ("rush3", "Rush 3 or fewer", style.SERIES[3], "D", (0, (4, 2)))]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.0))
xs = np.arange(len(ORDER))
for key, lab, col, mk, ls in series:
    ys = DEF[key].reindex(ORDER).values
    ax.plot(xs, ys, color=col, lw=2, ls=ls, marker=mk, ms=5.5, zorder=3)
    # direct labels at the right end replace a legend
    ax.text(xs[-1] + 0.12, ys[-1], f"{lab}  {100 * ys[-1]:.0f}%", va="center", fontsize=7.2, color=col,
            fontweight="bold")
ax.set_xticks(xs, [f"3rd & {b}" for b in ORDER], fontsize=8)
ax.set_xlim(-0.25, 4.6)
ax.set_ylim(0, 0.5)
ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(plt.FuncFormatter(lambda y, _: f"{100 * y:.0f}%"))
ax.tick_params(axis="y", labelsize=7.5)
ax.set_ylabel("Share of third-down dropbacks", fontsize=8)
ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
ax.spines["bottom"].set_bounds(0, 3)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 51.5: What NFL defenses did on third-down dropbacks, by yards to go, 2023–2025 regular seasons: how often they had six or more defensive backs on the field (dime or quarter personnel), blitzed (five or more rushers), played Cover 0 (man coverage with no deep safety) and rushed three or fewer. Dime grows with the distance; Cover 0 shrinks; the blitz peaks at 7 to 10 yards and falls away at 11 or more, where rushing three (dashed) becomes more common. Rates are shares of charted dropbacks; Cover 0 is a share of dropbacks with a charted coverage. Source: nflverse participation data (FTN charting).





Personnel. Defenses had six or more defensive backs on the field for 11% of third-and-short dropbacks, 42% at 7 to 10 yards and 45% at 11 or more, against 8% on first and second down.8 The dime back replaces a linebacker: he covers better and tackles worse, and on a down when the offense is very likely to throw that is a good trade. It is also a bet, and the draw above is how the offense makes the defense pay when the bet is wrong.
Pass rushers. The same logic applies up front. A 330-pound run-stopping tackle who is excellent on first-and-10 is wasted on third-and-9, so many defenses replace him with a lighter, quicker rusher, or put four edge rushers on the field together, with two of them lined up inside over the guards. Steve Spagnuolo’s 2007 Giants had a package of four pass rushers that Sports Illustrated later called his “Four Aces”; by 2011 the Giants’ version, four defensive ends on third-and-long, was known as their “NASCAR” package, for its speed.9 Most NFL defenses now have some version of it, and many rosters carry a rusher or two who play mostly on passing downs. And the most common third-down “pressure” is not a blitz at all: it is four rushers running a stunt, an end and a tackle crossing paths so that one of them comes free through a gap the protection thought was covered (The Pass Rush). A front of four quick rushers is built for exactly that.
Calls. Third down is also where a defense spends the calls it has been saving. The chart shows their shape by distance; the rest of this chapter takes the families in turn: sitting at the sticks, 2-Man, pressure, Cover 0, rushing three, and spying the quarterback.






NoteFilm room: the third-down back, Patriots 2018–2019



The offensive half of the package has faces too. Under Bill Belichick and Josh McDaniels the Patriots kept a running back whose main job was third down: first picking up blitzers in pass protection, then catching passes and running the option routes out of the backfield that linebackers struggle to cover. James White was New England’s most-targeted receiver on third down in both 2018 and 2019, the target on 26% of Tom Brady’s third-down throws to a named receiver across the two seasons.10 What to notice: on third down, watch which back comes into the game. If it isn’t the starter, the substitution is a statement: protection and routes, not runs.

title: Third Down: The Money Down
section: Sticks defense: keep it in front
text:
Sticks defense: keep it in front
The simplest third-down defense is the one that makes the offense’s own target its landmark. If the offense needs 12 yards, the defense can give up 11. Coaches call it playing the sticks: zone defenders drop to (or just past) the line to gain, keep every receiver in front of them, and tackle the catch short of it.


Show the Python
def c3_def(to_go, under_d, cb_drop, cb_d, fs_d, fs_drop):
    dfn = four_down() + [
        D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -2.2, "W"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, 2.2, "M"),
        D("NB", "NB", 5.0, -10.0, "$"), D("SS", "SS", 7.5, 10.0, "SS"),
        D("LCB", "CB", cb_d, -15.8, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", cb_d, 15.8, "CB"), D("FS", "FS", fs_d, 0.0, "FS")]
    p = Play(spread(), dfn, los=40, to_go=to_go)
    for k in ("LDE", "LDT", "RDT", "RDE"):
        p.rush(k, pts=[(-1.6, 0.0)])
    zs = (6.0, 8.0) if under_d < 9 else (5.0, 8.0)
    p.drop("NB", (under_d, -11.5), zone=zs); p.drop("WILL", (under_d, -4.5), zone=zs)
    p.drop("MIKE", (under_d, 4.5), zone=zs); p.drop("SS", (under_d, 11.5), zone=zs)
    p.drop("LCB", (cb_drop, -15.5), zone=(8.0, 9.5)); p.drop("RCB", (cb_drop, 15.5), zone=(8.0, 9.5))
    p.drop("FS", (fs_drop, 0.0), zone=(8.0, 12.0))
    return p


fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.5, 4.0))
for ax, (tg, ud, cbx, cbd, fsd, fsx, title) in zip(axes, [
        (4, 6.0, 14.0, 5.5, 11.0, 15.0, "3rd & 4: underneath squeezes to 6"),
        (12, 12.5, 18.5, 8.0, 15.5, 20.5, "3rd & 12: underneath sinks to the sticks")]):
    p = c3_def(tg, ud, cbx, cbd, fsd, fsx)
    fld = p.draw(ax=ax, lateral=(-21, 21), window=(-7.0, 27.0), title=False, width_in=3.2)
    clean(fld.ax); ruler(fld, p, fs=5.5)
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=7.8, loc="left", color=style.INK)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()








Figure 51.6: The same Cover 3 at two distances (illustrative). Cover 3 is a zone defense with three deep defenders, each guarding a third of the field’s width (here the two cornerbacks and the free safety), and four underneath. Left, third-and-4: the four underneath defenders squeeze to about 6 yards, the depth where a sticks route would break, so they can drive forward on the throw and tackle short of the line to gain; the deep defenders play tighter. Right, third-and-12: the same four sink to 12 or 13 yards, right on the line to gain (orange), and the cornerbacks and free safety play deeper, because nothing short of 12 yards hurts. The shaded ovals are the zones; the numbers on the left edge count yards past the line of scrimmage.





Why does this work? Because the offense’s routes have to be finished to be useful. A curl at 14 yards takes about two seconds to run; a defender who starts at 12 and only has to take one step and tackle has almost no ground to cover. And the defense doesn’t need to stop the catch, only the extra yard. This is very likely part of the reason for the dip in the past-the-sticks chart at throws aimed right at the line: the defender standing on the line to gain catches the receiver there.
What does it give up? Everything short. A sticks defense on third-and-12 hands the offense an open 6-yard route on almost every snap, which is fine until the offense is in four-down territory and happy to take it, or has a receiver who can make a man miss. It also gives the quarterback time, because the underneath defenders are reading him rather than rushing him. And it asks for good tackling: a defense that misses the first tackle at the sticks has turned a stop into a first down. The cure for the short completion is a fast defense that rallies to it; for the time, mixing in pressure; for the tackling, there is no scheme.

Man under, two deep: 2-Man
Zone at the sticks has a cousin built on man coverage. In 2-Man (also called Cover 5), two safeties split the deep field in halves and the five defenders underneath play man, usually in trail technique: a step behind the receiver and on his inside hip, daring him to run past, because a safety is waiting over the top. It is the classic third-and-medium-to-long man call against option-route offenses. The underneath defender can sit on the short break, the sticks route, with no fear of the deep ball, and the receiver who turns upfield runs into a safety. Defenses played it on 8% to 9% of charted third-and-4-to-10 dropbacks in 2023–2025, against 5% on early downs.11
The price is the rush and the middle. Two deep and five in man leaves four rushers and nobody to spy or rob, so a quarterback who escapes the pocket has open grass in front of him: the man defenders are running with their receivers, backs turned. That is why 2-Man is a favourite against pocket passers and a risk against quarterbacks who run (the spy, below, is the answer to that). The pre-snap tell is two high safeties with the cornerbacks and the nickel tight and inside their receivers; the trap is that the same picture can turn into a two-deep zone at the snap.

title: Third Down: The Money Down
section: Pressure on third down: simulated pressure and the blitz
text:
Pressure on third down: simulated pressure and the blitz
The second family is pressure. Zone Blitzes, Fire Zones, and Simulated Pressure built the tools; here is why third down is where they live.
On third down the quarterback has to hold the ball until a route past the sticks is open, so every fraction of a second the defense takes away is worth more than on any other down. Pressure that forces the ball out early forces it out short, usually to a hot receiver in front of the line to gain, and on third-and-8 a hot throw that gains five is a defensive win.
That is why the blitz peaks at third-and-7 to 10. In 2023–2025 defenses sent five or more rushers on 38% of third-and-7 to 10 dropbacks, against 25% on first and second down. At that distance the hot throw is short of the sticks, so the defense can live with it; the routes that convert take time to develop, so pressure can kill them. At 11 or more the blitz rate falls to 17%: the defense doesn’t need to force the ball out, because a short throw already loses. At 4 to 6, blitzing is more dangerous, because the hot throw can convert, so blitz rates there are lower, and most defenses that do blitz play man coverage behind it, not zone (the third-down chart in Zone Blitzes, Fire Zones, and Simulated Pressure counts it).
Simulated pressure fits third down even better. It shows a blitz, gets the protection to commit and the quarterback to plan a hot throw, then rushes four from unexpected places and drops seven, often with a lineman sitting in exactly the short window the hot throw was aimed at. On third-and-long the quarterback who throws hot into that window gains nothing, and the one who waits for a route past the sticks is facing a rusher his protection didn’t count. To see why “didn’t count” matters, look at the other side of the ball.

The offense’s answer: count, slide, keep the back in
Remember the quarterback in the opening, pointing at a safety and shouting. He was counting. Before every third-down snap the offense names the defenders it thinks can rush, picks one as the reference point (the Mike identification), and every blocker counts his man from him, so all of them block the same picture (Pass Protection). On third down that call does most of the work:

Slide toward the threat. The line slides toward the side the extra rusher is most likely to come from, blocking gaps rather than men, so a stunt or a late blitzer runs into a blocker.
Six-man protection. The back stays in to take the first extra rusher (the half-slide is the everyday version), which answers a five-man pressure with six blockers. The cost is one fewer receiver, on the down when the offense most needs a man open.
Hot and sight adjust. When the defense brings more than the protection can block, the quarterback throws hot to the receiver whose defender just blitzed, and a receiver who sees the same blitz may cut his route short (sight adjust). That is the defense’s bet: the hot throw is fast, and on third-and-8 it is usually short.

So when a simulated pressure walks a safety down and then drops him, it isn’t just “showing blitz.” It is attacking the count: the protection slid toward the safety, the back was told to check him, and the fourth rusher comes from the other side, where the count left a gap. Simulated pressures are designed to beat the protection’s counting rules (“who’s the fifth?”), and that is why third down is where they live.






NoteFilm room: Chiefs 2024 — Spagnuolo saves it for third down



Steve Spagnuolo, the Chiefs’ defensive coordinator since 2019 (and still in 2026), is the clearest modern case of a coordinator whose pressure is situational. In 2024 the Chiefs sent five or more rushers on 32% of first- and second-down dropbacks, already above the league’s typical rate (median 23%); on third down it was 42%, the second-highest rate in the NFL (league median 28%). In 2025 the pattern held: 32% early, 37% on third down. The 2025 Chiefs also played Cover 0 on 11.2% of their charted third-down dropbacks, the most in the league.12 The two calls go together: the all-out blitz with no deep safety, kept for third down, when a hot throw that doesn’t get to the line ends the drive.
What to notice: on a Chiefs third down, count the defenders within five yards of the line before the snap, then count again after it. Spagnuolo’s famous calls are the six-man zeros (Blitzing breaks down the ones from Super Bowl LVIII), but most of his third downs show that look and bring four or five.
And the honest footnote: pressure is a bet, not a guarantee. The 2024 Chiefs allowed third-down conversions on 43% of opponents’ third downs, only the 24th-best rate in the league, in a 15–2 season. A blitz that gets home ends the drive; one that doesn’t leaves a receiver alone.

title: Third Down: The Money Down
text:
Cover 0: all in
The most aggressive third-down call is Cover 0: man coverage on every eligible receiver, nobody deep, and everyone else rushing. Man Coverage and Blitzing drew it; this section is about when.
Across the league it is above all a short-yardage call. On third-and-1 to 3, Cover 0 was played on 9% of charted dropbacks in 2023–2025; on third-and-11 or more, 2%. Why short? Two reasons.

A completion costs less. With nobody deep, any completion that beats its man can go a long way. But on third-and-2 the defense loses the down on almost any completion anyway, so the bet risks less than on third-and-10, where a short completion is still a stop and the defense would be giving up its safe outcome to gamble.
Every defender is close to the line, which helps against the run. On third-and-short the offense might run; Cover 0 puts eight or nine defenders within a few yards of the ball.

Some coordinators use it at longer distances too, for a third reason: it forces the decision now. A quarterback facing six rushers and no safety has well under two seconds. He must throw hot, against tight man coverage, before the route has developed. On third-and-2 that hot throw can convert, but on third-and-6 or 7 the routes fast enough to beat the rush mostly end short of the line. That is the Cover 0 of the film rooms below. Spagnuolo’s Chiefs and Flores’s Dolphins called it on short third downs like everyone else, but kept calling it on long ones, where most of the league nearly stops: on third-and-7 or longer, the 2021 Dolphins played Cover 0 on 24% of charted dropbacks (first in the NFL; league median 3%), and the 2025 Chiefs on 10% (second; median 2%).13 They were betting that the hot throw would land short. The league habit (short yardage, for the run and because the completion converts anyway) and theirs (medium and long, because the completion lands short) are two answers to the same question: where is the quick completion least damaging?
What it gives up is everything behind it. A Cover 0 blitz that doesn’t get home is one broken tackle away from a touchdown, and offenses that see it coming (both safeties walking down, corners pressed, linebackers mugged in the A gaps) answer with slants, rubs, and protection that keeps an extra blocker in.






NoteFilm room: Dolphins 2021 — Brian Flores’s third-down zeros



Brian Flores spent fifteen seasons in Bill Belichick’s New England organisation (four in scouting, then eleven on the coaching staff) before becoming Miami’s head coach (2019–2021), and his Dolphins played Cover 0 more than anyone. In 2020 they played it on 17% of charted third-down dropbacks, level with Belichick’s Patriots (17%) at the top of the league; in 2021 on 28%, the most in the NFL and more than four times the league median (7%).14
The signature night came on Thursday, November 11, 2021, when the 2–7 Dolphins beat the 6–2 Ravens 22–10 in Miami. Flores sent five or more rushers on 52% of Lamar Jackson’s 48 charted dropbacks and played Cover 0 on 17 of them, with his safeties walked up as rushers or man defenders, and Baltimore converted 2 of 14 third downs. The Ravens’ own columnist described an offense “overwhelmed by relentless blitzes.”15
What to notice: before the snap, count the deep safeties. If there are none, and the corners are pressed, it is Cover 0 or a disguise of it, and the ball has to come out in well under two seconds. Flores kept the same idea in Minnesota (he has been the Vikings’ defensive coordinator since 2023, and still is in 2026), where the Cover 0 look is as often a disguise as a call.

title: Third Down: The Money Down
text:
Rush three, drop eight
At the other end of the dial is a call that sounds like giving up: rush three, drop eight. Three rushers, eight defenders in coverage, usually on third-and-long.


Show the Python
def rush3_play():
    dfn = [D("LDE", "DE", 1.0, -4.0, "E"), D("NT", "NT", 1.0, 0.0, "N"), D("RDE", "DE", 1.0, 4.0, "E"),
           D("OLB", "OLB", 1.0, -6.6, "B"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 6.5, 0.8, "M"),
           D("NB", "NB", 6.0, -9.5, "$"), D("DB", "DB", 6.0, 9.5, "D"), D("SS", "SS", 11.0, 6.0, "SS"),
           D("LCB", "CB", 8.0, -15.8, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 8.0, 15.8, "CB"), D("FS", "FS", 15.0, 0.0, "FS")]
    p = Play(spread(), dfn, los=40, to_go=12)
    for k in ("LDE", "NT", "RDE"):
        p.rush(k, pts=[(-2.0, 0.0)])
    # protection: tackles on the ends, center and left guard double the nose, right guard looks for work
    p.block("LT", pts=[(-1.3, -0.5)]); p.block("RT", pts=[(-1.3, 0.5)])
    p.block("LG", pts=[(-0.8, 0.8)]); p.block("C", pts=[(-0.7, 0.0)]); p.block("RG", pts=[(-1.2, 0.9)])
    p.route("X", r.curl(13.5)); p.route("Z", r.curl(13.5))
    p.route("H", r.dig(14.5, 8)); p.route("Y", r.seam(17))
    p.route("RB", [(0, 0), (2.5, 3.4), (8.0, 3.7)], side=-1)       # check, then release past the line
    zs = (5.0, 7.5)
    p.drop("NB", (12.0, -13.0), zone=zs); p.drop("OLB", (11.5, -6.0), zone=zs); p.drop("MIKE", (13.0, 0.0), zone=zs)
    p.drop("SS", (11.5, 6.0), zone=zs); p.drop("DB", (12.0, 13.0), zone=zs)
    p.drop("LCB", (18.5, -16.0), zone=(7.0, 11.0)); p.drop("RCB", (18.5, 16.0), zone=(7.0, 11.0))
    p.drop("FS", (21.0, 0.0), zone=(7.0, 12.0))
    return p


p = rush3_play()
fld = p.draw(lateral=(-22, 22), window=(-7.5, 27.0), title=False)
clean(fld.ax); ruler(fld, p)
say(fld, p, 24.7, -11.0, "five underneath at 11–13 yards:\nevery window at the sticks is filled", fontsize=6.5)
say(fld, p, 24.7, 12.0, "three deep at 18–21 yards:\nnothing gets over the top", fontsize=6.5)
point_to(fld, p, (-4.8, 10.5), (-1.9, 2.5), "three rushers, five blockers: C and LG\ndouble the nose, RG looks for work")
point_to(fld, p, (-4.6, -13.5), (3.0, -5.3), "checkdown: open,\nabout 10 yards short")
plt.show()








Figure 51.7: Rush three, drop eight on third-and-12 (illustrative). Three linemen rush; a stand-up edge player (B) who looked like a fourth rusher drops instead. Behind them, five underneath defenders sink to 11 to 13 yards, right on the line to gain (orange), and three deep defenders sit at 18 to 21 yards. The offense runs a typical third-and-long pattern: curls at the sticks outside, a dig at 13 from the left slot, and the tight end up the seam to hold the deep middle. Every one of those windows has a defender in it. The offense has five blockers for three rushers, so the center and left guard double the nose and the right guard looks for work, and the back’s checkdown is wide open, about 10 yards short.





The logic is the sticks defense taken to its limit. On third-and-12 the offense needs a completion past 12 yards, and eight defenders can put a body in every window at that depth and still keep three deep. The quarterback is offered the checkdown and little else.
The price is time. Three rushers against five blockers will rarely get home quickly: the offense has two spare linemen to double-team the best rusher, and the quarterback can hold the ball for four seconds or more. Given that long, receivers can run a second route, and a quarterback who can move will find the gaps in the rush and scramble through them. That is why rush-three calls often come with the next section’s idea attached, a defender assigned to the quarterback, and why defenses mix them with pressure: a quarterback who sees three rushers on one third-and-long can’t assume he’ll get time on the next.
How rare is it, and does it work? Across 2023–2025 defenses rushed three or fewer on 8% of third-and-11-or-more dropbacks and 4% at 7 to 10. On third-and-7 or longer, offenses converted 21% against three or fewer rushers, 24% against four and 31% against five or more.16 Sack rates run the way you’d expect: 7.7% with three rushers, 12.4% with five or more.
Read those conversion rates carefully, because they seem to say the blitz is the worst call on third-and-long. Most of that is the distance hiding inside the average. Three-man rushes come mostly on the very longest downs, which are the hardest to convert whatever the defense does, and blitzes mostly at 7 to 10, which are easier. Hold the distance still and the gap nearly closes: on third-and-7 to 10 alone, offenses converted 31% against four rushers and 34% against five or more. So the blitz doesn’t stop third-and-long more often than a four-man rush, on average. It does change how the down ends: more sacks, more hurried throws, and the occasional receiver left alone. That near-tie is roughly what you’d expect if coordinators are mixing their calls well. If one call were clearly better, everyone would call it more, offenses would prepare for it, and its edge would shrink. The blitz earns its place by being one option in a mix the quarterback can’t predict, not by winning every time it is called.
Some defenses lean on it. Brian Flores’s 2023 Vikings, the league’s heaviest blitzers that season, also rushed three or fewer on 30% of their third-and-7-or-longer dropbacks, the most in the NFL: a defense that might send seven or three, from the same look. In 2025 the leaders were Jesse Minter’s Chargers (19%; Minter is the Ravens’ head coach in 2026) and Kelvin Sheppard’s Lions (18%).






ImportantWhy it exists: rush three, drop eight



What it solves: on third-and-long the offense needs a completion past the sticks, so the defense puts its numbers where the completion has to happen, and accepts a free short throw. What it gives up: the pass rush. With only three rushing, the quarterback gets time, and time eventually beats any coverage. It works best against quarterbacks who don’t run and offenses without a receiver who can turn a checkdown into twelve yards, and it works only as one call in a mix.

title: Third Down: The Money Down
text:
The spy
The last family answers a problem that third down’s own calls create. Drop eight into coverage, or even seven, and the coverage covers everyone except the man with the ball. Play man coverage, and it is worse: every man defender is running with his receiver, back turned to the quarterback, so nobody sees him take off. (Zone defenders at least face the quarterback and can come up when he runs.) A quarterback who can run looks downfield, sees every receiver covered, sees the rush lanes open, and goes. Scrambles were only 6% of third-down dropbacks in 2021–2025, but on third-and-7 to 10 they converted 48% of the time, against 32% for dropbacks as a whole.17 Against the quarterbacks who scramble most, that is a weapon a defense has to plan for.
The defense’s answer is the spy (or QB spy): a defender assigned not to a receiver or a rush lane but to the quarterback himself. He stands at linebacker depth, usually 5 to 7 yards off the ball and in front of the quarterback, keeps his eyes on him, and mirrors him. If the quarterback throws, the spy has done nothing, which is the price. If he runs, the spy meets him.


Show the Python
def spy_play():
    dfn = four_down(lde=-6.4, rde=6.4) + [
        D("MIKE", "MIKE", 6.0, 0.0, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.0, -5.5, "W"),
        D("NB", "NB", 5.0, -9.5, "$"), D("SS", "SS", 6.0, 9.5, "SS"),
        D("LCB", "CB", 2.0, -15.8, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 2.0, 15.8, "CB"), D("FS", "FS", 14.0, 0.0, "FS")]
    p = Play(spread(rb_w=1.6), dfn, los=40, to_go=6)
    # routes: outs set a yard and a half past a third-and-6 line (offsets from a 1.5-yard-deep slot)
    p.route("X", r.go(14)); p.route("Z", r.go(14)); p.route("H", r.out(9.0, 4)); p.route("Y", r.out(9.0, 4))
    for dk, ok in (("LCB", "X"), ("RCB", "Z"), ("NB", "H"), ("SS", "Y")):
        p.man(dk, ok)
    p.drop("FS", (16.0, 0.0))
    timed(p, "RB", [(0.8, -4.0, 2.6)], "block")                      # six-man protection: the back stays in
    # the quarterback: drop, hold, then step up toward the left B gap
    timed(p, "QB", [(0.7, -7.0, 0.0), (1.5, -7.0, 0.0), (2.3, -4.0, -2.4)], "run")
    # the line: pass sets; the tackles are pushed back by the ends, the guards and center hold the inside
    timed(p, "LT", [(0.6, -2.0, -4.2), (1.8, -3.3, -4.8), (2.3, -3.6, -5.0)], "block")
    timed(p, "LG", [(0.6, -1.8, -1.5), (2.3, -2.4, -1.4)], "block")
    timed(p, "C", [(0.6, -1.8, 0.3), (2.3, -2.2, 0.4)], "block")
    timed(p, "RG", [(0.6, -1.8, 1.9), (2.3, -2.4, 2.2)], "block")
    timed(p, "RT", [(0.6, -2.0, 4.2), (1.8, -3.3, 4.8), (2.3, -3.6, 5.0)], "block")
    # the rush: ends stay outside their tackles (contain), tackles push into the guards
    timed(p, "LDE", [(0.6, -0.8, -5.8), (1.8, -2.4, -6.2), (2.3, -2.8, -6.4)], "rush")
    timed(p, "RDE", [(0.6, -0.8, 5.8), (1.8, -2.4, 6.2), (2.3, -2.8, 6.4)], "rush")
    timed(p, "LDT", [(0.6, -0.6, -0.8), (2.3, -1.1, -0.6)], "rush")
    timed(p, "RDT", [(0.6, -0.6, 2.3), (2.3, -1.1, 3.0)], "rush")
    # the spy: shuffles with the quarterback's shoulders, then starts to close
    timed(p, "MIKE", [(1.5, 6.0, 0.0), (2.0, 5.6, -0.8), (2.3, 4.9, -1.4)], "path")
    p.highlight("MIKE", color=PURPLE)
    return p


spy = spy_play()
T_SPY = 2.3
MEET = (2.1, -3.3)
fld = snapshot(spy, T_SPY, lateral=(-21, 21), window=(-9.5, 18.5), ruler_fs=6.3)
ax = fld.ax
PPs = lambda d, w: fld.xy(*spy.to_abs(d, w))  # noqa: E731
at = lambda k: tuple(float(v) for v in spy.position(k, T_SPY))  # noqa: E731
# the next half-second: the quarterback's escape and the spy's angle, and where they meet
for key, end, col, lw in (("QB", (MEET[0] - 0.5, MEET[1]), style.OFFENSE_DARK, 2.4),
                          ("MIKE", (MEET[0] + 0.4, MEET[1] + 0.2), PURPLE, 2.2)):
    x0, y0 = PPs(*at(key)); x1, y1 = PPs(*end)
    ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((float(x0), float(y0)), (float(x1), float(y1)), arrowstyle="-|>",
                                 mutation_scale=12, color=col, lw=lw, ls=(0, (3, 2)), shrinkA=8, shrinkB=1,
                                 zorder=9))
xm, ym = PPs(*MEET)
ax.plot([float(xm)], [float(ym)], marker="x", ms=10, mew=2.6, color=style.INK, zorder=12)
point_to(fld, spy, (12.4, 6.6), at("MIKE"), "the spy (M): eyes on the\nQB, shuffling, now closing")
point_to(fld, spy, (1.8, -13.5), MEET, "spy meets him here:\n2 yards past the line,\nshort of the sticks", shrink=5)
point_to(fld, spy, (-7.6, 10.0), at("RDE"), "ends rush in their lanes,\noutside the tackles: contain")
point_to(fld, spy, (-7.6, -9.5), at("QB"), "quarterback steps up\ntoward the B gap")
point_to(fld, spy, (11.4, -9.2), at("LCB"), "man defenders run with their\nreceivers, backs to the quarterback")
plt.show()








Figure 51.8: A spy on third-and-6, 2.3 seconds after the snap (simulated, illustrative; faint lines show where each player has been, dashed arrows where the quarterback and the spy go next). The defense plays Cover 1, man coverage on every receiver who goes out, with one deep safety; it rushes four and assigns the Mike linebacker (purple ring) to the quarterback. The back has stayed in to block, so the Will who had him waits. The man defenders have turned and run with their receivers, backs to the quarterback. The ends have rushed in their lanes, pushing the tackles back from the outside so the quarterback can’t escape around them. He steps up toward the B gap (between the left guard and tackle), and the spy, who has shuffled with him from 6 yards, is already closing: he meets him (×) about two yards past the line, short of the line to gain. In an ordinary Cover 1 this Mike might have been the robber; using him as a spy costs the defense that help.





Who spies? Someone fast enough to match a running quarterback and big enough to tackle him: usually a linebacker, sometimes a safety or nickel back against the fastest quarterbacks, occasionally a defensive lineman who “rushes” by stepping up and sitting in the middle. A linebacker assigned to the back can also be a green dog (some staffs say hug or add-on), who joins the rush only if the back stays in to block (Linebackers and the Second Level). The spy comes with a rush plan too: against a running quarterback the rushers play a mush rush (some say cage rush), staying square in their rush lanes and pushing the blockers back into the quarterback instead of racing around them (The Pass Rush). The ends keep contain, the pocket shrinks around him but doesn’t open, and the spy is the last line if he finds a crease anyway.
The trade is the familiar one: the spy is a defender who isn’t covering anyone. In Cover 1 he usually replaces the robber, so the middle of the field loses its best in-cut defender; in zone he is one fewer underneath player. A spy can also be used. Offenses run a receiver right at him to make him choose, or send the back on a route he has to respect, and a linebacker spying a quarterback who is faster than he is can be outrun to the sideline. Like every third-down call, it works best as one of several from the same look.






NoteFilm room: two spies for Lamar Jackson, 2024 and 2025



Lamar Jackson, the most dangerous running quarterback of his era, sees spies as often as anyone, and two games a year apart show both sides of the bargain.
Chiefs 2024, opening night (September 5). Kansas City moved linebacker Leo Chenal all over its front (in the box, on the defensive line and over the slot) and used him to spy Jackson in key moments, mirroring him and running him down on scrambles.18 It didn’t stop the running: Jackson carried 16 times for 122 yards, including 10 scrambles, and on third down he ran 5 times for 39 yards and 3 conversions. The Chiefs won anyway, 27–20, in a game decided on its final snap.
Lions 2025, Week 3 (September 22, Monday Night Football). Detroit’s coordinator Kelvin Sheppard, who had earlier said publicly that he didn’t like using a spy, built a plan around one and made it hard to find. Jackson ran 7 times for 35 yards, was sacked 7 times, and the Lions won in Baltimore, 38–30. Sheppard gave the credit not to the spy but to the disguise around it: “it’s because we’re making everything look the same,” he said, “and when you do that, it’s impossible to know who’s coming, who’s the spy, who’s in coverage.”19
What to notice: before a third-and-medium snap against a running quarterback, look for the linebacker who sits straight in front of him at 5 or 6 yards and doesn’t move with any receiver. After the snap, watch him: a spy shuffles with the quarterback’s shoulders. A green-dog rusher who comes forward late is the same idea, disguised.

section: The third-down dial at a glance
text:
The third-down dial at a glance
Put the chapter’s pieces side by side. The distance sets the menu for both sides; the pre-snap picture tells you which item is likely, but only some calls have a reliable tell, because the defense works hard to make the rest look alike.









Distance
Offense’s usual tools
Defense’s usual calls
What you can see before the snap




Short (1–3)
Power run, sneak, quick man-beaters (slant, rub)
Tight man (Cover 1), Cover 0, a packed box
No deep safety, pressed corners, linebackers mugged in the A gaps: Cover 0 or a disguise of it


Medium (4–6)
Option routes, mesh, rubs, matchups, empty
Cover 1 with a robber, mugs and disguise, some pressure
One deep safety, defenders tight on receivers; the robber or a mug shows where help is


Long (7–10)
Sticks routes past the line, six-man protection, hot throws
Blitz and simulated pressure, 2-Man, sticks zone
Dime personnel; defenders walked up to the line (blitz or sim: you usually can’t tell which); two deep with tight, inside defenders suggests 2-Man


Very long (11+)
Screen, draw, safe completion, a shot
Sticks zone, rush three/drop eight
Six or more defensive backs, soft corners, two or three deep; only three linemen with a hand down hints at rush three


Any distance, running QB
Scramble, designed run, routes at the spy
Spy, mush rush
A linebacker in front of the quarterback at 5–7 yards, lined up on nobody

51  Third Down: The Money Down

title: Third Down: The Money Down
text:
Is third down a skill?
Third down feels like the purest test of a team, and it is a big one. But it is also a small sample: a team faces roughly 200 to 230 third downs a season, and every one is a coin weighted by distance. Two consequences are worth knowing.
First, early downs decide a lot of third down. A team that is on schedule faces third-and-3, not third-and-9, and converts more often without being any better at third down. How do we know? With a correlation, a number between 0 and 1 (for this kind of comparison) that measures how well one season’s figure lines up with the next: 0 means last year tells you nothing about this year, 1 means it tells you everything, and anything around 0.2 or 0.3 is a weak link, real but swamped by luck. Across 2016–2025, a team’s success rate on first and second down predicted its third-down conversion rate the next season (correlation 0.33) nearly as well as its own third-down rate did (0.39).20 Neither is strong, and the early-down number, which comes from about four times as many plays, does almost as well.
Second, defensive third-down numbers are noisy. A defense’s third-down conversion rate allowed carried over from one season to the next with a correlation of only 0.20: barely more than nothing. A defense that “gets off the field” one year often doesn’t the next, which is a reason to judge third-down defenses on what they do (pressure, coverage, tackling) more than on the conversion rate alone. Offenses are more stable, but the gap between the best and worst is still modest: in 2025 the best offense converted 51% of its third downs, the worst 32%.
None of that makes third down unimportant; it makes it consequential and noisy at once, which is exactly what you’d expect of a single high-stakes snap. Expected Points, EPA, and Success Rate has the tools to measure it.

title: Third Down: The Money Down
section: Film room: the Patriots’ option routes
text:
Film room: the Patriots’ option routes






NoteFilm room: Patriots 2009–2019 — Welker, Edelman and the sticks



The Patriots of the Tom Brady era built much of their third-down offense on slot receivers running option routes set just past the sticks (Passing Game Fundamentals and The Quick Game introduce the route and Wes Welker). The data shows what that meant on third down.

Wes Welker, 2009–2012. Welker was New England’s most-targeted receiver on third down in 4 of those 4 seasons and the target on 28% of Brady’s third-down throws to a named receiver. Those throws converted 48% of the time, against 39% for third-down targets across the league. And the typical Welker target was thrown exactly to the line to gain: the median distance between the throw’s depth and the sticks was 0 yards. That looks like a contradiction: throws aimed right at the line are the chart’s weak spot. Welker beat the dip for the two reasons the dip exists. It comes from balls thrown into a defender sitting at the sticks; the option route against zone finds the gap between two of them and sits down in it, facing the quarterback. And it comes from defenders who have time to close; Brady threw as Welker settled, before anyone could. Caught on the line with nobody in front of him, a receiver only has to turn and fall forward.
Julian Edelman, 2013, 2016 and 2019 (the three seasons in which he played all 16 games; he missed 2017 injured): 26% of third-down targets, converting 45% against a league 41%.21

Why did it work? Because the option route attacks the defense’s third-down plan at its core. Against man coverage the slot defender has to choose a side, and the receiver breaks the other way; against zone the receiver sits down in the gap at the sticks, facing the quarterback. Brady could throw before the break was finished, because he and his receiver read the same defender. What to notice on old Patriots third downs: the slot receiver’s first few steps are the same every time; the break comes at the sticks; the ball is in the air before he turns.

title: Third Down: The Money Down
text:
Watch for it on Sunday






TipWatch for it



Past the sticks? On every third down for one half, make a prediction before the snap and check it after.

Say the bucket out loud: short (1–3), medium (4–6), long (7–10) or very long (11+). Then make the base-rate call: short, run or quick pass; medium, quick man-beater; long, a route past the sticks against pressure; very long, a safe completion or a draw.
Read the offense. Did the best receiver move to the slot? Is the back still in the backfield (likely to stay in and block a blitzer) or did the offense go empty (five out, and the quarterback has to beat any extra rusher himself)?
Read the package. How many defensive backs came on? Did a big tackle leave for a pass rusher? How many defenders are within five yards of the line, and how many deep? No deep safety means Cover 0; three or four deep with linemen standing up means the defense may drop eight. Then watch the quarterback point and shout: he is setting the protection’s count, and the defense is trying to make that count wrong.
Find a spy. Against a running quarterback, look for a linebacker or safety sitting in front of him who isn’t lined up on any receiver.
Predict the target: past the line, or short of it? Then, after the play, note where the ball was caught relative to the orange line, and who made the tackle.
For your log: for each third down, write the bucket, your prediction (past or short), what happened, and the number of rushers. Over a game you’ll see the defense’s third-down personality (pressure, sticks, or both) and whether the offense’s targets live past the line or short of it.

title: Third Down: The Money Down
text:
Predict the play






TipPredict the play 1: third-and-3 at midfield





Show the Python
dfn = four_down(ldt=-2.75, rdt=2.75) + [
    D("MIKE", "MIKE", 1.6, -1.0, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 1.6, 1.0, "W"),
    D("NB", "NB", 0.9, -9.0, "$"), D("SS", "SS", 6.0, 8.6, "SS"), D("FS", "FS", 6.5, -3.0, "FS"),
    D("LCB", "CB", 0.9, -15.0, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 0.9, 15.0, "CB")]
p = Play(spread(), dfn, los=55, to_go=3)
p.highlight("FS", "SS")
fld = p.draw(lateral=(-21, 21), window=(-7.0, 11.0), title=False)
clean(fld.ax); ruler(fld, p, upto=10)
plt.show()








Figure 51.9: Third-and-3 near midfield. The offense is in 11 personnel, 2x2, with the back beside the quarterback. The defense has the Mike (M) and Will (W) standing in the A gaps, the nickel ($) pressed on H, both corners pressed, and both safeties (green rings) walked down to 6 or 7 yards.





What is the defense likely to do, and what should the offense want to have called?






TipAnswer





A Cover 0 blitz is the likeliest reading: man on every receiver, nobody deep, six or more rushing. Count the deep players: none. Both corners and the nickel are pressed, which usually means man coverage. With the two linebackers mugged in the A gaps and both safeties walked down, the defense has up to eight possible rushers and no one to protect against a long completion. That only makes sense on a short-yardage down, which is where the league calls Cover 0 most (the Cover 0 section has the rates). It could still be a disguise: one safety may bail at the snap into a Cover 1, and one of the mugged linebackers may drop.
What the offense wants is a quick throw that beats tight man coverage before the rush arrives: a slant from X or Z against an outside-leverage corner, a rub between H and the back, or a quick out. A run is live only if the offense can account for the mugged linebackers, with a blocker for each of them, and against this look the quick throw is the better bet. Even the quarterback sneak runs straight into the two linebackers standing in its gaps; it becomes a better call once one of them shows he is dropping. What the offense should not have called is a slow-developing route past the sticks: on third-and-3 it doesn’t need one, and against six rushers it won’t get time.











TipPredict the play 2: third-and-13 from the 20





Show the Python
dfn = four_down() + [
    D("MIKE", "MIKE", 7.5, 0.8, "M"),
    D("NB", "NB", 7.0, -9.5, "$"), D("DB", "DB", 7.0, 9.5, "D"), D("SS", "SS", 15.5, 9.0, "SS"),
    D("LCB", "CB", 8.0, -15.8, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 8.0, 15.8, "CB"), D("FS", "FS", 15.5, -9.0, "FS")]
p = Play(spread(), dfn, los=30, to_go=13)
fld = p.draw(lateral=(-21, 21), window=(-7.0, 18.5), title=False)
clean(fld.ax); ruler(fld, p)
plt.show()








Figure 51.10: Third-and-13 from the offense’s own 20. The defense has four linemen down (E, T, T, E), one linebacker (M) at 7.5 yards, and six defensive backs: the nickel ($) and the dime back (D) 7 yards off the slots, the corners 8 off, and two safeties 15 to 16 yards deep, one on each half of the field.





How many will rush, where will the coverage sit, and what would you call if you were the offense?






TipAnswer





Most likely four rushers, with a two-deep coverage behind them and everything underneath sinking to the sticks. This is the third-and-very-long package: dime personnel, two safeties deep, corners off, and only one linebacker. At 11 or more yards, defenses rushed exactly four on about 76% of charted dropbacks in 2023–2025, so the base call is four. Behind it, two safeties high usually means a two-deep zone (Cover 2 or quarters) or 2-Man. Either way, expect the underneath defenders to drop to 12 or 13 yards, so that every route that converts runs into a defender and every route that’s open is short. Two catches: a simulated pressure looks exactly like this until the snap (an end drops, the Mike or a defensive back rushes), and an end who drops turns it into rush three. The picture tells you the distance-based call, not the exact one.
The offense’s options are the third-and-long menu. If it wants the first down, the soft spot of a two-deep shell is the middle of the field between and under the safeties, 14 to 18 yards deep: a dig or a seam, thrown on time. If it wants the possession, the draw and the screen are built for this picture: a light box, one linebacker who will drop, rushers chasing upfield. From its own 20, a 9-yard draw that sets up a punt from the 29 is a reasonable outcome, and an interception at the 35 is the disaster to avoid.











TipPredict the play 3: third-and-5 against a quarterback who runs





Show the Python
dfn = four_down(lde=-6.4, rde=6.4) + [
    D("MIKE", "MIKE", 6.2, 0.0, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 3.7, -3.2, "W"),
    D("NB", "NB", 2.0, -8.6, "$"), D("SS", "SS", 2.5, 8.6, "SS"),
    D("LCB", "CB", 1.2, -15.6, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 1.2, 15.6, "CB"), D("FS", "FS", 14.0, 0.0, "FS")]
p = Play(spread(), dfn, los=60, to_go=5)
p.highlight("MIKE")
fld = p.draw(lateral=(-21, 21), window=(-7.0, 16.5), title=False)
clean(fld.ax); ruler(fld, p, upto=15)
plt.show()








Figure 51.11: Third-and-5 at midfield; the quarterback is one of the league’s best runners. The defense presses the corners and walks the nickel ($) and the strong safety (SS) up on the slots, with one deep safety (FS). Four linemen are down, the Will (W) is at about 4 yards over the back, and the Mike (M, green ring) stands 6 yards deep, directly in front of the quarterback, lined up on no one.





What is the Mike’s job, what coverage is behind him, and where is the offense’s best throw?






TipAnswer





The Mike is probably a spy, in Cover 1. Every receiver has a defender pressed or tight on him (the corners on X and Z, the nickel on H, the safety on Y, the Will on the back), one safety is deep, and the Mike is lined up on nobody, square to the quarterback at spy depth. Against a quarterback who runs on third-and-5, the defense has given up its robber to keep him in the pocket.
Where to throw: not right in front of the spy. His eyes are on the quarterback, so he sees every throw that crosses his face at 5 to 8 yards, and spies rob those throws all the time. The good throws are the ones he can’t get to:

Behind him and in front of the free safety: a dig or an over route at 10 to 14 yards. In Cover 1 with no robber, that is the space the defense emptied, and the spy can’t turn and run back to it while watching the quarterback.
Away from leverage, outside: an out or option-out by a slot receiver whose defender is aligned inside him, toward the sideline the spy can’t reach.
Make the spy choose: send the back on a route right at him, or a receiver across his face, so that covering the route means leaving the quarterback.

And the quarterback still has his legs: a spy who is slower than him has to be right about the angle.

title: Third Down: The Money Down
text:
Takeaways

Third down decides drives, about three points of expected value on one snap, and the league converts about two in five, every year. The distance is the whole story: short third downs are converted most of the time, very long ones rarely.
The distance is information, so both sides specialise. Defenses add defensive backs and pass rushers as the distance grows; offenses set their routes by the line to gain, put their best receiver where he can win, count the protection, and keep a third-down back.
Aim a yard or two past the sticks. Third-down throws aimed there convert most often; throws short of the line rarely do, except on third-and-short, in four-down territory, or when the yards after the catch are the plan. Option routes, rubs and mesh exist to win that yard against man coverage, which costs the defense flags as well as catches.
The defense picks a point on a dial: Cover 0 and tight man on short yardage, pressure (real and simulated) and 2-Man on third-and-7 to 10, sticks defense and rush three/drop eight on very long, and a spy when the quarterback can run. Each call gives something up, none wins on average once the distance is held still, and the best defenses show the same look for all of them.
Third-and-long is often about the possession, not the down. Screens and draws rarely convert, but they avoid disasters, shorten punts, and keep the rush honest for the next one.
Third down is consequential and noisy. Early-down success predicts it nearly as well as past third-down success does, and defensive third-down rates barely carry over year to year.

title: Red Zone, Goal Line, Two-Point Plays, and Short Yardage (Including the Tush Push)
text:
The field runs out
Third-and-goal from the 6. For three quarters this offense has gone up and down the field: its receivers have been open, its quarterback has had time, its average play has gained six yards. Now, with the end zone close enough to hit with a thrown helmet, it gains one yard on first down, nothing on second, and on third the quarterback holds the ball, finds nobody, and throws it out of the back of the end zone. The kicker comes on. The announcer sighs about “red-zone efficiency” as if the offense had lost its nerve. It didn’t. The field got smaller, and a smaller field is a different game: some plays stop working, others start, and the defense gets to do things it could never do at midfield. This chapter is about that different game, from the 20-yard line to the last inch.
You’ll be able to:
How to read the diagrams. Offense is blue circles, defense orange squares, and left and right always mean the offense’s. On offense, Q is the quarterback, R the running back, F a fullback, X and Z the wide receivers, H the slot receiver (in the heavy goal-line pictures, H is instead a wing: a tight end or H-back lined up a step off the line, just outside the end man), Y and U tight ends, and P a pusher in the tush push; C is the center, G a pulling guard, and the other linemen are unlettered unless a picture needs them. On defense, E and T are the ends and tackles of the defensive line, N a nose tackle, M, W and S linebackers, CB a cornerback, $ the nickel back (the fifth defensive back), and SS and FS the safeties. Solid blue arrows are routes, the thick dark arrow is the ball carrier, lines ending in a short bar are blocks, dotted orange lines are man-coverage assignments, dashed orange lines are a defender’s path, and brown dashes are the ball in the air. The shaded rectangle at the top of most pictures is the end zone.
Start with geometry, because everything in this chapter follows from it. The red zone is the last 20 yards before the goal line. Behind the goal line is the end zone, 10 yards deep, and behind that the end line, the back edge of the playable field. A pass caught beyond the end line is out of bounds. So from the opponent’s 20, the offense has at most 30 yards to work with; from the 10, 20 yards; from the 2, where two-point tries are snapped, 12.
Show the Python
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 5.3))
fld = Field(ax=ax, orient="vertical", los=50, window=(25, 70), numbers=True)   # x = 75 .. 120
for t_ in list(ax.texts):                     # keep the yard numbers on the left only (arrows go on the right)
    if t_.get_position()[0] > FW / 2:
        t_.remove()


def band(x0, x1, alpha, color=style.DEFENSE):

Figure 52.1: The last 35 yards of the field, offense moving up the page. The red zone starts at the 20; inside the 10 and inside the 5, the offense and defense change personnel and plays. Two snaps happen at fixed spots: the extra-point kick from the 15 and the two-point try from the 2. The arrows on the right show the whole depth the defense has to protect, from the ball to the end line, from three spots: it shrinks from 30 yards to 12.
Why does that matter so much? Because of what defenses do between the 20s. A normal defense spends its safeties, and sometimes its corners, on the deepest part of the field, 15, 25, 40 yards away, because a receiver who gets behind everyone there scores. The defense has to keep its depth. Near the goal line that problem disappears: the end line protects the deepest part of the field for free. It is the twelfth defender that never misses a tackle. Every defender who had been guarding grass 30 yards downfield is now available to do something else: crowd the receivers, cover a man, or rush. That is the compressed field: less grass to defend, the same eleven defenders to defend it.
Show the Python
def cover3_panel(ax, los, deep_d, deep_c, deep_h, under_d, window, title):
    off = spread(y_pos="TE")
    dfn = dline() + [D("MIKE", "MIKE", under_d, -4.0, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", under_d, 4.0, "W"),
                     D("NB", "NB", under_d - 0.5, -12.5, "$"), D("SS", "SS", under_d - 0.5, 12.5, "SS"),
                     D("LCB", "CB", deep_d, -16.5, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", deep_d, 16.5, "CB"),
                     D("FS", "FS", deep_d + 0.5, 0.0, "FS")]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=los, to_go=None)
    fld = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=(-21.5, 21.5), window=window)
    for w in (-17.8, 0.0, 17.8):
        oval(fld, p, (deep_c, w), (deep_h, 17.6))
    for w, wid in ((-4.0, 7.5), (4.0, 7.5), (-12.5, 9.0), (12.5, 9.0)):
        oval(fld, p, (under_d, w), (5.0, wid))
    panel_title(ax, title)
    return p, fld

# at the 10: underneath zones run to the goal line, the deep zones sit between the goal line and the end line
p, f = cover3_panel(axes[1], opp(10), 12.5, 15.2, 8.2, 7.0, (-6.5, 22.6), "At the opponent's 10")
(xh0, yh0), (xh1, yh1) = P(f, p, 9.2, -8.4), P(f, p, 11.4, -8.4)
axes[1].annotate("", (float(xh1), float(yh1)), xytext=(float(xh0), float(yh0)),
                 arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="<->", color=OD, lw=0.9), zorder=6)
say(f, p, 10.3, -3.4, "hole: 1–2 yd", fontsize=6.4, color=OD)
say(f, p, 20.4, 0.0, "end line: nothing behind them", fontsize=6.4, color=OD, box=False)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=1.0)
field_legend(axes[0], ["area"], fs=6.8, y=-0.01)
plt.show()








Figure 52.2: If the defense stays in zone: the same Cover 3 (three deep defenders, four underneath; see the Cover 3 chapter) at midfield and at the opponent’s 10, with each defender drawn where he ends his drop. Left: at midfield the deep defenders must keep backing up, because there are 30-odd yards of field behind them, so a hole about five yards tall opens between the underneath zones and the deep ones. That hole is where intermediate routes are caught. Right: at the 10 the end line caps the deep zones, so the deep defenders can stop at the goal line and sit almost on top of the underneath layer. The hole between the levels shrinks to a yard or two, and all seven zones fit into the 20 yards in front of the end line. Shaded ovals are zones.
Defenses use that freedom in three big ways, and you can see all three on any red-zone snap.
Deep zones shrink, then disappear. A zone defense asks defenders to guard areas. The picture above shows what happens if the defense stays in zone: the deep areas get squeezed against the end line until they are barely deeper than the underneath ones, the hole between the two layers closes, and the spaces between defenders, the “windows” a quarterback throws into, get small. But a zone with nothing behind it is wasting its deep defenders, which is why, inside the 10, many defenses stop pretending: with no deep middle to protect, they bring the safeties down. In FTN’s charting of 2023–2025 dropbacks, two-deep shells (Cover 2, Cover 4 and their relatives, which keep two safeties deep) were called on 43% of plays outside the red zone but only 18% inside the 5.1
Man coverage and press take over. Man coverage’s great weakness is the receiver who beats his man deep, with no help behind. Near the goal line, “deep” doesn’t exist: a receiver who runs past his man runs out of the end zone. So defenses play much more man coverage, and much more of it press, with the defender a yard from the receiver at the snap, jamming him to wreck the timing. In Man Coverage you saw that charters label roughly four in five dropbacks inside the 5 as man, and that Cover 0 (man coverage with nobody deep at all) becomes the single most common call there.
The box fills up. Every defender not needed in deep coverage can line up near the ball. That squeezes the run game: the extra defenders take away the cutback lanes and the creases a running back finds between the 20s.
The freed defenders have two more jobs, both from Man Coverage. A safety who no longer needs to stay deep can rob the middle: in a Cover 1 robber or lurk call he sits a few yards deep in the middle of the end zone, reading the quarterback, waiting for the slant or the crossing route. And a defense with a defender to spare can double the best target: a bracket, two defenders on one star tight end or receiver, is expensive at midfield and affordable when nobody is needed deep.
The offense suffers in quieter ways too. Its deep routes are gone, so the threat that stretches the defense vertically, the one that keeps safeties honest between the 20s, is gone with them. Every route is shorter, so every throw arrives with defenders closer to the catch point. Yards after the catch shrink, because there are fewer yards left to gain. And the playbook narrows: concepts that need 15 or 20 yards of depth to develop (the deep crosser, the post, most of Dropback Concepts) simply don’t fit.
One rule quietly tilts the last few yards toward the run. A touchdown is scored the instant any part of the ball, held by a runner, breaks the plane of the goal line, the invisible wall rising from its front edge. A quarterback stopped dead on a sneak scores if he got the ball over the line before he was stopped. A receiver has a harder test: to make a catch in the end zone he must control the ball and get both feet (or a knee) down in bounds, and every red-zone throw near the sideline or the end line is a fight with that boundary as well as with the defender.2

title: Red Zone, Goal Line, Two-Point Plays, and Short Yardage (Including the Tush Push)
text:
ImportantWhy it exists



The compressed field isn’t a scheme; it’s a consequence of the rulebook’s geometry. But it explains a whole family of schemes. Defenses get more aggressive near the goal line because the end line gives them deep help for free: man coverage, press and Cover 0 are cheap there in a way they never are at midfield. Offenses answer with plays that win quickly and close to the line (slants, rubs, fades thrown before the safety can help, quarterback runs) or that create a numbers advantage the defense can’t cover. The trade: everything is faster and more crowded, so mistakes cost more. A tipped ball near the goal line is an interception risk in a crowd; a one-yard loss on third-and-goal can be the difference between seven points and three.



What each yard is worth
The numbers make the squeeze concrete. Across the 2022–2025 regular seasons, 6,881 drives ran at least one play inside the opponent’s 20. Of those, 57% ended in a touchdown and 29% in a field goal; the rest ended in turnovers, failed fourth downs, missed kicks or the end of a half.3 That 4-point gap between a touchdown (with its extra point) and a field goal is the whole economics of the red zone, and it is why coaches judge their red-zone offense by the share of trips that end in touchdowns, not by yards.
Look closer and the value of each yard is steep. The chart follows every drive that reached a first-and-goal and asks how often it ended in a touchdown, depending on where that first-and-goal was snapped.


Show the Python
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 2.9))
ys = FG_TD.index.astype(int)
vals = FG_TD["mean"].values * 100
bars = ax.bar(ys, vals, color=style.SERIES[0], width=0.7)
for b, v, n in zip(bars, vals, FG_TD["size"].values):
    ax.text(b.get_x() + b.get_width() / 2, v + 1.5, f"{v:.0f}%", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=7.5,
            color=style.INK)
ax.set_xticks(ys)
ax.set_xticklabels([f"{y}" for y in ys], fontsize=8)
ax.set_xlabel("First-and-goal snapped from the opponent's ... yard line", fontsize=8)
ax.set_ylabel("Drives ending in a TD", fontsize=8)
ax.set_ylim(0, 105)
ax.set_yticks([0, 25, 50, 75, 100])
ax.set_yticklabels(["0%", "25%", "50%", "75%", "100%"], fontsize=7.5)
ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
ax.invert_xaxis()
ax.set_title("Touchdown rate after first-and-goal, by starting yard line", fontsize=9.5)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 52.3: How often a drive scored a touchdown after reaching first-and-goal at each yard line, 2022–2025 regular seasons. From the 1, nine drives in ten score; from the 10, under six in ten. The bars count only the first first-and-goal snap of each drive, so a drive that moved from the 8 to the 2 counts at the 8. Data: nflverse play-by-play.





Read the chart from left to right, the way the offense moves. From the 10 to the 5, each yard gained adds about 3 percentage points of touchdown chance; from the 2 to the 1, it adds about 7. Those last yards are the hardest to gain and the most valuable, which is why the last part of this chapter is devoted to plays designed to gain exactly one.
The playbook shifts with the field. In neutral situations (first to third down, neither team running away with the game, outside the last two minutes of a half), offenses passed on 55% of plays between the 11 and the 20, a little below the 59% everywhere farther out, but on only 41% inside the 5.4 Near the goal line the run comes back, for reasons you will see: when there are only a few yards to gain, a play that gains them by force is as good as a play that gains them by deception.






CautionCommon misconception



“At the goal line, smart teams pass; running into a crowd is old-fashioned.” From the 1, passing and handing off come out about even, and the quarterback sneak beats both. In 2022–2025, dropbacks snapped from the 1 scored on 52% of plays and ordinary runs on 55%, while quarterback sneaks scored on 67%.5 (These are rates per play; the 90% in the chart above is per drive, which gets up to four tries. The sneak section returns to why one yard at the goal line is harder than one yard anywhere else.) A pass needs a receiver to beat tight man coverage in a tiny space; a run needs one yard. Neither play is always right, and the best goal-line offenses keep both alive so the defense can’t sell out against either.

title: Red Zone, Goal Line, Two-Point Plays, and Short Yardage (Including the Tush Push)
text:
Red-zone pass concepts
Because the field is short and the coverage is tight and usually man, red-zone pass plays share a style. They are quick (the ball is out in a second or two), they attack a specific matchup or leverage, and many of them are built to create separation that man coverage can’t prevent, rather than to find holes in zones. Here are the six you will see most.

The fade
The fade is the simplest red-zone pass and the most argued-about. The receiver releases outside his defender and runs for the back corner of the end zone; the quarterback throws the ball high and outside, over the receiver’s outside shoulder, toward the pylon, to a spot where only the receiver can catch it. It needs room, so the receiver usually lines up with five to eight yards between himself and the sideline: room for the ball to land outside him and still in bounds, with space for both feet. Line up much wider and there is no room for the ball; much narrower, and the safety in the middle has a shorter run to help. And it needs a matchup: a tall receiver with strong hands, ideally against a smaller corner.
Why does it fit the red zone? The fade beats a pressed corner with no deep help outside, and the compressed field produces plenty of those. If the corner lines up inside the receiver (inside leverage, to take away the slant), the receiver releases outside, and the corner is left chasing from behind and inside, unable to see the ball. The safety is usually in the middle of the end zone, too far away to arrive before a ball that is in the air for barely a second.


The back-shoulder throw
Against a corner who has learned to run with the fade, stride for stride and over the top, the back-shoulder throw is the answer. The quarterback throws short and behind the receiver, to his back (outside) shoulder. The receiver, reading the throw, stops, turns back to the ball and catches it, while the defender, running full speed with his back to the quarterback, is carried a step or two past. A defender taught to take away the deep ball can’t take this away without opening the deep ball again.


Show the Python
def fade_panel(ax, kind):
    off = [O("C", "C", LINE_D, 0.0), O("LG", "LG", LINE_D, -1.6, ""), O("LT", "LT", LINE_D, -3.2, ""),
           O("QB", "QB", GUN, 0.0, "Q"), O("X", "WR", LINE_D, -19.5)]
    cb_w = -18.7
    dfn = [D("CB", "CB", 1.1, cb_w, "CB"), D("FS", "FS", 11.5, -6.0, "FS"), D("T", "DT", 1.0, -0.8, "T"),
           D("E", "DE", 1.0, -4.4, "E")]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=opp(8), to_go=None)
    if kind == "fade":
        route_to(p, "X", (2.0, -20.4), (8.0, -21.6), (13.6, -22.3))
    else:
        route_to(p, "X", (2.5, -19.9), (10.5, -20.0), (9.3, -21.2))
    p.highlight("X")
    fld = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=(-26.67, 1.6), window=(-6.5, 18))
    goal_marks(fld, p, -3.0)
    if kind == "fade":
        branch(fld, p, [(1.1, -18.7), (5.0, -19.8), (11.6, -21.0)], color=style.DEFENSE)
        branch(fld, p, [(11.5, -6.0), (12.2, -10.0), (12.8, -13.0)], color=style.DEFENSE)
        throw(fld, p, (-5.0, 0.0), (13.0, -22.2), rad=-0.15)
        say(fld, p, 16.0, -15.4, "over the outside\nshoulder, to the pylon", fontsize=6.4, color=style.BALL)
        say(fld, p, 4.6, -14.0, "corner trails\nunderneath", fontsize=6.4, color=DD)
        say(fld, p, 14.6, -6.5, "safety too\nfar inside", fontsize=6.4, color=DD)
        panel_title(ax, "Fade: win outside, throw over the top")
    else:
        branch(fld, p, [(1.1, -18.7), (5.0, -18.9), (12.5, -19.1)], color=style.DEFENSE)
        throw(fld, p, (-5.0, 0.0), (9.2, -21.0), rad=-0.1)
        say(fld, p, 14.4, -13.2, "corner runs with\nhis back to the ball", fontsize=6.4, color=DD)
        say(fld, p, 4.4, -10.5, "thrown low and behind;\nX stops and turns", fontsize=6.4, color=style.BALL)
        say(fld, p, 9.6, -12.0, "caught in\nthe end zone", fontsize=6.4, color=OD)
        panel_title(ax, "Back-shoulder: throw behind him")
    return fld
