fade_panel(axes[1], "bs")
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=1.0)
field_legend(axes[0], ["route", "react", "pass"], fs=6.6, ncol=3, y=-0.01)
plt.show()








Figure 52.4: Two throws from one route, from the opponent’s 8 (the goal line is 8 yards up the page). X is lined up about 7 yards from the sideline. Left, the fade: the corner (CB) presses with inside leverage, so X releases outside and the ball is dropped over his outside shoulder toward the back pylon, where the corner, trailing underneath, can’t see it and the safety in the middle of the end zone can’t reach it in time. Right, the back-shoulder throw: this corner runs with X stride for stride, on his inside hip, to take away the fade. The ball is thrown early, low and behind X’s outside shoulder, away from the corner; X stops, turns back and catches it a yard or two deep in the end zone, near the sideline, while the corner, running with his back to the ball, is carried past. Short of the goal line, a back-shoulder catch is just a new set of downs.





The fade is famous for being thrown too often. It looks easy (one receiver, one defender, a jump ball) and it fails a lot: the ball has to be put in a small space near the sideline and the end line, and a corner who stays on the receiver’s hip can knock it away at the last moment. In 2022–2025, passes thrown into the end zone toward the outside from inside the 10, a rough stand-in for fades and back-shoulder throws that the public data can’t separate, were completed 40% of the time, against 68% for throws that stayed short of the goal line. But a completion in the end zone is a touchdown, and a short completion usually isn’t: per throw, the end-zone throws scored 40% of the time and the short ones 26%.6 So the fade is not a bad play. It fails more often than it works, but when it works it ends the drive in the best possible way; a short completion often just moves the ball a few yards closer and leaves another down to win. The danger is the offense that has nothing else and throws it on every third-and-goal, where a defense that knows it is coming can sit on it.
Contact helps the fade too. Defensive pass interference in the end zone gives the offense a first down at the 1, the most valuable spot on the field (nine drives in ten score from there, as the first-and-goal chart showed), so a corner who grabs a fading receiver is gambling too. The other way round, penalties near the goal line lose their teeth: half the distance means a 5-yard foul on the 4 moves the ball only 2 yards.






NoteFilm room: Green Bay Packers, the Rodgers–Nelson years (2010s)



The back-shoulder throw belongs to many quarterbacks, but its most famous partnership was Aaron Rodgers and Jordy Nelson in Mike McCarthy’s Green Bay offense. The Packers’ Hall of Fame profile of Nelson notes that the throw began as a red-zone play and that the two of them took it all over the field; Nelson, 6-foot-3, described it as a reaction rather than a set call: no signal, no pre-snap adjustment, just the ball arriving behind him when the corner ran too well.7 What to notice: the receiver’s head. On a fade he keeps running and looks up late; on a back-shoulder throw he snaps his head around early, sinks his hips, and the corner keeps running. If you see a corner win a fade early in a game, watch for the back-shoulder throw against him next time.




The slant, and leverage
If the corner shades outside to take away the fade, the receiver has the inside, and the quick slant (two steps up, then a sharp break inside) is the answer. It is caught a yard or two into the end zone, in the space between the corner and whoever is playing the middle, before either can close. Often a second receiver runs to the flat underneath it, the slant-flat pairing from Quick Game, so the defender between them can’t take both. Put the two together and you have the red zone’s first lesson about leverage: the corner can take away the fade or the slant, not both, and the receiver’s release attacks the side he gives up.
Defenses know the odds, and most red-zone corners play inside leverage on purpose. They use the sideline and the end line as help and concede the fade, the lowest-percentage throw on the field, to take away the slant, a high-percentage one thrown at their backs. The leverage game is a bet on both sides: the corner bets the quarterback can’t make the hard throw, and the offense bets on its receiver against that corner.
The slant’s risk lives in the middle of the field. The throw goes inside, where linebackers and safeties stand, so a defender who reads it can jump in front. That’s what happened on the most famous red-zone slant ever thrown, coming up in the film room on rubs.


The sprint-out
The fourth concept moves the quarterback. On a sprint-out he takes the snap and runs toward one sideline, with a group of routes flooding that side at three depths: high (a corner route to the back pylon), middle (an out at the goal line) and low (a flat route in front of the goal line). The sprint-out does three things near the goal line. It cuts the field in half, so the quarterback reads only one side. It moves the launch point away from the middle of the pocket, where interior rushers come free quickest. And it makes the quarterback a runner, so the defender in the flat faces a choice: cover the receiver in front of him, or come up to stop the quarterback. Either answer is wrong.


Show the Python
def slant_panel(ax):
    off = spread()
    dfn = dline() + [D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.0, -1.5, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.0, -6.0, "W"),
                     D("NB", "NB", 3.0, -9.5, "$"), D("SS", "SS", 3.5, 9.5, "SS"),
                     D("LCB", "CB", 1.1, -15.9, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 1.1, 15.9, "CB"),
                     D("FS", "FS", 11.0, -2.0, "FS")]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=opp(5), to_go=None)
    route_to(p, "X", (1.8, -15.0), (6.4, -9.8))
    route_to(p, "H", (0.9, -9.8), (2.7, -12.4), (3.1, -18.0))
    p.highlight("X")
    fld = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=(-21.5, 3.5), window=(-6.5, 15))
    goal_marks(fld, p, -19.0)
    branch(fld, p, [(1.1, -15.9), (3.6, -15.6), (5.2, -12.6)], color=style.DEFENSE)
    branch(fld, p, [(4.0, -6.0), (5.0, -7.6), (5.6, -8.6)], color=style.DEFENSE)
    branch(fld, p, [(3.0, -9.5), (3.8, -11.6), (4.2, -14.2)], color=style.DEFENSE)
    say(fld, p, -2.8, -11.4, "H to the flat\npulls the $ out", fontsize=6.2, color=OD)
    throw(fld, p, (-5.0, 0.0), (6.0, -10.3), rad=0.08)
    say(fld, p, -3.6, -17.4, "corner shades\noutside", fontsize=6.4, color=DD)
    say(fld, p, 8.6, -12.6, "caught a yard\ninto the end zone", fontsize=6.4, color=OD)
    point_to(fld, p, (8.2, -2.6), (5.0, -7.2), "the danger:\nW jumps it", fontsize=6.4, color=DD)

def sprint_panel(ax):
    off = line5() + [O("QB", "QB", GUN, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", GUN, 1.5, "R"),
                     O("X", "WR", LINE_D, -15.0), O("Y", "TE", LINE_D, 4.8),
                     O("H", "WR", OFF_BALL, 10.0), O("Z", "WR", OFF_BALL, 14.5)]
    dfn = dline(w=(-5.4, -0.8, 2.4, 6.0)) + [
        D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.0, 0.5, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.0, -4.5, "W"),
        D("NB", "NB", 3.0, 10.5, "$"), D("SS", "SS", 8.0, 9.0, "SS"),
        D("LCB", "CB", 5.0, -15.0, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 4.5, 17.0, "CB"),
        D("FS", "FS", 11.0, -3.0, "FS")]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=opp(7), to_go=None)
    move_to(p, "QB", (-5.6, 2.6), (-4.6, 6.6), (-3.8, 8.2), kind="run")
    move_to(p, "RB", (-3.4, 4.6), (-0.4, 5.8), kind="block")
    route_to(p, "Z", (4.5, 15.0), (12.8, 18.0))
    route_to(p, "Y", (5.4, 4.8), (6.6, 14.8))                 # middle: out at the goal line
    route_to(p, "H", (0.6, 10.9), (1.2, 16.4))                # low: the flat
    for k in ("LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT"):
        p.block(k, pts=[(-0.6, 1.0)])
    p.highlight("NB")
    fld = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=(-7.0, 21.0), window=(-6.5, 17))
    goal_marks(fld, p, 1.5)

Figure 52.5: Two quick red-zone answers. Left, from the 5, slant-flat: the corner shades outside to take away the fade, so X takes the inside on a slant, caught a yard into the end zone. H runs to the flat underneath, which pulls the nickel ($) outside and empties the slant’s window. The danger is the linebacker (W): if he reads the throw and drives on it, the slant becomes an interception. Right, from the 7, a sprint-out: the quarterback runs right behind the running back’s block, with three routes flooding that side at three depths: high (Z to the back pylon), middle (Y’s out at the goal line) and low (H to the flat). The nickel ($), ringed, has the flat. If he widens with H, the quarterback runs inside him (green); if he comes up for the quarterback, the ball goes to H, or to Y above him.







Rubs: the man-beater’s home field
The rub is the red zone’s signature pass. A rub route is a route designed to cross close to a teammate’s, so a defender chasing one receiver has to go around the other. Near the goal line it is at its most powerful, for a simple reason: the compressed field produces the man coverage rubs are built to beat. A zone defender doesn’t care if two receivers cross in front of him; a man defender who has to follow one particular receiver does.
Offenses set up rubs with alignment. Two receivers lined up one behind the other (a stack) or three in a tight triangle (a bunch) put their defenders close together, where any crossing route creates traffic. Watch the animation (the frame strip in print): the front man in a stack runs a slant inside, the back man runs out toward the pylon, and the nickel back covering the back man has to get through the slant to follow him. The stack can be run either way round: the front man can run the “pick” and the back man the slant, as Seattle did in the Super Bowl coming up below. What matters is that one receiver’s route crosses the path of the other’s defender.


Show the Python
def rub_play():
    off = line5() + [O("QB", "QB", GUN, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", GUN, -1.5, "R"),
                     O("X", "WR", LINE_D, -15.0), O("Y", "TE", LINE_D, -4.8),
                     O("Z", "WR", LINE_D, 11.0), O("H", "WR", -2.2, 11.4)]
    dfn = dline(w=(-6.4, -0.8, 2.4, 5.0)) + [
        D("MIKE", "MIKE", 3.5, 1.0, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 3.5, -4.0, "W"),
        D("NB", "NB", 2.0, 9.4, "$"), D("RCB", "CB", 1.0, 12.3, "CB"),
        D("LCB", "CB", 1.0, -15.6, "CB"), D("SS", "SS", 2.5, -5.5, "SS"),
        D("FS", "FS", 9.5, 1.0, "FS")]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=opp(4), to_go=None)
    for k in ("LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT"):
        p.block(k, pts=[(-1.0, 0.0)])
    for k in ("WDE", "WDT", "SDT", "SDE"):
        p.rush(k, pts=[(-1.4, 0.0)], speed=2.0)
    p.dropback(1.0)
    route_to(p, "Z", (1.0, 11.0), (4.0, 7.2), (5.6, 5.0), speed=6.5)
    route_to(p, "H", (-0.4, 12.6), (1.4, 15.0), (4.0, 18.2), (6.0, 20.2), speed=6.0)
    p.pass_to("H", t=0.95)
    tc = catch_time(p)
    set_tracks(p, {
        # the corner presses Z from outside and trails him inside, about a yard and a half behind
        "RCB": ease([(0.0, 1.0, 12.3), (0.3, 1.1, 12.0), (0.6, 1.4, 10.9), (1.0, 2.9, 8.7), (1.5, 3.9, 7.4),
                     (tc, 4.4, 6.6)]),
        # the nickel starts two yards off, inside H; Z's slant crosses his path, so he goes over the top
        "NB": ease([(0.0, 2.0, 9.4), (0.3, 2.6, 9.9), (0.6, 3.6, 10.6), (1.0, 4.2, 12.0), (1.4, 4.8, 13.8),
                    (1.8, 6.0, 15.6), (tc, 7.6, 17.2)]),
        "MIKE": ease([(0.0, 3.5, 1.0), (0.6, 3.6, 2.4), (1.6, 3.8, 4.0)]),
    }, t_end=tc + 0.1)
    return p


def catch_time(p, which=0):
    """When the ball arrives, the way gridiron times a pass (ball speed and the receiver's path)."""
    from gridiron.play import BALL_SPEED, _interp
    kf, _, _ = p._compile()
    kind, to, te = [e for e in p.ball_events if e[0] == "pass"][which]
    start, t_arr = p.ball_position(te), te + 0.5
    for _ in range(4):
        t_arr = te + float(np.linalg.norm(_interp(kf[to], t_arr) - start)) / BALL_SPEED
    return round(t_arr, 1)


def rub_deco(t, fld, p):
    if t <= 0:
        goal_marks(fld, p, 4.0, end=False)


RUB = rub_play()
RUB_TC = catch_time(RUB)
RUB_T = [0.0, 0.6, 1.0, RUB_TC]
RUB_N = ["Stack: Z in front, H behind.\nCB presses Z; $ sits inside on H.",
         "Z slants inside, right across\nthe $'s path; H breaks outside.",
         "Ball out. The $ has to go over\nthe top of Z: a step behind.",
         "H catches it toward the corner,\nthree yards clear of the $."]
RUB_LAT, RUB_WIN = (-3.0, 23.5), (-7.0, 12.0)
if PDF:
    strip_grid(RUB, RUB_T, RUB_N, RUB_LAT, RUB_WIN, rings=(("NB", style.THIRD),), ltg=False, mr=0.62,
               deco=rub_deco)
    plt.show()
else:
    video(RUB, RUB_LAT, RUB_WIN, RUB_TC + 0.1, rings=(("NB", style.THIRD),), notes=RUB_N, times=RUB_T, ltg=False,
          mr=0.62, deco=rub_deco)

Figure 52.6: A stack rub against man coverage from the opponent’s 4, simulated (BDB-format tracking generated by gridiron, not recorded). Z, the front of the stack, breaks into a slant after one step. H, a step behind him, runs out toward the corner of the end zone. The corner (CB) presses Z and goes with him. The nickel ($, ringed green), two yards off and inside H, has to cross Z’s path to follow H outside; Z never blocks him, he just runs his route, and the paths cross within about two yards of the line, but the nickel must go over the top of Z and loses a step. The ball is out at 1.0 second (panel 3), before the nickel has recovered; by the catch, toward the corner of the end zone, H is about three yards clear and the nickel is chasing from above and inside, behind the throw.




When does a rub become a pick? The receiver in front may run his route; he may not block. The NFL calls offensive pass interference on a receiver who deliberately initiates contact with a defender more than one yard past the line of scrimmage, before the pass is touched, to get a teammate open. So offenses teach the rub man to run through the defender’s path rather than at the defender, and to keep running, and they design the crossing to happen as close to the line as they can. Officials judge intent at full speed, and a quarterback can’t know in advance whether the flag will come, which is part of why rubs are both effective and maddening.
How defenses answer. The cleanest answer is not to be in pure man. Against a stack or bunch, defenders can play a banjo: instead of each locking onto one receiver before the snap, they decide at the release, the outside defender taking whoever breaks outside and the inside defender whoever breaks inside, so nobody has to fight through the traffic. Another answer is to stop the rub at its source: a defender who jams the front receiver at the line knocks the traffic out of the way before it can form. That second answer decided a Super Bowl.






NoteFilm room: Seattle vs. New England, Super Bowl XLIX (2014 season)



February 1, 2015, Glendale, Arizona. The Patriots led 28–24, and Seattle had the ball second-and-goal at New England’s 1 with about 26 seconds left and one timeout. Seattle had three wide receivers on the field; New England sent in its goal-line defense. Instead of handing off to Marshawn Lynch, Seattle threw. Pete Carroll said afterward that the goal-line personnel gave his receivers the better matchups, and that he wanted to use the down while keeping enough clock for all of his remaining plays. The receivers were stacked on the right: Jermaine Kearse in front, to run a pick route, and Ricardo Lockette behind him, to slant inside. Patriots cornerback Brandon Browner, lined up on the front man, jammed Kearse at the line, so the rub never happened, and rookie Malcolm Butler, off the ball on the back man, drove in front of Lockette and intercepted Russell Wilson’s pass at the goal line. “I remembered the formation they were in, two receivers stacked,” Butler said; “I just knew they were going to [a] pick route.” New England won 28–24.8 What to notice: every ingredient of this chapter. A stack rub against man coverage near the goal line, the picture in the frame strip above with the routes swapped; a slant thrown into the middle, where defenders live; and the defense’s two answers to the rub: a press jam that removed the traffic, and an off defender who had studied the formation. The call was second-guessed for years, but the concept was a standard one. It failed because one defender beat the rub at the line and another read it.




The shovel pass
The shovel pass is a run play that happens to be a pass. The quarterback takes the snap and moves sideways along the line, as if rolling out or keeping the ball; a teammate (a tight end, a back, sometimes a slot receiver) comes across just in front of him, behind the line of scrimmage, and the quarterback flips the ball to him underhand. The receiver then runs behind a pulling lineman into the gap the defense has just vacated.


Show the Python

p = Play(off, dfn, los=opp(9), to_go=None)

p.highlight("SDE")
p.highlight("LG", color=style.SERIES[6])

branch(fld, p, [(LINE_D, -1.6), (-1.5, -1.4), (-1.6, 2.4), (0.4, 3.6), (2.6, 3.0)], color=style.SERIES[6], lw=2.0,
       dash="-", z=4.5)                                   # the puller's path, in his ring colour

say(fld, p, -2.6, 5.0, "1", fontsize=8.5, color=DD, weight="bold")
say(fld, p, -3.7, 1.0, "2", fontsize=8.5, color=style.BALL, weight="bold")
say(fld, p, 6.6, 2.0, "3", fontsize=8.5, color=OD, weight="bold")
fld.ax.text(0.5, -0.005, "1  the unblocked end chases the QB     2  underhand flip: a forward pass, caught behind the line"
            "     3  Y follows the pulling guard", transform=fld.ax.transAxes, ha="center", va="top", fontsize=6.8,
            color=style.INK)
field_legend(fld.ax, ["route", "carrier", "block", "pass"], fs=6.8, y=-0.045)

Figure 52.7: A shovel pass from the opponent’s 9. The play-side end (E, ringed green) is left unblocked on purpose; he rushes at the quarterback, who steps right as if to run or throw. The left guard (G, ringed purple, his path in purple) pulls behind the line and turns up through the hole to block the Will linebacker. The tight end (Y), lined up on the left, crosses behind the line just behind the guard, takes an underhand flip from the quarterback (brown dashes), a forward pass caught behind the line of scrimmage, and follows the guard up into the gap the unblocked end has just left. The running back swings the other way, and H’s route takes the nickel ($) out of the picture.





Why does it work so well near the goal line? Because goal-line defenses are built to attack. Defensive ends charge upfield at a rolling quarterback; linebackers fly toward the first thing they see. The shovel pass turns that aggression into empty space: the end who chases the quarterback has taken himself out of the gap the ball is about to come through.
The flip is a forward pass, and that has two consequences. The good one: a dropped shovel is merely an incomplete pass, not a fumble. The constraint: because it counts as a pass, the offensive linemen may not run upfield until it is thrown. The NFL’s ineligible-downfield rule applies to every forward pass, even one caught behind the line: no lineman may be more than a yard past the line before the throw unless he got there while blocking.9 So the flip comes fast, while the linemen are still fighting at the line, and only then does the pulling guard lead the way up the field. College spread offenses made the shovel option famous; in the NFL it is a change-up, used a few times a season, usually near the goal line or on a short third down. Andy Reid’s Kansas City offenses have used it for years: the go-ahead touchdown in a 27–20 win over Philadelphia in September 2017 was a 15-yard shovel to tight end Travis Kelce, from a look that for its first half-second resembled a quarterback keep.10

title: Red Zone, Goal Line, Two-Point Plays, and Short Yardage (Including the Tush Push)
section: Two-point plays: designing a play from the 2
text:
Two-point plays: designing a play from the 2
After a touchdown, the scoring team gets one more snap, a try. It can kick an extra point for one point or run a play from the 2-yard line for two: the two-point conversion. The NFL adopted it in 1994, borrowing it from college football (which snaps its try from the 3) and from the American Football League, the NFL’s 1960s rival, which had used it throughout its ten seasons. In 2015 the league moved the extra-point kick back to the 15-yard line, turning a near-automatic kick into a 33-yard attempt, and began letting the defense score two points by returning a failed try to the other end zone.11 (The rules are unchanged for 2026: still snapped from the 2.) Whether to go for two, and when the scoreboard demands it, belongs to The Clock, the Two-Minute Drill, and Fourth Down. This section is about what to call.
From 2015 to 2025, NFL teams converted 47% of their 1,297 regular-season two-point tries (counting only tries that produced a run or a pass, not the ones wiped out by penalties). Runs converted 55% of the time, passes 44%, yet teams passed on about 73% of tries.12 (Is going for two worth it at all? Two points times 47% is about 0.94 points a try, almost exactly what the 94% extra-point kick is worth. That near-tie is why the scoreboard, not the average, decides, and it is 10-04’s subject.) Why not run every time?
Part of the answer is selection. The teams that run on two-point tries are mostly the ones built to: a running quarterback, a heavy line, a reliable short-yardage play. Passes include the desperate tries late in games, when everyone knows the offense needs two and the defense has called its best pass defense. The bigger part is game theory. A two-point try is a single snap the defense knows is coming, from a spot it has studied all week. If an offense ran every time, defenses would load the box with every man they have, and the run rate would fall. The value of a two-point play depends on what the defense expects, and the best calls are ones that work against more than one defense.
The defense’s side of the try looks like any goal-to-go snap. It matches the offense’s personnel rather than bringing in a goal-line package: on the 2023–2025 tries charted with personnel, the defense had five or more defensive backs on the field 71% of the time and a goal-line group of three or fewer only 9%, because most offenses went for two with three wide receivers. Its coverage is the red zone’s, only more so: 72% of charted two-point dropbacks faced man coverage.13
That gives a simple design rule for a two-point play: two good options that put one defender in conflict, ideally a run threat and a pass, or a man-beater and a zone-beater on the same snap. Here are four common shapes. (The public data can’t say which shape converts best: play-by-play records the run or the pass, not the concept, so the case for each is in the football, not in a success rate.)


Show the Python
def tp_base(variant):
    if variant == "bunch":
        off = line5() + [O("QB", "QB", GUN, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", GUN, -1.5, "R"),
                         O("X", "WR", LINE_D, -15.0), O("H", "WR", LINE_D, 8.0),
                         O("Y", "TE", -2.2, 6.4), O("Z", "WR", -2.2, 9.6)]
    elif variant == "snag":
        off = line5() + [O("QB", "QB", GUN, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", GUN, 1.5, "R"),
                         O("X", "WR", LINE_D, -15.0), O("Y", "TE", LINE_D, 4.8),
                         O("H", "WR", OFF_BALL, 8.5), O("Z", "WR", OFF_BALL, 13.0)]
    elif variant == "sprint":
        off = line5() + [O("QB", "QB", GUN, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", GUN, 1.5, "R"),
                         O("X", "WR", LINE_D, -15.0), O("Y", "TE", LINE_D, 4.8),
                         O("H", "WR", OFF_BALL, 11.5), O("Z", "WR", OFF_BALL, 14.5)]
    else:
        off = [O("LG", "LG", LINE_D, -1.6, "G") if q.key == "LG" else q for q in line5(names=True)]
        off = off + [O("QB", "QB", GUN, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", GUN, 1.5, "R"),
                                   O("X", "WR", LINE_D, -15.0), O("Y", "TE", LINE_D, 4.8),
                                   O("H", "WR", OFF_BALL, 9.5), O("Z", "WR", OFF_BALL, 14.5)]
    return off

                        D("RCB", "CB", 2.6, 15.2, "CB"), D("LCB", "CB", 4.0, -15.0, "CB"),

    else:

                        D("NB", "NB", 2.6, 10.6, "$"), D("SS", "SS", 7.0, 6.0, "SS"),
                        D("RCB", "CB", 4.0, 15.2, "CB"), D("LCB", "CB", 4.0, -15.0, "CB"),
                        D("FS", "FS", 9.0, -3.0, "FS")]

    lat, win = (-6.5, 17.5), (-6.5, 12)

        route_to(p, "H", (4.6, 8.0), (9.6, 13.4))

    elif variant == "snag":
        route_to(p, "Z", (4.6, 13.0), (5.0, 9.8))
        route_to(p, "H", (4.6, 8.5), (9.6, 15.0))
        route_to(p, "RB", (-3.6, 5.5), (0.8, 15.6))
        fld = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=lat, window=win)
        tri = [(5.0, 9.8), (9.6, 15.0), (0.8, 15.6), (5.0, 9.8)]
        xs, ys = P(fld, p, np.array([q[0] for q in tri]), np.array([q[1] for q in tri]))
        ax.fill(xs, ys, color=style.THIRD, alpha=0.12, zorder=1.7)
        ax.plot(xs, ys, color=READ_GREEN, lw=1.0, ls=(0, (2, 2)), zorder=1.8)
        say(fld, p, -5.0, 11.4, "shaded: 3 receivers\nv 2 defenders", fontsize=6.3, color=READ_GREEN)
    elif variant == "sprint":
        move_to(p, "QB", (-5.5, 2.6), (-4.6, 6.0), (-3.4, 8.0), kind="run")
        move_to(p, "RB", (-3.8, 3.0), (-1.6, 3.6), kind="block")                 # stays in: inside protection
        move_to(p, "Y", (0.4, 6.0), kind="block")                                 # seals the end inside
        route_to(p, "Z", (2.6, 13.6), (9.4, 13.0))                                # clears the corner
        route_to(p, "H", (1.0, 12.0), (1.6, 15.0))                                # the end-zone flat
        p.highlight("NB")
        fld = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=lat, window=win)
        branch(fld, p, [(-3.4, 8.0), (-1.4, 8.6), (2.2, 8.8)], color=style.THIRD, lw=1.6)
        point_to(fld, p, (8.8, 9.4), (2.6, 10.6), "flat defender:\nH or the QB?", fontsize=6.4, color=READ_GREEN)
    else:
        move_to(p, "QB", (-4.0, 0.6), (-2.4, 3.2), (-0.6, 4.6), (1.4, 4.9), (3.6, 4.9), kind="run")
        move_to(p, "RB", (-3.2, 4.6), (0.0, 6.1), kind="block")                 # kicks out the end
        move_to(p, "LG", (-1.6, -1.4), (-1.6, 2.6), (0.2, 4.2), (2.6, 2.0), kind="pull")   # leads for the Mike
        move_to(p, "C", (0.2, -0.5), kind="block")                               # back on the backside tackle
        move_to(p, "LT", (-1.2, -3.4), kind="block")                             # hinge
        move_to(p, "RG", (0.6, 1.2), (2.8, -2.6), kind="block")                  # climbs to the backside Will
        move_to(p, "RT", (0.3, 2.7), kind="block")                               # down on the 3-technique
        move_to(p, "Y", (0.4, 3.4), kind="block")                                # down, with the tackle
        move_to(p, "H", (1.6, 10.4), kind="block")
        move_to(p, "Z", (3.0, 14.4), kind="block")
        p.highlight("QB")
        p.highlight("LG", color=style.SERIES[6])
        fld = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=lat, window=win)
        branch(fld, p, [(LINE_D, -1.6), (-1.6, -1.4), (-1.6, 2.6), (0.2, 4.2), (2.6, 2.0)], color=style.SERIES[6],
               lw=2.0, dash="-", z=4.5)
        say(fld, p, -4.4, 11.6, "the back blocks:\n10 blockers, 1 runner", fontsize=6.4, color=OD)
    panel_title(ax, title, fs=8.2)
    return fld


fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(6.6, 6.2))
tp_panel(axes[0, 0], "bunch", "A  Bunch rub (vs man)")
tp_panel(axes[0, 1], "snag", "B  Snag triangle (vs zone)")
tp_panel(axes[1, 0], "sprint", "C  Sprint-out option")
tp_panel(axes[1, 1], "power", "D  QB power")
fig.tight_layout(h_pad=1.4, w_pad=1.0)
plt.show()








Figure 52.8: Four two-point shapes from the 2 (the goal line is 2 yards up the page; the end line 12). A, bunch rub against man: Y and Z cross just behind H, the point man (the front receiver of the bunch), so the defenders covering them must sort out the traffic; any hesitation leaves one open. B, snag against zone: three receivers make a triangle (shaded) against the two defenders in that area: H’s corner route high, Z’s snag in the middle (five yards, then sit down facing the quarterback) and the back’s flat route low. C, sprint-out option: the tight end seals the end inside, the back stays in to protect, and the quarterback runs at the flat defender (the nickel, $, ringed), who must choose between H in the end-zone flat and the quarterback running (green); Z’s vertical route clears the corner away. D, QB power, blocked as in Option Football: the tight end and right tackle double-team the tackle in front of them, the right guard climbs to the backside linebacker, the running back, who would otherwise carry, kicks out the end, and the pulling guard (G, ringed purple, his path in purple) leads through the hole for the Mike, with the quarterback right behind him through the hole between the tight end’s down block and the back’s kick-out. Everyone else blocks too: ten blockers for one runner.





Each shape answers a defensive call. Against the man coverage that dominates the goal line, the bunch rub (A) is the classic: three receivers starting close together, two crossing just behind the third, and three defenders who must either fight through traffic or switch assignments perfectly. Against zone, the snag triangle (B), from Quick Game (the snag itself is a receiver who runs five yards and sits down facing the quarterback), puts three receivers in one area guarded by two defenders: whichever receiver the defenders leave, the quarterback throws to. The sprint-out option (C) doesn’t care much which coverage it gets, because it attacks one defender with two threats. And the quarterback run (D), the extra-hat idea from Option Football, gives the offense one more blocker than a handoff can, which matters most when two yards is all it needs.
Notice what’s missing: deep routes, long developing reads, anything that needs a second and a half to come open. From the 2 the end line is 12 yards away, and a pass rush arrives in about two and a half seconds. Two-point plays are designed to be decided by the quarterback’s first look.






NoteFilm room: New England, Super Bowl LI (2016 season)



Down 28–3 in the third quarter against Atlanta, the Patriots needed two two-point conversions just to tie, and got both. The first, after Danny Amendola’s touchdown catch made it 28–18 with about six minutes left, was a direct snap to running back James White: Brady stood in the shotgun, White motioned in beside him, the center snapped the ball straight to White, and he ran it up the middle for 28–20. The second, after White’s own 1-yard touchdown run with 57 seconds left, was a quick throw from Tom Brady to Amendola for 28–28. New England won in overtime, 34–28.14 What to notice: two different answers on the same night, a run with the quarterback out of the play and a quick pass; a defense that had seen one couldn’t sit on it the next time. Why take the quarterback out of a run, when this chapter keeps saying a running quarterback adds a blocker? Because Brady was never a running threat, so the extra-hat arithmetic didn’t apply to him. What the direct snap bought was speed and surprise: the ball went straight to the runner, with no handoff, against a defense set up to stop a Brady pass.

section: Goal-line personnel: the biggest people on the field
text:
Goal-line personnel: the biggest people on the field
Inside the 3 or so, both teams change their players. The offense brings in its heaviest personnel: two or three tight ends, a fullback, sometimes a sixth offensive lineman (a jumbo package) who has to report as eligible: tell the referee, who announces it, because a lineman’s number normally makes him an ineligible receiver. And sometimes the extra body is a defensive lineman playing fullback. The most famous of those was William “The Refrigerator” Perry, the Chicago Bears’ rookie defensive tackle, who scored a 1-yard touchdown in Super Bowl XX in January 1986.15 The idea is simple arithmetic: every receiver taken off the field is replaced by a blocker, so the offense can match the defense body for body near the ball.
The defense answers in kind with a goal-line defense: extra linemen and linebackers in place of defensive backs, everyone lined up close to the ball, every gap along the line filled before the snap. The two classic shapes are the 6-2 (six down linemen, two linebackers, three defensive backs) and the 5-3 (five down linemen, three linebackers, three defensive backs). Both put eight defenders within about three yards of the ball.
Why two shapes? Against an offense with a tight end at each end of the line there are eight gaps to fill (A, B, C and D on each side, from The Language of the Run Game). The 6-2 puts six of those eight defenders on the line, in the gaps, low, and lets the two linebackers fill the last two: it is the stronger shape right at the ball, built to win the first yard by force. The 5-3 takes one lineman off the line and adds a third linebacker. It gives up a little of that force, but it gains a defender standing up, who can see the play, fill whichever gap the run goes to, or pick up a tight end or fullback who slips out for a pass. So the 6-2 suits the last yard against an offense that just pounds the ball, and the 5-3 suits a defense that fears play-action from the same look.


Show the Python
def jumbo():
    return line5(split=1.55) + [O("QB", "QB", -2.0, 0.0, "Q"), O("FB", "FB", -4.2, 0.0, "F"),
                                 O("RB", "RB", -6.4, 0.0, "R"), O("Y", "TE", LINE_D, 4.65),
                                 O("U", "TE", LINE_D, -4.65, "U"), O("W", "TE", -2.0, 6.3, "H")]


def gl_panel(ax, kind):
    if kind == "62":
        dfn = [D("E1", "DE", 0.9, -6.0, "E"), D("T1", "DT", 0.9, -3.9, "T"), D("T2", "DT", 0.9, -0.85, "T"),
               D("T3", "DT", 0.9, 0.85, "T"), D("T4", "DT", 0.9, 3.9, "T"), D("E2", "DE", 0.9, 6.3, "E"),
               D("LB1", "LB", 2.8, -2.3, "M"), D("LB2", "LB", 2.8, 2.3, "W"),
               D("CB1", "CB", 2.4, -8.2, "CB"), D("CB2", "CB", 2.6, 8.4, "CB"), D("SS", "SS", 5.0, 4.6, "SS")]
        notes = [("6 linemen +\n2 LBs: 8 gaps", (-4.6, -7.0))]
    else:
        dfn = [D("E1", "DE", 0.9, -5.3, "E"), D("T1", "DT", 0.9, -2.3, "T"), D("N", "NT", 0.9, 0.0, "N"),
               D("T2", "DT", 0.9, 2.3, "T"), D("E2", "DE", 0.9, 5.5, "E"),
               D("LB1", "LB", 2.8, -3.6, "W"), D("LB2", "LB", 2.8, 0.0, "M"), D("LB3", "LB", 2.8, 3.8, "S"),
               D("CB1", "CB", 2.4, -8.2, "CB"), D("CB2", "CB", 2.6, 8.4, "CB"), D("SS", "SS", 5.0, -1.9, "SS")]
        notes = [("5 linemen,\n3 linebackers", (-4.6, -7.0))]
    p = Play(jumbo(), dfn, los=opp(1), to_go=None)
    fld = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=(-10.5, 10.5), window=(-8.0, 8.5))
    for text, at in notes:
        say(fld, p, at[0], at[1], text, fontsize=6.6, color=DD)
    say(fld, p, 6.8, -5.0, "end zone", fontsize=6.6, color=style.MUTED, box=False)
    panel_title(ax, "6-2 goal line" if kind == "62" else "5-3 goal line")
    return fld


fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 3.7))
gl_panel(axes[0], "62")
gl_panel(axes[1], "53")
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=1.0)
plt.show()








Figure 52.9: Goal-line personnel on both sides, ball on the 1. The offense is in 23 personnel (a fullback F and a running back R, plus three tight ends: Y and U on the line and H as a wing just outside Y), with tight line splits. Left, a 6-2 goal-line defense: six linemen in the gaps along the line, low, the two linebackers filling the last two gaps, and three defensive backs for the tight ends and the wing. Right, a 5-3: a nose tackle (N) on the center, four more linemen, three linebackers. Both fill every gap from tight end to tight end at the snap. The defenders’ letters show their usual positions; on goal-line snaps the labels matter less than the gaps.





Football coaches have a three-word rule for this part of the field: low man wins. When two big men collide at the line, the one whose pads are lower gets under the other, lifts him and drives him back. On an ordinary down that matters; at the goal line it is almost everything, because the play will be decided within a yard of the ball. So goal-line defensive linemen often line up in four-point stances, both hands on the ground, and fire under the blockers, aiming to knock the offensive line back into the backfield and create a pile the runner can’t cross. Linebackers fill whatever gap is left, often by going over the top of the pile.
What does the offense run into all that? Mostly the same handful of downhill runs you met in Gap and Power Runs, and the simplest is the one below: the iso, a fullback leading into a gap onto the one linebacker who fills it.


Show the Python
p = Play(jumbo(), [D("E1", "DE", 0.9, -6.0, "E"), D("T1", "DT", 0.9, -3.9, "T"), D("T2", "DT", 0.9, -0.85, "T"),
                   D("T3", "DT", 0.9, 0.85, "T"), D("T4", "DT", 0.9, 3.9, "T"), D("E2", "DE", 0.9, 6.3, "E"),
                   D("LB1", "LB", 2.8, -2.3, "M"), D("LB2", "LB", 2.8, 2.3, "W"),
                   D("CB1", "CB", 2.4, -8.2, "CB"), D("CB2", "CB", 2.6, 8.4, "CB"), D("SS", "SS", 5.0, 4.6, "SS")],
         los=opp(1), to_go=None)
move_to(p, "RG", (0.1, 1.0), kind="block")                 # down on the A-gap tackle
move_to(p, "RT", (0.2, 4.2), kind="block")                 # out on the C-gap tackle
for k, w in (("LT", -3.3), ("LG", -1.7), ("C", -0.4)):
    move_to(p, k, (0.1, w), kind="block")
move_to(p, "Y", (0.2, 5.9), kind="block")
move_to(p, "U", (0.2, -5.6), kind="block")
move_to(p, "FB", (-3.0, 0.9), (-0.6, 1.9), (1.5, 2.2), kind="block")    # leads through the B gap onto W
move_to(p, "RB", (-5.0, 1.1), (-2.6, 2.5), (-0.6, 2.7), (0.9, 2.6), kind="run")   # follows him into the hole
p.highlight("LB2")
fld = draw(p, width_in=5.6, lateral=(-10.0, 10.0), window=(-8.0, 7.2))
branch(fld, p, [(2.8, -2.3), (3.1, -0.6), (2.6, 0.9)], color=style.DEFENSE)
point_to(fld, p, (5.2, -4.4), (3.1, -0.8), "M: over the top", fontsize=6.6, color=DD)
point_to(fld, p, (-5.6, 5.4), (-1.8, 1.4), "F leads into\nthe B gap", fontsize=6.6, color=OD)
say(fld, p, 5.4, 7.4, "end zone", fontsize=6.6, color=style.MUTED, box=False)
field_legend(fld.ax, ["carrier", "block", "react", "ring"], fs=6.6, ncol=4, y=-0.01)
plt.show()








Figure 52.10: The run a goal-line defense is built to stop: an iso from the I formation against the 6-2, ball on the 1. The right guard blocks the A-gap tackle down and the right tackle blocks the C-gap tackle out, which opens the right B gap; the fullback (F) leads through it onto the linebacker who fills it (W, ringed), and the running back (R) follows him in, needing only to get the ball across the goal line a yard away. The other linebacker (M) tries to come over the top of the pile. Every other blocker simply fires low into the man in front of him. At the goal line this is low man wins in its purest form: whoever gets lower at the hole wins it.











ImportantWhy it exists



A goal-line defense exists because near the goal line the run is a real threat on every snap and the pass has little room to hurt you. Trading cornerbacks and safeties for linemen and linebackers trades coverage, which the compressed field has made cheap, for gap control and size, which the last yard has made precious. What it gives up: coverage. Goal-line defenses are built to stop a run up the middle, and their worst nightmare is the play that looks exactly like that run and isn’t: the play-action pass to a tight end or a fullback slipping out, or a quarterback rollout to the edge where fewer defenders are standing. That is why, when heavy personnel does throw near the goal line, it almost always fakes the run first: inside the 3 in 2023–2025, offenses with one wide receiver or none passed on only 28% of snaps, but 66% of those dropbacks were play-action, against 31% from lighter groupings.16

title: Red Zone, Goal Line, Two-Point Plays, and Short Yardage (Including the Tush Push)
text:
The quarterback sneak
The shortest play in football is the QB sneak. The quarterback takes the snap under center and immediately drives forward behind his center, usually into one of the gaps beside him, to gain a yard or less. No handoff, no fake, no read.
It is the most reliable play in the book for one yard, and the reasons are worth spelling out:

The ball starts closest to the line. On a handoff, the ball goes backward to a running back five to seven yards deep, who then has to gain all of that back before he gains anything. On a sneak, the ball is a foot behind the line when the quarterback has it.
It is the fastest play there is. The ball goes from the center’s hands to the quarterback’s and forward in a fraction of a second, before linebackers can read the play and fill.
The quarterback is the extra blocker’s dividend. On every other run, the quarterback hands off and stops being a factor; on the sneak he is the runner, so every other player can block, the same extra-hat arithmetic as QB power.
The defense can’t see it coming any differently. A quarterback under center on third-and-1 might sneak, hand off, or fake and throw. Defenses have to defend all three.

And its blocking is simple. Coaches call it wedge blocking: every lineman drives low and forward toward the center’s hip, so the front moves as one block with no seams for a defender to slip through, often with the center and a guard double-teaming whoever lines up over the ball. The quarterback’s coaching point is just as simple: follow the center’s backside into the first crease. And the cadence, the quarterback’s call that tells his line when the ball will be snapped, is a weapon either way. A quick count snaps the ball on the first sound, before the defense has settled into its stances; a hard count, a long, loud call with a sudden bark meant to draw the defense offside, aims for the free yard without snapping it at all.


Show the Python
SNEAK_SPLIT = 1.3          # nearly foot to foot: the push line closes its splits


def sneak_off(push, p_d=-2.8):
    """Short-yardage offense: tight splits, tight ends on both ends of the line, the quarterback under center."""
    off = line5(split=SNEAK_SPLIT) + [O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0.0, "Q"), O("Y", "TE", LINE_D, 3.95),
                                      O("U", "TE", LINE_D, -3.95, "U"), O("W", "TE", -1.7, 5.4, "H")]
    if push:
        off += [O("P1", "RB", p_d, -0.75, "P"), O("P2", "TE", p_d, 0.75, "P")]
    else:
        off += [O("RB", "RB", -6.2, 0.0, "R"), O("FB", "FB", -4.1, 0.0, "F")]
    return off


def short_def():
    """A short-yardage front: six linemen low (two in the A gaps beside the center), three linebackers."""
    return [D("E1", "DE", 0.9, -5.4, "E"), D("T1", "DT", 0.9, -2.3, "T"), D("T2", "DT", 0.9, -0.75, "T"),
            D("T3", "DT", 0.9, 0.75, "T"), D("T4", "DT", 0.9, 2.3, "T"), D("E2", "DE", 0.9, 5.4, "E"),
            D("MIKE", "LB", 2.6, -1.4, "M"), D("WILL", "LB", 2.6, 1.4, "W"), D("SAM", "LB", 2.3, 6.4, "S"),
            D("CB1", "CB", 3.0, -8.0, "CB"), D("SS", "SS", 5.0, 0.0, "SS")]


def carrier_arrow(fld, p, pts):
    """The ball carrier's path through the pile: drawn over the markers but see-through, so the letters
    it crosses stay readable."""
    xs, ys = P(fld, p, np.array([q[0] for q in pts]), np.array([q[1] for q in pts]))
    fld.ax.plot(xs, ys, color=OD, lw=2.2, alpha=0.55, zorder=11, solid_capstyle="round")
    fld.ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((xs[-2], ys[-2]), (xs[-1], ys[-1]), arrowstyle="-|>", mutation_scale=12,
                                     color=OD, lw=2.2, zorder=11))


def sneak_panel(ax, push):
    p = Play(sneak_off(push, p_d=-3.2), short_def(), los=opp(35), to_go=1)
    for k in ("LG", "C", "RG"):
        p.block(k, pts=[(0.6, 0.0)])
    if push:
        p.highlight("P1", "P2")
    fld = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=(-9.5, 9.5), window=(-7.0, 6.5))
    if push:
        carrier_arrow(fld, p, [(-1.9, 0.0), (-0.2, 0.0), (2.0, 0.0), (2.6, 0.0)])
        say(fld, p, -4.9, -4.0, "2 pushers, tight\nbehind the QB", fontsize=6.6, color=READ_GREEN, weight="bold")
    else:
        carrier_arrow(fld, p, [(-1.9, 0.0), (-0.3, 0.4), (2.0, 0.4), (2.6, 0.4)])
        say(fld, p, -3.6, -4.0, "QB alone:\nfollow the center", fontsize=6.6, color=OD)
    panel_title(ax, "Tush push" if push else "Quarterback sneak")
    return fld


fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 3.5))
sneak_panel(axes[0], False)
sneak_panel(axes[1], True)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=1.0)
plt.show()








Figure 52.11: Two ways to gain a yard, third-and-1, from the same heavy formation: tight ends Y and U on the ends of the line, a wing (H) outside Y, and tight line splits. Left, the classic quarterback sneak: the quarterback (Q) alone under center, a fullback (F) and running back (R) deep, so the defense has to respect a handoff. At the snap the center and guards drive forward and the quarterback follows his center into the nearest crease, here the right A gap, between center and guard. Right, the tush push: the same sneak, but the backs have been replaced by two pushers (P) lined up almost against the quarterback’s hips (drawn a little apart here so the letters show), who drive into him at the snap and shove the whole pile forward. The defense, crowding the A gaps, lines up the same way against both. The yellow line is the line to gain, one yard away.











NoteFilm room: Tom Brady (2000–2022) and Josh Allen (2018–2025)



Two quarterbacks show the two ways to be a great sneaker. Tom Brady, a 6-foot-4 pocket passer who was never fast and never needed to be, won with timing. Counting every run he made with a yard or less to go, regular season and playoffs, nflverse play-by-play has Brady carrying 187 times and gaining the first down or the touchdown on 86% of them; almost all were sneaks.17 The Patriots often ran it on a quick count, and Brady was over the center’s back before the linebackers had moved. Josh Allen, one of the biggest and strongest quarterbacks in the league, wins with size: he sneaks, pushes and runs QB power with equal comfort, and Buffalo ran the second-most sneaks of 2022–2025. On every Allen carry for the Bills with a yard or less to go, nflverse has him converting 86% of 181 tries, essentially level with Brady’s career mark.18 What to notice: on old Patriots film, how quickly the ball is snapped; on Bills film, where Allen goes. A pure sneak goes straight ahead; Allen often bounces a step to the A or B gap where the pile is softest, using his size like a running back’s.

title: Red Zone, Goal Line, Two-Point Plays, and Short Yardage (Including the Tush Push)
text:
The tush push
The tush push is a quarterback sneak with help from behind. Two or three teammates (usually a running back and a tight end, sometimes a third player) line up directly behind the quarterback, and at the snap they drive into him and push. The offensive line fires low and forward; the quarterback, crouched behind his center, surges into the line; the pushers add their weight from behind, and the whole mass moves forward, usually just far enough. Philadelphia fans called it the Brotherly Shove.


Show the Python
def push_play():
    """Keyframes for every body at the snap, first contact, mid-push and the finish. The pile moves as a
    block, so each moment is placed by hand to keep engaged players about a yard and a quarter apart."""
    p = Play(sneak_off(True), short_def(), los=opp(35), to_go=1)
    K = {   # key: [(d, w) at t = 0.4, 0.8, 1.2]
        "LT": [(-0.25, -2.6), (0.05, -2.75), (0.3, -2.85)], "LG": [(-0.15, -1.3), (0.45, -1.5), (0.9, -1.65)],
        "C": [(-0.1, 0.0), (0.55, -0.35), (1.5, -0.75)], "RG": [(-0.15, 1.3), (0.55, 1.5), (1.5, 1.75)],
        "RT": [(-0.25, 2.6), (0.3, 2.8), (0.6, 2.95)], "U": [(-0.4, -3.95), (-0.2, -4.1), (0.0, -4.2)],
        "Y": [(-0.4, 3.95), (-0.2, 4.1), (0.0, 4.2)], "W": [(-1.5, 5.2), (-1.3, 5.1), (-1.1, 5.0)],
        "QB": [(-1.5, 0.05), (0.0, 0.5), (1.6, 0.7)],
        "P1": [(-2.4, -0.6), (-1.0, -0.05), (0.4, 0.05)], "P2": [(-2.4, 0.8), (-1.0, 1.25), (0.4, 1.4)],
        "E1": [(1.0, -5.5), (1.05, -5.55), (1.1, -5.6)], "T1": [(0.95, -2.4), (1.2, -2.6), (1.5, -2.8)],
        "T2": [(0.95, -0.8), (1.6, -1.2), (2.5, -1.7)], "T3": [(0.95, 0.85), (1.6, 1.8), (2.5, 2.6)],
        "T4": [(0.95, 2.4), (1.35, 3.1), (1.8, 3.65)], "E2": [(1.0, 5.6), (1.05, 5.8), (1.1, 5.9)],
        "MIKE": [(2.4, -1.3), (2.9, -0.8), (3.6, -0.3)], "WILL": [(2.4, 1.3), (2.8, 1.0), (3.4, 1.3)],
        "SAM": [(2.3, 6.3), (2.4, 6.1), (2.6, 6.0)], "SS": [(4.8, 0.0), (4.7, 0.2), (4.6, 0.4)],
        "CB1": [(3.0, -8.0), (3.0, -7.8), (3.0, -7.6)],
    }
    tr = {}
    for k, pts in K.items():
        q = p.players[k]
        tr[k] = ease([(0.0, q.d, q.w)] + [(t, d, w) for t, (d, w) in zip((0.4, 0.8, 1.2), pts)])
    set_tracks(p, tr, t_end=1.3)
    return p


def push_ball(t, fld, p):
    """The ball, held out in front of the quarterback once he has it."""
    if t <= 0.05:
        return
    d, w = p.position("QB", t)
    bd = d + 0.75
    x, y = P(fld, p, bd, w)
    fld.ax.add_patch(Ellipse((float(x), float(y)), 0.55, 0.85, fc=style.BALL, ec="white", lw=0.6, zorder=12))


PUSH = push_play()
PUSH_T = [0.0, 0.4, 0.8, 1.2]
PUSH_N = ["Under center, two pushers\nstacked behind the QB.",
          "Snap: the line fires low into\nthe linemen before they rise.",
          "QB slides in behind the center;\npushers drive into his back.",
          "The pile carries the ball\nwell past the line to gain."]
PUSH_LAT, PUSH_WIN = (-7.2, 7.2), (-4.6, 5.0)
if PDF:
    strip_grid(PUSH, PUSH_T, PUSH_N, PUSH_LAT, PUSH_WIN, rings=(("QB", style.THIRD),), mr=0.55, deco=push_ball)
    plt.show()
else:
    video(PUSH, PUSH_LAT, PUSH_WIN, 1.3, rings=(("QB", style.THIRD),), notes=PUSH_N, times=PUSH_T,
          t_start=-0.3, mr=0.55, deco=push_ball)





  
  Your browser does not support the video tag.



Figure 52.12: The tush push, simulated (BDB-format tracking generated by gridiron, not recorded): third-and-1 at the opponent’s 35. 1: the quarterback (ringed) is under center with two pushers (P) directly behind him. 2: at the snap, the offensive line fires low into the defensive linemen before they can rise. 3: the center and right guard drive the two A-gap tackles back and apart, opening a seam between them; the quarterback slides into it and the pushers drive into his back, while the linebackers (M, W) come forward to meet the pile at the top. 4: the pile, still moving as one, carries the ball (brown) more than a yard past the yellow line. The whole play is decided in about a second, and the front of the pile moves only a yard or two. Markers are drawn a little smaller than in the other diagrams so that engaged players stay visible.




Why does a shove from behind help that much? Physics, mostly. A sneak is a pushing contest at the line: the offense’s linemen and quarterback against the defense’s linemen and linebackers, both sides trying to move a pile a yard. Two pushers behind the quarterback add a few hundred pounds of driving force at exactly the point of the contest, and they add it immediately, at the snap, before the defense’s second level can arrive. The defense can’t add the same force, because its extra bodies have to come from the other side of a pile they can’t get into. And the quarterback, pushed from behind, can stay low and keep his feet driving instead of being stopped upright by the first linebacker to hit him.
Notice what the push gives up. A plain sneak hides inside a formation that could also hand off or throw; the push announces itself, because nobody lines up two players against the quarterback’s hips for anything else. The push trades disguise for force, and over one yard, force wins far more often than not.

How it became legal: assisting the runner
For most of the NFL’s history, the tush push was illegal. The rule on assisting the runner said teammates could not push or pull a ball carrier forward, a 10-yard foul. In the mid-2000s (accounts differ by a year) the NFL removed “push” from the rule and kept the ban on pulling. The reason was practical: in a pile, officials could never tell who was pushing whom (a runner, a teammate in contact with the runner, the pile itself), so the rule was close to unenforceable. As Mike Pereira, another former officiating chief, put it, pushing “became really too difficult to officiate,” so the league simply made it legal.19 Pulling is still a foul: a teammate who grabs the runner’s arm or jersey and hauls him forward costs his team 10 yards. Watch for it in a tush-push pile. The college rulebook followed in 2013.20
The timing carries a footnote of its own. On October 15, 2005, USC’s Matt Leinart scored the winning touchdown at Notre Dame with running back Reggie Bush shoving him across the goal line from behind, the “Bush Push.” College rules still banned pushing then, no flag was thrown, and the play became a legend: the illegal, unforgettable ancestor of a play that is now legal in the NFL.21
For more than 15 years after the change, NFL teams pushed runners only in passing, as piles formed. Then the Philadelphia Eagles turned it into a designed play.






NoteFilm room: Philadelphia Eagles, 2022–2025



Starting in 2022, Philadelphia ran the push more often and more reliably than anyone had, with the right ingredients: Jalen Hurts, a quarterback with exceptional leg strength; center Jason Kelce, small for a center but famously quick off the ball and low; an elite line around him, including right tackle Lane Johnson; and line coach Jeff Stoutland (with the Eagles through 2025), who drilled the timing. On 1 yard to go, FTN’s charters flagged 51% of the Eagles’ 2022–2025 snaps as quarterback sneaks or pushes, against a league median of 14%; counting every Hurts carry with a yard or less to go, nflverse has him converting 83% of 179 tries.22 Kelce retired after the 2023 season; Cam Jurgens, a guard in 2023, took over at center in 2024, and the play kept working.23 Hurts scored the first touchdown of Super Bowl LIX (February 2025, a 40–22 win over Kansas City) on a tush push.24 What to notice: the snap. The Eagles’ line moves as one at the exact instant of the snap, and the defensive linemen are already being driven back before they have risen out of their stances. The push from behind finishes a play that the line’s timing has mostly won already. (The Eagles’ push as a talent and coaching advantage, and how it compares with the rest of the league, is the subject of The Eagles: Trenches, RPOs, and the Tush Push.)




The ban debate
The push’s success made it controversial. Critics made three arguments: safety (a pile of the heaviest players on the field driving forward with heads down), aesthetics (a near-automatic yard is dull football), and fairness (one team’s mastery of a play is a reason to rethink it). Defenders of the play answered that injuries on it were rare, that other teams could copy it, and that you don’t ban a play for being executed well.
In 2025 Green Bay proposed a ban. Its first version, barring teammates from pushing the quarterback immediately at the snap, was tabled at the spring league meeting; a broader revision, barring any pushing, pulling, lifting or assisting of the runner except by blocking opponents, came to a vote on May 21, 2025, and failed 22–10, two votes short of the 24 needed (rule changes need three-quarters of the 32 owners). The league tightened its officiating guidance instead. In practice that meant watching for linemen who move before the snap (a false start, easy to miss when everyone is crouched shoulder to shoulder) and for players lined up in or across the neutral zone, the ball-length strip between the two lines; the officiating department’s own training video in September 2025 said an Eagles guard should have been flagged for moving early on one push.25 For 2026, no team proposed a ban; the competition committee’s co-chairman said in February 2026 that he didn’t expect one, and the league said it would only “lightly” revisit how the play is officiated. The tush push is legal for the 2026 season.26






CautionCommon misconception



“The tush push is unstoppable.” It isn’t, and the next section’s numbers show that. Defenses stop it by winning the snap: crowding both A gaps beside the center, timing the count so their linemen are moving first, and sending linebackers over the top to meet the quarterback before the pile moves. (Leaping over the pile is legal on a running play; many fans assume it isn’t.27) Defensive linemen also try to jump the snap count, accepting the occasional offside penalty for the chance of getting into the backfield early. What the push does is shift the odds of a one-yard contest, and on one yard that shift is worth a great deal.




Does it work? The sneak in the data
FTN’s charting service marks every play it thinks was a quarterback sneak (is_qb_sneak), and the flag covers the plain sneak and the push alike, because FTN does not chart them separately. So the numbers below are for sneaks of every kind.28
On 1 yard to go, 2022–2025 regular seasons, sneaks gained the first down or the touchdown 81% of the time (1,089 plays). Other runs on 1 yard to go converted 70%, and passes 58%. A gap of 11 percentage points on a play that decides whether a drive lives is an enormous difference. With 2 yards to go, sneaks were far rarer and far less successful (54% of 37), which tells you what the play is for: the last yard, not the last two. A sneak is a pile moving forward, and a pile of a dozen big men moves a yard, maybe a yard and a half, before it stalls (watch the frame strip above). Ask it for two and it usually stops short.
You have now met three numbers for “one yard”: sneaks from the 1 scored on 67% of plays, sneaks on any 1-yard-to-go snap converted 81%, and drives with first-and-goal at the 1 scored 90% of the time. They measure different things. The drive number is highest because a drive gets up to four tries at the yard. And the yard before the goal line is harder than the yard before a first down: there the defense’s back line is the goal line itself, so it can put every defender within a few yards of the ball, and it brings in its goal-line personnel to do it. In the middle of the field, a defense crowding the line on third-and-1 still has to worry about a pass over its head.


Show the Python
T = TEAM.sort_values("n", ascending=True)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 6.2), sharey=True, gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1, 1.25]})
ypos = np.arange(len(T))
cols = [style.SERIES[0] if t == "PHI" else (style.SERIES[1] if t == "BUF" else style.BASELINE) for t in T.index]
axes[0].barh(ypos, T["n"], color=cols, height=0.7)
for y, n in zip(ypos, T["n"]):
    axes[0].text(n + 2, y, f"{n}", va="center", fontsize=6.5, color=style.INK_2)
axes[0].set_yticks(ypos)
axes[0].set_yticklabels(T.index, fontsize=6.8)
axes[0].set_xlabel("Sneaks run", fontsize=8)
axes[0].set_title("How many", fontsize=9)
axes[0].set_xlim(0, T["n"].max() * 1.18)
axes[0].grid(axis="y", visible=False)
ok = T["n"] >= 15
se = np.sqrt(T["rate"] * (1 - T["rate"]) / T["n"])
for y, (t, row), s, c, keep in zip(ypos, T.iterrows(), se, cols, ok):
    if not keep:
        continue
    lo, hi = max(0, row["rate"] - 1.645 * s), min(1, row["rate"] + 1.645 * s)
    axes[1].plot([lo * 100, hi * 100], [y, y], color=c if c != style.BASELINE else style.MUTED, lw=1.4,
                 alpha=0.6)
    axes[1].plot([row["rate"] * 100], [y], marker="o", ms=5, color=c if c != style.BASELINE else style.INK_2)
axes[1].axvline(SN12_RATE * 100, color=style.INK_2, lw=1.0, ls=(0, (4, 3)))
axes[1].text(SN12_RATE * 100 + 0.8, 1.0, f"league\n{SN12_RATE * 100:.0f}%", fontsize=6.8,
             color=style.INK_2, va="center")
axes[1].set_xlim(45, 102)
axes[1].set_xlabel("Converted (first down or TD), %", fontsize=8)
axes[1].set_title("How often it worked", fontsize=9)
axes[1].grid(axis="y", visible=False)
for ax in axes:
    ax.tick_params(labelsize=7)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.8)
plt.show()








Figure 52.13: Quarterback sneaks (including tush pushes) on 1 or 2 yards to go, by team, 2022–2025 regular seasons. Left: how many each team ran. Right: the share that gained a first down or a touchdown, with a bar showing the range that chance alone could easily produce (a 90% interval) around each team’s rate; teams with fewer than 15 attempts are left out of the right panel. The dashed line is the league rate. Philadelphia (blue) ran far more than anyone; Buffalo (orange) was second. Data: nflverse play-by-play joined to FTN charting (is_qb_sneak).





Two lessons hide in that chart. First, volume, not rate, is what separates the teams. Most teams’ conversion rates overlap once you account for sample size: 40 sneaks is not enough to tell an 80% team from an 85% team. What differs enormously is how often teams call the play. The Eagles stand alone at one end; at the other, Kansas City was charted with 1 in four seasons, because Andy Reid’s offense almost never asks Patrick Mahomes to sneak.
If the sneak converts that often, why don’t the other teams run it more? None of the reasons is foolish. The sneak puts the quarterback, usually the most valuable and most expensive player on the roster, at the bottom of a pile of the biggest men on the field. Many modern offenses live in the shotgun, so their quarterback rarely takes a snap under center, and the sneak is a play they would have to practise specially. And the play needs a line that can win the first half-second together, which not every team has. A coach weighing a few extra yards a season against those costs can reasonably say no.
Second, a high rate is partly selection. Teams sneak when the distance is truly short, often inches rather than a full yard (the play-by-play records both as “1 to go”), and most teams sneak only when they like the look. That explains a puzzle you may have noticed. The push adds hundreds of pounds of force, yet Philadelphia’s sneak rate in the chart sits close to the league line, and Hurts’s mark in the film room is no better than Brady’s or Allen’s on their own. The Eagles called the play on about half of all their 1-yard downs: on full yards as well as inches, against defenses that knew it was coming and lined up to stop it. Other teams sneaked only when the spot and the look were good. Comparing the two rates compares a play run every time with a play run only when it was easy, which is why the Eagles’ rate is more impressive than it looks. How much the push really adds once you account for that is a harder question, taken up in the Eagles case study.

title: Red Zone, Goal Line, Two-Point Plays, and Short Yardage (Including the Tush Push)
section: Putting it together: a red-zone possession
text:
Putting it together: a red-zone possession
Here is how the pieces fit on one drive. First-and-10 at the opponent’s 18: the defense still has some depth to protect, so you’ll see two-high safeties, zone coverage and the offense’s normal playbook. A completion to the 7 makes it first-and-goal, and the picture changes: the safeties come down, the corners press, and the coverage is mostly man. The offense answers with quick throws: a slant or a fade on the outside if it likes a matchup, a rub from a bunch if it sees man, a sprint-out if it wants an easy read. Inside the 3, both teams change personnel: jumbo against goal-line defense. Now it’s a run, a quarterback sneak or push, or the play-action pass that the heavy personnel sets up. And if the drive ends in a touchdown, there’s one more decision: kick, or one more play from the 2.






TipWatch for it on Sunday: fade or rub?



When the ball crosses the 20

Count the safeties. Two deep at the 18 is normal; one or none inside the 10 means the defense has traded depth for bodies near the ball.
Look at the corners’ depth. A corner a yard off the receiver is pressing: expect man coverage.

Inside the 10: read the receivers’ splits

A receiver alone, wide, with 5 to 8 yards to the sideline? That spacing is for a fade or back-shoulder throw. Check the corner’s leverage: lined up inside him, think fade; outside him, think slant.
Receivers bunched or stacked, tight to the formation? That’s rub territory. Predict a crossing pattern against man, and watch whether the defenders switch (banjo) or chase through the traffic.
The quarterback in the gun with receivers flooded to one side? Look for a sprint-out to that side.

Inside the 3

Heavy personnel on both sides? Watch the quarterback: under center with players stacked directly behind him is a tush push; a fullback and tailback deep behind him is a handoff or play-action.
On the push, watch the snap and the first half-second, not the pile: whichever line fires first and lower usually wins.

After a touchdown

If the offense stays on the field, guess the concept before the snap from its formation: bunch (rub), spread with a back beside the quarterback (QB run or sprint-out), or heavy (run or play-action).

For your prediction log (01-06): inside the 10, write one word before each snap, from the splits alone: fade (fade or back-shoulder), rub, quick (slant or out), sprint (sprint-out) or run.

text:
Predict the play






TipPredict the play 1: the receiver alone





Show the Python
off = line5() + [O("QB", "QB", GUN, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", GUN, -1.5, "R"),
                 O("X", "WR", LINE_D, -19.5), O("Y", "TE", LINE_D, 4.8),
                 O("H", "WR", OFF_BALL, 9.0), O("Z", "WR", OFF_BALL, 14.5)]
dfn = dline() + [D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.0, 1.5, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.0, -3.5, "W"),
                 D("NB", "NB", 3.5, 9.5, "$"), D("SS", "SS", 6.0, 6.5, "SS"),
                 D("RCB", "CB", 2.0, 15.0, "CB"), D("LCB", "CB", 1.1, -18.3, "CB"),
                 D("FS", "FS", 11.0, 4.0, "FS")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=opp(7), to_go=None)
fld = draw(p, lateral=(-26.67, 17.5), window=(-7.0, 17))
goal_marks(fld, p, -9.0)
plt.show()








Figure 52.14: Second-and-goal at the opponent’s 7. Three receivers to the right, X alone on the left. Read the corner and the safeties before you read the answer.





Where is the ball most likely going, and what would change your answer after the snap?






TipAnswer





To X on the left, most likely a fade. Everything about the alignment points there. X is alone on his side, lined up with about 7 yards to the sideline, exactly the room a fade needs. The corner is pressing a yard off him and lined up a step inside him: inside leverage, which takes away the slant and gives up the outside release. And the safety help has rotated toward the three receivers on the right: the strong safety has walked over them and the free safety sits in the end zone just outside the right hash, much too far away to reach a ball thrown toward the left pylon a second after the snap. The three receivers on the right are there partly to pull that help away. Coaches call this a “backside” or isolation fade.
What would change it: if the corner ran with X stride for stride over the top, the better throw is the back-shoulder: thrown early, behind X’s outside shoulder, and caught a yard or two deep in the end zone. If the corner had lined up outside X, the slant would be open instead. And if the free safety had stayed in the middle or shaded left, the quarterback would likely work the three-receiver side, where the defense would then be short a man.











TipPredict the play 2: call the two-point play





Show the Python
off = line5() + [O("QB", "QB", GUN, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", GUN, 1.5, "R"),
                 O("X", "WR", LINE_D, -15.0), O("H", "WR", OFF_BALL, -9.0),
                 O("Y", "TE", OFF_BALL, 9.0), O("Z", "WR", LINE_D, 15.0)]
dfn = dline() + [D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.0, 0.5, "M"),
                 D("LCB", "CB", 1.0, -14.4, "CB"), D("NB", "NB", 1.6, -8.4, "$"),
                 D("DB", "DB", 1.6, 8.4, "$"), D("RCB", "CB", 1.0, 14.4, "CB"),
                 D("SS", "SS", 5.6, -6.8, "SS"), D("FS", "FS", 5.6, 6.8, "FS")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=opp(2), to_go=None)
fld = draw(p, lateral=(-19.0, 19.0), window=(-7.0, 12))
x0, y0 = P(fld, p, 5.0, -4.6)
x1, y1 = P(fld, p, -0.2, 4.6)
fld.ax.add_patch(Rectangle((min(x0, x1), min(y0, y1)), abs(x1 - x0), abs(y1 - y0), fc=style.MUTED, alpha=0.08,
                           ec=style.MUTED, lw=0.8, ls=(0, (3, 2)), zorder=1))
say(fld, p, 5.7, 0.0, "the box", fontsize=6.6, color=style.INK_2, box=False)
plt.show()








Figure 52.15: A two-point try from the 2. The offense is in the shotgun with two receivers on each side and the running back beside the quarterback. The defense has brought in six defensive backs: one on each receiver, pressed or close, and two safeties standing in the end zone. Count the defenders in the box between the tight ends’ spots, within five yards of the ball.





You have the four shapes from the two-point figure (A–D) on your call sheet. Which one do you call against this look, and why?






TipAnswer





D, the quarterback run (QB power), with the sprint-out option (C) as the second choice. Count the box: four linemen and one linebacker, five defenders. Count your blockers on a quarterback run: five linemen plus the running back, six, and the quarterback carries the ball. That is one more blocker than the box has defenders, the extra-hat arithmetic, and the two safeties are standing three or four yards deep in the end zone, so the runner needs only two yards before they arrive. The defense has bet everything on stopping a pass: a defender on every receiver and two more behind them. The bunch rub (A) and the snag (B) would throw into that bet.
What would change it: a safety walking down into the box before the snap (or, harder to see, timing his run to arrive at the snap). Then the count is even and the pass becomes the better bet, because a defender has left the coverage. That trade, the defense guessing and the offense counting, is the whole two-point game. Most defenses avoid this look for exactly this reason: on the 2023–2025 two-point tries in the participation data, they had six or seven defenders in the box on 71% of them.











TipPredict the play 3: second-and-goal at the 1





Show the Python
dfn = [D("E1", "DE", 0.9, -6.0, "E"), D("T1", "DT", 0.9, -3.9, "T"), D("T2", "DT", 0.9, -0.85, "T"),
       D("T3", "DT", 0.9, 0.85, "T"), D("T4", "DT", 0.9, 3.9, "T"), D("E2", "DE", 0.9, 6.3, "E"),
       D("LB1", "LB", 2.6, -2.3, "M"), D("LB2", "LB", 2.6, 2.3, "W"),
       D("CB1", "CB", 1.8, -7.4, "CB"), D("CB2", "CB", 1.8, 8.2, "CB"), D("SS", "SS", 2.8, 5.0, "SS")]
p = Play(jumbo(), dfn, los=opp(1), to_go=None)
fld = draw(p, width_in=5.2, lateral=(-10.5, 10.5), window=(-8.0, 7.0))
say(fld, p, 5.0, -5.0, "end zone", fontsize=6.6, color=style.MUTED, box=False)
plt.show()








Figure 52.16: Second-and-goal at the opponent’s 1. On first down the offense ran an iso from this same formation and was stopped short. Same personnel on both sides: the offense in 23 personnel (Y and U on the line, H as a wing, the fullback and running back stacked behind the quarterback under center); the defense in its 6-2 goal-line defense. This time its three defensive backs have crept up close to the line.





The defense has packed everyone in to stop the run. What call makes it pay, and which offensive player should you watch?






TipAnswer





Play-action from the same look. The quarterback fakes the iso to the running back behind the fullback; the line fires out exactly as it did on first down, so every defender’s eyes go to the pile. Then a tight end who seemed to be blocking slips into the end zone: Y or U blocks for a count and releases, or the wing, H, leaks to the corner of the end zone. Watch the backside tight end, U. On a run he blocks the end in front of him; on play-action he chips the end and releases, and the defensive back responsible for him, crept up to help against the run, is the one who has to see it.
This is exactly what goal-line offenses do. Inside the 3 in 2023–2025, offenses with one wide receiver or none passed on only 28% of snaps, but 66% of those passes came off a run fake. What could go wrong: a defense in a 5-3 has an extra linebacker standing up who can see the release, and a quarterback under center who fakes and turns his back has very little time against a front built to get into the backfield. One more run is never a bad answer either; the threat of the pass is what keeps those three defensive backs honest.

title: Red Zone, Goal Line, Two-Point Plays, and Short Yardage (Including the Tush Push)
text:
Takeaways

Near the goal line the end line becomes the deepest defender. The compressed field squeezes zones, frees safeties to come down, and makes man coverage, press and Cover 0 cheap. The offense loses its deep threat, and every throw arrives into a crowd.
Red-zone pass concepts win quickly and close: the fade and back-shoulder throw against press with no outside help, the slant when the corner takes away the fade, rubs from stacks and bunches against man, the shovel pass against an attacking front, and the sprint-out that puts a flat defender in conflict.
A good two-point play gives the offense two answers that put one defender in conflict, so it works against more than one defensive call. Runs have converted more often than passes since 2015, partly because of who chooses to run, and a try is worth about what the kick is, so the scoreboard decides.
Goal-line defenses (6-2, 5-3) trade defensive backs for linemen and linebackers and fill every gap; low man wins. Their weakness is the play that looks like the run and isn’t, which is why heavy personnel that throws near the goal line almost always fakes a run first.
The QB sneak is the best one-yard play in football: the ball starts closest to the line, the play is instant, and the quarterback-as-runner adds a blocker. The tush push adds pushers behind him; it has been legal since the NFL removed the ban on pushing the runner in the mid-2000s (2005 or 2006; pulling is still a foul), survived a 22–10 ban vote in 2025, and is legal in 2026.
In the data, a little under six red-zone trips in ten end in touchdowns; a first-and-goal from the 1 scores about nine times in ten (a drive gets four tries); and sneaks convert about four in five on 1 yard to go, but only about half the time on 2. Teams differ far more in how often they sneak than in how well, and the teams that sneak most face the hardest looks.

Builds on: Third Down (situational packages, the sticks), Contact Rules and Penalties as Strategy (pass interference and the rub-versus-pick line), Option Football (the quarterback as the extra hat), Man Coverage (Cover 0, press, banjo, robbers and brackets), Quick Game (slant-flat, snag, leverage) and Dropback Concepts (rub routes).

The Clock, the Two-Minute Drill, and Fourth Down: whether to go for two, the two-point chart, and when a short fourth down is worth the risk, which leans on the sneak numbers here.
The Eagles: Trenches, RPOs, and the Tush Push: the tush push as a talent and coaching edge, and how the Eagles compare with the rest of the league.
Appendix B, the Concept Atlas and Appendix C, the Defensive Atlas: one-page cards for the red-zone, two-point and short-yardage concepts, and for the goal-line fronts.

If you want to go deeper: Chris B. Brown’s The Art of Smart Football on red-zone passing and the leverage game; ESPN’s and the Packers’ pieces on the back-shoulder throw cited in this chapter; and any season’s goal-line snaps on the All-22 film, watched with nothing but the corners’ leverage and the receivers’ splits in mind.






NoteGo deeper



From simulation to real tracking data. The two animations in this chapter (the rub and the tush push) are gridiron simulations written in NFL Big Data Bowl (BDB) coordinates. The 2025 Big Data Bowl release (2022 season, weeks 1–9) has every player’s position ten times a second, before and after the snap, so you can find real quarterback sneaks and tush pushes (the Eagles ran plenty in those weeks) and draw them with the same code. The data lives on Kaggle and needs your own free login, so this cell is not run when the book is built.


Show the Python (real Big Data Bowl tracking; not run in the build)
import pandas as pd
from gridiron import bdb, show_animation

plays = pd.read_csv("data/bdb/plays.csv")
# short-yardage quarterback runs: 1 yard to go, play description names the quarterback up the middle
sneaks = plays[(plays["yardsToGo"] <= 1)
               & plays["playDescription"].str.contains("up the middle|sneak", case=False, na=False)
               & plays["playDescription"].str.contains("Hurts|Allen", na=False)]
print(len(sneaks), "candidate sneaks")
g, pl = sneaks.iloc[0][["gameId", "playId"]]

trk = bdb.load_tracking("data/bdb/tracking_week_*.csv")
one = bdb.prepare(trk, plays, game_id=g, play_id=pl)
show_animation(one, times=[-0.5, 0.0, 0.5, 1.0, 1.5])   # same call as the simulated plays
