title: The Clock, the Two-Minute Drill, and Fourth Down
text:
The clock is a currency, and the two teams want opposite things
Super Bowl LVIII, fourth quarter. San Francisco has just kicked a field goal to lead 19–16, and Kansas City takes over at its own 25 with 1:53 on the clock and two timeouts. It sounds like plenty of time. Is it? Seventy-five yards from a touchdown and about 40 from a long field goal, 113 seconds is less than it looks: a completion over the middle costs about 20 of them, a sack more, an incompletion only five. Over the next 107 seconds Kansas City will run eleven snaps, call one timeout, get two plays out of bounds and kick a field goal with three seconds left. Then the game goes to an overtime whose rules were rewritten after a Chiefs game two years earlier. This chapter explains every one of those choices, and the fourth-down revolution that changed how coaches spend the other 58 minutes.
You’ll be able to:
For 56 minutes of a typical game the clock is background noise. Then, at some point in the fourth quarter (and again at the end of the first half), it becomes the most important player on the field. The reason is simple: possessions are scarce, and time is what possessions are made of. A team that is behind needs plays per second: as many snaps as it can squeeze into the time left. A team that is ahead wants seconds per play: the fewest snaps, each taking as long as possible, so the opponent gets the ball back late or never.
Everything in this chapter follows from those two goals, and from one fact you met in the first chapter: the clock keeps running after a ball carrier is tackled in bounds and stops after almost everything else. So the first skill is pricing. How many seconds does each kind of play cost a team in a hurry? You can measure it. The play-by-play data records the game clock at every snap, so the gap between two snaps is what the first play, and whatever happened after it, cost.
Show the Python
lab = list(PRICE)
vals = [PRICE[k] for k in lab]
cols = [style.SERIES[0], style.SERIES[0], style.SERIES[2], style.SERIES[1], style.SERIES[1]]
note = ["the clock stops at once", "the clock stops at once (late in a half)", "...and costs a timeout",
        "...and costs a down", "the dearest: no stoppage at all"]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.3))
y = np.arange(len(lab))[::-1]
ax.barh(y, vals, color=cols, height=0.6, zorder=2)
for yi, v, k, n in zip(y, vals, lab, note):
    ax.text(v + 0.5, yi, f"{v:.0f} s", va="center", fontsize=8, color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")
    ax.text(v + 3.6, yi, f"[{PRICE_N[k]:,}]  {n}", va="center", fontsize=7, color=style.INK_2)
ax.set_yticks(y, lab, fontsize=8)
ax.set_xlim(0, 52)
ax.set_xticks([0, 10, 20, 30])
ax.set_xlabel("Game-clock seconds from this snap to the next (median)")
ax.set_title("Late in a half, every way a play can end has a price")
ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
plt.show()








Figure 53.1: What a play costs a hurrying offense. Median game-clock seconds from one snap to the next, for offenses trailing or tied in the last two minutes of the first half and the last two minutes of the game (2016-2025 regular seasons, no penalties; numbers in brackets are plays). An incompletion or a catch that goes out of bounds costs only the five or six seconds the play itself takes. A catch in bounds keeps the clock running while everyone sprints back to the line: about 16 seconds if the offense then spikes the ball (which also uses up a down), about 21 if it lines up and runs a real play. A timeout stops the bleeding for the price of the timeout. Source: nflverse play-by-play.
Read it as a price list. The cheapest plays are the ones that stop the clock by themselves: an incomplete pass, or a completion where the receiver gets out of bounds. Each costs only the five or six seconds the play takes. The expensive one is the catch in bounds, because the clock keeps running while eleven players run back to the line, the officials spot the ball and the quarterback relays the next call. That costs about 21 seconds if the offense simply runs its next play. Offenses have two ways to cut the bill. A timeout brings the cost back down to the play itself (6 seconds) but spends one of only three. A spike, which you’ll meet properly below, stops the clock about 16 seconds after the previous snap, and spends a down instead.
That is why two-minute offenses throw toward the sideline, why defenses protecting a lead try to tackle receivers inside the field, and why coaches hoard timeouts like cash. A team with 1:53 and two timeouts can afford roughly five or six in-bounds completions and a few incompletions. That is enough for 50 or 60 yards. It is not as much as it sounds.

title: The Clock, the Two-Minute Drill, and Fourth Down
text:
The out-of-bounds clock rule
One line in the price list has a condition attached. “Out of bounds stops the clock” is true only late in a half. The full rule, which this course calls the out-of-bounds clock rule, is this: when a runner goes out of bounds, the officials stop the clock, put the ball back on the hash, and restart the clock when the referee signals the ball ready for play, well before the next snap. The exceptions are the moments when time matters most. After the two-minute warning of the first half, and inside the last five minutes of the game, the clock stays stopped until the snap. One more case follows the same “until the snap” rule at any time of the game: if a runner goes out of bounds on a play where the ball changed hands (an interception or punt return that ends out of bounds, say), the clock waits for the new offense’s first snap.1


Show the Python
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 2.1))
blank(ax)
ax.set_xlim(-1, 61)
ax.set_ylim(-3.2, 5.2)
for q in range(4):
    x0 = q * 15
    ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x0, 0), 15, 2, fc=style.SURFACE, ec=style.BASELINE, lw=1, zorder=1))
    ax.text(x0 + 7.5, 1.0, f"Q{q + 1}", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=8.5, color=style.INK_2, zorder=4)
for x0, w, txt in [(28, 2, "last 2:00\nof the half"), (55, 5, "last 5:00\nof the game")]:
    ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x0, 0), w, 2, fc=STOP_C, ec=style.DEFENSE_DARK, lw=1.2, zorder=2))
    ax.text(x0 + w / 2, 2.4, txt, ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=7, color=DC, fontweight="bold",
            linespacing=1.1)
ax.plot([30, 30], [-0.4, 2.6], color=style.INK_2, lw=1.4, zorder=3)
ax.text(30, 4.9, "halftime", ha="center", va="top", fontsize=7, color=style.INK_2)
ax.text(14, -0.9, "out of bounds: clock restarts on the ready signal (seconds later)", ha="center",
        va="top", fontsize=7, color=style.INK_2)
ax.text(45, -0.9, "inside the shaded windows: clock\nstopped until the snap", ha="center", va="top",
        fontsize=7, color=DC, linespacing=1.1)
plt.show()








Figure 53.2: When does getting out of bounds actually save time? The game’s 60 minutes, quarter by quarter. In the white stretches (most of the game), a runner who goes out of bounds stops the clock only for the few seconds it takes to re-spot the ball; it restarts on the referee’s ready signal. In the shaded windows (after the two-minute warning of the first half, and the last five minutes of the fourth quarter) it stays stopped until the next snap. The rule’s asymmetry is deliberate: the fourth-quarter window is wider because the end of a game decides the result.





Why the general rule? Because the league wants the clock to keep moving for most of the game (television windows are three hours), and because without it any team could stop the clock for free all game long with five-yard sideline throws. So for 55 minutes out of bounds saves only a few seconds. Why the exception? Because late in a half the league wants a comeback to be possible: the rule hands the trailing team a lifeline, letting it save time without spending timeouts as long as it can get the ball to the sideline. One detail closes a loophole: a fumble that goes out of bounds restarts the clock on the ready signal at any time of the game, so nobody can fumble out of bounds on purpose to stop it.
Two more clock facts that surprise new viewers. A first down does not stop the NFL clock, ever. If you also watch college football, you’ll have seen the clock pause after a first down; since 2023 college does that only in the last two minutes of each half, but the NFL never does.2 And the two-minute warning is a free timeout for both teams. It comes after the last play snapped before 2:00, so a play snapped at 2:05 that ends at 1:58 is followed by a full stoppage.3 Trailing offenses plan around it (they would rather snap at 2:05 than at 1:55); leading offenses try to burn the clock right down to it, so that the warning stops a clock that has already done its work.






CautionCommon misconception



“He stepped out of bounds, smart: that stopped the clock.” In the third quarter, or with 7:00 left in the fourth, it barely did: the clock started again as soon as the ball was spotted, usually 25 or more seconds before the next snap. A runner who fights for two extra yards in bounds early in the fourth quarter is not costing his team time. The same play at 4:30 is a different story.

title: The Clock, the Two-Minute Drill, and Fourth Down
text:
The two-minute drill
The two-minute drill is the hurry-up offense with a deadline: a team that needs points before a half ends, usually with the clock already inside the two-minute warning. Teams practise it every week as its own script, because almost every rule of normal play-calling changes:

No huddle, two plays at a time. The quarterback gets two calls through his helmet radio, so after the first one the offense can line up and snap the second without waiting. The radio cuts out when the play clock reaches 15 seconds,4 and in a hurry-up there often isn’t time for a call at all, so the quarterback carries a menu on his wristband and calls one-word “clock” plays that the whole offense knows.
Throw outside. Routes break toward the sideline (outs, comebacks, corner routes) so that the catch ends out of bounds. Receivers are coached to secure the ball, take one more step, and get out: never turn upfield for two extra yards and get tackled in bounds.
Middle of the field only with a plan. A catch over the middle is worth taking if it gains a lot or if the offense has a timeout to spend. Otherwise it is the dearest line on the price list.
No sacks. A sack loses yards and keeps the clock running. Quarterbacks throw the ball away instead (out of bounds, past the line of scrimmage, or near a receiver) and accept the lost down. (Hold on to that rule: the four-minute offense below turns it exactly upside down.)
Know the finish line. The real target is usually not the end zone but field-goal range: the yard line from which the kicker has a good chance, with enough time left to get the field-goal unit on. That normally means a stopped clock. Teams also practise a running-clock field goal for emergencies, under names like “fire” or “Mayday”: the unit sprints on and kicks off a live clock. Kansas City’s special-teams coordinator Dave Toub has said about 17 seconds is as fast as it can realistically be done in a game.5 It works, but nobody plans on it.



Show the Python
off = offense("gun_2x2")
dfn = [Player(k, pos, "def", d, w) for k, pos, d, w in [
    ("DLE", "DE", 1.0, -4.5), ("DLT", "DT", 1.0, -1.2), ("DRT", "DT", 1.0, 1.8), ("DRE", "DE", 1.0, 4.8),
    ("MIKE", "MIKE", 7.0, 0.5), ("LCB", "CB", 8.0, -17.2), ("RCB", "CB", 8.0, 17.2),
    ("NB", "NB", 8.0, -8.0), ("DB", "DB", 8.0, 8.5), ("FS", "FS", 17.0, -10.0), ("SS", "SS", 17.0, 10.0)]]
p2m = Play(off, dfn, los=50, to_go=10)
p2m.dropback(2.0)
p2m.route("X", r.out(12, 6))
p2m.route("Z", r.comeback(15))
p2m.route("H", r.corner(11))
p2m.route("Y", r.seam(19))
p2m.route("RB", [(0, 0), (2.5, 4.5), (6.3, 11.0)], side=-1)   # to the flat, past the line, outside the numbers
p2m.highlight("X", "Z")
fld = p2m.draw(window=(-8, 25), lateral="full", title=False)
no_numbers(fld)
nl, nr = p2m.ball_y + 14.6, p2m.ball_y - 14.6           # the tops of the numbers, roughly
band(fld, p2m.los - 8, p2m.los + 25, nl, FIELD_WIDTH, style.SERIES[0], alpha=0.10)
band(fld, p2m.los - 8, p2m.los + 25, 0, nr, style.SERIES[0], alpha=0.10)
say(fld, p2m, 17.5, -21.8, "catch, step\nout: clock\nstops", color=OC, fs=6.4)
say(fld, p2m, 17.5, 21.8, "catch, step\nout: clock\nstops", color=OC, fs=6.4)
say(fld, p2m, 22.0, 3.0, "catch in here and get tackled:\nthe clock runs (about 20 s)\nunless you call a timeout",
    color=style.INK, fs=6.6)
say(fld, p2m, 13.5, -1.5, "soft zones: the defense\ngives the short stuff", color=DC, fs=6.3)
plt.show()








Figure 53.3: The two-minute menu. The offense (blue) has the ball near midfield and needs about 25 yards to reach field-goal range; the defense (orange) sits back in a soft two-deep zone, corners eight yards off, and invites throws underneath. To the left the call is a real concept, a three-level ‘flood’ of one sideline: H’s corner route goes over the cornerback, X’s 12-yard out sits under the deep safety, and the back (R) runs to the flat underneath, so whichever defender the quarterback reads, one of the three is open near the sideline. To the right, Z runs a comeback at 15 (straight up the field, then back toward the sideline) against the off corner, and Y a seam up the middle. The shaded lanes between the numbers and the sideline are where a catch can end out of bounds and stop the clock.





What does the defense do about it? It plays the same game backwards: it sits deep enough that nothing gets behind it, keeps its cornerbacks outside the receivers so the sideline routes are contested, and tackles in bounds. That tug-of-war, offense pulling the ball outside and defense pushing it inside, is the whole two-minute drill in one sentence.






ImportantWhy it exists



The two-minute drill exists because the clock rules are asymmetric. The offense can stop the clock (incompletions, out of bounds, timeouts, spikes); the defense can only stop it with timeouts and by forcing incompletions. So the trailing offense, uniquely, gets to control the pace of the end of a half. The drill is the set of habits that turns that control into points, and it has to be rehearsed because the habits contradict normal football: throw away from the open middle, give up yards for seconds, and never take a sack.


The drill has a long history in big games. In the 1958 NFL Championship Game, Johnny Unitas drove the Baltimore Colts into position for Steve Myhra’s tying field goal with seven seconds left, and the Colts won in the first sudden-death overtime in NFL history (sudden death: the first team to score in the extra period wins).6 In January 1987 John Elway’s Broncos went 98 yards in Cleveland, starting with 5:32 left (“The Drive”), to force overtime in the AFC Championship Game. The most famous two-minute drive of the modern era, Tom Brady’s in Super Bowl XXXVI, gets its own look later in the chapter, because it began with a famous broadcaster telling him not to try it.

The spike
A spike is the quarterback taking the snap and immediately throwing the ball into the ground. It is an incomplete pass, so the clock stops. Why isn’t it intentional grounding, which is exactly “throwing the ball away to avoid a loss with no receiver nearby”? Because the rulebook carves out an exception for it: a quarterback under center (the rulebook says within one yard of the snapper) may stop the clock legally if, immediately upon receiving the snap, he begins a continuous throwing motion and throws the ball directly into the ground. If he waits, he may not: a delayed spike is grounding. Nor may a quarterback in the shotgun: a spike from five yards deep is intentional grounding.7 That rule gives you one of the best tells in football. When a team that has been in the shotgun all day sprints to the line and the quarterback steps up under center, the spike is coming.
The spike play itself takes about 1 second of clock. (The price list’s 16 seconds for “catch in bounds, then a spike” is snap to snap, and almost all of it is the sprint back to the line before the spike.) What a spike really costs is a down. Spiking on first down is cheap (second-and-10 is fine in a two-minute drill); spiking on second down leaves only one real play before fourth down; spiking on third down is almost always a mistake. Teams spike about 72 times a season in all. You will see it most often in the sequence the price list describes: an in-bounds completion, a frantic sprint to the line, the quarterback under center, and the ball slammed into the turf with 15 to 20 seconds gone.
When should a team with a timeout spike instead of using the timeout? When there is time for more plays after it. A timeout is the more valuable token, because it keeps the down. Coaches spend timeouts late, for the field goal (the kicking unit needs a stopped clock to run onto the field) or for a catch in the middle near the end, and use the spike to keep them.






NoteGo deeper: the fake spike



Once everyone expects a spike, the threat of one is a weapon. On November 27, 1994, against the Jets, Dan Marino ran to the line at the Jets’ 8 with under 40 seconds left, shouted “Clock! Clock!”, made the spike motion, and instead threw a touchdown to Mark Ingram while the defense straightened up; the Dolphins won 28–24.8 The fake spike still shows up occasionally, and it is why a defense facing a hurried line-up can never completely relax. It works only because the real spike is so common.




Timeouts and the 10-second runoff
Timeouts are the scarcest resource in the two minutes: three per half, and none carry over. Their value depends on when they are used. A timeout early in a half saves the 20-odd seconds between plays, but those seconds rarely matter. The same timeout in the last minute can be the difference between a field goal and no field goal. That’s why you’ll hear announcers criticise a coach for “wasting” a timeout on a substitution mix-up in the third quarter: it is the end-of-half timeout he’s spending. The flip side is the end of the first half. Timeouts left over at halftime simply vanish, so coaches spend them much more freely in the second quarter’s last two minutes than they would in the fourth.
The rules guard the clock against cheap tricks. After the two-minute warning of either half, if the offense stops the clock by breaking a rule (a false start or other foul while the clock is running, intentional grounding, an illegal forward pass, a backward pass thrown out of bounds, spiking the ball after a play has ended), the officials take ten seconds off the game clock, the 10-second runoff, and restart it on the ready signal. The offense may spend a timeout instead, if it has one, and the defense may decline the runoff along with the yardage penalty.
The defense has its own version, with a different penalty. It is never charged a runoff; if it fouls to stop the clock, the clock simply restarts on the ready signal. But a trailing defense out of timeouts might be tempted to jump offside on purpose with, say, 0:20 left, just to freeze the clock. So in the last 40 seconds of a half, if the defense has no timeouts left, a defensive foul that stops the clock gives the offense a choice: take the yardage and play on, or have the half end right there. A leading offense will usually end it.9
Injuries are on the same list. After the two-minute warning an injury stoppage costs the injured player’s team one of its timeouts (unless an opponent’s foul caused the injury, or the play was a score, a free kick or a turnover). A team with none left is treated as having taken an illegal extra timeout: if it has the ball, the defense may run ten seconds off the clock, and if it is the defense, in the last 40 seconds the offense may end the half.10 The rule exists to stop players from faking injuries to stop the clock.
The runoff also applies when a replay changes a stopped clock into a running one after the two-minute warning. If a receiver ruled out of bounds is shown to have been tackled in bounds, the clock should never have stopped, so ten seconds come off, and neither team can decline them (either can use a timeout to prevent them). Either half can end on a runoff, and one famous game did.






NoteFilm room: Falcons at Lions, 2017 — ended by a runoff



Week 3 of the 2017 season, Atlanta led Detroit 30–26 in the last seconds. Detroit had no timeouts. On third-and-goal from the 1 with 12 seconds left, Matthew Stafford hit Golden Tate on a short pass, and the officials signalled touchdown. The booth reviewed it (all scoring plays are reviewed), and the replay showed Tate down short of the goal line, at the 1. A touchdown stops the clock; a runner tackled in bounds does not. The clock had stopped with eight seconds left; under the replay rule it goes back to the moment the play should have ended and then runs ten seconds, and with fewer than ten seconds left the game is simply over.11 What to notice: the Lions lost not because the play failed by a foot, but because they had no timeout to absorb the runoff. A single timeout saved for the end would have bought one more snap from the 1.




An annotated two-minute drive
Back to the opening scene. Here is every snap of Kansas City’s drive at the end of regulation in Super Bowl LVIII, plotted the way a clock manager thinks about it: time on one axis, field position on the other.


Show the Python
lv = raw[(raw.game_id == "2023_22_SF_KC") & (raw.qtr == 4) & (raw.half_seconds_remaining <= 113)].copy()
snaps = lv[(lv.posteam == "KC") & lv.play_type.isin(["pass", "run", "field_goal"])].copy()
snaps["t"] = snaps.half_seconds_remaining
snaps["own"] = 100 - snaps.yardline_100                      # yards from KC's own goal line
KEY = {3769: "1st & 10 KC 25: Kelce 9, in bounds",
       3794: "2nd & 1: Mahomes scramble 3, out of bounds",
       3816: "1st & 10: Gray 12, in bounds",
       3841: "1st & 10: Watson 8, in bounds",
       3866: "2nd & 2: incomplete",
       3889: "3rd & 2: McKinnon 7, first down;\n    KC timeout at 0:40",
       3914: "1st & 10 SF 36: Mahomes scramble 3,\n    in bounds (timeout kept)",
       3943: "2nd & 7: incomplete",
       3966: "3rd & 7: Kelce 22, pushed out at the\n    SF 11; SF timeout at 0:10 (two\n    49ers DBs hurt on the play)",
       3994: "1st & 10: incomplete",
       4027: "2nd & 10: Butker 29-yd field goal,\n    19-19 with 0:03 left"}
running = {3769: True, 3794: False, 3816: True, 3841: True, 3866: False, 3889: True, 3914: True,
           3943: False, 3966: False, 3994: False}
# snaps on the same yard line a few seconds apart: spread them along the time axis (never off their yard line)
NUDGE = {3866: 1.8, 3889: -1.8, 3943: 1.8, 3966: -1.8, 3994: 2.6, 4027: -2.6}
fig = plt.figure(figsize=(6.6, 3.9))
ax = fig.add_axes([0.09, 0.13, 0.52, 0.78])
kx = fig.add_axes([0.63, 0.05, 0.37, 0.88])
blank(kx)
pts = snaps[["play_id", "t", "own"]].values.copy()
pts[:, 1] += [NUDGE.get(int(pid), 0.0) for pid in pts[:, 0]]
for (pid, t0, y0), (_, t1, y1) in zip(pts[:-1], pts[1:]):
    c = GREEN if running[int(pid)] else style.DEFENSE
    ax.plot([t0, t1], [y0, y1], color=c, lw=2.2, zorder=2, solid_capstyle="round")
for i, (pid, t, y) in enumerate(pts, start=1):
    ax.scatter([t], [y], s=100, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, zorder=4, edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.8)
    ax.text(t, y, str(i), ha="center", va="center", fontsize=6.3, color="white", fontweight="bold", zorder=5)
for t, txt in [(40, "KC timeout"), (10, "SF timeout")]:
    ax.axvline(t, color=style.INK_2, lw=0.9, ls=(0, (3, 2)), zorder=1)
    ax.text(t - 1.2, 18, txt, fontsize=6.2, color=style.INK_2, ha="left", va="bottom", rotation=90)
ax.axhline(65, color=style.LINE_TO_GAIN, lw=1.2, zorder=1)
ax.text(114, 66.5, "long field-goal range begins\n(about the SF 35)", fontsize=6.2, color="#9a6a00", ha="left",
        va="bottom", linespacing=1.05)
ax.set_xlim(116, -2)
ax.set_ylim(15, 98)
ax.set_xticks([113, 90, 60, 30, 0], ["1:53", "1:30", "1:00", "0:30", "0:00"], fontsize=7.5)
ax.set_yticks([25, 40, 50, 60, 75, 89], ["KC 25", "KC 40", "50", "SF 40", "SF 25", "SF 11"], fontsize=7.5)
ax.set_xlabel("Game clock", fontsize=8)
ax.set_ylabel("Ball on", fontsize=8)
ax.set_title("Kansas City's last drive of regulation", fontsize=9.5)
ax.legend(handles=[Line2D([], [], color=GREEN, lw=2.2, label="clock ran to next snap"),
                   Line2D([], [], color=style.DEFENSE, lw=2.2, label="clock stopped")],
          loc="upper left", fontsize=6.5)
for i, pid in enumerate(KEY, start=1):
    yy = 0.97 - (i - 1) * 0.088
    kx.scatter([0.03], [yy], s=80, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, transform=kx.transAxes, clip_on=False)
    kx.text(0.03, yy, str(i), transform=kx.transAxes, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=6, color="white",
            fontweight="bold")
    kx.text(0.09, yy, KEY[pid], transform=kx.transAxes, ha="left", va="center", fontsize=6.4, color=style.INK,
            linespacing=1.05)
plt.show()








Figure 53.4: Super Bowl LVIII (February 11, 2024), Kansas City’s drive at the end of regulation, trailing 19-16. Each dot is a snap, placed at its game clock and the ball’s spot; the line to the next dot is green when the clock kept running between the snaps and orange when it was stopped. Kansas City used the cheap stoppages (three incompletions, a scramble and a catch that went out of bounds), spent only one of its two timeouts, after a first down near midfield, and kicked the tying field goal with three seconds left, still holding a timeout in case it needed one for the kick. Source: nflverse play-by-play, game 2023_22_SF_KC.





Four things are worth noticing, because they are what good clock management looks like.

The cheap plays came early. The first snap was a 9-yard catch in bounds, and then Mahomes, facing second-and-1, scrambled and got out of bounds. Inside the last five minutes, that stopped the clock until the next snap. The drive used about 40 seconds to reach midfield, and Kansas City still had both timeouts.
One timeout, when the price was high. After a third-down conversion at the 49ers’ 36 with the clock running, the Chiefs called their timeout at 0:40, saving about 20 seconds at the moment the seconds started to matter.
A timeout in the pocket. After Mahomes’s scramble to the 33 stayed in bounds, Kansas City didn’t use its last timeout; it hurried to the line and threw incomplete at 0:21. The timeout was insurance: as long as the Chiefs held it, any catch, anywhere, could be followed by a field goal.
The decisive catch went out of bounds. On third-and-7 with 16 seconds left, Travis Kelce caught a pass and was pushed out at the 11, stopping the clock at 0:10. Two 49ers defensive backs were hurt on the play, and San Francisco’s timeout at 0:10 came with the clock already stopped; after the two-minute warning an injury stoppage costs the injured player’s team a timeout, as you saw above. One more shot at the end zone, an incompletion, and Harrison Butker tied the game with three seconds left.12

Notice also what San Francisco did before the drive, because it is the clock decision people still argue about. Tied 16–16, the 49ers faced third-and-5 at the Chiefs’ 35 right after the two-minute warning, and threw incomplete. A run that stayed in bounds would probably not have gained the first down either, but it would have kept the clock running: Kansas City would have had to spend one of its timeouts or watch about 40 seconds disappear before the field goal. Instead the clock stopped, the 49ers kicked a 53-yarder on fourth-and-5 at 1:57 to lead by three, and the Chiefs got the ball back with 1:53 and both of their remaining timeouts, which, as the chart shows, was enough. Kicking on fourth-and-5 was defensible (it is at the edge of the “go zone” you’ll meet below, and a field goal at least forced Kansas City to score); the costly call was the third-down incompletion that came before it.

title: The Clock, the Two-Minute Drill, and Fourth Down
section: The four-minute offense: when the clock is on your side
text:
The four-minute offense: when the clock is on your side
Flip the situation. You lead by six with four minutes left and you have the ball. Now every second the clock runs is a second the other team can’t use. The four-minute offense is the two-minute drill in reverse:

Run the ball, and run it inside, where the ball carrier will be tackled in bounds. A 3-yard run that keeps the clock moving beats a 12-yard pass that might fall incomplete.
Use the whole play clock. Snap with one or two seconds left on the 40-second clock. A first down then costs the opponent about 40 seconds per play, or about two minutes per set of downs, if it has no timeouts.
Ball security over yards, and stay in bounds. A fumble or an interception hands the opponent both the ball and the clock. Backs are coached to go down in bounds rather than fight toward the sideline, and the quarterback to slide, or even to take a sack, rather than throw an incompletion that stops the clock. It is the two-minute drill’s “no sacks” rule turned upside down.
First downs end games. The point of the drive is not points; it is a fresh set of downs, each worth roughly two more minutes. Teams sometimes stay in bounds or even go down short of the goal line, rather than score and give the ball back.

The defense’s counter is timeouts, used immediately after each running play stays in bounds, and everything it can do to force an incompletion or a punt. A defense with three timeouts and the two-minute warning to come can stop the clock four times; with none, it can only hope for a stop.

The kneel-down arithmetic
At some point the leading team doesn’t need any more yards. It only needs the clock to run out, and the safest play in football is the quarterback kneeling down. Each kneel uses a down and takes about two seconds, and the clock keeps running afterwards, because the quarterback is “tackled” in bounds. Between kneels the offense lets the 40-second play clock run almost to zero. In the play-by-play, consecutive kneels with no timeout between them come about 39 seconds apart.
So the question every leading team asks when it gets a first down late in the game is: can we kneel it out from here? It has three kneels to use, and then one more thing working for it: after the third kneel the offense doesn’t have to snap again until the 40-second play clock runs out. If the game clock hits zero first, the game ends without a fourth-down play. It’s arithmetic.


Show the Python
PLAYCLK, KNEEL, LAST = 39, 2, 40
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 2.9))
rows = []
for n_to in range(4):
    segs, t, used = [], 0, 0
    clock_running = True
    for kneel in range(3):
        if clock_running:
            segs.append((t, PLAYCLK, "pc"))
            t += PLAYCLK
        segs.append((t, KNEEL, "kn"))
        t += KNEEL
        if used < n_to:
            used += 1
            segs.append((t, 0, "to"))
            clock_running = False
        else:
            clock_running = True
    if clock_running:                                   # the fourth-down play clock runs out the game
        segs.append((t, LAST, "last"))
        t += LAST
    rows.append((n_to, segs, t))
for n_to, segs, total in rows:
    yy = 3 - n_to
    for x0, w, kind in segs:
        if kind == "pc":
            ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x0, yy - 0.28), w, 0.56, fc=RUN_C, ec=GREEN, lw=0.8))
        elif kind == "kn":
            ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x0, yy - 0.28), w, 0.56, fc=style.OFFENSE_DARK, ec="none"))
        elif kind == "last":
            ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x0, yy - 0.28), w, 0.56, fc=style.SURFACE, ec=GREEN, lw=0.8, hatch="////"))
        else:
            ax.plot([x0 + 0.6, x0 + 0.6], [yy - 0.42, yy + 0.42], color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, lw=2.2)
    txt = f"game over from ≤ {mmss(total)}" if n_to < 3 else f"≤ {mmss(total)}; else a 4th-down snap"
    ax.text(total + 2.5, yy, txt, va="center", fontsize=7.6, color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")
ax.set_yticks([3, 2, 1, 0], ["0 timeouts", "1 timeout", "2 timeouts", "3 timeouts"], fontsize=8)
ax.set_ylabel("Defense has")
ax.set_xlim(0, 228)
ax.set_ylim(-1.75, 3.6)
ax.set_xticks([0, 30, 60, 90, 120, 150], ["0:00", "0:30", "1:00", "1:30", "2:00", "2:30"])
ax.set_xlabel("Game clock used by three kneels and the last play clock (first down, clock running)")
ax.set_title("How much clock three kneel-downs can kill")
ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
ax.legend(handles=[Patch(fc=RUN_C, ec=GREEN, label="play clock runs (≈39 s)"),
                   Patch(fc=style.OFFENSE_DARK, label="kneel (≈2 s)"),
                   Patch(fc=style.SURFACE, ec=GREEN, hatch="////", label="4th-down play clock (≈40 s)"),
                   Line2D([], [], color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, lw=2.2, label="defense timeout")],
          loc="lower center", fontsize=6.8, ncol=4, bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, -0.02), frameon=False)
plt.show()








Figure 53.5: The kneel-down arithmetic. The leading team has first-and-10, the clock is running and the play clock is fresh. Each kneel lets the play clock run down (green, about 39 seconds) and then takes about two seconds (dark blue). After the third kneel the play clock runs one last time before a fourth-down snap would be due (hatched, about 40 seconds): if the game clock reaches zero during it, the game is over. Every timeout the defense has left stops the clock after a kneel (orange tick), and the next snap starts it again at once, so that play clock costs the defense nothing. The total at the end of each bar is the most time a first down can have on the clock and still end the game: about 2:43 with no defensive timeouts, 2:04 with one, 1:25 with two. With three, the last timeout stops the clock after the third kneel, so there is no final play-clock run; the kneels alone cover only about 0:45, and above that the offense must snap on fourth down.





The rule of thumb that falls out, in the form a coach would use on the sideline: after the two-minute warning, a first down ends the game if the defense has zero or one timeout left. With two, it ends the game from about 1:25; with three, from about 0:45. Each of the first two timeouts is worth about 40 seconds; the third is worth more, because it also takes away that last free run of the play clock. That is why a defense down by four with 2:30 left will start calling timeouts after the first running play, not wait. And it is why a timeout is worth more to the team without the ball late in the game: it is the only thing that converts the offense’s play clock back into usable time.
Two wrinkles. If the first down comes shortly before the two-minute warning, the clock will stop at 2:00 anyway, so start the count at 2:00 and treat the warning as one more defensive timeout (it stops the clock for free, just as a timeout would). And if the arithmetic comes up a few seconds short, so that fourth down arrives with time still on the clock, the offense doesn’t kneel a fourth time (that would hand over the ball at the spot). It snaps and burns the clock: the quarterback takes the snap and runs backward or sideways until the seconds are gone, or the punter does the same, or the team simply punts deep.
One famous finish shows the leading team taking this arithmetic to its logical end. In December 2007, the Eagles led Dallas 10–6 when Brian Westbrook broke a run into the clear with Dallas out of timeouts; he deliberately went down at the 1 instead of scoring, and Donovan McNabb knelt three times to end the game.13 Run the numbers the way the chart does. The clock ran from 2:19 to the two-minute warning. From 2:00, the warning counts as one stoppage and Dallas had no timeouts, so read the chart’s one-timeout row: a first down at about 2:04 or less ends the game, and 2:00 is less. McNabb knelt at 2:00, 1:15 and 0:30, and the game clock ran out during the last play clock. A touchdown would have given Dallas the ball back with about two minutes left; the kneels gave it nothing.
The same arithmetic explains one of the strangest sights in football, a defense that lets the offense score. In Super Bowl XLVI the Patriots led the Giants 17–15, and the Giants had the ball at the New England 6 with about a minute left. New England had one timeout. Played normally, the Giants would run the clock down to the last seconds and kick a chip-shot field goal (a very short, near-certain kick) to win, and Tom Brady would never touch the ball again. So Bill Belichick told his defense to let Ahmad Bradshaw score, and Bradshaw, who tried to stop at the 1, fell into the end zone with 57 seconds left.14 Down 21–17 with 57 seconds and a timeout beat down 18–17 with no time at all. (It didn’t work: Brady’s last drive fell short.) Westbrook and Bradshaw are the same idea from opposite sides: the team with the ball valued the clock more than six points, and the defense paid six points to get the clock back.


The victory formation
The kneel is so routine that it has its own formation, the victory formation, and announcers call the play a kneel-down.


Show the Python
vf = [Player(k, pos, "off", d, w, label=lab) for k, pos, d, w, lab in [
    ("LT", "LT", -0.7, -3.2, ""), ("LG", "LG", -0.7, -1.6, ""), ("C", "C", -0.7, 0.0, "C"),
    ("RG", "RG", -0.7, 1.6, ""), ("RT", "RT", -0.7, 3.2, ""), ("U", "TE", -0.7, -4.8, "U"),
    ("Y", "TE", -0.7, 4.8, "Y"), ("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0.0, "Q"), ("LB_", "RB", -3.3, -1.5, "R"),
    ("RB_", "FB", -3.3, 1.5, "F"), ("DEEP", "S", -13.0, 0.0, "D")]]
vd = [Player(k, pos, "def", d, w) for k, pos, d, w in [
    ("E1", "DE", 1.0, -5.2), ("T1", "DT", 1.0, -1.6), ("T2", "DT", 1.0, 1.6), ("E2", "DE", 1.0, 5.2),
    ("M", "MIKE", 4.5, 0.0), ("S_", "SAM", 4.5, 4.5), ("W", "WILL", 4.5, -4.5),
    ("C1", "CB", 6.0, -10.0), ("C2", "CB", 6.0, 10.0), ("FS", "FS", 10.0, -5.0), ("SS", "SS", 10.0, 5.0)]]
pv = Play(vf, vd, los=70, to_go=None)
pv.highlight("QB")
fld = pv.draw(window=(-16.5, 12.5), lateral=(-15.5, 15.5), title=False)
no_numbers(fld)
say(fld, pv, -3.0, -9.6, "quarterback: snap,\ndrop to one knee", color=OC, fs=6.6)
lead(fld, pv, (-2.6, -6.6), (-2.0, -0.9))
say(fld, pv, -6.6, 6.9, "two backs: protect\nthe ball, block leaks", color=OC, fs=6.6)
lead(fld, pv, (-5.8, 4.0), (-3.9, 2.2))
say(fld, pv, -13.0, 7.6, "deep back: stops a\nfumble return", color=OC, fs=6.6)
lead(fld, pv, (-13.0, 4.4), (-13.0, 0.9))
say(fld, pv, -2.4, 10.0, "tight splits, both\nends attached", color=OC, fs=6.6)
lead(fld, pv, (-1.6, 7.6), (-0.9, 5.6))
plt.show()








Figure 53.6: The victory formation. Seven blockers on the line in tight splits (no gaps for a defender to shoot), both tight ends attached. The quarterback (Q) is under center; two backs stand just behind him on either side, close enough to block a defender who slips through and to fall on the ball if the snap is fumbled. One deep player (D, often a safety or a receiver) stands 12 or more yards back as a last line of defense: if the ball somehow comes loose and a defender scoops it up, he is the only one who can stop a touchdown return. The quarterback takes the snap and kneels; the defense usually doesn’t rush hard, by an unwritten rule, and a defense that has given up often stays in its base alignment, as here.





The formation’s history is a cautionary tale. On November 19, 1978, the Giants led the Eagles 17–12 with about 30 seconds left and the ball. Instead of kneeling, they handed off; quarterback Joe Pisarcik and fullback Larry Csonka botched the exchange, Eagles cornerback Herman Edwards picked up the loose ball and ran it in, and Philadelphia won 19–17. The “Miracle at the Meadowlands” cost the Giants’ offensive coordinator his job the next day, and teams across the league began kneeling, in a formation built to make that fumble impossible.15
By convention the defense doesn’t fight a kneel-down. When the Buccaneers’ Greg Schiano had his defense charge into the Giants’ victory formation in September 2012, knocking Eli Manning to the ground, Tom Coughlin confronted him at midfield and the incident became a league-wide argument about sportsmanship. Schiano’s defence was that the game wasn’t over until the clock hit zero, which is true; the convention survives because a fumble on a kneel is so unlikely that rushing it mostly risks injuries.16






NoteMadden vs. real life



In Madden, “kneel” is a button you press once the clock math works. In a real game somebody has to do the math, under noise, with the play clock running: down, distance, the opponent’s timeouts, whether the two-minute warning is still to come. NFL staffs keep a clock-management card for exactly this (often a dedicated assistant or the “game management” coach in the booth), and head coaches have been fired over getting it wrong. When a broadcast shows a coach on the headset at 2:15 with the offense jogging to the line, he is usually being read that card.

title: The Clock, the Two-Minute Drill, and Fourth Down
section: End of the half: points versus risk
text:
End of the half: points versus risk
The last minute of the first half has its own logic. There is no next possession to protect against (the second half starts with a kickoff and fresh timeouts), so a team with the ball and time faces a narrower question: is a shot at points worth the risk of giving the opponent the ball with time to use it?
Three questions settle most of these calls:

How far to field-goal range, and how many plays do I have? From the price list: with one timeout, 45 seconds is about four or five plays if half of them go out of bounds or fall incomplete. If those plays can plausibly gain 30 yards, go.
What happens if it goes wrong? An interception or a three-and-out deep in your own territory gives the opponent a short field. Backed up at your own 10 with 40 seconds, most coaches kneel.
Who gets the ball to start the second half? If you will receive the second-half kickoff, scoring at the end of the half is a double score opportunity: points just before the break, then the ball again immediately. That’s a big reason most coaches defer when they win the coin toss.

Put numbers on one. You have the ball at your own 30 with 0:45 left in the first half and one timeout, and your kicker is good from the opponent’s 35 (a 53-yarder). That is 35 yards in about five plays, realistic if the offense throws outside and uses its timeout well, and the downside (an interception at your own 35 with 30 seconds left) gives the opponent a long field-goal try at worst. Most modern coaches would go. Move the same situation back to your own 10 with no timeouts, and it is 55 yards in three or four plays with a turnover now handing the opponent a short field: kneel.
The most famous “points or risk?” argument came at the end of a game. In Super Bowl XXXVI, with the score tied and the Patriots starting at their own 17 with 1:21 and no timeouts, the broadcast’s John Madden said they should run out the clock: “You have to play for overtime now.” Bill Belichick and Tom Brady went for it anyway.17 Madden was not wrong about the risk; he was underrating the price list. Two short throws to the running back in bounds, then a spike on first down at 0:41, the textbook spike: an in-bounds catch, a sprint to the line, the clock stopped for the price of a cheap down. Then a third throw to the back that was pushed out of bounds, an incompletion, and Troy Brown’s 23-yard catch that went out of bounds had the ball at the Rams’ 36 with 21 seconds left. One more catch in bounds, six yards to the 30, a second spike at 0:07, and Adam Vinatieri kicked the 48-yard winner as time ran out.

The Hail Mary
When there is time for only one snap and the end zone is out of field-goal range, there is one play left: the Hail Mary. Four or five receivers sprint to one spot in or near the end zone, the quarterback buys time and throws as high and as far as he can, and everyone converges on the ball. The name comes from the Cowboys’ 1975 playoff game at Minnesota, when Roger Staubach threw a 50-yard winner to Drew Pearson and told reporters afterward that he had closed his eyes and said a Hail Mary.18


Show the Python
off = offense("gun_2x2")
off = [pl.moved(w=-17.0) if pl.key == "X" else pl.moved(w=17.0) if pl.key == "Z" else pl for pl in off]
off = [pl.moved(d=-5.0, w=1.5) if pl.key == "RB" else pl for pl in off]
hmd = [Player(k, pos, "def", d, w, label=lab) for k, pos, d, w, lab in [
    ("E1", "DE", 1.0, -3.5, None), ("N", "NT", 1.0, 0.5, None), ("E2", "DE", 1.0, 4.0, None),
    ("W", "WILL", 12.0, -8.0, None), ("M", "MIKE", 12.0, 0.0, None), ("D", "DB", 12.0, 8.0, None),
    ("C1", "CB", 18.0, -15.0, None), ("C2", "CB", 18.0, 15.0, None),
    ("S1", "FS", 36.0, -5.0, None), ("S2", "SS", 36.0, 5.0, None), ("G", "NB", 40.0, 0.0, "$")]]
hmp = Play(off, hmd, los=62, to_go=None)
hmp.dropback(3.0)
SPOT = 50.0                      # two yards deep in the end zone (the goal line is 48 yards away)
T_THROW = 4.3
# receivers: the diamond around the jumper (absolute (d, w) from the line of scrimmage)
for key, end, spd in [("Y", (SPOT, 0.5), 8.8),          # jumper
                      ("H", (SPOT - 3.0, 0.0), 8.6),    # front tipper
                      ("Z", (SPOT + 3.0, 0.5), 9.2),    # back tipper / trailer
                      ("X", (SPOT - 1.5, -3.0), 9.0),   # side
                      ("RB", (SPOT - 1.5, 3.5), 8.8)]:  # side
    hmp.route(key, [(end[0] - 2.0, end[1] * 1.3), end], absolute=True, speed=spd)
# defense: DBs at or above the jump point, a deeper goalie, underneath players to the front of the pile
for key, to, delay, spd in [("S1", (SPOT + 1.0, -1.6), 0.4, 4.5), ("S2", (SPOT + 1.0, 2.4), 0.4, 4.5),
                            ("C1", (SPOT + 2.0, -4.6), 0.0, 7.0), ("C2", (SPOT + 1.5, 5.2), 0.0, 7.0),
                            ("G", (SPOT + 5.5, 0.0), 0.6, 4.5), ("W", (SPOT - 4.0, -3.5), 0.2, 6.6),
                            ("M", (SPOT - 5.5, 0.5), 0.2, 6.6), ("D", (SPOT - 4.6, 4.4), 0.2, 6.6)]:
    hmp.drop(key, to, delay=delay, speed=spd)
for key in ("E1", "N", "E2"):
    hmp.rush(key, speed=3.6)
hmp.pass_to("Y", t=T_THROW)
# when does the ball arrive? (first moment it reaches the jumper)
_ts = np.arange(T_THROW, T_THROW + 6.0, 0.05)
T_ARR = float(next(t for t in _ts if np.linalg.norm(hmp.ball_position(t) - hmp.position("Y", t)) < 0.6))
if PDF:
    # print: the whole play at the snap (left), then two close-ups of the landing spot (right)
    from gridiron import draw_frame
    trk = hmp.to_tracking(t_after=0.8)
    trk["_id"] = trk.displayName
    tmap = trk.groupby("frameId")["time"].first()
    fig = plt.figure(figsize=(6.6, 5.3))
    axL = fig.add_axes([0.0, 0.0, 0.45, 0.93])
    no_numbers(hmp.draw(ax=axL, window=(-10, 60), lateral=(-19.5, 19.5), title=False))
    axL.set_title("The plan, at the snap", fontsize=8.5, color=style.INK, loc="left")
    for t, (x0, y0), ttl in [(T_ARR - 0.6, (0.47, 0.5), f"+{T_ARR - 0.6:.1f} s: the crowd sets up, ball coming down"),
                             (T_ARR, (0.47, 0.0), f"+{T_ARR:.1f} s: the ball arrives at the jumper")]:
        axr = fig.add_axes([x0, y0, 0.53, 0.43])
        fr = Field(ax=axr, orient="vertical", los=hmp.los, window=(38, 60), lateral=(hmp.ball_y - 12.5, hmp.ball_y + 12.5))
        no_numbers(fr)
        fid = int((tmap - t).abs().idxmin())
        near = trk[trk.x >= hmp.los + 39.0]                       # only what is inside the close-up
        draw_frame(fr, near[near.frameId == fid], near[(near.frameId <= fid) & (near.frameId >= fid - 10)],
                   fr.pts_per_yard())
        # the ball: where it is now, with a dotted trace of the last half-second of its flight
        trace = [tuple(map(float, fr.xy(*hmp.to_abs(*hmp.ball_position(tt))))) for tt in np.linspace(t - 0.5, t, 6)
                 if hmp.ball_position(tt)[0] >= 38.5]
        if len(trace) > 1:
            axr.plot(*zip(*trace), color=style.BALL, lw=1.2, ls=(0, (1.5, 1.5)), zorder=11)
        bd, bw = hmp.ball_position(t)
        if t == T_ARR:
            bd, bw = bd + 1.1, bw + 0.9      # at the jumper's raised hands, so his letter stays readable
        bx, by = map(float, fr.xy(*hmp.to_abs(bd, bw)))
        axr.add_patch(Ellipse((bx, by), 0.75, 1.15, fc=style.BALL, ec="white", lw=0.8, zorder=12))
        if t == T_ARR:
            for (d_, w_), (pd0, pw0), txt in [((SPOT, -8.6), (SPOT, -0.5), "jumper (Y)"),
                                             ((SPOT + 5.5, -8.6), (SPOT + 5.5, -0.9), "goalie ($)"),
                                             ((SPOT + 3.0, 8.6), (SPOT + 3.0, 1.4), "back tipper (Z)"),
                                             ((SPOT - 3.0, 8.6), (SPOT - 3.0, 1.0), "front tipper (H)")]:
                xx, yy = map(float, fr.xy(*hmp.to_abs(d_, w_)))
                lx, ly = map(float, fr.xy(*hmp.to_abs(pd0, pw0)))
                axr.plot([xx, lx], [yy, ly], color=style.MUTED, lw=0.6, zorder=8)
                axr.text(xx, yy, txt, fontsize=6.2, color=style.INK_2, ha="center", va="center", zorder=9,
                         bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.15", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none", alpha=0.95))
        axr.set_title(ttl, fontsize=8, color=style.INK, loc="left")
    plt.show()
else:
    show_play(hmp, times=[0.0, 2.5, T_THROW, T_ARR])

Figure 53.7: A Hail Mary from the opponent’s 48 with four seconds left (simulated tracking, BDB format). The five receivers (blue) race to one spot about two yards deep in the end zone and set up in a diamond with named jobs: Y is the jumper at the spot, H the front tipper about three yards short of him, Z the back tipper about three yards deeper, and X and the back (R) the two sides. The defense (orange) rushes three and drops eight: its safeties and corners get to the spot first and go up at or above the jump point to bat the ball down, one more defender ($) waits deeper as the ‘goalie’, and the three underneath droppers (W, M, D) collapse to the front of the pile to swat tips. The quarterback buys time with a deep drop and throws at a little over four seconds, as receivers need about five to six seconds to cover 50 yards; the ball is in the air for about three more. In print, the left panel shows everyone’s path from the snap and the right panels close in on the landing spot as the ball comes down and arrives (faint tails show the last second of movement).




How often does it work? Over the last ten regular seasons, throws of 35-plus air yards from 40 or more yards out in the last eight seconds of a half, the play-by-play’s best proxy for a Hail Mary, numbered 217. They produced a touchdown 6% of the time and an interception 20% of the time.19 One in seventeen sounds hopeless, but the alternative at 0:04 is zero, and an interception on the last play costs almost nothing. From deep in its own half (its own 30, say), even a strong arm can’t reach the end zone, so teams switch to a hook-and-lateral or a multi-lateral “river” play and hope someone breaks free.
Two rules make the last play stranger than it looks. First, a half never ends while the ball is in play: if the clock hits 0:00 while the ball is in the air, the play finishes. That is why a team with four seconds left can run a play that lasts eight. Second, a half cannot end on an accepted defensive foul. If the defense commits pass interference or holds on the last play, the offense gets the yardage and one more untimed down. (An offensive foul gives no such extension.)20 That is why you’ll see the pile in the end zone watched by every official on the field, why defenders are coached to go up for the ball and never through the receiver, and why a flag on a Hail Mary is the most dramatic flag in football.


The prevent defense
The defense’s mirror image is the prevent defense: rush three (sometimes four), drop eight, and play everyone deep, conceding the short completion in order to take away the long one and tackle in bounds.


Show the Python
off = offense("gun_2x2")
pd_ = [Player(k, pos, "def", d, w) for k, pos, d, w in [
    ("E1", "DE", 1.0, -3.8), ("N", "NT", 1.0, 0.0), ("E2", "DE", 1.0, 3.8),
    ("U1", "NB", 11.0, -18.5), ("U2", "WILL", 9.5, -4.5), ("U3", "MIKE", 9.5, 4.5), ("U4", "DB", 11.0, 18.5),
    ("D1", "CB", 21.0, -18.0), ("D2", "FS", 24.0, -6.0), ("D3", "SS", 24.0, 6.0), ("D4", "CB", 21.0, 18.0)]]
pp = Play(off, pd_, los=50, to_go=None)
pp.dropback(2.0)
for key in ("X", "H", "Y", "Z"):
    pp.route(key, r.go(29))
pp.route("RB", [(1.0, 7.0), (8.5, 8.5)], frame="field")
for key in ("D1", "D2", "D3", "D4"):
    pp.zone(center=(pp.players[key].d + 3.0, pp.players[key].w), size=(10.0, 11.0))
for key, dw in (("E1", -1.0), ("N", 0.0), ("E2", 1.0)):
    pp.rush(key, pts=[(-3.8, dw)])
pp.highlight("RB")
fld = pp.draw(window=(-8, 35), lateral="full", title=False)
no_numbers(fld)
say(fld, pp, 32.0, 0.0, "nothing gets over the top", color=DC, fs=6.8)
say(fld, pp, 5.5, -20.6, "sideline sink:\nno catch gets\nout of bounds", color=DC, fs=6.2)
say(fld, pp, 5.5, 20.6, "sideline sink:\nno catch gets\nout of bounds", color=DC, fs=6.2)
say(fld, pp, 13.0, 0.0, "underneath layer: rally and\ntackle the catch in bounds", color=DC, fs=6.6)
say(fld, pp, 5.5, -4.6, "free: short throws\nin front of them", color=OC, fs=6.6)
say(fld, pp, -5.0, 14.0, "three rushers:\nall the time he wants", color=DC, fs=6.4)
plt.show()








Figure 53.8: A prevent defense against four vertical routes, with 25 seconds left and the offense out of timeouts. Three rushers; four deep defenders (shaded zones) 20 to 25 yards off the ball, so that nothing can be thrown over them; four more underneath at 10 or 11 yards. The two outside underneath players ($ and D) are the key: they line up outside the wide receivers and sink toward the sideline, so that any catch that could get out of bounds is contested, and the two linebackers (W and M) take the middle. The open space is in front of them: the back’s checkdown at about 4 yards (R, ringed) and anything short of the underneath layer is free, but a catch in the middle that stays in bounds keeps the clock running, which is a win for the defense.





The prevent has a bad reputation. “The only thing the prevent defense prevents is winning” is one of football’s oldest lines, and every fan has watched a team give up 60 yards in 90 seconds while playing it. The criticism is fair when the defense goes soft too early. With two minutes left and timeouts in hand, an offense can take the free 12-yard completions all the way down the field, because the prevent concedes yards to save time and the offense has time to spare. With 15 seconds left and no timeouts, the same coverage is exactly right: there is time for one or two plays, so the only thing that can beat you is a long one. The prevent is a clock-dependent call, like everything else in this chapter. What it trades away is yards; what it buys is the end of the game. The trade is good only when the clock makes yards cheap.
You’ll rarely hear a coach say “prevent.” On the field it usually shows up as a dime (six defensive backs) or quarter (seven) package, with three rushers and deep zones. The vocabulary of the whole last two minutes varies like that from staff to staff: the spike call is often just “clock” (Marino shouted “Clock! Clock!” before his fake), the running-clock field goal is “fire” on one team and “Mayday” on another, and the four-minute offense is also called the four-minute drill. Listen for the idea, not the word.


Two rare plays that decide games

Sidebar plate: the intentional safety
An intentional safety gives the opponent two points on purpose. It sounds absurd until you see the situation it’s for: you lead late, you’re about to punt from your own end zone, and the punt is the most dangerous play you could run. The punter is standing almost on the end line, rushers have the shortest possible path to him, and a block or a long return can lose the game. So instead the punter takes the snap, runs around his own end zone burning seconds, and steps out of the back of it. The opponent gets two points; you then kick off from your own 20. (In Super Bowl XLVII the Ravens’ blockers held the rushers on purpose to buy their punter more seconds, since a hold in your own end zone costs only the safety you are already taking. The rulebook now closes that door: multiple fouls on one down to manipulate the clock cost 15 yards, and the clock is reset to where it was at the snap.21)


Show the Python
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(6.6, 5.1))
LAT = (6.0, 45.3)
yb = MIDDLE

for dy in (-6.4, 6.4):                                         # the wings, a yard off the line
    draw_marker(axa, *map(float, fa.xy(10.3, yb + dy)), "off", "", ppa)
draw_marker(axa, *map(float, fa.xy(6.2, yb)), "off", "PP", ppa)  # personal protector
draw_marker(axa, *map(float, fa.xy(1.8, yb)), "off", "P", ppa)
for dy in (-7.5, -3.3, 3.3, 7.5):
    draw_marker(axa, *map(float, fa.xy(13.2, yb + dy)), "def", "", ppa)
land = ezs + 9
axa.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch(fa.xy(1.8, yb), fa.xy(land, yb - 2), arrowstyle="-|>", mutation_scale=10,
                              color=style.BALL, lw=1.3, ls=(0, (2, 2)), connectionstyle="arc3,rad=-0.15", zorder=6))
axa.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch(fa.xy(land, yb - 2), fa.xy(ezs, yb - 8), arrowstyle="-|>",
                              mutation_scale=10, color=DC, lw=2.2, zorder=6))
lab(fa, 3, yb + 13.5, "punter at the end line, about 10 yards\ndeep: the rush is 3-4 yards closer than usual", ha="left")
lab(fa, 24, yb + 6.0, "punt", color=style.INK_2)
lab(fa, ezs + 4, yb - 12.0, "return", color=DC)
lab(fa, ezs - 14, yb + 7.5, f"opponent's drive starts\naround your {S['ezp_start']} (median)", color=DC)
axa.plot(*zip(*[tuple(map(float, fa.xy(x, y))) for x, y in [(ezs, yb + 4.6), (ezs, yb - 8)]]), color=DC, lw=1.0,
         ls=(0, (2, 2)), zorder=5)

# B: the safety and the safety kick

axb.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch(fb.xy(100, yb - 4), fb.xy(ret, yb - 9), arrowstyle="-|>",
                              mutation_scale=10, color=DC, lw=2.2, zorder=6))
lab(fb, 1.0, yb - 13.0, "punter runs out of the\nend zone: 2 points,\nseconds off the clock", ha="left")

lab(fb, 70, yb + 16.2, "coverage lines up on the opponent's 40", color=OC, fs=6.4)
lab(fb, ret + 12, yb - 13.0, f"returned to the opponent's\nown {S['sk_start']} (median)", color=DC)
axb.set_title("B. Take the safety, then kick from the 20", loc="left", fontsize=9, fontweight="bold", color=style.INK)
fig.tight_layout(h_pad=1.2)
plt.show()








Figure 53.9: The intentional safety, as a trade (offense moving left to right; small numbers are yard lines). A: punting from your own end zone, ball at the 2. The punter can stand only about ten yards deep, at the end line, instead of his usual 14 or 15, so the rush is three or four yards closer than on a normal punt, and a bad snap or a muffed catch is a safety or a touchdown. Even when it goes right, the punt (dotted) and the return (solid) leave the opponent’s drive starting near midfield in the punting team’s territory: the median of 2015-2025 punts from inside the 5 is marked (course calculation). B: taking the safety instead. The punter runs out of the back of the end zone (two points to the opponent, and several seconds off the clock); then the safety kick, from your own 20 with the 2026 kickoff alignment (the kicking team’s coverage players line up on the receiving team’s 40, as on every kickoff), has to reach the landing zone between the receiving team’s 20 and its goal line, and is returned to about the receiving team’s own 34 (median, marked). The safety buys about 20 yards of field position and removes the block-and-return risk, for two points.





In field position alone, the swap is worth about 20 yards, and it also removes the chance of a blocked punt. The usual version, the clock-killer, needs two things. The lead must be three or more, so that the two points don’t tie the game. And the clock must be nearly gone, so that the opponent’s drive after the kick has time for one or two plays at most. That second condition matters most with a lead of exactly three: the safety cuts it to one, so any field goal would now lose the game, and the swap is safe only if there is no time left to get into range. The best-known example is the Ravens’ in Super Bowl XLVII, covered in Downs, Distance, and Field Position.
The boldest safety used a different logic entirely, and the team taking it was behind. On Monday Night Football in November 2003, Bill Belichick’s Patriots trailed Denver 24–23 with 2:51 left and fourth down at their own 1. Long snapper Lonie Paxton snapped the ball through the end zone on purpose: 26–23 Broncos. The free kick from the 20 pushed Denver back to its own 15; New England used two timeouts to force a three-and-out, got the ball back at its own 42 after the punt, and Brady threw the winning touchdown to David Givens with 36 seconds left.22 This was the field-position safety: not a way to end the game, but a bet that two points were a fair price for moving the next exchange of possessions 20-odd yards up the field. It only works with timeouts in hand and a defense that can get a stop, which is why you almost never see it. Modern teams use the simpler version in the final seconds: the Chiefs took one with 15 seconds left in a January 2025 divisional-round win over Houston, and the Eagles with six seconds left against Tampa Bay in 2025.23


Sidebar plate: the fair-catch kick
After any fair catch, the receiving team may choose a fair-catch kick instead of a snap: a place kick (held, with no tee) or a drop kick (dropped and kicked on the bounce) for three points, taken from the spot of the catch, with the defense lined up ten yards away. There is no snap: the holder kneels at the spot itself, not seven yards behind a line. And there is no realistic rush, because, as on a kickoff, the defenders may not cross their line until the ball is kicked. Two details make it interesting. The kick is eight yards shorter than a field goal from the same line of scrimmage (spot plus 10 for the end zone, instead of plus 18), and the period can be extended for it: if time runs out during the punt on which the fair catch is made, the receiving team may still take the kick.24


Show the Python

draw_marker(ax, *map(float, fc.xy(63, MIDDLE)), "off", "H", ppy)
draw_marker(ax, *map(float, fc.xy(60.6, MIDDLE + 1.4)), "off", "K", ppy)
for dy in (-7, -4.5, -2, 0.5, 3, 5.5, 8):
    draw_marker(ax, *map(float, fc.xy(73.6, MIDDLE + dy)), "def", "", ppy)
for x, c, lab in [(73, style.DEFENSE_DARK, "defense's line:\n10 yards away"), (55, style.MUTED, "where a holder would kneel\nfor a field goal from scrimmage")]:
    fc._line([x, x], [12.5, 41.0], color=c, lw=1.2, ls=(0, (4, 2)), zorder=2)
ax.text(*fc.xy(74.5, 15.0), "defense lines up 10 yards\naway, can't cross until\nthe ball is kicked", fontsize=6.6, color=DC, ha="left", va="center",
        bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.2", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none"), zorder=9)
ax.text(*fc.xy(54.0, 15.5), "a field goal from\na snap here:\n47 + 18 = 65 yards", fontsize=6.6, color=style.INK_2,
        ha="right", va="center", bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.2", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none"), zorder=9)
ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch(fc.xy(63, MIDDLE), fc.xy(118.5, MIDDLE), arrowstyle="-|>", mutation_scale=10,
                             color=style.BALL, lw=1.4, ls=(0, (2, 2)), connectionstyle="arc3,rad=-0.12", zorder=6))
for dy in (-3.08, 3.08):                                      # goalposts on the end line
    fc._line([119.6, 119.6], [MIDDLE + dy - 0.1, MIDDLE + dy + 0.1], color=style.INK, lw=3)
fc._line([119.6, 119.6], [MIDDLE - 3.08, MIDDLE + 3.08], color=style.INK, lw=1.6)
ax.text(*fc.xy(96, 37.4), "fair catch, spotted at the DEN 47\nkick from the spot: 47 + 10 = 57 yards",
        fontsize=7, color=OC, ha="center", va="center", fontweight="bold",
        bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.25", fc=style.SURFACE, ec=style.BASELINE, lw=0.6), zorder=9)
ax.text(*fc.xy(114.0, 16.0), "end line\nand posts", fontsize=6.4, color=style.INK_2, ha="center", va="center")
plt.show()








Figure 53.10: The fair-catch kick, as Cameron Dicker made it for the Chargers on December 19, 2024. Denver punted from deep in its own end with eight seconds left in the first half; the Chargers fair-caught the ball, and a 15-yard foul on the punting team for interfering with the fair catch moved the spot to the Denver 47 as time expired. The Chargers chose the fair-catch kick: the holder put the ball down at the 47 itself, the defense lined up 10 yards away, and Dicker’s kick needed to travel 47 + 10 = 57 yards. A field goal from a snap at the same line would have been a 65-yarder.





Dicker’s 57-yarder was the first successful fair-catch kick in the NFL since 1976. Attempts are rare because the circumstances are: the fair catch has to come near the end of a half (otherwise the team would rather keep the drive alive) and close enough for a 55- to 65-yard kick. But with modern kickers making long field goals routinely, coaches now keep it on the end-of-half card, and you should too. Watch for a punt from deep in a team’s own territory in the last ten seconds of a half: if the returner signals for a fair catch near midfield, the kicking unit may run on with no snapper.

title: The Clock, the Two-Minute Drill, and Fourth Down
text:
Fourth down: the go-for-it decision
For most of NFL history, fourth down was a kicking down. Inside field-goal range you kicked; outside it you punted; you went for it on fourth-and-inches near midfield, or when you were losing late. The go-for-it decision, the choice among going for it, kicking and punting, has since become the most visible place where analytics changed football.
The argument is an expected-points argument, and you have the tools for it from Downs, Distance, and Field Position. Take fourth-and-2 at the opponent’s 36:

Punt: the opponent takes over somewhere around its own 10, a situation worth a little to it. You’ve traded a scoring chance for field position.
Field goal: a 54-yarder. Modern kickers make those about 74% of the time (2023–2025); a miss gives the opponent the ball at the spot of the kick, its own 44.
Go for it: teams converted fourth-and-2 58% of the time in 2021–2025. Success keeps a drive alive inside field-goal range; failure gives the opponent the ball at its own 36.

Now put the expected-points values from that chapter on each outcome (nflverse’s model, first-and-10 values averaged over 2021–2025; a value for the opponent counts as negative for you):








Choice
What can happen
Expected points




Go
58%: first-and-10 at the opponent’s 34, worth 3.5; otherwise the opponent’s ball at its own 36, worth 1.8 to it
+1.3


Field goal
74%: 3 points, then the opponent’s ball after the kickoff (about its own 30, worth 1.4 to it); otherwise its ball at its own 44, worth 2.2
+0.6


Punt
the opponent’s ball at about its own 10, worth 0.2 to it
-0.2



Going for it is worth about 0.7 points more than kicking and 1.5 more than punting. The reason is visible in the table: success is worth a lot (a first down inside field-goal range is a drive that usually scores), and failure costs less than it feels like. The opponent gets the ball at its own 36 instead of its own 10, a difference of only about 1.6 points. Real models refine every number (this kicker, these offenses, the score, the clock), and the gap shrinks or grows, but it rarely flips here. The economist David Romer made exactly this case in a 2006 paper with a mischievous title, “Do Firms Maximize? Evidence from Professional Football,” and concluded that NFL teams punted and kicked far more often than the numbers justified.25 For a decade coaches mostly ignored him. Then the data went public, a generation of analysts built fourth-down models (Ben Baldwin’s open model and its bot, which grades every fourth down live, is the best known), and teams hired their own analysts.26 The modern decision tools use win probability (the chance of winning the game from this score, clock and field position), not just expected points, so they know when the score makes a field goal worth more than its three points. That model is built in Win Probability and Decision Analysis; this chapter sticks to what the decisions look like and why they changed.


Show the Python
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.4))
for i, ccol in enumerate(GO.columns):
    ax.plot(GO.index, GO[ccol], color=style.SERIES[i], lw=2, marker="o", ms=3.5, label=ccol)
ax.axvspan(2017.5, 2025.5, color=style.GRID, alpha=0.35, zorder=0)
ax.text(2018.0, 0.012, "the aggression era", fontsize=7.5, color=style.INK_2, ha="left", va="center")
for ccol, yy, off_ in [(GO.columns[0], GO.iloc[-1, 0], 0.012), (GO.columns[1], GO.iloc[-1, 1], -0.014)]:
    ax.text(2025.3, yy + off_, pct(yy), fontsize=7.5, color=style.INK, ha="right", va="center", fontweight="bold")
ax.set_xlim(2009.6, 2025.6)
ax.set_ylim(0, 0.26)
ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(plt.FuncFormatter(lambda v, _: f"{v:.0%}"))
ax.set_xticks(range(2010, 2026, 2))
ax.set_ylabel("Share of fourth downs: went for it")
ax.set_title("Fourth down stopped being a kicking down")
ax.legend(loc="upper left", fontsize=7.5)
plt.show()








Figure 53.11: How often NFL teams went for it on fourth down, 2010-2025 regular seasons: all fourth downs (punts, field-goal tries and plays that went for it, including fakes), and the neutral ones, in the first three quarters with each team’s win probability between 20% and 80%, where the decision is a choice rather than desperation. The neutral rate hovered around 5-8% through 2017, climbed to about 15% by 2021, dipped in 2022-2023, and reached about 17% in 2025. Fourth downs wiped out by a pre-snap penalty are not counted. Source: nflverse play-by-play.





The neutral go rate more than doubled, from 6% in 2010 and 7% in 2017 to 17% in 2025; across all fourth downs it went from 13% to 23%. The turn came in 2018, the season after Doug Pederson’s Eagles won a Super Bowl with fourth-down conversions in the biggest moments, including the “Philly Special” in Super Bowl LII, a trick play on fourth-and-goal from the 1 in which the tight end threw a touchdown pass to quarterback Nick Foles.27 It is tempting to tell the story as one coach and one trick play. The truer story is the slow arrival of evidence: public models, analysts on every staff, owners asking questions, and a generation of head coaches who had grown up with the arguments.
Why did the rate dip in 2022 and 2023 before rising again? Nobody has a proven answer. One change is easy to see in the data: teams began trying long field goals far more often, 182 attempts of 50 yards or more in 2021, 224 in 2022 and 279 in 2024, as kickers’ range grew. A fourth down at the opponent’s 35 that would have been a go a few years earlier could now be a reasonable kick, so some of the dip is probably the kicking option getting better rather than coaches losing their nerve.
Where did the extra attempts come from? Not from fourth-and-long in your own territory, which still almost nobody tries. They came from short yardage around midfield, where teams used to punt, and from short yardage inside field-goal range, where they used to kick. The fringe just outside kicking range, which Early Downs and Field Zones calls four-down territory, already saw teams go on fourth-and-1 and 2 a decade ago; the change there is on fourth-and-3, where the go rate roughly doubled.


Show the Python

         "own\n21-30", "own\n1-20"]
HM["zone"] = pd.cut(HM.yardline_100, ZEDGES, labels=ZLABS)
cmap = LinearSegmentedColormap.from_list("blues", ["#f4f8fd"] + style.SEQUENTIAL_BLUE)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 3.9), sharey=True)
for ax, (lo, hi) in zip(axes, [(2010, 2012), (2023, 2025)]):
    sub = HM[HM.season.between(lo, hi)]
    tab = sub.pivot_table(index="ytg", columns="zone", values="go", aggfunc="mean", observed=False)
    n = sub.pivot_table(index="ytg", columns="zone", values="go", aggfunc="size", observed=False)
    tab = tab.where(n >= 15)[ZLABS[::-1]]
    n = n[ZLABS[::-1]]
    ax.imshow(tab.values, cmap=cmap, vmin=0, vmax=0.9, aspect="auto")
    for i in range(tab.shape[0]):
        for j in range(tab.shape[1]):
            v = tab.values[i, j]
            if np.isfinite(v):
                ax.text(j, i, f"{100 * v:.0f}", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=6.3,
                        color="white" if v > 0.5 else style.INK)
    ax.set_xticks(range(len(ZLABS)), ZLABS[::-1], fontsize=5.8)
    ax.set_yticks(range(10), [str(k) if k < 10 else "10+" for k in range(1, 11)], fontsize=7)
    ax.set_title(f"{lo}-{hi}", fontsize=9, loc="center")
    ax.grid(False)
    ax.tick_params(length=0)
axes[0].set_ylabel("Yards to go on fourth down")
fig.supxlabel("Ball on (offense moving left to right)", fontsize=8, color=style.INK_2)
fig.suptitle("Go-for-it rate (%), first three quarters", x=0.01, ha="left", fontsize=10, fontweight="bold")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 53.12: Go-for-it rate by yards to go and field position, first three quarters only (so that late-game desperation doesn’t count), 2010-2012 versus 2023-2025 regular seasons. Each cell shows the share of fourth downs on which the offense went for it; cells with fewer than 15 fourth downs are left blank. The biggest changes are on short yardage (fourth-and-1 to 4) between your own 40 and the opponent’s 40, and inside field-goal range, where fourth-and-1 and 2 used to mean a kick. The opponent’s 30-39, too far for an easy kick and too close for a good punt, was already a go zone on fourth-and-1 a decade earlier. Fourth-and-long in your own half barely moved. Source: nflverse play-by-play.






Fourth-down rules of thumb
You don’t need a model to make a decent call from the couch. These heuristics agree with the public models in most situations, for an average offense and kicker, with the score close and plenty of time left. Keep one thing straight: they are what the models recommend, not what teams do. Teams are still more conservative than the models, so on Sunday you’ll often see a punt or a kick where the rule below says go.

Fourth-and-1: go almost anywhere past your own 30, and in many models even deeper. Teams converted 68% of fourth-and-1s in 2021–2025 (this includes the QB sneak and tush push, which convert more often still).
Fourth-and-2 or 3: go from about midfield in. Conversion rates were 58% and 50%.
The opponent’s 30 to 40 is the “go zone.” It is too far for a sure field goal and too close for a good punt (a punt from the 35 nets only about 25 yards, and 15 if it bounces into the end zone), so the models usually say go there even on fourth-and-4 or 5 (converted 50%). Teams still go on those only about 30% of the time (the heatmap’s 2023–2025 panel); that gap between the models and the sideline is where the next round of the aggression shift will come from, if it comes.
Inside the opponent’s 5: go on fourth-and-goal from the 1 or 2 unless the score says three points matter more than seven. A failed try still leaves the opponent pinned at its own goal line.
Long yardage in your own half: punt. Fourth-and-6 to 10 converts only about 34% of the time, and failure gives the opponent a short field.
Then let the score and clock override everything. Trailing late, go more; leading late, the value of the clock (and of making the opponent need two scores) can flip a go into a kick.

Two things these rules leave out are what make real decisions hard: your offense and kicker are not average, and the opponent’s offense matters (if they score at will, possessions are worth more, so go). That’s why two smart coaches can disagree about the same fourth down.






CautionCommon misconception



“Going for it and failing proves it was the wrong call.” A fourth-and-2 that converts 58% of the time fails 42% of the time. Judge the decision by the odds when it was made, not by the result; the film room below shows why that is harder than it sounds.








NoteFilm room: Lions 2021-2025, Dan Campbell’s fourth downs



No coach has been more associated with fourth-down aggression than Dan Campbell, hired by Detroit in 2021. In the first three quarters of games from 2022 to 2025, the Lions went for it on 28% of their fourth downs, the highest rate in the league (the league average was 15%; next were the Eagles at 20%), and they led the league in that rate in four of the five seasons from 2021 to 2025.28 Campbell made aggression part of the team’s identity from his first season, and for most of those seasons the conversions and points it produced were part of why Detroit’s offense was one of the best in football.
The game everyone remembers went the other way. In the NFC Championship Game on January 28, 2024, at San Francisco, Detroit led 24–7 at halftime. Midway through the third quarter, leading 24–10, the Lions went for it on fourth-and-2 from the 49ers’ 28 instead of trying a 46-yard field goal, and threw incomplete. Late in the game, trailing 27–24, they went for it on fourth-and-3 from the 30 instead of a tying 48-yarder, and threw incomplete again. San Francisco scored after both, and won 34–31.
What to notice: those were exactly the kind of calls the heuristics call close, a short fourth down at the edge of field-goal range, with a strong kicker available. Reasonable people (and models) disagreed about them before the snap; after the snap, the results made them look like blunders. The fair evaluation is the whole record, and on the whole record Detroit’s aggression was a net positive for years. The lesson for a viewer is to separate the decision from the dice, and to notice that the most aggressive coach in the league still faced exactly the trade-off this chapter describes, possessions against points, every week.
