section: Two-point decisions and the two-point chart
text:
Two-point decisions and the two-point chart
After a touchdown the scoring team chooses between the extra point (a 33-yard kick since the league moved it back in 2015) and a two-point conversion (one play from the 2). Since 2015 the kick has been good 94.3% of the time and the two-point try has succeeded 48% of the time, so the expected points are almost the same: 0.94 for the kick, 0.95 for the try.29 When two choices are worth the same on average, the score decides. That’s the job of the two-point chart: a table, keyed by the margin right after the touchdown, of when two points are worth more than one. Coaches have carried versions of it for half a century; the NFL added the two-point try in 1994.30


Show the Python
CH = {-11: "K", -10: "G", -9: "C", -8: "G", -7: "K", -6: "K", -5: "G", -4: "C", -3: "K", -2: "G", -1: "C",
      1: "G", 2: "C", 3: "K", 4: "K", 5: "G", 6: "K", 7: "K", 8: "K", 9: "C", 10: "C", 11: "K", 12: "G",
      13: "K", 14: "K", 15: "G"}
FC = {"G": style.SERIES[0], "K": style.GRID, "C": "#f5cf6b"}
TC = {"G": "white", "K": style.INK, "C": style.INK}
WORD = {"G": "GO", "K": "kick", "C": "close"}
WHY = {-10: "→ down 8:\none score", -9: "→ 7 or 8:\nboth one\nscore", -8: "see\ntext",
       -5: "→ down 3:\nFG ties", -4: "FG wins\nor FG\nties?", -2: "→ tie", -1: "win now\nor play\nfor OT?",
       1: "→ up 3:\nFG only\nties", 2: "→ up 4:\nFG can't\ntie", 5: "→ up 7:\nTD only\nties",
       9: "→ up 11,\nor up 9\nif it fails", 10: "→ up 12:\nTD+2+FG\nno longer\nties",
       12: "→ up 14:\ntwo TDs\nonly tie", 15: "→ up 17:\nthree\nscores"}
WHY_LOW = {}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(6.6, 4.1))
for ax, rng, title in [(axes[0], range(-11, 0), "Trailing after the touchdown by"),
                       (axes[1], range(1, 16), "Leading after the touchdown by")]:
    blank(ax)
    keys = list(rng)
    ax.set_xlim(-0.6, 15.6)
    ax.set_ylim(-2.15, 1.05)
    for i, m in enumerate(keys):
        c = CH[m]
        ax.add_patch(FancyBboxPatch((i - 0.44, -0.4), 0.88, 0.95, boxstyle="round,pad=0.02,rounding_size=0.12",
                                    fc=FC[c], ec="white", lw=1))
        ax.text(i, 0.25, f"{abs(m)}", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=9, fontweight="bold", color=TC[c])
        ax.text(i, -0.17, WORD[c], ha="center", va="center", fontsize=6.4, color=TC[c])
        if m in WHY:
            # stagger the notes of neighbouring tiles so they never touch
            low = (m - 1) in WHY and (m - 1) in keys and not WHY_LOW.get(m - 1, False)
            WHY_LOW[m] = low
            y0 = -1.32 if low else -0.5
            if low:
                ax.plot([i, i], [-0.44, y0 + 0.04], color=style.MUTED, lw=0.6)
            ax.text(i, y0, WHY[m], ha="center", va="top", fontsize=5.6, color=style.INK_2, linespacing=1.05)
    ax.text(-0.5, 0.95, title, ha="left", va="center", fontsize=8.5, fontweight="bold", color=style.INK)
fig.tight_layout(h_pad=0.4)
plt.show()








Figure 53.13: A simple two-point chart for late in a game, when only one or two more scores are likely. Find the margin right after the touchdown, before the try; the small note under a tile says what the try changes. ‘Go’ (blue) means two points turn the margin into a better number: tying (down 2), making a field goal enough to tie (down 5), keeping it a one-score game (down 10), or making the opponent need more than it otherwise would (up 1, 5, 12 and 15). ‘Kick’ (grey) means the extra point is as good or better. ‘Close’ (yellow) means the two options are worth about the same, so the time left and the two teams decide; the text explains each. Down 8, the most debated case, is explained in the text too. Earlier in a game, kick unless you think your two-point play beats 50%.





The logic in each “go” box is the same: does two points move the margin across a line that matters? The lines are the numbers the other team can reach in one possession, 3 (a field goal) and 7 or 8 (a touchdown with a kick or a two-pointer).
The yellow boxes are the honest ones: the arithmetic comes out about even, so the situation decides. The one you’ll see most often on television is down 1 after a late touchdown. Kick, and you are tied and probably headed to overtime, roughly a coin flip. Go for two, and about half the time you win right now; the other half you lose. Those are almost the same number, so coaches lean on everything else: a tired defense or a hot offense says go; a road team that fears overtime says go; a great kicker and a strong overtime offense say kick; and if the opponent will get the ball back with time to score again, a lead of one point is worth less than it looks. Down 4 is similar: kicking leaves you down 3, where a field goal ties; a successful try leaves you down 2, where a field goal wins, and a miss leaves you needing a touchdown. Up 2, 9 and 10 are the leading team’s versions: each try either removes one of the opponent’s tying or winning combinations or, if it fails, hands it one.
The famous modern case is trailing by 8 after a touchdown, which happens when you were down 14 and score. The traditional answer was “kick, cut it to 7, and hope for another touchdown and overtime.” The analytics answer is “go for two now.” Make it (about half the time) and you trail by 6, so your next touchdown and extra point win the game in regulation. Miss it and you trail by 8, so you need a touchdown and a two-pointer to tie, but you know that now and can plan the rest of the game around it. Over the two touchdowns, going early wins outright about half the time you get both scores and goes to overtime some of the rest; kicking twice almost always goes to overtime, a coin flip. With a two-point success rate near 48%, going early wins about 60% of the games in which you score both touchdowns, against about 50% for kicking, and it also tells you before the last drive what you need.
Like the fourth-down rules, the chart assumes few scores remain. Early in a game, with many possessions to come, the margin will change again before it matters, so teams simply take the better expected value, which since 2015 has been close to a tie. A team with a great short-yardage offense (the Eagles of the tush-push era, for example) should go for two more often than the chart says.

title: The Clock, the Two-Minute Drill, and Fourth Down
text:
Overtime
The overtime rules have changed more in the last fifteen years than almost any other part of the game, and the reason is visible in one game. Under the old sudden-death rule (in the regular season from 1974), the first team to score in overtime won. That gave a big edge to the team that won the coin toss, and the edge grew as offenses improved. The league chipped away at it: in 2010 (playoffs) and 2012 (regular season) a field goal on the first possession no longer ended the game, but a touchdown still did; in 2017 regular-season overtime was cut from 15 minutes to 10.31 Then came the January 2022 divisional-round game in Kansas City, the “thirteen seconds” game covered in The Game in Fifteen Minutes: the Chiefs won the toss, drove for a touchdown, and Josh Allen never touched the ball. That spring the league changed playoff overtime so that both teams get a possession. In 2025 it extended the rule to the regular season.


Show the Python
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.6, 4.6))
blank(ax)
ax.set_xlim(0, 100)
ax.set_ylim(0, 78)
box(ax, 50, 73, 58, 7, "Tied after four quarters: new coin toss", ec=style.INK_2, bold=True, fs=8.5)
box(ax, 50, 59.5, 62, 10, "Team A's first possession", sub="(the team that receives the kickoff)",
    fs=8.3, sub_fs=6.8)
arrow(ax, (50, 69.4), (50, 64.6))
box(ax, 10, 44.5, 19, 16, "B's defense\nscores", sub="(a safety or\na return TD):\nTeam B wins", fs=7.2, sub_fs=6.4,
    fc=STOP_C, ec=style.DEFENSE_DARK)
arrow(ax, (30, 54.4), (14, 52.7))
box(ax, 60.5, 44.5, 76, 10.5, "Team B gets its possession, whatever Team A did",
    sub="A scored a TD: B needs a TD to tie (or a TD plus a two-pointer to win at once).\nA kicked a FG: B needs a FG to tie, a TD wins.   A didn't score: any score by B wins.",
    fs=7.6, sub_fs=6.2)
arrow(ax, (57, 54.4), (57, 49.8))
box(ax, 57, 29, 70, 9, "Both have had the ball: ahead wins; tied, the next score wins",
    fs=7.6, ec=style.INK_2)
arrow(ax, (57, 39.2), (57, 33.6))
box(ax, 30, 11.5, 40, 13, "Regular season", sub="one 10-minute period\n2 timeouts each\nstill tied at 0:00: a tie",
    fs=8, sub_fs=6.6, fc=MAYBE_C, ec="#c99a00", bold=True)
box(ax, 74, 11.5, 40, 13, "Playoffs", sub="15-minute periods until\nsomeone wins; 3 timeouts\nper two periods",
    fs=8, sub_fs=6.6, fc=RUN_C, ec=GREEN, bold=True)
arrow(ax, (45, 24.4), (33, 18.2))
arrow(ax, (69, 24.4), (72, 18.2))
ax.text(51, 21.5, "if the clock\nruns out", fontsize=6.6, color=style.INK_2, ha="center", va="center", linespacing=1.05)
plt.show()








Figure 53.14: NFL overtime as of the 2026 season. A new coin toss; the winner usually chooses to receive or kick. Both teams are guaranteed the chance of one possession, except that if the kicking team’s defense scores on the first possession (a safety, or an interception or fumble returned for a touchdown) it wins at once. The opening kickoff itself counts as the receiving team’s chance: if the receiving team fumbles it and the kicking team recovers, the receiving team has had its possession. After both have had the ball, the team ahead wins; if it is still tied, the next score of any kind wins. The regular season and the playoffs differ in what happens when time runs out: the regular season has one 10-minute period and can end in a tie (two timeouts each), while the playoffs play as many 15-minute periods as needed (three timeouts per ‘half’ of two periods).





The details are in the rulebook’s Rule 16; the strategy follows from three facts.32
Second possession is information. The team that gets the ball second knows exactly what it needs. If the first team kicked a field goal, the second can use all four downs in its own territory, because a punt is no longer an option worth taking. If the first team scored a touchdown, the second must too, and then decide whether to kick and play on or go for two and win on the spot.
First possession is a potential third possession. If the game is still tied after both teams have had the ball, the next score wins, and the team that received first is the one most likely to get the ball next. In the playoffs, with unlimited time, that potential third possession has real value; in the regular season’s 10-minute period, it often never comes.
The clock is a weapon in the regular season. Ten minutes is short. A first team that drives slowly for a field goal can leave the second team with four or five minutes and the need for points; a long drive by the second team can run the clock out, and the game ends in a tie (which counts as half a win and half a loss in the standings).33
Two edge cases complete the picture. If Team B’s defense scores on Team A’s first possession, with a safety or an interception or fumble returned for a touchdown, B wins on the spot: it has now had the ball too, and it’s ahead. And because the kickoff itself counts as A’s chance, a kicking team that recovers the opening kickoff has used up A’s possession. Since 2026 an onside kick may be declared at any time, so a team could try one to open overtime; onside kicks are recovered rarely enough that this is a curiosity, not a strategy.
That is why there’s no consensus on whether to receive. Analytics researchers still tend to find a small edge in receiving, mostly because of that possible third possession; many coaches and former players on television prefer kicking off, for the information and the free use of fourth down. The edge either way is small, it depends on the two offenses, and the regular season’s 10-minute clock makes the third possession less likely.34






NoteFilm room: Chiefs 2023 season — Super Bowl LVIII overtime



Super Bowl LVIII was the first Super Bowl played under the 2022 playoff overtime rule (and only the second to reach overtime at all, after LI). After Butker’s tying kick (see the timeline earlier in the chapter), San Francisco won the coin toss and chose to receive. It drove from its own 25 to the Kansas City 9 over more than seven minutes and kicked a 27-yard field goal: 22–19.
Now Kansas City knew everything. A field goal would tie and send the game to sudden death; a touchdown would win. On fourth-and-1 at its own 34, with the season on the line, the Chiefs called a timeout and then went for it (a punt would have meant that any San Francisco score won the game), and Mahomes ran for eight yards. On third-and-1 at the 49ers’ 32 he scrambled for 19 more. The drive ended with a three-yard touchdown pass to Mecole Hardman with three seconds left in the first overtime period: 25–22, Kansas City.
What to notice: the 49ers’ choice to receive, debated for weeks afterwards, followed the old sudden-death instinct. Under the new rule a first-possession touchdown no longer ends the game, so receiving first mainly bought San Francisco a possible third possession; it also meant the 49ers drove without knowing what they needed, and settled for three points. Deferring would have handed that information to them. Notice too how the second team plays four-down football from its own 34: the rule changed what fourth down means. And notice that the team with the information still spent a timeout to use it well: knowing what you need doesn’t make the clock free.

title: The Clock, the Two-Minute Drill, and Fourth Down
section: Film room: the clock manager’s reputation
text:
Film room: the clock manager’s reputation






NoteFilm room: Eagles 2004 and Chiefs 2015 — Andy Reid’s slow drives



Andy Reid is now remembered for one of the best two-minute offenses in football, but for most of his career “clock management” was the phrase his critics reached for. The two examples you’ll hear most:

Super Bowl XXXIX (2004 season). Reid’s Eagles trailed New England 24–14 with 5:40 left and the ball. They drove for a touchdown, but the drive took 3:52 of clock, with the clock running between many of the snaps, and the Eagles held two timeouts the entire way. They scored with 1:48 left, failed on the onside kick, and got the ball back only at their own 4 with 46 seconds left.
AFC Divisional Round, January 16, 2016 (2015 season). Reid’s Chiefs trailed the Patriots 27–13 and took over at their own 20 with 6:29 left. The touchdown came with 1:13 left: a 16-play drive that used 5:16, with the clock running between many of the snaps and all three timeouts unused. The onside kick failed, and New England knelt out the game.35

What to notice: both drives scored. The problem was the price. Trailing by two scores, a team needs two possessions, and the second one has to come from the time the first one leaves. Price the drives with the chapter’s list. Many of their snaps were incompletions or plays out of bounds, which cost the same whatever the tempo, so the slow snaps were the ones after a play ended in bounds: 7 of them for the Eagles, with a median of 33 seconds to the next snap, and 8 for the Chiefs, median 29 seconds, against about 21 for a hurry-up snap. That is about 60 seconds of clock given away by the Eagles and 61 by the Chiefs. Add the timeouts never used (each worth about 15 seconds more than even a hurried snap), and the Eagles left roughly 1:30 on the table and the Chiefs roughly 1:46: in each case about the time a second possession, after an onside kick or a defensive stop, would have needed.
The postscript is the more interesting part. The Chiefs of the Mahomes era made the clock their weapon: the thirteen-seconds game, the Super Bowl LVIII regulation drive charted above, and a long run of end-of-half scores. The coach was the same; the quarterback, the play design, and the team’s investment in game management were not. Reputations in this area lag reality by years in both directions.

Coach the clock: one flowchart

    sub="timeout right after each in-bounds run.\nAhead or tied, with the offense set to run\nthe clock down for a sure field goal at\nthe gun? Let them score; get the ball back",

Figure 53.15: A clock decision flowchart for the last two minutes of a half. Left: the team with the ball needs points and time. After each play, first ask whether the clock is running; if it is, decide how much the next snap is worth and choose the cheapest stoppage that gets it (a hurry-up snap, a spike that spends a down, or a timeout that spends a timeout). Right: the team with the lead and the ball spends time instead. Bottom right, the defense: a trailing defense’s main tool is its timeouts; a defense that is ahead (or tied) and facing a near-certain go-ahead field goal at the final gun can let the offense score, to get the ball back with time left (Super Bowl XLVI). The bottom row is the end of the line: kneel when the arithmetic works, take the field goal with the clock stopped, or throw the Hail Mary when there is only one snap left.

title: The Clock, the Two-Minute Drill, and Fourth Down
text:
Watch for it on Sunday






TipWatch for it on Sunday: coach the clock



In the last two minutes of each half, call the clock decision before the team makes it. Keep three numbers in your head from the score bug: time left, each team’s timeouts, and the yard line versus field-goal range (add 18).

After every play, say “running” or “stopped” before the broadcast tells you, and remember the out-of-bounds rule only bites after the first-half two-minute warning and in the last five minutes.
Trailing offense, clock running: predict hurry-up, spike or timeout. Spike on first or second down with time for more plays; timeout when there’s time for only one or two, or when the kicking unit has to come on. The tell for a spike: a shotgun quarterback stepping up under center.
Watch the receivers’ feet. On a sideline catch, does he get out, or turn upfield for two more yards? Did the defender push him out (a gift) or tackle him in bounds (a win for the defense)?
Leading team with a first down: do the kneel math. After the two-minute warning it’s over if the defense has 0 or 1 timeout; with 2 it needs about 1:25 or less, with 3 about 0:45. If it works, call the victory formation before it lines up.
Trailing defense: predict when it calls timeouts. A good one calls them right after the leading team’s first-down and second-down runs, not at the end.
Fourth down before the snap: go, kick or punt? Use the heuristics: fourth-and-1 almost always go; opponent’s 30 to 40 is the go zone; long yardage in your own half, punt.
After a touchdown late: find the margin and check the two-point chart (down 2, 5, 8 or 10; up 1, 5, 12 or 15: expect them to go). Down 1 is the coin flip: watch which way the coach leans.
At the end of the first half: who receives the second-half kickoff? That team will push harder for a late score.

title: The Clock, the Two-Minute Drill, and Fourth Down
text:
Predict the play






TipPredict the play 1: spike or snap?





Show the Python
off = offense("gun_2x2")
MOVE = {"QB": dict(d=-1.9), "X": dict(d=-3.2, w=-13.5), "Z": dict(d=-2.6, w=13.8), "H": dict(d=-3.4, w=-8.0),
        "Y": dict(d=-2.8, w=7.6)}
off = [pl.moved(**MOVE[pl.key]) if pl.key in MOVE else pl for pl in off]
p1 = Play(off, defense("nickel", "two_high", offense("gun_2x2")), los=84, to_go=10)
p1.highlight("QB")
fld = p1.draw(window=(-10, 21.5), lateral="full", title=False)
no_numbers(fld)
scorebug(fld.ax, 0.985, 0.985, ["Q4  0:31 (running)", "AWAY 18   HOME 20", "1st & 10   ball on HOME 26",
                                "AWAY timeouts: 0"], fs=6.4, ha="right")
say(fld, p1, -7.0, -14.5, "receivers still\nhurrying to the line", color=OC, fs=6.6)
say(fld, p1, -6.9, 7.0, "gun team, QB now under\ncenter: the spike tell", color=OC, fs=6.6)
lead(fld, p1, (-5.9, 4.2), (-2.4, 0.8))
say(fld, p1, 17.5, -8.0, "a field goal from here: 26 + 18 = 44 yards", color=style.INK, fs=6.8, box_ec=style.BASELINE)
plt.show()








Figure 53.16: Fourth quarter, 0:31 and running. The offense trails 20-18 and has no timeouts. It just completed a 12-yard pass to the opponent’s 26 (first-and-10), snapped at about 0:36, and the receiver was tackled in bounds. The offense, a shotgun team all day, is sprinting back to the line: the receivers are still a couple of yards short of their spots, and the quarterback has stepped up under center. Its kicker is good from about 50 yards. A field goal from here would be a 44-yarder.





Spike now, or snap a real play? And what has to be true before the field goal?






TipAnswer





Spike now. The field goal has to come with the clock stopped. With no timeouts, the only ways to stop the clock are an incompletion, getting out of bounds, or a spike, and a field-goal unit running on with the clock moving needs about 17 seconds at the very best, which this offense won’t have.
Price the options from the snap of the completion, at about 0:36. Spike: about 16 seconds snap to snap, so the clock stops at about 0:20 and it’s second-and-10. A real play instead: a hurried snap comes about 21 seconds later, at about 0:15. If that play is a catch in bounds, say at the 18, it ends around 0:10 with the clock running, and the spike that would have to follow needs about 16 seconds from that snap: the clock hits zero first. Game over. A sack or a run stuffed in bounds ends it the same way. The spike is the cheap, certain stoppage; that’s why the quarterback is already under center.
After the spike there is a real choice, and coaches split on it. Kick now: a 44-yarder, made about 84% of the time in 2023–2025. Or take one quick shot first: a ball-out-fast throw to the sideline, or a throwaway, costs about six seconds and stops the clock; ten yards turns it into a 34-yarder, made about 97% of the time. The shot is worth it only if it can’t end in bounds or in a sack: with no timeouts and about 0:14 left, a sack ends the game. (If the offense had a timeout, it would save it for the kick and still spike now.)











TipPredict the play 2: can they kneel it out?





Show the Python
pk_off = offense("i_form_22")
pk_def = [Player(k, pos, "def", d, w) for k, pos, d, w in [
    ("E1", "DE", 1.0, -6.0), ("T1", "DT", 1.0, -1.6), ("T2", "DT", 1.0, 1.6), ("E2", "DE", 1.0, 6.0),
    ("W", "WILL", 3.0, -3.2), ("M", "MIKE", 3.0, 0.6), ("S_", "SAM", 2.0, 7.6),
    ("C1", "CB", 2.5, -9.0), ("C2", "CB", 2.0, 15.0), ("FS", "FS", 5.5, -4.5), ("SS", "SS", 5.0, 4.5)]]
pk = Play(pk_off, pk_def, los=45, to_go=10)
fld = pk.draw(window=(-11, 12.5), lateral=(-19, 19), title=False)
no_numbers(fld)
scorebug(fld.ax, 0.015, 0.33, ["Q4  1:40 (running)", "HOME 24   AWAY 20", "1st & 10   ball on HOME 35",
                               "AWAY timeouts: 1"], fs=6.4, ha="left")
say(fld, pk, 9.0, -12.5, "everyone within five\nyards of the ball", color=DC, fs=6.6)
plt.show()








Figure 53.17: Fourth quarter, 1:40 and running, after a first-down run. The offense leads 24-20 with first-and-10 at its own 35, and is back in its heavy two-back, two-tight-end look with a fresh 40-second play clock. The defense has one timeout left, and has everyone crowded within about five yards of the ball. The two-minute warning has already passed.





Can the offense kneel three times and end the game? What should the defense do with its timeout?






TipAnswer





Yes: three kneels end it, and the timeout can’t stop that. Use the kneel chart’s one-timeout row: after the two-minute warning, a first down at about 2:04 or less ends the game, and 1:40 is less. Expect the offense to switch to the victory formation now.
The arithmetic, step by step. Kneel 1: the offense lets the play clock run, snaps at about 1:01 and the kneel ends at about 0:59. The defense calls its timeout. Kneel 2 starts the clock on the snap and ends at about 0:57. With no timeouts left, the play clock runs again: kneel 3 at about 0:18, ending around 0:16. Now it’s fourth down with 16 seconds left and a 40-second play clock, so the game clock reaches zero before the offense has to snap again. Game over, without a fourth-down play.
The defense needed two timeouts here to force a fourth-down snap, and even then it would get the ball back with only seconds left. It doesn’t matter when it calls the one it has; any order gives the same arithmetic. Its only real hope is the one its alignment shows: everyone crowding the ball in case the snap is fumbled, which is exactly what the victory formation is built to prevent.











TipPredict the play 3: fourth-and-2 at the 36





Show the Python
off = offense("gun_2x2")
d3 = defense("nickel", "single_high", off, press=True)
d3 = [pl.moved(d=5.5, w=3.0) if pl.key == "SS" else pl.moved(d=1.5) if pl.pos == "CB" else pl for pl in d3]
p3 = Play(off, d3, los=74, to_go=2)
fld = p3.draw(window=(-10, 17), lateral="full", title=False)
no_numbers(fld)
scorebug(fld.ax, 0.985, 0.265, ["Q2  6:00", "HOME 10   AWAY 10", "4th & 2   ball on AWAY 36",
                               "FG: 36 + 18 = 54 yards"], fs=6.4, ha="right")
say(fld, p3, 3.6, 21.0, "line to gain", color="#9a6a00", fs=6.6)
say(fld, p3, 10.5, -14.0, "corners pressed,\none deep safety", color=DC, fs=6.6)
plt.show()








Figure 53.18: Second quarter, 6:00 left, tied 10-10. The offense faces fourth-and-2 at the opponent’s 36 (yellow line: the line to gain). It has kept its regular 11-personnel offense on the field. The defense is in its nickel package but has changed its look: both corners pressed on the receivers, one deep safety, and the other safety walked down near the line with the nickel back, so seven defenders stand within about six yards of the ball. A field goal from here would be a 54-yarder; the kicker’s career long is 55.





Punt, kick or go? What do the two teams’ personnel and alignment tell you about the decision?






TipAnswer





Go for it, and both teams have told you so. By every rule of thumb in the chapter, this is a go: fourth-and-2 converts about 58% of the time; the 36 is in the opponent’s 30-to-40 “go zone”, where a punt nets only about 25 yards and a 54-yard kick near this kicker’s limit misses often (the league made 50- to 54-yarders 74% of the time in 2023–2025, and a kicker near his career long will do worse) and hands the opponent the ball at its own 44. It is the exact situation of the chapter’s expected-points table, where going was worth about 0.7 points more than kicking. In 2023–2025, teams in the first three quarters went for it on 57% of fourth-and-2s between the opponent’s 31 and 40, against 36% in 2013–2015.
The offense’s clue is its personnel: no punter or kicker jogging on, the regular offense lined up with the quarterback in the shotgun. Some teams line up to go and then take a delay-of-game penalty or call a timeout if they can’t draw the defense offside, so wait for the snap; but a team that keeps 11 personnel on the field on fourth-and-2 has usually made its decision on the sideline. The defense’s clue is its shell: it has read the same situation, given up on deep help, and put seven men near the line with the corners pressed, to take away the run and the quick throws that need only 2 yards. Expect a quick pass against that press (a slant, or two receivers crossing to shake their corners) or a run designed for exactly 2 yards, from the short-yardage menu in Red Zone, Goal Line, Two-Point Plays, and Short Yardage.

53  The Clock, the Two-Minute Drill, and Fourth Down

title: The Clock, the Two-Minute Drill, and Fourth Down
text:
Takeaways

The clock is a currency. Late in a half the trailing team wants plays per second and the leading team wants seconds per play. Price every play: an incompletion or a catch out of bounds costs about 5–6 seconds, a catch in bounds about 21, unless a spike (a down) or a timeout pays for it.
Out of bounds stops the clock until the snap only late: after the two-minute warning of the first half and in the last five minutes of the game. The 10-second runoff punishes an offense that stops the clock illegally, and can end a half.
The two-minute drill throws outside, avoids sacks, spikes on early downs and saves timeouts for the end. The four-minute offense does the opposite: runs inside, snaps at the end of the play clock, and treats first downs, not points, as the goal. After the two-minute warning a first down ends the game against a defense with 0 or 1 timeout left; with 2 it needs about 1:25 or less, with 3 about 0:45.
End-of-half calls weigh points against the risk of a short field for the opponent. The prevent defense is right only when the clock makes yards cheap; the Hail Mary scores about one time in seventeen. The intentional safety and fair-catch kick are rare but decide games.
Fourth down became a decision: the neutral go rate more than doubled from 2017 to 2025, because the expected-points arithmetic favours going far more often than coaches used to. Fourth-and-1 is almost always a go, the opponent’s 30–40 is the go zone (in the models, if not yet on every sideline), and good decisions still fail often.
Two points and overtime follow the score. The two-point chart asks whether two points cross a line that matters (down 2, 5, 8, 10; up 1, 5, 12, 15). Overtime gives both teams a possession; the second team plays with information, the first with a possible third possession.

Builds on: The Game in Fifteen Minutes (when the clock runs and stops, timeouts, the two-minute warning, the “thirteen seconds” game); Downs, Distance, and Field Position (expected points and the Super Bowl XLVII safety); In-Game Adjustments and Tempo (tempo and the hurry-up); Field Goals, Extra Points, and the Punting Game (field-goal range, the extra point and the fair catch); Kickoffs, Returns, and the Dynamic Kickoff (the safety kick’s alignment, squib and onside kicks late in games); Officiating, Replay, and the Rules of the Ball (grounding and late-game replay); and Red Zone, Goal Line, Two-Point Plays, and Short Yardage (the plays behind fourth-and-short and two-point decisions).

title: From the Single Wing to the 1970s Scoring Drought (1906–1977)
text:
Reading this part: action and reaction
Watch an NFL game today and sooner or later a running back walks up behind the center, five yards deep, with the quarterback split out wide like a receiver. The center snaps the ball through the air straight to the back, an extra lineman stands on one side of the line, and a second back is already sprinting across the formation. The broadcaster calls it the wildcat and treats it as a gimmick. A fan from 1935 would call it Saturday: it is the single wing, the formation football was built on. Now jump to 1977. NFL teams scored 17.2 points a game that season, the fewest since 1942, and not one receiver in the league reached 1,000 yards. How did football get from the single wing to the T-formation to the pro passing games of the 1960s, and then, with all that passing knowledge, grind to a near-halt? This chapter is the first half of that story, told the way it happened: every offensive idea, the defense’s answer, and the rules that tilted the board.
You’ll be able to…
Every chapter so far has met a scheme in its present form and given it a short history sidebar. This part of the book connects those sidebars into one story, and the story has a shape: an offense finds an advantage, the defense builds an answer, and when the defense gets too far ahead, the rule-makers step in. The single wing was football’s answer to a game with almost no passing. The T answered the single wing’s slowness. Platoons and Paul Brown made the T a specialist’s offense. The umbrella and the 4-3 answered Brown’s passes; the Flex answered Lombardi’s runs. The AFL (the American Football League, a rival league of the 1960s) went looking for points in the passing game, and by the 1970s the defenses had caught up with everyone. Hold on to that rhythm and the dates take care of themselves.

title: From the Single Wing to the 1970s Scoring Drought (1906–1977)
section: 1906: a pass nobody wanted to throw
text:
1906: a pass nobody wanted to throw
Football in 1905 was a shoving match. The ball was snapped, and the offense’s whole team crashed into the defense in a mass, with ball carriers pushed and pulled forward by their own teammates. That season, by the count usually cited, 19 players died nationwide, and President Theodore Roosevelt, a fan who wanted the game saved rather than banned, pressed the colleges to reform it. Among the changes the rules committee adopted on April 6, 1906, was one meant to spread the players out: the forward pass became legal.1
It was legal, but nobody wanted to throw it, and the reason was the rulebook. The early rules made a pass a gamble with lopsided odds. A pass that hit the ground untouched could cost the offense the ball (from 1907, a 15-yard penalty instead), it had to cross the line of scrimmage at least five yards to either side of the center, and a pass caught in the end zone was not a touchdown but a touchback. Some early versions also limited how far downfield a pass could be caught. Think about that as a coach: a run that fails costs you a down; a pass that fails can cost you the ball. Most coaches ran.
The rules eased slowly. In 1912 the colleges added the 10-yard end zone, a fourth down and the six-point touchdown, and dropped the limit on how far a pass could travel. A year later a small Catholic school from Indiana, Notre Dame, beat Army at West Point by throwing the ball around, with Gus Dorais passing to an end named Knute Rockne; the two had practiced it on a beach the summer before, while working as lifeguards. Newspapers loved it. Coaches mostly didn’t change.2
The professional league that became the NFL was founded in 1920 and took its rules from the colleges, and for its first dozen years it played the same cautious, running game. Two rule changes in 1933 and 1934 finally made the pass a normal play. The trigger was a controversial touchdown in the 1932 playoff game, played indoors on a shortened field because of a blizzard: Chicago’s Bronko Nagurski faked a run, backed up a step and threw a short touchdown pass, and Portsmouth argued that he hadn’t been the required five yards behind the line. For 1933 the NFL broke with the college rulebook and allowed a forward pass from anywhere behind the line of scrimmage. The same off-season it added hash marks (lines in the field from which every play starts, so the ball was no longer spotted beside the sideline) and moved the goalposts up to the goal line to encourage field goals. And from 1934, a second incomplete pass in the same set of downs no longer cost five yards.3 Meanwhile the ball itself got slimmer through the 1920s and ’30s, easier to grip and spiral.
You can see the effect in the scoring. In 1932 an NFL team scored 8.2 points a game; by 1948 it was 23.2, close to three times as many (the points chart later in this chapter shows the whole curve). The pass was not the only cause, since the T-formation and free substitution arrived in the same years (both are coming up), and the season-by-season passing numbers for the 1930s are too patchy to split the credit. But the direction is clear: by the peak years of the 1950s and ’60s, NFL teams threw on about half their plays.4 Offenses needed a player who could throw.

text:
The single wing: power and deception from a direct snap
For the first decades of the forward pass, the formation that ran football was the single wing. It is usually credited to Glenn “Pop” Warner at the Carlisle Indian Industrial School around 1907, where Jim Thorpe played tailback for him; Warner called it the Carlisle formation, and the name single wing came later from the one “wing” back lined up outside the end.5


Show the Python
def single_wing():
    return check_legal([
        P("WE", "TE", LINE_D, -3.2, "E"), OL("WT", -1.6), OL("C", 0.0, "C"), OL("WG", 1.6), OL("SG", 3.2),
        OL("ST", 4.8), P("SE", "TE", LINE_D, 6.4, "E"),
        P("QB", "TB", -5.0, 0.6, "T"), P("FB", "FB", -4.4, 2.8, "F"), P("BB", "HB", -2.1, 4.0, "B"),
        P("WB", "HB", -1.6, 8.3, "W")])


sw = Play(single_wing(), None, los=40, to_go=None)
sw.highlight("QB", color=BACK_RING)
fld = draw_play(sw, lateral=(-16.0, 18.0), window=(-10.5, 5.8))
(x0, y0), (x1, y1) = XY(fld, sw, 0.0, 0.0), XY(fld, sw, -4.2, 0.55)
fld.ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((x0, y0), (x1, y1), arrowstyle="-|>", mutation_scale=9, color=style.BALL,
                                 lw=1.3, ls=(0, (2, 2)), zorder=5, connectionstyle="arc3,rad=0.25"))
label(fld, sw, "unbalanced line: four men to the right\nof the center, two to the left", (3.7, -5.4))
label(fld, sw, "wingback (W): a yard off\nthe line, outside the end", (3.7, 11.6), target=(-1.6, 8.3))
label(fld, sw, "tailback (T): takes the snap about\n5 yards deep; runs, passes or hands off",
      (-8.6, -6.6), target=(-5.0, 0.6))
label(fld, sw, "direct snap: the ball\nflies back to him", (-2.8, -8.2), target=(-2.4, 0.35))
label(fld, sw, "fullback (F): fakes,\nspins or runs", (-8.6, 8.4), target=(-4.4, 2.8))
label(fld, sw, "blocking back (B):\nthe lead blocker", (-4.4, 12.4), target=(-2.1, 4.0))
plt.show()








Figure 54.2: The single wing (strength to the offense’s right; an illustrative alignment, since depths varied by team). The line is unbalanced: four men to the right of the center (both guards, a tackle and the end) and only two (a tackle and the end) to its left, so the play side has more blockers than a balanced line. This is the guard-over version; many teams moved a tackle over instead. Seven men are on the line, and the two at its ends (E) are eligible. There is no quarterback under center: the center snaps the ball through the air (dashed brown) to the tailback (T, aqua ring) about five yards deep, who can run, pass or hand off. The fullback (F) stands beside him, the blocking back (B), called the quarterback in its day, just behind the line, and the wingback (W) a yard off the line outside the right end.





Read it from the back, the way Classic Formations taught you to read any formation. There’s no one under center. The tailback, the star, stands four or five yards deep and takes a direct snap, a long toss between the center’s legs. Beside him is the fullback, a power runner and faker. Up near the line is the blocking back, who was called the quarterback but almost never threw: his job was to lead the play and call the signals. And just outside the end is the wingback, a runner on reverses and a receiver on passes. The line is unbalanced: one lineman from the weak side moves over to the strong side, so four players stand to the right of the center and only two, a tackle and an end, to its left. In the picture it’s a guard (both guards, a tackle and the end on the right); many teams moved a tackle over instead, which made the strong side guard, tackle, tackle, end. Either way the point was the same.

Why it existed
The single wing was built for a game in which the run was everything and the pass was an occasional surprise, and it solved that game’s problems well.
More blockers than the defense had defenders at the point of attack. Look at the right side of the line in the picture: both guards, a tackle and the end, the wingback and the blocking back, plus the fullback, all on one side. The signature play, the off-tackle power, sent nearly all of them at one spot, and the formation was built so that the key defender there could be double-teamed.
A runner who could also throw. Because the tailback caught the snap standing up, five yards deep, every run started as a possible pass, and every pass as a possible run. The great tailbacks were triple-threat players: they could run, pass and punt, which in the low-scoring game of the era was as valuable as anything else they did.
Deception from the backfield. With the ball snapped to either deep back, the backs could spin, fake and hand off behind the line. The single wing’s spinner plays (the fullback takes the snap, turns his back to the defense and either keeps it or hands to a back circling behind him) and its reverses to the wingback were built to make the defense guess.
A note on the letters in the next three pictures. They show the defenses of the 1930s and ’40s, which used the era’s names: E end, T tackle, G guard, L linebacker, H halfback (a defensive back), S safety. Defenders are always orange squares and offensive players blue circles, so a blue T is the single wing’s tailback and an orange T is a defensive tackle. From the Lombardi section on, the 4-3 letters of Part 5 take over: S, M and W are the Sam, Mike and Will linebackers, and the safeties are FS and SS.


Show the Python
def era_six_man():
    """A six-man front of the 1930s, shifted toward the single wing's strong (right) side."""
    return [D("DE_L", "DE", 1.3, -5.0, "E"), D("DT_L", "DT", 1.3, -2.4, "T"),
            D("DG_L", "DT", 1.3, 0.3, "G"), D("DG_R", "DT", 1.3, 3.0, "G"),
            D("DT_R", "DT", 1.3, 5.6, "T"), D("DE_R", "DE", 1.3, 9.0, "E"),
            D("LB_L", "LB", 4.0, -0.6, "L"), D("LB_R", "LB", 4.0, 5.0, "L"),
            D("HB_L", "DB", 8.0, -11.5, "H"), D("HB_R", "DB", 7.5, 11.6, "H"), D("S", "S", 13.5, 1.5, "S")]


sw_pw = [OL("WG", 1.6, "G") if q.key == "WG" else q for q in single_wing()]
pw = Play(sw_pw, era_six_man(), los=40, to_go=None)
# the defense reacts first (blocks aim at where these men end up)
pw.path("DT_R", [(2.2, 4.6)], absolute=True, delay=0.15, speed=1.6)     # driven inside by the double team
pw.path("DE_R", [(0.8, 9.9)], absolute=True, delay=0.1, speed=2.5)      # steps upfield, gets kicked out
pw.path("LB_R", [(3.2, 6.9)], absolute=True, delay=0.45, speed=3.0)     # fills the hole
pw.path("LB_L", [(3.2, 1.6)], absolute=True, delay=0.45, speed=3.0)
pw.path("HB_R", [(6.0, 10.6)], absolute=True, delay=0.6, speed=4.0)
pw.path("S", [(10.0, 6.5)], absolute=True, delay=0.6, speed=4.5)
# the blocks
pw.block("SE", pts=[(2.6, -0.5)], speed=2.2)                  # end: down on the tackle
pw.block("WB", pts=[(2.2, -2.6)], speed=2.6)                  # wingback: the other half of the double team
pw.block("ST", target="DG_R", speed=2.0)
pw.block("C", target="DG_L", speed=2.0)
pw.block("WT", target="DT_L", speed=2.0)
pw.block("SG", target="LB_L", speed=3.0)
pw.block("BB", target="DE_R", speed=4.0)                      # blocking back: the kick-out
pw.block("FB", pts=[(2.4, 2.4), (6.4, 4.6)], speed=5.5, delay=0.2)    # fullback: lead through the hole
pw.pull("WG", [(-1.2, 0.4), (-1.5, 3.6), (0.9, 5.6), (5.2, 8.8)], speed=5.2)  # inside guard pulls and leads
pw.run("QB", [(-4.6, 2.2), (-2.8, 5.4), (0.2, 7.5), (3.0, 8.4), (7.0, 8.6)], absolute=True, delay=0.45,
       speed=7.0)


def count_panel(fld, i):
    """Frame 1 only: shade the strong side and count blockers against defenders."""
    if i != 0:
        return
    (xa, ya), (xb, yb) = XY(fld, pw, -5.9, 0.9), XY(fld, pw, 8.6, 13.1)
    fld.ax.add_patch(Rectangle((min(xa, xb), min(ya, yb)), abs(xb - xa), abs(yb - ya), fc=style.OFFENSE,
                               alpha=0.07, ec=style.OFFENSE, lw=0.6, ls=(0, (3, 2)), zorder=0.6))
    label(fld, pw, "right of the ball:\n7 blockers, 5 defenders", (6.6, 5.6), fs=6.8)


animation_or_strip(pw, [0.0, 0.6, 1.4, 2.6], lateral=(-6.0, 13.5), window=(-6.3, 9.3),
                   rings=[("QB", BACK_RING), ("WG", style.OFFENSE_DARK)], mark_r=0.58, extra=count_panel,
                   notes=["count: seven blockers\nto five defenders",
                          "double team, kick-out;\nthe inside guard (G) pulls",
                          "fullback and guard lead\nthrough the hole",
                          "the tailback follows\nhis blockers"])





  
  Your browser does not support the video tag.



Figure 54.3: The single wing’s bread-and-butter play, the off-tackle power to the strong side, against a six-man front of the era (six linemen, two linebackers L, two defensive halfbacks H and a safety; an illustrative reconstruction; the far-side halfback and the safety are beyond the top and left of the picture). (1) Count before the snap: right of the ball the offense has seven blockers (shaded) against five defenders. (2) The snap has flown back to the tailback (T, aqua ring). The right end and the wingback double-team the defensive tackle (orange T), the blocking back (B) kicks out the defensive end (E), and the inside guard (G, dark ring), the one next to the center, pulls behind the line to lead. (3) The fullback (F) and the guard lead through the hole onto the linebacker and the halfback. (4) The tailback follows his blockers off the tackle’s outside hip.






What it gave up
Everything in the single wing was slow. The snap traveled five yards through the air before anything could happen, the tailback started from a standstill, and the play took a long time to reach the line. The defense could see who had the ball; it couldn’t always see what he would do with it, but it knew where to look. And the formation demanded one extraordinary athlete: a tailback who ran, passed, punted and often played defense too. A team without one had no offense.
The defenses of the era matched it man for man. Six or seven linemen stood shoulder to shoulder, with one or two linebackers behind them and three defensive backs, as in the picture: a run defense with a little pass insurance.

text:
1940: 73–0 and the T’s takeover
The T-formation was older than the single wing. What was new in 1940 was a version of it that worked. Classic Formations drew the T-formation and explained its logic: the quarterback’s hands under the center, an instant snap, backs who hit the line at full speed, and a ball handler who can fake to one back and give to another with his back to the defense. Here is how it took over.


Show the Python
def t_formation():
    return check_legal(line5() + [
        P("LE", "TE", LINE_D, -6.2, "E"), P("RE", "TE", LINE_D, 6.2, "E"),
        P("QB", "QB", UC, 0.0, "Q"), P("LH", "HB", -4.6, -3.0, "H"), P("FB", "FB", -4.6, 0.0, "F"),
        P("RH", "HB", -4.6, 3.0, "H")])


LAT, WIN = (-10.5, 13.5), (-9.2, 2.2)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 6.6 / 2 * (WIN[1] - WIN[0]) / (LAT[1] - LAT[0]) + 0.35))
for ax, (form, name) in zip(axes, [(single_wing(), "Single wing: direct snap"),
                                   (t_formation(), "T-formation: under center")]):
    pl = Play(form, None, los=40, to_go=None)
    pl.highlight("QB", color=BACK_RING)
    fl = pl.draw(ax=ax, lateral=LAT, window=WIN, title=False)
    hide_yard_numbers(ax)
    ax.set_title(name, fontsize=9, color=style.INK, loc="left", fontweight="bold")
    if form[0].key == "WE":
        (x0, y0), (x1, y1) = XY(fl, pl, 0.0, 0.0), XY(fl, pl, -4.2, 0.55)
        ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((x0, y0), (x1, y1), arrowstyle="-|>", mutation_scale=8, color=style.BALL,
                                     lw=1.2, ls=(0, (2, 2)), zorder=5, connectionstyle="arc3,rad=0.25"))
        label(fl, pl, "the snap flies\n5 yards", (-7.2, -6.0), target=(-2.6, 0.35), fs=6.6)
        label(fl, pl, "unbalanced:\n4 right, 2 left", (-7.4, 9.6), fs=6.6)
    else:
        label(fl, pl, "hand-to-hand snap:\nthe ball is out at once", (-7.4, -5.6), fs=6.6)
        label(fl, pl, "balanced line:\nthe same both sides", (-7.4, 9.0), fs=6.6)
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.005, right=0.995, top=0.9, bottom=0.01, wspace=0.04)
plt.show()








Figure 54.4: The two formations side by side, at the same scale (illustrative alignments). Left, the single wing: an unbalanced line, the ball snapped through the air to a tailback (T, aqua ring) about five yards deep, and three backs stacked to the strong side. Right, the T: a balanced line, the quarterback (Q, aqua ring) with his hands under the center, and three backs in a row about four and a half yards behind him. The T’s ball is in the quarterback’s hands the instant it moves, and the backs, all the same depth, can hit either side of the line.





The difference is all in the first second. The single wing’s tailback has to catch a five-yard toss before he can do anything; the T’s quarterback has the ball the instant the center moves it, and he can hand it to a back who is already moving toward the line.
The Chicago Bears’ coach and owner, George Halas, had stuck with a version of the T through the single-wing years, and his coach of 1930–32, Ralph Jones, is usually credited with adding a back in motion before the snap and spreading the ends and the backs to give it room. Clark Shaughnessy, a bookish, obsessive coach who worked with Halas as a consultant, refined it further. In 1940 Shaughnessy installed his version at Stanford, which had gone 1–7–1 the year before; Stanford went undefeated and won the Rose Bowl. In Chicago, Halas had found the quarterback the system needed: Sid Luckman, a single-wing tailback at Columbia, whom the Bears turned into a T quarterback who could take the snap, turn, fake, and drop back to throw.6






NoteFilm room: Chicago Bears, December 8, 1940



Three weeks before the 1940 NFL Championship Game, Washington had beaten the Bears 7–3, and its owner, George Preston Marshall, told reporters the Bears were “crybabies and quitters when the going got tough.” Halas pinned the articles up for his players. Shaughnessy, meanwhile, studied the game film and saw that Washington’s linebackers shifted with the Bears’ man in motion, so he drew up plays that went back the other way. On the Bears’ second play from scrimmage, fullback Bill Osmanski ran 68 yards for a touchdown. The final was 73–0, still the most lopsided result in NFL history. The Bears scored 11 touchdowns, ten different players scored, and Chicago intercepted 8 passes. Asked whether it would have been different if his receiver had caught a sure touchdown pass Washington dropped early in the game, Washington’s quarterback Sammy Baugh is supposed to have said: “Sure. The final score would have been 73–7.”7
What to notice (in the NFL Films highlights): how fast the backs reach the line after the snap, and how often the play goes away from where the motion man went.




Show the Python

            D("DG_R", "DT", 1.2, 1.25, "G"), D("DT_R", "DT", 1.0, 3.8, "T"), D("DE_R", "DE", 1.0, 7.4, "E"),

       absolute=True, speed=5.5, delay=0.1)

(3) The quarterback (Q) turns, the fullback (F) fakes a dive to the right, and the ball goes to the left halfback (aqua ring), who has taken a jab step right and now cuts back left. (4) The linebackers, still flowing toward the motion and the fake, are on the wrong side of the hole.




The rout settled the argument. Within a decade almost every college and pro team had switched to the T, and the Pittsburgh Steelers, the NFL’s last single-wing team, gave it up after the 1952 season.8






CautionCommon misconception



“Halas and Shaughnessy invented the T-formation.” They didn’t, and they never claimed to. A tight T with the quarterback under center was one of football’s oldest formations, and the Bears had used one all along. What Jones, Halas and Shaughnessy built was the modern T: man-in-motion, wider spacing, quick-hitting plays designed to make a defense commit, and a quarterback trained to fake and throw. The lesson repeats through this whole part of the book: formations are rarely invented; they’re re-equipped for a new problem.



Why the T won
The T’s advantages were speed and deception, and both came from the snap. The single wing’s tailback needed a second just to receive the ball; the T’s quarterback had it instantly, and his backs could be at the line in the time it took a single-wing snap to arrive. But the deepest reason was the quarterback. In the single wing, the man who threw also had to run, block and often punt. In the T, one player did nothing but handle the ball and throw it, from a few yards behind his line, facing his receivers after a short drop. That made him a specialist, and specialists improve faster than generalists. Every modern quarterback descends from Luckman more than from any single-wing tailback.


What the T gave up, and what football did about it
The T as the Bears ran it had two tight ends and three backs: lots of runners and almost no width. Over the next decade coaches pulled its players outward into the pro set of two backs, a tight end and two wide receivers (Classic Formations has the family tree, including Shaughnessy’s 1949 Rams flanking Elroy Hirsch wide9). The other thing the T needed was a different kind of roster, and that required a change in the rules.

title: From the Single Wing to the 1970s Scoring Drought (1906–1977)
text:
Platoon football: the specialist arrives
Until the 1940s the rules made substitution hard: a player who left the game generally couldn’t come back in the same quarter, so the same eleven men played offense and defense. The star tailback was also a defensive back. The quarterback tackled. Linemen had to be big enough to block and quick enough to chase.
Free substitution changed all of that. The colleges allowed it in 1941, and the NFL in 1943, both partly because the war had thinned rosters. In 1945 Michigan’s Fritz Crisler, facing a much stronger Army team, used it to send in separate units for offense and defense, and the idea spread. The NFL made unlimited substitution permanent in 1950. The colleges went the other way for a while: in 1953 they went back to limited substitution, mostly over cost, because fielding two full units had pushed dozens of small schools to drop football altogether, and they didn’t restore free substitution until 1965. That gap is part of why the pros pulled ahead in specialization.10
The two-way player didn’t vanish overnight. In 1960 injuries pushed the Philadelphia Eagles to use Chuck Bednarik, a 12-year veteran, on both sides of the line again, at center and linebacker. In that season’s championship game he played 58 of the 60 minutes and made the game-saving tackle, wrestling Green Bay’s Jim Taylor to the ground as time ran out. He is remembered as one of the last of the NFL’s two-way stars.11
That is platoon football: separate groups of players for offense and defense, and eventually for kicking plays and particular situations.

Why it mattered
Platooning sounds like a roster rule. It was really a revolution in what a player could be.

Bodies could specialize. An offensive lineman no longer needed to chase a halfback; he could get bigger and stronger and learn to pass block. A defensive back no longer needed to run the ball; he could be the fastest man on the field and learn to cover.
Skills could specialize. A T quarterback could spend his whole practice throwing. A defensive end could spend his rushing. The pass-catching end became a receiver who ran routes for a living.
Coaching could specialize. Two units meant two sets of schemes, and soon two sets of coaches: the ancestors of today’s offensive and defensive coordinators.

Everything after this point in the chapter is an argument between specialists.






NoteMadden vs. real life



In Madden you never think about who plays defense when your offense is on the field: there are 53 players and the game substitutes for you. For football’s first half-century that roster didn’t exist. NFL roster limits ran from about 20 players in the early 1930s to the low and mid-30s in the ’40s, and the best players stayed on the field for both halves of every possession.12 The whole modern idea of personnel groupings (Part 2) depends on free substitution. Before 1943 there were no groupings to choose between: to borrow the phrase in a different sense, a team’s “11 personnel” was simply its eleven best players, and they were the defense too.

section: Paul Brown: football becomes a profession
text:
Paul Brown: football becomes a profession
The coach who did the most with those specialists was Paul Brown. He had built winners at Massillon (Ohio) High School and at Ohio State, where his 1942 team won the national championship, and in 1946 he became head coach of a new professional team named after him, the Cleveland Browns of the All-America Football Conference (AAFC), a rival league. The Browns won all four AAFC championships (1946–49). When the AAFC folded and the Browns joined the NFL in 1950, the established league assumed they would be humbled. In their first NFL game, against the two-time defending champion Philadelphia Eagles, the Browns won 35–10. They won the NFL title that season and again in 1954 and 1955, and they played in the championship game in each of their first ten seasons (AAFC and NFL) with Otto Graham at quarterback.13
Brown’s innovations matter more than his trophies, because almost all of them are still standard:

A full-time, year-round coaching staff, at a time when many assistants were part-timers.
The playbook as a textbook. Players got detailed books of formations and plays, attended classroom sessions, and took written tests on them. Brown also gave them intelligence tests.
Film study. Brown is credited with being the first coach to use game film to scout opponents, breaking down what the other team did before playing it.
Measurable athletes. He timed players over 40 yards, a distance he adopted at Ohio State in 1941, by the usual account because it was about how far a player ran on a punt cover (his son Mike remembers it as simply the longest sprint a player usually had to make). The 40-yard dash is still the most famous number at the NFL Combine.
The draw play, which Brown dated to an accident in 1946: Otto Graham, about to be sacked, handed the ball to his fullback, Marion Motley, who ran through a defense that had dropped back for a pass. (A draw play is a run disguised as a pass: the linemen show pass protection, then the ball goes to a back.)
Integration. In 1946 Brown signed Motley and guard Bill Willis, two of the first Black players in modern pro football.


The coach calls the plays
The innovation that changed the game most directly was who called the plays. Before Brown, the quarterback called them in the huddle. Brown called them from the sideline, and to get his calls in, he rotated two guards on every play: each messenger guard came in with the call and the other went out. Guards were the natural men to shuttle. Two guards of similar size and skill could swap every play without changing what the offense could do, whereas swapping a back or a receiver would have changed the personnel on the field, and the quarterback had to stay in to run the play. One of them, from 1953 to 1959, was a smart, undersized lineman named Chuck Noll, who, Brown said, soon could have called the plays himself; Noll later coached the 1970s Steelers. In 1956 Brown went further and tested a radio receiver in his quarterback’s helmet. The Detroit Lions spotted the transmitter during a preseason game, and Commissioner Bert Bell banned the device after a handful of games. The NFL legalized helmet radios in 1994.14
A coach choosing every play from the sideline is so normal now (see What a Play Really Is) that it’s easy to miss how radical it was. It moved the brain of the offense from the field to the staff, and it made the game plan, built from film during the week, the center of football. Every coordinator with a laminated call sheet works in a system Paul Brown designed.






NoteFilm room: Cleveland Browns vs. Philadelphia Eagles, 1950



The Browns’ first NFL game, on September 16, 1950, was the AAFC champion against the NFL champion, and Otto Graham passed for 346 yards and three touchdowns in a 35–10 win. The Eagles’ coach, Greasy Neale, whose five-man Eagle defense had won the previous two NFL titles, grumbled that the Browns were like a basketball team, all they did was throw. When the teams met again on December 3, in rain in Cleveland, Brown answered him: the Browns won 13–7 without a single official pass attempt. (The two passes Graham threw were both called back by penalties.) No NFL team since has played a whole game without attempting a pass.15
What to notice: the point Brown was making. A team whose opponent can only stop one thing doesn’t have to do only one thing. The pass had become a weapon because it was no longer the only weapon.

section: The defense answers: Steve Owen’s umbrella
text:
The defense answers: Steve Owen’s umbrella
First, what had the defense done about the T? Through the 1940s, most teams’ answer was more men on the line and more men deep. The most successful version was Greasy Neale’s Eagle defense in Philadelphia, a 5-2-4 from 1947: five linemen, with a middle guard head-up on the center, two linebackers behind them, and four defensive backs instead of the three of the single-wing era, the extra one for the T’s passes. The Eagles won the 1948 and 1949 titles with it. Odd and Hybrid Fronts follows the five-man line from there to the 3-4. Its soft spot was the middle: with no linebacker over the center, a quick pass over the middle guard’s head had room.16 Keep that in mind; it comes back in a few pages.
Brown’s passing game created a problem defenses of 1950 had never had to solve. Most NFL teams still lined up with five or six linemen and only three or four defensive backs, and the Browns sent out receivers like Dante Lavelli and Mac Speedie, plus a flanker, plus backs who ran routes. There were more receivers than defenders who could cover them.
The first team to solve it was the New York Giants. Their head coach, Steve Owen, a heavyset Oklahoman who had been coaching the Giants since 1930 and had won the NFL title in 1934 and 1938, built a defense for the 1950 Browns that looked like a run defense and played like a pass defense. Owen called it a 6-1-4, and in his own words, on many plays it became “a 4-1-6 in reality.” The secret was the two defensive ends: they lined up on the line of scrimmage like linemen, and at the snap they could drop back into pass coverage. The four defensive backs behind them, spread in an arc like the ribs of an umbrella, gave the defense its name: the umbrella defense. One of those defensive backs, a young Texan named Tom Landry, explained it to the others and taught it on the field.17


Show the Python
def browns_t():
    return check_legal(line5() + [
        P("QB", "QB", UC, 0.0, "Q"), P("FB", "FB", -4.6, 0.0, "F"), P("HB", "HB", -4.6, 2.4, "H"),
        P("X", "WR", LINE_D, -12.0), P("Y", "TE", LINE_D, 9.6, "Y"), P("Z", "WR", OFF_BALL, 14.5)])


def umbrella_def():
    return [D("dLE", "DE", 1.0, -6.4, "E"), D("dLT", "DT", 1.0, -3.4, "T"), D("dLG", "DT", 1.0, -1.0, "G"),
            D("dRG", "DT", 1.0, 1.0, "G"), D("dRT", "DT", 1.0, 3.4, "T"), D("dRE", "DE", 1.0, 6.4, "E"),
            D("M", "MIKE", 4.0, 0.0, "M"),
            D("LH", "DB", 7.0, -12.5, "H"), D("RH", "DB", 7.0, 13.5, "H"),
            D("LS", "S", 11.5, -5.0, "S"), D("RS", "S", 11.5, 5.5, "S")]


um = Play(browns_t(), umbrella_def(), los=35, to_go=None)
um.dropback(5.0)
um.route("X", [(0, 0), (12.0, 0), (10.8, -1.5)])        # curl
um.route("Y", [(0, 0), (11.0, 0), (11.0, 5.0)])         # sideline out
um.route("Z", [(0, 0), (15.0, -0.5)])                   # go
um.route("HB", [(0, 0), (-0.6, 3.5), (1.5, 8.0)], side=1)  # swing to the flat
um.block("FB", pts=[(0.6, -1.5)], speed=2.0)
um.drop("dLE", (6.5, -11.0), delay=0.1)
um.drop("dRE", (6.0, 12.4), delay=0.3)
um.drop("M", (8.5, 0.5), delay=0.15)
um.drop("LH", (13.5, -13.6), delay=0.1)
um.drop("RH", (13.6, 12.0), delay=0.1)
um.drop("LS", (16.8, -5.0), delay=0.1)
um.drop("RS", (16.8, 5.5), delay=0.1)
for k in ("dLT", "dLG", "dRG", "dRT"):            # four rush and meet the blockers
    um.path(k, [(-0.1, um.players[k].w)], absolute=True, speed=1.5)
for k in ("LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT"):
    um.block(k, pts=[(-1.4, 0.0)], speed=1.2)
animation_or_strip(um, [0.0, 0.7, 1.4, 2.2], lateral=(-15.0, 17.0), window=(-8.5, 19.5),
                   rings=[("dLE", KEY_RING), ("dRE", KEY_RING)], mark_r=0.9, width_in=5.6,
                   notes=["snap: a 6-1-4, six men\non the line",
                          "the two ends turn and drop",
                          "the ends reach the flats;\nthe umbrella opens",
                          "a 4-1-6: four rush,\nseven cover"])





  
  Your browser does not support the video tag.



Figure 54.6: Owen’s umbrella against a Browns-style pass (an illustrative reconstruction: the Browns’ formation and routes varied). (1) Before the snap the Giants show a 6-1-4: six men on the line, one linebacker (M) and four defensive backs (two halfbacks H, two safeties S) in an arc, the umbrella. The two ends (E, orange rings) stand at the ends of the line. (2–3) At the snap the ends drop into the short outside zones (the flats), the linebacker drops to the middle, and the halfbacks and safeties retreat, the halfbacks staying shallower and wider so the arc keeps its umbrella shape. (4) Against the pass it is now a 4-1-6: four rushers and seven defenders in coverage, more than the five receivers the offense can send. Against a run, those same two ends are the defense’s edge (contain) players, which is the umbrella’s trade: an end who drops on a run has left the edge open. Offense: Q quarterback, F fullback, H halfback, X and Y split ends, Z flanker.




It worked. On October 1, 1950, the Giants beat the Browns 6–0, the first time Cleveland had ever been shut out, and they beat them again, 17–13, later in the season. Cleveland lost only those two games and then beat the Giants 8–3 in a playoff on the way to the title, but the umbrella had shown what mattered: a defense that can change its shape after the snap can show one thing and play another. That’s the seed of every disguise in Part 6.
The trade, as always, was real. An umbrella end who dropped into coverage on a run play was out of position, and on a pass the defense rushed only four men instead of the six the era was used to. Against a team with a dangerous runner who could hit a draw (Brown had Motley), dropping the ends could be expensive.

From the umbrella to the 4-3
The 4-3 came from two different parents, each of which gave up a lineman.
The first parent is the umbrella. Its dropping ends were really linebackers who started on the line. Stand them up for good and the 6-1-4 becomes four linemen, three linebackers (the two ends and the one linebacker) and four defensive backs.
The second parent is the five-man front of the Eagle family. Its weak spot, you’ll remember, was the middle. In 1954 the Bears’ middle guard, Bill George, kept getting beaten by quick passes thrown over his head, so he started standing up and backing off the line at the snap. Do that in a 5-2-4 and it becomes four linemen, three linebackers (the two and George) and four defensive backs. George is usually named as the first true middle linebacker, though the Hall of Fame itself says no one can be sure which middle guard first dropped back.18


Show the Python
def tier(ax, x0, rows, moved=(), title=""):
    """rows: counts per level (DL, LB, DB); moved: (row, index) pairs to ring."""
    ys = [0.0, -1.0, -2.0]
    for r, (n, y) in enumerate(zip(rows, ys)):
        xs = [x0 + (i - (n - 1) / 2) * 0.55 for i in range(n)]
        for i, x in enumerate(xs):
            ax.add_patch(RegularPolygon((x, y), 4, radius=0.2, orientation=np.pi / 4, fc=style.DEFENSE_TINT,
                                        ec=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.0, zorder=3))
            if (r, i) in moved:
                ax.add_patch(Circle((x, y), 0.27, fc="none", ec=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.6, zorder=4))
    ax.text(x0, 0.75, title, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=8.6, fontweight="bold", color=style.INK)
    ax.text(x0, -2.75, "-".join(str(n) for n in rows), ha="center", va="center", fontsize=8.0, color=style.INK_2)


fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.6, 2.1))
ax.set_xlim(-0.2, 12.2); ax.set_ylim(-3.1, 1.1); ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.axis("off")
tier(ax, 1.85, (6, 1, 4), moved={(0, 0), (0, 5)}, title="Umbrella (1950)")
tier(ax, 6.0, (4, 3, 4), title="4-3 (Landry, 1956)")
tier(ax, 10.15, (5, 2, 4), moved={(0, 2)}, title="Eagle-style 5-2-4")
for xa, xb, txt in [(3.75, 4.85, "ends\nstand up"), (8.65, 7.15, "middle guard\nstands up")]:
    ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((xa, -1.0), (xb, -1.0), arrowstyle="-|>", mutation_scale=11,
                                 color=style.INK_2, lw=1.2))
    ax.text((xa + xb) / 2, -0.45, txt, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=6.8, color=style.INK_2)
plt.show()








Figure 54.7: Two roads to the 4-3 (a schematic, not to scale; each row is a level of the defense: linemen, linebackers, defensive backs). Left, Owen’s 6-1-4 umbrella: stand its two ends up (orange rings) and they become outside linebackers. Right, the 5-2-4 Eagle-style front: stand the middle guard up (orange ring) and he becomes the middle linebacker. Both arrive at the same place, in the middle: four linemen, three linebackers, four defensive backs.





Landry took both moves at once: the umbrella’s idea of ends who could play off the line became his outside linebackers, and George’s stand-up middle guard became his middle linebacker. Four linemen, three linebackers and four defensive backs: the 4-3. Landry, by then the Giants’ defensive coach, made it the Giants’ base defense in 1956, built around a rookie middle linebacker from West Virginia, Sam Huff. The Giants won the 1956 championship, much of the league copied the defense the following season, and Huff became so famous that CBS made a television documentary about him, The Violent World of Sam Huff (1960, an episode of Walter Cronkite’s The Twentieth Century). The 4-3 would be the NFL’s standard defense for the next two decades.19 A First Look at Defense and Even Fronts cover how it lines up today.
Why did the 4-3 win? Because it was the first defense balanced for both threats. Four linemen are enough to rush a passer; three linebackers can stop a run or drop into coverage; four defensive backs can cover the receivers that platoon football had produced. It was the defense equivalent of the pro set: good at everything, great at nothing in particular.

text:
Lombardi’s sweep and Landry’s Flex

The offense: run to daylight
Vince Lombardi arrived in Green Bay in 1959 as a 45-year-old assistant who had never been a head coach in the NFL. (He had been the Giants’ offensive coach, across the hall from Landry, in the 1950s.) His Packers won five NFL championships in seven seasons, 1961–67, including the first two Super Bowls, and the play everyone associated with them was the power sweep. Gap and Power Runs draws it block by block; here is the version that matters for the history.


Show the Python
def pro_set_red():
    """Split backs set wide apart (Lombardi's 'Red'), tight end and flanker to the right."""
    return check_legal(line5() + [
        P("QB", "QB", UC, 0.0, "Q"), P("HB", "HB", -5.0, -2.8, "H"), P("FB", "FB", -5.0, 2.8, "F"),
        P("Y", "TE", LINE_D, TE_W, "Y"), P("X", "WR", LINE_D, -14.0), P("Z", "WR", OFF_BALL, 11.0)])


def base43_60s(fix=None):
    d = [D("WDE", "DE", 1.0, -4.0, "E"), D("WDT", "DT", 1.0, -0.8, "T"), D("SDT", "DT", 1.0, 2.4, "T"),
         D("SDE", "DE", 1.0, 4.2, "E"), D("SAM", "SAM", 3.6, 6.4, "S"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.3, 0.6, "M"),
         D("WILL", "WILL", 4.3, -3.2, "W"), D("LCB", "CB", 7.0, -14.0, "C"), D("RCB", "CB", 7.0, 11.0, "C"),
         D("FS", "FS", 12.0, -6.0, "FS"), D("SS", "SS", 11.0, 7.5, "SS")]
    fix = fix or {}
    return [q.moved(**fix[q.key]) if q.key in fix else q for q in d]


sweep_off = [OL(q.key, q.w, "G") if q.key in ("LG", "RG") else q for q in pro_set_red()]
sweep = Play(sweep_off, base43_60s(), los=35, to_go=None)
sweep.path("MIKE", [(3.4, 4.0)], absolute=True, delay=0.4, speed=3.5)
sweep.block("Y", target="SAM")
sweep.block("RT", target="SDT")
sweep.block("C", target="WDT")
sweep.block("LT", pts=[(0.9, 0.5)])
sweep.block("FB", target="SDE", speed=4.0)
sweep.pull("RG", [(-0.6, 0.6), (-0.7, 5.9), (2.2, 8.4), (6.0, 9.4)], speed=5.0)     # onside guard: the corner
sweep.pull("LG", [(-1.5, 1.2), (-1.6, 6.6), (1.6, 7.2), (3.8, 5.3)], speed=5.0)     # offside guard: up inside
sweep.block("Z", target="SS", speed=3.0)
sweep.path("QB", [(-2.7, -1.1), (-3.2, -1.6)], absolute=True, speed=3.0)
sweep.handoff("HB", t=0.8)
sweep.run("HB", [(-5.1, -0.6), (-6.0, 2.4), (-4.0, 5.3), (-0.6, 6.4)], absolute=True, speed=6.2)
sweep.highlight("HB", color=BACK_RING)
sweep.highlight("LG", "RG", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK)
fld = draw_play(sweep, lateral=(-16.5, 19.0), window=(-8.0, 15.5))
dashed_arrow(fld, sweep, [(-0.6, 6.4), (2.8, 6.0), (6.4, 5.4)])
dashed_arrow(fld, sweep, [(-0.6, 6.4), (2.6, 8.6), (6.2, 11.8)])
label(fld, sweep, "daylight: inside\nthe Sam", (8.6, 3.6), color=THREAT)
label(fld, sweep, "or outside\nhim", (8.9, 14.6), color=THREAT)
label(fld, sweep, "right guard: kicks out\nor logs the corner", (13.0, 13.4), target=(5.3, 9.3))
label(fld, sweep, "left guard: turns up\ninside, on the Mike", (9.0, -9.0), target=(3.7, 4.4))
label(fld, sweep, "the halfback reads\nthe Sam's block here", (-6.4, 11.4), target=(-0.6, 6.4))
label(fld, sweep, "split backs, set wide", (-6.6, -7.0))
plt.show()








Figure 54.8: Lombardi’s power sweep to the right from split backs (an illustrative reconstruction against a 1960s 4-3; landmarks varied). Both guards (G, dark rings) pull: the right guard to the first defender outside (here the cornerback), the left guard turning up inside for the pursuit (the Mike). The fullback (F) blocks the defensive end, the tight end (Y) takes the Sam linebacker (S), and the flanker (Z) blocks the strong safety. The halfback (H, aqua ring) takes the handoff, presses the edge about a yard outside the tight end and reads the block on the Sam there: if the Sam is driven outside, he cuts inside it; if the Sam fights inside, he runs around it. That choice is ‘running to daylight.’





The sweep’s genius was that it didn’t need to fool anyone. Lombardi drilled it until every block was automatic, and the runner was given a lane, not a hole. A hole is a fixed spot the play is designed to hit (“between the guard and the tackle”), and the back runs there whatever happens. A lane is wherever the defense isn’t once the blocks are made: the blockers take defenders the way they want to go, and the back finds the opening the blocks create. Lombardi’s own phrase for it, and the title of his 1963 book, was run to daylight. The defense knew the sweep was coming, and the Packers ran it anyway.
Underneath the sweep was a blocking idea that defenses found maddening, which coaches of the era called option blocking (not to be confused with the option offense, where the quarterback reads a defender). Here the blocker has the choice. Say the tight end’s job is the Sam linebacker. If the Sam steps outside, the tight end doesn’t fight to move him back in; he rides him farther outside, and the runner cuts inside. If the Sam steps inside, the tight end seals him there, and the runner goes around. Block the man where he goes, not to a spot, and let the runner read the result. The pulling guards read the same block: the right guard logs the cornerback inside or kicks him out, depending on which side of him he can reach, and the left guard turns up through whichever seam the tight end’s block has opened. A defense built on linemen charging hard into the backfield, each guessing his own way, helped option blocking. The harder a lineman charged, the easier he was to push past the hole, and the daylight appeared behind him.


The answer: the Flex
Tom Landry left the Giants to become the first head coach of the expansion Dallas Cowboys in 1960. His problem, as the Cowboys grew into contenders, was Green Bay. His answer, developed in the mid-1960s (sources date its first use anywhere from 1964 to 1966), was the Flex defense.20


Show the Python
flex_fix = {"SDE": dict(d=2.2, w=4.2), "WDT": dict(d=2.2, w=-0.9), "SDT": dict(w=2.4), "WDE": dict(w=-4.0),
            "SAM": dict(d=3.4, w=5.7), "MIKE": dict(d=4.6, w=0.8), "WILL": dict(d=4.6, w=-2.4)}
box_off = [q for q in pro_set_red() if q.key not in ("X", "Z")]               # zoomed on the box
box_def = [q for q in base43_60s(flex_fix) if q.key not in ("LCB", "RCB", "FS", "SS")]
fx = Play(box_off, box_def, los=35, to_go=None)
fx.highlight("SDE", "WDT", color=KEY_RING)
fld = draw_play(fx, lateral=(-10.5, 10.5), window=(-6.6, 10.6))
LANES = [("C", -4.8, -3.2), ("B", -3.2, -1.6), ("A", -1.6, 0.0), ("A", 0.0, 1.6), ("B", 1.6, 3.2),
