Figure 54.9: Landry’s Flex against the same split-backs formation (illustrative; which two linemen flexed changed with the formation and with what Dallas expected the offense to do; zoomed on the box, so the wide receivers are out of the picture). Two of the four defensive linemen (orange rings) line up about a yard off the ball, where they can read the blocks before they move; the other two stay on the line and charge into their gaps. The shaded lanes are the gaps between blockers (A next to the center, then B, C and D outward), and each lane has one defender standing in it: the ends (E) in the C gaps, the tackles (T) and the Mike (M) in the A and B gaps, the Will (W) in the weak-side B gap and the Sam (S) outside the tight end. A runner looking for daylight finds a defender already in every lane. Offense: Q quarterback, H halfback, F fullback, Y tight end.





In the Flex, two of the four defensive linemen line up about a yard off the ball while the other two stay on the line. The flexed linemen are in no hurry to charge: they read the blocks in front of them, then step into the gap they’re assigned. The linemen on the line attack their gaps. Linebackers fill the rest. The result is a defense in which every gap has an owner who is already standing in it before the runner arrives, which is exactly what run-to-daylight blocking can’t handle: there is no daylight to run to.
Why does a single yard matter so much? Think about it from the blocker’s side. Option blocking works on a defender who is already moving: you take his momentum and add to it. A flexed lineman isn’t moving. The yard of space means the blocker has to travel to reach him, which takes a moment, and in that moment the defender sees where the block is coming from. And because he hasn’t committed to a direction, there is no momentum for the blocker to use. A blocker trying to push a flexed defender “the way he wants to go” finds that he doesn’t want to go anywhere until he knows where the ball is.
But the two linemen on the ball do charge, so why weren’t they option-blocked? Because their charge is into an assigned gap, not a free-lance guess at where the play is going. A tackle who knows he owns the A gap gets there and holds it; if he is pushed past it, the flexed man behind him is reading that very block and steps into the space he left. The on-ball men, in other words, are there to occupy blockers and keep their own gaps, and the flexed men clean up behind them. Landry built it partly around the quickness of his great defensive tackle, Bob Lilly, who could play on the ball and get into his gap before a blocker touched him.
Why flex only two, and not all four? Because somebody still has to take on the blockers at the snap and threaten the quarterback. A line with all four men standing a yard off the ball reading would give the offense a free first step everywhere and no pass rush at all. Which two flexed changed with the offense’s formation and with where Dallas expected the run.
The Flex was Landry’s style in one picture: precise, rule-bound, analytical. Players learned exactly which step to take with which foot, which some of them hated. Its price was the pass rush from the Flex itself: linemen standing back reading blocks aren’t rushing the quarterback. So Dallas used it as a run-down defense, almost always on first down but mostly only in running situations on second and third, and on clear passing downs the linemen lined up on the ball and rushed. They could rush, too: the Cowboys’ defense of the 1970s, nicknamed the Doomsday Defense, had Harvey Martin, credited unofficially with 23 sacks in 1977.21 Dallas reached two straight NFL Championship Games against Green Bay, and later won Super Bowls after the 1971 and 1977 seasons with the Flex behind them. You have met its descendant: the idea that every defender owns a gap is the core of gap integrity and run fits.






NoteFilm room: Green Bay Packers vs. Dallas Cowboys, December 31, 1967



The 1967 NFL Championship Game, the “Ice Bowl,” was played in Green Bay in a temperature of about −13°F. It was Lombardi’s offense against Landry’s Flex for the second year in a row (Green Bay had won the 1966 title game 34–27). Trailing 17–14 late in the fourth quarter, the Packers drove the length of the field. The play that got them to the goal line was built to beat the Flex. On a call the Packers named 54-Give, which Lombardi called the “sucker” play, left guard Gale Gillingham pulled to his right as if it were the sweep. Bob Lilly, taught to read the guard in front of him and follow him, did exactly that, and fullback Chuck Mercein ran straight through the space Lilly had left, from the Dallas 11 to the 3. Then, with seconds left and the ball inside the 1-yard line, Bart Starr conferred with Lombardi and kept the ball on a quarterback sneak: he followed guard Jerry Kramer’s block (a double-team with center Ken Bowman) on Dallas tackle Jethro Pugh and scored with 13 seconds left. Green Bay won 21–17 and went on to win Super Bowl II.22
What to notice (NFL Films’ footage is everywhere): Mercein’s run. A defense that reads and follows blocks can be led away by a block that lies, which is the counterpunch to every read-and-react defense: an influence or “sucker” play. You’ll also notice how rarely either team breaks a long run; the frozen field explains as much of that as the Flex does.

section: Sid Gillman and the vertical passing game
text:
Sid Gillman and the vertical passing game
While Lombardi and Landry argued about the run, Sid Gillman was building the passing game you watch today. As a young man in Minneapolis, Gillman worked in his family’s movie theater and cut the football clips out of the newsreels so he could study them at home on a projector. He became the coach most associated with film study, and he used it to take passing apart. He coached the Los Angeles Rams (1955–59) and then the Chargers of the new AFL (1960–69), who won the 1963 AFL championship 51–10 over Boston.23
Gillman’s idea, in one sentence: use all of the field, deep and wide, so that the defense can’t protect all of it. Defenses of the 1950s and early ’60s were happy to let an offense throw short in front of them, and for a good reason: a short completion was a few yards and a tackle. To score that way an offense had to string together a long series of plays without an incompletion on a key down, a penalty or an interception (and interceptions were far more common then than now), so the defense’s first job was to stop the long ball and wait for the drive to die. Gillman threw deep first, with fast receivers like Lance Alworth, to push the safeties back, and then attacked the room that left underneath: intermediate routes, and backs released into the flats. As Al Davis, who coached under him, put it, people thought of the passing game as vertical, the length of the field, “but Sid also thought of it as horizontal.”
The mechanism under the slogan was timing. Gillman tied each route to the quarterback’s drop: on a five-step drop, the first receiver’s route was built to break just as the quarterback finished his last step, so the ball could leave before the receiver turned around, and the next receiver’s route came open a beat later for the next read.24 A defense can’t cover a throw that arrives before it has seen the receiver’s break. That idea, routes and drops on one clock, is what Don Coryell and Bill Walsh inherited.
He was building it, mostly, against man-to-man coverage. Much of the era’s pass defense, and especially the AFL’s, was man-to-man with a free safety behind it; the AFL is where the bump-and-run, a cornerback pressing his receiver and jamming him at the line, took hold in the 1960s, with Oakland’s Willie Brown its best-known practitioner. Beating man coverage is about getting one receiver open against one defender, and the whole-field spacing gave Gillman’s receivers room to do it. Remember that when you reach the 1970s: the defenses’ answer to the passing decade was to stop playing man and play zones as a team.


Show the Python
gl = Play(pro_set_red(), base43_60s({"FS": dict(d=12.0, w=-8.0)}), los=30, to_go=None)
gl.dropback(7.0)
gl.route("Z", [(0, 0), (6.0, 0.4), (27.0, 1.6)])
gl.route("X", [(0, 0), (16.0, 0), (14.0, 2.8)])
gl.route("Y", [(0, 0), (13.0, 0), (13.0, -8.4)])
gl.route("HB", [(0, 0), (2.0, 3.4), (8.0, 9.7)], side=-1)
gl.route("FB", [(0, 0), (2.0, 3.0), (8.0, 6.7)], side=1)
gl.drop("SS", (21.0, 9.5), delay=0.2)

Figure 54.10: Gillman’s principle with his AFL Chargers: stretch the defense deep and wide at once (an illustrative pass from split backs against a 1960s 4-3 with two safeties deep, not a specific Chargers play). The flanker’s go route (Z) runs at the deep safety (SS) and drives him back; the split end’s comeback (X) and the tight end’s dig (Y) settle in the intermediate band the safeties have just left (the dashed squares show where the safeties finish); the halfback and fullback release to the flats, so the linebackers have someone short to worry about on both sides. Three depths and the full width, on every pass: the defense can’t be everywhere.





Gillman’s coaching descendants are a who’s who of the next chapter: Al Davis (whose Raiders threw deep for thirty years), Chuck Noll, Bill Walsh (who coached under Davis in Oakland) and Dick Vermeil, and Don Coryell studied him closely. When you meet Air Coryell and the West Coast offense, you are meeting Gillman’s grandchildren. The vertical and horizontal stretches of Part 4 are his vocabulary.






NoteFilm room: San Diego Chargers, 1963 AFL Championship Game



On January 5, 1964, Gillman’s Chargers beat the Boston Patriots 51–10 in San Diego. The star was halfback Keith Lincoln, who ran for 206 yards on 13 carries and led the team with 123 receiving yards, the kind of two-way threat out of the backfield that Gillman’s spread-the-field passing game created room for.25
What to notice: how wide the Chargers’ receivers and backs spread the Patriots, and how many of the big plays come from backs running routes against linebackers.

title: From the Single Wing to the 1970s Scoring Drought (1906–1977)
text:
The AFL: a passing laboratory
In August 1959 a young Texan named Lamar Hunt, who had been refused an NFL expansion team, founded a league of his own. The AFL (American Football League) began play in 1960 with eight teams, and it needed fans, so it needed points.
The AFL was looser in almost every way. It added the two-point conversion (the NFL would not adopt it until 1994), put players’ names on their jerseys (a habit the NFL later copied), and shared its television money equally, including, from 1965, a five-year NBC contract worth $36 million that kept the league alive. Because it was scrambling for talent, it took players the NFL had overlooked: quarterbacks cut by NFL teams, small-college stars, and many players from historically Black colleges that NFL scouts had largely ignored.26
Why call it a passing laboratory? Because its best offenses built their identity on throwing deep to wide receivers. Gillman’s Chargers, the plate above, were the model: Alworth deep, the tight end and the backs underneath, every throw timed to the drop. Al Davis took the same idea to Oakland in 1963 and made the deep ball the Raiders’ trademark for decades: stretch the field vertically and use every eligible receiver.27 Quarterbacks like John Hadl, Len Dawson and Daryle Lamonica threw deep and often. The points chart below shows the result: in each of its first five seasons AFL teams outscored NFL teams, by close to three points a game in 1960 and 1961, and by about one point a game in 1962–64. And the AFL’s defenses answered in kind, with the bump-and-run corners you met above. The arms race of the next decade was rehearsed here.

Hank Stram’s Chiefs
The most inventive AFL coach after Gillman was Hank Stram, who led the Dallas Texans and then the Kansas City Chiefs from 1960 to 1974 and won three AFL titles (1962, 1966 and 1969). Stram’s contributions to the passing game and to everything around it:

The moving pocket. The protection shifted with a quarterback who set up somewhere other than straight behind the center, so the rushers had a moving target and the quarterback got a clear throwing lane. Part 4’s bootlegs and sprint-outs are its heirs.
New formations. He is credited with being the first pro coach to use both the I-formation and the two-tight-end offense.
The triple stack on defense. Linebackers hid directly behind defensive linemen, so the offense couldn’t tell which gap each would attack.
Talent from where others weren’t looking. He drafted heavily from historically Black colleges: defensive tackle Buck Buchanan (Grambling) and linebacker Willie Lanier (Morgan State) are both in the Hall of Fame.

In Super Bowl IV Stram wore a microphone for NFL Films, usually described as a first for a pro coach, and it caught him gleefully telling his team to keep “matriculating the ball down the field,” and the Chiefs beat Minnesota 23–7.28


The merger
The two leagues spent the early 1960s bidding against each other for players, and when the Jets signed Alabama quarterback Joe Namath on January 2, 1965, for a reported $427,000, the NFL owners decided the war was too expensive. The leagues announced a merger on June 8, 1966: a common draft, a championship game between them (the first, in January 1967, became known as Super Bowl I), and a single league from 1970. The NFL’s champions won the first two Super Bowls easily. Then the AFL won the next two: Namath’s Jets beat the Baltimore Colts 16–7 in Super Bowl III, and Stram’s Chiefs beat the Vikings in Super Bowl IV. When the merger took effect in 1970, the AFL’s ten teams (eight originals plus two later additions, Miami in 1966 and Cincinnati in 1968) and three NFL teams (the Colts, Browns and Steelers) formed the American Football Conference.
The AFL’s lasting gift was proof. Wide-open passing offenses could win championships, not just entertain, and the merged league inherited the coaches, quarterbacks and ideas to play that way. That makes what happened next all the stranger.


Meanwhile in the NFL: the 1960 shotgun
The NFL had its own experiment. On November 27, 1960, San Francisco’s coach, Red Hickey, lined his quarterback up about seven yards behind the center, a long direct snap away, with the backs and receivers spread around him. It was “really just a new version of an old formation,” the single wing’s direct snap with a passer instead of a runner, and Hickey called it the shotgun. As a heavy underdog the 49ers upset the Colts 30–22. In 1961 Hickey rotated three quarterbacks (John Brodie, Billy Kilmer and Bobby Waters) through it and started 4–1, including 49–0 over Detroit and 35–0 over the Rams. On October 22, 1961, the Bears found an answer, beat San Francisco 31–0, and Hickey shelved the formation.29 (What the Bears did is the second Predict-the-play drill below; try it before you look it up.) The shotgun returned in Dallas in 1975 as a passing-down weapon, and Formation Rules tells the rest; today’s NFL offenses spend most of their snaps in it.

The 1970s scoring drought

def league_ppg():
    from gridiron.data import CACHE
    path = CACHE / "fivethirtyeight_nfl_games.csv"
    try:
        if not path.exists():
            CACHE.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
            pd.read_csv(URL).to_csv(path, index=False)
        g = pd.read_csv(path)
        g = g[(g["playoff"] == 0) & g["season"].between(1932, 1977)].copy()
        g["league"] = "NFL"
        g.loc[g["season"].between(1960, 1969) & g["team1"].isin(AFL_TEAMS), "league"] = "AFL"
        g.loc[g["season"].between(1946, 1949) & g["team1"].isin(AAFC_TEAMS), "league"] = "AAFC"
        g["pts"] = g["score1"] + g["score2"]
        out = g.groupby(["league", "season"]).agg(pts=("pts", "sum"), games=("pts", "size"))
        out["ppg"] = out["pts"] / (2 * out["games"])
        return out["ppg"].unstack(0)
    except Exception:

        afl = pd.Series(FALLBACK["AFL"], index=range(1960, 1970))
        return pd.DataFrame({"NFL": nfl, "AFL": afl})

Figure 54.11: Points per team per game, regular season, 1932–1977. NFL (blue) and, for its ten seasons, the AFL (orange). Scoring nearly tripled between 1932 and 1948 as the passing rules loosened and the T arrived, held near 21–22 through the 1950s and ’60s, and then fell through the 1970s (shaded) to 17.2 in 1977, the lowest since 1942, despite rule changes in 1972, 1974 and 1977 (marked) meant to raise it. Computed from every game’s final score (AAFC games of 1946–49 excluded; course calculation, see the note).





Read the curve in three pieces. From 1932 to 1948, scoring nearly tripled: the 1933 passing rule, the end of the incompletion penalty, the T, and platoon football all pushed the same way. Through the 1950s and ’60s it held steady, around 21 or 22 points a game in the NFL and a little more in the AFL, with offense and defense trading innovations. Then, after the merger, it fell: 19.3 in 1970, 18.2 in 1974, and 17.2 in 1977, the lowest since 1942. In 1977 no receiver in the NFL gained 1,000 yards.30 The book calls this the 1970s scoring drought. (Older writing sometimes borrows baseball’s term “dead-ball era”; it’s the same decade.)
The passing numbers tell the same story from the other side. In 1977 NFL teams threw just 25 passes a game, against 29.4 in 1954; only 42 percent of their plays were passes, and they ran 37.4 times a game, a modern-era record. A pass gained 6.5 yards per attempt, down from about 7.4 in 1956–65, and from 1970 through 1977 more than five of every hundred passes were intercepted.31 Throwing had become both less rewarding and riskier, so teams did less of it.

Why the defense got ahead
No single cause, but five that reinforced each other.
1. Receivers could be hit all the way down the field. Until 1974 a defender could chuck a receiver (hit or shove him with his hands) anywhere on the field, as often as he liked, until the ball was thrown. A receiver who has to fight through a linebacker at 5 yards, a safety at 12 and a cornerback all the way can’t run his route on time, and a timing passing game depends on routes run on time.
2. Pass blockers couldn’t use their hands. Offensive linemen of the era had to keep their hands close to their chests while pass blocking, and couldn’t extend their arms to push a rusher away, while defensive linemen could use their hands freely, including the head slap, a swat to the side of a blocker’s helmet (legal until 1977). Pass protection was a fight with one side’s hands tied.
3. The great four-man lines. The 4-3 had matured, and the decade’s best teams were built on their defensive lines: the Steelers’ “Steel Curtain,” the Vikings’ “Purple People Eaters,” Dallas’s Doomsday, and early in the decade the Rams’ “Fearsome Foursome” (Deacon Jones, its most famous member, was traded after the 1971 season). Four rushers who could win without help let seven defenders cover.32
4. Zone coverage grew up. Defenses had learned to play zones as a team. The best-known version was the two-deep shell Bud Carson had begun developing as Georgia Tech’s head coach and brought to Pittsburgh in 1972 (Cover 2): corners jamming receivers at the line, safeties over the top, and, in Pittsburgh, a middle linebacker (Jack Lambert, from 1974) who ran deep down the middle, the ancestor of Tampa 2. The 1976 Steelers allowed 28 points in their last nine games, with five shutouts.33 Zones that are combined with unlimited chucking are close to airtight.
5. Offenses played it safe. When passing is that hard, the sensible strategy is to run, punt and win the field-position battle, and many coaches did. The game turned into a contest of whose defense would blink first.


Why then? What changed around 1970
Notice something odd about that list. Causes 1 and 2 are old rules. Defenders had been allowed to chuck receivers downfield, and blockers had been forbidden to extend their arms, all through the 1950s and ’60s, when the NFL scored 21 or 22 points a game and the AFL more. Rules that didn’t change can’t by themselves explain a fall. What they can explain is why the fall, once it started, was so hard to reverse. So what was new?

Zones met the chuck rule. Against man coverage, a receiver had one defender to beat, and the man hitting him was the man covering him. In a team zone, the receiver runs through several defenders’ areas, and under the old rules each of them could hit him on the way. The rule was the same; its value to the defense multiplied as defenses moved from man toward zone. That shift is the late-1960s and early-‘70s story of cause 4 (Carson’s Cover 2 reached the NFL in 1972), and it was the defenses’ answer to the Gillman-style passing that had beaten man coverage in the 1960s.
The defensive talent caught up. The AFL’s early scoring edge probably owed something to thin defenses in a new league. By 1969 its scoring had fallen back to the NFL’s level (the orange line on the chart), and after the common draft (from 1967) and the merger, every team drew from the same talent pool. The great four-man lines of cause 3 were built in exactly those years.
Coaches took the hint. Once the first two changes made passing riskier, the safe, run-first strategy of cause 5 won games (the 1972 Dolphins went 17–0 with it), and winning strategies get copied.

The constants (the chuck rule and the blockers’ hands) were the fuel; the new zones and the new defensive talent were the spark. That’s why the cure, when it came, had to change the constants.
New defenses kept coming, too. In 1972 Miami’s Bill Arnsparger moved a linebacker around his front in the package that became the 53 defense, and in 1974 the New England Patriots and Houston Oilers began using the 3-4 as a base defense, a story Odd and Hybrid Fronts tells in full.






NoteFilm room: Miami Dolphins, 1972



The only team in NFL history to finish a full season unbeaten and untied, the 1972 Dolphins went 17–0 and beat Washington 14–7 in Super Bowl VII. They did it in the most 1970s way imaginable: with a dominant running game (Larry Csonka and Mercury Morris both ran for 1,000 yards, a first for two teammates) and a defense so lacking in stars that it was called the “No-Name Defense.” Their starting quarterback, Bob Griese, broke his leg in the fifth game, and 38-year-old Earl Morrall started most of the rest of the season.34
What to notice: how few passes Miami threw and how rarely it needed to. When defenses rule, the team that never turns the ball over and never gives up a big play wins. And watch any 1970s Steelers highlight for the other half of the era: how far downfield defensive backs are still allowed to hit receivers, and how quickly quarterbacks give up and throw short. That’s what the rule-makers were trying to change.




The fixes that failed
The league saw the problem early and tried to fix it, three times.
1972: the hash marks. The NFL had first painted hash marks in 1933, 10 yards in from each sideline, and moved them to 20 yards in 1945. In 1972 it moved them in again, to 23 yards, 1 foot, 9 inches from each sideline, the width of the goalposts. A ball spotted on a hash used to leave the offense a cramped short side and a vast wide side; now the field was almost symmetrical.


Show the Python
W = 160 / 3


def hash_panel(ax, hash_in, title):
    ax.set_xlim(-1.5, W + 1.5)
    ax.set_ylim(-5.5, 13.0)
    ax.set_aspect("equal")
    ax.axis("off")
    ax.add_patch(Rectangle((0, 0), W, 10, fc=style.TURF, ec=style.BASELINE, lw=1.0))
    for yl in (0, 5, 10):
        ax.plot([0, W], [yl, yl], color=style.BASELINE, lw=0.8 if yl != 5 else 0.5)
    for x in (hash_in, W - hash_in):
        for yy in np.arange(1, 10, 1):
            if yy % 5:
                ax.plot([x, x], [yy - 0.25, yy + 0.25], color=style.INK, lw=1.3)
    ax.add_patch(Ellipse((hash_in, 5.0), 1.3, 0.8, fc=style.BALL, ec="white", lw=0.6, zorder=5))
    for x0, x1, y, txt in [(0, hash_in, -1.6, f"{hash_in:.1f} yd"), (hash_in, W, -1.6, f"{W - hash_in:.1f} yd")]:
        ax.annotate("", xy=(x0, y), xytext=(x1, y), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="<->", color=style.INK_2, lw=0.9))
        ax.text((x0 + x1) / 2, y - 1.5, txt, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=7.6, color=style.INK)
    ax.text(hash_in, 11.1, "ball on the hash", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=7.0, color=style.INK_2)
    ax.text(0.0, 12.9, title, ha="left", va="bottom", fontsize=9.0, fontweight="bold", color=style.INK)
    ax.text(hash_in / 2, 5.0, "short\nside", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=7.0, color=style.INK_2,
            style="italic")
    ax.text((hash_in + W) / 2 + 3.0, 5.0, "wide side", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=7.0,
            color=style.INK_2, style="italic")


fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 1.95))
hash_panel(axes[0], 20.0, "1945–1971")
hash_panel(axes[1], 70.75 / 3, "From 1972")
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.01, right=0.99, top=0.93, bottom=0.02, wspace=0.08)
plt.show()








Figure 54.12: The 1972 hash-mark change, with the ball on the left hash in both panels (to scale; the field is 53⅓ yards wide). Left, 1945–1971: the hashes were 20 yards in from each sideline, so a play from the hash left 20 yards to the short (boundary) side and 33⅓ yards to the wide (field) side. Right, from 1972: the hashes moved to 23 yards, 1 foot, 9 inches (about 23.6 yards) from each sideline, just 18½ feet apart, leaving about 23.6 yards to the short side and 29.75 to the wide side. More room to the short side meant more room for running plays and quick throws in either direction.





It helped the run more than the pass, and the reason is the sideline. Before 1972, a ball on the hash left only 20 yards to the short side, and a defense could treat that sideline as an extra defender: a sweep or an option run that way ran out of room fast, so in practice the offense ran to the wide side and the defense knew it. With the ball nearly in the middle, a run could go either way with room to spare, and the defense had to honor both. A pass, which travels over the defense rather than around it, gained much less: the long throw to the wide side got a few yards shorter, and that was about it. In 1973 Buffalo’s O. J. Simpson ran for 2,003 yards, the first 2,000-yard rushing season in NFL history. Scoring barely moved.35
1974: the package. With a rival league (the short-lived World Football League) advertising a more exciting game, the NFL’s competition committee passed its biggest set of changes in decades, aimed, in its own words, at making long touchdown drives more achievable:36

The goalposts moved from the goal line to the back of the end zone, ten yards farther away, so a drive that stalled at the 20 was no longer an easy field goal. That sounds like a way to cut scoring, and at first it was. The idea was that fewer cheap field-goal tries would mean more fourth-down attempts and more drives played out for touchdowns (the same logic, half a century early, as the go-for-it argument in The Clock, the Two-Minute Drill, and Fourth Down), and more room in the end zone for passes now that the posts weren’t standing in it.
Kickoffs moved back from the 40 to the 35, so more of them could be returned.
A missed field goal went back to the line of scrimmage (or to the 20 if the kick came from inside it), so a long attempt was no longer free.
Offensive holding dropped from 15 yards to 10, and receivers lined up wide could no longer be cut at the knees.
The first chuck rule: once a receiver was 3 yards past the line of scrimmage, a defender could contact him only once.

That last item introduces this chapter’s last term. A chuck rule is any rule limiting how a defender may hit or shove a receiver running his route. The 1974 version was sometimes called the “Isaac Curtis rule,” after the fast, slender Cincinnati receiver whom Miami’s defense had knocked down as often as it could in a 1973 playoff game; the Bengals’ owner, Paul Brown, sat on the rules committee and lobbied for the change. In 1977 the league tightened it so that a defender could contact a receiver only once in all, and banned the head slap.37
Look at the chart again and you’ll see that 1974, the package’s first season, is itself a dip, from 19.4 to 18.2. The goalposts explain it. Field-goal attempts fell from more than 860 in 1973 to 553 in 1974.38 If about three in five of those lost kicks would have gone in, that is something like 180 field goals, or roughly 1.5 points per team per game, more than the whole 1974 drop. The touchdowns the committee hoped would replace them came a year later: scoring rose to 20.6 in 1975. Then it fell again, to 19.2 in 1976 and 17.2 in 1977.


Why the fixes failed
Look at what the 1972 and 1974 changes touched: where the ball was spotted, where the goalposts stood, how kicks were returned, how far a penalty walked off. Each was sensible. None changed the basic arithmetic of a pass play. Under the 1974 rule a defender could still jam a receiver as he left the line and hit him again once he crossed 3 yards; an offensive lineman still couldn’t extend his arms to protect his quarterback. As long as the receiver couldn’t get open on time and the quarterback couldn’t stand in the pocket long enough to wait for him, the passing game that the AFL had proved could win stayed too risky to build an offense around. The rules had nibbled at the edges of the defense’s advantage without touching its center.
The 1977 rule looks, at first, like the real fix: one contact and no more, plus no head slap. Why did scoring hit bottom that very season? Because where the contact came was still up to the defender. He could spend it at the line, or he could save it for the moment that hurt most: 15 yards downfield, just as the receiver planted to make his break. One well-timed hit there wrecks a timed route as surely as five scattered ones. And the other half of the problem was untouched: banning the head slap took one weapon from the rushers, but the blockers still couldn’t extend their arms.
The changes that finally worked, in 1978, went straight at both halves. Contact with receivers was allowed only within 5 yards of the line (the Mel Blount rule), so past that point a receiver could run his route untouched and arrive on time; and pass blockers were allowed to extend their arms and open their hands. That’s the next chapter, and the scoring chart turns upward from there.






ImportantWhy it exists: the rules are the third player



This chapter’s history has three actors, not two. Offenses innovate, defenses answer, and the rules decide which side the board tilts toward. The 1906 pass rules held the forward pass back for a generation; the 1933 and 1934 changes released it; free substitution made the T a specialist’s offense; and the drought of the 1970s ended only when the league changed the rules of contact. Whenever you read about a scheme “taking over” the NFL, ask what rule made it possible. You’ll ask it again in Contact Rules and Penalties as Strategy.

title: From the Single Wing to the 1970s Scoring Drought (1906–1977)
text:
What survives
Not one of this chapter’s formations is a base offense in today’s NFL, and almost all of their ideas are still on the field.

The single wing’s direct snap became the shotgun, now the formation of most NFL snaps, and lives on in its purest form in the wildcat and in every direct snap to a running back on the goal line. Its spinners and reverses are the ancestors of today’s jet sweeps and misdirection.
The T’s under-center quarterback never left: it is the base of play-action, and under-center snaps rose to about a third of NFL plays in 2025.
Paul Brown’s organization (staffs, playbooks, film, sideline play-calling) is simply how football is run.
The umbrella’s idea, showing one structure and playing another after the snap, is the heart of modern disguise and simulated pressure.
The 4-3 remains one of the two families of base front, and the Flex’s gap ownership is how every defense now teaches run fits.
Gillman’s deep-and-wide passing is the grammar of every passing concept in Part 4.
The AFL’s two-point conversion arrived in the NFL in 1994, and its spirit, that you win by scoring, won the argument in 1978.

title: From the Single Wing to the 1970s Scoring Drought (1906–1977)
text:
Watch for it on Sunday






TipWatch for it: spot the ancestor



Pick one quarter of a game and hunt for the old ideas hiding in modern plays.

A direct snap to a running back. A back alone behind the center, the quarterback split wide or gone, maybe an extra lineman on one side: that’s the single wing, now called the wildcat. Note which side the extra blocker is on and whether the play went there.
Someone running across the formation at the snap. A jet or fly motion is the single wing’s wingback on a reverse, or the T’s man in motion. Watch whether the ball goes with him or the other way, like the 1940 Bears’ counter.
A buck sweep or a toss with two guards pulling. That’s Lombardi’s sweep (and the Wing-T’s cousin of it). Watch the back: does he cut inside or outside the last block? That’s running to daylight.
A defensive end who drops into coverage. When an edge player who lined up on the line turns and runs to the flat, you’ve seen Owen’s umbrella move, seventy-five years later.
The quarterback under center with two backs behind him. It’s the T’s descendant, and in 2025 it usually meant a run or a play-action pass.
Log it. Write down each ancestor you spot and what happened on the play. One wildcat, one jet motion counter and one dropping end is a good quarter’s hunting.

text:
Predict the play






TipPredict the play 1: spot the ancestor



Third-and-1 near midfield, 2025. The offense breaks the huddle into this:


Show the Python
wc_off = check_legal([
    OL("LG", -OL_SPLIT), OL("C", 0.0, "C"), OL("RG", OL_SPLIT), OL("RT", 2 * OL_SPLIT), OL("LT", 3 * OL_SPLIT),
    P("Y", "TE", LINE_D, 4 * OL_SPLIT + 1.0, "Y"), P("X", "WR", LINE_D, -12.0),
    P("RB", "RB", -5.0, 0.0, "R"), P("H", "RB", -5.0, -4.5, "H"), P("QB", "QB", OFF_BALL, 13.0, "Q"),
    P("Z", "WR", OFF_BALL, -7.5, "Z")])
wc_def = base43_60s({"WDE": dict(w=-3.2), "WDT": dict(w=-0.9), "SDT": dict(w=3.0), "SDE": dict(w=5.9),
                     "SAM": dict(d=3.6, w=8.6), "MIKE": dict(d=4.4, w=1.6), "WILL": dict(d=4.4, w=-2.6),
                     "LCB": dict(w=-12.0), "RCB": dict(w=13.0, d=6.5), "FS": dict(d=11.5, w=-1.0),
                     "SS": dict(d=7.5, w=-7.5)})
q1 = Play(wc_off, wc_def, los=50, to_go=None)
q1.motion("H", to=(-4.5, -1.7))
q1.highlight("RB", color=BACK_RING)
q1.highlight("LT", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK)
fld = draw_play(q1, lateral=(-16.5, 17.5), window=(-8.0, 14.0))
plt.show()








Figure 54.13: Drill 1: a direct-snap look. The running back (R, aqua ring) stands about five yards behind the center; the quarterback (Q) is split wide to the right, off the line. The line is unbalanced: the left tackle (dark ring) has lined up outside the right tackle, beside the tight end (Y). Before the snap, a second back (H) starts in motion from the left (arrow). It is third-and-1. Defense: E = end, T = tackle, S/M/W = linebackers, C = cornerbacks, FS/SS = safeties.





What old formation is this, and where do you expect the ball to go?






TipAnswer





It’s the single wing in modern clothes, the look broadcasters call the wildcat. Every piece has an ancestor: the direct snap to a runner five yards deep (the single-wing tailback), the unbalanced line with an extra lineman on one side (the single wing’s four-men-to-one-side line), and a second back crossing the formation at the snap (the wingback’s reverse, or the 1940 T’s man in motion).
The likeliest play is a run to the strong side, the right. On third-and-1 the offense wants a yard. To the right of the center it has three linemen and a tight end, a blocker for each of the four defenders on that side (counting the Mike, who is nearly over the center), with the motion man arriving as a fifth: the single wing’s off-tackle power, with more blockers than defenders at the point of attack.
Look at the defense, too. The unbalanced line moved the offense’s strength to the right after the huddle, and this defense hasn’t moved with it: the strong safety is still over on the left, across from Z. That is the modern reason the look works. An unbalanced line forces the defense to re-declare its strength before the snap, and a defense that doesn’t shift is outnumbered.
The counter-threat is the motion man. If the defense slides right to stop the power, the ball can go to H on his sweep, or the runner can fake to him and keep it, exactly the spinner-and-reverse logic that kept 1930s defenses honest. And because the quarterback split wide is still an eligible receiver, one defender has to cover him, which takes a man out of the box. What makes the modern version a gimmick rather than a base offense is the pass: few running backs can throw well enough to make the defense respect it, which is why the single wing’s triple-threat tailback mattered so much.











TipPredict the play 2: October 22, 1961



San Francisco’s shotgun has carried the 49ers to a 4–1 start, including shutouts of 49–0 and 35–0. The 49ers line up in it against the Bears: quarterback about seven yards deep, receivers spread. The Bears’ middle linebacker, Bill George, has walked up from his usual spot.


Show the Python
sg_off = check_legal(line5() + [
    P("QB", "QB", -7.0, 0.0, "Q"), P("FB", "FB", -5.5, 2.2, "F"), P("X", "WR", LINE_D, -14.0),
    P("H", "HB", OFF_BALL, -7.5, "H"), P("Y", "TE", LINE_D, 6.5, "Y"), P("Z", "WR", OFF_BALL, 13.5)])
sg_def = base43_60s({"MIKE": dict(d=1.0, w=0.0), "WDT": dict(w=-2.2), "SDT": dict(w=2.4), "WDE": dict(w=-4.4),
                     "SDE": dict(w=4.6), "SAM": dict(d=4.6, w=6.2), "WILL": dict(d=4.6, w=-5.6),
                     "LCB": dict(w=-14.0), "RCB": dict(w=13.5), "FS": dict(d=12.5, w=-7.0),
                     "SS": dict(d=10.0, w=7.5)})
q2 = Play(sg_off, sg_def, los=40, to_go=None)
q2.highlight("MIKE", color=KEY_RING)
fld = draw_play(q2, lateral=(-17.5, 17.5), window=(-9.5, 15.0))
plt.show()








Figure 54.14: Drill 2: the 1961 shotgun (an illustrative alignment) against the Bears’ 4-3, with middle linebacker Bill George (M, orange ring) walked up onto the line, head-up on the center. The quarterback (Q) is about seven yards deep; one back (F) stands beside him; the other backs and ends are spread. Defense: E = end, T = tackle, S/W = outside linebackers, C = cornerbacks, FS/SS = safeties.





What is the Bears’ plan, and why does it work against this formation in particular?






TipAnswer





Rush the center. In the shotgun the center has the hardest job on the field: he must look between his legs, throw a seven-yard snap accurately, and only then lift his head to block. A defender lined up directly over him gets a head start every time. With George on the center, either the center loses the one-on-one, or a guard has to help, and then someone else is free.
Why it works here: the 1961 shotgun had almost no running threat to punish an aggressive rush. A quarterback seven yards deep with a single back beside him can’t hand off quickly or threaten a quick dive, so the defense could commit to the pass rush. With pressure up the middle arriving before receivers spread across a wide field could get open, the 49ers had nowhere to go: the Bears won 31–0, and Hickey retired the formation. The modern shotgun survives because offenses solved both problems: quarterbacks set up about five yards deep, not seven, and there is a real run game (and the RPO) from it, so a defense that sends everyone at the center pays for it.











TipPredict the play 3: third-and-8, 1977



Third-and-8 at the offense’s own 35, third quarter, 1977. The offense is in split backs with a tight end and two wide receivers; the defense is a two-deep 4-3 with both cornerbacks squeezed up tight on the receivers.


Show the Python
q3_def = base43_60s({"LCB": dict(d=1.2, w=-14.9), "RCB": dict(d=1.2, w=13.4), "FS": dict(d=12.5, w=-9.5),
                     "SS": dict(d=12.5, w=9.5)})
q3_off = pro_set_red()
q3_off = [q.moved(w=12.5) if q.key == "Z" else q for q in q3_off]
q3 = Play(q3_off, q3_def, los=45, to_go=8)
q3.highlight("LCB", "RCB", color=KEY_RING)
fld = draw_play(q3, lateral=(-17.5, 17.5), window=(-8.0, 16.0))
plt.show()








Figure 54.15: Drill 3: third-and-8 in 1977. Offense: split backs (H and F), tight end Y, receivers X and Z. Defense: a 4-3 with two deep safeties (FS, SS) about 12 yards deep and both cornerbacks (C, orange rings) pressed tight on the receivers at the line, from an outside shade, so they can jam them inside toward the safeties.





What are the defense’s advantages under the 1977 rules, and what is the offense’s most sensible call?






TipAnswer





The defense’s advantages are the rulebook’s. Those pressed corners can jam the receivers at the line, and under the 1977 rule they get one legal contact on each, used right where it hurts the timing most. Seven defenders are in coverage behind them in a two-deep zone, the safeties over the top. Up front, four rushers can use their hands freely (the head slap is gone in 1977, but blockers still can’t extend their arms), so the quarterback doesn’t have long.
The offense’s sensible call is something short and safe: a quick pass to a back or the tight end underneath the zone, or a draw that punishes the four rushers for charging, and then a punt if it comes up short.
If you’ve read Cover 2 and Tampa 2, your first instinct may have been the classic Cover 2 beaters: smash (a corner route over the squatting cornerback) or the hole shot down the sideline between the corner and the safety. In 1977 both die before they start. The corner route needs the receiver to get off the line clean and break on time, and here he is jammed at the snap by a corner who is spending his one legal contact right where it hurts. The hole shot needs the quarterback to hold the ball while a deep route develops, behind blockers who can’t extend their arms. A 15-yard throw against this defense in 1977 asks a jammed receiver to get open in time behind a protection that can’t hold up. That’s the drought in one snap: on third-and-8, the most rational play was to try for a first down without risking an interception, and punt. A year later, with contact limited to 5 yards and blockers allowed to extend their arms, the same third-and-8 became a throwing down again.

title: From the Single Wing to the 1970s Scoring Drought (1906–1977)
text:
Takeaways

Football’s history is action, reaction and rules. Offenses innovate, defenses answer, and the rule-makers tilt the board. The forward pass, legal from 1906, didn’t matter until the rules stopped punishing it (1933–34).
The single wing was built for power and deception from a direct snap; the T beat it with speed and a specialist passer. The 1940 Bears’ 73–0 made the switch, and platoon football (permanent in the NFL from 1950) made the specialist possible.
Paul Brown turned football into a profession: full-time staffs, playbooks, film, measurable athletes, and plays called from the sideline. Every modern staff runs on his model.
The 4-3 was the defense’s answer to the pro passing game, and it had two parents. Owen’s umbrella showed a 6-1-4 and played a 4-1-6 (its ends became outside linebackers); Bill George stood up the five-man front’s middle guard (the middle linebacker); Landry combined them in 1956, then built the Flex in the 1960s to take away Lombardi’s daylight by giving every gap an owner.
Gillman and the AFL proved the passing game could win, using the whole field, deep and wide, and the merged league inherited their ideas.
The 1970s drought came from old rules meeting new defenses. Defenders could hit receivers downfield and pass blockers couldn’t extend their arms, as they always had; what was new was team zone coverage (which let several defenders each take a shot at a receiver) and defensive talent spread across one merged league. The 1972 hash marks, the 1974 package and even 1977’s one-contact rule left the arithmetic of a pass play alone, so scoring fell to 17.2 in 1977. Only 1978’s five-yard limit and open-handed pass blocking changed it.

crumbs: Part 11: History
54  From the Single Wing to the 1970s Scoring Drought (1906–1977)

title: 1978 and the Passing Revolution (1978–1999)
text:
Where the story starts: the 1977 problem
Put on a game from the early 1970s. The picture looks familiar: two wide receivers, a tight end, two backs, a quarterback under center. Then watch a receiver run a route. A linebacker hits him as he leaves the line, a safety hits him again eight yards downfield, and nobody throws a flag, because none of it is illegal. Watch an offensive tackle pass-block: his fists are balled against his chest and his elbows are out, like a man shielding himself in a crowd. The league trimmed that downfield contact twice in the mid-1970s and it made little difference: in 1977 NFL teams averaged 17.2 points a game, the fewest since 1942. Twenty-one years later a single team, the 1998 Minnesota Vikings, scored 556 points, a league record at the time. What happened in between? The answer starts with two short changes to the rulebook in March 1978, and with the twenty years of move and counter-move they set off, a story in which every offensive idea you now see on Sundays met a defensive answer, and every answer started the next round.
You’ll be able to:
The previous chapter ended with the defenses on top, and the recap is short. Until 1974 a defender could hit a receiver anywhere on the field until the ball was in the air, and a pass blocker had to keep his hands in to his chest and block with his forearms and shoulders. The league trimmed downfield contact in 1974, and in 1977 it allowed each receiver to be contacted only once and banned the head slap that pass rushers like Deacon Jones had used to stun blockers.1 None of it worked. In 1977 teams scored 17.2 points a game; only 40 percent of offensive plays were passes; and 5.7 percent of passes were intercepted, more than one in eighteen.
Why didn’t “only once” fix it? Because the defense chose where to spend its one hit. A pass play is a timed contract: the receiver promises to be at a spot at a moment, and the quarterback throws to the spot. One collision at 8 yards, from a linebacker the receiver had to run past anyway, was enough to make him half a second late, and a late receiver on a timed throw means an incompletion or an interception. The 1977 rule cut the number of hits but left the one that mattered. And for the pass blockers nothing had changed at all.
The league had reasons to care beyond taste. In October 1977 Pete Rozelle signed television contracts with all three networks that would carry every regular-season game from 1978, then the largest television package ever negotiated, and an expanded 16-game schedule was coming with them.2 A sport selling itself to a national audience every week needed points, and points in the 1970s came mostly from long, grinding drives that defenses were winning more often every season.

title: 1978 and the Passing Revolution (1978–1999)
text:
Spring 1978: two rules, one direction
In March 1978 the owners passed a package of changes. Two of them did almost all the work.3

The receiver goes free: the Mel Blount rule
The first rule drew a line five yards past the line of scrimmage. Inside that line, a defender squared up in front of a receiver may still contact him, jamming him, rerouting him, knocking him off the line, and he may stay on him (the rule’s word was maintain contact) until the receiver gets level with him or crosses the five-yard line. It is not a one-hit rule; it is a five-yard zone. Beyond it, while the quarterback still has the ball, a defender may not initiate contact that impedes the receiver: no shove, no chuck, no collision. Once the ball is thrown, any contact that interferes is pass interference, as before. (Today’s rulebook adds one condition worth knowing for old and new film alike: the restriction holds only while the quarterback is in the pocket with the ball. Once he scrambles out of it, defenders may chuck receivers downfield again; see Contact Rules and Penalties.) That five-yard zone is the Mel Blount rule (1978): a defender may contact a receiver only within five yards of the line, before the throw. The name honors, if that is the word, Pittsburgh’s 6-foot-3 cornerback Mel Blount, the 1975 defensive player of the year, whose bump-and-run coverage was so physical that the league’s answer was named after him. Some accounts attach the nickname to the 1977 one-chuck rule instead; the five-yard rule of 1978 is the one most people mean.4


Show the Python
def blount_panel(ax, era):
    off = [p for p in line("short") if p.key in ("C", "RG", "RT")] + [
        O("Y", "TE", -0.7, 4.8, "Y"), O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0.0, "Q")]
    dfn = [D("SAM", "LB", 1.0, 7.0, "S"), D("MIKE", "LB", 4.5, 2.2, "M"), D("SS", "S", 15.0, 10.4, "SS"),
           D("DT", "DT", 1.0, T("3"), "T"), D("DE", "DE", 1.0, T("5") + 0.3, "E")]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=None)
    if era == "old":
        go_to(p, "Y", (16.5, 9.6), kind="route", via=[(1.0, 5.3), (2.6, 6.4), (7.6, 5.5), (9.2, 7.6), (12.0, 7.9)])
        go_to(p, "MIKE", (7.4, 4.8), kind="path")
        go_to(p, "SS", (12.8, 8.6), kind="path")
    else:
        go_to(p, "Y", (17.5, 5.1), kind="route", via=[(1.0, 5.3), (2.4, 5.2)])
        go_to(p, "MIKE", (8.5, 3.2), kind="path")
        go_to(p, "SS", (16.5, 7.4), kind="path")
    p.highlight("Y")
    fld = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=(-3.6, 12.6), window=(-3.4, 19.0), title=False)
    band(fld, p, 0.0, 5.0, -3.6, 12.6, color=GREEN, alpha=0.09 if era == "new" else 0.0,
         lw=0.0 if era == "old" else 0.9)
    if era == "old":
        for (d, w), lab, (td, tw) in [((1.0, 5.3), "hit 1", (2.5, 4.0)), ((7.6, 5.5), "hit 2", (7.2, 2.9)),
                                       ((12.0, 7.9), "hit 3", (11.0, 10.2))]:
            spot(fld, p, d, w, ms=9)
            say(fld, p, td, tw, lab, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7, weight="bold")
        x2, y2 = _P(fld, p, 7.6, 5.5)
        ax.add_patch(Circle((float(x2), float(y2)), 1.15, fc="none", ec=style.DEFENSE_DARK, lw=1.3, zorder=7.5))
        say(fld, p, 6.0, 9.4, "1977: the one\nlegal hit", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.6)
        say(fld, p, 16.6, 3.2, "Y arrives late,\noff his path", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
        title(ax, "Before 1978: hit him downfield\n(any number of times before 1974)")
    else:
        spot(fld, p, 1.0, 5.3, ms=9)
        say(fld, p, 2.5, 4.0, "hit", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7, weight="bold")
        say(fld, p, 2.6, -0.3, "first 5 yards:\ncontact allowed", color=GREEN, fontsize=6.8)
        say(fld, p, 11.0, 1.2, "past 5 yards:\nhands off until\nthe ball is thrown", color=style.INK_2, fontsize=6.8)
        say(fld, p, 16.6, 1.6, "Y arrives on\ntime, on his path", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
        title(ax, "From 1978: contact only in\nthe first 5 yards")
    ruler(fld, p, depths=(5, 10, 15))
    return fld


fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.4, 4.9))
blount_panel(axes[0], "old")
blount_panel(axes[1], "new")
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=1.0)
plt.show()








Figure 55.1: The 1978 contact rule, on one tight end’s seam route (illustrative). Left, before 1978: the Sam (S) hits Y at the line, the Mike (M) knocks him off his path at 8 yards, and the strong safety hits him again at 12, so he arrives late and wide of where his quarterback expects him. Before 1974 all three hits were legal. Under the 1977 one-contact rule only one was, so the defense let Y off the line clean and saved its hit for the Mike at 8 yards (hit 2, outlined), which alone is enough to make him late. Right, from 1978: contact is legal only in the green zone, the first five yards past the line. Past it the Mike and the safety may not touch Y until the ball is thrown, so he runs his seam on time and on his path.





Figure 55.1 shows what changed for the defense. Before, every defender between the receiver and his landmark was a potential speed bump. A zone defense could re-route receivers: knock crossers off their paths, steer a tight end toward a waiting safety, and destroy the timing a passing game depends on. After 1978, only the defenders near the line got a shot, and only once the receiver was past them was he free. A linebacker dropping to 8 yards could no longer hit the tight end running past him. He had to cover him, with his feet, and linebackers built to take on guards are not built to run with tight ends.
The deepest effect was on timing. A route that can be disrupted anywhere can’t be thrown on a count, because the quarterback never knows when his receiver will arrive. A route that can be disrupted only in the first five yards can be. If the receiver gets a clean release, he will be at 12 yards, breaking toward the sideline, at the same moment on Sunday that he was in Wednesday’s practice. The quarterback can throw to the spot before the receiver turns around. Every timing route you have met in this book, from the quick game to the dropback concepts, assumes that.


The blocker gets his hands: open-hand pass protection
The second rule was about the other end of the play. From 1978 an offensive lineman pass-blocking could extend his arms and open his hands. That sounds like a technicality; it changed the geometry of the pocket. A blocker restricted to his chest and forearms meets the rusher body to body, and a rusher who gets his shoulder past the blocker’s hip is past him. A blocker who can extend his arms meets the rusher at arm’s length and can steer him: feel which way he is going and push him further that way, past the quarterback, while staying between him and the passer. That is the punch of Pass Protection, and it doesn’t exist without the 1978 rule. Holding (grabbing and restricting the rusher) stayed illegal. What changed is that a lineman could now meet the rusher with extended arms and open hands instead of his chest and forearms.
More time in the pocket matters most to the throws that take the longest. A three-step drop and a quick slant need little protection; a seven-step drop and a 20-yard post need a lot. So the second rule pointed the same way as the first: toward the deep and intermediate passing game the 1970s defenses had strangled.






ImportantWhy it exists



The two rules attacked the 1970s defensive advantage from both ends at once. The Blount rule took away the defense’s best way to wreck a route (hitting the receiver), and the hands rule took away its best way to wreck the quarterback’s clock (beating a blocker who couldn’t use his arms). The league’s stated aim, in the Hall of Fame’s words, was to “open up the game.” What the rules gave up was a style of defense. A team built on big, physical defensive backs who won by contact, like the Steelers who gave the rule its name, now had to win with speed and position instead. And the Steelers are the first example of the chapter’s theme, that the team that adapts first wins: Pittsburgh won the next two Super Bowls with a passing game. Terry Bradshaw was the league’s MVP in 1978 and threw for 318 yards and four touchdowns in the 35–31 win over Dallas in Super Bowl XIII.5




And the rest of the package
Three smaller changes rode along, and each fits the same story. The schedule grew from 14 games to 16 and a second wild card was added in each conference, which meant more games to televise. The league added a seventh official, the side judge, partly to rule on what happens downfield: a new contact rule needs someone standing where the contact happens. And the next spring, in 1979, officials were told to blow the whistle as soon as a quarterback was “clearly in the grasp” of a tackler, the first of many rules protecting the passer that the league’s investment in passing would require.6






CautionCommon misconception



“The Mel Blount rule outlawed bump-and-run coverage.” It didn’t. Inside five yards a cornerback can still jam a receiver at the line, and teams have played press coverage ever since, from the 1980s Raiders to Seattle’s press Cover 3 of the 2010s. What the rule removed was the second, third and fourth hit downfield, the ones that let a zone defense steer receivers wherever it wanted. It was also not the last word. Officials let a good deal of downfield contact go in the years that followed, the league renewed its emphasis on the rule in its 1994 package (later in this chapter), and it was called strictly only from 2004, the “Ty Law rule” of Coverage Fundamentals. On old film, expect to see more contact past five yards than the rulebook allowed.








NoteMadden vs. real life



In a video game the rulebook is fixed, and the best plays are the best plays forever. In the NFL the rulebook is rewritten every spring, and schemes chase the rewrites. The 1978 changes are the clearest example in the sport’s history: no coach invented a play that ended the 1970s scoring drought. The owners did, by changing what a defender was allowed to do with his hands, and then the coaches spent twenty years finding out what that made possible. When a rule changes, ask the question this chapter asks over and over: what did this take away, and from whom?

text:
What the numbers did
How big was the change? Season-level league totals answer that. Pro Football Reference keeps a year-by-year table of league averages, and Figure 55.2 draws four of its rates for every season from 1970 to 1999.7 Rates matter here, not totals, because the schedule grew from 14 to 16 games in 1978 and two seasons (1982 and 1987) were cut short by strikes.


Show the Python (league averages, 1970-1999)
# Pro Football Reference, "NFL League Year-by-Year Averages" (per team per game, and season totals).

                  cmp_pct=100 * LEAGUE.cmp / LEAGUE.att, int_pct=100 * LEAGUE.int / LEAGUE.att)

]

    ax.axvspan(1969.5, 1977.5, color=style.GRID, alpha=0.45, lw=0, zorder=0)

                    color=style.INK, ha=ha, va="center", zorder=4,

for ax in axes.flat:

    ax.text(1973.5, hi - 0.03 * (hi - lo), "before\n1978", fontsize=6.6, color=style.INK_2, ha="center", va="top")
for ax in axes[0]:
    lo, hi = ax.get_ylim()
    ax.text(1978.4, lo + 0.02 * (hi - lo), "1978 rules", fontsize=6.6, color=style.INK_2, ha="left", va="bottom")
    ax.text(1994.4, lo + 0.02 * (hi - lo), "1994\npackage", fontsize=6.6, color=style.MUTED, ha="left", va="bottom")
for ax in axes[1]:
    ax.set_xticks([1970, 1978, 1986, 1994, 1999])

plt.show()








Figure 55.2: The NFL’s passing game, 1970 to 1999: four league-wide rates by season, from Pro Football Reference’s league averages. The shaded years are before the 1978 rules (dashed line); the dotted line marks the 1994 rule package. Passes as a share of plays jumped from 40% in 1977 to 49% in 1980 and kept rising. Interceptions per 100 passes fell from 5.7 to 3.4 over twenty years. Net yards per pass attempt rose from 5.2 to 6.0 and then stopped. Scoring rose from 17.2 points to the low 20s, sagged in the early 1990s and rose again after 1994.





Read Figure 55.2 panel by panel.

Passes as a share of plays (top right) is the cleanest signal, and the biggest. In 1977 teams threw on 40 percent of their plays. By 1980 it was 49 percent, and after 1983 it never went below half again. Offenses decided, almost at once, that throwing had become a better deal.
Interceptions (bottom left) fell from 5.7 per 100 passes in 1977 to 4.6 in 1979 and 1980, and kept falling for twenty years, to 3.4 in 1999. A receiver who can’t be knocked off his route is where the quarterback expects him to be, and a ball thrown to the right spot is harder to intercept. Completion rate rose too, from 51 percent in 1977 to 56 percent in 1980.
Net yards per pass attempt (bottom right: passing yards minus sack yardage, divided by attempts plus sacks) jumped from 5.2 in 1977 to 6.0 in 1980 and then stopped. Through the 1980s and 1990s it wandered between 5.7 and 6.1. Each throw got a little better, once, and then the defenses caught up with it.
Points (top left) went from 17.2 to 20.5 in three seasons. Note 1978 itself: only 18.3. The rules arrived that season, but the offenses that exploited them took a year or two to arrive.

The pattern in those last two panels is the theme of this chapter. A rule change opens a gap, the offense pours into it, and then the defense adapts and the efficiency gain levels off. What stays is the volume: teams kept throwing more, because once the defense adjusted to stop the pass, it had less left over to stop the run. And at the far right of the points panel is the next round of the same cycle: scoring sagged to 18.7 in 1992 and 1993, and the league changed the rules again (the 1994 package, later in this chapter).
Averages show the floor of the new game, not its ceiling. The best offenses ran far ahead of the league line: in 1984 Dan Marino threw for 5,084 yards, and in 1998 the Vikings scored 556 points, 34.8 a game against a league average of 21.3. Both were records at the time.

section: Offense’s first answer: Air Coryell stretches the field deep
text:
Offense’s first answer: Air Coryell stretches the field deep
The coach most ready for 1978 was already in the league. Don Coryell had built pass-first offenses at San Diego State in the 1960s and with the St. Louis Cardinals from 1973, and on September 25, 1978, four games into the season, he took over the San Diego Chargers. Coryell’s offense, built on Sid Gillman’s idea that a defense should be made to cover every blade of grass, put receivers in motion, lined them up all over the formation, and made the deep throw the first option on most passing plays. His quarterback, Dan Fouts, had spent five unremarkable seasons in San Diego. In 1979 he threw for 4,082 yards, breaking Joe Namath’s single-season record of 4,007; in 1981 he threw for 4,802, and he became the first quarterback to pass for 4,000 yards in three straight seasons, and San Diego led the league in passing yards every season from 1978 to 1983.8
The offense needed a different kind of tight end, and Coryell had one. Kellen Winslow, a first-round pick in 1979, was big enough to line up next to the tackle and fast enough to run with safeties. Coryell split him out, put him in motion, and threw to him down the seams. A tight end who can’t be hit past five yards and can outrun a linebacker is exactly the matchup the new rules created.


Show the Python
# ------------------------------------------------------------- Air Coryell: 896 against Cover 2
off = line("short") + [O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0.0, "Q"), O("FB", "FB", -4.5, 0.0, "F"), O("RB", "RB", -7.0, 0.0, "R"),
                       O("Y", "TE", -0.7, 4.8, "Y"), O("X", "WR", -0.7, -14.0, "X"), O("Z", "WR", -1.5, 14.0, "Z")]
p = Play(off, era_43(off, "two"), los=30, to_go=None)
p.route("X", r.post(stem=10))
p.route("Y", r.seam(22))
p.route("Z", r.dig(depth=16.5, width=13))
p.dropback(7.0)
p.drop("FS", (19.0, -9.0), zone=(9, 16), label="deep half")
p.drop("SS", (19.0, 9.0), zone=(9, 16), label="deep half")
p.players["LCB"] = p.players["LCB"].moved(d=5.0)
p.players["RCB"] = p.players["RCB"].moved(d=5.0)
for k in ("SAM", "MIKE", "WILL"):
    q = p.players[k]
    p.drop(k, (10.0, q.w * 1.6 if k != "MIKE" else -1.6))
for k in ("LCB", "RCB"):
    q = p.players[k]
    p.drop(k, (7.0, q.w * 1.07))
for k in ("LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT"):
    p.block(k, pts=[(-1.2, 0.0)])
p.block("FB", pts=[(0.2, -2.0)])
p.block("RB", pts=[(1.6, 2.6)])
p.pass_to("Y", t=2.75)
p.highlight("Y")
fld = draw(p, width_in=5.6, lateral=(-18.5, 18.5), window=(-10.5, 25.5), title=False)
ruler(fld, p, depths=(5, 10, 15, 20))
say(fld, p, -8.4, 3.6, "7-step drop", fontsize=7)
say(fld, p, 22.6, -2.7, "X: 8 (post)", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7, weight="bold")
say(fld, p, 22.4, 7.2, "Y: 9 (go)", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7, weight="bold")
say(fld, p, 17.0, 14.3, "Z: 6 (dig)", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7, weight="bold")
say(fld, p, -5.6, -11.0, "seven block:\nline + both backs", fontsize=6.8)
plt.show()








Figure 55.3: Air Coryell: ‘896’ from a two-back I formation against Cover 2 (illustrative). In the digit system X runs an 8 (a post), Y, the tight end (ringed), a 9 (a go, up the seam), and Z a 6 (a dig at 15 yards). Both backs and the line stay in to block, seven blockers, while the quarterback takes a seven-step drop. The ball goes to Y in the seam between the two deep safeties, each responsible for half the field. The linebackers drop to about 10 yards and the corners, who start 5 yards off, sink a couple of yards to guard the short outside zones (the flats); none of them may touch a receiver once he is five yards past the line.





Figure 55.3 is a Coryell-style call in the digit system of Offensive Systems: “896” gives X an 8 (a post), Y a 9 (a go, here up the seam), and Z a 6 (a dig). Three receivers attack three spots deep, and against the two deep safeties of Cover 2 the tight end’s seam splits them. Cover 2 has an answer on paper: the Mike is taught to run with the tight end up the seam. Before 1978 he could slow him down by hitting him on the way; now he has to keep up with a tight end like Winslow by running, and he can’t. Notice what pays for it: both backs stay in to block, seven blockers for a seven-step drop, so the quarterback has time to let the deep routes develop.
Why it works, and what it costs. Air Coryell answers the 1978 rules with depth. Receivers who can’t be rerouted can be sent long, and blockers who can use their hands can hold up long enough for them to get there. The cost is everything a deep passing game always costs: long drops, longer protection, fewer receivers in routes, and interceptions when the throw is late. Coryell’s Chargers had famously poor defenses and never reached a Super Bowl. His ideas lasted anyway. They ran through his assistants (Joe Gibbs, Ernie Zampese) to Norv Turner’s Dallas offenses of the 1990s and to Mike Martz’s 1999 St. Louis Rams, the “Greatest Show on Turf.”






NoteFilm room: San Diego Chargers 1981 — the Epic in Miami



The game: the AFC divisional playoff at the Miami Orange Bowl on January 2, 1982. San Diego led 24–0 in the first quarter, Miami came back to lead, and the Chargers won 41–38 in overtime. Fouts completed 33 of 53 passes for 433 yards, all NFL playoff records at the time; Winslow caught 13 passes, also a playoff record, for 166 yards, and blocked a field goal at the end of regulation that would have won it for Miami. Both teams finished exhausted in the Florida heat, and the game is still ranked among the best ever played.9
What to notice: the Chargers’ receivers lining up anywhere (Winslow wide, in the slot, in motion), the depth of the routes, and how often the first read is downfield. Then notice the defenses: still mostly in base personnel with four defensive backs, so wherever Winslow lines up, a linebacker or a safety has to cover him past five yards, where he can’t be touched. Watch Miami keep changing who covers him. That mismatch is the 1978 rule change on film.

section: Offense’s second answer: Walsh stretches it sideways
text:
Offense’s second answer: Walsh stretches it sideways
Bill Walsh read the same rules the other way. Walsh had built a short passing game in Cincinnati in the early 1970s, as an assistant to Paul Brown, around a quarterback who couldn’t throw deep (the story is in Passing Fundamentals). In January 1979 the San Francisco 49ers, 2–14 in 1978, made him their head coach. They went 2–14 again in his first season, but in the third round of the 1979 draft he had taken a Notre Dame quarterback, Joe Montana. Three seasons later the 49ers beat Cincinnati 26–21 in Super Bowl XVI.10


Show the Python
# ------------------------------------------------------------- West Coast: slant-flat with a shallow cross
off = line("short") + [O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0.0, "Q"), O("HB", "RB", -5.0, -2.2, "H"), O("FB", "FB", -5.0, 2.2, "F"),
                       O("Y", "TE", -0.7, 4.8, "Y"), O("X", "WR", -0.7, -13.0, "X"), O("Z", "WR", -1.5, 13.0, "Z")]
dfn = [q.moved(w=-7.0) if q.key == "WILL" else q for q in era_43(off, "one")]   # Will as the weak curl-flat player
p = Play(off, dfn, los=30, to_go=None)
p.dropback(3.2)
p.route("X", [(0, 0), (1.8, 0), (7.6, -6.2)], speed=6.5)                 # slant: break at ~1 yd, catch at ~7
p.run("X", [(4.4, 3.4)])
p.route("HB", [(0, 0), (1.6, 2.6), (5.6, 7.4), (7.6, 11.4)], side=-1)    # flat: outside X's alignment, 2-3 yd deep
p.route("Y", [(0, 0), (2.5, -1.0), (3.5, -7.0)])
p.route("Z", r.curl(12))
for k in ("LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT"):
    p.block(k, pts=[(-1.0, 0.0)])
p.block("FB", pts=[(2.6, 0.9)])
p.drop("LCB", (11.5, -14.2))
p.drop("WILL", (3.6, -12.2), speed=4.2)
p.drop("MIKE", (8.0, 1.0))
p.pass_to("X", t=1.0)
p.highlight("X", "WILL")
fld = draw(p, width_in=6.0, lateral=(-18.5, 16.5), window=(-7.5, 16.5), title=False)
ruler(fld, p, depths=(5, 10, 15))
say(fld, p, 11.6, -2.6, "run after the catch", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
say(fld, p, 7.6, -9.6, "slant", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7, weight="bold")
say(fld, p, 0.8, -16.0, "flat", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7, weight="bold")
point_to(fld, p, (10.4, -10.4), (3.6, -12.2), "W widens:\nslant or flat?", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
say(fld, p, -5.9, 5.6, "3-step drop:\nball out in ~1 s", fontsize=6.8)
plt.show()








Figure 55.4: The West Coast idea: a quick slant with a flat route outside it, from the pro set, against Cover 3 (illustrative). The quarterback takes a three-step drop and throws in about a second. X runs the slant, breaking inside at 5 or 6 yards and catching the ball at about 7; the halfback (H) runs to the flat, outside X’s alignment; the tight end (Y) crosses underneath; the fullback (F) steps up to block and the line blocks. The Will linebacker (W, ringed) is the one defender between them. He can’t cover both, so as he widens toward the flat the window opens inside him and the ball goes to X (ringed) on the slant, in front of the corner, who has bailed to his deep third. The thick arrow is X’s run after the catch.





Walsh’s offense treats the short pass as a run. Figure 55.4 is the idea in its plainest form: a three-step drop, and the ball out in about a second to X on a quick slant, while the halfback runs to the flat outside him and the tight end crosses underneath. The Will linebacker can’t cover both the slant and the flat, a horizontal stretch, so whichever he chooses, the quarterback throws the other. The receiver catches the ball in stride, already running, and the yards come after the catch.
The quick slant is only the front door. The heart of Walsh’s offense was the five-step drop thrown on time, with high-low reads (one receiver deep and one short in the same area, so a defender who takes one leaves the other) and with the backs as real receivers rather than last-resort outlets. In 1985 Roger Craig became the first player to run for 1,000 yards and catch passes for 1,000 more in the same season.11
Why the 1978 rules made it work, and which rule did what. Be careful here, because the slant and the flat in Figure 55.4 live mostly inside the five-yard zone, where contact stayed legal. A corner can still jam X at the line, which is why pressing the receivers is still a defense’s first answer to a quick passing game. What the Blount rule gave Walsh was everything just past that line. X breaks inside at about 5 yards and catches the ball at 7, and the Will, who used to be allowed to knock him off his path as he crossed, can now only try to beat him to the spot; on a timed throw he never will. And most of Walsh’s offense lived further out still: crossing routes, digs and hooks at 8 to 15 yards, thrown off the five-step drop, running straight through the linebackers’ zones where re-routing used to happen. The hands rule did the rest. A timing offense needs the pocket to hold for exactly as long as the drop, every time, and blockers who could extend their arms could promise that. Walsh’s offense is the timing game at its purest: drops matched to route depths, the ball thrown to the spot before the receiver turns, and a progression the quarterback can run in a second and a half. It needs less protection than Coryell’s, throws fewer interceptions, and turns a 5-yard completion into a 15-yard gain. The cost is that it needs an extremely accurate quarterback and receivers who run every route to the inch, and that it is long and hard to learn: the West Coast play calls you met in Offensive Systems spell out every receiver’s job because the timing has no slack.
Walsh’s 49ers won Super Bowls after the 1981, 1984 and 1988 seasons, and his assistants carried the system everywhere (the coaching tree is in Case Study: Bill Walsh’s 49ers and the West Coast Offense). Between them, Coryell and Walsh defined the two ways to pass after 1978: stretch the defense vertically, or stretch it horizontally. Nearly every passing game since mixes the two.

title: 1978 and the Passing Revolution (1978–1999)
section: Defense’s first answer: more defensive backs
text:
Defense’s first answer: more defensive backs
Defenses answered the new passing game first with personnel. Offenses that meant to throw on half their plays wanted more receivers out in their routes, and they found them two ways. Some split a tight end or a back out wide, as Coryell split Winslow. Others took the second back off the field and sent on a third wide receiver, a set Sid Gillman had used since the 1960s, though teams didn’t use three-wide sets routinely, on any down, until the 1990s (the run-and-shoot and the K-Gun, later in this chapter).12 Either way, a linebacker covering that third receiver was a losing matchup. The fix was to take a linebacker off and put a fifth defensive back on: the nickel. The idea was older than 1978 (it is usually traced to Philadelphia assistant Jerry Williams around 1960, named by George Allen, and popularized by Don Shula and Bill Arnsparger’s Miami Dolphins in the 1970s),13 but after 1978 it went from a special package to an everyday one. In long-yardage situations defenses went further, to the dime: six defensive backs.
Each substitution is a trade. A nickel defense has one fewer player built to take on blockers, so it is softer against the run. And substitution became a game of its own: offenses changed their personnel to draw a defense into the wrong package, the substitution matching of Personnel Groupings. A defense in nickel against two tight ends is too light; a defense in base against three receivers is too slow. Hold on to that trade; it decides the K-Gun story later in this chapter.

title: 1978 and the Passing Revolution (1978–1999)
section: Defense’s second answer: Arnsparger’s 53 and the 3-4
text:
Defense’s second answer: Arnsparger’s 53 and the 3-4
The second answer was about the front, and it had started in Miami before 1978. Bill Arnsparger, Don Shula’s defensive coordinator, asked the Dolphins to trade for a Cleveland linebacker named Bob Matheson before the 1971 season, and built a package around him. Matheson lined up at the end of the line on the tight end’s side, standing up. On some snaps he rushed the passer like a defensive end; on others he dropped into coverage like a linebacker. The package was named for his jersey number: the 53 defense, Arnsparger’s front in which one hybrid player decided, snap by snap, whether the defense was a 4-3 or a 3-4. The package dates from the start of the 1972 season, and the 1972 Dolphins, Arnsparger’s “No-Name Defense” (Tom Landry’s name for a unit with no stars), went 17–0.14


Show the Python
# ------------------------------------------------------------------ the 53
off = line("short") + [O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0.0, "Q"), O("HB", "RB", -5.0, -2.2, "H"), O("FB", "FB", -5.0, 2.2, "F"),
                       O("Y", "TE", -0.7, 4.8, "Y"), O("X", "WR", -0.7, -13.0, "X"), O("Z", "WR", -1.5, 13.0, "Z")]
dfn = [D("WE", "DE", 1.0, T("5", -1), "E"), D("NT", "NT", 1.0, 0.0, "N"), D("SE", "DE", 1.0, T("5"), "E"),
       D("M53", "LB", 1.2, T("9") + 0.4, "53"), D("WLB", "LB", 4.2, -5.0, "L"),
       D("ILB1", "LB", 4.5, -1.2, "L"), D("ILB2", "LB", 4.5, 2.6, "L"),
       D("LCB", "CB", 7.0, -13.0, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 7.0, 13.0, "CB"),
       D("FS", "FS", 12.5, -3.0, "FS"), D("SS", "SS", 11.0, 3.6, "SS")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=None)
p.highlight("M53")
fld = draw(p, width_in=6.2, lateral=(-16.5, 16.5), window=(-7.5, 14.5), title=False)
band(fld, p, 0.1, 1.9, T("5", -1) - 1.1, T("5") + 1.1, color=style.DEFENSE, alpha=0.10, lw=0.8)
dashed(fld, p, [(1.2, 6.2), (-1.6, 6.9), (-4.4, 3.4)], color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, lw=1.6, dash="-")
dashed(fld, p, [(1.2, 6.2), (4.5, 7.6), (7.6, 9.6)], color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, lw=1.6)
say(fld, p, -4.2, 9.6, "rush: a fourth\nlineman (a 4-3)", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7.2)
say(fld, p, 10.3, 9.8, "or drop: a fourth\nlinebacker (a 3-4)", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7.2)
say(fld, p, 2.6, -7.4, "three linemen, hands down", fontsize=7)
say(fld, p, 6.1, -4.6, "three linebackers off the ball", fontsize=7)
plt.show()








Figure 55.5: Arnsparger’s 53 (illustrative, against a 1970s pro set). Three linemen have a hand down (shaded); Bob Matheson, number 53 (ringed), is the only player standing at the end of the line, outside the tight end; the other three linebackers (L) are off the ball. At the snap he either rushes, making a four-man line (a 4-3), or drops into coverage, making four linebackers (a 3-4). The blockers have to decide before the snap whether to account for him, and they can’t know which he will do.





Look at Figure 55.5 from the quarterback’s side. Before the snap there are three linemen with a hand on the ground and a fourth man standing at the end of the line. Is it four rushers or three? The quarterback and his blockers have to decide where Matheson is going before he goes, and they have no way to know. If they block him and he drops, a blocker is wasted and a linebacker is covering a receiver they thought was open. If they ignore him and he rushes, he is a free rusher. Arnsparger’s own phrase for what the 53 gave him, in a later interview, was the ability to “rush five guys and cover with six” from a look that showed neither. He called it “safe pressure,” and it is the seed of the zone blitz.
What made the 53 special was where it hid the choice. Matheson came on the field as part of an ordinary-looking group, and he was the only standing end, so the offense had one question to answer and no substitution to warn it. The rest of the league took the alignment more than the trick. Through the mid-1970s, teams stood up the two ends of the Oklahoma 5-2 (five linemen and two linebackers, the classic college front) and called it a 3-4. Chuck Fairbanks’s 1974 Patriots and Bum Phillips’s Oilers were among the first to make it their base defense (the competing origin claims are laid out in Odd and Hybrid Fronts), and by the late 1970s and early 1980s it was the league’s most common base defense.
The 3-4 fitted the post-1978 game for a reason that had nothing to do with the nose tackle. A 3-4 has two standing players at the ends of the line, its outside linebackers, and either one can rush or drop, so the 53’s question gets asked on both edges on every snap. What the 3-4 gives up is the 53’s surprise: the offense sees three linemen and four linebackers come on the field and knows what it faces, even if it doesn’t know who is coming. And the 3-4 creates a place on the field for a particular kind of athlete, a linebacker who is really a pass rusher, the stand-up edge. In 1981 the most famous one of all arrived.
