title: 1978 and the Passing Revolution (1978–1999)
section: Lawrence Taylor and the blind side
text:
Lawrence Taylor and the blind side
The New York Giants took Lawrence Taylor from North Carolina with the second pick of the 1981 draft and played him at outside linebacker in their 3-4. He was the league’s defensive player of the year as a rookie, again in 1982, and a third time in 1986, when he had 20.5 sacks and became the first defensive player voted the league’s MVP unanimously. Bill Parcells, his defensive coordinator and then head coach, and Bill Belichick, the Giants’ defensive coordinator from 1985, built the defense around the fact that no one could block him.15
Taylor’s speed broke the way offenses protected the passer. Through the 1970s, a blitzing linebacker was a running back’s problem: the back stayed in to block whichever linebacker came. A running back blocking Lawrence Taylor was a mismatch, and teams spent the 1980s inventing better answers. San Francisco’s Walsh, in a January 1982 playoff game against the Giants, assigned his best blocker, guard John Ayers, to him, which other teams copied; then coaches moved the job to the tackle, and in the end to whole protection schemes built around where Taylor was (the slide, the chip and the help side of Pass Protection).
Where Taylor lined up mattered as much as how fast he was. He rushed most often from the defense’s right side, the offense’s left (he was the Giants’ right outside linebacker), and that is where a right-handed quarterback is most exposed. Nearly every starting quarterback threw right-handed, so a defense could count on it.


Show the Python
# ------------------------------------------------------------------ the blind side
off = line("short") + [O("QB", "QB", -7.5, 0.0, "Q"), O("Y", "TE", -0.7, 4.8, "Y")]
dfn = [D("LE", "OLB", 1.0, -6.8, "E"), D("LDT", "DT", 1.0, T("3", -1), "T"), D("RDT", "DT", 1.0, T("3"), "T"),
       D("RE", "DE", 1.0, T("9") + 0.4, "E")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=None)
go_to(p, "LE", (-9.2, -1.5), kind="rush", via=[(-2.4, -7.6), (-5.6, -6.0), (-8.0, -3.8)])
go_to(p, "RE", (-5.4, 3.0), kind="rush", via=[(-2.4, 7.2), (-4.8, 5.4)], speed=4.0)
go_to(p, "LT", (-3.4, -5.0), kind="block", via=[(-1.6, -4.0)])
go_to(p, "RT", (-2.8, 4.9), kind="block", via=[(-1.4, 3.8)])
for k in ("LG", "C", "RG"):
    p.block(k, pts=[(-1.0, 0.0)])
p.block("Y", pts=[(-0.4, 0.8)])
p.highlight("LT", "LE")
fld = draw(p, width_in=6.0, lateral=(-13.5, 13.5), window=(-13.5, 6.5), title=False)
qx, qy = (float(v) for v in _P(fld, p, -7.5, 0.0))
fld.ax.add_patch(Wedge((qx, qy), 9.0, -35, 140, fc=style.THIRD, alpha=0.12, ec=style.THIRD, lw=0.8, zorder=1))
fld.ax.add_patch(Wedge((qx, qy), 6.0, 150, 285, fc=style.DEFENSE, alpha=0.13, ec=style.DEFENSE, lw=0.8,
                       ls=(0, (3, 2)), zorder=1))
say(fld, p, 3.6, 8.4, "what he sees\nas he sets to throw", color=GREEN, fontsize=7)
say(fld, p, -11.6, -5.0, "his blind side:\nbehind his left shoulder", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
say(fld, p, 4.0, -7.4, "the most dangerous rusher\nlines up over here", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
point_to(fld, p, (-3.2, -10.6), (-0.7, -3.2), "left tackle", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7.2, shrink=9)
say(fld, p, -9.6, 3.6, "right-handed QB\nat the top of his drop", color=style.INK_2, fontsize=6.8)
plt.show()








Figure 55.6: Why the left tackle matters (illustrative). A right-handed quarterback at the top of his drop. As he sets to throw, his left shoulder points downfield and his eyes go with it, so he can see the area shaded green but not the area shaded orange, behind his left shoulder. The edge rusher on the right (the defense’s left) comes at him where he can see and avoid him. The one on the left (ringed) comes from the blind side, and if he beats the left tackle (ringed) around the edge, he arrives unseen, from inside the orange area. Defenses put their best pass rusher on that side, so offenses put their best pass blocker there to meet him.





Figure 55.6 shows why. A right-handed quarterback dropping back from under center turns his body to the right as he drops, and when he sets to throw, his left shoulder points at his target and his eyes go downfield. Everything coming from behind his left shoulder is outside his field of view. A rusher from the right side is in front of him or at the edge of his vision, and he can step up or slide away from it. A rusher from the left arrives unseen, at full speed, at a quarterback holding the ball away from his body. That produces fumbles and injuries, the most famous of them Taylor’s 1985 sack that ended Joe Theismann’s career, told in The Twenty-Two.
The result was a new idea of the offensive line. The blind-side tackle is the tackle who protects the side the quarterback can’t see: the left tackle for a right-handed passer. Teams began to put their best pass blocker there, to draft him early and, once a salary cap made every dollar a choice (later in this chapter), to pay him like it. Two caveats keep the idea honest. For a left-handed quarterback (Steve Young in San Francisco, Mark Brunell in Jacksonville in the 1990s) the blind side is the right. And the side matters less once defenses learned to move their best rusher around, as they all do now, and once quarterbacks played from the shotgun and turned less on the drop; today the right tackle is paid almost as well. The blind side still pulls: when a team has to choose, its best pass protector usually plays on the left.

title: 1978 and the Passing Revolution (1978–1999)
section: Gibbs: one back, two tight ends, and the counter trey
text:
Gibbs: one back, two tight ends, and the counter trey
Taylor’s division rival had the most direct answer. Joe Gibbs, Coryell’s former offensive coordinator in San Diego, became Washington’s head coach in 1981 and played the Giants twice a year. Gibbs’s solution, in his own words, was a game plan built for one man: “We had to try in some way have a special game plan just for Lawrence Taylor… he’s one person that we learned the lesson the hard way. We lost ball games.”16 He took the second back out of the backfield and put him beside the tackle as an extra blocker. Playbooks of the time labelled the backs Q, H and F, so the new player kept his letter: the H-back, a tight end or fullback who lines up a step off the line, outside the tackle, where he can block an edge rusher, chip him and release into a route, or go in motion to the other side. With a second tight end on the line, the formation became the one-back, two-tight-end set (12 personnel) that Washington made its base: the ace of Classic Formations.
The one-back formation answered more than Taylor. With one back, the defense couldn’t key a fullback to find the run. With two tight ends and an H-back, the offense had extra blockers at the line who could also go out for passes, so the same formation threatened both. And it fitted the run game Washington built behind its huge offensive line, the “Hogs”: the counter trey, the guard-and-tackle counter of Gap Schemes, in which the back steps one way and two backside linemen pull the other way to lead him (the language of those runs is in The Language of the Run Game).
Gibbs won three Super Bowls, after the 1982, 1987 and 1991 seasons, with three different starting quarterbacks (Joe Theismann, Doug Williams and Mark Rypien), which says something about how much of the offense was the system.

title: 1978 and the Passing Revolution (1978–1999)
section: Buddy Ryan’s 46, and how the one-back attacked it
text:
Buddy Ryan’s 46, and how the one-back attacked it
While Gibbs was building his offense, Chicago’s defensive coordinator Buddy Ryan was building the defense meant to destroy offenses like it. The 46 put eight men near the line, covered the center and both guards with a nose and two 3-techniques (the bear front), stacked both outside linebackers on the tight end’s side, and usually played man coverage behind a blitz. It was designed against the two-back offenses of the early 1980s, and against them it was devastating. A two-back, one-tight-end offense has seven blockers at most (five linemen, the tight end and the fullback) and an obvious strong side, the tight end’s; the 46 put eight defenders near the line and aimed its stack at that side. The arithmetic was simply against the offense: the 1985 Bears allowed the fewest points in the league and beat New England 46–10 in Super Bowl XX (the full plate and Ryan’s story are in Even Fronts).17
The 46’s strength was its aggression and its alignment rules: both outside linebackers go to the tight end. Against a one-back team with two tight ends, the rule becomes a question: which tight end? Whichever side the defense chooses, the other side has fewer defenders, and a counter run pulls two extra blockers to exactly that side.
Follow Figure 55.7. The defense sets its stack to the in-line tight end, Y, on the right: two outside linebackers (W and S) out there, plus the Mike over the right tackle. On the left the offense faces only the end, a tackle, the nose and the strong safety (SS), who in the 46 plays like a linebacker. The H-back lines up on that side. At the snap the back jabs right, toward the stack, and the Mike, reading him, steps that way too. Then the right guard and right tackle pull left. Count the left side now: the guard kicks out the end, the left tackle and left guard block down on the tackle and the nose, the H-back takes the safety, and the pulling tackle leads through the hole onto the Mike. Five blockers for five defenders, and the back has a hole. The two linebackers stacked on the tight end, the players who make the 46 so dangerous against plays toward them, are out of the play: Y’s block walls off the Will at the line, and the Sam, the one man the play leaves unblocked, can only chase from behind. After the handoff the quarterback usually carries out a fake the other way, a bootleg toward the stack, to make that unblocked man hesitate.
Notice what the offense gives up to do this. The center has to block back on the 3-technique the right guard leaves, the hardest block on the play: in the 46 that tackle is coached to slant inside and penetrate, and a pulling guard leaves him a gap to do it, so if the center doesn’t cut him off, the play dies from behind before it starts. The bear front is hard on every gap scheme for that reason, since it covers all three interior linemen, and teams that ran counter at it often pulled the guard and the H-back instead of the guard and the tackle (GH counter, in Gap Schemes), which keeps the tackle home to help on the backside. And the play only works if the defense commits to one side. The 46 had answers of its own: it could set its stack to the H-back, or flip it when he went in motion, or blitz the side the counter was headed for. The more famous way to beat it was not a run at all but spreading out and throwing quickly, which is how Miami handed the 1985 Bears their only loss (see Even Fronts). That is the pattern of this whole era. The offense found a formation that forced the defense to declare, and the defense found a way to declare late.


Show the Python (simulated play, video on the web, frame strip in print)
def one_back_vs_46():
    """Gibbs-style one-back (12 personnel: Y in-line right, H-back off the left tackle) against the 46,
    which sets its two outside linebackers to the in-line tight end. Counter trey (GT counter) left."""
    off = line("short") + [O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -7.0, 0.0, "R"),
                           O("Y", "TE", -0.7, 4.8, "Y"), O("H", "TE", -1.5, -4.6, "H"),
                           O("X", "WR", -0.7, -14.0, "X"), O("Z", "WR", -1.5, 13.0, "Z")]
    bear = [D("WE", "DE", 1.0, -(3.2 + 1.5), "E"), D("WT", "DT", 1.0, T("3", -1), "T"), D("NT", "NT", 1.0, 0.0, "N"),
            D("ST", "DT", 1.0, T("3", 1), "T"), D("WILL", "LB", 1.3, 4.1, "W"), D("SAM", "LB", 1.4, 6.0, "S"),
            D("MIKE", "LB", 4.5, 3.2, "M"), D("SS", "S", 4.5, -3.2, "SS"),
            D("LCB", "CB", 1.2, -14.0, "C"), D("RCB", "CB", 1.2, 13.0, "C"), D("FS", "S", 10.0, -1.6, "FS")]
    p = Play(off, bear, los=35, to_go=None)
    # backfield: counter step right, then the handoff going left; the QB fakes a bootleg the other way
    go_to(p, "QB", (-3.9, -0.4), kind="path", speed=3.5)
    go_to(p, "QB", (-5.0, 4.0), kind="path", delay=0.55, speed=4.5)
    go_to(p, "RB", (-4.4, -0.9), kind="path", via=[(-6.6, 1.2)], speed=3.9)
    go_to(p, "RB", (5.6, -5.4), kind="run", via=[(-1.4, -3.4), (0.8, -4.4)], speed=5.0)
    p.handoff("RB", t=1.1)
    # play side: block down (each block ends just short of its man, so the markers touch, not overlap)
    go_to(p, "LT", (-0.1, -3.1))
    go_to(p, "LG", (-0.2, -1.1))
    go_to(p, "H", (0.9, -3.9), speed=3.2, delay=0.05)
    # backside: the center cuts off the slanting 3-technique; Y hinges on the Will and walls him off
    go_to(p, "C", (-0.4, 0.4))
    go_to(p, "Y", (0.0, 4.5))
    # the pullers: guard kicks out the end man, tackle wraps through the hole for the Mike
    go_to(p, "RG", (-0.6, -4.8), kind="pull", via=[(-1.6, 1.2), (-1.9, -3.0)])
    go_to(p, "RT", (2.9, -1.6), kind="pull", via=[(-2.3, 2.6), (-2.6, -3.6), (0.4, -4.0)], speed=6.6, delay=0.1)
    # receivers clear the corners away
    p.route("X", r.go(18)); p.route("Z", r.go(18))
    p.man("LCB", "X"); p.man("RCB", "Z")
    # defense: the bear front slants and penetrates; the backside 3-technique (ST) shoots the guard's gap
    go_to(p, "WE", (-0.2, -6.0), kind="rush", speed=1.5)
    go_to(p, "WT", (0.6, -1.9), kind="rush", speed=1.2)
    go_to(p, "NT", (0.6, 0.0), kind="rush", speed=1.0)
    go_to(p, "ST", (0.5, 1.3), kind="rush", speed=3.0)
    go_to(p, "WILL", (1.1, 4.0), kind="rush", speed=1.0)
    go_to(p, "SAM", (-1.4, 5.8), kind="rush", via=[(0.4, 6.9)], speed=4.8)
    go_to(p, "SAM", (-1.7, 0.7), kind="path", delay=0.35, speed=4.0)
    go_to(p, "MIKE", (4.3, 4.0), kind="path", speed=3.0)
    go_to(p, "MIKE", (4.1, -0.8), kind="path", delay=0.3, speed=4.4)
    go_to(p, "SS", (1.9, -3.0), kind="path", delay=0.45, speed=4.0)
    go_to(p, "FS", (6.1, -5.4), kind="path", delay=1.0, speed=4.2)
    return p


P46 = one_back_vs_46()


def tags(fld, p, t, i):
    first = i == 0 or (i == -1 and t < 0.3)
    hole = i in (2, 3) or (i == -1 and t >= 1.3)
    last = i == 3 or (i == -1 and t >= 2.3)
    if first:
        say(fld, p, 3.6, 7.2, "both OLBs\nto the TE", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.6)
        say(fld, p, -3.6, -5.4, "H-back", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.6)
    if hole:
        band(fld, p, -0.4, 2.6, -4.6, -3.4, color=GREEN, alpha=0.24, lw=1.1)
    if i == 2:
        say(fld, p, 3.4, -6.0, "the hole", color=GREEN, fontsize=6.6, weight="bold")
        say(fld, p, 2.9, 2.6, "C cuts off\nthe slant", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.4)
    if last:
        say(fld, p, -3.4, 2.6, "S: unblocked,\nchasing", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.4)
        say(fld, p, -6.4, 5.6, "Q fakes\nthe boot", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.4)


MOMENTS = [
    (0.0, "", "Both OLBs (W, S) are stacked on Y.\nLeft of the ball: E, T, N and SS."),
    (0.45, "counter step", "R jabs right, toward the stack;\nM steps with him. G and T pull."),
    (1.45, "pullers arrive", "G kicks out E; H takes SS; T and G block\ndown; C cuts off the slanting T."),

Figure 55.7: The counter trey from a one-back, two-tight-end set against the 46 (simulated, BDB-format tracking; illustrative, not a specific play). The 46 sets both outside linebackers (W, S) and the Mike to the in-line tight end, Y, on the right. 1: left of the ball are only the end, a 3-technique, the nose and the strong safety, with the H-back lined up across from them. 2: the back (green ring) jabs right toward the stack and the Mike steps with him, while the right guard and right tackle (purple rings) pull left. 3: the guard kicks out the end, the left tackle and guard block down, the H-back takes the safety, and the center cuts off the backside 3-technique, who slants into the gap the pulling guard left. The shaded green box is the hole. 4: the pulling tackle leads onto the Mike and the back is through the hole with only the free safety ahead. Y has walled off the Will at the line; the Sam, the one man left unblocked, can only chase from behind, slowed by the quarterback’s fake bootleg toward him. Faint lines are each player’s path so far.










NoteFilm room: Washington 1987 — Super Bowl XXII



The game: Washington 42, Denver 10, at San Diego on January 31, 1988. Denver led 10–0 after the first quarter. Washington then scored 35 points in the second quarter, still the Super Bowl record: Doug Williams, the first Black quarterback to start and win a Super Bowl, threw four touchdown passes in that quarter alone and finished with 340 yards, and rookie Timmy Smith, making his first NFL start, ran for a Super Bowl record 204 yards.18
What to notice: the one-back sets with two tight ends, the H-back moving before the snap, and Smith’s long runs, which come behind pulling linemen after a step the wrong way: the counter trey. Denver played Joe Collier’s 3-4, with standing outside linebackers at the ends of the line, and a counter that kicks out the end man and wraps a tackle onto a linebacker is built to gash exactly that front. Then watch Ricky Sanders’s two touchdown catches in the same quarter, of 80 and 50 yards, and ask yourself whether you could have told run from pass before the snap. That uncertainty is the point of the formation.


The rivalry went on after Ryan left Chicago to coach the Philadelphia Eagles (1986–1990): his Eagles knocked nine Washington players out of a November 1990 game, the “Body Bag Game,” and Washington beat them in the playoffs eight weeks later, after which the Eagles fired Ryan.19

title: 1978 and the Passing Revolution (1978–1999)
section: Spreading the field: the run-and-shoot and the K-Gun
text:
Spreading the field: the run-and-shoot and the K-Gun
By the late 1980s the next offensive answer was simply more receivers. If the 46 and the blitz-heavy defenses of the decade were built to win with numbers near the line, an offense could take the numbers away by spreading out.
The run-and-shoot went furthest: four wide receivers, one back, no tight end, and routes chosen after the snap from what the coverage did. Mouse Davis and June Jones, its two great teachers, brought it to the NFL, and between 1989 and the mid-1990s it was the base offense of the Detroit Lions, the Houston Oilers and the Atlanta Falcons. Warren Moon led the league in passing yards for Houston in 1990 and 1991. The defenses’ answer was the one Ryan always preached: hit the quarterback. Four receivers meant only five or six blockers, and blitzes that brought more rushers than that forced the quarterback to throw before the routes had sorted themselves out. Ryan, by then Houston’s defensive coordinator, called his own team’s run-and-shoot the “chuck and duck,” and the feud ended with him swinging at its coordinator, Kevin Gilbride, on the sideline in January 1994.20 The language and the reads of the run-and-shoot are in Offensive Systems.
Buffalo’s version was more durable. The K-Gun was a no-huddle offense run with three wide receivers, one tight end and one back (11 personnel), most often with quarterback Jim Kelly in the shotgun a few yards behind the center, calling the plays at the line.21 Its weapon was the clock between plays. A defense matches the offense’s personnel by substituting when the offense does; when the offense doesn’t substitute and doesn’t huddle, the defense has no time to change, and is stuck with whatever it had on the field when the drive started (the history, including the 1989 attempt to penalize the no-huddle, is in In-Game Adjustments and Tempo). The 1990 Bills went 13–3, scored a league-high 428 points and beat the Raiders 51–3 in the AFC Championship Game. They went on to play in four straight Super Bowls, and lost all four.


Show the Python
def spread_panel(ax, kind):
    if kind == "rs":
        off = line("short") + [O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -5.5, 0.0, "R"),
                               O("X", "WR", -0.7, -15.0, "X"), O("H", "WR", -1.5, -8.0, "H"),
                               O("S", "WR", -1.5, 8.0, "S"), O("Z", "WR", -0.7, 15.0, "Z")]
        ttl, notes = "Run-and-shoot: four wide, no tight end", [(-4.2, -8.6, "slot"), (-4.2, 8.6, "slot")]
    else:
        off = line("short") + [O("QB", "QB", -5.0, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -5.0, 1.6, "R"),
                               O("Y", "TE", -0.7, 4.8, "Y"), O("X", "WR", -0.7, -15.0, "X"),
                               O("H", "WR", -1.5, -8.5, "H"), O("Z", "WR", -1.5, 14.0, "Z")]
        ttl, notes = "K-Gun: three wide, a tight end, no huddle", [(-7.0, -2.4, "shotgun"), (1.6, 4.8, "TE")]

Figure 55.8: How to spot the two spread offenses of the late 1980s and early 1990s on old film (illustrative alignments). Top, the run-and-shoot: four wide receivers, two of them slots (H, S) a step off the line inside the outside receivers, one back, and no tight end, so only five linemen and the back to block. Bottom, the K-Gun: three wide receivers (X, H, Z), a tight end (Y) and a back, with the quarterback most often in the shotgun, and no huddle between plays. The run-and-shoot spreads the defense with its personnel; the K-Gun freezes the defense’s personnel with its tempo.





Figure 55.8 shows the two together. The tell for the run-and-shoot is the empty spot where a tight end should be, with two slot receivers standing a step off the line. The tell for the K-Gun is the tight end still attached to the line with three receivers around him, and above all the offense walking straight back to the line after the whistle while the defense’s sideline stays put.






NoteFilm room: New York Giants 1990 — Super Bowl XXV



The game: Giants 20, Bills 19, at Tampa on January 27, 1991, decided when Scott Norwood’s 47-yard field goal try went wide right with eight seconds left. The Giants were heavy underdogs to the K-Gun, which had scored 95 points in two playoff games.22
What to notice: both of the Giants’ game plans answer the no-huddle. On defense, Bill Belichick played extra defensive backs to take away Buffalo’s passing game, had them play Buffalo’s receivers physically wherever the rules allowed, and told his players, who had been the league’s best run defense, that they would win if Thurman Thomas ran for more than 100 yards. Thomas ran for 135 and the Giants won. On offense, Parcells kept the K-Gun on the sideline: the Giants held the ball for 40 minutes and 33 seconds, still the Super Bowl record. You can’t use tempo while you’re standing on the sideline. Belichick’s defensive plan is now in the Pro Football Hall of Fame.

title: 1978 and the Passing Revolution (1978–1999)
section: Safe pressure: the zone blitz meets the spread
text:
Safe pressure: the zone blitz meets the spread
The spread offenses beat man-coverage blitzes with hot throws: when more rushers come than the protection can block, the quarterback throws immediately to the receiver the blitzer left, and with four or five receivers spread wide, someone is always open for a moment. The 1990s defensive answer went back to Arnsparger’s idea of safe pressure: rush five, but from places the protection doesn’t expect, and drop a lineman into the throwing lane the quarterback expects to be open. The zone blitz gave a defense the pressure of a blitz without the man coverage that hot throws punish.
Who invented it is disputed. Some histories credit Arnsparger’s Miami defenses, in the 1970s or in his second stint in the 1980s with the “Killer B’s” (named for how many of its players’ surnames began with B); others credit Dick LeBeau, Cincinnati’s coordinator from 1984, who studied Arnsparger and turned the idea into a system. This book gives Arnsparger the idea and LeBeau the system (the case is laid out in Zone Blitzes). It became famous in Pittsburgh, where Dom Capers and LeBeau built “Blitzburgh”: the 1994 Steelers led the league with 55 sacks. Capers then took it to the expansion Carolina Panthers in 1995, and in their second season those Panthers went 12–4 and reached the NFC Championship Game.23

title: 1978 and the Passing Revolution (1978–1999)
section: 1994: the league tilts the board again
text:
1994: the league tilts the board again
Look back at the points panel of Figure 55.2. By 1992 and 1993 scoring had fallen to 18.7 points a game, the lowest since 1978, as the zone blitz, better pass rushers and faster defenses caught up. The owners responded as they had in 1978: in March 1994 they adopted a package of changes “to increase offensive production.” It modified line play and the roughing-the-passer rule, adopted the neutral zone infraction (a defender who enters the neutral zone and draws a flinch stops the play dead), and, in the part that matters most to this chapter, renewed the emphasis on “downfield chucking”: the 1978 five-yard rule was still on the books, and officials were told to call it. It also made two changes that are easy to see on any broadcast.24
The two-point conversion. After a touchdown, a team may now try to score two points by running or passing the ball into the end zone from the 2-yard line, instead of kicking for one. College football had used it since 1958 and the American Football League all through the 1960s; the NFL waited until 1994, 24 seasons after the merger, to adopt it. The first one in NFL history was scored by Cleveland’s punter and holder Tom Tupa, running in a faked kick in the opening week of 1994.25
The decision is a small expected-points problem, the kind Expected Points teaches. Kicking was worth almost exactly one point: from 1999 to 2014 (the seasons in nflverse data before the extra point was moved back in 2015), NFL kickers made 98.8 percent of extra points. Going for two succeeded 46.9 percent of the time, which is worth 2 × 0.469 ≈ 0.94 points.26 So on average the kick was slightly better, and teams went for two only a few times a season each.
The two-point try is a situational weapon, because late in a game what matters is not points but the chance of winning. Suppose you trail by 8 and score a touchdown with no time left. Kick, and you lose by 1: a near-certain point that is worth nothing. Go for two, and about 47 times in 100 you tie and go to overtime, roughly a coin flip, so about a 23 percent chance to win instead of none. The same logic runs the other way: score to go up by 1 late, and a kick puts you up 2, where a field goal still beats you, while a two-pointer puts you up 3, where a field goal only ties. Coaches carry a two-point chart that works through every score in this way; it is in Clock and Game Management.
Kickoffs from the 30. The kicking spot moved back five yards, from the 35 to the 30. A kickoff from five yards further back lands five yards shorter, so fewer kicks reach the end zone and more are returned: in 1993 only 68 percent of kickoffs were returned; in 1994, 88 percent. Why does a return help the offense? A touchback then put the ball at the 20, but the average return did better: in the seasons from 1999 to 2010, when the league still kicked off from the 30, a returned kickoff started the offense at about its own 28, eight yards better, and now and then a return went the distance. More returns meant better starting field position, which is what the package was for. (The kickoff spot went back to the 35 in 2011, and the kickoff has since been rebuilt entirely; see Kickoffs and Returns.)27
Scoring rose to 20.3 points a game in 1994 and 21.5 in 1995. The 1978 pattern again: the rules open a gap, and offenses move in.

section: Free agency and the salary cap: changing how teams are built
text:
Free agency and the salary cap: changing how teams are built
The last two changes of the era weren’t about the field at all, and they may have changed the game more than any rule about hands. Until 1993, an NFL player whose contract ended could not simply sign with another team. Through the 1980s the league’s rules made movement rare, and from 1989 to 1992 a system called Plan B let each team protect 37 players and leave only the rest free to sign elsewhere. Players sued, under the antitrust laws, which forbid competing businesses to agree among themselves not to compete; the players’ case was that the teams had done exactly that, agreeing not to bid for one another’s players. In 1992 a federal jury in a case brought by eight players, led by the Jets’ Freeman McNeil, agreed that Plan B violated those laws, and in January 1993 the league and the players settled the remaining suits with a seven-year agreement that rebuilt the system.28

Free agency (1993)
Free agency (1993) is the system, in force since March 1, 1993, that lets a veteran whose contract has expired sign with any team. What counts is accrued seasons: a player earns one for each season he spends at least six regular-season games on full pay status. Today a player with four or more accrued seasons and an expired contract is an unrestricted free agent, free to sign anywhere. With three, he is a restricted free agent: other teams may bid, but his old team can keep him by matching the offer. With fewer than three, he is an exclusive-rights free agent: if his old team offers him a one-year minimum contract, he can’t negotiate with anyone else.29 The first great free-agent signing showed what it could do. Reggie White, the best defensive end of his era, left Philadelphia in 1993 for a four-year, $17 million contract with Green Bay that made him the third-highest-paid player in the league, and after the 1996 season he set a Super Bowl record with three sacks as the Packers won Super Bowl XXXI.30


The salary cap (1994)
In exchange, the owners got the salary cap: a hard limit, the same for every team, on what a club may count against its player payroll in a season, set each year from a share of league revenue. It began in 1994 at $34.6 million per team, higher than the expected $32 million because a new television deal with a new network, Fox, raised league revenue. It is a hard cap: no team may exceed it for any reason.31






ImportantWhy it exists



The two came as a pair, and each answers the other’s problem. Free agency gave players the right to sell their services to the highest bidder; the cap kept the richest owners from simply buying every good player, which the league feared would end competitive balance. The trade the players made was a fixed share of revenue in return for movement; the trade the teams made was freedom to spend in return for a ceiling that made every contract a choice against every other.


The cap counts money by rules of its own, and one of them shapes every big contract. A signing bonus is paid when the contract is signed, but it counts against the cap spread evenly over the years of the contract (today, over at most five). Without that rule a team could pay a huge bonus in a year it had room and show only small salaries afterwards. With it, the same rule became the tool teams use to push cap charges into future years: turn this year’s salary into a bonus and most of its cap charge moves into later seasons. Under a hard cap the fights are not over whether money counts but when. Denver learned that the hard way: in 2004 the league fined the Broncos $950,000 and took a third-round pick for agreements, in 1996 to 1998, that deferred players’ salaries with interest and, the league ruled, got around the cap.32
How the cap changed football strategy. You will see three of its effects in almost every chapter of this book.

Positions got prices. Under a cap, paying one player means not paying another, so teams had to decide which positions are worth the most. The answers that emerged in the 1990s still hold: quarterback first, then the players who decide whether the quarterback has time, the pass rusher and the blind-side tackle. The cap is what turned Lawrence Taylor’s effect into a salary structure. Building a Roster follows that logic to today’s contracts.
Rosters churned, so systems had to travel. With players moving every spring, a team could no longer assume its starters had spent five years learning its playbook. Offenses and defenses had to be teachable to a newcomer in one off-season, which rewarded concept-based languages (one word for a whole pattern, the Erhardt-Perkins idea) and coaches who could install fast. Coaches moved too, and took their systems with them; the coaching trees of Part 12 are a product of the same mobility.
Depth got thinner, and cheap players got valuable. A team at the cap can’t stockpile veterans, so the draft, where players are cheap for their first contract, became the most valuable source of talent, and specialists who play only in certain packages (a third-down pass rusher, a nickel corner) are bought cheaply rather than kept on the roster as insurance.

title: 1978 and the Passing Revolution (1978–1999)
text:
Where the era landed: 1998 and 1999
By the end of the 1990s, each of the era’s big ideas had a winner. In 1998 the Denver Broncos went 14–2 behind Mike Shanahan’s offense, which married Walsh’s play-action passing to the outside-zone running Alex Gibbs had brought to Denver in 1995 (the story is in Zone Running). Terrell Davis ran for 2,008 yards, and John Elway, in his last game, was the MVP of a 34–19 win over Atlanta in Super Bowl XXXIII.33 The same season the Minnesota Vikings, coached by Dennis Green, a former Walsh assistant, and with a rookie receiver named Randy Moss, scored 556 points, then the most in league history, before losing the NFC Championship Game in overtime.34 And in 1999 the St. Louis Rams, running Mike Martz’s Coryell-descended offense, the “Greatest Show on Turf,” beat the Tennessee Titans 23–16 in Super Bowl XXXIV.35
Two champions and a record-setter, and every line of descent from 1978 is in them: Walsh’s timing game married to Alex Gibbs’s zone running (which came down a different line altogether) in Denver, a Walsh-tree offense with a vertical threat in Minnesota, and Coryell’s vertical game in St. Louis. Meanwhile the defenses had their nickel and dime packages, their 3-4 edge rushers and their zone blitzes, and were waiting for the next rule change. The next round of the story, the spread offenses that came up from college and the defenses built to stop them, is in The College Laboratory and Dynasties and Counterpunches.

text:
Watch for it on Sunday






TipWatch for it: classic film



Find a full game from the 1980s or early 1990s (NFL Films and the league’s own YouTube channel post many; Super Bowls XX, XXII and XXV are easy to find) and chart the first quarter with what you now know.

Personnel and formation. Count the backs and tight ends on every snap. How often is it the pro set or the I with two backs? When does a third receiver appear, and does the defense answer with a fifth defensive back? Is anyone lined up as an H-back, a step off the line beside the tackle?
The front. Three linemen with hands down and two standing at the ends (a 3-4), or four down (a 4-3)? If you see the center and both guards covered and a safety walked up into the box, you’re looking at the 46.
The best pass rusher. Find him before the snap. Which side is he on, and what does the offense do about it: an H-back next to his tackle, a back staying in, a tight end chipping him?
Contact on receivers. Watch a receiver past five yards. Does anyone touch him before the ball is thrown? After 1978 that is a foul, but officials let a good deal go until the league ordered strict enforcement in 2004, so expect to see more contact than the rulebook allowed.
The clock between plays. Does the offense huddle? If it doesn’t, does the defense manage to substitute?
Then flip to a game from this season and run the same list. Note what has faded (the two-back pro set, the 46, the seven-step drop) and what survived (the slant-flat, the counter, the stand-up edge rusher, the zone blitz). The huddle survived too: in 2025, NFL offenses went no-huddle on only about 8 percent of charted plays.37

plt.show()








Figure 55.10: Predict the play 1. 1986: one back, a tight end (Y) on the right, and an H-back who could line up in either dashed circle. The Giants are in a 3-4; their best pass rusher, number 56 (ringed), stands at the end of the line on the offense’s left, and he may walk across to the dashed square outside the tight end before the snap.





It’s 1986, and your right-handed quarterback is about to face the Giants. They are in their 3-4, and their best pass rusher, number 56, is standing at the end of the line on your left. You have one running back, a tight end on the right, and an H-back you can line up on either side. Where do you put the H-back, and what does he do at the snap? And if 56 walks across before the snap to stand outside your tight end, on the side your quarterback faces, what do you do then?






TipAnswer





On the left, next to the left tackle. Number 56 is lined up over your quarterback’s blind side, so that is where you need an extra man. At the snap the H-back chips him: hits him as he comes off the edge, then releases into a short route if nothing else comes. That gives the left tackle help against a rusher he can’t block alone, and gives the quarterback a check-down when the H-back releases. This is the job Joe Gibbs created the position for.
If 56 shifts right, the H-back goes with him, in motion across the formation, and sets up beside the tight end. Now your quarterback can see 56 coming, but seeing him isn’t the same as blocking him: he is still the rusher who beats one blocker, and the right tackle with a tight end and an H-back beside him can chip him twice. The left tackle is left alone with the other outside linebacker (B), which is a fair fight. Defenses learned to move their best rusher around for exactly this reason, to make the offense show where its help goes. The rule is the one from Pass Protection: find the best rusher first and put help where he is. The blind side matters because that is where he usually lines up, not for its own sake.

Figure 55.11: Predict the play 2. 1990: Buffalo in the shotgun with three wide receivers (X, H, Z), a tight end and a back, no huddle, against a base 3-4 that was on the field when the drive began. The slot receiver H and the linebacker over him (B) are ringed.





It’s 1990, first-and-10. Buffalo has just picked up a first down and hurried to the line without a huddle, Kelly in the shotgun: three wide receivers (the slot receiver on the left is H, here a receiver, not an H-back), a tight end, one back. The defense had its base 3-4 on the field when the drive started, and the offense hasn’t given it time to change. Where will Jim Kelly look, and what should the defense have done before the drive began?






TipAnswer





At the slot receiver on the left (H). The only player to cover him in a base defense is a linebacker, the highlighted B, and a wide receiver against a linebacker in space is the matchup the K-Gun was built to create. On first-and-10 the offense can do anything, so it takes the matchup: expect a quick throw to H, a slant or an option route that breaks away from the linebacker’s leverage. Base 3-4 personnel is built to stop the run, which is exactly why the K-Gun threw against it. Had the defense been in nickel instead, the call flips: Kelly hands to Thurman Thomas, on a draw or a trap, against a lighter box. That is why there was no right package to start the drive in.
The fix had to come before the drive, because once the offense stops huddling, the defense can only substitute when the offense does, and the offense won’t wait. A defense facing the K-Gun had to pick its package before the drive and live with it, and nickel or dime meant accepting the trade: lighter against the run. That is exactly what Belichick’s Giants did in Super Bowl XXV, with extra defensive backs on the field and a promise to let Thurman Thomas run. And the Giants’ offense took away the other ingredient tempo needs: the ball. You can’t hurry the next snap if you aren’t on the field.

Figure 55.12: Predict the play 3. 1979: the Cover 2 a defense would have called in 1977, against a two-back pro set. The tight end (Y, ringed) gets a clean release and runs up the seam between the two deep halves as the Mike (M, ringed) drops to about 8 yards in the middle.





It’s 1979, and the defense calls the Cover 2 it played in 1977: two deep safeties and five underneath. The tight end, Y, gets off the line clean and releases up the seam between the two safeties, and the Mike drops straight back to about 8 yards in the middle. In 1977 the Mike would have spent the defense’s one hit on Y right there (the previous chapter’s drill showed why). What can he do now, where is the ball going, and what does the defense have to change?






TipAnswer





He can’t touch him. Past five yards the Mike may not initiate contact with Y. He has to turn and run with Y, a linebacker chasing a tight end up the field, or let him go and hope a safety gets there. Neither safety can, because each is responsible for his own half of the field, and the seam is exactly between them. The ball goes to Y at 18 to 20 yards, in the hole that every Cover 2 has in the deep middle.
What the defense has to change: it needs someone in the deep middle. It can play a single safety there (Cover 3, or man coverage with a free safety), put a faster defensive back on the tight end, or, the answer that came to define a style of defense, make the Mike run: in Tampa 2 he sprints to the deep middle at the snap, turning Cover 2 into three deep in the middle of the field (Cover 2 and Tampa 2). That linebacker needed a sprinter’s speed, which is one more way the 1978 rules changed what a defensive player looks like.

title: 1978 and the Passing Revolution (1978–1999)
text:
Takeaways

Two 1978 rules opened the passing game from both ends. The Mel Blount rule stopped defenders from hitting receivers past five yards, which made timed routes possible; open-hand pass blocking gave the quarterback more time. Passes went from 40 percent of plays in 1977 to half of them by the early 1980s, and interceptions fell for twenty years.
The offense split into two answers. Air Coryell stretched the field deep with protection and big receivers; Walsh’s West Coast offense stretched it sideways with short, timed throws that worked like runs, living in the 5-to-15-yard band the Blount rule had cleared and behind blockers who could now use their hands. Gibbs’s one-back, two-tight-end offense, the run-and-shoot and the K-Gun built on both.
Every defensive answer answered something specific: nickel and dime for the third receiver; the 53 and the 3-4 for disguising who rushes; the 46 for two-back offenses; the zone blitz for hot throws. The 3-4 also made room for a new player, the stand-up edge rusher, and Lawrence Taylor broke protections that blocked linebackers with running backs, until the H-back and slide protections answered him. Each new answer created the next question.
The blind side made the left tackle a premium position, because a right-handed quarterback can’t see what comes from behind his left shoulder, and because the best rushers lined up there.
The league rewrote the rules again when defenses caught up: the 1994 package added the two-point conversion and moved kickoffs back to the 30.
Free agency (1993) and the salary cap (1994) changed how teams are built: positions got prices, systems had to be teachable fast, and cheap drafted players became the most valuable kind.

title: The College Laboratory: Wing-T, Wishbone, Air Raid, Spread Option, and the RPO
text:
Why college invents and the NFL borrows
Saturday night, third-and-6. The offense snaps the ball eleven seconds after the last play ended. Four receivers stand spread across a field whose hash marks seem to sit almost on the sideline; the ball is on the left one, and the whole offense seems to have drifted to the wide side of the field. The quarterback, five yards behind the center, puts the ball in his running back’s belly, watches a defensive end, pulls the ball, takes two steps, and flips it to a slot receiver bowing backward toward the sideline. Twelve yards. The next afternoon you watch an NFL team run almost the same play: same read, same flip, same receiver. The NFL version is a little quicker, the line looks a little different, and the announcer calls it “a college concept.” He is right, and he could have said the same thing about half the plays in the game. Where did they come from, why does college football keep inventing them, and why do some make the jump to Sunday while others never do?
You’ll be able to:
How to read the diagrams. The offense always moves up the page, and left and right mean the offense’s left and right.
Watch enough football and a pattern appears. Almost every offensive idea that changed the NFL in the last thirty years, the shotgun spread run game, the zone read, the pistol, the RPO, the spread no-huddle, the Air Raid’s handful of pass concepts, arrived from college (the NFL had flirted with the no-huddle in the K-Gun era; college made it an identity), often a decade or more after it was born there. The traffic runs the other way much less often. That isn’t because college coaches are smarter. It is because college football is a different environment, and four features of that environment reward invention.

title: The College Laboratory: Wing-T, Wishbone, Air Raid, Spread Option, and the RPO
text:
1. More teams, and bigger talent gaps
The NFL has 32 teams drawing from one talent pool, with a draft and a salary cap built to keep them roughly equal (1978 and the Passing Revolution tells how the cap arrived). College football has more than 130 teams in its top division alone, the Football Bowl Subdivision (FBS), and hundreds more below it, and no mechanism at all to keep them equal.1 Every year a few programs sign most of the best high-school players, and everyone else has to play them.
That gap is the mother of invention. A coach who can’t recruit the bigger, faster players has two choices: lose, or change the problem. Almost every lineage in this chapter starts with a coach in the second group: Bill Yeoman at Houston with an offensive line that couldn’t block, LaVell Edwards at BYU with no chance of out-recruiting the Southwest’s powers, Hal Mumme and Mike Leach at tiny Iowa Wesleyan, Rich Rodriguez at Glenville State, a Division II school in West Virginia. Their inventions all do the same thing in different ways: they change the arithmetic so that the defense’s better players have more to defend than they have bodies, or have to make a decision they aren’t trained for.
The NFL has talent gaps too, but small ones. When the other team’s players are as good as yours, a gimmick that exploits a mismatch is worth less, and a scheme that gets your quarterback hit is worth much less.


2. A wider field
College hash marks are 40 feet apart, 60 feet in from each sideline; NFL hash marks are 18 feet 6 inches apart, the width of the goal posts. The field is the same size. What changes is where the ball can start, and that changes everything about spacing. With the ball on a college hash, the short (boundary) side is 20 yards wide and the wide (field) side 33. Before 1993 the college hashes sat even wider, a third of the way across (53 feet 4 inches from each sideline, the high-school spot), so the wishbone and veer offenses of this chapter played with a boundary under 18 yards wide.2 The Game in Fifteen Minutes drew the same four-receiver formation on both fields.
A wide field is a gift to a horizontal offense, one that stretches a defense from sideline to sideline. With 33 yards to the field side, a defense that wants to cover four receivers spread across it has to send defenders a long way from the ball, out of the box (the area near the ball where runs are defended). With 20 yards to the boundary, the offense can put a single receiver into the short side and dare a cornerback to cover him alone, with no room to help. Option and spread offenses were made for that geometry. The NFL’s narrow hashes put the ball near the middle almost every snap, which makes the field more symmetrical and takes away some of the leverage.


3. Rules that tolerate the run-pass blur
College rules have been friendlier to offenses that mix run and pass on the same snap. The biggest difference is the ineligible downfield rule from Run-Pass Options: in college an offensive lineman may be up to three yards past the line when a pass that crosses it is thrown, and the rule doesn’t apply at all to passes caught behind the line; in the NFL, the limit is one yard on any forward pass.3 Three yards is room to run-block for a beat and still throw. It is the reason college RPOs can be “run first, throw later,” and the reason the college game grew so many plays that are a run and a pass at once. Other college rules nudge the same way: one foot in bounds makes a sideline catch easier, and a defensive pass interference foul costs at most 15 yards, which changes the math of a deep throw (the rules section near the end puts them all side by side).


4. Roster churn, practice limits and tempo
A college roster turns over every four or five years, and the best players leave sooner. NCAA rules cap the hours a team can make players practice in season.4 A system that has to be taught to a new quarterback every two or three years, in limited hours, rewards simplicity: a small number of plays repeated until they are automatic, which is exactly what the Air Raid and the spread option were. Simplicity, in turn, makes tempo possible. A team that runs twelve concepts can call them with one word or one hand signal and snap the ball before the defense has substituted or even lined up. College football’s clock (for decades it stopped after every first down) gave fast teams more snaps to use it on.


The filter: what the NFL keeps
Those same four forces explain what doesn’t cross. The NFL is a filter, and an idea has to survive four tests to get through it.

The quarterback test. NFL quarterbacks are the most expensive players in the sport, and every hit is a risk the team can’t insure. Ideas that hit the quarterback on most snaps (the triple option, the wishbone) stop at the border; ideas that hit him occasionally (the zone read) cross as a change-up.
The talent test. NFL defenders are fast enough, and evenly enough spread across the league, that a scheme built on a mismatch has to work against the best defense on the schedule, not the average one.
The rules test. The one-yard rule, two feet in bounds and the spot-foul DPI all change how an idea plays on Sunday. Some ideas cross in modified form (the RPO, with quicker throws); some don’t.
The people test. Ideas reach the NFL most easily inside players. A quarterback who ran the zone read for four years arrives knowing how; a coach who designed it has to convince an NFL building to change.

The rest of the chapter follows the ideas through that filter. Here is the map.


Show the Python
ROWS = [  # idea, who, college debut, NFL arrival (None = not as a system), side, NFL note
    ("Split-T option", "Faurot, Missouri", 1941, None, "off", "never as a system"),
    ("Wing-T", "Nelson, Maine and Delaware", 1950, 2017, "off", "jet-motion era: Rams, 49ers"),
    ("Veer, triple option", "Yeoman, Houston", 1965, 2012, "off", "option reads: the 2012 wave"),
    ("Wishbone", "Bellard, Texas", 1968, None, "off", "never"),
    ("BYU passing game", "Edwards, BYU", 1972, None, "off", "carried by its QBs and coaches"),
    ("Air Raid", "Mumme and Leach", 1989, 2019, "off", "Kingsbury's Cardinals"),
    ("Zone read", "Rodriguez", 1991, 2012, "off", "Griffin, Kaepernick, Wilson"),
    ("3-3-5 stack", "Dunn, Memphis", 1991, None, "def", "college only"),
    ("Match quarters", "Saban, Michigan State", 1995, 2018, "def", "the two-high boom"),
    ("Pistol", "Ault, Nevada", 2005, 2012, "off", "Washington, 49ers"),

    ("Up-tempo spread", "Kelly, Oregon", 2007, 2013, "off", "spread-run tempo: Kelly's Eagles"),
    ("Three-high safeties", "Heacock, Iowa State", 2017, None, "def", "college first"),
]
style.apply()
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.8, 4.5))
n = len(ROWS)
for i, (idea, who, cy, ny, side, note) in enumerate(ROWS):

    col = style.OFFENSE if side == "off" else style.DEFENSE

        ax.plot([cy, ny], [y, y], color=col, lw=2.2, alpha=0.45, zorder=2, solid_capstyle="round")
        ax.scatter([ny], [y], s=34, marker="D", facecolor=style.SURFACE, edgecolor=col, lw=1.6, zorder=4)
        ax.text((cy + ny) / 2, y + 0.17, f"{ny - cy} years", fontsize=6.6, color=style.INK_2, ha="center",
                va="bottom")

    else:
        ax.text(cy + 2.4, y, note, fontsize=6.6, color=style.MUTED, va="center", ha="left", style="italic")
ax.set_yticks(range(n))
ax.set_yticklabels([f"{r[0]}  ({r[1]})" for r in ROWS][::-1], fontsize=7.2)

ax.set_ylim(-0.7, n - 0.3)

ax.tick_params(axis="x", labelsize=7.5)

ax.tick_params(axis="y", length=0)
h = [Line2D([], [], marker="o", ls="", color=style.INK_2, ms=5.5, label="college debut"),
     Line2D([], [], marker="D", ls="", markerfacecolor=style.SURFACE, markeredgecolor=style.INK_2, ms=5,
            label="NFL mainstream")]
ax.legend(handles=h, loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.45, -0.07), ncol=2, fontsize=7.2, frameon=False)

plt.show()








Figure 56.1: Seventy years of borrowing: notice the long lags and how many diamonds bunch between 2012 and 2019. Each row is one college invention: the dot is roughly its college debut, the diamond when the idea became mainstream in the NFL, the label on the line the lag. Blue rows are offense, orange defense. Rows with no diamond never crossed as a system, or crossed only inside the people who learned them (BYU). Dates are approximate; several ideas, the RPO above all, have more than one claimed inventor.





Two things jump out. First, the lag. Ideas that crossed took a decade or two: the zone read about twenty years, the Air Raid thirty, the Wing-T’s motion game closer to seventy. Second, the timing of the crossings is bunched. Almost everything arrived between 2012 and 2019, as the first generation of NFL players who had spent their whole careers in shotgun spread offenses reached the league and as NFL coaches ran out of reasons to resist (the shotgun data near the end of the chapter shows what those reasons were). First, the ideas, in roughly the order they were born.

section: The option line: split-T, veer, wishbone, flexbone
text:
The option line: split-T, veer, wishbone, flexbone
Option Football taught how the option works: leave a defender unblocked, read him, and give the ball to whoever he isn’t playing. The history of that idea is a history of college coaches finding new backfields from which to run it.
It begins in 1941 with Don Faurot at Missouri, who widened the T-formation’s line splits and built the split-T, a series of dives, quarterback keeps and pitches that worked like a modern option. Bud Wilkinson took it to Oklahoma, and Oklahoma’s split-T teams won 47 straight games in the 1950s (03-04 has the details). The split-T never became an NFL offense, but it fixed the pattern for the next seventy years: option football is what you run when the other team’s linemen are bigger than yours.
The veer (Houston, 1965). Bill Yeoman’s Houston teams of the mid-1960s couldn’t block the defensive tackles, so Yeoman stopped trying: the play-side tackle released inside and the quarterback read the first defender outside him, giving to a diving halfback or keeping. That is the veer, and with the other halfback trailing as a pitch man it is the triple option. It made Houston one of the highest-scoring teams in the country: in 1968 the Cougars beat Tulsa 100–6.5
The wishbone (Texas, 1968). Two years later, Texas offensive coordinator Emory Bellard moved the split-T’s fullback up close behind the quarterback and set the two halfbacks deeper and wider behind him: the wishbone of Classic Formations. Darrell Royal’s Longhorns won 30 straight games with it; Oklahoma and Alabama copied it; and through the 1970s it was the most feared offense in college football.6
The wishbone’s genius was that every back had a job on every play, to either side: dive, lead or pitch. The defense had to assign someone to each of three runners on both sides of the formation, with every assignment perfect, and do it without knowing which way the play was going until the snap. In 1971 Oklahoma’s wishbone averaged 472.4 rushing yards a game, still the major-college record.7 Here is the play to one side.


Show the Python
def wishbone_off():
    off = line5() + [O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0.0, "Q"), O("FB", "FB", -3.6, 0.0, "F"),
                     O("LH", "RB", -5.2, -2.6, "H"), O("RH", "RB", -5.2, 2.6, "H"),
                     O("Y", "TE", -0.7, 4.8, "Y"), O("X", "WR", -0.7, -15.0, "X")]
    check_legal(off)
    return off


def wishbone_def():
    return [D("BE", "DE", 1.0, technique("5", -1), "5"), D("BT", "DT", 1.0, technique("2i", -1), "2i"),
            D("RT_", "DT", 1.0, technique("1", 1), "1"), D("RE", "DE", 1.0, technique("5", 1), "5"),
            D("WILL", "WILL", 1.0, -7.8, "W"), D("SAM", "SAM", 1.0, 6.4, "S"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, -0.8, "M"),
            D("SS", "SS", 7.5, -10.0, "SS"), D("FS", "FS", 12.5, 1.5, "FS"),
            D("LCB", "CB", 6.5, -15.0, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 7.0, 10.0, "CB")]


p = Play(wishbone_off(), wishbone_def(), los=35, to_go=None)
go_to(p, "LT", (3.4, -1.3), via=[(0.0, -2.9)])           # veer release to the Mike
go_to(p, "LG", (0.5, -1.1))                               # on the 2i
go_to(p, "C", (0.4, 0.5))                                 # back on the 1
go_to(p, "RG", (2.8, 1.6), via=[(0.2, 1.7)])              # climb for backside pursuit
go_to(p, "RT", (0.4, 3.7))
go_to(p, "Y", (0.6, 5.7))
go_to(p, "LH", (6.3, -10.0), via=[(-3.6, -6.4), (-0.6, -10.2)])   # arc around #2 to #3
go_to(p, "X", (5.4, -14.8))

       label_at=(6.5, -2.7), fontsize=7)

       label_at=(6.5, -6.6), fontsize=7)

       label_at=(2.4, -14.0), fontsize=7)

    say(f, p, d, w, num, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=8.5, weight="bold")
say(f, p, 11.9, -5.6, "1 = dive key (first read)\n2 = pitch key (second read)\n3 = alley: the lead halfback\n"
    "4 = deep: the split end", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
point_to(f, p, (-5.0, 6.6), (-5.4, 2.0), "pitch man starts\non the far side", fontsize=6.6)
point_to(f, p, (-5.4, -13.8), (-3.4, -6.6), "lead halfback arcs\naround #2 to #3", fontsize=6.6)
panel_title(f.ax, "The wishbone triple option", size=10)
plt.show()








Figure 56.2: The wishbone triple option to the split-end side (the offense’s left). Notice that every play-side defender is either blocked or read. The left tackle releases inside to the Mike, leaving the 5-technique unblocked as the dive key (#1); the Will, on the line outside him, is the pitch key (#2). The fullback (F) dives; the near halfback arcs around #2 to block the safety in the alley (#3); the split end (X) blocks the cornerback (#4). The far halfback sprints behind the quarterback to become the pitch man, about four yards outside him and a yard deeper, so #2 can’t cover both. The quarterback rides the dive reading #1, then, if he keeps, runs at #2.





Why did it fade? The same forces that made it, in reverse. Defenses got faster through the 1970s and 1980s, and fast defenders who play their assignments shrink the margins the triple option lives on. The best high-school quarterbacks wanted to pass, because passers were what the NFL drafted, and the programs that could recruit them stopped needing a talent equalizer. And it was hard to come from behind with an offense that threw a dozen times a game. Oklahoma won its last national title with the wishbone in 1985; by the 1990s the formation survived mostly at the service academies (Army, Navy and Air Force).8
The flexbone (late 1970s and 1980s). The wishbone’s last descendant fixed its biggest weakness, width. By standing the two halfbacks just off the line as slotbacks (A-backs), the flexbone spread the defense like a passing formation while keeping three runners near the ball; one A-back’s pre-snap motion became the pitch. Its invention is disputed. The name is usually traced to Fisher DeBerry’s Air Force teams of the 1980s (the wishbone, he is said to have remarked, needed to be more flexible), and Ken Hatfield, DeBerry’s predecessor there, ran a version at Arkansas later in the decade. Paul Johnson, Georgia Southern’s offensive coordinator from 1985, is the coach most credited with building it into a full system, and the formation itself is the double-slot set of the run-and-shoot (more on that offense below) with the option added. Johnson’s Navy and Georgia Tech teams are its modern face (02-03).9
Put the four option backfields side by side and the idea’s survival strategy is plain: the three threats never change; only where the threats start does.


Show the Python
def keys():
    return [D("K1", "DE", 1.0, -4.0, "1"), D("K2", "OLB", 1.0, -7.8, "2")]


def bf_split():
    off = line5() + [O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0.0, "Q"), O("LH", "RB", -4.6, -2.2, "H"), O("RH", "RB", -4.6, 2.2, "H")]
    return off, [((-4.6, -2.2), [(-3.0, -2.4), (2.6, -2.7)], "run"),
                 ((-4.6, 2.2), [(-5.0, 0.0), (-4.2, -5.6), (-2.6, -9.6)], "path")], (-2.5, -1.3)


def bf_bone():
    off = line5() + [O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0.0, "Q"), O("FB", "FB", -3.6, 0.0, "F"),
                     O("LH", "RB", -5.2, -2.6, "H"), O("RH", "RB", -5.2, 2.6, "H")]
    return off, [((-3.6, 0.0), [(-2.4, -1.6), (2.6, -2.5)], "run"),
                 ((-5.2, 2.6), [(-5.6, 0.2), (-4.4, -5.8), (-2.8, -9.8)], "path"),
                 ((-5.2, -2.6), [(-3.4, -6.2), (-0.6, -10.4), (3.2, -10.6)], "path")], (-2.4, -1.2)


def bf_flex():
    off = line5() + [O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0.0, "Q"), O("FB", "FB", -4.6, 0.0, "B"),
                     O("LA", "RB", -1.6, -5.2, "A"), O("RA", "RB", -1.6, 5.2, "A")]
    return off, [((-4.6, 0.0), [(-2.6, -1.6), (2.6, -2.5)], "run"),
                 ((-1.6, 5.2), [(-3.6, 1.6), (-4.4, -2.0), (-3.8, -6.4), (-2.6, -9.6)], "path"),
                 ((-1.6, -5.2), [(-0.8, -8.6), (0.4, -10.6), (3.2, -10.6)], "path")], (-2.4, -1.2)


def bf_spread():
    off = line5() + [O("QB", "QB", -5.0, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -5.0, -2.6, "R"), O("H", "WR", -1.5, -9.0, "H")]
    return off, [((-5.0, -2.6), [(-3.7, -1.4), (-3.2, 0.6), (2.6, 1.8)], "run"),
                 ((-1.5, -9.0), [(-2.9, -10.2), (-2.8, -12.8)], "path")], (-5.0, 0.0)


PANELS = [("Split-back veer (Houston, 1965)", bf_split, (-1.6, -5.0), (-2.7, -9.0)),
          ("Wishbone (Texas, 1968)", bf_bone, (-1.6, -5.2), (-2.9, -9.2)),
          ("Flexbone (1980s)", bf_flex, (-0.9, -4.4), (-2.8, -9.2)),
          ("Spread option (2000s)", bf_spread, (-2.4, -4.2), (-2.8, -12.0))]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(6.6, 5.0))
for ax, (title, fn, toss_from, toss_to) in zip(axes.flat, PANELS):
    off, paths, mesh = fn()
    dfn = keys() if fn is not bf_spread else [D("K1", "DE", 1.0, -4.0, "1"), D("K2", "NB", 3.0, -6.8, "2")]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=None)
    f = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=(-14.6, 7.2), window=(-6.6, 4.8), title=False)
    for start, pts, kind in paths:
        full = [start] + pts
        if kind == "run":
            branch(f, p, full, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, lw=2.2, dash="-")
        else:
            branch(f, p, full, color=style.OFFENSE, lw=1.4, dash="-")
    qb = p.players["QB"]
    if fn is bf_spread:
        branch(f, p, [(-5.0, 0.0), (-4.4, -1.4), (-2.6, -4.4), (0.4, -6.0), (3.4, -6.2)], color=GREEN, lw=1.8)
    else:
        branch(f, p, [(qb.d, 0.0), mesh, (-1.0, -4.2), (0.6, -6.0), (3.4, -6.2)], color=GREEN, lw=1.8)
    pitch_arc(f, p, toss_from, toss_to)
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=8.6, loc="left", color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")
fig.tight_layout(h_pad=0.8, w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()








Figure 56.3: One idea, four backfields: the three threats never change, only where they start. Offense only, plus the read keys (#1 dive, #2 pitch), option to the offense’s left. In the three under-center panels the inside runner (thick dark arrow) hits just inside #1, the quarterback (green) keeps outside him, and the pitch man (thin arrow, brown arc) stays about four yards outside and a yard deeper than the quarterback: the backside halfback (veer), the far halfback (wishbone), the backside A-back in motion (flexbone). In the spread option the give goes away from the read, and the third threat is a bubble screen: the pitch has become a pass.





What crossed into the NFL from this line was never a formation. It was the idea in the last panel: a quarterback who reads one defender instead of blocking him, run from the shotgun, with a third threat that can be a throw. That idea needed thirty more years and two more inventions, the spread offense and the zone read, before it could reach Sunday.






NoteFilm room: Oklahoma 1971



The 1971 Sooners, coached by Chuck Fairbanks with Barry Switzer as offensive coordinator, are the wishbone at its peak: quarterback Jack Mildren, halfback Greg Pruitt and the 472-yard rushing average. Their most famous game is the one they lost, 35–31 to Nebraska in Norman on Thanksgiving Day, the “Game of the Century” between the top two teams in the country.10
What to notice on the replays that circulate online: count the defenders Nebraska puts on each side of the ball, and watch how often a Nebraska defender who did his one job perfectly still ended up tackling a man without the ball. Then watch the pitch man’s spacing on the long runs: four or five yards outside the quarterback and a yard deeper, so the pitch key can never take both.

title: The College Laboratory: Wing-T, Wishbone, Air Raid, Spread Option, and the RPO
section: The Wing-T and BYU: misdirection and the passing equalizer
text:
The Wing-T and BYU: misdirection and the passing equalizer
Not every college lineage was an option. Two others, one running and one passing, fed the NFL more quietly.
The Wing-T (Maine and Delaware, about 1950). Dave Nelson crossed the T-formation with the single wing’s wingback to make the Wing-T, and his successor at Delaware, Tubby Raymond, ran it for 36 seasons.11 Its logic, taught in Perimeter Runs and Misdirection, is series football: several plays that start with the same backfield action and end differently, so a defense that flows to the first thing it sees is punished. The buck sweep, the trap, the counter and the waggle (the quarterback fakes the sweep and rolls out the other way to pass) all start the same way. The Wing-T itself never became an NFL offense, but its logic did, twice: through high-school coaches such as Gus Malzahn, who ran its series from the shotgun at Auburn (below), and through the NFL’s jet-motion era of the late 2010s. Sean McVay’s Rams and Kyle Shanahan’s 49ers ran what is, in effect, a Wing-T series with a receiver in the wingback’s role: the jet sweep one way, then the same motion with a handoff the other way, then the same motion with a bootleg pass off it. The defense that flows to the motion is punished, which is the Wing-T’s whole idea (03-05 has the film rooms). That is why the timeline gives the Wing-T an NFL diamond in 2017, while admitting it is the idea, not the formation, that crossed.
BYU (1972 to 2000). LaVell Edwards took over a Brigham Young program in Provo, Utah, that had no hope of out-recruiting the big programs, and decided to throw. Through the 1970s and 1980s BYU passed when almost nobody else in college football did, spreading the ball to backs and tight ends with timing routes and crossing patterns, and produced a line of record-setting quarterbacks: Gifford Nielsen, Marc Wilson, Jim McMahon, Steve Young, Robbie Bosco and Ty Detmer, who won the Heisman Trophy in 1990. In 1984 BYU went 13–0 and won the national title.12
BYU’s passing game didn’t cross into the NFL as a system. It crossed in people, which is the first example of a pattern this chapter keeps finding. McMahon won a Super Bowl with the 1985 Bears and Young two MVP awards with the 49ers; Mike Holmgren, BYU’s quarterbacks coach in the early 1980s, went to San Francisco and later built the Packers’ West Coast offense; Andy Reid played offensive line for Edwards; and Norm Chow, Edwards’s assistant for 27 years and his play-caller from 1982, became one of college football’s most celebrated offensive coordinators at USC and, briefly, the Tennessee Titans’.13 And BYU’s spacing and crossing routes became the raw material of the next lineage.
The run-and-shoot (Portland State, 1975 to 1980). The NFL side of this offense is in 11-02; its roots are a textbook small-school story. Glenn “Tiger” Ellison designed it as a high-school coach in Middletown, Ohio, and Mouse Davis, after 15 seasons coaching high school in Oregon, refined it as Portland State’s head coach, where June Jones and then Neil Lomax set passing records. Davis carried it to the USFL’s Houston Gamblers in 1984 and the Detroit Lions in 1988.14






ImportantWhy it exists



Every lineage so far answers the same problem: the other team has better players. The option answers it by reading a defender instead of blocking him (one fewer man to beat), the Wing-T by making the defense guess wrong about where the ball is going (defenders who flow the wrong way don’t count), and BYU’s passing game by spreading the ball to five receivers so a bigger, slower defense has to cover all of them. Each trade is real. The option gives up the passing game and puts the quarterback in harm’s way; the Wing-T gives up width and demands huge practice time for its fakes; the passing game gives up the clock (every incompletion stops it, so a passing team can’t sit on a lead) and asks a quarterback to be very good. College coaches could make those trades because their alternative was losing. NFL coaches, whose players are evenly matched, usually take the idea and leave the trade.

title: The College Laboratory: Wing-T, Wishbone, Air Raid, Spread Option, and the RPO
section: The Air Raid: subtraction as a strategy
text:
The Air Raid: subtraction as a strategy
Hal Mumme was the head coach at Iowa Wesleyan, an NAIA school (a small-college association outside the NCAA’s divisions) in Mount Pleasant, Iowa, when he hired a law-school graduate turned coach named Mike Leach as his offensive coordinator in 1989. Their plan, borrowed openly from BYU and then pushed much further, was to throw on almost every down from four- and five-receiver sets, with very wide line splits, and to run very few plays practised an enormous number of times. Leach gave it its name, helped by an old air-raid siren that a fan sounded after touchdowns (accounts differ on whether that began at Iowa Wesleyan or at their next stop). The pair took it to Valdosta State (1992–1996) and then to Kentucky, where in 1998 quarterback Tim Couch became a consensus All-American and, the next spring, the first pick in the NFL draft.15
Offensive Systems explains the Air Raid’s language (one-word calls, a slim playbook) and Dropback Concepts draws its signature concepts: mesh, the shallow cross, Y-cross and four verticals. What matters for this chapter is why a small menu was a weapon:

Repetition beats variety when your players are worse. A quarterback who has read the same mesh concept against every coverage ten thousand times throws it before the defender has finished deciding.
A small menu travels. It can be taught quickly to a new quarterback every two or three years, and it fits on a wristband or in a hand signal, which makes the no-huddle easy.
Spreading five receivers shrinks the box, so even a pass-first team can run the ball against a light front (more on that arithmetic in the next section).

Leach became Texas Tech’s head coach in 2000 and spent a decade there, then Washington State and Mississippi State, until his death in December 2022. His tree became the Air Raid’s distribution network: Dana Holgorsen, Sonny Dykes, Kliff Kingsbury and Lincoln Riley among many others.16 Riley’s Oklahoma and USC offenses produced three Heisman-winning quarterbacks who went first in the NFL draft: Baker Mayfield (2017 Heisman), Kyler Murray (2018) and Caleb Williams (2022).17






NoteFilm room: Texas Tech vs. Texas, November 1, 2008



Leach’s best team, quarterback Graham Harrell and receiver Michael Crabtree, beat top-ranked Texas 39–33 in Lubbock when Crabtree caught a pass near the sideline, kept his feet and scored with one second left.18
What to notice: count the plays. Texas Tech’s offense ran a handful of concepts all night from spread formations with very wide line splits. Wide splits widen the gaps between the defensive linemen too, which makes stunts harder to run, forces the defense to show where its pressure is coming from, and opens clear throwing windows for a quarterback on a quick three- or five-step drop. And watch where the ball went: short and quick to the sideline, again and again, to receivers who caught it and ran, until the defense crept up and the vertical route behind them came open.


The Air Raid’s route into the NFL ran through its quarterbacks and coaches. Patrick Mahomes played for Kingsbury at Texas Tech; Kingsbury became the Cardinals’ head coach in 2019, hired straight from college with no NFL coaching experience to bring the Air Raid with him,19 and later Washington’s offensive coordinator with Jayden Daniels (04-08 has that film room). Mesh, the shallow cross and four verticals are now in every NFL playbook. What the NFL left at the border was the pure system: the very wide line splits that NFL pass rushers would knife through, the near-total absence of a power run game, and the refusal to go under center.

title: The College Laboratory: Wing-T, Wishbone, Air Raid, Spread Option, and the RPO
section: The spread offense: a philosophy, not a formation
text:
The spread offense: a philosophy, not a formation
By the late 1990s these lineages were converging on one idea, and it’s worth naming exactly, because the word gets used loosely. A spread offense lines up in the shotgun with three or four receivers spread across the field so that the defense must send defenders out of the box to cover them, then attacks the space that leaves, with quick passes, with option reads, or with both. Spread and Modern Formations drew the distinction: a spread formation is a picture every NFL team uses; a spread offense is the whole system built on that picture.
The core of the philosophy is arithmetic, the hat math of the run game (count blockers against defenders; the side with more wins) applied to the whole field.


Show the Python
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.8, 4.6))
# left: I-formation vs 8-man box
off_i = line5() + [O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0.0, "Q"), O("FB", "FB", -4.5, 0.0, "FB"), O("RB", "RB", -7.0, 0.0, "R"),
                   O("Y", "TE", -0.7, 4.8, "Y"), O("X", "WR", -0.7, -15.0, "X"), O("Z", "WR", -1.5, 15.0, "Z")]
check_legal(off_i)
dfn_i = [D("SDE", "DE", 1.0, technique("7", 1), "7"), D("SDT", "DT", 1.0, technique("3", 1), "3"),
         D("WDT", "DT", 1.0, technique("1", -1), "1"), D("WDE", "DE", 1.0, technique("5", -1), "5"),
         D("SAM", "SAM", 4.0, 6.4, "S"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, 0.8, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -3.0, "W"),
         D("SS", "SS", 6.0, 3.6, "SS"), D("FS", "FS", 12.5, 0.0, "FS"),
         D("LCB", "CB", 7.0, -15.0, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 7.0, 15.0, "CB")]
p = Play(off_i, dfn_i, los=35, to_go=None)
f = draw(p, ax=axes[0], lateral=(-12.5, 12.5), window=(-8.6, 14.0), title=False)
box_shade(f, p, -0.2, 7.2, -6.2, 8.4)
say(f, p, 9.4, -9.0, "8 in the box\nv 7 blockers", color=GREEN, fontsize=7.2, weight="bold")
say(f, p, -5.0, -6.6, "Q hands off:\nblocks nobody", fontsize=6.6)
panel_title(axes[0], "1970s: I-formation v eight in the box", size=8.6)
# right: spread vs nickel
dfn_s = [D("BE", "DE", 1.0, technique("5", -1), "5"), D("BT", "DT", 1.0, technique("3", -1), "3"),
         D("PT", "DT", 1.0, technique("1", 1), "1"), D("PE", "DE", 1.0, technique("5", 1), "5"),
         D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -2.4, "W"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, 2.0, "M"),
         D("NB", "NB", 4.5, -6.6, "NB"), D("SS", "SS", 4.5, 6.6, "SS"),
         D("LCB", "CB", 6.5, -16.0, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 6.5, 16.0, "CB"), D("FS", "FS", 12.5, 0.0, "FS")]
p = Play(spread10(), dfn_s, los=35, to_go=None)
check_legal(spread10())
p.highlight("NB", color=style.DEFENSE); p.highlight("SS", color=style.DEFENSE)
f = draw(p, ax=axes[1], lateral=(-12.5, 12.5), window=(-8.6, 14.0), title=False)
box_shade(f, p, -0.2, 7.2, -4.6, 4.6)
say(f, p, 9.4, -9.0, "6 in the box\nv 5 blockers\n+ the QB's read", color=GREEN, fontsize=7.2, weight="bold")
say(f, p, -5.4, 7.6, "apex defenders:\nbox or slot?", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.6)
panel_title(axes[1], "2000s: four wide v six in the box", size=8.6)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()








Figure 56.4: Why spread out to run? Count the shaded box in each panel. Left, a 1970s-style I-formation (21 personnel; FB the fullback) against a 4-3 with the strong safety down: eight in the box against seven blockers, and the quarterback, who just hands off, blocks nobody, so one defender is always free. Right, a four-receiver spread (10 personnel) against nickel: the receivers have pulled five defenders wide, two of them apex defenders (NB and SS, ringed) halfway between the box and the slots. Six in the box against five linemen, and the quarterback’s read makes it six against six. If an apex defender steps in to make it seven, the slot outside him is uncovered. (Wide receivers and cornerbacks are outside both pictures.)





That is the whole idea in one picture. Spreading out is a way to run the ball, not only a way to throw it: four receivers take five defenders out of the box, and a defense that brings one back in leaves a receiver alone. The spread then needs one more thing to finish the job, because six defenders against five blockers is still one free man. Two answers emerged, and they split the spread into two families:

Spread to pass (the Air Raid, and Joe Tiller’s Purdue offense with Drew Brees, which Tiller himself called “basketball on grass”):20 accept the free man and throw quickly to whoever the defense left alone.
Spread to run (Rich Rodriguez, Urban Meyer and their heirs): make the quarterback a runner, so the read takes care of the free man. That is the spread option, next.

The NFL had plenty of the first family of its own (Air Coryell, the K-Gun, later the 2007 Patriots). What it imported from college was mostly the second, the spread run game, as the shotgun data near the end of the chapter shows.






CautionCommon misconception



“The spread is a passing offense.” Some spread offenses are, but the most influential ones were run-first. Rich Rodriguez’s West Virginia, Urban Meyer’s Florida and Gus Malzahn’s Auburn won with the run game, using the spread to empty the box and the quarterback’s legs to win the numbers.
