title: The College Laboratory: Wing-T, Wishbone, Air Raid, Spread Option, and the RPO
section: The spread option: Rodriguez, Meyer and the quarterback’s legs
text:
The spread option: Rodriguez, Meyer and the quarterback’s legs
The spread option is a spread offense whose run game is built on option reads from the shotgun. Its origin story is one of the best in football, and 03-04 tells it: at Glenville State in 1991, Rich Rodriguez’s quarterback fumbled a zone-play handoff in practice, picked the ball up, saw the backside end crashing down on the running back, and ran where the end had been.21 Rodriguez saw the mistake was a play. The zone read married the option’s read to the most common run in football, inside zone, and to the shotgun, where the quarterback could see the read key and the receivers at once.
Rodriguez took it to Tulane and Clemson as an offensive coordinator, then to West Virginia as head coach (2001–2007), where quarterback Pat White and running back Steve Slaton made it the most dangerous running offense in the country. Urban Meyer, at Bowling Green, Utah and Florida, built his own spread option on the same principles, with bigger quarterbacks who could run between the tackles: Alex Smith, whose unbeaten 2004 Utah team won the Fiesta Bowl before Smith went first in the 2005 draft, and Tim Tebow, the 2007 Heisman winner, whose Florida teams won national titles in the 2006 and 2008 seasons.22
What made the spread option more than the zone read was what Rodriguez attached to it. With four receivers spread out, the defense’s apex defenders (the ones ringed in Figure 56.4) are stuck between the box and the slots. Rodriguez’s quarterbacks read two defenders on the same side: the end, to give or keep, and then the apex defender, to keep or throw a bubble screen to the slot. It is the triple option’s logic with the pitch replaced by a pass.






NoteFilm room: West Virginia, Sugar Bowl, January 2, 2006



Rodriguez’s West Virginia, with a freshman quarterback, Pat White, and a freshman running back, Steve Slaton, beat Georgia 38–35 in the Sugar Bowl, played that year in Atlanta while New Orleans recovered from Hurricane Katrina. Slaton ran for 204 yards, a Sugar Bowl record.23
What to notice: on the zone reads, find the backside end first, then the apex defender over the slot. Georgia’s defense, built to beat the power-running teams of the SEC (the Southeastern Conference), had fast, big defenders, and it still spent the night a step late, because every snap asked two of them to make a decision they usually didn’t get to practise.




Show the Python
def zrb_defense():
    return [D("BE", "DE", 1.0, technique("5", -1), "5"), D("BT", "DT", 1.0, technique("3", -1), "3"),
            D("PT", "DT", 1.0, technique("1", 1), "1"), D("PE", "DE", 1.0, technique("5", 1), "5"),
            D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -2.4, "W"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, 2.0, "M"),
            D("NB", "NB", 4.5, -7.0, "NB"), D("SS", "SS", 4.5, 7.0, "SS"),
            D("LCB", "CB", 6.5, -16.0, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 6.5, 16.0, "CB"), D("FS", "FS", 12.5, 0.0, "FS")]


p = Play(spread10(), zrb_defense(), los=35, to_go=None)
go_to(p, "LT", (0.45, -2.75), via=[(-0.3, -3.0)])
go_to(p, "LG", (3.0, -1.6), via=[(-0.3, -1.4), (0.6, -1.5)])
go_to(p, "C", (0.5, 0.45))
go_to(p, "RG", (3.1, 2.0), via=[(-0.3, 1.9), (0.7, 2.0)])
go_to(p, "RT", (0.55, 3.75))
go_to(p, "X", (5.0, -15.8))
go_to(p, "H", (-2.2, -14.8), "route", via=[(-3.0, -10.6)])        # the bubble: bow back, then widen
p.highlight("BE", color=style.DEFENSE); p.highlight("NB", color=style.DEFENSE)
f = draw(p, lateral=(-17.6, 9.6), window=(-7.6, 10.4), title=False, width_in=5.5)
# the two reads, numbered in order
read_line(f, p, (-5.0, 0.0), (1.0, -4.3), num="1", at=0.45)
read_line(f, p, (-5.0, 0.0), (4.5, -7.0), num="2", at=0.78)
# give: the back starts from his own spot, crosses in front of the quarterback (the mesh) and runs inside zone
branch(f, p, [(-5.4, -2.4), (-3.8, -0.4), (-2.4, 1.1), (0.6, 1.2), (4.6, 0.5)], color=style.OFFENSE_DARK,
       label="give if the\nend stays", label_at=(7.6, 0.6), fontsize=6.8)
# keep: the quarterback pulls and runs outside the crashing end, inside the widening nickel
branch(f, p, [(-5.0, 0.0), (-4.2, -2.2), (-2.4, -4.9), (0.4, -6.0), (3.2, -5.6), (6.8, -4.6)], color=GREEN,
       label="keep if the\nnickel widens", label_at=(8.8, -6.6), fontsize=6.8)
pitch_arc(f, p, (-4.3, -2.0), (-2.5, -13.4), rad=0.16)
say(f, p, -5.8, -13.4, "throw the bubble if\nthe nickel takes Q", color=style.BALL, fontsize=6.8, weight="bold")
point_to(f, p, (-6.4, 3.6), (-4.4, -1.3), "mesh: Q rides the\nball in R's belly", fontsize=6.4, shrink=2)
point_to(f, p, (8.0, -12.6), (4.6, -7.2), "read 2: the\napex nickel", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.6)
point_to(f, p, (2.6, -12.4), (0.7, -4.6), "read 1:\nthe end", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.6)
panel_title(f.ax, "Zone read with the bubble attached", size=10)
plt.show()








Figure 56.5: The zone read with the bubble attached, as Rodriguez’s West Virginia teams ran it: two reads (numbered green lines), three possible ball carriers. The line zones right and leaves the left end unblocked. Read 1: if the end stays wide, R takes the handoff at the mesh, crossing in front of Q (dark dashed arrow). If the end crashes, Q pulls the ball and makes read 2, the apex nickel: if the nickel widens with H’s bubble, Q keeps (green arrow) into the space both defenders left; if the nickel comes up at Q, he throws the bubble (brown arc) to H behind X’s block. The triple option from the shotgun, with a pass as the third option.





Here are the two branches that come out after the end crashes, in motion.

def zrb_play(nickel_widens):
    p = Play(spread10(), zrb_defense(), los=35, to_go=None)
    # defense first (blocks aim at where they end up)

section: Pistol, tempo and the RPO: the 2000s laboratory
text:
Pistol, tempo and the RPO: the 2000s laboratory
Three more inventions finished the modern college offense, and each one came from a coach looking for an edge the others didn’t have.
The pistol (Nevada, 2005). Chris Ault put his quarterback about four yards behind the center, between under-center and shotgun depth, with the running back directly behind him. The pistol (02-02) kept the shotgun’s view for the quarterback’s read while letting the back run downhill to either side, so the defense couldn’t tell the play’s direction from his alignment. In 2009 Nevada had three 1,000-yard rushers, one of them the quarterback, Colin Kaepernick.24
Tempo (Oregon, Auburn and many others). Chip Kelly, Oregon’s offensive coordinator from 2007 and head coach from 2009 to 2012, ran the spread option at a pace college football had never seen: plays signalled from the sideline with picture boards (big posters whose pictures code the play), the ball snapped as soon as the officials allowed. Kelly went 46–7 as Oregon’s head coach.25 Gus Malzahn, a former Arkansas high-school coach who had learned offense from the Delaware Wing-T book, combined tempo, the shotgun and Wing-T misdirection; as Auburn’s offensive coordinator he won the 2010 national title with quarterback Cam Newton (the play we now call the inverted veer was one of their signatures), and as head coach he won the 2013 Iron Bowl on the “Kick Six.”26 In-Game Adjustments and Tempo explains what tempo does to a defense: it freezes the defense’s personnel and its calls, and wears it down.
Why did tempo work so much better on Saturday? Partly the clock, which (as the first section said) stopped after every first down until 2023, handing a fast team even more snaps. Partly the roster: a college team’s backups are much weaker than its starters, so a defense that can’t substitute, or has to play its second string because the first is exhausted, loses more than an NFL defense would. And partly the menu: tempo needs the small, signal-sized playbook the spread already had.
Defenses fought back with the only tool they had left, the rulebook. In October 2012 Nick Saban, whose Alabama defenses were built to substitute by situation, complained about no-huddle offenses and asked, “Is this what we want football to be?”27 In 2014 the NCAA’s rules committee proposed making offenses wait until 10 seconds had run off the play clock before snapping, so defenses could substitute; after an outcry from coaches, the proposal was tabled before it could be voted on.28 The offense had won the argument. The best evidence came from the critic himself. Saban’s Alabama, the most dominant defensive program of the 2010s, lost games to up-tempo spread teams (including Malzahn’s Auburn on the Kick Six and Ohio State’s spread offense in the playoff that ended the 2014 season), and Saban answered by hiring offensive coordinators who brought spread and up-tempo ideas, starting with Lane Kiffin in 2014. By 2020 his national champions were an up-tempo, RPO-heavy spread offense that set a school scoring record.29
The RPO (everyone, 2000s–2010s). Put a quick throw on a running play and you have the RPO. Run-Pass Options tells its tangled origin story (Air Raid tags, Rodriguez’s bubbles, Meyer’s accidental discovery at Utah, Brett Favre’s claim to have done it on his own) and why no single inventor can be named. The laboratory conditions explain why it was college that made it routine: the three-yard rule from the first section let linemen run-block while the quarterback decided, and a bubble or now screen thrown behind the line wasn’t covered by it at all. Art Briles’s Baylor teams took the RPO to an extreme, with receivers split almost to the sideline and the quarterback, Robert Griffin III in 2011, reading defenders on the run and the throw on the same snap.30

title: The College Laboratory: Wing-T, Wishbone, Air Raid, Spread Option, and the RPO
text:
The defense strikes back
Every offensive idea in this chapter created a problem for defenses, and college defenses, facing a spread offense almost every week, solved those problems first. Four answers matter.

The 3-3-5 stack: speed and mystery
The first answer was simply to match the offense’s speed with defensive backs. The 3-3-5 stack has three down linemen, three linebackers stacked directly behind them, and five defensive backs, two of whom are hybrids, safeties who play like linebackers, aligned outside the box over the slots. Joe Lee Dunn is usually credited with its first modern version, at Memphis in 1991, born of the familiar college reason: he didn’t have enough big defensive linemen, so he swapped one for a defensive back.31 (Be careful with the name. Odd and Hybrid Fronts explains that NFL coaches use “3-3-5” for something else: a five-man line in nickel, not this stack.)


Show the Python
def stack_def():
    return [D("LE", "DE", 1.0, technique("5", -1), "5"), D("N", "NT", 1.0, 0.0, "N"),
            D("RE", "DE", 1.0, technique("5", 1), "5"),
            D("WILL", "WILL", 4.6, technique("5", -1), "W"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.6, 0.0, "M"),
            D("SAM", "SAM", 4.6, technique("5", 1), "S"),
            D("SP", "DB", 5.0, -7.2, "SP"), D("BA", "DB", 5.0, 7.2, "BA"),
            D("FS", "FS", 12.5, 0.0, "FS"), D("LCB", "CB", 7.0, -16.0, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 7.0, 16.0, "CB")]


fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.8, 4.2))
for ax, version in zip(axes, ("A", "B")):
    p = Play(spread10(), stack_def(), los=35, to_go=None)
    if version == "A":
        go_to(p, "LE", (-1.2, -2.4), "rush", speed=4.0)           # slant inside, through the B gap
        go_to(p, "N", (-0.8, 1.0), "rush", speed=4.0)             # slant to the right A gap
        go_to(p, "RE", (-1.2, 4.6), "rush", speed=4.0)            # contain rush
        go_to(p, "MIKE", (-1.9, -0.8), "rush", speed=5.0, via=[(1.0, -0.6)])   # left A gap
        go_to(p, "WILL", (-2.0, -4.4), "rush", speed=5.0, via=[(1.0, -4.3)])   # left C gap
        go_to(p, "SAM", (8.6, 3.6), "path", speed=4.0)
        go_to(p, "SP", (8.2, -6.6), "path", speed=4.0)
        go_to(p, "BA", (8.6, 8.6), "path", speed=4.0)
        p.highlight("MIKE", color=style.DEFENSE); p.highlight("WILL", color=style.DEFENSE)
        title = "Pressure 1: Mike and Will"
    else:
        go_to(p, "LE", (-1.2, -4.8), "rush", speed=4.0)
        go_to(p, "N", (-0.8, -1.0), "rush", speed=4.0)
        go_to(p, "RE", (-1.2, 2.4), "rush", speed=4.0)
        go_to(p, "SAM", (-1.9, 4.0), "rush", speed=5.0, via=[(1.0, 4.4)])
        go_to(p, "BA", (-2.0, 5.6), "rush", speed=5.5, via=[(1.2, 6.8)])
        go_to(p, "MIKE", (7.5, 5.5), "path", speed=4.0)          # rotates to the pressure side: walls F
        go_to(p, "WILL", (7.8, -1.0), "path", speed=4.0)         # the middle hook
        go_to(p, "SP", (8.0, -8.5), "path", speed=4.0)           # weak curl/flat
        p.highlight("SAM", color=style.DEFENSE); p.highlight("BA", color=style.DEFENSE)
        title = "Pressure 2: Sam and bandit"
    f = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=(-11.5, 11.5), window=(-6.8, 14.4), title=False)
    panel_title(ax, title, size=8.8)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()








Figure 56.7: The 3-3-5 stack against a four-receiver spread: same picture, different five rushers. Both panels start from one alignment: a nose and two 5-techniques, three linebackers stacked behind them, two hybrid safeties (SP, BA) over the slots, one deep free safety (cornerbacks out of the picture). Left: the line slants right while the Mike and Will blitz the gaps it vacated. Right: the line slants left, the Sam and bandit come from the right, and the Mike rotates toward the pressure to wall off the slot: three under, three deep. A protection set for the first picture is wrong for the second.





The stack’s weapons are speed (an extra defensive back against an extra receiver) and mystery: with eight potential rushers and only three hands in the dirt, a protection scheme that counts the defenders on the line before the snap counts only three. (The hybrid safeties’ names are a dialect: spur and bandit are the names West Virginia’s stack made familiar; other staffs say star, rover, viper, or simply strong and weak safety, so expect a broadcast to use any of them.) Its price is size. Three linemen against five offensive linemen can be pushed around, which is why the stack thrived in conferences full of spread passing offenses and struggled against teams that lined up with tight ends and ran straight at it: double-team a down lineman, climb to a stacked linebacker who has no one in front of him, and the light front has nothing left. West Virginia, under Rodriguez’s defensive coordinator Jeff Casteel, paired the stack with the spread option, so the Mountaineers practised against the offense they defended.32 The NFL never adopted it as a base defense; NFL offensive lines are too good to give away a lineman every down.


Quarters and pattern matching: the college two-high
The second answer was in the secondary. Against spread offenses that ran option and play-action from the same looks on wide college hashes, a defense that put a safety in the box got beaten deep, and one that kept two safeties deep got run over. Quarters with pattern matching let it do both: two safeties 10 to 12 yards deep who read the receivers in front of them, carry the vertical routes and fit the run from depth when it shows. Quarters and Match Coverage tells this history in full: Nick Saban’s pattern-match rules, developed as Bill Belichick’s coordinator in Cleveland and refined at Michigan State, LSU and Alabama; Mark Dantonio and Pat Narduzzi’s Michigan State; Iowa’s long-running split-field quarters; Gary Patterson’s 4-2-5 at TCU.
This is the one lineage that made a round trip. Its roots were in an NFL building (Cleveland in the early 1990s), it matured on college fields against the spread, and when NFL offenses went spread in the late 2010s, NFL defenses went back to the college quarters coaches for the answer. NFL Next Gen Stats measured split-safety coverage on 32.9% of dropbacks in 2018 and 42.0% in 2025, the highest since tracking began.33


Tite and mint: walling off the middle
The third answer was a front built for the spread’s favourite run. With five or six defenders in the box, a defense can’t afford to let inside zone’s double teams climb to the linebackers. The tite front puts a nose on the center and two 4i-techniques on the tackles’ inside shoulders, so every interior lineman is covered and nobody climbs cleanly (05-03 draws it). Kirby Smart’s Georgia calls the same picture the mint front, and Georgia’s defenses won national titles in the 2021 and 2022 seasons with it as a base.34 It is also a case of parallel evolution rather than borrowing: Vic Fangio’s NFL defenses were running their own tite against the same spread run games, and the two traditions met in the middle.


Three-high: Iowa State’s answer to the Air Raid
The newest answer came from the conference where the Air Raid lived. By 2017 the Big 12 (Texas, Oklahoma and their neighbours on the Plains) was a league of spread passing offenses, and Iowa State, under head coach Matt Campbell and defensive coordinator Jon Heacock, was losing shootouts. After a 44–41 overtime loss to Iowa in the third game of 2017, Heacock and Campbell used the bye week to throw out the playbook, and against Texas they lined up in a 3-3-5 with three safeties deep. In the very next game Iowa State, a 31-point underdog with a walk-on backup quarterback, went to Norman and beat third-ranked Oklahoma, Baker Mayfield’s team, 38–31.35
A three-high safety defense shows three safeties deep before the snap, usually from a 3-3-5. It is built on one bet: make the offense run the ball against a light box, and fill the box late.


Show the Python
def three_high_def():
    return [D("LE", "DE", 1.0, technique("4i", -1), "4i"), D("N", "NT", 1.0, 0.0, "N"),
            D("RE", "DE", 1.0, technique("4i", 1), "4i"),
            D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -5.8, "W"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.6, 0.0, "M"), D("SAM", "SAM", 4.5, 5.8, "S"),
            D("LCB", "CB", 7.0, -16.0, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 7.0, 16.0, "CB"),
            D("LS", "SS", 9.5, -9.5, "LS"), D("FS", "FS", 12.0, 0.0, "FS"), D("RS", "SS", 9.5, 9.5, "RS")]


def tight(players):
    """Narrow the spread for a half-page panel: wideouts and corners at 13 yards, slots at 8 (Air Raid splits vary)."""
    W = {"X": -13.0, "Z": 13.0, "H": -8.0, "F": 8.0, "LCB": -13.0, "RCB": 13.0, "LS": -8.6, "RS": 8.6,
         "WILL": -5.2, "SAM": 5.2}
    return [q.moved(w=W[q.key]) if q.key in W else q for q in players]


fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.8, 5.2))
# against the pass
p = Play(tight(spread10()), tight(three_high_def()), los=35, to_go=None)
for k in ("X", "Z"):
    p.route(k, [(0, 0), (17.0, 0.4)])
for k in ("H", "F"):
    p.route(k, [(0, 0), (16.5, -0.6)])
p.route("RB", [(0, 0), (-0.4, 3.0), (1.5, 6.0)], side=-1)
p.dropback(2.0)
for k, end in [("LE", (-1.6, -3.4)), ("N", (-1.2, 0.6)), ("RE", (-1.6, 3.4))]:
    go_to(p, k, end, "rush")
for k, end in [("LCB", (15.5, -13.4)), ("RCB", (15.5, 13.4)), ("LS", (15.0, -7.6)), ("RS", (15.0, 7.6)),
               ("FS", (16.0, 0.0)), ("WILL", (7.5, -6.6)), ("MIKE", (7.0, 0.0)), ("SAM", (7.5, 6.6))]:
    go_to(p, k, end, "path")
f = draw(p, ax=axes[0], lateral=(-15.0, 15.0), window=(-9.4, 19.6), title=False, numbers=True)
rb_end = (p.players["RB"].d + 1.5, p.players["RB"].w - 6.0)
pitch_arc(f, p, (-7.0, 0.0), rb_end, rad=0.2)
say(f, p, rb_end[0] - 3.4, rb_end[1] + 1.0, "check-down", color=style.BALL, fontsize=6.6, weight="bold")
say(f, p, 17.9, -3.8, "5 deep", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7, weight="bold")
say(f, p, 10.4, -3.4, "3 under", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7, weight="bold")
panel_title(axes[0], "Pass: eight drop", size=8.8)
# against the run
p = Play(tight(spread10()), tight(three_high_def()), los=35, to_go=None)
go_to(p, "LT", (0.6, -2.6), via=[(-0.3, -3.0)])
go_to(p, "LG", (0.6, -0.9), via=[(-0.3, -1.4)])
go_to(p, "C", (0.6, 0.3))
go_to(p, "RG", (0.6, 1.9), via=[(-0.3, 1.9)])
go_to(p, "RT", (2.6, 2.2), via=[(0.3, 3.4)])
go_to(p, "WILL", (3.4, -3.8), "path")                   # backside apex squeezes
go_to(p, "SAM", (3.9, 4.6), "path")                     # playside apex fits
go_to(p, "X", (5.4, -12.6), delay=0.1)                  # stalk the corners
go_to(p, "Z", (5.4, 12.6), delay=0.1)
go_to(p, "H", (3.0, -5.0), delay=0.1)                   # slots block the apex players
go_to(p, "F", (3.6, 5.6), delay=0.1)
go_to(p, "RB", (2.6, 1.4), "run", via=[(-4.3, -0.6), (-1.2, 1.2)])
go_to(p, "FS", (3.4, 1.2), "path")
go_to(p, "MIKE", (3.1, 2.5), "path")
p.highlight("FS", color=style.DEFENSE)
f = draw(p, ax=axes[1], lateral=(-15.0, 15.0), window=(-9.4, 19.6), title=False, numbers=True)
point_to(f, p, (16.4, 6.4), (8.0, 0.7), "the 'flyover':\nthe middle safety\nfills the run", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK,
         fontsize=6.6)
panel_title(axes[1], "Run: a safety flies down", size=8.8)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()








Figure 56.8: The three-high safety defense: one pre-snap picture, two answers. Before the snap: two 4i-techniques and a nose, the Mike behind them (four in the box), the Will and Sam at apex spots halfway to the slots, two cornerbacks, and three safeties (LS, FS, RS) 9 to 12 yards deep (receiver splits drawn a little tight to fit the page). Left, against a pass: eight drop (five deep, three under) and three rush, so four vertical routes run into five deep defenders and the quarterback settles for the check-down. Right, against inside zone: the receivers block the corners and the apex players, the Will squeezes, and the middle safety (ringed) flies down after the snap, so the box ends up with one more defender than it showed.





Why does that work against the Air Raid in particular? Because the Air Raid’s whole menu is built to find the hole in a two-high or one-high shell: the seam against Cover 3, the deep middle against Cover 2, the crossers underneath against man. Against five deep defenders and three underneath, there is no deep hole, and the offense’s best answer, running the ball against a light box, is something many pure passing offenses were least prepared to do. The cost is the run defense if the safety is late: count four in the box and two apex players who may or may not get there, against five linemen and a running back with a head start. Iowa State’s version spread through the Big 12 and beyond (Kansas’s offensive coordinator called Iowa State “the originators”), and three-safety looks became a regular part of college defense.36 NFL defenses have mostly borrowed the personnel (a third safety on the field, the big nickel of A First Look at Defense) and the habit of disguising the shell before the snap (06-06), rather than the full college package. The likely reason is the same filter as always: the bet only pays if a safety arrives on time against NFL backs running behind NFL linemen, and a three-man rush gives an NFL quarterback all day to find the soft spot underneath. The margins that make three-high work against a Big 12 Air Raid are too thin on Sunday.

Three patterns run through Table 56.1.
Players carry ideas better than coaches. The ideas that crossed fastest arrived inside quarterbacks: the zone read with Griffin, Kaepernick and Wilson in 2012, the Air Raid with Mahomes (a starter from 2018), the designed quarterback run game with Lamar Jackson. College head coaches who tried to bring whole systems with them had a much harder time. Steve Spurrier (Washington, 2002–2003), Nick Saban (Miami, 2005–2006), Chip Kelly (Philadelphia, 2013–2015, then San Francisco), Urban Meyer (Jacksonville, 2021) and Matt Rhule (Carolina, 2020–2022) all left the NFL with losing or near-.500 records, none lasting more than four seasons, while ideas from their college offenses and defenses stayed behind.37 The NFL takes the play and sends back the coach.
The NFL adapts what it keeps. The RPO crossed, but as a quick-throw RPO, because the one-yard rule won’t let linemen run-block while the quarterback waits. The zone read crossed, but as a few plays a game, because the quarterback test is harsh. The Air Raid crossed, but inside offenses that also go under center, use tight ends and run power. Every idea arrives a little smaller.
The crossing has a rhythm. Ideas arrive in waves when a generation of players makes them unavoidable, and then the NFL’s defenses answer and the wave recedes. The zone read surged in 2012 and receded by 2014 (Dynasties and Counterpunches tells that story), though only the quarterback keep receded: the shotgun handoff it had made respectable stayed, which is why the run line in the chart below keeps climbing after 2014. The shotgun spread rose for twenty years and has just started to give ground to the under-center game (The Modern Era). Here is that long wave in data.


Show the Python
from gridiron.data import pbp

style.apply()
cols = ["season", "season_type", "play_type", "shotgun", "down", "qb_scramble"]
sg = pbp(list(range(1999, 2026)), columns=cols)
sg = sg[(sg["season_type"] == "REG") & sg["play_type"].isin(["pass", "run"]) & sg["down"].notna()].copy()
sg["kind"] = np.where((sg["play_type"] == "pass") | (sg["qb_scramble"] == 1), "pass", "run")
rate = sg.groupby(["season", "kind"])["shotgun"].mean().unstack() * 100
SG_ALL = sg.groupby("season")["shotgun"].mean() * 100

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.8, 3.9))
ax.plot(rate.index, rate["pass"], color=style.SERIES[0], lw=2.2, marker="o", ms=3)
ax.plot(rate.index, rate["run"], color=style.SERIES[1], lw=2.2, marker="o", ms=3)
ax.text(2025.4, rate.loc[2025, "pass"], "passes", color=style.SERIES[0], fontsize=8, va="center")
ax.text(2025.4, rate.loc[2025, "run"], "runs", color=style.SERIES[1], fontsize=8, va="center")
EVENTS = [  # season, series, label, label position (x, y), vertical alignment
    (2008, "run", "Wildcat (Dolphins,\nfrom Arkansas)", (2006.6, 13.5), "bottom"),
    (2012, "run", "read-option wave:\nGriffin, Kaepernick,\nWilson, Newton", (2014.4, 3.0), "bottom"),
    (2013, "pass", "Kelly's Eagles\n(Oregon tempo)", (2009.2, 86.0), "bottom"),
    (2018, "run", "RPO boom (2016-18):\nReid's Chiefs, the\nEagles' Super Bowl LII", (2021.8, 14.0), "bottom"),
    (2018, "pass", "Mahomes (Texas Tech)\nis NFL MVP", (2016.0, 93.0), "bottom"),
    (2023, "run", "peak: half of\nall runs", (2021.6, 60.0), "bottom"),
]
for yr, ser, txt, xy, va in EVENTS:
    ax.annotate(txt, (yr, rate.loc[yr, ser]), xytext=xy, fontsize=6.8, color=style.INK_2, ha="center",
                va=va, arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=style.MUTED, lw=0.7, shrinkB=3))
ax.set_ylim(0, 105)
ax.set_xlim(1998.5, 2028.5)
ax.set_xticks(list(range(2000, 2026, 5)))
ax.set_ylabel("% of plays from the shotgun", fontsize=8)
ax.tick_params(labelsize=7.5)
ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 56.9: The spread’s long arrival: the share of NFL plays snapped from the shotgun, 1999–2025 (regular season), shown separately for passes (dropbacks, scrambles included) and runs, with some of the college imports of the text marked. The passing game moved to the shotgun first; the run game followed only once offenses learned to run from it, with zone reads, the pistol and RPOs. Shotgun runs went from about 2% of runs in 1999 to half of them in 2023, before the under-center revival of 2024–2025. The pistol is counted as shotgun in this data. Data: nflverse play-by-play via nflreadpy (the shotgun flag).





Read Figure 56.9 as two stories. The passing line is the spread formation arriving: from about 19% of dropbacks in 1999 to 55% in 2009, as offenses learned what college coaches had learned, that a quarterback who starts five yards deep sees the defense better and gets the ball out faster. That shift needed no college import at all; the 2007 Patriots, the most famous spread passing offense of its era, were run by NFL lifers. The running line is the college story. In 2011, only 14% of NFL runs came from the shotgun: the NFL used the gun to pass and went under center to run. That was a reasoned choice, and it answers the question the timeline left open. Formation Rules listed what the shotgun costs a run game: the back beside the quarterback takes the handoff moving sideways rather than downhill, a five-yard snap can be fumbled, and play-action is less convincing when the quarterback never turns his back. For a quarterback who never kept the ball, those costs bought nothing. The zone read changed the arithmetic: once the quarterback’s read made a shotgun run plus-one, the costs were worth paying. Then the read-option wave and Chip Kelly’s Eagles arrived, and shotgun runs jumped to 32% in 2013. The spread run game, the zone read, the pistol and then the RPO, had crossed. By 2023 the shotgun accounted for 50% of runs and 72% of all plays. In 2025 both lines fell back (to 66% of all plays), as NFL offenses went back under center to run and play-action, the latest counterpunch, told in The Modern Era. Two cautions: the play-by-play’s shotgun flag comes from the official gamebook descriptions, which probably recorded it less consistently in the early seasons, and it can’t tell a spread-option shotgun run from a plain shotgun handoff.38
The borrowing hasn’t stopped. Pre-snap motion, the Wing-T’s oldest tool, was on 63.9% of NFL plays in 2025 by PFF’s count, up from 37.6% in 2014,39 and The Modern Era follows what is crossing now.






NoteFilm room: Washington at New Orleans, September 9, 2012



Robert Griffin III’s first NFL game, a 40–32 win over the Saints, is this chapter’s opening scene played for real. Washington’s attack “borrowed liberally from concepts Griffin used at Baylor,” NFL.com reported that week, and Mike Shanahan described how it worked: “we had running plays called and all of a sudden they gave us certain looks to take the running game away, and we threw a couple of bubbles early.”40
What to notice: take one of those snaps apart and every piece has a college birthplace. The quarterback four yards deep with the back behind him is Ault’s pistol (Nevada, 2005); the unblocked backside end he reads is Rodriguez’s zone read (Glenville State, 1991); the bubble attached to it is West Virginia’s third option; and putting run and throw on one call is Baylor’s packaged play. Then notice what Sunday changed: the bubble comes out on the quarterback’s first look, before any lineman can drift a yard downfield. The run side of that offense is in Option Football and the packaged plays in Run-Pass Options.

section: Saturday versus Sunday: the rules that shape each game
text:
Saturday versus Sunday: the rules that shape each game
You can’t watch a college game well without the rulebook differences, because many of the strategies in this chapter exist because of them. Here they are side by side, current for the 2026 seasons. (The full reference version lives in Appendix E.)



Table 56.2: The college and NFL rules that most change strategy, as of the 2026 seasons. Sources in the notes below the table’s discussion.











Rule
NFL (2026)
College (2026)
What it changes on the field




Hash marks
70 ft 9 in from each sideline; 18 ft 6 in apart
60 ft from each sideline; 40 ft apart
College has a true wide side and short side on most snaps; formations and play calls are built around it


Catch at the sideline
Two feet (or another body part) in bounds
One foot (or any body part) in bounds
Sideline throws are easier to complete in college


Ineligible linemen downfield on a pass
No more than 1 yard, on any forward pass
No more than 3 yards, and only on passes that cross the neutral zone
College RPOs can run-block longer and throw deeper (Drill 3)


Defensive pass interference
Spot foul, automatic first down
15 yards from the previous spot (or the spot, if shorter), automatic first down
A deep NFL throw into tight coverage can “win” 40 yards on a flag; in college the flag is capped


Offensive pass interference
10 yards
10 yards (15 until 2025)
Cut for 2026, matching the NFL


Clock after a first down
Keeps running
Stops only in the last two minutes of each half (stopped all game until 2023)
Pre-2023 college games had many more snaps; tempo offenses profited


Two-minute warning
Yes
Yes, since 2024 (the “two-minute timeout”)
Late-half clock strategy now looks similar


Ball carrier down
When touched by an opponent while on the ground
As soon as a knee or other body part touches the ground, touched or not
No “get up and keep running” in college


Overtime
One 10-minute period in the regular season (15 in the playoffs); both teams get the ball; then sudden death
Alternating possessions from the 25; a two-point try is required after a touchdown from the second overtime; alternating two-point plays from the third
College overtime is a series of short-field possessions; strategy becomes two-point math


Targeting / hits to the head
15 yards; ejection only for flagrant hits (use-of-helmet rule since 2018)
15 yards and automatic ejection; for 2026, a first offense no longer carries a suspension into the next game
College defenders must change their tackling target or lose a starter


Kickoffs
The “dynamic kickoff” (since 2024), built to be returned
Traditional kickoff; a fair catch inside the 25 is a touchback at the 25
Many college kickoffs end in a fair catch or a touchback


Fair-catch kick
Allowed for decades (rarely used)
New for 2026
A free 3-point try after a fair catch near midfield, now in both games


Motion
One player, not moving forward at the snap
The same
Differences you see in motion are usage, not law


Helmet communication
Quarterback and one defender (green dot) since 1994 and 2008
One player per side (FBS), since 2024
College offenses used sideline signals and picture boards for decades, which is part of why tempo grew there






Most rows explain themselves; four deserve a sentence on why.
The hash marks are the one you can see from your couch. Offenses put their strength into the wide field, defenses set their coverage by field and boundary rather than by formation (hence split-field quarters, 06-06), and college kickers sometimes waste a down centering the ball before a field goal.41
The three-yard rule, the one-foot catch and the capped DPI all favour offenses that throw in rhythm off the run and to the sideline; Drill 3 below puts the first two on one play.42 The NFL’s spot-foul DPI pushes the other way, making a deep throw into tight coverage a reasonable gamble (Contact Rules and Penalties measures it).
The clock and the headsets are where college has moved toward the NFL. The 2023 clock change took away roughly seven or eight snaps a game, and the two-minute timeout followed for 2024;43 helmet radios arrived in 2024 too, one player per side, cut off at 15 seconds as in the NFL.44 Before that, an offense that already signalled every play from the sideline lost nothing by going fast, one more reason tempo grew up on Saturday.
Overtime, targeting and kickoffs change the late game. College overtime since 2021 is a series of possessions from the 25 that turns into alternating two-point plays from the third overtime45 (the NFL’s version is in Clock and Game Management). A targeting foul ejects the player; for 2026, in a one-year trial, a first foul no longer carries into the next game.46 And while the NFL rebuilt its kickoff in 2024 to bring the return back (Kickoffs and Returns), college has let a fair catch inside the 25 come out to the 25 since 2018,47 and for 2026 adopted the fair-catch kick, the old NFL rule that allows a free field goal try from the spot of a fair catch.48






NoteMadden vs. real life



In a video game, every college team has roughly the same playbook menus. Real college football is closer to a hundred different sports: on one Saturday a service academy runs the flexbone triple option, an Air Raid team throws 60 times from five-receiver sets, and an SEC power lines up under center with two tight ends. NFL teams, drawing from one talent pool under one set of rules, are far more alike. That variety is the laboratory, and it makes a college game the best place to see a concept in its purest form.








TipWatch for it



Saturday versus Sunday. Watch one college game and one NFL game on the same weekend, and list three structural differences you can see. Some places to look:
Before the snap

Where is the ball? In college it usually sits on a hash 20 yards from one sideline. Do the receivers go to the wide field or the short side? Does the defense line up by field and boundary, or by formation?
How fast is the next snap? Time a few series from whistle to snap. College tempo teams snap in 10 to 15 seconds; how many NFL teams do?
Who is in the backfield? Count the snaps under center, and the option looks (a back beside the quarterback, an unblocked end).
How many safeties are deep? Look for three safeties back, and for three-down-lineman fronts with stacked linebackers.

After the snap

On a run with a throw attached, watch the linemen: in college they may be two or three yards downfield when the ball is thrown; in the NFL the throw comes out before they can get there.
On a sideline catch, count the feet. One in college, two in the NFL.
On a long pass-interference flag, where does the ball go? Fifteen yards in college; the spot of the foul in the NFL.
On a runner who slips, watch the whistle: a college ball carrier is down the moment a knee touches, touched or not, so there is no getting up to keep running.
On a targeting flag, check who leaves: in college the player is ejected, and a defense without its best safety for the rest of the game plays differently.
In college overtime, from the second overtime on, watch the two-point plays: the playbook shrinks to each offense’s best short-yardage call.

For your prediction log (01-06): on every college option or RPO look, write who the quarterback is reading, and how many defenders are in the box against how many blockers.

text:
Predict the play






TipPredict the play



Drill 1: count the Saturday box. First-and-10 at midfield in a Big 12 game. The ball is on the left hash. The offense lines up in a four-receiver spread with the running back beside the quarterback. The defense shows three down linemen, a Mike linebacker over the ball, the Will cheated in toward the box on the short side, the Sam out over the slot on the wide side, and three safeties deep. Count the box against the blockers. Is the offense more likely to run or pass, what kind of play, and what is the defense counting on?


Show the Python
off = spread10()
ball_y = FIELD_WIDTH - 20.0          # the offense's left hash on a college field
OFF_W = {"X": -13.0, "H": -7.4, "Z": 20.0}
off = [q.moved(w=OFF_W[q.key]) if q.key in OFF_W else q for q in off]
DEF_AT = {"LCB": (7.0, -13.0), "RCB": (7.0, 20.0), "WILL": (4.5, -3.6), "SAM": (4.5, 8.2),
          "LS": (8.0, -6.5), "FS": (13.0, 2.0), "RS": (11.6, 11.0)}   # shaded to the field, by field and boundary
dfn = [q.moved(d=DEF_AT[q.key][0], w=DEF_AT[q.key][1]) if q.key in DEF_AT else q for q in three_high_def()]
check_legal(off)
with hashes_at(20.0):
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=60, ball_y=ball_y, to_go=10, title="Drill 1: 1st and 10, ball on the left hash")
    f = p.draw(lateral="full", window=(-7.0, 15.0), width_in=6.0)
clean(f.ax, numbers=True, hashes=False)
box_shade(f, p, -0.2, 7.0, -4.4, 4.4)
say(f, p, 12.0, -13.5, "short side:\n20 yards", fontsize=6.8)
say(f, p, 12.0, 25.0, "wide side: 33 yards", fontsize=6.8)
point_to(f, p, (-5.2, 17.6), (-3.0, 13.33), "college hash", fontsize=6.6, shrink=1)
plt.show()








Figure 56.10: Drill 1: a four-receiver spread (10 personnel) against three-high, on a college field with the ball on the left hash (hash marks drawn at college width). The shaded strip is the box.













TipAnswer





Count it: five in the box against five blockers plus a read. Three linemen, the Mike and the cheated-in Will are in the box; the Sam is out over the wide-side slot. The offense has five linemen, and on a zone read the quarterback reads one box defender instead of blocking him, so five linemen take the other four with one to spare: the offense is plus-one. Expect a run, most likely a read (a zone read, or an RPO that reads the Will), because the defense has invited it.
What the defense is counting on is the three safeties: on a run, one of them, usually the middle one, comes down after the snap to fill, so the box gains a defender by the time the back gets there (Figure 56.8). That’s the bet of the three-high: give the offense a light box, take away everything deep, and tackle the run late. If the safety is a step slow, the run is a big gain; if he’s on time, the offense has run into a six-man box it didn’t see, and the plus-one is gone.
Bonus: why you knew it was college. The ball is 20 yards from the left sideline, not 23.6: college hash marks. The offense put a receiver out on the numbers of a 33-yard wide side; the defense set its safeties by field and boundary (the short-side safety tighter, the middle one shaded to the wide side, the wide-side safety wider); and the three-safety shell is a college look.









TipPredict the play



Drill 2: the wishbone count. A wishbone team runs the triple option to its split-end side (the offense’s left). On the first four snaps, the defense’s left end (the 5-technique) has squeezed down hard on the fullback every time, and the outside linebacker standing on the line outside him has run straight at the pitch man every time. Before the next snap, name #1, #2, #3 and #4, and predict who will carry the ball.


Show the Python
p = Play(wishbone_off(), wishbone_def(), los=35, to_go=None, title="Drill 2: who carries it?")
p.highlight("BE", color=style.DEFENSE); p.highlight("WILL", color=style.DEFENSE)
f = draw(p, lateral=(-19.0, 11.5), window=(-6.6, 13.6), width_in=4.6)
plt.show()








Figure 56.11: Drill 2: wishbone, triple option to the left. The two defenders who have been doing the same thing every snap are ringed; the prompt says what each has done.













TipAnswer





#1 is the 5-technique (the dive key), #2 the Will standing on the line outside him (the pitch key), #3 the strong safety in the alley (the lead halfback’s block), and #4 the cornerback (the split end’s block). Use the quarterback’s two reads in order:

#1 squeezes the dive, so the quarterback pulls the ball. The fullback carries out his fake and takes #1 with him.
#2 widens to take the pitch man, so the quarterback keeps and turns up inside him.

The quarterback carries it, up the seam between #1 (who is tackling a fullback with no ball) and #2 (who is covering a halfback with no ball), with #3 and #4 blocked outside. A defense that does the same thing every snap has stopped playing option defense, which is why wishbone teams ran the triple until a defender changed his mind, and why defensive coaches, as 03-04 showed, learned to mix up who took whom.









TipPredict the play



Drill 3: one play, two rulebooks. An offense runs an RPO: the line run-blocks inside zone, the outside receiver on the right runs a go route to clear the cornerback, and the quarterback pulls the ball and throws to the slot receiver on a seam-corner (a seam route that bends toward the sideline). He catches it 17 yards downfield, right at the sideline, with one foot down before stepping out. At the moment of the throw, the right guard, who came off a double team toward a linebacker, is 2½ yards past the line of scrimmage, still not touching anyone. What is the ruling in a college game? In an NFL game?


Show the Python
dfn = [q.moved(d=0.3) if q.key in ("BE", "BT", "PT", "PE") else q.moved(w=17.4) if q.key == "RCB" else q
       for q in zrb_defense()]
p = Play(spread10(), dfn, los=35, to_go=None, title="Drill 3: legal on Saturday? On Sunday?")
go_to(p, "LT", (0.45, -2.75), via=[(-0.3, -3.0)])
go_to(p, "LG", (0.5, -1.2), via=[(-0.3, -1.4)])
go_to(p, "C", (0.5, 0.45))
go_to(p, "RG", (2.5, 1.6), via=[(-0.3, 1.9), (0.7, 2.0)])
go_to(p, "RT", (0.55, 3.75))
p.route("F", [(0, 0), (11.0, -0.4), (18.5, 17.0)])
p.route("Z", [(0, 0), (19.0, 0.4)])
go_to(p, "RCB", (17.5, 17.4), "path")
go_to(p, "RB", (-3.6, 1.4), "path", via=[(-4.4, 0.0)])
f = draw(p, lateral=(-11.0, 30.5), window=(-6.8, 21.4), width_in=6.2)
pitch_arc(f, p, (-4.4, 0.6), (16.6, 25.6), rad=0.07)     # the throw, bowed away from the line
for d, txt in ((1.0, "NFL limit: 1 yard"), (3.0, "college limit: 3 yards")):
    (x0, y0), (x1, y1) = _P(f, p, d, -11.0), _P(f, p, d, 26.65)
    f.ax.plot([x0, x1], [y0, y1], color=style.INK_2, lw=0.9, ls=(0, (4, 2)), zorder=2)
    say(f, p, d + (0.0 if d > 2 else -0.15), 21.0, txt, fontsize=6.6, color=style.INK)
box_shade(f, p, 1.0, 3.0, -11.0, 26.65, color=style.OFFENSE, alpha=0.05)
point_to(f, p, (8.0, -1.4), (2.5, 1.6), "RG: 2½ yards\ndownfield", fontsize=6.6, shrink=2)
point_to(f, p, (11.4, 21.0), (17.0, 26.0), "caught with one\nfoot in bounds", fontsize=6.6, shrink=4)
say(f, p, 7.0, 28.6, "side-\nline", fontsize=6.4, color=style.INK_2)
plt.show()








Figure 56.12: Drill 3: the RPO at the moment of the throw (the defensive linemen are drawn engaged at the line). The dashed lines mark 1 and 3 yards past the line of scrimmage; the right guard’s block ends between them. F catches the seam-corner at the right sideline.













TipAnswer





College: a legal 17-yard completion. The guard is inside the three-yard limit, and a pass that crosses the neutral zone is exactly what the college rule allows him to be up to three yards beyond. One foot in bounds is a catch in college.
NFL: no gain. One foot in bounds isn’t a catch in the NFL, so the pass is incomplete. There is also a flag: the guard is more than a yard downfield when a forward pass is thrown, which is illegal man downfield (04-06). The defense chooses: five yards and replay the down, or decline and take the incompletion. Note the planted detail: had the guard still been blocking the man he engaged at the line, the NFL would have let him be carried past a yard, but he had left that block to climb and wasn’t touching anyone.
That is why NFL RPOs look different, and it closes this chapter’s opening scene: the Sunday version of the college play was a little quicker, and its line looked a little different, because the throw has to come out in about a second, before any lineman can drift a yard. The deep seam a college team runs off the same action shows up on Sunday only as play-action, with the linemen pass-blocking.

title: The College Laboratory: Wing-T, Wishbone, Air Raid, Spread Option, and the RPO
text:
Takeaways

College football is the sport’s laboratory because of its environment: huge talent gaps across hundreds of programs, wide hash marks, rules like the three-yard ineligible limit that tolerate the run-pass blur, and roster churn and tempo that reward small, repeatable systems.
The offensive lineages share one aim, changing the arithmetic for the team with lesser players: the option (split-T, veer, wishbone, flexbone, spread option) reads a defender instead of blocking him; the Wing-T makes him guess; BYU and the Air Raid spread the ball to five receivers and repeat a few plays endlessly; the spread offense empties the box so the run game has numbers.
The spread option is the triple option rebuilt from the shotgun, with the pitch replaced by a throw; add the three-yard rule and tempo and you have the modern college RPO offense.
Defenses answered with speed and disguise (the 3-3-5 stack), two-high match coverage (quarters, which made a round trip back to the NFL), fronts that wall off inside zone (tite and mint) and three-high safeties that concede the light-box run and fill it late.
The NFL is a filter: ideas that hit the quarterback, rely on a talent gap or need college rules arrive smaller or not at all. Players carry ideas across better than coaches, which is why the big crossings (2012’s read option, 2017’s RPOs, the Air Raid’s concepts) came with young quarterbacks.

If you want to go deeper: Chris B. Brown’s The Art of Smart Football and The Essential Smart Football (the zone read, the Air Raid and the 3-3-5’s birth, among much else); Tim Layden’s Blood, Sweat and Chalk, whose chapters on the wishbone, the veer, BYU, the zone read and the spread are told largely in the coaches’ own words; S. title: Dynasties and Counterpunches (2000-2016)
text:
The shape of the era
February 2, 2014, Super Bowl XLVIII. The Denver Broncos arrive with the highest-scoring offense the NFL has ever seen: 606 points, 55 touchdown passes from Peyton Manning, five players with ten or more touchdowns. Seattle’s defense lines up the way it has all season, one safety deep in the middle, cornerbacks pressed on the receivers’ noses, a strong safety rolled down near the line, and does almost nothing fancy. Final score: Seattle 43, Denver 8. The broadcast keeps asking what Seattle did to Manning, and this chapter will answer that near the end. But the better question is older and bigger: how did the league get to a point where the greatest passing offense in history and a defense built to stop exactly that met in the final game? The answer is seventeen seasons of punch and counterpunch. A defense dominates, an offense finds the seam in it, the rules lean one way, a coach reinvents his team, the defense answers, and every answer becomes the next thing to beat. This chapter tells that story, from the Tampa 2 dynasty to the read-option wave, and shows you how to see its leftovers on any Sunday.
You’ll be able to…
Reading the diagrams: offense is blue circles (X, Y, Z, H receivers; F a second tight end; Q quarterback; R running back); defense is outlined squares (E and T ends and tackles, N the nose tackle; O a 3-4 outside linebacker; M the Mike, W the Will, S the Sam; $ the nickel back; CB corners; FS and SS safeties). Solid arrows are routes and runs, dashed arrows defenders’ movements, dotted lines man-coverage assignments, tees blocks. The dark blue line is the line of scrimmage and the orange line the line to gain.
Start with the whole board. The figure below lays the seventeen seasons side by side: offensive moves on the left, defensive answers on the right, and in the middle the rule changes and new ideas that tilted the field. Read down a column to follow one side, then look across: an answer usually lands a season or two after the move it answers (the 2012 read option, and the 2013 word on hitting the quarterback). Very little happened in isolation.

    x, col, tint = COLS[key]
    for yr, text in items:
        ax.text(x, yr, text, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=6.4, color=style.INK, linespacing=1.15,
                bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.32", fc=tint, ec=col, lw=0.8), zorder=3)
plt.show()








Figure 57.1: The era at a glance, 2000-2016. Offensive moves (blue, left), defensive answers (orange, right), and the rules and ideas in between (grey, centre). Each item is placed at its season; a Super Bowl is listed under the season it ended (Super Bowl XLVIII, played in February 2014, belongs to 2013). The New England dynasty runs through the whole picture, on both sides of the ball.
The New England Patriots are the thread through all of it: three titles in four seasons at the start (2001, 2003, 2004), two more at the end (2014 and 2016), and in between a team that kept changing shape.1 Three forces push on every row.
The defenses that won titles late in the era (the 2013 Seahawks, the 2015 Broncos) won by answering those forces with new kinds of players: press corners who could run, safeties who could hit, and pass rushers who were neither linemen nor linebackers. That is the arc. Now the details, in roughly the order they happened.

title: Dynasties and Counterpunches (2000-2016)
text:
Defenses built on speed and simplicity, Tampa 2 above all, which made offenses earn every yard.
Rules that favoured the passing game, starting with a crackdown on downfield contact in 2004 and continuing with new protections for quarterbacks and receivers.
Offenses that turned personnel into a weapon: the no-huddle, the tight end who could be a receiver one snap and a blocker the next, and, from college, the quarterback who could run.

title: Dynasties and Counterpunches (2000-2016)
section: Tampa 2, and the quarterback who solved it
text:
Tampa 2, and the quarterback who solved it
At the turn of the century the most copied defense in football was Tony Dungy and Monte Kiffin’s Tampa 2: Cover 2 and Tampa 2 has its whole anatomy. In one paragraph: four fast linemen rush, two safeties guard the deep halves, two squat corners take the flats, and a rangy middle linebacker drops straight down the middle of the field at the snap to close the hole between the safeties (coaches call that deep middle strip the pipe). The defense keeps everything in front, tackles immediately, and waits for the offense to make a mistake. Its Mikes were rare athletes, Shelton Quarles in Tampa and later Brian Urlacher in Chicago, because the whole scheme rested on one linebacker who could run with receivers. In 2002 Tampa Bay allowed the fewest points in the league and won Super Bowl XXXVII 48-21, intercepting the league MVP, Rich Gannon, five times. Dungy wasn’t there to see it: the Buccaneers had fired him after the 2001 season, and Jon Gruden coached the title team, with Kiffin still running Dungy’s defense.2 By the middle of the decade Dungy’s Colts, Lovie Smith’s Bears and a string of imitators were running versions of it.
Why it won. Tampa 2 was a bet about the offenses of its day. In 2000 many NFL offenses still lined up with two backs and a tight end on early downs, threw short timing routes, and ran into a defense whose linebackers were faster than any blockers who could reach them. Against that, a defense of smaller, quicker players who all knew one simple scheme cold was terrifically hard to drive the ball against. Its weak spots, the deep middle behind the Mike, the sideline between corner and safety, the open middle at 12 to 15 yards when the Mike runs, were real, but hitting them took an accurate quarterback, patience, and a receiver who could beat a linebacker 20 yards downfield. In 2000 few offenses had all three.
Then Dungy moved to Indianapolis in 2002 and found the quarterback who did. He brought Tampa 2 with him as the Colts’ defense, so from then on Peyton Manning practised against it every day. That mattered because the league was full of it: Dungy’s own assistants and imitators were installing it all over the NFL, so the Colts’ offense under coordinator Tom Moore had to be built to beat exactly that kind of defense, and it had the perfect sparring partner across the practice field.3 Three things made it work.

A small playbook, run fast and changed at the line. The Colts often went without a huddle, which kept the defense from substituting and from disguising much, and Manning chose or changed the play at the line of scrimmage after seeing the defense. A defense whose whole philosophy was simple calls, played fast found itself playing simple calls against a quarterback who knew them all.
A run game that made the linebackers step up. The Colts’ bread-and-butter run was a stretch play (outside zone) to Edgerrin James, and their play-action passes were built to look exactly like it for the first second.
A tight end who ran like a receiver. Dallas Clark, a 2003 first-round pick, was not a blocker who could catch. He was a receiver in a tight end’s body, and he was fast enough to make a linebacker running down the middle of the field look slow.

Put those together and you get the play that ate Tampa 2.


Show the Python
def manning_play():
    off = offense("singleback")
    off = [p.moved(w=-9.0, d=-1.5) if p.key == "H" else p for p in off]
    dfn = [D("WDE", "DE", 1.0, -5.4, "E"), D("WDT", "DT", 1.0, -0.7, "T"), D("SDT", "DT", 1.0, 2.35, "T"),
           D("SDE", "DE", 1.0, 5.6, "E"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, 0.3), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, 6.2),
           D("NB", "NB", 5.0, -8.3), D("LCB", "CB", 5.5, -16.3, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 5.5, 16.3, "CB"),
           D("FS", "FS", 13.0, -9.5), D("SS", "SS", 13.0, 9.5)]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=40, to_go=10)
    for k in ("LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT"):          # run-action: the line steps right, as on the stretch
        p.block(k, pts=[(0.25, 1.4)])
    for k in ("WDE", "WDT", "SDT", "SDE"):       # the rush engages the line (kept short so markers don't overlap)
        p.rush(k, pts=[(-0.5, 0.0)], speed=1.5)
    p.path("QB", [(-3.0, 1.6), (-3.2, 2.2)], absolute=True, speed=4.0)     # fake to the back...
    p.path("QB", [(-7.0, 0.8)], absolute=True, speed=4.5)                   # ...then finish the drop
    p.path("RB", [(-5.5, 2.6), (-2.0, 6.0)], absolute=True, speed=6.0)      # the back sells the stretch
    p.route("Y", r.path((3.0, 0.3), (12.0, -3.0), (30.0, -6.2)), speed=7.0)  # Clark's seam, bending to the pipe
    p.route("X", r.go(30)); p.route("Z", r.go(30)); p.route("H", r.path((25.0, 1.0)))
    p.pass_to("Y", t=2.4)
    # the Mike: reads run, steps up, then turns and runs (late)
    p.path("MIKE", [(3.0, 1.6)], absolute=True, speed=2.6)
    p.path("MIKE", [(9.0, 2.2), (24.0, 2.0)], absolute=True, speed=6.0, delay=0.15)
    p.path("WILL", [(3.4, 6.6)], absolute=True, speed=3.0)
    p.drop("WILL", (9.5, 9.0), speed=5.0)
    p.drop("NB", (10.0, -9.0))
    # Tampa 2 corners with no flat threat sink under the outside receivers ("squeezing the hole")
    p.drop("LCB", (6.0, -15.8), speed=1.3); p.drop("LCB", (14.0, -16.5), speed=3.2)
    p.drop("RCB", (6.0, 15.8), speed=1.3); p.drop("RCB", (14.0, 16.5), speed=3.2)
    p.drop("FS", (22.0, -13.0), speed=4.4); p.drop("SS", (21.0, 11.5), speed=4.4)
    p.path("SS", [(24.0, 3.0)], absolute=True, speed=5.0, delay=0.1)
    p.highlight("MIKE", "Y")
    return p


seam = manning_play()
_, _catch = seam.pass_target_spot()
T_ARR = next(t for t in np.arange(2.4, 6.0, 0.02) if np.linalg.norm(seam.ball_position(t) - _catch) < 0.3)
SEAM_T = [0.0, 0.8, 2.4, round(float(T_ARR) + 0.04, 2)]
if PDF:
    strip(seam, SEAM_T, ["Snap · stretch look, Cover 2 shell", "+0.8 s · the Mike steps up to the fake",
                         "+2.4 s · Y is past him: throw", f"+{SEAM_T[3]:.1f} s · in the pipe, between the safeties"],
          lateral=(-20.5, 20.5), window=(-9.5, 28.5),
          notes_at={1: [("run fake", (-5.8, 6.4))], 3: [("Mike\ntrails", (15.5, 6.0))]})
    plt.show()
else:
    show_animation(seam, times=SEAM_T)





  
  Your browser does not support the video tag.



Figure 57.2: Manning against the Tampa 2 Mike, simulated (an illustration of the idea, not a specific Colts play). Snap: the Colts (11 personnel, under center) show their stretch run to the right; the defense shows a nickel Cover 2 with the Mike (M, ringed) 4.5 yards off the ball. +0.8 s: the Mike reads run and takes two steps up and toward the fake, as a linebacker must against the league’s best run game. The tight end, Y (ringed), is already level with him. +2.4 s: Manning has finished the fake and his seven-step drop. The Mike has turned to carry the seam, but he is three or four yards behind Y. Each safety has two vertical routes in his half (X’s go and H’s vertical on the left, Z’s go on the right, with the corners sinking under the outside receivers), so neither can come to the middle, and Manning throws. +3.6 s: the ball arrives about 23 yards downfield in the pipe, the strip of deep middle between the two safeties, with the Mike four or five yards behind and the strong safety a step late. One false step by one defender is the whole play.




Follow the ringed Mike. Nothing he does is wrong. He reads his keys, sees the line step and the back run toward the sideline, and comes up to fill his gap, because a Tampa 2 Mike who ignores the run gets run over. By the time he sees the quarterback pull the ball back and turns to run, the tight end has a three- or four-yard head start, and a linebacker cannot make up three yards on a receiver over the next fifteen. Meanwhile the vertical routes outside have done their job: the free safety has X and H running at his half, the strong safety has Z, and the corners have sunk under the outside men instead of helping in the middle, so neither safety can cheat toward the pipe. The ball goes over the Mike and under the safeties.
That is the general shape of beating any defense, and it is worth stating once: find the player with two jobs and make him do the wrong one first. Tampa 2’s Mike has a run job and a deep-pass job, and play-action puts them in the wrong order. Against a big, slow, blocking tight end the Mike could survive his false step. Against a receiver-speed tight end he couldn’t. And if a defense answered by telling the Mike to bail at the snap, the Colts ran the stretch into a box one defender lighter. Manning’s line-of-scrimmage checks were the last turn of the screw: he could see which answer the defense had chosen before the snap and pick the play that beat it.






NoteFilm room: Colts at Buccaneers, October 6, 2003 — Dungy comes home



Dungy’s first trip back to Tampa as the Colts’ head coach was a Monday night game against the defending champions and the defense he had built. For 55 minutes the Buccaneers’ Tampa 2 won: Ronde Barber jumped a throw to Marvin Harrison and returned it for a touchdown that made it 35-14 Tampa Bay with 5:09 left. Then the game turned, though not the way legend tells it. Brad Pyatt returned the kickoff 90 yards to the Tampa 12, and a short run scored. The Colts recovered an onside kick, and Harrison caught a 28-yard touchdown. Tampa recovered the second onside kick but had to punt, and on the Colts’ last drive a roughing-the-passer penalty on Warren Sapp and a 52-yard catch by Harrison set up the tying run with 35 seconds left. In overtime Mike Vanderjagt missed a 40-yard field goal, but Simeon Rice was flagged for unsportsmanlike conduct on the kick, and the retry from 29 yards won it, 38-35.4
What to notice: first, how well Tampa 2 played the league’s best offense for most of the night. Barber’s interception is the kind of play the scheme is built for: a corner sitting short, reading the quarterback and driving on the throw. Then notice what the comeback was made of. It wasn’t a patient dismantling of the coverage. It was a short field after a kick return, two penalties, and Manning’s two-minute operation from the shotgun, with Harrison catching the deep balls. That is a fair summary of the early Dungy-Manning years against Tampa 2 teams: the scheme held until the Colts found one or two plays it didn’t cover, and then Manning made them count.


A season later the Colts’ offense was the best in the league, and Manning’s 2004 season (49 touchdown passes and a 121.1 passer rating, both records at the time) is still one of the great quarterback years.5 But it did not happen in a vacuum. Something else changed in 2004, and it changed the whole league.

title: Dynasties and Counterpunches (2000-2016)
section: 2004: the rule that tilted the field
text:
2004: the rule that tilted the field
On January 18, 2004, in the AFC Championship Game, the New England Patriots beat the Colts 24-14 and intercepted Manning four times, three of them by cornerback Ty Law (safety Rodney Harrison had the other). New England’s defensive backs played the Colts’ receivers the way defensive backs had always played big games: they bumped, held and rerouted them well past the line of scrimmage, and the officials let them. Colts president Bill Polian sat on the league’s competition committee (the group of owners, team executives and coaches that proposes rule changes and tells officials what to stress), and he complained loudly. For the 2004 season the league made illegal contact a point of emphasis: an instruction to officials to enforce an existing rule more strictly. The rule itself was old. Since 1978 a defender may contact a receiver only within 5 yards of the line of scrimmage; beyond that, while the quarterback is still in the pocket with the ball, contact that impedes the receiver is illegal contact, a 5-yard penalty with an automatic first down. (Once the ball is thrown, pass interference takes over.) The emphasis covered defensive holding too. What changed was that officials started throwing the flag: the counts differ by source, but illegal-contact calls went from the high 70s in 2003 to about 190 in 2004 (STATS counted 76 and 190; Cover 2 and Tampa 2 quotes another count, 79 and 191). Patriots fans still call it the “Ty Law rule.”6
Why it mattered so much. A flag that was rarely called is, in practice, not a rule. For decades defenders had been able to shape routes with their hands: knock a receiver off his stem at 7 yards, lean on him at 10, give him a shove as he broke. Every Cover 2 and Tampa 2 depended on some of that, because the coverage needs receivers to arrive late and in the wrong place. Take the hands away beyond 5 yards and every route arrives on time, and a timing offense like Manning’s lives on routes that arrive on time. The change also made man coverage harder. A press corner used to be able to jam a receiver at the line and then ride him with his hands for another 10 yards. Now he gets one shot, inside 5 yards, and after that he has to run with the receiver, usually from the receiver’s inside shoulder (inside leverage, which takes away the slant and the middle of the field), not wrestle him.
Here is what the league’s passing game did next.


Show the Python (league efficiency by season, nflverse play-by-play 1999-2016)
from gridiron.data import nfl, pbp

COLS_PBP = ["season", "season_type", "play_type", "qb_dropback", "epa", "pass_attempt", "sack", "two_point_attempt",
            "complete_pass", "passing_yards", "pass_touchdown", "interception", "down", "qb_scramble",
            "aborted_play", "rusher_player_id", "passer_player_id", "ydstogo", "posteam", "yards_gained", "success"]
PB = pbp(range(1999, 2026), columns=COLS_PBP)
PB = PB[PB["season_type"] == "REG"]
PLAYS = PB[PB["play_type"].isin(["pass", "run"]) & PB["down"].notna()].copy()

# EPA per dropback (passes, sacks, scrambles) and per designed run, by season
EFF = pd.DataFrame({
    "dropback": PLAYS[PLAYS["qb_dropback"] == 1].groupby("season")["epa"].mean(),
    "run": PLAYS[PLAYS["qb_dropback"] == 0].groupby("season")["epa"].mean(),
})

# league passer rating, from the standard NFL formula, on pass attempts (no sacks, no two-point tries)
_pa = PB[(PB["pass_attempt"] == 1) & (PB["sack"] == 0) & (PB["two_point_attempt"] == 0) & PB["down"].notna()]
_g = _pa.groupby("season").agg(att=("pass_attempt", "size"), cmp=("complete_pass", "sum"),
                                yds=("passing_yards", "sum"), td=("pass_touchdown", "sum"),
                                ints=("interception", "sum"))
_c = lambda s: s.clip(0, 2.375)  # noqa: E731
EFF["rating"] = (_c((_g.cmp / _g.att - 0.3) * 5) + _c((_g.yds / _g.att - 3) * 0.25)
                 + _c(_g.td / _g.att * 20) + _c(2.375 - _g.ints / _g.att * 25)) / 6 * 100




Show the Python
E = EFF.loc[1999:2016]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 3.0))
ax = axes[0]
ax.axvspan(2003.5, 2004.5, color=style.LINE_TO_GAIN, alpha=0.18, lw=0)
ax.axhline(0, color=style.BASELINE, lw=0.9)
ax.plot(E.index, E["dropback"], marker="o", ms=3.5, color=style.SERIES[0], label="Dropbacks")
ax.plot(E.index, E["run"], marker="o", ms=3.5, color=style.SERIES[1], label="Designed runs")
ax.text(2016.6, E["dropback"].iloc[-1], "dropbacks", fontsize=7, color=style.SERIES[0], va="center")
ax.text(2016.6, E["run"].iloc[-1], "runs", fontsize=7, color=style.SERIES[1], va="center")
ax.set_xlim(1998.5, 2019.2)

ax.set_ylabel("expected points added per play", fontsize=7.5)

for yr, dy in ((2002, 1.6), (2003, -2.2), (2004, 1.6), (2016, 1.6)):
    ax.text(yr, E.loc[yr, "rating"] + dy, f"{E.loc[yr, 'rating']:.1f}", ha="center", fontsize=6.8,
            color=style.INK)
ax.set_ylim(74, 93)
ax.set_xlim(1998.5, 2017)
ax.set_title("League passer rating", fontsize=9)
ax.set_ylabel("passer rating", fontsize=7.5)
for a in axes:
    a.tick_params(labelsize=7)
    a.set_xticks([2000, 2004, 2008, 2012, 2016])
    a.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=1.5)
plt.show()








Figure 57.3: The passing boom, 1999-2016. Left: expected points added (EPA) per play, for dropbacks (passes, sacks and scrambles) and for designed runs, league-wide in the regular season. Throwing was already worth more than running in 1999; after 2004 the gap widened, as dropbacks became steadily more valuable and runs did not. Right: the league’s passer rating (the box-score formula on a 0-158.3 scale), which jumped four and a half points in 2004, the first season of the illegal-contact emphasis (shaded). Part of that jump was a rebound from a weak 2003, and 2005 and 2006 fell back to about 80, so one season proves little; the steady climb of about nine points from 2006 to 2016 is the story. Source: nflverse play-by-play.





Read the chart in three parts.7

2004 was a jump, but read it carefully. League passer rating (the familiar box-score formula that combines completion rate, yards, touchdowns and interceptions per attempt on a scale of 0 to 158.3; about 80 was league average then, about 90 today) rose from about 78 to about 83 in a single season, and EPA per dropback went from negative to positive. Look at the chart and you’ll see that 2003 was itself a dip: against 2002 (about 80), the 2004 rise is closer to two and a half points, and 2005 fell back. Manning had a historic year, and seasons bounce. So the 2004 number alone proves little. The officials’ foul counts are the firmer evidence that the rule changed what defenders could get away with, and the longer trend shows what it added up to.
Then the rise kept going. From 2007 the league passer rating climbed almost every season. Every rule change of the next decade pointed the same way: a 2009 directive that a defender knocked to the ground may not lunge at a quarterback’s legs (issued after Tom Brady’s knee was wrecked by such a hit in the 2008 opener), a 2009 rule against hits to the head of a “defenseless” receiver and wider protections after it, stricter roughing-the-passer enforcement.8 By 2016 the league passer rating was near 89, and a quarterback who would have been average in 2000 was below average.
Running didn’t keep up. EPA per designed run barely moved. The gap between a dropback and a run grew by about two-thirds across the era, and the share of plays that were passes crept up with it. Every coach in the next section was making the same calculation: the field had tilted toward the passing game, so the question was how to throw more, and better, without getting your quarterback hurt.

Why is the run line below zero in every season, and does that mean running is pointless? No. Below zero means the average run leaves the offense in a slightly worse spot than it started: a typical 3- or 4-yard run on first-and-10 leaves second-and-6 or -7, which is worth a little less than the first-and-10 was. But runs win the plays averages hide (third-and-1, the goal line, running out the clock with a lead), and the passing game’s best weapon, play-action, works only because the defense has to respect the run, as the Colts’ stretch showed. Expected Points and Success Rate takes the run-versus-pass numbers apart.






CautionCommon misconception



“The NFL changed the rules in 2004.” Not quite, and the difference matters if you want to understand how the league works. The 5-yard contact limit had been in the rulebook since 1978. In 2004 the league told officials to call it. Most of the NFL’s big strategic shifts work that way: a “point of emphasis” or a new interpretation changes the game as much as a new rule does, and it can quietly fade a few seasons later. When a broadcaster says “they’re calling it tighter this year,” take it seriously.


As Cover 2 and Tampa 2 points out, the change helped Dungy’s quarterback and hurt Dungy’s scheme. The fade was slow, not sudden: two Tampa 2 teams, Dungy’s Colts and Lovie Smith’s Bears, met in Super Bowl XLI after the 2006 season, and Manning was its MVP.9 But the copies around the league thinned out over the next few years, and within a decade almost nobody played Tampa 2 as a base defense. The team that rebuilt itself most completely around the new rules, though, was not the Colts. It was the team that had beaten them.

title: Dynasties and Counterpunches (2000-2016)
section: New England: the team that kept changing shape
text:
New England: the team that kept changing shape
Bill Belichick’s Patriots won three Super Bowls in four seasons (XXXVI, XXXVIII and XXXIX, after the 2001, 2003 and 2004 seasons) with a different team almost every year, and what stayed constant was not a scheme but a habit: decide what this opponent, this season, can’t handle, and become that. Those first champions were built on defense and on game plans rebuilt for each opponent; you’ve already seen their secondary take apart Manning in January 2004. The full case study is Belichick and Game-Plan Football. Here are the three offensive shapes that mattered to the league’s arms race.
The language underneath. The Patriots’ offense spoke Erhardt-Perkins, the concept-based play-calling system (Offensive Systems and Languages has it): one word names a whole pass pattern, and the same word works from any formation. “Ghost,” for example, tells the three receivers on one side to run a vertical, an 8-yard out and a flat, counting from the sideline in. From a two-tight-end set those three might be a receiver, a tight end and a fullback; from an empty set, three receivers; from a bunch, three players stacked together. Nobody learns a new play. That is what made the next two shapes possible: a team whose concepts work from any formation and any personnel group can change both every week without teaching a new playbook.
2007: the spread. Before the 2007 season New England traded for two receivers, Randy Moss (from Oakland, for a fourth-round pick) and Wes Welker (from Miami), and became something the NFL had not seen from a contender: a spread offense, often from the shotgun with three and four receivers, Moss running past people outside and Welker running option routes from the slot (routes where the receiver chooses his break after the snap, depending on how the defender plays him). The Patriots scored 589 points, a record at the time; Brady threw 50 touchdown passes and Moss caught 23, both records; they won all sixteen regular-season games.10 The 2007 Patriots were the NFL’s first great answer to the 2004 rules: spread the field, put the ball in the air, and make the defense cover all 53 yards of width with defenders who couldn’t touch anyone past 5 yards.
The counterpunch: four men who could get there. They lost the Super Bowl. In Super Bowl XLII, on February 3, 2008, the New York Giants beat them 17-14, and they did it with the oldest answer to a spread passing game: a four-man pass rush good enough to get home without blitzing. Defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo’s Giants had a surplus of defensive ends (Michael Strahan, Osi Umenyiora and Justin Tuck; Mathias Kiwanuka, an end moved to linebacker that year, had broken his leg in November), and on passing downs he put three or even four ends on the field at once, with Tuck sliding inside over a guard. (Four years later, when the Giants beat New England in another Super Bowl, their players had a name for that speed package: “NASCAR.”) They sacked Brady five times and hit him again and again.11 Two details make it a lesson rather than a highlight. First, the pressure came up the middle as well as around the edges: an end lined up over a guard, plus stunts between the rushers, put defenders in Brady’s face, where a pocket passer can’t step up to escape. Second, the arithmetic: if four rushers win, seven defenders can cover the five receivers a spread puts out, with two left over to help. Spagnuolo blitzed plenty in other situations; the point of the four-end package was not to need to on passing downs. Spagnuolo, more than eighteen years later, is still coordinating a defense on that idea, in Kansas City.

2010-2012: two tight ends, and the move tight end
Three years later the Patriots changed shape again, in almost the opposite direction. In the 2010 draft they took two tight ends: Rob Gronkowski in the second round and Aaron Hernandez in the fourth. By 2011 they were the core of the offense. Gronkowski was the most complete tight end in football, a 6-foot-6, 265-pound blocker who caught 17 touchdown passes and gained 1,327 receiving yards that season, both records for a tight end.12 Hernandez was something else: a tight end in name who lined up in the slot, out wide, next to the tackle, and in the backfield as a running back. In a playoff game against Denver in January 2012 he took a handoff on the Patriots’ first drive and ran 42 yards.13
Hernandez was the archetype of a player the whole league would soon want, the move tight end, also called the joker: a tight end who doesn’t have a fixed spot, so the defense can’t plan for where he’ll be. (The diagrams label him F; many staffs call the move tight end the F, the H or the U, and the in-line tight end the Y. Some defensive staffs use “joker” for a hybrid defender instead, so the word depends on which side of the ball is talking.) The point of him is not any one route. It is the decision he forces on the defense before the snap.
Recall the rule of substitution from Personnel Groupings: the offense sends its players on first, the defense answers with its own, and only then does the offense pick a formation. With 12 personnel on the field, a defense normally chooses between two answers, and the move tight end makes both of them wrong.


Show the Python
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 4.5))

# Left: nickel on the field -> stay tight, run at the nickel back with Hernandez leading
offA = line5() + [O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -7.0, 0.0, "R"), O("Y", "TE", -0.7, 4.8, "Y"),
                  O("F", "TE", -4.0, 2.4, "F"), O("X", "WR", -0.7, -14.0, "X"), O("Z", "WR", -1.5, 12.5, "Z")]
nick = [D("WDE", "DE", 1.0, -4.3, "E"), D("WDT", "DT", 1.0, -0.7, "T"), D("SDT", "DT", 1.0, 2.35, "T"),
        D("SDE", "DE", 1.0, 5.6, "E"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -2.4), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, 1.6),
        D("NB", "NB", 3.6, 8.0, "$"), D("LCB", "CB", 6.5, -14.0, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 6.5, 13.5, "CB"),
        D("FS", "FS", 12.0, -6.0), D("SS", "SS", 12.0, 7.0)]
a = Play(offA, nick, los=35, to_go=10)
a.block("Y", pts=[(1.0, 1.1)])                          # reach: get outside the end and seal him in
a.block("RT", target="SDT")                             # RT and RG: the 3-technique, then up to the Mike
a.block("RG", target="MIKE")
for k in ("C", "LG", "LT"):                             # backside: cut off the defenders away from the play
    a.block(k, pts=[(0.6, 1.2)])
a.block("Z", target="RCB")
a.pull("F", [(2.6, 4.0), (6.2, 5.2)], target="NB")     # arc around Y's block to the nickel back
a.run("RB", [(-5.2, 3.6), (-2.6, 8.8), (1.8, 11.0), (9.5, 11.6)], absolute=True, delay=0.4)
a.highlight("Y", "F", color=TE_RING)
a.highlight("NB", color=style.DEFENSE)

# Right: base on the field -> empty, find the linebackers

b = Play(offB, base, los=35, to_go=10)
for k, t in (("WILL", "F"), ("SAM", "Y"), ("SS", "RB"), ("LCB", "X"), ("RCB", "Z")):
    b.man(k, t)
b.route("F", r.path((3.0, 0.8), (5.5, 4.0)))           # an option route: the Will is inside, so break out
b.route("Y", r.path((12.0, -0.6)))
b.drop("MIKE", (8.5, -1.5))                             # the Mike drops to rob the middle
b.highlight("Y", "F", color=TE_RING)
b.highlight("WILL", "SAM", color=style.DEFENSE)
fb = b.draw(ax=axes[1], lateral=(-17.5, 17.5), window=(-9.5, 15.5), title=False)
