title: Case Study: The Shanahan Tree
text:
The data fingerprint
How would you recognise this offense from data alone, without watching a snap? Four measurements do most of the work: how often the quarterback is under center, how often he fakes a handoff, how much the receivers gain after the catch, and (to check that all this produces anything) how efficient the offense is.

Under center and play-action
The chart below sorts the 2025 play-callers into two generations. The first generation are the coaches who worked on the Shanahans’ or Kubiaks’ own staffs and called plays in 2025: Kyle Shanahan (49ers), Sean McVay (Rams), Matt LaFleur (Packers), Mike McDaniel (Dolphins) and Klint Kubiak (Seahawks); the tree section below traces how each got there. The second generation came up on McVay’s Rams staffs: Kevin O’Connell (Vikings), Zac Taylor (Bengals), Liam Coen (Jaguars), and two coordinators who called plays in 2025, Zac Robinson in Atlanta and Nick Caley in Houston.14


Show the Python
FP_SEASONS = [2022, 2023, 2024, 2025]
ftn = nfl().load_ftn_charting(FP_SEASONS).to_pandas()
fp = PLAYS[PLAYS["season"].isin(FP_SEASONS)].merge(
    ftn[["nflverse_game_id", "nflverse_play_id", "qb_location", "is_play_action", "is_motion"]],
    left_on=["game_id", "play_id"], right_on=["nflverse_game_id", "nflverse_play_id"])
fp["uc"] = fp["qb_location"].eq("U")
FP = fp.groupby(["season", "posteam"]).agg(uc=("uc", "mean"), motion=("is_motion", "mean"))
FP = FP.join(fp[fp["qb_dropback"] == 1].groupby(["season", "posteam"]).agg(pa=("is_play_action", "mean")))
for col in ("uc", "pa", "motion"):
    FP[col + "_rk"] = FP.groupby(level="season")[col].rank(ascending=False, method="min").astype(int)
LG_UC = fp.groupby("season")["uc"].mean()

CORE = {"SF": "49ers (Shanahan)", "LA": "Rams (McVay)", "GB": "Packers (LaFleur)",
        "MIA": "Dolphins (McDaniel)", "SEA": "Seahawks (Kubiak)"}
MCVAY = {"MIN": "Vikings", "CIN": "Bengals", "JAX": "Jaguars", "ATL": "Falcons", "HOU": "Texans"}
f25 = FP.xs(2025, level="season")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.6, 4.3))
rest = f25[~f25.index.isin(list(CORE) + list(MCVAY))]
ax.scatter(rest["uc"], rest["pa"], s=34, color=style.BASELINE, edgecolor=style.SURFACE, lw=0.8, zorder=2,
           label="other offenses")
ax.scatter(f25.loc[list(MCVAY), "uc"], f25.loc[list(MCVAY), "pa"], s=46, color=style.SERIES[2],
           edgecolor=style.SURFACE, lw=0.8, zorder=3, label="second generation (from McVay's staffs)")
ax.scatter(f25.loc[list(CORE), "uc"], f25.loc[list(CORE), "pa"], s=62, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK,
           edgecolor=style.SURFACE, lw=0.8, zorder=4, label="first generation")
LABEL_OFF = {"SF": (7, -10), "LA": (-6, 8), "GB": (-6, 9), "MIA": (-7, -8), "SEA": (7, 4),
             "MIN": (7, 2), "CIN": (-7, 0), "JAX": (7, -4), "ATL": (7, -6), "HOU": (7, 2)}
LABEL_AT = {"GB": (0.405, 0.292), "MIA": (0.205, 0.292)}     # crowded spots: label in open space, with a leader
for tm, off_ in LABEL_OFF.items():
    lab = CORE.get(tm, MCVAY.get(tm))
    r = f25.loc[tm]
    if tm in LABEL_AT:
        ax.annotate(lab, (r["uc"], r["pa"]), xytext=LABEL_AT[tm], textcoords="data", fontsize=6.8,
                    color=style.INK, fontweight="bold", ha="center", va="center",
                    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=style.INK_2, lw=0.6, shrinkA=2, shrinkB=4))
        continue
    ax.annotate(lab, (r["uc"], r["pa"]), xytext=off_, textcoords="offset points", fontsize=6.8,
                color=style.INK if tm in CORE else style.INK_2, fontweight="bold" if tm in CORE else "normal",
                ha="left" if off_[0] > 0 else "right", va="center")
s24 = FP.loc[(2024, "SEA")]
ax.annotate("", (f25.loc["SEA", "uc"], f25.loc["SEA", "pa"]), xytext=(s24["uc"], s24["pa"]),
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, lw=1.1, ls=(0, (3, 2)),
                            shrinkA=3, shrinkB=6))
ax.annotate("Seattle 2024", (s24["uc"], s24["pa"]), xytext=(0, -9), textcoords="offset points", fontsize=6.4,
            color=style.INK_2, ha="center", va="top")
ax.axvline(f25["uc"].median(), color=style.MUTED, lw=0.8, ls=(0, (3, 2)), zorder=1)
ax.axhline(f25["pa"].median(), color=style.MUTED, lw=0.8, ls=(0, (3, 2)), zorder=1)
ax.text(f25["uc"].median() + 0.004, 0.147, "league median", fontsize=6.4, color=style.INK_2, ha="left", va="bottom")
ax.text(0.103, f25["pa"].median() + 0.002, "league median", fontsize=6.4, color=style.INK_2, ha="left", va="bottom")
ax.yaxis.set_major_locator(plt.MultipleLocator(0.05))
ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(plt.FuncFormatter(lambda v, _: f"{v:.0%}"))
ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(plt.FuncFormatter(lambda v, _: f"{v:.0%}"))
ax.set_xlabel("Quarterback under center (share of plays), 2025", fontsize=8)
ax.set_ylabel("Play-action (share of dropbacks)", fontsize=8)
ax.tick_params(labelsize=7.5)
ax.legend(loc="upper left", fontsize=7, handletextpad=0.2)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 61.4: The 2025 fingerprint: how often each offense put the quarterback under center (share of runs and passes) against how often it used play-action (share of dropbacks), from FTN’s charting. Dark blue: the five first-generation play-callers (Shanahan, McVay, Matt LaFleur, McDaniel and Klint Kubiak). Green: five play-callers who came up on McVay’s Rams staffs. Grey: the rest of the league. The dashed lines are the league medians. Four of the five first-generation teams sit right of the under-center median, the Rams at the far corner of both; McDaniel’s Dolphins, the speed-and-motion branch, worked mostly from the shotgun and pistol. The dashed arrow is the one 2024 element: Seattle’s move from 2024 to 2025, Klint Kubiak’s one season as play-caller. The second generation is spread out: a coaching tree passes on ideas, not a single formula. Data: nflverse play-by-play joined to FTN charting, regular seasons.





The core of the family is easy to spot in Figure 63.6. In 2025 the Rams put Stafford under center on 59% of their plays, the most in the league, and used play-action on 35% of dropbacks, also the most. The 49ers were under center on 46% (6th). Seattle made the most dramatic move of any team in the chart: under center on 22% of plays in 2024, 25th in the league, and on 53% in 2025, 2nd, the year Klint Kubiak arrived as offensive coordinator. One new play-caller, and the fingerprint moved across the whole chart.
Two surprises are worth noticing. The first is San Francisco’s play-action rate, which in FTN’s charting is ordinary: 22% of dropbacks in 2025, 21st in the league, and in the bottom half in every season from 2022 to 2025. FTN’s play-action flag counts snaps with a fake handoff, and the 49ers fake less than you’d guess: their “it all looks the same” effect comes less from the fake itself than from the formation, the personnel and the motion that the runs, the passes and the boots all share. Where the 49ers are extreme is motion (2nd in 2025, 2nd, 2nd and 3rd in the three seasons before) and personnel. The second surprise is how scattered the second generation is: the Bengals under Zac Taylor are a shotgun passing team, and Atlanta in 2025 was under center less than almost anyone. A coaching tree hands down a way of thinking and a vocabulary, not a formation chart.


Show the Python (where 49ers runs ended up, 2019-2025)
_r = PLAYS[(PLAYS["play_type"] == "run") & (PLAYS["qb_scramble"] != 1) & PLAYS["season"].between(2019, 2025)]
_out = _r.groupby("posteam")["run_gap"].apply(lambda g: g.eq("end").mean())
OUT_SF, OUT_RK, OUT_LG = _out["SF"], int(_out.rank(ascending=False, method="min")["SF"]), _r["run_gap"].eq("end").mean()


One thing the fingerprint can’t show is how often the 49ers run wide zone. Public play-by-play doesn’t record the blocking scheme, only where the run ended up, and by that measure San Francisco looks ordinary: 26% of its runs from 2019 to 2025 were charted outside the tackles, 12th in the league, against 23% for the league. That isn’t a contradiction. A wide-zone run is aimed outside, but the back cuts wherever the crease is, and a run that bends back inside is charted as an inside run. The scheme is in the aim, not the destination, which is why the charting services that grade blocking schemes from film are the only source for it.
The fingerprint has also been spreading beyond the tree. League-wide, quarterbacks were under center on 27% of plays in 2023 and 34% in 2025 by FTN’s charting, the reversal of a decade-long slide toward the shotgun.15 Offenses that are not in the tree have been borrowing its habits.


YAC over expected


Show the Python
ngs = nfl().load_nextgen_stats(seasons=list(range(2018, 2026)), stat_type="receiving").to_pandas()
ngs = ngs[(ngs["week"] == 0) & (ngs["season_type"] == "REG") & ngs["team_abbr"].notna()].copy()
ngs["tot"] = ngs["avg_yac_above_expectation"] * ngs["receptions"]
NGS_T = ngs.groupby(["season", "team_abbr"]).agg(tot=("tot", "sum"), rec=("receptions", "sum")).reset_index()
NGS_T["yacoe"] = NGS_T["tot"] / NGS_T["rec"]
NGS_T["rank"] = NGS_T.groupby("season")["yacoe"].rank(ascending=False).astype(int)
NGS_SF = NGS_T[NGS_T["team_abbr"] == "SF"].set_index("season")["rank"]

POOL = CATCH[CATCH["season"].between(2019, 2025)].groupby("posteam")["yacoe"].mean().sort_values()
SF_SEASONS = list(range(2017, 2026))
sf_y = YR.xs("SF", level="posteam").loc[SF_SEASONS]

fig, (a1, a2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 4.9), gridspec_kw=dict(width_ratios=[1, 1.35]))
cols = [style.SERIES[0] if t == "SF" else style.BASELINE for t in POOL.index]
a1.barh(np.arange(len(POOL)), POOL.values, color=cols, height=0.72)
a1.set_yticks(np.arange(len(POOL)), POOL.index, fontsize=6.2)
a1.axvline(0, color=style.INK_2, lw=0.8)
a1.set_xlim(-0.85, 1.12)
a1.set_title("All teams, 2019–2025", fontsize=9)
a1.set_xlabel("YAC over expected per catch (yards)", fontsize=7.5)
a1.tick_params(axis="x", labelsize=7)
a1.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
a1.annotate(f"{POOL['SF']:+.2f}", (POOL["SF"], len(POOL) - 1), xytext=(-3, 0), textcoords="offset points",
            ha="right", va="center", fontsize=7, color="white", fontweight="bold")
a1.set_ylim(-0.7, len(POOL) - 0.3)

x = np.arange(len(SF_SEASONS))
a2.bar(x, sf_y["yacoe"].values, color=[style.SERIES[0] if v > 0 else style.SERIES[1] for v in sf_y["yacoe"]],
       width=0.66)
a2.axhline(0, color=style.INK_2, lw=0.8)
for xi, s, v, rk in zip(x, SF_SEASONS, sf_y["yacoe"].values, sf_y["rank"].values):
    a2.text(xi, v + (0.06 if v >= 0 else -0.06), ordinal(int(rk)), ha="center",
            va="bottom" if v >= 0 else "top", fontsize=7.2, color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")
    ng = f"NGS\n{ordinal(int(NGS_SF[s]))}" if s in NGS_SF.index else "NGS\nn/a"
    a2.text(xi, -1.02, ng, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=6.2, color=style.MUTED)
a2.set_xticks(x, [str(s) for s in SF_SEASONS], fontsize=7)
a2.set_ylim(-1.25, 2.3)
a2.set_title("49ers by season (rank of 32)", fontsize=9)
a2.set_ylabel("YAC over expected per catch (yards)", fontsize=7.5)
a2.tick_params(axis="y", labelsize=7)
a2.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=1.2)
plt.show()

NUM1 = int((sf_y.loc[2018:2023, "rank"] == 1).sum())








Figure 61.5: YAC over expected, the 49ers’ signature. Left: every team’s yards after the catch per completion above nflverse’s expected YAC, pooled over the 2019–2025 regular seasons; San Francisco (blue) is first by a wide margin. Right: the 49ers season by season, 2017–2025, with their rank among the 32 teams above each bar (nflverse model) and below it in grey the rank by Next Gen Stats’ tracking-based model (available from 2018; NGS team values are reception-weighted averages of the receivers it lists). Both models put San Francisco first in most seasons from 2018 to 2023. The 2025 drop came in a season when the receiving corps changed and Mac Jones started about half the games. Data: nflverse play-by-play; NGS receiving via nflreadpy.







Show the Python (the 2021 Deebo Samuel row, which NGS lists without a team)
_n = nfl().load_nextgen_stats(seasons=list(range(2018, 2026)), stat_type="receiving").to_pandas()
_n = _n[(_n["week"] == 0) & (_n["season_type"] == "REG") & (_n["receptions"] >= 40)]
DEEBO = _n[(_n["player_display_name"] == "Deebo Samuel") & (_n["season"] == 2021)].iloc[0]
DEEBO_RANK = int((_n["avg_yac_above_expectation"] > DEEBO["avg_yac_above_expectation"]).sum()) + 1
REC_MED, REC_P90 = _n["avg_yac_above_expectation"].quantile([0.5, 0.9])


No team in the period comes close to San Francisco in Figure 61.5. From 2019 to 2025 the 49ers’ receivers gained +0.89 yards after the catch per reception beyond what nflverse’s model expected, against +0.54 for the next team, KC. They ranked first in every one of the six seasons from 2018 to 2023, a stretch that began with C. J. Beathard and Nick Mullens throwing to Kittle in 2018. Among receivers with 40 or more catches from 2018 to 2025, Deebo Samuel’s 2021 ranks 1st in Next Gen Stats’ YAC over expected: +5.2 yards per catch above what the tracking model expected. For scale: the median receiver-season in that group is +0.5 and one in ten beats +1.7, so Samuel’s season is an outlier even among individuals. Team numbers are much smaller because they average every catch by every receiver, the tight end’s six-yard out included; a team half a yard per catch above expectation is very good, and the 49ers’ seven-year average was +0.89.
The two models agreeing matters. nflverse’s model doesn’t know where the defenders were, so it credits the 49ers for space the design created; Next Gen Stats’ model does know, and it still ranked them first in most of those seasons, so their receivers were also doing more with the space than the space alone predicts. Design and players, together. The 2025 bars are the reminder that YAC is partly personnel: Deebo Samuel was traded to Washington before the 2025 season, and Mac Jones started about half the games.16


Does it produce points?
All of that would be trivia if the offense weren’t good. Figure 61.6 shows where San Francisco’s offense ranked in EPA per play in each season from 2019 to 2025, with the quarterbacks who took its dropbacks.


Show the Python
RANK_SEASONS = list(range(2019, 2026))
sf_rank = [int(RANK[(s, "SF")]) for s in RANK_SEASONS]
sf_epa = [float(TEAM_EPA[(TEAM_EPA["season"] == s) & (TEAM_EPA["posteam"] == "SF")]["epa"].iloc[0]) for s in RANK_SEASONS]
sfd = DROP[(DROP["posteam"] == "SF") & DROP["passer"].notna()]


def qb_line(season):
    c = sfd[sfd["season"] == season]["passer"].value_counts(normalize=True)
    names = [c.index[0]] + [n for n in c.index[1:2] if c[n] >= 0.25]
    return ",\n".join(n.split(".", 1)[1] for n in names)


N_QB = sfd[sfd["season"].isin(RANK_SEASONS)].groupby("season")["passer"].agg(lambda c: c.value_counts().index[0]).nunique()
N_QB_ALL = len({n for s_ in RANK_SEASONS for n in qb_line(s_).replace(",\n", "|").split("|")})
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.6, 3.5))
ax.axhspan(0.5, 10.5, color=style.OFFENSE_TINT, alpha=0.55, zorder=0, lw=0)
ax.text(len(RANK_SEASONS) - 0.62, 10.0, "top ten", fontsize=7, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, va="bottom", ha="right")
x = np.arange(len(RANK_SEASONS))
ax.plot(x, sf_rank, color=style.SERIES[0], lw=2, marker="o", ms=8, mec=style.SURFACE, mew=1.5, zorder=3)
for xi, rk, e in zip(x, sf_rank, sf_epa):
    ax.annotate(f"{ordinal(rk)}\n{e:+.2f}", (xi, rk), xytext=(0, 10), textcoords="offset points",
                ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=7, color=style.INK)
ax.set_xticks(x, [f"{s}\n{qb_line(s)}" for s in RANK_SEASONS], fontsize=7)
ax.set_ylim(33, -4)
ax.set_yticks([1, 8, 16, 24, 32])
ax.set_ylabel("EPA per play rank (1 = best)", fontsize=8)
ax.tick_params(axis="y", labelsize=7.5)
ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 61.6: San Francisco’s offense, EPA per play rank among the 32 teams, 2019–2025 regular seasons (all runs and passes; 1st = most efficient), with the quarterbacks who took the most dropbacks each season beneath (a second name if he took at least a quarter of them). Six of the seven seasons are in the top ten (shaded), with the dropbacks spread across several quarterbacks. The outlier, 2020, was a season of injuries in which three quarterbacks started. Data: nflverse play-by-play.





Six of seven seasons in the top ten, including first in 2023 (Purdy’s league-leading season, with McCaffrey the Offensive Player of the Year), with three different quarterbacks leading the team in dropbacks along the way and four taking at least a quarter of them in some season. Before 2019 the system was still being built: the 49ers ranked 16th in 2017 and 24th in 2018, with Hoyer, Beathard, Garoppolo and Mullens all starting games. That steadiness across passers is the strongest single piece of evidence for the system’s claim. It isn’t proof (the 49ers also had elite players at tight end, running back, receiver and left tackle in most of those seasons), but no other offense of the period stayed this efficient through this much change at quarterback.






NoteFilm room: San Francisco 49ers 2019



The game: the NFC Championship Game against Green Bay, January 19, 2020, the purest wide-zone game of the era. San Francisco won 37–20 while Jimmy Garoppolo threw eight passes (six completions) and was sacked once. The 49ers ran 42 times for 285 yards, and Raheem Mostert had 220 of them and four touchdowns.17
What to notice:

The same track to both sides. Watch the five linemen’s first step and the back’s path on run after run: it is the same play aimed left, right, and left again, with the fullback (Kyle Juszczyk) leading outside.
The backside end. Find him on each run: nobody blocks him, and he spends the afternoon chasing from behind.
How little the offense needed to pass. Eight throws is the system’s base play doing all of the work, because the defense never made it stop.









NoteFilm room: Atlanta Falcons 2016



The season: Kyle Shanahan’s second and last as Atlanta’s offensive coordinator. The Falcons led the NFL with 540 points, Matt Ryan was named MVP, and they reached Super Bowl LI, where they led New England 28–3 in the third quarter and lost 34–28 in the first overtime in Super Bowl history.18
What to notice:

This is the system before San Francisco: outside zone with two backs who could both run and catch (Devonta Freeman and Tevin Coleman), bootlegs off it, and play-action shots to Julio Jones. The fullback ingredient is already here too: Patrick DiMarco made the Pro Bowl after Kyle’s first Atlanta season (2015).19
Watch the running backs as receivers. Much of the Shanahan YAC game in its later 49ers form (the back leaking out of the backfield, the screen against a blitz) is already here.
Watch Ryan’s feet on play-action. He turns his back to the defense under center, carries out the fake, and throws to a receiver who is already open, often crossing. It is the “easy throw” in action.
The clip the critics cite. Super Bowl LI, fourth quarter, Atlanta up 28–20 with 3:56 left and the ball on New England’s 23 after a Julio Jones catch: on second-and-11 Ryan dropped back and was sacked for a 12-yard loss, and a holding penalty on the next snap pushed Atlanta out of field-goal range. A field goal would have made it a two-score game; New England tied it and won in overtime.20









NoteFilm room: Miami Dolphins 2023



The season: Mike McDaniel’s second as Miami’s head coach. McDaniel spent most of his career on Kyle Shanahan’s staffs (in Houston, Washington, Cleveland, Atlanta and San Francisco, where he was run-game coordinator and then, in 2021, offensive coordinator) and brought the system to Miami in 2022 with a twist: speed. In Week 3 of 2023 the Dolphins beat Denver 70–20; Tua Tagovailoa led the league with 4,624 passing yards and Tyreek Hill had 1,799 receiving yards.21
What to notice:

Motion on almost every snap, much of it at the snap, the most of any team in the league (by FTN’s charting Miami was first in motion in 2022, 2023 and 2025). Three weeks into 2023, ESPN’s tracking had Miami with a man in motion at the snap on 59% of plays, the highest rate for any team since ESPN began counting in 2017.22
The fullback. Miami was the league leader in 21 personnel in 2022 and 2023 by nflverse’s data, with Alec Ingold leading wide zone and slicing on boots, but Miami’s backs and receivers were sprinters, so the same ideas produced longer plays.
The limit. The Dolphins’ offense faded late in 2023 and fell to the bottom half of the league in EPA per play in 2024 and 2025, and McDaniel was fired in January 2026. A system can raise a team’s floor; it doesn’t guarantee a ceiling, and it doesn’t protect a coach.









NoteFilm room: Los Angeles Rams 2018 and 2025



The seasons: two versions of Sean McVay’s offense, seven years apart. In 2018 the Rams went 13–3 and reached Super Bowl LIII with Jared Goff, running the whole offense out of one personnel group (11 personnel on about 93% of plays, 08-02’s film room). In 2025, with Matthew Stafford at 37, the Rams were first in the league in both under-center rate and play-action rate and second in EPA per play, and Stafford was MVP.
What to do: watch one game from each. In 2018 count the snaps in 11 personnel and notice how much of the deception comes from receivers’ splits and motion, not substitutions; that is McVay’s answer to the personnel problem the 49ers solved with a fullback. In 2025 watch the play-action passes from under center and see how quickly Stafford’s eyes come back downfield after the fake and the ball comes out on the first hitch of his drop. Then compare the two quarterbacks on third-and-long: that is the debate from earlier, on film.








NoteFilm room: Seattle Seahawks 2025



The season: Klint Kubiak’s only year as Seattle’s offensive coordinator, under defensive head coach Mike Macdonald, ending in Super Bowl LX: Seattle 29, New England 13. Kenneth Walker III ran 27 times for 135 yards and was the game’s MVP.23
What to notice:

The fingerprint on film. Seattle went from the bottom third of the league in under-center rate in 2024 to near the top in 2025 (Figure 63.6), and in the Super Bowl the quarterback was under center on about half the snaps, as he had been all year.
Wide zone as the base play, with Walker as the one-cut back: press the aiming point, cut once, go.
The pairing. When Seattle has run from a look two or three times, watch the backside end on the next snap from it; that is when the boot and the play-action come. Seattle’s 2025 quarterback was Sam Darnold (see Figure 61.3).

61  Case Study: The Shanahan Tree

title: Case Study: The Shanahan Tree
text:
The tree in 2025 and 2026
A coaching tree is the family of coaches descended from one head coach, traced through who worked on whose staff. The Walsh case study draws the whole Walsh tree, of which this family is the largest modern branch: Mike Shanahan was Seifert’s coordinator in San Francisco before he went to Denver. This section zooms in on the part of it that calls plays today.
The family has two roots in the Denver building of the 1990s. Gary Kubiak, Mike Shanahan’s coordinator, carried the system to Houston as head coach (2006–13) and back to Denver, where he won Super Bowl 50 after the 2015 season; his sons Klint and Klay are coaches in it now. Kyle Shanahan took it through Houston, Washington, Cleveland and Atlanta to San Francisco. The decisive moment was the Washington staff of 2010–13, under Mike Shanahan with Kyle as offensive coordinator: Sean McVay coached the tight ends, Matt LaFleur the quarterbacks, and Mike McDaniel (from 2011) was an offensive assistant and then the receivers coach. All four became NFL head coaches.24 (That Washington offense also produced one of the scheme’s purest seasons: in 2012 Alfred Morris, a sixth-round rookie, ran for 1,613 yards in wide zone, beside rookie quarterback Robert Griffin III and the read-option plays the staff borrowed from Baylor, which The College Laboratory covers.)25
From there it branched. McVay’s own staffs in Los Angeles produced head coaches Zac Taylor (Bengals, 2019), Kevin O’Connell (Vikings, 2022) and Liam Coen (Jaguars, 2025). LaFleur took the system to Green Bay in 2019; Aaron Rodgers won two MVPs in it. Kyle’s 49ers staffs produced McDaniel (Dolphins, 2022), Mike LaFleur (Matt’s brother) and Brian Fleury, and they gave Klint Kubiak a season on the staff before he went on to run offenses in New Orleans and Seattle.
Staffs change every winter, and this one changed a lot. Figure 61.7 lays out who held which job in the 2025 season and the 2026 season.


Show the Python
# (coach, how he joined the family, 2025 job, 2026 job, calls plays 2025, calls plays 2026)
MOVES = [
    ("Kyle Shanahan", "Mike Shanahan's son; Kubiak's Texans", "49ers head coach", "49ers head coach", True, True),
    ("Klay Kubiak", "Gary Kubiak's son, Klint's brother", "49ers OC", "49ers OC", False, False),
    ("Brian Fleury", "49ers staff 2019–25", "49ers run-game coordinator & TEs", "Seahawks OC", False, True),
    ("Klint Kubiak", "Gary Kubiak's son, Klay's brother", "Seahawks OC", "Raiders head coach", True, True),
    ("Mike McDaniel", "Kyle's staffs, Houston to SF", "Dolphins head coach", "Chargers OC", True, True),
    ("Bobby Slowik", "49ers 2017–22; Texans OC 2023–24", "Dolphins senior pass-game coordinator", "Dolphins OC", False, False),
    ("Kevin Stefanski", "Vikings OC 2019, Gary Kubiak advising", "Browns head coach", "Falcons head coach", False, False),
    ("Sean McVay", "Washington staff 2010–16", "Rams head coach", "Rams head coach", True, True),
    ("Mike LaFleur", "Kyle's staffs; Matt's brother", "Rams OC", "Cardinals head coach", False, True),
    ("Matt LaFleur", "Washington, Atlanta; McVay's OC 2017", "Packers head coach", "Packers head coach", True, True),
    ("Kevin O'Connell", "McVay's OC 2020–21", "Vikings head coach", "Vikings head coach", True, True),
    ("Liam Coen", "McVay's Rams staffs", "Jaguars head coach", "Jaguars head coach", True, True),
    ("Zac Taylor", "McVay's Rams 2017–18", "Bengals head coach", "Bengals head coach", True, True),
    ("Nick Caley", "from McVay's Rams staff", "Texans OC", "Texans OC", True, False),
]
W, H = 6.6, 0.34 * len(MOVES) + 0.75
fig = plt.figure(figsize=(W, H))
ax = fig.add_axes([0, 0, 1, 1])
ax.set_xlim(0, W); ax.set_ylim(0, H); ax.axis("off")
X_NAME, X25, X26, CW, CH = 0.06, 1.84, 4.26, 2.28, 0.27
ax.text(X25 + CW / 2, H - 0.2, "2025 season", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=8.5, fontweight="bold",
        color=style.INK)
ax.text(X26 + CW / 2, H - 0.2, "2026 season", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=8.5, fontweight="bold",
        color=style.INK)
ax.text(X_NAME, H - 0.2, "Coach (how he joined the family)", ha="left", va="center", fontsize=7.6,
        fontweight="bold", color=style.INK_2)
for i, (name, root, j25, j26, c25, c26) in enumerate(MOVES):
    y = H - 0.55 - i * 0.34
    changed = j25 != j26
    ax.text(X_NAME, y + 0.055, name, fontsize=7.4, fontweight="bold", color=style.INK, va="center")
    ax.text(X_NAME, y - 0.085, root, fontsize=5.8, color=style.INK_2, va="center")
    for xc, job, calls, hot in [(X25, j25, c25, False), (X26, j26, c26, changed)]:
        ax.add_patch(FancyBboxPatch((xc, y - CH / 2), CW, CH, boxstyle="round,pad=0.01,rounding_size=0.05",
                                    fc=style.DEFENSE_TINT if hot else style.SURFACE,
                                    ec=style.DEFENSE if hot else style.BASELINE, lw=1.1 if hot else 0.7))
        ax.text(xc + 0.07, y, job, fontsize=6.6, color=style.INK, va="center",
                fontweight="bold" if hot else "normal")
        if calls:
            ax.text(xc + CW - 0.07, y, "calls plays", fontsize=5.6, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, va="center",
                    ha="right", style="italic")
    ax.annotate("", (X26 - 0.03, y), xytext=(X25 + CW + 0.03, y),
                arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=style.DEFENSE if changed else style.BASELINE, lw=0.9))
plt.show()








Figure 61.7: Recent staff moves: the Shanahan family’s play-callers and coordinators, 2025 season vs 2026 season (staffs as of October 2026). Each row is one coach; the left card is his 2025 job, the right card his 2026 job (OC: offensive coordinator). Orange cards changed over the winter. ‘Calls plays’ marks the coach who called his offense’s plays that season; it is left off where the coach didn’t call them (Stefanski handed Cleveland’s play-calling to Tommy Rees during 2025, and Rees calls Atlanta’s in 2026) or where no report confirms who does. The family lost a head coach in Miami and gained three, in Las Vegas, Arizona and Atlanta; Miami’s offense stays in the family under Slowik, and Seattle replaced one family play-caller with another.





Read Figure 61.7 with the season labels in mind, because the two lists are easy to blur.
In the 2025 season the family’s play-callers ran the 49ers (Kyle Shanahan), the Rams (McVay, with Mike LaFleur as offensive coordinator), the Packers (Matt LaFleur), the Dolphins (McDaniel), the Seahawks (Klint Kubiak, as offensive coordinator under defensive head coach Mike Macdonald), and, a generation down, the Vikings, Jaguars and Bengals, plus coordinators from McVay’s staffs calling plays in Atlanta and Houston. The season ended with the family everywhere: the NFC Championship Game was Seattle against the Rams, 31–27, and Seattle went on to win Super Bowl LX 29–13 over New England.26
In the 2026 season the map is different. Miami fired McDaniel in January and he became the Chargers’ offensive coordinator and play-caller; Klint Kubiak became the Raiders’ head coach after his one season in Seattle and kept calling plays; Mike LaFleur left the Rams to become the Cardinals’ head coach and calls their plays; Seattle replaced Kubiak with Brian Fleury, the 49ers’ run-game coordinator and tight ends coach, so the Seahawks stayed in the family. Miami’s offense did too: the new head coach, Jeff Hafley, is a defensive coach, and his offensive coordinator is Bobby Slowik, who spent 2017–22 on Kyle Shanahan’s staffs and 2025 on McDaniel’s. A third branch runs through Gary Kubiak himself: Kevin Stefanski called the 2019 Vikings’ plays with Kubiak beside him as adviser, the season Kubiak’s zone scheme came to Minnesota, coached Cleveland from 2020 to 2025, and is Atlanta’s head coach in 2026. In San Francisco, Shanahan still calls the plays with Klay Kubiak as offensive coordinator, in Los Angeles Nathan Scheelhaase was promoted to replace Mike LaFleur, and in Houston Nick Caley is still the coordinator.27 Whether the 2026 branches are working is too early to say; this chapter’s data stops with the 2025 season.
The lesson of the moves board is how the system spreads: not by teams copying film, but by assistants leaving with the playbook and the vocabulary in their heads. That is also why the family’s offenses differ. A coordinator who leaves takes the ideas, but he builds them around his own quarterback, his own roster and his own instincts, which is how a shotgun team in Cincinnati and an under-center team in Los Angeles can share a grandfather.

title: Case Study: The Shanahan Tree
text:
How defenses answered
A system this successful for this long gets studied by every defensive staff in the league. Their answers fall into four groups, and you will see all four on any Sunday.
1. Change the front. The bear in Figure 61.1 is the oldest answer: cover the interior linemen so nobody can climb. Its cousin is the tite front (a nose and two linemen on the tackles’ inside shoulders), which walls off the middle and asks the edges to win; and its opposite is a wide four-man front with a quick 3-technique who penetrates before the guard’s reach can land (05-01 animates it). Odd and Hybrid Fronts explains why no single front stops both zone runs, so defenses change fronts by opponent and by down. The offense’s counter is everything in this chapter: the fullback, the unblocked backside end and the boot, and the change-ups from the bear section (split zone, crack-toss, duo and counter) out of the same looks when the front is built for zone.
2. Keep two safeties deep and play the run with fewer men. The most important defensive trend of the 2020s, the two-high shell, is partly an answer to this family. Play-action and bootlegs work best against a defense that brings a safety down to stop the run, so defenses led by Vic Fangio and his descendants kept both safeties deep, accepted a light box, and trusted bigger fronts to hold up against the run. Two-high coverage rose from 32.9% of snaps in 2018 to 42.0% in 2025 by Next Gen Stats’ count, the highest since tracking began.28 The fight between that idea and this one is the subject of Fangio’s Two-High Revolution and Macdonald’s Answer, and of The Modern Era.
3. Take away the middle and make the quarterback hold the ball. The crossing routes that produce all that YAC run through the middle of the field at linebacker depth. Fill that area with defenders, rush with stunts that take a moment to develop, and the quarterback who wanted to throw to a receiver on the move is holding the ball. The most famous example is New England’s plan in Super Bowl LIII, which held McVay’s Rams to 3 points; The Belichick case study draws it.
4. Hunt the tells. An offense built on looking the same can be beaten if it doesn’t quite look the same. Defensive staffs grade the running back’s depth, the fullback’s alignment, the receivers’ splits and the direction of the motion, looking for any detail that separates the run from the boot. That is the self-scouting war of 08-02: the offense’s job is to keep its tendencies balanced inside each look, and the defense’s job is to find the one look that isn’t.
And the system answered back. When defenses went light and two-high, the family ran the ball more and got heavier (in 2025 offenses used fewer than three wide receivers on 41.7% of plays, the highest rate in the Next Gen Stats era), and when the bear came, the boots came with it.29 When defenses took away the crossers, McVay went and got a quarterback who could beat them from the pocket.

61  Case Study: The Shanahan Tree

title: Case Study: The Shanahan Tree
text:
What survives
Ideas from this family are now just how offense is played in much of the NFL, including by teams with no connection to it:

Under center is back, led by this family (the numbers are in the fingerprint section).
Motion is universal. PFF counted a shift or motion on 63.9% of plays in 2025, up from 38.4% in 2016; every team but one used it on at least half its plays.30
Heavier personnel is back, for the same reason the 49ers kept a fullback: to make light defenses pay.
YAC as a design goal. Receivers are now scouted and drafted for what they do after the catch, and offenses design throws to catch them on the move.
The illusion of complexity (few plays, many looks; many plays, one look) is standard teaching on almost every offensive staff, inside the tree and out.

What may not survive is the specific balance. The 2025 Rams leaned harder on play-action from under center than anyone, while the 49ers’ play-action rate was ordinary, and the 2025 second generation in Cincinnati and Atlanta looks more like a spread offense than like Denver in 1998. A tree spreads by mutating. That is also how you will know it is still alive: the family resemblance will be in the questions the offense asks a defense, not in any one formation.






TipWatch for it



On Sunday: same look, different plays. Pick one Shanahan-family offense (in 2026: the 49ers, Rams, Packers, Vikings, Jaguars, Bengals, Texans, the Seahawks under Fleury, the Raiders under Klint Kubiak, the Cardinals under Mike LaFleur, the Chargers under McDaniel, the Dolphins under Slowik or the Falcons under Stefanski) and keep a simple chart for one half.
Before each snap

Write the look: personnel (count the backs and tight ends), where the quarterback is (under center or shotgun), and the motion (none, across, jet, orbit). For example, “21, under center, Z across.”
Is there a fullback? If so, where is he: offset to the tight end (the base look) or away from it? A fullback’s alignment is one of the tells defensive staffs grade, so when it changes, note what follows.

In the first second

Do all five linemen step the same way? (Zone.) Does the back run toward the tight end? (Wide zone, or a fake of it.)
Find the backside end and watch him. Does he chase the back, or stay home?

After the play

Write what the play turned out to be: wide zone, gap run, bootleg, keeper, play-action shot, dropback.
If it was a pass, where was the receiver when he caught it: moving or standing, and with how much space ahead? That is YAC by design.

At halftime

For each look, list the different plays run from it. A good Shanahan-family half has several plays from each look; a look that produced only one play is a tendency the defense can find (and so can you). When a look has produced a run or two and the backside end has been chasing, start watching for the bootleg from that look.

A template:








Look (personnel, alignment, motion)
Plays seen
Backside end




21, under center, Z across
wide zone R, wide zone R, boot L
chased twice


11, gun, jet from left
jet sweep, play-action cross
stayed home

title: Case Study: The Shanahan Tree
text:
Predict the play






TipPredict the play



Drill 1. First-and-10 from your own 35, third quarter. The offense is in 21 personnel, the quarterback under center, the fullback offset to the tight end, who is lined up on the left this time. The defense shows the bear again: the center and both guards covered, eight in the box, one deep safety. On the offense’s last three wide-zone runs toward the tight end, the backside end (on the right, ringed) crashed hard down the line after the back, and one of those runs lost two yards anyway. What is the offense’s best call, and which way will it go?


Show the Python
p = Play(off21(strength="left"), bear(s=-1), los=35, to_go=10)
p.highlight("BE", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK)
f = draw(p, lateral=(-13.5, 13.5), window=(-9.0, 15.0))
plt.show()








Figure 61.8: Drill 1: 21 personnel, offset I, the tight end on the left; a bear front with the strong safety in the box and one deep safety. The backside end (ringed) is on the offense’s right.











TipAnswer





A bootleg to the right (the side away from the tight end), probably naked, with the keeper built in. Wide zone here goes left, toward the tight end, so the play’s backside is the offense’s right, where the end has been crashing. Three runs have taught him to chase, and he is the defender the offense leaves unblocked against the bear. The quarterback fakes wide zone left, keeps the ball and rolls right behind him: the fullback slices into the right flat, the tight end crosses from left to right behind the linebackers who flowed with the fake, and if nobody comes up to stop him, the quarterback runs. First-and-10 is the ideal down for it: the defense expects run, and a short completion keeps the offense on schedule.
Why not run wide zone again? Against the bear it was losing yards; the defense has the numbers. The offense’s answer is not to block the bear better but to punish the habit the bear’s backside end has fallen into.











TipPredict the play



Drill 2. Second-and-6, early in the first quarter. The offense has one back and one tight end (11 personnel), the tight end in-line on the left, the quarterback under center and the receivers in tight splits (lined up 9–10 yards from the ball, well inside the numbers, instead of out near the sideline). Before the snap the Z, a slot receiver on the right, goes in jet motion from right to left (dashed). The defense keeps two deep safeties and nobody runs across with the motion; there are six defenders in the box. Run or pass, and which way?


Show the Python
off = named_line(offense("singleback"))
SPOTS = {"Y": (-0.7, -4.8), "H": (-1.5, -10.0), "X": (-0.7, 10.5), "Z": (-1.5, 7.2)}   # Y on the left
off = [q.moved(d=SPOTS[q.key][0], w=SPOTS[q.key][1]) if q.key in SPOTS else
       (q.moved(label="R") if q.key == "RB" else q) for q in off]
dfn = [D("LE", "DE", 1.0, -5.7, "9"), D("LT3", "DT", 1.0, -technique("3"), "3"),
       D("RT1", "DT", 1.0, technique("1"), "1"), D("RE", "DE", 1.0, technique("5"), "5"),
       D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.6, -1.4, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.6, 2.4, "W"),
       D("NB", "NB", 5.5, 7.8, "NB"), D("LCB", "CB", 6.5, -10.5, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 6.5, 10.5, "CB"),
       D("FS", "FS", 12.5, -6.5, "FS"), D("SS", "SS", 12.5, 6.5, "SS")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=6)
p.motion("Z", to=(-2.6, 1.6))
f = draw(p, lateral=(-14.0, 14.0), window=(-9.0, 15.0))
plt.show()








Figure 61.9: Drill 2: 11 personnel under center, the Y in-line on the left, receivers in tight splits (H, the third receiver, and X about 10 yards from the ball); the Z, a slot receiver on the right, goes in jet motion to the left (the dashed arrow ends where he will be at the snap, just behind the quarterback). The defense: a four-man front (a 9 outside the Y, a 3, a 1 and a 5) and two linebackers in the box, a nickel back (NB) who stays outside where the Z started, two cornerbacks and two deep safeties. Nobody follows the motion.











TipAnswer





A run. Count the box: six defenders against six blockers (five linemen and the tight end), with both safeties 12 yards deep. That is a light box, and the system’s standing answer to two-high safeties is to run the ball at them. The motion told the quarterback two more things: nobody ran across with the Z, so the coverage is very likely zone, and the safeties didn’t rotate down, so the box is staying light.
Which way is the play-caller’s choice, and both answers are textbook in this family:

Wide zone left, toward the motion (or the jet sweep itself, handed to the Z). The Z is just behind the quarterback at the snap and keeps running through the mesh toward the left sideline. He doesn’t block anyone; he is a threat, and the defender on the left edge has to respect a jet sweep for a beat, which is a beat he isn’t attacking the run.
Fake the jet, wide zone right, away from it. The fake drags the Will and the nickel back toward the motion and thins the right side, where the run is going.

If you said “run,” you read the picture; the direction is the bonus question.











TipPredict the play



Drill 3. First-and-10, a series after the bootleg in Drill 1 went for 22 yards. Same 21-personnel look, tight end on the left, quarterback under center. The defense has changed two things. It now shows two deep safeties before the snap, and when the Z goes in motion across the formation to the right, one safety spins down into the box on that side while the other runs to the middle of the field. And the backside end on the right is no longer chasing: on the last two runs he squeezed down the line, square, with his eyes on the quarterback. The offense’s last two wide-zone runs gained 3 and 2 yards. What should the offense call?


Show the Python
off3 = off21(strength="left")
d3 = [q.moved(d=12.5, w=8.5) if q.key == "SS" else (q.moved(d=12.5, w=-8.5) if q.key == "FS" else q)
      for q in bear(s=-1)]
p = Play(off3, d3, los=35, to_go=10)
p.motion("Z", to=(-1.5, 6.6))
p.drop("SS", (5.4, 6.6), label=None)
p.drop("FS", (14.0, 0.0), label=None)
p.highlight("BE", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK)
f = draw(p, lateral=(-13.5, 13.5), window=(-9.0, 16.5))
say(f, p, 9.0, 10.6, "spins down\non the motion", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
say(f, p, 14.0, -4.6, "rotates to\nthe middle", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
say(f, p, -3.4, 9.2, "squeezes,\neyes on the QB", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
plt.show()








Figure 61.10: Drill 3: the same 21-personnel look, the Z in motion across to the right (dashed blue). Before the snap the defense shows two deep safeties; as the Z moves, the right-side safety spins down into the box and the other rotates to the deep middle (dashed orange), leaving eight in the box and one deep safety still moving at the snap. The backside end (ringed) squeezes with his eyes on the quarterback.











TipAnswer





A play-action shot from under center, with max protection: two deep routes against the one safety. Put the two changes together. The naked boot is off the table, because the end who used to chase is squeezing and would be waiting for the quarterback. Wide zone is running into eight in the box, which is what the spin was for. But the spin has a price: one safety is left to cover the whole deep field, and at the snap he is still running to the middle. That is the picture the yankee concept from 04-05 is built for: fake wide zone, keep the fullback and the back in to protect, and send two receivers deep, a post from one side and a deep over from the other. The linebackers and the safety who came down step up for the fake; the lone deep safety can take only one of the two routes, and the quarterback throws the other.
Why not the protected boot? It’s a fine safe call, and a good one on second-and-long. But it attacks the short and middle areas the eight-man box is already crowding; on first-and-10 with one deep safety still moving, the shot is the bigger reward. This back-and-forth, base play, constraint, a new answer, a new constraint, is sequencing, and it is how a Shanahan play-caller spends a game.

title: Case Study: The Shanahan Tree
text:
Takeaways

Two problems, one family. Gibbs’s and Mike Shanahan’s 1990s Broncos built wide zone and the bootleg to block defenses that never stood still; Kyle Shanahan’s 2017 49ers added the fullback, motion and YAC passing to beat fast, light defenses without a star quarterback.
Four ingredients, one picture. Wide zone moves the defense sideways, the fullback forces a personnel choice, motion makes the defense answer first, and YAC passes throw into the space all of that empties. The same few looks carry all of it.
Leave a man free on purpose, then punish him. Against a bear front the offense can’t block everyone, so it leaves the backside end and beats him with the bootleg-keeper when he crashes; when he squeezes, the cutback, split zone and the protected boot are waiting. The defense’s answer to the base play sets up the constraint play.
The system raises the quarterback’s floor, and the ceiling is still argued. Several quarterbacks were much more efficient inside the family than outside it; even the 49ers’ third-and-long success is designed. Goff thrived in a cousin offense in Detroit, and EPA can’t see the difference McVay paid for in Stafford: the plays after the design breaks are a coach’s judgment, not a number.
The fingerprint: under center and in motion, 21 or heavy personnel (49ers), play-action at the top of the league (Rams), and receivers who gain far more after the catch than the catch predicts. From 2019 to 2025 the 49ers were first in YAC over expected by a wide margin and top ten in EPA per play in six of seven seasons.
Label every staff by season. In 2025 the family’s first generation called plays in San Francisco, Los Angeles, Green Bay, Miami and Seattle (Super Bowl LX champions), with McVay’s former assistants calling them in Minnesota, Jacksonville, Cincinnati, Atlanta and Houston. In 2026 Kubiak (Las Vegas) and Mike LaFleur (Arizona) are head coaches who call plays, McDaniel calls the Chargers’ plays, Fleury Seattle’s, Slowik coordinates Miami’s offense and Stefanski is Atlanta’s head coach.

Chris B. Brown, The Art of Smart Football (2015) and his Grantland piece on Gary Kubiak’s Houston run game (2012) are the best short introductions to the Gibbs zone system. Alex Gibbs’s own clinic video, “Outside Zone, Tight Zone, Boots and Thoughts on the Power,” is still sold to coaches. title: Case Study: Andy Reid and the Kansas City Chiefs
text:
The problem: a West Coast coach in a league that was changing
Super Bowl LIV, February 2, 2020, in Miami Gardens. Kansas City trails San Francisco 20–10 with 7:13 left, and it is third-and-15 at the Chiefs’ own 35. The 49ers have the best pass rush in the building and a coverage that keeps everything in front of it. A completion short of 15 yards is worth nothing, and an incompletion means a punt with seven minutes left and the game slipping away. On the sideline Patrick Mahomes asks his coaches whether there is time to run a play called “Wasp.” There is. He takes the snap, retreats, keeps retreating, and from 14 yards behind the line, with a 49ers defensive tackle arriving, throws the ball 57 yards through the air to Tyreek Hill near the left sideline. Forty-four yards. Kansas City scores three touchdowns in the last seven minutes and wins its first Super Bowl in fifty years.1 Why did Andy Reid’s offense have a play built for third-and-15? Why would a quarterback ask for the slowest-developing route on the call sheet, with the league’s best rush coming? And how did a 61-year-old coach who learned his NFL football in Green Bay in the early 1990s end up running the most modern offense in the sport? This chapter is about the team that answered those questions better than anyone for seven years, and about what happened when opponents found answers of their own.
You’ll be able to…
Andy Reid was born in Los Angeles in 1958, played offensive tackle at Brigham Young under LaVell Edwards (whose teams threw the ball when almost nobody in college did), and coached offensive linemen at four colleges from 1983 to 1991 before Mike Holmgren hired him in Green Bay in 1992. Holmgren was one of Bill Walsh’s assistants from the 49ers, so Reid learned the West Coast offense from its second generation: tight ends coach and assistant line coach first, then quarterbacks coach for Brett Favre in 1997 and 1998. In January 1999 the Philadelphia Eagles made him, at 40, the second-youngest head coach in the league. He stayed fourteen seasons, won 130 regular-season games, reached five NFC Championship Games (four in a row from 2001 to 2004) and lost Super Bowl XXXIX to New England, 24–21. After a 4–12 season the Eagles let him go on the last day of 2012. Four days later Kansas City hired him.2
The team he took over had gone 2–14. The first five Kansas City seasons were the kind most coaches would frame: 11–5, 9–7, 11–5, 12–4 and 10–6, with Alex Smith, a quarterback acquired from San Francisco, playing efficient, careful football. They also carried a ceiling you can see in the playoff results. A 45–44 loss at Indianapolis in January 2014, after leading by 28 in the third quarter. A 27–20 loss at New England two years later. An 18–16 home loss to Pittsburgh. A 22–21 home loss to Tennessee in January 2018, after leading 21–3 at halftime.3 From 2013 to 2016 the Chiefs’ offense ranked between 9th and 15th in the league in EPA per play: good, never frightening. (The 2017 offense, 3rd, is the exception, and the next two sections explain it; the chart in the data-fingerprint section shows the whole run.)
That ceiling had a schematic shape. The classic West Coast offense is a machine for completing passes: three- and five-step drops, routes timed to the quarterback’s last step, throws spread across the width of the field so that a 6-yard completion works like a run. It needs a quarterback who throws on time and accurately, and Smith did. What it doesn’t do by itself is produce explosive plays, and by the middle 2010s NFL defenses had grown very good at the thing a timing offense needs least: keeping everything in front of them and tackling the catch. A team that has to drive 75 yards in twelve completed passes gives a defense twelve chances to win a down. Reid’s problem in Kansas City was how to keep the efficiency and add the explosions, without blowing up the system his staff and players already knew.
Show the Python

    ("Head coach", [(2013, 2027, "Andy Reid", style.OFFENSE_DARK)]),
    ("Offensive\ncoordinator", [(2013, 2016, "Doug Pederson", style.OFFENSE), (2016, 2018, "Matt Nagy", style.SEQUENTIAL_BLUE[2]),
                                (2018, 2023, "Eric Bieniemy", style.OFFENSE), (2023, 2026, "Matt Nagy", style.SEQUENTIAL_BLUE[2]),
                                (2026, 2027, "", style.OFFENSE)]),
    ("Quarterback", [(2013, 2018, "Alex Smith", style.MUTED), (2018, 2027, "Patrick Mahomes", style.OFFENSE_DARK)]),
    ("Defensive\ncoordinator", [(2013, 2019, "Bob Sutton", style.MUTED), (2019, 2027, "Steve Spagnuolo", style.DEFENSE)]),
]
SB = {2019: "W", 2020: "L", 2022: "W", 2023: "W", 2024: "L"}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 2.75))
for i, (row, spans) in enumerate(ROWS):
    y = len(ROWS) - i
    ax.text(2012.85, y, row, ha="right", va="center", fontsize=7.6, color=style.INK, linespacing=1.0)
    for a, b, lab, col in spans:
        ax.add_patch(FancyBboxPatch((a + 0.04, y - 0.32), b - a - 0.08, 0.64,
                                    boxstyle="round,pad=0,rounding_size=0.12", fc=col, ec="none"))
        ax.text((a + b) / 2, y, lab, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=7.2, color="white", fontweight="bold")

        linespacing=1.0)

            color=style.OFFENSE_DARK if res == "W" else style.INK_2, fontweight="bold" if res == "W" else "normal")

        linespacing=1.0)

Figure 62.1: The Reid years in Kansas City at a glance. Reid has been head coach since 2013; he calls the plays himself (except for a stretch of 2017 when he handed them to Matt Nagy), and his offensive coordinator relays and helps build them. Coordinators: Doug Pederson (2013–2015), Matt Nagy (co-coordinator with Brad Childress in 2016, sole coordinator in 2017), Eric Bieniemy (2018–2022), Nagy again (2023–2025) and, from 2026, Bieniemy again. Defense: Bob Sutton (2013–2018), Steve Spagnuolo (2019 to now). The Mahomes years produced five Super Bowl trips in six seasons (W = won, L = lost).
A word on who does what, because it confuses almost everyone. Reid is the play-caller: he chooses the play and says a short name for it into his headset. The offensive coordinator finds it on his own copy of the sheet and relays the full call to the quarterback (The Game Plan describes the two-step relay and Reid’s famous oversized play card). The coordinator also builds the weekly plan, coaches the quarterbacks and runs meetings, which is why Reid’s coordinators keep leaving for head-coaching jobs: Doug Pederson won a Super Bowl as Philadelphia’s head coach two seasons after leaving, and Matt Nagy became the Bears’ head coach after 2017. The one exception to Reid calling plays came in late 2017, when a slump of six losses in seven games led him to hand the calls to Nagy for the rest of the season.
So what changes when the coordinator changes? Not the voice on the headset. The coordinator shapes which plays reach Reid’s card each week, how the quarterbacks are taught to read them and how the meetings run, and nobody outside the building can isolate that effect in the data. That is why this chapter names the coordinators by season (the figure above) but explains the offense through Reid, Mahomes and the players around them.

section: The scheme answer, part 1: keep the West Coast bones
text:
The scheme answer, part 1: keep the West Coast bones
Reid didn’t throw the old offense away. Watch a Chiefs game from any season and you will still see its skeleton:

Horizontal stretches. Routes that spread defenders sideways, so a linebacker can’t cover both a flat route and a short in-cut. The quick game (The Quick Game) is pure West Coast, and so are the running back’s checkdowns.
The tight end and the back as receivers. Walsh’s offenses threw to everybody. Reid’s have always fed a tight end (Brent Celek and the young Zach Ertz in Philadelphia, Travis Kelce in Kansas City) and a receiving back.
Long, descriptive calls. “2-3 Jet Chip Wasp” is a West Coast sentence: “2-3 Jet” most likely names the protection (the Chiefs have never said), “Chip” tells the back to hit a rusher before he releases, and “Wasp” is one receiver’s route. The language is the family resemblance, even when the plays look nothing like Walsh’s (Offensive Systems shows the call broken into its parts).
A big menu, installed weekly. Reid draws new plays on index cards early in the week, and his opening script is built from them (The Game Plan tells the story). That habit comes from Walsh too, who scripted his openers and treated the playbook as something rebuilt for each opponent (Case Study: Walsh’s 49ers).







ImportantWhy it exists



The West Coast core is what makes the rest possible. A team that can complete a 6-yard pass on any down doesn’t fall behind schedule, and a team that stays on schedule can afford to call its odd, risky, creative plays when it chooses, not when it is desperate. The bones are the insurance policy. What they give up is speed to the end zone: a pure timing offense needs many plays to score, and every play is another chance for a sack, a penalty or a turnover.

title: Case Study: Andy Reid and the Kansas City Chiefs
section: The scheme answer, part 2: graft the college game onto it
text:
The scheme answer, part 2: graft the college game onto it
The second source arrived on purpose. When Reid came to Kansas City in 2013 he brought Brad Childress, his old Philadelphia coordinator and former Vikings head coach, and gave him a title the NFL had never seen: spread game analyst. Childress’s job for three seasons was to study the college spread offenses of the time (the zone read, the packaged plays that would soon be called RPOs, the empty and trips formations) and work out what would survive in the NFL. In 2016 Childress and quarterbacks coach Matt Nagy became co-coordinators; in 2017 Nagy had the job alone, and the Chiefs built a large part of their offense on run-pass options, years before most of the league did.4
You know the RPO from Run-Pass Options: the linemen block a run, and the quarterback, holding the ball against the running back’s belly at the mesh point (the instant of the possible handoff; not the crossing-route concept also called “mesh”), watches one defender who can’t do two jobs. If that defender comes down to stop the run, the quarterback pulls the ball and throws into the space he just left. If he stays out to cover the pass, the back gets the ball against a box the offense has blocked.
Why read anyone at all? Because of the box count (A First Look at Defense). Five linemen can block five men. Even against two deep safeties, the defense keeps six in the box, and inside zone handles the sixth the way Zone Running taught: it leaves the backside end unblocked, because the run is going away from him and he can only chase it from behind. That leaves one more defender who can get to the ball: the apex player on the play side, who stands between the box and the receivers. He is the seventh man, the one the offense has no blocker for, so the quarterback reads him instead.


Show the Python
def rpo_play():
    off = oline() + [
        O("QB", "QB", -5.0, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -5.0, -2.0, "R"),
        O("X", "WR", -0.7, -15.0, "X"), O("H", "WR", -1.5, -9.0, "H"),
        O("KELCE", "TE", -1.5, 8.5, "87"), O("Z", "WR", -0.7, 15.0, "Z"),
    ]
    dfn = [
        D("LDE", "DE", 1.0, -5.2), D("LDT", "DT", 1.0, -2.4), D("RDT", "DT", 1.0, 0.7), D("RDE", "DE", 1.0, 4.6),
        D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.8, 1.0), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.6, -3.0), D("APEX", "NB", 4.5, 6.4),
        D("LCB", "CB", 7.0, -15.0, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 7.0, 15.5, "CB"),
        D("FS", "FS", 13.0, -8.0), D("SS", "SS", 13.0, 8.0),
    ]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=40, to_go=10)
    # inside zone to the right: five linemen block five of the six in the box; the backside end is left alone
    p.block("LT", "WILL"); p.block("LG", "LDT"); p.block("C", "RDT"); p.block("RG", "MIKE"); p.block("RT", "RDE")
    p.run("RB", [(-4.1, 0.6), (-1.5, 2.2), (3.0, 1.8)], absolute=True)
    p.read("APEX")
    p.route("KELCE", [(0, 0), (5.5, 0.0), (5.0, -0.6)])
    p.route("Z", r.go(9)); p.route("H", r.go(9)); p.route("X", r.go(9))
    p.path("APEX", [(2.2, 3.9)], absolute=True, speed=3.0)
    p.highlight("APEX", "KELCE")
    return p


rpo = rpo_play()
fld = rpo.draw(window=(-8.5, 14.0), lateral=(-19.5, 19.5), width_in=6.5, title=False)
no_numbers(fld.ax)
say(fld, rpo, 9.4, 12.6, "If the apex defender ($) comes\ndown on the run: throw to 87", 6.8)
say(fld, rpo, -6.9, 6.0, "If he stays: hand off", 6.8)
say(fld, rpo, 8.6, -2.5, "Six in the box,\nfive blockers", 6.8)
pointer(fld, rpo, "Backside end: left\nunblocked, the run\ngoes away from him", (-5.0, -11.5), (0.3, -5.2), fs=6.6)
plt.show()








Figure 62.2: The college graft in one picture: an inside-zone RPO of the kind Kansas City ran more than any other team in 2025 (illustrative). Two deep safeties leave six defenders in the box (E, T, T, E, M, W) against five linemen. Inside zone to the right blocks five of them and leaves the backside end (E, far left) alone, because the run is going away from him. The seventh defender who could reach the run is the nickel ($), standing in the apex between the right tackle and the tight end (87): the offense has no blocker for him, so the quarterback reads him instead (dashed green line). If he comes down to fill the run (orange arrow), the quarterback pulls the ball and throws to 87, whose 5-yard hitch settles in the space the nickel just left. If he stays, it is a handoff with every play-side defender blocked.





Why would a West Coast coach want this? Because the RPO solves the same problem the West Coast offense was invented to solve, more cheaply. Walsh’s short passes were a way to get the ball to a skill player in space without asking the line to win a long pass-protection rep. An RPO does that and makes the defense wrong on every snap: a run against a light box or a pass against a defender who has just stepped toward the line. Alex Smith, who had played in Urban Meyer’s spread-option offense at Utah, was well suited to it. The 2017 Chiefs led the league in passer rating behind him, rookie Kareem Hunt won the rushing title, and the offense jumped from 15th in EPA per play to 3rd.






NoteFilm room: Chiefs 2017 — the opener at New England



The game. Thursday night, September 7, 2017, the NFL’s season opener, at Foxborough against the defending champions. Kansas City won 42–27. Alex Smith threw for 368 yards and four touchdowns, including a 75-yard bomb to Tyreek Hill, and Kareem Hunt, a third-round rookie who had fumbled on his first NFL carry, finished with 148 rushing yards, 98 receiving yards and three touchdowns.5
What to notice: how often the “run” and the “pass” are the same play. Watch Smith at the mesh: his eyes are not on the back but on a linebacker or a slot defender, and the Patriots’ defenders are a half-step late all night because each of them is responsible for two things. Then watch Hill. A receiver that fast changes what a safety can do on every snap, a theme that becomes the whole first era of the Mahomes years.


The third piece came in the 2017 draft. Kansas City traded up from 27th to 10th, giving Buffalo its first-round pick, a third-rounder and its 2018 first, to take Patrick Mahomes from Texas Tech.6 Mahomes had played three seasons for Kliff Kingsbury in an Air Raid offense: shotgun, four and five receivers, reads of the whole field, throws from every arm angle. He sat behind Smith for a year. When he took over in 2018, Reid didn’t make him a West Coast quarterback. He met him halfway. The Chiefs played from the shotgun on 81% of their snaps that season, against a league average of 64%, and stayed around 80% for the next seven years: about as far from the under-center Shanahan offenses of the same era as a West Coast descendant could get (Case Study: The Shanahan Tree).

title: Case Study: Andy Reid and the Kansas City Chiefs
section: The scheme answer, part 3: the menu, and the plays nobody else has
text:
The scheme answer, part 3: the menu, and the plays nobody else has
The third source is Reid himself. On the first-quarter drive of Super Bowl LIV that put Kansas City ahead, facing fourth-and-1 at the San Francisco 5, the Chiefs lined up with three players stacked behind Mahomes; Mahomes turned a full circle, the others spun and reset, and running back Damien Williams took a direct snap and ran for 4 yards and a first down. Reid had found the play on old film of the 1948 Rose Bowl, Michigan against USC, and the Chiefs had been practicing it since spring.7 Three years later, two fourth-quarter touchdowns in Super Bowl LVII came on a return-motion play called “Corn Dog”: a receiver motions in toward the ball, his man-to-man defender follows him, and at the snap the receiver turns and runs back out toward the sideline, leaving the defender stopped, turning around and a stride behind. A year after that, the winning touchdown of Super Bowl LVIII came on a relative of it built for a defense that had studied Corn Dog; its first option was a shovel pass, another piece of the menu8 (Motion and Shifts draws the return motion, and What Beats What tells both stories).
How do you spot a play built for one opponent on a broadcast? You can’t be certain from the couch, but the tells are consistent: a formation or motion you haven’t seen from Kansas City all season (three players stacked behind the quarterback, a receiver reversing his motion), usually on fourth down, in the red zone or in a big game, where a coach spends a play he has been saving.






CautionCommon misconception



“The Chiefs win with trick plays.” They win with an ordinary core and use the strange plays as seasoning. In FTN’s charting, a trick play (reverses, flea-flickers, throwback passes and the like) was 1.5% of Kansas City’s plays in 2022, fourth in the league, but 0.5% in 2023 (26th), 0.9% in 2024 (9th) and 0.1% in 2025 (30th).9 What the Chiefs did far more than almost anyone was throw screens: between 6% and 10% of their plays from 2022 to 2025, never lower than seventh in the league. Screens are the West Coast’s way of punishing a pass rush, and they are the trick plays that work every week. The famous plays are memorable because they are rare; the screens are invisible because they are constant.


What the big menu buys is subtler than surprise. A defense prepares for an opponent by studying its tendencies: from this formation, with this motion, they run this. Reid’s offense shows the same handful of concepts from so many formations, shifts and motions that the tendency table gets thin. The illusion of complexity (Constraint Theory and Sequencing) usually describes a small playbook dressed up to look big. Reid runs a genuinely big one, and his players carry it because the core underneath doesn’t change.

title: Case Study: Andy Reid and the Kansas City Chiefs
section: Patrick Mahomes and the defensive arithmetic
text:
Patrick Mahomes and the defensive arithmetic
Every pass defense is built on a clock. A four-man rush reaches an NFL quarterback, on average, in something under three seconds; the coverage has to hold for that long, and then the rush finishes the play. Defensive coordinators design coverages around that budget: zone defenders drop to spots they can hold for two and a half or three seconds, man defenders play technique they can sustain for that long. When the clock runs out, the quarterback has to throw it away, take a sack or improvise, and for almost everyone improvising is a losing bet.
Here is that bet in numbers. Coverages are built for about three seconds; to count only throws that are clearly past that budget, the numbers below use four seconds as the cutoff. From 2018 to 2025, NFL passes thrown in under four seconds averaged about +0.17 EPA per attempt. Passes thrown after four seconds or more averaged about −0.03: a bad play, on average, before you even count the sacks the long-held ball produces. Now look at one quarterback.


Show the Python
thr = ATT[ATT.season >= 2018].merge(PART, left_on=["game_id", "play_id"], right_on=["nflverse_game_id", "play_id"])
thr = thr[thr.time_to_throw.notna()]
thr["late"] = thr.time_to_throw >= 4.0
q = thr.groupby(["passer", "late"]).epa.agg(["mean", "size"]).unstack()
q.columns = ["early", "late", "n_early", "n_late"]
q = q[q.n_late >= 150].copy()
LG_EARLY, LG_LATE = thr[~thr.late].epa.mean(), thr[thr.late].epa.mean()
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 4.0))
ax.axhline(LG_LATE, color=style.BASELINE, lw=0.9, zorder=1)
ax.axvline(LG_EARLY, color=style.BASELINE, lw=0.9, zorder=1)
oth = q.drop(index="P.Mahomes")
ax.scatter(oth.early, oth.late, s=oth.n_late / 6, color=style.GRID, edgecolor=style.MUTED, lw=0.6, zorder=2)
m = q.loc["P.Mahomes"]
ax.scatter([m.early], [m.late], s=m.n_late / 6, color=style.OFFENSE, edgecolor=style.SURFACE, lw=0.8, zorder=3)
ax.annotate(f"Mahomes\n{int(m.n_late)} late throws", (m.early, m.late), xytext=(10, -2), textcoords="offset points",
            fontsize=7.4, color=style.INK, va="center")
for nm, dx, dy in (("J.Winston", 8, 0), ("J.Burrow", 8, -2), ("D.Prescott", 8, 2), ("J.Allen", -8, 6),
                   ("L.Jackson", 8, 0), ("A.Rodgers", 8, 0), ("T.Brady", 8, 0)):
    if nm in q.index:
        rr = q.loc[nm]
        ax.annotate(nm.split(".")[-1], (rr.early, rr.late), xytext=(dx, dy), textcoords="offset points", fontsize=7,
                    color=style.INK_2, ha="left" if dx > 0 else "right", va="center")
ax.text(LG_EARLY + 0.004, ax.get_ylim()[0] + 0.01, "league average,\nunder 4 s", fontsize=7.2, color=style.INK_2,
        va="bottom", linespacing=1.0)
ax.text(ax.get_xlim()[0] + 0.004, LG_LATE + 0.01, "league average, 4 s or longer", fontsize=7.2, color=style.INK_2)
ax.set_xlabel("EPA per attempt on throws released in under 4 seconds", fontsize=8.5)
ax.set_ylabel("EPA per attempt on throws after 4+ seconds", fontsize=8.5)
ax.tick_params(labelsize=7.5)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 62.3: Throwing late. Every quarterback with at least 150 pass attempts released four or more seconds after the snap, 2018–2025 regular seasons (dots sized by those late throws). Horizontal: EPA per attempt on throws released in under four seconds; vertical: on throws released after four seconds or more. The grey lines are the league averages. What to look at: for nearly every quarterback the late throws are worth much less than the quick ones; Mahomes (blue, top right) is the exception, and he threw more late passes than anyone on the chart. Jameis Winston’s late throws rate higher on a much smaller, mostly 2018–2019 sample. Sacks are not included (the charting doesn’t time them; see the text). Data: nflverse play-by-play and NGS time to throw (2018–2022) and FTN (2023–2025) via nflreadpy.





Patrick Mahomes’s throws after four seconds, all 674 of them from 2018 to 2025, were worth about +0.30 EPA each: slightly more than his on-time throws (+0.28), and about a third of a point more per throw than the league’s late throws.10 He threw late about half again as often as the average quarterback.
A sceptic should ask about sacks, because a quarterback who holds the ball also gets sacked holding it, and the charting behind the chart doesn’t record a time for sacks, so they can’t be added to it. Two other measures can include them. First, Mahomes was sacked on 4.5% of his dropbacks from 2018 to 2025, against 6.4% for everyone else: the long-held ball didn’t turn into sacks the way it does for most quarterbacks. Second, FTN’s charting from 2022 records whether the quarterback left the pocket, and that count includes sacks and scrambles. Mahomes was outside the pocket on about 23% of his dropbacks through 2025 (the league, 18%), sacked on about 7% of those (the league, 8%), and those dropbacks were worth +0.31 EPA each, more than double his in-pocket plays, while the league’s out-of-pocket dropbacks were worth roughly nothing.11 Sacks included, holding the ball didn’t cost him. (A note on denominators, since this chapter uses three: EPA per attempt counts only passes thrown; per dropback adds sacks and scrambles, so it is usually a little lower; per play adds the runs too. Compare numbers only within one kind.) (Quarterback Play has the league-wide picture and the left-handed flip in Denver that Reid calls Mahomes’s best play.)
Think about what that does to a defensive coordinator’s arithmetic. Every coverage call is a bet that the rush gets home before the coverage breaks. Against most quarterbacks the bet pays twice: the quick throws are contested, and the late ones are bad. Against Mahomes, the late half of the bet doesn’t pay. So the defense has to change something, and every change costs:

Cover longer. Play coverage that holds for five seconds, not three. That usually means more defenders in coverage and fewer rushing, which gives the quarterback even more time.
Rush with discipline. Keep the rushers in rush lanes so he can’t escape outside, instead of winning with speed around the edge. That gives up the fastest route to a sack.
Spy him. Assign one defender to mirror him (spy). That defender is not covering anyone.
Get there sooner. Blitz, so the ball has to come out before four seconds. That leaves fewer defenders in coverage, and against a quarterback who sees the field, more open receivers.

None of these is free, and the Chiefs’ offense was built to collect on each one. The four-second plays aren’t luck. They come from the scramble drill: rules every receiver follows the moment the quarterback leaves the pocket, so the improvisation is organised on both ends.


Show the Python
def scramble_play():
    off = oline() + [
        O("QB", "QB", -5.0, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -5.0, -1.8, "R"),
        O("X", "WR", -0.7, -16.0, "X"), O("H", "WR", -1.5, -9.0, "H"),
        O("KELCE", "TE", -1.5, 8.0, "87"), O("Z", "WR", -0.7, 16.0, "Z"),
    ]
    dfn = [
        D("LDE", "DE", 1.0, -5.0), D("LDT", "DT", 1.0, -0.8), D("RDT", "DT", 1.0, 2.4), D("RDE", "DE", 1.0, 5.6),
        D("MIKE", "MIKE", 5.0, 1.0), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -3.5),
        D("LCB", "CB", 6.0, -16.0, "CB"), D("NB", "NB", 5.0, -8.4), D("SS", "SS", 6.0, 7.2),
        D("RCB", "CB", 6.0, 16.0, "CB"), D("FS", "FS", 14.0, 0.0),
    ]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=40, to_go=7)
    for k in ("LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT"):
        p.block(k, pts=[(-1.4, 0.0)], speed=1.0)
    # the play as called: a dropback against man coverage
    p.dropback(2.0)
    p.route("X", [(0, 0), (16.0, 0.0), (22.0, 0.8)])
    p.route("X", [(25.0, -7.0)], absolute=True, speed=3.0)                  # deep: keep climbing, drift toward the QB
    p.route("H", [(0, 0), (11.0, 0.0), (12.0, -6.0)])                       # a dig...
    p.route("H", [(15.0, 4.5)], absolute=True, speed=4.0)                   # ...that keeps crossing toward the scramble
    p.route("KELCE", [(0, 0), (9.0, -1.0), (8.5, -2.0)], speed=6.5)          # settle inside his man
    p.route("KELCE", [(10.5, 16.0)], absolute=True, speed=5.0, delay=1.5)    # scramble: work to the QB's sideline
    p.route("Z", [(0, 0), (12.0, 0.0), (10.8, -0.8)])                        # a curl...
    p.route("Z", [(24.0, 17.5)], absolute=True, speed=6.5, delay=1.2)        # ...that turns up the sideline
    p.route("RB", [(0, 0), (-1.0, 2.5), (1.5, 6.0)], side=-1, speed=5.0)
    # the pocket breaks: the left end beats the tackle, the QB slides, then breaks out to his right
    p.rush("LDE", pts=[(-5.5, 2.5), (-8.2, 4.8)], speed=2.9)
    p.path("LDE", [(-7.6, 7.2)], absolute=True, speed=4.0)
    p.rush("LDT", pts=[(-1.6, 0.0)], speed=1.2)
    p.rush("RDT", pts=[(-1.6, 0.0)], speed=1.2)
    p.rush("RDE", pts=[(-3.8, -1.2)], speed=1.6)
    p.path("RDE", [(-5.8, 8.6)], absolute=True, speed=3.5, delay=0.6)
    p.path("QB", [(-7.5, 2.5)], absolute=True, speed=4.3, delay=1.9)
    p.path("QB", [(-6.8, 11.0)], absolute=True, speed=6.0)
    p.pass_to("KELCE", t=4.45)
    # man coverage, with a hole player (the Mike) who comes up when the QB leaves the pocket
    p.man("LCB", "X"); p.man("NB", "H"); p.man("RCB", "Z"); p.man("WILL", "RB")
    p.path("SS", [(8.4, 4.6)], absolute=True, speed=4.0)                    # inside leverage: sits on the in-break
    p.path("SS", [(9.4, 12.6)], absolute=True, speed=4.4, delay=3.0)       # late to turn and chase
    p.drop("MIKE", (8.0, 2.0), speed=3.0)
    p.path("MIKE", [(0.8, 8.0)], absolute=True, speed=5.0, delay=1.9)       # ...and comes up for the QB
    p.drop("FS", (17.0, 1.5), speed=2.0)
    p.path("FS", [(19.0, 7.0)], absolute=True, speed=2.0, delay=1.0)
    p.highlight("QB", "KELCE")
    return p


scr = scramble_play()
SCR_T = [2.2, 3.3, 4.45, 5.45]
if PDF:
    NOTES = {
        0: [(19.0, -11.0, "Everyone covered", 6.8)],
        1: [(-8.6, -10.0, "The pocket breaks:\nout to the right", 6.6)],
        2: [(16.0, 12.5, "Z turns his curl\nup the sideline", 6.4)],
    }
    POINTERS = {
        2: [("87 slides to\nthe QB's side", (3.0, 15.5), None)],
        3: [("His man (SS) sat inside;\n87 breaks out a step clear", (12.6, 4.5), None),
            ("M comes up for the QB:\nthe middle opens for H", (-7.6, -9.5), "MIKE")],
    }
    labels = ["+2.2 s · the play as called", "+3.3 s · the escape", "+4.45 s · the scramble drill",
              "+5.45 s · the catch"]
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(6.5, 6.9))
    for i, (ax, t) in enumerate(zip(axes.flat, SCR_T)):
        f_ = snapshot(scr, t, ax, (-10.0, 28.0), (-20.0, 20.5), notes=NOTES.get(i, ()))
        for txt, at, who in POINTERS.get(i, ()):
            pointer(f_, scr, txt, at, tuple(scr.position(who or "KELCE", t)), fs=6.2)
        ax.set_title(labels[i], fontsize=8.5, loc="left", color=style.INK)
    fig.tight_layout(h_pad=0.4, w_pad=0.3)
    strip_legend(fig, y=0.01, offense="Offense")
    plt.show()
else:
    show_animation(scr, times=SCR_T)

Figure 62.4: The scramble drill (an illustrative play, not a specific one): four rushers and man coverage (Cover 1), with the free safety deep and the Mike linebacker (M) sitting in the hole underneath. At 2.2 seconds every receiver is covered and the ball should be gone or thrown away. Instead the left end (E) beats the tackle, the quarterback slides away from him and breaks out to his right. The receivers follow the drill’s rules: the deep receivers keep climbing (X drifts toward the quarterback’s side), the intermediate receivers work back toward the sideline he is running to (Z turns his curl up the sideline; the tight end, 87, slides out along with him), and the crossing route (H) keeps crossing. The defenders, playing man with their backs to the quarterback, have to turn and chase. The strong safety (SS), 87’s man, had been sitting on the inside of him to take away the in-cut; when 87 breaks back outside toward the scramble, the safety has to turn and run, and the throw beats him to the sideline with 87 a step clear. Meanwhile the Mike has to choose between his zone and the quarterback; he comes up, which opens the middle for H as well.










ImportantWhy it exists



The scramble drill turns a broken play into a second play with its own rules, and the second play favours the offense. Man defenders run with their backs to the ball, so when their receivers change direction they lose a step turning to find them. Zone defenders have dropped to spots chosen for a throw that was supposed to come at two and a half seconds, and the spots are now wrong. The cost is on the offense’s side too: receivers have to learn the rules and trust that the quarterback follows them, and a quarterback who extends plays will take sacks and make some awful throws. For most passers the trade is a loss. For a few it is a weapon, and Kansas City built around one.
