65  Case Study: The Lions — Ben Johnson's Offense and Dan Campbell's Aggression

title: Case Study: The Lions — Ben Johnson’s Offense and Dan Campbell’s Aggression
text:
Ben Johnson: the designer
Ben Johnson is an unlikely NFL play-caller in the best sense. He was a walk-on quarterback at North Carolina who graduated with degrees in mathematics and computer science and worked briefly as a software developer before going into coaching: graduate assistant and then tight ends coach at Boston College, seven seasons on the Miami Dolphins’ offensive staff (quarterbacks, tight ends and receivers), and then Detroit in 2019 as an offensive quality-control coach, the job of breaking down film and data for the coaches above him.7 Campbell’s arrival in 2021 kept him and made him passing-game coordinator. When the offense sputtered under coordinator Anthony Lynn, Campbell took over the play-calling at midseason, leaning on Johnson for the plan; after the season Lynn left and Johnson became the offensive coordinator and play-caller.8
The results came fast. Detroit’s offense ranked 23rd in EPA per play in 2021, 6th in 2022, 6th in 2023 and 3rd in 2024, when the Lions went 15–2 and led the league with 564 points. Goff, the castoff, threw for 4,629 yards and 37 touchdowns that year. Johnson was named the AP’s Assistant Coach of the Year for 2024.9
How much of that was Goff and how much was Johnson? The cleanest look is the same quarterback under different play-callers, measured in EPA per dropback (every pass, sack and scramble), against the league average in the same seasons:

Rams, 2019–2020 (Sean McVay calling): +0.06, league +0.06. An average starter over those two seasons.
Lions, 2021 (Lynn, then Campbell): -0.06.
Lions, 2022–2024 (Johnson): +0.18, league +0.02, and +0.28 in 2024 alone.
Lions, 2025 (Morton, then Campbell): +0.17, league +0.04.

Goff kept most of the gain after Johnson left, so it wasn’t all scheme: he and his receivers had become a very good passing team. But his best season came in Johnson’s last one, and it fell back by more than a third without him. Read it as a quarterback the system suited, in a system that got the most out of him.
What was his offense? Not one invention. Its base was familiar: a zone and gap run game behind Sewell and a strong interior line, play-action off it, and quick, timed throws to St. Brown and LaPorta. What made it Johnson’s was a set of habits layered on top that made every snap look like several others. Here are the four that show up most clearly on film and in the data, with what each buys and costs.

Habit 1: the quarterback goes back under center
In the 2010s the shotgun took over the NFL. Johnson’s Lions went the other way: in 2022 their quarterback was under center on 47% of their runs and passes, the highest share in the league, and in 2024 on 54%, again the highest.10
For comparison, the league average was 32% in 2022, fell to 27% in 2023 and was 29% in 2024. That 2023 dip is real, not a charting quirk: the play-by-play’s own shotgun flag rose from 68% to 72% of plays the same year. 2023 was the shotgun’s high-water mark, and the league-wide turn back toward under center came after it, in 2024 and 2025. Detroit was already there.
Why go back? Because under center, a run and a pass begin with the same motion. The quarterback turns his back to the defense, the running back comes downhill toward him, and for the first second the linebackers can’t see the ball. From the shotgun, the run fake is a sideways mesh the defense reads more easily. Under center is a disguise before it is anything else, and the payoff is play-action. In 2024 the Lions used a run fake on 35% of their dropbacks, the league’s highest share (league 23%).
Did it pay? Careful here, because play-action flatters everyone. It is called on run-friendly downs, against defenses set to stop the run, so it beats ordinary dropbacks across the whole league. The fair test compares Detroit’s edge with the league’s edge on the same downs. On first and second down in 2022–2024, a run fake was worth +0.07 EPA per dropback to the rest of the league, and +0.19 to Detroit: nearly three times the league’s edge.
The under-center split needs the same care. Detroit’s plays from under center averaged +0.11 EPA, its shotgun plays +0.10: no difference. That comparison can’t show the disguise working, because the two groups are different plays in different situations (most under-center snaps are runs, most shotgun snaps passes). What the numbers do show is narrower. Going under center more than anyone cost Detroit nothing, and when it threw from under center it threw unusually well: +0.31 EPA per dropback, against +0.10 for the rest of the league on the same kind of snap.
The costs are real. On a run fake the quarterback turns his back to the defense and loses sight of the coverage for about a second, so he comes out of the fake re-reading it. That is why play-action passes, Johnson’s included, are usually built as simple high-low reads to defined landmarks (the deep crosser, the post, the flat) rather than full-field progressions. And on a true dropback without a fake, the quarterback needs a beat longer to set up than from the shotgun, which is why under-center teams lean on play-action rather than pure drop-back passing.


Habit 2: bodies, and the lineman who might be a receiver
Johnson loved heavy personnel (extra tight ends) and jumbo sets with a sixth offensive lineman, and he made that sixth lineman a weapon by having him report eligible. Formation Rules counted the numbers: Detroit reported a lineman on 170 runs and passes from 2022 to 2024, third most in the league, and passed on about 35% of them against about 24% for the league.
A reported lineman sends the defense two messages at once. “Big formation” says run, so linebackers and a safety creep toward the line. “Eligible” says this 300-pounder might go out for a pass, so somebody has to account for him. Figure 65.2 shows the two plays that make the defense pay for each message.


Show the Python
def jumbo_look():
    off = line5() + [O("T70", "OL", -0.7, 4.8, "70"), O("U", "TE", -0.7, -4.8, "U"),
                     O("X", "WR", -1.5, -12.0, "X"), O("Z", "WR", -1.5, 9.5, "Z"),
                     O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -7.0, 0.0, "R")]
    dfn = [D("LE", "DE", 1.0, -4.0, "E"), D("LT_", "DT", 1.0, -0.7, "T"), D("RT_", "DT", 1.0, 2.35, "T"),
           D("RE", "DE", 1.0, 5.6, "E"), D("SAM", "SAM", 3.8, 7.4, "S"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.4, 1.2, "M"),
           D("WILL", "WILL", 4.4, -2.8, "W"), D("SS", "SS", 7.0, 4.2, "SS"), D("FS", "FS", 13.5, -0.5, "FS"),
           D("LCB", "CB", 6.5, -12.0, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 6.5, 10.5, "CB")]
    return off, dfn


def fake(ax, P, pts):
    """A run fake: a thin dotted arrow, so it can't be mistaken for the ball carrier's thick one."""
    xy = np.array([P(d, w) for d, w in pts])
    ax.plot(xy[:, 0], xy[:, 1], color=style.OFFENSE, lw=1.3, ls=(0, (1, 1.6)), zorder=4)
    ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch(tuple(xy[-2] + 0.75 * (xy[-1] - xy[-2])), tuple(xy[-1]), arrowstyle="-|>",
                                 mutation_scale=9, color=style.OFFENSE, lw=1.0, zorder=4))

p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=5)
go(p, "QB", [(-2.7, -1.2), (-5.2, 2.4), (-5.0, 6.8)], speed=5.0)             # fake, then boot right

# --- right: the bait ---
off, dfn = jumbo_look()

go(p, "FS", [(19.0, -3.0)], speed=3.0)                                       # stays with the post
go(p, "RCB", [(16.0, 11.0)], speed=5.0)

for k in ("LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT", "T70"):
    go(p, k, [(0.0, p.players[k].w + 0.6)], "block", speed=1.5)
p.pass_to("Z", t=2.8)

Figure 65.2: One jumbo look, two answers (illustrative). Six offensive linemen; #70 has reported eligible and lines up as the right end, where a tight end would stand, and the defense has walked its strong safety (SS) down to make eight in the box against the run. Left, the leak, a bootleg with three levels: the running back fakes left (dotted: he never gets the ball), the linebackers flow with him, and the quarterback boots right. U, the backside tight end, crosses the field at 8 to 10 yards, Z clears the corner deep, and #70 blocks for a count and then slips into the flat behind the linebackers. Nobody blocks the right end once #70 releases, so the throw has to come on time. Right, the bait, a play-action ‘Yankee’ concept: the fake goes right, toward #70, and the safety and linebackers attack it. X’s post holds the deep safety in the middle, the left corner bails deep, and Z’s deep crossing route is caught under that corner and outside the hash, in the space the bitten defenders left. Both plays start from exactly the same picture; the defense has to guess which message to believe.





The left play is the one fans remember, because the catch is funny. The right one is the one that does damage, and it is far more common. That trade is the whole design: the reported lineman is mostly a threat, and the offense cashes the threat by throwing somewhere else.
What does jumbo cost? Every lineman you add is a receiver you take off. With six linemen on the field, one of the five eligible players is a 320-pound tackle who catches a few passes a season, so the real receiving threats drop to three or four, and the defense can answer with its own big bodies (an extra linebacker instead of a nickel back) without fear of being spread out. The boot in the left panel shows a second cost: once #70 releases, nobody blocks the end on that side, so the quarterback has to throw on time or pull up. And there is a rule tax. Play-action from a run look asks the linemen to fire off the ball as if it were a run, and a lineman who is more than a yard past the line when a forward pass is thrown beyond it is an ineligible man downfield: five yards, and the play doesn’t count. The more the pass looks like a run, the closer the blockers come to that line. It is the foul that wiped out the Sewell lateral described below.






CautionCommon misconception



“Reporting a tackle eligible is a trick play.” Mostly it isn’t. Across the league, a reported lineman usually means a run, and Detroit ran on about two of every three such snaps. The report is a cheap way to add a blocker who is also a possible receiver, and the passes it sets up usually go to the regular receivers. The genuinely tricky part, a throw to the lineman himself, is the rare constraint play that keeps the threat honest.








NoteFilm room: Lions at Cowboys, December 30, 2023



Back to the opening play, now with the vocabulary. The official play-by-play tells the story in one line: “70-D.Skipper reported in as eligible… 16-J.Goff pass to 68-T.Decker is complete. ATTEMPT SUCCEEDS. PENALTY on DET-68-T.Decker, Illegal Touch Pass.” Backup tackle Dan Skipper (#70) and Decker (#68) had both gone toward referee Brad Allen; Decker said afterwards that he reported, Skipper said he hadn’t said a word, and Allen said that number 70 had reported. The retry moved back five yards and failed, and so did one more after a Dallas penalty.
The procedure is short, which is why it can go wrong. The player wearing a lineman’s number must report his change of status to the referee, and the referee “will inform the defensive team”; in practice he turns to the defense and usually announces it on his microphone.11 In practice the officials go by what the referee heard and announced. If two linemen walk toward him, the number he announces is the one treated as eligible, whatever the coaches meant, and that is what happened in Arlington.
The same game shows the rest of the identity. Earlier, on fourth-and-2 from their own 28, the Lions ran a fake punt: a direct snap to linebacker Jalen Reeves-Maybin, who threw 31 yards to Khalil Dorsey. When the two teams met again in October 2024, in a 47–9 Detroit win, the Lions ran a hook-and-lateral that ended with Penei Sewell carrying the ball to the Dallas 3. It was called back because center Frank Ragnow was an ineligible man downfield, and it was widely read as a joke at the expense of the 2023 game.12
What to notice: the play was a good idea that died on a procedure, a risk every reporting play carries. The lesson Detroit took was not to stop reporting linemen; they kept doing it for two more seasons. The lesson for a viewer is to listen for the referee’s announcement, and then watch the safeties rather than the lineman.




Habit 3: shift, set, motion: make the defense declare twice
Before a defense can stop a play, it has to agree on what it’s looking at: which side is the strength, which linebacker has which gap, who covers whom. Every shift asks it to agree again. Johnson’s offense layered two kinds of movement: first a shift that changed the formation (a tight end trading sides, a receiver tightening his split), then, after the required one-second freeze, a man in motion at the snap. Figure 65.3 runs one such sequence in simulation.


Show the Python
def shift_play():
    off = line5() + [O("Y", "TE", -0.7, 4.8, "Y"), O("X", "WR", -0.7, -14.0, "X"), O("U", "TE", -1.6, -6.2, "U"),
                     O("Z", "WR", -1.5, 13.0, "Z"), O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -7.0, 0.0, "R")]
    dfn = [D("LE", "DE", 1.0, -4.1, "E"), D("LT_", "DT", 1.0, -0.7, "T"), D("RT_", "DT", 1.0, 2.35, "T"),
           D("RE", "DE", 1.0, 5.7, "E"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -3.2, "W"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, 0.8, "M"),
           D("SAM", "SAM", 3.8, 6.4, "S"), D("LCB", "CB", 6.5, -14.0, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 6.5, 13.0, "CB"),
           D("FS", "FS", 12.0, -8.0, "FS"), D("SS", "SS", 12.0, 8.0, "SS")]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=10)
    # pre-snap paths (for positions); their timing is set by retime() below
    pre(p, "U", [(-3.3, -3.0), (-3.3, 3.5), (-1.6, 6.4)])
    pre(p, "Z", [(-1.5, 9.0), (-3.0, 4.0), (-3.0, 0.2)])
    for k, to in [("SAM", (3.6, 8.2)), ("RCB", (6.5, 9.8))]:
        pre(p, k, [to])
    pre(p, "MIKE", [(4.5, 2.8), (4.5, 0.9)])
    pre(p, "WILL", [(4.5, -1.0), (4.5, -3.0)])
    pre(p, "FS", [(8.0, -8.4)])
    pre(p, "SS", [(12.6, 2.5)])
    # after the snap
    go(p, "Z", [(-2.8, -8.0), (0.5, -13.5)], speed=8.0)                     # the fake jet sweep
    go(p, "QB", [(-2.4, -0.6), (-4.2, 1.4)], speed=6.0)                      # fake to Z, hand to R
    go(p, "RB", [(-4.6, 1.8), (-1.6, 3.7), (2.4, 4.3), (9.5, 4.6)], "run", speed=6.4, delay=0.3)
    p.handoff("RB", t=0.8)
    for k, dw in [("LT", -0.6), ("LG", 0.6), ("C", 0.7), ("RG", 0.7), ("RT", 0.6)]:
        go(p, k, [(0.3, p.players[k].w + dw)], "block", speed=1.5)
    go(p, "Y", [(0.4, 5.5)], "block", speed=1.6)
    go(p, "U", [(2.4, 7.4)], "block", speed=2.6)
    go(p, "X", [(3.4, -13.6)], "block", speed=4.0)
    go(p, "WILL", [(3.6, -4.8)], speed=3.5)                                  # first steps: chase the jet
    go(p, "MIKE", [(4.0, -0.4), (3.4, 2.8)], speed=3.5)                      # ... then back to the run, late
    go(p, "SAM", [(3.3, 8.4)], speed=2.0)
    go(p, "FS", [(5.6, -10.4)], speed=4.0)
    go(p, "LCB", [(4.8, -12.0)], speed=3.0)
    go(p, "SS", [(10.5, 3.4)], speed=3.0, delay=0.4)
    go(p, "LE", [(0.6, -3.2)], speed=1.5)
    go(p, "RE", [(1.0, 6.6)], speed=1.0)
    # the schedule: shift (-6.8 to -4.6), defense re-declares, everyone set, jet motion from -1.3
    retime(p, "U", [(-6.8, -1.6, -6.2), (-6.0, -3.3, -3.0), (-5.2, -3.3, 3.5), (-4.6, -1.6, 6.4)])
    retime(p, "Z", [(-6.8, -1.5, 13.0), (-5.6, -1.5, 13.0), (-4.6, -1.5, 9.0), (-1.3, -1.5, 9.0),
                    (-0.65, -3.0, 4.0), (0.0, -3.0, 0.2)])
    retime(p, "SAM", [(-6.8, 3.8, 6.4), (-4.4, 3.8, 6.4), (-3.4, 3.6, 8.2)])
    retime(p, "RCB", [(-6.8, 6.5, 13.0), (-4.4, 6.5, 13.0), (-3.4, 6.5, 9.8)])
    retime(p, "MIKE", [(-6.8, 4.5, 0.8), (-4.3, 4.5, 0.8), (-3.4, 4.5, 2.8), (-0.9, 4.5, 2.8), (0.0, 4.5, 0.9)])
    retime(p, "WILL", [(-6.8, 4.5, -3.2), (-4.3, 4.5, -3.2), (-3.4, 4.5, -1.0), (-0.9, 4.5, -1.0), (0.0, 4.5, -3.0)])
    retime(p, "FS", [(-6.8, 12.0, -8.0), (-1.0, 12.0, -8.0), (0.0, 8.0, -8.4)])

Figure 65.3: Shift, set, motion (simulated, in Big Data Bowl tracking format; illustrative, not a specific Lions play). 1: two tight ends, one on each side; the defense sets its strength toward Y. 2: the shift: U walks across behind the quarterback to a wing beside Y and Z tightens his split, so Y, U and Z form a tight bunch on the right. 3: the defense re-declares: the Sam slides out over U, the Mike and Will shuffle right, the right corner moves in over Z. Everyone on offense is set for a full second, as the rules require. 4: Z comes back in jet motion; the left safety spins down toward him and the right safety rotates to the middle (two-high becomes one-high), and the linebackers bump left. 5: at the snap the quarterback fakes the jet sweep to Z. 6: a handoff to R on an outside-zone-style run to the bunch side, behind U and Y. The safety who started over that side is now in the middle, the Will chased the jet and the Mike got back late: the run hits the side the defense just thinned. Dashed outlines are where players began.




Count what the defense had to do in under seven seconds: identify a two-tight-end formation and set its strength; watch two players move at once, re-identify the strength and slide three players; recognise a jet motion and rotate its safeties; and then, at the snap, decide whether the jet was real. Each of those is a call that must be heard by eleven people in a loud stadium. Each is a chance for one of them to be a step late or in the wrong gap. A defense that answers every movement correctly has still been made to show its answers, which tells the quarterback who is likely to be where.






ImportantWhy it exists



Shifts and motion buy information and mistakes. The defense’s adjustment reveals its coverage (a defender who travels with motion suggests man; a safety who spins suggests a rotation), though less reliably than it used to, since by the mid-2020s many zone defenses also “bump” a linebacker or safety across with the motion man. That is part of why Johnson layered a shift first: two adjustments are harder to fake than one. And every re-declaration is a chance for a miscommunication. Layering a shift and a motion means the defense has to answer twice on one snap. The cost: the offense must be perfectly drilled too. After a shift every player has to be still for a full second before anyone goes in motion, or it is a five-yard illegal shift, and the more players move, the more ways there are to get it wrong. It also burns play clock, which is why these sequences cluster on plays where the offense broke the huddle early.


Johnson’s Lions were not the league’s heaviest motion team by volume. FTN (a company that hand-charts every NFL play, in data the course loads through nflverse) logged motion on 59% of Detroit’s plays in 2024, 6th in the league. The Rams led, at 77%, but the two teams moved for different reasons. The Rams lined up with three wide receivers on 85% of their 2024 plays, so their motion mostly moved receivers around one familiar personnel group; Detroit used three receivers on only 55% (league 63%), with tight ends, a sixth lineman or two backs the rest of the time. The distinctive thing was the combination: motion plus shifts plus under center plus heavy personnel, so the same eleven players could arrive at many different formations, and the defense, having substituted for one personnel group, could rarely substitute its way out of the formation it ended up facing.


Habit 4: trick plays as constraint plays
Every team has a few trick plays. Johnson’s Lions ran them more than anyone and treated them as part of the system rather than a surprise package. FTN’s charters flagged 61 Detroit snaps as trick plays from 2022 to 2025, the most in the league (the next team had 56), and those snaps averaged +0.76 EPA, against +0.11 for everyone’s trick plays.13 The samples are small, a few dozen plays, so read the EPA as “worked often” rather than as a precise number.
The logic is constraint theory. A trick play isn’t random. It is a constraint play built on a specific habit the defense has learned from your film: a cornerback who always rallies to a short catch, a defense that ignores the running back as a passer, a safety who flies at every run fake. The offense’s own self-scout tells it which of its plays the defense has studied hardest, and the trick play starts as exactly that play. The 2024 season shows the pattern: the same catch-and-pitch idea four times, and three different non-quarterbacks throwing.
FTN flagged 17 Detroit snaps as trick plays in the 2024 regular season. Table 65.2 isn’t all of them: 8 were runs by wide receivers (end-arounds and reverses), and the table keeps the two kinds this chapter is about, the laterals and the throws by players who aren’t the quarterback.
Two rules make those plays possible. First, anyone can throw a forward pass (it has to be thrown from behind the line, and only one per play), so a receiver or a running back can be the passer. Second, anyone can catch a backward pass, a lateral or a pitch, including a lineman who hasn’t reported, because the eligibility rules apply only to forward passes.14 (Both are covered in Officiating, Replay, and the Rules of the Ball.) That is how a right tackle like Sewell can take a toss: the toss goes backward, as a backward pass. The running-back throws have a favourite home near the goal line, where the ball can be snapped straight to the back (a direct snap, the idea behind the wildcat) with the quarterback split out as a receiver. The defense then has to account for a back who can run behind an extra blocker, a quarterback who can catch, and tight ends who are eligible but block on almost every goal-line snap, and it tends to forget that the back can throw.


Show the Python

Notice two things in the table. The hook-and-lateral kept working after opponents had surely seen it on film, because the defense’s habit it attacks, swarming the receiver who has just caught a short pass, is one no coach wants to un-teach. And the last two rows are the cost of the habit: in the season’s biggest game, two trick plays, one a 20-yard gain and one intercepted in the fourth quarter.
The most famous of them is Figure 65.4: on a Monday night in Santa Clara, St. Brown caught a pass a yard past the line of scrimmage and pitched it to Jameson Williams, who ran 41 more yards for a touchdown.


Show the Python
def hook_play():
    off = line5() + [O("QB", "QB", -5.0, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -5.0, -1.6, "R"), O("X", "WR", -0.7, -15.0, "X"),
                     O("Y", "TE", -1.5, -8.0, "Y"), O("H", "WR", -1.5, 8.0, "H"), O("Z", "WR", -0.7, 14.5, "Z")]
    dfn = [D("LE", "DE", 1.0, -4.0, "E"), D("LT_", "DT", 1.0, -1.0, "T"), D("RT_", "DT", 1.0, 1.0, "T"),
           D("RE", "DE", 1.0, 4.0, "E"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -2.5, "W"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, 2.2, "M"),
           D("NB", "NB", 6.5, 8.4, "NB"), D("RCB", "CB", 7.5, 15.0, "CB"), D("LCB", "CB", 7.5, -15.0, "CB"),
           D("SS", "SS", 13.5, 10.0, "SS"), D("FS", "FS", 13.5, -8.0, "FS")]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=58, to_go=12)
    go(p, "Z", [(2.3, 14.6), (1.9, 14.2)], "route", speed=7.0)
    p.dropback(1.5)
    p.pass_to("Z", t=0.75)
    go(p, "H", [(-0.9, 10.6), (0.5, 13.0), (0.7, 15.2), (4.0, 17.5), (10.0, 19.0), (17.5, 19.8)], "route",
       speed=6.6, delay=0.85)
    p.pitch("H", t=2.0)                          # about half a second after the catch, as the tacklers close
    # the rally: they stop in a triangle around Z (outside, inside, over the top) rather than on one spot
    go(p, "RCB", [(2.8, 15.4), (2.5, 15.6)], speed=5.0, delay=0.9)
    go(p, "NB", [(2.9, 12.3), (2.6, 12.6)], speed=5.6, delay=0.95)
    go(p, "SS", [(5.6, 13.2), (4.6, 13.8)], speed=7.0, delay=0.85)
    go(p, "MIKE", [(3.2, 8.6)], speed=4.5, delay=0.9)
    for k in ("LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT"):
        go(p, k, [(-0.8, p.players[k].w)], "block", speed=1.2)
    p.highlight("Z", "H")
    return p

    """Draw the offense's right sideline (w = 26.65 with the ball in the middle of the field)."""

    ax.plot([x0, x1], [y0, y1], color=style.INK_2, lw=1.6, zorder=2.5)
    if label:
        say(ax, P, 15.5, 24.0, "sideline", fs=5.8, color=style.INK_2)


HOOK = hook_play()
show_play(HOOK, [0.0, 1.65, 2.05, 2.95],
          ["1. Snap: Z hitches, H starts late", "2. The catch: three defenders rally to Z",
           "3. The pitch, backward, to H", "4. H has the sideline"],
          phases([(0.7, "Z runs a short hitch; H starts late"), (1.5, "Quick throw to Z"),
                  (2.0, "Three defenders rally to the catch"), (2.4, "Pitch to H, backward"),
                  (9, "H has the sideline")]),
          lateral=(-6.0, 28.4), window=(-7.5, 19.5), ghosts=("RCB", "NB", "SS"), ghost_t=0.0, trail_from=0.0,
          annot={0: lambda ax, P: sideline(ax, P, True), 1: sideline, 2: sideline, 3: lambda ax, P: sideline(ax, P, True)})

Figure 65.4: The hook-and-lateral (simulated, in Big Data Bowl tracking format; illustrative, not the exact alignment the Lions used). Z is the outside receiver, St. Brown in the real play; H, inside him, is Jameson Williams. It is third-and-12, so the defense sits back near the sticks: the corner about 7 yards off, the nickel (NB) about 6, the strong safety about 13, all ready to rally forward to anything short. 1: at the snap Z runs a two-yard hitch, turning back to the quarterback; H starts late on a flat path toward the sideline. 2: the quarterback throws quickly to Z, and the three nearest defenders (the corner, the nickel and the safety) all rally to the catch: tackling the man with the ball is what they are trained to do. 3: as H passes just behind him, Z pitches the ball backward to H. A backward pass can be thrown to anyone, at any time, so this is legal anywhere on the field. 4: three defenders have converged on the wrong man, and H has the space along the sideline to himself. The pitch has to go backward or level, or it is an illegal forward pass. The left side of the formation (a receiver, a tight end, a corner and the free safety) is off the picture to the left; it plays no part.










NoteMadden vs. real life



In a video game a trick play is a menu option you pick when you’re feeling lucky. In the NFL it is a scheduled part of the week. A trick play is usually installed against one opponent’s habit, practised all week, and called when the situation matches the film: the right down, the right hash, the right defensive call. Coaches think of it like any other tendency breaker: it exists because the offense has been predictable on purpose, and it works only if the play it imitates has been run often enough that the defense trusts its read.

title: Case Study: The Lions — Ben Johnson’s Offense and Dan Campbell’s Aggression
text:
Dan Campbell’s fourth down
Johnson designed the plays; Campbell decided when to keep the offense on the field. The case for going for it on fourth down, and the rules of thumb, are in The Clock, the Two-Minute Drill, and Fourth Down. This section asks the case-study questions: how aggressive were the Lions, compared with whom, and did it pay?


Show the Python
fig, (a, b) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.7, 3.4), gridspec_kw=dict(width_ratios=[1.12, 1]))
yrs = list(range(2018, 2026))
a.fill_between(yrs, GR.quantile(0.1, axis=1).loc[yrs], GR.quantile(0.9, axis=1).loc[yrs], color=style.GRID,
               alpha=0.9, lw=0, label="middle 80% of teams")
a.plot(yrs, LGR.loc[yrs], color=LEAGUE, lw=1.6, label="league")
a.plot(yrs, GR.loc[yrs, "DET"], color=LIONS, lw=2.2, marker="o", ms=3.6, label="Lions")
a.axvline(2020.5, color=style.INK_2, lw=0.8, ls=(0, (3, 2)))
a.text(2020.65, 0.012, "Campbell\nhired", fontsize=6.8, color=style.INK_2, va="bottom")
a.set_ylim(0, 0.40)
a.set_xticks(yrs[::2])
a.yaxis.set_major_formatter(plt.FuncFormatter(lambda v, _: f"{v:.0%}"))
a.set_ylabel("Neutral fourth downs: went for it", fontsize=8)
a.set_title("Go rate", fontsize=9.5)
a.legend(loc="upper left", fontsize=6.8, frameon=True, facecolor=style.SURFACE, edgecolor="none", framealpha=1.0)

tg = TEAMGAIN.copy()
b.axhline(0, color=style.BASELINE, lw=0.9)
b.axhline(GOS.gain.mean(), color=LEAGUE, lw=0.9, ls=(0, (3, 2)))
b.text(tg.n.min() - 2, GOS.gain.mean() + 0.06, "league average", fontsize=6.5, color=style.INK_2, va="bottom")
b.text(tg.n.min() - 2, -0.06, "same as kicking", fontsize=6.5, color=style.INK_2, va="top")
other = tg.drop("DET")
b.scatter(other.n, other.per, s=16, color=style.MUTED, alpha=0.7, lw=0)
named = tg.loc[["PHI", "KC", "CHI"]]
b.scatter(named.n, named.per, s=22, color=style.INK_2, lw=0, zorder=4)
b.scatter([tg.loc["DET", "n"]], [tg.loc["DET", "per"]], s=42, color=LIONS, zorder=5)
for t, name, dx, dy, ha in [("DET", "Lions", -3, 0.12, "right"), ("PHI", "Eagles", 3, 0.0, "left"),
                            ("KC", "Chiefs", 3, 0.0, "left"), ("CHI", "Bears", 3, -0.05, "left")]:
    b.text(tg.loc[t, "n"] + dx, tg.loc[t, "per"] + dy, name, fontsize=7, ha=ha, va="center",
           color=LIONS if t == "DET" else style.INK, fontweight="bold" if t == "DET" else "normal")

b.set_ylabel("Points gained per attempt vs kicking", fontsize=8)
b.set_title("Value per attempt", fontsize=9.5)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=1.2)
plt.show()








Figure 65.5: Left: how often each team went for it on a neutral fourth down (first three quarters, win probability 20–80%, so the decision is a choice rather than desperation), 2018–2025. The shaded band is the middle 80% of teams each season. Detroit was a below-average team on this measure before Campbell, jumped in 2021, and led the league in 2022, 2023 and 2024. Right: a rough value check, 2021–2025, first three quarters. Each dot is a team: how many times it went for it (across) against the average points gained per attempt (up), estimated as the attempt’s EPA minus the league’s average EPA on punts and field goals from the same distance and field position. Detroit went for it more than anyone, and on average each attempt was worth a little more than the league’s, but less per attempt than teams like Philadelphia (whose tries leaned heavily on the tush push) and Kansas City. The Bears are labelled because they come back at the end of the chapter. Almost every team sits above zero because teams mostly go when they like their chances, so read the dots against each other, not against the zero line. Across teams there is no clear slope between how often a team goes and what each go is worth. Fakes from punt formation count as attempts. Source: nflverse play-by-play.





Three readings of Figure 65.5.
The habit came first, the good team second. Detroit’s neutral go rate was 9% in 2020, below the league. In Campbell’s first season it was 25%, 3rd in the league, for a team that won three games: the underdog logic from the start of this chapter. (Detroit led the league in raw attempts that year; by this rate, which strips out desperate situations, it was a whisker behind the leader’s 26%.) Then it stayed near a third of neutral fourth downs, first in the league in 2022, 2023 and 2024 (33% in 2024, against a league average of 14%), after Detroit had become a favourite. That is the more interesting decision, because the variance argument no longer applies. A favourite going for it is betting on the expected-points case alone, and on its own offense.
It paid, by a rough yardstick, though mostly in one season. Detroit converted 56% of its attempts in 2021–2025 (the league converted 54%). Converting is the wrong test, though, as 10-04 argued: what matters is the attempt compared with the kick it replaced. So compare each of Detroit’s 114 first-three-quarter attempts with what the league’s punts and field goals produced from the same spots. The attempts come out about 67 points ahead over five seasons, 4th in the league over the period. That total is lumpy: about 31 came in 2024 alone, and the other four seasons averaged about 9.
The total is a net figure, and the bad tail is inside it. The conversions gained about 216 points against kicking; the 47 failures gave back about 148. Each failure hands the opponent a short field, and the ones that come late in close games are the ones fans remember. The yardstick is also crude. Teams go for it when they like their chances, so the attempts are a selected sample, and that same selection is why the league average go in Figure 65.5 looks worth +0.45 points over kicking: the average go looks good partly because teams only go when it looks good. A proper answer needs a win-probability model of each decision, which is built in Win Probability and Decision Analysis. But the direction for Detroit is not in doubt.
The more you go, the less each go is worth. Detroit’s value per attempt (+0.59 points) was only a little above the league’s (+0.45), and well below the Eagles (+1.11) and the Chiefs (+1.45). The reason shows up inside Detroit’s own attempts. The first fourth downs a coach adds are the obvious ones, fourth-and-1 or 2 near midfield; the next ones are closer calls, and 26% of Detroit’s attempts came with four or more yards to go, against 19% for the league. Detroit’s attempts with one to three yards to go were worth +0.77 points each against kicking; its attempts with four or more were worth +0.10. That is diminishing returns: each extra, longer attempt is still slightly positive on average, but adds far less than the short ones, and it fails more often. (The right panel of Figure 65.5 can’t show this on its own: across teams, attempts and value per attempt are nearly uncorrelated, 0.06, because teams differ in far more than aggressiveness.)






CautionCommon misconception



“Campbell is a gambler.” A gambler takes bets with negative expected value for the thrill. Campbell’s fourth-down record is a long series of bets with positive expected value, some of which lost, a few of them in playoff games. The fair criticism is narrower: in a handful of late, high-leverage spots (the 2023 NFC Championship Game, covered in 10-04, is the famous one), the models themselves called the decision close, and a coach with a strong kicker might reasonably have kicked. Judge the habit by the whole record, and the close calls by the odds before the snap.


The habit extended past the field. Detroit’s front office took its aggressive streak to the league’s rule-making meetings: a Lions proposal produced the 2024 rule that gives a coach a third challenge when either of his first two succeeds (it had required both),15 and in 2025 the Lions proposed letting wild-card teams with better records be seeded above division winners, a proposal withdrawn before a vote.16 A team that thinks in expected value tends to notice where the rules leave value on the table.

title: Case Study: The Lions — Ben Johnson’s Offense and Dan Campbell’s Aggression
text:
How opponents responded
Defenses had answers, and they were the standard ones for this kind of offense. None of them is specific to Detroit’s opponents in any one game; they are what defensive coaches teach against under-center play-action, jumbo and heavy motion:

Keep the backside end home. On a run fake away from him, the end on the boot side doesn’t chase; he stays to meet the bootlegging quarterback. That is the reason the leak in Figure 65.2 has to come out on time.
Give the reported lineman an owner. A linebacker or the walked-down safety takes #70 if he releases, so the leak is covered and the bait still has to beat the defenders underneath.
Play single-high and accept the risk. Two deep safeties stop the play-action shots but leave a light box for the run game, so many defenses chose the other trade: a safety down, eight in the box, and a deep shot given up now and then. Detroit saw two-high coverage on 36% of its 2024 dropbacks against a league average of 39% (23rd of 32 teams, where 1st means the most two-high), so slightly more single-high than most. The gap is small, so read it as a lean, not a strategy.
Simplify against motion. Instead of rotating with every shift and motion, a defense can “lock” its coverage (nobody travels, nobody rotates) and play the call it started with, accepting a worse match-up in exchange for no busts.

None of these took the offense away: it ranked 6th, 6th and 3rd in EPA per play from 2022 to 2024. The worst day came in January 2025, in the divisional round against Washington. Detroit, the 15–2 top seed, lost 45–31 after turning the ball over five times: four interceptions, one of them returned for a touchdown, and a lost fumble. Two of the trick plays in the table above came in that game. It wasn’t a scheme answer so much as the bad tail of a high-variance team arriving on the worst day, against a Detroit defense that had been gutted by injuries since October: Aidan Hutchinson broke his leg in the 47–9 win at Dallas, and by December the injured defenders also included Alim McNeill, Alex Anzalone and Carlton Davis.17
The league’s response was the more durable one, and it came in two forms. The first was imitation, though the Lions were one influence among several (by 2025 the Rams took more snaps from under center than anyone): league-wide, the share of plays from under center went from about 27% in 2023 to about 34% in 2025, heavy personnel climbed to a decade high, and the neutral fourth-down go rate kept rising.18 The second was the coaching market. Within three days in January 2025, the Lions lost both coordinators to head-coaching jobs: Johnson to the Chicago Bears, a division rival, and defensive coordinator Aaron Glenn to the New York Jets.19 That is the usual price of success for a staff, and it set up what economists call a natural experiment: nobody designed it, but the same ideas now had one coach removed and two teams to compare. The rest of this chapter runs that comparison.

title: Case Study: The Lions — Ben Johnson’s Offense and Dan Campbell’s Aggression
text:
After Johnson: Detroit in 2025 and 2026
Campbell hired John Morton, a veteran assistant, as offensive coordinator and play-caller, and Kelvin Sheppard replaced Glenn as defensive coordinator. After a loss to Minnesota in Week 9, Campbell took the play sheet himself, starting with a 44–22 win over Washington.20 The Lions finished 9–8 and missed the playoffs. The offense was still good, 7th in EPA per play, with the same quarterback, receivers and running backs, but no longer great, and it looked more like everyone else’s (though still well above the league’s habits): under center 48% of the time (from 54%), play-action on 25% of dropbacks (from 35%). What a Play Really Is compares the offense under Morton and under Campbell in detail. After the season Morton was fired, and the Lions hired Drew Petzing, previously the Cardinals’ coordinator, as their third offensive coordinator in three years; Sheppard stayed on defense.21
The data in this chapter stop at the end of 2025, and the 2026 season is only weeks old as this is written, so it is too early to say what Petzing’s offense is. The test is easy to run yourself as the season goes on: if Detroit’s under-center and play-action rates in Figure 65.6 climb back toward their 2024 levels, the habits belonged to the building; if they stay near the league average, they left with Johnson.

title: Case Study: The Lions — Ben Johnson’s Offense and Dan Campbell’s Aggression
text:
What transferred to Chicago
The Bears Johnson inherited were a classic Detroit-2021 problem: 5–12 in 2024, an offense 26th in EPA per play, and a rookie quarterback, Caleb Williams, sacked 68 times. In 2025 they went 11–6, won the NFC North, beat Green Bay 31–27 in the wild-card round (the franchise’s first playoff win since the 2010 season) and lost to the Rams 20–17 in overtime in the divisional round.22 The offense jumped to 8th in EPA per play; Williams was sacked 24 times, and his EPA per dropback rose from -0.09 to +0.07.
How much of that is Johnson? Figure 65.6 compares the two teams’ fingerprints before and after he moved.


Show the Python
METRICS = [("Under center (% of plays)", HAB["uc"] * 100, HABL["uc"] * 100, "{:.0f}%"),
           ("Play-action (% of dropbacks)", HAB["pa"] * 100, HABL["pa"] * 100, "{:.0f}%"),
           ("Motion (% of plays)", HAB["mo"] * 100, HABL["mo"] * 100, "{:.0f}%"),
           ("Reported linemen (per 100 plays)", HAB["rep"], HABL["rep"], "{:.1f}"),
           ("Trick plays (per 100 plays)", HAB["tr"], HABL["tr"], "{:.1f}"),
           ("Neutral 4th-down go rate (%)", GR.loc[2022:] * 100, LGR.loc[2022:] * 100, "{:.0f}%")]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 2, figsize=(6.6, 5.6))
for ax, (title, tab, lg, fmt) in zip(axes.flat, METRICS):
    rows = [("Lions", LIONS, tab.loc[[2024, 2025], "DET"].values),
            ("Bears", BEARS, tab.loc[[2024, 2025], "CHI"].values),
            ("League", style.MUTED, lg.loc[[2024, 2025]].values)]
    hi = max(max(v) for _, _, v in rows)
    for i, (team, col, v) in enumerate(rows):
        y = 2 - i
        ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((v[0], y), (v[1], y), arrowstyle="-|>", mutation_scale=10, color=col, lw=1.9,
                                     shrinkA=3, shrinkB=1))
        ax.plot([v[0]], [y], marker="o", ms=3.8, color=col, mfc="white", mew=1.3)
        up = v[0] < v[1]
        ax.text(v[0] + (-1 if up else 1) * 0.03 * hi, y + 0.33, fmt.format(v[0]), fontsize=6.3,
                ha="right" if up else "left", va="center", color=style.INK_2)
        ax.text(v[1] + (1 if up else -1) * 0.03 * hi, y + 0.33, fmt.format(v[1]), fontsize=6.3,
                ha="left" if up else "right", va="center", color=style.INK if team == "League" else col,
                fontweight="bold")
    ax.set_yticks([2, 1, 0], ["Lions", "Bears", "League"], fontsize=7.2)
    ax.set_ylim(-0.55, 2.75)
    ax.set_xlim(0, hi * 1.3)
    ax.tick_params(axis="x", labelsize=6.6)
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=8.2)
    ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
fig.legend(handles=[Line2D([], [], color=style.INK_2, marker="o", mfc="white", lw=1.6, label="2024 → 2025")],
           loc="lower center", ncol=1, fontsize=7, frameon=False, bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, 0.0))
fig.tight_layout(h_pad=0.9, w_pad=1.4, rect=(0, 0.04, 1, 1))
plt.show()








Figure 65.6: What moved with Ben Johnson. Each arrow runs from a 2024 value to the 2025 value, for the Lions, the Bears and the league as a whole (grey), so you can see how much of a team’s change was just the league moving. Under center, play-action and trick plays jumped in Chicago in Johnson’s first season, to near the top of the league, and fell back in Detroit without him. Motion rose in Chicago by about twice the league’s rise, but not to the top. Reported linemen rose in Chicago but only to about the league’s new, higher level: that habit moved least. The fourth-down habit belonged to the other coach: Detroit stayed far more aggressive than the league under Campbell, while Chicago’s go rate rose about as much as the league’s did. Play-action is a share of dropbacks; under center and motion are shares of runs and passes; reported linemen and trick plays are per 100 runs and passes (a report from the official play-by-play; FTN’s trick-play flag); the go rate uses neutral fourth downs as in the previous figure. FTN doesn’t chart shifts, so the shift habit can’t be measured this way. Sources: FTN charting via nflverse; nflverse play-by-play.





The picture is unusually clean for football data, at least for the three most visible habits. In one offseason, Chicago went from 17th to 5th in under-center rate (28% to 48%), from 29th to 2nd in play-action share (18% to 31%), and from 28th to 1st in trick-play rate. Detroit’s numbers moved the other way. Those habits were the play-caller’s, and they travelled with him.
The other two habits moved less. Chicago’s motion rate rose from 46% to 58% of plays (12th in the league), about twice the league’s rise, but not to the top. Reported linemen rose from 1.1 to 4.0 per 100 plays, in a year when the whole league jumped from 2.4 to 4.5, so Chicago ended up slightly below the league average. A habit that depends on personnel (a sixth lineman Johnson trusts as a blocker and as a decoy) takes longer to install than one that depends on the play sheet. Shifts can’t be measured from FTN’s public charting at all.
The fourth-down habit didn’t travel the same way. Detroit’s neutral go rate fell from 33% to 25% but stayed 5th in the league under Campbell; Chicago’s rose from 17% to 21%, in a season when the whole league rose. Aggression on fourth down had been the head coach’s.
What the fingerprint can’t tell you is how much of Chicago’s improvement came from the scheme. The Bears also rebuilt the middle of their offensive line before 2025, trading for guards Joe Thuney and Jonah Jackson (a Lions starter in Johnson’s first two seasons as coordinator) and signing center Drew Dalman,23 and Williams was in his second season, when most young quarterbacks improve. The sack total falling from 68 to 24 belongs to all three. In short: the play-caller’s signature habits transferred at once, the personnel-dependent ones partly; the results transferred substantially, with help.

title: Case Study: The Lions — Ben Johnson’s Offense and Dan Campbell’s Aggression
text:
What survives
The Johnson-Campbell Lions lasted four seasons as a unit, from 2021 to 2024, and they leave a few ideas that have outlasted the staff.

Under center is a disguise, not a throwback. The Lions, with the Rams, showed that a modern passing offense can take a large share of its snaps from under center at no cost, and throw unusually well off the run fake, because the fake and the run look the same. The league followed.
Personnel is a message you can lie with. A reported lineman, a third tight end, a jumbo set: each tells the defense something, and an offense can choose whether to deliver on it.
Make the defense answer twice. Shifts layered with motion turn a single snap into two or three communication tests. Most defenses pass most of them; the offense only needs the occasional failure.
Trick plays are part of the system. Built on the defense’s habits and the offense’s own self-scout, they are constraint plays with a sense of humour, and their cost is visible on the bad days.
Fourth-down aggression became normal, and its edge got smaller. When one team goes for it a third of the time, it’s a strategy; when the league catches up, the remaining edge is in choosing which fourth downs, which is a harder skill to see from the stands.
A rebuild can choose variance. A bad team that plays to the expected-value math and accepts the ugly failures can turn into a good team that keeps doing it, which is what Detroit did.

title: Case Study: The Lions — Ben Johnson’s Offense and Dan Campbell’s Aggression
text:
Watch for it on Sunday






TipWatch for it: the trick detector



Pick a Lions or Bears game (or any team that runs a lot from under center) and flag every snap with something unusual in it.

Before the snap, listen. “Number 70 is reporting as eligible”: note the down and distance. Then watch the safeties, not the lineman. If they creep down, expect the run fake and a throw behind them.
Count the movements. One mark for a shift, one for a motion. Snaps with two or more marks are the ones where the defense has to communicate twice; look for a defender still pointing or moving at the snap.
Find the odd alignment. A quarterback split wide, a running back alone in the backfield taking a direct snap, a receiver stacked right behind another one a yard off the line, a tackle at the end of the line. Write down what the defense did about it.
After the snap: who caught the first ball? On a short catch near the sideline, keep your eyes on the player behind the catcher. If someone is trailing at full speed, the hook-and-lateral is on.
On fourth down, guess first. Before the offense decides, say go, kick or punt using the rules of thumb from 10-04. Then compare with what the coach did, and note whether he was more or less aggressive than you.
At the end of the game, count your flags and how many of them gained yards. You have just charted a team’s disguise rate, the raw material for a tendency report.

title: Case Study: The Lions — Ben Johnson’s Offense and Dan Campbell’s Aggression
text:
Predict the play






TipPredict the play



Drill 1. Second-and-5 at your own 35, first quarter. The offense comes out in Figure 66.9: six offensive linemen, number 70 has reported eligible and stands at the right end of the line, the quarterback is under center and the defense has walked a safety down, with only one deep safety left. You have seen this offense run from this look three times already today. What is the most likely play, and where is the ball going?


Show the Python
off, dfn = jumbo_look()
dfn = [q.moved(d=6.2, w=5.6) if q.key == "SS" else q for q in dfn]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=45, to_go=5, title="Drill 1: number 70 has reported eligible")
p.highlight("SS", color=style.DEFENSE)
p.highlight("T70")
fld = p.draw(width_in=5.6, lateral=(-15.5, 15.5), window=(-9.5, 17.5))
no_numbers(fld.ax)
P = P_of(fld, p)
point_to(fld.ax, P, (10.2, 9.8), (6.2, 5.6), "safety walked down:\neight in the box")
point_to(fld.ax, P, (-5.6, 8.4), (-0.7, 4.8), "#70 reported eligible")
point_to(fld.ax, P, (15.0, 7.4), (13.5, -0.5), "one deep safety", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK)
plt.show()








Figure 65.7: Drill 1: jumbo with a reported tackle (#70), second-and-5. The strong safety (ringed) has come down to about six yards deep, just outside #70, making eight defenders in the box; one deep safety remains.











TipAnswer





A play-action pass behind the safety, most likely to a receiver crossing into the space he left. Everything in the picture says run: second-and-5 (a run-friendly down), six linemen, a quarterback under center, and you’ve seen runs from it. The defense agrees, which is why the safety is down. That is the bait half of Figure 65.2. With eight defenders committed to the run and one deep safety in the middle, the space behind the linebackers and outside the deep safety is open for a moment after the run fake.
Why not the leak to #70, the player the question is about? Look where the safety walked down: just outside #70. A lineman slipping into the flat would run straight into him. The leak is the backup, and it’s best when the walked-down safety is on the other side and the linebackers flow hard away from #70. A plain run is still possible, but the offense has spent three snaps teaching this defense to bring the safety down. Detroit cashed exactly this kind of setup in Week 18 of 2023: on second-and-5 with Dan Skipper reported eligible, Goff faked the run and hit St. Brown for a 70-yard touchdown (the play is in Formation Rules).











TipPredict the play



Drill 2. Fourth-and-4 at the opponent’s 35, second quarter, score tied. Figure 66.10 shows the field. Your kicker makes about two-thirds of his kicks from 50 to 54 yards. What would the 2022–2024 Lions have done, what would a typical NFL team have done, and if Detroit goes for it, what will the offense look like?


Show the Python
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.6, 2.6))
LOS, Y0 = 110 - 35, 26.65
fld = Field(ax=ax, orient="horizontal", los=LOS, window=(-24, 46), to_go=4, numbers=False, hashes=True,
            lateral=(13.0, 40.3))
ax.add_patch(Ellipse((LOS, Y0), 1.6, 1.0, fc=style.BALL, ec="white", lw=0.6, zorder=9))
for x, lab in [(60, "50"), (70, "40"), (80, "30"), (90, "20"), (100, "10"), (110, "G")]:
    ax.text(x, 15.0, lab, fontsize=8, ha="center", va="center", color=style.MUTED, fontweight="bold", zorder=6,
            bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.15", fc=style.TURF, ec="none"))
ax.annotate("", xy=(120, 35.2), xytext=(LOS - 8, 35.2), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="<->", color=style.INK_2, lw=1.0))
ax.text((LOS - 8 + 120) / 2, 37.6, "field goal: about a 53-yard kick (holder ~8 yards back; posts at the end line)",
        fontsize=7.0, ha="center", va="center", color=style.INK,
        bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.2", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none"))
ax.annotate("", xy=(LOS + 4, 21.0), xytext=(LOS, 21.0),
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, lw=1.4))
ax.text(LOS + 5.0, 21.0, "4 yards for a first down", fontsize=7.2, ha="left", va="center",
        color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.2", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none"))
ax.text(LOS - 1.6, 28.6, "fourth-and-4,\nball on the\nopponent's 35", fontsize=7.0, ha="right", va="center",
        color=style.INK, bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.2", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none"))
ax.text(115, 24.0, "end\nzone", fontsize=7.4, ha="center", va="center", color=style.INK_2)
plt.show()








Figure 65.8: Drill 2: fourth-and-4 at the opponent’s 35 (offense moving left to right). A field goal from here is about a 53-yard kick: 35 yards to the goal line, 10 more to the goalposts at the back of the end zone, and about 8 for the snap and hold. A punt would net perhaps 20 to 25 yards.











TipAnswer





Detroit goes for it; most teams don’t; and the play will be a shotgun pass. This is the “go zone” from 10-04: the opponent’s 30 to 40, too far for a comfortable field goal (a 53-yarder at two-thirds or less) and too close for a punt to gain much, so the models usually say go even on fourth-and-4 or 5. Teams mostly ignore that. On fourth-and-3 to 5 between the opponent’s 30 and 40 in the first three quarters of 2022–2024, the league went for it 40% of the time and Detroit 73% (a small sample, 11 snaps). This is exactly where Campbell’s habit differed from everyone else’s: not on fourth-and-1, where most teams now go, but on the medium-yardage calls the models like and the sidelines still fear.
The play is the surprise. You might expect the under-center, play-action identity, and on fourth-and-1 or 2 you’d be partly right: Detroit was under center on 61% of those attempts (league 51%) and used play-action on 15% (league 9%). But on fourth-and-3 to 5, Detroit was in the shotgun on all 31 of its attempts in 2022–2024, and 94% were dropbacks, just like the league. When the down and distance tell the defense “pass”, there is nothing left to disguise, and even this offense lines up to throw. The menu isn’t one play.











TipPredict the play



Drill 3. Second-and-goal from the 3. The offense lines up in Figure 66.11: the running back is alone in the shotgun spot, the quarterback is split out in the left slot, and there are two tight ends to the right, one on the line and one on the wing, with a receiver outside them. What is the default play, what is the trick, and whom should the defense not forget?


Show the Python
off = line5() + [O("RB", "RB", -5.0, 0.0, "R"), O("QB", "QB", -1.5, -8.0, "Q"), O("X", "WR", -0.7, -13.0, "X"),
                 O("Y", "TE", -0.7, 4.8, "Y"), O("U", "TE", -1.6, 6.4, "U"), O("Z", "WR", -1.5, 12.5, "Z")]
# seven on the line: X, the five linemen and Y, so Y (the end) is eligible; U, Z, Q and R are backs
dfn = [D("LE", "DE", 0.9, -4.0, "E"), D("LT_", "DT", 0.9, -1.0, "T"), D("RT_", "DT", 0.9, 1.0, "T"),
       D("RE", "DE", 0.9, 5.6, "E"), D("WILL", "WILL", 3.0, -2.6, "W"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 3.0, 1.2, "M"),
       D("SAM", "SAM", 2.6, 7.6, "S"), D("NB", "NB", 2.6, -8.4, "NB"), D("LCB", "CB", 2.0, -13.0, "CB"),
       D("RCB", "CB", 2.0, 12.5, "CB"), D("FS", "FS", 6.5, -1.0, "FS")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=107, to_go=None, title="Drill 3: a direct snap at the 3")
fld = p.draw(width_in=5.6, lateral=(-15.5, 15.5), window=(-8.5, 13.0))
no_numbers(fld.ax)
P = P_of(fld, p)
point_to(fld.ax, P, (-5.4, -11.5), (-1.5, -8.0), "the quarterback,\nsplit out")
point_to(fld.ax, P, (-6.4, 6.4), (-5.0, 0.0), "direct snap\nto the back")
plt.show()








Figure 65.9: Drill 3: a direct snap to the running back (R) at the 3-yard line, with the quarterback (Q) split out in the left slot and two tight ends (Y at the end of the line, U on the wing) to the right. X is on the line at the left end; Z is a yard off the line, outside U. Illustrative alignment.











TipAnswer





The default is a run by the back who takes the snap, behind the wing tight end as an extra blocker; the trick is a pass by that back; and the men not to forget are the tight ends. This is the direct-snap look from the trick-play section. The back can run without a handoff, which gives the offense an extra blocker in the count, and the quarterback, standing in the slot as a receiver, takes a defender with him. The defense’s eyes go to the back and to the quarterback (everyone knows the quarterback can catch out there). What it tends to forget is that the back can throw, and that the tight ends, the players who block on almost every goal-line snap, are eligible: Y is the end of the line and U is a back on the wing. In Week 5 of 2025 at Cincinnati, Detroit took a direct snap to David Montgomery on second-and-3 from the 3, and Montgomery threw a touchdown pass to tight end Brock Wright.24 If the defense covers the quarterback and the back’s run, a tight end is the most likely target.

title: Case Study: The Lions — Ben Johnson’s Offense and Dan Campbell’s Aggression
text:
Takeaways

Detroit’s 2021 rebuild had two halves: build the lines and the core through the draft (Sewell, Hutchinson, St. Brown, Gibbs, LaPorta), and choose variance as an underdog. The fourth-down aggression came before the good team did.
Ben Johnson’s offense (2022–2024) was a familiar run and play-action base with four habits on top: the quarterback under center (the league’s highest share in 2022 and 2024), heavy and jumbo personnel with a reported lineman, shifts layered with motion, and trick plays built as constraint plays. Each makes one snap look like several; each costs drilling time, play clock and the occasional disaster.
Campbell’s fourth downs led the league in neutral go rate in 2022–2024 and, by a rough yardstick, gained about 67 points over kicking in five seasons, most of it in 2024. The extra, longer attempts were worth far less than the short ones: aggression has diminishing returns.
Defenses used the standard counters (a boot-side end who stays home, an owner for the reported lineman, more single-high, simpler motion rules), and the offense still ranked near the top every year. What finally broke it up was the coaching market: other teams hired its coordinators. Johnson went to the Bears and Glenn to the Jets in January 2025. Detroit then went through Morton, Campbell calling plays and, in 2026, Petzing: three coordinators in three years.
What transferred: in one season Chicago’s under-center, play-action and trick-play rates jumped to near the top of the league and Detroit’s fell back; motion and reported linemen moved less. The play-caller’s signature habits moved with him, the fourth-down habit stayed with the head coach, and the Bears’ results moved with help from a rebuilt line and a second-year quarterback.

Connections
Builds on: The Modern Era (the under-center revival and the motion boom); The Clock, the Two-Minute Drill, and Fourth Down (the go-for-it decision and the 2023 NFC title game); Formation Rules (reporting eligible and the eligible tackle); Motion and Shifts; Play-Action, Bootlegs, and Screens; and Constraint Theory.
Sets up: Win Probability and Decision Analysis, where the rough fourth-down yardstick here becomes a proper model; Tendencies, PROE, and Charting, for building fingerprints like Figure 65.6 for any team; and Building a Roster, for the draft-and-develop side of the rebuild.
See also (case studies): The Shanahan Tree, the other under-center, play-action family; The Eagles: Trenches, RPOs, and the Tush Push, the other great fourth-down team of the era; and Andy Reid and the Kansas City Chiefs, the league’s longest-running trick-play laboratory.
If you want to go deeper: the Lions’ and Bears’ All-22 from 2024 and 2025, watched with only the pre-snap movement in mind; Ben Baldwin’s open fourth-down model and its weekly team rankings (nfl4th); and the FTN charting data in nflverse, which lets you rebuild Figure 65.6 for any coordinator who changes teams.

title: Case Study: Fangio’s Two-High Revolution and Macdonald’s Answer
text:
The problem: one deep safety was a promise the offense could cash
Santa Clara, February 2026. In the days before Super Bowl LX, the Patriots’ offensive coordinator, Josh McDaniels, was asked what made Seattle’s defense so hard to prepare for. His answer wasn’t about a star pass rusher or a blitz package. It was about a picture. “If we have the ball for 70 snaps in the game,” he said, “65 of them are gonna look the same before the ball’s snapped.”1 Then the game was played, and the picture held. Drake Maye, the league’s MVP runner-up, was sacked six times. New England didn’t score until the fourth quarter. Seattle sent more than four rushers on only 8 of New England’s 53 dropbacks, and its safeties almost always started deep. A defense that looked the same every snap, rushed four, and still took the quarterback apart: how? This chapter is the story of the two coaches who built that idea, the older one who made “keep two safeties back” the league’s default and the younger one who found what was still missing from it.
You’ll be able to…
To see why two coaches built what they built, start with what NFL defenses looked like in 2017.
The dominant defense of the 2010s was Seattle’s Cover 3: one safety deep in the middle, the other walked down as an eighth man near the line. It was simple, fast and physical, and for a while it was the best defense in football. But it made a promise before every snap. With one safety deep, the defense had already committed its eighth defender to the run and told the quarterback where the deep help was: in the middle, and only there.
Two kinds of offense learned to cash that promise. Sean McVay’s and Kyle Shanahan’s play-action offenses pulled the eighth man forward with a run fake and threw into the space he left, and Patrick Mahomes punished the other half: with one deep safety, any receiver outside that safety’s reach was one-on-one deep. (The Modern Era tells both stories in full.)
The defensive problem had a precise shape. A one-high defense decides before the snap who will stop the run and where the deep help is, and modern offenses had learned to make that decision cost something on every play. The fix had to do three things at once:
Two safeties back solves the first. The other two are hard. Vic Fangio spent most of a long career working out how to do them.

title: Case Study: Fangio’s Two-High Revolution and Macdonald’s Answer
section: Vic Fangio: four decades in the room
text:
Vic Fangio: four decades in the room
Victor John Fangio was born in 1958 in Dunmore, Pennsylvania, a small town next to Scranton. He started coaching at his old high school in 1979, worked as a graduate assistant at North Carolina, and got his first professional job in 1984 as a defensive assistant for the Philadelphia Stars of the USFL. In 1986 he followed the Stars’ head coach, Jim Mora, to the NFL’s New Orleans Saints as linebackers coach, where he coached one of the most famous linebacker groups ever assembled (Rickey Jackson, Sam Mills, Pat Swilling and Vaughan Johnson, the “Dome Patrol”). From there he spent more than twenty years as a coordinator nobody outside the profession knew: the expansion Carolina Panthers (1995–1998), the Colts, the expansion Texans, a stint as an assistant in Baltimore, a year at Stanford under Jim Harbaugh, the 49ers (2011–2014) and the Bears (2015–2018). He was 60 when Denver made him a head coach for the first time, in 2019.2
Those who have worked for him describe a coach of the old school in most things: long meetings, padded practices, clips of hard hits in the film session. When he took over the Eagles’ defense in 2024 he told the players, in effect, that it wasn’t their fault they didn’t know how to work, “But that’s going to change now that I’m here.” At his introductory press conference he put it more broadly: “People are not expecting as much out of players as we used to expect.”3 He is also, by every account, a relentless student of the opponent’s habits, the coach who notices that a tight end’s alignment gives away the run that is coming.
What makes his career unusual is that his defense got more modern as he got older. The ideas that made him famous were not new, and he didn’t claim to have invented them: two-deep coverages and quarters had been staples in college (Michigan State, TCU and Nick Saban’s teams; see Quarters and the Two-High Match Family), and odd fronts are as old as the 3-4. What he did was assemble them into one system that answered the specific problem of the late 2010s NFL, and teach it to a generation of assistants.






NoteMadden vs. real life



In a video game you pick a defense from a menu: “Cover 4,” “Cover 3 Sky,” “Mid Blitz.” Each call has its own alignment, so the alignment is the call. A Fangio defense works the other way round. It starts from one alignment and has many calls that all begin there. The quarterback isn’t choosing between plays he can see; he is choosing between plays he has to imagine.

section: The scheme answer: five connected decisions
text:
The scheme answer: five connected decisions
Fangio’s defense is often summed up as “two-high,” which is like summing up a car as “four wheels.” It is five decisions that only work together. Each solves one part of the problem and creates a cost that the next decision pays.
Reading the diagrams: offense is blue circles (X, Z, H receivers; Y and U tight ends; Q quarterback; R running back; C center). Defense is outlined squares: E an edge player, 0 a nose tackle on the center, 4i a lineman on a tackle’s inside shoulder, T a defensive tackle, M and W linebackers, $ the nickel back, S a third safety, CB a cornerback, FS and SS the safeties. Shaded ovals are zone areas; dashed orange arrows are zone drops; solid orange arrows are rushes. A green ring marks the player to watch, and a purple ring a second one. The thick blue line is the line of scrimmage and the thick yellow-orange line the first-down marker. The small numbers on the left edge give the depth in yards past the line of scrimmage.


Show the Python
p = Play(eleven_attached(), tite_quarters(), los=35, to_go=10)
for k, to in (("LE", (-2.4, -3.6)), ("L4", (-2.6, -1.6)), ("NT", (-2.8, 0.3)), ("R4", (-2.6, 2.0))):
    go_to(p, k, to, "rush", speed=3.0)
p.drop("RE", (6.5, 11.0), zone=(7, 10))
p.drop("MIKE", (8.0, -0.5), zone=(7, 9))
p.drop("NB", (6.5, -11.5), zone=(7, 10))
for k, to in (("LCB", (17.5, -19.5)), ("RCB", (17.5, 19.5))):
    p.drop(k, to, zone=(10, 12.6))
for k, to in (("FS", (15.0, -6.0)), ("SS", (15.0, 6.0))):     # match-quarters safeties: slow, short, reading #2
    p.drop(k, to, speed=1.5)
for w in (-6.6, 6.6):
    p.zone((17.5, w), (10, 12.6))
p.highlight("FS", "SS")
fld = p.draw(lateral=(-26.6, 26.6), window=(-8.5, 25))
no_numbers(fld.ax)
ruler(fld, p, top=20)
ax, P = fld.ax, P_of(fld, p)
box_outline(ax, P, -1.4, 6.3, -6.6, 6.9, "the box: six vs. six", (-3.0, -11.0))
point_to(ax, P, (-4.6, 17.5), (1.0, 5.7), "the TE-side edge\nlines up to rush,\nthen drops")
point_to(ax, P, (22.2, -15.0), (15.0, -6.0), "safeties ~12 deep:\nread #2, cover him\nor fit the run", ha="center")
say(ax, P, 22.6, 13.2, "deep quarters", fs=6.8, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, weight="bold")
plt.show()








Figure 66.1: The tite front with quarters behind it, against 11 personnel (illustrative, not a specific Eagles or Bears call). The offense has three receivers, a tight end (Y) attached on the right and a back: six blockers counting the five linemen and Y. The defense is in its five-man nickel tite: a nose (0) on the center, two 4i-techniques on the tackles’ inside shoulders, and a stand-up edge (E) outside each tackle, the right one outside the tight end, with one linebacker (M) behind them. This is Fangio’s base-defense front with a nickel in place of a linebacker, and it became the everyday nickel of his former assistant Brandon Staley; Fangio’s own nickel more often kept two linebackers (decision 2). Either way: six defenders in the box (dashed rectangle) against six blockers, with nobody spare. The two safeties stand about 12 yards deep, outside the hashes; the corners (CB) are 7 to 9 yards off with outside leverage. After the snap, four rush (solid arrows), the tight-end-side edge drops into the right curl-flat area, the Mike and the nickel ($) take the middle and left underneath, and the corners bail to their deep quarters. The safeties (ringed) do not bail: they shuffle a couple of yards, flat-footed, reading the inside receiver on their side (#2: H on the left, Y on the right). If #2 runs deep, the safety takes him in his deep quarter (shaded); if #2 blocks, the safety comes downhill and fits the run.






Decision 1: keep two safeties deep, and show it every time
Two safeties at 12 to 14 yards take away the explosive pass. A receiver who runs past a corner still has a safety over the top of him on his side of the field, not one safety trying to cover all of it. That is the reason anyone plays two-high. Fangio’s twist is the every time. His safeties line up at about the same depth and width whatever the call, so the shell that answers “where is the deep help?” gives the same answer every snap. Ed Donatell, who coached with Fangio for eleven seasons, described the goal as “delayed identification”: the quarterback shouldn’t know the coverage until his first or second step of the drop.4
What it costs: two safeties back means two fewer defenders near the line. Someone else has to stop the run. That is decision 2.


Decision 2: accept a light box, and build a front that can hold it
Against 11 personnel (one back, one tight end, three receivers) a two-high nickel defense usually has six defenders in the box against six blockers. The old answer to “six against six” was “bring a safety down.” Fangio’s answer was to make the six good enough. The front he favored on early downs, the tite, puts five men on the line (in Figure 66.1: E, 4i, 0, 4i, E) so that every interior gap has a lineman in it. On paper the offense still has a spare blocker: the guards are uncovered. In practice the nose on the center and the 4is in the B gaps keep both guards busy helping on them, so neither can climb cleanly to the lone linebacker (Odd and Hybrid Fronts draws this against inside zone). The nose must hold both A gaps on his own; the 4is must take on the guards and tackles without being moved. Then the safeties fit the run late, from depth, arriving at five or six yards instead of two.
Against three receivers, Fangio’s own everyday nickel was a close cousin. His Bears and Eagles usually took the nose off and kept two inside linebackers behind four linemen, a 2-4-5: by this book’s count both inside linebackers were on the field for 80% of Chicago’s nickel snaps in 2018 (Danny Trevathan and Roquan Smith) and 84% of Philadelphia’s in 2024 (Zack Baun and Nakobe Dean). The box count is the same six against six. The five-man nickel tite with one linebacker is that idea pushed further, and it is the version Staley and others in the tree made their everyday nickel.5 Both are drawn in Figure 66.3, later in the chapter.
Why it exists: a run that gains five yards is not a disaster; a pass that gains forty is. Fangio’s whole defense prices those two outcomes honestly. He would rather give up 4.5 yards a carry than a deep touchdown, because the long drive gives the offense ten more chances to make a mistake.
What it costs: rushing yards, sometimes a lot of them, and an enormous bill for interior linemen. A light-box defense with ordinary defensive tackles gets pushed around. Every Fangio defense that worked had at least one interior lineman who didn’t need help: Justin Smith in San Francisco, Akiem Hicks and Eddie Goldman in Chicago, Jalen Carter and Jordan Davis in Philadelphia.


Decision 3: rush four, from the same places
With six in the box and two safeties deep, there is nobody left over to blitz without breaking the coverage. So the default is a four-man rush, and it has to win on its own. The 2018 Bears traded for Khalil Mack a week before the season to make sure it would. Blitzing is not banned, but it is rare: by this book’s count from the charting data, Fangio’s 2018 Bears sent five or more on 21% of dropbacks (28th-most in the league), his 2024 Eagles on 19% (28th), and his 2025 Eagles on 19% (31st).6
In the tite, four rush and the fifth man on the line drops: usually the edge on the tight-end side (as in Figure 66.1), sometimes a 4i or the nose on a creeper call that sends a linebacker in his place. That is a small disguise, but a readable one. The same five players stand on the line in the same spots every snap, so after a few series an offense knows who the dropper can be and where the four will come from. Hold on to that: it is the gap Macdonald’s defense fills.
What it costs: if the four can’t get home, a patient quarterback can sit behind good protection and pick at the underneath zones. Fangio’s defense accepts that trade too, on the theory that ten-play drives against a good rush and good tacklers usually stall.


Decision 4: play match quarters and Cover 6, so the safeties can do both jobs
The coverage behind it is the quarters family from Quarters and the Two-High Match Family, and this is where the run problem is really solved. A quarters safety reads the inside receiver on his side (#2). If #2 runs a route, the safety covers him; if #2 blocks, the safety becomes a run defender, coming downhill into the alley outside the edge (he is the alley player). So the “missing” eighth man is not missing. He is standing 12 yards deep, waiting for the offense to tell him whether the play is a run. That is the decisive difference from the old eighth-man defense: the extra run defender decides after the snap, from what the play shows him, so the play-action fake that beat the walked-down safety has a harder time fooling him.
The match in match quarters is pattern matching: each defender starts in a zone, but once the receivers show their routes he takes the one who enters his area and covers him like man coverage. The zone tells the safety where to start; #2’s route tells him whom to take.
Fangio’s family has a split-field version too, under two names. Cover 6 is quarter-quarter-half with the Cover 2 half on the side away from the passing strength (the side with more wide receivers: in Figure 66.1 the left, where the nickel lines up), the usual arrangement. Cover 8 flips it and puts the half toward the passing strength.7 The flip moves the help to where the offense has more receivers. On the two-receiver side the corner squats in the flat (a cloud corner) to sit on the quick outs and hitches that side is built to throw, with a safety taking the whole deep half over him; on the tight-end side the safety keeps his quarters read on Y, where the run strength is. The analyst Cody Alexander calls this targeted coverage. The alternative is a defense that drops each safety into a fixed zone and rotates the same way whatever the offense shows. A targeted defense decides, call by call, which side gets the Cover 2 help and puts it there. (The numbers are dialect: many college staffs, Saban’s among them, use 6 and 7 for different calls; Coverage Fundamentals has the table.)
What it costs: the read safety obeys a rule, and a rule can be used against him. A tight end who blocks for a count and then releases behind the safety who came downhill (play-action), or an RPO that reads the safety directly, punishes the rule. And the run help arrives late, at four or five yards, not at the line.


Decision 5: rotate late, so the shell lies
The last decision is what turns a sound defense into a frustrating one. Broadcasters and film-room coaches call the two-high shell middle of the field open (MOFO) and a one-high shell middle of the field closed (MOFC). From the same open picture, one safety can rotate down at the snap and the other run to the deep middle, closing it: the call has become Cover 3 (or Cover 1). One version Fangio leans on is a weak rotation: the safety on the side away from the passing strength comes down, and the other one runs to the middle. Alexander has written it up as Fangio’s “Cover 9.”8 The quarterback who saw two safeties and threw to the open middle finds a safety sitting in it.


Show the Python
def shell_play():
    return Play(eleven_attached(), tite_quarters(), los=35, to_go=None)


def ending(kind):
    p = shell_play()
    if kind == "quarters":
        p.drop("RE", (6.5, 11.0), zone=(6.5, 9.5)); p.drop("MIKE", (8.0, -0.5), zone=(6.5, 8.5))
        p.drop("NB", (6.5, -11.5), zone=(6.5, 9.5))
        for k, to in (("LCB", (17.0, -17.0)), ("RCB", (17.0, 17.0))):
            p.drop(k, to, zone=(9, 11.0))
        for k, to in (("FS", (15.0, -6.0)), ("SS", (15.0, 6.0))):
            p.drop(k, to, speed=1.5)
        for w in (-5.8, 5.8):
            p.zone((17.0, w), (9, 11.0))
    elif kind == "cover6":
        p.drop("LCB", (4.0, -17.5), zone=(5.5, 9)); p.drop("NB", (8.5, -10.0), zone=(6, 8.5))
        p.drop("FS", (17.5, -11.5), zone=(10, 22.5)); p.drop("MIKE", (8.0, 0.5), zone=(6, 8))
        p.drop("RE", (6.5, 11.0), zone=(6, 9))
        p.drop("SS", (15.0, 6.0), speed=1.5); p.zone((17.0, 5.8), (9, 11.0))
        p.drop("RCB", (17.0, 17.0), zone=(9, 11.0))
    else:  # weak rotation: SS down, FS to the middle, corners to thirds
        p.drop("SS", (8.5, 5.5), zone=(6, 8)); p.drop("FS", (17.5, 0.0), zone=(9, 15.0))
        p.drop("LCB", (17.5, -15.5), zone=(9, 14.5)); p.drop("RCB", (17.5, 15.5), zone=(9, 14.5))
        p.drop("NB", (6.5, -12.5), zone=(6, 9)); p.drop("MIKE", (8.0, -4.0), zone=(6, 7.5))
        p.drop("RE", (5.0, 13.0), zone=(5, 8))
        p.highlight("SS")
    return p


fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(6.6, 4.9))
panels = [(None, "A · Before the snap: two-high, every time"), ("quarters", "B · Quarters (Cover 4)"),
          ("cover6", "C · Cover 8: the half to the two-receiver side"),
          ("weak", "D · Weak rotation to Cover 3")]
for ax, (kind, title) in zip(axes.flat, panels):
    p = shell_play() if kind is None else ending(kind)
    if kind is None:
        p.highlight("FS", "SS")
    fld = p.draw(ax=ax, lateral=(-23.5, 23.5), window=(-7.5, 22.5), title=False)

    elif kind == "quarters":

    elif kind == "cover6":

        ax.plot([xa, xb], [ya, yb], color=style.INK_2, lw=0.9, ls=(0, (3, 2)), zorder=2.5)
        say(ax, P, 20.0, -11.5, "deep half", fs=6.2, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK)
        say(ax, P, 20.0, 11.5, "quarters", fs=6.2, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK)
