fig.tight_layout(h_pad=0.8, w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()








Figure 66.2: One shell, three endings (illustrative). Panel A is the picture the quarterback sees before the snap: the same as the previous figure, two safeties 12 to 13 yards deep and the corners 7 off. Panels B to D are three calls that all start from it; in each, four linemen rush (not drawn) and seven cover. B, quarters: the corners bail to deep quarters, the safeties shuffle and read #2 with the deep quarters behind them (shaded), three defenders underneath. C, Cover 8, Fangio’s name for Cover 6 with the half toward the passing strength (the two-receiver side, where the nickel is): on the left the corner squats in the flat and the free safety takes the whole deep half; on the right, quarters. D, the weak rotation to Cover 3 that Cody Alexander attributes to Fangio: the safety on the side away from the two receivers, here the strong safety (SS, ringed), comes down to the curl and hook area; the free safety runs to the deep middle and both corners bail to deep thirds, so the open middle the quarterback saw before the snap is closed. Weak here means away from the two-receiver side, which in this formation is the tight end’s side, so the rotating safety also becomes an eighth run defender where the run strength is. The defenders’ starting spots are the same in all four panels; only their first steps after the snap differ.





Why it exists: a two-high shell that is always two-high coverage is a puzzle the quarterback solves once. A shell that is two-high or one-high depending on the call is a puzzle he has to solve after the snap, every snap, while the four-man rush is coming. Rotation is what makes decision 1’s “every time” pay off.
What it costs: every rotation is a small play of its own with a way to go wrong. A safety who rotates down has a long way to travel, and a defense that rotates often sometimes busts (a bust is a blown assignment: two defenders take the same receiver, or nobody takes him). And the charting data stops calling it two-high. That point matters for the data later in this chapter, so hold on to it: Fangio’s 2024 Eagles built their calls from a two-high shell, but after the snap they played a two-high coverage on only 34% of dropbacks, 27th in the league (The Modern Era has the full film room). The coverage charts measure what was played, not what was shown.






ImportantWhy it exists: the system in one sentence



Make the offense earn it slowly. Take away the big pass with two deep safeties; stop the run with a front that wins its own fights and safeties who fit late; get pressure without sending more than four; and decide the coverage at the snap, so the offense can’t call its answer in advance. Every part is a trade: rushing yards for explosive plays, a blitz for a sound coverage, pre-snap clarity for post-snap uncertainty. It works only if the front holds and the four can rush.








CautionCommon misconception



“Fangio invented two-high defense.” He didn’t, and he has never claimed to. Quarters was a college staple in the 2000s and Saban’s pattern-match coverages go back to his years with Bill Belichick in Cleveland in the early 1990s (Quarters and the Two-High Match Family).9 Fangio’s contribution was the package: an odd front that let a light box hold, a four-man rush, a coverage family that let the safeties play the run, and a rotation habit that made the shell lie, all taught as one system to assistants who then spread it. Credit for a scheme in football is almost always shared.

title: Case Study: Fangio’s Two-High Revolution and Macdonald’s Answer
text:
Signature seasons: Chicago 2018 and Philadelphia 2024






NoteFilm room: Chicago Bears 2018 — the system arrives



Fangio’s fourth Bears defense was the one the league noticed. Chicago allowed 283 points, the fewest in the NFL; it led the league with 27 interceptions and 36 takeaways; and by this book’s count it allowed the fewest EPA per opponent dropback, while blitzing less than all but four teams. Its runs-against-light-boxes rate (62% of designed runs met six or fewer in the box) was the highest in the league. Fangio was the AP’s Assistant Coach of the Year, and Denver hired him as head coach in January 2019.10
What to notice: on 2018 Bears film, watch the front before the coverage. Against three receivers: Hicks and Goldman (or Bilal Nichols) inside, often in 4i-techniques so the guards can’t climb cleanly, Mack and Leonard Floyd standing up on the edges, and Danny Trevathan and Roquan Smith behind them: six in the box against three-receiver sets. Then watch the two safeties, Eddie Jackson and Adrian Amos, at the snap. On a run they come downhill late and arrive in the alley; on a pass they often stay deep and let the receivers come to them. That December the Bears held the Rams, the league’s best offense, to six points (the game is the film room in The Modern Era).


The Denver years (2019–2021) are the other half of the record, and they matter for the argument. As head coach, Fangio went 19–30 with no playoff appearances. His defenses were good (third-fewest points allowed in 2021) but not dominant, ranking 15th, 14th and 18th in EPA per dropback allowed. The weak link was the one the system leans on hardest: by this book’s count Denver’s pressure rate ranked 31st, 25th and 19th, so the four-man rush rarely got home. The lesson the league drew was not that the system failed. It was that a system built on a four-man rush and an interior front lives or dies on its players, and that a defensive head coach without a quarterback has a ceiling.11






NoteFilm room: Philadelphia Eagles 2024 and Super Bowl LIX — the system at full strength



After a year as an Eagles consultant (2022) and one as Miami’s coordinator (2023), Fangio took over a Philadelphia defense that had ranked 30th in scoring. In 2024 it allowed the fewest yards in the league and the second-fewest points, and, by this book’s count, ranked 1st in EPA per designed run allowed, while meeting 66% of opponents’ designed runs with six or fewer in the box (3rd-most).12
Then it played the best version of the problem the system was built for: Patrick Mahomes in the Super Bowl. In Super Bowl LIX (February 9, 2025; Eagles 40, Chiefs 22) the charting shows four or fewer rushers on 42 of Kansas City’s 42 dropbacks, and the coverage charted as quarters (Cover 4) on 25 of them. Mahomes was sacked 6 times. The Eagles didn’t need to blitz the best quarterback in football. They needed four rushers who could win and seven defenders who kept everything in front of them, and they had both.13
What to notice: in the Super Bowl LIX replay, count the rushers on each Chiefs dropback, then watch the safeties. Two deep, almost every snap; the deep ball never comes; Mahomes holds the ball looking for something downfield, and the four-man rush gets there.


Philadelphia’s 2025 defense was not as dominant (5th in points allowed), and the Eagles lost in the wild-card round to San Francisco. Fangio remains their defensive coordinator in 2026, at 68.14

section: The tree: how the system spread, and why results varied
text:
The tree: how the system spread, and why results varied
A scheme spreads through people. A coaching tree is usually drawn by who worked for whom, but this one is better drawn by who took the idea: a two-high shell, a light box held by the front, four rushers, and coverage targeted to what the offense shows. Most of these coaches sat in Fangio’s meetings; one never did.

Brandon Staley coached Fangio’s outside linebackers in Chicago (2017–2018) and Denver (2019), then became the Rams’ coordinator for one season, 2020. With Aaron Donald inside and Jalen Ramsey moving around the secondary, the Rams allowed the fewest points in the league, 296, and, by this book’s count, the fewest EPA per dropback. The Rams under Staley added a lot of visible disguise to the system; that season is the film room of Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage. Staley then became the Chargers’ head coach (2021–2023), and his defenses there ranked 29th, 21st and 24th in points allowed.
Ed Donatell, Fangio’s secondary coach for years, ran Denver’s defense under him (2019–2021) and then Minnesota’s (2022), which finished 28th in points allowed; he was let go after one season.
The Rams’ line of succession: Staley’s Rams staff included Ejiro Evero (safeties coach, later Denver’s coordinator in 2022 and Carolina’s since 2023) and Chris Shula (the Rams’ coordinator since 2024). Joe Barry, another Fangio-tree coach, took the system to Green Bay (2021–2023), where his defenses ranked between 10th and 17th in points allowed.
Sean Desai, a Bears assistant through Fangio’s years there, became Chicago’s coordinator (2021, 22nd in points allowed) and then Philadelphia’s (2023). His 2023 Eagles finished 30th; that is the defense Fangio inherited, and a year later, with largely the same ideas, it was second.
Jesse Minter is the branch that shows the idea traveling without the man. He never worked for Fangio; he worked beside Mike Macdonald on the Ravens’ defensive staff (2017–2020), succeeded him as Michigan’s coordinator (2022–2023), and ran the Chargers’ defense (2024–2025) with the same targeted split-field coverage. His 2024 Chargers allowed 301 points, the fewest in the league. He is the Ravens’ head coach in 2026.15

The record across the tree is uneven, and that is the most useful thing about it. The 2020 Rams (Donald, Ramsey), the 2024 Eagles (Carter, Davis, a deep secondary) and the 2024 Chargers led the league; Staley’s 2021 Chargers were 29th in points allowed and Evero’s 2024 Panthers 32nd, last. Carolina lost its best interior lineman, Derrick Brown, to a season-ending knee injury in Week 1 of 2024 and its veteran linebacker Shaq Thompson to a torn Achilles in Week 4, and by this book’s count ranked 32nd in pressure rate and 32nd in EPA per designed run.16 A light-box defense without the interior lineman who doesn’t need help is the failure case of decision 2. With Brown back for 2025, the same coordinator’s defense rose to 15th. The same ideas, run by coaches who understood them, produced the best and the worst defenses in football. The system decides how you will be beaten (slowly, on the ground, underneath), not whether. Its outcomes are set by the front four and the safeties.
There is also a reason the tree mattered more than any single coach. By 2021 offenses were facing some version of this defense almost every week. NFL Next Gen Stats counted two-high coverage on 32.9% of dropbacks in 2018 and 42.0% in 2025, the highest in its records, with every defense above 30%.17 When everyone plays the same defense, the defense that wins is the one that plays it with something the offense hasn’t seen. That is where Macdonald comes in.

section: Mike Macdonald: the student who added the missing piece
text:
Mike Macdonald: the student who added the missing piece
Mike Macdonald was born in Boston in 1987, grew up a Patriots fan, and finished high school outside Atlanta. He went to the University of Georgia to study finance, graduated summa cum laude, and stayed on as a graduate assistant and quality-control coach in the football program (2010–2013) while earning a master’s degree. He joined the Baltimore Ravens as an intern in 2014, and over seven seasons worked his way through defensive assistant, defensive backs coach and linebackers coach. In 2021 Jim Harbaugh hired him as Michigan’s defensive coordinator; Michigan’s scoring defense went from 95th in the country to 8th and the team reached the College Football Playoff. John Harbaugh brought him back to Baltimore as coordinator in 2022. In January 2024, at 36, he became the Seahawks’ head coach, the youngest in the league at the time, and he kept calling the defensive plays himself, with Aden Durde as his coordinator.18
He never worked on Fangio’s staff. But he came of age as a coach in the years when Fangio’s ideas were taking over the league, and his defenses start from the same place: two safeties back, a light box, a four-man rush most of the time. What he saw was the weakness that a universal defense creates. If everybody plays two-high, offenses learn to beat two-high. They spread it with three receivers and run into the six-man box; they put on extra tight ends and run into it with seven blockers; they throw quickly before the four-man rush arrives; they read the safeties after the snap. A Fangio defense is deliberately simple up front and complicated behind: few complex fronts, and, in the words of Eagles linebacker Zack Baun, “a lot of exotic stuff coverage-wise.”19 Offenses, once they had seen enough of it, knew exactly what the four-man rush and the six-man box would look like before the snap.
Macdonald’s answer was to make the front, the rushers and the personnel as hard to read as the coverage.

title: Case Study: Fangio’s Two-High Revolution and Macdonald’s Answer
text:
Multiplicity: one picture, many plays
Multiplicity is building a defense so that one pre-snap picture can become many different plays: several fronts, rushers and coverages that all start from the same look, and players who can play several roles, so the offense learns little before the snap. It is the opposite of a defense that wins by doing a few things the same way every snap.
Fangio’s defense is multiple mainly in one dimension, the coverage. Macdonald’s is multiple in four:

The coverage, decided at the snap, as in Fangio’s system. Seattle in 2025 played two-high coverage after the snap on 52% of dropbacks (3rd-most). Next Gen Stats counted 54.8% from Week 14 through the Super Bowl, the highest of any playoff team, and described Cover 6 as Macdonald’s beloved call.20
The front. Fangio’s front also puts five on the line and drops one, but it is the same five in the same spots, so the offense soon learns who the dropper can be (decision 3). Macdonald changes who is on the line: a linebacker walked up into an A gap, an edge standing up over a guard, a safety on the line outside the tight end. Any of the five may drop, and the protection can’t be set from the picture. In Macdonald’s own words, “We put five on the line and drop a guy.”21 Figure 66.3 draws the difference.
The rushers. Four rush, nearly always, but which four is not known. This is where his reputation for simulated pressure comes from, and it needs a correction, from the coach himself: “I’m going to disappoint you guys: We do not run a lot of simulated pressures,” he said on Seattle radio in November 2025. Seattle has them, and “it’s a great tool,” but by his definition a sim (simulated pressure) is a specific thing, four rushers with one of them a player the protection didn’t count, and it isn’t a major part of the plan. What is constant is the threat: a pressure look on snap after snap, with five or six who could come and four who do.22 (The data section below squares this with the 2023 Ravens’ reputation in Zone Blitzes.)
The personnel. Macdonald’s defenses are built on defensive backs who can play two or three positions: Kyle Hamilton in Baltimore; Devon Witherspoon, Julian Love and the rookie Nick Emmanwori in Seattle. When three safeties are on the field (a big nickel) and any of them can line up deep, in the slot or in the box, the personnel stops telling the offense what is coming. Before the Super Bowl, Macdonald said that with Emmanwori on the field, “when we go to dime, we’re really a nickel [4-3] team.”23 Decoded: Emmanwori is a safety who plays like a linebacker, so a six-DB package behaves like a five-DB one, and an offense that subs in receivers to face a light dime finds a nickel’s box instead.

Figure 66.4: Who is on the field on defense, 2025 regular season (all opponent runs and passes with charted personnel). Fangio’s Eagles play two packages (nickel and base) on more than nine snaps in ten. Macdonald’s Seahawks played five- and six-DB packages built around a third safety: the big nickel on more than half their snaps, and dime on about one in six (every Seattle dime snap also had three or more safeties). Across the league, about a quarter of snaps had three or more safeties on the field. Same two-high philosophy, very different bodies: the Seahawks’ third safety is the piece that lets the same picture become a different front or a different rusher. Source: nflverse participation data (FTN charting), course calculation.





The personnel is also the clearest record of how Macdonald built the Seattle defense. His first Seahawks defense, in 2024, was good, not great: 11th in points allowed and 12th in EPA per dropback, by this book’s count. It played the big nickel on only 6% of snaps. In 2025, with the rookie Emmanwori, that share was 56%, and the defense was 1st in points and 1st against the run. Next Gen Stats ties the late-season jump in split-safety coverage to a second piece, Julian Love’s return from injured reserve in Week 14.24 Same coach, same ideas; the second year had the bodies that let one picture hide more.
Put the four together and you get McDaniels’s complaint. Sixty-five of seventy snaps look the same, two safeties deep, a crowded line, three safeties somewhere, and from that one picture the defense can play quarters with a four-man rush from the usual spots, Cover 6 with a linebacker rushing and an edge dropping, Cover 3 with a safety rotating down, or, rarely, a real blitz. The quarterback can’t set the protection with confidence and can’t pick a side of the field with confidence. He has to find out after the snap, which is the slowest and most dangerous time to find anything out.






ImportantWhy it exists



Fangio’s system hides the coverage; Macdonald’s hides everything. Once two-high became the league’s default, its predictability became the weakness. Offenses knew a Fangio-style defense would rush four from known spots and leave six in the box, so they could set protections, plan quick throws and build run plays for that exact box. Multiplicity takes those pre-snap certainties away without giving up the two-high coverage that stops explosive plays. The cost is complexity: a defense this multiple needs smart, versatile players (expensive and rare), a lot of practice time, and a play-caller who can manage it all in real time. The call reaches the field through one radio helmet, the green dot, and the other ten have to hear it, adjust it to motion, and check out of it together. When that communication fails, the busts are spectacular: a receiver running free because two defenders each thought the other had him.



The double lie, step by step
Here is the idea in one play: a pressure look and a two-high shell before the snap, a different rush and a different coverage after it. It is drawn the way Seattle’s own description suggests, five on the line with one of them dropping, plus a late safety rotation, and it uses panel C of Figure 66.3.


Show the Python
def double_lie():
    off = eleven_2x2()
    dfn = [D("LE", "OLB", 1.0, -5.6, "E"), D("LT_", "DT", 1.0, T("3", -1), "T"), D("RT_", "DT", 1.0, T("2i", 1), "T"),
           D("RE", "OLB", 1.0, 5.6, "E"), D("MIKE", "LB", 4.6, 0.6, "M"), D("WILL", "LB", 5.0, 3.6, "W"),
           D("NB", "NB", 5.0, -8.5, "$"), D("LCB", "CB", 8.5, -15.6, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 8.5, 15.6, "CB"),
           D("FS", "FS", 13.0, -7.5, "FS"), D("SS", "SS", 13.0, 7.5, "SS")]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=40, to_go=7)
    # pre-snap: the Mike walks into the left A gap (mugged, about 2 yards off the ball), the Will creeps
    p.motion("MIKE", to=(2.0, -0.8), speed=1.6)
    p.motion("WILL", to=(3.5, 3.0), speed=0.8)
    # offense: dagger-style concept to the right (Y clears up the seam, Z digs under him), a go and a hitch left
    p.route("Z", [(4, 0), (12, 0), (12, -11)], absolute=False)
    p.route("Y", [(9, 0.0), (16.5, -1.0)]); p.route("X", [(19.5, 0)]); p.route("H", [(5, 0)])
    p.dropback(2.5)
    p.pass_to("Z", t=2.1)
    # protection: the line blocks the men on it; the back is responsible for the Will if he comes
    for k, to in (("LT", (-1.4, -4.6)), ("LG", (-1.3, -2.2)), ("C", (-1.2, -0.7)), ("RG", (-1.3, 1.5)),
                  ("RT", (-1.6, 4.4))):
        go_to(p, k, to, "block", speed=1.5)
    go_to(p, "RB", (-3.3, 2.5), "path", speed=2.0, delay=0.3)
    # the rush: both tackles, the left end and the Will
    go_to(p, "LE", (-1.0, -5.2), "rush", speed=2.0); go_to(p, "LT_", (-0.4, -2.4), "rush", speed=1.2)
    go_to(p, "RT_", (-0.4, 1.4), "rush", speed=1.2)
    go_to(p, "WILL", (-0.6, 2.6), "rush", speed=3.6, delay=0.1)
    go_to(p, "WILL", (-2.6, 2.4), "rush", speed=2.2)
    # the drops: the Mike backs out to the hook, the right edge walls Y and carries him up the seam
    p.drop("MIKE", (7.5, -1.5), speed=4.0, delay=0.15)
    p.drop("RE", (10.0, 8.6), speed=4.2, delay=0.1)
    p.drop("NB", (6.5, -12.0), speed=4.0)
    # the rotation: SS down to the hole, FS to the deep middle (shaded to the seam), corners to deep thirds
    p.drop("SS", (10.5, 3.4), speed=4.0, delay=0.15)
    p.drop("FS", (17.5, 3.0), speed=5.5, delay=0.1)
    p.drop("LCB", (17.0, -16.5), speed=4.8); p.drop("RCB", (16.0, 15.0), speed=4.8)
    p.highlight("SS")
    p.highlight("RE", color=PURPLE)
    return p


DL = double_lie()
DL_T0 = DL._compile()[1]
DL_T = [-1.8, 0.0, 1.1, 3.0]
show_play(DL, DL_T,
          ["1 · −1.8 s: two-high; the Mike walks\ninto the A gap, the Will creeps",
           "2 · Snap: five on the line,\nsix could come",
           "3 · +1.1 s: M and E drop, W rushes;\nSS down, FS to the middle",
           "4 · +3.0 s: four rushed, seven covered:\nthe dig meets the robber"],
          phases([(-0.05, "Before the snap: two-high shell; five on the line, the Will creeping"),
                  (0.6, "The snap: the Mike and the right edge drop; the Will rushes"),
                  (2.05, "The rotation: SS to the hole, FS to the deep middle (Cover 3 robber)"),
                  (9.0, "The dig to Z is thrown into the robber")]),
          annot={2: lambda ax, P: point_to(ax, P, (-6.0, 4.6), tuple(DL.position("WILL", 1.1)), "W rushes", fs=6.2),
                 3: lambda ax, P: (point_to(ax, P, (14.0, 12.0), tuple(DL.position("Z", 3.0)), "dig (Z)", fs=6.2),
                                   point_to(ax, P, (13.5, -8.5), tuple(DL.position("SS", 3.0)), "robber (SS)",
                                            fs=6.2))},
          ghosts=("MIKE", "RE", "WILL", "SS", "FS"), ghost_t=DL_T0, lateral=(-19.5, 19.5), window=(-8.5, 21.5))





  
  Your browser does not support the video tag.



Figure 66.5: The double lie (simulated, BDB-format tracking generated by gridiron; illustrative, not a specific Seahawks call). Third-and-7. 1: before the snap the defense shows two-high, and the Mike (M) walks up into the left A gap: with the four linemen that is five on the line, and the Will (W) creeps to about three and a half yards, so six could rush. The nickel ($) could just as well be Seattle’s third safety; the picture is the same. 2: at the snap nothing has moved in the secondary. 3: the lie about the rush. The Mike backs out to the hook and the right edge (E, purple ring) drops to wall off the tight end (Y), while the Will rushes through the right B gap and the back steps up to block him. Four rush: one of them (W) a player the protection had to guess about, and two of the six it counted (M, E) are in coverage. The lie about the coverage: the strong safety (SS, green ring) comes down to the hole, the short middle at about 10 yards, and the free safety runs to the deep middle, so two-high has become Cover 3 with a robber. 4: the dropped edge has carried Y up the seam until the free safety, shaded to that side, takes him. The quarterback, who saw an open middle before the snap and a blitz threat to his left, throws the dig to Z; it arrives where the robber is. Dashed outlines show where the defenders started.




Count the lies. Before the snap the quarterback saw five on the line and a creeping Will: six possible rushers for six blockers. The line takes the five men on it, which leaves the Will to the back. But nobody knows before the snap whether the Will is coming, so the back has to stay in and wait to find out; that is the guess. If the Will drops, the back blocks nobody, and either way he isn’t running a route, so four receivers face seven defenders. The quarterback also saw two safeties deep with an open middle, so the dig behind the linebackers looked like the right throw. After the snap there were four rushers, two of the “rushers” were in coverage (the Mike in the short middle, exactly where a hot throw would go), and the open middle had a robber in it. Neither lie is new. Fire zones have dropped linemen since the 1990s (Zone Blitzes), and two-high rotation is Fangio’s. The modern step is doing both from the same picture, with the same personnel, and mixing them with plays on which nothing changes at all, so the quarterback can never assume a lie.






CautionCommon misconception



“Macdonald’s defense is a blitz defense.” It’s the opposite. Seattle sent five or more rushers on 22% of dropbacks in 2025 (25th-most of 32) and his 2023 Ravens on 21%. What looks like a blitz is usually a pressure look: more players near the line than will rush. The pressure comes from where the four come from and when the offense finds out, not from how many there are.








NoteFilm room: Baltimore Ravens 2023 — multiplicity with a third safety



Macdonald’s second Ravens defense allowed 280 points, the fewest in the league, and led the NFL with 60 sacks while blitzing at a below-average rate. (Its charted pressure rate was only 18th, near the middle; the sacks came from finishing: by this book’s count Baltimore turned pressures into sacks at the 2nd-highest rate in the league.) Its signature was personnel: by this book’s count Baltimore had five defensive backs on the field, three or more of them safeties, on about three snaps in four, with Kyle Hamilton, a 6-foot-4 safety, as the piece that decided what each snap was: deep safety, slot defender, linebacker or rusher (A First Look at Defense has the personnel film room; Zone Blitzes has the pressure film room).25
What to notice: on a 2023 Ravens passing down, find number 14 before the snap, then find him one second after. Then do the same for the biggest defensive lineman. The less their pre-snap spots predict their post-snap jobs, the more multiple the defense is.

Super Bowl LX: Seattle against Drake Maye, dropback by dropback
Macdonald’s second Seattle team went 14–3, allowed 292 points (the fewest in the league) and, by this book’s count, ranked 1st in EPA per designed run allowed. It reached Super Bowl LX against a New England offense led by Drake Maye, second in the MVP vote, and coordinated by McDaniels, who had spent two weeks studying the picture he said would look the same 65 times.26


Show the Python
FAM_C = {"two": style.DEFENSE, "one": style.OFFENSE, "other": style.MUTED}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.6, 2.7))

for q in (1, 2, 3, 4):

    y = 4 - q
    ax.text(-0.9, y, f"Q{q}", ha="right", va="center", fontsize=8.5, fontweight="bold", color=style.INK)

        ax.add_patch(FancyBboxPatch((i + 0.06, y - 0.32), 0.88, 0.64, boxstyle="round,pad=0,rounding_size=0.1",
                                    fc=FAM_C[r.fam], ec="white", lw=0.6))
        n = r.number_of_pass_rushers
        ax.text(i + 0.5, y, "" if pd.isna(n) else f"{int(n)}", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=6.6,
                color="white", fontweight="bold")

        if mark:
            ax.text(i + 0.5, y + 0.5, mark, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=6.4, fontweight="bold",
                    color=style.INK)

            ax.plot(i + 0.5, y + 0.47, "o", ms=2.6, color=style.INK)
ax.legend(handles=[Patch(color=style.DEFENSE, label="two-high coverage"),
                   Patch(color=style.OFFENSE, label="one-high coverage"),
                   Patch(color=style.MUTED, label="combination"),
                   Line2D([], [], marker="o", ls="", ms=3, color=style.INK, label="pressured")],
          loc="lower center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, -0.12), ncol=4, fontsize=7, frameon=False)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 66.6: Every New England dropback in Super Bowl LX (Seahawks 29, Patriots 13), in order, one row per quarter. The fourth-quarter row is the longest because New England, trailing, went no-huddle and threw on almost every snap. Each square is one dropback: orange if Seattle’s coverage was charted as two-high after the snap (Cover 2, 2-Man, quarters, Cover 6), blue if one-high (Cover 1, Cover 3, Cover 9, Cover 0), grey if charted as a combination. The number in the square is how many rushed. Marks above the squares: S a sack, I an interception, T a New England touchdown; a dot means the quarterback was pressured. Seattle rushed four on almost every snap and played two-high on most of them; New England’s only points came in the fourth quarter, much of it in no-huddle catch-up mode. Source: nflverse play-by-play and participation (FTN charting); course calculation. Charted labels, not tracking: other charters may code some snaps differently.





Read Figure 66.6 row by row.

Four rushers, on six dropbacks in seven. Seattle rushed exactly four on 45 of New England’s 53 dropbacks and five or more on only 8. The pressure came anyway: Maye was pressured or sacked on 15 dropbacks and sacked 6 times: twice by defensive tackle Byron Murphy II, twice by edge rusher Derick Hall (the second a strip-sack), once by Rylie Mills and once by Witherspoon.
Two-high, mostly, and a lot of Cover 2. Of the dropbacks with a single coverage label, 37 of 51 were charted two-high, led by 16 Cover 2 and 13 Cover 6, with 9 Cover 1 snaps mixed in. The Cover 2 is mostly a fourth-quarter story: 10 of those snaps came in the fourth quarter, with Seattle ahead and New England in the hurry-up. Cover 2 sits the corners on the short outside throws and keeps two safeties over the top, so everything stays in front of the defense and the clock keeps running, which is what a team with a lead wants. The deep ball never came: New England’s longest completion before the fourth quarter gained 21 yards.
The run never mattered. Seattle didn’t stay light against the run: of New England’s 13 designed runs, 9 met seven or more defenders in the box and only 4 met six or fewer. The running backs carried 13 times for 42 yards, and once New England fell behind it stopped running. Multiplicity includes the option to be heavy (the data section below shows the 2023 Ravens doing the same all season). Seattle’s own offense, meanwhile, controlled the clock: Kenneth Walker III ran 27 times for 135 yards and was named MVP.
The scoreboard. Seattle led 9–0 at halftime and 12–0 after three quarters, all on Jason Myers field goals. Through three quarters New England averaged -0.67 EPA per dropback. For scale, the median NFL defense in 2025 allowed +0.05 per dropback over the season (Table 66.1), so this was a collapse. The fourth quarter looks different on Figure 66.6: trailing, New England went no-huddle on 57% of its snaps and threw on almost all of them, so the row has 28 dropbacks against 7 to 10 in the others, and its EPA per dropback rose to -0.01 against a defense content to keep everything in front of it. The first T is New England’s first points, with 12:33 left: a 35-yard touchdown pass from Maye to Mack Hollins against Cover 6. Then come the two I’s. Julian Love intercepted a deep throw down the middle against a four-man rush, and Uchenna Nwosu sealed the game with a 45-yard interception return for a touchdown, on one of Seattle’s rare five-man rushes, with Witherspoon blitzing. The last T is Rhamondre Stevenson’s late touchdown catch.27







NoteFilm room: Super Bowl LX — the picture and the plays



What to notice: watch any five New England third downs from the first half. Before the snap, look at Seattle’s safeties and count the defenders near the line. The picture barely changes: two deep, a crowded line, a third safety somewhere in the middle. Then, at the snap, count who actually rushes (almost always four) and where the safeties end up. On the third-and-15 in the first quarter, Witherspoon, a cornerback, was the sixth rusher and got the sack. On others, nobody came but the four linemen and the coverage was Cover 2 or Cover 6. Same picture, different plays: that is McDaniels’s 65 out of 70, and Maye, a quarterback who had torn the league apart in 2025, spent three quarters finding out after the snap what he was facing.

Three patterns stand out in Table 66.1.

None of these defenses blitzes much. Every one sits in the bottom half of the league in five-man rushes, most of them near the bottom. Both philosophies are four-man-rush philosophies. Their pressure rates rank from 4th to 18th: from the top of the league to its middle, despite rarely blitzing. The point of the system is to make four rushers enough, and the middle of the league is often enough when the coverage behind it holds.
Most of them play light boxes, and the best of them stopped the run anyway. Most rank near the top of the league for runs against six or fewer in the box: the light-box bargain of decision 2. Yet 6 of the seven rank in the top ten in EPA allowed per designed run (the Run EPA column), the 2025 Seahawks first. The clear exception on box count is the 2023 Ravens, who met most runs with seven or more in the box: being multiple includes the option to be heavy.
The two-high column doesn’t separate them, and it can’t. The 2023 Ravens and 2024 Eagles were in the bottom half of the league in two-high coverage after the snap (22nd and 27th); the 2025 Seahawks near the top. All three are known for starting from two-high shells. That is decision 5’s warning paid off: the difference between “showed” and “played” is the disguise itself, and no column in the public data records what a defense showed.

Now the whole league: two-high rate against pressure rate, every team for the three FTN-charted seasons, with the blitz rate alongside, so you can see where the two philosophies sit in the league.


Show the Python
SC = TEAM.loc[[2023, 2024, 2025]].reset_index()
HL = {(2024, "PHI"): ("PHI '24", style.SERIES[0]), (2025, "PHI"): ("PHI '25", style.SERIES[0]),

                  (2024, "SEA"): (0.011, -0.004), (2025, "SEA"): (0.011, 0.007)}}

Figure 66.7: Every NFL defense, 2023-2025 (96 team-seasons, FTN charting, regular seasons). Left: two-high coverage after the snap (across) against pressure rate (up). Right: blitz rate, five or more rushers (across), against the same pressure rate. Grey dots are other teams; the Fangio and Macdonald defenses are colored and labelled. On the left the named defenses are spread across the range: two-high coverage isn’t what unites them. On the right they cluster on the low-blitz side, most of them at or above the league’s middle in pressure rate; BAL ’23 sits below it, but finished more of its pressures as sacks than almost anyone (see the Ravens film room). That side of the chart, pressure without the blitz, is the common ground of the two philosophies. Dashed lines are the medians of all 96. Source: nflverse play-by-play and participation; course calculation.






What the data can’t see: the disguise
The column every reader of this chapter most wants, how often a defense showed one shell and played another, isn’t in any free public file: the nflverse charting has no field for the safeties’ alignment before the snap. (Some charting services estimate the shell by eye, and Next Gen Stats has published a pre-snap disguise model, but neither is open data.) There is one way to measure it yourself: tracking data. The 2025 Big Data Bowl released every frame of every play from Weeks 1–9 of the 2022 season, including the frames before the snap, together with the charted coverage. With it you can call the shell from the safeties’ depth and width at the snap and compare it with the coverage label, play by play. Tracking Data and the Big Data Bowl builds this from the ground up; 06-06 shows the safety-rotation figure that comes out of it. The cell below is the core of that calculation (it isn’t run here, because the Big Data Bowl files aren’t distributed with this book).28


Show the Python (shell at the snap vs coverage after it, from real Big Data Bowl 2025 tracking: not run here)
import pandas as pd
from gridiron import bdb

trk = bdb.load_tracking("data/bdb/tracking_week_*.csv")      # BDB 2025: 2022 season, Weeks 1-9
plays = pd.read_csv("data/bdb/plays.csv")
players = pd.read_csv("data/bdb/players.csv")
# raw coordinates on purpose: absoluteYardlineNumber is in the same (unflipped) frame as x
TWO_HIGH = {"Cover-2", "2-Man", "Quarters", "Cover-6 Right", "Cover 6-Left"}
ONE_HIGH = {"Cover-0", "Cover-1", "Cover-1 Double", "Cover-3", "Cover-3 Seam", "Cover-3 Cloud Left",
            "Cover-3 Cloud Right", "Cover-3 Double Cloud"}             # drop Red Zone, Goal Line, Bracket, Prevent, Misc.
plays = plays[plays.pff_passCoverage.isin(TWO_HIGH | ONE_HIGH)]

snap = trk[trk.frameType == "SNAP"].merge(players[["nflId", "position"]], on="nflId")
snap = snap.merge(plays[["gameId", "playId", "defensiveTeam", "absoluteYardlineNumber", "pff_passCoverage"]],
                  on=["gameId", "playId"])
saf = snap[snap.position.isin(["FS", "SS"])].copy()
saf["depth"] = (saf.x - saf.absoluteYardlineNumber).abs()     # yards off the line of scrimmage
# shell at the snap: how many safeties are 10+ yards deep
shell = (saf.groupby(["gameId", "playId", "defensiveTeam", "pff_passCoverage"])
            .depth.apply(lambda d: "two-high" if (d >= 10).sum() >= 2 else "one-high").rename("shell")
            .reset_index())
shell["played"] = shell.pff_passCoverage.map(lambda c: "two-high" if c in TWO_HIGH else "one-high")
shell["lie"] = shell.shell != shell.played
print(shell.groupby("defensiveTeam").lie.mean().sort_values(ascending=False).head(10))   # each team's "lie rate"


Two cautions keep that calculation honest. Defenses that rotate before the snap (during the cadence) will be caught at the snap already in their real shell and count as honest, so the lie rate measures late rotation only. And the coverage labels are a charter’s judgment, which can differ between services: the Next Gen Stats article cited earlier says Julian Love’s fourth-quarter interception in Super Bowl LX did not come against split-safety coverage, while FTN’s charting labels the same play 2-Man, a two-high coverage. Treat any lie rate as an estimate with a few percentage points of noise either way.
You can still make a back-of-envelope guess for Seattle. If McDaniels is roughly right that about nine snaps in ten look the same (two-high before the snap), and Seattle played two-high after the snap on 52% of dropbacks, then it rotated out of its shell on at least 38% or so of dropbacks, before counting any lie about the rush. It is an estimate built on a coach’s quote, but it shows the scale.
There is one more number the data offers, as a caution. FTN’s charting counts how many rushers on each play were not regular linemen or edge rushers, and the rate of four-man rushes that included one is the closest public proxy for simulated pressure. By it, the 2025 Seahawks ranked 21st of 32 and the 2025 Eagles 2nd, the reverse of each coach’s reputation, and exactly what Macdonald said (“We do not run a lot of simulated pressures”).29
That looks like a contradiction of Zone Blitzes, whose 2023 Ravens film room calls Baltimore one of the league’s heaviest users of simulated pressure. It mostly isn’t, for three reasons. Different team and season: the same proxy puts the 2023 Ravens 13th, around the middle, not near the bottom like the 2025 Seahawks. Different counting: 07-03’s ranking came from PFF’s charting through Week 6 of 2023, as Cody Alexander reported it, while this proxy depends on how FTN’s charters tag each rusher, and a dropped tackle with a safety rushing in his place is exactly the snap two charters can code differently. Different things: much of what reporters called sim pressure was a pressure look, five or six possible rushers with four coming from the usual spots, which no public column records. The fair reading is that Macdonald’s defenses show the threat far more often than they run a true sim.

title: Case Study: Fangio’s Two-High Revolution and Macdonald’s Answer
text:
How offenses responded
The two-high era produced its own counter-revolution on offense, told as history in The Modern Era. Here is how each answer maps onto the five decisions, and how a multiple defense changes the math.

Run into the light box (attacks decision 2). Against six in the box, add a seventh blocker: a second tight end, a fullback, or the quarterback as a runner. In 2025, offenses used fewer than three wide receivers on 41.7% of plays, the highest since Next Gen Stats began tracking personnel, and snaps under center climbed back to about a third.30 A defense that answers by bringing a safety down is one-high again; one that stays two-high is outnumbered. Macdonald’s response was to make the extra defender a safety who looks like a deep player (the third safety of the big nickel), so the offense can’t tell from the personnel whether it has the numbers.
Use motion and tempo to force the picture early (attacks decisions 1 and 5). Motion at the snap makes safeties declare before they can disguise, and tempo denies them time to set the picture. New England went no-huddle on much of its fourth quarter in Super Bowl LX, partly from necessity, and moved the ball more against a defense with less time to disguise and every reason to keep it in front.
Throw before the rush and the rotation arrive (attacks decision 3). Quick throws and screens beat a four-man rush that needs two and a half seconds, and beat a robber who needs a second to get to the hole (the short middle, 10 to 15 yards deep). The cost is that quick throws are short throws; it is exactly what the two-high defense is willing to give up.
Read the safeties after the snap, and throw away from the rotation (attacks decision 5). A two-way concept pairs a route combination that beats two-high coverage on one side with one that beats one-high on the other, so the quarterback picks after the snap (Concepts Versus Coverages).
Make the read safety wrong (attacks decision 4). Play-action that shows the safety a blocking tight end, then releases the tight end behind him; RPOs that read the safety directly. This is the cost named in decision 4, cashed.
A quarterback who extends plays. Every one of these defenses is built on a timed four-man rush and zone coverage that keeps the ball in front. A quarterback who escapes the rush turns a covered play into a scramble, and zone defenders with their eyes on the quarterback can’t also chase him. In the Super Bowl, Maye’s 4 scrambles gained 38 yards, some of New England’s best plays of the night.

Defenses answered the answers. When offenses went heavy, defenses played more base and big nickel: base defense rose to 29.7% of snaps in 2025, up from 20.5% in 2023.31 When offenses moved at the snap, defenses rehearsed rotating late from motion. When offenses threw quickly, defenses taught their underneath players to break on the ball and tackle. The cycle hasn’t ended; it has just sped up.






CautionCommon misconception



“Two-high defenses are soft against the run.” By this book’s count the 2024 Eagles ranked 1st and the 2025 Seahawks 1st in EPA allowed per designed run, both while meeting most runs with six or fewer in the box. A light box is a choice about who stops the run (the front and late-arriving safeties), not a decision to stop it less. It does give up more yards per carry on average than a loaded box, and it fails badly when the interior linemen aren’t good enough.

Sources: course fact sheet (team announcements and wire reports), cited in the notes.





The Seattle line is the one to watch. The defense’s architect and play-caller is unchanged, so the multiplicity should be too. The question for 2026 is the other side of the ball: the Kubiak run game that kept Seattle’s defense fresh and ahead on the scoreboard is now Brian Fleury’s, and the 2026 season is the first test of whether it survives the coordinator who built it.32

title: Case Study: Fangio’s Two-High Revolution and Macdonald’s Answer
section: What survives, and what offenses do next
text:
What survives, and what offenses do next
By 2026 the two-high counterrevolution is no longer a counter anything. It is the default. What survives of Fangio’s system is almost all of it: the two-high shell as the starting picture, the light box held by the front, the four-man rush, quarters and Cover 6 as everyday coverages, and the rotation at the snap. What survives of Macdonald’s is the next layer, which the rest of the league is now copying: three-safety personnel, pressure looks without the blitz, and the conviction that the front should be as hard to read as the coverage.
What do offenses do next? These are predictions, not facts, but each follows from the logic of this chapter, and you can check them against the 2026 season as it unfolds.

More blockers the offense controls. If a multiple defense hides its run defenders among three safeties, the offense’s cleanest counter is to count blockers it controls: 12 and 13 personnel, fullbacks, and quarterbacks who run. Expect the 2025 rise in heavy personnel to continue.
Faster declarations. Motion at the snap, tempo, and fake snap counts all try to make the defense show its real picture before the ball moves. Expect more of all three, especially no-huddle on early downs, which takes away the time a multiple defense needs to set its disguise.
Plays that don’t care. Concepts that work against both two-high and one-high (two-way reads, quick game paired with a deep shot) take the disguise out of play by making the coverage irrelevant.
Attack the dropper and the rotator. Every pressure look ends with someone dropping who doesn’t usually cover, and every rotation ends with a safety arriving late to a spot. Offenses will target the defensive lineman in coverage and the area the rotating safety left.
Quarterbacks who decide after the snap. In the end, multiplicity is a test of how fast a quarterback can process what he sees after the snap. Offenses will keep paying for the quarterbacks who can, and building simpler reads for those who can’t.

And defenses will answer again. The likeliest next step is the one Macdonald has already taken: more players who can do more things, so the same personnel can play every call. The cost of that strategy is in the roster, and it is covered in Building a Roster.

title: Case Study: Fangio’s Two-High Revolution and Macdonald’s Answer
text:
Watch for it on Sunday






TipWatch for it: the disguise audit



Pick one defense (Seattle or Philadelphia is ideal) and chart one half of passing downs on paper. You need three columns and about 25 rows.

Column 1, at the snap: the shell. Two-high or one-high? Count the safeties 10 or more yards deep as the ball is snapped (the center’s head goes down), not when the offense first sets: many defenses spin a second before the snap, and that is a pre-snap rotation, not a lie. Note anything unusual: a linebacker in an A gap, five on the line, a safety creeping.
Column 2, one second after the snap: what it became. Is the middle of the field closed (one deep safety) or open (two)? How many rushed (count the defenders who crossed the line)? Did anyone who looked like a rusher drop?
Column 3: the lie. Mark R if the shell changed (two-high to one-high or back), P if the rush changed (a pressure look that sent four, or a quiet look that sent five), RP for both, and S for same. A worked row: “2-high, M in the A gap, 5 on the line | 1-high, 4 rushed, M dropped | RP.”

At the end, compute the defense’s lie rate: the share of rows that aren’t S. Then split it. A Fangio defense should lie mostly with R (the coverage); a Macdonald defense with both R and P. For scale, one charted NFL defense built around disguise (Evero’s Carolina, by MatchQuarters’ count) rotated out of its two-high shell on about half the snaps that started there (Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage). Use the high, wide replay for column 2; the live angle often cuts off the safeties.

title: Case Study: Fangio’s Two-High Revolution and Macdonald’s Answer
text:
Predict the play






TipPredict the play



Drill 1: six against six. First-and-10 from your own 35. You are the offense, in 11 personnel with the tight end attached on the right. The defense shows its base picture: tite front, one linebacker, two safeties at 12 yards.


Show the Python
p1 = Play(eleven_attached(), tite_quarters(), los=35, to_go=10)
p1.highlight("FS", "SS")
fld = p1.draw(lateral=(-26.6, 26.6), window=(-8, 17))
no_numbers(fld.ax)
ruler(fld, p1, top=15)
plt.show()








Figure 66.9: Drill 1: first-and-10. 11 personnel, tight end (Y) attached on the right, back (R) offset right. The defense: nickel tite (E, 4i, 0, 4i, E), one linebacker (M), the nickel ($) inside the left slot, corners 7 off, safeties about 12 deep (ringed). Count the box.





The numbers say run: six blockers, six in the box, and the two deep safeties are 12 yards away. Which run do you call, and what is the defense counting on to stop it?








TipAnswer





A run that doesn’t go where the tite is strongest: wide, or with a seventh blocker. The tite is built to stop inside runs. The nose and the two 4is wall off the A and B gaps, and the Mike is free to fill whatever gap is left. An inside zone into that wall is the run the defense wants you to call. Two better choices:

Outside zone or a toss to the tight-end side, which asks the edge (E) to hold up against Y and puts the ball in the alley, where the strong safety has to come 12 yards to tackle. A tite pulls its linemen inside to choke the inside runs, which empties the gaps outside the tackles (05-03’s section “Inside zone or outside zone? How a front chooses” in Odd and Hybrid Fronts draws it). It may gain five; that is the bargain.
Add a seventh blocker without changing personnel: motion Z down into a wing or a crack block, or read the backside edge with the quarterback (a zone read), so one defender is left unblocked on purpose. The motion isn’t free, though: a match-quarters corner usually travels with Z or trades assignments with his safety, so the extra blocker brings an extra defender with him.

What the defense is counting on: that its interior linemen win their one-on-ones, and that the safeties tackle in space. And there is a trap. If Y blocks, the strong safety’s read says “run” and he comes downhill, so the same picture is a play-action opportunity: fake the run, release Y behind the safety.









TipPredict the play



Drill 2: the crowded line. Third-and-7 at midfield. Seattle shows two safeties deep, both linebackers walked up, and five defenders on the line.


Show the Python
d2 = double_lie()
p2 = Play([pl for pl in d2.players.values() if pl.side == "off"],
          [pl.moved(d=2.0, w=-0.8) if pl.key == "MIKE" else pl.moved(d=3.5, w=2.2) if pl.key == "WILL" else pl
           for pl in d2.players.values() if pl.side == "def"], los=50, to_go=7)
p2.highlight("WILL")
fld = p2.draw(lateral=(-25, 25), window=(-8, 17))
no_numbers(fld.ax)
ruler(fld, p2, top=15)
plt.show()








Figure 66.10: Drill 2: third-and-7. 11 personnel, 2x2. The defense: two safeties 13 deep; four linemen, plus the Mike (M) walked up into the left A gap about two yards off the ball, for five on the line; the Will (W, ringed) at about three and a half yards over the right guard; the nickel ($) over the left slot. Six possible rushers against six blockers (five linemen and the back).





How many will rush, and what should the quarterback plan to do?








TipAnswer





Most likely four, and the coverage is unknown until the snap. Seattle rushed exactly four on 76% of opponents’ dropbacks in 2025 and on 45 of 53 in the Super Bowl. Six could come, so the protection has to account for six (five linemen and the back), but expect one or two of the crowded players to drop, and expect the dropper to land in the short middle, right where a quick hot throw against a blitz would go.
The plan, then:

Don’t throw hot to the short middle the Mike appears to vacate. That is exactly where he drops.
Protect six, and give the back the Will. The line takes the five on it, and the back is responsible for the Will if he comes; if the Will drops, the back check-releases (waits a beat, then runs a short route).
Attack the dropper. If a lineman or edge drops (here, most likely the right edge), throw into his zone: a quick out or stick route by Y, or a seam the dropped edge has to carry. An edge rusher is rarely the quickest man in coverage.
Then read the safeties. If one rotates down (as in Figure 66.5), throw away from him, outside the numbers on the side he left. If both stay deep, the throws that beat two-high are open: a curl-flat combination outside, or a dig under the safeties if the Mike drops shallow.

This is what “finding out after the snap” means, and it is the moment the defense was built to win.









TipPredict the play



Drill 3: the heavy answer. First-and-10. The offense comes out in 12 personnel, quarterback under center, both tight ends attached. The defense stays in its nickel two-high shell.


Show the Python
dfn3 = [D("LE", "DE", 1.0, -5.7, "E"), D("L3", "DT", 1.0, T("3", -1), "T"), D("R1", "DT", 1.0, T("1", 1), "T"),
        D("RE", "DE", 1.0, 5.7, "E"), D("MIKE", "LB", 4.6, 1.5, "M"), D("WILL", "LB", 4.6, -2.5, "W"),
        D("NB", "NB", 5.5, -9.0, "$"), D("LCB", "CB", 7.0, -14.6, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 7.0, 14.6, "CB"),
        D("FS", "FS", 12.5, -7.5, "FS"), D("SS", "SS", 12.5, 7.5, "SS")]
p3 = Play(twelve_under_center(), dfn3, los=30, to_go=10)
p3.highlight("FS", "SS")
fld = p3.draw(lateral=(-26.6, 26.6), window=(-9, 17))
no_numbers(fld.ax)
ruler(fld, p3, top=15)
plt.show()








Figure 66.11: Drill 3: first-and-10. 12 personnel under center: tight ends U (left) and Y (right) attached, X and Z off the ball, a single back. The defense is still in nickel: a four-man line, two linebackers (M, W), the nickel ($), corners, and two safeties about 12 deep (ringed). Count blockers and box defenders.





Who has the numbers in the run game, and what are the defense’s options before the ball is snapped?








TipAnswer





The offense does, before the snap: seven blockers (five linemen and two tight ends) against six in the box (four linemen and two linebackers; the nickel is outside the box over the left side). The defense has four answers, and each one is the trade this chapter has been about:

Let the reads do it. This is the main reason quarters exists. Each safety’s #2 is a tight end: U for the free safety, Y for the strong safety. If U and Y block, both safeties read run at once and fit (Y’s side into the alley, U’s side into the cutback), so the defense has eight run defenders after the snap without showing them before it. The price: the safeties arrive at four or five yards, not at the line, and the play-action trap from Drill 1 is now available on both sides.
Match the personnel. Sub to base (a third linebacker, or Fangio’s 3-4 tite) when 12 personnel comes on. Across the league, base defense rose to 29.7% of snaps in 2025 for exactly this reason (see “How offenses responded”). The cost is a slower defense on the field if the offense then spreads out.
Bring a safety down before the snap to make it seven against seven. Now the defense is one-high, and 12 personnel under center is the formation built for play-action shots against exactly that (the safety who came down is the one the fake pulls forward).
Rotate a safety down at the snap: stay two-high in the picture and add a seventh run defender only after the snap. That only works if the front can hold for the half-second the safety needs, which is why these defenses pay so much for interior linemen.

If the defense simply stays as it is and loses the numbers, the likeliest run goes to the right, away from the nickel: on the left, the nickel is a seventh defender close enough to fit; on the right, nobody is outside the edge but a safety 12 yards away. A Macdonald defense has one more answer you can’t see here: a third safety in the nickel’s spot, a safety who can play like a linebacker, so the box count the offense made before the snap may be wrong. That is what the big nickel is for.









TipPredict the play



Drill 4: whose defense is it? Two third-and-9 pictures against the same 2x2 formation. One is the kind of picture a Fangio defense shows, the other the kind a Macdonald defense shows.


Show the Python
def picture_mac():
    dfn = [D("LE", "OLB", 1.0, -5.6, "E"), D("LT_", "DT", 1.0, T("3", -1), "T"), D("RT_", "DT", 1.0, T("2i", 1), "T"),
           D("RE", "OLB", 1.0, 5.6, "E"), D("MIKE", "LB", 2.0, -0.8, "M"), D("WILL", "LB", 3.5, 2.6, "W"),
           D("S3", "SS", 5.5, -8.5, "S"), D("LCB", "CB", 7.0, -15.6, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 7.0, 15.6, "CB"),
           D("FS", "FS", 13.0, -7.5, "FS"), D("SS", "SS", 13.0, 7.5, "SS")]
    return Play(eleven_2x2(), dfn, los=40, to_go=9)


def picture_fangio():
    dfn = [D("LE", "OLB", 1.0, -5.6, "E"), D("L4", "DL", 1.0, T("4i", -1), "4i"), D("R4", "DL", 1.0, T("4i", 1), "4i"),
           D("RE", "OLB", 1.0, 5.6, "E"), D("MIKE", "LB", 4.7, 1.6, "M"), D("WILL", "LB", 4.7, -1.8, "W"),
           D("NB", "NB", 5.0, -8.5, "$"), D("LCB", "CB", 7.0, -15.6, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 7.0, 15.6, "CB"),
           D("FS", "FS", 12.5, -7.5, "FS"), D("SS", "SS", 12.5, 7.5, "SS")]
    return Play(eleven_2x2(), dfn, los=40, to_go=9)


fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 2.75))
for ax, (fn, title) in zip(axes, ((picture_mac, "Picture 1"), (picture_fangio, "Picture 2"))):
    p4 = fn()
    fld = p4.draw(ax=ax, lateral=(-19.5, 19.5), window=(-7.5, 16.5), title=False)
    no_numbers(fld.ax)
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=8.4, color=style.INK, loc="left", pad=3, fontweight="bold")
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.8)
plt.show()








Figure 66.12: Drill 4: two pre-snap pictures. Picture 1: four linemen, the Mike (M) walked up into the left A gap, the Will (W) creeping over the right guard, a third safety (S) over the left slot, two safeties deep. Picture 2: two linemen in 4i-techniques with a stand-up edge (E) outside each, two linebackers (M, W) off the ball, the nickel ($) over the left slot, two safeties deep. Both are two-high.





Which picture belongs to which coach, and what is the one thing you would watch at the snap in each?








TipAnswer





Picture 1 is the Macdonald picture; Picture 2 is the Fangio picture. Picture 2 is honest up front: four on the line, two linebackers off the ball, a cornerback at nickel. The protection can be set from it, and the four who rush are the four on the line. The question it poses is the coverage, so at the snap watch the two safeties: do both stay deep (quarters or Cover 6/8), or does one come down (a rotation to Cover 3)?
Picture 1 poses three questions at once. There is a linebacker on the line, a creeping Will and a third safety where the nickel would be, so six could rush and the third safety could be a blitzer, a slot defender or a deep player. At the snap, watch the Mike and the third safety first. Whoever doesn’t rush tells you where the dropper is, and that is where the hot throw would go and where the quarterback must not throw. Then watch the safeties, because the coverage is still undecided.
Both coaches show both kinds of picture sometimes; this is a tendency, not a rule. But if you can tell which question a defense is asking, you know where to look.

title: Case Study: Fangio’s Two-High Revolution and Macdonald’s Answer
text:
Takeaways

The problem was the pre-snap commitment. One-high defenses had to decide the eighth run defender and the deep help before the snap, and McVay-era offenses and Mahomes punished that commitment every week.
Fangio’s answer is five decisions that pay for each other: two safeties back to stop explosive plays; a light box held by a tite front that wins its own fights; a four-man rush; quarters and Cover 6 so the safeties fit the run after the snap; and late rotation so the shell can lie. It works only when the interior linemen and the four rushers are good enough, which is why his tree produced both the best and the worst defenses in the league.
Macdonald’s answer is multiplicity: keep the two-high coverage, but make the front, the rushers and the personnel as hard to read as the coverage. Fangio puts the same five on the line; Macdonald changes who the five are. Same picture, many plays. It is a four-man-rush defense, not a blitz defense, and by his own account not even a heavy simulated-pressure defense; its pressure comes from pressure looks and uncertainty.
Super Bowl LX was the system on the biggest stage: four rushers on nearly every snap, mostly two-high coverage, six sacks, and no New England points for three quarters.
The public data shows the common ground (low blitz rates, pressure without the blitz, light boxes, strong run defense) but not the disguise. Measuring the lie takes tracking data or your own eyes.
Offenses answer by counting blockers they control, forcing early declarations and deciding after the snap. Heavy personnel, motion at the snap, tempo and quarterbacks who process fast are the counters, and defenses will answer them with even more versatile players.

Super Bowl LX, early in the second quarter.1 Seattle has second-and-10 at its own 24, and Kenneth Walker III takes the handoff around the left end for 30 yards before he is pushed out of bounds at the New England 46. On the broadcast it is a highlight. Every chart in this book was built from lines like that one. title: Working with nflverse Data in Python
section: nflverse: free football data, and why it exists
text:
nflverse: free football data, and why it exists
nflverse is a volunteer, open-source project that publishes free, cleaned NFL data and the packages that load it. Its centrepiece is play-by-play data, usually shortened to pbp: one row for every play of every game since the 1999 season, about 48,000 rows a season, each with a few hundred columns.
Where does it come from? The raw material is the league’s own play-by-play record of each game, which nflfastR reads from the NFL’s game-data feeds: the play descriptions entered by each game’s official statistics crew, the same text printed in the gamebook a reporter picks up after the game.2 That record says what happened in words and a handful of fields. nflverse turns it into a table, fixes its inconsistencies (team abbreviations that changed when franchises moved, plays logged out of order, penalties enforced from odd spots) and then adds the columns that make it useful for analysis: who was the passer and the receiver, expected points and EPA, win probability, completion probability and more. Those model columns are the reason the data matters. Anyone can count yards; EPA on every play since 1999, free, is what let public analysts argue with professional ones.
The project has a short, busy history. It began at Carnegie Mellon, where the statisticians Maksim Horowitz, Ronald Yurko and Samuel Ventura built nflscrapR, an R package that scraped the league’s game data and fitted the first widely used open-source expected-points and win-probability models.3 In April 2020 Ben Baldwin and Sebastian Carl released nflfastR, a much faster rebuild with new models that now reaches back to 1999, and the family of packages that grew up around it took the name nflverse.4 None of these people built it for a team. The data exists because a handful of people with statistics training, who also happened to love football, decided it should be free for anyone.
For Python users, the loader is nflreadpy: one function per table, each returning a Polars data frame. It replaced nfl_data_py, the older Python package, which is now archived; its own README says it is deprecated in favour of nflreadpy and will get no further maintenance.5 In October 2026 the current release of nflreadpy is 0.1.5 (November 2025), and the repository is still active.6
Drawing code (boxes, arrows, label positions, font sizes) is about matplotlib, not football or data, so this chapter keeps it in helper functions that are folded away in the web version (“Show the plotting code”) and left out of the printed one. Every line that loads, filters, joins or counts data is shown; each chart cell ends by handing its numbers to a plot_… function.


Show the presentation helpers and the drawing code for the three illustrations
def md_table(df, digits=2):
    """Show a small DataFrame as a Markdown table (presentation plumbing, not football)."""
    out = df.copy()
    for c in out.select_dtypes("number"):
        whole = (out[c].dropna() % 1 == 0).all()                # downs, yard lines, counts
        sep = "" if c in ("season", "week", "play_id") else ","  # 2025, not 2,025
        out[c] = out[c].map(lambda v: f"{v:{sep}.{0 if whole else digits}f}")
    align = ["---:" if pd.api.types.is_numeric_dtype(df[c]) else ":---" for c in df]
    rows = [list(out.columns), align] + out.astype(str).values.tolist()
    return Markdown("\n".join("| " + " | ".join(map(str, r)) + " |" for r in rows))


def drop_numbers(ax):
    """Remove the painted yard numbers from a gridiron field (they sit under wide players)."""
    for txt in list(ax.texts):
        if txt.get_text().strip().isdigit():
            txt.remove()


def show_animation_clean(trk, times, title, to_go):
    """gridiron's show_animation, minus the painted yard numbers (frame strip in print)."""
    from gridiron.animate import animate, frame_strip
    if os.environ.get("RTG_FORMAT", "").lower() in ("pdf", "typst", "print"):
        fig = frame_strip(trk, times=times, title=title, to_go=to_go)
        for ax in fig.axes:
            drop_numbers(ax)
        plt.show()
        return
    anim = animate(trk, title=title, to_go=to_go)
    drop_numbers(anim._fig.axes[0])
    html = (anim.to_html5_video(embed_limit=40).replace("<video ", '<video style="max-width:100%;height:auto" ')
            if shutil.which("ffmpeg") else anim.to_jshtml(default_mode="once"))
    plt.close(anim._fig)
    display(HTML(html))


def canvas(w, h, xlim, ylim):
    """A figure whose single axes fills the whole canvas (no margins), axis lines off."""
    fig = plt.figure(figsize=(w, h))
    ax = fig.add_axes([0.005, 0.005, 0.99, 0.99])
    ax.set_xlim(*xlim)
    ax.set_ylim(*ylim)
    ax.axis("off")
    return fig, ax


def draw_flow():
    """Sources -> nflverse -> your Python -> this book."""
    fig, ax = canvas(6.5, 3.9, (0, 100), (0, 62))

def draw_schema(examples, counts, desc):
    """Six column families, each with Walker's values for a few of its columns."""
    TINTS = {"Keys": "#ecebe5", "Situation before the snap": style.OFFENSE_TINT,
             "What happened": "#dff3ea", "Model estimates": "#fbecc9", "Players": "#f7dfe9",

                      "2026, after the season"], fontsize=6.6, ncol=3,

Here is how the pieces fit together, from the stadium to the pictures in this book:

draw_flow()
plt.show()







Figure 67.1: Where this book’s numbers and pictures come from. What to notice: nothing in the nflverse column records football itself; nflverse republishes three suppliers’ records and adds its own models. Left: the three suppliers (the league’s official play-by-play, Next Gen Stats tracking from chips in the players’ shoulder pads, and FTN’s human charters), plus the Big Data Bowl’s tracking samples, which you download from Kaggle yourself. nflfastR turns the league’s record into a clean table and adds the model columns; nflverse publishes everything as free files. In Python, nflreadpy downloads them as Polars data frames, and the course’s gridiron.data wrapper caches them and hands over pandas. Charts use gridiron.style; diagrams and animations use gridiron’s Play and Field, fed either by a hand-drawn play or by real tracking frames through gridiron.bdb.





Hold on to the shape of that picture. nflverse is a republisher, not a source: it does not chart games itself. The play-by-play reflects what the league’s statisticians wrote. The personnel and formation data reflect what Next Gen Stats (the league’s tracking system, which follows radio chips in every player’s shoulder pads; see Tracking Data and the Big Data Bowl) or FTN’s charters recorded. When those suppliers make a mistake, or change how they record something, nflverse inherits it. The models, on the other hand, are nflverse’s own. When this book quotes EPA or win probability, it is quoting nflfastR’s models, which are good, public and documented, but are one model among several. ESPN’s win probability on a broadcast is a different model and will not match to the decimal.






ImportantWhy it exists



Before free play-by-play, serious football analysis lived inside teams and a few paid services. You could read that “teams pass too much on first down” but you could not check it. A public, reproducible table changes the argument: anyone can run the numbers, find the flaw in someone else’s, and publish a better version. The cost is that you inherit the data’s quirks, and this chapter is mostly about those quirks. The trade is worth it.

text:
Installing nflreadpy and loading your first season
On your own machine, the whole setup is one install and two lines of Python:

# In a terminal:   pip install nflreadpy pandas pyarrow      (or: uv add nflreadpy pandas pyarrow)
import nflreadpy as nfl

plays = nfl.load_pbp([2025])      # a Polars DataFrame, one row per play
plays_pd = plays.to_pandas()      # the same data as pandas (needs pyarrow)

The first call downloads the season from nflverse’s GitHub releases, a Parquet file of about 20 megabytes, so it takes a few seconds. Every loader takes a list of seasons, a single season, or True for everything available.
This book wraps nflreadpy in a tiny module, gridiron.data, so that every chapter shares one cache on disk. nfl() returns the nflreadpy module, already pointed at that cache, and pbp(seasons, columns=[...]) loads seasons, keeps the columns you name and hands back pandas. Without gridiron, the plain nflreadpy versions are:

import nflreadpy as nfl                                    # instead of  nflr = nfl()
hist = nfl.load_pbp(seasons).select(cols).to_pandas()      # instead of  pbp(seasons, columns=cols)


nflr = nfl()                       # the nflreadpy module, pointed at data/cache
raw25 = nflr.load_pbp([2025])      # Polars
print(type(raw25).__name__, f"{raw25.height:,} rows x {raw25.width} columns")

DataFrame 48,771 rows x 372 columns



Polars or pandas?
nflreadpy returns Polars data frames. Polars is a newer data-frame library, written in Rust, that stores each column as one block of memory and runs operations in parallel; on a ten-season load it is noticeably faster than pandas and uses less memory. Most Python tutorials, and most of this book, use pandas, because it is what most readers know. You can work in either. Here is the same question, “how often did offenses pass on each down in the 2025 regular season?”, asked both ways:

# Polars: chain expressions on the frame nflreadpy returned
by_down_pl = (
    raw25.filter((pl.col("season_type") == "REG")
                 & pl.col("play_type").is_in(["pass", "run"])
                 & pl.col("down").is_not_null())
    .group_by("down")
    .agg(pl.col("pass").mean().alias("pass_rate"), pl.len().alias("plays"))
    .sort("down")
)
print(by_down_pl)

# pandas: convert once, then the familiar idioms
df25 = raw25.to_pandas()
reg25 = df25[(df25.season_type == "REG") & df25.play_type.isin(["pass", "run"])
             & df25.down.notna()]
print(reg25.groupby("down")["pass"].agg(pass_rate="mean", plays="size").round(3))

shape: (4, 3)
┌──────┬───────────┬───────┐
│ down ┆ pass_rate ┆ plays │
│ ---  ┆ ---       ┆ ---   │
│ f64  ┆ f64       ┆ u32   │
╞══════╪═══════════╪═══════╡
│ 1.0  ┆ 0.497722  ┆ 14267 │
│ 2.0  ┆ 0.617417  ┆ 10863 │
│ 3.0  ┆ 0.785032  ┆ 6801  │
│ 4.0  ┆ 0.6678    ┆ 882   │
└──────┴───────────┴───────┘
      pass_rate  plays
down                  
1.0       0.498  14267
2.0       0.617  10863
3.0       0.785   6801
4.0       0.668    882


The answers are identical, as they should be. To make the conversion painless, convert after you have selected the columns you need (raw25.select([...]).to_pandas()), because a 372-column frame is mostly columns you will never touch; gridiron.data.pbp(seasons, columns=[...]) does exactly that. And remember that Polars has no index: if pandas code does .loc[...] on the result of a groupby, it is relying on the index pandas created, which Polars never had.


The cache, and the current season
nflreadpy keeps what it downloads. By default the cache lives in memory for 24 hours, so a second load in the same session is instant and a new session downloads again. The course instead caches on disk for a year, so the book can be rebuilt without fetching ten seasons every time:

from nflreadpy.config import update_config

update_config(cache_mode="filesystem", cache_dir="data/cache",
              cache_duration=60 * 60 * 24 * 365)     # seconds; the course keeps files a year

A year is right for completed seasons, which change rarely. It is wrong for the season in progress. nflverse refreshes the current season’s play-by-play as games are played, so during the season you want a short cache (say cache_duration=6 * 60 * 60, six hours) or a fresh download (nflreadpy.clear_cache()). The Sunday notebook at the end of the chapter does exactly that.






CautionCommon misconception



“The Python package for NFL data is nfl_data_py.” It was, and thousands of tutorials and notebooks still use it (import nfl_data_py as nfl; nfl.import_pbp_data([2023])). It is now archived and unmaintained, so it will drift away from the data as nflverse changes its files. Use nflreadpy: the function names start with load_ instead of import_, it returns Polars instead of pandas, and otherwise the data is the same nflverse data.

Anatomy of a play-by-play row
Here is Walker’s run as nflverse records it, a handful of its 372 columns:

walker = df25[(df25.game_id == "2025_22_SEA_NE") & (df25.play_id == 1015)].iloc[0]
MEANING = {"game_id": "season _ week _ away team _ home team", "play_id": "the play's number in the game",
           "qtr": "quarter", "time": "game clock at the snap", "posteam": "team with the ball",
           "down": "down", "ydstogo": "yards to the line to gain",
           "yardline_100": "yards to the opponent's goal line", "play_type": "kind of play",
           "yards_gained": "yards gained on the play", "ep": "expected points before the snap",
           "epa": "expected points added by the play",
           "wp": "offense's win probability before the snap"}
FMT = {"play_id": "{:.0f}", "qtr": "{:.0f}", "down": "{:.0f}", "ydstogo": "{:.0f}",
       "yardline_100": "{:.0f}", "yards_gained": "{:.0f}", "ep": "{:.2f}", "epa": "{:+.2f}",
       "wp": "{:.2f}"}
md_table(pd.DataFrame({"column": list(MEANING),
                       "value": [FMT.get(c, "{}").format(walker[c]) for c in MEANING],
                       "meaning": list(MEANING.values())}))

Read it left to right and it is a scorebug plus a result. game_id names the game (season, week, away team, home team: Seattle was the designated away team), and play_id numbers the play within it. Seattle (posteam, the team with the ball) has second down (down) and 10 to go (ydstogo) at its own 24, which nflverse writes as yardline_100 = 76; the next section explains why. The play was a run that gained 30 yards. Before the snap the situation was worth 0.12 expected points (ep); the run added 2.62 (epa), because it turned second-and-10 deep in Seattle’s half into first-and-10 in New England’s. Before the snap, nflfastR’s win probability model gave Seattle a 53% chance of winning (wp), its estimate from the score, the clock, the down, distance and field position, and the timeouts left. It deliberately ignores the betting line; a sister column, vegas_wp, folds in the pre-game point spread and, because Seattle was favoured, gives it 72%.
The other 359 columns fall into a few families. You will use perhaps forty of them regularly, so it pays to know which family to look in. The book sorts them with a few name patterns (folded below; the sorting is the book’s, not nflverse’s):


Show the column-family patterns and the example values
KEYS = {"play_id", "game_id", "old_game_id", "home_team", "away_team", "season_type", "week",
        "game_date", "season", "nfl_api_id", "order_sequence"}
SITUATION = {"posteam", "posteam_type", "defteam", "side_of_field", "yardline_100", "yrdln",
             "quarter_seconds_remaining", "half_seconds_remaining", "game_seconds_remaining",
             "game_half", "qtr", "down", "goal_to_go", "time", "ydstogo", "home_timeouts_remaining",
             "away_timeouts_remaining", "posteam_timeouts_remaining",
             "defteam_timeouts_remaining", "total_home_score", "total_away_score",
             "posteam_score", "defteam_score", "score_differential"}
MODEL = r"(^|_)(ep|epa|wp|wpa|cp|cpoe|xpass|pass_oe)$|_prob$|^xyac|_epa$|_wpa$|^vegas|_wp$"
PLAYERS = r"player_id|player_name|_player_|jersey|^(passer|rusher|receiver|name|id)$|_id$|fantasy"
GAME = (r"^drive|^fixed_drive|^series|stadium|roof|surface|^temp$|^wind$|weather|_line$|coach"
        r"|^(location|result|total|div_game|start_time|time_of_day|home_score|away_score)$"
        r"|home_opening_kickoff|end_clock_time|end_yard_line")


def family(col):
    if col in KEYS:
        return "Keys"
    if col in SITUATION:
        return "Situation before the snap"
    if re.search(MODEL, col):
        return "Model estimates"
    if re.search(GAME, col):
        return "Drive and game"
    if re.search(PLAYERS, col):
        return "Players"
    return "What happened"


def schema_examples(w):
    """A few columns per family, with this row's values, for the schema picture."""
    return {
        "Keys": [("game_id", w.game_id), ("play_id", f"{w.play_id:.0f}"), ("season", w.season),
                 ("week", w.week), ("season_type", w.season_type)],
        "Situation before the snap": [("posteam", w.posteam),
                                      ("qtr · time", f"{w.qtr:.0f} · {w.time}"),
                                      ("down", f"{w.down:.0f}"), ("ydstogo", f"{w.ydstogo:.0f}"),
                                      ("yardline_100", f"{w.yardline_100:.0f}")],
        "What happened": [("play_type", w.play_type), ("yards_gained", f"{w.yards_gained:.0f}"),
                          ("shotgun", f"{w.shotgun:.0f}"), ("run_location", w.run_location),
                          ("first_down", f"{w.first_down:.0f}")],
        "Model estimates": [("ep", f"{w.ep:.2f}"), ("epa", f"{w.epa:+.2f}"), ("wp", f"{w.wp:.2f}"),
                            ("wpa", f"{w.wpa:+.3f}"), ("xpass", f"{w.xpass:.2f}")],
        "Players": [("rusher", w.rusher), ("rusher_jersey_number", f"{w.rusher_jersey_number:.0f}"),
                    ("rusher_player_id", w.rusher_player_id), ("passer", "(none)"),
                    ("…", "≈100 more")],
        "Drive and game": [("drive", f"{w.drive:.0f}"), ("series", f"{w.series:.0f}"),
                           ("fixed_drive_result", w.fixed_drive_result),
                           ("spread_line", f"{w.spread_line:+.1f}"), ("roof", w.roof)],
    }



fam = pd.Series({c: family(c) for c in raw25.columns})
counts = fam.value_counts()
print(counts.to_string())
draw_schema(schema_examples(walker), counts, walker.desc)
