plt.show()








Figure 71.5: The NFL’s business calendar (approximate dates; exact days shift each year). The league year turns over in mid-March, when contracts expire, free agency opens, and trades agreed since the end of the season can finally be processed. Tags are placed in the two weeks before, and a tagged player has until mid-July to sign a long-term deal; compensatory picks are awarded in March; the draft comes in late April and fifth-year options are due in early May; the June 1 date changes how releases count; rosters are cut to 53 in late August; the trade deadline falls in early November, after Week 9; and waivers run all year. Blue: acquiring players; orange: deadlines and cuts.






Free agency: unrestricted and restricted
When a contract expires, what happens depends on the player’s accrued seasons, the seasons in which he spent at least six regular-season games on full pay status (on the active roster, inactive, or on injured reserve).

An unrestricted free agent (UFA) has four or more accrued seasons. He may sign with anyone, and his old team gets nothing back except possibly a compensatory pick a year later (explained below). This is the market most fans picture: the first days of the league year in March, when the best players sign big deals, usually agreed during a two-day negotiating window just before it that broadcasters call “legal tampering”.
A restricted free agent (RFA) has exactly three. His team can offer him a one-year tender at one of several set prices. He may then sign an offer sheet with another team, but his old team can match it; if it doesn’t, it receives a draft pick whose round depends on the tender. Offer sheets are rare, because teams don’t like giving up picks to pry a player loose. (With fewer than three seasons, a player can be kept for a minimum salary and can’t negotiate elsewhere at all.)

Why free agency exists: it is the players’ half of the 1993 bargain that also created the cap (see 11-02). What it costs teams: free agents are usually paid for what they did on their last team, at the peak of their market, and a bidding war means the team that “wins” is the one that valued him most, often too much. Analysts call that the winner’s curse, and it’s why patient teams treat free agency as a way to fill specific holes rather than to build a roster.


The franchise and transition tags
What if the player is a star and the team can’t agree on a long-term deal? It can tag him.
The franchise tag is a one-year contract that a team may impose on one expiring player a year. Its price is set by formula: roughly the average of the five largest cap numbers at his position, or 120 percent of his previous salary, whichever is higher. The usual non-exclusive tag lets other teams bid, but his team may match, and if it doesn’t it receives two first-round picks, a price that almost always ends the conversation; the pricier exclusive tag forbids talking to other teams at all.
The transition tag is the cheaper version, priced from the top ten salaries at the position. Other teams can sign the player to an offer sheet, and his team gets only the right to match, with no compensation if it lets him go.6
Why tags exist: to let a team keep a great player for one more season while the two sides keep negotiating; a tagged player and his team have until mid-July to agree on a long-term deal, or he plays the year on the tag. What a tag costs: a full year of top-of-market salary, fully guaranteed, with no cap-friendly bonus structure, and a player who usually feels he has been denied his long-term security. Tagging the same player again costs more each time. Washington tagged quarterback Kirk Cousins in 2016 and again in 2017, then let him walk; Minnesota signed him in 2018 to a three-year, $84 million contract that was fully guaranteed, the first multi-year fully guaranteed deal for a quarterback and a direct result of the leverage two tags had given him.7
Because the tag is priced by position, it is also where scheme meets money. In 2014 the Saints tagged Jimmy Graham as a tight end, at about $7 million; Graham argued that he lined up in the slot or out wide so often that he was really a receiver, whose tag was about $12.3 million. An arbitrator ruled that a tight end detached from the line in the slot is still doing a tight end’s job, and Graham lost.8 The label on a player’s role is worth millions, which is the idea Scheme and Fantasy picks up.


Compensatory picks
A team that loses more good free agents than it signs gets a consolation prize. The compensatory pick formula looks at every unrestricted free agent who left or arrived the previous year, ranks each by his new contract’s average salary, playing time and honors, and awards up to 32 extra picks league-wide, at the end of rounds 3 through 7, at most four per team. Since 2017 the picks can be traded.9 The idea is to repay a team for talent it developed and then lost on the open market.
Why it matters for strategy: the formula nets the two lists. Every qualifying free agent a team signs cancels out one it lost, roughly matched by contract size. Only players whose contracts ran out count; a player who was released doesn’t count on either side. So a team can choose to let its own free agents walk, sign only veterans other teams have cut, and collect the picks.10 The Baltimore Ravens are the model: they have received more compensatory picks than any other franchise since the system began in 1994, and their roster is built on letting expensive veterans walk at the right time.11


Trades and the trade deadline
A trade moves a contract, not just a player. The acquiring team takes over his remaining salary and cap hits; the trading team keeps any signing-bonus proration it has not yet counted, as dead money. When a broadcast says a team “ate” money to make a deal work, that is what it means: it took a dead-money charge so that the other team would take the player. Trades also cluster around the new league year in March, because a trade agreed after the season can’t be processed until then, and because that is when next year’s cap numbers start to count.
The trade deadline is the last day of the season on which trades are allowed: since 2024, the Tuesday after Week 9.12 After it, a contender can add only free agents, waiver claims and its own practice squad. So contenders use the deadline to rent a veteran for a playoff run, paying with future picks, and sellers turn a player who won’t be part of their next good team into a pick that might be.


Waivers
When a team releases a player with fewer than four accrued seasons (and, after the trade deadline, any player, so that a contender can’t sign a veteran whom a rival releases to get around the deadline), he goes on waivers: for about a day, every other team may claim him and take over his contract as it stands. If several teams claim him, the one with the worst record wins. A player nobody claims becomes a free agent and can choose his next team. Waivers matter most on cut-down day in late August, when hundreds of players are released at once and every front office combs the list for someone better than its own 53rd man.






NoteFilm room: Los Angeles Rams, 2021



The build: the Rams of 2021 are the boldest trade-built champion of the cap era. In March they made official the trade for quarterback Matthew Stafford, sending Detroit Jared Goff, a 2021 third-round pick and their first-round picks in 2022 and 2023. They already had cornerback Jalen Ramsey, acquired in 2019 for two first-round picks and a fourth. At the trade deadline they added edge rusher Von Miller for a 2022 second- and third-round pick. A week later Cleveland released Odell Beckham Jr. Because the deadline had passed, even a veteran had to go through waivers; nobody claimed his contract, which made him a free agent free to pick his team, and he chose Los Angeles.13 On February 13, 2022, the Rams beat Cincinnati 23–20 in Super Bowl LVI: Beckham caught the game’s first touchdown, Miller had two sacks, and Stafford threw three touchdown passes.
What to notice: the currency. The Rams paid in future draft picks, which a team with a short window values least, and spent them on premium positions (a quarterback, a cornerback, an edge rusher) rather than on depth. The bill came later: the Rams did not make a first-round pick in any draft from 2017 through 2023 (their first after Jared Goff in 2016 was Jared Verse, 19th overall in 2024), and went 5–12 in 2022 with an injured, expensive roster. They drafted their way back (Puka Nacua was a 2023 fifth-round pick) and were back in the playoffs in 2023. A trade-built roster wins a window; it doesn’t build a pipeline.

title: Building a Roster: Positional Value, the Cap, Free Agency, and the Draft
section: The draft: the cheapest good players in football
text:
The draft: the cheapest good players in football

The rookie wage scale and the fifth-year option
Before 2011, top draft picks negotiated like free agents, and the price had run away: the 2010 first overall pick, quarterback Sam Bradford, signed a six-year deal worth up to $78 million with $50 million guaranteed before playing a down, more than many proven veteran quarterbacks earned. The 2011 collective bargaining agreement ended that with the rookie wage scale. Every draft slot now carries a set four-year contract value, falling steeply from the first pick to the last, with little left to negotiate. Drafted players cannot sign an extension until after their third regular season.14
First-round picks come with one extra year of team control. The fifth-year option lets the team add a fifth season at a set price, decided after the player’s third season (by early May). Since the 2020 agreement the option is fully guaranteed once exercised, and its price depends on how much the player has played and whether he made Pro Bowls, so teams now decline it for players they aren’t sure of.
Together these rules create the rookie-contract window: the years in which a good young player is paid far less than a veteran of his quality. For a star it usually lasts three seasons, not four or five, because the first moment an extension is allowed (after year 3) is also the moment his team rushes to lock him up before his price climbs further. For most positions the window is a nice bonus. For a quarterback it is the most valuable asset in the sport, as Figure 71.3 showed, and teams with a young starter build their entire cap plan around it.


Draft value charts: what is a pick worth?
To trade picks, teams need a common price list. The original draft value chart was built for the Dallas Cowboys in the early 1990s, under head coach Jimmy Johnson, from past trades and judgment: at Johnson’s request, Cowboys vice president Mike McCoy drew it up before the club’s run of draft-day trades in 1991.15 The Jimmy Johnson chart gives the first pick 3,000 points, the 16th 1,000, the 32nd 590, the 64th 270 and the 100th 100. Teams still use it or close cousins, and a trade that “balances on the chart” is still how deals get done. (Separately, each team ranks the prospects themselves on its draft board, its own ordered list of players; the chart prices the slots, the board decides whom to take in them.)
But the chart describes what teams pay for picks, not what the picks produce. In 2005 two behavioral economists, Cade Massey and Richard Thaler (Thaler later won a Nobel prize for work on how people make predictable mistakes), asked whether the prices were right. They measured each pick’s surplus value: what a player produces minus what he is paid. Their answer, published as “The Loser’s Curse,” was that teams badly overvalue the top of the draft. A top pick is more likely to become a star, but he is also paid far more, and teams are overconfident in their ability to tell the stars apart. By surplus value, they found, picks gained value through the first round, because a pick’s cost fell faster down the round than the production teams could expect from it, and the best value in the draft sat in the second round.16 The curse of the title: the worst team earns the first pick, and the first pick is overpriced.
Their data came from before the rookie wage scale, when top picks were far more expensive. We can redo the idea for the current era with contract data. For every player drafted from 2011 to 2020, take what the market paid him on his next contract (as a share of the cap) as the measure of what he turned out to be worth, and take his rookie salary as what he cost. Surplus is the difference. Why the next contract? Because when a rookie deal ends, 32 front offices that watched him for four years bid on him, and the price they settle on is the best available summary of how good he was; a player nobody would pay counts as zero. The two halves come from different years on purpose: value from the 2011–2020 classes, because later classes haven’t all reached a second contract yet, and cost from 2021–2025 rookie deals, because those are today’s prices. Figure 71.6 compares that curve with the Johnson chart.


Show the Python
fig, (a1, a2) = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(6.5, 5.6), sharex=True)
a1.plot(PICKS, 100 * JJ / JJ_TOP10, color=style.SERIES[1], lw=2.2, label="Jimmy Johnson chart")
a1.plot(PICKS, 100 * SURPLUS / SV_TOP10, color=style.OFFENSE, lw=2.4,
        label="Surplus value (contracts, 2011–2020 classes)")
a1.axhline(100, color=style.BASELINE, lw=0.8, zorder=0)
for pk in (32.5, 64.5):
    a1.axvline(pk, color=style.BASELINE, lw=0.8, ls=(0, (3, 3)), zorder=0)
for pk in (16, 32, 64, 100):
    a1.scatter([pk], [jj_rel(pk)], s=14, color=style.SERIES[1], zorder=4)
    a1.scatter([pk], [sv_rel(pk)], s=14, color=style.OFFENSE, zorder=4)
    if pk < 100:     # below-left of a falling curve sits clear of the line
        a1.text(pk * 0.93, jj_rel(pk) - 4, f"{jj_rel(pk):.0f}", fontsize=6.8, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK,
                ha="right", va="top")
    else:            # near the floor: above-right instead, so it stays off the x-axis
        a1.text(pk * 1.07, jj_rel(pk) + 5, f"{jj_rel(pk):.0f}", fontsize=6.8, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK)
    a1.text(pk * 1.07, sv_rel(pk) + 5, f"{sv_rel(pk):.0f}", fontsize=6.8, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK)
a1.annotate(f"picks 2–3: only {N23} players,\n{N23_BUST} were paid less on their\nnext deal than as rookies",
            (2.5, sv_rel(2.5) - 2), (3.4, 36), fontsize=6.3, color=style.INK_2, ha="center", va="center",
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=style.INK_2, lw=0.6))
a1.annotate(f"No. 1: {N1_QB} of 10 were QBs", (1.0, sv_rel(1)), (1.6, 182), fontsize=6.6, color=style.INK_2,
            va="center", arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=style.INK_2, lw=0.6))
a1.set_ylabel("% of an average top-10 pick", fontsize=8)
a1.set_ylim(0, 200)
a1.legend(fontsize=7, loc="upper right")
a1.text(36, 118, "round 2", fontsize=6.6, color=style.INK_2)
a1.text(70, 118, "round 3 on", fontsize=6.6, color=style.INK_2)
a2.fill_between(PICKS, 100 * COST, 100 * VALUE, where=VALUE > COST, color=style.OFFENSE, alpha=0.15, lw=0)
a2.plot(PICKS, 100 * VALUE, color=style.OFFENSE, lw=2.2, label="value: next contract, % of cap per year")
a2.plot(PICKS, 100 * COST, color=style.INK_2, lw=2.0, ls=(0, (4, 2)), label="cost: rookie scale, % of cap per year")
a2.text(9, 100 * (VALUE[8] + COST[8]) / 2, "surplus", fontsize=7.5, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, ha="center",
        va="center")
a2.set_ylabel("% of the salary cap per year", fontsize=8)
a2.legend(fontsize=7, loc="upper right")
a2.set_xscale("log")
a2.set_xticks([1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 32, 64, 100, 160, 256])
a2.set_xticklabels(["1", "2", "5", "10", "20", "32", "64", "100", "160", "256"])
a2.set_xlabel("Overall pick (log scale)", fontsize=8)
for ax in (a1, a2):
    ax.tick_params(labelsize=7)
    ax.set_xlim(1, 256)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 71.6: Two price lists for the draft. Top: each pick’s value as a percentage of an average top-ten pick, by the Jimmy Johnson chart (orange) and by surplus value (blue, smoothed). Both are scaled to the top ten as a group rather than to No. 1, because No. 1 is only ten players, mostly quarterbacks. They agree that the first pick is special. Right after it the blue curve dips at picks 2 and 3: that is twenty players, several of them busts, and it is noise, not a reason to prefer No. 6 to No. 3; read the blue curve as roughly flat from pick 2 to the mid-teens. After that the two part ways. The Johnson chart says the 32nd pick is worth about a third of a top-ten pick; by surplus it is worth about 60 percent, and the 64th pick about 40 percent rather than 15. Bottom: where the surplus comes from, in percent of the salary cap per season: the rookie wage scale (cost, 2021–2025 contracts) falls far faster than what those players went on to earn on their next contract (value, 2011–2020 draft classes; zero for a player who never signed one). The shaded gap is surplus. Both panels use a log scale for the pick, because value changes fastest at the top. Data: Over the Cap contract data via nflverse.





The two curves agree on the first pick and disagree about almost everything after it. Ignore the blue dip at picks 2 and 3: it is 20 players, 6 of them quarterbacks, and 7 of them were paid less on their next contract than on their rookie deal. With ten players a pick, a couple of busts move the line. The real pattern is that the surplus curve is nearly flat from pick 2 to the mid-teens, while the Johnson chart falls by half over the same stretch. Measured against an average top-ten pick, the Johnson chart prices the 32nd pick at 32 percent and the 64th at 15; by surplus they keep about 61 and 43 percent. The bottom panel shows why: the rookie scale makes the first pick cost about 4.4% of the cap a year, about 7 times what a third-round pick costs, but what the players turn out to be worth falls far more gently. The modern data softens Massey and Thaler’s “curse”: the wage scale made the top picks cheaper, so picks no longer gain value as you move down the first round and the very top is no longer a bad deal. But their main finding survives: the Johnson chart drops far too fast after the first few picks, so a team trading down for more picks is usually buying more value than the chart says, and a team trading up is usually paying more.
Two caveats keep this honest. “Next contract” is a rough measure of value: it misses players who were excellent and then hurt, and it credits players paid on reputation. And the top of the curve rests on very few players, mostly quarterbacks: 7 of the ten first overall picks from 2011 to 2020.
So when does the disagreement not matter? In two places. At the very top, both price lists agree that No. 1 is special. And when the player is a quarterback the team is genuinely sure of, because a franchise quarterback on a rookie deal is worth more than either chart’s price, so a team convinced it has found one can rationally pay almost anything; that is why the biggest trade-ups are for quarterbacks. Everywhere else, and above all in trades that bundle several picks or future first-rounders, the choice of chart decides who won. The catch in the quarterback exception is that the conviction is often wrong, as the next film room shows.






NoteFilm room: Brock Purdy and the 49ers, 2021–2025



The setup: In March 2021 the 49ers traded up from the 12th pick to the 3rd, giving Miami the 12th pick, their first-round picks in 2022 and 2023, and a 2022 third-rounder, and used it on quarterback Trey Lance. Lance started four games in two seasons, broke his ankle in 2022, and was traded to Dallas in August 2023 for a fourth-round pick. The quarterback who took his job was Brock Purdy, the 262nd and last pick of the 2022 draft, whose four-year rookie contract was worth $3.7 million in total.17


Show the Python
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.0))
yrs = PURDY.index.values
caps = PURDY.cap.values
ax.axvspan(2021.5, 2024.5, color=style.THIRD, alpha=0.13, zorder=0)
ax.text(2023, max(caps) * 0.93, "rookie-contract window", ha="center", fontsize=7.5, color=GREEN)
bars = ax.bar(yrs, caps, color=[style.THIRD if y <= 2024 else style.OFFENSE for y in yrs], width=0.62, zorder=2)
for y_, c_ in zip(yrs, caps):
    lab = f"${c_:.1f}M" if c_ < 10 else f"${c_:.0f}M"
    if y_ in CAP:
        lab += f"\n{100 * c_ / CAP[y_]:.1f}% of cap"
    ax.text(y_, c_ + max(caps) * 0.02, lab, ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=6.4, color=style.INK)
ax.set_xticks(yrs)
ax.set_xticklabels([str(y) for y in yrs], fontsize=7.2)
ax.set_ylabel("Cap hit, $ millions", fontsize=7.8)
ax.set_ylim(0, max(caps) * 1.22)
ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
ax.tick_params(axis="y", labelsize=7)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 71.7: Brock Purdy’s cap hits, 2022–2030, in $ millions, with each year’s share of that year’s salary cap above the bar where the cap is known. The three rookie-contract seasons (shaded) cost the 49ers less than half a percent of the cap each. The five-year extension signed in May 2025 is shaped like most big contracts: a modest first year, then rising hits as the cap grows. Years after 2026 are as scheduled at signing and will change if the deal is restructured. Data: Over the Cap via nflverse.





What to notice: what the window bought. A top-ten quarterback contract costs about 22% of the cap (Figure 71.1); Purdy cost under half a percent, so the 49ers had a fifth of their cap to spend elsewhere. In 2023 they paid Christian McCaffrey, Nick Bosa, Trent Williams, Fred Warner, George Kittle and Deebo Samuel at the same time, and they reached the Super Bowl. (Whether Purdy or Kyle Shanahan’s system earned those numbers is the “system quarterback” debate of Quarterback Play; the cap didn’t care.) As a seventh-rounder Purdy had no fifth-year option, so the window was always going to close once he became eligible for an extension after his third season. In May 2025 it closed: a five-year extension worth up to $265 million, $53 million a year, about 19% of the cap when signed, with $100 million fully guaranteed at signing. The same team, in the same two drafts, paid three first-round picks for the quarterback the Johnson chart loved and got its starter with a pick no chart valued at all. The lesson is not that late picks beat early ones; it is how uncertain the draft is, and why surplus value says to collect more chances rather than pay heavily for one.

section: Evaluating players: what scouts grade, and what the stopwatch can’t see
text:
Evaluating players: what scouts grade, and what the stopwatch can’t see
Every pick starts with an evaluation, and the core of evaluation is still film: area scouts watch every snap a prospect played in college and grade him against what his position demands. Figure 71.8 is a condensed version of the traits most NFL scouting departments grade.


Show the Python
CARDS = [
    ("Quarterback", ["Processing: reads the coverage, finds\nthe open man on time",
                     "Accuracy and ball placement,\nnot just completion %",
                     "Arm: velocity and every throw\nto the far sideline"],
     "hand size (grip in cold,\nwet weather); little else", "poise when the pocket\ncollapses"),
    ("Offensive tackle", ["Length: arms 34 in. or more to\nkeep rushers off his body",
                          "Anchor: absorbs a bull rush\nwithout giving ground",
                          "Feet: pass sets (kick-slide,\njump sets) to mirror speed"],
     "arm length, 10-yd split,\nshort shuttle", "hand timing and\nrecovery"),
    ("Edge rusher", ["Get-off: first-step burst\nat the snap",
                     "Bend: dips under the tackle's\nreach at full speed",
                     "Hands and a plan:\nmoves and counters"],
     "10-yard split, 3-cone,\nlength", "motor in the\nfourth quarter"),
    ("Interior DL", ["Quickness to shoot a gap\n(one-gap) or strength to\ncontrol a blocker (two-gap)",
                     "Leverage: plays low",
                     "Hands to shed blocks"],
     "weight, arm length,\n10-yd split, bench", "playing low when\ntired"),
    ("Wide receiver", ["Release against press",
                       "Route craft: tempo, breaks,\nhow he sets up a defender",
                       "Hands and catch radius;\nrun after the catch"],
     "40-yard dash, height,\nvertical jump", "separation against\nNFL corners"),
    ("Cornerback", ["Press, mirror and hip turn:\nopens to run without a false step",
                    "Long speed: can run with\na go route for 40 yards",
                    "Ball skills; eyes in zone;\ntackling in run support"],
     "40-yard dash, height,\narm length, 3-cone", "recovering after\nbeing beaten"),
]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.6, 6.8))
ax.set_xlim(0, 2)
ax.set_ylim(0, 3)
ax.axis("off")
for i, (pos, traits, proxy, unseen) in enumerate(CARDS):
    col, row = i % 2, 2 - i // 2
    x0, y0 = col + 0.03, row + 0.04
    ax.add_patch(FancyBboxPatch((x0, y0), 0.94, 0.92, boxstyle="round,pad=0.0,rounding_size=0.03",
                                fc=style.SURFACE, ec=style.BASELINE, lw=0.9))
    ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x0, y0 + 0.8), 0.94, 0.12, fc=style.OFFENSE, ec="none"))
    ax.text(x0 + 0.03, y0 + 0.86, pos, fontsize=8.6, fontweight="bold", color="white", va="center")
    ax.text(x0 + 0.03, y0 + 0.75, "GRADED ON FILM", fontsize=5.8, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontweight="bold")
    yy = y0 + 0.70
    for t in traits:
        nl = t.count("\n") + 1
        ax.text(x0 + 0.05, yy, "• " + t.replace("\n", "\n   "), fontsize=6.4, color=style.INK, va="top")
        yy -= 0.058 * nl + 0.025
    ax.plot([x0 + 0.03, x0 + 0.91], [y0 + 0.235, y0 + 0.235], color=style.GRID, lw=0.8)
    ax.text(x0 + 0.03, y0 + 0.205, "STAND-IN NUMBERS", fontsize=5.8, color=GREEN, fontweight="bold", va="top")
    ax.text(x0 + 0.03, y0 + 0.165, proxy, fontsize=6.2, color=style.INK_2, va="top")
    ax.text(x0 + 0.50, y0 + 0.205, "THE STOPWATCH MISSES", fontsize=5.8, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK,
            fontweight="bold", va="top")
    ax.text(x0 + 0.50, y0 + 0.165, unseen, fontsize=6.2, color=style.INK_2, va="top")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 71.8: What scouts grade, position by position (a composite of common scouting criteria, not one team’s form). For each position: the traits that decide the grade, the measurement or drill that stands in for them, and what no stopwatch can see. Notice how much of each card is about processing, technique and movement in pads rather than raw speed: that is why the combine adjusts grades rather than sets them. The drills named under ‘stand-in numbers’ are explained in the next section.





A few words on those cards are terms of art. A lineman’s anchor is his ability to stop a bull rush, sinking his weight and holding his ground instead of being driven back into the quarterback (Pass Protection). An edge rusher’s get-off is his first-step explosion at the snap, and bend is his ability to dip his shoulder and turn the corner around a tackle at full speed without slowing down (The Pass Rush). Processing, for a quarterback, is how quickly he reads the coverage and knows where to throw. Motor is effort that doesn’t fade late in games; hand timing is when a tackle shoots his punch, too early and the rusher swats it away, too late and he is already beaten; catch radius is how far from his body a receiver can still catch the ball. Hand size is the quarterback’s only real stand-in number because scouts believe a bigger hand holds a cold, wet ball better and fumbles less. Notice that the first trait on almost every card is one no stopwatch measures.

The combine and pro days
Film is graded through the fall. In February and March come the measurements. The NFL Scouting Combine brings more than 300 invited prospects (319 in 2026) to Indianapolis, where it has been held since 1987, for a week of medical exams, interviews with teams, body measurements (height, weight, arm length, hand size) and timed drills.18 Each drill stands in for a football trait:

40-yard dash, with a 10-yard split: long speed for receivers, backs and corners; the split, the first ten yards, is the closest number to a lineman’s or edge rusher’s burst off the snap.
Vertical and broad jump: lower-body explosiveness.
Bench press (reps of 225 pounds): upper-body strength endurance, mostly for linemen.
Three-cone drill and 20-yard short shuttle: change of direction, the ability to stop, bend and restart, which matters for edge rushers turning the corner and corners mirroring routes.

A pro day is the campus version, held in March and April for a school’s prospects with NFL scouts and coaches watching. Players who skipped drills at the combine run them here, usually on their own familiar turf and often with friendlier timing, so experienced evaluators treat pro-day numbers as slightly optimistic.


RAS: putting the numbers on one scale
A 4.6 forty is slow for a cornerback and astonishing for a 300-pound tackle, so raw numbers can’t be compared across positions. RAS, the Relative Athletic Score created by the analyst Kent Lee Platte, solves that by converting each measurement into a percentile among every player measured at the same position since 1987, then combining them into one score from 0 to 10. A 5 is average for the position; 8 is very good; 9 and above is elite.19
Is it useful? Figure 71.9 builds a simplified RAS-style score from the nflverse combine data and asks what it predicts.


Show the Python
COMB = nfl().load_combine().to_pandas()


def _inches(s):
    try:
        f_, i_ = str(s).split("-")
        return int(f_) * 12 + int(i_)
    except ValueError:
        return np.nan


COMB["htin"] = COMB.ht.map(_inches)
POSGRP = {"DE": "Edge", "EDGE": "Edge", "CB": "Cornerback"}
MEAS = {"htin": 1, "wt": 1, "forty": -1, "vertical": 1, "broad_jump": 1, "bench": 1, "cone": -1, "shuttle": -1}
cmb = COMB[COMB.pos.isin(POSGRP)].copy()
cmb["grp"] = cmb.pos.map(POSGRP)
for k, sgn in MEAS.items():
    cmb[k + "_p"] = cmb.groupby("grp")[k].transform(lambda s, sgn=sgn: (sgn * s).rank(pct=True))
cmb["nmeas"] = cmb[list(MEAS)].notna().sum(axis=1)
cmb["score"] = 10 * cmb[[k + "_p" for k in MEAS]].mean(axis=1)
cmb = cmb[(cmb.nmeas >= 5) & cmb.season.between(2006, 2018) & cmb.pfr_id.notna()]
dp = DRAFT_PICKS.dropna(subset=["pfr_player_id"]).drop_duplicates("pfr_player_id")
RAS = cmb.merge(dp[["pfr_player_id", "pick", "round", "seasons_started"]], left_on="pfr_id",
                right_on="pfr_player_id", how="inner")
BANDS = ["bottom\nquarter", "second", "third", "top\nquarter"]
RAS["band"] = RAS.groupby("grp").score.transform(lambda s: pd.qcut(s, 4, labels=False))
RAS["band"] = pd.Categorical.from_codes(RAS.band.astype(int), BANDS)
RAS["early"] = np.where(RAS["round"] <= 2, "rounds 1–2", "rounds 3–7")
RAS["starter3"] = RAS.seasons_started.fillna(0) >= 3
R_RAS_PICK = np.corrcoef(RAS.score, RAS.pick)[0, 1]
# What score range each quarter covers (pooled; the quarters are cut within each position, so this is a guide)
_cuts = RAS.groupby("band", observed=True).score.agg(["min", "max"])
BAND_TICKS = [f"{b}\n({lo:.1f}–{hi:.1f})" for b, (lo, hi) in zip(BANDS, _cuts.values)]

fig, (a1, a2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 3.2), gridspec_kw=dict(width_ratios=[1, 1.25]))
mp = RAS.groupby("band", observed=True).pick.median()
a1.bar(range(len(mp)), mp.values, color=style.MUTED, width=0.6, zorder=2)
for i, v in enumerate(mp.values):
    a1.text(i, v + 3, f"{v:.0f}", ha="center", fontsize=7, color=style.INK)
a1.set_xticks(range(len(mp)))
a1.set_xticklabels(BAND_TICKS, fontsize=6.4)
a1.set_xlabel("Athletic score, quarter of the position", fontsize=7.5)
a1.set_ylabel("Median overall pick", fontsize=7.5)
a1.set_title("Drafted earlier", fontsize=8.5)
a1.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
tab = RAS.groupby(["early", "band"], observed=True).agg(rate=("starter3", "mean"), n=("starter3", "size")).reset_index()
for j, (grp, c) in enumerate((("rounds 1–2", style.OFFENSE), ("rounds 3–7", style.SERIES[1]))):
    t = tab[tab.early == grp]
    xs = np.arange(len(t)) + (j - 0.5) * 0.36
    se = 100 * 1.96 * np.sqrt(t.rate * (1 - t.rate) / t.n)       # 95% interval for each share
    a2.bar(xs, 100 * t.rate, 0.34, color=c, label=grp, zorder=2)
    a2.errorbar(xs, 100 * t.rate, yerr=se, fmt="none", ecolor=style.INK_2, elinewidth=0.8, capsize=2, zorder=3)
    for xv, (r_, n_, e_) in zip(xs, zip(t.rate, t.n, se)):
        a2.text(xv, 100 * r_ + e_ + 1.5, f"{100 * r_:.0f}", ha="center", fontsize=6.4, color=style.INK)
        a2.text(xv, -6.5, f"n={n_}", ha="center", fontsize=5.4, color=style.MUTED)
a2.set_xticks(range(4))
a2.set_xticklabels(BAND_TICKS, fontsize=6.4)
a2.set_ylim(-9, 108)
a2.set_ylabel("% who started 3+ seasons", fontsize=7.5)
a2.set_xlabel("Athletic score, quarter of the position", fontsize=7.5)
a2.set_title("Became starters", fontsize=8.5)
a2.legend(fontsize=6.8, loc="upper left")
a2.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
for ax in (a1, a2):
    ax.tick_params(labelsize=7)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
_e = tab[tab.early == "rounds 1–2"].set_index("band")
RAS_LO, RAS_HI = _e.rate.iloc[0], _e.rate.iloc[-1]
RAS_N_LO, RAS_N_HI = int(_e.n.iloc[0]), int(_e.n.iloc[-1])
RAS_CI = 100 * 1.96 * np.sqrt(RAS_LO * (1 - RAS_LO) / RAS_N_LO)      # +/- points on the smaller bar








Figure 71.9: What an athletic score predicts, and what it doesn’t. A simplified RAS-style score (each of height, weight, 40-yard dash, vertical, broad jump, bench, three-cone and shuttle converted to a percentile within the position, averaged and scaled 0–10; at least five measurements required) for edge rushers and cornerbacks at the 2006–2018 combines who were drafted. Left: better athletes are drafted earlier: teams already price athleticism in. Both panels split the players into quarters by their score within the position. Tick labels give each quarter’s range of scores. Right: the share who became starters for three or more seasons, split by when they were drafted, with 95% intervals (the thin bars). Within each draft-round group the top quarter did start more often than the bottom quarter, but each bar is only a few dozen players and the intervals overlap widely: the score adds something after the draft order is set, but far less precisely than the bars alone suggest. Data: nflverse combine and draft-pick data (Pro Football Reference).





The left panel shows that teams already draft by athleticism: the correlation between the score and the pick number is -0.34 (negative because a better score means an earlier, lower-numbered pick). The right panel is more interesting than a shrug. Among players taken in the first two rounds, the top quarter of athletes became three-year starters 71% of the time and the bottom quarter 50%, which looks like a big edge. But those bars are 62 and 26 players, so each is uncertain by about 19 percentage points either way, and the gap could be much smaller than it looks. A fair reading: athleticism still helps a little after teams have priced it in, and nobody should bet heavily on the size of that help. Athletic scores tell you who can play the position at NFL speed; they can’t tell you who processes a coverage, plays with his hands, or keeps improving. So treat RAS as a filter, not a ranking: a very low score at a premium position is a real warning, and a very high score on a player with thin film is a bet on coaching. Some players beat their numbers for a career. Others, the “workout warriors,” turn a great combine into a high pick and never play like it.

title: Building a Roster: Positional Value, the Cap, Free Agency, and the Draft
section: Scheme fit: the same player, different value
text:
Scheme fit: the same player, different value
Here is where X’s and O’s come back. Scheme fit is how well a player’s body and skills match what a particular scheme asks of his position. Because schemes ask different things, the same prospect can be a first-round talent on one board and a fourth-rounder on another, and a smart team shops where its scheme makes it the only serious buyer.

Offensive line: move your feet or move the man


Show the Python (field-diagram helpers for the scheme-fit pictures)
def O(key, pos, d, w, label=None):
    return Player(key, pos, "off", d, w, label=key if label is None else label)


def D(key, pos, d, w, label=None):
    return Player(key, pos, "def", d, w, label=label)


def oline(show=("C",)):
    """Five offensive linemen; only the ones in `show` carry a label."""
    return [O(k, k, -0.7, w, k if k in show else "")
            for k, w in zip(["LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT"], (-3.2, -1.6, 0.0, 1.6, 3.2))]


def clean(ax):
    """Zoomed diagrams: drop the yard numbers (they would sit outside the window) and clip all text."""
    for t in list(ax.texts):
        if t.get_text().isdigit() and t.get_alpha() == 0.55:
            t.remove()
        else:
            t.set_clip_on(True)


def fdraw(p, ax, **kw):
    fld = p.draw(ax=ax, **kw)
    clean(ax)
    return fld


def go_to(p, key, end, kind="block", via=(), speed=None, delay=0.0):
    """Move `key` through absolute (d, w) points `via` to `end`, as a block, path or run."""
    start = np.array(p._cur(key))
    pts = [tuple(np.array(q) - start) for q in (*via, end)]
    if kind == "block":
        return p.block(key, pts=pts, speed=speed, delay=delay)
    return {"path": p.path, "run": p.run, "pull": p.pull}[kind](key, pts, speed=speed, delay=delay)


def fsay(fld, p, d, w, text, color=style.INK_2, fontsize=7.0, ha="center", bold=False):
    x, y = fld.xy(*p.to_abs(d, w))
    fld.ax.text(x, y, text, fontsize=fontsize, color=color, ha=ha, va="center", zorder=9,
                fontweight="bold" if bold else "normal",
                bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.22", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none", alpha=0.93))


def fpoint(fld, p, frm, to, text, color=style.INK_2, fontsize=6.8, ha="center"):
    (x0, y0), (x1, y1) = fld.xy(*p.to_abs(*frm)), fld.xy(*p.to_abs(*to))
    fld.ax.annotate("", (x1, y1), (x0, y0), zorder=8,
                    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=color, lw=0.8, shrinkA=6, shrinkB=4, mutation_scale=8))
    fld.ax.text(x0, y0, text, fontsize=fontsize, color=color, ha=ha, va="center", zorder=9,
                bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.22", fc=style.SURFACE, ec=color, lw=0.6))


def pair(width=6.6, height=4.6):
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(width, height))
    return fig, axes


A wide-zone team and a gap team ask their linemen to do opposite things. Outside zone (wide zone) asks every lineman to step sideways at the snap and reach the defender in front of him: to get his body across a man who is already lined up outside him. That is a race, and it rewards quick feet, balance and athleticism over size. A gap scheme such as power asks the play-side linemen to down block, driving a defender sideways off his spot from an angle, and asks a guard to pull and lead through the hole. That rewards mass and power, plus one guard who can run. Figure 71.10 puts the two side by side.


Show the Python
def front_43():
    return [D("LE", "DE", 1.0, technique("5", -1), "5"), D("LT1", "DT", 1.0, technique("1", -1), "1"),
            D("R3", "DT", 1.0, technique("3", 1), "3"), D("RE", "DE", 1.0, technique("9", 1), "9"),
            D("WILL", "WILL", 4.6, -2.8, "W"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.6, 1.2, "M"), D("SAM", "SAM", 4.4, 6.4, "S")]


def ol_base(fb=False, show=("C",)):
    off = oline(show) + [O("Y", "TE", -0.7, 4.8, "Y"), O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -7.0, 0.0, "R")]
    if fb:
        off += [O("FB", "FB", -4.5, 0.0, "F")]
    return off


LAT, WIN = (-6.5, 11.0), (-8.5, 10.0)
fig, (axl, axr) = pair(6.7, 5.0)
p = Play(ol_base(show=("C", "RG", "RT")), front_43(), los=35, to_go=None, title="Outside zone: win the race")
# wide-zone rules against this front: C + RG combo the 3 (RG keeps him, C climbs to the Mike), the uncovered RT
# climbs to the Sam, Y reaches the 9, LG cuts off the 1, LT climbs to the Will; the backside 5 is left alone.
go_to(p, "LT", (3.5, -2.3), via=[(-1.0, -2.6), (0.6, -2.4)])
go_to(p, "LG", (0.1, 0.0), via=[(-1.0, -0.7)])
go_to(p, "C", (3.6, 1.4), via=[(-0.9, 0.9), (0.6, 1.6)])
go_to(p, "RG", (0.25, 3.05), via=[(-1.05, 2.5)])
go_to(p, "RT", (3.4, 5.8), via=[(-1.0, 4.0), (1.0, 4.7)])
go_to(p, "Y", (0.3, 6.45), via=[(-1.0, 5.7)])
go_to(p, "RB", (3.6, 4.3), "run", via=[(-6.2, 2.6), (-2.2, 5.0)])
p.handoff("RB", t=0.6)
p.highlight("RG", color=PURPLE)
f = fdraw(p, axl, lateral=LAT, window=WIN)
fsay(f, p, 8.2, -2.4, "every first step\nis sideways", fontsize=6.4, color=GREEN)
fpoint(f, p, (-3.8, -3.2), (-1.05, 2.4), "RG must get his\nhead across the 3:\nfeet, quickness", color=PURPLE,
       fontsize=6.0)

# power right against the same front: RG + RT double the 3 and RG comes off to the Will, C blocks back on the 1,
# the fullback kicks out the end man on the line (the 9), Y climbs to the Sam, and the left guard pulls up
# through the hole for the Mike
p2 = Play(ol_base(fb=True, show=("C", "LG", "RG", "RT")), front_43(), los=35, to_go=None,
          title="Power: move the man")
go_to(p2, "RT", (0.75, 2.85), via=[(-0.3, 3.0)])
go_to(p2, "RG", (3.7, -1.9), via=[(-0.25, 1.95), (0.55, 1.85), (1.8, 0.2)])
go_to(p2, "C", (0.3, -0.45), via=[(-0.5, -0.25)])
go_to(p2, "LT", (-1.6, -3.5), via=[(-1.1, -2.6)])
go_to(p2, "Y", (3.7, 6.0), via=[(0.6, 5.0)])
go_to(p2, "FB", (0.4, 5.05), via=[(-3.4, 2.6), (-1.6, 4.4)])
go_to(p2, "LG", (3.6, 1.9), "pull", via=[(-1.8, -1.2), (-2.9, 0.4), (-2.9, 2.8), (-1.2, 4.0), (1.3, 4.0)])
go_to(p2, "RB", (5.6, 3.8), "run", via=[(-5.6, 1.0), (-3.4, 3.5), (0.2, 4.0), (2.4, 4.1)])
p2.handoff("RB", t=0.9)
p2.highlight("LG", color=PURPLE)
f2 = fdraw(p2, axr, lateral=LAT, window=WIN)
fsay(f2, p2, 8.2, -2.4, "double teams and down\nblocks move a man", fontsize=6.4, color=GREEN)
fpoint(f2, p2, (-6.4, -3.4), (-2.6, -0.6), "the puller: big\nand able to run", color=PURPLE, fontsize=6.0)
fpoint(f2, p2, (-2.6, 8.0), (0.3, 5.3), "F kicks\nout the 9", fontsize=6.0)
fsay(f2, p2, 6.9, 8.0, "Y up to\nthe Sam", fontsize=6.0)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 71.10: Why a wide-zone team and a gap team draft different linemen (illustrative, against the same 4-3 front with the strength to the tight end). Left, outside zone right: every blocker’s first step is sideways. The right guard (ringed) has to get his body across a 3-technique who starts outside him while the center steps with him and then climbs to the Mike; the uncovered right tackle climbs to the Sam, the tight end reaches the 9, and the backside end (5) is left alone, because the back is running away from him. That is a race won with feet and quickness. Right, power right: the right guard and tackle double-team the 3-technique and drive him off the ball, then the guard comes off to the Will; the center blocks back on the 1, the fullback kicks out the end man on the line (the 9), the tight end climbs to the Sam, and the left guard (ringed) pulls around and leads through the hole for the Mike. Those blocks are won with mass and leg drive, and the puller is a big man who must also run. Typical builds: wide-zone linemen often weigh about 295–315 pounds, gap linemen 315–340.





That’s why a wide-zone team will happily draft a 300-pound guard who ran well in the shuttle and a gap team will pass on him for a 330-pounder who moves people. The weights in the caption are rough tendencies, not rules: teams draft for what the player does on film, and a heavy man who moves well fits anywhere. (The 49ers film room below shows how small the real difference in average weight is.)


Defensive line: two-gap nose or one-gap 3-technique
The same split runs through the defensive front. In a two-gap defense, often a 3-4 with a nose tackle head-up on the center, the lineman’s job is to strike the blocker, control him, and be ready to shed into either gap beside him (two-gap play). In a one-gap attacking front, the 3-technique on the guard’s outside shoulder owns a single gap and shoots into it at the snap (one-gap play). DL Techniques and Gap Control taught both jobs; Figure 71.11 shows what each asks of a body.


Show the Python
def threefour():
    return [D("LE", "DE", 1.0, technique("4", -1), "4"), D("NT", "NT", 1.0, 0.0, "N"),
            D("RE", "DE", 1.0, technique("4", 1), "4"),
            D("LOLB", "OLB", 1.2, -5.9, "E"), D("ROLB", "OLB", 1.2, 6.5, "E"),
            D("LILB", "ILB", 4.6, -1.9, "M"), D("RILB", "ILB", 4.6, 2.1, "W")]


def fourman():
    return front_43()


fig, (axl, axr) = pair(6.7, 4.2)
off = oline() + [O("Y", "TE", -0.7, 4.8, "Y"), O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -7.0, 0.0, "R")]
p = Play(off, threefour(), los=35, to_go=None, title="Two-gap nose: absorb and control")
go_to(p, "C", (0.0, 0.0)); go_to(p, "RG", (-0.05, 0.85), via=[(-0.5, 1.3)])
p.highlight("NT", color=PURPLE)
f = fdraw(p, axl, lateral=(-8.0, 8.0), window=(-8.0, 7.5))
for w in (-1.0, 1.0):     # the nose owns both A gaps: he can shed to either side
    (x0, y0), (x1, y1) = f.xy(*p.to_abs(0.95, 0.35 * np.sign(w))), f.xy(*p.to_abs(0.15, w))
    f.ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((x0, y0), (x1, y1), arrowstyle="-|>", mutation_scale=9, color=PURPLE, lw=1.6,
                                   zorder=8))

fpoint(f, p, (4.9, -5.8), (1.5, -0.5), "both A gaps:\nmass, anchor,\nlong arms", color=PURPLE, fontsize=6.0)

p2 = Play(off, fourman(), los=35, to_go=None, title="One-gap 3-technique: penetrate")
go_to(p2, "R3", (-2.6, 2.5), "path", via=[(0.2, 2.45)], speed=4.0)
go_to(p2, "LT1", (-2.2, -0.85), "path", via=[(0.2, -0.8)], speed=4.0)
p2.highlight("R3", color=PURPLE)
f2 = fdraw(p2, axr, lateral=(-8.0, 8.0), window=(-8.0, 7.5))
fsay(f2, p2, 2.55, 2.4, "B", color=GREEN, fontsize=6.6, bold=True)
fpoint(f2, p2, (-5.0, 5.6), (-2.5, 2.7), "one gap, fast:\nget-off,\nquickness", color=PURPLE, fontsize=6.0)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 71.11: Two defensive-line jobs, two body types (illustrative). Left, a two-gap 3-4 (E: the stand-up edge players, its outside linebackers): the nose (ringed) lines up head-up on the center and must absorb him, often a guard as well, and still be able to shed into either A gap. He needs mass, a strong anchor and long arms, so classic two-gap noses are often 320–340 pounds or more. Right, a one-gap four-man front: the 3-technique (ringed) is shaded on the right guard’s outside shoulder and attacks the B gap at the snap. He needs first-step quickness and leverage more than bulk, so he is often 285–315 pounds. A team switching from one front to the other has to rebuild its defensive line.





Pure two-gap 3-4 defenses are rare now, but the heavy nose came back another way: the tite front (Odd and Hybrid Fronts) puts a nose on the center and two linemen on the tackles’ inside shoulders to wall off inside runs, and it needs a big man in the middle again. The Eagles drafted both archetypes in back-to-back first rounds: Jordan Davis (No. 13 in 2022, 341 pounds at the combine), a nose, and Jalen Carter (No. 9 in 2023, 314 pounds), a penetrating 3-technique.20
The edge has the same split. A 4-3 defensive end plays with his hand in the dirt and must hold up against tackles in the run game, so teams like him heavier, around 255–280 pounds; a 3-4 outside linebacker stands up, rushes from wider and sometimes drops into coverage, so he can be lighter and quicker, around 240–260. But defenses played their base personnel on only about 30 percent of snaps in 2025, and spent the rest with five or more defensive backs,21 so whatever the base front is called, the live split today is less “4-3 end or 3-4 linebacker” than “run-down edge or pass-rush specialist”.


Cornerbacks: press or off
Cornerbacks split by technique, not by man versus zone. A team whose corners play press, jamming the receiver at the line, wants long, physical corners with the hips to turn and the long speed to run with a go route, whether they then play man or bail into a zone. Pete Carroll’s Seattle teams of the 2010s, the league’s signature press Cover 3 defense (Coverage Fundamentals), drafted outside corners with long arms and nearly all of them six feet or taller.22 A team whose corners play off coverage, with a cushion and their eyes in the backfield, can live with shorter corners who read the play and break on the ball quickly. The clearest case is the Cover 2 squat corner, who sits about five to seven yards off, keeps the flat and hands the deep ball to a safety: Ronde Barber, listed at 5 feet 10, played that role in Tampa Bay’s Tampa 2 on his way to the Hall of Fame.23 Figure 71.12 shows both jobs.


Show the Python
def cb_play(press=True):
    off = oline(()) + [O("QB", "QB", -5.0, 0.0, "Q"), O("X", "WR", -0.7, -15.0, "X"),
                       O("RB", "RB", -5.0, -1.6, "R")]
    dfn = [D("CB", "CB", 1.0 if press else 6.0, -15.0 if press else -16.0, "C")]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=None,
             title="Press-man: stay on his hip" if press else "Cover 2 squat: sink, then drive")
    p.route("X", [(3, 0.6), (16, 0.8)], side=None)
    if press:
        go_to(p, "CB", (14.5, -14.0), "path", via=[(2.5, -14.3)], speed=7.0)
    else:
        p.route("RB", [(2.0, -3.5), (6.5, -10.9)], frame="field")
        go_to(p, "CB", (3.2, -12.7), "path", via=[(8.6, -15.6)], speed=4.2)
        p.zone((3.4, -14.2), (5.5, 9.5))
        p.read("QB", key="CB")
        p.pass_to("RB", t=1.6)
    p.highlight("CB", color=PURPLE)
    return p


LAT_CB, WIN_CB = (-21.5, 4.5), (-7.0, 19.5)
fig, (axl, axr) = pair(6.7, 4.6)
p = cb_play(True)
f = fdraw(p, axl, lateral=LAT_CB, window=WIN_CB)
fpoint(f, p, (7.5, -6.0), (1.6, -14.3), "jam, then run:\nlength, strength,\nlong speed", color=PURPLE, fontsize=6.0)
p2 = cb_play(False)
f2 = fdraw(p2, axr, lateral=LAT_CB, window=WIN_CB)
fpoint(f2, p2, (11.5, -6.0), (8.4, -15.0), "sink, then drive:\nvision, quick\nbreak on the ball", color=PURPLE,
       fontsize=6.0)
fsay(f2, p2, 16.8, -9.0, "safety takes\nhim deep", fontsize=6.0)
fsay(f2, p2, 1.9, -17.6, "flat", fontsize=6.4, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 71.12: Two cornerback jobs (illustrative; the outside receiver on the offense’s left). Left, press-man: the corner (ringed) is a yard off the receiver, jams him, then turns and runs with him on his hip, no matter where he goes. Length, strength and long speed decide it. Right, a Cover 2 squat corner: he lines up six yards off with outside leverage, reroutes the receiver, sinks a few yards while the safety takes the go route over the top, and drives on the throw to the running back in the flat. The dashed line is his eyes, on the quarterback. Vision, footwork and a quick break on the ball decide it, so a shorter corner can thrive.







The archetypes, in real numbers
Figure 71.13 puts real combine measurements behind these archetypes. Each dot is one prospect; the shaded regions are drawn by hand to show where each kind of team tends to shop. They are a picture of the idea, not a finding: the 49ers film room below checks the offensive-line version against what teams actually drafted.


Show the Python
c = COMB[COMB.season.between(2006, 2026)].copy()
# combine "OLB" mixes 3-4 rushers with off-ball 4-3 linebackers: keep only OLBs who became NFL pass rushers
_sacks = DRAFT_PICKS.dropna(subset=["pfr_player_id"]).drop_duplicates("pfr_player_id").set_index("pfr_player_id").def_sacks
c["nfl_sacks"] = c.pfr_id.map(_sacks).fillna(0)
edge = c[c.pos.isin(["DE", "EDGE"]) | ((c.pos == "OLB") & (c.nfl_sacks >= 10))]
panels = [

]

# A team-level check on the OL archetype: linemen drafted 2017-2025 by Shanahan-tree play-callers (49ers,
# Rams, Packers from 2019, Dolphins from 2022; PFR team codes) against everyone else's.
_ol = DRAFT_PICKS[DRAFT_PICKS.position.isin(["T", "G", "C", "OL", "OT", "OG"]) & DRAFT_PICKS.season.between(2017, 2025)]

             | ((_ol.team == "MIA") & (_ol.season >= 2022)))
WZ = _ol.groupby("wz").agg(n=("pick", "size"), wt=("wt", "mean"), sh=("shuttle", "mean"))
SF_OL_WT = _ol[_ol.team == "SFO"].wt.mean()








Figure 71.13: Body types by position and scheme: every combine prospect measured 2006–2026 at four positions (dots), with the typical scheme archetypes shaded (illustrative regions, not hard cut-offs). Offensive linemen: wide-zone teams shop on the lighter, quicker side (upper left: the shuttle axis is flipped so faster times sit higher), gap teams on the heavier side. Interior defensive linemen (combine DT and NT; the generic ‘DL’ label used since 2018 is left out because it mixes ends and tackles): two-gap noses are the heaviest men in the draft; one-gap 3-techniques are 20 to 50 pounds lighter. Edge rushers (combine DE and EDGE, plus combine OLBs who went on to at least 10 NFL sacks, so that off-ball linebackers are left out): hand-down 4-3 ends are heavier than stand-up 3-4 outside linebackers. Cornerbacks: press-man teams want height (and length, which the combine measures but this data set does not include); off-coverage teams can take shorter players. Data: nflverse combine data (Pro Football Reference).











NoteFilm room: San Francisco 49ers, 2017–2025



The pattern: Kyle Shanahan’s 49ers run the purest wide-zone offense in the league (the Shanahan case study tells its history), and they have mostly filled their offensive line from the middle of the draft. From 2017 to 2025 they drafted ten offensive linemen; only two went in the first two rounds (Mike McGlinchey ninth overall in 2018 and Aaron Banks in the second round in 2021), and the rest came from rounds 3 to 7: Dominick Puni (third round, 2024), who started as a rookie, Spencer Burford (fourth, 2022), Colton McKivitz (fifth, 2020) and others.24
What to notice: it isn’t that the 49ers draft small linemen. Their picks with combine weights average about 311 pounds. Widen the lens to all four Shanahan-tree offenses (the 49ers, the Rams, the Packers from 2019 and the Dolphins from 2022) and the archetype shows up, but faintly: their 40 drafted linemen averaged 311 pounds and a 4.67-second shuttle, against 314 pounds and 4.73 for everyone else. A few pounds and a few hundredths of a second: the real difference is movement on film (the ability to reach and climb), which a stopwatch barely catches. They buy it at mid-round prices and trust their coaching to turn those players into starters. And where positional value says to pay, they paid: in 2020 they traded for left tackle Trent Williams rather than wait for one to develop. Cheap, scheme-specific depth inside; a premium price at the premium position. That is positional value and scheme fit working together.








NoteFilm room: Philadelphia Eagles, 2014–2025



The Eagles took the opposite route to an elite line: they paid for it. Using the same contract data as Figure 71.2, Philadelphia’s offensive line took a larger share of its player spending than the league average in every season from 2014 to 2025, as Figure 71.14 shows. They spent picks on it too: Lane Johnson went fourth overall in 2013, and Landon Dickerson and Cam Jurgens in the second round in 2021 and 2022. But the line’s best bargains were developed: Jason Kelce was a sixth-round pick, and Jordan Mailata, an Australian rugby league player who had never played American football, a seventh-rounder in 2018, both under offensive line coach Jeff Stoutland, who held the job from 2013 through the 2025 season. The high spending is largely the price of keeping what they built: Kelce, Johnson, Mailata and Dickerson all signed second contracts in Philadelphia.25 The Eagles case study tells how that line made the scheme possible.

ax.set_ylabel("OL share of player\ncap spending (%)", fontsize=7.5)

Philadelphia was above the league in every season, and in half of them by five percentage points or more, roughly an extra starter’s salary committed to the line each year. Dead money is excluded. text:
The 53, the 48 and the practice squad
The last layer of roster building is the rulebook for who may play on Sunday. A team carries up to 90 players in the spring and summer, cuts to 53 in late August, and then manages several lists at once. Figure 71.15 lays them out.


Show the Python
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.6, 4.3))
ax.set_xlim(0, 10)
ax.set_ylim(0, 7.0)
ax.axis("off")

    ax.add_patch(FancyBboxPatch((x, y), w, h, boxstyle="round,pad=0.02,rounding_size=0.12", fc=fc, ec=ec, lw=1.2))

    ax.text(x + 0.15, y + h - 0.62, body, fontsize=6.6, color=style.INK_2, va="top", linespacing=1.35)


box(0.2, 0.25, 6.0, 6.35, "53-man roster", "", style.SURFACE, style.OFFENSE)
box(0.45, 2.1, 3.3, 3.2, "Game-day actives: 48",
    "dress and may play\n(at least 8 offensive linemen;\notherwise 47)", style.OFFENSE_TINT, style.OFFENSE)
box(3.95, 3.45, 2.05, 1.85, "Inactives", "the rest of the 53;\nannounced 90 min\nbefore kickoff",

    "practices with the team, not on the 53;\nany team may sign one to its 53;\n+1 international player exemption",
    "#fdf3e6", GOLD)

Figure 71.15: How an NFL roster is organized during the season (rules as of 2026). The 53-man roster is the pool; on game day up to 48 of them may be active (if at least eight are offensive linemen), with the rest inactive. A third quarterback from the 53 may also dress as the emergency third quarterback without counting toward the 48. The practice squad (16 players, plus an international player exemption) practices with the team and can be elevated for a game, two a game and up to three times per player per season. Injured reserve removes a player from the 53 (red arrow); he must miss at least four games, and a team may bring back up to eight players a season. The gold arrow is an elevation from the practice squad to the game-day roster.





Game-day actives. A team may dress 48 of its 53, provided at least eight are offensive linemen (otherwise 47); the rest are declared inactive about 90 minutes before kickoff. Who sits is a weekly game-plan decision. A team facing a run-heavy opponent might dress a fifth defensive tackle instead of a sixth receiver, and the inactive list on Sunday morning is one of the best free clues to the plan.
The practice squad. Each team keeps 16 players on its practice squad (plus one exemption for an international player). They practice with the team but are not on the 53, and any other team may sign one to its 53 at any time. A practice squad elevation moves one of them up for a single game: a team may elevate two a game, each player at most three times a season, and he reverts to the practice squad afterward without going through waivers. That is how a team covers a Saturday injury without cutting anyone, and it’s why a “practice squad” kicker can make a game-winning field goal.26
Injured reserve (IR) takes an injured player off the 53 so his spot can be filled. During the season a player placed on IR must sit out at least four games, and a team can bring back a limited number of players a year (eight); everyone else stays out for the season. The rule creates a real decision: put a player with a six-week injury on IR, freeing his spot for a healthy body, or keep him on the 53 and play a man short for a month and a half.
The emergency third quarterback. Since 2023 a team may dress a third quarterback from its 53 without counting him among the 48, and he may enter only if both of the other quarterbacks are injured or ejected. The rule was a direct answer to the 2022 NFC Championship Game, in which San Francisco lost its starter to an elbow injury and then its backup to a concussion; with a running back as the only other option, the injured starter went back in, barely able to throw.27

title: Building a Roster: Positional Value, the Cap, Free Agency, and the Draft
text:
Watch for it on Sunday






TipWatch for it: the cap check



Pick one team before its game (Over the Cap and Spotrac have free team pages) and do a five-minute cap check. On an Over the Cap team page, the cap hit is the Cap Number column, and a Dead Money & Cap Savings section shows, for each player, what cutting him would leave as dead money and save, with separate “Cut (pre-June 1)” and “Cut (post-June 1)” views. Use the pre-June 1 view for March decisions.
Before kickoff

Find the five biggest cap hits. Are they at premium positions (QB, edge, receiver, interior pass rusher, tackle, corner)? A top-five hit at running back, linebacker or safety is a team paying for a player, not a position.
Find the dead money. A large number means a recent mistake or a recent release; it tells you which era of the roster the team is paying for.
Is the quarterback on a rookie contract? If so, look for the team spending the savings: expensive veterans elsewhere, a deadline trade. If not, look for bargains and late-round starters around him.
Check the inactives (posted 90 minutes before kickoff) and any practice-squad elevations announced the day before. They tell you the game plan’s priorities and who is hurt.

During the game

When a veteran with a big cap hit plays poorly, ask the cap question: what would releasing him save, and how much dead money would it leave? A small dead-money figure next to a big cap hit is a player likely to be released or asked to take a pay cut in March.
When a young player on a rookie deal plays well at a premium position, you are watching his team’s cap plan for the next three years.

The prediction: before the season ends, name the one contract the team will restructure (a star it plans to keep, with a large base salary next year) and the one it will cut (an older player at a lower-value position whose cap hit far exceeds his dead money). Check in March.

text:
Predict the play
In this chapter the “play” is a front-office move. The pictures are a cap table, a trade offer and a scheme.






TipPredict the play 1: the March squeeze

Figure 71.16: An invented team’s eight largest cap hits for next season, in $ millions (bar length), with the dead money each would leave if he were released before June 1 (red part of the bar) and the cap saved by releasing him (number at the right). The team is $14 million over next year’s cap. Ages are next season’s. The quarterback’s $52 million is $40 million of base salary plus $12 million of prorated signing bonus, with three seasons left on his deal.





The team must clear $14 million before free agency opens in March. Which moves clear it most cheaply? On the radio, one caller says to cut the quarterback, the single biggest saving on the board; another says to cut the 32-year-old left tackle. Why are both wrong?








TipAnswer





Release the running back and the linebacker ($20 million saved); don’t touch the quarterback or the left tackle.
Start with the cuts that are cheap and sensible. The running back saves $12 million against $2 million of dead money, at the position the market values least, at an age when backs decline fast. That isn’t quite enough, so add the linebacker ($8 million saved, $1 million dead), another low-value position and another player past 30: $20 million cleared. (The top-51 rule trims that a little, since two minimum-salary players move up into the 51 that count, but it still clears 14.) Both are pre-June 1 releases on purpose: a post-June 1 designation would leave their cap hits on the books until June 2, after free agency has opened.
The other lever is a restructure. Turning $30 million of the quarterback’s $40 million base salary into a bonus spread over his three remaining seasons counts $10 million a year, so next year’s hit falls by $20 million. The cost is the future: his next two cap hits each rise by $10 million, and his dead money grows by $20 million on top of the $36 million already there, which makes him almost impossible to cut. Fine for a quarterback the team is sure of; a trap for one it isn’t. Most teams would make the two cheap cuts and save the restructure for when they need room to add someone.
Now the callers. Cutting the quarterback saves $16 million but leaves $36 million of dead money and no starter, and replacing a starting quarterback costs far more than $16 million. The left tackle is the subtler trap: $15 million saved, but tackle is a premium position, replacements are expensive, and the quarterback needs protecting. If he is still good, the hole costs more to fill than the cut saves. The edge rusher and cornerback are young premium players with heavy dead money, extension candidates rather than cuts; the receiver, at 30, is more likely to be asked to take a pay cut.

By each chart, how much did Chicago overpay? What would have to be true for the trade to be right anyway, and what hidden risk sits in that 2022 first-rounder?








TipAnswer





By the Johnson chart, Chicago paid about 54 percent more than No. 11 was worth. By surplus value, it gave up about 2.1 times what it received.
The two charts disagree about how much a pick in the teens and a future first are worth next to No. 11. The Johnson chart thinks No. 11 is worth half again as much as No. 20, so a future first on top looks like a hefty but normal premium. On the surplus curve No. 11 is worth only about 23 percent more than No. 20, and a mid-round first is worth nearly as much as No. 11, so giving both for it is a steep price.
What would make it right anyway? The quarterback exception: if the player at No. 11 is a franchise quarterback, he is worth more than either chart’s price. The pick was Justin Fields.
The hidden risk is the future first. A team that trades up for a rookie quarterback is betting on being good next year, and if the quarterback struggles, the team is bad and the pick it gave away lands near the top. Chicago won 6 games in 2021, and the 2022 first it sent away became No. 7. Priced at its real slot, the trade cost 2,446 Johnson points, about 2.0 times No. 11. Figure 71.17: A team’s most-called run (illustrative), from under center with a fullback. Read the blockers’ first steps to name the run. The team needs a right guard (ringed); two prospects are on its board at the same pick.





Both prospects grade as starters. First, name the run from the first steps of the blockers. Then: which prospect does this team draft, what does that choice cost it, and why might the other be the better pick for a different team?








TipAnswer





It is outside zone, and the team takes Prospect B. Every lineman’s first step is sideways and to the right, with the back aiming wide and cutting up: that is outside zone. The right guard’s job is to reach a 3-technique who lines up outside him while the center steps with him on a combination block and then climbs to a linebacker. That is a race, and B’s quickness (a 4.45 short shuttle is excellent for a guard) and film (“quick to reach and climb”) are exactly the traits it rewards.
The cost is in pass protection. B gives ground to big bull rushers, and the team will have to cover for it: help from the center on obvious passing downs, a quicker passing game, and play-action and boots that move the launch point away from the defensive tackle. A wide-zone team can live with that because its run game and its play-action both ask him to move, not to stand still and absorb a 330-pound man head-on.
Prospect A is the better gap lineman: heavy, long, with a stout anchor, and able to move a defender off his spot on a down block, the power-team skill. On a gap team’s board he may be the higher-rated player, and on this team’s board he is a worse fit who would spend his first year trying to win races he isn’t built for. That’s scheme fit: the same pick, two right answers, depending on what the team runs. It also explains why a wide-zone team can often draft B a round later than his talent suggests. Fewer teams are shopping for him.

title: Building a Roster: Positional Value, the Cap, Free Agency, and the Draft
text:
Takeaways

Positional value is real, but price is not value. The market pays quarterbacks most by far, then edge rushers and receivers, then interior pass rushers, corners and tackles. Yet a team’s share of spending on any position barely predicts winning (r near zero, 2014–2025), while quarterback play predicts it strongly (r about 0.7). Value comes from getting play above your price.
A contract is a cap schedule, not a number. Signing bonuses are paid up front but prorated over up to five years; restructures and void years borrow cap space from the future; releasing a player accelerates his remaining proration as dead money, which is why cutting a star can save almost nothing.
Every acquisition route has a currency. Free agency costs cap space at peak prices; tags buy one year at a top-of-market price; trades cost picks and move contracts; compensatory picks reward letting players go; waivers and the practice squad are how teams find the 53rd man.
The draft is the cheapest source of good players, and the Johnson chart overprices the top. Surplus value (production minus rookie cost) falls far more gently than the chart, so trading down usually buys value and trading up usually pays a premium, except, sometimes, for a franchise quarterback.
The rookie-contract window is the biggest edge in roster building. A star quarterback on a rookie deal, like Purdy in 2022–2024, frees a fifth or more of the cap to spend on everyone else.
Scheme decides who is worth drafting. Wide-zone and gap teams want different linemen, two-gap and one-gap fronts want different tackles, press and off teams want different corners. RAS and the combine filter for athleticism; film and fit decide the pick.

title: Building a Roster: Positional Value, the Cap, Free Agency, and the Draft
text:
Connections
Builds on: Expected Points, EPA and Success Rate (EPA per dropback, and why passing outweighs running, the root of positional value); The Game Plan (matchup hunting, which only works with the players a front office bought); The 1978 Liberation (where free agency and the cap came from); Zone Running, Gap and Power Runs, DL Techniques and Gap Control, Odd and Hybrid Fronts, Coverage Fundamentals and Cover 2 and Tampa 2 (the jobs behind scheme fit).
Sets up: Scheme and Fantasy: Reading Usage, Not Box Scores, which takes the same idea (what a scheme asks of each position) and turns it into fantasy usage: snap share, target share and the roles that predict points. The case studies show these choices in full: the Eagles paying for the lines, the 49ers and the Shanahan tree drafting for wide zone, and the Chiefs living through the end of a rookie-contract window. The Capstone puts the cap check into a full game-day routine.






NoteGo deeper



For contracts, Over the Cap (overthecap.com, which also hosts the full collective bargaining agreement by article) and Spotrac are the standard free references; Jason Fitzgerald and Brad Spielberger’s work at Over the Cap explains cap mechanics with real deals. Cade Massey and Richard Thaler’s “The Loser’s Curse” (Management Science, 2013) is readable and still the foundational paper on draft value. Andrew Brandt, a former Packers executive, writes about the business of football for Sports Illustrated and teaches it at Villanova. For scouting, Kent Lee Platte’s ras.football explains RAS and lets you look up any prospect, and Pat Kirwan’s Take Your Eye Off the Ball has a front-office view of how rosters are assembled. To extend this chapter’s data, change the position groups in the first code cell, or swap "PHI" for any team in Figure 71.14.

title: Scheme and Fantasy: Reading Usage, Not Box Scores
text:
Outputs and inputs: why the box score misleads
Week 1, Sunday night. You check your fantasy team. The tight end you drafted in the sixth round was on the field for 52 of his team’s 61 snaps and caught one pass for 7 yards. Your league-mate’s backup running back played 14 snaps and scored twice, both times from the 1-yard line. On Monday the talk is all touchdowns: the backup is a waiver-wire must, your tight end a bust. A coach looking at the same game would ask different questions. On how many of those 52 snaps did your tight end run a route, and on how many was he blocking a defensive end? Why was the backup the one in the game at the 1-yard line, and is that a role the play-caller will keep giving him? The box score records what happened. Usage (who is on the field, who goes out for a pass, who the ball is aimed at, how often the team throws at all) records what the scheme intended to happen, and intentions repeat from week to week far more reliably than outcomes. This chapter teaches you to read usage, to trace it back to the scheme and the play-caller who produce it, and to predict how it moves when the play-caller changes.
You’ll be able to…
Reading the diagrams: offense is blue circles (X and Z wide receivers; Y and U tight ends, ringed in gold; F a fullback; Q quarterback; R running back); defense is outlined squares. Solid arrows are routes and runs, short arrows ending in a bar are blocks, dashed lines defenders’ movements. The dark blue line is the line of scrimmage. The charts come from nflverse data; the notes under each one say which seasons and filters it uses.
A fantasy point is the end of a chain. For a wide receiver, the chain runs like this: his team runs a certain number of plays (pace); some fraction of them are passes (the play-caller’s tendency, adjusted by the score); on some of those passes he is on the field and running a route rather than blocking or standing on the sideline (route participation); on some of those routes the ball is thrown to him (target share), some of them deep (air-yards share); and on some of those targets he catches the ball, gains yards and, now and then, scores. Every link before the catch is mostly usage, and usage is set by people: the coordinator who designs the plays, the play-caller who chooses them on game day, and the quarterback who decides where the ball goes. The links after it are mostly efficiency, which belongs to the player, plus a large dose of luck.
The reason to care about the difference is that the two halves behave very differently over time. The next figure takes every wide receiver and tight end with at least 50 targets in both 2024 and 2025 and asks a simple question of each statistic: if you knew a player’s 2024 number, how well would it predict his 2025 number?
Show the Python
def stab_frame(u):
    u = u[u.pos.isin(["WR", "TE"])].copy()
    u["tpg"], u["ypg"] = u.tgt / u.games, u.yds / u.games
    u["ypt"], u["tdpg"], u["catch"] = u.yds / u.tgt, u.td / u.games, u.rec / u.tgt
    u = u[u.tgt >= 50]
    return u.loc[u.groupby("pid").tgt.idxmax()].set_index("pid")


STAB = stab_frame(U24).join(stab_frame(U25), lsuffix="_24", rsuffix="_25", how="inner")
METRICS = [("tgt_share", "Target share", "use"), ("ay_share", "Air-yards share", "use"),
           ("tpg", "Targets per game", "use"), ("wopr", "WOPR", "use"),
           ("route_part", "Route participation (est.)", "use"),
           ("ypg", "Receiving yards per game", "mix"), ("catch", "Catch rate", "eff"),
           ("yprr", "Yards per route run (est.)", "eff"), ("ypt", "Yards per target", "eff"),
           ("tdpg", "Touchdowns per game", "td")]
vals = [(lab, STAB[f"{k}_24"].corr(STAB[f"{k}_25"]), grp) for k, lab, grp in METRICS]
COLORS = {"use": style.OFFENSE, "mix": style.MUTED, "eff": style.DEFENSE, "td": style.SERIES[7]}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 3.6))
for i, (lab, v, grp) in enumerate(vals[::-1]):
    ax.barh(i, v, color=COLORS[grp], height=0.62)
    ax.text(v + 0.012, i, f"{v:.2f}", va="center", fontsize=8, color=style.INK)
ax.set_yticks(range(len(vals)))
ax.set_yticklabels([v[0] for v in vals[::-1]], fontsize=8.5, color=style.INK)
ax.set_xlim(0, 0.85)
ax.set_xlabel("Correlation, 2024 value with 2025 value (same player)")
ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
ax.legend(handles=[Line2D([], [], color=COLORS[g], lw=6, label=l) for g, l in
                   [("use", "Opportunity (usage)"), ("mix", "Volume × efficiency"), ("eff", "Efficiency"),
                    ("td", "Touchdowns")]],
          loc="lower right", fontsize=8)
ax.set_title(f"How well does last season predict this season? (n = {len(STAB)})", fontsize=10)
plt.show()








Figure 72.1: Usage repeats; touchdowns don’t. Each bar is the correlation between a player’s 2024 and 2025 value of the statistic, for the 78 wide receivers and tight ends with 50 or more targets in both regular seasons (a player who changed teams counts with the team where he drew more targets). A correlation of 1 would mean the 2024 number predicts 2025 perfectly; 0, not at all. Blue bars measure opportunity, orange bars what the player did with each chance, the grey bar a mix of the two (yards per game is volume times efficiency), the red bar touchdowns. With 78 players, a correlation is uncertain by roughly ±0.08, so bars within about 0.1 of each other are not really different. Only players who kept a 50-target role in both seasons are included, so players who lost their role are missing. Route participation and yards per route run are estimated from on-field dropbacks (see the note on where route counts come from). Data: nflverse play-by-play and participation, this book’s calculation.
The opportunity numbers (target share, air-yards share, targets per game, WOPR, route participation) all correlate at about 0.64 to 0.70 from one season to the next. Be careful about what the chart does not say. Receiving yards per game (0.62) is almost as sticky, but it isn’t a pure efficiency number: it is volume times efficiency, so it inherits most of its stability from the volume. Catch rate (0.59) is sticky because it is partly a role too: a slot receiver who runs short routes catches a high share of his targets every year, and a deep threat a low one. The numbers that really wobble are the per-chance ones. Yards per target sits near 0.45, and touchdowns per game, the statistic that swings a fantasy week more than any other, correlate at only 0.25.
In plain terms, a receiver’s share of his team’s targets is mostly a fact about his role, and his role is decided before the season by the scheme, the depth chart and the quarterback’s trust. Whether a given target turns into a 40-yard catch or a touchdown depends on the coverage, the throw, the defender’s hand and a dozen things that don’t repeat. One honest caveat: the chart includes only receivers who kept a real role in both seasons, the survivors. A player who lost his job isn’t in it, so treat these correlations as “if the role holds”, which is exactly the question a scheme change raises.2

title: Scheme and Fantasy: Reading Usage, Not Box Scores
text:
ImportantWhy it exists



Usage stats exist because fantasy players and analysts kept being fooled by box scores. A season of touchdowns makes a player look like a star; a season of near-misses makes an equally used player look ordinary. The next season, the touchdowns are dealt out again more or less at random, while the opportunity that produced them carries over. Reading usage is the habit of pricing a player on the part of his production that will repeat. The trade-off: usage tells you about the chances, not the talent. A player who gets the ball constantly and does nothing with it will eventually lose the role, so the efficiency numbers still matter. They are just slower to trust.








NoteMadden vs. real life



In Madden, a player’s ratings drive what he does on the field: a 95-overall receiver gets open and makes plays. In a real offense, the ball goes where the play was designed to send it, read by the quarterback in the order the play-caller drew it. A great receiver in a run-first offense that rotates its receivers can finish behind an average one in a pass-first offense that never takes him off the field. The talent is the same; the opportunity is not, and opportunity is drawn on the play-caller’s call sheet, not in the player’s ratings.
